tags.vgi.doc_llm: The Microsoft 365 Defender / Sentinel security functions. Each is an incremental watermark feed over the Microsoft Graph security API — incidents (with correlated alerts) or alerts_v2 — cursored by a safety-lagged lastUpdateDateTime `ge` boundary. A scan returns rows updated since the supplied `since` cursor, followed by one marker row whose _watermark_next column is the cursor to persist for the next scan. Omit `since` for a bounded cold start (now − lookback). Capture is at-least-once (the lag window re-reads late rows); apply idempotently by id. `status` is a lifecycle field, never a tombstone.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Defender security watermark functions

Two incremental feeds over the Microsoft Graph security API: incidents (`/security/incidents`, `$expand=alerts`, returning changed incidents with their alerts) and alerts (`/security/alerts_v2`, returning changed alerts).

Both share the same shape: read data rows with `WHERE _row_kind <> 'marker'` (equivalently `_watermark_next IS NULL`), and take the next cursor from the single marker row's `_watermark_next`. The incidents feed interleaves `_row_kind` values `incident` and `alert`; the alerts feed emits only `alert` and is the authoritative source for alert completeness. Each requires an app-only `azure_graph` secret.

vgi.example_queries.description: Cold-start sync of open high-severity incidents
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id, display_name, severity, status FROM azure.main.security_incidents() WHERE _row_kind = 'incident' AND severity = 'high' AND status = 'active'

vgi.example_queries.description: Incremental incident sync from a saved watermark
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id, display_name, status FROM azure.main.security_incidents(since := '<_watermark_next>') WHERE _row_kind = 'incident'

vgi.example_queries.description: Read the watermark cursor to persist for the next scan
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT _watermark_next FROM azure.main.security_incidents() WHERE _row_kind = 'marker'

vgi.example_queries.description: Authoritative alert feed, high severity only
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id, title, severity, category FROM azure.main.security_alerts() WHERE _row_kind = 'alert' AND severity = 'high'

vgi.example_queries.description: Active incidents ranked by how many distinct MITRE ATT&CK techniques their alerts carry in the authoritative security_alerts feed (incidents with no technique-tagged alert in the window are omitted)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT i.id, i.display_name, i.severity, count(DISTINCT t.technique) AS technique_count, list_sort(list(DISTINCT t.technique)) AS techniques FROM azure.main.security_incidents() AS i JOIN (SELECT incident_id, unnest(mitre_techniques) AS technique FROM azure.main.security_alerts() WHERE _row_kind = 'alert') AS t ON t.incident_id = i.id WHERE i._row_kind = 'incident' AND i.status = 'active' GROUP BY i.id, i.display_name, i.severity ORDER BY technique_count DESC, i.id

vgi.example_queries.description: For incidents whose expanded alert set was capped (_alerts_truncated), list every alert from the authoritative security_alerts feed updated in the same lookback window
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT a.incident_id, a.id AS alert_id, a.title, a.severity, a.status FROM azure.main.security_alerts() AS a WHERE a._row_kind = 'alert' AND a.incident_id IN (SELECT id FROM azure.main.security_incidents() WHERE _row_kind = 'incident' AND _alerts_truncated) ORDER BY a.incident_id, a.id

## security_incidents

Microsoft 365 Defender / Sentinel incidents as an incremental watermark feed backed by the Microsoft Graph `/security/incidents` endpoint (`$expand=alerts`). The row stream interleaves incident rows (`_row_kind = 'incident'`) with their correlated alert rows (`_row_kind = 'alert'`, `incident_id` = parent), closed by one marker row (`_row_kind = 'marker'`) whose `_watermark_next` is the cursor to persist.

workers.doc_md:
## Microsoft Entra Directory

Incremental (delta) access to Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) directory objects via Microsoft Graph: users (including removals), groups and devices, each as an incremental change feed.

Each feed returns changed objects plus a single marker row (`_row_kind = 'marker'`) whose `_delta_next` column holds the verbatim `@odata.deltaLink` to persist and replay on the next scan. Call with no arguments for a full sync; pass `delta_token := '<link>'` for an incremental sync. An app-only `azure_graph` secret (Microsoft Entra client credentials) is required.

### Sources and references

- [Microsoft Graph delta query overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/delta-query-overview) — how `@odata.deltaLink` change tracking works
- [user: delta](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/user-delta) — users feed
- [group: delta](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/group-delta) — groups feed
- [device: delta](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/device-delta) — devices feed
- [Register an app](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity-platform/quickstart-register-app) — create the app-only client credentials, then grant `User.Read.All` / `Group.Read.All` / `Device.Read.All`

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The Microsoft Entra ID directory delta functions. Each function is an incremental change feed for one object type — users, groups, or devices — driven by Microsoft Graph's delta query. A scan returns rows for objects created/updated (change_type 'upsert') or deleted (change_type 'removed') since the supplied delta_token, followed by one marker row whose _delta_next column is the cursor to persist for the next scan. Omit delta_token for a full sync; the $select projection is pinned for the life of a token.

workers.doc_md:
## Microsoft 365 Content Delta

Incremental (delta) access to Microsoft 365 content via Microsoft Graph: OneDrive / SharePoint document-library files and folders as a per-drive change feed (with removals and an opt-in, short-lived download capability column), and SharePoint list items as a per-list change feed (with removals; `$expand=fields` materializes user-defined columns).

Each feed returns changed items plus a single marker row (`_row_kind = 'marker'`) whose `_delta_next` column holds the verbatim `@odata.deltaLink` to persist and replay on the next scan. Call with no `delta_token` for a full sync; pass `delta_token := '<link>'` for an incremental sync. Each invocation is a single-resource cursor atom — the caller holds the `{resourceId -> deltaLink}` map. An app-only `azure_graph` secret (Microsoft Entra client credentials) is required.

### Sources and references

- [driveItem: delta](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/driveitem-delta) — the OneDrive / SharePoint drive change feed
- [listItem: delta](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/listitem-delta) — the SharePoint list-item change feed
- [Selected permissions (Sites.Selected)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/permissions-selected-overview) — the least-privilege per-site grant
- [Register an app](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity-platform/quickstart-register-app) — create the app-only client credentials for the `azure_graph` secret

agent_tasks: List the files in the OneDrive / SharePoint document library with drive id '<driveId>', showing each file's name and size.
After scanning a drive with drive_items, how do I get the cursor to use for the next incremental sync?
Using a previously saved delta cursor, fetch only the SharePoint list items in site '<siteId>' list '<listId>' that changed since the last scan, including which ones were removed.
What kinds of Microsoft 365 content can I sync with this catalog, and which table function serves each?

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The Microsoft 365 content delta functions. Each function is an incremental change feed for one kind of resource — a document library's driveItems, or a SharePoint list's listItems — driven by Microsoft Graph's delta query. A scan returns rows for items created/updated (change_type 'upsert') or deleted (change_type 'removed') since the supplied delta_token, followed by one marker row whose _delta_next column is the cursor to persist for the next scan. Omit delta_token for a full sync; the $select / $expand / $top projection is pinned for the life of a token. Each call is a single-resource cursor atom — the {resourceId -> deltaLink} map is held by the caller.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Microsoft 365 content delta functions

Delta table functions over two kinds of Microsoft 365 resource — a OneDrive / SharePoint document library's driveItems and a SharePoint list's listItems — each returning the changed items plus a delta cursor.

Both share the same shape: read data rows with `WHERE _row_kind IS NULL`, and take the next cursor from the single marker row's `_delta_next`. The document-library feed can additionally opt into a short-lived `_download_url` capability column via `include_download_url := true`. Each requires an app-only `azure_graph` secret.

vgi.example_queries.description: Incremental sync of a drive from a saved cursor (upserts and removals)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id, change_type, name FROM azure.main.drive_items('<driveId>', delta_token := '<@odata.deltaLink>')

vgi.example_queries.description: Include the opt-in short-lived download capability URL
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id, name, _download_url FROM azure.main.drive_items('<driveId>', include_download_url := true) WHERE _row_kind IS NULL AND change_type = 'upsert'

vgi.example_queries.description: Full sync of a SharePoint list's items
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id, name, web_url, last_modified_date_time FROM azure.main.sharepoint_list_items('<siteId>', '<listId>') WHERE _row_kind IS NULL

vgi.example_queries.description: Read the delta cursor to persist for a drive's next sync
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT _delta_next FROM azure.main.drive_items('<driveId>') WHERE _row_kind = 'marker'

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
The result schema depends on the `include_download_url` argument.

### Default (`include_download_url := false`)

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | VARCHAR | The item's id. NULL on the marker row. |
| `change_type` | VARCHAR | `upsert` (created/updated) or `removed` (deleted). NULL on the marker row. |
| `removed_reason` | VARCHAR | For removed rows, the `@removed.reason` (`changed` or `deleted`); NULL otherwise. |
| `name` | VARCHAR | The item's name (file/folder name, or the list item's Title). NULL on removed tombstones and the marker row. |
| `size` | BIGINT | The item's size in bytes. NULL for folders, removed tombstones, and the marker row. |
| `web_url` | VARCHAR | Browser URL to the item. NULL on removed tombstones and the marker row. |
| `last_modified_date_time` | VARCHAR | ISO 8601 last-modified timestamp. NULL on removed tombstones and the marker row. |
| `_row_kind` | VARCHAR | NULL for data rows; `marker` for the single trailing cursor row. |
| `_delta_next` | VARCHAR | On the marker row, the verbatim `@odata.deltaLink` to persist and replay as this resource's next cursor; NULL on data rows. |

### With `include_download_url := true`

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | VARCHAR | The item's id. NULL on the marker row. |
| `change_type` | VARCHAR | `upsert` (created/updated) or `removed` (deleted). NULL on the marker row. |
| `removed_reason` | VARCHAR | For removed rows, the `@removed.reason` (`changed` or `deleted`); NULL otherwise. |
| `name` | VARCHAR | The item's name (file/folder name, or the list item's Title). NULL on removed tombstones and the marker row. |
| `size` | BIGINT | The item's size in bytes. NULL for folders, removed tombstones, and the marker row. |
| `web_url` | VARCHAR | Browser URL to the item. NULL on removed tombstones and the marker row. |
| `last_modified_date_time` | VARCHAR | ISO 8601 last-modified timestamp. NULL on removed tombstones and the marker row. |
| `_download_url` | VARCHAR | Only present when `include_download_url := true`. A short-lived, pre-authed, no-bearer download capability URL for live file rows; NULL for folders, removed tombstones, and the marker row. |
| `_row_kind` | VARCHAR | NULL for data rows; `marker` for the single trailing cursor row. |
| `_delta_next` | VARCHAR | On the marker row, the verbatim `@odata.deltaLink` to persist and replay as this resource's next cursor; NULL on data rows. |

arguments.name: drive
arguments.description: REQUIRED. The Microsoft Graph drive id of the OneDrive / SharePoint document library to scan (the `driveId`).

arguments.name: delta_token
arguments.description: A previously persisted `@odata.deltaLink` (the `_delta_next` value from a prior scan's marker row for THIS drive), replayed verbatim to return only what changed since. Empty (the default) performs a full sync.

arguments.name: include_download_url
arguments.description: Opt-in only. When `true`, adds a `_download_url` column carrying a short-lived, pre-authed, no-bearer capability URL for each live file row (never folders or removed tombstones). Omitted from the schema entirely when `false` (the default) — SECURITY: this URL bypasses RBAC if leaked.

arguments.name: page_size
arguments.description: Best-effort Microsoft Graph `$top` page size for the initial full sync (Graph may not honor it). Defaults to 200.

arguments.name: select_fields
arguments.description: Comma-separated Microsoft Graph `$select` projection of driveItem fields to fetch on the initial full sync. Pinned for the life of a delta token (baked into the server's deltaLink). Defaults to `id,name,size,webUrl,lastModifiedDateTime`. (Named `select_fields` rather than `select` because `select` is a reserved SQL keyword and cannot be used bare as a named argument.)

examples: SELECT id, name, size, web_url FROM azure.main.drive_items('<driveId>') WHERE _row_kind IS NULL
SELECT id, change_type, name FROM azure.main.drive_items('<driveId>', delta_token := '<@odata.deltaLink>')
SELECT id, name, _download_url FROM azure.main.drive_items('<driveId>', include_download_url := true) WHERE _row_kind IS NULL AND change_type = 'upsert'
SELECT _delta_next FROM azure.main.drive_items('<driveId>') WHERE _row_kind = 'marker'

workers.doc_md:
## Microsoft Entra Governance

Security-governance snapshots of a Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) tenant via Microsoft Graph: Conditional Access policy posture (state, targets, grant/session controls), directory role assignments (active plus PIM-eligible, told apart by an `assignment_kind` discriminator), and app / service-principal credential hygiene (password and key credentials with scan-time expiry).

Each surface is a full-pull snapshot (no delta cursor, no marker row): every scan returns the complete current state, so refresh by replacing the target table wholesale. An app-only `azure_graph` secret (Microsoft Entra client credentials) is required.

### Sources and references

- [List Conditional Access policies](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/conditionalaccessroot-list-policies) — `conditional_access_policies`
- [List role assignments](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/rbacapplication-list-roleassignments) — active directory-role assignments
- [List role eligibility schedule instances](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/rbacapplication-list-roleeligibilityscheduleinstances) — PIM-eligible assignments
- [List applications](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/application-list) — app credential metadata (service principals are read the same way)
- [Register an app](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity-platform/quickstart-register-app) — create the app-only client credentials, then grant `Policy.Read.All`, `RoleManagement.Read.Directory` and `Application.Read.All`

example_queries.title: conditional_access_policies_bind_probe
example_queries.description: Bind conditional_access_policies and expose its result columns (credential-free; drop LIMIT 0 and attach an azure_graph secret to pull real policies)
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, display_name, state FROM azure.main.conditional_access_policies() LIMIT 0;

example_queries.title: role_assignments_bind_probe
example_queries.description: Bind role_assignments and expose its result columns (credential-free; attach an azure_graph secret to pull real assignments)
example_queries.sql: SELECT assignment_kind, principal_id, role_display_name FROM azure.main.role_assignments() LIMIT 0;

example_queries.title: app_credentials_bind_probe
example_queries.description: Bind app_credentials and expose its result columns (credential-free; attach an azure_graph secret to pull real credentials)
example_queries.sql: SELECT owner_display_name, credential_type, end_date_time, days_until_expiry, is_expired FROM azure.main.app_credentials() LIMIT 0;

example_queries.description: Enabled Conditional Access policies
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, display_name, state FROM azure.main.conditional_access_policies() WHERE state = 'enabled'

example_queries.description: PIM-eligible directory role assignments
example_queries.sql: SELECT role_display_name, principal_id, status FROM azure.main.role_assignments() WHERE assignment_kind = 'eligible'

example_queries.description: Credentials expiring within 30 days
example_queries.sql: SELECT owner_display_name, credential_type, end_date_time, days_until_expiry FROM azure.main.app_credentials(expiring_within_days := 30) ORDER BY days_until_expiry

example_queries.description: Already-expired app & service-principal credentials
example_queries.sql: SELECT owner_kind, owner_display_name, credential_type, end_date_time FROM azure.main.app_credentials() WHERE is_expired

example_queries.description: Directory-role holders (active or PIM-eligible) that an enabled Conditional Access policy explicitly excludes by user id — the break-glass / exclusion audit
example_queries.sql: WITH excluded AS (SELECT ca.display_name AS policy_name, x.principal_id FROM azure.main.conditional_access_policies() AS ca, unnest(from_json(ca.excluded_users_json, '["VARCHAR"]')) AS x(principal_id) WHERE ca.state = 'enabled') SELECT e.policy_name, r.role_display_name, r.principal_id, r.assignment_kind FROM excluded AS e JOIN azure.main.role_assignments() AS r ON r.principal_id = e.principal_id ORDER BY e.policy_name, r.role_display_name, r.principal_id, r.assignment_kind

example_queries.description: Held directory roles that no enabled Conditional Access policy targets by role (conditions.users.includeRoles), with the number of distinct holders; policies scoped to all users are not counted
example_queries.sql: WITH targeted AS (SELECT DISTINCT t.role_id FROM azure.main.conditional_access_policies() AS ca, unnest(from_json(json_extract(ca.raw_json, '$.conditions.users.includeRoles'), '["VARCHAR"]')) AS t(role_id) WHERE ca.state = 'enabled') SELECT r.role_display_name, count(DISTINCT r.principal_id) AS holders FROM azure.main.role_assignments() AS r WHERE r.role_definition_id NOT IN (SELECT role_id FROM targeted) GROUP BY r.role_display_name ORDER BY holders DESC, r.role_display_name

example_queries.description: Credentials held directly on a service principal that also holds a directory role, expiring within 30 days or already expired (soonest first), with the roles it holds
example_queries.sql: WITH privileged AS (SELECT principal_id, string_agg(DISTINCT role_display_name, ', ' ORDER BY role_display_name) AS roles FROM azure.main.role_assignments() GROUP BY principal_id) SELECT c.owner_display_name, p.roles, c.credential_type, c.end_date_time, c.days_until_expiry FROM azure.main.app_credentials(expiring_within_days := 30) AS c JOIN privileged AS p ON p.principal_id = c.owner_id WHERE c.owner_kind = 'servicePrincipal' ORDER BY c.days_until_expiry, c.owner_display_name, c.credential_type

example_queries.description: All directory role assignments (active and PIM-eligible)
example_queries.sql: SELECT assignment_kind, role_display_name, principal_id FROM azure.main.role_assignments

example_queries.description: Only PIM-eligible (not yet activated) assignments
example_queries.sql: SELECT role_display_name, principal_id, status FROM azure.main.role_assignments WHERE assignment_kind = 'eligible'

example_queries.description: Active assignment count per directory role
example_queries.sql: SELECT role_display_name, count(*) FROM azure.main.role_assignments WHERE assignment_kind = 'active' GROUP BY role_display_name ORDER BY count(*) DESC

example_queries.description: All Conditional Access policies with their state
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, display_name, state FROM azure.main.conditional_access_policies

example_queries.description: Only the enabled (enforced) policies
example_queries.sql: SELECT display_name FROM azure.main.conditional_access_policies WHERE state = 'enabled'

example_queries.description: Grant controls for each enabled policy
example_queries.sql: SELECT display_name, grant_controls_json FROM azure.main.conditional_access_policies WHERE state = 'enabled'

example_queries.description: All Conditional Access policies with their state
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, display_name, state FROM azure.main.conditional_access_policies()

example_queries.description: Only the enabled (enforced) policies

## Entra governance snapshot functions

Snapshot functions over three governance surfaces of a Microsoft Entra tenant: Conditional Access (one row per policy), directory roles (active ∪ PIM-eligible assignments), and credential hygiene (one row per app / service-principal password or key credential).

All are full-pull snapshots (no `_row_kind` marker, no delta cursor): every scan is the complete current state. Refresh by replacing the target table. Each requires an app-only `azure_graph` secret.

vgi.example_queries.description: Enabled Conditional Access policies
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id, display_name, state FROM azure.main.conditional_access_policies() WHERE state = 'enabled'

vgi.example_queries.description: PIM-eligible directory role assignments
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT role_display_name, principal_id, status FROM azure.main.role_assignments() WHERE assignment_kind = 'eligible'

vgi.example_queries.description: Credentials expiring within 30 days
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT owner_display_name, credential_type, end_date_time, days_until_expiry FROM azure.main.app_credentials(expiring_within_days := 30) ORDER BY days_until_expiry

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT owner_kind, owner_display_name, credential_type, end_date_time FROM azure.main.app_credentials() WHERE is_expired

vgi.example_queries.description: Directory-role holders (active or PIM-eligible) that an enabled Conditional Access policy explicitly excludes by user id — the break-glass / exclusion audit
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH excluded AS (SELECT ca.display_name AS policy_name, x.principal_id FROM azure.main.conditional_access_policies() AS ca, unnest(from_json(ca.excluded_users_json, '["VARCHAR"]')) AS x(principal_id) WHERE ca.state = 'enabled') SELECT e.policy_name, r.role_display_name, r.principal_id, r.assignment_kind FROM excluded AS e JOIN azure.main.role_assignments() AS r ON r.principal_id = e.principal_id ORDER BY e.policy_name, r.role_display_name, r.principal_id, r.assignment_kind

vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH targeted AS (SELECT DISTINCT t.role_id FROM azure.main.conditional_access_policies() AS ca, unnest(from_json(json_extract(ca.raw_json, '$.conditions.users.includeRoles'), '["VARCHAR"]')) AS t(role_id) WHERE ca.state = 'enabled') SELECT r.role_display_name, count(DISTINCT r.principal_id) AS holders FROM azure.main.role_assignments() AS r WHERE r.role_definition_id NOT IN (SELECT role_id FROM targeted) GROUP BY r.role_display_name ORDER BY holders DESC, r.role_display_name

vgi.example_queries.description: Credentials held directly on a service principal that also holds a directory role, expiring within 30 days or already expired (soonest first), with the roles it holds
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH privileged AS (SELECT principal_id, string_agg(DISTINCT role_display_name, ', ' ORDER BY role_display_name) AS roles FROM azure.main.role_assignments() GROUP BY principal_id) SELECT c.owner_display_name, p.roles, c.credential_type, c.end_date_time, c.days_until_expiry FROM azure.main.app_credentials(expiring_within_days := 30) AS c JOIN privileged AS p ON p.principal_id = c.owner_id WHERE c.owner_kind = 'servicePrincipal' ORDER BY c.days_until_expiry, c.owner_display_name, c.credential_type

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## app_credentials

Flattened inventory of every password (client secret) and key (certificate) credential on the tenant's applications and service principals, with a scan-time expiry snapshot (`days_until_expiry`, `is_expired`). No secret material is returned — metadata only.

Pass `expiring_within_days := 30` to keep only credentials expiring within the next 30 days (already-expired credentials have a negative `days_until_expiry` and stay in), or omit the argument for the full inventory. Order by `days_until_expiry` to surface the most urgent rotations first. Runnable, copy-pasteable queries live in this function's example queries.

workers.title: Azure Monitor Log Analytics
workers.subtitle: Run KQL queries against Azure Monitor Log Analytics workspaces from SQL, with incremental watermark pulls.
workers.summary: Azure Monitor / Log Analytics KQL passthrough (loganalytics_query) — vgi-azure-loganalytics
workers.doc_md:
## Azure Monitor Log Analytics

KQL passthrough to an Azure Monitor / Log Analytics workspace, exposed as one DuckDB table function.

- **`loganalytics_query`** — run verbatim KQL against a workspace; each Kusto row is returned as one JSON `result` string, with an optional `TimeGenerated` watermark for incremental pulls.

Pass the KQL text and workspace GUID (both required). For a snapshot, set `timespan` (an ISO-8601 duration/range, default `P1D`). For incremental use, project `TimeGenerated` in the KQL and pass `since := '<prior _watermark_next>'`; the function then emits the changed rows plus a single marker row (`_row_kind = 'marker'`) whose `_watermark_next` column is the cursor to persist and replay. An app-only `azure_graph` secret (Microsoft Entra client credentials) with workspace read access is required.

### Sources and references

- [Azure Monitor Log Analytics API overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/logs/api/overview) — the query API and its authentication
- [Query - Execute REST API](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/rest/api/loganalytics/dataaccess/query/execute) — the endpoint `loganalytics_query` calls
- [Kusto Query Language (KQL) reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/kusto/query/) — the query language passed through verbatim
- [Register an app](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity-platform/quickstart-register-app) — create the app-only client credentials for the `azure_graph` secret

example_queries.title: query_bind_probe
example_queries.description: Bind loganalytics_query and expose its result columns (credential-free; drop LIMIT 0 and attach an azure_graph secret to run the KQL against a real workspace)
example_queries.sql: SELECT result, _row_kind, _watermark_next FROM azure.main.loganalytics_query('AzureActivity | take 1', '00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000') LIMIT 0;

example_queries.description: Snapshot: the 100 most recent audit-log entries over the last day
example_queries.sql: SELECT result FROM azure.main.loganalytics_query('AuditLogs | take 100', '<workspace-guid>') WHERE _row_kind IS NULL

example_queries.description: Last-day ingested GB per table from the Usage table, joined to loganalytics_tables for each table's category (NULL for tables outside the curated index), largest first
example_queries.sql: SELECT u.result->>'DataType' AS table_name, t.category, CAST(u.result->>'IngestedGB' AS DOUBLE) AS ingested_gb FROM azure.main.loganalytics_query('Usage | summarize IngestedGB = sum(Quantity) / 1000 by DataType', '<workspace-guid>') u LEFT JOIN azure.main.loganalytics_tables t ON t.table_name = u.result->>'DataType' WHERE u._row_kind IS NULL ORDER BY ingested_gb DESC, table_name

example_queries.description: Curated tables from loganalytics_tables (other than Usage itself) with no ingestion recorded in the workspace's Usage table over the last day (e.g. a diagnostic setting or agent that is not sending data)
example_queries.sql: SELECT t.table_name, t.category FROM azure.main.loganalytics_tables t WHERE t.table_name <> 'Usage' AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM azure.main.loganalytics_query('Usage | summarize IngestedGB = sum(Quantity) / 1000 by DataType', '<workspace-guid>') u WHERE u._row_kind IS NULL AND u.result->>'DataType' = t.table_name) ORDER BY t.category, t.table_name

example_queries.description: Count sign-in events by result type over the last hour
example_queries.sql: SELECT result FROM azure.main.loganalytics_query('SigninLogs | summarize count() by ResultType', '<workspace-guid>', timespan := 'PT1H') WHERE _row_kind IS NULL

example_queries.description: Incremental pull replaying a saved TimeGenerated watermark
example_queries.sql: SELECT result FROM azure.main.loganalytics_query('SigninLogs | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName', '<workspace-guid>', since := '<prior _watermark_next>') WHERE _row_kind IS NULL

example_queries.description: Read the watermark cursor to persist for the next incremental scan
example_queries.sql: SELECT _watermark_next FROM azure.main.loganalytics_query('SigninLogs | project TimeGenerated', '<workspace-guid>', since := '2026-01-01T00:00:00Z') WHERE _row_kind = 'marker'

example_queries.description: List every curated table and its category
example_queries.sql: SELECT table_name, category FROM azure.main.loganalytics_tables ORDER BY category, table_name

example_queries.description: Get the starter KQL for the identity tables
example_queries.sql: SELECT table_name, sample_kql FROM azure.main.loganalytics_tables WHERE category = 'identity' ORDER BY table_name

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Log Analytics query function

| Function | Purpose | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `loganalytics_query` | Run verbatim KQL against a workspace | one JSON `result` per Kusto row (+ optional watermark) |

Read data rows with `WHERE _row_kind IS NULL`; on an incremental (`since`) pull, take the next cursor from the single marker row's `_watermark_next`. Requires an app-only `azure_graph` secret with read access to the target workspace.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Run an arbitrary Kusto (KQL) query against an Azure Monitor / Log Analytics workspace and get the results back as SQL rows. The KQL text (`kql`) is sent verbatim to the workspace (`workspace`, a GUID); each Kusto result row is returned as one JSON `result` string (all its projected columns encoded together, since the output schema is fixed for any KQL). A snapshot call reads a `timespan` window (default P1D). For incremental use, project `TimeGenerated` in the KQL and pass `since := '<prior _watermark_next>'`: the function returns rows newer than that watermark (at-least-once within a safety lag) followed by one marker row whose `_watermark_next` is the cursor to persist. Requires an app-only `azure_graph` secret with workspace read access.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## loganalytics_query

KQL passthrough to an Azure Monitor / Log Analytics workspace. The `kql` text is sent verbatim; each Kusto result row comes back as one JSON `result` string. Read data rows by filtering `_row_kind IS NULL`. For incremental pulls, project `TimeGenerated`, pass `since`, and take the next cursor from the marker row's `_watermark_next` (the marker row is the one whose `_row_kind` equals `marker`).

A snapshot call reads the `timespan` window (default `P1D`); an incremental call projects `TimeGenerated`, passes `since`, and takes the next cursor from the marker row's `_watermark_next`. Aggregations (`summarize`) run server-side in the workspace and come back one JSON `result` per group. Large result sets (>~500k rows / 64MB) must be time-sliced by the caller via `timespan` or `since`. Requires an app-only `azure_graph` secret with workspace read access.

workers.doc_md:
## Azure Resource Graph

Whole-estate Azure inventory via Azure Resource Graph (ARG), exposed as one DuckDB table function.

- **`resourcegraph_query`** — run one KQL query across the ARM estate; returns one JSON `result` string per resource (a point-in-time snapshot, no change feed).

The KQL string is required (positional); optionally scope to specific subscriptions and tune the ARG page size. Each result row is a JSON object — extract fields with `json_extract(result, '$.name')` or the `->` / `->>` operators. An app-only `azure_graph` secret (Microsoft Entra client credentials, Reader on the target subscriptions) is required to fetch data.

### Sources and references

- [Azure Resource Graph overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/governance/resource-graph/overview) — what ARG indexes
- [Resources REST API](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/rest/api/azureresourcegraph/resourcegraph/resources/resources) — the `Microsoft.ResourceGraph/resources` endpoint `resourcegraph_query` calls
- [Resource Graph query language](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/governance/resource-graph/concepts/query-language) — supported KQL tables and operators
- [Register an app](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity-platform/quickstart-register-app) — create the app-only client credentials, then grant Reader on the target subscriptions

example_queries.title: resourcegraph_bind_probe
example_queries.description: Bind resourcegraph_query and expose its result column (credential-free; drop LIMIT 0 and attach an azure_graph secret to run the KQL against your estate)
example_queries.sql: SELECT result FROM azure.main.resourcegraph_query('Resources | project name, type, location') LIMIT 0;

example_queries.description: Count resources by type across the estate
example_queries.sql: SELECT result ->> 'type' AS type, count(*) FROM azure.main.resourcegraph_query('Resources | project type') GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC

example_queries.description: Count resources per subscription by display name: join a Resources count per subscriptionId to the subscription rows of ResourceContainers
example_queries.sql: WITH subs AS (SELECT result ->> 'subscriptionId' AS subscription_id, result ->> 'name' AS subscription_name FROM azure.main.resourcegraph_query('ResourceContainers | where type =~ ''microsoft.resources/subscriptions'' | project subscriptionId, name')) SELECT s.subscription_name, CAST(r.result ->> 'n' AS BIGINT) AS resources FROM azure.main.resourcegraph_query('Resources | summarize n = count() by subscriptionId') r JOIN subs s ON s.subscription_id = r.result ->> 'subscriptionId' ORDER BY resources DESC, s.subscription_name

example_queries.description: Find resources deployed in a different region than their resource group (global and location-less resources excluded): join Resources to the resource-group rows of ResourceContainers
example_queries.sql: WITH rgs AS (SELECT result ->> 'subscriptionId' AS subscription_id, lower(result ->> 'name') AS resource_group, result ->> 'location' AS group_location FROM azure.main.resourcegraph_query('ResourceContainers | where type =~ ''microsoft.resources/subscriptions/resourcegroups'' | project subscriptionId, name, location')) SELECT g.resource_group, r.result ->> 'name' AS name, r.result ->> 'type' AS type, r.result ->> 'location' AS location, g.group_location FROM azure.main.resourcegraph_query('Resources | where isnotempty(location) and location != ''global'' | project name, type, resourceGroup, location, subscriptionId') r JOIN rgs g ON g.subscription_id = r.result ->> 'subscriptionId' AND g.resource_group = lower(r.result ->> 'resourceGroup') WHERE r.result ->> 'location' <> g.group_location ORDER BY g.resource_group, name

example_queries.description: List storage accounts with their resource group
example_queries.sql: SELECT result ->> 'name' AS name, result ->> 'resourceGroup' AS resource_group FROM azure.main.resourcegraph_query('Resources | where type =~ ''microsoft.storage/storageaccounts'' | project name, resourceGroup')

example_queries.description: Query a single subscription by GUID
example_queries.sql: SELECT result FROM azure.main.resourcegraph_query('Resources | project name, location', subscriptions := '00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000')

example_queries.description: List every curated KQL recipe with what it returns
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, description FROM azure.main.kql_recipes ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: First 100 resources as JSON, projecting name, type, and location
example_queries.sql: SELECT result FROM azure.main.resourcegraph_query('Resources | project name, type, location') LIMIT 100

example_queries.description: Count resources by type across the whole estate
example_queries.sql: SELECT result ->> 'type' AS type, count(*) AS n FROM azure.main.resourcegraph_query('Resources | project type') GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY n DESC

example_queries.description: List storage account names alongside their resource group
example_queries.sql: SELECT result ->> 'name' AS name, result ->> 'resourceGroup' AS resource_group FROM azure.main.resourcegraph_query('Resources | where type =~ ''microsoft.storage/storageaccounts'' | project name, resourceGroup') ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Scope the query to one subscription GUID with a 500-resource page size
example_queries.sql: SELECT result FROM azure.main.resourcegraph_query('Resources | project name, location', subscriptions := '00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000', page_size := 500)

workers.doc_md:
## Microsoft Entra ID Protection Risk

Incremental access to the Microsoft Entra ID Protection risk feed via Microsoft Graph, exposed as DuckDB table functions: current per-user and per-workload-identity risk state (the source of truth for the verdict) and the immutable stream of risk detection events.

Each function returns data rows plus a single marker row (`_row_kind = 'marker'`) whose `_watermark_next` column holds the ISO-8601 instant to persist and replay as the next scan's `since`. Call with no arguments for a full sync from epoch; pass `since := '<_watermark_next>'` for an incremental sync. Always reconcile a detection event against the affected user's current risk state for the verdict. Requires an app-only `azure_graph` secret, the three `Identity*.Read.All` Graph permissions, and an Entra ID P2 license.

### Sources and references

- [Microsoft Entra ID Protection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/id-protection/overview-identity-protection) — what user/workload risk means and the P2 licensing requirement
- [Identity Protection Graph API overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/resources/identityprotection-overview) — the riskyUsers / riskyServicePrincipals / riskDetections resources
- [List riskyUsers](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/riskyuser-list) — `risky_users`
- [List riskDetections](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/riskdetection-list) — `risk_detections`
- [List riskyServicePrincipals](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/identityprotectionroot-list-riskyserviceprincipals) — `risky_service_principals`

example_queries.title: risky_users_bind_probe
example_queries.description: Bind risky_users and expose its result columns (credential-free; drop LIMIT 0 and attach an azure_graph secret to sync real data)
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, user_principal_name, risk_level, risk_state FROM azure.main.risky_users() LIMIT 0;

example_queries.title: risk_detections_bind_probe
example_queries.description: Bind risk_detections and expose its result columns (credential-free; attach an azure_graph secret to sync real data)
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, user_id, risk_event_type, detected_date_time FROM azure.main.risk_detections() LIMIT 0;

example_queries.title: risky_service_principals_bind_probe
example_queries.description: Bind risky_service_principals and expose its result columns (credential-free; attach an azure_graph secret to sync real data)
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, app_id, display_name, risk_level, risk_state FROM azure.main.risky_service_principals() LIMIT 0;

example_queries.description: Users currently at risk
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, user_principal_name, risk_level FROM azure.main.risky_users() WHERE _row_kind IS NULL AND risk_state = 'atRisk'

example_queries.description: Incremental sync of risk detections from a saved watermark
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, user_id, risk_event_type FROM azure.main.risk_detections(since := '<_watermark_next>') WHERE _row_kind IS NULL

example_queries.description: Reconcile detections against the current per-user verdict (mandatory §2c join)
example_queries.sql: SELECT d.id, d.risk_event_type, u.risk_state AS current_verdict FROM azure.main.risk_detections() d JOIN azure.main.risky_users() u ON d.user_id = u.id WHERE d._row_kind IS NULL AND u._row_kind IS NULL ORDER BY d.id

example_queries.description: Detections whose own risk_state is stale: the detection still says one thing (e.g. atRisk) while the user's current verdict in risky_users has moved on (e.g. remediated or confirmedCompromised)
example_queries.sql: SELECT d.id, d.user_principal_name, d.risk_event_type, d.risk_state AS detection_state, u.risk_state AS current_verdict FROM azure.main.risk_detections() d JOIN azure.main.risky_users() u ON d.user_id = u.id WHERE d._row_kind IS NULL AND u._row_kind IS NULL AND d.risk_state IS DISTINCT FROM u.risk_state ORDER BY d.detected_date_time DESC, d.id

example_queries.description: Triage list: every user currently atRisk or confirmedCompromised with their number of risk detections, the latest detection time, and the distinct detection types (users with no detections show 0)
example_queries.sql: SELECT u.user_principal_name, u.risk_level, u.risk_state, count(d.id) AS detections, max(d.detected_date_time) AS last_detected, list(DISTINCT d.risk_event_type ORDER BY d.risk_event_type) FILTER (WHERE d.id IS NOT NULL) AS event_types FROM azure.main.risky_users() u LEFT JOIN azure.main.risk_detections() d ON d.user_id = u.id AND d._row_kind IS NULL WHERE u._row_kind IS NULL AND u.risk_state IN ('atRisk', 'confirmedCompromised') GROUP BY u.user_principal_name, u.risk_level, u.risk_state ORDER BY detections DESC, u.user_principal_name

example_queries.description: High-risk service principals
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, app_id, display_name FROM azure.main.risky_service_principals() WHERE _row_kind IS NULL AND risk_level = 'high'

example_queries.description: List every risk feed and the table function that serves it
example_queries.sql: SELECT collection, table_function FROM azure.main.risk_collections ORDER BY collection

example_queries.description: Find the state feeds and their watermark field
example_queries.sql: SELECT collection, watermark_field FROM azure.main.risk_collections WHERE kind = 'state'

example_queries.description: Full sync of all risky service principals (data rows only)
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, app_id, display_name, risk_level, risk_state FROM azure.main.risky_service_principals() WHERE _row_kind IS NULL

example_queries.description: Read the watermark to persist for the next sync
example_queries.sql: SELECT _watermark_next FROM azure.main.risky_service_principals() WHERE _row_kind = 'marker'

example_queries.description: Full sync of all risk detections (data rows only)
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, user_id, risk_event_type, detected_date_time FROM azure.main.risk_detections() WHERE _row_kind IS NULL

example_queries.description: Read the watermark to persist for the next sync
example_queries.sql: SELECT _watermark_next FROM azure.main.risk_detections() WHERE _row_kind = 'marker'

example_queries.description: Full sync of users currently at risk (data rows only)
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, user_principal_name, risk_level, risk_state FROM azure.main.risky_users() WHERE _row_kind IS NULL AND risk_state = 'atRisk'

example_queries.description: Incremental sync replaying a previously saved watermark
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, user_principal_name, risk_detail FROM azure.main.risky_users(since := '<_watermark_next>') WHERE _row_kind IS NULL

## Entra ID Protection risk functions

Two kinds of feed: **state** feeds (one mutable row per user or service principal, watermarked on `risk_last_updated_date_time`) and an **event** feed of immutable detections (watermarked on `detected_date_time`). The `risk_collections` view indexes them without credentials.

Every feed shares the same shape: read data rows with `WHERE _row_kind IS NULL`, and take the next cursor from the single marker row's `_watermark_next`. Each requires an app-only `azure_graph` secret and an Entra ID P2 license.

arguments.name: page_size

arguments.name: safety_lag

A detection's riskState transitions in place without moving detectedDateTime, so this cursor never re-surfaces a verdict change — consumers MUST join userId <-> risky_users.id and read the CURRENT verdict there (§2c), never act on the detection's own (possibly stale) riskState.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Immutable detection EVENTS from Microsoft Entra ID Protection via Microsoft Graph — each row is one risk detection (e.g. unfamiliarFeatures, anonymizedIPAddress) created once and never moved. Reach for it to answer 'what risk events fired, of what type, for which user, from where'. IMPORTANT: a detection's own risk_state transitions in place WITHOUT moving detected_date_time, so this cursor never re-surfaces a verdict change — consumers MUST join user_id <-> risky_users.id and read the CURRENT verdict there, never act on the detection's own (possibly stale) risk_state. Incremental via a lagged `TIMESTAMP` watermark on detected_date_time: pass since := <prior _watermark_next>, or omit since for a full sync from epoch. Read data rows with WHERE _row_kind IS NULL and persist the marker row's _watermark_next. Requires an app-only azure_graph secret with IdentityRiskEvent.Read.All and Entra ID P2.

functions.name: risky_users
functions.comment: Entra ID Protection risky users (current per-user risk STATE) via Microsoft Graph, lagged-watermark on riskLastUpdatedDateTime. SOURCE OF TRUTH for current riskState: any risk_detections row MUST be reconciled against the matching risky_users row (join userId <-> id) before acting — a detection's riskState can be stale (§2c). Absence from a page NEVER means 'cleared'; dismissal is a riskState field change, not a delete.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Current per-user risk STATE from Microsoft Entra ID Protection via Microsoft Graph. Reach for it to answer 'which users are risky right now and how bad', reading risk_level (low/medium/high/hidden) and risk_state (atRisk/confirmedCompromised/dismissed/remediated). This is the SOURCE OF TRUTH for the current verdict — any risk_detections row MUST be reconciled against the matching risky_users row (join risk_detections.user_id <-> risky_users.id) before acting, because a detection's own risk_state can be stale. Incremental via a lagged `TIMESTAMP` watermark on risk_last_updated_date_time: pass since := <prior _watermark_next>, or omit since for a full sync from epoch. Read data rows with WHERE _row_kind IS NULL and persist the marker row's _watermark_next as the next cursor. Requires an app-only azure_graph secret with IdentityRiskyUser.Read.All and an Entra ID P2 license.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## risky_users

Current per-user risk state from Microsoft Entra ID Protection, backed by Graph `identityProtection/riskyUsers` with a lagged-watermark cursor on `risk_last_updated_date_time`.

Read data rows with `WHERE _row_kind IS NULL`; persist the marker row's `_watermark_next` and replay it as `since` on the next scan. This table is the source of truth for the current verdict — reconcile any `risk_detections` row against it (join `user_id` <-> `id`).

vgi.example_queries.description: Full sync of users currently at risk (data rows only)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id, user_principal_name, risk_level, risk_state FROM azure.main.risky_users() WHERE _row_kind IS NULL AND risk_state = 'atRisk'

vgi.example_queries.description: Triage list: every user currently atRisk or confirmedCompromised with their number of risk detections, the latest detection time, and the distinct detection types (users with no detections show 0)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT u.user_principal_name, u.risk_level, u.risk_state, count(d.id) AS detections, max(d.detected_date_time) AS last_detected, list(DISTINCT d.risk_event_type ORDER BY d.risk_event_type) FILTER (WHERE d.id IS NOT NULL) AS event_types FROM azure.main.risky_users() u LEFT JOIN azure.main.risk_detections() d ON d.user_id = u.id AND d._row_kind IS NULL WHERE u._row_kind IS NULL AND u.risk_state IN ('atRisk', 'confirmedCompromised') GROUP BY u.user_principal_name, u.risk_level, u.risk_state ORDER BY detections DESC, u.user_principal_name

vgi.example_queries.description: Incremental sync replaying a previously saved watermark
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id, user_principal_name, risk_detail FROM azure.main.risky_users(since := '<_watermark_next>') WHERE _row_kind IS NULL

workers.summary: Microsoft Entra sign-in & directory audit logs via Graph (lagged-watermark cursor) — vgi-azure-signins
workers.doc_md:
## Microsoft Entra Audit & Sign-in Logs

Incremental (lagged-watermark) access to Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) audit and sign-in logs via Microsoft Graph, exposed as DuckDB table functions: interactive sign-in events (`/auditLogs/signIns`, requires Entra ID P1/P2) and directory audit / activity events (`/auditLogs/directoryAudits`, available more broadly).

Each function returns events in the requested time window plus a single marker row (`_row_kind = 'marker'`) whose `_watermark_next` column holds the ISO-8601 (already lag-adjusted) high-watermark to persist and replay via the `since` argument on the next scan. Call with no arguments to backfill; pass `since := '<watermark>'` for an incremental scan. Apply idempotently (dedup-by-id) because the safety-lag overlap re-emits the window tail. An app-only `azure_graph` secret is required.

### Sources and references

- [Microsoft Graph audit logs overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/resources/azure-ad-auditlog-overview) — the sign-in and directory-audit log resources and their licensing
- [List signIns](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/signin-list) — the `/auditLogs/signIns` endpoint
- [List directoryAudits](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/directoryaudit-list) — the `/auditLogs/directoryAudits` endpoint
- [Get access without a user (app-only auth)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/auth-v2-service) — set up the client-credentials app and grant `AuditLog.Read.All`

example_queries.title: signin_logs_bind_probe
example_queries.description: Bind signin_logs and expose its result columns (credential-free; drop LIMIT 0 and attach an azure_graph secret to sync real sign-in events)
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, created_date_time, app_display_name, user_principal_name, ip_address, status FROM azure.main.signin_logs() LIMIT 0;

example_queries.title: audit_logs_bind_probe
example_queries.description: Bind audit_logs and expose its result columns (credential-free; attach an azure_graph secret to sync real audit events)
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, created_date_time, app_display_name, user_principal_name, ip_address, status FROM azure.main.audit_logs() LIMIT 0;

example_queries.description: Backfill all available sign-in events
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, created_date_time, app_display_name, user_principal_name FROM azure.main.signin_logs() WHERE _row_kind IS NULL

example_queries.description: Incremental sign-in scan from a saved watermark
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, created_date_time, app_display_name FROM azure.main.signin_logs(since := '<prior _watermark_next>') WHERE _row_kind IS NULL

example_queries.description: Failed sign-ins per application (non-zero errorCode)
example_queries.sql: SELECT app_display_name, count(*) AS failures FROM azure.main.signin_logs() WHERE _row_kind IS NULL AND status <> '0' GROUP BY app_display_name ORDER BY failures DESC

example_queries.description: Read the sign-in watermark cursor to persist for the next scan
example_queries.sql: SELECT _watermark_next FROM azure.main.signin_logs() WHERE _row_kind = 'marker'

example_queries.description: Directory audit events grouped by logging service
example_queries.sql: SELECT app_display_name, count(*) AS events FROM azure.main.audit_logs() WHERE _row_kind IS NULL GROUP BY app_display_name ORDER BY events DESC

example_queries.description: Users with failed sign-ins who later initiated directory audit events: failed sign-in count, first failure time, and how many audit events they initiated after it (users with no later audit event are omitted)
example_queries.sql: WITH failed AS (SELECT user_principal_name, count(*) AS failed_signins, min(created_date_time::TIMESTAMPTZ) AS first_failure FROM azure.main.signin_logs() WHERE _row_kind IS NULL AND status <> '0' GROUP BY user_principal_name) SELECT f.user_principal_name, f.failed_signins, f.first_failure, count(*) AS audit_events_after FROM failed AS f JOIN azure.main.audit_logs() AS a ON a.user_principal_name = f.user_principal_name AND a.created_date_time::TIMESTAMPTZ > f.first_failure WHERE a._row_kind IS NULL GROUP BY f.user_principal_name, f.failed_signins, f.first_failure ORDER BY audit_events_after DESC, f.user_principal_name

example_queries.description: Directory audit events initiated from an IP address that also produced failed sign-ins, listing the users whose sign-ins failed from that IP (catches a different account acting from the same source)
example_queries.sql: SELECT a.id, a.created_date_time, a.app_display_name, a.user_principal_name AS initiated_by, a.status, s.failed_signin_users FROM azure.main.audit_logs() AS a JOIN (SELECT ip_address, list_sort(list(DISTINCT user_principal_name)) AS failed_signin_users FROM azure.main.signin_logs() WHERE _row_kind IS NULL AND status <> '0' GROUP BY ip_address) AS s ON s.ip_address = a.ip_address WHERE a._row_kind IS NULL ORDER BY a.created_date_time, a.id

example_queries.description: Per-user activity across both feeds: sign-ins, failed sign-ins, and directory audit events initiated (a user missing from one feed gets 0 there; app-initiated audit events with no user are excluded)
example_queries.sql: WITH s AS (SELECT user_principal_name, count(*) AS signins, count(*) FILTER (WHERE status <> '0') AS failed_signins FROM azure.main.signin_logs() WHERE _row_kind IS NULL GROUP BY user_principal_name), a AS (SELECT user_principal_name, count(*) AS audit_events FROM azure.main.audit_logs() WHERE _row_kind IS NULL AND user_principal_name IS NOT NULL GROUP BY user_principal_name) SELECT coalesce(s.user_principal_name, a.user_principal_name) AS user_principal_name, coalesce(s.signins, 0) AS signins, coalesce(s.failed_signins, 0) AS failed_signins, coalesce(a.audit_events, 0) AS audit_events FROM s FULL OUTER JOIN a ON a.user_principal_name = s.user_principal_name ORDER BY failed_signins DESC, audit_events DESC, user_principal_name

example_queries.description: List every audit feed and the table function that serves it
example_queries.sql: SELECT feed, table_function FROM azure.main.audit_feeds ORDER BY feed

example_queries.description: Find the Graph endpoint backing the sign-in feed
example_queries.sql: SELECT graph_endpoint FROM azure.main.audit_feeds WHERE table_function = 'signin_logs'

example_queries.description: Backfill all available directory audit events (data rows only)
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, created_date_time, app_display_name, user_principal_name, status FROM azure.main.audit_logs() WHERE _row_kind IS NULL

example_queries.description: Incremental scan replaying a previously saved high-watermark cursor
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, created_date_time, app_display_name FROM azure.main.audit_logs(since := '<prior _watermark_next>') WHERE _row_kind IS NULL

example_queries.description: Read the high-watermark cursor to persist for the next scan
example_queries.sql: SELECT _watermark_next FROM azure.main.audit_logs() WHERE _row_kind = 'marker'

example_queries.description: Replay a bounded historical window (since/until); the marker cursor here is replay-only, not the live watermark
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, created_date_time, app_display_name FROM azure.main.audit_logs(since := '2026-01-01T00:00:00Z', until := '2026-02-01T00:00:00Z') WHERE _row_kind IS NULL

example_queries.description: Backfill all available sign-in events (data rows only)
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, created_date_time, app_display_name, user_principal_name, status FROM azure.main.signin_logs() WHERE _row_kind IS NULL

example_queries.description: Narrow the feed server-side to failed sign-ins with an additive OData $filter
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, created_date_time, app_display_name FROM azure.main.signin_logs(filter := 'status/errorCode ne 0') WHERE _row_kind IS NULL

Each scan returns directory activity/change events whose createdDateTime falls in the requested window, followed by a marker row whose _watermark_next is the (already lag-adjusted) high-watermark to persist. ## audit_logs

Microsoft Entra ID directory audit logs as an incremental feed backed by Microsoft Graph's `/auditLogs/directoryAudits` endpoint, cursored by a lagged high-watermark on `createdDateTime`. workers.doc_md:
# Barcode & QR-Code Decoding and Generation for DuckDB

![ZXing logo](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/zxing/zxing/zxing-logo.png)

Read and write barcodes and QR codes directly in SQL: decode QR, EAN, UPC, Code 128, Code 39, Data Matrix, PDF417, Aztec and more out of image BLOBs, and generate scannable barcode PNGs from text — all over Apache Arrow, with no external service.

## What it does and who it's for

The `barcode` extension turns DuckDB into a complete barcode and QR-code toolkit. Data engineers, retail and logistics teams, and anyone holding a column of product photos or scanned documents can pull the encoded text and symbology out of images, or mint fresh barcode/QR images for labels, tickets, and links — entirely in SQL. Decoding is hardened against hostile or oversized input: a corrupt, empty, or giant image yields `NULL` (scalars) or zero rows (tables) instead of crashing the worker, so it is safe to run across untrusted data at scale.

## How it works

Decoding and encoding are powered by [`rxing`](https://github.com/rxing-core/rxing), the maintained Rust port of the venerable [ZXing](https://github.com/zxing/zxing) ("zebra crossing") library. Input rasters (PNG, JPEG, GIF, BMP, WebP) are converted to grayscale and scanned for one or many symbols; text is encoded into a bit matrix and rendered to a PNG `BLOB`. Full API documentation for the underlying library lives at [docs.rs/rxing](https://docs.rs/rxing). The worker streams everything over Apache Arrow IPC, so results flow back into DuckDB as native columns without intermediate files.

## When to reach for it

Reach for this worker to read product or QR codes out of a column of images, to fan a single image that holds several codes into one row per symbol, or to produce scannable barcode and QR PNGs for labels, tickets, and links — without leaving SQL or standing up an external service. Text encoding and image decoding round-trip cleanly, so you can both mint and re-read codes in one query. A quick round-trip looks like:

```sql
SELECT decode_barcode(generate_qr('https://query.farm'));
SELECT generate_barcode('5901234123457', 'EAN_13');
```

tags.vgi.doc_md:
# barcode.main

The primary schema of the barcode worker. It groups the barcode and QR-code capabilities into three areas: **decoding** symbols out of image data, **generating** scannable barcode/QR images from text, and **reference** lookups for the supported symbologies and the worker build.

Decoding accepts raster images (PNG, JPEG, GIF, BMP, WebP) and is hardened against hostile or oversized input — unreadable data yields `NULL` or zero rows rather than an error, so it is safe to run over untrusted data at scale. Generation returns a PNG `BLOB` and raises a clear error only for an unknown symbology or an unencodable payload.

workers.summary: US Bureau of Economic Analysis national, regional, industry and international economic accounts, such as GDP and personal income, as SQL tables with dataset and parameter discovery. Needs a free BEA API key.
workers.doc_md:
# vgi-bea

Discover BEA datasets, parameters and parameter values, then retrieve national, regional, industry and international economic accounts. Use a bea_api secret with api_key or BEA_API_KEY. BEA has no pagination: narrow parameters_json to fit a bounded response; max_rows explicitly caps returned rows. Numeric values retain published units; unit_multiplier is the base-10 exponent and is not applied automatically. Suppressed values become NULL, with original value_text and notes preserved. NULL arguments are rejected. Missing optional response fields return NULL. Upstream errors fail the query; SQL WHERE filters are local.

Queries use bounded HTTP responses and retries. Credentials stay out of continuation state. See README.md for deployment and operational limits.

## Sources and references

example_queries.description: Show the columns datasets() returns without an API key: binding the function with LIMIT 0 resolves its schema and makes no BEA API request

example_queries.description: Discover BEA datasets
example_queries.sql: SELECT dataset_name, description FROM bea.main.datasets() ORDER BY dataset_name

example_queries.description: Retrieve economic accounts
example_queries.sql: SELECT time_period, line_number, value, unit FROM bea.main.data('NIPA', '{"TableName":"T10101","Frequency":"A","Year":"2024"}') ORDER BY time_period, line_number

example_queries.description: Attach source footnote text to each 2024 real GDP growth line by joining data rows to notes on the note references they cite
example_queries.sql: SELECT TRY_CAST(d.line_number AS INTEGER) AS line_no, d.line_description, d.value, d.unit, n.note_text FROM bea.main.data('NIPA', '{"TableName":"T10101","Frequency":"A","Year":"2024"}') AS d LEFT JOIN bea.main.notes('NIPA', '{"TableName":"T10101","Frequency":"A","Year":"2024"}') AS n ON list_contains(string_split(d.note_ref, ','), n.note_ref) ORDER BY line_no, n.note_ref, n.note_text

example_queries.description: Compare each state's 2023 share of the 50-state-plus-DC personal income total (SAINC1 line 1) with its share of population (line 2) and the gap between them, largest income share first
example_queries.sql: WITH income AS (SELECT geo_fips, geo_name, round(100 * value / sum(value) OVER (), 2) AS income_share_pct FROM bea.main.data('Regional', '{"TableName":"SAINC1","LineCode":"1","GeoFips":"STATE","Year":"2023"}') WHERE geo_fips BETWEEN '01000' AND '56000'), population AS (SELECT geo_fips, round(100 * value / sum(value) OVER (), 2) AS population_share_pct FROM bea.main.data('Regional', '{"TableName":"SAINC1","LineCode":"2","GeoFips":"STATE","Year":"2023"}') WHERE geo_fips BETWEEN '01000' AND '56000') SELECT i.geo_fips, i.geo_name, i.income_share_pct, p.population_share_pct, round(i.income_share_pct - p.population_share_pct, 2) AS share_gap_pct FROM income AS i JOIN population AS p ON p.geo_fips = i.geo_fips ORDER BY i.income_share_pct DESC NULLS LAST, i.geo_fips

example_queries.description: Read source notes
example_queries.sql: SELECT note_ref, note_text FROM bea.main.notes('NIPA', '{"TableName":"T10101","Frequency":"A","Year":"2024"}') ORDER BY note_ref, note_text

## main

Discover BEA datasets, parameters and parameter values, then retrieve national, regional, industry and international economic accounts. Use a bea_api secret with api_key or BEA_API_KEY. BEA has no pagination: narrow parameters_json to fit a bounded response; max_rows explicitly caps returned rows. NULL arguments are rejected. Missing optional response fields return NULL. Upstream errors fail the query; SQL WHERE filters are local.

Discover source metadata before querying observations. Use named arguments to select upstream data and ORDER BY for deterministic output.

workers.tagline: Decode BGP MRT routing dumps in DuckDB with SQL — RouteViews/RIPE RIB and updates with AS-path and community helpers. A VGI worker.
workers.subtitle: Query RouteViews and RIPE RIS MRT archives (RIB snapshots and BGP updates) as SQL rows, with AS-path and community helpers.
workers.summary: Decode MRT routing dumps (BGP4MP updates + TABLE_DUMP_V2 RIB snapshots) into SQL rows, reusing the core INET type for prefixes and peer IPs.
workers.doc_md:
# bgp

Decode **MRT** routing dumps — the archive format RouteViews and RIPE RIS publish — directly in SQL. MRT comes in two flavors this worker reads: **BGP4MP** update streams (announcements, withdrawals, and session state changes) and **TABLE_DUMP_V2** RIB snapshots (a full routing table at one instant). Streaming them into rows turns route-leak / hijack / RIB-diff analysis into a JOIN in the engine instead of an ETL-to-Parquet step.

A source argument is a path (local / glob / `s3://` / `http(s)://`) or an inline `BLOB`; `.gz` / `.bz2` inputs auto-decompress. Prefixes, peer IPs, and next hops are DuckDB **INET** values (cast with `::INET`), so containment such as `prefix::INET <<= '203.0.113.0/24'` and prefix joins work directly. AS paths are `LIST(UINTEGER)` and BGP communities are `LIST(VARCHAR)`; scalar helpers operate on those columns. RPKI / route-origin validation is out of scope — JOIN the origin AS against your VRP table (ROV lives in vgi-netflow).

## Sources and references

- [RFC 6396](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6396) — the MRT routing information export format (BGP4MP and TABLE_DUMP_V2)
- [RFC 4271](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4271) — BGP-4, the protocol whose UPDATE messages and path attributes the rows carry
- [RFC 8092](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8092) — BGP large communities (`a:b:c`)
- [RouteViews archive](https://archive.routeviews.org/) and [RIPE RIS raw data](https://ris.ripe.net/docs/mrt/) — public MRT dumps to query
- [bgpkit-parser](https://github.com/bgpkit/bgpkit-parser) — the MRT decoding library this worker uses

Rank the inline RIB routes by AS-path length using the path_length helper on the emitted as_path column.

Diff the built-in sample RIB routes (example_rib) against announcements in the inline update stream: for each peer + prefix announced with a different AS path than the RIB held, compare hop count (path_length) and prepends (as_path_prepends) before and after (both paths got one hop shorter; one lost its prepend).

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## What this schema covers

MRT is the on-the-wire archive format route collectors such as RouteViews and RIPE RIS publish. It comes in two shapes: **BGP4MP** update streams — the announcements, withdrawals, and session-state changes a collector sees over time — and **TABLE_DUMP_V2** RIB snapshots, a full routing table frozen at one instant.

This schema streams those archives into relational rows, so route-leak, prefix-hijack, and RIB-diff analysis becomes a JOIN in the engine instead of an ETL-to-Parquet step. One kind of object streams an archive into rows; another operates on the AS-path and BGP-community values each row carries.

## Data model

Prefixes, peer IPs, and next hops are emitted in DuckDB's core **INET** physical layout, so cast them with `::INET` for containment such as `prefix::INET <<= '203.0.113.0/24'` and for joins against flow or geolocation data. AS paths surface as `UINTEGER[]` and communities as `VARCHAR[]`.

## When to reach for it

Reach for it for route-leak and prefix-hijack investigation, for diffing two RIB snapshots over time, and for origin-AS analysis. Since the catalog name matches the ATTACH name, calls qualify as `bgp.main.<name>(...)`. RPKI / route-origin validation is out of scope here — JOIN the origin AS against your own VRP table.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scan an MRT BGP4MP update stream (a RouteViews / RIPE RIS `updates.*` archive) into one row per BGP message: a prefix announcement, a withdrawal, or an FSM state change. `src` is a path — local, a glob, an `s3://` URL, or an `http(s)://` URL — or an inline `BLOB` of MRT bytes; gzip (`.gz`) and bzip2 (`.bz2`) inputs are decompressed transparently. Each row carries the timestamp, the reporting peer (peer_ip INET, peer_asn), the message_type ('announce' / 'withdraw' / 'state_change'), the prefix (INET), AS path (`LIST(UINTEGER)`), origin ASN, next hop (INET), communities (`LIST(VARCHAR)`), and — for state changes — old_state and new_state. prefix / peer_ip / next_hop are DuckDB INET values (cast with `::INET`) so containment and prefix joins work without parsing strings. Announcements and withdrawals stay in one stream so RIB churn can be reconstructed over time. A malformed record yields a row with NULL fields and a populated `error` column unless `strict => true`. This is the update-stream counterpart of read_rib.

functions.name: read_rib
functions.comment: Read an MRT TABLE_DUMP_V2 RIB snapshot into rows

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scan an MRT TABLE_DUMP_V2 RIB snapshot (a RouteViews / RIPE RIS `rib.*` archive) into one row per (prefix, peer) RIB entry. `src` is a path — local, a glob, an `s3://` URL, or an `http(s)://` URL — or an inline `BLOB` of MRT bytes; gzip (`.gz`) and bzip2 (`.bz2`) inputs are decompressed transparently. Each row carries the route timestamp, RIB view name, the reporting peer (peer_ip INET, peer_asn), the prefix (INET), the AS path (`LIST(UINTEGER)`), origin ASN, next hop (INET), communities (`LIST(VARCHAR)` — standard and large), MED, local pref, atomic-aggregate flag, and aggregator ASN. prefix / peer_ip / next_hop are DuckDB INET values (cast with `::INET`), so prefix containment (`prefix::INET <<= '203.0.113.0/24'`) and joins against vgi-netflow / geoip work without parsing strings. A malformed record yields a row with NULL fields and a populated `error` column unless `strict => true`. This is the RIB counterpart of read_updates.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Scan an MRT TABLE_DUMP_V2 RIB dump into rows: timestamp, view_name, peer_ip (INET), peer_asn, prefix (INET), as_path (`LIST(UINTEGER)`), origin_asn, next_hop (INET), communities (`LIST(VARCHAR)`), med, local_pref, atomic_aggregate, aggregator_asn, and an `error` capture column. `src` is a path / glob / `s3://` / `http(s)://` URL or a `BLOB`; `.gz`/`.bz2` auto-decompress. Cast INET columns with `::INET` for containment.

functions.name: peers
functions.comment: List the distinct peers / collectors in an MRT file

tags.vgi.doc_llm: List the distinct BGP peers in an MRT file: one row per (peer_ip, peer_asn, collector) triple. For a TABLE_DUMP_V2 RIB it returns every peer in the PEER_INDEX_TABLE, with the RIB view name as the `collector`; for a BGP4MP update stream it returns each distinct peer that produced a message, and `collector` is NULL (a raw update stream carries no collector name). Use it to enumerate vantage points before scanning a dump, or to join peer ASNs against attribution data.

functions.comment: Whether an AS path traverses a given ASN

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Return whether an AS path traverses a given ASN anywhere along it. NULL if the path is NULL. Use it to find every route that passes through a suspect transit AS (leak detection).

functions.comment: Parse a standard community 'asn:value' into a STRUCT(asn, value)

Returns a NULL struct for anything that is not a plain two-part community — a large community ('a:b:c'), a well-known mnemonic ('NO_EXPORT'), or NULL input. Use it to filter or group routes by community without a regex.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Parse a standard community into (asn, value), e.g. `community_parse('65001:100')` = {asn: 65001, value: 100}.

functions.comment: Number of AS hops in an AS path

vgi.example_queries.description: Diff the built-in sample RIB routes (example_rib) against announcements in the inline update stream: for each peer + prefix announced with a different AS path than the RIB held, compare hop count (path_length) and prepends (as_path_prepends) before and after (both paths got one hop shorter; one lost its prepend).

workers.title: Bureau of Labor Statistics
workers.tagline: Python VGI worker for BLS labor, employment, inflation and productivity data
workers.subtitle: Retrieve labor, employment, price and productivity series with period codes, footnotes, calculations and survey metadata.
workers.summary: US Bureau of Labor Statistics time series for employment, unemployment, prices, pay and productivity as SQL tables, keeping BLS period codes, footnotes and survey metadata. Works without a key; a free BLS registration key raises the limits.
workers.doc_md:
# vgi-bls

Retrieve labor, employment, price and productivity series with period codes, footnotes, calculations and survey metadata. Use a bls_api secret with api_key or BLS_API_KEY for registered access. Unregistered access has lower limits. Request explicit years and series identifiers; period codes retain annual averages and non-monthly frequencies without inventing dates. NULL arguments are rejected. Missing optional response fields return NULL. Upstream errors fail the query; SQL WHERE filters are local.

Queries use bounded HTTP responses and retries. Credentials stay out of continuation state. See README.md for deployment and operational limits.

## Sources and references

- [U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics](https://www.bls.gov/)
- [BLS Public Data API: getting started](https://www.bls.gov/developers/)
- [API v2 request and response signatures](https://www.bls.gov/developers/api_signature_v2.htm)
- [Register for a BLS API key](https://data.bls.gov/registrationEngine/)

example_queries.title: surveys_columns
example_queries.description: Show the columns surveys() returns without an API key: binding the function with LIMIT 0 resolves its schema and makes no BLS API request
example_queries.sql: SELECT * FROM bls.main.surveys() LIMIT 0;

example_queries.description: Discover BLS surveys
example_queries.sql: SELECT survey_abbreviation, survey_name FROM bls.main.surveys() ORDER BY survey_abbreviation

example_queries.description: Discover popular series
example_queries.sql: SELECT series_id FROM bls.main.popular_series(survey := 'CU') ORDER BY series_id

example_queries.description: Label popular series with the name of the survey they belong to; a BLS series identifier starts with its two-letter survey abbreviation
example_queries.sql: SELECT p.series_id, s.survey_abbreviation, s.survey_name FROM bls.main.popular_series() AS p JOIN bls.main.surveys() AS s ON s.survey_abbreviation = left(p.series_id, 2) ORDER BY p.series_id

example_queries.description: Retrieve labor statistics
example_queries.sql: SELECT year, period, value FROM bls.main.observations(['LNS14000000'], 2024, 2024) ORDER BY year, period

example_queries.description: Label 2024 annual averages (period M13) with each series' published title and seasonality; BLS publishes annual averages for not seasonally adjusted series such as LNU04000000 and CUUR0000SA0, and they require a BLS registration key
example_queries.sql: SELECT o.series_id, m.series_title, m.seasonality, o.value AS annual_average FROM bls.main.observations(['LNU04000000', 'CUUR0000SA0'], 2024, 2024, annual_average := true) AS o JOIN bls.main.series(['LNU04000000', 'CUUR0000SA0'], 2024, 2024) AS m USING (series_id) WHERE o.period = 'M13' ORDER BY o.series_id

example_queries.description: Inspect series metadata
example_queries.sql: SELECT series_id, series_title, seasonality FROM bls.main.series(['LNS14000000'], 2024, 2024) ORDER BY series_id

example_queries.description: Read latest observation
example_queries.sql: SELECT series_id, year, period, value FROM bls.main.latest('LNS14000000') ORDER BY year, period

example_queries.description: Compare the latest unemployment rate with the same period one year earlier and the change; the observations window (2023-2026) must include the year before the latest period, so move it forward as new years are published
example_queries.sql: SELECT l.year, l.period, l.value AS latest_value, p.value AS year_earlier_value, l.value - p.value AS change FROM bls.main.latest('LNS14000000') AS l JOIN bls.main.observations(['LNS14000000'], 2023, 2026) AS p ON p.series_id = l.series_id AND p.period = l.period AND p.year = l.year - 1 ORDER BY l.year, l.period

agent_tasks: Using bls.main.surveys, discover bls surveys. Use the arguments in this example and return the same columns: SELECT survey_abbreviation, survey_name FROM bls.main.surveys() ORDER BY survey_abbreviation
Using bls.main.popular_series, discover popular series. Use the arguments in this example and return the same columns: SELECT series_id FROM bls.main.popular_series(survey := 'CU') ORDER BY series_id

Using bls.main.observations, retrieve labor statistics. Use the arguments in this example and return the same columns: SELECT year, period, value FROM bls.main.observations(['LNS14000000'], 2024, 2024) ORDER BY year, period

Using bls.main.series, inspect series metadata. Use the arguments in this example and return the same columns: SELECT series_id, series_title, seasonality FROM bls.main.series(['LNS14000000'], 2024, 2024) ORDER BY series_id

Using bls.main.latest, read latest observation. Use the arguments in this example and return the same columns: SELECT series_id, year, period, value FROM bls.main.latest('LNS14000000') ORDER BY year, period

Using bls.main.popular_series (overall, no survey argument) and bls.main.surveys, count the popular series in each survey, matching a series to its survey by the series identifier's two-letter prefix. Return columns survey_abbreviation (VARCHAR), survey_name (VARCHAR) and popular_count (BIGINT), one row per survey that has at least one popular series, ordered by survey_abbreviation.

For BLS series CUUR0000SA0 in 2024, return its published series title from bls.main.series together with the highest monthly value from bls.main.observations (monthly periods M01-M12 only; ignore NULL values). Return one row with columns series_id (VARCHAR), series_title (VARCHAR) and peak_value (DOUBLE).
