Unregistered access has lower limits. Request explicit years and series identifiers; period codes retain annual averages and non-monthly frequencies without inventing dates. NULL arguments are rejected. Missing optional response fields return NULL. Upstream errors fail the query; SQL WHERE filters are local.

Discover source metadata before querying observations. Use named arguments to select upstream data and ORDER BY for deterministic output.

vgi.example_queries.description: Discover BLS surveys
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT survey_abbreviation, survey_name FROM bls.main.surveys() ORDER BY survey_abbreviation

vgi.example_queries.description: Discover popular series
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT series_id FROM bls.main.popular_series(survey := 'CU') ORDER BY series_id

vgi.example_queries.description: Label popular series with the name of the survey they belong to; a BLS series identifier starts with its two-letter survey abbreviation
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT p.series_id, s.survey_abbreviation, s.survey_name FROM bls.main.popular_series() AS p JOIN bls.main.surveys() AS s ON s.survey_abbreviation = left(p.series_id, 2) ORDER BY p.series_id

vgi.example_queries.description: Retrieve labor statistics
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT year, period, value FROM bls.main.observations(['LNS14000000'], 2024, 2024) ORDER BY year, period

vgi.example_queries.description: Label 2024 annual averages (period M13) with each series' published title and seasonality; BLS publishes annual averages for not seasonally adjusted series such as LNU04000000 and CUUR0000SA0, and they require a BLS registration key
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT o.series_id, m.series_title, m.seasonality, o.value AS annual_average FROM bls.main.observations(['LNU04000000', 'CUUR0000SA0'], 2024, 2024, annual_average := true) AS o JOIN bls.main.series(['LNU04000000', 'CUUR0000SA0'], 2024, 2024) AS m USING (series_id) WHERE o.period = 'M13' ORDER BY o.series_id

vgi.example_queries.description: Inspect series metadata
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT series_id, series_title, seasonality FROM bls.main.series(['LNS14000000'], 2024, 2024) ORDER BY series_id

vgi.example_queries.description: Read latest observation
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT series_id, year, period, value FROM bls.main.latest('LNS14000000') ORDER BY year, period

vgi.example_queries.description: Compare the latest unemployment rate with the same period one year earlier and the change; the observations window (2023-2026) must include the year before the latest period, so move it forward as new years are published
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT l.year, l.period, l.value AS latest_value, p.value AS year_earlier_value, l.value - p.value AS change FROM bls.main.latest('LNS14000000') AS l JOIN bls.main.observations(['LNS14000000'], 2023, 2026) AS p ON p.series_id = l.series_id AND p.period = l.period AND p.year = l.year - 1 ORDER BY l.year, l.period

workers.title: Bluesky Social
workers.tagline: Bluesky as ordinary DuckDB tables — a read-only VGI worker. Posts, threads, profiles, followers, likes, feeds, trends and the Jetstream firehose, over SQL.
workers.subtitle: Query Bluesky posts, threads, profiles, followers, feeds, trending topics and the live firehose.
workers.summary: Read-only Bluesky data: posts, threads, profiles, followers, likes, feeds and trending topics
workers.doc_md:
Bluesky is a decentralised social network built on the AT Protocol. This catalog reads its public AppView — the service that indexes the whole network — and returns what it serves as ordinary tables.

### Identifiers

- **Actors** are accounts. Each has a permanent `did` (`did:plc:...`) and a `handle` (`bsky.app`) that it can change. Every function taking an actor accepts either, as well as `@handle` or a pasted `https://bsky.app/profile/...` URL. Join and store on `did`.
- **Posts** are addressed by AT-URI, `at://<did>/app.bsky.feed.post/<rkey>`. Functions taking a post also accept the `https://bsky.app/profile/<handle>/post/<rkey>` URL the app shows.

### Timestamps

`created_at` on a post is what the author's app claimed and can be backdated; `indexed_at` is when Bluesky first saw it, and is the one to trust for ordering.

### Access and limits

No credentials are needed and none are accepted. Bluesky rate-limits anonymous traffic per IP; requests are retried with backoff, and the AppView's own 30-second `Cache-Control` is forwarded to the result cache, so repeating a query within half a minute is free.

example_queries.title: trends_are_ranked_from_one
example_queries.description: The trends table is populated and ranked from 1.
example_queries.sql: SELECT min(rank) = 1 AND count(*) > 0 FROM bluesky.main.trends;

example_queries.title: trends_and_scan_function_agree
example_queries.description: The `trends` table and the `all_trends` function behind it have the same shape.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM bluesky.main.trends) > 0 AND (SELECT count(*) FROM bluesky.main.all_trends()) > 0;

example_queries.title: profile_resolves_a_handle_to_its_did
example_queries.description: A handle resolves to the account's permanent DID.
example_queries.sql: SELECT did FROM bluesky.main.profile('bsky.app');

example_queries.title: profile_accepts_a_web_url
example_queries.description: A pasted bsky.app profile URL is accepted as an actor.
example_queries.sql: SELECT handle FROM bluesky.main.profile('https://bsky.app/profile/bsky.app');

example_queries.title: author_feed_is_the_authors
example_queries.description: Without reposts, an author feed holds only that author's posts.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The whole read-only Bluesky surface, in one schema. The `trends` table needs no arguments; everything else is a function keyed by a search query, an actor or a post. Point lookups — `profile()`, `post()`, `thread()` — compose under a correlated LATERAL; list functions stream a page at a time so a LIMIT stops them early, and drive joins rather than sit inside them.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One schema holding the whole read-only Bluesky surface.

### Where to start

Start from what you have. A topic leads to `trends` or post search; a name leads to account search and then a profile; an account leads to its timeline, its graph and its feeds; a post leads to its conversation and to who engaged with it.

### Two kinds of function

**Lookups** — a profile, a post, a thread — are blended: one registration serves a literal call and a correlated `LATERAL`, and they batch their requests, 25 profiles or posts per call.

**Listings** follow Bluesky's cursor one page per batch, so a `LIMIT` stops them early. That streaming is also why they cannot be the inner side of a `LATERAL`: drive a join from them, not into them.

### Counts versus listings

A large account has millions of followers and a viral post hundreds of thousands of likes. Profiles and posts carry the totals; list the individual accounts only when you need them, and put a `LIMIT` on it.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: What Bluesky currently reports as trending, up to 25 topics in rank order, with a headline, a one-line summary, a category and how many posts it has drawn. Reach for this first when asked what people are talking about. `status` says where each trend is in its lifecycle — 'trending', 'saturating' or 'cooling'.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Bluesky's current trending topics, one row per trend.

### Why this is a table and everything else is a function

It needs no key, it is small — never more than 25 rows — and it is a single unpaginated request. Nothing else here is any of those things.

### Going deeper

Each trend is backed by a feed in the web app (`trend_url`). To read what people are saying, pass the trend's `display_name` to `search_posts()`.

### Freshness

The AppView declares a 30-second `Cache-Control`, which is forwarded to the result cache.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Find accounts by name or topic. Matches handles, display names and bios, and returns them in Bluesky's relevance order. This is how to get from a name to a `did` or `handle` when you do not already know it; feed that into `profile()` for counts or `author_feed()` for posts.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Account search, in Bluesky's own relevance order.

### Streaming

Rows arrive one API page (100 accounts) at a time, so a `LIMIT` stops early. The cost is that this cannot be the inner side of a correlated `LATERAL` — drive a join from it, not into it.

### Counts are not here

Search returns the basic actor view, which carries no follower counts. Join to `profile()` under a LATERAL to add them.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Who reposted (boosted) a post. Reach for this to see who spread a post to their own followers. The endpoint does not timestamp reposts, so `interacted_at` is NULL. For just the total, use `post().repost_count`; for quote posts, `quotes()`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Accounts that reposted the given post.

### The post must be a literal

Pass the post as a literal AT-URI or bsky.app URL. DuckDB does not accept a subquery as this function's argument, and because it streams it cannot be the inner side of a `LATERAL` either — look the URI up first, then call this with it.

### Streaming

Rows arrive 100 at a time, most recent first, so a `LIMIT` stops early. For just the number, `post()` already carries the count.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Every post that quotes a given post, with its text and engagement. Reach for this to see what people said *about* a post, as opposed to replies (use `thread()`) or plain reposts (use `reposted_by()`). Each row's `quoted_uri` is the input post.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Quote posts of the given post, as full post rows.

### The post must be a literal

Pass the post as a literal AT-URI or bsky.app URL. DuckDB does not accept a subquery as this function's argument, and because it streams it cannot be the inner side of a `LATERAL` either — look the URI up first, then call this with it.

### Streaming

Rows arrive 100 at a time, most recent first, so a `LIMIT` stops early. For just the number, `post()` already carries the count.

vgi.example_queries.description: The most-liked quotes of bsky.app's pinned welcome post
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT author_handle, text, like_count FROM bluesky.main.quotes('at://did:plc:z72i7hdynmk6r22z27h6tvur/app.bsky.feed.post/3l6oveex3ii2l') ORDER BY like_count DESC LIMIT 20

functions.name: profile
functions.comment: One Bluesky account's profile and follower counts, by handle or DID

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The full profile of one account — bio, follower/following/post counts, and verification — by handle or DID. Reach for this to size up an account or to turn a handle into the permanent `did`. It composes under a correlated LATERAL, so it enriches the actors any other function returns with their counts.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per account that exists; an unknown or deleted account returns no row rather than an error.

### Handles versus DIDs

A handle (`bsky.app`) is a DNS name the account can change at any time; the `did` is permanent. Store and join on `did`. The `actor` column echoes the input exactly, so a LATERAL can still be matched back to what was passed in.

### Cost under LATERAL

Profiles are fetched 25 per request, so a LATERAL over 100 actors is four calls, not a hundred. Results are cached for the 30 seconds the AppView declares.

vgi.example_queries.description: The official Bluesky account's counts
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT handle, display_name, followers_count, follows_count, posts_count FROM bluesky.main.profile('bsky.app')

vgi.example_queries.description: Follower counts for every account a search finds, via LATERAL
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT p.handle, p.followers_count FROM (SELECT did FROM bluesky.main.search_actors('duckdb') LIMIT 20) a, LATERAL bluesky.main.profile(a.did) p ORDER BY p.followers_count DESC

functions.name: post
functions.comment: One Bluesky post with its current like, repost and reply counts

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A single post's text, author and live engagement counts, by AT-URI or bsky.app URL. Reach for this to check how a known post is doing, or to hydrate URIs that another query produced — the `quoted_uri` and `reply_parent_uri` columns, say. It composes under a correlated LATERAL.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per post that exists; a deleted or unknown post returns no row.

### Accepted references

Either the AT-URI (`at://did:plc:.../app.bsky.feed.post/3k...`) or the web URL the app shows (`https://bsky.app/profile/<handle>/post/<rkey>`). A handle is resolved to its DID first, because the batch endpoint behind this answers HTTP 500 to a handle-based URI.

### Cost under LATERAL

Posts are fetched 25 per request.

functions.name: jetstream
functions.comment: Bluesky's live firehose via Jetstream: every post, like, follow and more, time-boxed

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Everything happening on Bluesky right now — every post, like, repost, follow, block and profile change across the whole network — read live from Jetstream, Bluesky's JSON firehose. Reach for this for network-wide activity that no lookup can answer: what is being posted this minute, posting volume by language, which hashtags are spiking, the like rate. It listens for `seconds` (default 10) and ends, so every result is a time-boxed sample of a stream about 400 events a second strong. Filter with `collections`, or replay a recent window with `cursor` or a WHERE on `event_time`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
A bounded read of Bluesky's firehose, via Jetstream.

### What an event is

Nearly every row is a **commit**: a record created, updated or deleted in someone's repository. `collection` says what kind — `app.bsky.feed.post`, `app.bsky.feed.like`, `app.bsky.feed.repost`, `app.bsky.graph.follow`, `app.bsky.graph.block`, `app.bsky.actor.profile` and more. The whole record is in `record` as JSON; the post columns (`text`, `langs`, `hashtags`, …) are filled for posts, and `subject_uri` / `subject_did` for likes, reposts, follows and blocks. A few rows are `identity` or `account` events, which arrive regardless of any collection filter.

Events are raw: there are no author handles and no like counts here. Join a post's `uri` to `post()` or a `did` to `profile()` under a LATERAL to hydrate them.

### How long it runs

It stops at the first of: `seconds` of wall-clock listening (default 10), `max_events`, a `LIMIT`, or an upper bound on `event_time` / `time_us` in the WHERE clause. Rows arrive about once a second while it listens. The `seconds` clock starts once the connection is open, so connecting is not counted: each attempt times out after 10 seconds, and a live read moves on to another Jetstream instance (a read with a cursor stays on its own).

### Running without an end

`seconds => 0` streams until the query is cancelled, one batch per `batch_ms`. From a DuckDB client, run `SET streaming_buffer_size = '1KB'` and `SET enable_caching_operators = false` first. DuckDB otherwise buffers about 1 MB of a streaming result before handing it over, and caches the small chunks a selective filter (a keyword match) produces until it has 2048 rows — either way, rows would not reach you as they arrive.

### Listening for a topic

Jetstream filters by collection and account, not content. Match a topic in the WHERE clause — `text ILIKE '%duckdb%'` or `list_contains(hashtags, 'art')` — over `collections => 'app.bsky.feed.post'`. A niche topic can be quiet for minutes; replay a longer window with a WHERE on `event_time` to check.

### Replaying the recent past

Jetstream buffers roughly the last day and a half. Pass `cursor => epoch_us(now() - INTERVAL 10 MINUTE)`, or simply `WHERE event_time >= ...`, to start there; a range such as `WHERE event_time BETWEEN now() - INTERVAL 2 MINUTE AND now() - INTERVAL 1 MINUTE` replays exactly that minute and stops. Replay runs far faster than real time, but a long window still needs a larger `seconds`. A cursor older than the buffer starts at the oldest event without an error.

### Filters that are pushed to Jetstream

`WHERE collection = '...'` and `WHERE did = '...'` become Jetstream's own filters, so the unwanted events never cross the network. `collections` also takes a prefix wildcard, e.g. `'app.bsky.graph.*'`.

### Polling continuously

`time_us` is the cursor. Remember the highest `time_us` you have read and pass it back as `cursor`: the next call resumes with the event after it, so successive calls neither skip nor repeat anything. Each call returns up to `max_events` events or `seconds` of listening, whichever comes first, so `cursor => <last>, max_events => 1000` is one page of the stream. A call that finds nothing new returns no rows; keep the old cursor.

`time_us` is not unique: every operation of one commit (a post with its threadgate, say) is its own event with the same `time_us`. A call never stops partway through a commit — it may return a few events past `max_events` to finish one — so the cursor stays exact. A `LIMIT` can cut a commit, so page with `max_events`, not `LIMIT`.

Prefer `cursor =>` over `WHERE time_us > <last>` for this: `max_events` counts events read *before* any WHERE is applied, so the WHERE form spends one of them on the event you already have. Cursors are points on one Jetstream instance's clock, so a call with a cursor never fails over to another instance; set `BLUESKY_JETSTREAM_URL` to choose which one.

vgi.example_queries.description: Ten seconds of new posts from across the whole network
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT event_time, did, text, langs FROM bluesky.main.jetstream(collections => 'app.bsky.feed.post') WHERE operation = 'create'

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT collection, operation, count(*) AS events FROM bluesky.main.jetstream(seconds => 5) GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY events DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Posting volume by language over the last minute, replayed
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT lang, count(*) AS posts FROM (SELECT unnest(langs) AS lang FROM bluesky.main.jetstream(collections => 'app.bsky.feed.post', seconds => 60) WHERE event_time >= now() - INTERVAL 1 MINUTE AND event_time < now()) GROUP BY lang ORDER BY posts DESC LIMIT 10

functions.name: follows
functions.comment: Accounts a Bluesky account follows, most recent first

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Who an account follows, most recently followed first. Reach for this to see what an account reads or to find related accounts. For just the number, use `profile().follows_count`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Accounts the given actor follows, most recent first.

### Streaming, and why that matters here

A large account has millions of followers. Rows arrive one API page (100 accounts) at a time, so a `LIMIT` stops the walk early — but an aggregate such as `count(*)` over a large account will walk every page. Use `profile()`'s `followers_count` / `follows_count` for counts.

Because it streams, this cannot be the inner side of a correlated `LATERAL`.

functions.comment: A Bluesky post's full conversation: ancestors and replies, one row per post

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The whole conversation around one post, flattened to one row per post with a `depth` column: negative for the posts it replies to, 0 for the post itself, positive for replies. Reach for this to read a discussion, find the most-liked reply, or trace a reply back to the post that started it.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Bluesky returns a thread as a tree; this flattens it to rows ordered ancestors-first, then the post, then its replies depth-first.

### Reading `depth`

`0` is the post you asked about. `-1` is its parent, `-2` the grandparent, and so on up to the thread root. `1` is a direct reply, `2` a reply to a reply. `reply_parent_uri` links each row to the row above it in the tree.

### What is left out

Deleted posts and posts hidden by a block have no content, so they produce no row; replies beneath them still appear. Replies deeper than `depth` (default 6) are not fetched — raise it, up to 1000, for long chains.

vgi.example_queries.description: The most-liked direct replies to the official account's latest post
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT author_handle, text, like_count FROM bluesky.main.thread((SELECT uri FROM bluesky.main.author_feed('bsky.app', filter => 'posts_no_replies') WHERE reason IS NULL LIMIT 1), depth => 1) WHERE depth = 1 ORDER BY like_count DESC LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: Replies under the official account's latest post from its best-followed repliers, biggest first
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT t.author_handle, t.text, p.followers_count FROM bluesky.main.thread((SELECT uri FROM bluesky.main.author_feed('bsky.app', filter => 'posts_no_replies') WHERE reason IS NULL LIMIT 1)) t, LATERAL bluesky.main.profile(t.author_did) p WHERE t.depth > 0 ORDER BY p.followers_count DESC, t.uri LIMIT 10

functions.name: followers
functions.comment: Accounts that follow a Bluesky account, most recent first

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Who follows an account, most recent follows first. Reach for this to see an account's audience or recent follower growth. For just the number, use `profile().followers_count` — this lists them one by one and a large account has millions.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Accounts following the given actor, most recent first.

### Streaming, and why that matters here

A large account has millions of followers. Rows arrive one API page (100 accounts) at a time, so a `LIMIT` stops the walk early — but an aggregate such as `count(*)` over a large account will walk every page. Use `profile()`'s `followers_count` / `follows_count` for counts.

Because it streams, this cannot be the inner side of a correlated `LATERAL`.

functions.name: feed
functions.comment: The posts a Bluesky custom feed is currently serving, in feed order

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Read a custom feed — such as Discover, or any community feed — as its algorithm serves it to a logged-out visitor, in the feed's own ranking order. Reach for this to see what a feed is surfacing right now. Find feed URIs with `popular_feeds()` or `actor_feeds()`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
The posts a feed generator returns, hydrated into full post rows.

### Order is the feed's

Rows come back in the order the feed's algorithm ranked them, not by time. Keep that order with `row_number() OVER ()` before you sort by anything else.

### The feed must be a literal

Pass the feed as a literal AT-URI or bsky.app feed URL: DuckDB does not accept a subquery as this function's argument. Look the URI up first, then call this with it.

### Availability

A feed is computed by its publisher's own service; the AppView only forwards the request. A feed whose service is down fails, and feeds personalised to a logged-in viewer show their logged-out fallback.

functions.name: author_feed
functions.comment: A Bluesky account's posts and reposts, newest first

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Everything one account has posted or reposted, newest first — their profile timeline. Reach for this to analyse what an account talks about, how its posts perform, or how often it posts. Reposts are included and marked `reason = 'repost'`; filter `reason IS NULL` for the account's own posts only.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
The account's profile timeline, as the app shows it.

### Reposts are in here

A repost appears as the *original* post (with the original author) and `reason = 'repost'`. For only the account's own writing, add `WHERE reason IS NULL`, or `author_did = <their did>`.

### The `filter` argument

`posts_no_replies` drops replies at the source; `posts_with_media` and `posts_with_video` keep only posts with attachments; `posts_and_author_threads` keeps replies only when they continue the author's own thread.

### Streaming

Rows arrive 100 at a time, so a `LIMIT` stops early. It cannot be the inner side of a correlated `LATERAL`.

functions.name: search_posts
functions.comment: Full-text search over Bluesky posts

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Search every public Bluesky post by keyword, newest first (or by engagement with `sort => 'top'`); returns at most 100 posts per call. This is the way in when you have a topic rather than an account or a post: what people are saying about something, who is saying it, and how much it is being shared. Narrow with `author`, `lang`, `tag`, `domain`, `since` and `until` — or with an ordinary WHERE on `created_at` / `author_handle`, which is pushed to the API.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Bluesky's full-text post search.

### Query syntax

The query string supports Bluesky's search operators — `from:handle`, `mentions:handle`, `lang:en`, `domain:example.com`, `#hashtag`, `"exact phrase"` — and each also has a named argument.

### Filters that are pushed to the API

`WHERE author_handle = '...'` becomes the endpoint's `author` filter. An upper bound on `created_at` becomes `until`. A lower bound becomes `since` only when `indexed_at` is bounded too, because the endpoint filters on the earlier of the two timestamps — pass `since =>` explicitly to narrow by time at the source.

### At most 100 posts per search

Bluesky serves the first page of search results anonymously but refuses (HTTP 403) to page further without a login, so each call returns at most 100 posts. To see more, narrow the search — by `since`/`until` windows, `author`, `lang` or `tag` — and union several calls. This is a sample of a topic, not a census.

### Freshness

Search is served uncached by the origin; pass `cache_ttl => N` to cache.

workers.title: BOE Statistics
workers.tagline: Python VGI worker for Bank of England series, observations, provisional data, and publication revisions.
workers.subtitle: Discover Bank of England statistical series and retrieve observations with original periods, units and source metadata.
workers.summary: Bank of England statistics as SQL tables: interest rates, money, credit and other time series from the Bank of England Database, with series metadata and published revision history. No API key needed.
workers.doc_md:
# vgi-boe

Discover Bank of England statistical series and retrieve observations with original periods, units and source metadata. The upstream public data service needs no API key. SQL NULL arguments are rejected; missing source values become NULL. Use function arguments for source filtering; SQL WHERE filters are local. HTTP worker access can require a bearer token.

Queries use bounded HTTP responses and retries. Credentials stay out of continuation state. See README.md for deployment and operational limits.

## Sources and references

- [Bank of England Database](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/boeapps/database/)
- [Database help (codes and download parameters)](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/boeapps/database/help.asp)

example_queries.title: bank_rate_series
example_queries.description: Find the Official Bank Rate series code in the curated list (no network request)
example_queries.sql: SELECT series_code, title FROM boe.main.datasets(query := 'bank rate') ORDER BY series_code;

example_queries.description: Discover BoE series examples
example_queries.sql: SELECT series_code, title FROM boe.main.datasets(query := 'rate') ORDER BY series_code

example_queries.description: Inspect BoE series metadata
example_queries.sql: SELECT series_code, title, frequency FROM boe.main.series(['IUDBEDR'], start_date := '2024-01-02', end_date := '2024-01-05') ORDER BY series_code

example_queries.description: Read BoE observations
example_queries.sql: SELECT period, value FROM boe.main.observations(['IUDBEDR'], start_date := '2024-01-02', end_date := '2024-01-05') ORDER BY period

example_queries.description: Read BoE publication history
example_queries.sql: SELECT period, published_at, value FROM boe.main.revisions(['LPMAUZI'], start_date := '2024-01-01', end_date := '2024-03-31', updated_since := '2024-01-01') ORDER BY period, published_at

example_queries.description: Compare each 2024 month's first-published and current M4 change (LPMAUZI revisions) with that month's average Bank Rate (IUDBEDR observations), showing how much each estimate was revised
example_queries.sql: WITH m4 AS (SELECT observation_date AS month_end, arg_min(value, published_at) AS first_published, max(value) FILTER (WHERE is_current) AS current_value FROM boe.main.revisions(['LPMAUZI'], start_date := '2024-01-01', end_date := '2024-12-31', updated_since := '2024-01-01') GROUP BY observation_date), rate AS (SELECT date_trunc('month', observation_date) AS month_start, round(avg(value), 3) AS avg_bank_rate FROM boe.main.observations(['IUDBEDR'], start_date := '2024-01-01', end_date := '2024-12-31') GROUP BY ALL) SELECT strftime(m.month_end, '%Y-%m') AS month, r.avg_bank_rate, m.first_published, m.current_value, m.current_value - m.first_published AS total_revision FROM m4 AS m JOIN rate AS r ON r.month_start = date_trunc('month', m.month_end) ORDER BY month

example_queries.description: Discover the BoE series added in September 2024
example_queries.sql: SELECT series_code, title FROM boe.main.new_series(start_date := '2024-09-01', end_date := '2024-09-30') ORDER BY series_code

agent_tasks: Using boe.main.datasets, discover boe series examples. Use the arguments in this example and return the same columns: SELECT series_code, title FROM boe.main.datasets(query := 'rate') ORDER BY series_code

Using boe.main.series, inspect boe series metadata. Use the arguments in this example and return the same columns: SELECT series_code, title, frequency FROM boe.main.series(['IUDBEDR'], start_date := '2024-01-02', end_date := '2024-01-05') ORDER BY series_code

Using boe.main.observations, read boe observations. Use the arguments in this example and return the same columns: SELECT period, value FROM boe.main.observations(['IUDBEDR'], start_date := '2024-01-02', end_date := '2024-01-05') ORDER BY period

Using boe.main.revisions, read boe publication history. Use the arguments in this example and return the same columns: SELECT period, published_at, value FROM boe.main.revisions(['LPMAUZI'], start_date := '2024-01-01', end_date := '2024-03-31', updated_since := '2024-01-01') ORDER BY period, published_at

Using boe.main.new_series, discover the boe series added in september 2024. Use the arguments in this example and return the same columns: SELECT series_code, title FROM boe.main.new_series(start_date := '2024-09-01', end_date := '2024-09-30') ORDER BY series_code

For each Bank of England LPMAUZI (monthly M4 change) period from 2024-01-01 to 2024-03-31, using a revision baseline of 2024-01-01, return period (VARCHAR), releases (BIGINT: the number of revision rows published for that period), current_value (DOUBLE: the value of the current release) and bank_rate (DOUBLE: the latest non-NULL Official Bank Rate, series IUDBEDR, observed on or before the period's observation_date). Order by period.

workers.doc_md:
# vgi-boj

Discover Bank of Japan statistical series and retrieve observations with original periods, units and source metadata. The upstream public data service needs no API key. SQL NULL arguments are rejected; missing source values become NULL. Use function arguments for source filtering; SQL WHERE filters are local. HTTP worker access can require a bearer token.

Queries use bounded HTTP responses and retries. Credentials stay out of continuation state. See README.md for deployment and operational limits.

## Sources and references

- [BOJ Time-Series Data Search](https://www.stat-search.boj.or.jp/index_en.html)
- [BOJ statistics API manual (PDF)](https://www.stat-search.boj.or.jp/info/api_manual_en.pdf)

example_queries.title: interest_rate_databases
example_queries.description: List curated BoJ interest- and exchange-rate databases (no network request)
example_queries.sql: SELECT database, name FROM boj.main.datasets(query := 'rate') ORDER BY database;

example_queries.description: Discover BoJ series metadata
example_queries.sql: SELECT series_code, name, frequency FROM boj.main.series('IR01') ORDER BY series_code

example_queries.description: Group FM08 foreign exchange series under their hierarchy headings from layers, with the layer selection string to pass to layer_observations for each branch
example_queries.sql: SELECT top.name AS section, sub.name AS subsection, s.frequency, CASE WHEN sub.name IS NULL THEN s.layer1::VARCHAR ELSE s.layer1 || ',' || s.layer2 END AS layer, count(*) AS series_count FROM boj.main.series('FM08') AS s JOIN boj.main.layers('FM08') AS top ON top.layer1 = s.layer1 AND top.layer2 = 0 LEFT JOIN boj.main.layers('FM08') AS sub ON sub.layer1 = s.layer1 AND sub.layer2 = s.layer2 AND sub.layer2 <> 0 AND sub.layer3 = 0 GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY layer

example_queries.description: Discover BoJ hierarchy headings
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, layer1, layer2 FROM boj.main.layers('IR01') ORDER BY layer1, layer2, name

example_queries.description: Read BoJ observations by code
example_queries.sql: SELECT period, value, unit FROM boj.main.observations('IR01', ['MADR1Z@D'], start_period := '202401', end_period := '202401') ORDER BY period

example_queries.description: Read BoJ observations by hierarchy
example_queries.sql: SELECT series_code, period, value FROM boj.main.layer_observations('IR01', 'D', '1,1', start_period := '202401', end_period := '202401') ORDER BY series_code, period

example_queries.description: Compare each business day's uncollateralized overnight call rate (average, highest and lowest from FM01 layer 1) with the Basic Loan Rate from IR01 in March 2024, when the call rate turned positive, with the day's highest call rate's headroom below the Basic Loan Rate in basis points
example_queries.sql: SELECT c.period, max(c.value) FILTER (WHERE c.series_code = 'STRDCLUCON') AS call_avg, max(c.value) FILTER (WHERE c.series_code = 'STRDCLUCONH') AS call_high, max(c.value) FILTER (WHERE c.series_code = 'STRDCLUCONL') AS call_low, any_value(b.value) AS basic_loan_rate, round((any_value(b.value) - max(c.value) FILTER (WHERE c.series_code = 'STRDCLUCONH')) * 100, 1) AS headroom_bp FROM boj.main.layer_observations('FM01', 'D', '1', start_period := '202403', end_period := '202403') AS c JOIN boj.main.observations('IR01', ['MADR1Z@D'], start_period := '202403', end_period := '202403') AS b USING (period) WHERE c.value IS NOT NULL GROUP BY c.period ORDER BY c.period

Using the boj catalog, find the first day in July-August 2024 on which the Bank of Japan's Basic Loan Rate (IR01 series MADR1Z@D) was higher than on 1 July 2024. Return one row with columns period (VARCHAR, YYYYMMDD), basic_loan_rate (DOUBLE), call_rate (DOUBLE, the uncollateralized overnight call rate average, FM01 series STRDCLUCON, on that day) and gap_bp (DOUBLE, basic_loan_rate minus call_rate in basis points, rounded to 1 decimal).

workers.title: BSON Codec
workers.tagline: Read and write BSON in DuckDB with SQL — decode, encode, Extended JSON, ObjectId helpers and mongodump files. A VGI worker.
workers.subtitle: Query BSON documents and move them between files and tables.
workers.summary: BSON (Binary JSON) decode & encode plus Extended JSON v2, typed field extraction, mongodump/oplog/GridFS stream splitting, and raw BSON COPY import/export for SQL.
workers.doc_md:
# bson

Decode and encode **BSON** (Binary JSON, [bsonspec.org](https://bsonspec.org)) in SQL, with lossless typed handling of ObjectId, Decimal128, `UUID`-subtype Binary, and the Timestamp-vs-UTCDateTime footgun — plus correct **MongoDB Extended JSON v2** (canonical & relaxed). The value is in-engine decode of the raw BSON the live `mongo` connector never sees: **mongodump backups**, **oplog / change-stream** captures, **GridFS chunks**, and **BSON columns at rest**. The `bson_seq` / `mongodump_read` table functions fan a concatenated `.bson` stream into one row per document. **COPY FROM / TO** with `FORMAT '<catalog>.bson'` imports and exports local BSON files through one `BLOB` column, preserving bytes with strict validation. Imports stream bounded batches; exports stage in shared storage and atomically publish the output. No network, zero egress.

**Out of scope:** any live MongoDB connection (that is the `mongo` extension's job — this is the offline/at-rest complement) and FLE / Queryable-Encryption decryption (encrypted Binary subtypes stay opaque `BLOB`).

example_queries.description: Render a BSON document as canonical (lossless) Extended JSON v2.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.to_json(bson.main.from_json('{"a":1}'))

example_queries.description: Render the same document as relaxed, human-readable Extended JSON.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.to_json(bson.main.from_json('{"a":1}'), 'relaxed')

example_queries.description: Extract a nested leaf by dotted path without decoding the whole document.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.field(bson.main.from_json('{"o":{"sku":"abc"}}'), 'o.sku')

example_queries.description: Check that a tiny empty document is structurally well-formed.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (bson.main.well_formed(from_hex('0500000000'))).ok

example_queries.description: Report the top-level BSON type name of a document.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.type_of(bson.main.from_json('{"a":1}'))

example_queries.description: Fan a concatenated BSON stream into one row per document with its byte length.
example_queries.sql: SELECT idx, octet_length(doc) AS n FROM bson.main.bson_seq(from_hex('05000000000500000000')) ORDER BY idx

example_queries.description: Audit which BSON type every document's _id uses in a mongodump file body (three documents, inlined as hex and split with bson_seq), looking up its one-byte type code and Extended JSON wrapper in the bson_types registry.
example_queries.sql: SELECT t.type_name, t.type_byte, t.extjson_wrapper, count(*) AS docs FROM bson.main.bson_seq(from_hex('2f000000075f69640054759eb3c090d83494e2d804026e616d650006000000616c6963650010616765001e000000002d000000075f69640054759eb3c090d83494e2d805026e616d650004000000626f6200106167650019000000002f000000075f69640054759eb3c090d83494e2d806026e616d6500060000006361726f6c0010616765002900000000')) AS d JOIN bson.main.bson_types AS t ON t.type_name = bson.main.type_of(d.doc, '_id') GROUP BY t.type_name, t.type_byte, t.extjson_wrapper ORDER BY docs DESC, t.type_name

example_queries.description: Recover when each document in a mongodump file body (three documents, inlined as hex and split with bson_seq) was created from the timestamp embedded in its ObjectId _id, next to the document as relaxed Extended JSON.
Split a concatenated oplog-style BSON stream into documents and count the entries per operation type (i = insert, u = update).
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.field(s.doc, 'op') AS op, count(*) AS entries FROM bson.main.bson_seq(bson.main.from_json('{"op":"i","ns":"shop.orders"}') || bson.main.from_json('{"op":"u","ns":"shop.orders"}') || bson.main.from_json('{"op":"i","ns":"shop.users"}')) AS s GROUP BY op ORDER BY op

example_queries.description: Canonical Extended JSON round-trips BSON byte-for-byte (the migration guarantee).
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.from_json(bson.main.to_json(bson.main.from_json('{"a":1}'))) = bson.main.from_json('{"a":1}') AS roundtrips;

example_queries.description: A minimal empty document (05 00 00 00 00) is well-formed.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (bson.main.well_formed(from_hex('0500000000'))).ok AS ok;

example_queries.description: List the temporal BSON types and their Extended JSON wrappers.
example_queries.sql: SELECT type_name, type_byte, extjson_wrapper FROM bson.main.bson_types WHERE type_class = 'temporal' ORDER BY type_name

example_queries.title: copy_then_mongodump_read
example_queries.description: Write three documents to a mongodump-style .bson file with COPY ... TO, then read the file back with mongodump_read: one row per document with its zero-based idx, rendered as relaxed Extended JSON.
example_queries.sql:
COPY (SELECT bson.main.from_json(j) AS doc FROM (VALUES (1, '{"name":"alice","age":30}'), (2, '{"name":"bob","age":25}'), (3, '{"name":"carol","age":41}')) AS v(n, j) ORDER BY n) TO '/tmp/vgi_bson_example.bson' (FORMAT 'bson.bson');
SELECT idx, bson.main.to_json(doc, 'relaxed') AS doc_json FROM bson.main.mongodump_read('/tmp/vgi_bson_example.bson') ORDER BY idx;

example_queries.description: Diagnose a truncated document.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (bson.main.well_formed(from_hex('0500000001'))).kind AS kind

example_queries.description: Decode forcing JSON mode.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.decode(bson.main.from_json('{"a":1}'), 'json') AS d

example_queries.description: List the keys of a {a:1,b:2} document.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.keys(bson.main.from_json('{"a":1,"b":2}')) AS k

example_queries.description: Relaxed Extended JSON of {a:1}.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.to_json(bson.main.from_json('{"a":1}'), 'relaxed') AS j

example_queries.description: Validate a tiny empty BSON document (05 00 00 00 00).
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.is_valid(from_hex('0500000000')) AS ok

example_queries.description: Extract _id as a hex ObjectId.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.field(bson.main.from_json('{"_id":{"$oid":"54759eb3c090d83494e2d804"}}'), '_id', 'objectid') AS id

example_queries.description: Hex of a 12-byte ObjectId.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.objectid_hex(bson.main.objectid_from_hex('54759eb3c090d83494e2d804')) AS h

example_queries.description: Creation time of an ObjectId.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.objectid_timestamp('54759eb3c090d83494e2d804') AS created

example_queries.description: Encode a JSON document to BSON and hex it.
example_queries.sql: SELECT to_hex(bson.main.from_json('{"a":1}')) AS h

example_queries.description: 12-byte ObjectId from hex.
example_queries.sql: SELECT to_hex(bson.main.objectid_from_hex('54759eb3c090d83494e2d804')) AS b

example_queries.description: Read the (t, i) parts of a Timestamp.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (bson.main.timestamp_parts({'t': 1416994483, 'i': 2})).i AS inc

example_queries.description: Convert a Timestamp struct to a TIMESTAMPTZ.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.timestamp_to_ts({'t': 1416994483, 'i': 1}) AS ts

example_queries.description: Encode a struct to BSON and hex it.
example_queries.sql: SELECT to_hex(bson.main.encode({'a': 1, 'b': 'x'})) AS h

example_queries.description: Type of a nested ObjectId field.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bson.main.type_of(bson.main.from_json('{"_id":{"$oid":"54759eb3c090d83494e2d804"}}'), '_id') AS t

agent_tasks: Using the bson worker, confirm that the BSON encoding of the JSON document {"a":1} round-trips losslessly: rendering it to canonical MongoDB Extended JSON with to_json and parsing that back with from_json must reproduce the original BSON bytes. Return the single boolean result.
Using the bson worker, extract the value at the dotted path o.sku from the BSON encoding of the JSON document {"o":{"sku":"abc"}}.
Using the bson worker, return the creation time embedded in the ObjectId whose hexadecimal string is 54759eb3c090d83494e2d804.
Using the bson worker's is_valid function, return the single boolean telling whether the bytes produced by from_hex('0500000000') are exactly one well-formed BSON document.
Using the bson worker, split the concatenated BSON byte stream from_hex('05000000000500000000') into one row per contained document and return each document's zero-based index.

Using the bson worker, confirm that decode and to_json agree on the BSON encoding of {"a":1}: decode of those bytes must equal to_json of the same bytes in canonical mode. Return the single boolean result.
Using the bson worker, encode the DuckDB struct {'a': 1} to BSON bytes with the encode function and return the result as an uppercase hexadecimal string.
Using the bson worker, list the top-level field names, in document order, of the BSON encoding of the JSON document {"z":1,"a":2,"m":3}.
Using the bson worker, report the BSON type name at the field path _id of the document {"_id":{"$oid":"54759eb3c090d83494e2d804"}} encoded with from_json.
Using the bson worker's well_formed function, return the single boolean telling whether the failure kind it reports for the malformed bytes from_hex('0c00000010610001') is 'truncated'.
Using the bson worker, convert the ObjectId hex string 54759eb3c090d83494e2d804 to its 12 raw bytes with objectid_from_hex and then back to a hex string with objectid_hex; return that hex string.
Using the bson worker, read the increment (i) component from the BSON internal Timestamp struct {'t': 1416994483, 'i': 7} using timestamp_parts.
Using the bson worker, convert the BSON internal Timestamp struct {'t': 1416994483, 'i': 7} to a TIMESTAMPTZ from its seconds component using timestamp_to_ts.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## bson.main

The single schema of the `bson` worker. The catalog name matches the `ATTACH` name, so qualify calls as `bson.main.<name>`.

It covers the whole offline BSON surface, grouped into a few families: a BSON ↔ Extended JSON v2 **codec**, structural **validity** checks that stay total on hostile input, typed dotted-path **projection**, **ObjectId** and internal-**Timestamp** helpers, and **stream**-splitting table functions for mongodump / oplog / GridFS data.

The `vgi.categories` groupings show where each function fits; the codec's canonical Extended JSON round-trips byte-for-byte, making it the migration and diff surface for BSON at rest.

tables.name: bson_types
tables.comment: The BSON element-type registry: every BSON type, its one-byte type code, and its canonical Extended JSON v2 wrapper.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A static, credential-free reference view listing all 21 BSON element types: the type name `type_of` returns, the one-byte type code (0x01–0x13, plus 0xFF minKey and 0x7F maxKey), a coarse `type_class` for browsing, the canonical Extended JSON v2 wrapper the type serializes to, and a one-line note. Use it to map a `type_of` result to its wire code, to see how a type renders in canonical Extended JSON, or to spot the footguns — Timestamp (0x11) is a replication clock, not a wall-clock time; undefined / dbPointer / symbol are deprecated. It scans instantly with no argument, so it is the cheapest way to see real data from this worker.

functions.name: mongodump_read
functions.comment: Read a glob of mongodump `.bson` files into one row per document

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Read a glob of mongodump `.bson` files (each a concatenation of length-prefixed BSON documents) and fan them into one row per document: columns idx (`BIGINT`, per-file zero-based position), doc (`BLOB`, one document), and file (`VARCHAR`, the source path). Point it at a backup directory (e.g. '/backups/mydb/*.bson') to get every document joinable in SQL, then feed `doc` to decode / to_json / field. Stops cleanly at any trailing partial document. v1 reads local-filesystem globs; for a cloud dump, store one file's read_blob content in a DuckDB variable and split it with bson_seq over getvariable. The worker opens no sockets of its own.

functions.name: bson_seq
functions.comment: Split a concatenated length-prefixed BSON stream into one row per document

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Split a `BLOB` holding N concatenated length-prefixed BSON documents (each is `int32 length ++ body ++ 0x00`) into one row per document: columns idx (`BIGINT`, zero-based position) and doc (`BLOB`, the single document's bytes). This is exactly the wire shape of a mongodump `.bson` file body, an oplog batch, or a GridFS reassembly. Stops cleanly at the first malformed length prefix — partial trailing bytes are ignored (never panics). Feed `doc` to decode / to_json / field. The `stream` argument must be a constant (a literal, a constant expression, or getvariable(...)); DuckDB does not allow a column here, so it cannot be used LATERAL over a table of blobs — for local files use mongodump_read, or store one file's read_blob content in a DuckDB variable and pass that variable via getvariable.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Fan one constant concatenated length-prefixed BSON stream into rows of `(idx BIGINT, doc BLOB)`. Not LATERAL: pass a literal or `getvariable(...)`.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Diagnose a BSON blob and return `STRUCT(ok BOOL, error VARCHAR, kind VARCHAR)`. `kind` is one of truncated, length-mismatch, trailing-bytes, invalid-type, bad-cstring, bad-utf8, duplicate-key, nesting-limit, bad-decimal128, bad-subtype (NULL when ok). Never errors or panics on hostile input — a lying gigabyte length prefix or a 5000-deep document returns ok=false with the classified reason, so a bad row never crashes the scan.

functions.name: decode
functions.comment: Decode a BSON document to its richest form (Extended JSON in v1)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Decode a BSON document to its richest self-describing form and return it as text. `decode(doc)` is the zero-decisions codec: it always yields canonical MongoDB Extended JSON v2 — the lossless column that preserves ObjectId, Decimal128, `UUID`, and the Timestamp-vs-UTCDateTime distinction — and is exactly equivalent to `to_json(doc, 'canonical')`. Prefer `to_json` when you want to choose canonical vs relaxed rendering; reach for `decode` when you just want one stable lossless column and no mode decision. The optional `mode` ('auto', 'struct', 'map', 'json') is a forward-looking hint for the output shape you would like, but because a DuckDB scalar fixes its output column type at bind time with no data sample, all four currently materialize as the same canonical Extended JSON text — the argument does not yet change the result, so omit it unless you are signalling intent. For a typed projection of a known shape, cast the JSON or use `field(doc, path, as)` per leaf. Returns NULL for a malformed blob.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Decode BSON to its richest self-describing form → canonical Extended JSON (the stable lossless column). Equivalent to `to_json(doc, 'canonical')`; prefer `to_json` when you need the canonical/relaxed choice. `mode` ∈ {auto, struct, map, json} is a forward-looking shape hint that currently always returns the same Extended JSON text.

functions.name: is_valid

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Return TRUE iff the blob is exactly one well-formed BSON document per the BSON spec (declared length matches the bytes, types known, cstrings NUL-terminated, valid UTF-8, no trailing bytes). functions.name: field
functions.comment: Extract a BSON field by dotted path (inferred leaf rendering)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Extract one field from a BSON document by dotted path ('o._id', 'items.0.sku') without materializing the whole document, returning a `VARCHAR`. The optional `as` argument coerces the leaf to a cast-ready string: 'objectid' → 24-hex, 'decimal' → the canonical decimal literal (cast with `::DECIMAL(38,4)`), 'uuid' → canonical `UUID` (cast with `::UUID`), 'datetime'/'timestamp' → RFC 3339 (cast with `::TIMESTAMPTZ`), 'blob' → lowercase hex, 'json' → canonical Extended JSON. With no `as` (or NULL), the leaf is inferred (scalars render bare). A missing path → NULL. Lossless typed projection a naive JSON path would corrupt.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Extract a field by dotted path → `VARCHAR`. `as` ∈ {objectid, decimal, uuid, timestamp, datetime, blob, json} coerces the leaf to a cast-ready string; NULL infers.

functions.name: timestamp_parts
functions.comment: Return the raw (time, increment) pair of a BSON Timestamp as STRUCT(t,i)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Normalize a BSON internal Timestamp to `STRUCT(t UINTEGER, i UINTEGER)` — the raw (time-in-seconds, increment) pair of the 0x11 replication clock. `t` orders ops to the second; `i` breaks ties within the same second. Use timestamp_to_ts for a `TIMESTAMPTZ` from `t`. Returns a NULL struct for a NULL input.

functions.name: timestamp_to_ts
functions.comment: Convert a BSON Timestamp STRUCT(t,i) to a TIMESTAMPTZ (from `t`)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Convert a BSON internal Timestamp (the decoded `STRUCT(t, i)` replication clock) to a second-resolution `TIMESTAMPTZ` from its `t` (seconds-since-epoch) component — the oplog ordering clock. NOTE this is the MongoDB-internal 0x11 Timestamp, NOT the user-facing 0x09 UTCDateTime: a 0x11 value is a replication marker, not a wall-clock time. Returns NULL when the input struct has no integer `t`.
tags.vgi.doc_md: BSON Timestamp `STRUCT(t,i)` → `TIMESTAMPTZ` from the `t` seconds (the oplog clock).

tags.vgi.title: BSON Timestamp → TIMESTAMPTZ

arguments.name: ts
arguments.description: A BSON internal replication-clock value in its decoded (t, i) form — the (seconds, increment) pair.

examples: SELECT bson.main.timestamp_to_ts({'t': 1416994483, 'i': 1}) AS ts

functions.name: encode
functions.comment: Encode a DuckDB STRUCT/MAP value as a BSON document

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Encode a DuckDB value as a BSON document. `STRUCT` → embedded document; `MAP` → document; `LIST` → array; `TIMESTAMP`/`TIMESTAMPTZ` → UTCDateTime; `UUID` → Binary subtype 0x04; `BLOB` → Binary subtype 0x00; integers → Int32/Int64 by range; `DOUBLE` → Double; `DECIMAL` → Decimal128. workers.title: NOAA Buoys
workers.tagline: NOAA buoy and coastal-station observations as VGI SQL functions
workers.subtitle: NOAA NDBC buoy stations, latest observations and recent station histories for marine analysis.
workers.summary: NOAA National Data Buoy Center stations, latest marine observations and about 45 days of recent station history (wind, waves, pressure, temperatures, visibility, water level) as SQL tables in metric units. No API key needed.
workers.doc_md:
# NOAA Buoys

NOAA NDBC buoy stations, latest observations and recent station histories in SQL. Table functions return typed Arrow columns with UTC timestamps, source URLs and retrieval times. No API key is needed. Missing measurements become NULL; invalid arguments and unexpected upstream responses fail explicitly. Data is retrieved when a query executes. Use SQL to filter, aggregate and join stations to measurements. Wind speeds are m/s, waves are metres, periods seconds, temperatures Celsius and pressure hPa. Visibility is converted to metres and water level to metres relative to MLLW. The recent station file covers approximately 45 days; this worker does not read annual archives. Observation timestamps, not retrieval times, determine freshness.

## Data access

Use the main schema to discover stations and retrieve observations. Each response preserves its source URL and UTC retrieval time. Missing sensor values remain NULL.

## Sources and references

- [NOAA National Data Buoy Center](https://www.ndbc.noaa.gov/): the upstream station directory, latest-observation file and realtime station files this worker reads.
- [NDBC realtime data access](https://www.ndbc.noaa.gov/faq/rt_data_access.shtml): how the realtime2 station files are published.
- [NDBC measurement descriptions and units](https://www.ndbc.noaa.gov/faq/measdes.shtml): definitions of the source columns converted here.

example_queries.description: Discover stations with meteorological data
example_queries.sql: SELECT station_id, name, latitude, longitude FROM buoys.main.stations() WHERE has_met ORDER BY station_id LIMIT 20

example_queries.description: List directory stations flagged has_met that have no row in the latest observations file, with owner and station type
example_queries.sql: SELECT s.station_id, s.name, s.owner, s.station_type FROM buoys.main.stations AS s ANTI JOIN buoys.main.latest_observations() AS o USING (station_id) WHERE s.has_met ORDER BY s.station_id

example_queries.description: Find the largest reported seas and their wave periods
example_queries.sql: SELECT station_id, time, wave_height_m, dominant_period_s FROM buoys.main.latest_observations() WHERE wave_height_m IS NOT NULL ORDER BY wave_height_m DESC, station_id LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Name the 10 stations reporting the largest significant wave heights in the latest file, with owner, station type and dominant period
example_queries.sql: SELECT o.station_id, s.name, s.owner, s.station_type, o.time, o.wave_height_m, o.dominant_period_s FROM buoys.main.latest_observations() AS o JOIN buoys.main.stations AS s USING (station_id) WHERE o.wave_height_m IS NOT NULL ORDER BY o.wave_height_m DESC, o.station_id LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Inspect the latest measured waves and winds off Boston
example_queries.sql: SELECT time, wind_speed_mps, wave_height_m, dominant_period_s FROM buoys.main.observations('44013') WHERE wave_height_m IS NOT NULL ORDER BY time DESC LIMIT 24

example_queries.description: Summarise the 7 most recent days (session time zone) at buoy 44013 (daily peak wave height, mean wind speed, report count) with the directory name and coordinates that recent files omit
example_queries.sql: SELECT s.station_id, s.name, s.latitude, s.longitude, date_trunc('day', o.time) AS obs_day, max(o.wave_height_m) AS max_wave_height_m, avg(o.wind_speed_mps) AS mean_wind_speed_mps, count(*) AS reports FROM buoys.main.observations('44013') AS o JOIN buoys.main.stations AS s USING (station_id) GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY obs_day DESC LIMIT 7

example_queries.description: Show each non-missing measurement in station 46026's latest report as one row, with its output unit, NDBC source field, source unit and conversion scale
example_queries.sql: SELECT v.column_name, v.value, m.output_unit, m.source_field, m.source_unit, m.scale FROM (UNPIVOT buoys.main.latest_observations(station_id := '46026') ON COLUMNS(* EXCLUDE (station_id, time, latitude, longitude, source_url, fetched_at)) INTO NAME column_name VALUE value) AS v JOIN buoys.main.measurements AS m USING (column_name) ORDER BY v.column_name

example_queries.description: Discover stations with meteorological data
example_queries.sql: SELECT station_id, name FROM buoys.main.stations WHERE has_met ORDER BY station_id

example_queries.description: NDBC measurement fields, source units and conversion factors
example_queries.sql: SELECT column_name, source_unit, output_unit, scale FROM buoys.main.measurements WHERE column_name = 'visibility_m'

agent_tasks: List column_name, source_unit, output_unit and scale for visibility_m in the measurements reference table.
Using buoys.main.stations, list the first five station IDs and names ordered by station ID.
Using buoys.main.latest_observations, list the five stations with highest nonmissing wind_speed_mps, ordered by wind_speed_mps descending then station_id.
Using buoys.main.observations, list the five most recent nonmissing wave heights for station 44013, showing time and wave_height_m.

What is the highest significant wave height in buoy 44013's whole recent history (buoys.main.observations), and what is that station's name in the station directory? Save the answer with CREATE TEMP TABLE boston_peak AS SELECT ... with exactly one row and columns name (VARCHAR) and max_wave_height_m (DOUBLE).

What is the greatest visibility currently reported in buoys.main.latest_observations, expressed back in the NDBC source unit? Use the measurements reference table's scale for visibility_m to convert. Save the answer with CREATE TEMP TABLE max_visibility AS SELECT ... with exactly one row and one column visibility_nmi (DOUBLE).

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Read the NDBC active-station XML catalog, including partner and land stations. No arguments or API key. Returns station_id, name, coordinates, elevation_m, owner, program, station_type and capability booleans, plus source_url and fetched_at. IDs are lowercase strings. Missing attributes are NULL. tags.vgi.doc_md:
## NDBC Active Stations

Read the NDBC active-station XML catalog, including partner and land stations. No arguments or API key. Returns station_id, name, coordinates, elevation_m, owner, program, station_type and capability booleans, plus source_url and fetched_at. IDs are lowercase strings. Missing attributes are NULL. Active station metadata does not guarantee fresh measurements or a standard meteorological file. Filter for has_met and join station_id with observations() or latest_observations(). Coordinates here describe the catalog location, not a moving buoy's observation position.

### Result columns

| Column | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| station_id | NDBC station identifier in lowercase. |
| name | Station name. |
| latitude | Station latitude in decimal degrees. |
| longitude | Station longitude in decimal degrees. |
| elevation_m | Site elevation in metres above mean sea level when supplied. |
| owner | Organization responsible for the station. |
| program | NDBC or partner program. |
| station_type | NOAA station type, such as buoy, fixed or oilrig. |
| has_met | Whether NDBC lists meteorological observations for this station. |
| has_currents | Whether NDBC lists current observations; this worker reads standard meteorological data only. |
| has_water_quality | Whether NDBC lists water-quality observations. |
| has_dart | Whether this is a DART tsunami station. |
| source_url | Exact NOAA NDBC source URL. |
| fetched_at | UTC retrieval time; use time to assess measurement freshness. |

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Measurements Reference

A built-in reference for all supported NDBC meteorological measurements. Use column_name to connect a result column to its source_field, source_unit, output_unit and conversion scale. This deterministic table makes no network requests. Missing source measurements stay NULL before conversion. Wind and wave directions retain their source convention: where they come from, relative to true north.

### Result columns

| Column | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| column_name | Output measurement column. |
| source_field | NDBC text header field. |
| source_unit | Unit in the source NDBC data file. |
| output_unit | Unit in the worker result. |
| scale | Dimensionless conversion factor: multiply source values by this ratio to obtain output values. |

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT column_name, source_unit, output_unit, scale FROM buoys.main.measurements WHERE column_name = 'visibility_m'

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Read one station's recent standard meteorological file (approximately 45 days, coverage varies). Required station_id is case-insensitive. Named start_time/end_time are optional inclusive UTC ISO bounds ending in Z; defaults are empty strings. These filter the downloaded file and do not retrieve archives. Uses the same measurement units and columns as latest_observations(): UTC time, m/s winds, metre waves, second wave periods, Celsius temperatures, hPa pressure, visibility_m and water_level_m (MLLW). Handles separate hour/minute and drifting-station hhmm layouts by header name. Fixed-station files omit coordinates; join stations() by station_id if needed. Missing measurements are NULL, not zero. NULL arguments, malformed rows and unexpected units fail explicitly. HTTP 404 means no file is available. No API key required.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Recent NDBC Station History

Read one station's recent standard meteorological file (approximately 45 days, coverage varies). Required station_id is case-insensitive. Named start_time/end_time are optional inclusive UTC ISO bounds ending in Z; defaults are empty strings. These filter the downloaded file and do not retrieve archives. Uses the same measurement units and columns as latest_observations(): UTC time, m/s winds, metre waves, second wave periods, Celsius temperatures, hPa pressure, visibility_m and water_level_m (MLLW). Handles separate hour/minute and drifting-station hhmm layouts by header name. Fixed-station files omit coordinates; join stations() by station_id if needed. Missing measurements are NULL, not zero. NULL arguments, malformed rows and unexpected units fail explicitly. HTTP 404 means no file is available. No API key required.

### Result columns

| Column | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| station_id | NDBC station ID in lowercase; retain as text, including leading zeroes. |
| time | UTC observation timestamp supplied by NDBC; measurements may be stale. |
| latitude | Observation latitude in decimal degrees; NULL when absent from a station history file. |
| longitude | Observation longitude in decimal degrees; NULL when absent from a station history file. |
| wind_direction_deg | Direction wind comes from, clockwise degrees from true north. Missing MM becomes NULL. |
| wind_speed_mps | Measured wind speed in metres per second, at the station's anemometer height. Missing MM becomes NULL. |
| wind_gust_mps | Wind gust speed in metres per second. Missing MM becomes NULL. |
| wave_height_m | Significant wave height in metres; mean of the highest third of sampled waves. Missing MM becomes NULL. |
| dominant_period_s | Dominant wave period in seconds, at maximum wave energy. Missing MM becomes NULL. |
| average_period_s | Average wave period in seconds. Missing MM becomes NULL. |
| wave_direction_deg | Direction waves at the dominant period come from, degrees from true north. Missing MM becomes NULL. |
| pressure_hpa | Sea-level atmospheric pressure in hectopascals. Missing MM becomes NULL. |
| pressure_tendency_hpa | Signed pressure change over the preceding three hours, in hectopascals. Missing MM becomes NULL. |
| air_temperature_c | Air temperature in degrees Celsius. Missing MM becomes NULL. |
| water_temperature_c | Water temperature in degrees Celsius. Missing MM becomes NULL. |
| dew_point_c | Dew point in degrees Celsius. Missing MM becomes NULL. |
| visibility_m | Visibility in metres, converted from source nautical miles. Missing MM becomes NULL. |
| water_level_m | Water level in metres relative to MLLW, converted from source feet. Missing MM becomes NULL. |
| source_url | Exact NOAA NDBC source URL. |
| fetched_at | UTC retrieval time; use time to assess measurement freshness. |

workers.summary: Holiday, business-day, and recurrence calendar math for SQL
workers.doc_md:
# Calendar, Holiday & Recurrence Math in SQL

**`cal` brings public-holiday lookups, business-day arithmetic, and RFC-5545 (RRULE) recurrence expansion directly into DuckDB SQL — no ETL, no Python glue, just `SELECT`.** Ask whether a date is a holiday or a working day, name the holiday, add or count business days, or expand a recurrence rule into a series of timestamps, all as ordinary SQL expressions and table functions.

This VGI worker is for analysts, data engineers, and application developers who need correct calendar logic close to their data: payment and settlement date math, SLA and business-day deadlines, payroll and billing cycles, and scheduling and reminders. It exposes a single `cal` catalog (schema `main`) over Apache Arrow, so every function streams results back to DuckDB with native types — `DATE`, `TIMESTAMP`, and `TIMESTAMPTZ` round-trip cleanly. Coverage is global, not US-centric: hundreds of countries and their subdivisions are supported, and `'US'` is merely the default argument, not a limit.

The holiday and business-day engine is powered by the [holidays](https://github.com/vacanza/holidays) library ([docs](https://holidays.readthedocs.io/)), which models hundreds of national and subdivision calendars. Recurrence and Easter math come from [python-dateutil](https://github.com/dateutil/dateutil) ([docs](https://dateutil.readthedocs.io/)), whose `rrulestr` parser implements the [RFC-5545](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5545) recurrence grammar. For stock-exchange trading calendars (sessions, market hours, and schedules), see the companion [vgi-trading-calendar](https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-trading-calendar) worker.

Per-row questions are answered by scalar functions you can drop straight into a projection or predicate; set-returning questions — a year's holidays, a range of working days, an expanded recurrence — are table functions. Country/subdivision are ordinary arguments that default to `'US'`; the `supported_countries` table enumerates every valid `country`/`subdiv` code. Weekend-aware `is_business_day` differs from holiday-only `is_holiday`; recurrence rules must be bounded (`COUNT`/`UNTIL`) or they never terminate.

example_queries.title: is-christmas-a-holiday
example_queries.description: Whether 25 December 2026 is a US public holiday.
example_queries.sql: SELECT cal.main.is_holiday(DATE '2026-12-25') AS is_holiday;

example_queries.title: add-business-days
example_queries.description: Two US business days after 24 December 2026 (skips Christmas + weekend).
example_queries.sql: SELECT cal.main.add_business_days(DATE '2026-12-24', 2) AS due;

example_queries.title: weekly-recurrence
example_queries.description: The first four weekly occurrences from 1 January 2026.
example_queries.sql: SELECT seq, occurrence FROM cal.main.rrule(TIMESTAMP '2026-01-01', 'FREQ=WEEKLY;COUNT=4') ORDER BY seq;

example_queries.title: settlement-schedule-following
example_queries.description: Payment calendar: 1st-of-month 2026 payments from rrule, rolled forward to the next US business day when the 1st is not one, with the reason: the holiday name, or the weekday for weekend rolls.
example_queries.sql: WITH sched AS (SELECT r.seq, CAST(r.occurrence AS DATE) AS due FROM cal.main.rrule(TIMESTAMP '2026-01-01', 'FREQ=MONTHLY;BYMONTHDAY=1;COUNT=12') AS r) SELECT due, CASE WHEN cal.main.is_business_day(due) THEN due ELSE cal.main.add_business_days(due, 1) END AS settles_on, CASE WHEN NOT cal.main.is_business_day(due) THEN coalesce(cal.main.holiday_name(due), dayname(due)) END AS rolled_because FROM sched ORDER BY seq;

example_queries.description: Name of the US holiday on 4 July 2026.
example_queries.sql: SELECT cal.main.holiday_name(DATE '2026-07-04') AS holiday_name

example_queries.description: Is Christmas 2026 a US business day?
example_queries.sql: SELECT cal.main.is_business_day(DATE '2026-12-25') AS is_business_day

example_queries.description: How many US business days fall in January 2026.
example_queries.sql: SELECT cal.main.business_days_between(DATE '2026-01-01', DATE '2026-02-01') AS n

example_queries.description: Western Easter Sunday in 2026.
example_queries.sql: SELECT cal.main.easter(2026) AS easter_sunday

example_queries.description: ISO-8601 year-week label for 22 June 2026.
example_queries.sql: SELECT cal.main.iso_year_week(DATE '2026-06-22') AS iso_year_week

example_queries.description: US + California public holidays in 2026, projected and ordered.
example_queries.sql: SELECT date, name FROM cal.main.holidays(2026, country := 'US', subdiv := 'CA') ORDER BY date

example_queries.description: US business days in the 2026 year-end week, in order.
example_queries.sql: SELECT date FROM cal.main.business_days(DATE '2026-12-21', DATE '2026-12-31', country := 'US') ORDER BY date

example_queries.description: How many distinct countries the holiday functions support.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(DISTINCT country) AS countries FROM cal.main.supported_countries

example_queries.description: Capacity plan: US business days per month in 2026, with the holidays that fell on a weekday and so removed a working day (weekend holidays such as Saturday 4 July are left out).
example_queries.sql: WITH bd AS (SELECT date_trunc('month', date) AS month, count(*) AS business_days FROM cal.main.business_days(DATE '2026-01-01', DATE '2026-12-31', country := 'US') GROUP BY ALL), lost AS (SELECT date_trunc('month', date) AS month, count(*) AS weekday_holidays, string_agg(name, ', ' ORDER BY date) AS holiday_names FROM cal.main.holidays(2026, country := 'US') WHERE isodow(date) <= 5 GROUP BY ALL) SELECT strftime(bd.month, '%Y-%m') AS month, bd.business_days, coalesce(lost.weekday_holidays, 0) AS weekday_holidays, lost.holiday_names FROM bd LEFT JOIN lost USING (month) ORDER BY bd.month

example_queries.description: Cross-border settlement window: the days from 21 Dec 2026 to 8 Jan 2027 when both the US and the UK (GB) are open, i.e. US business days that are also GB business days.
example_queries.sql: SELECT b.date, dayname(b.date) AS weekday FROM cal.main.business_days(DATE '2026-12-21', DATE '2027-01-08', country := 'US') AS b WHERE cal.main.is_business_day(b.date, 'GB') ORDER BY b.date

example_queries.description: Sprint capacity: US business days in each ISO week from 30 Nov 2026 to 10 Jan 2027, labelled with iso_year_week (Christmas and New Year's Day cut W52 and W53 to 4 days).
example_queries.sql: SELECT cal.main.iso_year_week(b.date) AS iso_week, count(*) AS business_days, min(b.date) AS first_day, max(b.date) AS last_day FROM cal.main.business_days(DATE '2026-11-30', DATE '2027-01-10', country := 'US') AS b GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY iso_week

example_queries.description: Countdown: the US holidays on or after 13 November 2026, with how many US business days remain until each (business_days_between counts [start, end)).
example_queries.sql: SELECT h.date, h.name, cal.main.business_days_between(DATE '2026-11-13', h.date) AS business_days_away FROM cal.main.holidays(2026, country := 'US') AS h WHERE h.date >= DATE '2026-11-13' ORDER BY h.date

example_queries.description: Moveable feasts: the German holidays whose offset from easter() is the same in 2025, 2026 and 2027, i.e. the Easter-anchored ones, with that offset in days. Fixed-date holidays such as Labor Day drop out.
example_queries.sql: WITH h AS (SELECT date, name FROM cal.main.holidays(2025, country := 'DE') UNION ALL SELECT date, name FROM cal.main.holidays(2026, country := 'DE') UNION ALL SELECT date, name FROM cal.main.holidays(2027, country := 'DE')) SELECT name, min(date - cal.main.easter(year(date))) AS days_from_easter FROM h GROUP BY name HAVING count(*) = 3 AND count(DISTINCT date - cal.main.easter(year(date))) = 1 ORDER BY days_from_easter

example_queries.description: Cross-border closures: the 2026 dates that are a public holiday in both the US and GB, with each country's holiday name.
example_queries.sql: SELECT us.date, us.name AS us_holiday, gb.name AS gb_holiday FROM cal.main.holidays(2026, country := 'US') AS us JOIN cal.main.holidays(2026, country := 'GB') AS gb ON us.date = gb.date ORDER BY us.date

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Calendar, holiday & recurrence math

Holiday, business-day, and recurrence functions over Apache Arrow, exposed as ordinary DuckDB SQL.

**Key concepts**

- Scalar functions answer one question per row and slot into a projection or predicate.
- Table functions return sets of rows: a year's holidays, a range of working days, or an expanded recurrence.
- Country/subdivision are ordinary arguments; `'US'` is only a default, not a limit — coverage is global.
- `DATE`, `TIMESTAMP`, and `TIMESTAMPTZ` round-trip natively over Arrow.

**When to use it**

Reach for this schema for holiday and business-day date math (settlement, SLA, payroll, billing), calendar labels (Easter, ISO week / year-week), and RFC-5545 recurrence expansion. The `supported_countries` table enumerates the valid `country`/`subdiv` codes those functions accept.

functions.name: rrule
functions.comment: Expand an RFC-5545 recurrence rule (dateutil) into timestamps

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Expand an **RFC-5545 (iCalendar) recurrence rule** into concrete timestamps as `(seq, occurrence)` rows. Takes a `dtstart` timestamp and an RRULE string (e.g. `'FREQ=WEEKLY;COUNT=4'` or a full `'RRULE:...'`) positionally, plus optional named `count` and `until` bounds. Because an RRULE can be infinite, you **must** bound it -- either inside the rule (`COUNT=`/`UNTIL=`) or via the `count`/`until` arguments -- or it will not terminate. `seq` is the 0-based occurrence index. Parsing is via `dateutil.rrule`. Use it to materialize schedules: meetings, billing cycles, reminders, cron-like calendar events.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## rrule(dtstart, rule, count := ..., until := ...)

Expand an **RFC-5545 RRULE** into `(seq, occurrence)` timestamp rows.

Always bound the rule (`COUNT`/`UNTIL` in the string, or the `count`/`until` args) -- recurrences can be infinite. `seq` is the 0-based index. Backed by `dateutil.rrule`.

functions.name: holidays
functions.comment: All public holidays in a year (date, name, observed)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: List **every public holiday in a calendar year** as `(date, name, observed)` rows. Takes the year as a positional argument and optional named `country` (default `'US'`) and `subdiv` (state/province) arguments. The `observed` column is `true` when the row is an *observed-day shift* -- e.g. a holiday that falls on a weekend and is observed on the adjacent weekday. Coverage spans hundreds of countries via the `holidays` library; call `cal.supported_countries` to discover valid `country`/`subdiv` codes. Use it to build a holiday lookup table, join against transactions, or audit a jurisdiction's calendar.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## holidays(year, country := ..., subdiv := ...)

All **public holidays in a year** as `(date, name, observed)` rows.

`country` defaults to `'US'`; add `subdiv` for regional holidays. `observed` flags weekend-shift observances. See `cal.supported_countries` for valid codes.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT date, name FROM cal.main.holidays(2026, country := 'US') ORDER BY date

vgi.example_queries.description: US + California holidays in 2026, ordered by date
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT date, name FROM cal.main.holidays(2026, country := 'US', subdiv := 'CA') ORDER BY date

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT h.date, h.name, cal.main.business_days_between(DATE '2026-11-13', h.date) AS business_days_away FROM cal.main.holidays(2026, country := 'US') AS h WHERE h.date >= DATE '2026-11-13' ORDER BY h.date

vgi.example_queries.description: Moveable feasts: the German holidays whose offset from easter() is the same in 2025, 2026 and 2027, i.e. the Easter-anchored ones, with that offset in days. Fixed-date holidays such as Labor Day drop out.
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH h AS (SELECT date, name FROM cal.main.holidays(2025, country := 'DE') UNION ALL SELECT date, name FROM cal.main.holidays(2026, country := 'DE') UNION ALL SELECT date, name FROM cal.main.holidays(2027, country := 'DE')) SELECT name, min(date - cal.main.easter(year(date))) AS days_from_easter FROM h GROUP BY name HAVING count(*) = 3 AND count(DISTINCT date - cal.main.easter(year(date))) = 1 ORDER BY days_from_easter
