functions.name: business_days
functions.comment: Every business day in an inclusive [start, end] range

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Enumerate **every business (working) day in an inclusive `[start, end]` date range**, one per row -- weekdays that are not public holidays. Takes `start` and `end` positionally plus optional named `country` (default `'US'`) and `subdiv`. Both bounds are inclusive. Use it to expand a range into a working-day series you can join against, count, or window over (e.g. allocate workload across business days). For other jurisdictions pass `country`/`subdiv`; see `cal.supported_countries` for valid codes.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## business_days(start, end, country := ..., subdiv := ...)

Every **business day in the inclusive `[start, end]` range**, one per row.

Weekdays minus holidays; both bounds inclusive. `country` defaults to `'US'`. Expand a range into a working-day series for joins/counts.

vgi.example_queries.description: How many US business days fall in the 2026 year-end week (Christmas excluded)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS business_days FROM cal.main.business_days(DATE '2026-12-21', DATE '2026-12-31', country := 'US')

vgi.example_queries.description: The US business days of the 2026 year-end week, in order
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT date FROM cal.main.business_days(DATE '2026-12-21', DATE '2026-12-31', country := 'US') ORDER BY date

vgi.example_queries.description: Capacity plan: US business days per month in 2026, with the holidays that fell on a weekday and so removed a working day (weekend holidays such as Saturday 4 July are left out).
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH bd AS (SELECT date_trunc('month', date) AS month, count(*) AS business_days FROM cal.main.business_days(DATE '2026-01-01', DATE '2026-12-31', country := 'US') GROUP BY ALL), lost AS (SELECT date_trunc('month', date) AS month, count(*) AS weekday_holidays, string_agg(name, ', ' ORDER BY date) AS holiday_names FROM cal.main.holidays(2026, country := 'US') WHERE isodow(date) <= 5 GROUP BY ALL) SELECT strftime(bd.month, '%Y-%m') AS month, bd.business_days, coalesce(lost.weekday_holidays, 0) AS weekday_holidays, lost.holiday_names FROM bd LEFT JOIN lost USING (month) ORDER BY bd.month

vgi.example_queries.description: Cross-border settlement window: the days from 21 Dec 2026 to 8 Jan 2027 when both the US and the UK (GB) are open, i.e. US business days that are also GB business days.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT b.date, dayname(b.date) AS weekday FROM cal.main.business_days(DATE '2026-12-21', DATE '2027-01-08', country := 'US') AS b WHERE cal.main.is_business_day(b.date, 'GB') ORDER BY b.date

vgi.example_queries.description: Sprint capacity: US business days in each ISO week from 30 Nov 2026 to 10 Jan 2027, labelled with iso_year_week (Christmas and New Year's Day cut W52 and W53 to 4 days).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT cal.main.iso_year_week(b.date) AS iso_week, count(*) AS business_days, min(b.date) AS first_day, max(b.date) AS last_day FROM cal.main.business_days(DATE '2026-11-30', DATE '2027-01-10', country := 'US') AS b GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY iso_week

functions.name: easter
functions.comment: Western (Gregorian) Easter Sunday for a year

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Return the date of Western (Gregorian) **Easter Sunday** for a given calendar year. Easter is a *movable feast* whose date is derived from the ecclesiastical lunar calendar, so it cannot be computed with ordinary date arithmetic. Pass an integer year (e.g. `2026`) and get back a `DATE`; `NULL` years pass through as `NULL`. Useful for anchoring Easter-relative observances such as Good Friday (Easter - 2 days), Easter Monday (Easter + 1), Ascension, or Pentecost. This is the Gregorian/Western computus only -- Orthodox (Julian) Easter is not returned.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## easter

Western (Gregorian) **Easter Sunday** for a year.

Easter is a movable feast, so it needs the computus rather than plain date math. `easter(2026)` returns `DATE '2026-04-05'`.

Derive related days arithmetically: Good Friday is `easter(y) - 2`, Easter Monday is `easter(y) + 1`. Returns the Western/Gregorian date only.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Return the **ISO-8601 year-week label** such as `'2026-W26'` for a date. This combines the ISO week-numbering *year* with the ISO week number, which is the correct, unambiguous way to label a week: because ISO week 1 is anchored to the first Thursday, the ISO year can differ from the calendar year for dates near the year boundary (e.g. `2027-01-01` may be labelled `'2026-W53'`). ## iso_year_week

Combines the ISO week-numbering year with the zero-padded week so the label is unambiguous across year boundaries (a January date can be `'2025-W52'`). Returns a string -- handy as a `GROUP BY` key for weekly rollups.

functions.name: iso_week
functions.comment: ISO-8601 week number (1..53) for a date

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Return the **ISO-8601 week number** (1..53) for a date. Under ISO-8601, weeks start on Monday and week 1 is the week containing the first Thursday of the year, so the first few days of January can belong to week 52/53 of the *previous* ISO year (and the last days of December to week 1 of the *next*). This returns only the week component; pair it with `iso_year_week` when you need the disambiguating year. `NULL` dates pass through as `NULL`.

functions.name: add_business_days
functions.comment: Advance a date by N business days, skipping weekends + holidays (country 'US')

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Advance a date by **N business days in a country subdivision** (state/province/region), skipping weekends and that subdivision's public holidays. Pass the ISO-3166 country code plus a subdivision code (e.g. `'US','CA'`) as the third and fourth arguments. This four-argument overload honours *regional* holidays the national overload would miss -- e.g. advancing across California's Cesar Chavez Day skips it, whereas the plain `'US'` calendar does not. `N` may be negative to step backwards; the result is always a business day. Returns `DATE` per row (`NULL` inputs -> `NULL`). See `cal.supported_countries` for valid `(country, subdiv)` pairs.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## add_business_days(date, n, country, subdiv)

Advance `date` by **`n` business days in a subdivision** (e.g. `'US','CA'`).

Skips weekends + that subdivision's holidays; `n` can be negative. Per-row `DATE`. See `cal.supported_countries` for valid `(country, subdiv)` pairs.

vgi.example_queries.description: Two business days after 2026-12-24 (skips Christmas + weekend)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT cal.main.add_business_days(DATE '2026-12-24', 2)

vgi.example_queries.description: Two UK business days after 2026-12-24
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT cal.main.add_business_days(DATE '2026-12-24', 2, 'GB')

vgi.example_queries.description: Two California business days after 2026-03-30 (skips Cesar Chavez Day)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT cal.main.add_business_days(DATE '2026-03-30', 2, 'US', 'CA')

vgi.example_queries.description: Payment calendar: 1st-of-month 2026 payments from rrule, rolled forward to the next US business day when the 1st is not one, with the reason: the holiday name, or the weekday for weekend rolls.
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH sched AS (SELECT r.seq, CAST(r.occurrence AS DATE) AS due FROM cal.main.rrule(TIMESTAMP '2026-01-01', 'FREQ=MONTHLY;BYMONTHDAY=1;COUNT=12') AS r) SELECT due, CASE WHEN cal.main.is_business_day(due) THEN due ELSE cal.main.add_business_days(due, 1) END AS settles_on, CASE WHEN NOT cal.main.is_business_day(due) THEN coalesce(cal.main.holiday_name(due), dayname(due)) END AS rolled_because FROM sched ORDER BY seq

tags.vgi.title: Add Business Days In Subdivision

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Test whether a date is a **business (working) day in a country subdivision** (state/province/region) -- a weekday that is not a holiday under that subdivision's calendar. Pass the ISO-3166 country code plus a subdivision code (e.g. `'US','CA'`). Regional holidays count: `2026-03-31` is a weekday but, in California, it is Cesar Chavez Day and so is *not* a business day there. Returns `BOOLEAN` per row (`NULL` date -> `NULL`); see `cal.supported_countries` for valid pairs.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## is_business_day(date, country, subdiv)

True if `date` is a **working day in a subdivision** (e.g. `'US','CA'`).

Honours region-only holidays. Per-row `BOOLEAN`; see `cal.supported_countries` for valid `(country, subdiv)` pairs.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT cal.main.is_business_day(DATE '2026-12-25')

vgi.example_queries.description: Is Christmas 2026 a UK business day?
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT cal.main.is_business_day(DATE '2026-12-25', 'GB')

vgi.example_queries.description: Is Cesar Chavez Day a California business day?

vgi.example_queries.description: Cross-border settlement window: the days from 21 Dec 2026 to 8 Jan 2027 when both the US and the UK (GB) are open, i.e. US business days that are also GB business days.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT b.date, dayname(b.date) AS weekday FROM cal.main.business_days(DATE '2026-12-21', DATE '2027-01-08', country := 'US') AS b WHERE cal.main.is_business_day(b.date, 'GB') ORDER BY b.date

workers.title: US Vehicle Data
workers.tagline: US vehicle specs, EPA fuel economy, VIN decoding, recalls and crash ratings in DuckDB (Python)
workers.subtitle: EPA fuel economy, NHTSA VIN decoding, recalls, complaints and crash ratings for US vehicles.
workers.summary: US vehicle specifications, fuel economy and safety from keyless US-government sources: EPA fueleconomy.gov MPG and powertrain data since 1984, NHTSA vPIC VIN decoding, recalls, owner complaints and NCAP 5-Star crash ratings.
workers.doc_md:
# Cars: US vehicle specs, fuel economy and safety

**Keyless US-government vehicle data in DuckDB.** Look up EPA fuel economy and specifications for every US light-duty vehicle since 1984, decode VINs, and check recalls, owner complaints and crash ratings, then join them in SQL.

Sources (all US-government works in the public domain, no key needed):

- [EPA fueleconomy.gov web services and bulk data](https://www.fueleconomy.gov/feg/ws/index.shtml)
- [NHTSA vPIC API](https://vpic.nhtsa.dot.gov/api/) for VIN decoding, makes and models
- [NHTSA datasets and APIs](https://www.nhtsa.gov/nhtsa-datasets-and-apis) for recalls, complaints and 5-Star Safety Ratings

Join across sources on `model_year` and the upper-cased `make`. Vehicle colors are not included: there is no free official source for them.
workers.readme_sql:
-- Fuel economy and crash ratings for the 2020 Honda Accord, side by side.
SELECT v.model, v.combined_mpg, s.vehicle_description, s.overall_rating
FROM cars.main.vehicles(year := 2020, make := 'honda', model := 'accord') v
JOIN cars.main.safety_ratings('honda', 'accord', 2020) s
  ON s.model_year = v.model_year AND s.make = v.make AND s.model = upper(v.base_model)
ORDER BY v.combined_mpg DESC;

example_queries.description: Check whether the EPA file is cached and which model years it covers
example_queries.sql: SELECT cached, vehicle_rows, min_model_year, max_model_year FROM cars.main.cache_info()

example_queries.sql: SELECT status, vehicle_rows, max_model_year FROM cars.main.refresh_cache()

example_queries.description: Passenger-car makes whose names start with A
example_queries.sql: SELECT make FROM cars.main.makes(vehicle_type := 'car') WHERE make LIKE 'A%' ORDER BY make

example_queries.description: Honda's 2020 model lineup according to NHTSA
example_queries.sql: SELECT model FROM cars.main.models('honda', year := 2020) WHERE make = 'HONDA' ORDER BY model

example_queries.description: Decode one VIN and pick out make, model, year, body and plant country
example_queries.sql: SELECT d.make, d.model, d.model_year, d.body_class, d.plant_country FROM (SELECT cars.main.decode_vin('1HGCM82633A004352') AS d)

example_queries.description: Decode a small list of VINs into make, model, year and electrification
example_queries.sql: SELECT vin, make, model, model_year, electrification_level FROM cars.main.decode_vins((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('1HGCM82633A004352'), ('5YJ3E1EA7KF317000')) AS t(vin))) ORDER BY vin

example_queries.description: Air bag recalls for the 2003 Honda Accord, oldest first
example_queries.sql: SELECT campaign_number, report_received_date, component FROM cars.main.recalls('honda', 'accord', 2003) WHERE component LIKE 'AIR BAGS%' ORDER BY report_received_date, campaign_number

example_queries.description: The five components owners complain about most for the 2003 Honda Accord
example_queries.sql: SELECT component, count(*) AS complaints FROM (SELECT unnest(components) AS component FROM cars.main.complaints('honda', 'accord', 2003)) GROUP BY component ORDER BY complaints DESC, component LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Crash ratings for each tested 2024 Toyota Tundra cab and drive variant
example_queries.sql: SELECT vehicle_description, overall_rating, rollover_rating, rollover_risk FROM cars.main.safety_ratings('toyota', 'tundra', 2024) ORDER BY vehicle_description

example_queries.description: Count EV models and the longest EPA range per model year since 2020
example_queries.sql: SELECT model_year, count(*) AS ev_models, max(electric_range_miles) AS longest_range FROM cars.main.vehicles() WHERE powertrain = 'EV' AND model_year >= 2020 GROUP BY model_year ORDER BY model_year

example_queries.description: Decode a 2003 Honda VIN and return its trim

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The `main` schema holds every cars function. EPA fuel economy comes from a locally cached bulk file, so filtering and aggregating it is fast and offline after the first download. NHTSA functions call the live APIs per make, model and model year; they take those three values positionally and return zero rows for unknown vehicles. VIN decoding is available as a scalar returning a `STRUCT` for use inside projections, and as a table in-out function for decoding a query's VIN column into flat columns. Every result uses model_year `INTEGER` and upper-cased make as join keys.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

Vehicle data functions grouped by source:

- **Fuel economy** from EPA fueleconomy.gov, served from a local cache of the bulk file.
- **VIN decoding and model lists** from NHTSA vPIC.
- **Safety** (recalls, complaints, crash ratings) from NHTSA, per make, model and model year.
- **Cache** functions report and refresh the EPA file's vintage.

functions.name: vehicles
functions.comment: EPA fuel economy and specs for US vehicles since 1984, filterable by year, make and model

tags.vgi.doc_llm: EPA fuel economy and powertrain specifications for every light-duty vehicle sold in the US since model year 1984 (about 50,000 rows), from the fueleconomy.gov bulk file. One row per EPA vehicle configuration (model year x make x model x engine x transmission x drive). Optional named filters: `year := 2024`, `make := 'toyota'` (case-insensitive), `model := 'tundra'` (matches base_model or the full EPA model name, case-insensitive). Key columns: model_year, make (upper-cased join key), model, base_model, vehicle_class, drive, transmission, cylinders, engine_displacement_l, fuel_type, powertrain ('EV', 'Hybrid', 'Plug-in Hybrid', 'FFV', 'Diesel', 'CNG' or NULL for conventional), city_mpg/highway_mpg/combined_mpg (MPGe for EVs), *_secondary MPG for dual-fuel vehicles, electric_range_miles, co2_grams_per_mile, annual_fuel_cost_usd, fuel_economy_score, ghg_score, fueleconomy_url. The file is downloaded once (~2 MB) into a local cache and re-checked weekly; use `cache_info()` to see its vintage. Join to NHTSA functions on model_year and make; compare upper(base_model) with NHTSA's upper-case model names. No colors: no free official source.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## vehicles(year := NULL, make := NULL, model := NULL)

Every EPA-tested US light-duty vehicle since 1984 with MPG/MPGe, CO2, fuel cost, EV range and powertrain details, from the [fueleconomy.gov](https://www.fueleconomy.gov/feg/ws/index.shtml) bulk file (US government work, public domain).

- Named filters are applied before rows leave the worker; `make` and `model` are case-insensitive, and `model` matches the base model or full model name.
- `make` is upper-cased to join with the NHTSA functions.
- The ~2 MB file is cached locally (see `cache_info()` / `refresh_cache()`).

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Table in-out function: pass a subquery with a `VARCHAR` column `vin` (and optionally an `INTEGER` `model_year`), e.g. `decode_vins((SELECT vin FROM fleet))`. Returns one row per input row with the same columns as the `decode_vin` `STRUCT`, flattened: vin, make, model, model_year, trim, series, body_class, vehicle_type, doors, drive_type, primary_fuel, secondary_fuel, electrification_level, engine_cylinders, displacement_l, engine_hp, turbo, transmission_style, transmission_speeds, gvwr_class, manufacturer, plant_city, plant_state, plant_country, error_code, error_text, suggested_vin. functions.name: decode_vin
functions.comment: Decode a VIN with NHTSA vPIC into a STRUCT of make, model, year, body, engine and plant

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Decode US Vehicle Identification Numbers with NHTSA vPIC and return a `STRUCT` of key fields: vin, make (upper-cased), model, model_year, trim, series, body_class, vehicle_type, doors, drive_type, primary_fuel, secondary_fuel, electrification_level, engine_cylinders, displacement_l, engine_hp, turbo, transmission_style, transmission_speeds, gvwr_class, manufacturer, plant_city, plant_state, plant_country, error_code ('0' = clean), error_text, suggested_vin. Access fields with dot notation: `cars.main.decode_vin(vin).make`. Works over a column: VINs are de-duplicated and sent 50 per request. NULL or blank VIN gives NULL; partial VINs (with '*') decode what they can; a malformed VIN returns a struct with error_code '400'. Missing values mean NHTSA has no data, not that a feature is absent. For many columns at once use `decode_vins((SELECT vin ...))`. This overload also sends `model_year` (an integer, 1949-2100, constant or a column), which vPIC uses because VIN position 10 repeats every 30 years: `decode_vin(vin, model_year) FROM fleet` decodes each row with its own year.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## decode_vin(vin, model_year)

Same `STRUCT` as `decode_vin(vin)`, with the model year passed to vPIC.

workers.title: Causal Inference
workers.tagline: Causal inference — ATE/ATT & propensity (IPW/AIPW) for DuckDB (Python)
workers.subtitle: Estimate treatment effects (ATE, ATT) and propensity scores from observational data with IPW, regression adjustment, and AIPW.
workers.summary: Causal treatment-effect estimation (ATE, ATT, propensity scores) for SQL
workers.doc_md:
# Causal Inference in SQL: Treatment Effects, Propensity & Doubly-Robust Estimation

![DoWhy logo](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/py-why/dowhy/main/docs/source/_static/dowhy-logo-small.png)

**Estimate the causal effect of an intervention directly in DuckDB SQL** — average treatment effect (ATE), effect on the treated (ATT), and per-subject propensity scores — from observational cohort data, with confounders adjusted for automatically. This VGI extension turns causal questions like *"did the treatment actually work, after controlling for who was likely to get it?"* into a single SQL query.

Causal inference goes beyond correlation and naive group means: a simple difference between treated and untreated subjects is biased whenever the same factors that drive treatment also drive the outcome (confounding). The `causal` catalog corrects that bias using the standard toolkit of observational causal inference — inverse probability weighting (IPW), regression adjustment (the g-formula), and doubly-robust augmented IPW (AIPW) — so analysts, data scientists, and epidemiologists can run treatment-effect, impact, and intervention analysis where their data already lives, without exporting to a notebook.

Under the hood the estimators are powered by [scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/) ([source](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn)) for the propensity and outcome models and [statsmodels](https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/index.html) ([source](https://github.com/statsmodels/statsmodels)) for the regression and inference machinery, with an optional doubly-robust backend via [DoWhy](https://www.pywhy.org/dowhy/) ([source](https://github.com/py-why/dowhy)). Propensities come from an L2-regularized logistic model with score clipping that keeps near-perfect separation from blowing up the weights, and standard errors come from influence functions (IPW/AIPW), OLS (regression adjustment), or a seeded bootstrap (ATT) — every estimate is deterministic and reproducible.

## Estimands

Every estimator consumes a whole cohort as a `(SELECT ...)` relation plus named role arguments; **every column not named by a role is treated as a covariate/confounder and adjusted for**, and treatment must be binary `0/1`.

- **Average treatment effect** `E[Y(1)-Y(0)]`, returned one row per method: IPW, regression adjustment, and doubly-robust AIPW, each with a standard error and 95% confidence interval.
- **Average treatment effect on the treated** `E[Y(1)-Y(0)|T=1]` via IPW-ATT weighting, with a bootstrap standard error.
- **Per-row propensity** `e(X)=P(T=1|X)` from the logistic model, keyed by your `id` column.

Runnable, catalog-qualified demonstrations live in each object's example queries (and the schema's `vgi.example_queries`), so they are executed and coverage-checked rather than pasted inline here.

Estimates are causal only under the usual assumptions — **unconfoundedness** (no unmeasured confounders given the supplied covariates), **overlap** (`0 < e(X) < 1`), and **SUTVA**. Choosing the covariate set is your modeling decision; the worker estimates, it does not assume the assumptions hold.

example_queries.description: Average treatment effect by IPW, regression adjustment, and doubly-robust AIPW.
example_queries.sql:
WITH cohort AS (
  SELECT
    g                                                   AS id,
    (g - 30)::DOUBLE / 10.0                             AS x,
    CASE WHEN ((g * 7 + 3) % 10) < 5 + 3 * sign(g - 30) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS t,
    5.0 * (CASE WHEN ((g * 7 + 3) % 10) < 5 + 3 * sign(g - 30) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
      + 2.0 * ((g - 30)::DOUBLE / 10.0)                 AS y
  FROM generate_series(0, 60) AS s(g)
)
SELECT method, round(estimate, 2) AS estimate FROM causal.main.ate((SELECT t, y, x FROM cohort), treatment := 't', outcome := 'y') ORDER BY method

example_queries.description: Average treatment effect on the treated (ATT).
example_queries.sql:
WITH cohort AS (
  SELECT
    g                                                   AS id,
    (g - 30)::DOUBLE / 10.0                             AS x,
    CASE WHEN ((g * 7 + 3) % 10) < 5 + 3 * sign(g - 30) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS t,
    5.0 * (CASE WHEN ((g * 7 + 3) % 10) < 5 + 3 * sign(g - 30) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
      + 2.0 * ((g - 30)::DOUBLE / 10.0)                 AS y
  FROM generate_series(0, 60) AS s(g)
)
SELECT round(estimate, 2) AS att FROM causal.main.att((SELECT t, y, x FROM cohort), treatment := 't', outcome := 'y')

example_queries.description: The five subjects most likely to have been treated, by fitted propensity.
example_queries.sql:
WITH cohort AS (
  SELECT
    g                                                   AS id,
    (g - 30)::DOUBLE / 10.0                             AS x,
    CASE WHEN ((g * 7 + 3) % 10) < 5 + 3 * sign(g - 30) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS t,
    5.0 * (CASE WHEN ((g * 7 + 3) % 10) < 5 + 3 * sign(g - 30) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
      + 2.0 * ((g - 30)::DOUBLE / 10.0)                 AS y
  FROM generate_series(0, 60) AS s(g)
)
SELECT id, round(propensity, 3) AS propensity, treatment FROM causal.main.propensity_scores((SELECT id, t, x FROM cohort), treatment := 't', id := 'id') ORDER BY propensity DESC LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Naive treated-minus-control difference of means next to the doubly-robust ATE and the ATT: confounding by x inflates the naive contrast well above both adjusted estimates.
example_queries.sql:
WITH cohort AS (
  SELECT
    g                                                   AS id,
    (g - 30)::DOUBLE / 10.0                             AS x,
    CASE WHEN ((g * 7 + 3) % 10) < 5 + 3 * sign(g - 30) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS t,
    5.0 * (CASE WHEN ((g * 7 + 3) % 10) < 5 + 3 * sign(g - 30) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
      + 2.0 * ((g - 30)::DOUBLE / 10.0)                 AS y
  FROM generate_series(0, 60) AS s(g)
)
, naive AS (SELECT avg(y) FILTER (WHERE t = 1) - avg(y) FILTER (WHERE t = 0) AS diff FROM cohort), dr AS (SELECT estimate FROM causal.main.ate((SELECT t, y, x FROM cohort), treatment := 't', outcome := 'y') WHERE method = 'aipw'), treated AS (SELECT estimate FROM causal.main.att((SELECT t, y, x FROM cohort), treatment := 't', outcome := 'y')) SELECT round(naive.diff, 2) AS naive_diff, round(dr.estimate, 2) AS ate_aipw, round(treated.estimate, 2) AS att FROM naive CROSS JOIN dr CROSS JOIN treated

example_queries.description: Overlap trimming: keep only subjects whose fitted propensity lies in [0.2, 0.8] (44 of the 61), then re-estimate the ATE by every method on that trimmed cohort.
example_queries.sql:
WITH cohort AS (
  SELECT
    g                                                   AS id,
    (g - 30)::DOUBLE / 10.0                             AS x,
    CASE WHEN ((g * 7 + 3) % 10) < 5 + 3 * sign(g - 30) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS t,
    5.0 * (CASE WHEN ((g * 7 + 3) % 10) < 5 + 3 * sign(g - 30) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
      + 2.0 * ((g - 30)::DOUBLE / 10.0)                 AS y

## Causal treatment-effect estimation

Estimate the causal effect of a **binary treatment** on an outcome from observational cohort data, adjusting for measured confounders — directly in DuckDB SQL, with no export to a notebook.

### Key concepts

- **Confounding** biases a naive difference of group means whenever the factors that drive treatment also drive the outcome; adjustment corrects it.
- Estimators draw on the standard observational toolkit — inverse-probability weighting (IPW), regression adjustment (the g-formula), and doubly-robust augmented IPW (AIPW).
- Each call consumes a whole `(SELECT ...)` cohort relation plus named role arguments; every column not named by a role is treated as an adjusted-for covariate, and treatment must be binary `0/1`.

### When to use

Reach for these estimators for treatment-effect, impact, and intervention analysis where the data already lives. Estimates are causal only under unconfoundedness, overlap, and SUTVA.

Backed by scikit-learn and statsmodels, with deterministic, reproducible estimates.

# Estimator Method Reference

A small, self-contained registry of the estimator methods the `causal` worker exposes — one row per method. Use it to discover the worker's surface before calling a table function: which methods `ate` emits, which estimator is doubly-robust, and what each one estimates.

## Columns

- `method` — the estimator id (matches the `method` column emitted by `ate`).
- `function_name` — the function that produces the method (`ate`, `att`, or `propensity_scores`).
- `estimand` — the causal quantity: `ATE`, `ATT`, or the per-row propensity `e(X)`.
- `doubly_robust` — `TRUE` for AIPW (consistent if either nuisance model is correct).
- `description` — a one-line summary of the estimator.

The registry is backed by an inline `VALUES` relation, so it scans with no external data or credentials.

# Average Treatment effect on the Treated (ATT)

Estimate `E[Y(1) - Y(0) | T = 1]`: the average treatment effect **restricted to the units that actually received treatment**, via inverse-probability-of-treatment (IPW-ATT) weighting.

**Inputs.** A `(SELECT ...)` cohort relation as the first positional argument, plus named role args `treatment` (a binary 0/1 column) and `outcome` (a numeric column). Every remaining column is a covariate/confounder and is adjusted for. An optional `random_state` (default 0) seeds the propensity fit and the bootstrap.

**Output.** A single row: `estimate` (the ATT) and `std_error` (a deterministic, seeded bootstrap standard error).

**When to use.** When the policy question is about those who were treated -- e.g. 'how much did the program help the people who enrolled?' -- rather than the whole population (which is `ate`). The ATT and ATE coincide under a homogeneous effect but diverge with effect heterogeneity.

**Edge cases / assumptions.** Controls are reweighted by `e/(1 - e)`; the propensity model is regularized and clipped, so it stays finite under near-separation. Treatment must be exactly binary `{0, 1}`. Causal only under unconfoundedness, overlap on the treated, and SUTVA. The bootstrap is seeded (`random_state`), so the SE is reproducible.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# Average Treatment Effect (ATE)

Estimate the **average treatment effect** `E[Y(1) - Y(0)]` of a binary treatment on a numeric outcome from an observational cohort, adjusting for confounders.

**Inputs.** A `(SELECT ...)` cohort relation as the first positional argument, plus named role args `treatment` (a binary 0/1 column) and `outcome` (a numeric column). Every remaining column is treated as a covariate/confounder and is adjusted for. An optional `random_state` (default 0) seeds the deterministic propensity fit.

**Output.** Three rows, one per estimator: `ipw` (inverse-probability weighting, Hajek/self-normalized), `regression_adjustment` (g-formula via OLS), and `aipw` (doubly-robust). Each row has `estimate`, `std_error`, and a 95% Wald confidence interval (`ci_lower`, `ci_upper`).

**When to use.** Answering 'what is the overall effect of this intervention?' Comparing methods builds confidence: AIPW is doubly-robust, so it is consistent if *either* the propensity or the outcome model is correct.

**Edge cases / assumptions.** Treatment must be exactly binary `{0, 1}` or the call errors. Estimates are causal only under unconfoundedness (no unmeasured confounding given the covariates), overlap (`0 < e(X) < 1`), and SUTVA. With few rows or perfect separation the SEs widen but the regularized propensity model still returns finite estimates.

## Usage

## Notes

- Emits one row per method: `ipw`, `regression_adjustment`, `aipw`.
- Each row carries the point estimate, its standard error, and a 95% Wald confidence interval.
- `treatment` must be binary 0/1; every non-role column is an adjusted-for covariate. Estimates are causal only under unconfoundedness, overlap, and SUTVA.

functions.name: propensity_scores
functions.comment: Fit a logistic propensity model and emit per-row scores: (id, propensity, treatment). The id column is passed through and excluded from the covariates; every other column is a covariate. treatment must be binary 0/1.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# Propensity Scores

Fit a logistic **propensity model** `e(X) = P(T = 1 | X)` over the cohort and emit one row per input subject: its `id`, fitted `propensity`, and observed `treatment`.

**Inputs.** A `(SELECT ...)` cohort relation as the first positional argument, plus named role args `treatment` (a binary 0/1 column) and `id` (a row identifier passed through and **excluded** from the covariates). Every other column is a covariate fed to the logistic model. An optional `random_state` (default 0) seeds the deterministic fit.

**Output.** One row per input row: `id` (`BIGINT`), `propensity` (`DOUBLE` in `(0, 1)`), and `treatment` (`INTEGER` 0/1).

**When to use.** Diagnose overlap/positivity before estimating effects, build matched or weighted cohorts, or trim units with extreme scores. The scores are the same ones `ate`/`att` use internally for IPW.

**Edge cases / behaviors.** The logistic fit is L2-regularized and scores are clipped to `[1e-6, 1 - 1e-6]`, so perfect separation does not produce 0/1 scores or infinite weights. Treatment must be exactly binary `{0, 1}`. The output is unbounded (one row per subject) and is paged through the worker's offset cursor.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# propensity_scores

Per-row fitted propensity `e(X) = P(T = 1 | X)` from a regularized logistic model.

## Usage

Pass a cohort relation as the first positional argument and name the `treatment` and `id` roles; the `id` column is passed through and every other column is a covariate. A complete, runnable call is attached as this function's example query.

## Notes

- Emits one row per input subject: `(id, propensity, treatment)`.
- The `id` column is passed through and excluded from the covariates; every other column is a covariate.
- Scores are clipped to `(0, 1)`; use them for overlap diagnostics, matching, or weighting. `treatment` must be binary 0/1.

vgi.example_queries.description: The five subjects most likely to have been treated, by fitted propensity.
vgi.example_queries.sql:
WITH cohort AS (
  SELECT
    g                                                   AS id,
    (g - 30)::DOUBLE / 10.0                             AS x,
    CASE WHEN ((g * 7 + 3) % 10) < 5 + 3 * sign(g - 30) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS t,
    5.0 * (CASE WHEN ((g * 7 + 3) % 10) < 5 + 3 * sign(g - 30) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
      + 2.0 * ((g - 30)::DOUBLE / 10.0)                 AS y
  FROM generate_series(0, 60) AS s(g)
)
SELECT id, round(propensity, 3) AS propensity, treatment FROM causal.main.propensity_scores((SELECT id, t, x FROM cohort), treatment := 't', id := 'id') ORDER BY propensity DESC LIMIT 5

vgi.example_queries.description: Count subjects whose fitted propensity exceeds one half (an overlap check).
vgi.example_queries.sql:
WITH cohort AS (
  SELECT
    g                                                   AS id,
    (g - 30)::DOUBLE / 10.0                             AS x,
    CASE WHEN ((g * 7 + 3) % 10) < 5 + 3 * sign(g - 30) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS t,
    5.0 * (CASE WHEN ((g * 7 + 3) % 10) < 5 + 3 * sign(g - 30) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
      + 2.0 * ((g - 30)::DOUBLE / 10.0)                 AS y
  FROM generate_series(0, 60) AS s(g)
)
SELECT count(*) AS n_high_propensity FROM causal.main.propensity_scores((SELECT id, t, x FROM cohort), treatment := 't', id := 'id') WHERE propensity > 0.5

vgi.example_queries.description: Overlap trimming: keep only subjects whose fitted propensity lies in [0.2, 0.8] (44 of the 61), then re-estimate the ATE by every method on that trimmed cohort.
vgi.example_queries.sql:
WITH cohort AS (
  SELECT
    g                                                   AS id,
    (g - 30)::DOUBLE / 10.0                             AS x,
    CASE WHEN ((g * 7 + 3) % 10) < 5 + 3 * sign(g - 30) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS t,
    5.0 * (CASE WHEN ((g * 7 + 3) % 10) < 5 + 3 * sign(g - 30) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
      + 2.0 * ((g - 30)::DOUBLE / 10.0)                 AS y
  FROM generate_series(0, 60) AS s(g)
)
, ps AS (SELECT id, propensity FROM causal.main.propensity_scores((SELECT id, t, x FROM cohort), treatment := 't', id := 'id')) SELECT method, round(estimate, 2) AS estimate, round(std_error, 3) AS std_error FROM causal.main.ate((SELECT c.t, c.y, c.x FROM cohort AS c JOIN ps USING (id) WHERE ps.propensity BETWEEN 0.2 AND 0.8), treatment := 't', outcome := 'y') ORDER BY method

workers.title: CBOR & MessagePack
workers.tagline: Decode CBOR and MessagePack in DuckDB with SQL — with tag-aware COSE / CWT / WebAuthn structural decode. A VGI worker.
workers.subtitle: Decode and encode CBOR and MessagePack, inspect security payloads, and import or export row files from SQL.
workers.summary: CBOR (RFC 8949) / MessagePack decode & encode plus tag-aware COSE / CWT / WebAuthn structural decode and bulk COPY import/export for SQL.
workers.doc_md:
# cbor

Decode and encode **CBOR** (RFC 8949) and **MessagePack** in SQL, plus tag-aware structural decoders for **COSE** (RFC 9052), **CWT** (RFC 8392), **COSE_Key**, and **WebAuthn / FIDO2 / CTAP2** attestation. The byte codec is commodity; the value is the in-engine security-payload decode and the bulk SQL join surface (COSE `x5t`/`x5chain` and WebAuthn `x5c` join to `vgi-x509`). Scalar and blob-input table functions use no network or persisted state.

**Bulk files:** load and save row files with COPY.

```sql
COPY events FROM 'events.cbor' (FORMAT '<alias>.cbor');
COPY events TO 'events.mp' (FORMAT '<alias>.msgpack');
```

Replace `<alias>` with the attached catalog name (usually `cbor`). Both formats read and write worker-local files or `s3://` objects using DuckDB secrets; `http(s)://` is read-only. Reads stream and support globs. Exports stage batches in execution-scoped storage, then publish a temporary local file or multipart upload after encoding succeeds.

**Structural decode only:** no signature/MAC verification and no decryption (a downstream verifier consumes `cose_payload` + `cose_key`).

## Sources and references

- [RFC 8949](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8949) — Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR)
- [MessagePack specification](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack/blob/master/spec.md)
- [RFC 9052](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9052) — COSE structures; [IANA COSE registries](https://www.iana.org/assignments/cose/cose.xhtml) for algorithm, key-type and curve labels
- [RFC 8392](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8392) — CBOR Web Token (CWT)
- [W3C Web Authentication](https://www.w3.org/TR/webauthn-2/) — WebAuthn attestation objects

example_queries.description: Decode the CBOR array [1,2,3] to JSON.
example_queries.sql: SELECT cbor.main.to_json(from_hex('83010203')) AS j;

example_queries.description: Round-trip a JSON array through deterministic CBOR.
example_queries.sql: SELECT to_hex(cbor.main.from_json('[1,2,3]')) AS h;

example_queries.description: Structurally decode a COSE_Sign1 and read its algorithm name.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (cbor.main.cose_headers(from_hex('d28443a10126a04044deadbeef'))).alg AS alg;

example_queries.description: Render a CBOR array blob as JSON text.
example_queries.sql: SELECT cbor.main.to_json(from_hex('83010203')) AS json

example_queries.description: Show a tag-1 epoch timestamp in human-readable diagnostic (EDN) notation.
example_queries.sql: SELECT cbor.main.diagnostic(from_hex('c11a514b67b0')) AS edn

example_queries.description: Encode a JSON array into deterministic CBOR and hex it.
example_queries.sql: SELECT to_hex(cbor.main.from_json('[1,2,3]')) AS hex

example_queries.description: Check that an untrusted blob is well-formed CBOR.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (cbor.main.well_formed(from_hex('83010203'))).ok AS ok

example_queries.description: Pull the issuer claim out of a bare CWT claim set.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (cbor.main.cwt_claims(from_hex('a10169636f61703a2f2f6173'))).iss AS iss

example_queries.description: Fan a 3-item CBOR Sequence into one row per item.
example_queries.sql: SELECT idx, value FROM cbor.main.seq_decode(from_hex('010203')) ORDER BY idx

example_queries.description: Inventory COSE_Sign1-signed CWTs: the signing algorithm from each token's COSE header beside the subject and expiry from the claim set it signs, soonest expiry first.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (cbor.main.cwt_claims(t.token)).sub AS subject, (cbor.main.cose_headers(t.token)).alg AS alg, (cbor.main.cwt_claims(t.token)).exp AS expires FROM (VALUES (from_hex('d28443a10126a104426b31582aa3017668747470733a2f2f6973737565722e6578616d706c6502696465766963652d3432041a6955b90044deadbeef')), (from_hex('d28443a10127a104426b325828a3017568747470733a2f2f6f746865722e6578616d706c6502686465766963652d37041a6553f10044deadbeef'))) AS t(token) ORDER BY expires

example_queries.description: Migrate MessagePack frames to deterministic CBOR for byte-level dedupe: transcode each frame to CBOR, canonicalize it, and group by the canonical bytes. Frames 1 and 2 differ only in map key order, so they share one canonical encoding.
example_queries.sql: SELECT to_hex(cbor.main.canonical(cbor.main.msgpack_to_cbor(f.frame))) AS canonical_cbor, list(f.id ORDER BY f.id) AS frame_ids FROM (VALUES (1, from_hex('82a16201a16102')), (2, from_hex('82a16102a16201')), (3, from_hex('82a16103a16201'))) AS f(id, frame) GROUP BY canonical_cbor ORDER BY canonical_cbor

example_queries.description: Screen inbound blobs for deterministic encoding: classify malformed ones by failure kind, and flag well-formed ones whose map keys are not in canonical order (blob 2 is out of order, blob 3 is truncated).

It groups a commodity binary codec — CBOR and MessagePack rendered to and parsed from JSON, diagnostic (EDN) notation, canonical / core-deterministic re-encoding, semantic-tag inspection, and untrusted-input well-formedness checks that never crash the scan — with tag-aware structural decoders for the CBOR-based security payloads (COSE messages, CWT tokens, COSE keys, and WebAuthn authenticator data), plus table functions that fan a single CBOR Sequence or WebAuthn attestation object into rows, and bulk-copy formats that move whole tables in and out of CBOR and MessagePack row files. tags.vgi.doc_md:
## CBOR / MessagePack / security codec

The single schema for the `cbor` worker. The catalog name matches the `ATTACH` name, so qualify calls as `cbor.main.<fn>(...)` (or `SET search_path='cbor.main'`).

**Binary codec.** Render CBOR and MessagePack blobs to JSON or diagnostic (EDN) notation, parse them back, re-encode into canonical / core-deterministic forms, walk semantic tags, and run untrusted-input well-formedness checks that never crash a scan.

**Security payloads.** Tag-aware structural decoders explode the CBOR-based credential formats — COSE messages, CWT tokens, COSE keys, and WebAuthn authenticator data — into typed columns, and table functions fan a single CBOR Sequence or WebAuthn attestation object into rows.

**Bulk copy.** The `cbor` and `msgpack` bulk-copy formats move whole tables in and out of row files (one top-level item per row), in both directions under a single format name.

All decode is *structural only*: no signature/MAC verification and no decryption.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A browsable lookup table of the IANA COSE registries this worker knows: the signature/encryption/MAC/KDF algorithms (RFC 9053, e.g. -7 → ES256, -8 → EdDSA, 5 → 'HMAC 256/256'), the key types (`kty`, e.g. 1 → OKP, 2 → EC2, 3 → RSA), and the elliptic curves (`crv`, e.g. 1 → P-256, 6 → Ed25519, 8 → secp256k1). Columns are `registry` ('alg' | 'kty' | 'crv'), the signed numeric `id`, and the standard `name`. It is exactly the mapping the `cose_headers`, `cose_decode`, and `cose_key` decoders apply when they turn the raw numeric COSE labels into names, so you can join a decoded id back to its name, discover which algorithms are recognized, or reverse a name to its numeric label — no CBOR blob required to get started.

## cose_registry

The IANA COSE registries the worker recognizes, as a plain browsable table.

| column | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `registry` | VARCHAR | Which registry: `alg`, `kty`, or `crv`. |
| `id` | BIGINT | The signed numeric COSE label (algorithm ids are typically negative). |
| `name` | VARCHAR | The standard IANA name (e.g. `ES256`, `EdDSA`, `EC2`, `P-256`). |

This is the same numeric-label → name mapping the `cose_headers` / `cose_decode` / `cose_key` decoders apply, so a decoded `alg` id or `kty` joins straight back to its name here.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Decode a CBOR Sequence (RFC 8742 — a concatenation of zero or more CBOR items) into one row per item, with columns `idx` (`BIGINT`, zero-based position) and `value` (JSON). A truncated trailing item stops the sequence cleanly, returning the items parsed so far (never panics). The blob argument is a per-row input column, so the function works equally on a literal, on a whole column, and under a correlated LATERAL join — fanning each row's sequence out beside that row's other columns. A NULL or undecodable blob contributes no rows. To load a whole *file* of CBOR rows into a table, use the `cbor` bulk-copy format instead.

functions.name: msgpack_copy

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Bulk-move whole tables in and out of MessagePack data files — the row-file counterpart to the per-blob `msgpack_decode` scalar. The file is a concatenated MessagePack items: one top-level item per row, with no container header or footer, so it appends and streams. The same format name serves both directions, and a file written by one round-trips through the other. The `FORMAT` identifier is scoped by the ATTACH alias, so it reads `<alias>.msgpack`:

```sql
COPY (<query>) TO '<path>' (FORMAT '<alias>.msgpack');
COPY <table> FROM '<path>' (FORMAT '<alias>.msgpack');
```

With the default `row_format 'map'` each item is a map keyed by column name: self-describing, so on read the columns may appear in any order, a key absent from an item reads as NULL, and extra keys are ignored. `row_format 'array'` frames each row as an array of values in column order — more compact, but positional. Column values encode exactly as the `encode` scalar does (shortest-lossless integers and floats, `BLOB` as a byte string, `TIMESTAMP` as an epoch instant, `LIST` / `STRUCT` / `MAP` as arrays and maps) and decode back onto the COPY target's exact column types. A value that cannot be represented in its target column fails the COPY with a column-qualified message; `ignore_errors true` instead skips unusable rows and warns about skipped data. A decode error discards that file's unreadable remainder and continues with the next source; source-open failures still fail the COPY. Rows are written in source order, so an ordered source query keeps its ordering in the file.

**Paths resolve on the worker.** The file is opened by the worker process, so the path is interpreted against its filesystem and working directory — not the SQL client's. That is invisible when DuckDB spawns the worker locally, but a worker in a container or on another host cannot see the caller's paths: use a location both sides agree on (a mounted volume), and prefer absolute paths. A path the worker cannot open is reported with the directory it actually looked in.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Bulk import and export of MessagePack row files. The file is a concatenated MessagePack items — one item per row, no container header — so it appends, streams, and round-trips between the two directions. The `FORMAT` identifier is scoped by the ATTACH alias:

```sql
COPY (<query>) TO '<path>' (FORMAT '<alias>.msgpack');
COPY <table> FROM '<path>' (FORMAT '<alias>.msgpack');
```

`row_format 'map'` (the default) keys each row by column name; `row_format 'array'` is positional. On read, `ignore_errors true` skips unusable rows with warnings. A decode error discards that file's unreadable remainder and continues with the next source; source-open failures still fail the COPY. Writes preserve source order.

Paths are opened by the **worker** process, so they resolve against its filesystem and working directory rather than the client's — a containerized or remote worker needs a shared location, and absolute paths.

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
### Read direction — columns mirror the COPY target

The scan emits exactly the COPY target table's columns, in its declared order and types: DuckDB fixes them from the target and the reader projects each MessagePack item onto them, inserting no cast. There is no independent result schema, so the shape below is one worked variant — a target declared `(id INTEGER, name VARCHAR, seen TIMESTAMP)`.

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| id | INTEGER | The item's value for the `id` column — by key name under `row_format 'map'`, by position under `row_format 'array'`. |
| name | VARCHAR | The item's value for the `name` column. A nested value lands as its JSON text. |

functions.name: webauthn_attestation
functions.comment: Decode a WebAuthn attestation object into typed columns

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Decode a CTAP2 / WebAuthn attestation OBJECT ({fmt, attStmt, authData}) and shred it into typed columns: fmt, aaguid, sign_count, rp_id_hash, up, uv, cred_id, alg, sig, x5c (`LIST<BLOB>`), att_stmt (JSON). Parses the embedded authenticatorData and the format-specific attStmt (packed, fido-u2f, tpm, android-key, android-safetynet, apple, none). The `x5c` certificate chain is the join key to `vgi-x509` for AAGUID / vendor trust-anchor checks. The blob argument is a per-row input column, so this works equally on a literal, on a whole enrollment column, and under a correlated LATERAL join — shredding each row's attestation beside that row's own columns. Structural only — NO signature verification. A NULL blob, or one that is not a valid attestation object, contributes no rows.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Shred a WebAuthn attestation object into a row of (fmt, aaguid, sign_count, rp_id_hash, up, uv, cred_id, alg, sig, x5c, att_stmt) — per literal, per column, or under a correlated LATERAL join. Join `x5c` to `vgi-x509`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Shred a packed CTAP2 attestation object into one typed row.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT fmt, aaguid, sign_count, alg FROM cbor.main.webauthn_attestation(from_hex(''))

vgi.example_queries.description: Shred each enrollment's attestation object and join its algorithm name to the COSE registry to recover the numeric COSEAlgorithmIdentifier, checked against a relying-party allow-list of -7 (ES256) and -257 (RS256); the undecodable enrollment contributes no row.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT e.user_name, w.fmt, w.alg, r.id AS alg_id, r.id IN (-7, -257) AS alg_allowed FROM (VALUES ('alice', from_hex('')), ('bob', from_hex('00'))) AS e(user_name, att_obj), LATERAL cbor.main.webauthn_attestation(e.att_obj) AS w JOIN cbor.main.cose_registry AS r ON r.registry = 'alg' AND r.name = w.alg ORDER BY e.user_name

functions.name: to_json
functions.comment: Render a CBOR blob as canonical JSON text (byte strings as base64url)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Decode a CBOR (RFC 8949) blob and render it as a canonical JSON string. Always succeeds on well-formed input; it is necessarily lossy on the types JSON lacks — byte strings render as base64url, non-text map keys are stringified, and semantic tags are transparent (the inner value is shown). For the lossless typed path use `decode`; for a tag- and byte-preserving human view use `diagnostic`. Returns NULL for a malformed blob.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Render a CBOR blob as JSON text. Lossy on `BLOB`/non-string keys (base64url), tags transparent. `decode` is the lossless path, `diagnostic` the debug path.

vgi.example_queries.description: Migrate MessagePack frames to deterministic CBOR for byte-level dedupe: transcode each frame to CBOR, canonicalize it, and group by the canonical bytes. Frames 1 and 2 differ only in map key order, so they share one canonical encoding.

functions.comment: Re-encode CBOR into a deterministic core form (RFC 8949 §4.2.1)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Re-encode a CBOR blob into a deterministic form. `mode` is 'core' (default, RFC 8949 §4.2.1: shortest integers, map keys sorted by encoded-byte order) or 'ctap2' (CTAP2 canonical CBOR: keys sorted length-first then bytewise — required to recompute WebAuthn signatures). Idempotent and round-trips through `decode`. NULL on malformed input.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Deterministically re-encode CBOR. `mode` ∈ {core, ctap2}. Idempotent.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Diagnose a CBOR blob and return `STRUCT(ok BOOL, error VARCHAR, kind VARCHAR)`. `kind` is one of truncated, trailing-bytes, invalid-major, bad-utf8, duplicate-key, nesting-limit, reserved-simple (NULL when ok). workers.title: Crypto Market Data
workers.tagline: Crypto exchange market data (OHLCV, trades, order books, funding, open interest) across 100+ exchanges in DuckDB (Python, CCXT)
workers.subtitle: Candles, quotes, order books, trades and perpetual funding from 100+ crypto exchanges.
workers.summary: Public cryptocurrency market data from more than one hundred centralized exchanges through the CCXT library: candles, trades, quotes, order books, and perpetual funding and open interest. Every query is a live request to the exchange. No API key needed.
workers.doc_md:
# Crypto exchange market data

Unified public market data from more than one hundred centralized crypto exchanges, served to DuckDB through the MIT-licensed [CCXT](https://github.com/ccxt/ccxt) library: candles, quotes, order books, trades, listed markets, and perpetual-swap funding and open interest.

Exchanges are named by CCXT id and markets by CCXT's unified symbol (`BTC/USD` for spot, `BTC/USDT:USDT` for a USDT-settled perpetual). No credentials are used or accepted.

**Terms of use.** Every call is a live request from your machine to the exchange's public API. Nothing is cached or redistributed by this worker; you are the API caller, and each exchange's terms of use and geographic restrictions apply to you (for example, Binance.com refuses US IP addresses).

## Sources and references

- [CCXT on GitHub](https://github.com/ccxt/ccxt)
- [CCXT documentation (unified API, exchange ids)](https://docs.ccxt.com/)
- [ccxt on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/ccxt/)

example_queries.description: Daily BTC/USD candles on Coinbase for January 2025
example_queries.sql: SELECT ts, close, volume FROM ccxt.main.ohlcv('coinbase', 'BTC/USD', '1d', since := TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01', until := TIMESTAMP '2025-02-01') ORDER BY ts

example_queries.description: Buy versus sell volume in Kraken's most recent BTC/USD trades
example_queries.sql: SELECT side, count(*) AS trades, sum(amount) AS btc FROM ccxt.main.trades('kraken', 'BTC/USD') GROUP BY side ORDER BY side

example_queries.description: Compare BTC/USD on two US exchanges
example_queries.sql: SELECT exchange, last, ask - bid AS spread, quote_volume FROM ccxt.main.ticker(['kraken', 'coinbase'], 'BTC/USD') WHERE error IS NULL ORDER BY last

example_queries.description: Liquidity in the top 50 levels on each side of Kraken's BTC/USD book
example_queries.sql: SELECT side, sum(amount) AS btc, sum(price * amount) AS usd FROM ccxt.main.order_book('kraken', 'BTC/USD', depth := 50) GROUP BY side ORDER BY side

example_queries.description: BTC perpetual swaps listed on OKX
example_queries.sql: SELECT symbol, settle, contract_size FROM ccxt.main.markets('okx') WHERE type = 'swap' AND base = 'BTC' ORDER BY symbol

example_queries.description: Which of three exchanges publish funding-rate history
example_queries.sql: SELECT exchange, supported FROM ccxt.main.has(['kraken', 'okx', 'binance']) WHERE method = 'fetchFundingRateHistory' ORDER BY exchange

example_queries.description: Number of settlements and average annualized BTC perpetual funding on Binance over June 2025 (for a rolling window, pass start_date := current_date - INTERVAL 30 DAY)
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS settlements, avg(funding_rate_annualized) AS avg_apr FROM ccxt.main.funding_rates('binance', 'BTC/USDT:USDT', start_date := DATE '2025-06-01', end_date := DATE '2025-07-01')

example_queries.description: Rank venues by annualized BTC perpetual funding
example_queries.sql: SELECT exchange, funding_rate, interval_hours, funding_rate_annualized FROM ccxt.main.funding_rate(['binance', 'okx'], 'BTC/USDT:USDT') WHERE error IS NULL ORDER BY funding_rate_annualized DESC

example_queries.description: BTC perpetual open interest by venue, largest first
example_queries.sql: SELECT exchange, open_interest_value FROM ccxt.main.open_interest(['binance', 'okx'], 'BTC/USDT:USDT') WHERE error IS NULL ORDER BY open_interest_value DESC

example_queries.description: Exchanges that publish both funding history and open interest
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, name FROM ccxt.main.exchanges WHERE has_funding_rate_history AND has_open_interest ORDER BY id

example_queries.description: Current annualized BTC perpetual funding across Binance and OKX, weighted by each venue's open interest (funding_rate joined to open_interest)
example_queries.sql: SELECT sum(f.funding_rate_annualized * o.open_interest_value) / sum(o.open_interest_value) AS oi_weighted_apr, sum(o.open_interest_value) AS total_oi_usdt, count(*) AS venues FROM ccxt.main.funding_rate(['binance', 'okx'], 'BTC/USDT:USDT') AS f JOIN ccxt.main.open_interest(['binance', 'okx'], 'BTC/USDT:USDT') AS o USING (exchange) WHERE f.error IS NULL AND o.error IS NULL

example_queries.description: What a 2 BTC market buy on Kraken would cost: walk the ask side of the order book, then add the market's default taker fee from markets (filled_btc is below 2 if the book is too thin)
example_queries.sql: WITH asks AS (SELECT price, amount, sum(amount) OVER (ORDER BY level) - amount AS ahead FROM ccxt.main.order_book('kraken', 'BTC/USD', depth := 50) WHERE side = 'ask'), fill AS (SELECT sum(least(amount, greatest(2 - ahead, 0))) AS filled_btc, sum(price * least(amount, greatest(2 - ahead, 0))) AS cost_usd FROM asks) SELECT fill.filled_btc, fill.cost_usd / fill.filled_btc AS avg_fill_price, fill.cost_usd * (1 + m.taker) AS cost_with_taker_fee_usd FROM fill JOIN ccxt.main.markets('kraken') AS m ON m.symbol = 'BTC/USD'

example_queries.description: Funding settled each UTC day on Binance's BTC perpetual next to that day's open-to-close return of the perpetual itself, first week of 2025 (funding_rates joined to ohlcv)
example_queries.sql: WITH funding AS (SELECT CAST(ts AS DATE) AS day, sum(funding_rate) AS daily_funding FROM ccxt.main.funding_rates('binance', 'BTC/USDT:USDT', start_date := DATE '2025-01-01', end_date := DATE '2025-01-08') GROUP BY day), candles AS (SELECT CAST(ts AS DATE) AS day, close / open - 1 AS price_return FROM ccxt.main.ohlcv('binance', 'BTC/USDT:USDT', '1d', since := TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01', until := TIMESTAMP '2025-01-08')) SELECT day, daily_funding, price_return FROM funding JOIN candles USING (day) ORDER BY day

example_queries.description: The ten countries listed for the most exchanges
example_queries.sql: SELECT unnest(countries) AS country, count(*) AS exchanges FROM ccxt.main.exchanges GROUP BY country ORDER BY exchanges DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: ETH perpetual open interest on OKX
example_queries.sql: SELECT open_interest_amount FROM ccxt.main.open_interest('okx', 'ETH/USDT:USDT')

example_queries.description: Daily high-low range of ETH/USDT on OKX in the first week of 2025, from hourly candles
example_queries.sql: SELECT date_trunc('day', ts) AS day, max(high) - min(low) AS range_usdt FROM ccxt.main.ohlcv('okx', 'ETH/USDT', '1h', since := TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01', until := TIMESTAMP '2025-01-08') GROUP BY day ORDER BY day

example_queries.description: The current ETH/USDT price and 24-hour change on OKX
example_queries.sql: SELECT last, change_pct FROM ccxt.main.ticker('okx', 'ETH/USDT')

example_queries.description: Best bid and ask for ETH/USD on Coinbase
example_queries.sql: SELECT max(price) FILTER (side = 'bid') AS best_bid, min(price) FILTER (side = 'ask') AS best_ask FROM ccxt.main.order_book('coinbase', 'ETH/USD', depth := 1)

example_queries.description: Kraken's five most common quote currencies
example_queries.sql: SELECT quote, count(*) AS pairs FROM ccxt.main.markets('kraken') WHERE type = 'spot' AND active GROUP BY quote ORDER BY pairs DESC LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Kraken's support for every method this worker uses
example_queries.sql: SELECT method, status FROM ccxt.main.has('kraken') WHERE exposed_by_worker ORDER BY method

example_queries.description: Kraken supports candles but not funding history
example_queries.sql: SELECT method, supported FROM ccxt.main.has('kraken') WHERE method IN ('fetchOHLCV', 'fetchFundingRateHistory') ORDER BY method;

example_queries.description: Daily total ETH perpetual funding on Binance over the first two weeks of 2025
example_queries.sql: SELECT date_trunc('day', ts) AS day, sum(funding_rate) AS daily_funding FROM ccxt.main.funding_rates('binance', 'ETH/USDT:USDT', start_date := DATE '2025-01-01', end_date := DATE '2025-01-15') GROUP BY day ORDER BY day

example_queries.description: The next ETH perpetual funding settlement on OKX
example_queries.sql: SELECT funding_rate, next_funding_ts FROM ccxt.main.funding_rate('okx', 'ETH/USDT:USDT') WHERE error IS NULL

example_queries.description: Volume-weighted average price over Coinbase's most recent ETH/USD trades
example_queries.sql: SELECT sum(price * amount) / sum(amount) AS vwap, min(ts) AS first_trade FROM ccxt.main.trades('coinbase', 'ETH/USD')

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Table functions over CCXT's public market-data API. History functions page through a time window with a since-cursor and accept `TIMESTAMP`, `DATE` or ISO-8601 string bounds; snapshot functions return the current state and some accept a list of exchanges to compare them side by side, reporting a per-exchange failure in an error column instead of failing the query. Reference functions describe exchanges, markets and capabilities without fetching prices. A plain `TIMESTAMP` bound is read as UTC; for a relative window pass a `TIMESTAMPTZ` such as `now() - INTERVAL 1 DAY`, because `now()::TIMESTAMP` is local wall-clock time. The leading arguments are positional; the rest are named, written name := value. Funding rates are decimals per funding interval where positive means longs pay shorts, with an annualized column alongside.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

Public crypto market data through CCXT.

- **History** pages through a time window and streams one exchange page per batch.
- **Snapshots** return the current quote or book, and can fan out across exchanges.
- **Derivatives** cover perpetual funding (decimal per interval, positive = longs pay) and open interest.
- **Reference** data lists exchanges, markets and per-exchange capabilities.

## exchanges

A table: every CCXT exchange id with its name, countries and capabilities. Offline.

functions.name: ohlcv
functions.comment: OHLCV candles for one market on one exchange, backfilled over a time window

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Open/high/low/close/volume candles for one market. Positional arguments: exchange id (e.g. 'coinbase'), unified symbol (e.g. 'BTC/USD') and timeframe (e.g. '1h', '1d'). Named arguments: `since := TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01'` (inclusive start, UTC), `until := TIMESTAMP '2025-02-01'` (exclusive end, default now) and `max_rows` (default 100,000). With `since` the worker pages forward through the window with a cursor until it reaches `until`; without `since` it returns only the latest page of candles (the exchange's default count). `ts` is the candle's open time in UTC; prices are in the quote currency and volume in the base currency. Some exchanges keep only recent history (Kraken serves the latest 720 candles), so an old `since` can return fewer rows than the window implies; the worker then logs a warning naming the first candle the exchange returned. An unsupported timeframe is rejected at bind with the list the exchange offers.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## ohlcv(exchange, symbol, timeframe, since := …, until := …, max_rows := 100000)

Candles over `[since, until)`, paged with a since-cursor; one batch per exchange page.

Every call is a live request from your machine to the exchange's public API. Nothing is cached or redistributed by this worker; you are the API caller, and each exchange's terms of use and geographic restrictions apply to you (for example, Binance.com refuses US IP addresses).

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ts, close, volume FROM ccxt.main.ohlcv('coinbase', 'BTC/USD', '1d', since := TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01', until := TIMESTAMP '2025-02-01') ORDER BY ts

vgi.example_queries.description: Daily high-low range of ETH/USDT on OKX in the first week of 2025, from hourly candles
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT date_trunc('day', ts) AS day, max(high) - min(low) AS range_usdt FROM ccxt.main.ohlcv('okx', 'ETH/USDT', '1h', since := TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01', until := TIMESTAMP '2025-01-08') GROUP BY day ORDER BY day

functions.name: order_book
functions.comment: Order-book depth snapshot for one market: bids and asks by level

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A snapshot of one market's level-2 order book: one row per price level and side. Positional: exchange id and unified symbol; named `depth` (levels per side, default 20, up to 1000; exchanges may return fewer). `side` is 'bid' or 'ask', `level` 1 is the best price, `amount` is base currency. Use it for spread, mid price and liquidity within a price band.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## order_book(exchange, symbol, depth := 20)

Bids and asks by level, best first.

Every call is a live request from your machine to the exchange's public API. Nothing is cached or redistributed by this worker; you are the API caller, and each exchange's terms of use and geographic restrictions apply to you (for example, Binance.com refuses US IP addresses).

vgi.example_queries.description: Liquidity in the top 50 levels on each side of Kraken's BTC/USD book
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT side, sum(amount) AS btc, sum(price * amount) AS usd FROM ccxt.main.order_book('kraken', 'BTC/USD', depth := 50) GROUP BY side ORDER BY side

vgi.example_queries.description: Best bid and ask for ETH/USD on Coinbase
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT max(price) FILTER (side = 'bid') AS best_bid, min(price) FILTER (side = 'ask') AS best_ask FROM ccxt.main.order_book('coinbase', 'ETH/USD', depth := 1)

vgi.example_queries.description: What a 2 BTC market buy on Kraken would cost: walk the ask side of the order book, then add the market's default taker fee from markets (filled_btc is below 2 if the book is too thin)
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH asks AS (SELECT price, amount, sum(amount) OVER (ORDER BY level) - amount AS ahead FROM ccxt.main.order_book('kraken', 'BTC/USD', depth := 50) WHERE side = 'ask'), fill AS (SELECT sum(least(amount, greatest(2 - ahead, 0))) AS filled_btc, sum(price * least(amount, greatest(2 - ahead, 0))) AS cost_usd FROM asks) SELECT fill.filled_btc, fill.cost_usd / fill.filled_btc AS avg_fill_price, fill.cost_usd * (1 + m.taker) AS cost_with_taker_fee_usd FROM fill JOIN ccxt.main.markets('kraken') AS m ON m.symbol = 'BTC/USD'

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Settled funding rates of one perpetual swap over a window. Positional: exchange id (e.g. 'binance', 'okx', 'bybit') and the unified perpetual symbol ('BTC/USDT:USDT'). Named: `start_date` (inclusive, UTC), `end_date` (exclusive, default now), `max_rows`. `funding_rate` is a decimal per funding interval with the convention positive = longs pay shorts; `interval_hours` is inferred from the spacing of settlements (exchanges use 1, 4 or 8 hours and some switch); `funding_rate_annualized` multiplies by intervals per 365-day year. Without `start_date` only the latest page is returned. Retention differs by venue: Hyperliquid serves long history, OKX about three months, KuCoin about one, Gate 180 days, and Bitget only its latest page; when an exchange starts later than `start_date` the worker logs a warning and returns what the exchange has. Fails with a clear error on exchanges without fetchFundingRateHistory (spot-only venues such as Kraken or Coinbase).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## funding_rates(exchange, symbol, start_date := …, end_date := …, max_rows := 100000)

Settled funding of a perpetual, decimal per interval (positive = longs pay shorts) plus a simple annualized rate.

Every call is a live request from your machine to the exchange's public API. Nothing is cached or redistributed by this worker; you are the API caller, and each exchange's terms of use and geographic restrictions apply to you (for example, Binance.com refuses US IP addresses).

vgi.example_queries.description: Number of settlements and average annualized BTC perpetual funding on Binance over June 2025 (for a rolling window, pass start_date := current_date - INTERVAL 30 DAY)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS settlements, avg(funding_rate_annualized) AS avg_apr FROM ccxt.main.funding_rates('binance', 'BTC/USDT:USDT', start_date := DATE '2025-06-01', end_date := DATE '2025-07-01')

vgi.example_queries.description: Daily total ETH perpetual funding on Binance over the first two weeks of 2025
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT date_trunc('day', ts) AS day, sum(funding_rate) AS daily_funding FROM ccxt.main.funding_rates('binance', 'ETH/USDT:USDT', start_date := DATE '2025-01-01', end_date := DATE '2025-01-15') GROUP BY day ORDER BY day

vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH funding AS (SELECT CAST(ts AS DATE) AS day, sum(funding_rate) AS daily_funding FROM ccxt.main.funding_rates('binance', 'BTC/USDT:USDT', start_date := DATE '2025-01-01', end_date := DATE '2025-01-08') GROUP BY day), candles AS (SELECT CAST(ts AS DATE) AS day, close / open - 1 AS price_return FROM ccxt.main.ohlcv('binance', 'BTC/USDT:USDT', '1d', since := TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01', until := TIMESTAMP '2025-01-08')) SELECT day, daily_funding, price_return FROM funding JOIN candles USING (day) ORDER BY day

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Public executed trades for one market. Positional: exchange id and unified symbol. Named: `since` (inclusive start, UTC), `until` (exclusive end, default now) and `max_rows` (default 100,000). With `since` the worker pages forward with a cursor that keeps fills sharing a millisecond intact across page boundaries (exchanges that need an explicit window end, such as Coinbase, are walked in self-sizing time windows); without `since` it returns the exchange's most recent page. Many exchanges only serve recent trades publicly (hours to days), so a deep `since` may start later than requested. `side` is the taker side; `amount` is base currency; `cost` is price times amount.

workers.title: Character Encodings
workers.tagline: Detect text encoding & transcode to UTF-8 / fix mojibake for DuckDB (Rust)
workers.subtitle: Detect text encodings, convert legacy bytes to and from UTF-8, and repair mojibake.
workers.summary: Character-encoding detection and UTF-8 transcoding (mojibake repair).
workers.doc_md:
# charset — detect text encoding and transcode to UTF-8 in SQL

Detect the character encoding of raw bytes and transcode legacy or mojibake-garbled text into clean UTF-8 directly in DuckDB SQL — no Python preprocessing step and no manual `iconv` passes.

## What it does

`charset` is a [VGI](https://query.farm) worker that adds character-encoding detection and UTF-8 transcoding to DuckDB over Apache Arrow. It is built for data engineers and analysts wrangling text of unknown or mixed provenance: CSV and log dumps in legacy Windows code pages, scraped HTML, email archives, and columns that arrived double-encoded — the classic `CafÃ©`-instead-of-`Café` mojibake. Rather than shelling out to external tools, you detect, repair, and normalize encodings inline with ordinary SQL queries.

## How it works

Encoding detection is powered by Mozilla's [`chardetng`](https://github.com/hsivonen/chardetng) ([docs](https://docs.rs/chardetng)), the same heuristic Firefox applies to unlabelled legacy text. Decoding and encoding use [`encoding_rs`](https://github.com/hsivonen/encoding_rs) ([docs](https://docs.rs/encoding_rs)), the pure-Rust implementation of the [WHATWG Encoding Standard](https://encoding.spec.whatwg.org/) that Firefox ships for every web-platform codec. A byte-order-mark (BOM) check runs first; undecodable bytes within a known encoding become the U+FFFD replacement character rather than raising an error, while an unknown encoding *label* is rejected so typos surface immediately.

## When to reach for it

Reach for `charset` whenever a text column's bytes are of unknown, mixed, or legacy provenance: sniff the likely encoding and score how trustworthy that guess is, decode legacy bytes to UTF-8 either automatically or with an explicit codec label, re-encode UTF-8 back into a legacy codec for export, repair double-encoded mojibake, and check whether bytes are already clean UTF-8. Because detection is heuristic, confidence-check short or ambiguous samples before relying on a result. Empty or NULL input yields NULL everywhere.
workers.readme_sql:
LOAD vgi;
ATTACH 'charset' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'github-auto://Query-farm/vgi-charset@v0.4.1');
SET search_path = 'charset.main';

SELECT detect_encoding('\x63\x61\x66\xE9'::BLOB);    -- 'windows-1252'
SELECT detect_confidence('\x63\x61\x66\xE9'::BLOB);  -- 1.0
SELECT to_utf8('\x63\x61\x66\xE9'::BLOB);            -- 'café'
SELECT to_utf8_from('\x93\xFA\x96\x7B\x8C\xEA'::BLOB, 'shift_jis');  -- '日本語'
SELECT transcode('café', 'windows-1252');            -- BLOB \x63\x61\x66\xE9
SELECT fix_mojibake('CafÃ©');                         -- 'Café'
SELECT is_valid_utf8('café'::BLOB);                  -- true
SELECT * FROM supported_encodings();                 -- discovery: label

-- Compose them: which encodings can store 'naïve café' losslessly?
SELECT label FROM supported_encodings
WHERE label <> 'replacement'                         -- decode-only, no encoder
  AND to_utf8_from(transcode('naïve café', label), label) = 'naïve café'
ORDER BY label;                                      -- 14 labels, incl. windows-1252, UTF-16LE

example_queries.description: Triage a column of unlabelled bytes in mixed legacy encodings (produced here with transcode): detect each row's encoding and confidence, flag which rows are already UTF-8, and decode every row to UTF-8 text.
example_queries.sql: WITH raw AS (SELECT id, charset.main.transcode(txt, enc) AS bytes FROM (VALUES (1, 'Grüße aus München', 'windows-1252'), (2, 'Привет, как дела?', 'windows-1251'), (3, 'こんにちは世界', 'shift_jis'), (4, 'naïve café', 'utf-8')) AS t(id, txt, enc)) SELECT id, charset.main.detect_encoding(bytes) AS detected, charset.main.detect_confidence(bytes) AS confidence, charset.main.is_valid_utf8(bytes) AS already_utf8, charset.main.to_utf8(bytes) AS text FROM raw ORDER BY id

example_queries.description: List the supported encodings that can store 'naïve café' losslessly: encode it into each label with transcode, decode it back with to_utf8_from, and keep the labels whose round trip is exact (the decode-only 'replacement' encoding has no encoder, so it is skipped).
example_queries.sql: SELECT label FROM charset.main.supported_encodings WHERE label <> 'replacement' AND charset.main.to_utf8_from(charset.main.transcode('naïve café', label), label) = 'naïve café' ORDER BY label

example_queries.description: Before exporting names to a windows-1252 system, flag the ones that would not survive: encode each with transcode, decode the bytes back with to_utf8_from, and compare with the original.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, charset.main.to_utf8_from(charset.main.transcode(name, 'windows-1252'), 'windows-1252') = name AS fits_1252 FROM (VALUES ('Café Müller'), ('Łódź'), ('東京'), ('Smith')) AS t(name) ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Reproduce double-encoding mojibake (UTF-8 bytes from transcode misread as windows-1252 by to_utf8_from) and show fix_mojibake restoring the original text.
example_queries.sql: SELECT original, charset.main.to_utf8_from(charset.main.transcode(original, 'utf-8'), 'windows-1252') AS garbled, charset.main.fix_mojibake(garbled) AS repaired FROM (VALUES ('Café'), ('Ünïcödé'), ('“smart quotes” — dash')) AS t(original) ORDER BY original

example_queries.description: Detect the character encoding of windows-1252 bytes for "café".
example_queries.sql: SELECT charset.main.detect_encoding('\x63\x61\x66\xE9'::BLOB);

example_queries.description: Auto-detect and decode windows-1252 bytes to a UTF-8 string.

example_queries.sql: SELECT charset.main.to_utf8_from('\x93\xFA\x96\x7B'::BLOB, 'shift_jis');

Does this worker report full confidence — a score of exactly 1.0 — for the UTF-8 byte representation of the text 'hello'? Return only a single boolean value as one column.

## charset.main

Character-encoding detection and UTF-8 transcoding over Apache Arrow. The `main` schema groups its functions into detection (identify an encoding and score confidence), decoding (turn legacy or unlabelled bytes into clean UTF-8), encoding and repair (write UTF-8 back into a legacy codec and fix double-encoded mojibake), and discovery (enumerate supported encodings). Every function is catalog-qualified as `charset.main.<fn>(...)` and operates row-wise.

### Usage

```sql
SELECT charset.main.to_utf8('\x63\x61\x66\xE9'::BLOB); -- 'café'
```

vgi.example_queries.description: Triage a column of unlabelled bytes in mixed legacy encodings (produced here with transcode): detect each row's encoding and confidence, flag which rows are already UTF-8, and decode every row to UTF-8 text.
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH raw AS (SELECT id, charset.main.transcode(txt, enc) AS bytes FROM (VALUES (1, 'Grüße aus München', 'windows-1252'), (2, 'Привет, как дела?', 'windows-1251'), (3, 'こんにちは世界', 'shift_jis'), (4, 'naïve café', 'utf-8')) AS t(id, txt, enc)) SELECT id, charset.main.detect_encoding(bytes) AS detected, charset.main.detect_confidence(bytes) AS confidence, charset.main.is_valid_utf8(bytes) AS already_utf8, charset.main.to_utf8(bytes) AS text FROM raw ORDER BY id

vgi.example_queries.description: List the supported encodings that can store 'naïve café' losslessly: encode it into each label with transcode, decode it back with to_utf8_from, and keep the labels whose round trip is exact (the decode-only 'replacement' encoding has no encoder, so it is skipped).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT label FROM charset.main.supported_encodings WHERE label <> 'replacement' AND charset.main.to_utf8_from(charset.main.transcode('naïve café', label), label) = 'naïve café' ORDER BY label

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, charset.main.to_utf8_from(charset.main.transcode(name, 'windows-1252'), 'windows-1252') = name AS fits_1252 FROM (VALUES ('Café Müller'), ('Łódź'), ('東京'), ('Smith')) AS t(name) ORDER BY name

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## to_utf8

Auto-detects the encoding of a `BLOB` of text bytes and decodes it to a UTF-8 string in one step.

**How it works:** runs the same detection as `detect_encoding` (BOM, then `chardetng`) and decodes with `encoding_rs`. Bytes that are undecodable in the detected encoding become the `U+FFFD` replacement character rather than raising an error.

**Returns:** a `VARCHAR`; `NULL` for empty or `NULL` input.

**When to use:** the convenient default for unlabelled data. Use `to_utf8_from` instead when you already know the source codec and want to skip detection.

```sql
SELECT charset.main.to_utf8('\x63\x61\x66\xE9'::BLOB); -- 'café'
```

## is_valid_utf8

Tests whether a `BLOB` of bytes is already well-formed UTF-8.

**Returns:** `BOOLEAN` — `true` when every byte forms a valid UTF-8 sequence, `false` otherwise. An empty `BLOB` is valid UTF-8; `NULL` input returns `NULL`.

**When to use:** as a cheap pre-check to skip decoding/transcoding for data that is already clean, or to find rows that still need repair.

```sql
SELECT charset.main.is_valid_utf8('\x63\x61\x66\xC3\xA9'::BLOB); -- true
```

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Repair the classic double-encoding mojibake where UTF-8 text was mistakenly read as Latin-1/Windows-1252 and then re-stored as UTF-8, turning garbled sequences like 'CafÃ©' back into 'Café'. It only rewrites text when doing so strictly reduces mojibake markers, otherwise it returns the input unchanged. Returns NULL for NULL input.

## fix_mojibake

Repairs the classic *mojibake* failure where UTF-8 text was mistakenly read as Latin-1/Windows-1252 and then re-stored as UTF-8, leaving garbled sequences like `CafÃ©`.

**How it works:** re-encodes the text as Windows-1252 and re-decodes it as UTF-8, accepting the result **only** when it strictly reduces the number of mojibake markers. Otherwise it returns the input unchanged, so clean text and non-mojibake garble pass through untouched.

**Returns:** a `VARCHAR`; `NULL` for `NULL` input.

```sql
SELECT charset.main.fix_mojibake('CafÃ©'); -- 'Café'
```
