# cloudflare.zones.introspection

List available analytics datasets. Reads Cloudflare GET `/analytics/sql/introspection`, which takes no parameters.

## Endpoint

Returns the analytics dataset catalogue. By default, the response contains dataset names, titles, categories, descriptions, kinds, and hidden flags. Set `include_columns` to include each dataset's column names, descriptions, data types, and hidden flags. The caller must have Account Analytics Read permission on the account identified by `account_tag`. Dataset names, descriptions, and columns are the same for every authorized account. When `include_custom_attributes` or `include_attributes` is set, the response also includes attribute names and types discovered from that account's own data, which legitimately differs per caller. `attributes` is a replacement for `custom_attributes` that will eventually be removed; until then, set either flag independently to receive the corresponding field. `hidden` marks catalogue entries a client should de-emphasise. It has no effect on access: hidden datasets and columns are returned here and remain fully queryable.

The catalogue lists the datasets this deployment is able to describe, which is not a fixed list. Some datasets are described by the service that owns them and are listed only where that service is available, so the same account may see a different catalogue in different environments, and datasets may appear or disappear without a change to this API. Clients should query the catalogue rather than hard-coding it, and should not treat a dataset's absence as proof that it does not exist.

Workers Analytics Engine datasets are…

## Columns

| Column | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `datasets` | VARCHAR | Datasets visible through the Analytics SQL API. |

# cloudflare.zones.origin_h2_max_streams

Get Origin H2 Max Streams Setting. Reads the origin h2 max streams object at Cloudflare GET `/zones/{zone_id}/settings/origin_h2_max_streams`: one row, or none when it doesn't exist (404) or an argument is NULL. Arguments, in URL order: zone_id.

## Endpoint

Origin H2 Max Streams configures the max number of concurrent requests that Cloudflare will send within the same connection when communicating with the origin server, if the origin supports it. Note that if your origin does not support H2 multiplexing, 5xx errors may be observed, particularly 520s. Also note that the default value is `100` for all plan types except Enterprise where it is `1`. `1` means that H2 multiplexing is disabled.

# cloudflare.zones.scripts

List detected scripts. Returns every script from Cloudflare GET `/zones/{zone_id}/page_shield/scripts` for the given path ids, paginated. Arguments, in URL order: zone_id (each is also returned as a column). Optional named arguments sent to the API: exclude_urls, urls, hosts, order_by, prioritize_malicious, exclude_cdn_cgi, exclude_duplicates, status, page_url, export.

## Endpoint

Lists scripts detected on webpages in the zone, with filtering and pagination.

Returns 22 columns, described in the declared result schema.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT p.name AS zone, r.id, r.added_at FROM cloudflare.zones.zones p, cloudflare.zones.scripts(p.id) r

vgi.example_queries.description: Only scripts matching a exclude_urls: the named argument is sent to the API, which filters.

arguments.description: Zone id: the id column of cloudflare.zones.zones.

arguments.name: exclude_cdn_cgi
arguments.description: When true, excludes scripts seen in a `/cdn-cgi` path from the returned scripts. The default value is true.

arguments.name: exclude_duplicates
arguments.description: When true, excludes duplicate scripts. We consider a script duplicate of another if their javascript content matches and they share the same url host and zone hostname. In such case, we return the most recent script for the URL host and zone hostname combination.

arguments.name: exclude_urls
arguments.description: Excludes scripts whose URL contains one of the URL-encoded URLs separated by commas.

arguments.name: export
arguments.description: Export the list of scripts as a file, limited to 50000 entries. One of: `csv`.

arguments.name: hosts
arguments.description: Includes scripts that match one or more URL-encoded hostnames separated by commas. Wildcards are supported at the start and end of each hostname to support starts with, ends with and contains. If no wildcards are used, results will be filtered by exact match.

arguments.name: order_by
arguments.description: The field used to sort returned scripts. One of: `first_seen_at`, `last_seen_at`.

arguments.name: page_url
arguments.description: Includes scripts that match one or more page URLs (separated by commas) where they were last seen Wildcards are supported at the start and end of each page URL to support starts with, ends with and contains. If no wildcards are used, results will be filtered by exact match.

arguments.name: prioritize_malicious
arguments.description: When true, malicious scripts appear first in the returned scripts.

arguments.name: status
arguments.description: Filters the returned scripts using a comma-separated list of scripts statuses. Accepted values: `active`, `infrequent`, and `inactive`. The default value is `active`.

arguments.name: urls
arguments.description: Includes scripts whose URL contain one or more URL-encoded URLs separated by commas.

Preferred instructs Cloudflare to opportunistically send a Post-Quantum keyshare in the first message to the origin (for fastest connections when the origin supports and prefers PQ), supported means that PQ algorithms are advertised but only used when requested by the origin, and off means that PQ algorithms are not advertised.

# cloudflare.zones.cache_reserve_clear

# cloudflare.zones.tiered_caching

Get Tiered Caching setting. Reads the tiered caching object at Cloudflare GET `/zones/{zone_id}/argo/tiered_caching`: one row, or none when it doesn't exist (404) or an argument is NULL. Arguments, in URL order: zone_id.

## Endpoint

Tiered Cache works by dividing Cloudflare's data centers into a hierarchy of lower-tiers and upper-tiers. If content is not cached in lower-tier data centers (generally the ones closest to a visitor), the lower-tier must ask an upper-tier to see if it has the content. If the upper-tier does not have the content, only the upper-tier can ask the origin for content. This practice improves bandwidth efficiency by limiting the number of data centers that can ask the origin for content, which reduces origin load and makes websites more cost-effective to operate. Additionally, Tiered Cache concentrates connections to origin servers so they come from a small number of data centers rather than the full set of network locations. This results in fewer open connections using server resources.

Returns 5 columns, described in the declared result schema.

# cloudflare.zones.status

Get waiting room status. Reads the status object at Cloudflare GET `/zones/{zone_id}/waiting_rooms/{waiting_room_id}/status`: one row, or none when it doesn't exist (404) or an argument is NULL. Arguments, in URL order: zone_id, waiting_room_id.

## Endpoint

Fetches the status of a configured waiting room. Response fields include:
1. `status`: String indicating the status of the waiting room. The possible status are:
	- **not_queueing** indicates that the configured thresholds have not been met and all users are going through to the origin.
	- **queueing** indicates that the thresholds have been met and some users are held in the waiting room.
	- **event_prequeueing** indicates that an event is active and is currently prequeueing users before it starts.
	- **suspended** indicates that the room is suspended.
2. `event_id`: String of the current event's `id` if an event is active, otherwise an empty string.
3. `estimated_queued_users`: Integer of the estimated number of users currently waiting in the queue.
4. `estimated_total_active_users`: Integer of the estimated number of users currently active on the origin.
5. `max_estimated_time_minutes`: Integer of the maximum estimated time currently presented to the users.

Returns 7 columns, described in the declared result schema.

# cloudflare.zones.zone_name

Get Zone Hold by Zone Name. Fetches one zone name from Cloudflare GET `/zones/{zone_id}/hold/{zone_name}`: one row when it exists, none when the id is unknown (404) or an argument is NULL. Arguments, in URL order: zone_id, zone_name.

## Endpoint

Retrieve whether a given hostname is subject to a zone hold, and metadata about the hold.
This endpoint checks whether the given hostname (or any of its ancestor domains) is blocked
by an active zone hold. If a hold with `include_subdomains` is active on an ancestor domain,
that hold is returned. This endpoint is used internally by SSL/COMS to check hold status
during zone activation.

arguments.name: zone_id
arguments.description: Zone id: the id column of cloudflare.zones.zones.

arguments.name: domain
arguments.description: Filters the returned cookies that match the specified domain attribute.

arguments.name: export
arguments.description: Export the list of cookies as a file, limited to 50000 entries. One of: `csv`.

arguments.name: hosts
arguments.description: Includes cookies that match one or more URL-encoded hostnames separated by commas. Wildcards are supported at the start and end of each hostname to support starts with, ends with and contains. If no wildcards are used, results will be filtered by exact match.

arguments.name: http_only
arguments.description: Filters the returned cookies that are set with HttpOnly.

arguments.name: name
arguments.description: Filters the returned cookies that match the specified name. Wildcards are supported at the start and end to support starts with, ends with and contains. e.g. session*.

arguments.name: order_by
arguments.description: The field used to sort returned cookies. One of: `first_seen_at`, `last_seen_at`.

arguments.name: page_url
arguments.description: Includes connections that match one or more page URLs (separated by commas) where they were last seen Wildcards are supported at the start and end of each page URL to support starts with, ends with and contains. If no wildcards are used, results will be filtered by exact match.

arguments.name: path
arguments.description: Filters the returned cookies that match the specified path attribute.

arguments.name: same_site
arguments.description: Filters the returned cookies that match the specified same_site attribute. One of: `lax`, `strict`, `none`.

arguments.name: secure
arguments.description: Filters the returned cookies that are set with Secure.

arguments.name: type
arguments.description: Filters the returned cookies that match the specified type attribute. One of: `first_party`, `unknown`.

# cloudflare.zones.connections

List detected connections. Returns every connection from Cloudflare GET `/zones/{zone_id}/page_shield/connections` for the given path ids, paginated. Arguments, in URL order: zone_id (each is also returned as a column). Optional named arguments sent to the API: exclude_urls, urls, hosts, order_by, prioritize_malicious, exclude_cdn_cgi, status, page_url, export.

## Endpoint

Lists outbound connections made by webpages in the zone.

Returns 14 columns, described in the declared result schema.

vgi.example_queries.description: List connections for one zone (zone_id: the URL path id).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id, added_at, domain_reported_malicious FROM cloudflare.zones.connections('<zone_id>')

vgi.example_queries.description: Every connection across all of your zones, one API call per zone.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT p.name AS zone, r.id, r.added_at FROM cloudflare.zones.zones p, cloudflare.zones.connections(p.id) r

vgi.example_queries.description: Only connections matching a exclude_urls: the named argument is sent to the API, which filters.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id, added_at, domain_reported_malicious FROM cloudflare.zones.connections('<zone_id>', exclude_urls := '<exclude_urls>')

arguments.name: zone_id
arguments.description: Zone id: the id column of cloudflare.zones.zones.

arguments.name: exclude_cdn_cgi
arguments.description: When true, excludes connections seen in a `/cdn-cgi` path from the returned connections. The default value is true.

arguments.name: exclude_urls
arguments.description: Excludes connections whose URL contains one of the URL-encoded URLs separated by commas.

arguments.name: export
arguments.description: Export the list of connections as a file, limited to 50000 entries. One of: `csv`.

arguments.name: hosts
arguments.description: Includes connections that match one or more URL-encoded hostnames separated by commas. Wildcards are supported at the start and end of each hostname to support starts with, ends with and contains. If no wildcards are used, results will be filtered by exact match.

arguments.name: order_by
arguments.description: The field used to sort returned connections. One of: `first_seen_at`, `last_seen_at`.

arguments.name: page_url
arguments.description: Includes connections that match one or more page URLs (separated by commas) where they were last seen Wildcards are supported at the start and end of each page URL to support starts with, ends with and contains. If no wildcards are used, results will be filtered by exact match.

arguments.name: prioritize_malicious
arguments.description: When true, malicious connections appear first in the returned connections.

arguments.name: status
arguments.description: Filters the returned connections using a comma-separated list of connection statuses. Accepted values: `active`, `infrequent`, and `inactive`. The default value is `active`.

arguments.name: urls
arguments.description: Includes connections whose URL contain one or more URL-encoded URLs separated by commas.

workers.title: CloudQuery Source Plugins
workers.tagline: Run CloudQuery source plugins as DuckDB tables via Arrow (Go)
workers.subtitle: Every CloudQuery source plugin's tables as DuckDB tables, streamed as Arrow, with secret-held specs.
workers.summary: Host CloudQuery source plugins and query their tables from DuckDB: each plugin is a schema, each plugin table a table, streamed as Arrow from the plugin's sync. No CloudQuery CLI or destination database needed.
workers.doc_md:
# CloudQuery source plugins in DuckDB

Hosts [CloudQuery](https://www.cloudquery.io) source plugins and turns their tables into DuckDB tables, talking to each plugin directly over the plugin protocol v3 (gRPC + Arrow): no CloudQuery CLI, no destination database. Name plugins in the `plugins` ATTACH option; each becomes a schema, and its tables are queried like any other.

- **Plugins**: local binaries, GitHub release archives, CloudQuery Hub downloads (API key required), or a running plugin server. Archives are sha256-verified and cached.
- **Credentials**: a DuckDB secret of type `cloudquery`, never the ATTACH string.
- **Arrow end to end**: record batches from the plugin's sync go to DuckDB with their buffers intact; `UUID` and `JSON` columns keep their types.
- **Pushdown**: table selection and projection; CloudQuery plugins take no filters, so WHERE runs in DuckDB, and LIMIT cancels the sync.

attach_options.name: plugins
attach_options.description: Comma-separated CloudQuery source plugins to host, each `[schema=]ref`. A ref is a local plugin binary path, a CloudQuery Hub plugin (`cloudquery/xkcd@v1.6.1`, `hub:team/name`), a GitHub release (`github:cloudquery/test@v4.1.0`), or a running plugin server (`grpc:host:port`); append `#sha256:<hex>` to pin an archive. Each plugin becomes a schema named after it (or `schema`), holding one table per plugin table.

attach_options.name: spec
attach_options.description: Non-secret plugin specs: a JSON or YAML object keyed by schema, each value the plugin's own `spec:` object (`{"hackernews": {"item_concurrency": 10}}`). Used to discover tables at ATTACH and for every query. Never put credentials here: use CREATE SECRET (TYPE cloudquery, ...).

attach_options.name: cache_dir
attach_options.description: Directory for downloaded plugins (default: <user cache dir>/vgi-cloudquery/plugins). Binaries are kept with their verified sha256 and reused offline.

attach_options.name: hub_url
attach_options.description: CloudQuery Hub API base URL (default https://api.cloudquery.io); for mirrors and tests.

attach_options.name: github_url
attach_options.description: Base URL GitHub release downloads come from (default https://github.com); for mirrors and tests.

example_queries.description: Read a plugin table directly and aggregate it
example_queries.sql: SELECT category, count(*) AS items FROM cloudquery.main.scan('fixture', 'fixture_item') GROUP BY category ORDER BY category

example_queries.description: Stop the plugin's sync after 10 rows
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS fetched FROM cloudquery.main.scan('fixture', 'fixture_item', max_rows := 10)

example_queries.description: Download the CloudQuery test plugin from its GitHub release into the cache
example_queries.sql: SELECT ref, plugin_version, archive_sha256, from_cache FROM cloudquery.main.install_plugin('github:cloudquery/test@v4.1.0')

example_queries.description: The attached plugins and how many tables each serves
example_queries.sql: SELECT schema_name, plugin, plugin_version, table_count FROM cloudquery.main.plugin ORDER BY schema_name

example_queries.description: Child relations and their parents
example_queries.sql: SELECT schema_name, table_name, parent_table FROM cloudquery.main.plugin_table WHERE parent_table IS NOT NULL ORDER BY ALL

example_queries.description: Columns with CloudQuery extension types and their DuckDB types
example_queries.sql: SELECT table_name, column_name, cloudquery_type, duckdb_type FROM cloudquery.main.plugin_column WHERE cloudquery_type IN ('uuid', 'json', 'inet', 'mac') ORDER BY ALL

example_queries.description: Extension-typed columns of fixture_item
example_queries.sql: SELECT column_name, duckdb_type FROM cloudquery.main.plugin_column WHERE table_name = 'fixture_item' AND cloudquery_type IN ('uuid', 'json', 'inet', 'mac') AND column_name NOT LIKE '\_cq%' ESCAPE '\' ORDER BY ordinal;

example_queries.description: Child relations of the fixture plugin
example_queries.sql: SELECT table_name, parent_table FROM cloudquery.main.plugin_table WHERE parent_table IS NOT NULL ORDER BY table_name;

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The main schema introspects and reads the plugins of the current ATTACH; the plugin tables themselves live in one schema per plugin. Its tables report what the plugins option resolved to (versions, verified sha256 digests, spec JSON Schema), every plugin table with its parent relation and primary key, and every column with its CloudQuery and DuckDB types. scan(schema, table_name, max_rows := 0, strict := false) reads a plugin table directly, which is the way in when a table needs credentials only a secret holds; a plugin can also be downloaded into the cache ahead of use. Everything here reflects the current ATTACH and is empty when it named no plugins.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

Introspection of the plugins this ATTACH hosts: what the `plugins` option resolved to (version, source, verified sha256 digest, spec JSON Schema), which tables exist and how child relations hang off their parents (`_cq_parent_id` to `_cq_id`), and how each CloudQuery column type maps to DuckDB (`UUID` and `JSON` keep their types).

The plugin tables themselves live in one schema per plugin. Every read runs a plugin sync of just that table: plugins take no filters, so `WHERE` runs in DuckDB, while projection is pushed down and `LIMIT` stops the sync early. When a plugin's tables depend on credentials that only a `cloudquery` secret holds, read them with `scan` instead. Everything here is empty when the ATTACH named no plugins.

workers.doc_md:
# Source-Code Structure Analysis for DuckDB

![tree-sitter logo](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tree-sitter/tree-sitter/master/docs/src/assets/images/tree-sitter-small.png)

Parse, search, and measure source code directly in SQL: extract symbols, imports, comments, and string literals, count physical lines and function definitions, and run arbitrary tree-sitter queries across nine programming languages — all over Apache Arrow with no language server, no checkout, and no external services.

The `code` worker turns DuckDB into a lightweight code-intelligence engine for developers, data and platform engineers, and security or research teams who need to treat large codebases as queryable data. Point it at source held in any DuckDB table or file and get structured facts back as ordinary rows and columns. Because everything is just SQL, you can join code structure against commits, issues, ownership, or CVE data and compute metrics over an entire repository in a single query.

Parsing is powered by [tree-sitter](https://tree-sitter.github.io/), the fast, incremental, error-tolerant parsing library used by editors and code-search tools such as Neovim, Zed, and GitHub. Each call builds a concrete syntax tree and runs curated per-language tree-sitter queries, so extraction stays accurate even on incomplete or malformed input (garbage in yields empty results, never a crash). Supported languages are rust, python, javascript, typescript, go, java, c, cpp, and json. See the official [tree-sitter documentation](https://tree-sitter.github.io/tree-sitter/) and the [tree-sitter source on GitHub](https://github.com/tree-sitter/tree-sitter) for grammar and query details.

## Key concepts

Everything is exposed as ordinary SQL: scalar functions take a per-row source string (and, where parsing is needed, a `language` id) and return a value or a `VARCHAR[]` array; table functions take a constant source and return a result set you can join and aggregate. Language ids are lowercase (`rust`, `python`, `go`, …) and parsing is best-effort — malformed or truncated input yields empty results rather than an error, while an unknown language or a bad tree-sitter query is reported clearly.

## When to reach for it

Use the `code` worker whenever you want to treat source as data instead of text: build codebase metrics dashboards (size, complexity, function density), audit dependencies and import graphs, mine comments and TODOs, scan string literals for secrets, URLs, or missing license headers, and run structural code search with your own tree-sitter queries. Because the answers come back as rows, you can join them against commits, ownership, issues, or CVE data and compute over an entire repository in one query.
workers.readme_sql:
LOAD vgi;
ATTACH 'code' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'github-auto://Query-farm/vgi-code@v0.4.1');
SET search_path = 'code.main';

-- Infer a language from a filename.
SELECT language_of('main.rs');                 -- → 'rust'

-- Per-row analysis of a source column.
SELECT path,
       count_functions(content, language_of(path)) AS fns,
       loc(content, language_of(path))            AS code_lines
FROM files;

-- One import per row.
SELECT UNNEST(extract_imports(content, 'python')) FROM files;

-- The power feature: run any tree-sitter query.
SELECT UNNEST(ts_query(content, 'rust',
       '(function_item name: (identifier) @n)')) FROM files;

-- Structural symbols of one document (table function).
SELECT * FROM symbols('fn add(a:i32,b:i32)->i32{a+b}', 'rust');
-- kind     | name | start_line | end_line
-- function | add  |          1 |        1

-- Arbitrary query matches as rows.
SELECT * FROM ts_nodes('func A(){}', 'go', '(function_declaration) @f');

-- Combine them: a call graph from symbols' function spans + ts_nodes' call sites.
SELECT s.name AS caller, c.text AS callee
FROM symbols(E'fn main() {\n    run();\n}\nfn run() {\n    log();\n}\n', 'rust') AS s
JOIN ts_nodes(E'fn main() {\n    run();\n}\nfn run() {\n    log();\n}\n', 'rust',
              '(call_expression function: (identifier) @callee)') AS c
  ON c.start_line BETWEEN s.start_line AND s.end_line
WHERE s.kind = 'function'
ORDER BY c.start_line;
-- caller | callee
-- main   | run
-- run    | log

-- Discover what the worker can parse.
SELECT * FROM supported_languages();

# Source-code structure

The single schema of the `code` worker. It exposes source-code structure to SQL over Apache Arrow, powered by [tree-sitter](https://tree-sitter.github.io/): detect a file's language, measure it, and pull structural facts out of it without a checkout, language server, or external service.

Scalar functions work per row and return a value or a `VARCHAR[]` you can `UNNEST`; table functions take a constant source and return joinable result sets. Parsing supports rust, python, javascript, typescript, go, java, c, cpp and json. Language ids are lowercase; malformed or truncated input yields empty results rather than an error, while an unknown language or a bad query is reported clearly.

workers.title: Color Science & Accessibility
workers.tagline: Color science — RGB/HSL/LAB, CIEDE2000 ΔE & WCAG contrast for DuckDB (Rust)
workers.subtitle: Convert colors between hex, RGB, HSL and CIELAB, measure CIEDE2000 difference, and check WCAG contrast for accessibility.
workers.summary: Color science for SQL: color-space conversions, CIEDE2000 (ΔE00) color difference, and WCAG contrast/accessibility.
workers.doc_md:
# Color Science for SQL

Bring professional color science to DuckDB — convert between color spaces, measure perceptual color difference, and check accessibility contrast directly in SQL, with no application code required.

The `color` extension is a [VGI](https://query.farm) worker that adds sRGB hex, RGB, HSL and CIELAB color tools to DuckDB over Apache Arrow. It is built for designers, data engineers, and accessibility teams who need to normalize colors, build and de-duplicate palettes, compute [CIEDE2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_difference#CIEDE2000) (ΔE00) color differences, and audit [WCAG](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#contrast-minimum) contrast at warehouse scale.

## How it works

Every transform is implemented directly from the canonical specifications — [sRGB / IEC 61966-2-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SRGB) companding, the [CIELAB (D65)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CIELAB_color_space) color space, the Sharma–Wu–Dalal [CIEDE2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_difference#CIEDE2000) ΔE formula, and the [WCAG 2.x relative-luminance and contrast](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/contrast-minimum.html) definitions — so results match the standards exactly with zero external color dependencies. The same algorithms are available in open-source libraries such as the Rust [palette](https://github.com/Ogeon/palette) crate ([docs](https://docs.rs/palette)); here they run inside a fast, dependency-free worker. The 148 CSS named colors come from the [CSS Color Module Level 4](https://www.w3.org/TR/css-color-4/#named-colors) specification.

## Key concepts

Colors are represented as sRGB hex strings, integer RGB triples, HSL, or perceptually-uniform CIELAB. Perceptual similarity is measured with CIEDE2000 (ΔE00), where a value near 1 is roughly a just-noticeable difference. Accessibility is expressed as WCAG relative luminance (0–1) and contrast ratio (1–21), which classify into the WCAG conformance levels AAA, AA, AA Large and fail.

## When to use it

Reach for this worker whenever colors live in your data: normalizing user-entered or imported hex values, building and de-duplicating palettes, labeling arbitrary colors with their nearest name, or auditing foreground/background pairs for accessibility. Its functions are organized into four categories — conversion, color difference, accessibility, and reference.
workers.readme_sql:
LOAD vgi;
ATTACH 'color' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'github-auto://Query-farm/vgi-color@v0.5.1');
SET search_path = 'color.main';

SELECT to_hex(255, 0, 0);                       -- '#ff0000'
SELECT unnest(from_hex('#ff0000'));             -- r = 255, g = 0, b = 0
SELECT unnest(rgb_to_hsl(255, 0, 0));           -- h = 0, s = 1, l = 0.5
SELECT unnest(rgb_to_lab(255, 0, 0));           -- l ≈ 53.24, a ≈ 80.09, b ≈ 67.20
SELECT ROUND(delta_e('#ff0000', '#ff4500'), 2); -- 6.4 (CIEDE2000 ΔE)
SELECT ROUND(contrast_ratio('#000000','#ffffff'), 1);  -- 21.0
SELECT wcag_level('#000000', '#ffffff');        -- 'AAA'
SELECT is_dark('#222222');                      -- true (white text reads better)
SELECT nearest_color_name('#ff0000');           -- 'red'
SELECT name, hex FROM named_colors ORDER BY name; -- the 148 CSS named colors

example_queries.description: Format an RGB triple as a '#rrggbb' hex string.
example_queries.sql: SELECT color.main.to_hex(255, 99, 71)

example_queries.description: Parse a hex color into its red channel.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (color.main.from_hex('#ff6347')).r AS red

example_queries.description: Convert pure red to its HSL hue.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (color.main.rgb_to_hsl(255, 0, 0)).h AS hue

example_queries.description: Compute the WCAG contrast ratio between black and white.
example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(color.main.contrast_ratio('#000000', '#ffffff'), 1) AS ratio

example_queries.description: Classify the WCAG conformance level of dark-grey text on white.
example_queries.sql: SELECT color.main.wcag_level('#595959', '#ffffff') AS level

example_queries.description: Find the closest CSS named color to a hex value.
example_queries.sql: SELECT color.main.nearest_color_name('#ff6347') AS name

example_queries.description: List a few CSS named colors with their hex values.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, hex FROM color.main.named_colors() ORDER BY name LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Accessible shade finder: keep tomato's (#ff6347) HSL hue and saturation, step its lightness from 0.60 down to 0.30, and grade white text on each shade with contrast_ratio and wcag_level. Lightness 0.45 (#e52300, 4.59:1) is the lightest shade that reaches AA; 0.30 (#991700, 8.48:1) reaches AAA.
example_queries.sql: WITH base AS (SELECT color.main.rgb_to_hsl(c.r, c.g, c.b) AS hsl FROM (SELECT color.main.from_hex('#ff6347') AS c)), shades AS (SELECT t.k / 100 AS lightness, color.main.hsl_to_rgb(base.hsl.h, base.hsl.s, t.k / 100) AS rgb FROM base, range(30, 65, 5) AS t(k)), ladder AS (SELECT lightness, color.main.to_hex(rgb.r, rgb.g, rgb.b) AS hex FROM shades) SELECT lightness, hex, ROUND(color.main.contrast_ratio('#ffffff', hex), 2) AS ratio_on_white, color.main.wcag_level('#ffffff', hex) AS level FROM ladder ORDER BY lightness DESC

example_queries.description: Pick a readable label color for each background in a palette: is_dark chooses white text on dark backgrounds and black text on light ones, then contrast_ratio and wcag_level grade the pair. is_dark always picks the higher-contrast option, so every row reaches at least AA; the closest call is #e50914 with white text at 4.79:1, and mid-grey #808080 gets black text (5.32:1).
example_queries.sql: SELECT p.bg, CASE WHEN color.main.is_dark(p.bg) THEN '#ffffff' ELSE '#000000' END AS text_hex, ROUND(color.main.contrast_ratio(text_hex, p.bg), 2) AS ratio, color.main.wcag_level(text_hex, p.bg) AS level FROM (VALUES ('#e50914'), ('#e1306c'), ('#808080'), ('#4285f4'), ('#3b5998'), ('#ff9900')) AS p(bg) ORDER BY ratio, p.bg

example_queries.description: Which CSS named colors are safe for body text on a white page? Grade every named color as text on #ffffff with contrast_ratio and wcag_level, keep AA or better, and list the six lightest that still pass, starting with teal (4.77:1). Only 32 of the 148 names pass; most fail.
example_queries.sql: SELECT n.name, n.hex, ROUND(color.main.contrast_ratio(n.hex, '#ffffff'), 2) AS ratio, color.main.wcag_level(n.hex, '#ffffff') AS level FROM color.main.named_colors AS n WHERE color.main.wcag_level(n.hex, '#ffffff') IN ('AA', 'AAA') ORDER BY ratio, n.name LIMIT 6

example_queries.description: Palette de-duplication: join named_colors to itself, score every pair of names with different hex values by CIEDE2000 delta_e, and keep the pairs a viewer can barely tell apart (ΔE00 < 2). Five pairs qualify, from chartreuse / lawngreen (0.652) to moccasin / wheat (1.99).
example_queries.sql: SELECT name_a, name_b, hex_a, hex_b, ROUND(d, 3) AS delta_e FROM (SELECT a.name AS name_a, b.name AS name_b, a.hex AS hex_a, b.hex AS hex_b, color.main.delta_e(a.hex, b.hex) AS d FROM color.main.named_colors AS a JOIN color.main.named_colors AS b ON a.name < b.name AND a.hex <> b.hex) AS pairs WHERE d < 2 ORDER BY delta_e, name_a, name_b

example_queries.description: Color-harmony generator: convert #ff6347 to HSL, rotate its hue by 120, 180 and 240 degrees, convert each back with hsl_to_rgb and to_hex, and label it with nearest_color_name. Result: base #ff6347 tomato, triad 1 #47ff63 springgreen, complement #47e3ff skyblue, triad 2 #6347ff slateblue.
example_queries.sql: WITH base AS (SELECT color.main.rgb_to_hsl(c.r, c.g, c.b) AS hsl FROM (SELECT color.main.from_hex('#ff6347') AS c)), harmony AS (SELECT t.role, t.shift, color.main.hsl_to_rgb((base.hsl.h + t.shift) % 360, base.hsl.s, base.hsl.l) AS rgb FROM base, (VALUES ('base', 0), ('triad 1', 120), ('complement', 180), ('triad 2', 240)) AS t(role, shift)), palette AS (SELECT role, shift, color.main.to_hex(rgb.r, rgb.g, rgb.b) AS hex FROM harmony) SELECT role, hex, color.main.nearest_color_name(hex) AS nearest_name FROM palette ORDER BY shift

example_queries.description: Snap brand hex values to CSS names and flag which swaps are safe: nearest_color_name picks the name, joining named_colors recovers its hex, and delta_e measures the error; close_match is true when ΔE00 < 2. #ffd800 → gold (0.32) and #fafafa → white (1.0) are close; #f40009 → red (2.55), #4285f4 → dodgerblue (5.05) and #1da1f2 → dodgerblue (7.03) are visibly off.
example_queries.sql: SELECT p.hex, n.name AS css_name, n.hex AS css_hex, ROUND(color.main.delta_e(p.hex, n.hex), 2) AS delta_e, color.main.delta_e(p.hex, n.hex) < 2 AS close_match FROM (VALUES ('#fafafa'), ('#ffd800'), ('#f40009'), ('#4285f4'), ('#1da1f2')) AS p(hex) JOIN color.main.named_colors AS n ON n.name = color.main.nearest_color_name(p.hex) ORDER BY delta_e, p.hex

example_queries.description: HSL lightness is not perceived lightness: take the 18 named colors whose HSL lightness (rgb_to_hsl) is exactly 0.5 and sort them by CIELAB L* (rgb_to_lab). L* runs from 97.1 for yellow down to 32.3 for blue, so sort or match palettes by L*, not HSL l.
example_queries.sql: WITH rgb AS (SELECT n.name, n.hex, color.main.from_hex(n.hex) AS c FROM color.main.named_colors AS n), spaces AS (SELECT name, hex, color.main.rgb_to_hsl(c.r, c.g, c.b) AS hsl, color.main.rgb_to_lab(c.r, c.g, c.b) AS lab FROM rgb) SELECT name, hex, ROUND(lab.l, 1) AS lab_lightness FROM spaces WHERE ROUND(hsl.l, 3) = 0.5 ORDER BY lab_lightness DESC, name

example_queries.description: Look up the hex value of a specific CSS named color.
example_queries.sql: SELECT hex FROM color.main.named_colors WHERE name = 'tomato'

example_queries.description: Parse a hex color into its red, green and blue channels.

example_queries.description: Convert pure red into hue, saturation and lightness.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (color.main.rgb_to_hsl(255, 0, 0)).h AS hue, (color.main.rgb_to_hsl(255, 0, 0)).s AS saturation, (color.main.rgb_to_hsl(255, 0, 0)).l AS lightness;

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Color-science functions: convert between sRGB hex, RGB, HSL and CIELAB; measure CIEDE2000 (ΔE00) color difference; compute WCAG relative luminance and contrast ratio and classify WCAG conformance; test whether a color is dark; and look up the nearest CSS named color.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# color.main

Color science over Apache Arrow. Everything the `color` worker exposes lives in this single schema.

Three kinds of operation are available. **Conversions** move a color between representations — sRGB hex, RGB, HSL and CIELAB. **Color-difference** operations measure how far apart two colors look, using the perceptual CIEDE2000 (ΔE00) metric, and can map an arbitrary color to its nearest CSS name. **Accessibility** operations compute WCAG relative luminance and contrast ratios and classify conformance for text on a background.

Use this schema for color normalization, palette analysis and de-duplication, and WCAG contrast/accessibility auditing directly in SQL. The functions are grouped into four categories: conversion, color difference, accessibility, and reference.

vgi.example_queries.description: Format an RGB triple as a '#rrggbb' hex string.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT color.main.to_hex(255, 99, 71)

vgi.example_queries.description: Parse a hex color into its red channel.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT (color.main.from_hex('#ff6347')).r AS red

vgi.example_queries.description: Convert pure red to its HSL hue.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT (color.main.rgb_to_hsl(255, 0, 0)).h AS hue

vgi.example_queries.description: Compute the WCAG contrast ratio between black and white.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(color.main.contrast_ratio('#000000', '#ffffff'), 1) AS ratio

vgi.example_queries.description: Classify the WCAG conformance level of dark-grey text on white.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT color.main.wcag_level('#595959', '#ffffff') AS level

vgi.example_queries.description: Find the closest CSS named color to a hex value.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT color.main.nearest_color_name('#ff6347') AS name

vgi.example_queries.description: List a few CSS named colors with their hex values.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, hex FROM color.main.named_colors() ORDER BY name LIMIT 5

vgi.example_queries.description: Accessible shade finder: keep tomato's (#ff6347) HSL hue and saturation, step its lightness from 0.60 down to 0.30, and grade white text on each shade with contrast_ratio and wcag_level. Lightness 0.45 (#e52300, 4.59:1) is the lightest shade that reaches AA; 0.30 (#991700, 8.48:1) reaches AAA.
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH base AS (SELECT color.main.rgb_to_hsl(c.r, c.g, c.b) AS hsl FROM (SELECT color.main.from_hex('#ff6347') AS c)), shades AS (SELECT t.k / 100 AS lightness, color.main.hsl_to_rgb(base.hsl.h, base.hsl.s, t.k / 100) AS rgb FROM base, range(30, 65, 5) AS t(k)), ladder AS (SELECT lightness, color.main.to_hex(rgb.r, rgb.g, rgb.b) AS hex FROM shades) SELECT lightness, hex, ROUND(color.main.contrast_ratio('#ffffff', hex), 2) AS ratio_on_white, color.main.wcag_level('#ffffff', hex) AS level FROM ladder ORDER BY lightness DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Pick a readable label color for each background in a palette: is_dark chooses white text on dark backgrounds and black text on light ones, then contrast_ratio and wcag_level grade the pair. is_dark always picks the higher-contrast option, so every row reaches at least AA; the closest call is #e50914 with white text at 4.79:1, and mid-grey #808080 gets black text (5.32:1).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT p.bg, CASE WHEN color.main.is_dark(p.bg) THEN '#ffffff' ELSE '#000000' END AS text_hex, ROUND(color.main.contrast_ratio(text_hex, p.bg), 2) AS ratio, color.main.wcag_level(text_hex, p.bg) AS level FROM (VALUES ('#e50914'), ('#e1306c'), ('#808080'), ('#4285f4'), ('#3b5998'), ('#ff9900')) AS p(bg) ORDER BY ratio, p.bg

vgi.example_queries.description: Which CSS named colors are safe for body text on a white page? Grade every named color as text on #ffffff with contrast_ratio and wcag_level, keep AA or better, and list the six lightest that still pass, starting with teal (4.77:1). Only 32 of the 148 names pass; most fail.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT n.name, n.hex, ROUND(color.main.contrast_ratio(n.hex, '#ffffff'), 2) AS ratio, color.main.wcag_level(n.hex, '#ffffff') AS level FROM color.main.named_colors AS n WHERE color.main.wcag_level(n.hex, '#ffffff') IN ('AA', 'AAA') ORDER BY ratio, n.name LIMIT 6

vgi.example_queries.description: Palette de-duplication: join named_colors to itself, score every pair of names with different hex values by CIEDE2000 delta_e, and keep the pairs a viewer can barely tell apart (ΔE00 < 2). Five pairs qualify, from chartreuse / lawngreen (0.652) to moccasin / wheat (1.99).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name_a, name_b, hex_a, hex_b, ROUND(d, 3) AS delta_e FROM (SELECT a.name AS name_a, b.name AS name_b, a.hex AS hex_a, b.hex AS hex_b, color.main.delta_e(a.hex, b.hex) AS d FROM color.main.named_colors AS a JOIN color.main.named_colors AS b ON a.name < b.name AND a.hex <> b.hex) AS pairs WHERE d < 2 ORDER BY delta_e, name_a, name_b

vgi.example_queries.description: Color-harmony generator: convert #ff6347 to HSL, rotate its hue by 120, 180 and 240 degrees, convert each back with hsl_to_rgb and to_hex, and label it with nearest_color_name. Result: base #ff6347 tomato, triad 1 #47ff63 springgreen, complement #47e3ff skyblue, triad 2 #6347ff slateblue.
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH base AS (SELECT color.main.rgb_to_hsl(c.r, c.g, c.b) AS hsl FROM (SELECT color.main.from_hex('#ff6347') AS c)), harmony AS (SELECT t.role, t.shift, color.main.hsl_to_rgb((base.hsl.h + t.shift) % 360, base.hsl.s, base.hsl.l) AS rgb FROM base, (VALUES ('base', 0), ('triad 1', 120), ('complement', 180), ('triad 2', 240)) AS t(role, shift)), palette AS (SELECT role, shift, color.main.to_hex(rgb.r, rgb.g, rgb.b) AS hex FROM harmony) SELECT role, hex, color.main.nearest_color_name(hex) AS nearest_name FROM palette ORDER BY shift

vgi.example_queries.description: Snap brand hex values to CSS names and flag which swaps are safe: nearest_color_name picks the name, joining named_colors recovers its hex, and delta_e measures the error; close_match is true when ΔE00 < 2. #ffd800 → gold (0.32) and #fafafa → white (1.0) are close; #f40009 → red (2.55), #4285f4 → dodgerblue (5.05) and #1da1f2 → dodgerblue (7.03) are visibly off.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT p.hex, n.name AS css_name, n.hex AS css_hex, ROUND(color.main.delta_e(p.hex, n.hex), 2) AS delta_e, color.main.delta_e(p.hex, n.hex) < 2 AS close_match FROM (VALUES ('#fafafa'), ('#ffd800'), ('#f40009'), ('#4285f4'), ('#1da1f2')) AS p(hex) JOIN color.main.named_colors AS n ON n.name = color.main.nearest_color_name(p.hex) ORDER BY delta_e, p.hex

vgi.example_queries.description: HSL lightness is not perceived lightness: take the 18 named colors whose HSL lightness (rgb_to_hsl) is exactly 0.5 and sort them by CIELAB L* (rgb_to_lab). L* runs from 97.1 for yellow down to 32.3 for blue, so sort or match palettes by L*, not HSL l.
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH rgb AS (SELECT n.name, n.hex, color.main.from_hex(n.hex) AS c FROM color.main.named_colors AS n), spaces AS (SELECT name, hex, color.main.rgb_to_hsl(c.r, c.g, c.b) AS hsl, color.main.rgb_to_lab(c.r, c.g, c.b) AS lab FROM rgb) SELECT name, hex, ROUND(lab.l, 1) AS lab_lightness FROM spaces WHERE ROUND(hsl.l, 3) = 0.5 ORDER BY lab_lightness DESC, name

# named_colors

The discovery table of every CSS Color Module Level 4 named color. One row per color, with columns `name` (the color name, e.g. `tomato`) and `hex` (its lowercase `#rrggbb` sRGB value). Use it to list valid color names, look up a name's hex value, or browse the palette that backs `nearest_color_name`.

Grade every named color as text on #ffffff with contrast_ratio and wcag_level, keep AA or better, and list the six lightest that still pass, starting with teal (4.77:1). Only 32 of the 148 names pass; most fail.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT n.name, n.hex, ROUND(color.main.contrast_ratio(n.hex, '#ffffff'), 2) AS ratio, color.main.wcag_level(n.hex, '#ffffff') AS level FROM color.main.named_colors AS n WHERE color.main.wcag_level(n.hex, '#ffffff') IN ('AA', 'AAA') ORDER BY ratio, n.name LIMIT 6

vgi.example_queries.description: Palette de-duplication: join named_colors to itself, score every pair of names with different hex values by CIEDE2000 delta_e, and keep the pairs a viewer can barely tell apart (ΔE00 < 2). Five pairs qualify, from chartreuse / lawngreen (0.652) to moccasin / wheat (1.99).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name_a, name_b, hex_a, hex_b, ROUND(d, 3) AS delta_e FROM (SELECT a.name AS name_a, b.name AS name_b, a.hex AS hex_a, b.hex AS hex_b, color.main.delta_e(a.hex, b.hex) AS d FROM color.main.named_colors AS a JOIN color.main.named_colors AS b ON a.name < b.name AND a.hex <> b.hex) AS pairs WHERE d < 2 ORDER BY delta_e, name_a, name_b

workers.title: Multi-Codec Compression
workers.tagline: Compress and decompress blobs in DuckDB with SQL — zstd, gzip, brotli, lz4, snappy, xz, bzip2 with decompression-bomb guards. A VGI worker.
workers.subtitle: Compress, decompress, and identify zstd, gzip, brotli, lz4, snappy, xz, and bzip2 payloads stored in BLOB columns.
workers.summary: Multi-codec (de)compression over a DuckDB BLOB column — zstd, gzip, zlib, deflate, brotli, lz4, snappy, xz, lzma, bzip2 — with codec auto-detection and a decompression-bomb guard.
workers.doc_md:
# compress

**Multi-codec (de)compression over a DuckDB `BLOB` column** — `zstd`, `gzip`, `zlib`, `deflate`, `brotli`, `lz4` (frame + block), `snappy` (framed + raw), `xz`, `lzma`, `bzip2` — plus codec auto-detection by magic bytes, level control, and size/ratio introspection. Fills the one gap DuckDB core leaves open: core decompresses *files*, but there is no scalar to decode a *column* of compressed payloads at scan time. Decode a mixed-codec Kafka payload column, transcode a cold archive in place (gzip → zstd), or audit compression — all without leaving the engine.

**Security — decompression bombs.** Every decode path enforces a bounded `max_output_bytes` cap (default 256 MiB): a hostile high-ratio blob aborts that one row with a per-row error instead of OOMing the worker. Pure in-engine local CPU — no network, no state, zero egress.

## Sources and references

- [RFC 8878](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8878) — Zstandard
- [RFC 1952](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1952) — gzip; [RFC 1950](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1950) — zlib; [RFC 1951](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1951) — DEFLATE
- [RFC 7932](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7932) — Brotli
- [LZ4 frame format](https://github.com/lz4/lz4/blob/dev/doc/lz4_Frame_format.md) — and the [Snappy framing format](https://github.com/google/snappy/blob/main/framing_format.txt)
- [The .xz file format](https://tukaani.org/xz/format.html) — and [bzip2](https://sourceware.org/bzip2/)

example_queries.description: Decode a gzip'd HTTP body column to text at scan time.
example_queries.sql: SELECT compress.main.decompress(body_gz, 'gzip')::VARCHAR AS body FROM http_logs

example_queries.description: Identify the codec of each message in a mixed-codec column.
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, compress.main.detect_codec(value) AS codec FROM kafka_messages

example_queries.description: Auto-detect and decode a mixed-codec column with a 64 MiB/row cap.
example_queries.sql: SELECT compress.main.decompress_auto(value, 67108864) AS payload FROM kafka_messages

example_queries.description: Audit the zstd-19 compression ratio of a blob column.
example_queries.sql: SELECT avg(compress.main.ratio(blob, 'zstd', 19)) AS avg_ratio FROM report

example_queries.description: List every codec this build supports.
example_queries.sql: SELECT compress.main.codecs() AS codecs

example_queries.description: Rank every supported codec by compressed size and ratio on a sample JSON-lines payload, at each codec's default level (smallest output first).
example_queries.sql: SELECT codec, compress.main.compressed_size(p, codec) AS bytes_out, round(compress.main.ratio(p, codec), 3) AS ratio FROM (SELECT repeat('{"user":42,"event":"click","page":"/home"}' || chr(10), 200)::BLOB AS p), unnest(compress.main.codecs()) AS t(codec) ORDER BY bytes_out, codec

example_queries.description: Profile a mixed-codec message column: group messages by the codec sniffed from their magic bytes and total stored vs. decompressed bytes per codec (the headerless brotli message is detected as 'unknown' and left out).
example_queries.sql: WITH inbox AS (SELECT id, compress.main.compress(repeat(body, 20)::BLOB, codec) AS payload FROM (VALUES (1, 'zstd', 'temp=21.5;'), (2, 'gzip', 'temp=22.0;'), (3, 'zstd', 'temp=20.9;'), (4, 'bzip2', 'temp=23.1;'), (5, 'brotli', 'temp=19.8;')) AS t(id, codec, body)), sniffed AS (SELECT payload, compress.main.detect_codec(payload) AS codec FROM inbox) SELECT codec, count(*) AS messages, sum(octet_length(payload)) AS stored_bytes, sum(compress.main.decompressed_size(payload, codec)) AS raw_bytes FROM sniffed WHERE codec <> 'unknown' GROUP BY codec ORDER BY codec

example_queries.description: Before transcoding a gzip archive to zstd, compare each file's current gzip size with the size its decompressed contents would take as zstd level 19 (nothing is rewritten).
example_queries.sql: WITH archive AS (SELECT name, compress.main.compress(repeat(line, n)::BLOB, 'gzip') AS gz FROM (VALUES ('access.log', 'GET /index.html 200' || chr(10), 300), ('error.log', 'WARN disk 91% full' || chr(10), 40)) AS t(name, line, n)) SELECT name, octet_length(gz) AS gzip_bytes, compress.main.compressed_size(compress.main.decompress(gz, 'gzip'), 'zstd', 19) AS zstd_bytes FROM archive ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Triage payloads whose codec cannot be sniffed: for each blob detect_codec reports as 'unknown', list every supported codec it validates as a well-formed stream (the gzip blob is detectable, so it is skipped).
example_queries.sql: WITH uploads AS (SELECT id, compress.main.compress(body::BLOB, codec) AS payload FROM (VALUES (1, '{"status":"ok","items":[1,2,3]}', 'brotli'), (2, '{"status":"ok","items":[4,5,6]}', 'deflate'), (3, '{"status":"ok","items":[7,8,9]}', 'gzip')) AS t(id, body, codec)) SELECT id, codec FROM uploads, unnest(compress.main.codecs()) AS t(codec) WHERE compress.main.detect_codec(payload) = 'unknown' AND compress.main.is_valid(payload, codec) ORDER BY id, codec

example_queries.description: How big does this gzip blob expand to?

Codecs span zstd, gzip, zlib, deflate, brotli, lz4 (frame and block), snappy (framed and raw), xz, lzma, and bzip2. Every decode is bounded by a decompression-bomb guard (a per-row output-byte cap). tags.vgi.doc_md:
## compress.main

The single schema of the `compress` worker. The catalog name matches the `ATTACH` name, so calls are qualified with the `compress.main` prefix.

The surface is grouped into four navigable areas:

- **encode** — turn a `BLOB` into compressed bytes with a chosen codec and optional level.
- **decode** — recover the original bytes, with the codec named explicitly or auto-detected, under a decompression-bomb guard.
- **introspection** — measure compressed and decompressed size, compression ratio, and stream validity without materializing the output.
- **discovery** — identify a blob's codec and list the codecs this build supports.

Every codec — zstd, gzip, zlib, deflate, brotli, lz4, snappy, xz, lzma, and bzip2 — shares this one uniform surface over a `BLOB` column.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Decompress a `BLOB` with the named codec (the inverse of compress). The optional third argument max_output_bytes is the decompression-bomb guard: decoding aborts the row once output would exceed the cap and returns a per-row error, so the worker never OOMs. NULL/omitted uses the worker's configured default cap (the compress_max_output_bytes ATTACH option / env, default 256 MiB); pass a large value to opt out per call. functions.name: detect_codec
functions.comment: Return the codec name of a BLOB by magic bytes, or 'unknown'

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Return the codec name a `BLOB` is compressed with ('gzip', 'zstd', 'xz', …) by magic-byte match, validated against a trial decode of the leading block to reject weak-magic false positives. Returns 'unknown' when no signature matches — which includes every HEADERLESS codec (brotli, deflate, lz4_block, snappy_raw carry no magic and can never be detected; use the explicit decompress form for those). Cheap: inspects only the first few bytes plus a bounded trial. Never errors. NULL input → NULL.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Return the codec of a `BLOB` by magic bytes, e.g. `detect_codec(b)` → 'gzip', or 'unknown' for headerless/unrecognized input. Never errors.

vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH inbox AS (SELECT id, compress.main.compress(repeat(body, 20)::BLOB, codec) AS payload FROM (VALUES (1, 'zstd', 'temp=21.5;'), (2, 'gzip', 'temp=22.0;'), (3, 'zstd', 'temp=20.9;'), (4, 'bzip2', 'temp=23.1;'), (5, 'brotli', 'temp=19.8;')) AS t(id, codec, body)), sniffed AS (SELECT payload, compress.main.detect_codec(payload) AS codec FROM inbox) SELECT codec, count(*) AS messages, sum(octet_length(payload)) AS stored_bytes, sum(compress.main.decompressed_size(payload, codec)) AS raw_bytes FROM sniffed WHERE codec <> 'unknown' GROUP BY codec ORDER BY codec

workers.summary: Validate + normalize phone/email/IBAN/VAT/card/URL/postal fields for SQL
workers.doc_md:
# conform: Field Validation & Normalization in SQL

**Validate and normalize phone numbers, emails, IBANs, EU VAT numbers, credit-card numbers, URLs, and postal codes directly in DuckDB SQL** -- no UDF plumbing, no external service, and no network calls. The `conform` extension turns the data-cleaning steps you would normally script in Python into fast, set-based SQL functions, so you can check validity, standardize formatting, and extract field parts right where your data lives.

This catalog is built for anyone wrangling messy real-world contact, banking, and payment data: data engineers cleaning a CRM export, analysts deduplicating customer records, or pipelines that must reject malformed input before it lands. Every check is **offline, deterministic, and total** -- functions never raise on garbage (with one deliberate exception, an unknown postal-code country), returning `false` for `is_valid_*` and `NULL` for formatters and extractors. That makes the extension hermetic and safe to run over huge tables without DNS lookups or flaky I/O.

Under the hood, `conform` composes three best-in-class, battle-tested libraries. Phone parsing, validation, and E.164/national/international formatting come from [`phonenumbers`](https://github.com/daviddrysdale/python-phonenumbers) (the Python port of Google's [libphonenumber](https://github.com/google/libphonenumber)). IBAN, EU VAT, and the Luhn credit-card check come from [`python-stdnum`](https://github.com/arthurdejong/python-stdnum) ([documentation](https://arthurdejong.org/python-stdnum/)). Email syntax validation and normalization come from [`email-validator`](https://github.com/JoshData/python-email-validator). URL and postal-code handling are implemented in-process against per-country rules.

## What you get

The surface divides into three shapes -- **validity tests** that return a boolean, **normalizers/formatters** that rewrite a value into a canonical string (ideal for joining or deduplication), and **part extractors** that pull a single component (a domain, country, brand, or host) out of a well-formed value -- plus discovery tables that enumerate the phone regions and card brands the worker recognizes.

Phone and VAT functions take an optional ISO region/country argument (`'US'` and the EU-prefixed form are defaults); postal-code validation requires a country.

```sql
SELECT conform.main.normalize_email('Test@Example.COM');
SELECT conform.main.format_phone_e164('07911 123456', 'GB');
SELECT conform.main.mask_card('4111-1111-1111-1111');
```

INSTALL vgi FROM community; LOAD vgi;
ATTACH 'conform' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'uvx --from git+https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-conform@v0.4.1 vgi-conform-worker');

SELECT conform.is_valid_email('a@b.com');                  -- true
SELECT conform.normalize_email('Test@Example.COM');        -- 'Test@example.com'
SELECT conform.format_phone_e164('202-456-1111');          -- '+12024561111' (region 'US')
SELECT conform.format_phone_e164('07911 123456', 'GB');    -- '+447911123456'
SELECT conform.is_valid_iban('GB82 WEST 1234 5698 7654 32');-- true
SELECT conform.iban_country('GB82WEST12345698765432');     -- 'GB'
SELECT conform.is_valid_vat('DE136695976');                -- true
SELECT conform.card_brand('4111111111111111');             -- 'visa'
SELECT conform.mask_card('4111-1111-1111-1111');           -- '************1111'
SELECT conform.normalize_url('HTTP://Example.com:80/Path');-- 'http://example.com/Path'
SELECT conform.is_valid_postal_code('90210', 'US');        -- true

tags.vgi.doc_md:
# conform · main schema

Field validation, normalization, and extraction for email, phone, IBAN, EU VAT, credit-card, URL, and postal-code values, plus three discovery tables.

## What's here

The functions come in three shapes:

- **Validity tests** return `BOOLEAN` -- `true`/`false`, and `NULL` on `NULL` input.
- **Normalizers & formatters** return a canonical `VARCHAR` for storage, joining, or deduplication, or `NULL` for invalid input.
- **Part extractors** pull one component (a domain, country code, brand, or host) out of a well-formed value.

Two discovery tables enumerate the phone regions and card brands the worker recognizes.

## Conventions

All validation is **offline and deterministic** -- no DNS or network. Phone and VAT functions accept an optional ISO region/country argument; postal-code checks require a country.

functions.name: is_valid_postal_code
functions.comment: True if text matches a country's postal-code format (modest coverage: US, CA, GB, DE, FR, NL, AU, JP, IN, BR). Unknown country raises an error.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `is_valid_postal_code(text, country)`

Returns `BOOLEAN`: `true` when `text` matches the postal-code **format** for `country` (ISO-3166 alpha-2), `false` when it does not, `NULL` when `text` is `NULL`.

Coverage is intentionally modest -- a per-country regex table for US, CA, GB, DE, FR, NL, AU, JP, IN, BR. This is a **format** check, not deliverability validation. An **unknown** `country` raises an error (rather than silently returning `false`) so a country typo is not mistaken for an invalid code. `country` is a required constant.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# `is_valid_postal_code`

Format-check a postal code for a country.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT conform.is_valid_postal_code('90210', 'US');     -- true
SELECT conform.is_valid_postal_code('K1A 0B1', 'CA');   -- true
```

## Notes

- Supported: US, CA, GB, DE, FR, NL, AU, JP, IN, BR.
- Unknown `country` raises an error (caught typos, not silent `false`).

functions.comment: Normalized email address (lower-cased domain, etc.), or NULL if invalid

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `normalize_email(text)`

Returns `VARCHAR`: a **canonical** form of the email address (the domain lower-cased and IDNA-normalized; the local-part case left intact per the email standard), or `NULL` when `text` is invalid or `NULL`.

Validation is offline (no DNS). Use this before grouping, joining, or deduplicating on email so that `Test@Example.COM` and `Test@example.com` collapse to the same key (differently-cased local parts stay distinct). Combine with `is_valid_email` if you also need a validity flag.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# `normalize_email`

Canonicalize an email address for comparison / deduplication.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT conform.normalize_email('Test@Example.COM');  -- 'Test@example.com'
```

## Notes

- Lower-cases the domain; leaves the local-part case unchanged.
- Returns `NULL` for invalid or `NULL` input.

Returns `BOOLEAN`: `true` when the card number's digits pass the **Luhn** checksum, `false` otherwise, `NULL` when `text` is `NULL`. Separators (spaces, dashes) are ignored.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT conform.is_valid_card('4111 1111 1111 1111');  -- true
```

## Notes

- Luhn only -- not an authorization or existence check.
- Independent of `card_brand`.

## `is_valid_email(text)`

Returns `BOOLEAN`: `true` when `text` is a **syntactically** valid email address, `false` when it is not, and `NULL` when `text` is `NULL`.

Validation is **offline** -- it checks address syntax and normalizes the domain, but performs **no DNS or deliverability lookup**, so it is fast, deterministic, and never makes a network call.

Use it to gate or filter a column of user-supplied email values (`WHERE conform.is_valid_email(email)`), or as a quality check before loading contact data. Pair with `normalize_email` to canonicalize the values you keep.
tags.vgi.doc_md:

Test whether a string is a syntactically valid email address.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT conform.is_valid_email('a@b.com');   -- true
SELECT conform.is_valid_email('not-email');  -- false
```

## Notes

- Offline only -- no DNS / deliverability check.
- `NULL` in yields `NULL` out; any non-`NULL` invalid value yields `false`.

functions.name: url_host

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `url_host(text)`

Returns `VARCHAR`: the lower-cased **host** (domain) of a valid URL (e.g. `'www.example.com'`), or `NULL` when the URL is invalid or `NULL`.

Use it to group or filter by site/domain, build allow/deny lists, or join URL data on host. The port and userinfo are excluded; only the host is returned. Offline.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# `url_host`

Extract the (lower-cased) host from a URL.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT conform.url_host('https://WWW.Example.com/a');  -- 'www.example.com'
```

## Notes

- Host only (no port/userinfo); `NULL` for invalid URLs.

workers.doc_md:
# Cricket data

Query international and franchise cricket directly from SQL: match results, full batting and bowling cards, ball-by-ball deliveries, computed league tables with net run rate, season leaderboards, live scores and commentary, ICC rankings, and official ECB tables.

## Sources and licensing

Historical data comes from [Cricsheet](https://cricsheet.org) under ODC-By 1.0 and must be attributed. ESPN, ICC, and ECB endpoints are public but undocumented or unlicensed; the worker fetches them on demand, caches politely, and never rehosts them. It is not affiliated with any of these organisations or leagues.

Parameterized functions cover competition seasons, scorecards, ball-by-ball deliveries, computed standings, player aggregates, ESPN live cards, and ECB tables.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Cricket analytical data

Rows are match-, innings-, batter-innings-, bowler-innings-, delivery-, team-, or player-grain.

## Arguments

Cricsheet functions take a competition code first, then an optional season label and match id. ESPN functions take an event id (equal to the Cricsheet match id). ECB functions take a tournament id.

## Freshness

Cricsheet lags play by one to three days; ESPN live data is cached for 30 seconds, ICC rankings for six hours, and ECB data for ten minutes.

functions.name: standings
functions.comment: Computed league-stage table with points and net run rate from Cricsheet results

tags.vgi.doc_llm: League-stage points table for a franchise or domestic competition season, computed from Cricsheet results: played, won, lost, tied, no result, points, and net run rate. Knockout matches are excluded; super-over winners take the win. NULL season means the latest season. For official English tables with bonus points use ecb_standings().
tags.vgi.doc_md: Computed standings. Points use the competition's `points_for_win` (2, or 4 for The Hundred) and half that for a tie, draw, or no result. Net run rate charges an all-out side its full allocation. Penalty deductions and bonus points are not modelled, so official tables can differ.

functions.name: deliveries
functions.comment: Ball-by-ball deliveries for one match or one season from Cricsheet

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per delivery, wides and no-balls included: over, ball sequence, batter, bowler, runs off the bat, extras by type, boundary and wicket flags, and dismissal detail. Requires match_id or season. Use it for phase analysis (powerplay, death overs), matchups, and custom metrics.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Cricsheet ball-by-ball data. `over_number` starts at 1; `legal_ball_number` counts legal balls in the innings and is NULL for wides and no-balls. Either `match_id` or `season` is required.

vgi.example_queries.description: The last over of the IPL 2026 final.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT over_number, ball_in_over, bowler, batter, runs_total, is_wicket FROM cricket.main.deliveries('ipl', match_id := 1535465) WHERE innings_number = 2 ORDER BY over_number DESC, ball_in_over DESC LIMIT 6

vgi.example_queries.description: IPL 2026 sixes by bowler conceding them.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT bowler, count(*) AS sixes FROM cricket.main.deliveries('ipl', season := '2026') WHERE runs_batter = 6 AND is_boundary GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY sixes DESC LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: The IPL 2026 league table alongside each team's powerplay (overs 1-6) batting run rate and wickets lost, aggregated from deliveries() over the whole season.
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH pp AS (SELECT batting_team AS team, round(sum(runs_total) * 6.0 / count(*) FILTER (WHERE is_legal), 2) AS powerplay_run_rate, count(*) FILTER (WHERE is_wicket) AS powerplay_wickets FROM cricket.main.deliveries('ipl', season := '2026') WHERE over_number <= 6 AND NOT super_over GROUP BY team) SELECT s.position, s.team, s.points, pp.powerplay_run_rate, pp.powerplay_wickets FROM cricket.main.standings('ipl', season := '2026') s JOIN pp USING (team) ORDER BY s.position

workers.title: CVE & CVSS
workers.tagline: CVE/NVD lookup with offline CVSS scoring in DuckDB (Go)
workers.subtitle: Look up CVE records, flag known-exploited CVEs, score exploit likelihood, find open-source package advisories, and compute CVSS v3.1 scores.
workers.summary: Look up and prioritize CVEs: NVD records, CISA KEV, FIRST EPSS, OSV.dev, and offline CVSS scoring
workers.doc_md:
# CVE Lookup & Offline CVSS Scoring for DuckDB

**Query CVE / vulnerability data and compute CVSS v3.1 severity scores directly in SQL.** The `cve` extension turns DuckDB into a defensive vulnerability-management workbench: resolve advisories, search vulnerability descriptions, map products to the vulnerabilities that affect them, and score CVSS vectors offline — all without leaving your query editor.

This worker is built for security engineers, vulnerability-management and patch teams, threat researchers, and data analysts who need to enrich, triage, and report on software vulnerabilities at SQL speed. The live lookups read from the National Vulnerability Database (NVD) 2.0 REST API, which republishes and enriches the public CVE records curated by the MITRE-led CVE Program. The scoring math is a faithful, dependency-free implementation of the CVSS v3.1 base-metric equation maintained by FIRST, so a vector string always maps to the same base score and qualitative severity band that the official calculator produces.

The extension is organized in two complementary halves. **Offline CVSS scoring** runs with no network access at all: it parses a CVSS:3.1 vector string into its numeric base score and buckets any numeric score into its qualitative band (NONE, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, or CRITICAL), fully deterministic and safe for air-gapped or high-volume pipelines. **Live NVD 2.0 lookups** stream vulnerability records from the National Vulnerability Database and accept optional `base_url` and `api_key` arguments so you can target a mirror or raise NVD rate limits with a personal key.

Severity alone is a poor patch-priority signal, so the worker also brings **exploit intelligence**: the CISA **Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV)** catalog of CVEs with evidence of active exploitation (US government work, public domain), and FIRST's **Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS)** probability that a CVE is exploited in the next 30 days. For open-source dependencies, **OSV.dev** lookups list the advisories (GitHub Security Advisories, PyPI, Go, RustSec, npm, Maven and more) affecting a package version along with the versions that fix them (OSV data is CC-BY-4.0). Every network function takes an optional `base_url` override, and all of them join on the CVE id.

Reach for this worker whenever you need to attach severity to raw CVSS vectors, look up the details of a known advisory, discover vulnerabilities by keyword or by affected product, or join vulnerability data against your own asset inventory. CVEs still under analysis surface a SQL `NULL` score rather than a misleading zero.

## Learn more

- CVSS specification and scoring (FIRST): [first.org/cvss](https://www.first.org/cvss/) — [CVSS v3.1 specification document](https://www.first.org/cvss/v3-1/specification-document) and the [official CVSS v3.1 calculator](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3-1).
- CVE records and program (MITRE): [cve.org](https://www.cve.org) — source data in the [CVE List repository](https://github.com/CVEProject/cvelistV5).
- CISA KEV catalog: [cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog](https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog).
- EPSS (FIRST): [first.org/epss](https://www.first.org/epss/) and its [API](https://www.first.org/epss/api).
- OSV.dev: [osv.dev](https://osv.dev) and its [API docs](https://google.github.io/osv.dev/api/).
- This worker's source: [github.com/Query-farm/vgi-cve](https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-cve).

example_queries.description: Compute the CVSS v3.1 base score for the Log4Shell vector (9.8).
example_queries.sql: SELECT cve.main.cvss_base_score('CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H');

example_queries.description: Map a numeric CVSS base score to its qualitative severity band (CRITICAL).
example_queries.sql: SELECT cve.main.cvss_severity(9.8);

example_queries.description: Score a vector and bucket it into a severity band in one query.
example_queries.sql: SELECT cve.main.cvss_severity(cve.main.cvss_base_score('CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H'));

example_queries.description: Score an inventory of CVSS v3.1 vectors offline and count the assets in each severity band, keeping empty bands as zero-count rows.
example_queries.sql: WITH inventory(asset, vector) AS (VALUES ('web-01', 'CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H'), ('db-01', 'CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N'), ('kiosk-01', 'CVSS:3.1/AV:P/AC:H/PR:H/UI:R/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N'), ('app-02', 'CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H')), scored AS (SELECT asset, cve.main.cvss_base_score(vector) AS base_score FROM inventory) SELECT b.severity, count(s.asset) AS assets, string_agg(s.asset, ', ' ORDER BY s.asset) AS asset_list FROM cve.main.cvss_severity_bands b LEFT JOIN scored s ON s.base_score BETWEEN b.min_score AND b.max_score GROUP BY b.severity, b.min_score ORDER BY b.min_score;

example_queries.description: Browse the CVSS severity bands with their inclusive base-score ranges.
example_queries.sql: SELECT severity, min_score, max_score FROM cve.main.cvss_severity_bands ORDER BY min_score;

tags.vgi.doc_llm: CVE lookup, prioritization, and CVSS scoring functions. This schema groups four capability families: offline CVSS v3.1 scoring (parse a vector string into a numeric base score and bucket a score into its qualitative severity band) that runs with no network access; live NVD 2.0 REST API lookups (resolve advisories, keyword-search descriptions, and map products to their known vulnerabilities); exploit intelligence (whether CISA lists a CVE as actively exploited, and FIRST's EPSS probability that it will be exploited soon); and OSV.dev open-source advisories by package version or by advisory id. Every network function accepts an optional `base_url` named argument. Results share the CVE id as a join key, so the families combine to rank what to patch first: known-exploited, then likely-exploited, then most severe.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## `cve.main`

The single schema of the **cve** worker. It groups two kinds of functions:

- **Offline CVSS math** — implements the CVSS v3.1 base equation and severity banding with no network access, turning a vector string into a numeric base score and any score into a qualitative band.
- **Live NVD 2.0 lookups** — query the National Vulnerability Database to resolve advisories, search descriptions, and map products to their vulnerabilities, each accepting optional `base_url`/`api_key` arguments.
- **Exploit intelligence** — the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and FIRST EPSS exploitation probabilities, the strongest signals for patch prioritization.
- **Open-source advisories** — OSV.dev records for package versions and advisory ids (CC-BY-4.0).

Use this schema to enrich, triage, and report on software vulnerabilities directly from SQL.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Browsable, offline reference table of the five CVSS v3.1 qualitative severity bands (NONE, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL) and the inclusive base-score range each covers. tags.vgi.doc_md:
## `cvss_severity_bands`

A browsable reference table of the five **CVSS v3.1 qualitative severity bands** and the inclusive base-score range each covers — the discovery counterpart to the `cvss_severity` scalar. It is fully offline and deterministic.

| severity | min_score | max_score |
|---|---|---|
| NONE | 0.0 | 0.0 |
| LOW | 0.1 | 3.9 |
| MEDIUM | 4.0 | 6.9 |
| HIGH | 7.0 | 8.9 |
| CRITICAL | 9.0 | 10.0 |

Join it against a column of scores, or read it to learn the banding before calling `cvss_severity`.

functions.name: osv_query
functions.comment: List OSV.dev vulnerabilities affecting an open-source package (optionally one version)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Query OSV.dev, the distributed open-source vulnerability database (GitHub Security Advisories, PyPI, Go, RustSec, npm, Maven, OSS-Fuzz and more), for the vulnerabilities affecting a package given its ecosystem and name, optionally narrowed with version := 'x.y.z' to the advisories that affect exactly that version. Each row carries the OSV id, summary, details, aliases, the CVE ids among them, a CVSS vector, the source database severity, timestamps, and that package's affected version ranges and fixed versions. Paged via next_page_token and bounded to 1000 rows. OSV data is CC-BY-4.0.

functions.name: epss
functions.comment: Score CVEs with FIRST EPSS (probability of exploitation in the next 30 days)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Score a list of CVE identifiers with FIRST's Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS): the modeled probability (0-1) that each CVE is exploited in the wild within the next 30 days, plus its percentile rank among all scored CVEs. Pass a `VARCHAR[]` list literal; table-function arguments cannot be subqueries, so to score a dynamic set first store the list in a DuckDB variable and pass it with getvariable(). Ids are deduplicated (case-insensitively) and batched into as few API calls as the API's 2000-character cve parameter allows. Optional date := 'YYYY-MM-DD' returns historical scores. CVEs without an EPSS score are omitted. Data from FIRST (first.org/epss).
tags.vgi.doc_md: EPSS exploitation probability and percentile for a list of CVEs, e.g. `epss(['CVE-2021-44228'])`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Get today's EPSS exploitation probability and percentile for Log4Shell and Spring4Shell.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT cve_id, epss, percentile, date FROM cve.main.epss(['CVE-2021-44228', 'CVE-2022-22965']) ORDER BY epss DESC;

vgi.example_queries.description: Look up Log4Shell's historical EPSS score as published on 2023-03-01.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT cve_id, epss, percentile FROM cve.main.epss(['CVE-2021-44228'], date := '2023-03-01');

vgi.example_queries.description: Prioritize the CVEs affecting Apache Log4j 2.14.1: flag CISA known-exploited ones, attach EPSS exploitation probability, and rank exploited-first, then by EPSS and CVSS.
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH n AS (SELECT cve_id, cvss_score, cvss_severity FROM cve.main.cpe_cves('cpe:2.3:a:apache:log4j:2.14.1:*:*:*:*:*:*:*')) SELECT n.cve_id, n.cvss_score, n.cvss_severity, k.cve_id IS NOT NULL AS in_kev, k.known_ransomware_campaign_use, e.epss, e.percentile FROM n LEFT JOIN cve.main.kev() k ON k.cve_id = n.cve_id LEFT JOIN cve.main.epss(['CVE-2021-44228', 'CVE-2021-45046', 'CVE-2021-45105', 'CVE-2021-44832']) e ON e.cve_id = n.cve_id ORDER BY in_kev DESC, e.epss DESC NULLS LAST, n.cvss_score DESC NULLS LAST, n.cve_id;
