workers.title: DataHub Metadata Catalog
workers.tagline: DataHub datasets, schemas, lineage, owners, glossary and assertions as SQL in DuckDB (Python)
workers.subtitle: Datasets, columns, owners, glossary, lineage, assertions and usage from DataHub as SQL.
workers.summary: DataHub (open-source and DataHub Cloud) metadata catalog as SQL: datasets, columns, owners, tags, glossary, domains, lineage, assertions, profiles and usage, read through the DataHub GraphQL API.
workers.doc_md:
# DataHub metadata catalog

Read a [DataHub](https://datahub.com) metadata graph from DuckDB: datasets and their columns, dashboards, charts and pipelines; owners, tags, glossary terms, domains and data products; dataset- and column-level lineage; assertions with their pass/fail history; profiles, operations, usage and incidents.

It works with open-source DataHub and DataHub Cloud through the GraphQL API, authenticated with a personal access token kept in a `datahub` DuckDB secret (GMS_URL plus TOKEN).

Columns shared with the other data-catalog workers (`catalog_tool`, `id`, `platform`, `qualified_name`, `description`, `created_at`, `updated_at`, `url`) let you UNION catalogs and join them to lineage and BI workers on `qualified_name`.

example_queries.description: Snowflake datasets per schema (platform pushes down)
example_queries.sql: SELECT schema, count(*) AS tables FROM datahub.main.datasets WHERE platform = 'snowflake' GROUP BY schema ORDER BY tables DESC

example_queries.description: Datasets nobody owns
example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, domain FROM datahub.main.datasets WHERE len(owners) = 0 AND NOT deprecated ORDER BY qualified_name

example_queries.description: Columns tagged PII
example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, column_name FROM datahub.main.columns WHERE list_contains(tags, 'pii') ORDER BY qualified_name, column_name

example_queries.description: One dataset's schema (dataset_id pushes down)
example_queries.sql: SELECT column_name, native_data_type, nullable FROM datahub.main.columns WHERE dataset_id = 'urn:li:dataset:(urn:li:dataPlatform:snowflake,analytics.marts.fct_orders,PROD)' ORDER BY ordinal_position

example_queries.description: Datasets per schema container
example_queries.sql: SELECT c.qualified_name, count(d.id) AS datasets FROM datahub.main.containers c LEFT JOIN datahub.main.datasets d ON d.container_id = c.id WHERE c.subtype = 'Schema' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY datasets DESC

example_queries.description: Dashboards per BI tool and how many lack an owner
example_queries.sql: SELECT platform, count(*) AS dashboards, count(*) FILTER (WHERE len(owners) = 0) AS unowned FROM datahub.main.dashboards GROUP BY platform ORDER BY dashboards DESC

example_queries.description: The datasets each chart reads
example_queries.sql: SELECT c.name, e.upstream_qualified_name FROM datahub.main.charts c JOIN datahub.main.lineage_edges e ON e.downstream_id = c.id WHERE e.level = 'dataset' ORDER BY c.name

example_queries.description: Tasks per pipeline
example_queries.sql: SELECT f.name, count(j.id) AS tasks FROM datahub.main.data_flows f LEFT JOIN datahub.main.data_jobs j ON j.flow_id = f.id GROUP BY f.name ORDER BY tasks DESC

example_queries.description: Which datasets each Airflow task writes
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, unnest(output_dataset_ids) AS writes FROM datahub.main.data_jobs WHERE platform = 'airflow' ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Datasets owned per person or group
example_queries.sql: SELECT owner_name, count(*) AS datasets FROM datahub.main.owners WHERE entity_type = 'dataset' GROUP BY owner_name ORDER BY datasets DESC

example_queries.description: How many columns carry each tag
example_queries.sql: SELECT t.name, count(c.column_name) AS tagged_columns FROM datahub.main.tags t LEFT JOIN datahub.main.columns c ON list_contains(c.tags, t.name) GROUP BY t.name ORDER BY tagged_columns DESC

example_queries.description: Terms per top-level glossary node
example_queries.sql: SELECT parent_path[1] AS top_node, count(*) AS terms FROM datahub.main.glossary_terms GROUP BY top_node ORDER BY terms DESC

example_queries.description: Terms directly under each glossary node
example_queries.sql: SELECT n.name, count(t.id) AS terms FROM datahub.main.glossary_nodes n LEFT JOIN datahub.main.glossary_terms t ON t.parent_node_id = n.id GROUP BY n.name ORDER BY n.name

example_queries.description: Domains by asset count
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, asset_count FROM datahub.main.domains ORDER BY asset_count DESC

example_queries.description: Data products and assets per domain
example_queries.sql: SELECT domain, count(*) AS products, sum(asset_count) AS assets FROM datahub.main.data_products GROUP BY domain ORDER BY products DESC

example_queries.description: Assets owned per user
example_queries.sql: SELECT u.display_name, count(o.entity_id) AS owned FROM datahub.main.users u LEFT JOIN datahub.main.owners o ON o.owner_id = u.id GROUP BY u.display_name ORDER BY owned DESC

example_queries.description: Assets owned per team
example_queries.sql: SELECT g.name, count(o.entity_id) AS owned FROM datahub.main.groups g LEFT JOIN datahub.main.owners o ON o.owner_id = g.id GROUP BY g.name ORDER BY owned DESC

example_queries.description: Where each column of one table comes from (downstream_id pushes down)
example_queries.sql: SELECT upstream_qualified_name, upstream_column, downstream_column FROM datahub.main.lineage_edges WHERE level = 'column' AND downstream_id = 'urn:li:dataset:(urn:li:dataPlatform:snowflake,analytics.marts.fct_orders,PROD)' ORDER BY downstream_column

example_queries.description: Lineage edges by downstream entity type
example_queries.sql: SELECT downstream_type, count(*) AS edges FROM datahub.main.lineage_edges WHERE level = 'dataset' GROUP BY downstream_type ORDER BY edges DESC

example_queries.description: Assertions whose latest run failed
example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, assertion_type, description, last_run_at FROM datahub.main.assertions WHERE last_status = 'failed' ORDER BY last_run_at DESC

example_queries.description: Failure counts per dataset since a date (run_at pushes down)
example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed') AS failures, count(*) AS runs FROM datahub.main.assertion_results WHERE run_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00' GROUP BY qualified_name ORDER BY failures DESC

example_queries.description: Latest row count per dataset
example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, max_by(row_count, profiled_at) AS latest_rows FROM datahub.main.dataset_profiles GROUP BY qualified_name ORDER BY latest_rows DESC

example_queries.description: Last write per dataset (stalest first)
example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, max(operation_at) AS last_write FROM datahub.main.operations GROUP BY qualified_name ORDER BY last_write

example_queries.description: The ten most-queried datasets this month
example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, query_count, unique_user_count FROM datahub.main.usage WHERE time_range = 'MONTH' ORDER BY query_count DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Open incidents, newest first (state pushes down)
example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, title, priority, created_at FROM datahub.main.incidents WHERE state = 'ACTIVE' ORDER BY created_at DESC

example_queries.description: Datasets and dashboards about orders
example_queries.sql: SELECT entity_type, name, qualified_name FROM datahub.main.search('orders') WHERE entity_type IN ('dataset', 'dashboard') ORDER BY entity_type, name

example_queries.description: Snowflake datasets tagged PII (tag, type and platform all push down)
example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name FROM datahub.main.search('*', tag := 'pii') WHERE entity_type = 'dataset' AND platform = 'snowflake' ORDER BY qualified_name

example_queries.description: Every dataset a table depends on, nearest first
example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, degree FROM datahub.main.lineage('urn:li:dataset:(urn:li:dataPlatform:snowflake,analytics.marts.fct_orders,PROD)') WHERE entity_type = 'dataset' ORDER BY degree, qualified_name

example_queries.description: Charts and dashboards affected by a change to a raw table
example_queries.sql: SELECT entity_type, name FROM datahub.main.lineage('urn:li:dataset:(urn:li:dataPlatform:snowflake,analytics.raw.orders,PROD)', direction := 'downstream', max_hops := 5) WHERE entity_type IN ('chart', 'dashboard') ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Most-consumed upstream datasets by qualified name
example_queries.sql: SELECT datahub.main.dataset_qualified_name(upstream_id) AS source, count(*) AS consumers FROM datahub.main.lineage_edges WHERE level = 'dataset' AND upstream_type = 'dataset' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY consumers DESC

example_queries.description: Lineage edges per upstream platform
example_queries.sql: SELECT datahub.main.parse_dataset_urn(upstream_id).platform AS platform, count(*) AS edges FROM datahub.main.lineage_edges WHERE upstream_type = 'dataset' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY edges DESC

example_queries.description: A table's columns, looked up by platform and name
example_queries.sql: SELECT column_name, native_data_type FROM datahub.main.columns WHERE dataset_id = datahub.main.dataset_urn('snowflake', 'analytics.marts.fct_orders') ORDER BY ordinal_position

example_queries.description: Look up a DEV table by platform and name
example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, environment FROM datahub.main.datasets WHERE id = datahub.main.dataset_urn('bigquery', 'proj.ds.events', 'dev')

example_queries.description: The URN of a BigQuery table in DEV
example_queries.sql: SELECT datahub.main.dataset_urn('bigquery', 'proj.ds.events', 'dev') AS urn;

example_queries.description: The join key of a Snowflake table URN and of a Kafka topic URN
example_queries.sql: SELECT datahub.main.dataset_qualified_name('urn:li:dataset:(urn:li:dataPlatform:snowflake,ANALYTICS.Marts.FCT_ORDERS,PROD)') AS snowflake_table, datahub.main.dataset_qualified_name('urn:li:dataset:(urn:li:dataPlatform:kafka,Orders.Events,PROD)') AS kafka_topic;

example_queries.description: Platform, environment and schema of a Snowflake table URN
example_queries.sql: SELECT p.platform, p.environment, p.schema FROM (SELECT datahub.main.parse_dataset_urn('urn:li:dataset:(urn:li:dataPlatform:snowflake,ANALYTICS.Marts.FCT_ORDERS,PROD)') AS p);

tags.vgi.doc_llm: DataHub entities as tables plus traversal and search functions. Entity tables have one row per entity with `id` = its URN; child tables hang off a dataset (`dataset_id`) or any entity (`entity_id`). Lineage is available both as direct edges (dataset and column level) and as a multi-hop traversal function. Filtering a child table on `dataset_id = '<urn>'` (or IN) fetches just those datasets instead of scrolling the whole catalog; platform, environment, domain and container equality filters become DataHub search filters; time ranges on run, profile and operation timestamps become DataHub time windows. Offline scalars build and parse dataset URNs and derive the qualified_name join key without calling DataHub.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

DataHub entities as tables: assets, governance metadata, lineage, quality and usage.

Entity tables are keyed by URN (`id`); child tables reference their dataset through `dataset_id`. Filter on ids, platform, domain or environment and the filter runs inside DataHub's search.

Use the traversal function for multi-hop impact analysis and the search function for keyword discovery across entity types.

vgi.example_queries.description: Snowflake datasets per schema (platform pushes down)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT schema, count(*) AS tables FROM datahub.main.datasets WHERE platform = 'snowflake' GROUP BY schema ORDER BY tables DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Datasets nobody owns
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, domain FROM datahub.main.datasets WHERE len(owners) = 0 AND NOT deprecated ORDER BY qualified_name

vgi.example_queries.description: Columns tagged PII
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, column_name FROM datahub.main.columns WHERE list_contains(tags, 'pii') ORDER BY qualified_name, column_name

vgi.example_queries.description: One dataset's schema (dataset_id pushes down)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT column_name, native_data_type, nullable FROM datahub.main.columns WHERE dataset_id = 'urn:li:dataset:(urn:li:dataPlatform:snowflake,analytics.marts.fct_orders,PROD)' ORDER BY ordinal_position

vgi.example_queries.description: Datasets per schema container
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT c.qualified_name, count(d.id) AS datasets FROM datahub.main.containers c LEFT JOIN datahub.main.datasets d ON d.container_id = c.id WHERE c.subtype = 'Schema' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY datasets DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Dashboards per BI tool and how many lack an owner
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT platform, count(*) AS dashboards, count(*) FILTER (WHERE len(owners) = 0) AS unowned FROM datahub.main.dashboards GROUP BY platform ORDER BY dashboards DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: The datasets each chart reads
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT c.name, e.upstream_qualified_name FROM datahub.main.charts c JOIN datahub.main.lineage_edges e ON e.downstream_id = c.id WHERE e.level = 'dataset' ORDER BY c.name

vgi.example_queries.description: Tasks per pipeline
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT f.name, count(j.id) AS tasks FROM datahub.main.data_flows f LEFT JOIN datahub.main.data_jobs j ON j.flow_id = f.id GROUP BY f.name ORDER BY tasks DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Which datasets each Airflow task writes
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, unnest(output_dataset_ids) AS writes FROM datahub.main.data_jobs WHERE platform = 'airflow' ORDER BY name

vgi.example_queries.description: Datasets owned per person or group
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT owner_name, count(*) AS datasets FROM datahub.main.owners WHERE entity_type = 'dataset' GROUP BY owner_name ORDER BY datasets DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: How many columns carry each tag
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT t.name, count(c.column_name) AS tagged_columns FROM datahub.main.tags t LEFT JOIN datahub.main.columns c ON list_contains(c.tags, t.name) GROUP BY t.name ORDER BY tagged_columns DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Terms per top-level glossary node
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT parent_path[1] AS top_node, count(*) AS terms FROM datahub.main.glossary_terms GROUP BY top_node ORDER BY terms DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Terms directly under each glossary node
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT n.name, count(t.id) AS terms FROM datahub.main.glossary_nodes n LEFT JOIN datahub.main.glossary_terms t ON t.parent_node_id = n.id GROUP BY n.name ORDER BY n.name

vgi.example_queries.description: Domains by asset count
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, asset_count FROM datahub.main.domains ORDER BY asset_count DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Data products and assets per domain
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT domain, count(*) AS products, sum(asset_count) AS assets FROM datahub.main.data_products GROUP BY domain ORDER BY products DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Assets owned per user
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT u.display_name, count(o.entity_id) AS owned FROM datahub.main.users u LEFT JOIN datahub.main.owners o ON o.owner_id = u.id GROUP BY u.display_name ORDER BY owned DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Assets owned per team
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT g.name, count(o.entity_id) AS owned FROM datahub.main.groups g LEFT JOIN datahub.main.owners o ON o.owner_id = g.id GROUP BY g.name ORDER BY owned DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Where each column of one table comes from (downstream_id pushes down)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT upstream_qualified_name, upstream_column, downstream_column FROM datahub.main.lineage_edges WHERE level = 'column' AND downstream_id = 'urn:li:dataset:(urn:li:dataPlatform:snowflake,analytics.marts.fct_orders,PROD)' ORDER BY downstream_column

vgi.example_queries.description: Lineage edges by downstream entity type
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT downstream_type, count(*) AS edges FROM datahub.main.lineage_edges WHERE level = 'dataset' GROUP BY downstream_type ORDER BY edges DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Assertions whose latest run failed
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, assertion_type, description, last_run_at FROM datahub.main.assertions WHERE last_status = 'failed' ORDER BY last_run_at DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Failure counts per dataset since a date (run_at pushes down)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed') AS failures, count(*) AS runs FROM datahub.main.assertion_results WHERE run_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00' GROUP BY qualified_name ORDER BY failures DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Latest row count per dataset
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, max_by(row_count, profiled_at) AS latest_rows FROM datahub.main.dataset_profiles GROUP BY qualified_name ORDER BY latest_rows DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Last write per dataset (stalest first)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, max(operation_at) AS last_write FROM datahub.main.operations GROUP BY qualified_name ORDER BY last_write

vgi.example_queries.description: The ten most-queried datasets this month
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, query_count, unique_user_count FROM datahub.main.usage WHERE time_range = 'MONTH' ORDER BY query_count DESC LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: Open incidents, newest first (state pushes down)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, title, priority, created_at FROM datahub.main.incidents WHERE state = 'ACTIVE' ORDER BY created_at DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Datasets and dashboards about orders
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT entity_type, name, qualified_name FROM datahub.main.search('orders') WHERE entity_type IN ('dataset', 'dashboard') ORDER BY entity_type, name

vgi.example_queries.description: Snowflake datasets tagged PII (tag, type and platform all push down)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name FROM datahub.main.search('*', tag := 'pii') WHERE entity_type = 'dataset' AND platform = 'snowflake' ORDER BY qualified_name

vgi.example_queries.description: Every dataset a table depends on, nearest first
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, degree FROM datahub.main.lineage('urn:li:dataset:(urn:li:dataPlatform:snowflake,analytics.marts.fct_orders,PROD)') WHERE entity_type = 'dataset' ORDER BY degree, qualified_name

vgi.example_queries.description: Charts and dashboards affected by a change to a raw table
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT entity_type, name FROM datahub.main.lineage('urn:li:dataset:(urn:li:dataPlatform:snowflake,analytics.raw.orders,PROD)', direction := 'downstream', max_hops := 5) WHERE entity_type IN ('chart', 'dashboard') ORDER BY name

vgi.example_queries.description: Most-consumed upstream datasets by qualified name
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT datahub.main.dataset_qualified_name(upstream_id) AS source, count(*) AS consumers FROM datahub.main.lineage_edges WHERE level = 'dataset' AND upstream_type = 'dataset' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY consumers DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Lineage edges per upstream platform
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT datahub.main.parse_dataset_urn(upstream_id).platform AS platform, count(*) AS edges FROM datahub.main.lineage_edges WHERE upstream_type = 'dataset' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY edges DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: A table's columns, looked up by platform and name
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT column_name, native_data_type FROM datahub.main.columns WHERE dataset_id = datahub.main.dataset_urn('snowflake', 'analytics.marts.fct_orders') ORDER BY ordinal_position

vgi.example_queries.description: Look up a DEV table by platform and name
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, environment FROM datahub.main.datasets WHERE id = datahub.main.dataset_urn('bigquery', 'proj.ds.events', 'dev')

tables.name: lineage_edges
tables.comment: Every lineage edge, upstream to downstream, at dataset and column level

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per direct lineage edge. level = 'dataset': entity-to-entity edges into datasets, data jobs (tasks), charts and dashboards (upstream_id -> downstream_id, with relationship and created_at). level = 'column': DataHub fine-grained lineage (upstream_column -> downstream_column with transformation and query_id). Both ends carry type, platform, name and qualified_name (datasets), so join on qualified_name to other workers. Pushdown: downstream_id = / IN (fetches those entities' upstreams only), downstream_type, downstream_platform. For multi-hop traversal use lineage(id, direction, max_hops).

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT downstream_type, count(*) AS edges FROM datahub.main.lineage_edges WHERE level = 'dataset' GROUP BY downstream_type ORDER BY edges DESC

workers.title: dbt Artifacts
workers.tagline: dbt artifacts (manifest, run_results, catalog) and dbt Cloud runs as SQL in DuckDB (Go)
workers.subtitle: Stream dbt manifest, run results, catalog and freshness artifacts, and dbt Cloud runs, into stable SQL tables.
workers.summary: Query dbt artifacts (manifest, run results, catalog, source freshness) and dbt Cloud runs, jobs and Discovery metadata as SQL tables.
workers.doc_md:
# dbt

**dbt artifacts and dbt Cloud as SQL.** DuckDB's `read_json` turns a `manifest.json` into one row holding a project-specific `STRUCT` with one field per node, which is slow to infer, different for every project, and fully materialized before the first row. This worker streams the same file into flat tables whose columns do not change between projects or dbt releases (manifest schema v7 to v12), and skips unselected compiled SQL without decoding it, so the first rows of a 300 MB manifest arrive in well under a second.

The `main` schema reads artifact files you already have (local paths and globs, https URLs, the bundled `sample://` jaffle_shop artifacts, or a dbt Cloud run's artifacts) and needs no credentials. Run artifact triage first on an unfamiliar file: an unknown schema version becomes a row, not a crash. The `cloud` schema reads the dbt Cloud Admin and Discovery APIs with a `dbt_cloud` secret, and the `unified` schema exposes runs and task runs in the shape every orchestrator worker shares, so dbt runs union with Airflow, Dagster or Prefect runs.

See dbt's [artifact reference](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/artifacts/dbt-artifacts) and the [dbt Cloud API docs](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/dbt-cloud-apis/overview).

example_queries.description: Find your account id
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, name, plan FROM dbt.cloud.accounts ORDER BY id

example_queries.description: Active projects
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, name FROM dbt.cloud.projects WHERE state = 1 ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Deployment environments
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, name, deployment_type FROM dbt.cloud.environments WHERE type = 'deployment' ORDER BY id

example_queries.description: Scheduled jobs and their cron
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, name, schedule_cron FROM dbt.cloud.jobs WHERE schedule_enabled ORDER BY id

example_queries.description: Failure counts per job since a date
example_queries.sql: SELECT job_name, count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'Error') AS failed, count(*) AS runs FROM dbt.cloud.runs() WHERE created_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01' GROUP BY job_name ORDER BY failed DESC

example_queries.description: Recent successful runs of one job
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, status, duration_seconds FROM dbt.cloud.runs() WHERE job_id = 42 AND status = 'Success' ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Steps of a run
example_queries.sql: SELECT step_index, name, status FROM dbt.cloud.run_steps(70403103) ORDER BY step_index

example_queries.description: Top-level JSON artifacts of a run
example_queries.sql: SELECT path, artifact_url FROM dbt.cloud.run_artifacts(70403103) WHERE path LIKE '%.json' AND path NOT LIKE '%/%' ORDER BY path

example_queries.description: Models whose last execution failed
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, last_run_status, execution_time FROM dbt.cloud.models(environment_id := 218762) WHERE last_run_status = 'error' ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Test results in production by status
example_queries.sql: SELECT last_run_status, count(*) AS tests FROM dbt.cloud.tests(environment_id := 218762) GROUP BY last_run_status ORDER BY last_run_status

example_queries.description: Stale sources in production
example_queries.sql: SELECT unique_id, freshness_status, round(age_seconds / 3600) AS hours_old FROM dbt.cloud.sources(environment_id := 218762) WHERE freshness_status <> 'pass' ORDER BY unique_id

example_queries.description: Triage every artifact in a target directory
example_queries.sql: SELECT artifact_type, schema_version, dbt_version, support_status FROM dbt.main.artifact_info('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/*.json') ORDER BY artifact_type

example_queries.description: Manifest versions across several dbt releases
example_queries.sql: SELECT schema_version, dbt_version, node_count FROM dbt.main.artifact_info('sample://jaffle_shop/*/manifest.json') ORDER BY dbt_version

example_queries.description: Schema version of a manifest
example_queries.sql: SELECT dbt.main.manifest_version('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') AS version

example_queries.description: Models tagged marts
example_queries.sql: SELECT name FROM dbt.main.nodes('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') WHERE dbt.main.selector_match(unique_id, fqn, tags, materialized, 'tag:marts,resource_type:model') ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: See which atom of a selector is unsupported
example_queries.sql: SELECT term, kind, supported, reason FROM dbt.main.parse_selector('tag:finance,+fct_orders') ORDER BY term

example_queries.description: Model version from a unique_id
example_queries.sql: SELECT dbt.main.parse_unique_id('model.jaffle_shop.orders.v2').version AS version

example_queries.description: Canonical relation keys for every model
example_queries.sql: SELECT dbt.main.normalize_relation(db_name, db_schema, alias, NULL) AS relation FROM dbt.main.nodes('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') WHERE resource_type = 'model' ORDER BY relation

example_queries.description: Models downstream of stg_orders
example_queries.sql: SELECT unique_id, depth FROM dbt.main.descendants('model.jaffle_shop.stg_orders', manifest := 'sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') WHERE unique_id LIKE 'model.%' ORDER BY depth, unique_id

example_queries.description: Sources a model ultimately reads
example_queries.sql: SELECT unique_id, depth FROM dbt.main.ancestors('model.jaffle_shop.customers', manifest := 'sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') WHERE unique_id LIKE 'source.%' ORDER BY unique_id

example_queries.description: Supported manifest versions and the dbt releases that write them
example_queries.sql: SELECT schema_version, dbt_version_range FROM dbt.main.schema_versions WHERE artifact_type = 'manifest' AND supported ORDER BY schema_version

example_queries.description: Check an artifact against the support matrix
example_queries.sql: SELECT i.dbt_version, v.support_status FROM dbt.main.artifact_info('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') i JOIN dbt.main.schema_versions v USING (artifact_type, schema_version)

example_queries.description: Count models by materialization
example_queries.sql: SELECT materialized, count(*) AS models FROM dbt.main.nodes('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') WHERE resource_type = 'model' GROUP BY materialized ORDER BY materialized

example_queries.description: Models with no description, in a dbt 1.3 (v7) manifest
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, description FROM dbt.main.nodes('sample://jaffle_shop/v7/manifest.json') WHERE resource_type = 'model' AND description = '' ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Documented columns per node
example_queries.sql: SELECT unique_id, count(*) AS documented FROM dbt.main.node_columns('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') WHERE description <> '' GROUP BY unique_id ORDER BY unique_id

example_queries.description: Most depended-upon resources
example_queries.sql: SELECT depends_on_id, count(*) AS dependents FROM dbt.main.depends_on('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') GROUP BY depends_on_id ORDER BY dependents DESC, depends_on_id LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Macros used by each model
example_queries.sql: SELECT unique_id, depends_on_id FROM dbt.main.depends_on('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json', kind := 'macros') WHERE unique_id LIKE 'model.%' ORDER BY ALL

example_queries.description: Sources with freshness checks configured
example_queries.sql: SELECT unique_id, loaded_at_field FROM dbt.main.sources('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') WHERE freshness IS NOT NULL ORDER BY unique_id

example_queries.description: Which models feed each exposure
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, unnest(depends_on_ids) AS feeds_from FROM dbt.main.exposures('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') ORDER BY ALL

example_queries.description: List metrics and their type
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, metric_type, expression FROM dbt.main.metrics('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Semantic models and how many measures each defines
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, model_ref, json_array_length(measures) AS measures FROM dbt.main.semantic_models('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Groups and their owners

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Schema cloud reads a dbt Cloud account through its Admin API (v2 and v3) and its Discovery (metadata GraphQL) API, authenticated by a dbt_cloud secret holding TOKEN and ACCOUNT_ID, with BASE_URL for EMEA, APAC, cell-based or single-tenant hosts, an optional DISCOVERY_URL, and an optional default ENVIRONMENT_ID. The account's structure (projects, environments, job definitions) is exposed as tables; run history is a function whose job, environment, project, status and created_at filters become API query parameters and which takes an incremental cursor; per-run steps and saved artifact files are functions of a run id, and every saved artifact can be passed to the main schema's artifact functions as dbt-cloud://runs/<id>/<file>.json. Discovery functions return the applied state of an environment with the latest execution and freshness of each resource.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## cloud

Read-only dbt Cloud access with a `dbt_cloud` DuckDB secret (`TOKEN`, `ACCOUNT_ID`, and `BASE_URL` for non-US or single-tenant accounts).

Account structure is plain tables; run history filters on job, environment, project, status and creation date are sent to the Admin API, and an incremental cursor returns only runs newer than one you already have. A run's saved artifacts open directly in the `main` tables through `dbt-cloud://runs/<id>/manifest.json`.

The Discovery functions answer "what is the state of production": the latest status of every model and test, and the freshness of every source, for one environment.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Schema main reads dbt artifact files. Every table function takes the artifact path first (a local path or glob, an https:// URL, or dbt-cloud://runs/<run_id>/<file>.json), so two manifests (main and a pull request) can be compared in one query. Tables cover manifest.json (nodes, declared columns, dependency edges to nodes or macros, sources, exposures, the semantic layer, groups), run_results.json (node results and phase timings), catalog.json (warehouse-observed columns) and sources.json (freshness), normalized across manifest schema v7 to v12: fields a version lacks are NULL and adapter blobs such as config and meta stay JSON. Start with artifact triage on an unfamiliar file. Descendant/ancestor walks take a unique_id and the manifest path and run per row (LATERAL). Selector matching supports tag:, path:, fqn:, package:, resource_type:, config.materialized: and names; graph operators are errors. Scalar helpers split unique_ids, normalize relation names and read a manifest's schema version, and the supported artifact versions are themselves a table.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

Tables over dbt's four artifact files, normalized across manifest schema v7 to v12. Every function takes the artifact path as its first argument, so two manifests (main and a pull request) can be compared in one query; bind each file once as a view and join the views.

Fields a version lacks are `NULL`, adapter-specific blobs such as `config` and `meta` stay `JSON`, and the support matrix is itself a table. Graph closure is a per-row (LATERAL) walk, and node selection supports a strict, enumerated subset of dbt's selector grammar: unsupported terms are errors, never a silent false.

vgi.example_queries.description: Triage every artifact in a target directory
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT artifact_type, schema_version, dbt_version, support_status FROM dbt.main.artifact_info('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/*.json') ORDER BY artifact_type

vgi.example_queries.description: Manifest versions across several dbt releases
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT schema_version, dbt_version, node_count FROM dbt.main.artifact_info('sample://jaffle_shop/*/manifest.json') ORDER BY dbt_version

vgi.example_queries.description: Schema version of a manifest
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT dbt.main.manifest_version('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') AS version

vgi.example_queries.description: Models tagged marts
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name FROM dbt.main.nodes('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') WHERE dbt.main.selector_match(unique_id, fqn, tags, materialized, 'tag:marts,resource_type:model') ORDER BY name

vgi.example_queries.description: See which atom of a selector is unsupported
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT term, kind, supported, reason FROM dbt.main.parse_selector('tag:finance,+fct_orders') ORDER BY term

vgi.example_queries.description: Model version from a unique_id
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT dbt.main.parse_unique_id('model.jaffle_shop.orders.v2').version AS version

vgi.example_queries.description: Canonical relation keys for every model
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT dbt.main.normalize_relation(db_name, db_schema, alias, NULL) AS relation FROM dbt.main.nodes('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') WHERE resource_type = 'model' ORDER BY relation

vgi.example_queries.description: Models downstream of stg_orders
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT unique_id, depth FROM dbt.main.descendants('model.jaffle_shop.stg_orders', manifest := 'sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') WHERE unique_id LIKE 'model.%' ORDER BY depth, unique_id

vgi.example_queries.description: Sources a model ultimately reads
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT unique_id, depth FROM dbt.main.ancestors('model.jaffle_shop.customers', manifest := 'sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') WHERE unique_id LIKE 'source.%' ORDER BY unique_id

vgi.example_queries.description: Supported manifest versions and the dbt releases that write them
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT schema_version, dbt_version_range FROM dbt.main.schema_versions WHERE artifact_type = 'manifest' AND supported ORDER BY schema_version

vgi.example_queries.description: Check an artifact against the support matrix
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT i.dbt_version, v.support_status FROM dbt.main.artifact_info('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') i JOIN dbt.main.schema_versions v USING (artifact_type, schema_version)

vgi.example_queries.description: Count models by materialization
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT materialized, count(*) AS models FROM dbt.main.nodes('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') WHERE resource_type = 'model' GROUP BY materialized ORDER BY materialized

vgi.example_queries.description: Models with no description, in a dbt 1.3 (v7) manifest
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, description FROM dbt.main.nodes('sample://jaffle_shop/v7/manifest.json') WHERE resource_type = 'model' AND description = '' ORDER BY name

vgi.example_queries.description: Documented columns per node
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT unique_id, count(*) AS documented FROM dbt.main.node_columns('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') WHERE description <> '' GROUP BY unique_id ORDER BY unique_id

vgi.example_queries.description: Most depended-upon resources
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT depends_on_id, count(*) AS dependents FROM dbt.main.depends_on('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') GROUP BY depends_on_id ORDER BY dependents DESC, depends_on_id LIMIT 5

vgi.example_queries.description: Macros used by each model
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT unique_id, depends_on_id FROM dbt.main.depends_on('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json', kind := 'macros') WHERE unique_id LIKE 'model.%' ORDER BY ALL

vgi.example_queries.description: Sources with freshness checks configured
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT unique_id, loaded_at_field FROM dbt.main.sources('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') WHERE freshness IS NOT NULL ORDER BY unique_id

vgi.example_queries.description: Which models feed each exposure
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, unnest(depends_on_ids) AS feeds_from FROM dbt.main.exposures('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') ORDER BY ALL

vgi.example_queries.description: List metrics and their type
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, metric_type, expression FROM dbt.main.metrics('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') ORDER BY name

vgi.example_queries.description: Semantic models and how many measures each defines
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, model_ref, json_array_length(measures) AS measures FROM dbt.main.semantic_models('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') ORDER BY name

vgi.example_queries.description: Groups and their owners
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, owner_email FROM dbt.main.groups('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') ORDER BY name

vgi.example_queries.description: Macros defined by the project itself
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, path FROM dbt.main.macros('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') WHERE package_name = 'jaffle_shop' ORDER BY name

vgi.example_queries.description: Results of a run by status
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT status, count(*) AS nodes FROM dbt.main.run_results('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/run_results.json') GROUP BY status ORDER BY status

vgi.example_queries.description: Slowest model executions across an archive of runs
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT unique_id, round(execution_time, 3) AS seconds FROM dbt.main.run_results('sample://jaffle_shop/*/run_results.json') WHERE unique_id LIKE 'model.%' ORDER BY execution_time DESC LIMIT 5

vgi.example_queries.description: Count compile and execute phases in a run
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, count(*) AS phases FROM dbt.main.run_timings('sample://jaffle_shop/v12/run_results.json') GROUP BY name ORDER BY name

functions.name: nodes
functions.comment: Every node (model, test, seed, snapshot, analysis) in a dbt manifest.json, one row per node

tags.vgi.doc_llm: nodes(manifest) streams manifest.json's `nodes` map as one row per node with stable columns across manifest schema versions v7-v12: unique_id, resource_type, package_name, name, relation_name, db_name, db_schema, alias, materialized, tags, meta/config (JSON), raw_code, compiled_code, fqn, checksum, description, group_name, access, contract_enforced and more. tags.vgi.doc_md:
## nodes(manifest)

One row per entry of `manifest.json`'s `nodes` map, with the same columns for every manifest version. Bind the file once as a view and join the view; unselected `raw_code` and `compiled_code` are never decoded.

functions.name: descendants
functions.comment: Every node downstream of a unique_id in a manifest's DAG (the + suffix operator), per input row

tags.vgi.doc_llm: descendants(unique_id, manifest := ..., max_depth := 64, include_self := false) walks the manifest's child map from each input unique_id and returns root_id, unique_id, depth and the shortest path. It is a blended function: call it with a literal or LATERAL over a column of ids (FROM changed c, dbt.main.descendants(c.id, manifest := 'target/manifest.json')). It is the replacement for dbt's 'model+' / 'n+' selectors.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## descendants(unique_id, manifest := ..., max_depth := 64, include_self := false)

Downstream closure (blast radius).

vgi.example_queries.description: Models downstream of stg_orders
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT unique_id, depth FROM dbt.main.descendants('model.jaffle_shop.stg_orders', manifest := 'sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json') WHERE unique_id LIKE 'model.%' ORDER BY depth, unique_id

vgi.executable_examples.description: Models one hop downstream of stg_payments
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT unique_id FROM dbt.main.descendants('model.jaffle_shop.stg_payments', manifest := 'sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json', max_depth := 1) WHERE unique_id LIKE 'model.%' ORDER BY unique_id

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: root_id
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: The unique_id the walk started from (the input row).

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: unique_id
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: A node reached from root_id.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: depth
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Edges between root_id and unique_id (0 = the root itself when include_self).

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: path
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Shortest path from root_id to unique_id, both ends included.

SELECT unique_id FROM dbt.main.descendants('model.jaffle_shop.stg_payments', manifest := 'sample://jaffle_shop/v12/manifest.json', max_depth := 1) WHERE unique_id LIKE 'model.%' ORDER BY unique_id;

functions.name: selector_match
functions.comment: True when a node matches a dbt selector (an enumerated subset of dbt's grammar); unsupported terms fail at bind

tags.vgi.doc_llm: selector_match(unique_id, fqn, tags, materialized, selector) evaluates a constant dbt selector against one node per row, using the columns of dbt.main.nodes(...). Supported: tag:x, path:x, fqn:x, package:x, resource_type:x, config.materialized:x and bare names/globs; space-separated terms are a union, comma-joined atoms an intersection. Graph operators (+, n+, @), state:, result:, source_status: and --exclude raise a bind error naming the term; use descendants/ancestors, joins, or NOT selector_match(...) instead. Check a selector first with parse_selector.

## unified

The cross-orchestrator run shape: `orchestrator`, `run_id`, `pipeline`, `status`, `raw_status`, `trigger`, timing columns and a `url`.

Point it at an archive of `run_results.json` files to treat every dbt invocation as a run and every node result as a task, or leave the path out to read dbt Cloud runs; either way the rows union with the other orchestrator workers' `unified` tables.

workers.title: Disassembly & Malware Triage
workers.tagline: Disassemble and triage binaries in DuckDB with SQL — Capstone multi-arch disassembly, sections/imports/strings and heuristic ATT&CK capabilities. A VGI worker.
workers.subtitle: Disassemble binaries and shellcode, then triage their sections, imports,                  strings, and MITRE ATT&CK capabilities.
workers.summary: Disassemble PE/ELF/Mach-O binaries and shellcode into instruction rows, with section/import/string/capability triage for malware analysis.
workers.doc_md:
# Disasm — Disassembly & Malware Triage in SQL

**Disassemble PE/ELF/Mach-O binaries and raw shellcode directly in DuckDB SQL** — one instruction row per machine instruction, with section, import, string, and heuristic MITRE ATT&CK capability relations alongside. The `disasm` worker is driven by [Capstone](https://www.capstone-engine.org/) with container parsing by goblin, and is built for **fleet-scale, in-SQL triage**: disassemble and capability-tag thousands of samples and join the instruction stats and ATT&CK tags to the rest of your security tables — with no per-sample tooling and zero egress.

It pairs with `vgi-pe` (static PE/ELF/Mach-O metadata), `vgi-yara` (rule hits), and `vgi-ioc` (indicators) in a VGI security bundle. The worker is **pure static compute over the input `BLOB` — it never executes the sample**, making it safe for air-gapped / regulated malware repositories.

**How it works.** You supply a sample as inline bytes or a filesystem path; the worker sniffs the container, resolves architecture and mode, statically decodes the executable sections, and tags heuristic behaviours against MITRE ATT&CK — all as ordinary SQL relations you can filter, aggregate, and join. Nothing is ever run or emulated. See the [source repository](https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-disasm) for the full instruction/section/import/string/capability schema and licensing.

example_queries.description: Disassemble an x64 shellcode blob and project the instruction address, mnemonic, and operands.
example_queries.sql: SELECT address, mnemonic, op_str FROM disasm.main.disassemble(from_hex('554889e5c3'), arch := 'x86', mode := 'x64')

example_queries.description: Probe a blob by its magic bytes and read back just the detected container format.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (disasm.main.format(from_hex('7f454c46'))).container AS container

example_queries.description: Count the heuristic MITRE ATT&CK capability hits on a suspicious command line.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## The `disasm` worker

A static binary-analysis toolkit exposed as SQL. It turns an opaque executable — a PE, ELF, or Mach-O file, or a raw shellcode blob, supplied inline as a `BLOB` or as a filesystem path — into queryable relations.

### Key concepts

- **Static only.** Every decode is a pure parse; the sample is *never* executed or emulated.
- **Bounded & panic-free.** Malformed or hostile input yields empty or diagnostic output, never a crash.
- **Triage-oriented.** Beyond raw machine instructions you get container layout, imported symbols, printable strings, and heuristic MITRE ATT&CK capability tags.

### When to use it

Reach for this schema to disassemble shellcode or binaries, inspect a container's structure and entry point, or run first-pass malware triage entirely inside DuckDB.

functions.name: disassemble
functions.comment: Disassemble a binary or shellcode blob into one row per machine instruction (address, size, bytes, mnemonic, op_str, groups)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Disassemble the executable sections of a PE/ELF/Mach-O binary — or a raw shellcode blob — into one row per machine instruction via Capstone. Arch/mode auto-detect from the container, or pass arch (x86, arm, arm64, mips, ppc, sysz, riscv) and mode (x16, x32, x64, arm, thumb, big, little) explicitly (required for raw blobs). base seeds the address column and makes branch targets print absolute; section selects auto (every executable section), all (the whole blob as raw bytes), or a section name. Each row carries address, size, bytes, mnemonic, op_str, and a normalized groups `LIST<VARCHAR>` (call/jump/ret/int/privileged/branch_relative/fpu/sse/vm). Output is address-ordered and bounded; undecodable bytes become '.byte' rows so the sweep never stalls. The input is statically decoded, never executed.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Disassemble a binary or shellcode into instruction rows (`address`, `size`, `bytes`, `mnemonic`, `op_str`, `groups`) via [Capstone](https://www.capstone-engine.org/). Arch/mode auto-detect from a PE/ELF/Mach-O container, or pass `arch` / `mode` explicitly (required for raw shellcode). v1 uses a **linear sweep** from the start of each selected section — simple and deterministic, but it can mis-decode data interleaved in code; undecodable bytes become `.byte` rows and the sweep resumes, so it never stalls. Supported arches: x86 (16/32/64), arm, arm64, mips, ppc, sysz, riscv.

arguments.name: blob
arguments.description: The binary or shellcode to analyze: either the raw bytes supplied inline, or a filesystem path to the file to open and read. The bytes are statically decoded only — never executed.

arguments.name: arch
arguments.description: Override container detection or supply the arch for raw bytes: x86, arm, arm64, mips, ppc, sysz, or riscv. Required for a raw blob (no container to read).

arguments.name: mode
arguments.description: Decode mode: x16, x32, x64 (x86 width), arm or thumb (32-bit ARM), or big/little (endianness for the other arches).

arguments.name: base
arguments.description: Virtual/load address of the first byte (default = the section's VA, or 0 for a raw blob), so branch-relative operands print absolute targets.

arguments.name: section
arguments.description: What to sweep: 'auto' (every executable section, the default), 'all' (the whole blob as raw bytes at base), or a section name such as '.text' or '__text'.

functions.name: capabilities
functions.comment: Heuristic capability indicators mapped to MITRE ATT&CK (rule, attack_id, attack_name, severity, evidence) — not capa

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Surface lightweight, ATT&CK-tagged capability indicators for malware triage from three cheap signals: suspicious import names (e.g. VirtualAllocEx/WriteProcessMemory/CreateRemoteThread → T1055 Process Injection), interesting strings (PowerShell -enc, cmd.exe /c, autorun registry paths, VM-artifact names, ransom-note markers), and anti-analysis instruction patterns (rdtsc/cpuid timing, int3 / int 0x2d). One row per match with rule, attack_id, attack_name, severity (advisory only), and the matched evidence. This is a deliberate heuristic over curated reference tables — it is NOT a port of capa's rule engine. Input may be inline `BLOB` bytes or a `VARCHAR` path.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Lightweight, [MITRE ATT&CK](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/)-tagged capability indicators for malware triage (`rule`, `attack_id`, `attack_name`, `severity`, `evidence`), matched from three cheap signals — suspicious import names, interesting strings, and anti-analysis instruction patterns. A deliberate heuristic over curated reference tables; **not** a port of capa's rule engine.

vgi.example_queries.description: Surface ATT&CK-tagged capability indicators (rule, technique id, evidence) for a suspicious command line.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT rule, attack_id, evidence FROM disasm.main.capabilities('powershell.exe -EncodedCommand ZQA='::BLOB);

vgi.example_queries.description: Locate each string-based ATT&CK indicator in a sample: join capabilities() to strings() on the matched evidence to get the file offset of every flagged string (offsets 0, 18 and 56 here).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT c.rule, c.attack_id, c.severity, s."offset", s.value FROM disasm.main.capabilities('cmd.exe /c whoami\x00schtasks /create /tn upd /tr evil.exe\x00http://evil.example/c2'::BLOB) AS c JOIN disasm.main.strings('cmd.exe /c whoami\x00schtasks /create /tn upd /tr evil.exe\x00http://evil.example/c2'::BLOB) AS s ON s.value = c.evidence ORDER BY s."offset", c.rule;

vgi.executable_examples.description: A PowerShell -EncodedCommand string flags T1059.001.
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT attack_id FROM disasm.main.capabilities('powershell.exe -EncodedCommand ZQA='::BLOB) WHERE attack_id = 'T1059.001' LIMIT 1

functions.name: entrypoint
functions.comment: The container entry point and resolved (arch, mode): STRUCT(arch, mode, vaddr, file_off, section)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Resolve the container entry point and the (arch, mode) it implies: returns a `STRUCT(arch, mode, vaddr, file_off, section)`. vaddr is the entry virtual address, file_off its file offset, and section the section that contains it. For a Mach-O fat binary the primary (first) slice is reported. A raw blob returns NULL struct fields. Input may be inline `BLOB` bytes or a `VARCHAR` path.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Resolve a binary's entry point — `STRUCT(arch, mode, vaddr, file_off, section)`. NULL fields for a raw blob.

vgi.example_queries.description: Resolve a blob's entry point; a raw blob yields NULL fields.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT (disasm.main.entrypoint('not a binary'::BLOB)).arch AS arch;

vgi.example_queries.description: Check where a binary starts executing: join entrypoint() to sections() on the entry's section name to report that section's kind, exec flag and entropy (an entry point in a non-code or near-8-bit-entropy section suggests a packer; the fixture's entry is in __TEXT,__text, kind code).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ep.e.section, ep.e.vaddr AS entry_vaddr, s.kind, s.exec, round(s.entropy, 2) AS entropy FROM (SELECT disasm.main.entrypoint('test/sql/data/hello-macho-arm64') AS e) AS ep JOIN disasm.main.sections('test/sql/data/hello-macho-arm64') AS s ON s.name = ep.e.section ORDER BY s.vaddr;

tags.vgi.title: Resolve Entry Point

functions.comment: Probe a blob's container/arch without disassembling: STRUCT(container, arch, mode, bits, endian, entry)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Cheaply probe a blob's container and architecture WITHOUT disassembling: returns a `STRUCT(container, arch, mode, bits, endian, entry)`. container is one of pe, elf, macho, fat-macho, or raw. The fast pre-filter for 'is this even a binary I can disassemble' across a large scan. Input may be inline `BLOB` bytes or a `VARCHAR` path. A raw/unrecognized blob returns container='raw' with NULL detail fields.

workers.title: dlt Sources
workers.tagline: Run dlt sources, including the declarative REST API source, as DuckDB tables (Python)
workers.subtitle: Run dlt sources - the declarative rest_api source or any @dlt.source - as DuckDB tables.
workers.summary: Run dlt (dlthub) sources from DuckDB without a pipeline: the declarative rest_api source covers most REST APIs with a JSON config, and any @dlt.source package loads in an isolated environment.
workers.doc_md:
# dlt sources in DuckDB

Run any [dlt](https://dlthub.com) source and query its resources with SQL, without a pipeline or a destination.

Describe a REST API with dlt's declarative `rest_api` JSON config, or load any `@dlt.source` from a directory or a pip package into an isolated, cached environment. Credentials live in DuckDB secrets; items stream back as typed Arrow batches; dlt incremental cursors become arguments and filter pushdown.

Attach a source to see every resource as a table.

attach_options.name: source
attach_options.description: 'rest_api' or 'package.module:function'. Every selected resource becomes a table.

attach_options.name: config
attach_options.description: The rest_api JSON config or the source function's keyword arguments: JSON or a path.

attach_options.name: columns
attach_options.description: Column types per resource, {"resource": {"column": "TYPE"}}: JSON or a path.

attach_options.name: source_path
attach_options.description: Directory to import a module source from (the function argument `path`).

attach_options.name: pip_url
attach_options.description: pip requirement(s) installed into an isolated cached environment.

attach_options.name: python
attach_options.description: Python version for the pip_url environment, e.g. '3.12'.

attach_options.name: secret_name
attach_options.description: Name of the dlt secret to use; empty picks it by SCOPE.

attach_options.name: timeout_seconds
attach_options.description: Stop a source that produces nothing for this many seconds; 0 waits forever.

example_queries.description: List the resources a rest_api config defines
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, primary_key, incremental_cursor FROM dlt.main.resources('rest_api', config := '{"client": {"base_url": "https://pokeapi.co/api/v2/"}, "resources": ["pokemon", "berry"]}') ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: The column types a public REST endpoint's items map to
example_queries.sql: SELECT column_name, data_type FROM dlt.main.infer_columns('rest_api', resource := 'pokemon', config := '{"client": {"base_url": "https://pokeapi.co/api/v2/"}, "resources": ["pokemon"]}') ORDER BY ordinal

example_queries.description: Which resources the inferred ATTACH columns cover
example_queries.sql: SELECT json_keys(columns) AS resources FROM dlt.main.columns_json('rest_api', config := '{"client": {"base_url": "https://pokeapi.co/api/v2/"}, "resources": ["pokemon", "berry"]}')

example_queries.description: The five most-starred repositories of a GitHub organization via the rest_api source
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, stargazers_count FROM dlt.main.read_resource('rest_api', 'repos', config := '{"client": {"base_url": "https://api.github.com/"}, "resources": [{"name": "repos", "endpoint": {"path": "orgs/dlt-hub/repos"}}]}') ORDER BY stargazers_count DESC LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Count recently updated issues with a `dlt init github` verified source
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS issues FROM dlt.main.read_resource('github:github_reactions', 'issues', path := '/srv/dlt_project', config := '{"owner": "dlt-hub", "name": "dlt"}') WHERE updated_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01'

example_queries.description: Explore raw GitHub API items and pull one field out of the JSON
example_queries.sql: SELECT item->>'$.login' AS login FROM dlt.main.read_items('rest_api', 'members', config := '{"client": {"base_url": "https://api.github.com/"}, "resources": [{"name": "members", "endpoint": {"path": "orgs/dlt-hub/public_members"}}]}') ORDER BY login LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Read GitHub issues updated since a date and keep the cursor to resume from
example_queries.sql: SELECT items, last_value FROM dlt.main.final_state('rest_api', 'issues', config := '{"client": {"base_url": "https://api.github.com/repos/dlt-hub/dlt/"}, "resources": [{"name": "issues", "endpoint": {"path": "issues", "params": {"since": {"type": "incremental", "cursor_path": "updated_at", "initial_value": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z"}}}}]}')

example_queries.description: Normalize a decimal type text the way a columns override reads it
example_queries.sql: SELECT dlt.main.column_type('decimal(18,2)') AS duckdb_type

example_queries.description: See what a nested API object becomes before reading the resource
example_queries.sql: SELECT dlt.main.infer_type('{"user": {"login": "ada"}, "labels": ["bug"]}') AS duckdb_type

example_queries.description: dlt data types and a DuckDB type text
example_queries.sql: SELECT t, dlt.main.column_type(t) AS duckdb_type FROM (VALUES ('bigint'), ('text'), ('timestamp'), ('struct(login varchar)')) v(t) ORDER BY t;

example_queries.description: A nested object, a timestamp string and a list of labels
example_queries.sql: SELECT dlt.main.infer_type(v) AS duckdb_type FROM (VALUES ('{"login": "ada", "id": 1}'), ('"2026-01-01T00:00:00Z"'), ('["bug", "ui"]')) t(v) ORDER BY duckdb_type;

functions.name: read_resource
functions.comment: Run a dlt source (rest_api or any @dlt.source) and return one resource as a typed table

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Iterate one resource of a dlt source and return its items as a table (no pipeline, no destination). `source` is 'rest_api' (then `config` is the dlt rest_api JSON config: client.base_url, client.paginator, resources[].endpoint) or 'package.module:function' for any @dlt.source (then `config` is its keyword arguments; import it from `path` or install it with `pip_url` into an isolated cached env). `resource` is the resource name. Columns come from `columns` (JSON {name: type}), the resource's dlt column hints, then inference from the first `sample_rows` items: integers -> `BIGINT`, floats -> `DOUBLE`, ISO timestamps -> `TIMESTAMPTZ`, objects -> `STRUCT`, lists -> `LIST`, mixed -> `JSON`. Credentials come from a `dlt` secret (CONFIG JSON/TOML), never the query. Incremental: `initial_value`, `end_value`, `state` (from final_state); a WHERE <cursor> >= X filter becomes the incremental start (sent as the rest_api start_param).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## read_resource(source, resource, ...)

One resource of a dlt source as a typed table.

Use dlt's declarative `rest_api` source with a JSON config, or any installable `@dlt.source`. Credentials live in a `dlt` secret.

vgi.example_queries.description: The five most-starred repositories of a GitHub organization via the rest_api source
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, stargazers_count FROM dlt.main.read_resource('rest_api', 'repos', config := '{"client": {"base_url": "https://api.github.com/"}, "resources": [{"name": "repos", "endpoint": {"path": "orgs/dlt-hub/repos"}}]}') ORDER BY stargazers_count DESC LIMIT 5

vgi.example_queries.description: Count recently updated issues with a `dlt init github` verified source
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS issues FROM dlt.main.read_resource('github:github_reactions', 'issues', path := '/srv/dlt_project', config := '{"owner": "dlt-hub", "name": "dlt"}') WHERE updated_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01'

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
One column per item key, in this order: the resource's dlt column hints, then keys seen in the first `sample_rows` items. `columns := '{...}'` overrides any type. Typing rules:

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| hinted `decimal` column | DECIMAL(10,2) | a dlt column hint; `text`, `bigint`, `double`, `bool`, `timestamp`, `date`, `time`, `json`, `binary` map the same way (see column_type); primary keys are NOT NULL |
| integer key | BIGINT | whole numbers |
| number key | DOUBLE | numbers with a fraction (or mixed) |
| boolean key | BOOLEAN | true / false |
| timestamp key | TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE | ISO-8601 strings with a time; offset-less values are UTC |
| date key | DATE | ISO-8601 dates |
| text key | VARCHAR | other strings |
| object key | STRUCT(login VARCHAR, id BIGINT) | e.g. a nested user object; keys from the sample |
| array key | VARCHAR[] | e.g. a list of labels; elements typed by the same rules |
| mixed key | JSON | values of different types, or nesting deeper than 3 levels |
| Arrow `int32` column | INTEGER | resources that yield Arrow tables keep their Arrow types |

workers.title: DOCX Mail Merge
workers.tagline: Mail-merge SQL data into DOCX (optional PDF) for DuckDB (Python, docxtpl)
workers.subtitle: Fill Word templates from query rows to produce invoices, letters and other DOCX or PDF documents.
workers.summary: Mail-merge SQL data into DOCX templates -> filled documents (DOCX/PDF) as BLOBs.
workers.doc_md:
# docgen: DOCX Mail Merge and Document Generation in SQL

**Turn DuckDB query results into finished Word documents and PDFs — generate invoices, contracts, statements, and letters straight from SQL with mail-merge templates, no application code required.**

`docgen` is a VGI worker that does the inverse of text-extraction tools such as vgi-tika and vgi-pdf: rather than pulling text and structure *out* of documents, it pushes your SQL row data *into* DOCX (Microsoft Word) templates to produce filled, ready-to-send documents. Each rendered document is returned to DuckDB as a `BLOB`, so you can write it to a file, store it in a table, or stream it onward. It is built for anyone who needs to automate document production at query time — billing and finance teams generating invoices and account statements, operations teams producing contracts and form letters, and developers building reporting or notification pipelines directly on their data warehouse.

Rendering is powered by [docxtpl](https://github.com/elapouya/python-docx-template) ([documentation](https://docxtpl.readthedocs.io/)), which layers the [Jinja2](https://jinja.palletsprojects.com/) templating engine over [python-docx](https://github.com/python-openxml/python-docx) ([documentation](https://python-docx.readthedocs.io/)). You design a normal `.docx` template in Word using `{{ field }}` placeholders and `{% for %}` loops, and every field or column from your query becomes a template variable. Multi-document output is stitched together with [docxcompose](https://pypi.org/project/docxcompose/), and optional DOCX-to-PDF conversion is handled by a headless [LibreOffice](https://www.libreoffice.org/) when it is available on the host (PDF is always optional and never a hard dependency).

The catalog exposes two functions. The scalar `docgen_render(template, data[, pdf])` renders one document per row: pass a template — either a `VARCHAR` path (resolved directly, then under `$VGI_DOCGEN_TEMPLATES`) or inline `.docx` `BLOB` bytes — and a `STRUCT` of fields that become the Jinja2 variables, with an optional `pdf` flag. The table function `docgen_merge(relation, template := ..., [pdf := true])` consumes an entire relation and concatenates one render per input row into a single combined document, ideal for batch statement runs or multi-page contract packs.

The `sample_templates` discovery table lists every template the worker ships along with its absolute path and the placeholder fields it expects, so an agent can produce a real document without supplying a file of its own.

Untrusted bytes are magic-checked before rendering, and bad input degrades cleanly to NULL (scalar) or a visible error (merge).

## DOCX mail merge in SQL

Turn query results into finished Word documents. This schema mail-merges row data into `.docx` templates and returns each rendered file as a `BLOB`, so documents are produced at query time with no application code.

### Key concepts

- **Templates** are ordinary Word files with `{{ field }}` placeholders and `{% for %}` loops, powered by Jinja2 over python-docx.
- **Data** comes straight from your columns: every field or column becomes a template variable at render time.
- **Output** is a document `BLOB` — DOCX by default, or PDF when a headless LibreOffice is available on the host.

### When to use it

Reach for this schema to automate document production — invoices, account statements, contracts, and form letters — either one filled document per row or a whole relation merged into a single combined document. Untrusted input is magic-checked and degrades cleanly rather than crashing the worker.

## `sample_templates`

A **browsable table** (no arguments) listing the DOCX templates the worker ships, so an agent can render a real document without supplying a file. One row per bundled template:

- `name` (`VARCHAR`) -- logical template name, e.g. `sample_invoice`.
- `path` (`VARCHAR`) -- the absolute filesystem path to pass as the `template` argument of `docgen_render` / `docgen_merge`.
- `field_count` (`INTEGER`) -- how many placeholder fields the template has.
- `fields` (`VARCHAR`) -- the comma-separated `{{ placeholder }}` names; these are exactly the keys the `STRUCT` data argument must provide.
- `description` (`VARCHAR`) -- what the template is for.

Read `path` and `fields` from this table, then call `docgen_render(path, {field: value, ...})` to produce a document.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Mail-merge a **whole input relation into a SINGLE merged DOCX (or PDF) document**, returned as a one-row, one-column `BLOB`.

## What it does

`docgen_merge` is the "many rows -> one document" path. It consumes an entire input relation (passed positionally as a `(SELECT ...)` subquery), renders the named `template` once per row, and concatenates the results into one `.docx`, with a page break between rows. Every column of the relation is exposed to the template as a Jinja2 variable (`{{ column }}`). Because it is a buffering (Sink+Source) function, it sinks every input batch first and renders+merges once at finalize.

## When to use it

Use it to assemble one combined document from many rows -- a single PDF of all monthly statements, one Word file containing every contract. When you instead want a *separate* document per row, use the `docgen_render` scalar.

## Inputs and output

- `data` -- the input relation, a positional `(SELECT ...)` subquery; every column becomes a template variable.
- `template` -- named `VARCHAR` arg: path to a `.docx` template, resolved under `$VGI_DOCGEN_TEMPLATES`.
- `pdf` -- named `BOOLEAN` arg; `true` converts the merged document to PDF via headless LibreOffice.
- Returns a single `doc` `BLOB` row.

## Edge cases

An **empty input relation yields zero output rows** (no document). A missing/typo'd template name or an unavailable LibreOffice surfaces as a clean DuckDB error (the merge path fails loudly rather than emitting a silently empty file); the worker stays alive and serving afterwards.

Mail-merge **one DOCX (Microsoft Word) document per input row** from a template, returning each rendered file as a `BLOB`.

## What it does

The first argument is the template, accepted as **either** a `VARCHAR` path (resolved directly, then under `$VGI_DOCGEN_TEMPLATES`) **or** a `BLOB` of raw `.docx` bytes. The second argument is an arbitrary `STRUCT` of row data: every field becomes a Jinja2 variable in the template (`{{ field }}`), and nested lists/structs drive `{% for %}` loops and tables. An optional third boolean (`pdf`) converts the result to PDF via a headless LibreOffice when one is on PATH.

## When to use it

Use this scalar to produce a separate filled document for each row -- one invoice per customer, one letter per recipient, one statement per account. When you instead want a *single* document concatenating every row, use the `docgen_merge` table function.

## Inputs and output

- `template` -- `VARCHAR` path or `BLOB` `.docx` bytes.
- `data` -- `STRUCT`; fields become template variables.
- `pdf` (optional) -- `BOOLEAN`; `true` requests PDF output.
- Returns a `BLOB`: the rendered `.docx` (or PDF).

## Edge cases

Hostile or missing input degrades to `NULL`, never a crash: a `NULL` template or `NULL` data, a non-DOCX blob, a missing template file, a malformed template, a Jinja render error, and a requested-but-unavailable PDF conversion all yield `NULL`.

workers.title: VGI Ducks
workers.tagline: Duck sightings, spatial seasonal ranges, and weekly regional abundance in DuckDB via a TypeScript VGI worker
workers.subtitle: Query duck species, sightings, seasonal range polygons and weekly regional abundance using Cornell Lab of Ornithology data.
workers.summary: Duck species reference data, recent eBird sightings and nearby birding hotspots, plus eBird Status and Trends seasonal ranges, weekly regional abundance and migration calendars, all from the Cornell Lab of Ornithology. Sightings and hotspots need an eBird API key.
workers.doc_md:
# VGI Ducks

Duck data for birders and analysts from the Cornell Lab of Ornithology, in two families. Observation data comes from the eBird API 2.0: recent reported sightings of duck species near a point and the birding hotspots around it, which need an ebird DuckDB secret or EBIRD_API_KEY. Migration data comes from eBird Status and Trends: modeled seasonal range polygons and weekly relative abundance summarized over a WGS84 region, which need a separate ebirdst secret or EBIRDST_KEY, except Cornell's public yebsap-example sample. An offline species reference table (a bundled eBird 2026 taxonomy subset) supplies the species codes both families take. Observations are bounded recent snapshots with local wall-clock times and reported counts, not population estimates or a historical archive. Status and Trends values are modeled distributions for a model year (default 2023) whose species codes can differ from the current taxonomy; they are not individual tracks or live forecasts, so read coverage alongside abundance.

## How the parts fit

Look a duck up in the species table to get its eBird code, then pass that code to the observation or migration functions. Sightings and hotspots share eBird location identifiers, so a join shows which birding sites have reported ducks. Range polygons are WKB for DuckDB Spatial, and regional abundance takes a longitude/latitude polygon, so the two compose with any geometry you already have. Join with weather and tide workers to explore conditions at sighting locations.

## Caveats

Data are supplied by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology's [eBird](https://ebird.org) and its terms apply. The worker preserves source identifiers and review flags; a missing count is SQL NULL. Only species-level records are kept: hybrids, domestic forms and unidentified groups are excluded.

## Sources and references

- [eBird API 2.0 documentation](https://documenter.getpostman.com/view/664302/S1ENwy59): the API behind the sightings and hotspots functions; [request an eBird API key](https://ebird.org/api/keygen).
- [eBird Status and Trends](https://science.ebird.org/en/status-and-trends): the modeled ranges, abundance and migration data; [request Status and Trends data access](https://ebird.org/st/request) for the ebirdst key.

example_queries.description: Latest sighting per duck species near Boston (requires eBird key)
example_queries.sql: SELECT common_name, observed_at_local FROM ducks.main.recent_sightings(42.36, -71.06) ORDER BY common_name

example_queries.description: Latest Mallard sighting at each nearby location (requires eBird key)
example_queries.sql: SELECT location_name, reported_count, observed_at_local FROM ducks.main.recent_sightings(42.36, -71.06, species_code := 'mallar3') ORDER BY observed_at_local DESC, location_name

example_queries.description: Five nearest birding hotspots to Boston (requires eBird key)
example_queries.sql: SELECT location_name, distance_km FROM ducks.main.nearby_hotspots(42.36, -71.06) ORDER BY distance_km, location_name LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Inspect season dates in Cornell's public sample (requires network, not a key)
example_queries.sql: SELECT season, start_date, end_date, wraps_year FROM ducks.main.seasonal_ranges('yebsap-example') ORDER BY season

example_queries.description: Find seasonal ranges intersecting a point using DuckDB Spatial

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The one schema of the ducks worker. Start from the offline species table: it maps common and scientific names to the eBird species codes every other object takes, and flags extinct taxa, which observation requests reject. Observation functions read the live eBird API around a latitude/longitude within a small radius and a short lookback; migration functions read Cornell's modeled Status and Trends products for a species and model year. Explicit NULL arguments are rejected everywhere, and every result is bounded rather than an exhaustive archive.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

Everything the worker exposes lives here. Use the offline species table to find current eBird codes and scientific names, then pass a code to the live observation functions (eBird API key) or the modeled migration functions (Status and Trends key, or the public sample).

Observation results keep local times and unknown counts and cover only a recent lookback window; migration results are modeled seasonal patterns whose coverage should be checked before comparing weeks. Load DuckDB Spatial to work with the range geometry and region polygons.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Duck Species Reference

Offline reference of 140 duck species from the eBird 2026 taxonomy, including 9 flagged extinct taxa. Includes teals, eiders, mergansers, shelducks, whistling-ducks and Nettapus pygmy-geese. Excludes other geese and swans, hybrids, domestic forms and unidentified groups. Use species_code in recent_sightings; filter NOT extinct for living taxa. Taxonomy is versioned, not automatically refreshed. This is a worker scope convention, not a taxonomic clade. Names and identifiers are factual eBird reference data attributed to Cornell Lab of Ornithology; upstream terms apply separately from the code license.

### Result columns

| Column | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| species_code | Unique eBird 2026 species code, used in recent_sightings. |
| common_name | English common name in the bundled taxonomy. |
| scientific_name | Scientific binomial in the bundled taxonomy. |
| genus | Scientific genus. |
| family_name | Scientific family: Anatidae. |
| taxon_order | Unitless eBird taxonomic sort index; not a bird count. |
| extinct | Whether eBird marks the taxon extinct; false is not a conservation assessment. |
| taxonomy_version | Version of the bundled eBird taxonomy. |
| source_url | eBird species page URL. |

functions.name: weekly_abundance
functions.comment: Summarize weekly modeled relative abundance inside a geographic polygon with coverage counts

tags.vgi.doc_llm: weekly_abundance(species_code, region_wkt, data_year := 2023, resolution := '27km') summarizes every available weekly median relative-abundance band inside a WGS84 POLYGON or MULTIPOLYGON in longitude/latitude order. Polygon holes and multipart regions are respected; centers on boundaries are excluded. Equal Earth EPSG:8857 grid cells have equal area, so the mean weights selected modeled cell centers equally; it is not an exact area-clipped polygon mean or a bird population total. Zero predictions remain zero. NoData is excluded and reported through modeled_cell_count and coverage_fraction; no modeled cells gives NULL abundance. Changing coverage can affect week-to-week comparisons. Original band dates are preserved; no 52-week completeness is assumed. At most 2000 region vertices and 50000 cells in the bounding decode window are allowed. Regions spanning the antimeridian must be split into separate queries. Uses the eBird Status and Trends file API with a separate ebirdst TOKEN secret or EBIRDST_KEY. yebsap-example reads Cornell's public Yellow-bellied Sapsucker sample without credentials, only for 2023/27km; the sample is restricted to Michigan and is not duck data. Model-release species codes are not silently mapped to the offline 2026 taxonomy. data_year is explicit and defaults to 2023; unavailable products fail clearly. Responses are bounded to 128 MiB and all NULL arguments are rejected. These are modeled seasonal distributions, not individual migration tracks or live forecasts. Access/data terms apply. No key, signed URL or downloaded file is retained in table state.
