## Weekly Regional Duck Abundance

weekly_abundance(species_code, region_wkt, data_year := 2023, resolution := '27km') summarizes every available weekly median relative-abundance band inside a WGS84 POLYGON or MULTIPOLYGON in longitude/latitude order. Polygon holes and multipart regions are respected; centers on boundaries are excluded. Equal Earth EPSG:8857 grid cells have equal area, so the mean weights selected modeled cell centers equally; it is not an exact area-clipped polygon mean or a bird population total. Zero predictions remain zero. NoData is excluded and reported through modeled_cell_count and coverage_fraction; no modeled cells gives NULL abundance. Changing coverage can affect week-to-week comparisons. Original band dates are preserved; no 52-week completeness is assumed. At most 2000 region vertices and 50000 cells in the bounding decode window are allowed. Regions spanning the antimeridian must be split into separate queries. Uses the eBird Status and Trends file API with a separate ebirdst TOKEN secret or EBIRDST_KEY. yebsap-example reads Cornell's public Yellow-bellied Sapsucker sample without credentials, only for 2023/27km; the sample is restricted to Michigan and is not duck data. Model-release species codes are not silently mapped to the offline 2026 taxonomy. data_year is explicit and defaults to 2023; unavailable products fail clearly. Responses are bounded to 128 MiB and all NULL arguments are rejected. These are modeled seasonal distributions, not individual migration tracks or live forecasts. Access/data terms apply. No key, signed URL or downloaded file is retained in table state.

### Result columns

| Column | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| species_code | Species identifier from the selected model release. |
| product_species_code | Requested product identifier; yebsap-example identifies the public sample. |
| prediction_year | Model prediction year, not the current year. |
| week_date | Model week's date label in YYYY-MM-DD format; not an observed arrival date. |
| mean_relative_abundance | Mean expected birds per standardized 1-hour, 2-km checklist across modeled cells inside the region; NULL without modeled cells. |
| max_relative_abundance | Maximum expected birds per standardized checklist among modeled cells inside the region; NULL without modeled cells. |
| selected_cell_count | Count of native grid cell centers strictly inside the polygon and raster extent, including unmodeled cells. |
| modeled_cell_count | Count of selected cells with a finite prediction, including true zero abundance. |
| coverage_fraction | Modeled cell count / selected cell count (0–1); NULL when the region contains no raster cell centers. |
| resolution_km | Native Equal Earth grid spacing in km; no interpolation or upsampling. |
| region_wkb | Requested region as WGS84 polygon WKB; use ST_GeomFromWKB to map or join it. |
| geometry_crs | Region coordinate reference system: EPSG:4326, x=longitude and y=latitude. |
| source_product | Upstream weekly raster object path, without credentials. |

functions.name: nearby_hotspots
functions.comment: Find nearby eBird birding locations for all birds, with distance and reporting history

tags.vgi.doc_llm: nearby_hotspots(latitude, longitude, radius_km := 25, days_back := 0) reads eBird's nearby birding hotspots. These are locations for all birds, not evidence that ducks were seen there. Join location_id to recent_sightings for that evidence. all_bird_species_count counts all-time bird species, not ducks or individuals. days_back 0 omits the recency filter; 1–30 filters visits. WGS84 search coordinates are rounded to two decimals and distance_km is measured from that rounded center. Radius is limited to 0–50 km for consistency with sightings. Local dates retain original precision without assigning UTC; optional missing values become NULL. An ebird secret TOKEN or EBIRD_API_KEY is required. Explicit NULL arguments and responses reaching the 10000-record bound fail clearly.

functions.name: recent_sightings
functions.comment: Read the latest nearby sighting per duck species, or per location for a selected species

tags.vgi.doc_llm: recent_sightings(latitude, longitude, radius_km := 25, days_back := 14, species_code := '', hotspots_only := false, include_provisional := false) reads the eBird recent nearby API and keeps extant species in the bundled duck catalog. Empty species_code returns only the latest sighting per species across the search area. A species code selects the species-specific endpoint: latest sighting per location. Neither mode is an exhaustive checklist history. Observation times remain local strings with original date/minute precision; missing counts and flags are NULL. Coordinates are sent rounded to two decimal places; radius is 0–50 km, lookback 1–30 days. An extinct species_code is rejected. An ebird secret TOKEN or EBIRD_API_KEY is required. Results are a bounded recent snapshot, not a historical observation archive. Responses reaching the 10000-record cap fail rather than claiming completeness. All explicit NULL arguments are rejected. Upstream 429/5xx responses are retried with bounded backoff; no invented pagination or zero observations on failure.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Recent Nearby Duck Sightings

recent_sightings(latitude, longitude, radius_km := 25, days_back := 14, species_code := '', hotspots_only := false, include_provisional := false) reads the eBird recent nearby API and keeps extant species in the bundled duck catalog. Empty species_code returns only the latest sighting per species across the search area. A species code selects the species-specific endpoint: latest sighting per location. Neither mode is an exhaustive checklist history. Observation times remain local strings with original date/minute precision; missing counts and flags are NULL. Coordinates are sent rounded to two decimal places; radius is 0–50 km, lookback 1–30 days. An extinct species_code is rejected. An ebird secret TOKEN or EBIRD_API_KEY is required. Results are a bounded recent snapshot, not a historical observation archive. Responses reaching the 10000-record cap fail rather than claiming completeness. All explicit NULL arguments are rejected. Upstream 429/5xx responses are retried with bounded backoff; no invented pagination or zero observations on failure.

### Result columns

| Column | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| species_code | eBird code; joins to species.species_code. |
| common_name | English common name returned by eBird. |
| scientific_name | Scientific name returned by eBird. |
| location_id | eBird location identifier (join sightings to hotspots on this column). |
| location_name | eBird location display name; retain any access restrictions in the name. |
| latitude | Location latitude in WGS84 decimal degrees. |
| longitude | Location longitude in WGS84 decimal degrees. |
| distance_km | Great-circle distance in km from the API search center, rounded to 2 decimal degrees. |
| observed_at_local | Local observation date/time as supplied: YYYY-MM-DD or YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM. No timezone is implied. |
| reported_count | Reported individuals; NULL means present but uncounted/missing. Never a population estimate. |
| observation_valid | eBird obsValid flag, preserved independently of manual review. |
| observation_reviewed | eBird obsReviewed flag; false does not necessarily mean invalid. |
| location_private | eBird locationPrivate flag; a shared location is not permission to enter. |
| checklist_id | Source checklist identifier (subId), if supplied. |
| fetched_at | Time the worker retrieved this snapshot, UTC. |

functions.name: migration_calendar
functions.comment: Find all positive peak weeks in a region's modeled annual abundance curve

tags.vgi.doc_llm: migration_calendar has the same arguments, units, geometry rules and coverage semantics as weekly_abundance. It returns all tied weeks with the highest positive mean relative abundance in the region. A series with only zero or NULL values returns no peak rows. Peak abundance does not establish arrival/departure dates or a migration event; breeding or winter residence can cause the peak. Compare coverage_fraction and modeled_cell_count before interpreting changes. weekly_abundance(species_code, region_wkt, data_year := 2023, resolution := '27km') summarizes every available weekly median relative-abundance band inside a WGS84 POLYGON or MULTIPOLYGON in longitude/latitude order. Polygon holes and multipart regions are respected; centers on boundaries are excluded. Equal Earth EPSG:8857 grid cells have equal area, so the mean weights selected modeled cell centers equally; it is not an exact area-clipped polygon mean or a bird population total. Zero predictions remain zero. NoData is excluded and reported through modeled_cell_count and coverage_fraction; no modeled cells gives NULL abundance. Changing coverage can affect week-to-week comparisons. Original band dates are preserved; no 52-week completeness is assumed. At most 2000 region vertices and 50000 cells in the bounding decode window are allowed. Regions spanning the antimeridian must be split into separate queries. Uses the eBird Status and Trends file API with a separate ebirdst TOKEN secret or EBIRDST_KEY. yebsap-example reads Cornell's public Yellow-bellied Sapsucker sample without credentials, only for 2023/27km; the sample is restricted to Michigan and is not duck data. Model-release species codes are not silently mapped to the offline 2026 taxonomy. data_year is explicit and defaults to 2023; unavailable products fail clearly. Responses are bounded to 128 MiB and all NULL arguments are rejected. These are modeled seasonal distributions, not individual migration tracks or live forecasts. Access/data terms apply. No key, signed URL or downloaded file is retained in table state.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Peak Weeks of Regional Duck Abundance

migration_calendar has the same arguments, units, geometry rules and coverage semantics as weekly_abundance. It returns all tied weeks with the highest positive mean relative abundance in the region. A series with only zero or NULL values returns no peak rows. Peak abundance does not establish arrival/departure dates or a migration event; breeding or winter residence can cause the peak. Compare coverage_fraction and modeled_cell_count before interpreting changes. weekly_abundance(species_code, region_wkt, data_year := 2023, resolution := '27km') summarizes every available weekly median relative-abundance band inside a WGS84 POLYGON or MULTIPOLYGON in longitude/latitude order. Polygon holes and multipart regions are respected; centers on boundaries are excluded. Equal Earth EPSG:8857 grid cells have equal area, so the mean weights selected modeled cell centers equally; it is not an exact area-clipped polygon mean or a bird population total. Zero predictions remain zero. NoData is excluded and reported through modeled_cell_count and coverage_fraction; no modeled cells gives NULL abundance. Changing coverage can affect week-to-week comparisons. Original band dates are preserved; no 52-week completeness is assumed. At most 2000 region vertices and 50000 cells in the bounding decode window are allowed. Regions spanning the antimeridian must be split into separate queries. Uses the eBird Status and Trends file API with a separate ebirdst TOKEN secret or EBIRDST_KEY. yebsap-example reads Cornell's public Yellow-bellied Sapsucker sample without credentials, only for 2023/27km; the sample is restricted to Michigan and is not duck data. Model-release species codes are not silently mapped to the offline 2026 taxonomy. data_year is explicit and defaults to 2023; unavailable products fail clearly. Responses are bounded to 128 MiB and all NULL arguments are rejected. These are modeled seasonal distributions, not individual migration tracks or live forecasts. Access/data terms apply. No key, signed URL or downloaded file is retained in table state.

### Result columns

| Column | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| species_code | Species identifier from the selected model release. |
| product_species_code | Requested product identifier; yebsap-example identifies the public sample. |
| prediction_year | Model prediction year, not the current year. |
| week_date | Model week's date label in YYYY-MM-DD format; not an observed arrival date. |
| mean_relative_abundance | Mean expected birds per standardized 1-hour, 2-km checklist across modeled cells inside the region; NULL without modeled cells. |
| max_relative_abundance | Maximum expected birds per standardized checklist among modeled cells inside the region; NULL without modeled cells. |
| selected_cell_count | Count of native grid cell centers strictly inside the polygon and raster extent, including unmodeled cells. |
| modeled_cell_count | Count of selected cells with a finite prediction, including true zero abundance. |
| coverage_fraction | Modeled cell count / selected cell count (0–1); NULL when the region contains no raster cell centers. |
| resolution_km | Native Equal Earth grid spacing in km; no interpolation or upsampling. |
| region_wkb | Requested region as WGS84 polygon WKB; use ST_GeomFromWKB to map or join it. |
| geometry_crs | Region coordinate reference system: EPSG:4326, x=longitude and y=latitude. |
| source_product | Upstream weekly raster object path, without credentials. |

workers.title: Earth Observation Time Series
workers.tagline: vgi-earth-observation — Query Farm VGI worker with executable SQL notebook examples
workers.subtitle: Optical index and calibrated radar histories for geospatial SQL queries.
workers.summary: Satellite imagery histories for land parcels and regions from STAC catalogs: cloud-masked Sentinel-2 vegetation and water indices and calibrated Sentinel-1 radar backscatter, with change flags. Reads local STAC files or public STAC APIs; offline sample scenes are included.
workers.doc_md:
## GIS analysis

Build parcel vegetation or water-index histories from STAC ItemCollections or public STAC APIs. Align bands and categorical SCL masks, apply scale/offset metadata, exclude cloudy pixels, optionally form monthly pixel-median composites, and flag declines between adequately observed periods. Output parcel IDs join directly to ownership and weather tables. Synthetic offline assets ship in the wheel. Summarize prepared calibrated SAR intensity assets over polygon regions for time-series change analysis. Input region_id and geometry_wkb columns retain caller identity. Read local STAC ItemCollections or public STAC APIs, using vv/vh assets. This function accepts calibrated terrain-corrected linear power or decibel rasters, not raw radar, complex SLC, or an optical index. Convert dB pixels to linear power before spatial averaging, then report 10*log10(mean_power). Nonpositive linear power, nodata and nonfinite pixels are excluded. Pixel centres define membership. Keep platform, relative_orbit, orbit_state and polarization separate in temporal statistics. A viewing group's rasters must share CRS, resolution and pixel-grid alignment; differing extents are allowed. No resampling or additional speckle filter is performed. Missing observations are NULL, never zero. A change is not a damage probability. Coherence requires a separate phase-preserving SLC pipeline. Private asset signing is outside this function; use prepared local windows.

### SQL workflow

Pass query results to the main schema functions, retaining IDs for joins. Use bundled synthetic data to try the executable examples without network access. CRS, coverage, inference limits and resource bounds are explicit function parameters.

## Sources and references

- [STAC specification](https://stacspec.org/): the SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog items and API searches this worker reads.
- [Earth Search by Element 84](https://element84.com/earth-search/): the public STAC API whose `sentinel-2-l2a` Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs the optical examples use.
- [Sentinel-2 processing (SentiWiki)](https://sentiwiki.copernicus.eu/web/s2-processing): Level-2A surface reflectance and the Scene Classification (SCL) codes used for cloud masking.
- [Sentinel-1 RTC on Microsoft Planetary Computer](https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/dataset/sentinel-1-rtc): the radiometrically terrain-corrected radar collection the `sentinel-1-rtc` default names.
- [Rasterio](https://rasterio.readthedocs.io/): the GDAL-based raster library used to read and align assets.

arguments.name: clear_scl_classes
arguments.description: Comma-separated SCL codes treated as clear; default vegetation, bare soil, and water.

arguments.name: collections
arguments.description: Comma-separated collection IDs for STAC API search.

arguments.name: composite
arguments.description: Monthly pixel-median composites or individual observation-time composites.

arguments.name: decline_threshold
arguments.description: Minimum absolute negative index change to flag as a decline.

arguments.name: end_date
arguments.description: Inclusive UTC ISO observation end.

arguments.name: geometry_crs
arguments.description: Explicit CRS of all input parcel WKB geometries; XY axis order.

arguments.name: green_asset
arguments.description: STAC asset key for green reflectance when computing NDWI.

arguments.name: index_name
arguments.description: Normalized difference: NDVI=(NIR-red)/(NIR+red), NDWI=(green-NIR)/(green+NIR), NBR=(NIR-SWIR)/(NIR+SWIR).

arguments.name: max_change_gap_days
arguments.description: Maximum time separation between change-comparison observations.

arguments.name: max_cloud
arguments.description: Maximum scene-level cloud percentage; pixel cloud masks are still applied.

arguments.name: max_json_bytes
arguments.description: Maximum decoded bytes per STAC JSON page or static document.

arguments.name: max_pages
arguments.description: Hard STAC pagination bound; cyclic or excessive paging fails.

arguments.name: max_pixels
arguments.description: Maximum aligned bounding-window pixels per parcel; a 20 million pixel-scene memory cap also applies.

arguments.name: max_scenes
arguments.description: Hard scene limit; an oversized result fails instead of silently truncating.

arguments.name: max_source_pixels
arguments.description: Maximum native pixels per reflectance crop before cloud masking and resampling.

arguments.name: min_coverage
arguments.description: Minimum clear pixel fraction before a result participates in change detection.

arguments.name: nir_asset
arguments.description: STAC asset key for near-infrared reflectance.

arguments.name: offset_mode
arguments.description: auto honors Earth Search's already-applied BOA flag for GeoTIFF assets, otherwise uses band metadata. metadata always applies declared offsets; zero ignores offsets for independently verified harmonized data. Effective calibration is returned for audit.

arguments.name: red_asset
arguments.description: STAC asset key for red reflectance.

arguments.name: scl_asset
arguments.description: Required categorical Scene Classification Layer asset; never bilinearly resampled.

arguments.name: start_date
arguments.description: Inclusive UTC ISO observation start.

arguments.name: swir_asset
arguments.description: STAC asset key for shortwave infrared reflectance when computing NBR.

examples: SELECT parcel_id, round(mean_index, 2), decline FROM earth_observation.main.parcel_series((SELECT * FROM earth_observation.main.sample_parcels)) ORDER BY parcel_id, observed_at

WITH optical AS (SELECT parcel_id, count(*) FILTER (WHERE decline) AS ndvi_declines, min(delta_index) AS worst_ndvi_change FROM earth_observation.main.parcel_series((SELECT parcel_id, geometry_wkb FROM earth_observation.main.sample_parcels)) GROUP BY parcel_id), radar AS (SELECT region_id, relative_orbit, orbit_state, arg_max(mean_db, observed_at) - arg_min(mean_db, observed_at) AS vv_change_db FROM earth_observation.main.radar_series((SELECT parcel_id AS region_id, geometry_wkb FROM earth_observation.main.sample_parcels), polarizations := 'vv') WHERE status = 'ok' GROUP BY region_id, relative_orbit, orbit_state) SELECT o.parcel_id, o.ndvi_declines, round(o.worst_ndvi_change, 2) AS worst_ndvi_change, r.relative_orbit, r.orbit_state, round(r.vv_change_db, 1) AS vv_change_db FROM optical AS o JOIN radar AS r ON r.region_id = o.parcel_id ORDER BY o.parcel_id, r.relative_orbit, r.orbit_state
SELECT parcel_id, round(mean_index, 2), decline FROM earth_observation.main.parcel_series((SELECT * FROM earth_observation.main.sample_parcels)) ORDER BY parcel_id, observed_at;

WITH optical AS (SELECT parcel_id, count(*) FILTER (WHERE decline) AS ndvi_declines, min(delta_index) AS worst_ndvi_change FROM earth_observation.main.parcel_series((SELECT parcel_id, geometry_wkb FROM earth_observation.main.sample_parcels)) GROUP BY parcel_id), radar AS (SELECT region_id, relative_orbit, orbit_state, arg_max(mean_db, observed_at) - arg_min(mean_db, observed_at) AS vv_change_db FROM earth_observation.main.radar_series((SELECT parcel_id AS region_id, geometry_wkb FROM earth_observation.main.sample_parcels), polarizations := 'vv') WHERE status = 'ok' GROUP BY region_id, relative_orbit, orbit_state) SELECT o.parcel_id, o.ndvi_declines, round(o.worst_ndvi_change, 2) AS worst_ndvi_change, r.relative_orbit, r.orbit_state, round(r.vv_change_db, 1) AS vv_change_db FROM optical AS o JOIN radar AS r ON r.region_id = o.parcel_id ORDER BY o.parcel_id, r.relative_orbit, r.orbit_state;

workers.title: ECB Statistics
workers.tagline: Python VGI worker for European Central Bank datasets, SDMX metadata, observations, and revision history.
workers.subtitle: Discover European Central Bank statistical series and retrieve observations with original periods, units and source metadata.
workers.summary: European Central Bank statistics as SQL tables: exchange rates, interest rates, money, prices and other euro-area time series from the ECB Data Portal, with dataflow dimensions and code lists. No API key needed.
workers.doc_md:
# vgi-ecb

Discover European Central Bank statistical series and retrieve observations with original periods, units and source metadata. The upstream public data service needs no API key. SQL NULL arguments are rejected; missing source values become NULL. Use function arguments for source filtering; SQL WHERE filters are local. HTTP worker access can require a bearer token.

Queries use bounded HTTP responses and retries. Credentials stay out of continuation state. See README.md for deployment and operational limits.

## Sources and references

- [ECB Data Portal](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/)
- [ECB Data Portal API overview](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/help/api/overview)
- [API data queries (series keys and parameters)](https://data.ecb.europa.eu/help/api/data)

example_queries.title: exchange_rates_dataflow
example_queries.description: Look up the ECB exchange-rates dataflow (EXR) from the keyless ECB Data Portal API
example_queries.sql: SELECT flow, name FROM ecb.main.datasets(flow := 'EXR') ORDER BY flow;

example_queries.description: Discover ECB dimensions
example_queries.sql: SELECT dimension, position, codelist FROM ecb.main.dimensions('EXR') ORDER BY position NULLS LAST, dimension

example_queries.description: Discover ECB dimension codes
example_queries.sql: SELECT code, name FROM ecb.main.codes('CL_CURRENCY') WHERE code IN ('USD','EUR') ORDER BY code

example_queries.description: Inspect ECB series
example_queries.sql: SELECT series_key, title, unit FROM ecb.main.series('EXR', 'D.USD.EUR.SP00.A') ORDER BY series_key

example_queries.description: Every frequency at which the US dollar/euro reference rate is published, with the frequency name decoded from the CL_FREQ code list
example_queries.sql: SELECT s.frequency, f.name AS frequency_name, s.series_key FROM ecb.main.series('EXR', '.USD.EUR.SP00.A') AS s JOIN ecb.main.codes('CL_FREQ') AS f ON f.code = s.frequency ORDER BY s.series_key

example_queries.description: Read ECB observations
example_queries.sql: SELECT period, value, unit FROM ecb.main.observations('EXR', 'D.USD.EUR.SP00.A', start_period := '2024-01-02', end_period := '2024-01-05') ORDER BY period

example_queries.description: Average monthly ECB euro reference rates for Q1 2024 (USD, GBP, JPY), labelled with each currency's name from the CL_CURRENCY code list
example_queries.sql: SELECT c.code AS currency, c.name AS currency_name, round(avg(o.value), 4) AS avg_rate_per_eur, count(o.value) AS months FROM ecb.main.observations('EXR', 'M.USD+GBP+JPY.EUR.SP00.A', start_period := '2024-01', end_period := '2024-03') AS o JOIN ecb.main.codes('CL_CURRENCY') AS c ON c.code = split_part(o.series_key, '.', 2) GROUP BY c.code, c.name ORDER BY c.code

agent_tasks: Using ecb.main.datasets, discover ecb datasets. Use the arguments in this example and return the same columns: SELECT flow, name FROM ecb.main.datasets(flow := 'EXR') ORDER BY flow

Using ecb.main.dimensions, discover ecb dimensions. Use the arguments in this example and return the same columns: SELECT dimension, position, codelist FROM ecb.main.dimensions('EXR') ORDER BY position NULLS LAST, dimension

Using ecb.main.codes, discover ecb dimension codes. Use the arguments in this example and return the same columns: SELECT code, name FROM ecb.main.codes('CL_CURRENCY') WHERE code IN ('USD','EUR') ORDER BY code

Using ecb.main.series, inspect ecb series. Use the arguments in this example and return the same columns: SELECT series_key, title, unit FROM ecb.main.series('EXR', 'D.USD.EUR.SP00.A') ORDER BY series_key

Using ecb.main.observations, read ecb observations. Use the arguments in this example and return the same columns: SELECT period, value, unit FROM ecb.main.observations('EXR', 'D.USD.EUR.SP00.A', start_period := '2024-01-02', end_period := '2024-01-05') ORDER BY period

Using the ECB worker, find the highest daily ECB euro reference rate between 2024-01-02 and 2024-01-31 (inclusive) for the US dollar and the Japanese yen, each labelled with the currency's name from the ECB CL_CURRENCY code list. Return exactly the columns currency (ISO code, VARCHAR), currency_name (VARCHAR) and max_rate (DOUBLE), one row per currency, ordered by currency.

workers.tagline: Python VGI worker for EIA energy data, API v2 discovery, facets and legacy series
workers.subtitle: Explore EIA API v2 routes, facets and frequencies, then retrieve energy observations and legacy series with original dimensions and units.
workers.summary: US Energy Information Administration energy data from EIA API v2, covering electricity, petroleum, natural gas, coal and renewables, as SQL tables with route and facet discovery and the original units. Needs a free EIA API key.
workers.doc_md:
# vgi-eia

Explore EIA API v2 routes, facets and frequencies, then retrieve energy observations and legacy series with original dimensions and units. Use an eia_api secret with api_key or EIA_API_KEY. Discover routes and facets before querying observations. Numeric values retain published units; value_text preserves the original representation. page_size controls requests and max_rows=0 retrieves all matching rows. NULL arguments are rejected. Missing optional response fields return NULL. Upstream errors fail the query; SQL WHERE filters are local.

Queries use bounded HTTP responses and retries. Credentials stay out of continuation state. See README.md for deployment and operational limits.

## Sources and references

- [EIA Open Data](https://www.eia.gov/opendata/)
- [EIA API v2 documentation](https://www.eia.gov/opendata/documentation.php)
- [Register for a free EIA API key](https://www.eia.gov/opendata/register.php)

example_queries.title: routes_columns
example_queries.description: Show the columns routes() returns without an API key: binding the function with LIMIT 0 resolves its schema and makes no EIA API request
example_queries.sql: SELECT * FROM eia.main.routes(route := 'electricity') LIMIT 0;

example_queries.description: Discover EIA routes
example_queries.sql: SELECT route, name FROM eia.main.routes(route := 'electricity') ORDER BY route

example_queries.description: Inspect EIA dataset metadata
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, start_period, end_period FROM eia.main.metadata('electricity/retail-sales')

example_queries.description: Pair the retail-sales dataset's default frequency with that frequency's native period format and the advertised period range, to know how to write start_period and end_period
example_queries.sql: SELECT m.name, m.default_frequency, f.period_format, m.start_period, m.end_period FROM eia.main.metadata('electricity/retail-sales') AS m JOIN eia.main.frequencies('electricity/retail-sales') AS f ON f.frequency = m.default_frequency ORDER BY f.frequency

example_queries.description: Discover EIA frequencies
example_queries.sql: SELECT frequency, period_format FROM eia.main.frequencies('electricity/retail-sales') ORDER BY frequency

example_queries.description: Discover EIA measures
example_queries.sql: SELECT measure, units FROM eia.main.measures('electricity/retail-sales') ORDER BY measure

example_queries.description: Discover EIA dimensions
example_queries.sql: SELECT facet, description FROM eia.main.facets('electricity/retail-sales') ORDER BY facet

example_queries.description: Discover EIA dimension values
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, name FROM eia.main.facet_values('electricity/retail-sales', 'sectorid') ORDER BY id

example_queries.description: List every retail-sales sector ID and name with Colorado's 2024 annual average price, NULL for sectors with no published 2024 Colorado price
example_queries.sql: SELECT s.id AS sectorid, s.name AS sector, o.value AS cents_per_kwh FROM eia.main.facet_values('electricity/retail-sales', 'sectorid') AS s LEFT JOIN eia.main.observations('electricity/retail-sales', 'price', 'annual', facets_json := '{"stateid":["CO"]}', start_period := '2024', end_period := '2024') AS o ON o.dimensions_json ->> '$.sectorid' = s.id ORDER BY s.id

example_queries.description: Read EIA observations
example_queries.sql: SELECT period, value, units FROM eia.main.observations('electricity/retail-sales', 'price', 'monthly', facets_json := '{"stateid":["CO"],"sectorid":["RES"]}', start_period := '2024-01', end_period := '2024-03') ORDER BY period

example_queries.description: Colorado residential 2024 electricity price weighted by monthly retail sales, beside the simple average of the 12 monthly prices (cents per kilowatt-hour)
example_queries.sql: WITH price AS (SELECT period, value AS cents_per_kwh FROM eia.main.observations('electricity/retail-sales', 'price', 'monthly', facets_json := '{"stateid":["CO"],"sectorid":["RES"]}', start_period := '2024-01', end_period := '2024-12')), sales AS (SELECT period, value AS million_kwh FROM eia.main.observations('electricity/retail-sales', 'sales', 'monthly', facets_json := '{"stateid":["CO"],"sectorid":["RES"]}', start_period := '2024-01', end_period := '2024-12')) SELECT count(*) AS months, round(sum(price.cents_per_kwh * sales.million_kwh) / sum(sales.million_kwh), 2) AS weighted_price, round(avg(price.cents_per_kwh), 2) AS simple_average_price FROM price JOIN sales USING (period) ORDER BY months

example_queries.description: Read a legacy EIA series
example_queries.sql: SELECT period, value, units FROM eia.main.series('ELEC.SALES.CO-RES.A', start_period := '2022', end_period := '2024') ORDER BY period

agent_tasks: Using eia.main.routes, discover eia routes. Use the arguments in this example and return the same columns: SELECT route, name FROM eia.main.routes(route := 'electricity') ORDER BY route

Using eia.main.metadata, inspect eia dataset metadata. Use the arguments in this example and return the same columns: SELECT name, start_period, end_period FROM eia.main.metadata('electricity/retail-sales')

Using eia.main.frequencies, discover eia frequencies. Use the arguments in this example and return the same columns: SELECT frequency, period_format FROM eia.main.frequencies('electricity/retail-sales') ORDER BY frequency

Using eia.main.measures, discover eia measures. Use the arguments in this example and return the same columns: SELECT measure, units FROM eia.main.measures('electricity/retail-sales') ORDER BY measure

Using eia.main.facets, discover eia dimensions. Use the arguments in this example and return the same columns: SELECT facet, description FROM eia.main.facets('electricity/retail-sales') ORDER BY facet

Using eia.main.facet_values, discover eia dimension values. Use the arguments in this example and return the same columns: SELECT id, name FROM eia.main.facet_values('electricity/retail-sales', 'sectorid') ORDER BY id

Using eia.main.observations, read eia observations. Use the arguments in this example and return the same columns: SELECT period, value, units FROM eia.main.observations('electricity/retail-sales', 'price', 'monthly', facets_json := '{"stateid":["CO"],"sectorid":["RES"]}', start_period := '2024-01', end_period := '2024-03') ORDER BY period

Using eia.main.series, read a legacy eia series. Use the arguments in this example and return the same columns: SELECT period, value, units FROM eia.main.series('ELEC.SALES.CO-RES.A', start_period := '2022', end_period := '2024') ORDER BY period

Using the eia catalog's electricity/retail-sales dataset at annual frequency, compute Texas (stateid TX) residential (sectorid RES) average electricity spending per customer in 2023, in US dollars: the revenue measure (million dollars) times 1,000,000 divided by the customers measure for the same period. Save the answer as a temporary table tx_res_spend with exactly one row and one DOUBLE column dollars_per_customer.

WITH price AS (SELECT period, value AS cents_per_kwh FROM eia.main.observations('electricity/retail-sales', 'price', 'monthly', facets_json := '{"stateid":["CO"],"sectorid":["RES"]}', start_period := '2024-01', end_period := '2024-12')), sales AS (SELECT period, value AS million_kwh FROM eia.main.observations('electricity/retail-sales', 'sales', 'monthly', facets_json := '{"stateid":["CO"],"sectorid":["RES"]}', start_period := '2024-01', end_period := '2024-12')) SELECT count(*) AS months, round(sum(price.cents_per_kwh * sales.million_kwh) / sum(sales.million_kwh), 2) AS weighted_price, round(avg(price.cents_per_kwh), 2) AS simple_average_price FROM price JOIN sales USING (period) ORDER BY months

workers.title: Elasticsearch & OpenSearch
workers.tagline: Query Elasticsearch/OpenSearch as tables with search_after+PIT in DuckDB (Go)
workers.subtitle: Query Elasticsearch and OpenSearch indices as SQL tables with consistent deep pagination.
workers.summary: Query Elasticsearch/OpenSearch indices as SQL tables (PIT + search_after deep pagination via externalized scan state)
workers.doc_md:
# Elasticsearch & OpenSearch for DuckDB

![Elasticsearch logo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f4/Elasticsearch_logo.svg/250px-Elasticsearch_logo.svg.png)

Query [Elasticsearch](https://www.elastic.co) and [OpenSearch](https://opensearch.org) indices as live SQL tables over Apache Arrow — full-text search, the query DSL, and consistent deep pagination, straight from DuckDB SQL with no application code.

This VGI worker turns any Elasticsearch or OpenSearch cluster into queryable tables inside DuckDB. It is built for data engineers, analysts, and anyone who needs to read, filter, join, and export search-engine data without standing up a separate ETL pipeline or learning a client library. Point it at a cluster endpoint and an index (or an index pattern such as `logs-*`) and select the fields you want; the worker handles authentication, mapping introspection, pagination, and the translation of SQL filters into Elasticsearch query DSL for you. It works with both the commercial Elasticsearch distribution from Elastic and the Apache-2.0 licensed OpenSearch fork.

Under the hood the worker speaks the native Elasticsearch/OpenSearch REST API and JSON [query DSL](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/query-dsl.html) directly over HTTP. Large result sets are streamed using a [Point-In-Time (PIT)](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/point-in-time-api.html) snapshot combined with a `search_after` cursor, and that cursor is carried as externalized scan state — so a scan resumes cleanly across batch boundaries with no duplicated and no dropped documents, even across millions of hits. The `flavor` option selects the correct PIT dialect for OpenSearch versus Elasticsearch. See the [Elasticsearch documentation](https://www.elastic.co/docs) and the [OpenSearch documentation](https://opensearch.org/docs/latest/) for cluster-side details.

Reads support projection pushdown (only the requested fields are fetched via `_source` filtering), predicate pushdown (`term`, `terms`, `range`, and `exists` filters are compiled into the query DSL), a raw query-DSL escape hatch for anything more advanced, explicit `sort`, and basic-auth or API-key credentials. Every row carries the document `_id` and relevance `_score` alongside one typed column per source field. Typical use cases include exploring and aggregating log or product indices, joining search hits against local DuckDB tables or Parquet files, and exporting filtered subsets — for example projecting `name` and `price` from a `products` index, keeping only rows where `price` exceeds a threshold, and ordering by price. See the `es_search` function's examples for ready-to-run queries, and browse the `es_type_mapping` view to see how each Elasticsearch field type becomes a DuckDB column type.

example_queries.description: Bind the column schema for the products index from an explicit fields spec: the _id/_score meta columns plus one typed column per declared source field.
example_queries.sql: DESCRIBE SELECT _id, _score, name, price FROM elasticsearch.main.es_search('http://localhost:9200', 'products', fields => 'name:keyword,price:double');

tags.vgi.doc_md:
# elasticsearch.main

Elasticsearch and OpenSearch search over Apache Arrow. This schema turns a live cluster index into a SQL table you can read, filter, join, and export directly from DuckDB.

## Capabilities

- **Consistent deep pagination** using a Point-In-Time snapshot plus a `search_after` cursor carried as externalized scan state, so a scan resumes cleanly across batch boundaries with no duplicated or dropped documents.
- **Projection and predicate pushdown**: only requested fields are fetched via `_source` filtering, and `term`/`terms`/`range`/`exists` filters compile into the query DSL, with a raw query-DSL escape hatch for anything more advanced.
- **Both dialects and authentication**: the OpenSearch and Elasticsearch PIT dialects, plus basic-auth and API-key credentials.

## When to use it

Reach for this schema to explore or aggregate log and product indices, join search hits against local DuckDB tables or Parquet files, or export filtered subsets — without writing application code.

# es_type_mapping

A cluster-free reference view: one row per Elasticsearch/OpenSearch field type, giving the DuckDB column type `es_search` emits for it. Use it to predict a column's type before you run a search.

| ES type family | DuckDB type |
|---|---|
| `keyword`, `text`, `ip`, … | `VARCHAR` |
| `long`, `integer`, `short`, `byte` | `BIGINT` |
| `double`, `float`, `half_float` | `DOUBLE` |
| `boolean` | `BOOLEAN` |

| `object`, `nested`, `geo_*` | `VARCHAR` (raw JSON) |

Opens a Point-In-Time and pages through every matching document with search_after for consistent, resumable deep pagination over millions of hits. tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
The result always begins with two meta columns, then adds one column per indexed source field (from the explicit `fields` spec, or the introspected index mapping when `fields` is omitted). The per-field DuckDB type follows the `es_type_mapping` reference view.

## Always-present meta columns

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `_id` | VARCHAR | The Elasticsearch/OpenSearch document `_id`. Always present. |
| `_score` | DOUBLE | The relevance score for the hit; NULL when sorting suppresses scoring. Always present. |

## Source columns (example: `fields => 'name:keyword,price:double,created:date,meta:object'`)

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | VARCHAR | An ES `keyword`/`text` field. |
| `price` | DOUBLE | An ES `double`/`float` field. |
| `created` | TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE | An ES `date`/`date_nanos` field, parsed to a UTC microsecond timestamp. |
| `meta` | VARCHAR | An ES `object`/`nested`/`geo_*` field, surfaced as raw JSON text. |

workers.doc_md:
# VGI Elements

Periodic-table and isotope reference data that runs entirely offline: every value is bundled in the worker, so queries are deterministic and need no network or key.

## What you can do

- Look up element properties by atomic number, symbol or name, and normalize messy element columns.
- Compute molar masses of formulas such as `CuSO4·5H2O` or `K4[Fe(CN)6]`, and their mass percent.
- Explore isotopes and natural abundances, joined to the elements on `atomic_number`.

## Caveats

Atomic masses are in g/mol. For the twelve elements IUPAC publishes as an interval (H, Li, B, C, N, O, Mg, Si, S, Cl, Br, Tl) the worker uses IUPAC's conventional single value; for radioactive elements without a standard atomic weight it uses the longest-lived isotope's mass. Group, period and block are derived from the atomic number. Superheavy-element properties are sparse or predicted. NIST's table is the vintage published on its site and can lag the latest IUPAC revisions.

## Sources and references

- [PubChem Periodic Table](https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/periodic-table/) (NCBI/NLM): element properties.
- [NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions](https://www.nist.gov/pml/atomic-weights-and-isotopic-compositions-relative-atomic-masses): isotope masses, compositions and standard atomic weights.
- [IUPAC CIAAW](https://www.ciaaw.org/atomic-weights.htm): conventional atomic weights.

example_queries.description: Symbols of the first ten elements
example_queries.sql: SELECT z, elements.main.element_symbol(z) AS symbol FROM range(1, 11) t(z) ORDER BY z

example_queries.description: Name of element 118
example_queries.sql: SELECT elements.main.element_name(118) AS name

example_queries.description: Normalize symbols to names
example_queries.sql: SELECT s, elements.main.element_name(s) AS name FROM (VALUES ('fe'), ('AU'), ('Na')) t(s) ORDER BY s

example_queries.description: Atomic mass of iron
example_queries.sql: SELECT elements.main.atomic_mass(26) AS iron

example_queries.description: Ratio of gold's atomic mass to silver's
example_queries.sql: SELECT elements.main.atomic_mass('Au') / elements.main.atomic_mass('Ag') AS gold_to_silver

example_queries.description: Atomic number of oganesson
example_queries.sql: SELECT elements.main.atomic_number('oganesson') AS z

example_queries.description: Molar masses of water, aspirin and copper sulfate pentahydrate
example_queries.sql: SELECT f, round(elements.main.formula_mass(f), 3) AS g_per_mol FROM (VALUES ('H2O'), ('C9H8O4'), ('CuSO4·5H2O')) t(f) ORDER BY f

example_queries.description: Moles of sodium chloride in one kilogram
example_queries.sql: SELECT round(1000 / elements.main.formula_mass('NaCl'), 2) AS mol_per_kg

example_queries.description: Mass percent of each element in aspirin
example_queries.sql: SELECT element, count, round(100 * mass_fraction, 2) AS mass_percent FROM elements.main.formula_composition('C9H8O4') ORDER BY mass_percent DESC

example_queries.description: Atom counts of copper sulfate pentahydrate
example_queries.sql: SELECT element, count FROM elements.main.formula_composition('CuSO4·5H2O') ORDER BY element

example_queries.description: Natural isotopes of carbon and their abundance
example_queries.sql: SELECT nuclide, isotopic_composition FROM elements.main.isotopes WHERE symbol = 'C' AND isotopic_composition IS NOT NULL ORDER BY mass_number

example_queries.description: Elements with the most naturally occurring isotopes
example_queries.sql: SELECT e.symbol, count(*) AS natural_isotopes FROM elements.main.isotopes i JOIN elements.main.elements e USING (atomic_number) WHERE i.isotopic_composition IS NOT NULL GROUP BY e.symbol ORDER BY natural_isotopes DESC, e.symbol LIMIT 3

example_queries.description: The noble gases with their atomic masses
example_queries.sql: SELECT symbol, name, atomic_mass FROM elements.main.elements WHERE group_number = 18 ORDER BY atomic_number

example_queries.description: Element count and mean electronegativity per block
example_queries.sql: SELECT block, count(*) AS elements, round(avg(electronegativity_pauling), 2) AS avg_en FROM elements.main.elements GROUP BY block ORDER BY block

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The only schema of the elements worker. Start with the elements table (one row per element, key atomic_number, unique symbol) or the isotopes table (key atomic_number + mass_number) and join them on atomic_number. The lookup scalars accept a column and are vectorized; the numeric overloads take an atomic number, the text overloads a symbol or English name in any case. Scalars have no named arguments. Use formula_mass for one molar mass per row, and formula_composition(formula) for an element-by-element breakdown of one constant formula.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

Everything the worker exposes lives here: two bundled reference tables, element lookups and formula math.

Tables are read by name with no arguments and join on `atomic_number`. Scalars work on whole columns, so they also clean up and join free-text element data.

All values are a fixed offline snapshot of PubChem and NIST data; see the catalog documentation for how atomic masses are chosen.

tables.comment: Every nuclide in NIST's Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions table (3,352 isotopes) with relative atomic mass and natural abundance; bundled offline.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per nuclide, keyed by (atomic_number, mass_number); nuclide ('Fe-56') is also unique. relative_atomic_mass is NIST's mass in u with its uncertainty; relative_atomic_mass_estimated marks values NIST derives from systematic trends ('#'). isotopic_composition is the representative natural mole fraction, NULL for isotopes with no natural abundance; summing it per element gives about 1. tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Isotope Table

One row per nuclide, keyed by (atomic_number, mass_number); nuclide ('Fe-56') is also unique. relative_atomic_mass is NIST's mass in u with its uncertainty; relative_atomic_mass_estimated marks values NIST derives from systematic trends ('#'). isotopic_composition is the representative natural mole fraction, NULL for isotopes with no natural abundance; summing it per element gives about 1. NIST does not flag stability, so a NULL composition does not by itself mean an isotope is unstable. Deuterium (D) and tritium (T) appear as H-2 and H-3. Join to elements on atomic_number.

### Columns

| Column | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| atomic_number | INTEGER | Atomic number Z: count of protons in the nucleus; joins to elements.atomic_number. |
| symbol | VARCHAR | Element symbol (deuterium and tritium are listed under 'H'). |
| mass_number | INTEGER | Mass number A (protons + neutrons). |
| nuclide | VARCHAR | Nuclide label symbol-A, e.g. 'Fe-56', 'H-2'. Unique. |
| relative_atomic_mass | DOUBLE | NIST relative atomic mass of the nuclide in u (Da). |
| relative_atomic_mass_uncertainty | DOUBLE | Standard uncertainty of relative_atomic_mass in u; 0 for C-12, which is exact by definition. |
| relative_atomic_mass_estimated | BOOLEAN | True when NIST marks the mass '#' (estimated from systematic trends, not measured). |
| isotopic_composition | DOUBLE | Representative terrestrial isotopic composition as a mole fraction 0-1; NULL when the nuclide has no representative natural abundance (most radioactive isotopes). |
| isotopic_composition_uncertainty | DOUBLE | Standard uncertainty of isotopic_composition, in mole-fraction units (0-1); NULL when absent. |
| is_most_abundant | BOOLEAN | True for the isotope with the largest isotopic_composition of its element (false for elements with none). |

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT nuclide, isotopic_composition FROM elements.main.isotopes WHERE symbol = 'C' AND isotopic_composition IS NOT NULL ORDER BY mass_number

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT e.symbol, count(*) AS natural_isotopes FROM elements.main.isotopes i JOIN elements.main.elements e USING (atomic_number) WHERE i.isotopic_composition IS NOT NULL GROUP BY e.symbol ORDER BY natural_isotopes DESC, e.symbol LIMIT 3

vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT nuclide, isotopic_composition FROM elements.main.isotopes WHERE symbol = 'C' AND isotopic_composition IS NOT NULL ORDER BY mass_number
vgi.executable_examples.description: Natural isotopes of carbon and their abundance

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per element, Z = 1 (hydrogen) to 118 (oganesson), keyed by atomic_number; symbol is also unique. atomic_mass is a `DOUBLE` in g/mol suitable for arithmetic; standard_atomic_weight keeps NIST's published text with its uncertainty or interval. group_number, period and block are derived from Z (lanthanides and actinides have NULL group). tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Periodic Table

One row per element, Z = 1 (hydrogen) to 118 (oganesson), keyed by atomic_number; symbol is also unique. atomic_mass is a `DOUBLE` in g/mol suitable for arithmetic; standard_atomic_weight keeps NIST's published text with its uncertainty or interval. group_number, period and block are derived from Z (lanthanides and actinides have NULL group). Physical properties (electronegativity, radius, ionization energy, melting/boiling point in K, density in g/cm3, oxidation states, discovery year, CPK colour) come from PubChem; superheavy-element values are often NULL or predicted (properties_predicted). Data is a fixed bundled snapshot; no network is used.

### Columns

| Column | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| atomic_number | INTEGER | Atomic number Z (proton count), 1-118. Primary key. |
| symbol | VARCHAR | IUPAC chemical symbol, case-sensitive ('Fe'). |
| name | VARCHAR | English element name as published by PubChem ('Iron', 'Aluminum', 'Cesium'). |
| atomic_mass | DOUBLE | Atomic mass in g/mol (Da): see atomic_mass_basis. Fe = 55.845, C = 12.011 (conventional). |
| atomic_mass_basis | VARCHAR | Where atomic_mass comes from: 'standard_atomic_weight' (NIST value), 'conventional_atomic_weight' (IUPAC conventional value for interval elements) or 'longest_lived_isotope' (no stable isotopes). |
| standard_atomic_weight | VARCHAR | NIST standard atomic weight as published: '55.845(2)' (uncertainty in last digits), an interval '[12.0096,12.0116]', or '[98]' (mass number of the longest-lived isotope); NULL when none is assigned. |
| atomic_weight_notes | VARCHAR[] | NIST/IUPAC footnotes on the atomic weight: 'g' geologically exceptional samples, 'm' modified isotopic compositions in commercial material, 'r' range in natural composition. Empty when none. |
| group_number | INTEGER | IUPAC group 1-18 (derived from Z). NULL for the lanthanides (La-Lu) and actinides (Ac-Lr). |
| period | INTEGER | Period (row) 1-7, derived from Z. |
| block | VARCHAR | Periodic-table block 's', 'p', 'd' or 'f' (derived; La-Lu and Ac-Lr are 'f', matching group_number). |
| group_block | VARCHAR | PubChem category: 'Alkali metal', 'Alkaline earth metal', 'Transition metal', 'Post-transition metal', 'Metalloid', 'Nonmetal', 'Halogen', 'Noble gas', 'Lanthanide' or 'Actinide'. |
| electron_configuration | VARCHAR | Ground-state electron configuration, e.g. '[Ar]4s2 3d6'. |
| electronegativity_pauling | DOUBLE | Electronegativity on the dimensionless Pauling scale (fluorine 3.98); NULL where not measured. |
| atomic_radius_pm | DOUBLE | Atomic (van der Waals) radius in picometres, as given by PubChem. |
| ionization_energy_ev | DOUBLE | First ionization energy in electronvolts. |
| electron_affinity_ev | DOUBLE | Electron affinity in electronvolts; NULL where unknown. |
| oxidation_states | INTEGER[] | Common oxidation states (formal charge per atom, an integer count of electrons) as published by PubChem, e.g. [3, 2] for iron; NULL if none listed. |
| standard_state | VARCHAR | State at standard conditions: 'Solid', 'Liquid' or 'Gas' (expected state for superheavy elements). |
| properties_predicted | BOOLEAN | True when PubChem marks the state or electron configuration as predicted/expected (superheavies). |
| melting_point_k | DOUBLE | Melting point in kelvin. |
| boiling_point_k | DOUBLE | Boiling point in kelvin. |
| density | DOUBLE | Density in g/cm3 at standard conditions (gases too, so hydrogen is 0.00008988). |
| year_discovered | INTEGER | Year of discovery; NULL for elements known since antiquity (see discovered_in_antiquity). |
| discovered_in_antiquity | BOOLEAN | True for elements PubChem lists as discovered in 'Ancient' times. |
| cpk_hex_color | VARCHAR | CPK/Jmol molecular-model colour as 6 hex digits, e.g. 'E06633'; NULL if none. |

functions.name: formula_composition
functions.comment: Break a chemical formula into elements with atom counts and mass fractions

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Parse a chemical formula and return one row per element, in order of first appearance, with columns element, atomic_number, count (`BIGINT` atoms per formula unit), atomic_mass, mass (count * atomic_mass, g/mol) and mass_fraction (0-1, summing to 1). Groups in (), [] or {} multiply by their subscript; hydrate parts after '·', '*' or '.' are added with their coefficient, so 'CuSO4·5H2O' gives Cu 1, S 1, O 9, H 10. Symbols are case-sensitive. An invalid formula raises an error that names the problem and its position. sum(mass) equals formula_mass(formula). Multiply mass_fraction by 100 for mass percent.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## formula_composition(formula)

Elemental breakdown of a formula: atom counts, g/mol per element and mass fraction.

| Column | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| element | Element symbol. |
| atomic_number | Atomic number. |
| count | Atoms of the element per formula unit. |
| atomic_mass | Atomic mass in g/mol. |
| mass | count * atomic_mass in g/mol. |
| mass_fraction | Share of the formula mass, 0-1. |

functions.name: formula_mass
functions.comment: Molar mass in g/mol of a chemical formula: formula_mass('H2O') returns about 18.015

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Compute the molar mass (g/mol, `DOUBLE`) of a chemical formula by summing atomic_mass over its atoms. Supports nested (), [] and {} groups with subscripts, a leading coefficient ('2H2O'), and hydrates joined by '·', '*' or '.' with their own coefficient ('CuSO4·5H2O', 'CuSO4*5H2O'). Symbols are case-sensitive ('Co' is cobalt, 'CO' carbon monoxide). Charges, isotope labels (D, 13C) and fractional subscripts are not supported. An invalid formula returns NULL instead of failing the query; call formula_composition(formula) to see the error. Examples: H2O = 18.015, C9H8O4 (aspirin) = 180.159.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## formula_mass(formula)

Molar mass in g/mol. `formula_mass('C9H8O4')` is about 180.16.

Handles parentheses and brackets, coefficients and hydrates. Returns NULL for invalid input; `formula_composition` reports the reason.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT f, round(elements.main.formula_mass(f), 3) AS g_per_mol FROM (VALUES ('H2O'), ('C9H8O4'), ('CuSO4·5H2O')) t(f) ORDER BY f

vgi.example_queries.description: Moles of sodium chloride in one kilogram
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT round(1000 / elements.main.formula_mass('NaCl'), 2) AS mol_per_kg

workers.doc_md:
# Local Text Embeddings & Semantic Search in SQL

![fastembed logo](https://qdrant.tech/images/logo_with_text.png)

**Turn text into vector embeddings directly in DuckDB SQL** — generate fixed-length `FLOAT[]` embedding vectors and score them with cosine similarity for semantic search, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and nearest-neighbor ranking, all without leaving your query and without sending a single byte to an external API.

The **embed** extension brings sentence-transformer text embeddings to SQL for data engineers, RAG builders, and search teams who want vector search inside the database instead of a separate embedding service. Embeddings are computed **entirely in-process and offline** — there is no torch dependency, no GPU requirement, and no network call after the one-time model download — so the same query runs identically on a laptop, in CI, and in production.

Under the hood it is powered by [fastembed](https://github.com/qdrant/fastembed) from [Qdrant](https://qdrant.tech) (Apache-2.0), which runs quantized sentence-transformer models through [ONNX Runtime](https://onnxruntime.ai) ([source](https://github.com/microsoft/onnxruntime)). The configured default model is `BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5` (384-dimensional), downloaded on first use and cached locally. Set `VGI_EMBED_DEFAULT_MODEL` before startup to change it, or pass a model as the second argument to each embedding function. Use the same model for queries and documents. Vectors are returned over Apache Arrow as native DuckDB `FLOAT[]` lists, ready to index and rank with the [DuckDB VSS extension](https://duckdb.org/docs/extensions/vss.html).

## How it works

There are two embedding modes. *Symmetric* embedding maps any text to a vector for text-to-text comparison (dedup, clustering, classification). *Asymmetric* retrieval follows the query/passage convention these models are trained on: a short search query and a longer document are embedded with slightly different instruction prefixes so they land in the same space, which improves recall over plain symmetric embedding. Ranking is then just cosine similarity between vectors -- pure arithmetic, no model load. Model discovery and dimension lookups let you size a vector column or VSS index ahead of time.

```sql
-- A sentence is more similar to itself than to an unrelated one
SELECT embed.similarity(embed.embed('cat'), embed.embed('kitten')) AS score;
```

NULL or empty input text yields a NULL vector, and the model is loaded once and amortized across every row in a scan.

example_queries.description: Embed text into a FLOAT[] vector and check its length.
example_queries.sql: SELECT len(embed.main.embed('hello world')) AS dim

example_queries.description: Embed text with an explicitly chosen model.
example_queries.sql: SELECT len(embed.main.embed('hello world', 'BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5')) AS dim

example_queries.description: Score how related two short texts are (rounded for stable output).
example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(embed.main.similarity(embed.main.embed('cat'), embed.main.embed('kitten')), 3) AS score

example_queries.description: Rank a passage against a search query (asymmetric retrieval).
example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(embed.main.similarity(embed.main.embed_query('how do I reset my password'), embed.main.embed_passage('Reset your password in account settings.')), 3) AS score

example_queries.description: Look up the default model's vector dimension.
example_queries.sql: SELECT embed.main.embedding_dim('BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5') AS dim

example_queries.description: List the supported models and their dimensions.
example_queries.sql: SELECT model, dim FROM embed.main.supported_models() ORDER BY model

example_queries.description: Semantic search: embed the question once with embed_query, embed each corpus passage with embed_passage, rank by similarity and keep the top 2 (both password-help passages).
example_queries.sql: WITH docs(id, body) AS (VALUES (1, 'Reset your password from the account settings page.'), (2, 'Our office is closed on public holidays.'), (3, 'Invoices are emailed on the first day of each month.'), (4, 'Forgot your login? Use the password recovery link to sign in again.')), q AS (SELECT embed.main.embed_query('how do I reset my password') AS v) SELECT d.id, d.body, ROUND(embed.main.similarity(q.v, embed.main.embed_passage(d.body)), 3) AS score FROM docs AS d CROSS JOIN q ORDER BY score DESC, d.id LIMIT 2

example_queries.description: Zero-shot classification: embed each support ticket and each candidate label, then pick the label with the highest similarity per ticket (bug report / billing problem / feature request).
example_queries.sql: WITH tickets(ticket) AS (VALUES ('The app crashes every time I open the settings screen.'), ('I was charged twice for my subscription this month.'), ('Could you add a dark mode option?')), labels(label) AS (VALUES ('bug report'), ('billing problem'), ('feature request')) SELECT t.ticket, arg_max(l.label, embed.main.similarity(embed.main.embed(t.ticket), embed.main.embed(l.label))) AS label FROM tickets AS t CROSS JOIN labels AS l GROUP BY t.ticket ORDER BY t.ticket

example_queries.description: Near-duplicate detection: embed every title once, self-join the vectors and keep pairs whose similarity exceeds 0.8 (the two paraphrase pairs; the unrelated title matches nothing).
example_queries.sql: WITH titles(id, title) AS (VALUES (1, 'How to reset a forgotten password'), (2, 'Steps for resetting your lost password'), (3, 'Quarterly revenue grew by twelve percent'), (4, 'Revenue increased 12% this quarter'), (5, 'Best hiking trails near Denver')), v AS (SELECT id, title, embed.main.embed(title) AS vec FROM titles) SELECT a.title AS title_a, b.title AS title_b, ROUND(embed.main.similarity(a.vec, b.vec), 3) AS score FROM v AS a JOIN v AS b ON a.id < b.id WHERE embed.main.similarity(a.vec, b.vec) > 0.8 ORDER BY score DESC, a.id

example_queries.description: List the supported embedding models and their dimensions.
example_queries.sql: SELECT model, dim FROM embed.main.supported_models ORDER BY model

example_queries.description: Dimension of the default model.

example_queries.description: Dimension of the default model.
example_queries.sql: SELECT dim FROM embed.main.supported_models() WHERE model = 'BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5'

example_queries.description: Score how similar two embeddings are (rounded for stable output).
example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(embed.main.similarity(embed.main.embed('dog'), embed.main.embed('puppy')), 3) AS related

example_queries.description: Confirm a related pair ranks above an unrelated pair.
example_queries.sql: SELECT embed.main.similarity(embed.main.embed('dog'), embed.main.embed('puppy')) > embed.main.similarity(embed.main.embed('dog'), embed.main.embed('airplane')) AS related_wins

example_queries.sql: SELECT len(embed.main.embed_query('how do I reset my password')) AS dim

example_queries.sql: SELECT len(embed.main.embed_query('how do I reset my password', 'BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5')) AS dim

example_queries.sql: SELECT embed.main.embedding_dim('') AS dim;

## embed.main schema

The single schema of the embed worker. It groups the local text-embedding and vector-similarity surface into a few concepts: symmetric text-to-text embedding, the asymmetric query/passage convention used for retrieval, a pure-arithmetic cosine-similarity score, and model-discovery/dimension helpers for sizing vector columns and indexes.

Everything runs in-process via fastembed/ONNX (no torch, no network after the one-time model download). Use it to build semantic search and RAG pipelines that store and rank vectors with DuckDB VSS, all in SQL.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# embed.main

Local text-embedding and cosine-similarity functions over Apache Arrow, for semantic search and RAG with DuckDB.

## Overview

This schema holds the worker's scalar embedding and similarity helpers plus a model-discovery table. Embeddings are generated locally with fastembed on ONNX Runtime; the default model is `BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5` (384-dim). All three embedding functions accept a model as their second positional argument; `VGI_EMBED_DEFAULT_MODEL` sets the shared default before startup. Symmetric embedding is for text-to-text comparison; the query/passage pair is for asymmetric retrieval.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT embed.similarity(embed.embed('cat'), embed.embed('kitten')) AS score;
```

## Notes

- Use the query/passage pair for retrieval; use plain symmetric embedding for text-to-text comparison.
- NULL or empty text yields a NULL vector.

## supported_models()

List every embedding model the worker can use, one `(model, dim)` pair per row. Takes no arguments.

**When to use.** Use it to discover the valid values for the second argument of `embed(text, model)` (and for `embedding_dim(model)`) and to see each model's output dimension before you size a vector column or VSS index.

**Output.** Columns: `model` (`VARCHAR` -- the name to pass to `embed`/`embedding_dim`) and `dim` (`INTEGER` -- the `FLOAT[]` length the model produces). One row per supported model.

**Edge cases.** This is a discovery table function -- reference it in the query's table position, `embed.main.supported_models()`, rather than as a scalar. A parenthesis-free `supported_models` view exposes the same rows for plain browsing. Runnable, catalog-qualified examples are attached as example queries.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## similarity(a, b)

Compute the **cosine similarity** of two `FLOAT[]` vectors, a value in `[-1, 1]` where 1 means identical direction. This is pure arithmetic -- it loads no model and does no I/O -- so it is cheap to call over large joins.

**When to use.** Use it to rank or threshold embedding pairs: `ORDER BY similarity(embed_query(q), embed_passage(doc)) DESC` for retrieval, or a `WHERE similarity(...) > 0.8` cutoff for dedup/near-duplicate detection.

**Input/output.** Inputs: two `FLOAT[]` vectors (typically from `embed*`). Output: one `DOUBLE` per row. NULL, empty, or length-mismatched vector pairs yield NULL rather than an error.

**Edge cases.** A zero vector has undefined direction and yields NULL; vectors must be the same length to be comparable.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# similarity(a, b)

Cosine similarity of two `FLOAT[]` vectors, in `[-1, 1]` (pure arithmetic, no model).

## Usage

Feed two `FLOAT[]` vectors (typically from the `embed*` functions) to `similarity(a, b)` to get a `DOUBLE` in `[-1, 1]`; order retrieval candidates by it descending, or threshold it (e.g. `> 0.8`) for near-duplicate detection. Runnable, catalog-qualified examples are attached as example queries.

## Notes

- 1.0 = identical direction, 0 = orthogonal, -1 = opposite.
- NULL / empty / length-mismatch returns NULL.

## embed_query(text [, model])

Embed a *search query* for retrieval, applying the selected model's recommended query instruction prefix (for bge: `Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: `). This is the query side of asymmetric retrieval.

**When to use.** Use `embed_query` for the short user query and `embed_passage` for the corpus documents, then rank passages by `similarity(embed_query(q), embed_passage(doc))`. The prefix nudges the query vector toward the passages that answer it, improving recall over a plain symmetric `embed`.

**Input/output.** Input: one `VARCHAR` query per row and an optional constant `VARCHAR` model as the second positional argument. Output: one `FLOAT[]` per row (NULL/empty -> NULL), with the selected model's dimension. Omitting the model or passing an empty string uses `BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5`. Set `VGI_EMBED_DEFAULT_MODEL` before worker startup to change the default.

**Edge cases.** Use the same model for queries and passages; matching dimensions alone do not make embeddings compatible. Models without a query instruction prefix embed queries as-is.

## embed_passage(text [, model])

Embed a *document/passage* for retrieval. For bge-style retrieval models, passages get **no** instruction prefix (only queries do), and this function mirrors that convention exactly.

**When to use.** Use `embed_passage` for the corpus side of asymmetric retrieval and `embed_query` for the user query, then rank with `similarity(embed_query(q), embed_passage(doc))`. Pre-compute passage vectors once and store them (e.g. in a DuckDB VSS HNSW index).

**Input/output.** Input: one `VARCHAR` passage per row and an optional constant `VARCHAR` model as the second positional argument. Output: one `FLOAT[]` per row (NULL/empty -> NULL), with the selected model's dimension. Omitting the model or passing an empty string uses `BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5`. Set `VGI_EMBED_DEFAULT_MODEL` before worker startup to change the default. Use the same model for queries and passages.

**Edge cases.** Numerically this equals plain `embed` for bge (passages have no prefix); it exists as a named counterpart to `embed_query` so retrieval pipelines read symmetrically.
tags.vgi.doc_md:

## embed(text, model)

The two-argument arity overload of `embed`: embed text into a `FLOAT[]` vector using an *explicit* model name instead of the default. Call `supported_models()` to discover valid model names and their output dimensions.

**When to use.** Use this when you need a specific model -- a larger model for higher recall, or a model whose dimension matches an existing vector index. Otherwise use the one-argument `embed(text)`.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## embedding_dim(model)

Return the output dimension (the `FLOAT[]` length) a model produces, **without** loading the model or embedding anything. Pass `''` or NULL to get the default model's dimension.

**When to use.** Use it to size a vector column or index ahead of time (e.g. an `ARRAY[FLOAT, N]` / VSS HNSW index), or to validate that a chosen model matches an existing index width before re-embedding a corpus.

**Input/output.** Input: a `VARCHAR` model name (`''`/NULL = default). Output: `INTEGER` dimension, or NULL for an unknown model name (it does not raise).

**Edge cases.** Unknown model names return NULL rather than erroring, so a dirty model column won't abort a scan.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# embedding_dim(model)

Output dimension (vector length) for a model name -- `''`/NULL = the default model. No model is loaded.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT embed.embedding_dim('BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5');  -- 384
SELECT embed.embedding_dim('');                        -- default model dim
```

## Notes

- Unknown model name -> NULL (no error).
- Use to size a vector column / VSS index before embedding.

workers.doc_md:
## First Trust ETFs

First Trust US ETF data, exposed as DuckDB tables and a table function.

The **fund** is the unit of the data and is keyed by an exchange `ticker` (e.g. `FTCS`) — begin at the catalog to discover that key, then drill into a fund's deeper facts or its holdings. Holdings are the current published portfolio (First Trust does not publish historical holdings).

### Sources

- [First Trust ETF list](https://www.ftportfolios.com/retail/etf/etflist.aspx) — the fund lineup the catalog is read from.
- [Example fund summary (FTCS)](https://www.ftportfolios.com/Retail/Etf/EtfSummary.aspx?Ticker=FTCS) — the per-fund summary pages behind fund_details (holdings come from the matching EtfHoldings page).
- [First Trust legal information](https://www.ftportfolios.com/retail/legal.aspx) — terms that govern use of the site's data.

Data is provided for informational use; review First Trust's terms before redistribution.

example_queries.description: Top holdings of FTCS
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, ticker, weight_percent FROM firsttrust.main.holdings WHERE fund_ticker = 'FTCS' ORDER BY weight_percent DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: The three largest positions of every Alternative fund, with the fund's name — products picks the funds by category and holdings supplies their positions (futures, cash and fund-of-fund lines included)
example_queries.sql: SELECT p.ticker, p.fund_name, h.name, h.weight_percent FROM firsttrust.main.products p JOIN firsttrust.main.holdings h ON h.fund_ticker = p.ticker WHERE p.category = 'Alternative Funds' QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY p.ticker ORDER BY h.weight_percent DESC) <= 3 ORDER BY p.ticker, h.weight_percent DESC

example_queries.description: Reconcile FTCS's published holdings with its fund facts: reported holding count vs listed lines (which include cash), and the holdings' total market value as a percent of net assets

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Detailed portfolio holdings for First Trust ETFs as a hive-partitioned table. It is partitioned by fund_ticker (the FUND's ticker, distinct from the constituent `ticker` column): filter `WHERE fund_ticker = '…'` (or `fund_ticker IN (…)`) to pick funds, or scan with no filter to stream EVERY fund's holdings (~300 funds — slow, so prefer a filter). Rows come back weight-descending; weight_percent is in percent points (2.59 = 2.59%). Join on fund_ticker to products.ticker for fund-level facts.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## holdings

Detailed fund holdings as a **hive-partitioned table**, partitioned by `fund_ticker` (the fund's ticker). `fund_ticker` is distinct from `ticker` (the constituent's own ticker). Filter `WHERE fund_ticker = 'FTCS'` for one fund's holdings (see the example queries).

`WHERE fund_ticker IN ('FTCS','AIRR')` fans out per partition; an unfiltered scan streams every fund (~300 partitions — slow). First Trust publishes **current holdings only** (no historical dates). `weight_percent` is in percent points (2.59 = 2.59%).

workers.doc_md:
## Global X ETFs

Global X US ETF data, exposed as DuckDB tables.

The **fund** is the unit of the data and is keyed by an exchange `ticker` (e.g. `QYLD`) — begin at the catalog to discover that key, then drill into a fund's holdings. Holdings are the current published portfolio (Global X does not publish historical holdings).

### Sources

- [Global X ETF explorer](https://www.globalxetfs.com/explore) — the fund lineup the catalog is read from.
- [Example fund page (QYLD)](https://www.globalxetfs.com/funds/qyld) — a per-fund page with the facts and holdings exposed here.

Data is provided for informational use; review Global X's terms before redistribution.

example_queries.title: largest_etfs
example_queries.description: The largest Global X ETFs by net assets
example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, fund_name, net_assets FROM globalx.main.products ORDER BY net_assets DESC LIMIT 5;

example_queries.title: top_holdings
example_queries.description: The top holdings of the Global X Nasdaq 100 Covered Call ETF
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, ticker, weight_percent FROM globalx.main.holdings WHERE fund_ticker = 'QYLD' ORDER BY weight_percent DESC LIMIT 5;

example_queries.description: Ten largest Global X ETFs by net assets
example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, fund_name, net_assets FROM globalx.main.products ORDER BY net_assets DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Top holdings of QYLD
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, ticker, weight_percent FROM globalx.main.holdings WHERE fund_ticker = 'QYLD' ORDER BY weight_percent DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Join a fund's catalog facts to its top holdings (fund_ticker = products.ticker)
example_queries.sql: SELECT p.fund_name, p.net_assets, h.name AS holding, h.weight_percent FROM globalx.main.products p JOIN globalx.main.holdings h ON h.fund_ticker = p.ticker WHERE p.ticker = 'QYLD' ORDER BY h.weight_percent DESC LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: The ten Global X ETFs with the largest dollar position in NVIDIA, with each fund's name and sub-theme from products (scans every fund's holdings, so it takes a few seconds)
example_queries.sql: SELECT h.fund_ticker, p.fund_name, p.sub_theme, h.weight_percent, h.market_value FROM globalx.main.holdings h JOIN globalx.main.products p ON p.ticker = h.fund_ticker WHERE h.ticker = 'NVDA' ORDER BY h.market_value DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Portfolio overlap of QYLD (Nasdaq-100) and XYLD (S&P 500): how many constituents both hold (matched on SEDOL) and the overlap weight, the sum of the smaller weight of each shared holding
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS shared_constituents, round(sum(least(q.weight_percent, x.weight_percent)), 2) AS overlap_weight_percent FROM globalx.main.holdings q JOIN globalx.main.holdings x ON x.sedol = q.sedol WHERE q.fund_ticker = 'QYLD' AND x.fund_ticker = 'XYLD' AND q.sedol <> ''

example_queries.description: The most concentrated Thematic ETFs: weight in each fund's top 10 ticker-bearing holdings (cash and other untickered lines excluded), its number of such holdings, and its gross expense ratio (scans every fund's holdings, so it takes a few seconds)
example_queries.sql: WITH ranked AS (SELECT fund_ticker, weight_percent, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY fund_ticker ORDER BY weight_percent DESC) AS rnk FROM globalx.main.holdings WHERE ticker IS NOT NULL) SELECT p.ticker, p.fund_name, p.gross_expense_ratio_percent, count(*) AS constituents, round(sum(r.weight_percent) FILTER (WHERE r.rnk <= 10), 2) AS top10_weight_percent FROM globalx.main.products p JOIN ranked r ON r.fund_ticker = p.ticker WHERE p.sub_theme = 'Thematic' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY top10_weight_percent DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: The largest positions of the Copper Miners ETF
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, weight_percent, market_value FROM globalx.main.holdings WHERE fund_ticker = 'COPX' ORDER BY weight_percent DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Two funds at once (partition fan-out)
example_queries.sql: SELECT fund_ticker, name, weight_percent FROM globalx.main.holdings WHERE fund_ticker IN ('QYLD', 'COPX')

example_queries.description: Cheapest funds by gross expense ratio
example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, fund_name, gross_expense_ratio_percent FROM globalx.main.products ORDER BY gross_expense_ratio_percent LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Look up a single fund by ticker
example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, fund_name, gross_expense_ratio_percent FROM globalx.main.products WHERE ticker = 'QYLD'

example_queries.description: Top 10 holdings of QYLD, passing the fund ticker as the argument
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, weight_percent FROM globalx.main.holdings_scan(fund_ticker => 'QYLD') ORDER BY weight_percent DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Two funds at once via a pushed IN filter on the no-argument scan
example_queries.sql: SELECT fund_ticker, count(*) FROM globalx.main.holdings_scan() WHERE fund_ticker IN ('QYLD', 'COPX') GROUP BY fund_ticker

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Detailed portfolio holdings for Global X ETFs as a hive-partitioned table. It is partitioned by fund_ticker (the FUND's ticker, distinct from the constituent `ticker` column): filter `WHERE fund_ticker = '…'` (or `fund_ticker IN (…)`) to pick funds, or scan with no filter to stream EVERY fund's holdings (~116 funds — slow, so prefer a filter). Global X publishes CURRENT holdings only, so there is no historical as-of date; as_of_date is the published file's own date. Rows come back weight-descending; weight_percent is in percent points (0.74 = 0.74%). Join on fund_ticker to products.ticker for fund-level facts.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## holdings

Detailed fund holdings as a **hive-partitioned table**, partitioned by `fund_ticker` (the fund's ticker). `fund_ticker` is distinct from `ticker` (the constituent's own ticker). Filter `WHERE fund_ticker = 'QYLD'` for one fund's holdings (see the example queries).

`WHERE fund_ticker IN ('QYLD','COPX')` fans out per partition; an unfiltered scan streams every fund (~116 partitions — slow). Global X publishes **current holdings only** (no historical dates). `weight_percent` is in percent points (0.74 = 0.74%).

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## products

The Global X US ETF catalog as a base table — one row per fund. It takes no arguments; query it directly and filter with a WHERE clause (e.g. `WHERE theme = 'Fixed Income' ORDER BY net_assets DESC`; see the example queries). Percent columns (`*_percent`) are in **percent points** (a gross expense ratio of 0.60 means 0.60%). The ticker column is the key for the holdings table.
