tags.vgi.doc_llm: Functions that return Vanguard ETF data at two levels. At the catalog level you screen the whole lineup on key facts and resolve a fund's key. At the fund level you drill into one fund — its current holdings, its characteristics, and its distribution and NAV/price history. A fund is keyed by its exchange `ticker` (e.g. `VOO`); resolve the key at the catalog level first. Holdings are current-only (no historical as-of).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Vanguard fund data

Work happens at two levels. **Catalog level:** screen the lineup on key facts and find a fund's key. **Fund level:** drill into a single fund — its current constituents, characteristics, and time series. A fund is keyed by its exchange `ticker` (e.g. `VOO`).

Holdings are current-only: Vanguard reports one as-of date per fund, with no historical time travel.

vgi.example_queries.description: Cheapest Vanguard ETFs by expense ratio
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, long_name, expense_ratio_percent FROM vanguard.main.products ORDER BY expense_ratio_percent LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: Top holdings of VOO
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, name, weight_percent FROM vanguard.main.holdings WHERE fund_ticker = 'VOO' ORDER BY weight_percent DESC LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: Recent NAV history for VOO
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT as_of_date, nav FROM vanguard.main.nav_history('VOO', period := '1Y') ORDER BY as_of_date DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: NVIDIA's portfolio weight in four Vanguard equity ETFs alongside each fund's name and expense ratio (holdings joined to products); a fund that doesn't hold it (the value fund VTV) drops out
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT h.fund_ticker, p.long_name, p.expense_ratio_percent, h.holding_rank, h.weight_percent FROM vanguard.main.holdings h JOIN vanguard.main.products p ON p.ticker = h.fund_ticker WHERE h.fund_ticker IN ('VOO', 'VTI', 'VUG', 'VTV') AND h.ticker = 'NVDA' ORDER BY h.weight_percent DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Portfolio overlap between VOO and VUG: how many constituents they share and the overlapping weight (the sum, over shared stocks, of the smaller of the two funds' weights)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS shared_holdings, round(sum(least(a.weight_percent, b.weight_percent)), 2) AS overlap_percent FROM vanguard.main.holdings a JOIN vanguard.main.holdings b ON a.ticker = b.ticker WHERE a.fund_ticker = 'VOO' AND b.fund_ticker = 'VUG' AND a.ticker <> ''

vgi.example_queries.description: BND's trailing-12-month distribution yield (per-share distributions over the past year divided by the current price from products) next to its published SEC yield
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT p.ticker, p.price, p.yield_percent AS sec_yield_percent, count(*) AS payouts, round(sum(d.per_share_amount), 4) AS paid_per_share, round(100 * sum(d.per_share_amount) / p.price, 2) AS trailing_12m_yield_percent FROM vanguard.main.distributions('BND', start_date := (CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL 1 YEAR)::DATE) d CROSS JOIN vanguard.main.products p WHERE p.ticker = 'BND' GROUP BY p.ticker, p.price, p.yield_percent ORDER BY p.ticker

vgi.example_queries.description: VOO's approximate 1-year total return: the NAV change over the past year plus the distributions paid in the same window (payouts not reinvested)
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH nav AS (SELECT arg_min(nav, as_of_date) AS start_nav, arg_max(nav, as_of_date) AS end_nav FROM vanguard.main.nav_history('VOO', period := '1Y')), paid AS (SELECT sum(per_share_amount) AS per_share FROM vanguard.main.distributions('VOO', start_date := (CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL 1 YEAR)::DATE)) SELECT nav.start_nav, nav.end_nav, round(paid.per_share, 4) AS distributions_per_share, round(100 * (nav.end_nav / nav.start_nav - 1), 2) AS nav_return_percent, round(100 * ((nav.end_nav + paid.per_share) / nav.start_nav - 1), 2) AS total_return_percent FROM nav CROSS JOIN paid ORDER BY total_return_percent

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Detailed current portfolio holdings for Vanguard ETFs as a hive-partitioned table. It is partitioned by fund_ticker (the FUND's ticker, distinct from the constituent `ticker` column): filter `WHERE fund_ticker = '…'` (or `fund_ticker IN (…)`) to pick funds, or scan with no filter to stream EVERY fund's holdings (over a hundred funds — slow, so prefer a filter). Holdings are current-only — Vanguard reports a single as-of date (the as_of_date column), with no historical time travel. Rows come back weight-descending; weight_percent is in percent points (7.89 = 7.89%); bond funds also fill coupon/maturity/face. Join on fund_ticker to products.ticker for fund-level facts.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## holdings

Detailed **current** fund holdings as a **hive-partitioned table**, partitioned by `fund_ticker` (the fund's ticker). `fund_ticker` is distinct from `ticker` (the constituent's own ticker). Filter `WHERE fund_ticker = 'VOO'` for one fund, or scan with no filter to stream every fund (see the example queries).

`WHERE fund_ticker IN ('VOO','BND')` fans out per partition; an unfiltered scan streams every fund (over a hundred partitions — slow). Holdings are **current-only** (Vanguard reports one as-of date; no time travel). `weight_percent` is in percent points (7.89 = 7.89%).

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## products

The Vanguard US ETF catalog as a base table — one row per fund. It takes no arguments; query it directly and filter with a WHERE clause (e.g. `WHERE asset_class = 'Equity' ORDER BY expense_ratio_percent`; see the example queries). tags.vgi.doc_md:
## holdings_scan

The backing scan for the **`holdings` table** — prefer the table. Takes an optional `fund_ticker` argument: `holdings_scan(fund_ticker := 'VOO')` scans one fund. Hive-partitioned by `fund_ticker`: pass the fund as the argument, filter `WHERE fund_ticker = 'VOO'`, or scan with no argument to stream every fund (see the example queries). `fund_ticker` is distinct from the constituent `ticker` column. Holdings are current-only (no historical as-of).

functions.name: nav_history
functions.comment: Net-asset-value and market-price history for a fund over a look-back window — one row per observation with the NAV and the market (exchange) price. `fund` is a ticker; `period` picks the window (1M/1Y/5Y/10Y, default 1Y). Longer windows return coarser (weekly/monthly) points.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: NAV and market-price time series for a fund over a look-back window (period = 1M/1Y/5Y/10Y, default 1Y). Each row carries the NAV and the market (exchange) price for a date. Use it for NAV-based return series and NAV-vs-price comparison. Shorter windows are daily; 5Y thins to weekly and 10Y to monthly. This is fund NAV, not intraday candles.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## nav_history

NAV and market-price history over a look-back window. Pick the window with `period` (`1M`/`1Y`/`5Y`/`10Y`, default `1Y`); longer windows return coarser points (5Y weekly, 10Y monthly). This is **fund NAV**, not an intraday candle series (see the example queries).

vgi.example_queries.description: Daily VOO NAV over the past year
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT as_of_date, nav FROM vanguard.main.nav_history('VOO', period := '1Y') ORDER BY as_of_date DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: VOO's approximate 1-year total return: the NAV change over the past year plus the distributions paid in the same window (payouts not reinvested)
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH nav AS (SELECT arg_min(nav, as_of_date) AS start_nav, arg_max(nav, as_of_date) AS end_nav FROM vanguard.main.nav_history('VOO', period := '1Y')), paid AS (SELECT sum(per_share_amount) AS per_share FROM vanguard.main.distributions('VOO', start_date := (CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL 1 YEAR)::DATE)) SELECT nav.start_nav, nav.end_nav, round(paid.per_share, 4) AS distributions_per_share, round(100 * (nav.end_nav / nav.start_nav - 1), 2) AS nav_return_percent, round(100 * ((nav.end_nav + paid.per_share) / nav.start_nav - 1), 2) AS total_return_percent FROM nav CROSS JOIN paid ORDER BY total_return_percent

vgi.example_queries.description: 10-year NAV vs market-price series (monthly points)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT as_of_date, nav, market_price FROM vanguard.main.nav_history('VOO', period := '10Y') ORDER BY as_of_date

vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Valuation date.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: nav
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Net asset value per share.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: market_price
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Market (exchange) closing price that day.

arguments.description: The fund to look up, given as an exchange ticker like 'VOO'. Required, first positional argument.

arguments.name: period
arguments.description: The look-back window for the price series, one of 1M, 1Y, 5Y, 10Y. Defaults to 1Y. Shorter windows are daily; longer windows thin to weekly (5Y) or monthly (10Y).

examples: SELECT as_of_date, nav FROM vanguard.main.nav_history('VOO', period := '1Y') ORDER BY as_of_date DESC

WITH nav AS (SELECT arg_min(nav, as_of_date) AS start_nav, arg_max(nav, as_of_date) AS end_nav FROM vanguard.main.nav_history('VOO', period := '1Y')), paid AS (SELECT sum(per_share_amount) AS per_share FROM vanguard.main.distributions('VOO', start_date := (CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL 1 YEAR)::DATE)) SELECT nav.start_nav, nav.end_nav, round(paid.per_share, 4) AS distributions_per_share, round(100 * (nav.end_nav / nav.start_nav - 1), 2) AS nav_return_percent, round(100 * ((nav.end_nav + paid.per_share) / nav.start_nav - 1), 2) AS total_return_percent FROM nav CROSS JOIN paid ORDER BY total_return_percent
SELECT as_of_date, nav, market_price FROM vanguard.main.nav_history('VOO', period := '10Y') ORDER BY as_of_date

result_columns.description: Market (exchange) closing price that day.

functions.name: distributions
functions.comment: Recent distribution history for a fund — one row per distribution with record, reinvestment, and payable dates, the distribution type, the per-share amount, and the reinvestment price. `fund` is a ticker; bound the record-date range with start_date/end_date.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Distribution (dividend / capital-gain) history for a fund: record / reinvestment / payable dates, the distribution type, the per-share amount, and the reinvestment price. Amounts are per-share dollars, not percents. Bound the record-date range with start_date/end_date. Vanguard publishes only a rolling recent window — about the trailing 18 months (roughly 6 payouts for a quarterly payer, 18 for a monthly one) — so bounds outside it return no rows; derive them from CURRENT_DATE rather than hard-coding a calendar year.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## distributions

Recent distribution history, one row per distribution. Amounts are **per-share** dollars (not percentages). Bound the record-date range with `start_date`/`end_date` (see the example queries). Vanguard publishes only a rolling window of about the trailing 18 months, so bounds outside it return no rows.

vgi.example_queries.description: Recent VOO distributions
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT record_date, per_share_amount FROM vanguard.main.distributions('VOO') ORDER BY record_date DESC LIMIT 8

vgi.example_queries.description: Total distributions over the trailing year
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT sum(per_share_amount) AS total FROM vanguard.main.distributions('VOO', start_date := (CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL 1 YEAR)::DATE)

vgi.example_queries.description: BND's trailing-12-month distribution yield (per-share distributions over the past year divided by the current price from products) next to its published SEC yield
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT p.ticker, p.price, p.yield_percent AS sec_yield_percent, count(*) AS payouts, round(sum(d.per_share_amount), 4) AS paid_per_share, round(100 * sum(d.per_share_amount) / p.price, 2) AS trailing_12m_yield_percent FROM vanguard.main.distributions('BND', start_date := (CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL 1 YEAR)::DATE) d CROSS JOIN vanguard.main.products p WHERE p.ticker = 'BND' GROUP BY p.ticker, p.price, p.yield_percent ORDER BY p.ticker

vgi.example_queries.description: Distributions within a bounded record-day window
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT record_date, per_share_amount FROM vanguard.main.distributions('VOO', start_date := (CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL 1 YEAR)::DATE, end_date := (CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL 3 MONTH)::DATE) ORDER BY record_date

workers.doc_md:
## WisdomTree ETFs

WisdomTree US ETF data, exposed as DuckDB tables.

The **fund** is the unit of the data and is keyed by an exchange `ticker` (e.g. `DGRW`) — begin at the catalog to discover that key, then drill into a fund's holdings. Holdings are the current published portfolio (WisdomTree does not publish historical holdings).

### Sources

- [WisdomTree US ETFs](https://www.wisdomtree.com/us/products) — the fund lineup the catalog is read from.
- [WisdomTree terms of use](https://www.wisdomtree.com/us/terms) — terms that govern use of the site's data.

Data is provided for informational use; review WisdomTree's terms before redistribution.

example_queries.title: etf_lineup
example_queries.description: The WisdomTree US ETF lineup
example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, fund_name, asset_class FROM wisdomtree.main.products ORDER BY ticker LIMIT 5;

example_queries.title: top_holdings
example_queries.description: The top holdings of the WisdomTree U.S. Quality Dividend Growth Fund
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, ticker, weight_percent FROM wisdomtree.main.holdings WHERE fund_ticker = 'DGRW' ORDER BY weight_percent DESC LIMIT 5;

example_queries.description: Stocks held by the most WisdomTree Large Cap Value funds, with each stock's average weight across those funds (products category filter joined to holdings; scans every fund's holdings)
example_queries.sql: SELECT h.ticker, h.name, count(*) AS funds_holding, round(avg(h.weight_percent), 2) AS avg_weight_percent FROM wisdomtree.main.products p JOIN wisdomtree.main.holdings h ON h.fund_ticker = p.ticker WHERE p.category = 'Large Cap Value' AND h.asset_group = 'EQ' GROUP BY h.ticker, h.name ORDER BY funds_holding DESC, avg_weight_percent DESC, h.ticker LIMIT 10

workers.title: Windows Event Log Parser
workers.tagline: Parse Windows Event Logs (.evtx) into rows for DuckDB (Rust)
workers.subtitle: Parse Windows .evtx event-log files into queryable SQL rows for forensics and incident response.
workers.summary: Windows Event Log (.evtx) parsing for defensive DFIR — turn event-log files into queryable rows.
workers.doc_md:
# Windows Event Log (.evtx) Parsing in SQL

Query Windows Event Logs directly in DuckDB: this VGI extension turns binary `.evtx` files into Apache Arrow rows so you can run digital-forensics and incident-response (DFIR) analysis, threat hunting, and log triage entirely in SQL — no external tooling, no network access, no scripting.

## What it does

The Windows Event Log (`.evtx`, the binary `ElfFile` format that backs the Security, System, Application, PowerShell, and Sysmon channels) is the primary evidence source for Windows DFIR. This extension reads those files — including logs pulled from potentially compromised hosts — and exposes every event record as a queryable row, with convenience columns for the event id, provider, channel, source computer, severity level, and creation time, plus the complete original event preserved as JSON. It is built for incident responders, threat hunters, detection engineers, SOC analysts, and anyone who would rather join, filter, and aggregate event logs in SQL than wrangle them in a GUI.

## How it works

Parsing is powered by the battle-tested [`evtx`](https://github.com/omerbenamram/evtx) Rust crate (API docs on [docs.rs](https://docs.rs/evtx)), which decodes the BinXML chunks of the [Windows event-logging](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/eventlog/event-logging) format. Everything runs offline inside the worker — it never touches the network — and every entry point is hardened against hostile input: malformed, truncated, or deliberately corrupted files yield `NULL` / `false` / no rows and never crash the worker. Input may be supplied either inline as a `BLOB` (for example from `read_blob()`) or as a `VARCHAR` filesystem path.

## Working in SQL

Because every event becomes an ordinary row, you build timelines by filtering on provider and creation time, surface the noisiest activity by grouping and counting event ids, and pivot from triage to detection: the preserved event JSON composes with the companion `vgi-sigma` worker to run Sigma detection rules straight against your logs. The curated `windows_event_id_reference` view lets you look up what a given event id means and join it onto parsed records for readable timelines. Runnable, catalog-qualified queries for every function and the reference view are attached to each object and to this schema as example queries.
workers.readme_sql:
LOAD vgi;
ATTACH 'evtx' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'github-auto://Query-farm/vgi-evtx@v0.4.2');
SET search_path = 'evtx.main';

-- A small sample Security log, pinned to a release tag so it resolves anywhere.
-- Table-function arguments must be constants (not subqueries), so fetch the
-- bytes into a variable first; a local file can also be passed as a VARCHAR
-- path, e.g. evtx_records('Security.evtx').
SET VARIABLE evtx_sample = (SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-evtx/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/sample-security.evtx'));

-- One row per event record (7 rows for the sample).
SELECT record_id, event_id, provider, channel, time_created
FROM evtx_records(getvariable('evtx_sample'))
ORDER BY record_id;

-- Non-evtx bytes simply yield no rows.
SELECT count(*) FROM evtx_records('not a real evtx'::BLOB);  -- 0

-- Label each record with the built-in Windows Event ID reference
-- (meaning is NULL for ids the reference does not catalogue).
SELECT r.record_id, r.event_id, ref.name AS meaning
FROM evtx_records(getvariable('evtx_sample')) AS r
LEFT JOIN windows_event_id_reference AS ref USING (event_id, channel)
ORDER BY r.record_id;

-- How many records? Is it a real .evtx?
SELECT evtx_record_count(getvariable('evtx_sample'));  -- 7
SELECT is_valid_evtx(getvariable('evtx_sample'));      -- true

-- Compose with vgi-sigma over the preserved full event JSON:
--   SELECT * FROM evtx_records(getvariable('evtx_sample'))
--   WHERE sigma_match(event_json, '<rule yaml>');

example_queries.description: Validate that a file's bytes (a sample Security log fetched by URL) are a parseable .evtx before loading it.
example_queries.sql: SELECT evtx.main.is_valid_evtx((SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-evtx/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/sample-security.evtx')));

example_queries.description: Count how many event records a .evtx file (a sample Security log fetched by URL) contains.
example_queries.sql: SELECT evtx.main.evtx_record_count((SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-evtx/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/sample-security.evtx')));

example_queries.description: Explode a .evtx file into one row per event record, ordered by record id (the sample log's bytes are fetched by URL into a variable, since table-function arguments must be constants).
example_queries.sql: SET VARIABLE evtx_sample = (SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-evtx/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/sample-security.evtx')); SELECT record_id, event_id, provider, time_created FROM evtx.main.evtx_records(getvariable('evtx_sample')) ORDER BY record_id;

example_queries.description: Rank event ids by how often they occur to surface the noisiest activity.
example_queries.sql: SET VARIABLE evtx_sample = (SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-evtx/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/sample-security.evtx')); SELECT event_id, count(*) AS n FROM evtx.main.evtx_records(getvariable('evtx_sample')) GROUP BY event_id ORDER BY n DESC;

example_queries.description: Label each parsed record with its human-readable meaning by LEFT JOINing the event id reference onto evtx_records (meaning is NULL for ids the reference does not catalogue).
example_queries.sql: SET VARIABLE evtx_sample = (SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-evtx/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/sample-security.evtx')); SELECT r.record_id, r.event_id, ref.name AS meaning, r.time_created FROM evtx.main.evtx_records(getvariable('evtx_sample')) AS r LEFT JOIN evtx.main.windows_event_id_reference AS ref ON ref.event_id = r.event_id AND ref.channel = r.channel ORDER BY r.record_id;

example_queries.description: Hunt failed logons and lockouts: select the event ids from the reference by name, then pull the targeted account and source IP address out of each matching record's event_json.
example_queries.sql: SET VARIABLE evtx_sample = (SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-evtx/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/sample-security.evtx')); SELECT r.record_id, r.time_created, ref.name, r.event_json->>'$.Event.EventData.TargetUserName' AS target_user, r.event_json->>'$.Event.EventData.IpAddress' AS source_ip FROM evtx.main.evtx_records(getvariable('evtx_sample')) AS r JOIN evtx.main.windows_event_id_reference AS ref ON ref.event_id = r.event_id AND ref.channel = r.channel WHERE ref.name IN ('Failed logon', 'Account locked out') ORDER BY r.time_created, r.record_id;

example_queries.description: Triage a set of collected files (here a sample .evtx and a README fetched by URL): flag which ones are parseable .evtx logs and how many event records each holds (non-evtx files show valid = false and 0 records).
example_queries.sql: SELECT filename, evtx.main.is_valid_evtx(content) AS valid, evtx.main.evtx_record_count(content) AS records FROM read_blob(['https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-evtx/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/README.md', 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-evtx/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/sample-security.evtx']) ORDER BY filename;

example_queries.description: Look up the meaning and DFIR relevance of a single Windows event id.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, dfir_use FROM evtx.main.windows_event_id_reference WHERE event_id = 4688

example_queries.description: List the curated Security-channel event ids in numeric order.
example_queries.sql: SELECT event_id, name FROM evtx.main.windows_event_id_reference WHERE channel = 'Security' ORDER BY event_id

example_queries.description: Non-evtx bytes yield zero rows from evtx_records (hostile input is handled, never an error).
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS n FROM evtx.main.evtx_records('not a real evtx'::BLOB);

example_queries.description: Non-evtx bytes are reported as not valid (false), never an error.
example_queries.sql: SELECT evtx.main.is_valid_evtx('not a real evtx'::BLOB) AS valid;

example_queries.description: Non-evtx bytes count as zero event records (hostile input is handled).
example_queries.sql: SELECT evtx.main.evtx_record_count('not a real evtx'::BLOB) AS records;

## evtx.main

Windows Event Log (`.evtx`) parsing and inspection over Apache Arrow. This schema turns a `.evtx` file — supplied as inline `BLOB` bytes or a `VARCHAR` filesystem path — into queryable event rows so a whole log can be joined, filtered, and aggregated in SQL.

Alongside parsing, it lets you validate and size a log before loading it, and each event's full JSON is preserved so results compose with downstream detection tooling such as `vgi-sigma`.

Everything runs offline. All entry points tolerate hostile input — malformed, truncated, or non-evtx data yields empty or false results rather than an error — because event logs are routinely pulled from potentially compromised hosts.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## windows_event_id_reference

A curated lookup of well-known Windows Event IDs (Security auditing, the System service-control log, Sysmon, and PowerShell script-block logging) with a short name and a DFIR relevance note for each. Browse it to learn which ids matter — for example 4624 (successful logon), 4625 (failed logon), 4688 (process creation), or 7045 (service installed) — or join it onto parsed records by `event_id` to turn a raw timeline into a readable one. It is static data: it needs no `.evtx` file and touches no network.

vgi.example_queries.description: Look up the meaning and DFIR relevance of a single Windows event id.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, dfir_use FROM evtx.main.windows_event_id_reference WHERE event_id = 4688

vgi.example_queries.description: List the curated Security-channel event ids in numeric order.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT event_id, name FROM evtx.main.windows_event_id_reference WHERE channel = 'Security' ORDER BY event_id

vgi.example_queries.description: Hunt failed logons and lockouts: select the event ids from the reference by name, then pull the targeted account and source IP address out of each matching record's event_json.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SET VARIABLE evtx_sample = (SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-evtx/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/sample-security.evtx')); SELECT r.record_id, r.time_created, ref.name, r.event_json->>'$.Event.EventData.TargetUserName' AS target_user, r.event_json->>'$.Event.EventData.IpAddress' AS source_ip FROM evtx.main.evtx_records(getvariable('evtx_sample')) AS r JOIN evtx.main.windows_event_id_reference AS ref ON ref.event_id = r.event_id AND ref.channel = r.channel WHERE ref.name IN ('Failed logon', 'Account locked out') ORDER BY r.time_created, r.record_id;

workers.title: SHAP Model Explanations
workers.tagline: SHAP explanations for sklearn/XGBoost predictions in DuckDB (Python)
workers.subtitle: Explain scikit-learn and XGBoost model predictions with per-row SHAP values and global feature importance.
workers.summary: SHAP explanations for scikit-learn / XGBoost models as SQL functions.
workers.doc_md:
# SHAP Model Explanations in SQL

![SHAP logo](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/shap/shap/master/docs/artwork/shap_logo.png)

**Explainable AI for machine learning predictions, right inside DuckDB — compute SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) feature attributions for fitted scikit-learn and XGBoost models with plain SQL.**

The `explain` catalog turns model interpretability into a set of DuckDB/SQL table functions, so you can answer *why* a model made a prediction without leaving your database or writing any Python. It is built for data engineers, analysts, and ML practitioners who need transparent, auditable, per-prediction explanations — for model debugging, regulatory and fair-lending reviews, feature selection, or simply building trust in a model's output. Every explanation is computed over your data in place via Apache Arrow, so it composes naturally with joins, filters, and aggregates in ordinary SQL.

Under the hood the worker is powered by [SHAP](https://github.com/shap/shap), the reference implementation of Shapley-value feature attribution ([documentation](https://shap.readthedocs.io/en/latest/)), grounded in cooperative game theory's [Shapley values](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shapley_value). Importantly, vgi-explain does **not** train models — it *interprets* the self-contained *model* `BLOB` produced by the sibling `vgi-sklearn` ([scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/)) and `vgi-xgboost` ([XGBoost](https://xgboost.readthedocs.io/)) workers. SHAP automatically selects an appropriate explainer (e.g. TreeExplainer for tree ensembles), so explanations are exact and fast for the supported model families. Because a DuckDB table function accepts only one subquery argument (reserved for the feature relation), the model travels as a scalar `model` argument, usually held in a session variable and read with `getvariable('m')` — see the schema's and each function's example queries for ready-to-run SQL.

Three functions make up the surface. `shap_values` streams a feature relation and emits per-row, per-feature signed contributions in long format (with a contribution per class for multi-class classifiers), aligning input columns to the model's fitted features by name. `shap_base_value` returns the explainer's expected value — the model's baseline output that the per-feature contributions add onto, so that base value + sum(contributions) reproduces the prediction (SHAP's additivity property). `feature_importance` aggregates `mean(|SHAP|)` across a relation to produce a global, ranked importance of which features matter most, falling back to the model's native importances when no rows are supplied. Together they cover local (single-prediction) and global (whole-dataset) interpretability for the models you already serve from VGI.

example_queries.description: Read the model's expected (base) output — one row per class ('0' and '1') for this binary RandomForest classifier.
example_queries.sql: ["SET VARIABLE m = (SELECT model FROM read_parquet('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-explain/v0.2.0/test/fixtures/models.parquet') WHERE name = 'rf_clf')", "SELECT class, base_value FROM explain.main.shap_base_value(model := getvariable('m')) ORDER BY class"]

example_queries.description: Explain each row's prediction feature by feature (model held in session VARIABLE m).
example_queries.sql: ["SET VARIABLE m = (SELECT model FROM read_parquet('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-explain/v0.2.0/test/fixtures/models.parquet') WHERE name = 'rf_clf')", "SELECT id, feature, class, shap_value FROM explain.main.shap_values((SELECT id, signal, noise_a, noise_b FROM read_parquet('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-explain/v0.2.0/test/fixtures/features.parquet')), model := getvariable('m'), id := 'id') ORDER BY id, feature, class LIMIT 6"]

example_queries.description: Rank features by their average SHAP magnitude across the dataset (model in session VARIABLE m).
example_queries.sql: ["SET VARIABLE m = (SELECT model FROM read_parquet('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-explain/v0.2.0/test/fixtures/models.parquet') WHERE name = 'rf_clf')", "SELECT feature, rank, method FROM explain.main.feature_importance((SELECT id, signal, noise_a, noise_b FROM read_parquet('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-explain/v0.2.0/test/fixtures/features.parquet')), model := getvariable('m'), id := 'id') ORDER BY rank"]

example_queries.description: Reconstruct each row's predicted class-1 probability as the SHAP base value plus the sum of the row's per-feature contributions (SHAP additivity), joining shap_values to shap_base_value on class, and list the rows the model is least sure about (probability closest to 0.5).
example_queries.sql: ["SET VARIABLE m = (SELECT model FROM read_parquet('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-explain/v0.2.0/test/fixtures/models.parquet') WHERE name = 'rf_clf')", "WITH contrib AS (SELECT id, class, sum(shap_value) AS total_shap FROM explain.main.shap_values((SELECT id, signal, noise_a, noise_b FROM read_parquet('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-explain/v0.2.0/test/fixtures/features.parquet')), model := getvariable('m'), id := 'id') GROUP BY id, class) SELECT c.id, round(b.base_value, 4) AS base_value, round(c.total_shap, 4) AS total_shap, round(b.base_value + c.total_shap, 4) AS predicted_proba FROM contrib AS c JOIN explain.main.shap_base_value(model := getvariable('m')) AS b ON c.class IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b.class WHERE c.class = '1' ORDER BY round(abs(b.base_value + c.total_shap - 0.5), 4), c.id LIMIT 6"]

tags.vgi.doc_md:
# SHAP Explanations

Model-interpretability table functions that turn a fitted scikit-learn or XGBoost model into per-prediction and dataset-wide **SHAP** feature attributions. Every explanation is computed in place over Apache Arrow, so it composes with ordinary SQL joins, filters, and aggregates.

## What it covers

*Local* interpretability answers **why did the model predict this row?** by attributing the output to each input feature; *global* interpretability ranks **which features matter most** across a whole dataset. Multi-class classifiers report a contribution per class, and every attribution obeys SHAP additivity — a row's base value plus its feature contributions reconstruct the model's output.

## How models arrive

This schema does **not** train models: it *interprets* the self-contained model `BLOB` packed by the sibling `vgi-sklearn` / `vgi-xgboost` workers. Because a DuckDB table function reserves its single subquery slot for the feature relation, the model travels as a scalar `model` argument — typically held in a session VARIABLE and read with `getvariable('m')`.

# supported_models

A browsable, model-free reference of the estimator families this worker explains and the SHAP explainer selected for each. It takes no arguments and needs no model, so it is the cheapest way to check whether your estimator is supported before loading a model.

## Columns

- `model_family` (`VARCHAR`) -- tree ensemble, linear, or fallback family.
- `estimator_examples` (`VARCHAR`) -- example estimator classes in the family.
- `shap_explainer` (`VARCHAR`) -- the SHAP explainer chosen (`TreeExplainer` / `LinearExplainer` / `KernelExplainer`).
- `exactness` (`VARCHAR`) -- `exact` or `approximate`.
- `notes` (`VARCHAR`) -- how the explainer works and any caveats.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `shap_base_value`

Return the **SHAP base (expected) value** of a fitted scikit-learn / XGBoost model — the explainer's *expected output* over the background distribution. This is the anchor that every row's per-feature SHAP contributions (`shap_values`) add onto to reconstruct that row's prediction (SHAP additivity).

**When to use it.** Establish the model's baseline before reading local explanations: a row's prediction = base value + sum of its SHAP contributions. Pair it with `shap_values` whenever you present a per-row attribution.

**Inputs.** Just the scalar `model` `BLOB` (produced by vgi-sklearn / vgi-xgboost) — no feature relation. It is typically a session VARIABLE or an inline subquery.

**Outputs.** Columns `class`, `base_value`. One row per class (the `class` column carries the label) when the explainer reports one output per class — every multi-class model, and binary RandomForest / ExtraTrees / DecisionTree classifiers (two rows, '0' and '1'); a single row with `class = NULL` for regression and single-margin binary classifiers (XGBoost, GradientBoosting, HistGradientBoosting, LogisticRegression).

**Edge cases.** The model `BLOB` does not carry a background sample, so the base value is computed from a single zero feature vector — exact for tree / linear explainers, an approximation for models that require real background data. An invalid / untrusted `BLOB` raises a clear `invalid model: …` error.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# shap_base_value

The **SHAP base (expected) value** of a fitted scikit-learn / XGBoost model: the explainer's expected output — the anchor that a row's SHAP contributions add onto to reach its prediction.

## Usage

Takes only the scalar `model` `BLOB` (no feature relation), usually held in a session VARIABLE and read with `getvariable('m')` — pass it as `model := getvariable('m')`. A runnable end-to-end demonstration ships in this function's `vgi.executable_examples`.

## Notes

- One row per class when the explainer reports one output per class (multi-class, and binary RandomForest / ExtraTrees / DecisionTree); a single `class = NULL` row for single-output models.
- Computed from a zero background vector (exact for tree / linear explainers).
- `base_value + sum(shap_value)` reconstructs a row's model output.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `feature_importance`

Rank a fitted model's features by **global importance** — by default the **mean absolute SHAP value** (`mean(|SHAP|)`) of each feature over the feature relation you pass. This aggregates the per-row, per-feature attributions of `shap_values` into one number per feature: how much, on average, the feature moves the model's output.

**When to use it.** Answer *which features matter most overall?* — for model summaries, feature selection, or dashboards. SHAP-based importance is consistent and model-agnostic, unlike split-count / Gini heuristics.

**Inputs.** A feature relation (the single subquery argument) to average over; the scalar `model` `BLOB`; and an optional `id` column name to exclude from features. Features are aligned to the model's fitted columns by name.

**Outputs.** Columns `feature`, `importance`, `rank` (1 = most important), and `method` (`'mean_abs_shap'` or `'native'`).

**Edge cases.** If the passed relation has **zero rows**, the function falls back to the model's *native* importances (`feature_importances_`, or `|coef_|` for linear models) and sets `method = 'native'`; if the model exposes neither, that empty-relation call raises a clear error. An invalid / untrusted model `BLOB` raises `invalid model: …`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# feature_importance

**Global feature importance** for a fitted scikit-learn / XGBoost model: `mean(|SHAP|)` over the relation you pass, or the model's native importances when the relation is empty.

## Usage

Pass the feature relation as the single table argument and the model as the scalar `model` argument (usually a session VARIABLE read with `getvariable('m')`, passed as `model := getvariable('m')`); order the output by `rank`. A runnable end-to-end demonstration ships in this function's `vgi.executable_examples`.

## Notes

- `method = 'mean_abs_shap'` when rows are supplied; `'native'` when the relation is empty (uses `feature_importances_` / `|coef_|`).
- `rank` is 1-based, most important first.
- Features are aligned to the model's fitted columns by name.

vgi.example_queries.description: Rank features by their average SHAP magnitude across the dataset (model in session VARIABLE m).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SET VARIABLE m = (SELECT model FROM read_parquet('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-explain/v0.2.0/test/fixtures/models.parquet') WHERE name = 'rf_clf'); SELECT feature, rank, method FROM explain.main.feature_importance((SELECT id, signal, noise_a, noise_b FROM read_parquet('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-explain/v0.2.0/test/fixtures/features.parquet')), model := getvariable('m'), id := 'id') ORDER BY rank

vgi.example_queries.description: Compare each feature's global importance with the number of rows in which it is the dominant (largest |SHAP|) driver of the class-1 prediction, joining feature_importance to per-row shap_values.

functions.name: shap_values
functions.comment: Per-row, per-feature SHAP contributions in long format (one row per row x feature [x class])

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `shap_values`

Compute **per-row, per-feature SHAP contributions** for a fitted scikit-learn / XGBoost model, returned in **long format** — one output row per (input row x feature [x class]).

**When to use it.** Answer *why did the model predict this for this row?* — the signed `shap_value` for each feature shows how much that feature pushed the model's output up (positive) or down (negative), relative to the model's base value (see `shap_base_value`). Summing a row's contributions and the base value reconstructs the model's raw output (SHAP additivity).

**Inputs.** A feature relation as the single subquery argument; a `model` `BLOB` (scalar, produced by vgi-sklearn / vgi-xgboost), typically a session VARIABLE or an inline subquery; and an optional `id` column name to carry through (excluded from features). Features are aligned to the model's fitted columns **by name**, so input column order does not matter; the input must contain every feature the model expects.

**Outputs.** Columns `id`, `feature`, `class`, `shap_value`. When the explainer reports one output per class there is one row per class (the `class` column carries the label): every multi-class classifier, and binary classifiers explained on probabilities (scikit-learn RandomForest / ExtraTrees / DecisionTree, the KernelExplainer fallback) — those report both class '0' and class '1'. Regression and binary classifiers explained on a single margin (XGBoost, GradientBoosting, HistGradientBoosting, LogisticRegression) have one output with `class = NULL`.

**Edge cases.** An empty input relation yields zero rows. A missing feature column is an input-alignment failure and raises a clear `input is missing feature column(s) …` error (listing the model's expected features and the input's columns); a separate `invalid model: …` error is raised only for a malformed, truncated, or untrusted model `BLOB`. Neither crashes the worker.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# shap_values

Per-row, per-feature **SHAP contributions** for a fitted scikit-learn / XGBoost model, in **long format** (one row per input row x feature, and per class for multi-class classifiers).

## Usage

The model travels as the scalar `model` argument (a DuckDB table function allows only one subquery, reserved for the feature relation); it is usually held in a session VARIABLE and read with `getvariable('m')`. Pass the feature relation as the single table argument, the model as `model := getvariable('m')`, and optionally the id column as `id := 'row_id'`. Features are aligned to the model's fitted columns by name, so input order is irrelevant. A runnable end-to-end demonstration ships in this function's `vgi.executable_examples`.

## Notes

- Each row's contributions plus the model base value (`shap_base_value`) reconstruct the prediction (SHAP additivity).
- `class` is the class label when the explainer reports one output per class (every multi-class model; binary RandomForest / ExtraTrees / DecisionTree), `NULL` for single-output models (regression; binary XGBoost / GradientBoosting / logistic).
- A missing feature column raises an `input is missing feature column(s) …` error; a malformed or untrusted model `BLOB` raises an `invalid model: …` error.

workers.doc_md:
# Formula 1 results, standings, and timing

Query Formula 1 from SQL. Current tables cover this season's championships, calendar, and latest result. Parameterized functions reach back to 1950 for results and standings, and into 2023+ sessions for lap, stint, pit, weather, and race-control detail.

## Data model

Jolpica-F1 functions are keyed by `season`, `round`, and text ids (`driver_id`, `constructor_id`, `circuit_id`). OpenF1 functions are keyed by `session_key` and car `driver_number`; use `session_drivers()` to map numbers to names.

## Licence

Both sources publish their data under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0: attribute them, do not use the data commercially, and share derived datasets alike. This worker fetches on demand and does not rehost data. It is not affiliated with Formula 1 or the FIA.

## Sources and references

* [Jolpica-F1](https://jolpi.ca/): the Ergast-compatible API behind calendars, results, standings, and laps ([API docs](https://github.com/jolpica/jolpica-f1/tree/main/docs)).
* [OpenF1](https://openf1.org/): 2023+ session timing, stints, weather, and race control ([API docs](https://openf1.org/docs/)).
* [CC BY-NC-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/4.0/): the licence both sources publish under.

example_queries.title: current_driver_standings_are_populated
example_queries.description: The current drivers' championship has driver rows with stable identifiers.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) > 0 AND count(driver_id) = count(*) AS populated FROM f1.main.current_driver_standings;

example_queries.title: championship_points_are_ordered
example_queries.description: A higher championship position never has more points than a lower one.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bool_and(points <= prev_points) AS ordered FROM (SELECT points, lag(points) OVER (ORDER BY position) AS prev_points FROM f1.main.current_driver_standings WHERE position IS NOT NULL) WHERE prev_points IS NOT NULL;

example_queries.title: verstappen_2023_wins
example_queries.description: Max Verstappen won 19 Grands Prix in 2023.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS wins FROM f1.main.race_results(2023) WHERE position = 1 AND driver_id = 'max_verstappen';

example_queries.description: The current championship top ten.
example_queries.sql: SELECT position, driver_name, constructor_name, points, wins FROM f1.main.current_driver_standings ORDER BY position LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Points gap from each driver to the leader.
example_queries.sql: SELECT driver_name, points, max(points) OVER () - points AS gap_to_leader FROM f1.main.current_driver_standings ORDER BY position

example_queries.description: Championship top ten with each driver's finish and points in the latest Grand Prix.
example_queries.sql: SELECT s.position, s.driver_name, s.points, r.position AS last_race_finish, coalesce(r.points, 0) AS last_race_points FROM f1.main.current_driver_standings s LEFT JOIN f1.main.last_race_results r USING (driver_id) ORDER BY s.position LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Sprint winner against Grand Prix winner on every 2024 sprint weekend.
example_queries.sql: WITH sp AS (SELECT round, race_name, driver_name AS sprint_winner FROM f1.main.sprint_results(2024) WHERE position = 1), gp AS (SELECT round, driver_name AS grand_prix_winner FROM f1.main.race_results(2024) WHERE position = 1) SELECT round, race_name, sprint_winner, grand_prix_winner, sprint_winner = grand_prix_winner AS won_both FROM sp JOIN gp USING (round) ORDER BY round

example_queries.description: Max Verstappen's pace per stint in the 2024 Chinese Grand Prix, splitting his laps at each pit stop and leaving out in- and out-laps.
example_queries.sql: WITH stops AS (SELECT lap FROM f1.main.pit_stops(2024, 5) WHERE driver_id = 'max_verstappen'), laps AS (SELECT l.lap, l.lap_time_seconds, 1 + (SELECT count(*) FROM stops WHERE stops.lap < l.lap) AS stint FROM f1.main.lap_times(2024, 5, driver_id := 'max_verstappen') l) SELECT stint, min(lap) AS first_lap, max(lap) AS last_lap, min(lap_time_seconds) AS best_lap_seconds, median(lap_time_seconds) AS median_lap_seconds FROM laps WHERE lap NOT IN (SELECT lap FROM stops) AND lap NOT IN (SELECT lap + 1 FROM stops) GROUP BY stint ORDER BY stint

example_queries.description: Every driver's tyre sequence in the 2024 Bahrain Grand Prix (session 9472), in finishing order.
example_queries.sql: SELECT r.position, d.name_acronym, d.team_name, count(*) AS stints, string_agg(st.compound, ' > ' ORDER BY st.stint_number) AS strategy FROM f1.main.session_stints(9472) st JOIN f1.main.session_drivers(9472) d USING (driver_number) JOIN f1.main.session_result(9472) r USING (driver_number) GROUP BY r.position, d.name_acronym, d.team_name ORDER BY r.position NULLS LAST, d.name_acronym

## Formula 1 analytical data

Rows are explicitly driver-, constructor-, round-, lap-, stint-, stop-, or message-grain. Times are exact decimal seconds from Jolpica-F1 and `DOUBLE` seconds from OpenF1; published display strings are kept alongside.

Start with the `current_*` tables and `last_race_results`. Historical functions take `season` (and optionally `round`); OpenF1 session functions take a `session_key` found with `sessions()`.

functions.name: lap_times
functions.comment: Lap-by-lap times and running positions for one Grand Prix (1996 onwards)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per driver per lap of one race, with running position and lap time. Requires season and round; pass driver_id := '...' to fetch a single driver cheaply. A full race is roughly 1,000-1,400 rows fetched over 10-15 upstream pages.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Race lap times from 1996 onwards. Filtering by `driver_id` is pushed to the API and is much cheaper than filtering in SQL.

vgi.example_queries.description: Max Verstappen's laps in the 2024 Chinese Grand Prix.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT lap, position, lap_time FROM f1.main.lap_times(2024, 5, driver_id := 'max_verstappen') ORDER BY lap

vgi.example_queries.description: Max Verstappen's pace per stint in the 2024 Chinese Grand Prix, splitting his laps at each pit stop and leaving out in- and out-laps.
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH stops AS (SELECT lap FROM f1.main.pit_stops(2024, 5) WHERE driver_id = 'max_verstappen'), laps AS (SELECT l.lap, l.lap_time_seconds, 1 + (SELECT count(*) FROM stops WHERE stops.lap < l.lap) AS stint FROM f1.main.lap_times(2024, 5, driver_id := 'max_verstappen') l) SELECT stint, min(lap) AS first_lap, max(lap) AS last_lap, min(lap_time_seconds) AS best_lap_seconds, median(lap_time_seconds) AS median_lap_seconds FROM laps WHERE lap NOT IN (SELECT lap FROM stops) AND lap NOT IN (SELECT lap + 1 FROM stops) GROUP BY stint ORDER BY stint

functions.name: session_stints
functions.comment: Tyre stints (compound, laps, tyre age) for every driver in one OpenF1 session

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per stint per driver with tyre compound, first and last lap, and tyre age at the start. Use it to reconstruct race strategies.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Tyre stints for one session; `lap_end - lap_start + 1` is the stint length.

vgi.example_queries.description: Compound usage in the 2024 Bahrain Grand Prix.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT compound, count(*) AS stints, sum(lap_end - lap_start + 1) AS laps FROM f1.main.session_stints(9472) GROUP BY compound ORDER BY laps DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Every driver's tyre sequence in the 2024 Bahrain Grand Prix (session 9472), in finishing order.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT r.position, d.name_acronym, d.team_name, count(*) AS stints, string_agg(st.compound, ' > ' ORDER BY st.stint_number) AS strategy FROM f1.main.session_stints(9472) st JOIN f1.main.session_drivers(9472) d USING (driver_number) JOIN f1.main.session_result(9472) r USING (driver_number) GROUP BY r.position, d.name_acronym, d.team_name ORDER BY r.position NULLS LAST, d.name_acronym

workers.doc_md:
# RSS, Atom & JSON Feed Parser for DuckDB

Parse RSS, Atom, and JSON feeds directly in SQL — turn any syndication feed into queryable DuckDB rows over Apache Arrow, with zero glue code and automatic format detection.

This VGI extension brings **feed parsing to SQL** for data engineers, analysts, and anyone who needs to ingest news, blog, or podcast feeds without writing a custom scraper. Point it at an `http(s)` URL and it fetches the feed over HTTP, or hand it a raw RSS / Atom / JSON Feed document inline — either way the format is auto-detected, so a single query handles RSS 2.0, Atom, and JSON Feed alike. Missing or unparseable publish dates surface as `NULL` timestamps, absent text fields as empty strings, and malformed feeds raise a clean, actionable error rather than crashing your session.

Feed parsing and format auto-detection are powered by [gofeed](https://github.com/mmcdole/gofeed), a robust, widely-used Go feed parser (see the [gofeed API documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/mmcdole/gofeed)). It understands the [RSS 2.0 specification](https://www.rssboard.org/rss-specification), the [Atom Syndication Format (RFC 4287)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4287), and the [JSON Feed format](https://www.jsonfeed.org/), normalizing their differences into one consistent row shape. HTTP fetches are bounded by a timeout and a maximum response size so a query can never hang or exhaust memory on a hostile feed.

## SQL use cases & functions

Use `feed_items(input [, timeout_ms, max_items])` to get **one row per feed entry**, with `seq`, `guid`, `title`, `link`, `published`, `updated`, `author`, a `categories` list, `summary`, and `content` columns — ideal for monitoring news and blog feeds, building a podcast episode catalog, deduplicating items by GUID, or `UNNEST`-ing categories for tag analytics. Use `feed_info(input [, timeout_ms])` for a **single row of feed-level metadata**: `title`, `description`, `link`, detected `feed_type` (rss / atom / json), `language`, last `updated` time, and `item_count` — perfect for cataloging or health-checking a set of feeds.

New to the data? Browse the `feed_registry` view for a curated set of real, public feeds across all three formats, pick a `url`, and hand it to either table function. Runnable, network-free example queries are attached to each function and to the `main` schema.

Source code and issues: [github.com/Query-farm/vgi-feed](https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-feed).

example_queries.description: List the items parsed from an inline RSS 2.0 feed, ordered by position.
example_queries.sql: SELECT seq, title, link FROM feed.main.feed_items('<rss version="2.0"><channel><title>Query Farm Sample Feed</title><link>https://query.farm/</link><description>A small RSS feed used by vgi-feed examples</description><language>en-us</language><item><title>First Post</title><link>https://query.farm/first</link><category>news</category><category>release</category><description>The first sample entry</description></item><item><title>Second Post</title><link>https://query.farm/second</link><category>news</category><description>The second sample entry</description></item></channel></rss>') ORDER BY seq;

example_queries.description: Count the items in an inline feed.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS items FROM feed.main.feed_items('<rss version="2.0"><channel><title>Query Farm Sample Feed</title><link>https://query.farm/</link><description>A small RSS feed used by vgi-feed examples</description><language>en-us</language><item><title>First Post</title><link>https://query.farm/first</link><category>news</category><category>release</category><description>The first sample entry</description></item><item><title>Second Post</title><link>https://query.farm/second</link><category>news</category><description>The second sample entry</description></item></channel></rss>');

example_queries.description: Find the entries that are new since an earlier snapshot of the same feed by anti-joining the current feed_items against the snapshot's feed_items on link (returns Second Post; no network access).
example_queries.sql: SELECT cur.seq, cur.title, cur.link FROM feed.main.feed_items('<rss version="2.0"><channel><title>Query Farm Sample Feed</title><link>https://query.farm/</link><description>A small RSS feed used by vgi-feed examples</description><language>en-us</language><item><title>First Post</title><link>https://query.farm/first</link><category>news</category><category>release</category><description>The first sample entry</description></item><item><title>Second Post</title><link>https://query.farm/second</link><category>news</category><description>The second sample entry</description></item></channel></rss>') AS cur ANTI JOIN feed.main.feed_items('<rss version="2.0"><channel><title>Query Farm Sample Feed</title><item><title>First Post</title><link>https://query.farm/first</link></item></channel></rss>') AS prev ON cur.link = prev.link ORDER BY cur.seq

example_queries.description: Break a feed's entries down by category: join feed_info (feed title and reported item_count) to the UNNESTed categories from feed_items to get each category's entry count and its share of the feed (news 2 entries = 1.0, release 1 = 0.5; no network access).
example_queries.sql: SELECT f.title AS feed_title, c.category, count(*) AS entries, round(count(*) / f.item_count, 2) AS share_of_feed FROM feed.main.feed_info('<rss version="2.0"><channel><title>Query Farm Sample Feed</title><link>https://query.farm/</link><description>A small RSS feed used by vgi-feed examples</description><language>en-us</language><item><title>First Post</title><link>https://query.farm/first</link><category>news</category><category>release</category><description>The first sample entry</description></item><item><title>Second Post</title><link>https://query.farm/second</link><category>news</category><description>The second sample entry</description></item></channel></rss>') AS f CROSS JOIN (SELECT UNNEST(categories) AS category FROM feed.main.feed_items('<rss version="2.0"><channel><title>Query Farm Sample Feed</title><link>https://query.farm/</link><description>A small RSS feed used by vgi-feed examples</description><language>en-us</language><item><title>First Post</title><link>https://query.farm/first</link><category>news</category><category>release</category><description>The first sample entry</description></item><item><title>Second Post</title><link>https://query.farm/second</link><category>news</category><description>The second sample entry</description></item></channel></rss>')) AS c GROUP BY f.title, f.item_count, c.category ORDER BY entries DESC, c.category

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Syndicated feeds in SQL

Turn **RSS 2.0, Atom, and JSON Feed** documents into queryable entries and feed-level metadata, or generate feed documents from SQL rows.

### Ingestion

Supply an `http(s)` feed URL or inline feed text; the format is detected automatically. COPY FROM can also read worker-local files. Entries carry identifiers, titles, links, dates, authors, categories, summaries, and content. Feed metadata describes the document as a whole.

### Publishing

COPY TO writes RSS, Atom, or JSON Feed from query results. Supply feed metadata as COPY options and use ORDER BY to choose entry order. File paths refer to the worker's filesystem.

### Missing values

Missing/unparseable dates surface as NULL timestamps, absent text as empty strings, and missing categories as empty lists. Malformed feeds raise errors.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Curated Feed Registry

A browsable, zero-argument view listing well-known public **RSS / Atom / JSON** feeds — a starting point for discovery when you do not already have a feed URL in hand.

### Columns

- **`name`** — human-friendly feed name.
- **`url`** — the feed URL to hand to `feed_items(input)` or `feed_info(input)`.
- **`feed_type`** — the feed format (`rss`, `atom`, or `json`).
- **`category`** — a broad topic (Technology, News, Science, Security, Comics).
- **`description`** — a one-line summary of the feed.

### Notes

The registry is a static list, so it returns instantly with no network access. Pick a `url` here, then parse it with the feed table functions.

functions.name: write_jsonfeed_copy
functions.comment: Export SQL rows to a jsonfeed feed document using COPY TO

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Export jsonfeed using COPY TO a worker-local file. Source columns are matched by feed_items column names and types. title and link options are required; RSS also requires description. Optional language and author describe the feed. Use ORDER BY to choose item order. Missing item IDs are generated deterministically; Atom dates default to the export time.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Generate a jsonfeed feed

Export jsonfeed using COPY TO a worker-local file. Source columns are matched by feed_items column names and types. title and link options are required; RSS also requires description. Optional language and author describe the feed. Use ORDER BY to choose item order. Missing item IDs are generated deterministically; Atom dates default to the export time.

### Input and output

Alias and cast source columns to the item schema; subsets are supported. This is a sink with no result columns. DuckDB reports the COPY row count. Every item needs title, summary, or content; Atom requires a title. Empty input produces a valid empty feed.

### Example

```sql
COPY (SELECT 'First post' AS title, 'https://example.com/1' AS link)
TO '/tmp/posts.feed' (FORMAT 'feed.jsonfeed', title 'Posts', link 'https://example.com', description 'Recent posts');
```

### Limits

Only worker-local destinations are supported. Buffered input and encoded output are limited to 64 MiB, and exports to one million items. The destination is replaced after successful encoding.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Import auto feed items using COPY FROM an HTTP(S) URL or worker-local file. Target columns must be a subset of feed_items columns with matching names and types. timeout_ms defaults to 15000; max_items defaults to 0 (all items). Documents over 64 MiB or over one million items are rejected.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Import feed items

Import auto feed items using COPY FROM an HTTP(S) URL or worker-local file. Target columns must be a subset of feed_items columns with matching names and types. timeout_ms defaults to 15000; max_items defaults to 0 (all items). Documents over 64 MiB or over one million items are rejected.

### Column mapping

The destination table chooses the output schema. Use any subset of the item columns, in any order, with matching types. Dates are plain `TIMESTAMP`; categories are `VARCHAR[]`. Unknown columns and incompatible types are errors.

### Example

```sql
CREATE TABLE headlines (title VARCHAR, link VARCHAR);
COPY headlines FROM 'https://hnrss.org/frontpage' (FORMAT 'feed.auto', timeout_ms 5000);
```

functions.name: write_rss_copy
functions.comment: Export SQL rows to a rss feed document using COPY TO

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Export rss using COPY TO a worker-local file. Source columns are matched by feed_items column names and types. title and link options are required; RSS also requires description. Optional language and author describe the feed. Use ORDER BY to choose item order. Missing item IDs are generated deterministically; Atom dates default to the export time.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Generate a rss feed

Export rss using COPY TO a worker-local file. Source columns are matched by feed_items column names and types. title and link options are required; RSS also requires description. Optional language and author describe the feed. Use ORDER BY to choose item order. Missing item IDs are generated deterministically; Atom dates default to the export time.

### Input and output

Alias and cast source columns to the item schema; subsets are supported. This is a sink with no result columns. DuckDB reports the COPY row count. Every item needs title, summary, or content; Atom requires a title. Empty input produces a valid empty feed.

### Example

```sql
COPY (SELECT 'First post' AS title, 'https://example.com/1' AS link)
TO '/tmp/posts.feed' (FORMAT 'feed.rss', title 'Posts', link 'https://example.com', description 'Recent posts');
```

### Limits

Only worker-local destinations are supported. Buffered input and encoded output are limited to 64 MiB, and exports to one million items. The destination is replaced after successful encoding.

workers.title: FHIR R4 Connector
workers.tagline: Query HL7 FHIR R4 REST resources as tables in DuckDB (Go)
workers.subtitle: Query HL7 FHIR R4 REST servers from SQL: patients, observations, generic search, reads by id, and server capabilities.
workers.summary: Query HL7 FHIR R4 REST servers and return resources as rows
workers.doc_md:
# FHIR R4 in SQL

![HL7 FHIR logo](https://hl7.org/fhir/assets/images/fhir-logo-www.png)

**Query live HL7 FHIR R4 healthcare APIs directly from SQL** — turn any FHIR REST server into DuckDB tables and run analytics over patients, clinical observations, and server capabilities without writing a line of integration code.

The `fhir` catalog connects to any [HL7 FHIR R4](https://hl7.org/fhir/R4/) endpoint over plain REST/JSON and streams the resources back as DuckDB rows over Apache Arrow. FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) is the modern HL7 standard that powers EHR, EMR, and health-data interoperability across hospitals, payers, and digital-health platforms. This connector is for analysts, data engineers, and clinical-informatics teams who want to explore, validate, or extract FHIR data with familiar SQL instead of bespoke API clients — point a function at a service base URL (for example `https://hapi.fhir.org/baseR4`) and start querying.

Under the hood the worker speaks the FHIR R4 [RESTful API](https://hl7.org/fhir/R4/http.html) using nothing but the Go standard library, so it stays light and dependency-free while remaining faithful to the published [FHIR R4 specification](https://hl7.org/fhir/R4/) (build source at [HL7/fhir on GitHub](https://github.com/HL7/fhir)). It follows FHIR [search](https://hl7.org/fhir/R4/search.html) Bundle pagination automatically — every `link[].relation == "next"` page is fetched up to a safety cap — so a single query transparently spans many result pages. An optional OAuth bearer `token` argument unlocks protected endpoints, and non-2xx responses (including FHIR `OperationOutcome` bodies) surface as clean SQL errors rather than panics.

The connector turns a FHIR endpoint's core capabilities into SQL: pull clinical resources with their most-used fields flattened into typed columns, run a generic search across any resource type (Condition, Encounter, MedicationRequest, …) with an optional raw query string and `_count` page size, read an individual resource by its logical id, and discover which resource types and REST interactions a server supports from its [CapabilityStatement](https://hl7.org/fhir/R4/capabilitystatement.html). Flattened results always carry the untouched resource JSON alongside the typed columns, so nothing is lost — anything not surfaced as a column is still reachable with `json_extract`. Built on the [vgi-go](https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-go) SDK.

Not sure which endpoint to point at? Browse the built-in `fhir_servers` directory view for a curated list of public FHIR R4 base URLs, then hand one to any `fhir_*` function. Worked, runnable statements ship as each function's examples.
workers.readme_sql:
INSTALL vgi FROM community; LOAD vgi;

ATTACH 'fhir' AS fhir (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'github-auto://Query-farm/vgi-fhir@v0.4.1');

-- Patients (core fields flattened, full JSON in `raw`). Every search-backed
-- function STREAMS: it fetches one Bundle page per batch, so `LIMIT` stops the
-- scan after a single HTTP round-trip instead of crawling every page first.
SELECT id, family, given, gender, birth_date, active
FROM fhir.fhir_patients('https://r4.smarthealthit.org');

-- All observations (valueQuantity flattened; non-numeric values are NULL).
SELECT code, code_display, value, unit, subject
FROM fhir.fhir_observations('https://r4.smarthealthit.org');

-- Generic search of any resource type (id + full resource JSON).
SELECT id, resource
FROM fhir.fhir_search('https://r4.smarthealthit.org', 'Condition');

-- A raw search query string + a custom page size.
SELECT id
FROM fhir.fhir_search(
  'https://r4.smarthealthit.org', 'Patient',
  query := 'family=smith&gender=female',
  count := 50);

-- One resource by id.
SELECT resource
FROM fhir.fhir_read('https://r4.smarthealthit.org', 'Patient',
                    '45a69bf0-7116-4f9f-a1d9-29700439b4a4');

-- What the server supports.
SELECT resource_type, interactions
FROM fhir.fhir_capabilities('https://r4.smarthealthit.org');

-- Combine functions: one patient's Body Weight trend (fhir_observations),
-- labelled with their name (fhir_patients) by joining on the subject
-- reference. Table-function arguments must be literals, so both sides are
-- filtered to the same patient id.
SELECT p.given, p.family, o.effective[:10] AS measured_on,
       round(o.value, 1) AS weight_kg,
       round(o.value - lag(o.value) OVER (ORDER BY o.effective), 1) AS change_kg
FROM fhir.fhir_observations('https://r4.smarthealthit.org',
       query := 'patient=45a69bf0-7116-4f9f-a1d9-29700439b4a4&code=29463-7') AS o
JOIN fhir.fhir_patients('https://r4.smarthealthit.org',
       query := '_id=45a69bf0-7116-4f9f-a1d9-29700439b4a4') AS p
  ON o.subject = 'Patient/' || p.id
ORDER BY o.effective;

-- A bearer token for protected servers (named option on every function).

Reach for it when a question is about patients, clinical observations, or what a FHIR/EHR endpoint can do. tags.vgi.doc_md:
## FHIR R4 Query Functions

This schema groups every table function exposed by the **vgi-fhir** connector. Each function takes a FHIR R4 service *base URL* as its first argument and returns resources as DuckDB rows over Apache Arrow.

The functions cover the common ways to pull data from a FHIR R4 endpoint: listing clinical resources with their most-used fields flattened into typed columns, running a generic search across any resource type, reading an individual resource by its logical id, and inspecting the server's CapabilityStatement for the resource types and REST interactions it supports.

### Notes

- Bundle pagination (`link[].relation == "next"`) is followed automatically up to a safety cap.
- The flattened functions also expose the untouched resource JSON (`raw` / `resource`) so nothing is lost.
- An optional `token` named argument supplies an OAuth bearer token for protected endpoints.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## fhir_servers

A curated, credential-free directory of well-known **public HL7 FHIR R4** endpoints. It is a static list (no network access), so it always returns instantly and is the natural starting point for discovery: pick a `base_url` here and hand it to any `fhir_*` table function as its first argument.

### Columns

- `name` — human-friendly server name.
- `base_url` — the FHIR R4 service base URL (e.g. `https://hapi.fhir.org/baseR4`).
- `fhir_version` — the FHIR version served (all `4.0.1`).
- `requires_auth` — whether an OAuth bearer token is needed (all listed servers are open).
- `description` — what the endpoint is and what data it holds.

## fhir_read

Read a single FHIR R4 resource by its type and logical id — a direct `GET /{type}/{id}` against the server (the FHIR [read](https://hl7.org/fhir/R4/http.html#read) interaction).

### Usage

Call it with a FHIR R4 base URL, a resource type, and a logical id (for example `Patient` and a logical id listed by `fhir_patients`) to fetch that one resource as JSON; runnable statements are attached as this function's examples.

### Notes

- Returns exactly one row when the resource exists; a missing resource (HTTP 404) surfaces as a query error rather than an empty result.
- Supply `token` for endpoints that require authentication.

## fhir_patients

List [Patient](https://hl7.org/fhir/R4/patient.html) resources from a FHIR R4 server with the most-used demographic fields flattened into columns, while still returning the full resource JSON.

### Usage

Call it with a FHIR R4 base URL to list Patients with their core demographic fields flattened into columns; runnable statements are attached as this function's examples.

### Notes

- The `raw` column carries the untouched Patient JSON for fields not flattened here.

## fhir_observations

List [Observation](https://hl7.org/fhir/R4/observation.html) resources from a FHIR R4 server with the `valueQuantity` flattened into a numeric `value` plus `unit`, alongside status, code, display, effective time, and subject reference.

### Usage

Call it with a FHIR R4 base URL to list Observations with their numeric `value` and `unit` flattened out; runnable statements are attached as this function's examples.

Narrow to a single LOINC code with a raw `query` such as the heart-rate code, and keep only rows whose `value` is not null for numeric measurements.

### Notes

- Observations without a numeric `valueQuantity` (e.g. coded or string results) surface a **NULL** `value` rather than `0`.
- The `raw` column preserves the full Observation JSON, including components and reference ranges.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Read a FHIR R4 server's CapabilityStatement (/metadata) and list each resource type it exposes together with the REST interactions supported for that type (read, search-type, create, ...). Use to discover what an EHR/FHIR endpoint can do before querying it.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## fhir_capabilities

Read a server's [CapabilityStatement](https://hl7.org/fhir/R4/capabilitystatement.html) (`GET /metadata`) and list each resource type it exposes together with the REST interactions supported for that type.

### Usage

Call it with a FHIR R4 base URL to list every resource type the server exposes and the REST interactions it supports for each; runnable statements are attached as this function's examples.

### Notes

- `interactions` is a `VARCHAR[]`; `UNNEST` it to get one row per (resource type, interaction) pair.
- Use this first to discover what an unfamiliar EHR/FHIR endpoint supports before querying specific resource types.

vgi.example_queries.description: List every resource type a FHIR server supports and the REST interactions available for each.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT resource_type, interactions FROM fhir.main.fhir_capabilities('https://r4.smarthealthit.org');

vgi.example_queries.description: Expand the supported REST interactions to one row per (resource type, interaction).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT resource_type, UNNEST(interactions) AS interaction FROM fhir.main.fhir_capabilities('https://hapi.fhir.org/baseR4');

vgi.executable_examples.description: List Patients with core demographic fields flattened into columns.
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT id, family, given, gender, birth_date FROM fhir.main.fhir_patients('https://r4.smarthealthit.org') LIMIT 20

vgi.executable_examples.description: List numeric Observations with their code, value, and unit.
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT code, code_display, value, unit FROM fhir.main.fhir_observations('https://r4.smarthealthit.org') WHERE value IS NOT NULL LIMIT 20

vgi.executable_examples.description: Search Condition resources and return their logical ids.
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT id FROM fhir.main.fhir_search('https://r4.smarthealthit.org', 'Condition') LIMIT 20

vgi.executable_examples.description: Expand a server's supported resource types and REST interactions.
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT resource_type, UNNEST(interactions) AS interaction FROM fhir.main.fhir_capabilities('https://r4.smarthealthit.org')

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Search a single FHIR R4 resource type via the server's search endpoint, following Bundle next links across pages. Use for any resource type (Patient, Observation, Condition, ...) with an optional raw search query and page size.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## fhir_search

Run a FHIR R4 [search](https://hl7.org/fhir/R4/search.html) over a single resource type and return one row per matched resource.

### Usage

Call it with a FHIR R4 base URL and a resource type (for example `Condition`) to return one row per matched resource; runnable statements are attached as this function's examples.

Pass a raw `query` (e.g. `name=smith&_count=50`) and/or `count` to refine the search, and `token` for protected servers.

### Notes

- Follows Bundle `next` links across pages until exhausted or the safety cap is reached.
- The `resource` column holds the complete resource JSON, so any field not surfaced by the flattened functions is still reachable via `json_extract`.

vgi.example_queries.description: List the ids of all Condition resources on a FHIR R4 server (paging through Bundle next links).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id FROM fhir.main.fhir_search('https://r4.smarthealthit.org', 'Condition') LIMIT 20;

vgi.example_queries.description: Search Patients named 'smith' on the public HAPI R4 server, 100 per page, returning id plus the raw resource JSON.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id, resource FROM fhir.main.fhir_search('https://hapi.fhir.org/baseR4', 'Patient', query := 'name=smith', count := 100);

vgi.example_queries.description: Build one patient's problem list: search their Condition resources with fhir_search, join to fhir_patients on the subject reference, and report each condition's clinical status, onset date, and the patient's age in whole years at onset.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT p.given, p.family, json_extract_string(c.resource, '$.code.text') AS condition_name, json_extract_string(c.resource, '$.clinicalStatus.coding[0].code') AS clinical_status, CAST(json_extract_string(c.resource, '$.onsetDateTime')[:10] AS DATE) AS onset_date, date_sub('year', CAST(p.birth_date AS DATE), onset_date) AS age_at_onset FROM fhir.main.fhir_search('https://r4.smarthealthit.org', 'Condition', query := 'patient=45a69bf0-7116-4f9f-a1d9-29700439b4a4') AS c JOIN fhir.main.fhir_patients('https://r4.smarthealthit.org', query := '_id=45a69bf0-7116-4f9f-a1d9-29700439b4a4') AS p ON json_extract_string(c.resource, '$.subject.reference') = 'Patient/' || p.id ORDER BY onset_date, condition_name;
