functions.name: mt940_read
functions.comment: Read SWIFT MT940 customer statements into rows (one per statement).

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scan a glob of SWIFT MT940 (customer statement) text files into one row per statement (a file may hold several; statement_idx orders them). Columns include the account, statement/sequence numbers, signed opening and closing balances with their dates, and the line count. Use the raw column with mt940_lines(raw) to explode the :61: statement lines for reconciliation.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Read MT940 Statements

Scan a glob of SWIFT MT940 (customer statement) text files into one row per statement (a file may hold several; statement_idx orders them). Columns include the account, statement/sequence numbers, signed opening and closing balances with their dates, and the line count. Use the raw column with mt940_lines(raw) to explode the :61: statement lines for reconciliation.

The argument may be the **message text supplied inline** (handy for a single message or an example), a file path, or a glob that scans many files. All reads are local on the worker host — no network, no egress; payment data never leaves the machine. See the result columns for the full schema.

vgi.example_queries.description: Statement roll-forward check: explode each MT940 statement's :61: lines, net credits against debits, and compare opening balance + net movement with the reported closing balance (here STMT-2 is off by 50.50).
vgi.example_queries.sql:
SELECT transaction_ref, opening_balance, sum(CASE WHEN credit_debit IN ('D', 'RC') THEN -amount ELSE amount END) AS net_movement, closing_balance, opening_balance + net_movement = closing_balance AS balanced FROM iso20022.main.mt940_lines((SELECT transaction_ref, opening_balance, closing_balance, raw FROM iso20022.main.mt940_read('{1:F01X}{2:O940X}{4:
:20:STMT-1
:25:DE89370400440532013000
:28C:1/1
:60F:C260101EUR1000,00
:61:2601020102C500,00NTRFNONREF//BANK-A
:61:2601030103D250,50NMSCCUST-REF//BANK-B
:62F:C260103EUR1249,50
-}{1:F01X}{2:O940X}{4:
:20:STMT-2
:25:DE89370400440532013000
:28C:2/1
:60F:C260103EUR1249,50
:61:2601040104D100,00NMSCREF-2//BANK-C
:62F:C260104EUR1200,00
-}'))) GROUP BY transaction_ref, opening_balance, closing_balance ORDER BY transaction_ref

SELECT transaction_ref, account, ccy, closing_balance, line_count FROM iso20022.main.mt940_read('{1:F01ACMEDEFFAXXX0000000000}{2:O940DEUTDEFFXXXXN}{4:
:20:STMT-1
:25:DE89370400440532013000
:28C:12345/1
:60F:C260101EUR1000,00
:61:2601020102C500,00NTRFNONREF//BANK-A
EXTRA INFO
:86:GROCERY STORE PAYMENT
:61:2601030103D250,50NMSCCUST-REF//BANK-B
:86:?20RENT ?30BANK ?31ACC123
:62F:C260103EUR1249,50
:64:C260103EUR1249,50
-}') WHERE account IS NOT NULL

functions.name: camt054_entries
functions.comment: Explode camt.054 notification Ntry rows (one per entry; multi-TxDtls split; input columns passthrough).

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Explode the Ntry rows of camt.054 debit/credit notifications into one row per entry — identical column shape to camt053_entries, so reconciliation queries are portable. Pass a relation whose `raw` column (or the column named by `msg`) holds each notification, typically the output of camt054_read.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Explode camt.054 Entries

Explode the Ntry rows of camt.054 debit/credit notifications into one row per entry — identical column shape to camt053_entries, so reconciliation queries are portable. Pass a relation whose `raw` column (or the column named by `msg`) holds each notification, typically the output of camt054_read.

## Calling it

This is a table-in-out function: pass the relation to explode as a subquery, e.g. `camt054_entries((SELECT raw FROM <reader>('…')))`, or feed it any relation that exposes a `raw` message column (rename it with `msg := 'col'`). Every input column is passed through unchanged, repeated once per child row, so results correlate back to the parent.

## Result schema

The passthrough input columns come first, followed by the fixed child columns — their names, types, and meanings are documented in `vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md`, and a runnable call is in `vgi.executable_examples`. Local-only — no network, no egress.

vgi.executable_examples.description: Explode the entries of an inline camt.054 notification.
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT amount, credit_debit, end_to_end_id FROM iso20022.main.camt054_entries((SELECT '<Document xmlns="urn:iso:std:iso:20022:tech:xsd:camt.054.001.08"><BkToCstmrDbtCdtNtfctn><Ntfctn><Id>N</Id><Ntry><Amt Ccy="EUR">250.50</Amt><CdtDbtInd>DBIT</CdtDbtInd><NtryDtls><TxDtls><Refs><EndToEndId>E2E</EndToEndId></Refs></TxDtls></NtryDtls></Ntry></Ntfctn></BkToCstmrDbtCdtNtfctn></Document>' AS raw))

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
The result schema is **dynamic**: every column of the input relation you pass is returned first, unchanged and repeated once per child row, followed by the fixed child columns below. When the input is the output of a `*_read` function (or any relation that exposes a `raw` message column), that `raw` column is passed through too.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| raw | VARCHAR | Passthrough: the parent message text carried from the input relation (present whenever the input exposes a `raw` column). |

tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Read pacs.002 Payment Statuses

Scan a glob of ISO 20022 pacs.002 (FIToFIPmtStsRpt) XML files into one row per TxInfAndSts: the transaction status (ACSC/ACSP/RJCT/PDNG), status reason codes, and original references back to the pacs.008 it answers. Use it to reconcile payment acknowledgements / rejections.

The argument may be the **message text supplied inline** (handy for a single message or an example), a file path, or a glob that scans many files. All reads are local on the worker host — no network, no egress; payment data never leaves the machine. See the result columns for the full schema.

vgi.example_queries.description: Status reconciliation: join each pacs.008 credit transfer to the pacs.002 status report on UETR to see which payments settled (ACSC) and which were rejected, with the reason code.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT p.end_to_end_id, p.creditor_name, p.amount, p.ccy, s.tx_status, s.status_reason_code FROM iso20022.main.pacs008_read('<Document xmlns="urn:iso:std:iso:20022:tech:xsd:pacs.008.001.08"><FIToFICstmrCdtTrf><GrpHdr><MsgId>BATCH-7</MsgId></GrpHdr><CdtTrfTxInf><PmtId><EndToEndId>E2E-A</EndToEndId><UETR>0a1b2c3d-0000-4aaa-8bbb-00000000000a</UETR></PmtId><IntrBkSttlmAmt Ccy="EUR">1500.00</IntrBkSttlmAmt><Cdtr><Nm>WIDGETS SARL</Nm></Cdtr></CdtTrfTxInf><CdtTrfTxInf><PmtId><EndToEndId>E2E-B</EndToEndId><UETR>0a1b2c3d-0000-4aaa-8bbb-00000000000b</UETR></PmtId><IntrBkSttlmAmt Ccy="EUR">98000.00</IntrBkSttlmAmt><Cdtr><Nm>GADGETS GMBH</Nm></Cdtr></CdtTrfTxInf></FIToFICstmrCdtTrf></Document>') AS p LEFT JOIN iso20022.main.pacs002_read('<Document xmlns="urn:iso:std:iso:20022:tech:xsd:pacs.002.001.10"><FIToFIPmtStsRpt><GrpHdr><MsgId>STS-7</MsgId></GrpHdr><OrgnlGrpInfAndSts><OrgnlMsgId>BATCH-7</OrgnlMsgId></OrgnlGrpInfAndSts><TxInfAndSts><OrgnlUETR>0a1b2c3d-0000-4aaa-8bbb-00000000000a</OrgnlUETR><TxSts>ACSC</TxSts></TxInfAndSts><TxInfAndSts><OrgnlUETR>0a1b2c3d-0000-4aaa-8bbb-00000000000b</OrgnlUETR><TxSts>RJCT</TxSts><StsRsnInf><Rsn><Cd>AM04</Cd></Rsn></StsRsnInf></TxInfAndSts></FIToFIPmtStsRpt></Document>') AS s ON s.orig_uetr = p.uetr ORDER BY p.end_to_end_id

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Scan a glob of SWIFT MT103 (single customer credit transfer) text files into one row per message: ordering customer and beneficiary (name/account/BIC), the exact :32A: settled amount and currency, instructed amount, charges, remittance info, the derived end-to-end id, and the block-3 UETR. tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Read MT103 Credit Transfers

Scan a glob of SWIFT MT103 (single customer credit transfer) text files into one row per message: ordering customer and beneficiary (name/account/BIC), the exact :32A: settled amount and currency, instructed amount, charges, remittance info, the derived end-to-end id, and the block-3 UETR. Use it for payment ingestion and MT103<->pacs.008 migration-QA joins.

The argument may be the **message text supplied inline** (handy for a single message or an example), a file path, or a glob that scans many files. All reads are local on the worker host — no network, no egress; payment data never leaves the machine. See the result columns for the full schema.

vgi.example_queries.description: Migration QA: pair an MT103 with its pacs.008 twin on end_to_end_id and check that the settled amount, currency, and UETR agree in both formats.
vgi.example_queries.sql:
SELECT m.end_to_end_id, m.ccy, m.amount AS mt_amount, p.amount AS mx_amount, m.amount = p.amount AND m.ccy = p.ccy AS amount_match, m.uetr = p.uetr AS uetr_match FROM iso20022.main.mt103_read('{1:F01ACMEDEFFAXXX0000000000}{2:I103DEUTDEFFXXXXN}{3:{121:e3bf1c2a-1111-4aaa-8bbb-1234567890ab}}{4:
:20:TXN-REF-1
:23B:CRED
:32A:260101EUR1234,56
:50K:/DE89370400440532013000
ACME CORP
:59:/FR1420041010050500013M02606
WIDGETS SARL
:71A:SHA
:72:/EToE/E2E-REF-001
-}') AS m JOIN iso20022.main.pacs008_read('<Document xmlns="urn:iso:std:iso:20022:tech:xsd:pacs.008.001.08"><FIToFICstmrCdtTrf><GrpHdr><MsgId>PACS-MSG-1</MsgId></GrpHdr><CdtTrfTxInf><PmtId><EndToEndId>E2E-REF-001</EndToEndId><UETR>e3bf1c2a-1111-4aaa-8bbb-1234567890ab</UETR></PmtId><IntrBkSttlmAmt Ccy="EUR">1234.56</IntrBkSttlmAmt></CdtTrfTxInf></FIToFICstmrCdtTrf></Document>') AS p USING (end_to_end_id) ORDER BY m.end_to_end_id

vgi.executable_examples.description: Parse an inline MT103 credit transfer and read its exact settled amount, currency, and parties.
vgi.executable_examples.sql:
SELECT senders_ref, value_date, ccy, amount, beneficiary FROM iso20022.main.mt103_read('{1:F01ACMEDEFFAXXX0000000000}{2:I103DEUTDEFFXXXXN}{3:{121:e3bf1c2a-1111-4aaa-8bbb-1234567890ab}}{4:
:20:TXN-REF-1
:23B:CRED
:32A:260101EUR1234,56
:50K:/DE89370400440532013000
ACME CORP
:59:/FR1420041010050500013M02606
WIDGETS SARL
:70:INVOICE 998877
:71A:SHA
:72:/EToE/E2E-REF-001
-}') WHERE amount > 1000

tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Explode camt.053 Entries

Explode the Ntry rows of camt.053 statements (or any camt.053/054 documents) into one row per entry, with multi-TxDtls split by tx_idx and every input column passed through. Pass a relation whose `raw` column (or the column named by `msg`) holds each statement — typically the output of camt053_read — to get amount, credit/debit, dates, references, counterparty, and remittance for reconciliation.

## Calling it

This is a table-in-out function: pass the relation to explode as a subquery, e.g. `camt053_entries((SELECT raw FROM <reader>('…')))`, or feed it any relation that exposes a `raw` message column (rename it with `msg := 'col'`). Every input column is passed through unchanged, repeated once per child row, so results correlate back to the parent.

## Result schema

The passthrough input columns come first, followed by the fixed child columns — their names, types, and meanings are documented in `vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md`, and a runnable call is in `vgi.executable_examples`. Local-only — no network, no egress.

vgi.executable_examples.description: Explode the entries of an inline camt.053 statement.
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT amount, credit_debit, end_to_end_id FROM iso20022.main.camt053_entries((SELECT '<Document xmlns="urn:iso:std:iso:20022:tech:xsd:camt.053.001.08"><BkToCstmrStmt><Stmt><Id>S</Id><Ntry><Amt Ccy="EUR">500.00</Amt><CdtDbtInd>CRDT</CdtDbtInd><NtryDtls><TxDtls><Refs><EndToEndId>E2E</EndToEndId></Refs></TxDtls></NtryDtls></Ntry></Stmt></BkToCstmrStmt></Document>' AS raw))

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
The result schema is **dynamic**: every column of the input relation you pass is returned first, unchanged and repeated once per child row, followed by the fixed child columns below. When the input is the output of a `*_read` function (or any relation that exposes a `raw` message column), that `raw` column is passed through too.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| raw | VARCHAR | Passthrough: the parent message text carried from the input relation (present whenever the input exposes a `raw` column). |
| entry_idx | INTEGER | Ordinal of the Ntry within the statement. |
| tx_idx | INTEGER | Ordinal of the TxDtls within the entry. |
| amount | DECIMAL(38,9) | Ntry/Amt. |
| ccy | VARCHAR | Ntry/Amt/@Ccy. |
| credit_debit | VARCHAR | Ntry/CdtDbtInd (CRDT/DBIT). |

| account_servicer_ref | VARCHAR | Ntry/AcctSvcrRef. |

| bank_tx_family | VARCHAR | Ntry/BkTxCd/Domn/Fmly/Cd. |
| bank_tx_subfamily | VARCHAR | Ntry/BkTxCd/Domn/Fmly/SubFmlyCd. |
| bank_tx_proprietary | VARCHAR | Ntry/BkTxCd/Prtry/Cd. |
| end_to_end_id | VARCHAR | TxDtls/Refs/EndToEndId. |
| tx_id | VARCHAR | TxDtls/Refs/TxId. |
| uetr | VARCHAR | TxDtls/Refs/UETR. |

functions.comment: Return the raw text of an MT field by tag (newline-joined if repeatable)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Return the raw text of any SWIFT MT field by its tag (e.g. '50K', '59', '71F', '32A') from a message's block 4. Repeatable tags (e.g. '71F') are joined with a newline. A bare numeric prefix like '50' matches whichever option variant is present (50A/50F/50K). Returns NULL when the tag is absent or the message is unparseable. Works on any MT type despite the name; the message argument is inline text, a file path, or `BLOB` bytes.

arguments.name: tag
arguments.description: The SWIFT field tag to read from message block 4. Tags form an open vocabulary rather than a fixed set — a two-digit field number with an optional single option letter. functions.name: iso20022_validate
functions.comment: Validate an MT/MX message: STRUCT(ok BOOLEAN, errors VARCHAR[])

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Validate a SWIFT MT or ISO 20022 MX payment message and return a `STRUCT(ok BOOLEAN, errors VARCHAR[])`. It auto-detects the family and message type, then runs structural checks (balanced MT blocks / well-formed MX, mandatory tags & elements present) plus selected CBPR+ SR2025 field rules: BIC format, IBAN mod-97 checksum, ISO 4217 currency and minor-unit consistency, charge-bearer code sets, and UETR `UUID` shape. `ok` is true iff `errors` is empty; each error is a stable 'CODE: text' string you can unnest or list_contains. This is structural + field-level validation, NOT full CBPR+/HVPS+ network validation. The message argument is inline text, a file path, or `BLOB` bytes.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Validate an MT/MX message -> `STRUCT(ok BOOLEAN, errors VARCHAR[])` (structural + IBAN/BIC/currency/charge-bearer/UETR field rules). `ok` is true iff `errors` is empty.

workers.title: Jira and Confluence
workers.tagline: Jira issues with JQL pushdown, changelogs, sprints and Confluence pages (CQL) as SQL in DuckDB (TypeScript)
workers.subtitle: Atlassian Jira issues, sprints and projects plus Confluence pages as SQL, with JQL/CQL pushdown.
workers.summary: Atlassian Jira (Cloud and Data Center) and Confluence Cloud as SQL: issues, changelogs, sprints, projects, pages and spaces, read-only, with JQL and CQL pushdown.
workers.doc_md:
# Jira and Confluence

Query Atlassian Jira (Cloud or Data Center) and Confluence Cloud from DuckDB: issues with their changelog, comments, worklogs and links; projects, boards and sprints; site configuration; and Confluence spaces and pages. Read-only.

Create an `atlassian` secret with your site URL and an API token (Cloud), a personal access token (Data Center) or an OAuth access token. WHERE filters become JQL or CQL and only the columns you select are fetched, so filter and project early.

### Sources and references

- [Jira Cloud REST API v3](https://developer.atlassian.com/cloud/jira/platform/rest/v3/intro/) and the [enhanced JQL search](https://developer.atlassian.com/cloud/jira/platform/rest/v3/api-group-issue-search/#api-rest-api-3-search-jql-get)
- [Jira Data Center REST API v2](https://developer.atlassian.com/server/jira/platform/rest/v10000/intro/)
- [JQL reference](https://support.atlassian.com/jira-software-cloud/docs/use-advanced-search-with-jira-query-language-jql/)
- [Jira Software (Agile) REST API](https://developer.atlassian.com/cloud/jira/software/rest/intro/)
- [Confluence Cloud REST API v2](https://developer.atlassian.com/cloud/confluence/rest/v2/intro/) and [CQL](https://developer.atlassian.com/cloud/confluence/advanced-searching-using-cql/)
- [Rate limiting](https://developer.atlassian.com/cloud/jira/platform/rate-limiting/) and [API tokens](https://support.atlassian.com/atlassian-account/docs/manage-api-tokens-for-your-atlassian-account/)
workers.readme_sql:
CREATE SECRET jira (TYPE atlassian, SITE_URL 'https://acme.atlassian.net',
                    EMAIL 'you@acme.com', API_TOKEN '…');

-- Open bugs in ENG by priority: one JQL request
--   project = "ENG" AND issuetype = "Bug" AND statusCategory != Done
SELECT key, title, priority, assignee_display_name
FROM jira.main.issues()
WHERE project_key = 'ENG' AND issue_type = 'Bug' AND state = 'open'
ORDER BY priority, key;

-- Hours each ENG issue spent In Progress, from the status changelog.
SELECT issue_key, sum(epoch(next_at - changed_at)) / 3600 AS hours_in_progress
FROM (SELECT issue_key, changed_at, to_string,
             lead(changed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY issue_key ORDER BY changed_at) AS next_at
      FROM jira.main.issue_changelog(jql := 'project = ENG') WHERE field = 'status')
WHERE to_string = 'In Progress' AND next_at IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY issue_key;

-- Runbooks in the OPS Confluence space, as plain text (CQL: space = "OPS" AND label = "runbook").
SELECT title, body_text FROM jira.confluence.pages()
WHERE space_key = 'OPS' AND list_contains(labels, 'runbook');

example_queries.description: The issues() result columns (binds only; create an atlassian secret and drop LIMIT 0 for rows)

example_queries.description: The pages() result columns (binds only; create an atlassian secret and drop LIMIT 0 for rows)
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, space_key, title, last_modified_at FROM jira.confluence.pages() LIMIT 0;

example_queries.description: Runbooks in a space (space and label become CQL)
example_queries.sql: SELECT title, last_modified_at FROM jira.confluence.pages() WHERE space_key = 'OPS' AND list_contains(labels, 'runbook') ORDER BY title

example_queries.description: Full-text search, reading plain-text bodies
example_queries.sql: SELECT title, left(body_text, 200) AS preview FROM jira.confluence.pages(cql := 'text ~ "deploy"') WHERE type = 'page' ORDER BY title

example_queries.description: Edit history of a page
example_queries.sql: SELECT number, author_id, created_at, message FROM jira.confluence.page_versions(page_id := '1001') ORDER BY number

example_queries.description: Most used labels across pages
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, count(*) AS pages FROM jira.confluence.page_labels() GROUP BY name ORDER BY pages DESC, name

example_queries.description: Unresolved inline comments on a page
example_queries.sql: SELECT author_id, inline_selection, body_text FROM jira.confluence.page_comments(page_id := '1001') WHERE kind = 'inline' AND resolution_status = 'open' ORDER BY created_at

example_queries.description: Global spaces
example_queries.sql: SELECT key, name FROM jira.confluence.spaces WHERE type = 'global' ORDER BY key

example_queries.description: Open bugs in a project by priority (one JQL request: project, issuetype, statusCategory)
example_queries.sql: SELECT key, title, priority, assignee_display_name FROM jira.main.issues() WHERE project_key = 'ENG' AND issue_type = 'Bug' AND state = 'open' ORDER BY priority, key

example_queries.description: Issues per status category for one label (list_contains becomes labels = "backend")
example_queries.sql: SELECT status_category, count(*) AS issues FROM jira.main.issues() WHERE list_contains(labels, 'backend') GROUP BY status_category ORDER BY status_category

example_queries.description: Combine raw JQL with SQL filters: recently resolved issues of the current sprint
example_queries.sql: SELECT key, closed_at FROM jira.main.issues(jql := 'sprint in openSprints()') WHERE closed_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01' ORDER BY closed_at

example_queries.description: Status transitions of one issue in order (cycle-time building block)
example_queries.sql: SELECT changed_at, from_string, to_string, author_display_name FROM jira.main.issue_changelog(issue_key := 'ENG-1') WHERE field = 'status' ORDER BY changed_at

example_queries.description: Hours each issue of a project spent In Progress, from consecutive status changes
example_queries.sql: SELECT issue_key, sum(epoch(next_at - changed_at)) / 3600 AS hours_in_progress FROM (SELECT issue_key, changed_at, to_string, lead(changed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY issue_key ORDER BY changed_at) AS next_at FROM jira.main.issue_changelog(jql := 'project = ENG') WHERE field = 'status') WHERE to_string = 'In Progress' AND next_at IS NOT NULL GROUP BY issue_key ORDER BY issue_key

example_queries.description: Most talkative commenters in a project
example_queries.sql: SELECT author_display_name, count(*) AS comments FROM jira.main.issue_comments(jql := 'project = ENG') GROUP BY author_display_name ORDER BY comments DESC

example_queries.description: Read one issue's discussion as text
example_queries.sql: SELECT created_at, author_display_name, body FROM jira.main.issue_comments(issue_key := 'ENG-1') ORDER BY created_at

example_queries.description: Hours logged per person on one issue
example_queries.sql: SELECT author_display_name, sum(time_spent_seconds) / 3600.0 AS hours FROM jira.main.issue_worklogs(issue_key := 'ENG-2') GROUP BY author_display_name ORDER BY hours DESC

tags.vgi.doc_llm: pages(cql := NULL) searches Confluence content with CQL (/wiki/rest/api/search) and returns one row per page or blog post: id, type (page / blogpost), status, title, space_key, space_name, parent_id, author_id, author_display_name, created_at, version, last_modified_at, last_modified_by, labels, excerpt, body_storage (storage-format XHTML), body_text (plain text extracted from it), html_url. Use cql := 'text ~ "…"' or 'title ~ "…"' for full-text search. Bodies are fetched only when selected.
tags.vgi.doc_md:

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Jira as SQL. issues(jql := NULL, page_size := 100) is the main entry point: WHERE filters push into JQL (ANDed with jql), projection picks the fields= list. Per-issue collections (history, comments, worklogs, links) take issue_key = / IN or jql := and otherwise read every issue the JQL matches. Per-project collections take project_key and sprints take board_id; otherwise they fan out over every project / board. Site-wide configuration listings are unfiltered. Users are identified by accountId on Cloud and by username on Data Center.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main (Jira)

Issues from JQL search with SQL→JQL pushdown, per-issue history, comments, worklogs and links, projects and their components/versions/statuses, boards and sprints, and site metadata.

All objects need an `atlassian` secret.

vgi.example_queries.description: Open bugs in a project by priority (one JQL request: project, issuetype, statusCategory)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT key, title, priority, assignee_display_name FROM jira.main.issues() WHERE project_key = 'ENG' AND issue_type = 'Bug' AND state = 'open' ORDER BY priority, key

vgi.example_queries.description: Issues per status category for one label (list_contains becomes labels = "backend")
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT status_category, count(*) AS issues FROM jira.main.issues() WHERE list_contains(labels, 'backend') GROUP BY status_category ORDER BY status_category

vgi.example_queries.description: Combine raw JQL with SQL filters: recently resolved issues of the current sprint
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT key, closed_at FROM jira.main.issues(jql := 'sprint in openSprints()') WHERE closed_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01' ORDER BY closed_at

vgi.example_queries.description: Status transitions of one issue in order (cycle-time building block)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT changed_at, from_string, to_string, author_display_name FROM jira.main.issue_changelog(issue_key := 'ENG-1') WHERE field = 'status' ORDER BY changed_at

vgi.example_queries.description: Hours each issue of a project spent In Progress, from consecutive status changes
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT issue_key, sum(epoch(next_at - changed_at)) / 3600 AS hours_in_progress FROM (SELECT issue_key, changed_at, to_string, lead(changed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY issue_key ORDER BY changed_at) AS next_at FROM jira.main.issue_changelog(jql := 'project = ENG') WHERE field = 'status') WHERE to_string = 'In Progress' AND next_at IS NOT NULL GROUP BY issue_key ORDER BY issue_key

vgi.example_queries.description: Most talkative commenters in a project
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT author_display_name, count(*) AS comments FROM jira.main.issue_comments(jql := 'project = ENG') GROUP BY author_display_name ORDER BY comments DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Read one issue's discussion as text
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT created_at, author_display_name, body FROM jira.main.issue_comments(issue_key := 'ENG-1') ORDER BY created_at

vgi.example_queries.description: Hours logged per person on one issue
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT author_display_name, sum(time_spent_seconds) / 3600.0 AS hours FROM jira.main.issue_worklogs(issue_key := 'ENG-2') GROUP BY author_display_name ORDER BY hours DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Open issues that are blocked, and by what
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT issue_key, linked_issue_key, linked_issue_status FROM jira.main.issue_links(jql := 'statusCategory != Done') WHERE relationship = 'is blocked by' ORDER BY issue_key

vgi.example_queries.description: Components of a project with their leads
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, lead_display_name FROM jira.main.components(project_key := 'ENG') ORDER BY name

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT project_key, name, release_date FROM jira.main.versions() WHERE NOT released ORDER BY release_date

functions.name: issues
functions.comment: Jira issues matching a JQL search, with SQL filters pushed into the JQL and only selected fields fetched.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: issues(jql := NULL, page_size := 100) runs a Jira JQL search (Cloud enhanced search /rest/api/3/search/jql, or /rest/api/2/search on Data Center) and returns one row per issue. Prefer plain SQL WHERE filters: they are translated to JQL — project/repo (= / IN / !=), key (= / IN), id, status, status_category, state ('open' → statusCategory != Done), issue_type, is_subtask, priority, resolution, assignee, user_login (reporter) — = / IN and IS NULL (→ is EMPTY) where meaningful; list_contains on labels, components, fix_versions, affects_versions, assignees and sprint_ids; parent_key (Cloud); created_at / updated_at / closed_at ranges (widened by a day for JQL's minute precision and user time zone, then re-checked exactly); hoisted numeric custom fields (= and ranges via cf[id]). All clauses are ANDed with the jql argument. The projection becomes the fields= parameter. Use jql := for anything SQL cannot express (text ~, functions such as openSprints(), currentUser(), was/changed history predicates). Columns: repo/project_key, number, key, id, title/summary, state ('open'/'closed'), status, status_category, issue_type, is_subtask, priority, resolution, user_login (reporter id), reporter_display_name, assignee (accountId on Cloud, username on DC), assignee_display_name, assignees, labels, components, fix_versions, affects_versions, parent_key, sprint_ids, sprint_names, due_date, estimates/time spent in seconds, votes, watches, body (plain text), description_adf, html_url, created_at, updated_at, closed_at (resolution date), custom_fields (JSON by field name) plus any columns hoisted via the custom_fields ATTACH option. Names match the GitHub/GitLab workers for UNIONs.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## issues(jql := NULL, page_size := 100)

Jira issues from a JQL search. SQL filters are translated into JQL and ANDed with `jql`; only the selected columns' fields are requested.

Hoist custom fields into typed columns at ATTACH time:

```sql
ATTACH 'jira' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION '…', custom_fields 'story_points=Story point estimate:DOUBLE, team=Team');
```

**Pushdown:** project/repo (= / IN / !=), key (= / IN), id, status, status_category, state ('open' → statusCategory != Done), issue_type, is_subtask, priority, resolution, assignee, user_login (reporter) — = / IN and IS NULL (→ is EMPTY) where meaningful; list_contains on labels, components, fix_versions, affects_versions, assignees and sprint_ids; parent_key (Cloud); created_at / updated_at / closed_at ranges (widened by a day for JQL's minute precision and user time zone, then re-checked exactly); hoisted numeric custom fields (= and ranges via cf[id]). All clauses are ANDed with the jql argument. The projection becomes the fields= parameter.

vgi.example_queries.description: Open bugs in a project by priority (one JQL request: project, issuetype, statusCategory)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT key, title, priority, assignee_display_name FROM jira.main.issues() WHERE project_key = 'ENG' AND issue_type = 'Bug' AND state = 'open' ORDER BY priority, key

vgi.example_queries.description: Issues per status category for one label (list_contains becomes labels = "backend")
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT status_category, count(*) AS issues FROM jira.main.issues() WHERE list_contains(labels, 'backend') GROUP BY status_category ORDER BY status_category

vgi.example_queries.description: Combine raw JQL with SQL filters: recently resolved issues of the current sprint
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT key, closed_at FROM jira.main.issues(jql := 'sprint in openSprints()') WHERE closed_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01' ORDER BY closed_at

functions.comment: Field-level change history of Jira issues: status transitions, reassignments, edits (one row per changed field).

tags.vgi.doc_llm: issue_changelog(issue_key := NULL, jql := NULL) returns one row per changed field per changelog entry: issue_key, history_id, author (accountId / DC username), author_display_name, changed_at, field (e.g. 'status', 'assignee', 'Sprint'), field_id, field_type, from_value / from_string, to_value / to_string. For status transitions and cycle time filter WHERE field = 'status' and use from_string / to_string with changed_at. Pass issue_key (or WHERE issue_key IN (…)) for specific issues; otherwise jql picks the issues (every issue when omitted). Cloud pages /rest/api/3/issue/{key}/changelog; Data Center reads the search with expand=changelog.
tags.vgi.doc_md:

vgi.example_queries.description: Status transitions of one issue in order (cycle-time building block)

vgi.example_queries.description: Hours each issue of a project spent In Progress, from consecutive status changes
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT issue_key, sum(epoch(next_at - changed_at)) / 3600 AS hours_in_progress FROM (SELECT issue_key, changed_at, to_string, lead(changed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY issue_key ORDER BY changed_at) AS next_at FROM jira.main.issue_changelog(jql := 'project = ENG') WHERE field = 'status') WHERE to_string = 'In Progress' AND next_at IS NOT NULL GROUP BY issue_key ORDER BY issue_key

# Jolt JSON Transformation for DuckDB

**Reshape, rename, and restructure JSON directly in SQL** with declarative JSON-to-JSON transformations powered by [Bazaarvoice Jolt](https://github.com/bazaarvoice/jolt) — no imperative parsing code, no external ETL step, just a Jolt spec and a SQL query.

This extension brings Jolt's battle-tested declarative JSON transformation engine to DuckDB so data engineers, analysts, and API integrators can normalize, remap, flatten, and enrich JSON documents where the data already lives. Instead of writing language-specific code to walk and rebuild nested objects, you describe the *target shape* with a Jolt spec and let the engine do the structural work. It is ideal for cleaning up messy API responses, conforming event-stream payloads to a canonical schema, and reshaping nested records for downstream analytics — entirely inside your DuckDB pipeline.

Under the hood the worker embeds [Bazaarvoice Jolt](https://github.com/bazaarvoice/jolt) (Apache-2.0), the widely used JVM library for specification-driven JSON transformation. A Jolt **chainr** spec is a JSON array of ordered operations — `shift` (path-based copy/move of values into a new tree), `default` (supply missing keys), `remove`, `cardinality` (single↔list coercion), `sort`, and the `modify-*-beta` function operators — applied in sequence to transform an input document into an output document. The worker compiles each spec once per Arrow batch and reuses it across rows for efficient columnar execution. To learn the spec language hands-on, try the [interactive Jolt demo](https://jolt-demo.appspot.com/) and read the [Jolt documentation](https://github.com/bazaarvoice/jolt/blob/master/README.md).

## When to reach for it

Reach for this worker whenever a JSON document arrives in the wrong shape for what comes next: keys need renaming, values need lifting out of (or nesting into) deep structures, arrays need flattening or grouping, missing fields need sensible defaults, or a heterogeneous feed needs conforming to one canonical schema. Because the transformation is a declarative spec rather than procedural code, the same query adapts to new shapes by editing the spec — not by rewriting logic.

## Key concepts

- **Spec-driven.** You describe the *target* shape; Jolt does the structural walking. A full **chainr** spec is an ordered JSON array of operations, applied in sequence.
- **Operation vocabulary.** `shift` (path-based copy/move), `default` (supply absent keys), `remove`, `cardinality` (single↔list coercion), `sort`, and the `modify-*-beta` function operators.
- **Validation first.** Companion predicates let a pipeline check that a spec compiles and that a payload is well-formed JSON before attempting a transform, so bad rows can be filtered rather than fault the query.
- **Columnar & batched.** Each spec is compiled once per Arrow batch and reused across rows, and the document column is the data vector while the spec is a query constant.

A worked example — lift a deeply nested value up to a top-level key with a full chainr spec:

```sql
SELECT jolt.jolt_transform(
  '{"rating":{"primary":{"value":3}}}',
  '[{"operation":"shift","spec":{"rating":{"primary":{"value":"Rating"}}}}]');
```

Built and maintained by [Query.Farm](https://query.farm) for the [DuckDB](https://duckdb.org/) ecosystem.

Using this worker, test whether the literal text value not valid json is a well-formed JSON document. Pass that text straight to the worker's JSON-validity check and return the single boolean it produces.

Five raw signup payloads arrive as JSON text: {"usr":"a1","plan":"pro"}, {"usr":"b2"}, {"usr":"c3" (truncated), {"usr":"d4","plan":"team"} and {"usr":"e5"}. Using this worker, drop any payload that is not well-formed JSON, reshape the rest with a Jolt shift that moves usr to user.id and plan to user.tier, then apply a Jolt default so user.tier is "free" when it is missing. # Jolt transformation & validation

Declarative JSON→JSON transformation and validation over Apache Arrow, powered by [Bazaarvoice Jolt](https://github.com/bazaarvoice/jolt). This schema groups the worker's SQL functions for reshaping JSON documents and for guarding those transforms against malformed input.

## What lives here

- **Transformation** — reshape, rename, nest, flatten, and default JSON fields by describing the target shape as a Jolt spec instead of writing imperative traversal code.
- **Validation** — cheap, never-throwing predicates that check a spec compiles and a payload is well-formed JSON, so a pipeline can filter bad rows before transforming.

## When to use it

Use it to normalize messy API responses, conform event-stream payloads to a canonical schema, and restructure nested records for downstream analytics — all inside DuckDB, with no external ETL step. Transforms raise on malformed input, while the validation predicates never throw — pair them to guard a pipeline and filter bad rows before reshaping.

The default operation supplies values for keys that are **absent** from the input; existing keys are left untouched. Use it to normalize documents to a known shape (guaranteeing fields exist, supplying fallback defaults) before downstream processing.

# jolt_default

Apply one Jolt **default** operation — supply values for keys absent from the input document.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT jolt.main.jolt_default(
  '{"name":"widget"}',
  '{"inStock":true,"currency":"USD"}');
-- => {"name":"widget","inStock":true,"currency":"USD"}
```

Keys already present in the input win; the spec only fills gaps. The spec is the **bare** default spec object, not the chainr operation envelope.

## Notes

- Returns `VARCHAR` JSON; output key order is not guaranteed.
- NULL input row maps to a NULL result.
- Malformed input JSON or default spec raises an error.

# json_valid

Return whether a string parses as a well-formed JSON document.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT jolt.main.json_valid('{"a":[1,2,3]}');  -- true
SELECT jolt.main.json_valid('{oops');           -- false
```

## Notes

- Never throws: malformed JSON returns `false`, not an error.
- NULL input row maps to a NULL result.
- Pair with the transform scalars to filter out bad rows before transforming.

Apply a full [Bazaarvoice Jolt](https://github.com/bazaarvoice/jolt) **chainr** spec to a JSON document and return the transformed JSON string.

A chainr spec is a JSON **array** of operation entries, each `{"operation": <name>, "spec": <op-spec>}`, applied in order. Supported operations include `shift` (path-based copy/move), `default` (fill absent keys), `remove` (delete keys), `cardinality` (single↔list), `sort`, and the `modify-*-beta` function operations.

**Inputs:** `input_json` (`VARCHAR` or `BLOB` JSON document, taken as the data vector) and `spec_json` (a constant chainr spec, compiled once per batch and reused across rows).

**Output:** the transformed document as a JSON `VARCHAR`. A NULL input row yields NULL. Malformed input JSON or a malformed/invalid spec raises a DuckDB error. Use this as the headline function for arbitrary multi-step JSON restructuring; for a single operation prefer `jolt_shift` or `jolt_default`.

# jolt_transform

Apply a complete Jolt **chainr** specification to a JSON document, returning the restructured JSON.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT jolt.main.jolt_transform(
  '{"rating":{"primary":{"value":3}}}',
  '[{"operation":"shift","spec":{"rating":{"primary":{"value":"Rating"}}}}]');
-- => {"Rating":3}
```

The spec is a JSON array of operations (`shift`, `default`, `remove`, `cardinality`, `sort`, `modify-*-beta`) applied in sequence. The spec argument is a query constant: it is compiled once and reused for every row in the batch.

## Notes

- Returns `VARCHAR` JSON; key order in the output is not guaranteed by Jolt.
- NULL input row maps to a NULL result.
- Malformed input JSON or an invalid spec raises an error rather than returning NULL.

Compiled once per batch and reused for every input row; a malformed or invalid spec raises an error.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Test whether a string is a valid [Bazaarvoice Jolt](https://github.com/bazaarvoice/jolt) **chainr** spec, returning a `BOOLEAN`.

Returns `true` when the input both parses as JSON and compiles via `Chainr.fromSpec` (i.e. it is a JSON array of recognized operation entries). Returns `false` for malformed JSON, a non-array, or an unknown/invalid operation — it never raises an error, so it is safe as a guard or filter before calling `jolt_transform`.

**Input:** `spec_json` (`VARCHAR`/`BLOB`). **Output:** `BOOLEAN`, or NULL for a NULL input row.

# is_valid_jolt_spec

Return whether a string compiles as a Jolt chainr spec.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT jolt.main.is_valid_jolt_spec(
  '[{"operation":"shift","spec":{"a":"b"}}]');  -- true
SELECT jolt.main.is_valid_jolt_spec('not json');  -- false
```

## Notes

- Never throws: invalid input returns `false`, not an error.
- NULL input row maps to a NULL result.
- Use as a pre-flight check before `jolt_transform`, which does raise on an invalid spec.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Apply a single [Bazaarvoice Jolt](https://github.com/bazaarvoice/jolt) **shift** operation to a JSON document — the most common Jolt operation — and return the transformed JSON string.

A shift spec is a tree that mirrors the input: each leaf is an **output path** telling Jolt where to copy the matched input value. This is the convenience entry point for the single shift case; for multi-step pipelines use `jolt_transform`.

**Inputs:** `input_json` (`VARCHAR`/`BLOB` JSON, the data vector) and `shift_spec` (a constant **bare** shift spec object, NOT wrapped in the `{"operation":"shift",...}` chainr envelope). The `Shiftr` is built once per batch.

**Output:** the reshaped document as a JSON `VARCHAR`. NULL input row yields NULL; malformed input JSON or shift spec raises a DuckDB error.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# jolt_shift

Apply one Jolt **shift** operation — path-based copy/move of input values into an output tree.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT jolt.main.jolt_shift(
  '{"first":"Ada","last":"Lovelace"}',
  '{"first":"name.given","last":"name.family"}');
-- => {"name":{"given":"Ada","family":"Lovelace"}}
```

The spec is the **bare** shift spec object, not the chainr operation envelope. Wildcards (`*`), array indexing, and `@`/`#`/`$` references follow standard Jolt shift semantics.

## Notes

- Returns `VARCHAR` JSON; output key order is not guaranteed.
- NULL input row maps to a NULL result.
- Malformed input JSON or shift spec raises an error.

workers.title: Kalshi Prediction Markets
workers.tagline: Kalshi prediction-market data as ordinary DuckDB tables — a read-only VGI worker. Markets, order books, candlesticks, trades, events and the series catalog, over SQL.
workers.subtitle: Live and archived Kalshi prediction markets, with order books, prices, trades and settlements.
workers.summary: Read-only public data from Kalshi, a CFTC-regulated US prediction-market exchange whose contract prices read directly as event probabilities, covering live and archived markets. Market data needs no account or API key; the margin_* functions read your own perps account with one.
workers.doc_md:
Kalshi is a CFTC-regulated exchange for event contracts. A contract pays $1 if its question resolves YES and $0 if it resolves NO, so its price is the market's implied probability of that outcome.

### How the data is shaped

Kalshi nests in three levels, and nearly every question starts by picking one at the top:

- **Series** — a recurring question, such as KXBTCD for the Bitcoin daily price. This is the level the `series` table lists, and its ticker is the key almost everything else requires.
- **Event** — one occurrence of a series, with a single resolution date.
- **Market** — one strike within an event. This is what actually trades, and its ticker is what the per-market lookups take.

### Reading prices

Every `*_dollars` column is dollars per contract between 0 and 1, so a best bid of 0.62 is a 62% implied probability. They are `DECIMAL`, never `DOUBLE`: Kalshi sends exact fixed-point strings, and rounding them through a float would throw that away silently. Contract counts (`*_fp`) are decimals for the same reason.

### Access

No credentials are needed for market data. Kalshi's whole market-data surface is public. The four `margin_*` functions (`margin_positions`, `margin_balance`, `margin_risk`, `margin_funding_history`) read the key holder's own perps account and need a `kalshi` secret; RSA and Ed25519 keys both work, and a read-only key is the right kind. Order entry and transfers are out of reach: the worker has no write verb and its account paths are a fixed allowlist. Read-only by construction, not by configuration.

### Rate limits

Unauthenticated traffic is limited tightly enough that a handful of back-to-back requests draws an HTTP 429. A correlated `LATERAL` issues one request per input row, so a join across a whole series is hundreds of calls. Requests are retried with exponential backoff, and the per-market functions take a `cache_ttl` argument that turns repeated lookups of the same ticker into cache hits when a few seconds of staleness is acceptable.

### Sources

- [Kalshi](https://kalshi.com) — the exchange this data comes from.
- [Kalshi API documentation](https://docs.kalshi.com) — the public Trade API v2 this worker reads (`https://api.elections.kalshi.com/trade-api/v2`): series, events, markets, order books, candlesticks, trades, exchange status and the [historical archive](https://docs.kalshi.com/getting_started/historical_data).
- [Rate limits and tiers](https://docs.kalshi.com/getting_started/rate_limits) — the request budget that `cache_ttl` and the retry backoff are built around.
- [API keys](https://docs.kalshi.com/getting_started/api_keys) — needed for the `margin_*` account functions, or to sign market-data requests at a higher rate-limit tier, via a `kalshi` secret.
- [Perps API](https://docs.kalshi.com/perps_openapi.yaml) — the `/margin` endpoints the account functions read.

### Terms of use

The market data is Kalshi Inc.'s, not covered by this worker's MIT license, and is subject to the [Kalshi Data Terms of Use](https://kalshi-public-docs.s3.amazonaws.com/kalshi-data-terms-of-service.pdf) and the [Kalshi Developer Agreement](https://kalshi-public-docs.s3.amazonaws.com/Kalshi-Developer-Agreement.pdf). The Developer Agreement limits API use to facilitating a member's own trading on the exchange and restricts storing, aggregating or sharing the data without Kalshi's written authorization; read both before using this worker. This worker is not affiliated with or endorsed by Kalshi.

attach_options.name: auth

example_queries.title: series_catalog_is_populated
example_queries.description: The series catalog returns the whole exchange in one response.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) > 1000 FROM kalshi.main.series;

example_queries.title: series_and_scan_function_agree
example_queries.description: The `series` table and the `all_series` function behind it are the same rows.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM kalshi.main.series) = (SELECT count(*) FROM kalshi.main.all_series());

example_queries.title: markets_carry_their_series
example_queries.description: Every market row is stamped with the series it was fetched from.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bool_and(series_ticker = 'KXBTCD') FROM (SELECT series_ticker FROM kalshi.main.markets('KXBTCD') LIMIT 200);

example_queries.title: events_belong_to_their_series
example_queries.description: Events under a series all report that series.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bool_and(series_ticker = 'KXBTCD') FROM (SELECT series_ticker FROM kalshi.main.events('KXBTCD') LIMIT 100);

example_queries.title: a_limit_stops_the_scan_early
example_queries.description: A paged scan yields its first rows without walking every page — the property that keeps a LIMIT over a large series from wedging the client.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT ticker FROM kalshi.main.markets('KXBTCD') LIMIT 5);

example_queries.title: prices_are_exact_decimals
example_queries.description: Money comes back as DECIMAL, never a float.
example_queries.sql: SELECT typeof(yes_bid_dollars) FROM kalshi.main.markets('KXBTCD') LIMIT 1;

example_queries.title: orderbook_sides_are_yes_or_no
example_queries.description: A book flattens to labelled sides, or to nothing when it is empty.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bool_and(side IN ('yes', 'no')) IS NOT FALSE FROM (SELECT o.side FROM kalshi.main.markets('KXBTCD', status => 'open') m, LATERAL kalshi.main.orderbook(m.ticker) o LIMIT 50);

example_queries.description: Browse the crypto series catalog
example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, title, frequency FROM kalshi.main.series WHERE category = 'Crypto' ORDER BY ticker

example_queries.description: Open Bitcoin daily markets with their best quotes, busiest first
example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, title, yes_bid_dollars, yes_ask_dollars, volume_24h_fp FROM kalshi.main.markets('KXBTCD') WHERE status = 'active' ORDER BY volume_24h_fp DESC

example_queries.description: Order books for a whole series in one query, via LATERAL
example_queries.sql: SELECT m.ticker, o.side, o.price_dollars, o.count_fp FROM kalshi.main.markets('KXBTCD') m, LATERAL kalshi.main.orderbook(m.ticker, cache_ttl => 30) o WHERE m.status = 'active' ORDER BY m.ticker, o.side, o.price_dollars

example_queries.description: Hourly candles for every open market in a series, driven by markets()
example_queries.sql: SELECT m.ticker, c.end_period_ts, c.price_close_dollars FROM kalshi.main.markets('KXBTCD', status => 'open') m, LATERAL kalshi.main.candlesticks(m.series_ticker, m.ticker, period_interval => 60) c ORDER BY m.ticker, c.end_period_ts

example_queries.description: The most recent trades on an actively traded open market in a series
example_queries.sql: SELECT t.created_time, t.taker_side, t.yes_price_dollars, t.count_fp FROM (SELECT ticker FROM kalshi.main.markets('KXBTCD') WHERE status = 'active' AND volume_24h_fp > 100 LIMIT 1) m, LATERAL kalshi.main.trades(m.ticker, max_rows => 100) t ORDER BY t.created_time DESC

example_queries.description: Open Bitcoin events by strike date
example_queries.sql: SELECT event_ticker, title, strike_date FROM kalshi.main.events('KXBTCD', status => 'open') ORDER BY strike_date

example_queries.description: Upcoming Bitcoin events with their question and resolution date, plus the implied median read off each event's strike ladder: the highest strike still priced at even odds or better to settle above
example_queries.sql: SELECT e.event_ticker, e.title, e.strike_date, count(*) AS strikes, max(m.floor_strike) FILTER (WHERE (m.yes_bid_dollars + m.yes_ask_dollars) / 2 >= 0.5) AS implied_median, sum(m.open_interest_fp) AS open_interest FROM kalshi.main.events('KXBTCD', status => 'open') AS e JOIN kalshi.main.markets('KXBTCD', status => 'open') AS m ON m.event_ticker = e.event_ticker WHERE m.strike_type = 'greater' GROUP BY e.event_ticker, e.title, e.strike_date ORDER BY e.strike_date

example_queries.description: Ten recently settled Bitcoin markets that traded: what each paid next to the volume-weighted price it traded at
example_queries.sql: SELECT m.ticker, m.result, m.settlement_value_dollars, CAST(sum(t.yes_price_dollars * t.count_fp) / sum(t.count_fp) AS DECIMAL(18,4)) AS vwap_dollars, sum(t.count_fp) AS contracts FROM (SELECT ticker, result, settlement_value_dollars FROM kalshi.main.historical_markets('KXBTCD') WHERE volume_fp > 0 LIMIT 10) AS m, LATERAL kalshi.main.historical_trades(m.ticker) AS t GROUP BY m.ticker, m.result, m.settlement_value_dollars ORDER BY m.ticker

example_queries.description: An actively traded open market's current quote
example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, status, yes_bid_dollars, yes_ask_dollars FROM kalshi.main.market((SELECT ticker FROM kalshi.main.markets('KXBTCD') WHERE status = 'active' AND volume_24h_fp > 100 LIMIT 1))

example_queries.sql: SELECT market_settled_ts, trades_created_ts FROM kalshi.main.historical_cutoff

example_queries.sql: SELECT DATE '2026-08-01' >= market_settled_ts AS use_live_functions FROM kalshi.main.historical_cutoff

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The whole read-only Kalshi surface, in one schema. Work top-down: the `series` table lists every recurring question on the exchange and needs no arguments, so start there and take a series ticker. That ticker unlocks the tradeable contracts under it, and each contract's ticker in turn unlocks resting order-book depth, OHLC price history and the raw trade tape. Every function is keyed — none of them will scan the whole exchange for you — and every one composes under a correlated LATERAL, so a per-row lookup becomes a set-based query without a second registration.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One schema holding the whole read-only Kalshi surface.

### Finding your way in

Almost everything here is keyed, so the unkeyed `series` table is the way in: it lists every recurring question on the exchange, filterable by category. From a series ticker you reach the tradeable contracts, and from a contract ticker you reach depth, history and the trade tape.

Contracts carry a `series_ticker` column that Kalshi's own payload does not include — it is stamped on by the function that fetched them, so their output can feed the price-history lookup, which needs a series ticker as well as a contract ticker, without you repeating it by hand.

### Everything composes under LATERAL

Every function here is blended: one registration serves both a literal call and a correlated `LATERAL`, so a per-row lookup composes into a set-based query. That is also what makes it easy to issue hundreds of requests by accident — see the catalog notes on rate limits and the `cache_ttl` argument.

### The one real trap

Kalshi filters and reports contract status in two different vocabularies. The `status` **argument** accepts `unopened`, `open`, `closed` and `settled`; the `status` **column** reports `initialized`, `active`, `closed`, `determined`, `settled` and `finalized`. They are not interchangeable — filter with `status => 'open'`, but match the column against `'active'`. A wrong argument is a hard error from Kalshi; a wrong predicate silently matches nothing.

vgi.example_queries.description: Browse the crypto series catalog
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, title, frequency FROM kalshi.main.series WHERE category = 'Crypto' ORDER BY ticker

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, title, yes_bid_dollars, yes_ask_dollars, volume_24h_fp FROM kalshi.main.markets('KXBTCD') WHERE status = 'active' ORDER BY volume_24h_fp DESC

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT m.ticker, o.side, o.price_dollars, o.count_fp FROM kalshi.main.markets('KXBTCD') m, LATERAL kalshi.main.orderbook(m.ticker, cache_ttl => 30) o WHERE m.status = 'active' ORDER BY m.ticker, o.side, o.price_dollars

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT m.ticker, c.end_period_ts, c.price_close_dollars FROM kalshi.main.markets('KXBTCD', status => 'open') m, LATERAL kalshi.main.candlesticks(m.series_ticker, m.ticker, period_interval => 60) c ORDER BY m.ticker, c.end_period_ts

vgi.example_queries.description: The most recent trades on an actively traded open market in a series
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT t.created_time, t.taker_side, t.yes_price_dollars, t.count_fp FROM (SELECT ticker FROM kalshi.main.markets('KXBTCD') WHERE status = 'active' AND volume_24h_fp > 100 LIMIT 1) m, LATERAL kalshi.main.trades(m.ticker, max_rows => 100) t ORDER BY t.created_time DESC

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT event_ticker, title, strike_date FROM kalshi.main.events('KXBTCD', status => 'open') ORDER BY strike_date

vgi.example_queries.description: Upcoming Bitcoin events with their question and resolution date, plus the implied median read off each event's strike ladder: the highest strike still priced at even odds or better to settle above
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT e.event_ticker, e.title, e.strike_date, count(*) AS strikes, max(m.floor_strike) FILTER (WHERE (m.yes_bid_dollars + m.yes_ask_dollars) / 2 >= 0.5) AS implied_median, sum(m.open_interest_fp) AS open_interest FROM kalshi.main.events('KXBTCD', status => 'open') AS e JOIN kalshi.main.markets('KXBTCD', status => 'open') AS m ON m.event_ticker = e.event_ticker WHERE m.strike_type = 'greater' GROUP BY e.event_ticker, e.title, e.strike_date ORDER BY e.strike_date

vgi.example_queries.description: Ten recently settled Bitcoin markets that traded: what each paid next to the volume-weighted price it traded at
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT m.ticker, m.result, m.settlement_value_dollars, CAST(sum(t.yes_price_dollars * t.count_fp) / sum(t.count_fp) AS DECIMAL(18,4)) AS vwap_dollars, sum(t.count_fp) AS contracts FROM (SELECT ticker, result, settlement_value_dollars FROM kalshi.main.historical_markets('KXBTCD') WHERE volume_fp > 0 LIMIT 10) AS m, LATERAL kalshi.main.historical_trades(m.ticker) AS t GROUP BY m.ticker, m.result, m.settlement_value_dollars ORDER BY m.ticker

tables.name: historical_cutoff

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row saying where Kalshi's live endpoints stop and its archive begins. Read it before querying a date range: the live functions return no rows — not an error — for anything older, so an empty result is otherwise indistinguishable from a market that never traded. Compare a date against `market_settled_ts` for markets and candles, or `trades_created_ts` for the tape, and pick the live or the historical function accordingly.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row, four timestamps, because Kalshi archives each kind of data on its own schedule.

### Why this is a table and not a note in the docs

The boundary moves. Hardcoding a date works until it quietly does not, and the failure mode is an empty result rather than an error — which reads like an answer.

### Which column governs what

`market_settled_ts` covers markets and their candles; `trades_created_ts` covers the trade tape. The remaining two describe order and position archives, which this read-only worker does not expose; they are reported because Kalshi reports them.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT DATE '2026-08-01' >= market_settled_ts AS use_live_functions FROM kalshi.main.historical_cutoff

tables.name: exchange_status
tables.comment: Whether the exchange, and each venue within it, is open for trading

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Whether Kalshi is open for trading right now, one row per venue. Check this before concluding that an empty order book or an unmoving price means anything — outside trading hours it means the venue is closed. Kalshi runs several venues that open and close independently, so the exchange-wide flag alone is not the answer.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per trading venue, with the exchange-wide flags repeated on each.

### Read the venue, not just the exchange

Crypto trades around the clock while sports venues follow their seasons, so `exchange_active` does not tell you whether the contract you care about is tradeable. Match on `description`, or use the `*_overall` columns to ignore the distinction deliberately.

### Freshness

The most volatile thing Kalshi publishes, and it says so: `max-age=1`, the shortest TTL in the API. That directive is forwarded to the result cache rather than invented.

tables.comment: Every series on the exchange (small, slow-changing reference data)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The catalog of every recurring question on the exchange — around 13,600 rows, small and slow-changing. This is the discovery entry point: nearly every other object needs a series ticker, and this is where you find one. Filter by `category` to narrow to a topic such as Crypto, Politics or Economics.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Every series Kalshi lists, as an ordinary table — no argument required.

### Why this is a table and everything else is a function

It has no required key, it is small enough to return whole in one response, and it changes slowly. The market-data functions are none of those things, which is why they take a key.

### Where to go next

Take a `ticker` and pass it to `markets()` for the tradeable contracts, `events()` for resolution dates, or `candlesticks()` for price history.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The caller's own open perpetual-futures positions on Kalshi, one row per position: signed size (negative = short), entry price, unrealized P&L, maintenance margin used and fees. Requires a `kalshi` API-key secret. Join to `margin_risk()` on (subaccount, market_ticker) for the liquidation price, and to `margin_funding_history()` for funding paid or received.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Your open Kalshi perps positions, across every subaccount, including isolated ones. An isolated position lives in its own subaccount, so the subaccount number identifies it.

### Units

Prices are per contract, as Kalshi quotes them: KXGOLDPERP is 0.001 oz and KXBTCPERP 0.0001 BTC per contract, so divide by the contract size for a per-unit price.

### Credentials

Reads **your own** account, so it needs a `kalshi` secret. RSA and Ed25519 keys both work; create the key read-only in Kalshi's API key settings.

```sql
CREATE SECRET (TYPE kalshi, key_id '...',
    private_key '-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----...');
```

Without a secret the call fails rather than returning an empty result, so a missing key cannot read as a flat account.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Markets that have settled and been archived out of `markets()`. Reach for this for anything resolved — how a past question turned out, what it paid, how it was priced before it closed. Same columns as the live `markets()` plus `settlement_value_dollars`, so a query moves across the boundary by changing only the function name. Check `historical_cutoff` if you are unsure which side a date falls on; the live functions return nothing rather than erroring for anything older.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
The archive of settled markets.

### Why this is a separate function

Kalshi archives settled markets out of the live endpoints entirely. Asking `markets()` for something that settled last month returns no rows — not an error — so the split has to be visible rather than inferred.

### What it adds

`settlement_value_dollars` is what one contract actually paid: 1 for the winning side and 0 for the losing one, or a value in between for a scalar market. Every other column matches the live shape.

### Finding the boundary

`historical_cutoff` reports the timestamp where the archive begins. It moves, so read it rather than hardcoding a date.

vgi.example_queries.description: How recent Bitcoin daily markets settled
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, close_time, result, settlement_value_dollars FROM (SELECT ticker, close_time, result, settlement_value_dollars FROM kalshi.main.historical_markets('KXBTCD') LIMIT 50) ORDER BY close_time DESC, ticker

vgi.example_queries.description: Ten recently settled Bitcoin markets that traded: what each paid next to the volume-weighted price it traded at
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT m.ticker, m.result, m.settlement_value_dollars, CAST(sum(t.yes_price_dollars * t.count_fp) / sum(t.count_fp) AS DECIMAL(18,4)) AS vwap_dollars, sum(t.count_fp) AS contracts FROM (SELECT ticker, result, settlement_value_dollars FROM kalshi.main.historical_markets('KXBTCD') WHERE volume_fp > 0 LIMIT 10) AS m, LATERAL kalshi.main.historical_trades(m.ticker) AS t GROUP BY m.ticker, m.result, m.settlement_value_dollars ORDER BY m.ticker

vgi.example_queries.description: Settled markets whose last traded price disagreed with the outcome
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, last_price_dollars, settlement_value_dollars FROM kalshi.main.historical_markets('KXBTCD') WHERE abs(last_price_dollars - settlement_value_dollars) > 0.5

vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Lower bound of the range this contract settles YES on, exclusive. Set for 'greater' and 'between' strikes, NULL for 'less'. Units are the series' own — dollars for a price market, thousands of barrels for an inventory one.

vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Kalshi's structured key/value bag for this contract, and the only machine-readable form of what a 'custom' strike says — those markets carry NULL floor_strike and cap_strike because the outcome is categorical, not a number line. The key carries meaning as well as the value: KXFEDDECISION splits into {'Hike': '25'} and {'Cut': '25'}, which are opposite outcomes. functions.name: trades
functions.comment: Executed trades for a Kalshi market (the public tape)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Individual executed trades on one market — the public tape, newest first. Reach for this when you need actual prints rather than quotes or aggregated bars: trade-by-trade flow, taker direction, or a precise volume-weighted price. Use `candlesticks()` instead when bars are enough; the tape is far more rows.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per execution, with the trade quoted from both sides of the contract.

### Polling, and why there is no WebSocket

Kalshi's WebSocket `trade` channel pushes these, but a dropped connection is a gap you cannot recover. Polling with `min_ts` is lossless instead: the cursor is replayable, so a failed poll costs a retry rather than lost prints. Track the highest `created_time` you have seen and pass it as the next `min_ts`.

### Reading the price columns

`yes_price_dollars` and `no_price_dollars` are the same execution seen from each side and always sum to 1. `taker_side` tells you which side the aggressor bought, which is the direction signal.

### Volume

An active market can have a very long tape, so cap it with `max_rows` unless you genuinely want the whole history.

vgi.example_queries.description: The most recent trades on an actively traded open market in a series
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT t.created_time, t.taker_side, t.yes_price_dollars, t.count_fp FROM (SELECT ticker FROM kalshi.main.markets('KXBTCD') WHERE status = 'active' AND volume_24h_fp > 100 LIMIT 1) m, LATERAL kalshi.main.trades(m.ticker, max_rows => 100) t ORDER BY t.created_time DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Volume-weighted average price from the tape
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT sum(t.yes_price_dollars * t.count_fp) / sum(t.count_fp) AS vwap_dollars FROM (SELECT ticker FROM kalshi.main.markets('KXBTCD') WHERE status = 'active' AND volume_24h_fp > 100 LIMIT 1) m, LATERAL kalshi.main.trades(m.ticker, max_rows => 500) t

functions.name: events
functions.comment: Events under a Kalshi series (series_ticker required)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The layer between a series and its markets: one row per resolution date, with the strike date, settlement sources and whether its markets are mutually exclusive. Reach for this to find a specific `event_ticker` — which `markets()` accepts as a filter — without scanning every market in the series.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
A Kalshi series recurs; each occurrence is an event; each event carries many markets, one per strike. `KXBTCD` (Bitcoin daily) opens one event per day, and each event holds a market for every strike price.

### Narrowing from here

Take an `event_ticker` from this and pass it to `markets()` as its `event_ticker` argument to get just that day's strikes rather than the whole series. Note that has to be a literal or a scalar subquery: `event_ticker` is a named argument, and DuckDB does not allow a correlated column to be passed as one.

### Settlement sources

`settlement_sources` stays a nested list of `{name, url}` structs — flattening it would fan every event out into one row per source. Apply DuckDB's `unnest` to the column when you do want one row per source; the example queries show it. For the images as well, use `event_metadata()`.

### Paging

`/events` caps its page size at 200 rather than the usual 1000 and rejects anything larger outright. Rows stream a page at a time, so a `LIMIT` stops early.

vgi.example_queries.description: Open Bitcoin events by strike date
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT event_ticker, title, strike_date FROM kalshi.main.events('KXBTCD', status => 'open') ORDER BY strike_date

vgi.example_queries.description: Upcoming Bitcoin events with their question and resolution date, plus the implied median read off each event's strike ladder: the highest strike still priced at even odds or better to settle above
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT e.event_ticker, e.title, e.strike_date, count(*) AS strikes, max(m.floor_strike) FILTER (WHERE (m.yes_bid_dollars + m.yes_ask_dollars) / 2 >= 0.5) AS implied_median, sum(m.open_interest_fp) AS open_interest FROM kalshi.main.events('KXBTCD', status => 'open') AS e JOIN kalshi.main.markets('KXBTCD', status => 'open') AS m ON m.event_ticker = e.event_ticker WHERE m.strike_type = 'greater' GROUP BY e.event_ticker, e.title, e.strike_date ORDER BY e.strike_date

vgi.example_queries.description: Settlement sources for each open event, one row per source
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT event_ticker, unnest(settlement_sources).name AS source FROM kalshi.main.events('KXBTCD', status => 'open') ORDER BY event_ticker, source

tags.vgi.doc_llm: What an event settles against, flattened to one row per source, plus the images Kalshi displays for it. Reach for this to answer 'how is this decided?' — the named source is the thing that determines the outcome. Distinct from the `settlement_sources` column on `events()`, which is the summary inlined into the listing; the images only exist here.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per settlement source for one event.

### Why one row per source

An event can settle against more than one source. Flattening them means they join and aggregate like ordinary rows, at the cost of repeating the image columns — the same trade-off `orderbook()` makes with price levels. An event with no declared sources still returns one row, so a lookup always answers with its images rather than with nothing.

### Versus the events() column

`events()` carries a nested `settlement_sources` list, which is the right shape when you are already scanning events. This endpoint is the one that also has the images, and it is a point lookup rather than a scan.

functions.name: orderbook
functions.comment: Kalshi order book flattened to one row per side and price level

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Resting order-book depth for one market, flattened to one row per side and price level so it aggregates and joins like an ordinary table. Reach for this to see liquidity behind the best quote — spread, depth at a price, or the shape of one side. For just the top of book, `markets()` already carries the best bid and ask without a second request.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Kalshi returns the book as a nested object of `[price, count]` pairs; this flattens it to one row per (side, price level).

### Reading the two sides

A binary contract has two books that mirror each other: a YES bid at 0.40 is economically a NO ask at 0.60. Both sides are returned, labelled in `side`.

### An empty result is not an error

An unknown ticker is answered with HTTP 200 and two empty sides rather than a 404, so zero rows means 'no resting orders' *or* 'no such market' — check the ticker against `markets()` if that distinction matters.

### Cost under LATERAL

One request per input row. Over a whole series that is hundreds of calls into a rate-limited API, so pass `cache_ttl => N` to enable per-value memoization when a few seconds of staleness is acceptable.

functions.name: markets
functions.comment: Markets under a Kalshi series (series_ticker required)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The entry point to Kalshi's market data: one row per tradeable contract under a series, with its current quotes, volume and lifecycle state. Reach for this when you know the series (from the `series` table) and want the individual strikes. The series ticker is required, so start from `series` if you do not have one. Every deeper function keys off the `ticker` this returns, and the `series_ticker` it stamps on is what lets its output drive `candlesticks()` directly.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Markets are the tradeable contracts under one Kalshi series — a series like `KXBTCD` (Bitcoin daily) opens a new event each day, and each event carries many markets, one per strike price.

### Why the series ticker is required

An unfiltered market scan pages past 400,000 rows, roughly 398,000 of which are zero-volume `KXMVECROSSCATEGORY` parlay combinations, and takes minutes. Requiring the series keeps a naive unfiltered scan honest.

### The two status vocabularies

The `status` **argument** filters on `unopened`, `open`, `closed` or `settled`. The `status` **column** reports `initialized`, `active`, `closed`, `determined`, `settled` or `finalized`. They are not interchangeable: `status => 'open'` returns rows whose column reads `active`, and passing `active` as the filter is an error from Kalshi.

### Streaming

Rows arrive one API page at a time, so a `LIMIT` stops early instead of paying for the whole series. The cost of that is this cannot be used as the inner side of a correlated `LATERAL` — drive a join from it, not into it.

### Prices

All `*_dollars` columns are dollars per contract between 0 and 1, carried as `DECIMAL(18,4)` — Kalshi sends them as exact fixed-point strings and rounding them through a float would lose that.

### Reading a strike ladder

A series like `KXWTI` lists one market per threshold. `strike_type` says how to read the bounds — `greater` sets `floor_strike`, `less` sets `cap_strike`, `between` sets both — and the units are the series' own: dollars for a price market, thousands of barrels for an inventory one. Do not parse the threshold out of the ticker or the subtitle; `subtitle` is not always populated, and a ticker is not a contract.

Each row is `P(settles above floor_strike)`, so a ladder read in strike order is a survival curve and the implied median is where it crosses 0.5.

vgi.example_queries.description: Open Bitcoin daily markets with their best bid, busiest first
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, title, yes_bid_dollars, volume_24h_fp FROM kalshi.main.markets('KXBTCD') WHERE status = 'active' ORDER BY volume_24h_fp DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Ask Kalshi for only the open markets instead of filtering after the fact
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, status FROM kalshi.main.markets('KXBTCD', status => 'open') ORDER BY ticker

vgi.example_queries.description: The open Bitcoin daily markets carrying the most open interest
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, floor_strike, open_interest_fp FROM kalshi.main.markets('KXBTCD', status => 'open') ORDER BY open_interest_fp DESC, ticker LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: The implied probability curve for a price ladder, in strike order
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT floor_strike, (yes_bid_dollars + yes_ask_dollars) / 2 AS implied_probability FROM kalshi.main.markets('KXWTI', status => 'open') WHERE strike_type = 'greater' AND floor_strike IS NOT NULL ORDER BY floor_strike

functions.name: historical_candlesticks
functions.comment: Archived OHLC candlesticks for a settled Kalshi market

tags.vgi.doc_llm: OHLC bars for a market that has settled and been archived. The columns match the live `candlesticks()` exactly, but the signature does not: this takes only the market ticker, because the archive is not scoped by series. Reach for it to chart or backtest a resolved question.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Archived price history for one settled market.

### One ticker, not two

The live candlestick endpoint lives under a series and needs both tickers; the archive is keyed on the market alone. That is the only difference in how you call it — the returned columns are identical.

### No batched form

There is no archive equivalent of the batched live endpoint, so a LATERAL over many markets issues one request per market against a rate-limited API. Drive it from a narrow set of tickers.

### Default window

Without `end_ts`, each market's window ends at its own `close_time` (looked up in one request per 100 tickers), and without `start_ts` it starts 30 days earlier — so a market's whole life comes back however long ago it settled.

### Immutable, so cached

Nothing in the archive can change, so results are cached for a day regardless of what the window looks like — the live function's forming-candle problem cannot arise here.

vgi.example_queries.description: Hourly closing prices for the most recently settled market in a series
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT c.end_period_ts, c.price_close_dollars FROM (SELECT ticker FROM kalshi.main.historical_markets('KXBTCD') LIMIT 1) m, LATERAL kalshi.main.historical_candlesticks(m.ticker, period_interval => 60) c ORDER BY c.end_period_ts

vgi.example_queries.description: Hourly high and low for a settled market
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT end_period_ts, price_high_dollars, price_low_dollars FROM kalshi.main.historical_candlesticks('KXBTCD-26JUL0119-T68299.99', period_interval => 60) ORDER BY end_period_ts

functions.name: event
functions.comment: One Kalshi event by ticker

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A single event by its exact ticker, with the same columns `events()` returns. Use this when you already have an `event_ticker` — from a market row, say — and want its resolution date or settlement sources without scanning the series it belongs to. `events()` is the browse path; this is the lookup.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row for one event.

### When to use this instead of `events()`

`events()` needs a series ticker and returns every event under it. If you already hold an `event_ticker` — every market row carries one — this fetches just that event, and composes under a LATERAL driven by markets.

### What it does not return

Kalshi's response also carries the event's markets. They are not returned here: `markets(series, event_ticker => ...)` is the way to ask for those, and it paginates properly where the inlined copy does not.

functions.name: margin_risk
functions.comment: Your Kalshi perps leverage and estimated liquidation price per position (needs an API key)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Per-position risk for the caller's Kalshi perps: mark, notional, maintenance margin required, leverage and Kalshi's own estimated liquidation price, plus account-wide totals on every row. The way to answer 'how far is my position from liquidation'. Requires a `kalshi` API-key secret.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Kalshi's risk view of each open position. `estimated_liquidation_price` is Kalshi's estimate; it moves as funding and P&L change the position's equity.

### Units

Prices are per contract, as Kalshi quotes them: KXGOLDPERP is 0.001 oz and KXBTCPERP 0.0001 BTC per contract, so divide by the contract size for a per-unit price.

### Credentials

Reads **your own** account, so it needs a `kalshi` secret. RSA and Ed25519 keys both work; create the key read-only in Kalshi's API key settings.

```sql
CREATE SECRET (TYPE kalshi, key_id '...',
    private_key '-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----...');
```

Without a secret the call fails rather than returning an empty result, so a missing key cannot read as a flat account.

Either way it is the discovery starting point: a series ticker from here is the required key for `markets()`, `events()` and `candlesticks()`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
The whole Kalshi series catalog — roughly 13,600 rows, returned in a single unpaginated response.

### Prefer the table

The `series` catalog table is backed by this function, so it can be selected from directly, without parentheses. This function returns exactly the same rows; it is named `all_series` only so that the function and the table it backs can coexist in one schema.

### Where to go next

A series is the top of Kalshi's hierarchy: series → events → markets. Take a `ticker` from here and pass it to `markets()` or `events()`.
