functions.name: candlesticks
functions.comment: Kalshi OHLC candlesticks for a market (series and market ticker)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Historical OHLC price and quote bars for one market, at 1-minute, hourly or daily resolution. This is the time-series view — reach for it to chart or backtest how a contract's price moved, rather than where it stands now. It needs BOTH the series ticker and the market ticker, so drive it from `markets()`, whose `series_ticker` column exists precisely to feed this.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
OHLC bars for one market. Three nested Kalshi structs — traded `price`, `yes_bid` and `yes_ask` — are flattened into `price_*`, `yes_bid_*` and `yes_ask_*` column families.

### Both tickers are required

The endpoint lives under the series (`/series/{series}/markets/{ticker}/candlesticks`), not under the market, so the series ticker is not redundant. `markets()` stamps a `series_ticker` column on its output for exactly this.

### Periods with no trades

The `price_*` columns are NULL for any period that saw no trades — Kalshi sends an empty struct. The `yes_bid_*` and `yes_ask_*` columns still carry quotes, so prefer them when you need an unbroken series.

### Window and caching

`period_interval` is the bar width in minutes: 1, 60 or 1440. The window defaults to the last 24 hours. A window that ends in the past contains only closed bars, which can never change and are cached for a day; a window running up to now contains a still-forming bar and is never cached.

functions.name: historical_trades
functions.comment: Archived executed trades for a Kalshi market

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Executed trades from before the archive cutoff — the same tape as `trades()`, for markets old enough to have been moved out of it. Identical columns, so the two can be combined with UNION ALL to span the boundary. `trades()` answers with no rows, not an error, for anything this old, which is the mistake this function exists to prevent.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
The archived half of the public trade tape.

### Same shape as the live tape

Every column matches `trades()`, deliberately: a query spanning the cutoff can `UNION ALL` the two without reshaping either side.

### Where the boundary is

`historical_cutoff.trades_created_ts` is the moment the archive takes over. It advances, so read it rather than assuming a fixed date.

### Volume

An archived market's whole life is in here, so cap it with `max_rows` or a `min_ts`/`max_ts` window unless you want all of it.

vgi.example_queries.description: The last hundred archived trades on a settled market

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT taker_side, sum(count_fp) AS contracts FROM kalshi.main.historical_trades('KXBTCD-26JUL0119-T68299.99') GROUP BY taker_side ORDER BY taker_side

functions.name: all_historical_cutoff
functions.comment: The live/archive boundary (the scan backing `historical_cutoff`)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The single row that says where Kalshi's live endpoints stop and its archive begins. Read it before querying a date range: the live functions return no rows, rather than an error, for anything older than this, so an empty result is otherwise indistinguishable from 'nothing happened'. Prefer the `historical_cutoff` table, which scans this.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row, four timestamps — Kalshi archives each kind of data on its own schedule.

### Why it matters

Asking a live function for something older than its cutoff is not an error. It returns nothing, which reads exactly like a market that never traded. Comparing against this row is the only way to tell those apart.

### Which column

`market_settled_ts` governs markets and their candles; `trades_created_ts` governs the tape. The other two describe order and position archives, which this worker does not expose — they are here because Kalshi reports them and omitting them would misrepresent the response.

vgi.example_queries.description: Where does the archive begin?
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT market_settled_ts, trades_created_ts FROM kalshi.main.all_historical_cutoff()

vgi.example_queries.description: Is a date served by the live functions or the archive?
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT DATE '2026-08-01' >= market_settled_ts AS use_live_functions FROM kalshi.main.all_historical_cutoff()

vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Markets that settled before this are in the archive, not in markets().

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: trades_created_ts
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Trades executed before this are in the archive, not in trades().

vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Order archive boundary. Informational here: this worker exposes no order data.

vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Position archive boundary. Informational here: this worker exposes no positions.

functions.name: all_exchange_status
functions.comment: Exchange and per-venue trading status (the scan backing `exchange_status`)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Whether Kalshi is open for trading right now, per venue. Prefer the `exchange_status` table, which scans this. Worth checking before concluding that an empty order book or a stale quote means something — outside trading hours it means the venue is closed. Kalshi runs several venues (Default, Combos, Crypto, sports) that open and close independently, so this returns one row per venue plus the exchange-wide flags repeated on each.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per trading venue, plus the exchange-wide flags on every row.

### Why this is per-venue

Kalshi is not one market. Crypto trades around the clock while sports venues follow their seasons, so `exchange_active` on its own does not tell you whether the contract you care about is tradeable. Match the venue by its `description`, or read the `*_overall` columns to ignore the distinction.

### Freshness

This is the most volatile thing Kalshi publishes and it says so: `Cache-Control: public, max-age=1`, the shortest TTL anywhere in the API. That one second is forwarded to the result cache rather than invented here.

functions.name: market
functions.comment: One Kalshi market by ticker

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A single market's current snapshot, by exact ticker. Use this when you already have a ticker and want one fresh row; use `markets()` when you want to browse or filter a series. Same columns as `markets()`, so the two are interchangeable downstream. Quotes are live and uncached unless you pass `cache_ttl`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row for one market, refetched on every call.

### When to use this instead of `markets()`

`markets()` is the browse path and returns a whole series; this is the point lookup. It is also the cheaper way to re-check a single contract's quote, since it fetches one market rather than paging a series.

### Caching

Kalshi declares no freshness at all on this endpoint, so nothing is cached by default. Pass `cache_ttl => N` to cache for N seconds and enable per-value memoization — worth it when a `LATERAL` repeats the same ticker, at the cost of a quote up to N seconds stale.

vgi.example_queries.description: Current quote for one market by ticker
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ticker, status, yes_bid_dollars, yes_ask_dollars FROM kalshi.main.market((SELECT ticker FROM kalshi.main.markets('KXBTCD') WHERE status = 'active' AND volume_24h_fp > 100 LIMIT 1))

vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Contract mechanism, e.g. 'binary' or 'scalar'.

vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Secondary heading distinguishing this strike within its event.

vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Label describing what a YES holder is betting on.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: strike_type
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: How to read the strike bounds: 'greater' (floor only), 'less' (cap only), or 'between' (both). The machine-readable form of what `subtitle` says in prose.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: floor_strike
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Lower bound of the range this contract settles YES on, exclusive. Set for 'greater' and 'between' strikes, NULL for 'less'. Units are the series' own — dollars for a price market, thousands of barrels for an inventory one.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: cap_strike
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Upper bound of the range this contract settles YES on. Set for 'less' and 'between' strikes, NULL for 'greater'. Same units as floor_strike.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: custom_strike
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Kalshi's structured key/value bag for this contract, and the only machine-readable form of what a 'custom' strike says — those markets carry NULL floor_strike and cap_strike because the outcome is categorical, not a number line. The key carries meaning as well as the value: KXFEDDECISION splits into {'Hike': '25'} and {'Cut': '25'}, which are opposite outcomes. On an ordinary numeric strike it holds contract metadata instead — KXWTI sets front_month_contract and strike_date — so it is not exclusive with the strike columns. Read it rather than parsing yes_sub_title.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: price_ranges
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: The tick ladder: the price bands this market quotes in, each with its own step, in dollars. Needed to tell a one-tick spread from a wide one, because the step is not the same everywhere — a market may step by 0.001 in the tails and 0.01 in the middle, so the same 0.01 spread is one tick at 0.50 and ten at 0.02. Ordered by start; look up the band containing the price of interest.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: status
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Lifecycle state: initialized, active, closed, determined, settled or finalized. Note this is NOT the vocabulary the status filter argument accepts — filter with 'open' to select markets reading 'active'.

vgi.result_columns_schema.description: When the contract expires and settlement is final.

vgi.result_columns_schema.description: When Kalshi last changed this market's row. The staleness signal: a market whose quotes have not moved in weeks is priced but not traded, and volume alone does not distinguish that from one that simply had a quiet day.

workers.title: Kubernetes Cluster API
workers.tagline: Kubernetes pods, workloads, RBAC, events, CRDs and pod logs as SQL in DuckDB (Go)
workers.subtitle: A live Kubernetes cluster's pods, nodes, workloads, events, RBAC, logs and custom resources as SQL.
workers.summary: A live Kubernetes cluster's API as SQL: pods, nodes, workloads, services, events, RBAC, storage, logs, metrics and custom resources, read-only.
workers.doc_md:
# Kubernetes

Query a live [Kubernetes](https://kubernetes.io) cluster from DuckDB: pods and their containers, nodes, workloads, services, ingresses, events, storage, RBAC, container logs and metrics-server usage, with typed columns and server-side namespace, field-selector and label-selector filtering. Any other API resource, custom resources included, is readable through `resources(api_version, resource)` or as tables via the `resource_tables` ATTACH option.

Connect with a `kubernetes` secret holding a `KUBECONFIG` (and optional `CONTEXT`) or `SERVER` + `TOKEN` + `CERTIFICATE_AUTHORITY_DATA`. The local kubeconfig is read only when the ATTACH sets `use_local_kubeconfig true`.

Read-only by construction: the worker issues GET requests only. Secret values are never returned.

attach_options.name: use_local_kubeconfig
attach_options.description: Opt in to reading the local kubeconfig ($KUBECONFIG, else ~/.kube/config) when no kubernetes secret is set. Off by default: the worker never reads local credentials unless this is true.

attach_options.name: context
attach_options.description: Kubeconfig context to use (the local kubeconfig's or the secret's KUBECONFIG); overrides the secret's CONTEXT. Default the current-context.

attach_options.name: secret
attach_options.description: Name of the kubernetes secret to use when several exist (one ATTACH per cluster); default the unscoped kubernetes secret.

attach_options.name: resource_tables
attach_options.description: Comma-separated API resources to expose as tables in schema `resources`, each `group/version/resource` (e.g. `stable.example.com/v1/crontabs`, `v1/pods`), or `all` to expose every listable resource found by discovery (needs use_local_kubeconfig, since secrets are not available at ATTACH time). Each table has the metadata columns plus spec, status and object as JSON.

attach_options.name: configmap_values
attach_options.description: true to fill configmaps.data with the ConfigMap values; default false, which lists only the keys. Secret values are never returned.

attach_options.name: page_size
attach_options.description: Objects requested per list page (limit=), 1 to 5000; default 500. Pages are fetched lazily with the API's continue token.

example_queries.description: Namespaces with their pod security enforcement level
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, phase, labels['pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce'] AS enforce FROM kubernetes.main.namespaces ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Allocatable CPU cores and memory GiB per ready node
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, allocatable_cpu_millicores / 1000.0 AS cpu_cores, allocatable_memory_bytes / 2^30 AS memory_gib FROM kubernetes.main.nodes WHERE ready ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Pods not running or succeeded, with their reason
example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, name, phase, reason FROM kubernetes.main.pods WHERE phase NOT IN ('Running', 'Succeeded') ORDER BY namespace, name

example_queries.description: Containers that were OOM-killed last time they stopped
example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, pod_name, container_name, restart_count FROM kubernetes.main.pod_containers WHERE last_termination_reason = 'OOMKilled' ORDER BY restart_count DESC

example_queries.description: Deployments with fewer ready replicas than desired
example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, name, replicas, ready_replicas FROM kubernetes.main.deployments WHERE coalesce(ready_replicas, 0) < replicas ORDER BY namespace, name

example_queries.description: Old, scaled-down ReplicaSets kept per deployment
example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, owner_references[1].name AS deployment, count(*) AS old_replicasets FROM kubernetes.main.replicasets WHERE replicas = 0 GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY old_replicasets DESC

example_queries.description: StatefulSets mid-rollout
example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, name, current_revision, update_revision FROM kubernetes.main.statefulsets WHERE current_revision <> update_revision ORDER BY namespace, name

example_queries.description: DaemonSets not ready on every node
example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, name, desired_number_scheduled, number_ready FROM kubernetes.main.daemonsets WHERE number_ready < desired_number_scheduled ORDER BY namespace, name

example_queries.description: Failed jobs in the last day
example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, name, failed, start_time FROM kubernetes.main.jobs WHERE status = 'Failed' AND start_time > now() - INTERVAL 1 DAY ORDER BY start_time DESC

example_queries.description: CronJobs whose last scheduled run did not succeed
example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, name, schedule, last_schedule_time, last_successful_time FROM kubernetes.main.cronjobs WHERE last_successful_time IS NULL OR last_successful_time < last_schedule_time ORDER BY namespace, name

example_queries.description: Autoscalers pinned at their maximum
example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, name, target_kind, target_name, max_replicas FROM kubernetes.main.horizontalpodautoscalers WHERE current_replicas >= max_replicas ORDER BY namespace, name

example_queries.description: LoadBalancer services and their external addresses
example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, name, load_balancer_ingress FROM kubernetes.main.services WHERE type = 'LoadBalancer' ORDER BY namespace, name

example_queries.description: Ready and total endpoints per service
example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, service_name, sum(ready_count) AS ready, sum(endpoint_count) AS total FROM kubernetes.main.endpointslices GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY namespace, service_name

example_queries.description: Every routed host and path with its backend service
example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, name, r.host, r.path, r.service_name, r.service_port FROM kubernetes.main.ingresses, UNNEST(rules) AS u(r) ORDER BY r.host, r.path

example_queries.description: Namespaces with a default-deny ingress policy
example_queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT namespace FROM kubernetes.main.networkpolicies WHERE default_deny_ingress ORDER BY namespace

example_queries.description: ConfigMaps and how many keys each holds
example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, name, len(keys) AS key_count FROM kubernetes.main.configmaps ORDER BY key_count DESC, namespace, name

example_queries.description: Secrets by type
example_queries.sql: SELECT type, count(*) AS secrets FROM kubernetes.main.secrets GROUP BY type ORDER BY secrets DESC

example_queries.description: Service accounts that do not opt out of token automount
example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, name FROM kubernetes.main.serviceaccounts WHERE automount_service_account_token IS DISTINCT FROM false ORDER BY namespace, name

example_queries.description: Released or failed volumes still holding storage
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, phase, capacity_bytes / 2^30 AS gib, claim_namespace, claim_name FROM kubernetes.main.persistentvolumes WHERE phase IN ('Released', 'Failed') ORDER BY gib DESC

example_queries.description: Requested storage per storage class, in GiB
example_queries.sql: SELECT storage_class, sum(requested_bytes) / 2^30 AS gib FROM kubernetes.main.persistentvolumeclaims GROUP BY storage_class ORDER BY gib DESC

example_queries.description: The default storage class
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, provisioner, volume_binding_mode FROM kubernetes.main.storageclasses WHERE is_default ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Priority classes from highest to lowest
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, value, preemption_policy FROM kubernetes.main.priorityclasses ORDER BY value DESC

example_queries.description: Roles with the most rules
example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, name, len(rules) AS rule_count FROM kubernetes.main.roles ORDER BY rule_count DESC, namespace, name

example_queries.description: Cluster roles that grant every verb on every resource
example_queries.sql: SELECT name FROM kubernetes.main.clusterroles, UNNEST(rules) AS u(r) WHERE list_contains(r.verbs, '*') AND list_contains(r.resources, '*') ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Bindings that grant cluster-admin inside a namespace
example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, name, subjects FROM kubernetes.main.rolebindings WHERE role_name = 'cluster-admin' ORDER BY namespace, name

example_queries.description: Who is bound to cluster-admin
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, s.kind, s.name AS subject FROM kubernetes.main.clusterrolebindings, UNNEST(subjects) AS u(s) WHERE role_name = 'cluster-admin' ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Roles and cluster roles that can read secrets
example_queries.sql: SELECT role_kind, namespace, role_name FROM kubernetes.main.rbac_rules WHERE resource IN ('secrets', '*') AND verb IN ('get', 'list', 'watch', '*') AND api_group IN ('', '*') GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY ALL

example_queries.description: Roles granted to one service account
example_queries.sql: SELECT binding_kind, namespace, binding_name, role_kind, role_name FROM kubernetes.main.rbac_subjects WHERE subject_kind = 'ServiceAccount' AND subject_namespace = 'kube-system' AND subject_name = 'default' ORDER BY ALL

example_queries.description: Most frequent warning reasons
example_queries.sql: SELECT reason, sum(count) AS occurrences FROM kubernetes.main.events WHERE type = 'Warning' GROUP BY reason ORDER BY occurrences DESC

example_queries.description: Node CPU and memory utilisation against allocatable
example_queries.sql: SELECT n.name, m.cpu_usage_millicores / n.allocatable_cpu_millicores AS cpu_util, m.memory_usage_bytes / n.allocatable_memory_bytes AS mem_util FROM kubernetes.main.node_metrics m JOIN kubernetes.main.nodes n ON n.name = m.node_name ORDER BY cpu_util DESC

example_queries.description: Containers using more memory than they request
example_queries.sql: SELECT m.namespace, m.pod_name, m.container_name, m.memory_usage_bytes, c.memory_request_bytes FROM kubernetes.main.pod_metrics m JOIN kubernetes.main.pod_containers c USING (namespace, pod_name, container_name) WHERE m.memory_usage_bytes > c.memory_request_bytes ORDER BY m.memory_usage_bytes DESC

example_queries.description: Custom resource types (dotted groups outside *.k8s.io)
example_queries.sql: SELECT api_version, resource, kind FROM kubernetes.main.api_resources WHERE preferred AND "group" LIKE '%.%' AND "group" NOT LIKE '%k8s.io' ORDER BY ALL

example_queries.description: Kubernetes version of the cluster
example_queries.sql: SELECT git_version, platform FROM kubernetes.main.api_servers

example_queries.description: PodDisruptionBudgets and how many disruptions they allow
example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, name, (status->>'disruptionsAllowed')::INT AS allowed FROM kubernetes.main.resources('policy/v1', 'poddisruptionbudgets') ORDER BY allowed, namespace, name

example_queries.description: Last 50 lines of a pod's logs
example_queries.sql: SELECT timestamp, container, message FROM kubernetes.main.pod_logs('default', 'web-0', tail_lines := 50) ORDER BY timestamp

example_queries.description: Top CPU consumers per namespace
example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, sum(cpu_usage_millicores) AS millicores FROM kubernetes.main.pod_metrics GROUP BY namespace ORDER BY millicores DESC

example_queries.description: Recent events for one pod
example_queries.sql: SELECT last_seen, type, reason, message FROM kubernetes.main.events WHERE namespace = 'default' AND involved_kind = 'Pod' AND involved_name = 'web-0' ORDER BY last_seen

example_queries.description: TLS secrets in one namespace
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, keys FROM kubernetes.main.secrets WHERE namespace = 'default' AND type = 'kubernetes.io/tls' ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Average duration of completed jobs per CronJob
example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, cron_job, avg(duration_seconds) AS avg_seconds FROM kubernetes.main.jobs WHERE status = 'Complete' AND cron_job IS NOT NULL GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY avg_seconds DESC

example_queries.description: Running containers without a memory limit
example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, pod_name, container_name, image FROM kubernetes.main.pod_containers WHERE state = 'running' AND memory_limit_bytes IS NULL ORDER BY namespace, pod_name

example_queries.description: Hosts served without TLS
example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, name, unnest(hosts) AS host FROM kubernetes.main.ingresses WHERE len(tls) = 0 ORDER BY host

example_queries.description: Every exposed port
example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, name, p.port, p.protocol, p.target_port FROM kubernetes.main.services, UNNEST(ports) AS u(p) ORDER BY namespace, name, p.port

example_queries.description: Containers waiting in CrashLoopBackOff
example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, name, c.name AS container, c.restart_count FROM kubernetes.main.pods, UNNEST(containers) AS u(c) WHERE c.state_reason = 'CrashLoopBackOff' ORDER BY namespace, name

example_queries.description: CPU requested per node, in cores
example_queries.sql: SELECT node_name, sum(cpu_request_millicores) / 1000.0 AS cpu_cores FROM kubernetes.main.pods WHERE phase = 'Running' GROUP BY node_name ORDER BY cpu_cores DESC

example_queries.description: Nodes with a NoSchedule taint
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, t.key, t.effect FROM kubernetes.main.nodes, UNNEST(taints) AS u(t) WHERE t.effect = 'NoSchedule' ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Images deployed per namespace
example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, image, count(*) AS deployments FROM kubernetes.main.deployments, UNNEST(images) AS u(image) GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY namespace, image

example_queries.description: Who can exec into pods, via which binding
example_queries.sql: SELECT b.subject_kind, b.subject_name, r.role_name FROM kubernetes.main.rbac_rules r JOIN kubernetes.main.rbac_subjects b ON b.role_name = r.role_name AND b.role_kind = r.role_kind WHERE r.resource = 'pods/exec' AND r.verb IN ('create', '*') ORDER BY ALL

example_queries.description: cert-manager certificates that are not ready
example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, name, status->>'$.conditions[0].reason' AS reason FROM kubernetes.main.resources('cert-manager.io/v1', 'certificates') WHERE status->>'$.conditions[0].status' <> 'True' ORDER BY namespace, name

example_queries.description: Error lines from the crashed instance of a container
example_queries.sql: SELECT timestamp, message FROM kubernetes.main.pod_logs('default', 'worker-1', container := 'app', previous := true) WHERE message ILIKE '%error%' ORDER BY line_number

example_queries.description: Hugepages capacity per node, in bytes
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, kubernetes.main.quantity_value(capacity['hugepages-2Mi']) AS hugepages_bytes FROM kubernetes.main.nodes ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Parse CPU, memory and decimal quantities
example_queries.sql: SELECT q, kubernetes.main.quantity_value(q) AS value FROM (VALUES ('250m'), ('64Mi'), ('1G'), ('1.5Gi'), ('2'), ('bogus')) t(q) ORDER BY q;

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Schema main is a read-only view of a live Kubernetes cluster: one table per core object kind, plus functions for container logs, metrics-server usage and generic access to any API resource, custom resources included. Every query lists objects through the API server (nothing is cached), across all namespaces unless WHERE namespace = '...' (or IN) narrows it. Filter labels server-side with WHERE label_selector = 'app=web' (any kubectl selector syntax); labels['app'] also works but is filtered by the worker after listing. Container state (waiting/terminated reasons such as CrashLoopBackOff, restart counts) answers health questions; the flattened RBAC rule and subject tables answer access reviews; events show what happened recently. Secret values are never exposed, only their keys and metadata. Usage metrics need metrics-server in the cluster.

vgi.example_queries.description: Node CPU and memory utilisation against allocatable
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT n.name, m.cpu_usage_millicores / n.allocatable_cpu_millicores AS cpu_util, m.memory_usage_bytes / n.allocatable_memory_bytes AS mem_util FROM kubernetes.main.node_metrics m JOIN kubernetes.main.nodes n ON n.name = m.node_name ORDER BY cpu_util DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Containers using more memory than they request
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT m.namespace, m.pod_name, m.container_name, m.memory_usage_bytes, c.memory_request_bytes FROM kubernetes.main.pod_metrics m JOIN kubernetes.main.pod_containers c USING (namespace, pod_name, container_name) WHERE m.memory_usage_bytes > c.memory_request_bytes ORDER BY m.memory_usage_bytes DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Custom resource types (dotted groups outside *.k8s.io)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT api_version, resource, kind FROM kubernetes.main.api_resources WHERE preferred AND "group" LIKE '%.%' AND "group" NOT LIKE '%k8s.io' ORDER BY ALL

vgi.example_queries.description: Kubernetes version of the cluster
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT git_version, platform FROM kubernetes.main.api_servers

vgi.example_queries.description: PodDisruptionBudgets and how many disruptions they allow
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, name, (status->>'disruptionsAllowed')::INT AS allowed FROM kubernetes.main.resources('policy/v1', 'poddisruptionbudgets') ORDER BY allowed, namespace, name

vgi.example_queries.description: Last 50 lines of a pod's logs
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT timestamp, container, message FROM kubernetes.main.pod_logs('default', 'web-0', tail_lines := 50) ORDER BY timestamp

functions.name: pod_logs
functions.comment: Log lines of a pod's containers, with the runtime's timestamps (kubectl logs --timestamps)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: pod_logs(namespace, pod, container := NULL, previous := false, since_seconds := NULL, since_time := NULL, tail_lines := NULL, limit_bytes := 10485760) returns one row per log line: namespace, pod, container, line_number (1-based per container), timestamp (`TIMESTAMPTZ` recorded by the container runtime), message. With container NULL every app container of the pod is read (name init containers explicitly). previous := true reads the last terminated instance, which is what explains a CrashLoopBackOff (right after a crash, while the container is terminated, that is the current instance); containers without one are skipped. Use tail_lines or since_seconds to keep reads small; at most limit_bytes are read per container. Filter the lines with WHERE message LIKE / regexp_matches; those filters run in DuckDB after the read.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Pod Logs

`pod_logs(namespace, pod)` reads container logs like `kubectl logs --timestamps`: one row per line with the container, a line number, the runtime timestamp and the message.

Named arguments: `container`, `previous` (the crashed instance), `since_seconds`, `since_time`, `tail_lines` and `limit_bytes` (default 10 MiB per container).

vgi.example_queries.description: Last 50 lines of a pod's logs
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT timestamp, container, message FROM kubernetes.main.pod_logs('default', 'web-0', tail_lines := 50) ORDER BY timestamp

vgi.example_queries.description: Error lines from the crashed instance of a container
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT timestamp, message FROM kubernetes.main.pod_logs('default', 'worker-1', container := 'app', previous := true) WHERE message ILIKE '%error%' ORDER BY line_number

workers.subtitle: LaunchDarkly flags, targeting, segments, audit log, approvals, members and experiments as SQL tables.
workers.summary: LaunchDarkly feature management as SQL: projects, environments, flags and their targeting, segments, the audit log, approvals, members and experiments, read-only from the LaunchDarkly REST API.
workers.doc_md:
# LaunchDarkly

Query a LaunchDarkly account from DuckDB: feature flags and how they target each environment, change management (the audit trail, approvals and scheduled changes), access control and experimentation. Read-only.

Create a `launchdarkly` secret with an access token (`ACCESS_TOKEN`); set `BASE_URL` for the EU or Federal instance. Filters are translated into LaunchDarkly's `filter=`, audit-log `spec` and time window, so only matching rows cross the network; offset paging and rate-limit headers are handled for you.

### Sources and references

- [LaunchDarkly REST API](https://launchdarkly.com/docs/api) — the endpoints this worker reads
- [Feature flags API](https://launchdarkly.com/docs/api/feature-flags/get-feature-flags) — `filter`, `sort`, `env`, `summary`
- [Audit log API](https://launchdarkly.com/docs/api/audit-log/get-audit-log-entries) and [resource specifiers](https://launchdarkly.com/docs/home/account/roles/role-resources)
- [Rate limiting](https://launchdarkly.com/docs/api#rate-limiting) and [API versioning](https://launchdarkly.com/docs/api#versioning)
- [Access tokens](https://launchdarkly.com/docs/home/account/api) (personal and service tokens)
workers.readme_sql:
CREATE SECRET ld (TYPE launchdarkly, ACCESS_TOKEN 'api-…');

-- What changed on production flags in the hour before the incident?
-- (resource_kind + environment_key become the audit `spec`, date becomes after/before.)
SELECT date, actor, resource_key, title
FROM launchdarkly.main.audit_log()
WHERE resource_kind = 'flag' AND environment_key = 'production'
  AND date BETWEEN TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-14 09:00Z' AND TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-14 10:00Z'
ORDER BY date DESC;

-- Temporary flags that are fully launched in production and still referenced in code.
SELECT f.key, s.last_requested, count(r.path) AS code_refs
FROM launchdarkly.main.flags(project_key := 'default', environment_key := 'production') f
JOIN launchdarkly.main.flag_status(project_key := 'default', environment_key := 'production') s
  ON s.flag_key = f.key
LEFT JOIN launchdarkly.main.code_references(project_key := 'default') r ON r.flag_key = f.key
WHERE f.temporary AND s.status = 'launched'
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY code_refs DESC;

example_queries.description: How widely each flag is referenced in code

tags.vgi.doc_llm: LaunchDarkly REST API v2 collections as SQL. Account-wide collections (projects, access control, approvals, code-reference repositories) are tables; per-project and per-environment collections are table functions with project_key := / environment_key := (NULL = all) and optional named arguments. Flag and targeting-rule functions return one row per flag per environment. The audit log is time-windowed: filter on date (default lookback 30 days). All objects need a `launchdarkly` secret.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

LaunchDarkly collections: projects and environments, flags and targeting, change management, access and experimentation.

Account-wide collections are tables; per-project and per-environment collections are table functions that take the project and environment keys as named arguments or pushed filters and otherwise read them all.

All objects need a `launchdarkly` secret; filters push down into LaunchDarkly's filter syntax.

Project keys are the `project_key` argument of every per-project function. WHERE key = / IN (...) pushes down as `filter=keys:`; list_contains(tags, 'x') pushes down as `filter=tags:`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## projects

One row per LaunchDarkly project.

**Pushdown:** `key` (=, IN) → `filter=keys:a|b`; `list_contains(tags, …)` → `filter=tags:a+b`.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT key, name, tags FROM launchdarkly.main.projects ORDER BY key
vgi.example_queries.description: Every project

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT key, name FROM launchdarkly.main.projects WHERE list_contains(tags, 'web') ORDER BY key
vgi.example_queries.description: Projects tagged web (the tag filter is sent to LaunchDarkly)

functions.name: segments
functions.comment: Segments per project and environment: rules and included/excluded counts

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Segments of each project and environment (GET /api/v2/segments/{projectKey}/{environmentKey}): key, name, description, tags, unbounded (big segment), rule_count and rules (id, description, clause_count, weight, bucket_by), included_count / excluded_count (individually listed targets), timestamps and version. Member lists are not returned by default; include_members := true adds included_keys / excluded_keys. Arguments project_key / environment_key (NULL = all), query (fuzzy key/name/description search), page_size.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## segments(project_key := NULL, environment_key := NULL, query := NULL, include_members := false, page_size := 50)

One row per segment per environment.

**Pushdown:** `project_key`, `environment_key` (=, IN) pick the scopes; `key` (=, IN) → `filter=includedKeys anyOf [...]`; `list_contains(tags, …)` → `filter=tags anyOf [...]`; `unbounded` → `filter=unbounded equals …`; `query :=` → `filter=query equals "…"`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Production segments and their sizes
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT key, rule_count, included_count, excluded_count FROM launchdarkly.main.segments(project_key := 'default', environment_key := 'production') ORDER BY key

vgi.example_queries.description: Big segments in every environment (sent as filter=unbounded equals true)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT environment_key, key FROM launchdarkly.main.segments(project_key := 'default') WHERE unbounded ORDER BY ALL

functions.name: experiments
functions.comment: Experiments across every environment of each project, with the current iteration

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Experiments of each project across environments (GET /api/v2/projects/{projectKey}/experiments?expand=treatments): key, name, description, environment_key, maintainer_id, creation_date, archived_date, tags, type, methodology, data_source, and the current iteration: iteration_status (not_started / running / stopped), hypothesis, started_at, ended_at, randomization_unit, flag_keys, primary_metric_key, metric_keys, treatments (name, allocation_percent, baseline), winning_treatment_id, winning_reason. lifecycle_state := 'active' (default), 'archived' or 'active,archived'.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## experiments(project_key := NULL, lifecycle_state := 'active', page_size := 50)

One row per experiment.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT key, started_at FROM launchdarkly.main.experiments() WHERE iteration_status = 'running' ORDER BY started_at

functions.name: flags
functions.comment: Feature flags with their per-environment targeting state, one row per flag and environment

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Feature flags of each project (GET /api/v2/flags/{projectKey}?env=<env>&summary=0), one row per flag and environment. Flag-level columns: key, name, description, kind (boolean / multivariate), state (live / deprecated / archived), temporary, tags, maintainer_id / maintainer_email / maintainer_team_key, client-side availability, variations (index, id, name, value as text), default on/off variations, creation_date. Environment columns: targeting_on, off_variation, fallthrough_variation or fallthrough_rollout (weights in thousandths of a percent, 100000 = 100%), rule_count, target_count (individually targeted contexts), prerequisites (key, variation), last_modified, env_version, site_url. Like the LaunchDarkly API, archived flags are only returned when asked for: WHERE archived (or state = 'archived'). Arguments: project_key / environment_key (NULL = all, or push WHERE project_key/environment_key = ...), query (substring of key or name), evaluated_since_days, sort, page_size. Use flag_rules for the targeting rules themselves and flag_status for evaluation activity.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## flags(project_key := NULL, environment_key := NULL, query := NULL, evaluated_since_days := NULL, sort := NULL, page_size := 100)

One row per flag and environment, with the flag's targeting state in that environment.

**Pushdown:** `project_key`, `environment_key` (=, IN) pick the scopes; `key` (single =) → `filter=query:`; `list_contains(tags, …)` → `filter=tags:a+b`; `state` / `archived` / `deprecated` → `filter=state:`; `temporary` → `filter=type:`; `maintainer_id`, `maintainer_team_key` → `filter=maintainerId:` / `maintainerTeamKey:`; `client_side_using_environment_id` / `client_side_using_mobile_key` = true → `filter=sdkAvailability:`; `creation_date <` → `filter=creationDate:{"before":…}`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Production flags, most recently changed first
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT key, targeting_on, rule_count, last_modified FROM launchdarkly.main.flags(project_key := 'default', environment_key := 'production') ORDER BY last_modified DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Temporary flags switched on per environment (temporary is sent as filter=type:temporary)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT environment_key, count(*) FILTER (WHERE targeting_on) AS flags_on, count(*) AS flags FROM launchdarkly.main.flags(project_key := 'default') WHERE temporary GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY ALL

workers.title: libpostal
workers.tagline: International address parsing & normalization for DuckDB (Python, libpostal)
workers.subtitle: Parse and normalize international street addresses into house number, road, city, postcode and more.
workers.summary: Parse + normalize international postal addresses (libpostal) for SQL
workers.doc_md:
# International Address Parsing & Normalization in SQL

**Parse, standardize, and normalize free-form postal addresses from anywhere in the world directly in DuckDB SQL** — turn a messy one-line address string into clean, structured components (house number, road, unit, city, state, postcode, country) without leaving your query.

The `postal` catalog brings [libpostal](https://github.com/openvenues/libpostal) — the open-source statistical address parser trained on OpenStreetMap and open address data — to SQL. It is built for data engineers, analysts, and anyone doing geocoding pre-processing, address standardization, record linkage, entity resolution, or deduplication over customer, shipping, or location data. Because libpostal is trained on real addresses from [OpenStreetMap](https://www.openstreetmap.org) across hundreds of countries and languages, it handles international formats, transliteration, and local abbreviations far better than hand-written regular expressions or fixed format rules.

Under the hood this worker wraps libpostal's C library through its official Python binding, [pypostal](https://github.com/openvenues/pypostal), and exposes it over DuckDB's VGI interface. libpostal does two core things: it *parses* an address — using a sequence model to tag each token with a component label — and it *expands/normalizes* abbreviations into canonical forms (for example `St` → `street`, `E` → `east`, `Rd` → `road`), which is what makes two differently written versions of the same address comparable. All output is lower-cased; an empty string yields an empty result and `NULL` yields `NULL`, so the functions compose cleanly inside larger queries.

## Key concepts

- **Parsing** turns a one-line address into labeled components (house number, road, unit, city, state, postcode, country, and more). Labels are statistical and best-effort — a borough can come back as a city district rather than a city — so treat them as a strong signal, not a strict schema.
- **Normalization / expansion** rewrites abbreviations into canonical, fully-spelled-out forms and can return several valid variants for an ambiguous token; two addresses match when their expansion sets overlap.

## When to reach for it

Use this catalog for geocoding pre-processing, address standardization, record linkage, entity resolution, and deduplication over customer, shipping, or location data — anywhere you need messy free-form addresses made comparable directly in SQL, without shipping data to an external service.

Learn more from the [libpostal source repository](https://github.com/openvenues/libpostal) and its [installation and usage documentation](https://github.com/openvenues/libpostal#installation).
workers.readme_sql:
INSTALL vgi FROM community; LOAD vgi;
ATTACH 'postal' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'docker://ghcr.io/query-farm/vgi-libpostal:0.4.0');

-- Parse an address into a MAP of components (values are lower-cased)
SELECT postal.parse_address('1600 Pennsylvania Ave NW, Washington, DC 20500');
-- {road=pennsylvania ave nw, city=washington, state=dc, postcode=20500, house_number=1600}

SELECT postal.parse_address('10 Downing St, London SW1A 2AA, UK')['postcode'];  -- 'sw1a 2aa'
SELECT postal.address_city('1600 Pennsylvania Ave NW, Washington, DC 20500');   -- 'washington'

-- Normalize / expand abbreviations
SELECT UNNEST(postal.expand_address('120 E 96th St'));  -- '120 east 96th street', ...

-- Long-format parse: one (label, value) row per component
SELECT * FROM postal.parse_address_components('781 Franklin Ave, Brooklyn, NY 11216');

-- Discover the component labels libpostal can emit
SELECT label FROM postal.address_labels() ORDER BY label;

-- Compose them: find duplicate addresses -- same postcode AND overlapping
-- normalized expansions ('St' = 'Street', 'E' = 'East')
WITH customers(id, addr) AS (VALUES
    (1, '120 E 96th St, New York, NY 10128'),
    (2, '120 East 96th Street, New York NY 10128'),
    (3, '130 E 96th St, New York, NY 10128')),
keyed AS (SELECT id, postal.address_postcode(addr) AS postcode,
                 postal.expand_address(addr) AS forms FROM customers)
SELECT a.id AS id_a, b.id AS id_b
FROM keyed AS a JOIN keyed AS b
  ON a.postcode = b.postcode AND a.id < b.id AND list_has_any(a.forms, b.forms)
ORDER BY id_a, id_b;
-- (1, 2): 130 E 96th St shares the postcode but is a different building

example_queries.description: Parse a US address into a MAP of libpostal components.
example_queries.sql: SELECT postal.main.parse_address('1600 Pennsylvania Ave NW, Washington, DC 20500')

example_queries.description: Pull just the postcode out of a parsed UK address.
example_queries.sql: SELECT postal.main.parse_address('10 Downing St, London SW1A 2AA, UK')['postcode']

example_queries.description: Normalize an abbreviated address into one expansion per row.
example_queries.sql: SELECT UNNEST(postal.main.expand_address('120 E 96th St'))

example_queries.description: Extract a single component (the postcode) inline.
example_queries.sql: SELECT postal.main.address_postcode('781 Franklin Ave, Brooklyn, NY 11216')

example_queries.description: Long-format parse: one (label, value) row per component.
example_queries.sql: SELECT label, value FROM postal.main.parse_address_components('781 Franklin Ave, Brooklyn, NY 11216') ORDER BY label

example_queries.description: List the vocabulary of component labels libpostal can emit.
example_queries.sql: SELECT label FROM postal.main.address_labels() ORDER BY label

example_queries.description: Find duplicate customer addresses: block candidate pairs on the extracted postcode, then match when their libpostal normalized expansions overlap (pairs 1-2 and 3-4 match; 120 vs 130 E 96th St does not).
example_queries.sql: WITH customers(id, addr) AS (VALUES (1, '120 E 96th St, New York, NY 10128'), (2, '120 East 96th Street, New York NY 10128'), (3, '781 Franklin Ave, Brooklyn, NY 11216'), (4, '781 Franklin Avenue, Brooklyn NY 11216'), (5, '130 E 96th St, New York, NY 10128')), keyed AS (SELECT id, addr, postal.main.address_postcode(addr) AS postcode, postal.main.expand_address(addr) AS forms FROM customers) SELECT a.id AS id_a, b.id AS id_b, a.postcode FROM keyed AS a JOIN keyed AS b ON a.postcode = b.postcode AND a.id < b.id AND list_has_any(a.forms, b.forms) ORDER BY id_a, id_b

tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Address Parsing & Normalization

Turn free-form international postal addresses into structured, comparable data directly in SQL, powered by libpostal.

## What's here

- **Parsing** — break a full address string into labeled components, returned either as a `MAP` or as long-format `(label, value)` rows.
- **Component extraction** — pull a single field (city, road, postcode, state, unit, country, house number) inline in a projection.
- **Normalization** — expand abbreviations into canonical forms for fuzzy matching, joins, and deduplication.
- **Discovery** — list the vocabulary of component labels the parser can emit.

Output is lower-cased; an empty string yields an empty result and `NULL` yields `NULL`, so the functions compose cleanly inside larger queries.

# address_labels

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## parse_address_components

Table function: parse a single address string and emit one `(label, value)` **row per libpostal component**, in libpostal's order. This is the long-format complement to the `parse_address` `MAP` scalar.

**Use it when** you want to filter, join, or aggregate over address components in set-based SQL (e.g. `... WHERE label = 'city'`) rather than indexing a map.

**Argument:** `text` (`VARCHAR`) -- the address to parse. **Returns:** rows of `(label VARCHAR, value VARCHAR)`.

**Behaviors / edge cases:** values are lower-cased; labels are statistical and best-effort (see `address_labels()` for the full set). An empty / whitespace input yields **no rows** (not an error).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# parse_address_components

Parse an address into one `(label, value)` row per libpostal component -- the long-format complement to the `parse_address` `MAP` scalar.

## Result

Each returned row pairs a libpostal component `label` (such as `house_number`, `road`, `city`, `state`, or `postcode`) with its lower-cased `value`, in libpostal's own token order. Because it is a table function, you consume it in the `FROM` clause and can freely filter, join, or aggregate the component rows -- for example keeping only the `city` label, or counting how many components libpostal recovered. Runnable examples are carried in this object's example-query metadata.

## Notes

Values are lower-cased; empty/whitespace input yields no rows. See the `address_labels` discovery relation for the full label set.

## address_unit

Convenience scalar that parses an address with libpostal and returns just the **`unit`** component (apartment, suite, floor, or similar sub-address), or `NULL` when libpostal does not identify one.

**Use it when** you need the secondary/sub-premise designator. Equivalent to `parse_address(addr)['unit']`. Many addresses have no unit, so `NULL` is common and expected.

**Input:** one `VARCHAR` address per row. **Output:** a `VARCHAR` (lower-cased) or `NULL`. A `NULL` input yields `NULL`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# address_unit

Return the libpostal `unit` (apartment / suite / floor) component of an address.

```sql
SELECT postal.main.address_unit('Apt 5B, 120 E 96th St, New York, NY 10128');  -- apt 5b
```

## Notes

`NULL` is common -- most addresses have no unit. Returns `NULL` for `NULL` input. Shorthand for `parse_address(addr)['unit']`.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## parse_address

Parse a single free-form postal address string into a `MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)` of libpostal components, keyed by the component label libpostal assigns (`house_number`, `road`, `unit`, `city`, `state`, `postcode`, `country`, and more).

**Use it when** you have unstructured address text and need it broken into addressable fields for geocoding pre-processing, standardization, deduplication, or record linkage -- all inline in SQL.

**Input:** one `VARCHAR` address per row. **Output:** a `MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)`. Index a single field with `parse_address(addr)['city']`.

**Behaviors / edge cases:** libpostal is a statistical (OSM-trained) parser, so labels are best-effort and occasionally surprising (a borough may come back as `city_district`, not `city`). All values are **lower-cased**. An empty string parses to an empty map (not an error); a `NULL` input yields `NULL`. For the long-format `(label, value)` row shape, use the `parse_address_components` table function instead.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# parse_address

Parse a free-form postal address into a `MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)` of libpostal components.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT postal.main.parse_address('1600 Pennsylvania Ave NW, Washington, DC 20500');
SELECT postal.main.parse_address('10 Downing St, London SW1A 2AA, UK')['postcode'];
```

## Notes

- Keys are libpostal labels (`house_number`, `road`, `unit`, `city`, `state`, `postcode`, `country`, ...).
- Values are lower-cased; an empty string yields an empty map and `NULL` yields `NULL`.
- Labels are statistical and may vary across address styles; see `address_labels()` for the full label set.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## expand_address

Normalize a single address string into a `VARCHAR[]` of libpostal **expansions** -- canonical, fully-spelled-out forms where abbreviations and tokens are rewritten (`St` -> `street`, `E` -> `east`, `Ave` -> `avenue`).

**Use it when** you need to compare or deduplicate addresses that are written inconsistently. libpostal may return several equally valid normalizations (e.g. `st` could mean `street` or `saint`), so the result is a *list*; match two addresses if their expansion lists intersect.

**Input:** one `VARCHAR` address per row. **Output:** a `VARCHAR[]` of normalized strings. Use `UNNEST(...)` to get one expansion per row.

**Behaviors / edge cases:** output is lower-cased. An empty string yields an empty list (not an error); a `NULL` input yields `NULL`. This is normalization for matching -- it does not split the address into fields; use `parse_address` for that.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# expand_address

Normalize an address into a `VARCHAR[]` of libpostal expansions, rewriting abbreviations into canonical forms for matching and deduplication.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT postal.main.expand_address('120 E 96th St');
SELECT UNNEST(postal.main.expand_address('120 E 96th St'));
```

## Notes

- Multiple expansions can be returned for an ambiguous token.
- Output is lower-cased; an empty string yields an empty list and `NULL` yields `NULL`.
- For field extraction (not normalization), use `parse_address`.

workers.summary: Airborne LiDAR analysis over classified LAS/LAZ point clouds: building and tree-canopy heights within polygons, and vegetation encroaching on power lines within a 3D clearance distance. Uses the cloud's existing ASPRS classes; a sample point cloud is included.
workers.doc_md:
## GIS analysis

Read classified LAS/LAZ point clouds to estimate building and canopy heights above nearby classified ground, and find vegetation points within a three-dimensional clearance distance of supplied power-line geometry. Inputs and outputs retain caller feature IDs; horizontal coordinates and elevations must be metres. This worker uses existing ASPRS classifications: ground=2, vegetation=3/4/5, buildings=6.

### SQL workflow

Pass query results to the main schema functions, retaining IDs for joins. Use bundled synthetic data to try the executable examples without network access. CRS, coverage, inference limits and resource bounds are explicit function parameters.

## Sources and references

- [ASPRS LAS specification](https://github.com/ASPRSorg/LAS) (also published as an [OGC community standard](https://www.ogc.org/standards/las/)): the point-cloud format and the ground/vegetation/building classification codes this worker relies on.
- [laspy](https://laspy.readthedocs.io/): reads LAS files, with [LASzip](https://laszip.org/)-compatible LAZ decompression via lazrs.
- [SciPy cKDTree](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.spatial.cKDTree.html): the nearest-neighbour index behind ground lookup and clearance searches.
- [Shapely](https://shapely.readthedocs.io/): polygon and power-line geometry operations.

example_queries.description: Estimate heights above a known flat ground surface
example_queries.sql: WITH site(feature_id, geometry_wkb) AS (VALUES ('site', ST_AsWKB('POLYGON ((499995 4099995, 500045 4099995, 500045 4100045, 499995 4100045, 499995 4099995))'::GEOMETRY))) SELECT feature_id, round(building_p95_m, 1), canopy_max_m FROM lidar.main.height_metrics((SELECT * FROM site)) ORDER BY feature_id

example_queries.description: Run height_metrics twice over the bundled site, at the default 2 m and at a 15 m canopy threshold, and join the results: canopy cover is 0.077 and 0.038, so half of the canopy cells hold vegetation at least 15 m tall
example_queries.sql: WITH site(feature_id, geometry_wkb) AS (VALUES ('site', ST_AsWKB('POLYGON ((499995 4099995, 500045 4099995, 500045 4100045, 499995 4100045, 499995 4099995))'::GEOMETRY))), any_canopy AS (SELECT feature_id, canopy_cover_fraction AS cover_2m FROM lidar.main.height_metrics((SELECT * FROM site))), tall AS (SELECT feature_id, canopy_cover_fraction AS cover_15m FROM lidar.main.height_metrics((SELECT * FROM site), canopy_height_m := 15)) SELECT feature_id, round(cover_2m, 3) AS cover_2m, round(cover_15m, 3) AS cover_15m, round(cover_15m / cover_2m, 2) AS tall_share FROM any_canopy JOIN tall USING (feature_id) ORDER BY feature_id

example_queries.description: Find a tree return two metres below a conductor
example_queries.sql: WITH conductor(feature_id, geometry_wkb) AS (VALUES ('line', ST_AsWKB('LINESTRING Z (500025 4100030 120, 500040 4100030 120)'::GEOMETRY))) SELECT feature_id, round(clearance_m, 2) FROM lidar.main.vegetation_clearance((SELECT * FROM conductor)) ORDER BY feature_id, point_index

example_queries.description: Span vegetation report: join canopy height and cover from height_metrics over the right-of-way polygon with vegetation_clearance returns along the conductor (12 m search); Span 7 has 18 m canopy, one return within 3 m, two within 12 m, the closest at 2 m
example_queries.sql: WITH site(feature_id, geometry_wkb) AS (VALUES ('site', ST_AsWKB('POLYGON ((499995 4099995, 500045 4099995, 500045 4100045, 499995 4100045, 499995 4099995))'::GEOMETRY))), conductor(feature_id, geometry_wkb) AS (VALUES ('line', ST_AsWKB('LINESTRING Z (500025 4100030 120, 500040 4100030 120)'::GEOMETRY))), spans(span_id, corridor_id, conductor_id) AS (VALUES ('Span 7', 'site', 'line')), canopy AS (SELECT feature_id, canopy_max_m, canopy_cover_fraction FROM lidar.main.height_metrics((SELECT * FROM site))), returns AS (SELECT feature_id, count(*) FILTER (WHERE clearance_m <= 3) AS within_3m, count(*) AS within_12m, min(clearance_m) AS closest_m FROM lidar.main.vegetation_clearance((SELECT * FROM conductor), clearance_m := 12) GROUP BY feature_id) SELECT s.span_id, c.canopy_max_m, round(c.canopy_cover_fraction, 3) AS canopy_cover, coalesce(r.within_3m, 0) AS within_3m, coalesce(r.within_12m, 0) AS within_12m, round(r.closest_m, 2) AS closest_m FROM spans s JOIN canopy c ON c.feature_id = s.corridor_id LEFT JOIN returns r ON r.feature_id = s.conductor_id ORDER BY s.span_id

agent_tasks: Estimate building and canopy heights above ground for the site. Return feature_id, building p95 height rounded to 1 decimal and maximum canopy height, ordered by feature_id. The site is the polygon with feature_id 'site' covering x 499995-500045, y 4099995-4100045 in EPSG:32618; the conductor is the 3D line with feature_id 'line' from (500025, 4100030, 120) to (500040, 4100030, 120). Use the bundled classified point cloud (the default path).

Find vegetation returns within the default clearance of the conductor. Return feature_id and clearance rounded to 2 decimals, ordered by feature_id and point index. The site is the polygon with feature_id 'site' covering x 499995-500045, y 4099995-4100045 in EPSG:32618; the conductor is the 3D line with feature_id 'line' from (500025, 4100030, 120) to (500040, 4100030, 120). Use the bundled classified point cloud (the default path).

Screen the power-line corridor: find the maximum canopy height inside the site polygon, count the vegetation returns within 15 metres of the conductor and find the closest one. Return one row with columns canopy_max_m (DOUBLE), returns_within_15m (BIGINT) and closest_clearance_m (DOUBLE, rounded to 2 decimals). The site is the polygon with feature_id 'site' covering x 499995-500045, y 4099995-4100045 in EPSG:32618; the conductor is the 3D line with feature_id 'line' from (500025, 4100030, 120) to (500040, 4100030, 120). Use the bundled classified point cloud (the default path).

functions.name: vegetation_clearance
functions.comment: Find classified vegetation within a 3D power-line clearance distance

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Compare classified vegetation returns with supplied 3D LineString/MultiLineString conductor geometry. Return exact Euclidean distance, nearest conductor coordinate and original point index for each return within clearance_m. Input conductor Z and cloud Z must share a vertical datum and metre units. Two-dimensional lines fail. An empty result means no observed encroachments, not a certified safe corridor.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Vegetation conductor clearance

Compare classified vegetation returns with supplied 3D LineString/MultiLineString conductor geometry. Return exact Euclidean distance, nearest conductor coordinate and original point index for each return within clearance_m. Input conductor Z and cloud Z must share a vertical datum and metre units. Two-dimensional lines fail. An empty result means no observed encroachments, not a certified safe corridor.

vgi.example_queries.description: Find a tree return two metres below a conductor
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH conductor(feature_id, geometry_wkb) AS (VALUES ('line', ST_AsWKB('LINESTRING Z (500025 4100030 120, 500040 4100030 120)'::GEOMETRY))) SELECT feature_id, round(clearance_m, 2) FROM lidar.main.vegetation_clearance((SELECT * FROM conductor)) ORDER BY feature_id, point_index

vgi.example_queries.description: Span vegetation report: join canopy height and cover from height_metrics over the right-of-way polygon with vegetation_clearance returns along the conductor (12 m search); Span 7 has 18 m canopy, one return within 3 m, two within 12 m, the closest at 2 m
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH site(feature_id, geometry_wkb) AS (VALUES ('site', ST_AsWKB('POLYGON ((499995 4099995, 500045 4099995, 500045 4100045, 499995 4100045, 499995 4099995))'::GEOMETRY))), conductor(feature_id, geometry_wkb) AS (VALUES ('line', ST_AsWKB('LINESTRING Z (500025 4100030 120, 500040 4100030 120)'::GEOMETRY))), spans(span_id, corridor_id, conductor_id) AS (VALUES ('Span 7', 'site', 'line')), canopy AS (SELECT feature_id, canopy_max_m, canopy_cover_fraction FROM lidar.main.height_metrics((SELECT * FROM site))), returns AS (SELECT feature_id, count(*) FILTER (WHERE clearance_m <= 3) AS within_3m, count(*) AS within_12m, min(clearance_m) AS closest_m FROM lidar.main.vegetation_clearance((SELECT * FROM conductor), clearance_m := 12) GROUP BY feature_id) SELECT s.span_id, c.canopy_max_m, round(c.canopy_cover_fraction, 3) AS canopy_cover, coalesce(r.within_3m, 0) AS within_3m, coalesce(r.within_12m, 0) AS within_12m, round(r.closest_m, 2) AS closest_m FROM spans s JOIN canopy c ON c.feature_id = s.corridor_id LEFT JOIN returns r ON r.feature_id = s.conductor_id ORDER BY s.span_id

workers.title: LightGBM
workers.tagline: LightGBM for DuckDB/SQL — train/predict model registry, hyperparameter search, native categoricals, feature importance and SHAP, exposed as a VGI worker
workers.subtitle: Train, tune, evaluate, and explain gradient-boosted classifiers and regressors, with a saved-model registry.
workers.summary: LightGBM train/predict model registry, datasets, and interpretation for DuckDB/SQL
workers.doc_md:
# LightGBM for SQL

Exposes [LightGBM](https://lightgbm.readthedocs.io) to DuckDB/SQL as VGI functions:

- **Datasets** — toy datasets and generators
- **Models** — `fit`/`predict`, typed `fit_<estimator>`, cross-validation, grid/randomized search
- **Interpretation** — feature importance, SHAP `explain`, partial dependence, permutation importance

Models are stored as reusable BLOBs in a registry; native text serialization.

example_queries.description: Load the built-in iris dataset.
example_queries.sql: SELECT * FROM lightgbm.main.iris LIMIT 5;

example_queries.description: Fit a LightGBM classifier on iris, then predict with the fitted model.
example_queries.sql:
SET VARIABLE iris_model = (SELECT model FROM lightgbm.main.fit((SELECT * EXCLUDE (target_name) FROM lightgbm.main.iris), estimator := 'lgbm_classifier', target := 'target', id := 'sample_id'));
SELECT sample_id, prediction FROM lightgbm.main.predict((SELECT * FROM lightgbm.main.iris), model := getvariable('iris_model'), id := 'sample_id') LIMIT 5;

example_queries.description: Three-fold cross-validated accuracy of a LightGBM classifier on iris.
example_queries.sql: SELECT fold, score FROM lightgbm.main.cross_val_score((SELECT * EXCLUDE (target_name) FROM lightgbm.main.iris), estimator := 'lgbm_classifier', target := 'target', cv := 3);

example_queries.description: Grid-search a LightGBM classifier on iris over a tiny grid (3-fold).
example_queries.sql: SELECT params, mean_score, rank FROM lightgbm.main.grid_search((SELECT * EXCLUDE (target_name) FROM lightgbm.main.iris), target := 'target', cv := 3, estimator := 'lgbm_classifier', num_leaves := [15, 31], learning_rate := [0.1]) ORDER BY rank;

example_queries.description: Out-of-fold confusion matrix on iris with species names: 5-fold cross_val_predict joined back to iris for the true and the predicted species (setosa is never confused; versicolor and virginica are mixed up a handful of times)
example_queries.sql: SELECT a.target_name AS actual, l.target_name AS predicted, count(*) AS n FROM lightgbm.main.cross_val_predict((SELECT * EXCLUDE (target_name) FROM lightgbm.main.iris()), estimator := 'lgbm_classifier', target := 'target', id := 'sample_id', cv := 5) p JOIN lightgbm.main.iris() a USING (sample_id) JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT target, target_name FROM lightgbm.main.iris()) l ON l.target = p.prediction GROUP BY actual, predicted ORDER BY actual, predicted;

example_queries.description: Fit a LightGBM classifier on iris and return the training summary
example_queries.sql: SELECT estimator, task, n_samples, n_features, train_score FROM lightgbm.main.fit((SELECT * EXCLUDE (target_name) FROM lightgbm.main.iris), estimator := 'lgbm_classifier', target := 'target', id := 'sample_id')

example_queries.description: Do split-gain and permutation importance agree? Join the stored 'iris_clf' model's gain ranking to its permutation (accuracy-drop) ranking per feature; both put the two petal measurements first
example_queries.sql: SELECT f.feature, f.rank AS gain_rank, p.rank AS permutation_rank, round(f.importance, 1) AS gain, round(p.importance_mean, 4) AS accuracy_drop FROM lightgbm.main.feature_importance('iris_clf', importance_type := 'gain') f JOIN lightgbm.main.permutation_importance((SELECT * EXCLUDE (target_name) FROM lightgbm.main.iris()), model_name := 'iris_clf', target := 'target', random_state := 42) p USING (feature) ORDER BY f.rank

example_queries.description: Which features push each flower toward its own species? Join SHAP contributions from the stored 'iris_clf' to iris on sample and true class, then average |SHAP| per species and feature (petal length leads for all three species)
example_queries.sql: SELECT i.target_name, e.feature, round(avg(abs(e.shap_value)), 3) AS mean_abs_shap FROM lightgbm.main.explain((SELECT * EXCLUDE (target_name) FROM lightgbm.main.iris()), model_name := 'iris_clf', id := 'sample_id') e JOIN lightgbm.main.iris() i ON i.sample_id = e.sample_id AND i.target = e.class GROUP BY i.target_name, e.feature ORDER BY i.target_name, mean_abs_shap DESC

example_queries.description: How many models are saved
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS model_count FROM lightgbm.main.models

example_queries.description: Class balance
example_queries.sql: SELECT target_name, count(*) FROM lightgbm.main.breast_cancer GROUP BY target_name

example_queries.description: Range and mean of the one-year progression score
example_queries.sql: SELECT min(progression) AS lo, max(progression) AS hi, round(avg(progression), 1) AS mean FROM lightgbm.main.diabetes

example_queries.description: Average median house value by latitude band
example_queries.sql: SELECT round(latitude) AS lat, round(avg(median_house_value), 2) AS avg_value FROM lightgbm.main.california_housing GROUP BY lat ORDER BY lat

example_queries.description: Average alcohol per cultivar
example_queries.sql: SELECT target_name, round(avg(alcohol), 2) FROM lightgbm.main.wine GROUP BY target_name

example_queries.description: Row count per species
example_queries.sql: SELECT target_name, count(*) FROM lightgbm.main.iris GROUP BY target_name

example_queries.description: Randomized-search num_leaves x learning_rate on iris
example_queries.sql: SELECT params, mean_score, rank FROM lightgbm.main.randomized_search((SELECT sample_id, sepal_length_cm, sepal_width_cm, petal_length_cm, petal_width_cm, target FROM lightgbm.main.iris()), target := 'target', id := 'sample_id', n_iter := 2, cv := 2, estimator := 'lgbm_classifier', num_leaves := [15, 31, 63], learning_rate := [0.05, 0.1, 0.2]) ORDER BY rank

example_queries.description: Rank iris features by permutation importance for a stored model
example_queries.sql: SELECT feature, round(importance_mean, 4) AS importance_mean FROM lightgbm.main.permutation_importance((SELECT * EXCLUDE (target_name) FROM lightgbm.main.iris()), model_name := 'iris_clf', target := 'target', n_repeats := 1) WHERE rank <= 3 ORDER BY rank

example_queries.description: Mean and spread of a noisy 500-row, 3-feature regression target
example_queries.sql: SELECT round(avg(target), 3) AS mean_target, round(stddev(target), 3) AS sd_target FROM lightgbm.main.make_regression(n_samples := 500, n_features := 3, noise := 5.0)

example_queries.description: Class balance and mean first feature of a 500-row, 3-feature, 3-class sample
example_queries.sql: SELECT target, count(*) AS n, round(avg(feature_0), 3) AS avg_feature_0 FROM lightgbm.main.make_classification(n_samples := 500, n_features := 3, n_classes := 3) GROUP BY target ORDER BY target

example_queries.description: Row count and mean petal length per species
example_queries.sql: SELECT target_name, count(*) AS n, round(avg(petal_length_cm), 2) AS avg_petal_length_cm FROM lightgbm.main.iris() GROUP BY target_name ORDER BY target_name

example_queries.description: Mean petal length per species
example_queries.sql: SELECT target_name, avg(petal_length_cm) FROM lightgbm.main.iris() GROUP BY target_name

example_queries.description: Partial dependence of 'iris_clf' on petal length
example_queries.sql: SELECT feature_value, round(partial_dependence, 4) AS pd FROM lightgbm.main.partial_dependence((SELECT * EXCLUDE (target_name) FROM lightgbm.main.iris()), model_name := 'iris_clf', feature := 'petal_length_cm', grid_resolution := 5) WHERE class = 0 ORDER BY feature_value

example_queries.description: How many models the registry holds, and how many distinct estimators
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS n_models, count(DISTINCT estimator) AS n_estimators FROM lightgbm.main.models()

example_queries.description: Grid-search num_leaves x learning_rate on iris
example_queries.sql: SELECT params, mean_score, rank FROM lightgbm.main.grid_search((SELECT sample_id, sepal_length_cm, sepal_width_cm, petal_length_cm, petal_width_cm, target FROM lightgbm.main.iris()), target := 'target', id := 'sample_id', cv := 2, estimator := 'lgbm_classifier', num_leaves := [15, 31], learning_rate := [0.1]) ORDER BY rank

example_queries.description: Train a lgbm_regressor with named hyperparameters
example_queries.sql: SELECT model_name, task FROM lightgbm.main.fit_lgbm_regressor((SELECT * EXCLUDE (target_name) FROM lightgbm.main.iris()), model_name := 'm', target := 'target', id := 'sample_id', n_estimators := 100, num_leaves := 31)

example_queries.description: Train a lgbm_classifier with named hyperparameters
example_queries.sql: SELECT model_name, task FROM lightgbm.main.fit_lgbm_classifier((SELECT * EXCLUDE (target_name) FROM lightgbm.main.iris()), model_name := 'm', target := 'target', id := 'sample_id', n_estimators := 100, num_leaves := 31)

example_queries.description: Rank features by mean absolute SHAP contribution for a stored regressor 'diab_reg'
example_queries.sql: SELECT feature, round(avg(abs(shap_value)), 4) AS mean_abs_shap FROM lightgbm.main.explain((SELECT * FROM lightgbm.main.diabetes()), model_name := 'diab_reg', id := 'sample_id') GROUP BY feature ORDER BY mean_abs_shap DESC

example_queries.description: Delete a model by name; `dropped` is false when the name did not exist
example_queries.sql: SELECT model_name, dropped FROM lightgbm.main.drop_model('no_such_model')

example_queries.description: Check whether a model named 'iris_clf' is in the registry
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS found FROM lightgbm.main.model_info('iris_clf')

example_queries.description: Gain-based feature importance for a stored model
example_queries.sql: SELECT feature, round(importance, 3) AS importance FROM lightgbm.main.feature_importance('iris_clf', importance_type := 'gain') WHERE rank <= 5 ORDER BY rank

example_queries.description: Sample count and mean nucleus radius per diagnosis
example_queries.sql: SELECT target_name, count(*) AS n, round(avg(mean_radius), 2) AS avg_mean_radius FROM lightgbm.main.breast_cancer() GROUP BY target_name ORDER BY target_name

example_queries.description: Predict with the stored 'iris_clf' model
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, prediction FROM lightgbm.main.predict((SELECT * FROM lightgbm.main.iris()), model_name := 'iris_clf', id := 'sample_id') ORDER BY sample_id LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: 5-fold accuracy scores on iris
example_queries.sql: SELECT fold, score FROM lightgbm.main.cross_val_score((SELECT sample_id, sepal_length_cm, sepal_width_cm, petal_length_cm, petal_width_cm, target FROM lightgbm.main.iris()), estimator := 'lgbm_classifier', target := 'target', cv := 5)

example_queries.description: Range and mean of the one-year progression score
example_queries.sql: SELECT round(min(progression), 1) AS lo, round(max(progression), 1) AS hi, round(avg(progression), 1) AS mean FROM lightgbm.main.diabetes()

example_queries.description: Distribution of the 5-fold out-of-fold predictions on iris
example_queries.sql: SELECT prediction, count(*) AS n FROM lightgbm.main.cross_val_predict((SELECT sample_id, sepal_length_cm, sepal_width_cm, petal_length_cm, petal_width_cm, target FROM lightgbm.main.iris()), estimator := 'lgbm_classifier', target := 'target') GROUP BY prediction ORDER BY prediction

example_queries.description: Train a LightGBM classifier on iris and store it as 'iris_clf'
example_queries.sql: SELECT model_name, task, n_samples FROM lightgbm.main.fit((SELECT sample_id, sepal_length_cm, sepal_width_cm, petal_length_cm, petal_width_cm, target FROM lightgbm.main.iris()), model_name := 'iris_clf', estimator := 'lgbm_classifier', target := 'target', id := 'sample_id')

example_queries.description: Mean median-house-value per latitude band (downloads on first use)
example_queries.sql: SELECT round(latitude) AS lat, count(*) AS block_groups, round(avg(median_house_value), 3) AS avg_value FROM lightgbm.main.california_housing() GROUP BY lat ORDER BY lat

example_queries.description: The ten strongest wines with their cultivar
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, alcohol, flavanoids, target_name FROM lightgbm.main.wine() WHERE alcohol > 13.5 ORDER BY alcohol DESC LIMIT 10

agent_tasks: How many flowers of each species are in the built-in iris dataset? Return one row per species with columns named target_name and n, ordered by target_name.
How many wine samples are in the built-in wine-recognition dataset? Return a single row with one column named n.

Before trusting a tumour-screening model I need an honest out-of-sample number. Using the built-in Wisconsin breast-cancer data and all 30 cell-nucleus features, run 5-fold cross-validation with a LightGBM classifier and report the mean held-out accuracy. Round to 4 decimals and return a single row with one column named mean_cv_accuracy.

In the built-in California housing data, which one-degree latitude band (round the latitude to the nearest whole degree) has the highest average median house value? Return a single row with one column named lat.

Fit a LightGBM regressor on the diabetes dataset to predict the one-year progression score from the baseline measurements, then score those same rows with the fitted model and report the root-mean-squared error between the predictions and the actual scores. Round to 2 decimals and return a single row with one column named train_rmse.

I want a leakage-free accuracy for a LightGBM classifier on iris: predict every row from a model trained on the other folds (5 folds), then compare those out-of-fold predictions with the true labels. Round to 4 decimals and return a single row with one column named oof_accuracy.

I'm tuning a LightGBM classifier on iris. Sweep num_leaves over 7, 15 and 31 and learning_rate over 0.05 and 0.1 with 5-fold cross-validation, and report the best mean cross-validated accuracy across all those combinations. Round to 4 decimals and return a single row with one column named best_cv_accuracy.

The full grid is too big to sweep, so sample it instead: on iris, try 4 randomly chosen combinations of num_leaves (7, 15, 31, 63) and learning_rate (0.03, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2) with 3-fold cross-validation, using 42 as the sampling seed. How many combinations end up on the leaderboard? Return a single row with one column named n_combos.

Using the typed classifier fitter (the one that takes hyperparameters as named SQL arguments rather than JSON), train a LightGBM classifier on iris with target column 'target' and id column 'sample_id', and report the training summary's sample and feature counts. Return one row with columns named n_samples and n_features.

Using the typed regressor fitter, train a LightGBM regressor on the diabetes dataset (target column 'progression', id column 'sample_id') with 50 boosting rounds, and report the training summary's sample and feature counts. Return one row with columns named n_samples and n_features.
Fit a LightGBM regressor on the diabetes dataset and tell me which single baseline measurement the booster relies on most, measured by total split gain. Return one row with a column named feature.

Fit a LightGBM regressor on the diabetes dataset, then use per-row SHAP contributions to find the feature with the largest mean absolute contribution across all rows. Return one row with a column named feature.

Fit a LightGBM regressor on the diabetes dataset, then measure how much the model's score drops when each feature's values are shuffled (5 repeats, seed 42) and report the single most important feature by that measure. Return one row with a column named feature.

Fit a LightGBM regressor on the diabetes dataset, then show how the model's average predicted progression moves as BMI varies over a 20-point grid, and report the lowest and highest values on that curve, each rounded to 2 decimals. Return one row with columns named min_pd and max_pd.

Save a LightGBM classifier trained on iris under the name 'agent_iris_demo', confirm the registry can tell me which estimator and task it holds for that name, then delete it again. Return one row from the lookup with columns named estimator and task.

Train a LightGBM classifier on iris and store it as 'agent_scratch_model', then delete that model from the registry and confirm it is gone: report how many models in the registry are named 'agent_scratch_model' after the delete. Return a single row with one column named remaining.

Generate a synthetic classification dataset with 120 samples, 4 features, 3 classes and random_state 42, then report how many rows fall in each class. Return one row per class with columns named target and n, ordered by target.

For a tumour screen the costly mistake is calling a malignant tumour benign. On the built-in Wisconsin breast-cancer data, using all 30 cell-nucleus features, get leakage-free 5-fold out-of-fold predictions from a LightGBM classifier and count how many tumours that are actually malignant were predicted benign. Return a single row with one column named missed_malignant.

Generate a synthetic regression dataset with 90 samples, 3 features, noise 5.0 and random_state 42, then report how many rows it has and the standard deviation of its target rounded to 2 decimals. Return one row with columns named n and sd_target.
