All are DuckDB table functions.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# `main` schema

Every LightGBM function lives here, grouped by family:

- **datasets** — toy/generated data as table functions
- **models** — `fit`/`predict`, typed `fit_<estimator>`, cross-validation, grid/randomized search
- **interpretation** — feature importance, SHAP `explain`, partial dependence, permutation importance

Fit returns a reusable model `BLOB`; predict aligns features by name.

vgi.example_queries.description: Fit a LightGBM classifier on iris and return the training summary
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT estimator, task, n_samples, n_features, train_score FROM lightgbm.main.fit((SELECT * EXCLUDE (target_name) FROM lightgbm.main.iris), estimator := 'lgbm_classifier', target := 'target', id := 'sample_id')

vgi.example_queries.description: Out-of-fold confusion matrix on iris with species names: 5-fold cross_val_predict joined back to iris for the true and the predicted species (setosa is never confused; versicolor and virginica are mixed up a handful of times)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT a.target_name AS actual, l.target_name AS predicted, count(*) AS n FROM lightgbm.main.cross_val_predict((SELECT * EXCLUDE (target_name) FROM lightgbm.main.iris()), estimator := 'lgbm_classifier', target := 'target', id := 'sample_id', cv := 5) p JOIN lightgbm.main.iris() a USING (sample_id) JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT target, target_name FROM lightgbm.main.iris()) l ON l.target = p.prediction GROUP BY actual, predicted ORDER BY actual, predicted

vgi.example_queries.description: Do split-gain and permutation importance agree? Join the stored 'iris_clf' model's gain ranking to its permutation (accuracy-drop) ranking per feature; both put the two petal measurements first
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT f.feature, f.rank AS gain_rank, p.rank AS permutation_rank, round(f.importance, 1) AS gain, round(p.importance_mean, 4) AS accuracy_drop FROM lightgbm.main.feature_importance('iris_clf', importance_type := 'gain') f JOIN lightgbm.main.permutation_importance((SELECT * EXCLUDE (target_name) FROM lightgbm.main.iris()), model_name := 'iris_clf', target := 'target', random_state := 42) p USING (feature) ORDER BY f.rank

vgi.example_queries.description: Which features push each flower toward its own species? Join SHAP contributions from the stored 'iris_clf' to iris on sample and true class, then average |SHAP| per species and feature (petal length leads for all three species)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT i.target_name, e.feature, round(avg(abs(e.shap_value)), 3) AS mean_abs_shap FROM lightgbm.main.explain((SELECT * EXCLUDE (target_name) FROM lightgbm.main.iris()), model_name := 'iris_clf', id := 'sample_id') e JOIN lightgbm.main.iris() i ON i.sample_id = e.sample_id AND i.target = e.class GROUP BY i.target_name, e.feature ORDER BY i.target_name, mean_abs_shap DESC

functions.name: randomized_search
functions.comment: Cross-validated randomized search: sample n_iter hyperparameter combinations

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Runs a cross-validated randomized search over a LightGBM estimator, sampling `n_iter :=` random hyperparameter combinations (capped at the grid size) instead of exhausting the grid — cheaper than `grid_search` for large spaces. Same arguments: `estimator :=` names the estimator and each swept hyperparameter takes a list of candidate values; omitted params stay at their default. Set `target :=`, `cv :=` folds, `search_seed :=` for reproducible sampling, optional `id :=`. Returns the same leaderboard (`params`, `mean_score`, `std_score`, `rank`, `metric`) with the refit best model as a `model` `BLOB` on the best row (`WHERE model IS NOT NULL`).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**Cross-validated randomized search** — sample the hyperparameter space.

- `estimator := 'lgbm_classifier'` | `'lgbm_regressor'`, then one list per swept hyperparameter
- `n_iter :=` combinations to sample (capped at grid size), `search_seed :=` for reproducibility
- `target :=`, `cv :=` folds, optional `id :=`

Cheaper than `grid_search` on large grids; best model is a `model` `BLOB` on the best row.

vgi.example_queries.description: Randomized-search num_leaves x learning_rate on iris
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT params, mean_score, rank FROM lightgbm.main.randomized_search((SELECT sample_id, sepal_length_cm, sepal_width_cm, petal_length_cm, petal_width_cm, target FROM lightgbm.main.iris()), target := 'target', id := 'sample_id', n_iter := 2, cv := 2, estimator := 'lgbm_classifier', num_leaves := [15, 31, 63], learning_rate := [0.05, 0.1, 0.2]) ORDER BY rank

functions.name: permutation_importance
functions.comment: Model-agnostic feature importance: the drop in score when each feature is shuffled, ranked

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Computes model-agnostic permutation importance over an evaluation table: for each feature, shuffle its values `n_repeats :=` times and measure the resulting drop in the model's score; a larger drop means a more important feature. Returns one ranked row per feature (`feature`, `importance_mean`, `importance_std`, `rank`; rank 1 = most important). Identify the model with `model_name :=` or `model :=`, name the held-out `target :=` column, and optionally set `scoring :=` and `random_state :=`. Unlike `feature_importance` this measures impact on real predictions and respects feature correlations, but it needs labelled data and is slower.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**Permutation importance** — model-agnostic, ranked.

- Identify the model with `model_name :=` or `model :=`; name the `target :=` column
- `n_repeats :=` shuffles per feature, optional `scoring :=`, `random_state :=`
- Returns `(feature, importance_mean, importance_std, rank)`, sorted descending

Measures impact on real predictions (needs labels; slower than `feature_importance`).

vgi.example_queries.description: Rank iris features by permutation importance for a stored model
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT feature, round(importance_mean, 4) AS importance_mean FROM lightgbm.main.permutation_importance((SELECT * EXCLUDE (target_name) FROM lightgbm.main.iris()), model_name := 'iris_clf', target := 'target', n_repeats := 1) WHERE rank <= 3 ORDER BY rank

functions.name: make_regression
functions.comment: Generate a synthetic regression dataset

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Table function that synthesises a random linear regression problem (scikit-learn's `make_regression`). Control the shape with `n_samples`, `n_features`, `n_informative`, `noise`, and `random_state`; the output schema has a `sample_id`, one `feature_<i>` `DOUBLE` column per feature, and a continuous `DOUBLE` `target`. Use it to generate reproducible regression data of an arbitrary size with a tunable noise level for fit/predict, search, or interpretation demos.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**Synthetic regression generator** — a random linear problem with optional noise.

- Args: `n_samples`, `n_features`, `n_informative`, `noise`, `random_state`
- `sample_id` `INTEGER`, `target` `DOUBLE` (continuous)
- one `feature_<i>` `DOUBLE` column per feature (width set by `n_features`)

functions.name: partial_dependence
functions.comment: How a stored model's average prediction changes as one feature varies over a grid

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Computes the partial-dependence curve for one numeric feature: sweeps `feature :=` over a grid of `grid_resolution :=` points and reports the model's average prediction at each value, holding the rest of the buffered background table fixed. Returns `(feature_value, class, partial_dependence)` ordered along the grid; `class` is NULL for regression and the single binary curve, and is the class index (one curve per class) for multiclass. Identify the model with `model_name :=` or `model :=`. Numeric features only (categorical features raise a clear error). Use it to see the marginal effect and shape of a feature on the prediction.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**Partial dependence** — marginal effect of one feature.

- `feature :=` (numeric only) swept over `grid_resolution :=` points
- Identify the model with `model_name :=` or `model :=`; input is the background table
- Returns `(feature_value, class, partial_dependence)` along the grid

`class` is NULL for regression/binary, the class index for multiclass (one curve each).

vgi.example_queries.description: Partial dependence of 'iris_clf' on petal length
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT feature_value, round(partial_dependence, 4) AS pd FROM lightgbm.main.partial_dependence((SELECT * EXCLUDE (target_name) FROM lightgbm.main.iris()), model_name := 'iris_clf', feature := 'petal_length_cm', grid_resolution := 5) WHERE class = 0 ORDER BY feature_value

functions.name: grid_search
functions.comment: Cross-validated grid search; returns the leaderboard + refit best model `BLOB` on the best row

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Runs an exhaustive cross-validated grid search over a LightGBM estimator's hyperparameters and returns the leaderboard — one row per combination tried, with its `params` (JSON), `mean_score`, `std_score`, `rank` (1 = best), and `metric` (accuracy or r2). Pick the estimator with `estimator := 'lgbm_classifier'` or `'lgbm_regressor'`, then give each hyperparameter you want swept its own list of candidate values (`num_leaves := [15, 31]`, `learning_rate := [0.05, 0.1]`, `n_estimators := [100, 300]`, ...); anything you leave out stays at the estimator default. Set `target :=`, `cv :=` folds, optional `id :=`. The refit best model rides as a `model` `BLOB` on the single best row — grab it with `WHERE model IS NOT NULL`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**Cross-validated grid search** — exhaustive hyperparameter sweep.

- `estimator := 'lgbm_classifier'` | `'lgbm_regressor'`, then one list per swept hyperparameter (`num_leaves := [15, 31]`, `learning_rate := [0.05, 0.1]`, ...)
- `target :=`, `cv :=` folds, optional `id :=`
- Returns the leaderboard: `params`, `mean_score`, `std_score`, `rank`, `metric`

The refit best model is a `model` `BLOB` on the best row — `WHERE model IS NOT NULL`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Grid-search num_leaves x learning_rate on iris
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT params, mean_score, rank FROM lightgbm.main.grid_search((SELECT sample_id, sepal_length_cm, sepal_width_cm, petal_length_cm, petal_width_cm, target FROM lightgbm.main.iris()), target := 'target', id := 'sample_id', cv := 2, estimator := 'lgbm_classifier', num_leaves := [15, 31], learning_rate := [0.1]) ORDER BY rank

functions.name: fit_lgbm_regressor
functions.comment: Fit a lgbm_regressor with typed LightGBM hyperparameters; returns/stores the model

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Buffers a training table and fits a gradient-boosted decision-tree **regressor** (LightGBM's `LGBMRegressor`) with its key hyperparameters exposed as typed, named SQL arguments (`n_estimators`, `num_leaves`, `max_depth`, `learning_rate`, `min_child_samples`, `subsample`, `colsample_bytree`, `reg_alpha`, `reg_lambda`, `boosting_type`, ...). Equivalent to `fit(estimator := 'lgbm_regressor', ...)` but discoverable and type-checked in the catalog instead of a JSON `params` blob. Name the regression label with `target :=`, optionally carry an `id :=` through; every other column is a feature (string columns become LightGBM native categoricals and missing values flow through). Returns the same one-row summary with a reusable `model` `BLOB`, and persists to the registry when `model_name :=` is given. Feed the `BLOB` to `predict`/`explain`/`feature_importance`. Sentinel: `max_depth := 0` means unlimited.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**`fit_lgbm_regressor`** — fit a gradient-boosted decision-tree **regressor** (LightGBM's `LGBMRegressor`) with typed hyperparameters.

- Input: a training table `(SELECT ...)`; name the label with `target :=`, optional `id :=` passthrough
- Hyperparameters are named, typed SQL args (`n_estimators`, `num_leaves`, `max_depth`, `learning_rate`, `min_child_samples`, `reg_lambda`, ...) at LightGBM's defaults
- Returns the standard fit summary plus a reusable `model` `BLOB`; `model_name :=` also persists it

The discoverable, type-checked alternative to `fit(estimator := 'lgbm_regressor', ...)`. `max_depth := 0` = unlimited.

functions.name: explain
functions.comment: Per-row SHAP feature contributions, long format (row, [class], feature, shap_value, base_value)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Streams a table through a stored model and emits SHAP-style per-row prediction contributions (LightGBM's `pred_contrib`) in long format: one row per (input row, feature) with `feature`, `shap_value` (how much that feature pushed this row's raw margin away from the model's base), and `base_value` (the expected margin). Identify the model with `model_name :=` or `model :=` (a `BLOB`); name an `id :=` to tag every emitted row. For multiclass models an extra `class` column appears (one row per (row, class, feature)). Sum `shap_value` over a row's features and add `base_value` to recover the raw margin. Use it for local, per-prediction explanations.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**SHAP explanations** — per-row feature contributions, long format.

- Identify the model with `model_name :=` or `model :=`; optional `id :=` passthrough
- One row per (input row, feature): `feature`, `shap_value`, `base_value`
- Multiclass adds a `class` `BIGINT` column (one row per (row, class, feature))

`sum(shap_value) + base_value` = the row's raw margin. Local, per-prediction explanation.

vgi.example_queries.description: Rank features by mean absolute SHAP contribution for a stored regressor 'diab_reg'
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT feature, round(avg(abs(shap_value)), 4) AS mean_abs_shap FROM lightgbm.main.explain((SELECT * FROM lightgbm.main.diabetes()), model_name := 'diab_reg', id := 'sample_id') GROUP BY feature ORDER BY mean_abs_shap DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Which features push each flower toward its own species? Join SHAP contributions from the stored 'iris_clf' to iris on sample and true class, then average |SHAP| per species and feature (petal length leads for all three species)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT i.target_name, e.feature, round(avg(abs(e.shap_value)), 3) AS mean_abs_shap FROM lightgbm.main.explain((SELECT * EXCLUDE (target_name) FROM lightgbm.main.iris()), model_name := 'iris_clf', id := 'sample_id') e JOIN lightgbm.main.iris() i ON i.sample_id = e.sample_id AND i.target = e.class GROUP BY i.target_name, e.feature ORDER BY i.target_name, mean_abs_shap DESC

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
Long format: one row per (input row, feature). Naming `id :=` carries that input column through as the first column (the table below shows the common `sample_id` case), and a multiclass model adds a `class` column so there is one row per (input row, class, feature).

#### Always present

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `feature` | VARCHAR | Feature column name. |
| `shap_value` | DOUBLE | Contribution of the feature to the raw margin. |
| `base_value` | DOUBLE | Model base (expected) raw-margin value. |

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `class` | BIGINT | Class index the contribution belongs to (0-based). |

#### `id := '<column>'` passthrough

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sample_id` | INTEGER | The named id column, carried through as the first column. |

functions.name: feature_importance
functions.comment: Per-feature importance (split or gain) for a model, ranked

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Returns the booster's built-in per-feature importance for a stored model, one ranked row per feature (`feature`, `importance`, `rank`; rank 1 = most important, already sorted descending). Identify the model positionally by name (`feature_importance('m')`) or with `model :=` (a `BLOB`). Choose the `importance_type :=` — `gain` (default; total gain of the feature's splits) or `split` (the number of times the feature is used in a split). Features never used in a split report importance 0. A fast, model-native ranking; for a model-agnostic alternative use `permutation_importance`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**Booster feature importance** — model-native, ranked.

- Identify the model by name (`feature_importance('m')`) or `model :=` `BLOB`
- `importance_type :=` `gain` (default; total split gain) | `split` (split count)
- Returns `(feature, importance, rank)`, sorted by importance descending

Unused features score 0. See `permutation_importance` for a model-agnostic measure.

vgi.example_queries.description: Gain-based feature importance for a stored model
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT feature, round(importance, 3) AS importance FROM lightgbm.main.feature_importance('iris_clf', importance_type := 'gain') WHERE rank <= 5 ORDER BY rank

vgi.example_queries.description: Do split-gain and permutation importance agree? Join the stored 'iris_clf' model's gain ranking to its permutation (accuracy-drop) ranking per feature; both put the two petal measurements first
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT f.feature, f.rank AS gain_rank, p.rank AS permutation_rank, round(f.importance, 1) AS gain, round(p.importance_mean, 4) AS accuracy_drop FROM lightgbm.main.feature_importance('iris_clf', importance_type := 'gain') f JOIN lightgbm.main.permutation_importance((SELECT * EXCLUDE (target_name) FROM lightgbm.main.iris()), model_name := 'iris_clf', target := 'target', random_state := 42) p USING (feature) ORDER BY f.rank

functions.name: predict
functions.comment: Score a table through a stored model (model_name) or an inline model BLOB

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Streams a table through an already-fit LightGBM model and emits its predictions. Identify the model with either `model_name :=` (a registry name) or `model :=` (a `BLOB` from `fit`, passed via `SET VARIABLE` + `getvariable()` since a table function has only one subquery slot). Features are matched by name (order-independent; extra columns ignored; missing ones error at bind), and string/categorical columns are re-encoded exactly as at fit. The default output is the decoded `prediction` (the original label dtype for classifiers, value for regressors); the mutually exclusive modes `with_proba`, `output_margin`, and `pred_leaf` switch to per-class probabilities, the raw margin, or per-tree leaf indices respectively. Name an `id :=` column to carry it through.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**Predict with a stored model** — score a table row by row.

- Identify the model with `model_name :=` *or* `model :=` (a `fit` `BLOB`)
- Features aligned by name; an optional `id :=` is carried through
- Default output: `prediction` (label or value)
- `with_proba := true` → one `proba_<label>` column per class; `output_margin := true` → a `margin` `DOUBLE`; `pred_leaf := true` → a `leaf` `INTEGER[]` (one index per tree) — the three modes are mutually exclusive

vgi.example_queries.description: Predict with the stored 'iris_clf' model
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, prediction FROM lightgbm.main.predict((SELECT * FROM lightgbm.main.iris()), model_name := 'iris_clf', id := 'sample_id') ORDER BY sample_id LIMIT 10

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
The result shape depends on the prediction mode and on whether an `id` column is named. When `id :=` is given, that input column is carried through unchanged as the first column (the table below shows the common `sample_id` case). The prediction column itself is one of the mutually exclusive variants below: the default `prediction` (typed from the label dtype), `with_proba := true` (one `proba_<label>` column per class, classifiers only), `output_margin := true` (`margin`), or `pred_leaf := true` (`leaf`).

#### Default — classification with integer or boolean labels

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `prediction` | BIGINT | Predicted class label, decoded to the original label value. |

#### Default — classification with string labels

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `prediction` | VARCHAR | Predicted class label, decoded to the original label value. |

#### Default — regression

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `prediction` | DOUBLE | Predicted value. |

#### `with_proba := true` (classifiers only)

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `proba_<label>` | DOUBLE | Predicted probability of that class; one column per class, keyed by the original label. |

#### `output_margin := true`

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `margin` | DOUBLE | Raw (pre-link) margin score from the booster. |

#### `pred_leaf := true`

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `leaf` | INTEGER[] | Leaf index reached in each tree, one element per tree. |

#### `id := '<column>'` passthrough

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sample_id` | INTEGER | The named id column, carried through as the first column. |

functions.name: cross_val_score
functions.comment: Per-fold cross-validation scores (accuracy or R^2); no model is stored

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Runs k-fold cross-validation and returns the held-out score for each fold (one `(fold, score, metric)` row), without storing any model. Name the label with `target :=`, choose the `estimator :=`, set the number of folds with `cv :=` (default 5), and tune via JSON `params :=`. The metric is the estimator's own scorer — accuracy for classifiers, R^2 for regressors. Aggregate the rows (e.g. `avg(score)`) for a single cross-validated performance estimate or to compare estimators/hyperparameters.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**Cross-validated fold scores** — one row per fold, no model stored.

- `estimator :=`, `target :=`, `cv :=` folds (default 5), JSON `params :=`
- Returns `(fold, score, metric)` — the held-out score for each fold

Scorer is the estimator's own (accuracy / R^2). Take `avg(score)` for a single cross-validated estimate.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT fold, score FROM lightgbm.main.cross_val_score((SELECT sample_id, sepal_length_cm, sepal_width_cm, petal_length_cm, petal_width_cm, target FROM lightgbm.main.iris()), estimator := 'lgbm_classifier', target := 'target', cv := 5)

functions.name: cross_val_predict
functions.comment: Out-of-fold cross-validated predictions (no model is stored)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Computes out-of-fold cross-validated predictions for a training table without persisting any model. Each row is predicted by a model trained on the other folds (`cv :=` folds, default 5), so the result is an honest, leakage-free prediction per row — ideal for building a held-out prediction column to score with metrics or to stack. Name the label with `target :=`, pick the `estimator :=`, optionally carry an `id :=` through, and tune via JSON `params :=`. Classification labels of any dtype are decoded back to the original values.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**Cross-validated out-of-fold predictions** — no model is stored.

- Each row is predicted by a model fit on the *other* folds (`cv :=`, default 5)
- `estimator :=`, `target :=`, optional `id :=` passthrough, JSON `params :=`
- Returns one `prediction` per input row (label or value), leakage-free

Use it to make a held-out prediction column for metrics or model stacking.

vgi.example_queries.description: Out-of-fold confusion matrix on iris with species names: 5-fold cross_val_predict joined back to iris for the true and the predicted species (setosa is never confused; versicolor and virginica are mixed up a handful of times)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT a.target_name AS actual, l.target_name AS predicted, count(*) AS n FROM lightgbm.main.cross_val_predict((SELECT * EXCLUDE (target_name) FROM lightgbm.main.iris()), estimator := 'lgbm_classifier', target := 'target', id := 'sample_id', cv := 5) p JOIN lightgbm.main.iris() a USING (sample_id) JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT target, target_name FROM lightgbm.main.iris()) l ON l.target = p.prediction GROUP BY actual, predicted ORDER BY actual, predicted

vgi.example_queries.description: Distribution of the 5-fold out-of-fold predictions on iris

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
One row per input row. The `prediction` column's type follows the label dtype (classification decodes back to the original labels; regression is `DOUBLE`), and naming `id :=` carries that input column through as the first column (the table below shows the common `sample_id` case).

#### Classification with integer or boolean labels

| --- | --- | --- |
| `prediction` | BIGINT | Out-of-fold predicted class label, decoded to the original label value. |

#### Classification with string labels

| `prediction` | VARCHAR | Out-of-fold predicted class label, decoded to the original label value. |

#### Regression

functions.name: fit
functions.comment: Fit a LightGBM estimator; returns the model as a `BLOB` and stores it when model_name is given

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Buffers a training table, fits a LightGBM estimator (`estimator :=` one of `lgbm_classifier` or `lgbm_regressor`), and returns a one-row training summary whose `model` column is a self-contained `BLOB` (booster text + metadata). Name the label column with `target :=`; every other column except an optional `id :=` passthrough becomes a feature — string columns are used as LightGBM's native categorical features and NULLs are kept as missing values. Hyperparameters go in a JSON `params :=` string. Pass `model_name :=` to also persist the model to the registry; otherwise it lives only in the returned `BLOB`. Feed that `BLOB` to `predict`/`explain`/`feature_importance` via `SET VARIABLE` + `getvariable()`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**Fit a LightGBM model** — train and return a reusable model `BLOB`.

- Input: a training table `(SELECT ...)`; name the label with `target :=`, optionally an `id :=` passthrough
- `estimator :=` `lgbm_classifier` | `lgbm_regressor`; hyperparameters via JSON `params :=`
- Returns one row: `estimator`, `task`, `n_samples`/`n_features`/`n_classes`/`n_categorical`, `train_score`, `features`, and the `model` `BLOB`
- `model_name :=` also persists to the registry; string features are learned as native categoricals and classification labels of any dtype are decoded back on predict

workers.subtitle: Linear issues, history, comments, projects, cycles, initiatives and customers as SQL tables.
workers.summary: Linear issue tracking as SQL: issues with state history, comments, attachments and relations, plus teams, projects, cycles, initiatives and customers, read-only from the Linear GraphQL API.
workers.doc_md:
# Linear

Query a Linear workspace from DuckDB: issues with their full change history and discussion, the workspace's teams and workflow, planning (projects, cycles, initiatives, roadmaps), customer requests and the audit log. Read-only.

Create a `linear` secret with a personal API key (`API_KEY`) or an OAuth access token (`ACCESS_TOKEN`). WHERE filters become Linear filter inputs and only the columns you select are fetched, so filter and project early; rate limits and query complexity are handled for you.

### Sources and references

- [Linear GraphQL API](https://linear.app/developers/graphql) — the API this worker reads
- [Filtering](https://linear.app/developers/filtering) — the filter inputs SQL predicates become
- [Pagination](https://linear.app/developers/pagination) — relay `first` / `after` cursors
- [Rate limiting](https://linear.app/developers/rate-limiting) — request and complexity budgets
- [Public schema](https://github.com/linear/linear/blob/master/packages/sdk/src/schema.graphql) (MIT)
workers.readme_sql:
CREATE SECRET linear (TYPE linear, API_KEY 'lin_api_…');

-- Open ENG work by priority (one IssueFilter, only the selected fields fetched).
SELECT key, title, status, assignee
FROM linear.main.issues()
WHERE team_key = 'ENG' AND state = 'open'
ORDER BY priority, key;

-- Cycle time in hours: first move to a started state → completion, per issue.
SELECT issue_key, (epoch_ms(done) - epoch_ms(started)) / 3600000 AS cycle_time_hours
FROM (SELECT issue_key,
             min(created_at) FILTER (WHERE to_state_type = 'started')   AS started,
             max(created_at) FILTER (WHERE to_state_type = 'completed') AS done
      FROM linear.main.issue_history() WHERE team_key = 'ENG' GROUP BY issue_key)
WHERE done IS NOT NULL ORDER BY cycle_time_hours DESC;

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Linear as SQL. Table functions take named arguments: issues(include_archived := false, filter := NULL, page_size := 100) where filter is a raw Linear IssueFilter JSON object ANDed with the pushed WHERE filters. Per-issue functions (issue_key := NULL) read `issue(id:)` for the keys passed or pushed (= / IN); without keys the change-history function fans out over all issues (filter team_key to narrow it) while attachments and relations list the whole workspace, and comments push issue_key, team_key, user_login and time ranges into CommentFilter. Workspace objects (teams, workflow, planning, customers, audit log) are catalog tables with their own filter pushdown. All objects need a `linear` secret.

functions.name: issue_history
functions.comment: Change history of Linear issues: state transitions, reassignments, label and estimate changes

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per change to an issue (Issue.history): issue_key, team_key, created_at (when), actor, from_state / to_state (+ _type and _id), is_state_change, from/to assignee, priority, estimate, title, cycle, project and parent, added_labels / removed_labels and flags (archived, auto_closed, updated_description). Use it for cycle time and lead time: e.g. epoch(max(created_at) FILTER (WHERE to_state_type = 'completed')) - epoch(min(created_at) FILTER (WHERE to_state_type = 'started')) seconds per issue_key. Pass issue_key := 'ENG-1' or filter WHERE issue_key = / IN (…) to read specific issues; otherwise every issue is read (filter team_key = '…' to narrow the issues), nesting the first 50 entries of each issue in the issues page.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## issue_history(issue_key := NULL, include_archived := false, page_size := 50)

Every change to the selected issues, newest first.

**Pushdown:** `issue_key` / `issue_id` (=, IN) select which issues are read (`issue(id:)` each); otherwise `team_key` (=, IN) narrows the issues fanned out over.

vgi.example_queries.description: State transitions of one issue
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT created_at, actor, from_state, to_state FROM linear.main.issue_history(issue_key := 'ENG-1') WHERE is_state_change ORDER BY created_at

vgi.example_queries.description: Cycle time (first started → completed) per ENG issue
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT issue_key, (epoch(max(created_at) FILTER (WHERE to_state_type = 'completed')) - epoch(min(created_at) FILTER (WHERE to_state_type = 'started'))) / 3600 AS cycle_time_hours FROM linear.main.issue_history() WHERE team_key = 'ENG' GROUP BY issue_key ORDER BY issue_key

functions.name: issues
functions.comment: Linear issues, with SQL filters pushed into Linear's IssueFilter and GraphQL projection

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Every Linear issue the key can see (Query.issues, newest updatedAt first), one row each: key (ENG-123), number, repo / team_key, title, state ('open' / 'closed'), status (workflow state name), status_type, priority (0 none … 4 low) and priority_label, estimate, assignee / assignees / assignee_id, user_login (creator), labels, project, project_milestone, cycle_number, parent_key, due_date, body (Markdown description), html_url and the lifecycle timestamps created_at, updated_at, started_at, completed_at, canceled_at, closed_at. WHERE filters on those columns become Linear's IssueFilter (key / id IN uses Linear's identifier-aware id comparator; list_contains(labels, 'Bug') becomes labels.some.name; assignee IS NULL becomes assignee.null). filter := '<IssueFilter JSON>' adds a raw filter for anything else (e.g. '{"slaStatus": {"eq": "Breached"}}'). Archived issues need include_archived := true. Only the GraphQL fields of the selected columns are fetched.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## issues(include_archived := false, filter := NULL, page_size := 100)

Linear issues, one row each, paged with relay cursors and ordered by `updatedAt`.

**Pushdown:** `key`/`id` (=, IN), `repo`/`team_key` (=, IN, starts_with), `team_id`, `number`, `title` (=, starts_with), `state`, `status`, `status_type`, `state_id`, `priority`, `estimate`, `assignee`/`assignee_id`/`assignee_name`, `user_login`/`creator_id`, `list_contains(labels | label_ids, …)`, `project`/`project_id`, `project_milestone`, `cycle_number`/`cycle_id`, `parent_key`/`parent_id`, IS [NOT] NULL on the nullable relations and dates, and ranges on every timestamp → `IssueFilter`. Projection → the GraphQL selection.

vgi.example_queries.description: Open ENG issues by priority (both predicates become one IssueFilter)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT key, title, status, assignee FROM linear.main.issues() WHERE team_key = 'ENG' AND state = 'open' ORDER BY priority, key

vgi.example_queries.description: Issues created since October by workflow state
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT status, count(*) AS issues FROM linear.main.issues() WHERE created_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-10-01' GROUP BY status ORDER BY issues DESC

workers.doc_md:
# AI SQL for DuckDB

**Call LLMs and embed text directly in DuckDB SQL.** `vgi-llm` brings Snowflake Cortex AISQL-style functions -- completion, classification, filtering, extraction, sentiment, summarization, and group-level map-reduce -- to DuckDB over a pluggable provider (Anthropic, OpenRouter, OpenAI, or a local Ollama), plus **keyless** local embeddings and cosine similarity.

## Keyless first

```sql
-- No API key required: local ONNX embeddings + similarity
SELECT ai_similarity(ai_embed('cat'), ai_embed('kitten')) AS score;
```

Add one OpenRouter key (or run Ollama locally) to unlock cloud/local completions:

```sql
CREATE SECRET (TYPE llm, openrouter_api_key 'sk-or-...');
SELECT ai_complete('Write a haiku about DuckDB', 'openrouter/anthropic/claude-sonnet-5');
```

## Notes

- The model argument routes by prefix (`anthropic/…`, `openrouter/…`, `openai/…`, `ollama/…`).
- Empty/NULL input maps to NULL; a provider error or missing key raises a DuckDB error.
- Embeddings run locally (fastembed/ONNX); pair with the DuckDB VSS extension.

## Sources and references

- [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/docs) -- one key for hundreds of cloud models; browse model ids at [openrouter.ai/models](https://openrouter.ai/models)
- [Ollama](https://ollama.com/) -- run models locally for keyless completions
- [Claude API](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/overview) and [OpenAI API](https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference) -- the direct providers behind `anthropic/…` and `openai/…`
- [FastEmbed](https://github.com/qdrant/fastembed) -- the local ONNX embedding library behind `ai_embed`
- [Snowflake Cortex AISQL](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-cortex/aisql) -- the function family this worker mirrors

example_queries.title: embed_dimension
example_queries.description: Embed a string into a fixed-length FLOAT[] with the local default model (keyless).
example_queries.sql: SELECT len(llm.main.ai_embed('hello world')) AS dim;

example_queries.title: self_similarity
example_queries.description: A phrase is maximally similar to itself (keyless).
example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(llm.main.ai_similarity(llm.main.ai_embed('database'), llm.main.ai_embed('database')), 3) AS sim;

example_queries.title: prompt_template
example_queries.description: Build a prompt string by positional substitution (pure, no model).
example_queries.sql: SELECT llm.main.prompt('Translate {} into {}', 'hello', 'French') AS p;

example_queries.title: token_estimate
example_queries.description: Estimate a text's token count locally (no model call).
example_queries.sql: SELECT llm.main.ai_count_tokens('the quick brown fox') AS tokens;

example_queries.title: route_tickets_by_embedding
example_queries.description: Keyless zero-shot routing: embed each support ticket and each label's description with ai_embed, then pick the label with the highest ai_similarity per ticket via arg_max (billing / bug / feature, one row per ticket with its best score).
example_queries.sql: WITH tickets(ticket) AS (VALUES ('I was charged twice for my subscription this month'), ('The app crashes every time I upload a photo'), ('Please add a dark mode to the dashboard')), labels(label, hint) AS (VALUES ('billing', 'payments, invoices, refunds and charges'), ('bug', 'the software crashes or shows an error'), ('feature', 'a request for a new capability')), t AS (SELECT ticket, llm.main.ai_embed(ticket) AS v FROM tickets), l AS (SELECT label, llm.main.ai_embed(hint) AS v FROM labels) SELECT ticket, arg_max(label, llm.main.ai_similarity(t.v, l.v)) AS label, ROUND(max(llm.main.ai_similarity(t.v, l.v)), 3) AS score FROM t, l GROUP BY ticket ORDER BY ticket;

example_queries.title: prompt_token_budget
example_queries.description: Pre-flight cost estimate before calling a model: render one prompt per review row with prompt() and count its tokens locally with ai_count_tokens, plus the batch total (no model call, no key).
example_queries.sql: WITH reviews(id, product, review) AS (VALUES (1, 'laptop', 'Battery barely lasts two hours and the fan is loud.'), (2, 'headphones', 'Great sound, but the ear cushions started peeling after a month.'), (3, 'blender', 'Works fine.')) SELECT id, llm.main.ai_count_tokens(llm.main.prompt('Summarize this {} review in one sentence: {}', product, review)) AS prompt_tokens, SUM(prompt_tokens) OVER () AS total_tokens FROM reviews ORDER BY id;

example_queries.description: Embed text into a FLOAT[] vector (keyless local ONNX).
example_queries.sql: SELECT llm.main.ai_embed('hello world')

example_queries.description: Cosine similarity of two embeddings (keyless).
example_queries.sql: SELECT llm.main.ai_similarity(llm.main.ai_embed('cat'), llm.main.ai_embed('kitten'))

example_queries.description: Build a prompt string by safe template substitution (pure, no model).
example_queries.sql: SELECT llm.main.prompt('Summarize: {}', 'DuckDB is an in-process OLAP database')

example_queries.description: Count tokens locally with tiktoken (no model call).
example_queries.sql: SELECT llm.main.ai_count_tokens('the quick brown fox')

example_queries.description: Complete a prompt with the default provider.
example_queries.sql: SELECT llm.main.ai_complete('Write a haiku about DuckDB')

example_queries.description: Classify text into a subset of the given categories.
example_queries.sql: SELECT llm.main.ai_classify('my card was declined', ['billing','bug','feature']).labels

example_queries.description: Semantic search (keyless): embed the search phrase once with ai_embed and rank a table of documents by ai_similarity to it, keeping the top 2. The two database sentences outrank the unrelated ones.
example_queries.sql: WITH docs(doc) AS (VALUES ('DuckDB is an in-process analytical SQL database'), ('Paris is the capital of France'), ('Kittens are young cats'), ('PostgreSQL is a client-server relational database')), q AS (SELECT llm.main.ai_embed('embedded database for analytics') AS v) SELECT doc, ROUND(llm.main.ai_similarity(llm.main.ai_embed(doc), q.v), 3) AS score FROM docs, q ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 2

example_queries.description: Summarize with an explicit provider/model

example_queries.description: Classify with an explicit provider/model
example_queries.sql: SELECT llm.main.ai_classify(t, ['billing','bug'], 'ollama/llama3.2').labels FROM (VALUES ('my card was declined')) AS x(t)

example_queries.description: Embed text into a FLOAT[] vector (keyless)

example_queries.description: Embed with an explicitly chosen local model

example_queries.description: Cosine similarity of two texts (embedded locally)

example_queries.description: Cosine similarity of two texts with a chosen model
example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(llm.main.ai_similarity('cat', 'kitten', 'BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5'), 3) AS score

example_queries.description: Count tokens with a specific model's tokenizer

example_queries.description: Complete a prompt with an explicit provider/model
example_queries.sql: SELECT llm.main.ai_complete('Summarize DuckDB in one line', 'ollama/llama3.2')

example_queries.description: Overall + per-aspect sentiment
example_queries.sql: SELECT llm.main.ai_sentiment('The food was great but service was slow').overall

Compute the cosine similarity of the embedding of 'database' with itself, rounded to 3 decimals.

Use the prompt() function to render 'Hi {}' with the value 'Sam'.

Get the completion details for a short prompt and confirm the text field is populated.
Describe an image BLOB with the multimodal completion function.
Classify the text 'my card was declined' into one of billing, bug, or feature.
Decide whether 'How do I reset my password?' is a question using ai_filter.
Extract the age from 'Bob is 42' as JSON with an integer age field.
Analyze the sentiment of 'The food was great but service was slow' and read the overall label.
Summarize a short paragraph with ai_summarize.

Without calling an LLM (keyless embeddings only), route each support ticket to the closest label. Tickets: 'My parcel never arrived', 'I cannot log in after resetting my password', 'Where can I track my delivery?'. Labels and their descriptions: 'shipping' = 'delivery, tracking and lost parcels'; 'account' = 'login, password and profile settings'. Return two VARCHAR columns, ticket and label, one row per ticket, ordered by ticket.

Render the template 'Translate to French: {}' with prompt() for each of the phrases 'good morning', 'where is the train station?' and 'thank you very much', then return the total token count of the three rendered prompts using ai_count_tokens with its default tokenizer, as a single integer column total_tokens.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## llm.main schema

The single schema of the AI SQL worker. It groups the surface into a few concepts: free-form completion and summarization, structured outputs (classification, boolean filtering, extraction, sentiment), keyless local embeddings and cosine similarity for semantic search / RAG, group-level LLM map-reduce aggregates, and pure utilities (prompt templating and local token estimation). Completions route to a pluggable provider by a model-prefix string; embeddings and similarity run in-process with no key. Reach for the keyless embedding/similarity pair first (semantic search works with no setup), add a provider key only when you need generative completion or structured extraction.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# llm.main

AI functions over Apache Arrow for DuckDB: completion, structured output, embeddings, aggregates, and utilities.

## Overview

Completions call a pluggable LLM provider (Anthropic / OpenRouter / OpenAI / Ollama) chosen by a model-prefix string. Embeddings and `ai_similarity` run locally (fastembed/ONNX) with no key. The aggregates reduce a whole group to one answer via chunked map-reduce.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT ai_similarity(ai_embed('cat'), ai_embed('kitten')) AS score;
```

## Notes

- Empty/NULL input maps to NULL; a provider error or missing key raises a DuckDB error.
- Embeddings are keyless; completions need a key (or keyless Ollama).

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## ai_classify(input, categories[, model])

Classify each `input` text into one or more of the supplied `categories` (a `LIST<VARCHAR>`) and return `STRUCT{labels LIST<VARCHAR>}` -- the chosen labels drawn from your category set. The model is asked for strict JSON matching the struct; an unparseable reply -> NULL row.

**When to use.** Route/triage a column of text against a fixed taxonomy (support tickets, intents, topics). For a boolean keep/drop decision use `ai_filter`; for free-form fields use `ai_extract`.

**Input/output.** Inputs: `VARCHAR` text, `LIST<VARCHAR>` categories, optional model. Output: `STRUCT` with a `labels` list. NULL/empty input -> NULL (no model call); a provider failure, or a reply that is not the expected JSON, **raises** a DuckDB error.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## ai_embed(input[, model])

Embed each `input` text into a fixed-length `FLOAT[]` vector using a local ONNX model (fastembed) -- **no API key, no network** after the one-time model download. The default model (`BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5`) produces 384-dim vectors; pass a second argument to pick another supported model.

**When to use.** Semantic search, RAG, clustering, and dedup inside SQL: embed a corpus once, embed a query, and rank rows by `ai_similarity`. Pairs naturally with the DuckDB VSS extension.

**Input/output.** Input: one `VARCHAR` per row (+ optional model). Output: one `FLOAT[]` per row; NULL/empty text -> NULL vector.

functions.name: ai_similarity
functions.comment: Cosine similarity of two FLOAT[] vectors, in [-1, 1] (pure arithmetic); NULL on mismatch.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## ai_similarity(a, b)

Cosine similarity of two `FLOAT[]` vectors (typically from `ai_embed`), a `DOUBLE` in `[-1, 1]` where 1 means identical direction. Pure arithmetic -- **no model, no key, no I/O** -- so it is cheap over large joins.

**When to use.** Rank or threshold embedding pairs: `ORDER BY ai_similarity(ai_embed(q), ai_embed(doc)) DESC` for retrieval, or `WHERE ai_similarity(...) > 0.8` for near-duplicate detection.

**Input/output.** Inputs: two `FLOAT[]` vectors. Output: `DOUBLE`. NULL, empty, or length-mismatched pairs -> NULL (never an error).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# ai_similarity

Cosine similarity of two `FLOAT[]` vectors, in `[-1, 1]` (pure arithmetic, keyless).

## Notes

- 1.0 = identical direction, 0 = orthogonal, -1 = opposite.
- NULL / empty / length-mismatch returns NULL.

vgi.example_queries.description: Cosine similarity between two embeddings
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT llm.main.ai_similarity(llm.main.ai_embed('cat'), llm.main.ai_embed('kitten'))

vgi.example_queries.description: Semantic search (keyless): embed the search phrase once with ai_embed and rank a table of documents by ai_similarity to it, keeping the top 2. The two database sentences outrank the unrelated ones.
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH docs(doc) AS (VALUES ('DuckDB is an in-process analytical SQL database'), ('Paris is the capital of France'), ('Kittens are young cats'), ('PostgreSQL is a client-server relational database')), q AS (SELECT llm.main.ai_embed('embedded database for analytics') AS v) SELECT doc, ROUND(llm.main.ai_similarity(llm.main.ai_embed(doc), q.v), 3) AS score FROM docs, q ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 2

vgi.example_queries.description: Cosine similarity of two texts (embedded locally)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(llm.main.ai_similarity('cat', 'kitten'), 3) AS score

vgi.example_queries.description: Cosine similarity of two texts with a chosen model
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(llm.main.ai_similarity('cat', 'kitten', 'BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5'), 3) AS score

functions.name: ai_count_tokens
functions.comment: Count tokens per text with a local tiktoken tokenizer (no network); BIGINT.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## ai_count_tokens(input[, model])

Count the number of tokens in each `input` text with a **local tiktoken** tokenizer and return a `BIGINT` -- **no** network/provider call, so it is fast, deterministic, and free. The optional `model` argument selects the tokenizer: OpenAI/GPT-family models are counted **exactly**; other models (Anthropic, Ollama, ...) use `o200k_base`, a strong cross-model estimate. Use it to budget prompts, chunk long text, or estimate cost before calling a model.

**Input/output.** Input: one `VARCHAR` per row. Output: `BIGINT` token count (>= 1 for non-empty text). NULL/empty input -> NULL. For exact Anthropic counts use the provider's own token-count API.

functions.name: ai_count_tokens
functions.comment: Count tokens per text with the tokenizer for an explicit model (local, no network); BIGINT.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## ai_count_tokens(input[, model])

Count the number of tokens in each `input` text with a **local tiktoken** tokenizer and return a `BIGINT` -- **no** network/provider call, so it is fast, deterministic, and free. The optional `model` argument selects the tokenizer: OpenAI/GPT-family models are counted **exactly**; other models (Anthropic, Ollama, ...) use `o200k_base`, a strong cross-model estimate. Use it to budget prompts, chunk long text, or estimate cost before calling a model.

**Input/output.** Input: one `VARCHAR` per row. Output: `BIGINT` token count (>= 1 for non-empty text). NULL/empty input -> NULL. For exact Anthropic counts use the provider's own token-count API.

## ai_complete_image(prompt, image[, model])

Multimodal completion: send a text `prompt` together with an `image` (a `BLOB` of PNG/JPEG/GIF/WebP bytes) to a vision-capable model and return the text reply as `VARCHAR`. Use it to caption, describe, OCR, or answer questions about images stored in a column.

functions.name: ai_extract
functions.comment: Extract structured JSON from text per a JSON-Schema string; returns a JSON VARCHAR.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## ai_extract(input, response_format[, model])

Extract structured data from each `input` text according to a `response_format` -- a JSON Schema string describing the fields you want -- and return the model's JSON result as a `VARCHAR`. Parse it with DuckDB's JSON functions (`->`, `json_extract`, `from_json(..., schema)`).

**When to use.** Pull typed fields (names, dates, amounts, nested objects) out of unstructured text. For a fixed label set use `ai_classify`; for a boolean use `ai_filter`.

**Input/output.** Inputs: `VARCHAR` text, a constant JSON-Schema string, optional model. Output: a JSON `VARCHAR`. NULL/empty input -> NULL (no model call); a provider failure, or a reply that is not a JSON object, **raises** a DuckDB error. The schema is sent to the provider as a structured-output constraint when supported.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# ai_extract

Schema-driven extraction from text to a JSON `VARCHAR`.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT ai_extract(
  'Invoice 42 for $9.99 due 2026-01-01',
  '{"type":"object","properties":{"amount":{"type":"number"}}}'
)::JSON->>'amount';
```

## Notes

- `response_format` is a JSON-Schema string (a positional constant).
- Output is a JSON string; NULL/empty input -> NULL, an unparseable reply raises.

functions.name: ai_complete
functions.comment: LLM text completion for each prompt row (default model); NULL on empty input, errors raise.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## ai_complete(prompt[, model])

Send each row's `prompt` to a large language model and return its text reply as a `VARCHAR`. The optional second argument selects the provider/model (`anthropic/…`, `openrouter/…`, `openai/…`, `ollama/…`, or a bare model id for the default provider); omit it to use the configured default.

**When to use.** Free-form generation, rewriting, or answering over a column of prompts. For a structured result use `ai_classify` / `ai_extract` / `ai_sentiment`; for a yes/no filter use `ai_filter`.

**Input/output.** Input: one `VARCHAR` prompt per row. Output: one `VARCHAR` per row. NULL/empty prompt -> NULL (no model call); a provider error or a missing key **raises** a DuckDB error -- it is not swallowed to NULL. Calls are fanned across a bounded thread pool, so a wide column completes concurrently.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## ai_filter(predicate, input[, model])

Evaluate a natural-language `predicate` against each `input` text and return a `BOOLEAN` -- true when the predicate holds, false when it does not. Designed for `WHERE` and `CASE`: keep only the rows an LLM judges to match a condition you phrase in plain English.

**When to use.** Semantic filtering that a `LIKE`/regex can't express ("is this review angry?", "does this mention a refund?"). For the matched labels use `ai_classify`; for extracted fields use `ai_extract`.

**Input/output.** Inputs: `VARCHAR` predicate, `VARCHAR` text, optional model. Output: `BOOLEAN`. NULL/empty input, or an answer with no clear yes/no, -> NULL (excluded by a `WHERE`); a provider failure or missing key **raises** a DuckDB error.

functions.name: prompt
functions.comment: Safely substitute positional args into a template ({} / {n}); pure, no model call.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## prompt(template, args...)

Build a prompt string from a `template` and one or more positional `args` by **safe** positional substitution: `{}` (sequential) and `{n}` (explicit index), with `{{`/`}}` escapes. This is **pure** -- it calls **no** model -- so it is the cheap building block for assembling prompts from columns before feeding them to `ai_complete` / `ai_classify` / etc. Unlike Python `str.format`, it rejects format specs and attribute/index access, so a template can never traverse object attributes or trigger a giant-width allocation.

**Input/output.** Inputs: a `VARCHAR` `template` and >= 1 further column values (any type). Output: one `VARCHAR` per row. A NULL template, a malformed placeholder, or an out-of-range index -> NULL row.
tags.vgi.doc_md:

## Notes

Analyse the sentiment of each `input` text and return `STRUCT{overall VARCHAR, categories LIST<STRUCT{name VARCHAR, sentiment VARCHAR}>}`. `overall` is one of positive/negative/neutral/mixed; `categories` breaks sentiment down by aspect the model detects (e.g. price, service). The model is asked for strict JSON; an unparseable reply -> NULL row.

**Input/output.** Input: one `VARCHAR` per row (+ optional model). Output: one sentiment `STRUCT` per row; NULL/empty input -> NULL (no model call). A provider failure, or a reply that is not the expected JSON, **raises** a DuckDB error.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## ai_summarize_agg(input)

Summarize a whole column of text within each `GROUP BY` group into one coherent `VARCHAR` summary per group. It is `ai_agg` with a fixed summarize task: rows are buffered and reduced via chunked map-reduce, so a group larger than the model's context window still yields one summary.

**When to use.** "One summary per category over all its rows" -- grouping a text column and summarizing each group. For a custom instruction use `ai_agg`; for a per-row summary use `ai_summarize`.

**Input/output.** Input: a `VARCHAR` column. Output: one `VARCHAR` summary per group. An empty group yields NULL; a provider failure is raised. Keys come from a CREATE SECRET (TYPE llm) or env vars (or keyless Ollama).

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## ai_agg(input, task)

Aggregate a whole column of text within each `GROUP BY` group by applying a natural-language `task` to all the rows at once, returning one `VARCHAR` answer per group. It is a hierarchical **chunked map-reduce**: rows are buffered, split into context-sized chunks, each chunk mapped to a partial answer, then the partials reduced with your task -- so a group larger than the model's context window still produces a single answer.

**When to use.** One summary, theme, or answer per category over all its rows -- grouping a text column and applying a task such as listing the top complaints to each group. For a per-row answer use `ai_complete`; for a plain summary-per-group use `ai_summarize_agg`.

**Input/output.** Inputs: a `VARCHAR` column and a constant `task` string. Output: one `VARCHAR` per group. A group with no rows yields NULL; a provider failure is raised as a DuckDB error. Keys come from a CREATE SECRET (TYPE llm) or provider env vars (or keyless Ollama).

workers.subtitle: LogQL log and metric queries, log lines with pushdown, stream metadata and ruler state from Grafana Loki.
workers.summary: Query Grafana Loki and Grafana Cloud Logs from DuckDB: LogQL log and metric queries as typed rows, log lines with SQL filters pushed into LogQL, stream metadata, ruler rules and alerts, and offline LogQL tools.
workers.doc_md:
# Loki in DuckDB

Run LogQL against Grafana Loki and get typed rows back: log lines with `TIMESTAMPTZ` and exact nanosecond timestamps, stream labels hoisted into columns and kept as a `MAP`, structured metadata and parsed fields as maps; metric queries in the same long layout as vgi-prometheus, so logs-derived and Prometheus metrics UNION.

- **query_range / query**: arbitrary LogQL; log results are paged past the 5000-line limit, metric ranges chunked under 11,000 points.
- **logs**: SQL `WHERE` filters become stream matchers, line filters and the time window; every filter is re-applied exactly.
- **Metadata**: labels, values, streams, index stats, volume, detected fields and labels, patterns.
- **Ruler**: LogQL rules and active alerts.
- **LogQL tools**: quote, classify and inspect LogQL offline; validate on the server.

Credentials come from a `loki` DuckDB secret (bearer token or basic auth, optional tenant header).

example_queries.description: Log lines per level for the checkout app in the hour before 01:00 UTC
example_queries.sql: SELECT labels['level'] AS level, value AS lines FROM loki.main.query('sum by (level) (count_over_time({app="checkout"}[1h]))', time := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 01:00:00+00') ORDER BY level

example_queries.description: Current log volume per app in one namespace
example_queries.sql: SELECT labels['app'] AS app, round(value, 3) AS lines_per_second FROM loki.main.query('sum by (app) (rate({namespace="shop"}[5m]))') ORDER BY lines_per_second DESC

example_queries.description: Checkout error lines mentioning a timeout in a two-hour window
example_queries.sql: SELECT ts, pod, line FROM loki.main.query_range('{app="checkout", level="error"} |= "timeout"', TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00', TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 02:00:00+00') ORDER BY ts

example_queries.description: Checkout log lines per level in half-hour buckets, summed
example_queries.sql: SELECT labels['level'] AS level, sum(value) AS lines FROM loki.main.query_range('sum by (level) (count_over_time({app="checkout"}[30m]))', TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00', TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 02:00:00+00', step := 1800) GROUP BY level ORDER BY level

example_queries.description: Declined-payment errors per pod; app and level become stream matchers, the LIKE a |= line filter and the ts range the request window
example_queries.sql: SELECT pod, count(*) AS errors FROM loki.main.logs('{namespace="shop"}') WHERE app = 'checkout' AND level = 'error' AND line LIKE '%declined%' AND ts >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00' AND ts < TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 02:00:00+00' GROUP BY pod ORDER BY pod

example_queries.description: The five newest checkout lines with a logfmt-parsed status; ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 5 becomes a backward query with limit 5
example_queries.sql: SELECT ts, parsed['status'] AS status, line FROM loki.main.logs('{app="checkout"} | logfmt', start_date := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00', end_date := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 02:00:00+00') ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Which stream labels the shop namespace uses
example_queries.sql: SELECT label FROM loki.main.labels(match := '{namespace="shop"}', start_date := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00', end_date := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 02:00:00+00') ORDER BY label

example_queries.description: How many distinct stream label names were seen in the last six hours
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS label_names FROM loki.main.labels()

example_queries.description: Apps logging in the shop namespace
example_queries.sql: SELECT value AS app FROM loki.main.label_values('app', match := '{namespace="shop"}', start_date := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00', end_date := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 02:00:00+00') ORDER BY app

example_queries.description: How many namespaces logged in the last six hours
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS namespaces FROM loki.main.label_values('namespace')

example_queries.description: Stream cardinality per app in one namespace
example_queries.sql: SELECT app, count(*) AS streams FROM loki.main.series('{namespace="shop"}', start_date := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00', end_date := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 02:00:00+00') GROUP BY app ORDER BY streams DESC, app

example_queries.description: Which pods and levels the checkout app has streams for
example_queries.sql: SELECT labels['pod'] AS pod, level FROM loki.main.series('{app="checkout"}', start_date := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00', end_date := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 02:00:00+00') ORDER BY pod

example_queries.description: How much data a selector would read before running the query
example_queries.sql: SELECT streams, entries, bytes FROM loki.main.index_stats('{namespace="shop"}', start_date := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00', end_date := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 02:00:00+00')

example_queries.description: Size of one app's logs over the last hour
example_queries.sql: SELECT round(bytes / 1e6, 1) AS megabytes FROM loki.main.index_stats('{app="bulk"}')

example_queries.description: Log volume per namespace, largest first
example_queries.sql: SELECT labels['namespace'] AS namespace, bytes FROM loki.main.volume('{namespace=~".+"}', target_labels := 'namespace', start_date := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00', end_date := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 02:00:00+00') ORDER BY bytes DESC, namespace

example_queries.description: The five noisiest apps in a namespace over the last hour
example_queries.sql: SELECT labels['app'] AS app, bytes FROM loki.main.volume('{namespace="shop"}', target_labels := 'app', top_n := 5) ORDER BY bytes DESC

example_queries.description: Fields inside the payments app's JSON lines, with types and parsers
example_queries.sql: SELECT field, type, cardinality, parsers FROM loki.main.detected_fields('{app="payments"}', start_date := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00', end_date := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 02:00:00+00') ORDER BY field

example_queries.description: logfmt fields in a namespace's recent lines, most distinct first
example_queries.sql: SELECT field FROM loki.main.detected_fields('{namespace="shop"}') WHERE list_contains(parsers, 'logfmt') ORDER BY cardinality DESC

example_queries.description: Stream labels of one namespace by cardinality
example_queries.sql: SELECT label, cardinality FROM loki.main.detected_labels(query := '{namespace="shop"}', start_date := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00', end_date := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 02:00:00+00') ORDER BY cardinality DESC, label

example_queries.description: High-cardinality stream labels over the last hour
example_queries.sql: SELECT label FROM loki.main.detected_labels() WHERE cardinality > 100 ORDER BY label

example_queries.description: The most frequent line shapes of one app
example_queries.sql: SELECT pattern, sum(count) AS lines FROM loki.main.patterns('{app="bulk"}', start_date := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 01:00:00+00', end_date := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 02:00:00+00') GROUP BY pattern ORDER BY lines DESC

example_queries.description: Which patterns appear in the most five-minute buckets over the last hour
example_queries.sql: SELECT pattern, count(*) AS buckets FROM loki.main.patterns('{namespace="shop"}', step := 300) GROUP BY pattern ORDER BY buckets DESC

example_queries.description: Every LogQL alerting rule with its state
example_queries.sql: SELECT group_name, rule_name, state, active_alerts FROM loki.main.rules(rule_type := 'alert') ORDER BY group_name, rule_name

example_queries.description: Which stream labels each rule's LogQL selects on
example_queries.sql: SELECT rule_name, loki.main.selector_labels(query) AS labels_used FROM loki.main.rules() ORDER BY rule_name

example_queries.description: Active LogQL alerts with severity
example_queries.sql: SELECT alert_name, state, labels['severity'] AS severity FROM loki.main.alerts() ORDER BY alert_name

example_queries.description: Firing alerts per severity
example_queries.sql: SELECT labels['severity'] AS severity, count(*) AS alerts FROM loki.main.alerts() WHERE state = 'firing' GROUP BY severity ORDER BY alerts DESC

example_queries.description: Which Loki version the server runs
example_queries.sql: SELECT version, revision FROM loki.main.build_info()

example_queries.description: Whether the server is new enough for detected_fields()
example_queries.sql: SELECT version >= '3.0' AS has_detected_fields FROM loki.main.build_info()

example_queries.description: Canonical form of a LogQL metric query
example_queries.sql: SELECT valid, formatted FROM loki.main.format_query('sum(rate({app="x"}|="a"[5m]))by(b)')

example_queries.description: The parser's message for an unclosed stream selector
example_queries.sql: SELECT valid, error FROM loki.main.format_query('{app="x" |= "a"')

example_queries.description: Build a LogQL query from SQL strings with correct escaping
example_queries.sql: SELECT '{app=' || loki.main.logql_quote('checkout') || '} |= ' || loki.main.logql_quote('error="payment declined"') AS logql

example_queries.description: How many ruler rules are metric queries
example_queries.sql: SELECT loki.main.query_type(query) AS kind, count(*) AS rules FROM loki.main.rules() GROUP BY kind ORDER BY kind

example_queries.description: The stream selectors every ruler rule reads
example_queries.sql: SELECT rule_name, unnest(loki.main.stream_selectors(query)) AS selector FROM loki.main.rules() ORDER BY rule_name

example_queries.description: Which stream labels the most rules depend on
example_queries.sql: SELECT l AS label, count(*) AS rules FROM loki.main.rules(), unnest(loki.main.selector_labels(query)) u(l) GROUP BY l ORDER BY rules DESC

example_queries.description: Classify three queries
example_queries.sql: SELECT q, loki.main.query_type(q) AS kind FROM (VALUES ('{app="x"} |= "err"'), ('sum by (app) (rate({app="x"}[5m]))'), ('{app="x"')) t(q) ORDER BY q;

example_queries.description: Selectors of a ratio query; braces in a template string are skipped
example_queries.sql: SELECT loki.main.stream_selectors('sum(rate({app="api", level="error"} | line_format "{{.msg}}" [5m])) / sum(rate({app="api"}[5m]))') AS selectors;

example_queries.description: Quote strings with quotes, backslashes and a tab
example_queries.sql: SELECT s, loki.main.logql_quote(s) AS literal FROM (VALUES ('plain'), ('say "hi"'), ('C:\temp'), ('a' || chr(9) || 'b')) t(s) ORDER BY s;

example_queries.description: Labels of a two-selector query
example_queries.sql: SELECT loki.main.selector_labels('sum(count_over_time({namespace="shop", app=~"check.*"} | json [5m])) / sum(count_over_time({namespace="shop"}[5m]))') AS labels;

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The main schema holds every function. Table functions that call the server take an optional secret_name named argument (default: the loki secret whose scope matches). Window arguments are start_date/end_date (query_range takes start and end positionally); log windows are [start, end). Log rows: read a stream label with labels['name'], a parsed field with parsed['name'] (add | json or | logfmt to the LogQL), structured metadata with structured_metadata['name']. In logs(), list a stream label in label_columns to get a pushdown column. The LogQL scalars take one `VARCHAR` expression and need no secret.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

Table functions call the Loki HTTP API named by a `loki` secret (bearer token or basic auth, optional `X-Scope-OrgID` tenant); pass `secret_name` to choose between several. Scalars inspect LogQL locally and need no secret.

Conventions: log rows carry `ts` (`TIMESTAMPTZ`) and exact `ts_ns`, common stream labels hoisted into columns, all labels in a `labels` map, and `structured_metadata` and `parsed` maps. Windows are `start_date`/`end_date`, half-open `[start, end)`. Log results are paged past Loki's 5000-line limit with de-duplication, and metric results use the same long layout as vgi-prometheus so the two UNION.

Reach for `logs` when you want SQL filters pushed into LogQL (label matchers, line filters, the time window, newest-first `LIMIT`), and for `query_range` when you need arbitrary LogQL such as parsers, `line_format` or metric aggregations.

functions.name: query_range
functions.comment: Run a LogQL log or metric query over a time range: log lines paged past the server limit, or metric series as long rows

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Run any LogQL over a time range (/loki/api/v1/query_range). Positional args: logql, start (`TIMESTAMPTZ`, inclusive), end. The output schema depends on the query kind, decided when the query is bound: a LOG query (starts with a stream selector, e.g. '{app="x"} |= "err" | json') returns one row per log line: ts `TIMESTAMPTZ`, ts_ns `BIGINT` (exact nanoseconds), job, namespace, pod, app, level (stream labels, NULL when absent), labels `MAP` (all stream labels), line, structured_metadata `MAP`, parsed `MAP` (labels extracted by | json, | logfmt, ... in your query); end is exclusive. A METRIC query (count_over_time, rate, sum by, ...) returns vgi-prometheus's long layout: result_type, metric (NULL), job, instance, labels, ts, value `DOUBLE`, histogram (NULL), string_value, so it UNIONs with Prometheus data; end is the last evaluation time. Named args: max_lines (stop after N log lines; default all), direction ('backward' newest first, default, or 'forward'), step (metric step seconds; default Loki's), page_size (default 5000, the server limit), chunk_seconds (default 3600), max_points_per_chunk (default 11000), secret_name. Log pages advance from the last timestamp with de-duplication, so every line is returned exactly once. Put parsing and label filters in the LogQL; use logs() to have SQL WHERE filters pushed into the query instead.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## query_range(logql, start, end, max_lines := NULL, direction := 'backward', step := NULL, ...)

Log queries return log rows (paged past the server's 5000-line limit); metric queries return the vgi-prometheus long layout (chunked under the 11,000-point limit). The cursor is resumable over HTTP.

vgi.example_queries.description: Checkout error lines mentioning a timeout in a two-hour window
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ts, pod, line FROM loki.main.query_range('{app="checkout", level="error"} |= "timeout"', TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00', TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 02:00:00+00') ORDER BY ts

vgi.example_queries.description: Checkout log lines per level in half-hour buckets, summed
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT labels['level'] AS level, sum(value) AS lines FROM loki.main.query_range('sum by (level) (count_over_time({app="checkout"}[30m]))', TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00', TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 02:00:00+00', step := 1800) GROUP BY level ORDER BY level

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
The columns depend on the LogQL kind.

**Log query** (`{...}` with an optional pipeline):

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `ts` | TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE | Entry or sample timestamp (UTC, microsecond precision; ts_ns keeps nanoseconds). |
| `ts_ns` | BIGINT | Entry timestamp in Unix nanoseconds (Loki's full precision). |
| `job` | VARCHAR | Value of the 'job' label; NULL when absent. |
| `namespace` | VARCHAR | Value of the 'namespace' label; NULL when absent. |
| `pod` | VARCHAR | Value of the 'pod' label; NULL when absent. |
| `app` | VARCHAR | Value of the 'app' label; NULL when absent. |
| `level` | VARCHAR | Value of the 'level' label; NULL when absent. |
| `labels` | MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR) | Every label of the stream or series as MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR). Read one with labels['name']. |
| `line` | VARCHAR | The log line as returned (after any line_format in the query). |
| `structured_metadata` | MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR) | Structured metadata of the entry (e.g. trace_id, detected_level); empty map when none. |
| `parsed` | MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR) | Labels extracted by parsers in the query (| json, | logfmt, | regexp, | pattern); empty map when none. |

**Metric query** (same as vgi-prometheus `query_range`):

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `result_type` | VARCHAR | LogQL result type: vector, matrix or scalar. |
| `metric` | VARCHAR | The __name__ label; NULL for Loki results (kept so metric rows UNION with vgi-prometheus). |
| `job` | VARCHAR | Value of the 'job' label; NULL when absent. |
| `instance` | VARCHAR | Value of the 'instance' label; NULL when absent. |
| `labels` | MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR) | Every label of the stream or series as MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR). Read one with labels['name']. |
| `ts` | TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE | Entry or sample timestamp (UTC, microsecond precision; ts_ns keeps nanoseconds). |
| `value` | DOUBLE | Sample value; NaN, +Inf and -Inf are kept. |
| `histogram` | STRUCT(count DOUBLE, sum DOUBLE, buckets STRUCT(lower DOUBLE, upper DOUBLE, count DOUBLE, lower_inclusive BOOLEAN, upper_inclusive BOOLEAN)[]) | Always NULL for Loki; present so metric rows UNION with vgi-prometheus query_range. |
| `string_value` | VARCHAR | Value of a string result; NULL otherwise. |

functions.name: logs

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Read log lines as typed rows with SQL WHERE filters pushed into LogQL. Positional arg (optional): a LogQL log query (stream selector plus optional pipeline such as '| json' or '| logfmt'); omit it to build the selector from filters. Named: label_columns (extra stream labels as `VARCHAR` columns, e.g. 'cluster'), start_date/end_date (window, default the last hour; end exclusive), max_lines, direction ('backward' default or 'forward'), page_size (default 5000), chunk_seconds (default 3600), secret_name. Columns: ts `TIMESTAMPTZ`, ts_ns `BIGINT`, job, namespace, pod, app, level, label_columns..., labels `MAP` (all stream labels), line `VARCHAR`, structured_metadata `MAP`, parsed `MAP` (fields from parsers in the query). Pushdown: =, <>, IN, IS [NOT] NULL, LIKE, NOT LIKE, prefix/suffix/contains on label columns become stream matchers; contains(line,'x'), line LIKE '%x%', prefix/suffix/= on line become '|= "x"' line filters and NOT contains / NOT LIKE '%x%' become '!= "x"'; ts and ts_ns comparisons become the request window; ORDER BY ts [DESC] LIMIT n sets the direction and limit. Every filter is re-applied exactly, so results always match the SQL. Loki needs at least one non-empty stream matcher (e.g. app = 'x' or a selector argument). Filters on labels['x'], parsed[...] or structured_metadata[...] run in DuckDB; list a stream label in label_columns to push it, or write parser filters into the LogQL argument (e.g. '{app="api"} | json | status >= 500').
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## logs(selector := '{}', label_columns := '', start_date, end_date, max_lines, direction, ...)

Typed log rows. SQL filters on stream-label columns become stream matchers, filters on `line` become LogQL line filters, `ts` ranges become the request window, and `ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT n` becomes a backward query with a limit. Every filter is also re-applied exactly by the worker.

functions.name: logs

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Read log lines as typed rows with SQL WHERE filters pushed into LogQL. Positional arg (optional): a LogQL log query (stream selector plus optional pipeline such as '| json' or '| logfmt'); omit it to build the selector from filters. Named: label_columns (extra stream labels as `VARCHAR` columns, e.g. 'cluster'), start_date/end_date (window, default the last hour; end exclusive), max_lines, direction ('backward' default or 'forward'), page_size (default 5000), chunk_seconds (default 3600), secret_name. Columns: ts `TIMESTAMPTZ`, ts_ns `BIGINT`, job, namespace, pod, app, level, label_columns..., labels `MAP` (all stream labels), line `VARCHAR`, structured_metadata `MAP`, parsed `MAP` (fields from parsers in the query). Pushdown: =, <>, IN, IS [NOT] NULL, LIKE, NOT LIKE, prefix/suffix/contains on label columns become stream matchers; contains(line,'x'), line LIKE '%x%', prefix/suffix/= on line become '|= "x"' line filters and NOT contains / NOT LIKE '%x%' become '!= "x"'; ts and ts_ns comparisons become the request window; ORDER BY ts [DESC] LIMIT n sets the direction and limit. Every filter is re-applied exactly, so results always match the SQL. Loki needs at least one non-empty stream matcher (e.g. app = 'x' or a selector argument). Filters on labels['x'], parsed[...] or structured_metadata[...] run in DuckDB; list a stream label in label_columns to push it, or write parser filters into the LogQL argument (e.g. '{app="api"} | json | status >= 500').

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Evaluate a LogQL metric expression at one instant (GET /loki/api/v1/query) and return one row per result series. Positional arg: the LogQL text, which must be a metric query (count_over_time, rate, sum by, ...); Loki rejects log queries here, so use query_range or logs for log lines. tags.vgi.doc_llm: query_type(logql) returns 'log' when the query selects log lines (it starts with a stream selector, optionally in parentheses: '{app="x"} | json'), 'metric' when it computes samples (count_over_time, rate, sum by, vector, ...), and NULL when the text is lexically broken (unterminated string, unbalanced brackets). query_range() uses the same rule to choose its output columns: log rows or metric rows. It lexes LogQL (strings, comments, brackets, stream selectors) but is not Loki's full parser; use format_query() for server-side validation.

workers.summary: Looker metadata and usage as SQL: dashboards, tiles, Looks, folders, users, connections, LookML explores and lineage, schedules, alerts and System Activity, read-only.
workers.doc_md:
# Looker

Query a Looker instance from DuckDB: dashboards and tiles, Looks, folders, users, groups, roles, connections, LookML models / explores / fields, explore-to-table lineage, git branches, schedules, alerts, and usage from System Activity. Read-only.

Create a `looker` secret with your API host (`BASE_URL`) and an API key pair (`CLIENT_ID`, `CLIENT_SECRET`). Filters become Looker search parameters and System Activity filters; secrets such as connection passwords, git credentials and schedule recipients are never returned.

### Sources and references

- [Looker API 4.0 reference](https://cloud.google.com/looker/docs/reference/looker-api/latest) — the endpoints this worker reads
- [API authentication](https://cloud.google.com/looker/docs/api-auth) — client id / secret login
- [System Activity](https://cloud.google.com/looker/docs/system-activity-pages) — the usage model behind content_usage and query_history
- [run_inline_query](https://cloud.google.com/looker/docs/reference/looker-api/latest/methods/Query/run_inline_query) and [filter expressions](https://cloud.google.com/looker/docs/filter-expressions)
workers.readme_sql:
CREATE SECRET looker (TYPE looker,
    BASE_URL 'https://acme.cloud.looker.com',
    CLIENT_ID '…', CLIENT_SECRET '…');

-- Dashboards nobody opened in 90 days, with their folder.
SELECT title, folder_path, owner, last_viewed_at
FROM looker.main.dashboards
WHERE NOT deleted AND last_viewed_at < now() - INTERVAL 90 DAY
ORDER BY last_viewed_at;

-- Slowest explores this week (System Activity, filters pushed into the inline query).
SELECT model, explore, count(*) AS runs, avg(runtime_seconds) AS avg_s
FROM looker.main.query_history
WHERE created_at >= now() - INTERVAL 7 DAY AND result_source = 'query'
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY avg_s DESC LIMIT 10;

-- Which warehouse tables feed which dashboards (join with dbt / OpenLineage on table names).
SELECT DISTINCT t.table_schema, t.table_name, d.title
FROM looker.main.explore_tables t
JOIN looker.main.dashboard_elements e ON e.model = t.model_name AND e.explore = t.explore_name
JOIN looker.main.dashboards d ON d.id = e.dashboard_id
WHERE t.model_name = 'thelook';
