tags.vgi.doc_llm: Looker API 4.0 collections exposed as tables, grouped into content, administration, LookML lineage, delivery and usage categories, plus two functions that run a saved Look or query and return typed rows. Usage tables read the System Activity model: filter their date column to choose the window. Tables that expand per explore or per query make one API call per item, so filter model_name, explore_name or id when you can. Identifiers join across tables (a tile's query_id to the queries table, an explore's model to its LookML project). All objects need a `looker` secret.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

Every Looker collection this worker reads is a table here, plus two functions that return the typed results of a saved Look or query.

All objects need a `looker` secret. Filters push down into Looker search parameters and System Activity inline-query filters; tables that fan out per explore or per query make one API call per item, so filter on the model, explore or id when you can. Connection passwords, git credentials and schedule recipients are never returned.

tables.name: query_history
tables.comment: Every query Looker ran: runtime, source, status, user, model and explore, from System Activity.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per query run from Looker's System Activity (`system__activity` model, `history` explore) via a read-only inline query. Columns: tool, history_id, created_at, completed_at, runtime_seconds, status (complete, error, killed, running …), source (dashboard, explore, api4, scheduled_task, look, …), result_source (query, cache, …), connection_name, dashboard_id, look_id, query_id, model, explore, user_id, user_email, message (error text). The window comes from WHERE created_at bounds (default: the last 7 days), read newest-first in 7-day inline queries (smaller when a chunk is large). status, source, model, explore, user_email, connection_name, dashboard_id and look_id filters (= / IN) push down. Needs see_system_activity.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Query runs with runtimes, for performance and adoption analysis. Filter `created_at` to choose the window (default last 7 days).

**Pushdown:** `created_at` bounds become the `history.created_time` filter (default last 7 days; read newest-first in 7-day chunks that shrink when a chunk nears the 50,000-row cap); `status`, `source`, `model`, `explore`, `user_email`, `connection_name`, `dashboard_id` and `look_id` (`=` / `IN`) become inline-query filters.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Daily usage of each dashboard and Look from Looker's System Activity (`system__activity` model, `history` explore) via a read-only inline query. workers.title: Data Masking & De-identification
workers.tagline: FF1 format-preserving encryption, HMAC tokenization & redaction for DuckDB (Rust)
workers.subtitle: Encrypt, tokenize, or redact card numbers, SSNs, emails, and other PII in query results.
workers.summary: Reversible format-preserving encryption, deterministic tokenization, and irreversible partial redaction of sensitive values.
workers.doc_md:
# Mask: Data Masking, Format-Preserving Encryption & PII De-identification in SQL

![RustCrypto logo](https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/22351541?s=240)

**Mask** brings production-grade data masking to DuckDB — reversible format-preserving encryption (FPE), deterministic tokenization, and irreversible redaction of sensitive values, all callable as plain SQL scalar functions over Apache Arrow. It is built for data engineers, analysts, and privacy teams who need to de-identify PII such as credit card numbers, Social Security numbers, email addresses, and account IDs directly in their queries, views, and pipelines, with no external service or pre-processing step.

Under the hood, Mask uses real, vetted, permissively-licensed cryptography — never hand-rolled ciphers. Format-preserving encryption is implemented with the NIST [SP 800-38G](https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/sp/800-38g/final) **FF1** algorithm from the [`fpe`](https://github.com/str4d/fpe) crate ([docs](https://docs.rs/fpe)), keyed with AES-256 from the [RustCrypto `aes`](https://github.com/RustCrypto/block-ciphers) crate ([docs](https://docs.rs/aes)). Deterministic tokenization uses HMAC-SHA-256, and keys are derived with SHA-256, both from the [RustCrypto](https://github.com/RustCrypto) hashing and MAC crates ([`hmac`](https://docs.rs/hmac), [`sha2`](https://docs.rs/sha2)). FPE preserves a value's *shape*: a 16-digit card stays a Luhn-valid 16-digit card, an SSN stays SSN-shaped, and an email keeps its `@domain` — so masked data still passes format validation and flows through schemas unchanged.

Mask offers three complementary de-identification strategies, and you choose between them based on whether the original value must be recoverable later. **Reversible format-preserving encryption** protects a value under a secret key while keeping its shape, so authorized holders of the key can recover it and downstream format checks still pass — ideal for masked views, reversible data sharing, and generating referentially-consistent synthetic test data that mirrors production shape. **Deterministic tokenization** replaces an identifier with a stable, non-reversible HMAC-SHA-256 pseudonym so equal inputs always map to equal tokens and masked columns stay joinable across tables for analytics without ever exposing the real value. **Irreversible redaction** stars out the sensitive portion of a value for human-facing display, keeping only a small non-secret hint such as the last four digits. Mask supports GDPR- and HIPAA-driven anonymization and pseudonymization workflows; note that key management (KMS/HSM, rotation) is intentionally out of scope — the worker simply takes a key. Learn more about [format-preserving encryption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Format-preserving_encryption) and the [RustCrypto](https://www.rustcrypto.org/) project that powers Mask.

example_queries.description: Build a masked view of a customer table in one query: a joinable token for the email (mask_token), display-safe email and card hints (mask_redact), and a reversibly encrypted, still SSN-shaped SSN (mask_fpe).
example_queries.sql: SELECT c.id, mask.main.mask_token(c.email, 'my-secret-key') AS customer_key, mask.main.mask_redact(c.email, 'email') AS email_display, mask.main.mask_redact(c.card, 'last4') AS card_display, mask.main.mask_fpe(c.ssn, 'ssn', 'my-secret-key') AS ssn_protected FROM (VALUES (1, 'alice@example.com', '4012888888881881', '123-45-6789'), (2, 'bob@example.org', '5555555555554444', '987-65-4321')) AS c(id, email, card, ssn) ORDER BY c.id;

example_queries.description: Join an orders extract that was shared with emails replaced by tokens back to the customer table by tokenizing the customer emails with the same key, then total spend per customer showing only the redacted email (alice 200, bob 65, carol 15).
example_queries.sql: WITH customers(email, region) AS (VALUES ('alice@example.com', 'EU'), ('bob@example.org', 'US'), ('carol@example.net', 'US')), shared_orders AS (SELECT mask.main.mask_token(o.email, 'my-secret-key') AS customer_key, o.amount FROM (VALUES ('alice@example.com', 120), ('bob@example.org', 40), ('alice@example.com', 80), ('carol@example.net', 15), ('bob@example.org', 25)) AS o(email, amount)) SELECT mask.main.mask_redact(c.email, 'email') AS customer, c.region, SUM(s.amount) AS total_spend FROM customers AS c JOIN shared_orders AS s ON s.customer_key = mask.main.mask_token(c.email, 'my-secret-key') GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY total_spend DESC;

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The `main` schema of the mask worker groups its data-masking scalar functions into three complementary strategies. Reversible format-preserving encryption keeps a value's shape while protecting it under a secret key, so authorized key holders can recover it. Deterministic tokenization produces stable, non-reversible pseudonyms that stay joinable across tables. Irreversible redaction stars out the sensitive portion of a value for display. Pick format-preserving encryption when you must reverse the value, tokenization when you need joinable pseudonyms, and redaction for one-way display masking. Format-preserving encryption alone is reversible under the key; tokenization and redaction are one-way, and tokenization additionally keeps equal inputs equal so masked columns remain joinable.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# mask.main

Data-masking scalar functions over Apache Arrow, grouped into three complementary strategies:

- **Format-preserving encryption** — reversibly protect a value under a key while keeping its shape (a card stays a Luhn-valid 16-digit card).
- **Tokenization** — replace an identifier with a stable, non-reversible HMAC-SHA-256 pseudonym that stays joinable across tables.
- **Redaction** — irreversibly star out the sensitive portion of a value for display.

Only format-preserving encryption is reversible (under the same key); tokenization and redaction are one-way, and tokenization keeps equal inputs equal so masked columns stay joinable.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `mask_token(value, key)`

Produces a stable, **one-way pseudonym** for a value using **HMAC-SHA-256** under a secret `key`, returned as a hex string. The mapping is deterministic: the same `value` and `key` always yield the same token.

### When to use
Choose tokenization when you need to de-identify an identifier *and* keep it joinable. Because identical inputs map to identical tokens, you can replace an account ID or email with its token in two different tables and still join on it — referential integrity is preserved without ever exposing the original. Unlike `mask_fpe`, this is **not reversible**; unlike `mask_redact`, it does not preserve the input's shape.

### Inputs
- `value` — the identifier to tokenize (`VARCHAR`). NULL passes through to NULL.
- `key` — secret key string; the HMAC key is domain-separated from the FPE key.

### Output
A hexadecimal HMAC-SHA-256 token (`VARCHAR`). The original value cannot be recovered from it.

### Behavior & edge cases
- Deterministic and collision-resistant; same input+key ⇒ same token across runs and tables, so it is safe for joins.
- **Caution:** deterministic tokens are frequency-analyzable on low-cardinality columns — equal inputs always produce equal tokens.
- NULL input → NULL; an empty `key` raises an error.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Deterministic Tokenize

`mask_token(value, key)` returns a stable, non-reversible HMAC-SHA-256 pseudonym for a value, as a hex string.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT mask.main.mask_token('customer-42', 'my-secret-key');
```

The same input and key always produce the same token, so tokens stay joinable across tables.

## Notes

- Tokens are one-way: the original value cannot be recovered (use `mask_fpe` if you need reversibility).
- Deterministic output is frequency-analyzable on low-cardinality data.
- NULL in → NULL out; an empty key is an error.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `mask_redact(value, mode)`

Irreversibly **partially masks** a value for display, replacing the sensitive portion with `*` characters while keeping a small, non-secret hint visible. No key is involved and the original value cannot be recovered.

### When to use
Use this for human-facing display masking — showing the last four digits of a card on a receipt, the first character of an email in a UI, or fully starring a column in an export. It is the simplest masking strategy; choose `mask_token` instead when you need joinable pseudonyms, or `mask_fpe` when you need to reverse the transform later.

### Inputs
- `value` — the string to redact (`VARCHAR`). NULL passes through to NULL.
- `mode` — redaction strategy (see below).

### Modes
| mode | keeps | example |
|---|---|---|
| `last4` | last four characters | `4012888888881881` → `************1881` |
| `first4` | first four characters | `4012888888881881` → `4012************` |
| `email` | first local char + `@domain` | `alice@example.com` → `a****@example.com` |
| `all` | nothing | `secret` → `******` |

### Behavior & edge cases
- Irreversible: the starred characters are discarded, not encrypted.
- NULL input → NULL; an unknown `mode` raises an error.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Irreversible Partial Redaction

`mask_redact(value, mode)` partially masks a value for display by starring out the sensitive portion. It is one-way — the original cannot be recovered.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT mask.main.mask_redact('4012888888881881', 'last4'); -- ************1881
SELECT mask.main.mask_redact('alice@example.com', 'email'); -- a****@example.com
```

## Modes

- `last4` — keep only the last four characters.
- `first4` — keep only the first four characters.
- `email` — keep the first local character plus the `@domain`.
- `all` — star out everything.

## Notes

- For joinable pseudonyms use `mask_token`; for reversible masking use `mask_fpe`.
- NULL in → NULL out; an unknown mode is an error.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `mask_fpe(value, format, key)`

Reversibly encrypts a sensitive string under a secret `key` using **FF1 format-preserving encryption** (FF1 over AES-256), so the ciphertext keeps the *shape* of the input and can be substituted wherever the original was used.

### When to use
Reach for this when you need to de-identify PII but downstream consumers still expect the original format — masked views over cards/SSNs/emails, generating referentially-consistent test data, or sharing data while keeping it reversible for authorized holders of the key. If you never need to recover the value, prefer `mask_token` (one-way pseudonym) or `mask_redact` (display masking).

### Inputs
- `value` — the string to encrypt (`VARCHAR`). NULL passes through to NULL.
- `format` — shape profile: `card`, `ssn`, `digits`, `alnum`, or `email`.
- `key` — secret key string; the AES key is derived from it via SHA-256.

### Output
A `VARCHAR` ciphertext with the same shape as the input. `card` stays a Luhn-valid 16-digit number, `ssn` keeps its dashes, `email` keeps `@domain` and FPEs only the local part, `digits`/`alnum` keep their length and character class.

### Behavior & edge cases
- Reverse with `mask_unfpe` under the **same** `format` and `key`.
- **Small-domain pass-through:** FF1 refuses domains below 1,000,000 (radix 10 ⇒ fewer than 6 digits; radix 62 ⇒ fewer than 4 chars), so very short values are returned unchanged — they still round-trip.
- NULL input → NULL; an unknown `format` or an empty `key` raises an error.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Format-Preserving Encrypt

`mask_fpe(value, format, key)` reversibly encrypts a value while preserving its shape, using FF1 format-preserving encryption over AES-256.

## Usage

```sql
-- card stays a Luhn-valid 16-digit number
SELECT mask.main.mask_fpe('4012888888881881', 'card', 'my-secret-key');
-- SSN keeps its dashes
SELECT mask.main.mask_fpe('123-45-6789', 'ssn', 'my-secret-key');
```

The `format` profile selects the shape to preserve: `card`, `ssn`, `digits`, `alnum`, or `email`.

## Notes

- Reverse the transform with `mask_unfpe` under the same `format` and `key`.
- Values too short for FF1's minimum domain are passed through unchanged but still round-trip.
- NULL in → NULL out; an unknown format or empty key is an error.

## `mask_unfpe(value, format, key)`

The **inverse of `mask_fpe`**: recovers the original plaintext from a format-preserving ciphertext using FF1 decryption over AES-256.

### When to use
Use this on the authorized side of a masking pipeline to recover a value that was protected with `mask_fpe`. It only succeeds when you supply the **same** `format` profile and the **same** `key` that produced the ciphertext — a different key yields different (wrong) output, which is the point of keyed encryption.

### Inputs
- `value` — the format-preserving ciphertext to reverse (`VARCHAR`).
- `format` — the profile used to encrypt: `card`, `ssn`, `digits`, `alnum`, or `email`.
- `key` — the same secret key that was used with `mask_fpe`.

### Output
The recovered original `VARCHAR` value.

### Behavior & edge cases
- For `card`, decryption re-derives the Luhn check digit, so the original 16-digit number is reproduced exactly.
- Values that were passed through unchanged by `mask_fpe` (small-domain rule) decrypt to themselves.
- NULL input → NULL; an unknown `format` or an empty `key` raises an error.

# Format-Preserving Decrypt

`mask_unfpe(value, format, key)` reverses `mask_fpe`, recovering the original value from a format-preserving ciphertext.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT mask.main.mask_unfpe(
  mask.main.mask_fpe('123-45-6789', 'ssn', 'k'), 'ssn', 'k');
-- => '123-45-6789'
```

## Notes

- You must pass the same `format` and `key` used to encrypt; a different key produces incorrect output.
- `card` decryption re-derives the Luhn check digit so the round-trip is exact.
- NULL in → NULL out; an unknown format or empty key is an error.

# Match: Probabilistic Entity Resolution & Record Linkage in SQL

![Splink logo](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/7570107/85285114-3969ac00-b488-11ea-88ff-5fca1b34af1f.png)

**Match brings fuzzy entity resolution, record linkage, and deduplication directly into DuckDB SQL** -- point it at a messy relation, name the columns to compare, and get back clusters of rows that refer to the same real-world person, customer, contact, or product.

## What it does and who it's for

Real-world data is full of duplicates that exact `GROUP BY` and `JOIN` can never catch: `John Smith` vs `Jon Smith`, `j.smith@x.com` vs `J.Smith@x.com`, typos, nicknames, and transpositions. Match solves this *probabilistic matching* problem in plain SQL. It is built for data engineers, analysts, and data-quality teams who need to deduplicate customer master data, consolidate CRM contacts, link records across systems, or clean a product catalog -- without exporting to a separate Python pipeline. You stay in DuckDB; Match does the fuzzy matching and clustering and hands you back the same rows plus an entity label.

## How it works and the engine behind it

Match is powered by [Splink](https://github.com/moj-analytical-services/splink), the open-source probabilistic record-linkage library from the UK Ministry of Justice. Under the hood it uses the **Fellegi-Sunter** statistical model with fuzzy string comparisons (Jaro-Winkler for name-like columns, Levenshtein edit distance for the rest) to estimate, for every candidate pair of records, the probability that they describe the same entity. Pairs scoring above a threshold are linked, and connected components of linked records collapse into entity clusters. The default model is deterministic and robust on relations of any size, while `train := true` opts into Splink's unsupervised EM estimation for larger datasets. See the [Splink documentation](https://moj-analytical-services.github.io/splink/) and this [introduction to probabilistic linkage](https://www.robinlinacre.com/intro_to_probabilistic_linkage/) for the theory.

## SQL use cases and the function surface

Match exposes a single, focused table function, `match_resolve(relation, columns := '...', threshold := 0.5, train := false)`. Pass a relation as a subquery and the comparison columns; it returns every input row unchanged plus two appended columns: `cluster_id` (rows sharing it are the same entity) and `match_probability` (confidence per row). Use it to deduplicate a customer or contact list, link records that refer to the same organization, or detect duplicate products before a migration.

A typical call passes your rows as a parenthesised subquery and names the comparison columns -- `match_resolve(relation, columns := 'first_name,last_name,email')` -- then orders or groups the result by `cluster_id` to inspect each resolved entity or to count how many records collapsed into it. Fully runnable, coverage-checked queries live in the function's own example set (see `match.main.match_resolve`) and in the `main` schema examples.

## Notes

- The default model is deterministic and robust on relations of any size; `train := true` opts into Splink's unsupervised EM (weak on tiny inputs).
- This is a buffer-all-then-compute operator (entity resolution is an all-pairs problem), so block tightly for very large inputs.

example_queries.description: Resolve three records on name + email and inspect the entity each row was assigned to, grouped by cluster.
example_queries.sql: SELECT first_name, last_name, email, cluster_id FROM match.main.match_resolve((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('John','Smith','j@x.com'),('Jon','Smith','j@x.com'),('Jane','Doe','jane@y.com')) AS t(first_name,last_name,email)), columns := 'first_name,last_name,email') ORDER BY cluster_id, first_name

example_queries.description: Count how many records collapsed into each resolved entity, largest duplicate group first.
example_queries.sql: SELECT cluster_id, count(*) AS n FROM match.main.match_resolve((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('Ann','Lee'),('Anne','Lee'),('Bob','Ng')) AS t(first_name,last_name)), columns := 'first_name,last_name') GROUP BY cluster_id ORDER BY n DESC

example_queries.description: Build a golden record per entity: resolve the built-in sample_customers demo on name + email and collapse each cluster to one row (lowest record_id, the first-name spellings seen, email, city, and how many source records merged) -- the three Smith variants and two Doe variants each become one row, the two Jones stay separate.
example_queries.sql: SELECT min(record_id) AS golden_record_id, string_agg(DISTINCT first_name, ' / ' ORDER BY first_name) AS name_variants, any_value(last_name) AS last_name, any_value(email) AS email, any_value(city) AS city, count(*) AS source_records FROM match.main.match_resolve((SELECT record_id, first_name, last_name, email, city FROM match.main.sample_customers), columns := 'first_name,last_name,email') GROUP BY cluster_id ORDER BY golden_record_id

example_queries.description: Score the resolver against sample_customers' ground-truth expected_entity label: self-join the resolved rows into record pairs and count true/false positive and false negative links, with pairwise precision and recall (4 true links, no false ones: precision = recall = 1.0).
example_queries.sql: WITH resolved AS (SELECT record_id, expected_entity, cluster_id FROM match.main.match_resolve((SELECT record_id, first_name, last_name, email, expected_entity FROM match.main.sample_customers), columns := 'first_name,last_name,email')), pairs AS (SELECT a.cluster_id = b.cluster_id AS predicted_same, a.expected_entity = b.expected_entity AS actually_same FROM resolved AS a JOIN resolved AS b ON a.record_id < b.record_id) SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE predicted_same AND actually_same) AS true_pos, count(*) FILTER (WHERE predicted_same AND NOT actually_same) AS false_pos, count(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT predicted_same AND actually_same) AS false_neg, round(true_pos / nullif(true_pos + false_pos, 0), 3) AS precision, round(true_pos / nullif(true_pos + false_neg, 0), 3) AS recall FROM pairs

example_queries.description: Check what dropping email costs: resolve sample_customers on first + last name only at threshold 0.7 and count clusters per ground-truth entity -- Jane/Janet Doe still link, but the John/Jon/Johnny Smith variants split into three clusters (under-merging).
example_queries.sql: SELECT expected_entity, count(*) AS records, count(DISTINCT cluster_id) AS clusters FROM match.main.match_resolve((SELECT record_id, first_name, last_name, expected_entity FROM match.main.sample_customers), columns := 'first_name,last_name', threshold := 0.7) GROUP BY expected_entity ORDER BY expected_entity

example_queries.description: Count the sample records that belong to each ground-truth entity -- the planted duplicate groups match_resolve should reproduce.
example_queries.sql: SELECT expected_entity, count(*) AS records FROM match.main.sample_customers GROUP BY expected_entity ORDER BY records DESC, expected_entity

example_queries.description: Inspect just the messy Smith records (three spelling variants of one real person) to see the kind of duplication entity resolution targets.
example_queries.sql: SELECT record_id, first_name, last_name, email FROM match.main.sample_customers WHERE last_name = 'Smith' ORDER BY record_id

example_queries.description: Dedup on name + email; the John/Jon Smith rows share a cluster_id, Jane Doe is separate.
example_queries.sql: SELECT first_name, last_name, email, cluster_id, match_probability FROM match.main.match_resolve((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('John','Smith','john@x.com'),('Jon','Smith','john@x.com'),('Jane','Doe','jane@y.com')) AS t(first_name,last_name,email)), columns := 'first_name,last_name,email') ORDER BY cluster_id, first_name

example_queries.description: Surface only duplicate groups by clustering and keeping entities with more than one record.
example_queries.sql: SELECT cluster_id, count(*) AS rows_in_entity FROM match.main.match_resolve((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('John','Smith','john@x.com'),('Jon','Smith','john@x.com'),('Jane','Doe','jane@y.com'),('Jayne','Doe','jane@y.com'),('Bob','Ng','bob@z.com')) AS t(first_name,last_name,email)), columns := 'first_name,last_name,email') GROUP BY cluster_id HAVING count(*) > 1 ORDER BY rows_in_entity DESC

example_queries.description: Stricter resolution: raise the link threshold and keep only the more-confident matches.
example_queries.sql: SELECT first_name, last_name, cluster_id, match_probability FROM match.main.match_resolve((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('John','Smith','john@x.com'),('Jon','Smith','john@x.com'),('Jane','Doe','jane@y.com')) AS t(first_name,last_name,email)), columns := 'first_name,last_name,email', threshold := 0.9) WHERE match_probability >= 0.5 ORDER BY cluster_id, first_name

example_queries.description: Deduplicate three records on name + email; the two John/Jon Smith rows resolve to one cluster, Jane Doe to another.
example_queries.sql: SELECT first_name, last_name, cluster_id FROM match.main.match_resolve((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('John','Smith','john@x.com'),('Jon','Smith','john@x.com'),('Jane','Doe','jane@y.com')) AS t(first_name,last_name,email)), columns := 'first_name,last_name,email') ORDER BY cluster_id, first_name;

example_queries.description: Count how many distinct real-world entities remain after resolving five customer records (two of which are duplicates).
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(DISTINCT cluster_id) AS entities FROM match.main.match_resolve((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('Ann','Lee','ann@z.com'),('Anne','Lee','ann@z.com'),('Bob','Ng','bob@z.com')) AS t(first_name,last_name,email)), columns := 'first_name,last_name,email');

# sample_customers

A small, **browsable demo relation** of seven customer records with planted duplicates, so you can try entity resolution without supplying your own data.

## The planted story

- **Smith, John** -- rows 1-3 (`John` / `Jon` / `Johnny`, same email) are one real person with spelling variants.
- **Doe, Jane** -- rows 4-5 (`Jane` / `Janet`, same email) are one real person.
- **Jones** -- rows 6-7 (`Robert`, `Alice`) are *different* people who only share a surname -- the over-merge trap.

## Columns

`record_id`, `first_name`, `last_name`, `email`, `city`, and `expected_entity` (the ground-truth grouping label). Compare `expected_entity` against the `cluster_id` a resolver assigns to gauge quality.

## Notes

The relation is static and credential-free (VALUES-backed), so it scans instantly and is safe to use in docs, demos, and tests.

# match_resolve

Cluster the rows of a relation into **resolved entities** (deduplication / record linkage) using probabilistic matching.

## What it does

Buffers the whole input relation, scores every candidate record pair with [Splink](https://github.com/moj-analytical-services/splink)'s Fellegi-Sunter model (fuzzy Jaro-Winkler / Levenshtein comparisons), links pairs above the threshold, and groups linked records into clusters.

## Calling it

Signature: `match_resolve(relation, columns := '...', threshold := 0.5, train := false)`. The first positional argument is the relation to resolve, passed as a parenthesised subquery over your source rows; the runnable, coverage-checked examples are attached to this function's example set.

- `columns` — comma-separated comparison columns to match on (required).
- `threshold` — match-probability cutoff in `[0,1]` for linking pairs (default `0.5`).
- `train` — opt into Splink's unsupervised EM refinement (default `false`; weak on tiny inputs).

## Returns

Every input column unchanged, plus `cluster_id` (`VARCHAR`) and `match_probability` (`DOUBLE`).

## Notes

- Singletons get their own `cluster_id` and `match_probability = 1.0`.
- An empty input relation raises an error.
- This is a buffer-all-then-compute operator; block tightly for very large inputs.

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
The result schema is **dynamic**: it is the input relation's own columns, passed through unchanged, followed by two appended columns. The passthrough columns therefore vary with whatever relation you pass as the first argument; the two appended columns are always present. If the input already has a `cluster_id` or `match_probability` column, it is replaced by the produced one.

### Appended columns (always present)

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| cluster_id | VARCHAR | Resolved-entity id; rows sharing a cluster_id are the same entity (a singleton entity gets its own id). |
| match_probability | DOUBLE | Strongest pairwise match probability linking the row into its cluster, in [0, 1] (1.0 for a singleton). |

### Passthrough columns (vary by input) — shown for the (first_name, last_name, email) demo relation

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| first_name | VARCHAR | Echo of the like-named input column (a comparison column in this demo). |
| last_name | VARCHAR | Echo of the like-named input column (a comparison column in this demo). |
| email | VARCHAR | Echo of the like-named input column (a comparison column in this demo). |

workers.doc_md:
# Media Metadata Extraction in SQL with ffprobe

![FFmpeg logo](https://ffmpeg.org/ffmpeg-logo.png)

Inspect video, audio, and container files directly from DuckDB SQL: read codec, resolution, duration, bitrate, frame rate, and embedded metadata tags from MP4, MKV, MOV, WAV, MP3, WebM, and every other format that [FFmpeg](https://ffmpeg.org) can open — no manual transcoding, no external scripts.

This extension is for data engineers, media pipelines, and anyone who needs to take inventory of a media library, triage transcoding jobs, or run quality and conformance checks at scale. Instead of shelling out to a command-line tool and parsing JSON by hand, you query your media the same way you query any other table, and join the results against the rest of your warehouse.

## How it works

Under the hood the worker runs [ffprobe](https://ffmpeg.org/ffprobe.html), the media analyzer that ships with the [FFmpeg](https://github.com/FFmpeg/FFmpeg) project, in a sandboxed subprocess with bounded probe size and timeouts so that truncated or untrusted bytes can never hang a query. Every function accepts either a filesystem path (`VARCHAR`) or the raw media bytes (`BLOB`), so you can probe files on disk or `BLOB` columns already loaded into DuckDB. ffprobe's findings are surfaced over Apache Arrow as native SQL columns; missing or unparseable fields return NULL rather than erroring.

## What you can read

The worker groups its surface into a few kinds of reading:

- **Container-level facts** — one value per file, such as the format name, playback duration, overall bit rate, byte size, and how many elementary streams the file holds.
- **Video attributes** — for the first video track: its codec, pixel width and height, a combined resolution string, and the average frame rate.
- **Audio attributes** — for the first audio track, such as its codec.
- **Full enumeration** — table functions that return one row per elementary stream, and one row per format-level metadata tag, when you need every detail rather than a single summary value.

## When to use it

Reach for this worker whenever media files are part of your data and you want their technical metadata available in SQL: cataloguing an asset library, validating that uploads meet a resolution or codec policy, or driving transcoding decisions from a query rather than a bespoke script.

See the official [ffprobe documentation](https://ffmpeg.org/ffprobe.html) and the broader [FFmpeg documentation](https://ffmpeg.org/documentation.html) for details on the underlying analyzer.
workers.readme_sql:
INSTALL vgi FROM community; LOAD vgi;

ATTACH 'media' AS media (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'github-auto://Query-farm/vgi-media@v0.4.2');

-- Scalars take a file PATH or URL (VARCHAR) or media BYTES (BLOB). These read a
-- small sample MP4 (1 s, 320x240, 10 fps, H.264) committed to this repo.
SELECT media.media_format('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-media/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/tiny.mp4');   -- 'mov,mp4,m4a,3gp,3g2,mj2'
SELECT media.resolution('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-media/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/tiny.mp4');     -- '320x240'
SELECT media.duration('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-media/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/tiny.mp4');       -- 1.0 (seconds)
SELECT media.video_codec('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-media/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/tiny.mp4');    -- 'h264'

-- Probe a BLOB read into DuckDB:
SELECT media.media_format(content)
FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-media/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/tiny.mp4');

-- Table functions: one row per stream / per metadata tag.
SELECT * FROM media.media_streams('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-media/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/tiny.mp4');
SELECT * FROM media.media_tags('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-media/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/tiny.mp4');

-- Combine them: inventory a set of files (for a local folder use
-- FROM glob('/your/folder/*')), classifying each file as video or audio-only
-- from which codec is present.
SELECT parse_filename(file) AS file_name, media.media_format(file) AS format,
       CASE WHEN media.video_codec(file) IS NOT NULL THEN 'video'
            WHEN media.audio_codec(file) IS NOT NULL THEN 'audio-only' ELSE 'unknown' END AS kind,
       coalesce(media.video_codec(file), media.audio_codec(file)) AS codec,
       media.resolution(file) AS resolution, round(media.duration(file), 2) AS seconds
FROM (VALUES ('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-media/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/tiny.mp4'),
             ('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-media/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/silent.wav')) AS f(file)
ORDER BY file_name;

example_queries.description: List the container-level metadata tags of a media file as key/value rows, ordered by tag name.
example_queries.sql: SELECT key, value FROM media.main.media_tags('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-media/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/tiny.mp4') ORDER BY key

example_queries.description: Inventory a list of media files (here the two sample URLs; a local folder works the same through glob()): for each file, its container format, whether it is video or audio-only (from video_codec / audio_codec), the codec, the video resolution (NULL for audio-only), and the duration.
example_queries.sql: SELECT parse_filename(file) AS file_name, media.main.media_format(file) AS format, CASE WHEN media.main.video_codec(file) IS NOT NULL THEN 'video' WHEN media.main.audio_codec(file) IS NOT NULL THEN 'audio-only' ELSE 'unknown' END AS kind, coalesce(media.main.video_codec(file), media.main.audio_codec(file)) AS codec, media.main.resolution(file) AS resolution, round(media.main.duration(file), 2) AS seconds FROM (VALUES ('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-media/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/tiny.mp4'), ('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-media/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/silent.wav')) AS f(file) ORDER BY file_name

example_queries.description: One-row file card: container format and duration, the stream layout aggregated from media_streams (e.g. 'video:h264'), and the MP4 major_brand container tag from media_tags.
example_queries.sql: SELECT media.main.media_format('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-media/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/tiny.mp4') AS format, round(media.main.duration('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-media/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/tiny.mp4'), 2) AS seconds, (SELECT string_agg(s.type || ':' || s.codec, ', ' ORDER BY s.idx) FROM media.main.media_streams('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-media/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/tiny.mp4') AS s) AS stream_layout, (SELECT t.value FROM media.main.media_tags('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-media/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/tiny.mp4') AS t WHERE t.key = 'major_brand') AS major_brand

example_queries.description: Compare every stream's duration with the container's duration and show the drift in seconds (media_streams + duration); a non-zero drift flags a track that ends early or late, as in a truncated or badly remuxed file.
example_queries.sql: SELECT s.idx, s.type, s.codec, s.duration AS stream_seconds, media.main.duration('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-media/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/tiny.mp4') AS container_seconds, round(abs(s.duration - media.main.duration('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-media/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/tiny.mp4')), 3) AS drift_seconds FROM media.main.media_streams('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-media/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/tiny.mp4') AS s ORDER BY s.idx

example_queries.description: List every video-category function and its return type, alphabetically.

example_queries.description: Count how many functions fall into each navigation category.
example_queries.sql: SELECT category, count(*) AS n FROM media.main.media_functions GROUP BY category ORDER BY category

example_queries.description: List the container-level metadata tags (title, artist, encoder, ...) of a WAV file as key/value rows, ordered by tag name.

## Media metadata functions

Read technical metadata from video, audio, and container files over Apache Arrow, backed by ffprobe. Every function accepts either a media file path (`VARCHAR`) or the raw media bytes (`BLOB`), and missing or unparseable fields return NULL rather than erroring.

The surface is organised into a few groups:

- **Container** — one value per file: format, duration, bit rate, size, and stream count.
- **Video** — the first video track's codec, width, height, resolution, and frame rate.
- **Audio** — the first audio track's codec.
- **Enumeration** — table functions that return one row per elementary stream and one row per format-level metadata tag.

Use this schema for media inventory, transcoding triage, and quality or conformance checks in SQL.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Media function registry

A browsable, argument-free view that catalogues every media metadata function in this worker. Because every other object is a function that needs a media path or `BLOB` before it returns anything, this view is the entry point for discovery: read it to see the full surface and each function's return type, then call the function you need.

Columns:

- `name` — function name as called in SQL.
- `kind` — `scalar` or `table`.
- `category` — `container`, `video`, `audio`, or `enumeration`.
- `result_type` — the SQL type a scalar returns, or `TABLE` for a table function.
- `description` — a one-line summary.

For example, list only the video functions and their return types, or count how many functions fall into each category.

vgi.example_queries.description: List every video-category function and its return type, alphabetically.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, result_type FROM media.main.media_functions WHERE category = 'video' ORDER BY name

vgi.example_queries.description: Count how many functions fall into each navigation category.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT category, count(*) AS n FROM media.main.media_functions GROUP BY category ORDER BY category

workers.doc_md:
# Metabase

Query a Metabase site from DuckDB: collections, dashboards and their cards and tabs, saved questions, models and metrics with their SQL or MBQL, MBQL lineage to tables, databases, tables, fields, segments, users, groups, data permissions, subscriptions, alerts, revision history and usage. Read-only.

Create a `metabase` secret with your site URL (`BASE_URL`) and an `API_KEY` (or `USERNAME` and `PASSWORD`). Per-day usage and the query log come from Usage Analytics on Pro/Enterprise; OSS reports lifetime view counters. Connection passwords and recipients' addresses are never returned.

### Sources and references

- [Metabase API reference](https://www.metabase.com/docs/latest/api) — the endpoints this worker reads
- [API keys](https://www.metabase.com/docs/latest/people-and-groups/api-keys) — x-api-key authentication
- [Usage analytics](https://www.metabase.com/docs/latest/usage-and-performance-tools/usage-analytics) — the View log and Query log models behind content_usage and query_history (Pro/Enterprise)
- [Data permissions](https://www.metabase.com/docs/latest/permissions/data) — the levels in group_permissions
workers.readme_sql:
CREATE SECRET metabase (TYPE metabase,
    BASE_URL 'https://bi.acme.com',
    API_KEY 'mb_…');

-- Dashboards nobody opened in 90 days, with their collection.
SELECT title, folder_path, owner, last_viewed_at
FROM metabase.main.dashboards
WHERE NOT archived AND last_viewed_at < now() - INTERVAL 90 DAY
ORDER BY last_viewed_at;

-- Which warehouse tables feed which dashboards (MBQL questions).
SELECT DISTINCT d.dashboard_title, t.table_schema, t.table_name
FROM metabase.main.dashboard_cards d
JOIN metabase.main.card_tables t ON t.card_id = d.card_id
ORDER BY ALL;

-- Native SQL questions that mention a table you are about to drop.
SELECT id, title, native_sql FROM metabase.main.queries
WHERE query_type = 'native' AND native_sql ILIKE '%legacy_orders%';

-- Run a saved question with a filter value; columns come back typed.
SELECT * FROM metabase.main.run_card('41', parameters := '{"category": "Gizmo"}');

example_queries.title: dashboards_columns
example_queries.description: The dashboards columns (binds only; create a metabase secret and drop LIMIT 0 for rows)
example_queries.sql: SELECT tool, id, title, folder_path, owner, view_count, url FROM metabase.main.dashboards LIMIT 0;

example_queries.title: charts_columns
example_queries.description: The charts columns (binds only; create a metabase secret and drop LIMIT 0 for rows)
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, title, card_type, query_type, folder_path FROM metabase.main.charts LIMIT 0;

example_queries.description: Profile the columns of card 40
example_queries.sql: SUMMARIZE SELECT * FROM metabase.main.run_card('40')

example_queries.description: Run a native SQL question with a variable and profile the result
example_queries.sql: SUMMARIZE SELECT * FROM metabase.main.run_card('41', parameters := '{"category": "Gizmo"}')

example_queries.description: The collection tree, deepest paths last
example_queries.sql: SELECT folder_path, title, is_personal FROM metabase.main.folders WHERE NOT archived ORDER BY length(folder_path), folder_path

example_queries.description: Content per collection
example_queries.sql: SELECT f.folder_path, count(c.id) AS charts FROM metabase.main.folders f LEFT JOIN metabase.main.charts c ON c.folder_id = f.id GROUP BY f.folder_path ORDER BY charts DESC

example_queries.description: Most-viewed dashboards with their collection path
example_queries.sql: SELECT title, folder_path, owner, view_count FROM metabase.main.dashboards WHERE NOT archived ORDER BY view_count DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Dashboards nobody has opened in 90 days
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, title, owner, last_viewed_at FROM metabase.main.dashboards WHERE last_viewed_at < now() - INTERVAL 90 DAY ORDER BY last_viewed_at

example_queries.description: Cards per dashboard tab
example_queries.sql: SELECT dashboard_title, tab_name, count(*) AS cards, count(card_id) AS questions FROM metabase.main.dashboard_cards GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY dashboard_title, tab_name

example_queries.description: Which dashboard filters drive which card
example_queries.sql: SELECT d.card_title, m.parameter_id, m.target FROM metabase.main.dashboard_cards d, unnest(d.parameter_mappings) AS t(m) WHERE d.dashboard_id = '2' ORDER BY d.card_title

example_queries.description: Dashboards with the most tabs
example_queries.sql: SELECT dashboard_title, count(*) AS tabs, sum(card_count) AS cards FROM metabase.main.dashboard_tabs GROUP BY dashboard_title ORDER BY tabs DESC

example_queries.description: Cards by type and query kind
example_queries.sql: SELECT card_type, query_type, count(*) AS cards FROM metabase.main.charts WHERE NOT archived GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY cards DESC

example_queries.description: Most-viewed models
example_queries.sql: SELECT title, folder_path, view_count FROM metabase.main.charts WHERE card_type = 'model' ORDER BY view_count DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Native SQL questions that select from ORDERS
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, title, native_sql FROM metabase.main.queries WHERE query_type = 'native' AND native_sql ILIKE '%orders%' ORDER BY id

example_queries.description: My recently viewed dashboards
example_queries.sql: SELECT title, viewed_at FROM metabase.main.recent_views WHERE model = 'dashboard' ORDER BY viewed_at DESC

example_queries.description: Slowest questions over the last 7 days
example_queries.sql: SELECT card_id, count(*) AS runs, avg(runtime_seconds) AS avg_s, max(runtime_seconds) AS max_s FROM metabase.main.query_history WHERE card_id IS NOT NULL AND NOT cache_hit GROUP BY card_id ORDER BY avg_s DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Errors by source in a fixed window
example_queries.sql: SELECT source, count(*) AS errors FROM metabase.main.query_history WHERE status = 'error' AND created_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01' AND created_at < TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-08' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY errors DESC

example_queries.description: Active alerts and who receives them
example_queries.sql: SELECT card_title, send_condition, cron_schedules, recipient_count, recipient_domains FROM metabase.main.alerts WHERE active ORDER BY card_title

example_queries.description: Subscriptions that send outside the company domain
example_queries.sql: SELECT title, recipient_domains FROM metabase.main.subscriptions WHERE NOT archived AND len(list_filter(recipient_domains, lambda d: d <> 'example.com')) > 0 ORDER BY title

example_queries.description: Groups that can write native SQL, per database
example_queries.sql: SELECT group_name, database_name FROM metabase.main.group_permissions WHERE create_queries = 'query-builder-and-native' ORDER BY ALL

example_queries.description: Most-edited dashboards
example_queries.sql: SELECT entity_id, count(*) AS edits, max(changed_at) AS last_edit FROM metabase.main.revisions WHERE entity_type = 'dashboard' GROUP BY entity_id ORDER BY edits DESC

example_queries.description: History of one question
example_queries.sql: SELECT changed_at, user_name, description FROM metabase.main.revisions WHERE entity_type = 'card' AND entity_id = '41' ORDER BY changed_at

example_queries.description: Groups by size
example_queries.sql: SELECT title, member_count FROM metabase.main.groups ORDER BY member_count DESC

example_queries.description: Segments per table
example_queries.sql: SELECT s.title, s.definition_description, t.table_name FROM metabase.main.segments s JOIN metabase.main.tables t ON t.id = s.table_id ORDER BY s.title

example_queries.description: Largest tables by estimated rows
example_queries.sql: SELECT database_name, table_schema, table_name, estimated_row_count FROM metabase.main.tables WHERE active ORDER BY estimated_row_count DESC NULLS LAST LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Which warehouse tables feed each dashboard
example_queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT d.dashboard_title, t.table_schema, t.table_name FROM metabase.main.dashboard_cards d JOIN metabase.main.card_tables t ON t.card_id = d.card_id ORDER BY ALL

example_queries.description: Most-used tables across MBQL questions
example_queries.sql: SELECT table_name, count(DISTINCT card_id) AS cards FROM metabase.main.card_tables WHERE table_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY table_name ORDER BY cards DESC

example_queries.description: Admins and when they last logged in
example_queries.sql: SELECT display_name, email, last_login FROM metabase.main.users WHERE is_superuser AND is_active ORDER BY last_login DESC NULLS LAST

example_queries.description: Users who never logged in
example_queries.sql: SELECT email, created_at FROM metabase.main.users WHERE is_active AND last_login IS NULL ORDER BY created_at

example_queries.description: Foreign keys between tables
example_queries.sql: SELECT table_name, name, fk_target_field_name FROM metabase.main.fields WHERE semantic_type = 'type/FK' ORDER BY table_name, name

example_queries.description: Columns per semantic type in one database
example_queries.sql: SELECT semantic_type, count(*) AS fields FROM metabase.main.fields WHERE database_id = '1' GROUP BY semantic_type ORDER BY fields DESC

example_queries.description: Connections by engine
example_queries.sql: SELECT engine, count(*) AS databases, list(title ORDER BY title) AS names FROM metabase.main.connections GROUP BY engine ORDER BY databases DESC

example_queries.description: Most-viewed dashboards (per-day rows on Pro/Enterprise are summed)
example_queries.sql: SELECT content_id, title, sum(view_count) AS views FROM metabase.main.content_usage WHERE content_type = 'dashboard' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY views DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Daily views for one week (Usage Analytics only)
example_queries.sql: SELECT view_date, sum(view_count) AS views, max(user_count) AS peak_viewers FROM metabase.main.content_usage WHERE view_date >= DATE '2026-11-01' AND view_date < DATE '2026-11-08' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY view_date

example_queries.description: Which usage source content_usage will use
example_queries.sql: SELECT version, edition, usage_analytics FROM metabase.main.instance

example_queries.description: Questions built on another card (model reuse)
example_queries.sql: SELECT q.title, src AS source_card_id FROM metabase.main.queries q, unnest(q.source_card_ids) AS t(src) ORDER BY q.title

Tables that expand per dashboard, per database or per object make one API call per parent, so filter dashboard_id, database_id or entity_id when you can. tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per query execution from the Usage Analytics 'Query log' model (Pro / Enterprise with the audit_app feature; read with a read-only POST /api/dataset). OSS keeps no query log reachable through the API, so this table raises an error there (check metabase.main.instance.usage_analytics). Columns: tool, execution_id, created_at (start, UTC), runtime_seconds, result_rows, status ('complete' or 'error'), message (error text), source (dashboard, question, ad-hoc, pulse, csv-download …), is_native, cache_hit, card_id, dashboard_id, database_id, user_id, url. The window comes from WHERE created_at bounds (default: the last 7 days), read newest-first in pages of 2,000 rows.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Query executions with runtimes, for performance and adoption analysis (Pro/Enterprise Usage Analytics). Filter `created_at` to choose the window (default last 7 days).

**Pushdown:** `created_at` bounds become MBQL filters on the Query log `started_at` (default last 7 days); `card_id`, `dashboard_id`, `user_id`, `database_id` and `source` (`=` / `IN`) become MBQL filters.

vgi.example_queries.description: Slowest questions over the last 7 days
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT card_id, count(*) AS runs, avg(runtime_seconds) AS avg_s, max(runtime_seconds) AS max_s FROM metabase.main.query_history WHERE card_id IS NOT NULL AND NOT cache_hit GROUP BY card_id ORDER BY avg_s DESC LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: Errors by source in a fixed window
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT source, count(*) AS errors FROM metabase.main.query_history WHERE status = 'error' AND created_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01' AND created_at < TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-08' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY errors DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Most-used tables across MBQL questions

tables.name: content_usage
tables.comment: Views per dashboard and card: per day from Usage Analytics (Pro/Enterprise), else Metabase's lifetime counters (OSS).

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Usage of dashboards and cards. On Pro / Enterprise with Usage Analytics (instance.usage_analytics = true) it aggregates the 'View log' model: one row per (content_type, content_id, view_date) with view_count, user_count (distinct viewers) and last_viewed_at, usage_source 'usage_analytics'; the window comes from WHERE view_date bounds (default: the last 30 days, UTC days). On OSS (or without the feature) it returns one row per live dashboard and card with Metabase's lifetime view_count and last_viewed_at (cards: last_used_at), view_date and user_count NULL, usage_source 'lifetime_counters' — so a view_date filter returns no OSS rows. Columns: tool, content_type ('dashboard' or 'card' — other View log types such as 'table' and 'collection' pass through), content_id, title, view_date, view_count, user_count, last_viewed_at, usage_source, url.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Views per dashboard and question. Per day on Pro/Enterprise (Usage Analytics), lifetime counters on OSS. See `metabase.main.instance` for which applies.

**Pushdown:** Usage Analytics: `view_date` bounds become an MBQL filter on the View log timestamp (default last 30 days); `content_type` and `content_id` (`=` / `IN`) become MBQL filters; Metabase groups by day. OSS: `content_type` picks the dashboard and/or card listing.

vgi.example_queries.description: Most-viewed dashboards (per-day rows on Pro/Enterprise are summed)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT content_id, title, sum(view_count) AS views FROM metabase.main.content_usage WHERE content_type = 'dashboard' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY views DESC LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: Daily views for one week (Usage Analytics only)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT view_date, sum(view_count) AS views, max(user_count) AS peak_viewers FROM metabase.main.content_usage WHERE view_date >= DATE '2026-11-01' AND view_date < DATE '2026-11-08' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY view_date

workers.title: NTFS $MFT Forensic Timeline
workers.tagline: Forensic NTFS \$MFT timelines in DuckDB with SQL — file records, MACB timestamps, ADS, deleted entries and timestomp detection. A VGI worker.
workers.subtitle: Turn a collected NTFS $MFT into a SQL forensic timeline with full paths, timestomp flags, deleted records, and data streams.
workers.summary: Parse the NTFS $MFT into a forensic filesystem timeline: path reconstruction, the SI/FN MACB timestamp pair, timestomp detection, deleted-record recovery, and alternate data streams — straight into SQL.
workers.doc_md:
# mft — NTFS $MFT Forensic Timeline in SQL

Parse a collected NTFS **`$MFT`** (Master File Table) into a full forensic filesystem timeline — one row per FILE record — without a per-host CLI run and with **zero egress**. Built for DFIR / incident-response / threat-hunt teams who want to timeline thousands of collected `$MFT`s and join the result to known-bad paths, hashes, and rules in one query.

**Key concepts.** The `$MFT` is NTFS's index of every file and directory. Each FILE record carries the metadata this worker turns into columns: the full path reconstructed by walking parent references, logical and physical sizes, allocated / deleted and file / directory flags, alternate data streams, and inline resident content. Deleted-but-resident records are recovered by default.

**The timestomp engine.** `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` is user-writable (the Win32 `SetFileTime` API and anti-forensic tools rewrite it) while `$FILE_NAME` is kernel-only, so a standard-information timestamp that predates its file-name counterpart — naturally impossible — and whole-second values are strong anti-forensic tells. Both MACB timestamp quads are first-class columns.

Built on the permissively-licensed `mft` crate (omerbenamram); the NTFS on-disk layout is documented openly by Microsoft and the forensics community.

## Sources and references

- [Master File Table (Microsoft Learn)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/master-file-table)
- [libyal NTFS format documentation](https://github.com/libyal/libfsntfs/blob/main/documentation/New%20Technologies%20File%20System%20%28NTFS%29.asciidoc) — FILE records, attributes and timestamps
- [omerbenamram/mft](https://github.com/omerbenamram/mft) — the Rust `$MFT` parser this worker builds on ([docs.rs](https://docs.rs/mft))

example_queries.description: The headline forensic timeline: one row per FILE record with its reconstructed path and deleted flag.
example_queries.sql:
SET VARIABLE mft_sample = (SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft'));
SELECT entry, full_path, is_deleted FROM mft.main.read_mft(getvariable('mft_sample'))

example_queries.description: Hunt for timestomped records — the SI-vs-FN heuristic exposed as a plain WHERE clause.
example_queries.sql:
SET VARIABLE mft_sample = (SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft'));
SELECT full_path FROM mft.main.read_mft(getvariable('mft_sample')) WHERE is_timestomp_suspect

example_queries.description: Surface every alternate data stream (a classic malware hiding spot) via streams mode.
example_queries.sql:
SET VARIABLE mft_sample = (SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft'));
SELECT full_path, ads_name FROM mft.main.read_mft(getvariable('mft_sample'), mode := 'streams') WHERE ads_name IS NOT NULL

example_queries.description: Profile the attribute makeup of a whole $MFT: feed every record entry from the read_mft timeline into attributes(), label each attribute type with its purpose from the ntfs_attribute_types reference view, and count the records and attribute instances per type.
example_queries.sql:
SET VARIABLE mft_sample = (SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft'));
SELECT a.type_id, t.type_name, t.purpose, count(DISTINCT a.entry) AS records, count(*) AS instances FROM mft.main.attributes((FROM (SELECT getvariable('mft_sample') AS blob, entry FROM mft.main.read_mft(getvariable('mft_sample'))))) AS a JOIN mft.main.ntfs_attribute_types AS t ON t.type_id = a.type_id GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY a.type_id

example_queries.description: Explain each timestomp suspect in the read_mft timeline: re-score its $STANDARD_INFORMATION and $FILE_NAME MACB columns with timestomp() to list which heuristic reasons fired (the timeline itself only carries the is_timestomp_suspect flag).
example_queries.sql:
SET VARIABLE mft_sample = (SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft'));
SELECT full_path, si_created, fn_created, mft.main.timestomp({'created': si_created, 'modified': si_modified, 'accessed': si_accessed, 'mft_modified': si_mft_modified}, {'created': fn_created, 'modified': fn_modified, 'accessed': fn_accessed, 'mft_modified': fn_mft_modified}).reasons AS reasons FROM mft.main.read_mft(getvariable('mft_sample')) WHERE is_timestomp_suspect ORDER BY full_path

example_queries.description: Pair each path in the read_mft timeline with its DOS 8.3 short name, unnesting the full $FILE_NAME list that mft_record() decodes for the entry (the timeline keeps only the primary Win32 name).
example_queries.sql:
SET VARIABLE mft_sample = (SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft'));
SELECT t.full_path, f.name AS short_name FROM mft.main.read_mft(getvariable('mft_sample')) AS t, unnest(mft.main.mft_record(getvariable('mft_sample'), t.entry).fn) AS u(f) WHERE f.namespace = 'DOS' ORDER BY t.full_path

example_queries.description: Browse the whole NTFS attribute-type registry, lowest code first.
example_queries.sql: SELECT type_id, type_name, purpose FROM mft.main.ntfs_attribute_types ORDER BY type_id

example_queries.description: Look up the name and purpose of attribute type 128 (the $DATA attribute).
example_queries.sql: SELECT type_name, purpose FROM mft.main.ntfs_attribute_types WHERE type_id = 128

example_queries.description: List the $DATA streams (primary + each ADS) of one sample $MFT record.
example_queries.sql: SELECT entry, name, logical_size, resident FROM mft.main.streams((FROM (SELECT content AS blob, 22::UBIGINT AS entry FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft'))))

example_queries.description: List the $DATA streams of one sample $MFT record, surfacing the hidden ADS by name.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, logical_size, resident FROM mft.main.streams((FROM (SELECT content AS blob, 22::UBIGINT AS entry FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft')))) ORDER BY name NULLS FIRST;

example_queries.description: The headline timeline: one row per FILE record with its reconstructed path and deleted flag.
example_queries.sql:
SET VARIABLE mft_sample = (SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft'));
SELECT entry, full_path, is_deleted FROM mft.main.read_mft(getvariable('mft_sample')) ORDER BY entry;

example_queries.description: Hunt the sample $MFT for timestomped records — the SI-vs-FN mismatch is a plain WHERE clause.
example_queries.sql:
SET VARIABLE mft_sample = (SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft'));
SELECT full_path FROM mft.main.read_mft(getvariable('mft_sample')) WHERE is_timestomp_suspect ORDER BY full_path;

example_queries.description: Surface every alternate data stream by switching to streams mode.
example_queries.sql:
SET VARIABLE mft_sample = (SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft'));
SELECT full_path, ads_name FROM mft.main.read_mft(getvariable('mft_sample'), mode := 'streams') WHERE ads_name IS NOT NULL ORDER BY full_path;

example_queries.description: List every attribute (type, residency, ADS name, size) of one sample $MFT record.
example_queries.sql: SELECT entry, type_name, resident, name, logical_size FROM mft.main.attributes((FROM (SELECT content AS blob, 22::UBIGINT AS entry FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft'))))

example_queries.description: List every attribute (type, residency, ADS name, size) of one sample $MFT record.
example_queries.sql: SELECT type_name, resident, name, logical_size FROM mft.main.attributes((FROM (SELECT content AS blob, 22::UBIGINT AS entry FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft')))) ORDER BY attribute_id;

example_queries.description: Flag a record whose $STANDARD_INFORMATION quad predates its $FILE_NAME quad — the naturally-impossible ordering timestomping produces.
example_queries.sql: SELECT mft.main.timestomp({'created': TIMESTAMP '2009-01-01', 'modified': TIMESTAMP '2009-01-01', 'accessed': TIMESTAMP '2009-01-01', 'mft_modified': TIMESTAMP '2009-01-01'}, {'created': TIMESTAMP '2020-01-01', 'modified': TIMESTAMP '2020-01-01', 'accessed': TIMESTAMP '2020-01-01', 'mft_modified': TIMESTAMP '2020-01-01'}).suspect AS suspect

example_queries.description: Probe just the FILE-record header of one sample record (entry 12): signature, directory flag, and sequence number.
example_queries.sql: SELECT h.signature, h.is_dir, h.sequence FROM (SELECT mft.main.record_header((SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft')), 12) AS h)

example_queries.description: Fully decode one sample $MFT record, exposing its primary name and how many alternate data streams it carries.
example_queries.sql: SELECT r.fn[1].name AS primary_name, len(r.ads) AS ads_count FROM (SELECT mft.main.mft_record((SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft')), 22) AS r)

example_queries.description: Reconstruct the full filesystem path of one record (entry 20) in the sample $MFT.
example_queries.sql: SELECT mft.main.full_path((SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft')), 20) AS full_path

example_queries.description: Validate one sample record (entry 20) — a clean record reports ok = true with kind 'ok'.
example_queries.sql: SELECT w.ok, w.kind FROM (SELECT mft.main.well_formed((SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft')), 20) AS w)

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## The `mft` worker

Turns a collected NTFS `$MFT` into a forensic filesystem timeline you can query with SQL. Point it at a captured `$MFT` — a path, a glob across many hosts, or an in-memory `BLOB` — and it reconstructs what the filesystem looked like, and what was tampered with. Qualify calls as `mft.main.<fn>(...)`.

**Key concepts**

- *Path reconstruction* — parent-reference walking rebuilds absolute paths, flagging orphans and reference cycles.
- *MACB timelines* — the `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` and `$FILE_NAME` timestamp quads surfaced side by side.
- *Timestomp heuristic* — the user-writable-SI vs kernel-only-FN comparison that flags manipulated timestamps.
- *Recovery & robustness* — deleted-record recovery and never-panic decode over hostile or truncated input, plus attribute and `$DATA` / alternate-data-stream fan-out.

**When to use it** — DFIR triage, threat hunting, and incident response over Windows hosts.

tables.name: ntfs_attribute_types
tables.comment: Reference registry mapping each NTFS attribute type code to its canonical name and purpose — the vocabulary behind the `type_id` / `type_name` columns of the attributes() function. A static, credential-free lookup you can browse or join.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A browsable reference table (no arguments, no $MFT needed) listing the fifteen standard NTFS attribute type codes with their canonical `$`-prefixed name and a one-line purpose. Columns: `type_id` (`UINTEGER`, e.g. 128), `type_name` (`VARCHAR`, e.g. `$DATA`), `purpose` (`VARCHAR`). It is the vocabulary behind the `type_id` and `type_name` columns of the attributes() function — join or filter it to explain a record's attributes without parsing bytes. Type codes are the on-disk NTFS values (16 = 0x10 = $STANDARD_INFORMATION, 48 = 0x30 = $FILE_NAME, 128 = 0x80 = $DATA).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# `ntfs_attribute_types`

A static, browsable reference of the fifteen standard NTFS attribute type codes — the vocabulary behind the `type_id` / `type_name` columns of the `attributes()` function. No arguments, no `$MFT`, no network.

## Columns

- `type_id` (`UINTEGER`) -- the on-disk NTFS attribute type code, e.g. `128` (`0x80`).
- `type_name` (`VARCHAR`) -- the canonical `$`-prefixed name, e.g. `$DATA`.
- `purpose` (`VARCHAR`) -- a one-line description of what the attribute stores.

Join it to the `attributes()` output on `type_id` to label each attribute, or browse it on its own.

vgi.example_queries.description: Browse the whole NTFS attribute-type registry, lowest code first.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT type_id, type_name, purpose FROM mft.main.ntfs_attribute_types ORDER BY type_id

vgi.example_queries.description: Look up the name and purpose of attribute type 128 (the $DATA attribute).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT type_name, purpose FROM mft.main.ntfs_attribute_types WHERE type_id = 128

functions.name: read_mft
functions.comment: Parse a collected NTFS $MFT into a forensic filesystem timeline

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Parse a collected NTFS $MFT (Master File Table) into a full forensic filesystem timeline — one row per FILE record, with the path reconstructed from parent references, both the $STANDARD_INFORMATION and $FILE_NAME MACB timestamp quads (so the SI-vs-FN timestomp mismatch is a plain WHERE clause), logical/physical sizes, allocated/deleted and file/dir flags, alternate data streams, and resident file content. The first argument is a `VARCHAR` path or glob ('/cases/*/$MFT', 's3://…') or a `BLOB` of $MFT bytes. `host :=` scopes a collection (defaults to the source filename); `mode :=` is 'files' (one row per record, the default), 'streams' (one row per $DATA stream — primary + each ADS), or 'allocated' (live files only). Deleted but still-resident records are included by default — filter with WHERE is_allocated for live files only.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Parse a collected NTFS `$MFT` into a forensic timeline: one row per FILE record with reconstructed `full_path`, the SI + FN MACB quads, sizes, deleted/dir flags, ADS, and resident data. `read_mft(path_or_blob, host := …, mode := 'files'|'streams'|'allocated')`.

functions.comment: Score the SI-vs-FN timestomp heuristic over two MACB quads

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Score the anti-forensic SI-vs-FN timestamp heuristic over a $STANDARD_INFORMATION MACB quad `si` and a $FILE_NAME MACB quad `fn` (each a `STRUCT(created, modified, accessed, mft_modified)` of `TIMESTAMP`). Returns `STRUCT(suspect BOOLEAN, reasons LIST<VARCHAR>)`; reasons ⊆ {si-before-fn, si-creation-before-fn-creation, zero-subsecond, fn-newer-than-si, all-four-equal}. SI is user-writable (tools like timestomp edit it) while FN is kernel-only, so SI earlier than FN — naturally impossible — and whole-second SI values are strong tells. Composable over the read_mft si_* / fn_* columns.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Score the SI-vs-FN timestomp heuristic: `timestomp(si, fn)` → `STRUCT(suspect, reasons)`. reasons ⊆ {si-before-fn, si-creation-before-fn-creation, zero-subsecond, fn-newer-than-si, all-four-equal}.

vgi.example_queries.description: Flag a record whose $STANDARD_INFORMATION quad predates its $FILE_NAME quad — the naturally-impossible ordering timestomping produces.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT mft.main.timestomp({'created': TIMESTAMP '2009-01-01', 'modified': TIMESTAMP '2009-01-01', 'accessed': TIMESTAMP '2009-01-01', 'mft_modified': TIMESTAMP '2009-01-01'}, {'created': TIMESTAMP '2020-01-01', 'modified': TIMESTAMP '2020-01-01', 'accessed': TIMESTAMP '2020-01-01', 'mft_modified': TIMESTAMP '2020-01-01'}).suspect AS suspect

vgi.example_queries.description: Explain each timestomp suspect in the read_mft timeline: re-score its $STANDARD_INFORMATION and $FILE_NAME MACB columns with timestomp() to list which heuristic reasons fired (the timeline itself only carries the is_timestomp_suspect flag).

SET VARIABLE mft_sample = (SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-mft/v0.2.0/data/sample.mft'));
SELECT full_path, si_created, fn_created, mft.main.timestomp({'created': si_created, 'modified': si_modified, 'accessed': si_accessed, 'mft_modified': si_mft_modified}, {'created': fn_created, 'modified': fn_modified, 'accessed': fn_accessed, 'mft_modified': fn_mft_modified}).reasons AS reasons FROM mft.main.read_mft(getvariable('mft_sample')) WHERE is_timestomp_suspect ORDER BY full_path

workers.doc_md:
# Mixpanel

Query a Mixpanel project from DuckDB: raw events, segmentation, funnels and retention reports, user profiles, cohorts, the Lexicon data dictionary and annotations. Read-only.

Create a `mixpanel` secret with a service account (`USERNAME`, `SECRET`), the numeric `PROJECT_ID` and the data residency `REGION` (`us`, `eu` or `in`). Filters on event time, event name and common properties are sent to Mixpanel, so only matching events cross the network.

The `unified` schema shares its column names with the Amplitude and PostHog workers.

### Sources and references

- [Raw Event Export API](https://docs.mixpanel.com/reference/raw-event-export)
- [Query API](https://docs.mixpanel.com/reference/query-api): segmentation, funnels, retention, engage, cohorts
- [Segmentation expressions](https://docs.mixpanel.com/reference/segmentation-expressions) (the `where` syntax)
- [Lexicon Schemas API](https://docs.mixpanel.com/reference/lexicon-schemas-api) and [Annotations](https://docs.mixpanel.com/reference/annotations)
- [Service accounts](https://docs.mixpanel.com/docs/orgs-and-projects/service-accounts) and [rate limits](https://docs.mixpanel.com/reference/rate-limits)
workers.readme_sql:
CREATE SECRET mixpanel (TYPE mixpanel, USERNAME 'svc.reporting', SECRET '…', PROJECT_ID '123456', REGION 'eu');

-- Sign-ups per OS over three days: dates, event name and $os are all filtered by Mixpanel.
SELECT os, count(*) AS signups
FROM mixpanel.main.events()
WHERE event_name = 'Sign Up' AND os IN ('iOS', 'Android')
  AND event_time >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01' AND event_time < TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-04'
GROUP BY os;

-- Day-1 retention of each day's sign-ups.
SELECT cohort_date, retention_rate
FROM mixpanel.main.retention('2026-11-01', '2026-11-07', born_event := 'Sign Up')
WHERE period = 1 ORDER BY cohort_date;

-- The same query across tools.
SELECT tool, event_name, count(*) FROM mixpanel.unified.events
WHERE event_time >= now() - INTERVAL 1 DAY GROUP BY ALL
UNION ALL
SELECT tool, event_name, count(*) FROM amplitude.unified.events
WHERE event_time >= now() - INTERVAL 1 DAY GROUP BY ALL;

example_queries.description: The events() result columns (binds only; attach a mixpanel secret and drop LIMIT 0 for rows)
example_queries.sql: SELECT event_name, event_time, distinct_id, os, properties FROM mixpanel.main.events() LIMIT 0;

example_queries.title: segmentation_columns
example_queries.description: The segmentation() result columns (binds only; attach a mixpanel secret and drop LIMIT 0 for rows)
example_queries.sql: SELECT event, segment, period_start, value FROM mixpanel.main.segmentation('Sign Up', '2026-11-01', '2026-11-03') LIMIT 0;

example_queries.description: Sign-ups per operating system over three days (event name and dates are sent to Mixpanel)
example_queries.sql: SELECT os, count(*) AS signups FROM mixpanel.main.events() WHERE event_name = 'Sign Up' AND event_time >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01' AND event_time < TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-04' GROUP BY os ORDER BY signups DESC

example_queries.description: Revenue per user from Purchase events
example_queries.sql: SELECT distinct_id, count(*) AS purchases, sum((properties->>'revenue')::DOUBLE) AS revenue FROM mixpanel.main.events(from_date := '2026-11-01', to_date := '2026-11-03') WHERE event_name = 'Purchase' GROUP BY distinct_id ORDER BY revenue DESC

example_queries.description: Daily sign-ups over three days
example_queries.sql: SELECT period_start::DATE AS day, value AS signups FROM mixpanel.main.segmentation('Sign Up', '2026-11-01', '2026-11-03') ORDER BY day

example_queries.description: Sign-ups per operating system
example_queries.sql: SELECT segment AS os, sum(value) AS signups FROM mixpanel.main.segmentation('Sign Up', '2026-11-01', '2026-11-03', segment_by := 'properties["$os"]') GROUP BY os ORDER BY signups DESC

example_queries.description: Weekly conversion of each step of funnel 7509
example_queries.sql: SELECT step, event, count, round(overall_conv_ratio, 3) AS conversion FROM mixpanel.main.funnel(7509, '2026-11-02', '2026-11-08', unit := 'week') ORDER BY step

example_queries.description: Day-1 retention of each day's sign-ups
example_queries.sql: SELECT cohort_date, round(retention_rate, 3) AS day1 FROM mixpanel.main.retention('2026-11-01', '2026-11-03', born_event := 'Sign Up') WHERE period = 1 ORDER BY cohort_date

example_queries.description: Five most common events today
example_queries.sql: SELECT event, amount FROM mixpanel.main.top_events() ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Ten most common event names
example_queries.sql: SELECT event_name FROM mixpanel.main.event_names() ORDER BY rank LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Properties of Purchase events by frequency
example_queries.sql: SELECT property_name, count FROM mixpanel.main.top_event_properties('Purchase') ORDER BY count DESC

example_queries.description: Plans seen on Purchase events
example_queries.sql: SELECT value AS plan FROM mixpanel.main.event_property_values('Purchase', 'plan') ORDER BY rank

example_queries.description: Users on the pro plan (filtered by Mixpanel)
example_queries.sql: SELECT email, created_at FROM mixpanel.main.profiles(where_expr := 'properties["plan"] == "pro"') ORDER BY created_at

example_queries.description: Users per country
example_queries.sql: SELECT country_code, count(*) AS users FROM mixpanel.main.profiles() GROUP BY country_code ORDER BY users DESC

example_queries.description: Annotations since November 1 (the date bound is sent to Mixpanel)
example_queries.sql: SELECT annotation_time, description FROM mixpanel.main.annotations WHERE annotation_time >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01' ORDER BY annotation_time

example_queries.description: Hidden events in the Lexicon
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, description FROM mixpanel.main.schemas WHERE entity_type = 'event' AND is_hidden ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Properties defined for the Purchase event
example_queries.sql: SELECT property_name, data_type FROM mixpanel.main.schema_properties WHERE entity_type = 'event' AND entity_name = 'Purchase' ORDER BY property_name

example_queries.description: Cohorts by size
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, count FROM mixpanel.main.cohorts ORDER BY count DESC

example_queries.description: Saved funnels
example_queries.sql: SELECT funnel_id, name FROM mixpanel.main.funnels ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Active users per platform over three days
example_queries.sql: SELECT platform, count(DISTINCT distinct_id) AS users FROM mixpanel.unified.events WHERE event_time >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01' AND event_time < TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-04' GROUP BY platform ORDER BY users DESC

example_queries.description: Users per country
example_queries.sql: SELECT country, count(*) AS users FROM mixpanel.unified.users GROUP BY country ORDER BY users DESC

example_queries.description: Cohorts by size
example_queries.sql: SELECT tool, name, size FROM mixpanel.unified.cohorts ORDER BY size DESC

example_queries.description: Visible events of the tracking plan
example_queries.sql: SELECT event_name, description FROM mixpanel.unified.event_definitions WHERE NOT is_hidden ORDER BY event_name

example_queries.description: Properties per scope
example_queries.sql: SELECT scope, count(*) AS properties FROM mixpanel.unified.property_definitions GROUP BY scope ORDER BY scope

Choose the days with WHERE event_time >= / < ... (pushed down) or from_date := / to_date := ('YYYY-MM-DD'); with neither it reads the last lookback_days (7).
