workers.title: Global News Search
workers.tagline: Global news via GDELT (free) + NewsAPI for DuckDB (Python)
workers.subtitle: Search worldwide news articles from SQL via GDELT (free) or NewsAPI (with a key).
workers.summary: Global news search (GDELT by default; NewsAPI with a key) for SQL.
workers.doc_md:
# news

Global news search as a DuckDB/SQL VGI worker.

Query worldwide news coverage by free text and get one unified article schema (`title, url, domain, language, seendate, country, tone, source, extra`) regardless of provider, with a look-back window, optional country/language filters, and row-count paging.

**Providers**: `gdelt` (default, free, no key, worldwide) and `newsapi` (requires a `TYPE newsapi` secret with an `api_key`). The provider list and each provider's key requirement are queryable from SQL.

## Sources and references

- [The GDELT Project](https://www.gdeltproject.org/) and its [DOC 2.0 API](https://blog.gdeltproject.org/gdelt-doc-2-0-api-debuts/), which backs the default `gdelt` provider.
- [NewsAPI](https://newsapi.org/): the [`/v2/everything` endpoint](https://newsapi.org/docs/endpoints/everything) behind the `newsapi` provider; [register for an API key](https://newsapi.org/register) and review its [terms](https://newsapi.org/terms).

example_queries.description: List the available providers and their key requirements.
example_queries.sql: SELECT provider, requires_key FROM news.main.news_providers ORDER BY provider

example_queries.description: Fetch the 10 most recent headlines mentioning 'climate summit'.
example_queries.sql: SELECT title, url, domain, seendate FROM news.main.news_search('climate summit', count := 10)

example_queries.description: Rank domains by how many 'elections' articles they ran in the last two days.
example_queries.sql: SELECT domain, count(*) AS articles FROM news.main.news_search('elections', timespan := '2d', count := 50) GROUP BY domain ORDER BY articles DESC

example_queries.description: Find the outlets covering both 'climate' and 'election': join the 100 most recent past-day articles of two news_search calls on domain and rank domains by combined article count (page_size := 100 keeps each search to one GDELT request).
example_queries.sql: WITH climate AS (SELECT domain, count(*) AS climate_articles FROM news.main.news_search('climate', count := 100, page_size := 100, timespan := '1d') GROUP BY domain), election AS (SELECT domain, count(*) AS election_articles FROM news.main.news_search('election', count := 100, page_size := 100, timespan := '1d') GROUP BY domain) SELECT domain, climate_articles, election_articles FROM climate JOIN election USING (domain) ORDER BY climate_articles + election_articles DESC, domain LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Count how many providers are available.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# news_search

Search worldwide news coverage by free-text query and return a **unified article schema** regardless of which upstream provider served the rows. This is the worker's primary surface: use it whenever you need to find, filter, or analyze recent news articles directly from SQL.

## When to use

- Find which outlets/domains are covering a topic right now.
- Pull recent headlines with their URLs and publish times for a feed or digest.
- Measure coverage volume over a look-back window, per domain or source country.
- Filter coverage by source country or language.

## Inputs

- `query` (positional, required): the free-text search string.
- `provider :=` (default `'gdelt'`): `'gdelt'` (free, no key, worldwide) or `'newsapi'` (requires a `TYPE newsapi` DuckDB secret).
- `count :=` (default 25): total maximum rows across all internally-paged requests.
- `timespan :=` (default `'1d'`): look-back window such as `'6h'`, `'1d'`, `'2w'`.
- `country :=` / `language :=`: optional provider-mapped filters (empty = no filter).
- `page_size :=` (default 50): rows fetched per upstream request / per scan tick.

## Outputs

One row per article over `title, url, domain, language, seendate, country, tone, source, extra`. `seendate` is a real `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE`; `tone` is a `DOUBLE` sentiment slot that is currently always NULL (GDELT's article list carries no per-article tone and NewsAPI has no sentiment); `extra` carries provider-specific fields as a JSON string.

## Behavior & edge cases

- Results are paginated transparently across `process()` ticks: GDELT pages by time window (carrying the oldest `seendate` as the next window edge — a window-edge approximation, since GDELT has no deep cursor), NewsAPI pages by page number.
- An empty/blank `query` raises a clean error; an unknown `provider` lists the known ones. Upstream HTTP failures (rate limits, 5xx) surface as a clean DuckDB error.
- Missing provider fields map to `NULL`. GDELT is rate-limited (~1 request / 5s).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# News Article Search

`news_search(query, provider := ..., count := ..., timespan := ..., country := ..., language := ..., page_size := ...)` searches global news coverage and returns a single unified column set for every provider.

## Overview

Pass a free-text `query` and get back recent articles with their headline, URL, publisher domain, language, publish time, source country, a (currently NULL) sentiment tone, the originating provider, and a JSON `extra` blob of provider-specific fields. Runnable queries are attached as this function's example queries.

## Notes

- Default provider is **GDELT** (free, no API key).
- **NewsAPI** requires a `TYPE newsapi` DuckDB secret holding an `api_key`; never inline a key in SQL.
- `count` caps total rows; `page_size` controls the per-request fetch size.
- GDELT enforces a ~1 request / 5 seconds rate limit and has no deep cursor, so very large look-backs are approximated at window edges.

workers.doc_md:
# NFL scores, standings, and statistics

Query live and historical National Football League data from SQL.

## Data model

* **Live (ESPN):** scoreboards, standings, injuries, rosters, depth charts, and per-game box scores, drives, scoring plays, and play-by-play.
* **Analytics (nflverse, CC-BY 4.0):** schedules with lines and weather, play-by-play with EPA/WP, weekly and season player stats, team stats, snap counts, draft, combine, and Next Gen Stats.
* **Calendar (Sleeper):** the current season and week.

Data is fetched on demand, cached briefly in memory, and never rehosted. This worker is not affiliated with the NFL, ESPN, Disney, nflverse, or Sleeper.

## Sources and references

* [ESPN NFL](https://www.espn.com/nfl/): live scoreboards, standings, injuries, rosters and game detail.
* [nflverse](https://nflverse.nflverse.com/): analytics releases from [nflverse-data](https://github.com/nflverse/nflverse-data), licensed [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).
* [Sleeper API](https://docs.sleeper.com/): the current NFL season and week.

example_queries.title: opener_top_scrimmage_share
example_queries.description: CeeDee Lamb's 110 scrimmage yards were the largest share (35.8%) of either team's offense in the 2025 opener.
example_queries.sql: SELECT athlete_name, scrimmage_yards, pct_of_team_offense FROM (SELECT p.team_abbreviation, p.athlete_name, coalesce(p.rush_yards, 0) + coalesce(p.receiving_yards, 0) AS scrimmage_yards, t.total_yards AS team_total_yards, round(100.0 * (coalesce(p.rush_yards, 0) + coalesce(p.receiving_yards, 0)) / t.total_yards, 1) AS pct_of_team_offense FROM nfl.main.box_score_player('401772510') p JOIN nfl.main.box_score_team('401772510') t USING (team_id) WHERE p.rush_attempts > 0 OR p.receptions > 0 ORDER BY pct_of_team_offense DESC, p.athlete_name) ORDER BY pct_of_team_offense DESC LIMIT 1;

example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS rows FROM nfl.main.current_week;

example_queries.description: Each ball carrier's and receiver's yards from scrimmage in the 2025 season opener as a share of his team's total offense, joining the player box score to the team box score.
example_queries.sql: SELECT p.team_abbreviation, p.athlete_name, coalesce(p.rush_yards, 0) + coalesce(p.receiving_yards, 0) AS scrimmage_yards, t.total_yards AS team_total_yards, round(100.0 * (coalesce(p.rush_yards, 0) + coalesce(p.receiving_yards, 0)) / t.total_yards, 1) AS pct_of_team_offense FROM nfl.main.box_score_player('401772510') p JOIN nfl.main.box_score_team('401772510') t USING (team_id) WHERE p.rush_attempts > 0 OR p.receptions > 0 ORDER BY pct_of_team_offense DESC, p.athlete_name

example_queries.description: 2025 regular-season scoring leaders: points per game from the schedule's final scores beside each team's passing and rushing EPA and giveaways from team_stats.
example_queries.sql: WITH games AS (SELECT home_team, away_team, home_score, away_score FROM nfl.main.schedule(season := 2025) WHERE game_type = 'REG' AND home_score IS NOT NULL), points AS (SELECT team, count(*) AS games, avg(points) AS points_per_game FROM (SELECT home_team AS team, home_score AS points FROM games UNION ALL SELECT away_team, away_score FROM games) GROUP BY team) SELECT t.team, points.games, round(points.points_per_game, 1) AS points_per_game, round(t.passing_epa, 1) AS passing_epa, round(t.rushing_epa, 1) AS rushing_epa, t.interceptions + t.fumbles_lost AS giveaways FROM nfl.main.team_stats(season := 2025) t JOIN points USING (team) ORDER BY points_per_game DESC, t.team LIMIT 10

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One schema for live and historical NFL questions. Argument-free current tables and the team and player directories answer what is happening now. ESPN functions reach other weeks and seasons and, given an ESPN game id, the detail of one game: summary, team and player box scores, drives, scoring plays and play-by-play. nflverse functions carry the analytics (schedules with lines and weather, EPA and win-probability play-by-play, weekly and season statistics, snap counts, draft, combine and Next Gen Stats); each takes a season with optional week and team filters and downloads one cached release file. ESPN rows use ESPN ids, nflverse rows use GSIS player ids and nflverse team abbreviations; the nflverse schedule and player directory carry the ESPN ids that join the two.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## NFL data

Current tables answer live questions about this week's games, standings, injuries, the current week, teams, and players.

Parameterized ESPN functions take a season and week, a team abbreviation, or a game id. nflverse functions take a season with optional week and team filters and download one cached release file per call.

vgi.example_queries.description: Division tables in rank order.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT division, division_rank, team_name, wins, losses, ties, games_back FROM nfl.main.current_standings ORDER BY division, division_rank

vgi.example_queries.description: Current playoff field by conference seed.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT conference, playoff_seed, team_name, wins, losses FROM nfl.main.current_standings WHERE playoff_seed <= 7 ORDER BY conference, playoff_seed

vgi.example_queries.description: Each ball carrier's and receiver's yards from scrimmage in the 2025 season opener as a share of his team's total offense, joining the player box score to the team box score.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT p.team_abbreviation, p.athlete_name, coalesce(p.rush_yards, 0) + coalesce(p.receiving_yards, 0) AS scrimmage_yards, t.total_yards AS team_total_yards, round(100.0 * (coalesce(p.rush_yards, 0) + coalesce(p.receiving_yards, 0)) / t.total_yards, 1) AS pct_of_team_offense FROM nfl.main.box_score_player('401772510') p JOIN nfl.main.box_score_team('401772510') t USING (team_id) WHERE p.rush_attempts > 0 OR p.receptions > 0 ORDER BY pct_of_team_offense DESC, p.athlete_name

vgi.example_queries.description: 2025 regular-season scoring leaders: points per game from the schedule's final scores beside each team's passing and rushing EPA and giveaways from team_stats.
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH games AS (SELECT home_team, away_team, home_score, away_score FROM nfl.main.schedule(season := 2025) WHERE game_type = 'REG' AND home_score IS NOT NULL), points AS (SELECT team, count(*) AS games, avg(points) AS points_per_game FROM (SELECT home_team AS team, home_score AS points FROM games UNION ALL SELECT away_team, away_score FROM games) GROUP BY team) SELECT t.team, points.games, round(points.points_per_game, 1) AS points_per_game, round(t.passing_epa, 1) AS passing_epa, round(t.rushing_epa, 1) AS rushing_epa, t.interceptions + t.fumbles_lost AS giveaways FROM nfl.main.team_stats(season := 2025) t JOIN points USING (team) ORDER BY points_per_game DESC, t.team LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: First-round wide receivers drafted 2015-2020 who ran the combine 40-yard dash, fastest first, with career receiving yards and Pro Bowls, joining draft to combine on the Pro Football Reference id.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT d.season, d.pick, d.player_name, d.team, c.forty, d.rec_yards, d.pro_bowls FROM nfl.main.draft() d JOIN nfl.main.combine() c ON c.pfr_id = d.pfr_player_id WHERE d.position = 'WR' AND d.draft_round = 1 AND d.season BETWEEN 2015 AND 2020 AND c.forty IS NOT NULL ORDER BY c.forty, d.pick

vgi.example_queries.description: 2025 rookies with the most yards from scrimmage and where each was drafted, joining season stats to the players directory on the GSIS id (undrafted rookies show NULL draft columns).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT s.player_display_name, s.position, s.recent_team, p.draft_round, p.draft_pick, coalesce(s.rushing_yards, 0) + coalesce(s.receiving_yards, 0) AS scrimmage_yards FROM nfl.main.player_stats_season(season := 2025) s JOIN nfl.main.players p ON p.gsis_id = s.player_id WHERE p.rookie_season = 2025 ORDER BY scrimmage_yards DESC, s.player_display_name LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: 2025 rookies with the most yards from scrimmage and where each was drafted, joining season stats to the players directory on the GSIS id (undrafted rookies show NULL draft columns).

functions.name: box_score_player
functions.comment: Player box score for one NFL game, one row per player (ESPN)

tags.source: ESPN site/core/common API (undocumented; ESPN terms apply)
tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per player who recorded a stat, merging ESPN's passing, rushing, receiving, fumbles, defense, interception, return, kicking, and punting tables. Columns for categories a player did not record are NULL. The single positional argument is ESPN's game id as text (from scoreboard(), team_schedule(), or schedule().espn_game_id). Works for live and completed games.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Player box score for one NFL game, one row per player (ESPN). Backed by one cached ESPN game-summary request.

vgi.example_queries.description: Leading rushers in the 2025 season opener.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT athlete_name, team_abbreviation, rush_attempts, rush_yards, rush_touchdowns FROM nfl.main.box_score_player('401772510') WHERE rush_attempts > 0 ORDER BY rush_yards DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Each ball carrier's and receiver's yards from scrimmage in the 2025 season opener as a share of his team's total offense, joining the player box score to the team box score.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT p.team_abbreviation, p.athlete_name, coalesce(p.rush_yards, 0) + coalesce(p.receiving_yards, 0) AS scrimmage_yards, t.total_yards AS team_total_yards, round(100.0 * (coalesce(p.rush_yards, 0) + coalesce(p.receiving_yards, 0)) / t.total_yards, 1) AS pct_of_team_offense FROM nfl.main.box_score_player('401772510') p JOIN nfl.main.box_score_team('401772510') t USING (team_id) WHERE p.rush_attempts > 0 OR p.receptions > 0 ORDER BY pct_of_team_offense DESC, p.athlete_name

vgi.example_queries.description: 2025 regular-season scoring leaders: points per game from the schedule's final scores beside each team's passing and rushing EPA and giveaways from team_stats.
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH games AS (SELECT home_team, away_team, home_score, away_score FROM nfl.main.schedule(season := 2025) WHERE game_type = 'REG' AND home_score IS NOT NULL), points AS (SELECT team, count(*) AS games, avg(points) AS points_per_game FROM (SELECT home_team AS team, home_score AS points FROM games UNION ALL SELECT away_team, away_score FROM games) GROUP BY team) SELECT t.team, points.games, round(points.points_per_game, 1) AS points_per_game, round(t.passing_epa, 1) AS passing_epa, round(t.rushing_epa, 1) AS rushing_epa, t.interceptions + t.fumbles_lost AS giveaways FROM nfl.main.team_stats(season := 2025) t JOIN points USING (team) ORDER BY points_per_game DESC, t.team LIMIT 10

functions.name: play_by_play
functions.comment: Season play-by-play with EPA, win probability, and player ids (nflverse)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per play for an NFL season from nflverse (1999 onward), including expected points (ep, epa), win probability (wp, wpa), completion probability over expected (cpoe), success, down and distance, formation flags, and passer/rusher/receiver GSIS ids and names. Always pass season; add week and team (either side of the game) to limit the download-backed scan. Use play_by_play_game() for a live ESPN feed.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Curated nflverse play-by-play. The season file is downloaded once and cached in memory; filters apply before rows reach SQL. `posteam` is the offense. Join players to `players` on GSIS id.

vgi.example_queries.description: Passing EPA per dropback leaders for 2025 week 1.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT passer_player_name, count(*) AS dropbacks, round(avg(epa), 3) AS epa_per_play FROM nfl.main.play_by_play(season := 2025, week := 1) WHERE qb_dropback AND passer_player_name IS NOT NULL GROUP BY passer_player_name HAVING count(*) >= 20 ORDER BY epa_per_play DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Fourth-down attempts by Philadelphia in 2025.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT week, quarter, yards_to_go, play_type, first_down FROM nfl.main.play_by_play(season := 2025, team := 'PHI') WHERE down = 4 AND posteam = 'PHI' AND play_type IN ('run', 'pass') ORDER BY week

functions.name: player_game_log
functions.comment: One NFL player's per-game statistics for a season, one row per game and stat (ESPN)

tags.source: ESPN site/core/common API (undocumented; ESPN terms apply)
tags.vgi.doc_llm: Long-format game log from ESPN: one row per game per stat for an athlete and season, with week, opponent, home/away, result, category (passing, rushing, receiving, defensive, ...), stat key such as passingYards, and exact numeric value. Pivot or filter on stat. The athlete id is ESPN's (roster().athlete_id or players.espn_id).
tags.vgi.doc_md: ESPN athlete game log. Stats offered depend on the player's position.

vgi.example_queries.description: Patrick Mahomes's 2025 passing yards by week.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT week, opponent_abbreviation, result, value AS passing_yards FROM nfl.main.player_game_log(3139477, season := 2025) WHERE stat = 'passingYards' ORDER BY week

workers.summary: Read-only National Hockey League standings, schedules, scores, game detail, and player and team statistics from the NHL's public web and stats APIs
workers.doc_md:
# NHL standings, games, and statistics

Query current and historical National Hockey League data directly from SQL: standings, schedules and scores, season reports for every skater, goalie, and team, official leaderboards, rosters and player careers, and per-game box scores, play-by-play, and shift charts.

## Identifiers

Seasons are 8-digit ids (`20252026` is 2025-26). `game_type` is 2 for the regular season, 3 for the playoffs, and 1 for the preseason. Game ids are 10 digits (`2025020001`) and player ids 7 digits (`8478402`); `player_search()` finds them.

## Source

All access is read-only, keyless, and on demand from NHL.com's own backends; nothing is stored or rehosted. This project is not affiliated with the NHL.

* [NHL.com](https://www.nhl.com/) and [NHL Stats](https://www.nhl.com/stats/): the official sites backed by the `api-web.nhle.com` and `api.nhle.com/stats` APIs this worker calls.
* [NHL.com Terms of Service](https://www.nhl.com/info/terms-of-service): the terms that apply to NHL data.
* [NHL API Reference](https://github.com/Zmalski/NHL-API-Reference): a community reference for those endpoints.

example_queries.title: opener_final_score
example_queries.description: The 2025-26 opener (game 2025020001) ended Florida 3, Chicago 2.
example_queries.sql: SELECT home_team_abbrev, home_score, away_team_abbrev, away_score FROM nhl.main.scores(date := DATE '2025-10-07') WHERE game_id = 2025020001;

example_queries.title: opener_goal_events
example_queries.description: The opener's play-by-play contains its five goals.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS goals FROM nhl.main.play_by_play(2025020001) WHERE event_type = 'goal';

example_queries.title: current_standings_have_teams
example_queries.description: Today's standings list every NHL team with a team code.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) >= 32 AND count(team_abbrev) = count(*) AS populated FROM nhl.main.current_standings;

example_queries.description: Current division tables in official order.
example_queries.sql: SELECT division_name, division_rank, team_abbrev, points, games_played FROM nhl.main.current_standings ORDER BY division_name, division_rank

example_queries.description: Eastern Conference wild-card race.
example_queries.sql: SELECT wildcard_rank, team_abbrev, points, games_played FROM nhl.main.current_standings WHERE conference_name = 'Eastern' AND wildcard_rank > 0 ORDER BY wildcard_rank

example_queries.description: Goals for and against while each player was on the ice in the 2025-26 opener: play_by_play goals joined to the shift_chart interval that contains each goal's game_seconds.
example_queries.sql: WITH goals AS (SELECT game_seconds, event_owner_team_abbrev AS scoring_team FROM nhl.main.play_by_play(2025020001) WHERE event_type = 'goal') SELECT s.team_abbrev, s.player_name, count(*) FILTER (WHERE g.scoring_team = s.team_abbrev) AS on_ice_goals_for, count(*) FILTER (WHERE g.scoring_team <> s.team_abbrev) AS on_ice_goals_against FROM goals g JOIN nhl.main.shift_chart(2025020001) s ON g.game_seconds > s.start_seconds AND g.game_seconds <= s.end_seconds GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY on_ice_goals_for DESC, on_ice_goals_against, s.player_name

example_queries.description: Toronto's 2025-26 roster skaters with their season scoring: roster joined to skater_stats on player_id (a traded player's totals cover every club he played for).
example_queries.sql: SELECT r.sweater_number, r.player_name, r.position_code, s.games_played, s.goals, s.assists, s.points FROM nhl.main.roster('TOR', season := 20252026) r JOIN nhl.main.skater_stats(season := 20252026) s USING (player_id) WHERE r.position_group <> 'goalies' ORDER BY s.points DESC, r.player_name

example_queries.description: 2025-26 skaters with at least 50 points and 150 hits: skater_stats scoring joined to skater_realtime_stats physical play on player_id.
example_queries.sql: SELECT s.player_name, s.team_abbrevs, s.points, rt.hits, rt.blocked_shots FROM nhl.main.skater_stats(season := 20252026) s JOIN nhl.main.skater_realtime_stats(season := 20252026) rt USING (player_id) WHERE s.points >= 50 AND rt.hits >= 150 ORDER BY rt.hits DESC, s.player_name

example_queries.description: All NHL franchises alphabetically.
example_queries.sql: SELECT franchise_id, full_name FROM nhl.main.franchises ORDER BY full_name

example_queries.description: Every team that has played for the Avalanche/Nordiques franchise.
example_queries.sql: SELECT t.team_id, t.full_name, t.tricode FROM nhl.main.teams t JOIN nhl.main.franchises f USING (franchise_id) WHERE f.common_name = 'Avalanche'

example_queries.description: Seasons whose standings used the wild card, newest first.
example_queries.sql: SELECT season, standings_start, standings_end FROM nhl.main.standings_seasons WHERE wildcard_in_use ORDER BY season DESC

example_queries.description: Current save-percentage leaders.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rank, player_name, team_abbrev, value AS save_pct FROM nhl.main.current_goalie_leaders WHERE category = 'savePctg' ORDER BY rank

example_queries.description: Today's scoreboard.
example_queries.sql: SELECT away_team_abbrev, away_score, home_team_abbrev, home_score, game_state, period FROM nhl.main.current_scores ORDER BY start_time_utc

example_queries.description: This week's games in start order.
example_queries.sql: SELECT game_date, start_time_utc, away_team_abbrev, home_team_abbrev, venue FROM nhl.main.current_schedule ORDER BY start_time_utc

example_queries.description: Current scoring race.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rank, player_name, team_abbrev, value AS points FROM nhl.main.current_skater_leaders WHERE category = 'points' ORDER BY rank

example_queries.description: Final 2023-24 Atlantic Division table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT division_rank, team_name, wins, losses, ot_losses, points FROM nhl.main.standings(date := DATE '2024-04-18') WHERE division_name = 'Atlantic' ORDER BY division_rank

example_queries.description: Toronto's 2025-26 regular-season home results.
example_queries.sql: SELECT game_date, away_team_abbrev, away_score, home_score FROM nhl.main.team_schedule('TOR', season := 20252026) WHERE game_type = 2 AND home_team_abbrev = 'TOR' ORDER BY game_date

example_queries.description: The 2025-26 regular-season scoring leaders.
example_queries.sql: SELECT player_name, team_abbrevs, games_played, goals, assists, points FROM nhl.main.skater_stats(season := 20252026) ORDER BY points DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: 2025-26 playoff goal leaders.
example_queries.sql: SELECT player_name, team_abbrevs, goals FROM nhl.main.skater_stats(season := 20252026, game_type := 3) ORDER BY goals DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: The 2025-26 top-ten point scorers.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rank, player_name, team_abbrev, value AS points FROM nhl.main.skater_leaders(season := 20252026, category := 'points') ORDER BY rank

example_queries.description: Opening night of 2025-26 with shots on goal.
example_queries.sql: SELECT away_team_abbrev, away_score, home_team_abbrev, home_score, last_period_type FROM nhl.main.scores(date := DATE '2025-10-07') ORDER BY start_time_utc

example_queries.description: The first week of the 2025-26 regular season.

example_queries.sql: SELECT team_abbrev, player_name, count(*) AS shifts, sum(duration_seconds) AS seconds FROM nhl.main.shift_chart(2025020001) GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY seconds DESC

example_queries.description: Connor McDavid's NHL regular-season lines by season.
example_queries.sql: SELECT season, team_name, games_played, goals, assists, points FROM nhl.main.player_career(8478402) WHERE league_abbrev = 'NHL' AND game_type = 2 ORDER BY season

example_queries.description: Every goal in the 2025-26 opener with scorer and location.
example_queries.sql: SELECT period, time_in_period, event_owner_team_abbrev, primary_player_name, shot_type, x_coord, y_coord, away_score, home_score FROM nhl.main.play_by_play(2025020001) WHERE event_type = 'goal' ORDER BY sort_order

example_queries.description: Shot attempts by team and type of outcome.
example_queries.sql: SELECT event_owner_team_abbrev, event_type, count(*) AS events FROM nhl.main.play_by_play(2025020001) WHERE event_type IN ('goal', 'shot-on-goal', 'missed-shot', 'blocked-shot') GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY ALL

example_queries.description: 2025-26 save-percentage leaders with at least 40 games.
example_queries.sql: SELECT player_name, team_abbrevs, games_played, save_pct, goals_against_average FROM nhl.main.goalie_stats(season := 20252026) WHERE games_played >= 40 ORDER BY save_pct DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: The 2025-26 regular-season wins leaders.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rank, player_name, team_abbrev, value AS wins FROM nhl.main.goalie_leaders(season := 20252026, category := 'wins') ORDER BY rank

example_queries.description: Goaltending in the 2025-26 opener.
example_queries.sql: SELECT team_abbrev, player_name, decision, shots_against, saves, save_pct FROM nhl.main.box_score_goalies(2025020001) ORDER BY team_abbrev, toi_seconds DESC

example_queries.description: Connor McDavid's profile and NHL career totals.
example_queries.sql: SELECT player_name, current_team_abbrev, position, birth_date, draft_year, draft_overall_pick, career_games_played, career_points FROM nhl.main.player(8478402)

example_queries.description: All NHL franchises alphabetically.
example_queries.sql: SELECT franchise_id, full_name FROM nhl.main.all_franchises() ORDER BY full_name

example_queries.description: Skater lines from the 2025-26 opener, by points.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Argument-free current tables give today's standings, schedule, scores and stat leaders; reference tables of teams, franchises and seasons supply the ids the functions accept. Parameterized functions work at three levels: season reports for every skater, goalie and team; one player's profile, career and game log, found by name search; and one game's box score, play-by-play and shift chart, keyed by its 10-digit game id. Seasons are 8-digit ids such as 20252026.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## NHL analytical data

Rows are explicitly team-, game-, player-, player-season-, player-game-, event-, or shift-grain. Current tables reflect today; functions take seasons, dates, team codes, player ids, or game ids.

Reference tables (`teams`, `franchises`, `standings_seasons`) supply the identifiers the functions accept. Percentages are 0-1 fractions and times on ice come both as MM:SS text and as integer seconds.

functions.name: skater_stats
functions.comment: Season scoring summary for every NHL skater (goals, assists, points, TOI)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per skater for a season and game type: games, goals, assists, points, plus-minus, PIM, points per game, even-strength/power-play/shorthanded goals and points, game-winning and OT goals, shots, shooting %, faceoff %, and average TOI in seconds. Traded players have one combined row; team_abbrevs lists every club. Percentages are 0-1 fractions.
tags.vgi.doc_md: The NHL.com/stats skater summary report. `season` is an 8-digit id such as 20252026 (default current); `game_type` 2 regular season, 3 playoffs.

vgi.example_queries.description: The 2025-26 regular-season scoring leaders.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT player_name, team_abbrevs, goals FROM nhl.main.skater_stats(season := 20252026, game_type := 3) ORDER BY goals DESC LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: 2025-26 skaters with at least 50 points and 150 hits: skater_stats scoring joined to skater_realtime_stats physical play on player_id.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT s.player_name, s.team_abbrevs, s.points, rt.hits, rt.blocked_shots FROM nhl.main.skater_stats(season := 20252026) s JOIN nhl.main.skater_realtime_stats(season := 20252026) rt USING (player_id) WHERE s.points >= 50 AND rt.hits >= 150 ORDER BY rt.hits DESC, s.player_name

functions.name: play_by_play

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per game event in order (sort_order): faceoffs, shots on goal, missed and blocked shots, goals, hits, giveaways, takeaways, penalties, and stoppages, with period clock, game_seconds, situation code (strength), owning team, x/y rink coordinates in feet, shot type, and primary/secondary players with names. For a goal the primary player is the scorer and assists are in assist1/assist2.

vgi.example_queries.description: Goals for and against while each player was on the ice in the 2025-26 opener: play_by_play goals joined to the shift_chart interval that contains each goal's game_seconds.
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH goals AS (SELECT game_seconds, event_owner_team_abbrev AS scoring_team FROM nhl.main.play_by_play(2025020001) WHERE event_type = 'goal') SELECT s.team_abbrev, s.player_name, count(*) FILTER (WHERE g.scoring_team = s.team_abbrev) AS on_ice_goals_for, count(*) FILTER (WHERE g.scoring_team <> s.team_abbrev) AS on_ice_goals_against FROM goals g JOIN nhl.main.shift_chart(2025020001) s ON g.game_seconds > s.start_seconds AND g.game_seconds <= s.end_seconds GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY on_ice_goals_for DESC, on_ice_goals_against, s.player_name

workers.doc_md:
# Classical NLP for DuckDB SQL

![spaCy logo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/88/SpaCy_logo.svg)

Run **classical natural language processing in SQL** -- language detection, sentiment analysis, named entity recognition (NER), lemmatization, and tokenization -- directly over your text columns in DuckDB, with no LLM and no API key required. This worker turns the proven open-source NLP stack of [spaCy](https://spacy.io), [fastText](https://fasttext.cc/), and [VADER](https://github.com/cjhutto/vaderSentiment) into fast, deterministic SQL functions for bulk, cheap, per-row text enrichment.

## Who it is for

Data engineers and analysts who want to enrich large text tables -- product reviews, support tickets, articles, social posts -- without leaving SQL or paying per token. Because the underlying models are rule- and statistics-based rather than generative, output is reproducible and runs at column scale -- ideal *upstream* of, not as a replacement for, LLM workers.

## Key concepts

- **Models load once per worker process and are cached**, so the one-time model-load cost is amortized across every row of every query.
- **Language identification** uses Facebook's [fastText lid.176](https://fasttext.cc/docs/en/language-identification.html) model (176 languages). When you do not pin a language, each row is routed to the matching language pipeline automatically.
- **Sentiment** uses the lexicon-and-rule-based VADER scorer, tuned for English and social media text; it understands negation, intensifiers, and emoji.
- **Linguistic analysis** -- structured span extraction, part-of-speech tagging, sentence boundaries, noun-phrase mining, lemmatization, and Unicode normalization -- uses spaCy's small English pipeline (`en_core_web_sm`) by default; pin a language or name a specific model to override it.

## When to reach for it

Use it whenever you need to enrich or filter free text at scale in SQL: detect and segment multilingual corpora, score or bucket opinion, clean and canonicalize text so free-text keys join and group reliably, or split documents into structured rows you can aggregate and join back to their source. Attach the worker, then call the functions directly from SQL -- `nlp.main.detect_lang(body)`, `nlp.main.sentiment(body)`, or `nlp.main.entities((SELECT id, body FROM docs), id := 'id')`:

```sql
INSTALL vgi FROM community;
LOAD vgi;
ATTACH 'nlp' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'uv run nlp_worker.py');
```

Powered by spaCy ([source](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy) - [docs](https://spacy.io/usage)), fastText ([source](https://github.com/facebookresearch/fastText) - [docs](https://fasttext.cc/docs/en/language-identification.html)), and VADER ([source & docs](https://github.com/cjhutto/vaderSentiment)). Source for this worker: [Query-farm/vgi-nlp](https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-nlp).

example_queries.sql: SELECT id, ent_text, label FROM nlp.main.entities((SELECT 1 AS id, 'Apple is based in California.' AS body), id := 'id', lang := 'en')

example_queries.description: Split each review into sentences and score every sentence's sentiment to find the single most negative sentence per review -- pinpointing the complaint inside otherwise mixed feedback.
example_queries.sql: WITH reviews(id, body) AS (VALUES (1, 'The hotel location was perfect. The room was filthy and the staff were rude. Breakfast was fine.'), (2, 'Checkout was a frustrating mess. Otherwise it was a wonderful stay with a lovely view!')) SELECT id, arg_min(sentence, nlp.main.sentiment(sentence)) AS worst_sentence, round(min(nlp.main.sentiment(sentence)), 3) AS worst_score FROM nlp.main.sentences((SELECT id, body FROM reviews), id := 'id', lang := 'en') GROUP BY id ORDER BY id

example_queries.description: Extract the organizations (ORG entities) mentioned in each review, join them back to their review by id, and average the review sentiment per organization -- brand perception from free text.
example_queries.sql: WITH reviews(id, body) AS (VALUES (1, 'I love my new Apple laptop, the battery life is amazing.'), (2, 'Microsoft support was awful and rude.'), (3, 'The Apple store staff were friendly and quick to help.'), (4, 'Microsoft keeps crashing my laptop, which is incredibly frustrating.')) SELECT e.ent_text AS organization, count(*) AS mentions, round(avg(nlp.main.sentiment(r.body)), 3) AS avg_sentiment FROM nlp.main.entities((SELECT id, body FROM reviews), id := 'id', lang := 'en') AS e JOIN reviews AS r USING (id) WHERE e.label = 'ORG' GROUP BY e.ent_text ORDER BY avg_sentiment DESC

example_queries.description: Detect each document's language and look it up in the supported_languages table to see which default spaCy pipeline would process it -- documents in a language without one (here Swahili) get NULL and cannot be tokenized or run through NER without naming a model.
example_queries.sql: WITH docs(id, body) AS (VALUES (1, 'The quarterly report shows strong growth in every region.'), (2, 'Le rapport trimestriel montre une forte croissance dans toutes les régions.'), (3, 'Ripoti ya robo mwaka inaonyesha ukuaji mkubwa katika kila mkoa.')), detected AS (SELECT id, nlp.main.detect_lang(body) AS lang FROM docs) SELECT d.id, d.lang, s.spacy_model, s.spacy_model IS NOT NULL AS has_default_pipeline FROM detected AS d LEFT JOIN nlp.main.supported_languages AS s ON s.lang_code = d.lang ORDER BY d.id

example_queries.description: Keep only reviews labelled negative, extract their noun chunks, and lemmatize each chunk's head noun so 'rooms' and 'room' count together -- ranking the aspects that negative reviews mention.
example_queries.sql: WITH reviews(id, body) AS (VALUES (1, 'The rooms were dirty and the beds were terrible.'), (2, 'Awful service, and the room smelled bad.'), (3, 'The beds were comfortable and the view was great.'), (4, 'The breakfast was cold and the coffee was disgusting.')) SELECT nlp.main.lemmatize(lower(root), 'en') AS aspect, count(DISTINCT id) AS negative_reviews FROM nlp.main.noun_chunks((SELECT id, body FROM reviews WHERE nlp.main.sentiment_label(body) = 'neg'), id := 'id', lang := 'en') GROUP BY aspect ORDER BY negative_reviews DESC, aspect

agent_tasks: Identify the language of the text 'Bonjour tout le monde, comment allez-vous aujourd''hui?' and return its two-letter ISO-639 language code in a column named lang.

Decide whether the language detector is highly confident (more than 90%) that the text 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog' is English. Return a single boolean column named confident_english that is true only when the detected ISO-639 code is 'en' and the detection confidence exceeds 0.9.

Decide whether the sentence 'I absolutely love this product, it works wonderfully!' expresses positive sentiment. Using the compound sentiment score, return a single boolean column named is_positive that is true when the score is above the standard positive threshold of 0.05.
Classify the sentiment of the sentence 'This is the worst experience I have ever had' into a coarse label of negative, neutral, or positive, and return the label in a column named mood.
Produce a canonical, comparable form of the string '  Cafe   DELUXE  ' by applying Unicode normalization, lowercasing, and collapsing runs of whitespace. Return it in a column named canonical.

Lemmatize the English sentence 'The cats were running quickly', reducing each word to its dictionary base form. Decide whether the lemmatized result contains the base form 'run'. Return a single boolean column named has_run. Treat the text as English.

Remove English stop-words and punctuation from the sentence 'this is a really great movie'. Decide whether the content word 'great' survives the stop-word removal. Return a single boolean column named keeps_great. Treat the text as English.
Decide whether the sentence 'Apple was founded by Steve Jobs in California.' contains at least two named entities. Treat the text as English. Return a single boolean column named has_entities.

Tokenize the English sentence 'The quick brown fox jumps.' into individual tokens with part-of-speech tags. Decide whether it yields more than three tokens. Treat the text as English. Return a single boolean column named many_tokens.

Split the text 'First sentence here. Second one follows.' into sentences and decide whether it contains exactly two sentences. Treat the text as English. Return a single boolean column named two_sentences.

Extract the base noun phrases (noun chunks) from the English sentence 'The big red car drove down the long road.' and decide whether it yields at least two noun chunks. Treat the text as English. Return a single boolean column named has_chunks.

Determine whether this worker has a default spaCy pipeline for English (ISO-639 code 'en'), i.e. whether English text can be lemmatized and run through NER without naming a custom model. Return a single boolean column named supported.

Split the English review 'Our flight left on time. The seats were broken and the crew was hostile. The snacks were tasty.' into sentences, score the sentiment of each sentence, and return the 0-based position of the most negative sentence as a single INTEGER column named worst_index. Treat the text as English.

Detect the language of each of these four texts: 'The weather is lovely today and we are going to the beach.', 'Das Wetter ist heute schön und wir fahren an den Strand.', 'Cuaca hari ini sangat cerah dan kami akan pergi ke pantai bersama keluarga.', and 'Bugün hava çok güzel ve sahile gidiyoruz.'. Count how many of them are written in a language for which this worker has a default spaCy pipeline. Return a single BIGINT column named n_supported.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `supported_languages` (table)

One row per language that has a default spaCy pipeline, so the extraction table functions and the `lemmatize` / `strip_stopwords` scalars can process it without naming a model. Columns:

- `lang_code` (`VARCHAR`, primary key) -- the ISO-639 code you pass as the `lang` argument (or that per-row auto-detect must resolve to).
- `spacy_model` (`VARCHAR`) -- the default small spaCy pipeline that backs it.

Read this table directly to discover which languages can be lemmatized, tokenized, or run through NER. Note `detect_lang` recognizes far more languages (fastText covers 176) than have a spaCy pipeline installed -- this table lists only the latter. Backed by the identically-named table function, so the rows are identical.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# `supported_languages`

Discovery table of every language the worker has a default spaCy pipeline for, exposed as a regular table you can read without parentheses.

## Columns

- `lang_code` (`VARCHAR`, primary key) -- ISO-639 code accepted by the `lang` argument.
- `spacy_model` (`VARCHAR`) -- the default small spaCy model backing it.

Language detection (`detect_lang`) spans 176 languages via fastText, but only the languages listed here can be lemmatized, tokenized, or run through NER without naming a custom model.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Tokenization plus linguistic annotation as a table-in-out function: each input text row explodes into **one row per token**, each carrying its lemma, part-of-speech, fine-grained tag, stop-word flag, and dependency relation from the spaCy pipeline.

**When to use:** linguistic analysis, building token-level features, counting parts of speech, or filtering to content words -- anything that needs the words of a document as queryable rows.

**Input:** a `(SELECT ...)` relation passed positionally; `id := 'col'` names a passthrough key; `text :=`, `lang :=`, `model :=` pick the text column, pin the language, and override the model. **Output:** rows of `(token, lemma, pos, tag, is_stop, dep)` plus the optional id. Output order is not guaranteed -- add `ORDER BY` for determinism.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# tokens

Tokenizes a text column with spaCy and emits one row per token with rich annotations. Pass the input relation positionally; `id :=` names the join key copied onto every token row, and `text :=`, `lang :=`, `model :=` pick the text column, pin the language, and override the model.

Each row gives the token text, its lemma, coarse and fine POS tags, a stop-word flag, and its dependency label. Filter on `is_stop` or `pos` to isolate content words; use `id :=` to join tokens back to their source document.

functions.name: noun_chunks
functions.comment: Noun chunks per text row: (id, chunk, root) -- keyword/topic candidates

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Noun-phrase extraction as a table-in-out function: each input text row explodes into **one row per noun chunk** (a base noun phrase such as 'the long road'), each with its head/root token.

**When to use:** mine candidate keywords, topics, or product/feature mentions from free text without training a model -- noun chunks are a cheap, high-recall source of 'what this text is about'.

**Input:** a `(SELECT ...)` relation passed positionally; `id := 'col'` names a passthrough key; `text :=`, `lang :=`, `model :=` pick the text column, pin the language, and override the model. **Output:** rows of `(chunk, root)` plus the optional id. Text rows with no noun chunks emit nothing; output order is not guaranteed -- add `ORDER BY` for determinism.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# noun_chunks

Extracts base noun phrases from a text column with spaCy, emitting one row per chunk. Pass the input relation positionally; `id :=` names the join key copied onto every chunk row, and `text :=`, `lang :=`, `model :=` pick the text column, pin the language, and override the model.

Each row gives the noun-phrase text and its head token (`root`). Aggregate the chunks to surface frequent topics/keywords, or join back to the source via `id :=`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Explode a literal English document into noun_chunks, projecting its key columns
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT chunk, root FROM nlp.main.noun_chunks((SELECT 'The big red car drove down the long road.' AS body), lang := 'en')

vgi.example_queries.description: Keep only reviews labelled negative, extract their noun chunks, and lemmatize each chunk's head noun so 'rooms' and 'room' count together -- ranking the aspects that negative reviews mention.
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH reviews(id, body) AS (VALUES (1, 'The rooms were dirty and the beds were terrible.'), (2, 'Awful service, and the room smelled bad.'), (3, 'The beds were comfortable and the view was great.'), (4, 'The breakfast was cold and the coffee was disgusting.')) SELECT nlp.main.lemmatize(lower(root), 'en') AS aspect, count(DISTINCT id) AS negative_reviews FROM nlp.main.noun_chunks((SELECT id, body FROM reviews WHERE nlp.main.sentiment_label(body) = 'neg'), id := 'id', lang := 'en') GROUP BY aspect ORDER BY negative_reviews DESC, aspect

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: chunk
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: The noun-phrase text.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: root
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: The head/root token of the noun phrase.

functions.name: sentences
functions.comment: Sentences per text row: (id, sent_index, sentence) -- chunking for embeddings

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Sentence segmentation as a table-in-out function: each input text row explodes into **one row per sentence**, in document order, with a 0-based index.

**When to use:** chunk long documents into sentence-sized units before embedding/retrieval, sentence-level sentiment, or any per-sentence analysis.

**Input:** a `(SELECT ...)` relation passed positionally; `id := 'col'` names a passthrough key copied onto every sentence row; `text :=`, `lang :=`, `model :=` pick the text column, pin the language, and override the model. **Output:** rows of `(sent_index, sentence)` plus the optional id. The `sent_index` preserves order; output row order across documents is otherwise not guaranteed -- add `ORDER BY id, sent_index` for determinism.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# sentences

Splits a text column into sentences with spaCy, emitting one indexed row per sentence. Pass the input relation positionally; `id :=` names the join key copied onto every sentence row, and `text :=`, `lang :=`, `model :=` pick the text column, pin the language, and override the model.

Each row carries the 0-based `sent_index` and the trimmed sentence text. This is the standard first step for sentence-level embeddings or retrieval chunking; use `id :=` to keep sentences tied to their source document, and order by `id, sent_index` for determinism.

vgi.example_queries.description: Explode a literal English document into sentences, projecting its key columns
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT sent_index, sentence FROM nlp.main.sentences((SELECT 'First sentence here. Second one follows.' AS body), lang := 'en')

vgi.example_queries.description: Split each review into sentences and score every sentence's sentiment to find the single most negative sentence per review -- pinpointing the complaint inside otherwise mixed feedback.
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH reviews(id, body) AS (VALUES (1, 'The hotel location was perfect. The room was filthy and the staff were rude. Breakfast was fine.'), (2, 'Checkout was a frustrating mess. Otherwise it was a wonderful stay with a lovely view!')) SELECT id, arg_min(sentence, nlp.main.sentiment(sentence)) AS worst_sentence, round(min(nlp.main.sentiment(sentence)), 3) AS worst_score FROM nlp.main.sentences((SELECT id, body FROM reviews), id := 'id', lang := 'en') GROUP BY id ORDER BY id

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: sent_index
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: 0-based index of the sentence within the source text.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: sentence
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: The sentence text.

functions.name: entities
functions.comment: Named entities per text row: (id, ent_text, label, start_char, end_char)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Named-entity recognition as a table-in-out function: each input text row explodes into **one row per detected entity** (people, organizations, places, dates, money, ...) found by the spaCy NER pipeline.

**When to use:** pull structured mentions out of unstructured text -- e.g. every company named across a news corpus, or every date in a contract -- so you can aggregate, filter, or join on them.

**Input:** a `(SELECT ...)` relation passed positionally; `id := 'col'` names a passthrough key copied onto every emitted row (so you can join entities back to the source); `text :=`, `lang :=`, and `model :=` select the text column, pin the language, and override the model. **Output:** rows of `(ent_text, label, start_char, end_char)` plus the optional id. Text rows with no entities emit nothing; output order is not guaranteed -- add `ORDER BY` for determinism.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# entities

Runs spaCy named-entity recognition over a text column, emitting one row per entity span. Pass the input relation positionally and name the join key with `id :=` so every emitted entity carries the source row's id; `text :=`, `lang :=`, and `model :=` choose the text column, pin the language, and override the model.

Each output row carries the entity text, its type label (`PERSON`, `ORG`, `GPE`, `DATE`, `MONEY`, ...), and the character span within the source. Rows with no entities produce no output; add an `ORDER BY` for deterministic order.

vgi.example_queries.description: Explode a literal English document into entities, projecting its key columns
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ent_text, label FROM nlp.main.entities((SELECT 'Apple was founded by Steve Jobs in California.' AS body), lang := 'en')

vgi.example_queries.description: Extract the organizations (ORG entities) mentioned in each review, join them back to their review by id, and average the review sentiment per organization -- brand perception from free text.
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH reviews(id, body) AS (VALUES (1, 'I love my new Apple laptop, the battery life is amazing.'), (2, 'Microsoft support was awful and rude.'), (3, 'The Apple store staff were friendly and quick to help.'), (4, 'Microsoft keeps crashing my laptop, which is incredibly frustrating.')) SELECT e.ent_text AS organization, count(*) AS mentions, round(avg(nlp.main.sentiment(r.body)), 3) AS avg_sentiment FROM nlp.main.entities((SELECT id, body FROM reviews), id := 'id', lang := 'en') AS e JOIN reviews AS r USING (id) WHERE e.label = 'ORG' GROUP BY e.ent_text ORDER BY avg_sentiment DESC

vgi.executable_examples.description: Extract named entities from a literal document, keyed back to its id.
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT id, ent_text, label FROM nlp.main.entities((SELECT 1 AS id, 'Apple was founded by Steve Jobs in California.' AS body), id := 'id', lang := 'en')

vgi.executable_examples.description: Extract noun chunks from a literal document, keyed back to its id.
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT id, chunk, root FROM nlp.main.noun_chunks((SELECT 1 AS id, 'The big red car drove down the long road.' AS body), id := 'id', lang := 'en')

vgi.executable_examples.description: Extract the organizations (ORG entities) mentioned in each review, join them back to their review by id, and average the review sentiment per organization -- brand perception from free text.

functions.name: sentiment
functions.comment: Sentiment score in [-1, 1] (VADER lexicon; tuned for English/social text)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Score the sentiment of each text with VADER and return the **compound** value in `[-1, 1]`, where `-1` is maximally negative, `0` neutral, and `+1` maximally positive.

**When to use:** rank or aggregate opinion in reviews, comments, tweets, and other short social/English text -- e.g. `avg(nlp.sentiment(body))` per product.

**Input:** one `VARCHAR` column. **Output:** a `FLOAT` in `[-1, 1]`. NULL/empty input yields NULL. VADER is a lexicon-and-rules model tuned for English and social media; it understands emphasis, negation, and emoticons but is not a translator -- score non-English text only after detecting/translating it.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# sentiment

Returns the VADER compound sentiment score in `[-1, 1]` for each text. A typical use is per-group opinion tracking -- e.g. the average `nlp.sentiment(body)` per product, so you can rank which products reviewers feel best about.

VADER is purpose-built for English social text (handling negation, intensifiers, and emoji). For a coarse neg/neu/pos bucket instead of a number, use `nlp.sentiment_label`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Score the sentiment of a literal English string
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT nlp.main.sentiment('I absolutely love this, it is fantastic!') AS score

tags.vgi.title: Sentiment Compound Score

arguments.name: text
arguments.description: Text column to score

examples: SELECT nlp.main.sentiment('I absolutely love this, it is fantastic!') AS score

functions.name: detect_lang_conf
functions.comment: Confidence (0-1) of the detected language (fastText lid.176)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Return the fastText `lid.176` confidence (roughly 0-1) for the **top** language guess of each input string -- the companion probability to `detect_lang`.

**When to use:** gate downstream processing on identification quality, e.g. keep only rows the model is sure about with `WHERE nlp.detect_lang_conf(body) > 0.8`.

**Input:** one `VARCHAR` column. **Output:** a `FLOAT`. NULL/empty input yields NULL. Edge case: fastText occasionally reports a confidence marginally above 1.0 (e.g. ~1.00001), so do not assert a strict `<= 1.0` upper bound on the result.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# detect_lang_conf

Returns how confident the fastText `lid.176` model is in the language it picked for each text -- a float near the `[0, 1]` range. A common pattern is to keep only confidently-identified rows by filtering on `nlp.detect_lang_conf(body) > 0.8`.

Use alongside `nlp.detect_lang`. Note the confidence can read slightly above 1.0 for some inputs, so avoid a strict upper-bound assertion.

vgi.example_queries.description: Confidence of the top language guess for a literal string
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT nlp.main.detect_lang_conf('The quick brown fox') AS conf

tags.vgi.title: Detect Language Confidence Score

arguments.name: text
arguments.description: Text column to identify

examples: SELECT nlp.main.detect_lang_conf('The quick brown fox') AS conf

functions.name: sentiment_label
functions.comment: Coarse sentiment label: neg / neu / pos (VADER thresholds)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Bucket each text into a coarse three-way sentiment **label** -- `neg`, `neu`, or `pos` -- by thresholding the VADER compound score.

**When to use:** when you want a categorical opinion bucket for `GROUP BY` / filtering rather than a continuous number; cheaper to read in dashboards than the raw score.

**Input:** one `VARCHAR` column. **Output:** a `VARCHAR` in `{neg, neu, pos}`. NULL/empty input yields NULL. Same English/social-text caveats as `sentiment`; if you need the underlying magnitude, call `nlp.sentiment` instead.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# sentiment_label

Returns a coarse sentiment class -- `neg`, `neu`, or `pos` -- derived from the VADER compound score by thresholding at +/-0.05. A common use is to tally how many reviews fall into each `nlp.sentiment_label(body)` bucket for a dashboard.

Use this when a label is more convenient than the numeric `nlp.sentiment` score, for example to tally how many reviews fall into each mood bucket.

vgi.example_queries.description: Bucket a literal string into neg / neu / pos
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT nlp.main.sentiment_label('This is the worst experience ever') AS mood

tags.vgi.title: Sentiment Polarity Label

arguments.name: text
arguments.description: Text column to label

examples: SELECT nlp.main.sentiment_label('This is the worst experience ever') AS mood

functions.name: detect_lang
functions.comment: Detect the dominant language of each text (ISO-639 code, fastText lid.176)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Identify the dominant natural language of each input string and return its two-letter ISO-639-1 code (`en`, `fr`, `de`, `es`, ...), using the fastText `lid.176` model.

**When to use:** routing mixed-language corpora, filtering a table down to one language before applying English-only models (e.g. VADER sentiment), or building a language histogram with `GROUP BY`.

**Input:** one `VARCHAR` column. **Output:** a `VARCHAR` ISO-639 code. NULL or empty input yields NULL. Very short or ambiguous strings can be misclassified -- pair with `detect_lang_conf` and threshold on confidence when accuracy matters.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# detect_lang

Returns the ISO-639-1 language code of each text value, computed with the fastText `lid.176` identifier -- for example `fr` for `Bonjour le monde` and `en` for a plain English sentence.

Use it to segment a multilingual column before language-specific processing. Combine with `nlp.detect_lang_conf` to discard low-confidence guesses; very short snippets are inherently hard to classify.

vgi.example_queries.description: Identify the language of a literal string
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT nlp.main.detect_lang('The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog') AS lang

vgi.example_queries.description: Detect each document's language and look it up in the supported_languages table to see which default spaCy pipeline would process it -- documents in a language without one (here Swahili) get NULL and cannot be tokenized or run through NER without naming a model.
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH docs(id, body) AS (VALUES (1, 'The quarterly report shows strong growth in every region.'), (2, 'Le rapport trimestriel montre une forte croissance dans toutes les régions.'), (3, 'Ripoti ya robo mwaka inaonyesha ukuaji mkubwa katika kila mkoa.')), detected AS (SELECT id, nlp.main.detect_lang(body) AS lang FROM docs) SELECT d.id, d.lang, s.spacy_model, s.spacy_model IS NOT NULL AS has_default_pipeline FROM detected AS d LEFT JOIN nlp.main.supported_languages AS s ON s.lang_code = d.lang ORDER BY d.id

tags.vgi.title: Detect Language Code

arguments.name: text
arguments.description: Text column to identify

examples: SELECT nlp.main.detect_lang('The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog') AS lang

WITH docs(id, body) AS (VALUES (1, 'The quarterly report shows strong growth in every region.'), (2, 'Le rapport trimestriel montre une forte croissance dans toutes les régions.'), (3, 'Ripoti ya robo mwaka inaonyesha ukuaji mkubwa katika kila mkoa.')), detected AS (SELECT id, nlp.main.detect_lang(body) AS lang FROM docs) SELECT d.id, d.lang, s.spacy_model, s.spacy_model IS NOT NULL AS has_default_pipeline FROM detected AS d LEFT JOIN nlp.main.supported_languages AS s ON s.lang_code = d.lang ORDER BY d.id

functions.name: normalize
functions.comment: Normalize text: Unicode NFKC, lowercase, and collapse whitespace

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Canonicalize each text into a comparable form: apply Unicode **NFKC** normalization, casefold (aggressive lowercase), and collapse all runs of whitespace to single spaces (trimming the ends).

**When to use:** before equality joins, deduplication, or grouping on free-text keys so that visually-identical strings differing only in case, full/half-width forms, ligatures, or spacing compare equal.

**Input:** one `VARCHAR` column. **Output:** a normalized `VARCHAR`. NULL input yields NULL. This function is **pure Python** -- no spaCy/fastText model is loaded -- so it is the cheapest function in the worker and always available.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# normalize

Returns a canonical form of each text: Unicode NFKC + casefold + whitespace collapse -- e.g. `  Cafe   DELUXE  ` becomes `cafe deluxe`.

Use it to make free-text keys join and group reliably. Unlike the other cleaners this needs no model, so it runs everywhere with no setup.

vgi.example_queries.description: Canonicalize a messy literal string for dedup / matching
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT nlp.main.normalize('  Café   DELUXE	—  ') AS canonical

tags.vgi.title: Normalize Text Form

arguments.name: text
arguments.description: Text column to normalize

examples: SELECT nlp.main.normalize('  Café   DELUXE	—  ') AS canonical

functions.name: lemmatize
functions.comment: Lemmatize each text (tokens replaced by their dictionary form); language auto-detected

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Reduce every token to its lemma and return them space-joined, loading a **named** spaCy model rather than the default for the language.

**When to use:** when you need a particular model -- e.g. a larger/transformer model (`en_core_web_trf`) for higher accuracy, or a non-default model already installed in the worker environment.

**Inputs:** a `VARCHAR` text column, an ISO-639 `lang` (`''` ignores it when a model is given), and a `model` name. **Output:** a `VARCHAR` of space-joined lemmas. NULL/empty text yields NULL. The named model must be installed in the worker's environment, or the call errors at load time.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# lemmatize(text, lang, model)

Lemmatizes each text using an explicitly named spaCy model, giving full control over accuracy/speed trade-offs -- for instance naming `en_core_web_sm` for English or a larger `en_core_web_trf` transformer model.

The model must be present in the worker's Python environment. When the `lang` argument is empty the model name alone selects the pipeline.

vgi.example_queries.description: Lemmatize a literal string with per-row language auto-detect
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT nlp.main.lemmatize('The cats were running quickly') AS lemmas

vgi.example_queries.description: Lemmatize a literal string with the language pinned to English
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT nlp.main.lemmatize('The cats were running quickly', 'en') AS lemmas

vgi.example_queries.description: Lemmatize a literal string with an explicit spaCy model
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT nlp.main.lemmatize('The cats were running quickly', 'en', 'en_core_web_sm') AS lemmas

tags.vgi.title: Lemmatize Text (Explicit Model)

workers.doc_md:
# Notion

Query a Notion workspace from DuckDB: find pages and databases, read any database as a typed table (one column per property), and export page content as blocks, Markdown or plain text. Read-only.

Create a `notion` secret with an integration token and share the pages and databases you want with that integration. WHERE filters on database properties become Notion filter objects and only the properties you select are downloaded.

### Sources and references

- [Notion API reference](https://developers.notion.com/reference/intro) (version 2026-03-11)
- [Data sources and the 2025-09-03 upgrade](https://developers.notion.com/docs/upgrade-guide-2025-09-03)
- [Query a data source](https://developers.notion.com/reference/query-a-data-source) and [filter objects](https://developers.notion.com/reference/filter-data-source-entries)
- [Property values](https://developers.notion.com/reference/property-value-object) and [block types](https://developers.notion.com/reference/block)
- [Request limits](https://developers.notion.com/reference/request-limits) and [authorization](https://developers.notion.com/docs/authorization)
workers.readme_sql:
CREATE SECRET notion (TYPE notion, TOKEN 'ntn_…');   -- an internal integration secret

-- Open tasks due from November on. One request:
--   {"and":[{"property":"Status","status":{"equals":"In progress"}},
--           {"property":"Due","date":{"on_or_after":"…"}}]}
SELECT "Name", "Assignee", "Due".start AS due
FROM notion.main.query_database('https://www.notion.so/acme/Tasks-1a2b3c4d00004000800000000000d001')
WHERE "Status" = 'In progress' AND "Due".start >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01 00:00:00+00'
ORDER BY due;

-- Story points per assignee, joining the people column to the workspace users.
SELECT u.name, sum(t."Estimate") AS points
FROM notion.main.query_data_source('1a2b3c4d-0000-4000-8000-00000000d501') t, notion.main.users u
WHERE list_contains(t."Assignee", u.id)
GROUP BY u.name ORDER BY points DESC;

-- A page as Markdown, and its outline.
SELECT markdown FROM notion.main.page_markdown('1a2b3c4d-0000-4000-8000-00000000a001');
SELECT depth, text FROM notion.main.blocks('1a2b3c4d-0000-4000-8000-00000000a001')
WHERE type LIKE 'heading_%' ORDER BY path;

example_queries.sql: SELECT title, url, last_edited_time FROM notion.main.search(query := 'roadmap') WHERE object = 'page' ORDER BY last_edited_time DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.sql: SELECT object, count(*) AS n FROM notion.main.search() GROUP BY object ORDER BY object

example_queries.sql: SELECT property, type, column_name, sql_type FROM notion.main.data_source_schema('1a2b3c4d-0000-4000-8000-00000000d501') ORDER BY position

example_queries.description: Every select and status option, to know which values to filter on
example_queries.sql: SELECT property, unnest(options).name AS option FROM notion.main.data_source_schema('1a2b3c4d-0000-4000-8000-00000000d501') WHERE type IN ('select', 'status') ORDER BY property, option

example_queries.description: Task count and estimate total per status

example_queries.description: Where a page lives and when it last changed

example_queries.description: A page's non-empty properties as name / value pairs
example_queries.sql: SELECT property, type, text FROM notion.main.page_properties('1a2b3c4d-0000-4000-8000-00000000a001') WHERE text IS NOT NULL ORDER BY position

example_queries.description: A page's outline: its headings in document order
example_queries.sql: SELECT depth, type, text FROM notion.main.blocks('1a2b3c4d-0000-4000-8000-00000000a001') WHERE type LIKE 'heading_%' ORDER BY path

example_queries.description: How many to-do items on a page are ticked
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE checked) AS done, count(*) AS total FROM notion.main.blocks('1a2b3c4d-0000-4000-8000-00000000a001') WHERE type = 'to_do'

example_queries.description: Render a page to Markdown and measure it
example_queries.sql: SELECT title, length(markdown) AS chars FROM notion.main.page_markdown('1a2b3c4d-0000-4000-8000-00000000a001')

example_queries.description: A page's plain text split into words, if it mentions a launch
example_queries.sql: SELECT title, regexp_split_to_array(text, '\s+') AS words FROM notion.main.page_text('1a2b3c4d-0000-4000-8000-00000000a001') WHERE text ILIKE '%launch%'

example_queries.description: The discussion on a page, oldest first
example_queries.sql: SELECT display_name, text, created_time FROM notion.main.comments('1a2b3c4d-0000-4000-8000-00000000a001') ORDER BY created_time

example_queries.description: Every data source the integration can query, most recently edited first
example_queries.sql: SELECT title, property_count, database_id FROM notion.main.data_sources ORDER BY last_edited_time DESC

example_queries.description: Databases and how many data sources each holds
example_queries.sql: SELECT title, len(data_source_ids) AS sources, is_inline FROM notion.main.databases ORDER BY title

example_queries.description: People versus bots in the workspace
example_queries.sql: SELECT type, count(*) AS n FROM notion.main.users GROUP BY type ORDER BY type

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

A read-only view of a Notion workspace, scoped to what the integration behind the `notion` secret has been shared with. Discover pages and data sources by title, then query a data source as a typed table whose columns are its properties; `WHERE` predicates on those columns are pushed into Notion's own filter, so only matching rows come back.

Page content is available as structured blocks or rendered Markdown and plain text, alongside metadata, properties and comments. Ids accept dashed UUIDs, 32 hex digits or notion.so URLs, and people and relation columns hold ids you can join back to users or to another data source.

functions.name: query_data_source
functions.comment: Rows of a Notion data source as a typed table, one column per property

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Rows (pages) of a Notion data source as a typed table: one column per property, named exactly as in Notion (quote names with spaces or capitals: "Status", "Due date"), plus id, url, created_time, last_edited_time, created_by, last_edited_by and in_trash. Types: title / rich_text `VARCHAR` plain text (+ "<name>__json" raw rich text `JSON`), number `DOUBLE`, checkbox `BOOLEAN`, select / status `VARCHAR`, multi_select `VARCHAR[]`, people / relation `VARCHAR[]` of ids (join users or another data source), date `STRUCT("start", "end" TIMESTAMPTZ, time_zone, has_time)` (filter with "Due".start), created / last edited time `TIMESTAMPTZ`, files `STRUCT(name, type, url, expiry_time)[]`, unique_id `BIGINT`, formula / rollup by result type. Call data_source_schema(id) first to see the exact column names and types. WHERE on properties pushes down into Notion's filter (equality, ranges, IN, LIKE '%…%' / contains / suffix, list_contains, IS NULL, AND/OR); only the columns you select are downloaded. Ids may be given as notion.so URLs.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## query_data_source(data_source_id, notion_filter := NULL, notion_sorts := NULL, rich_text_json := true)

Each row is a page of the data source; each property becomes a typed column. `data_source_schema(id)` lists the columns. Pushdown: WHERE → Notion filter object (`and`/`or`, property conditions by type, `created_time`/`last_edited_time` timestamp filters), projection → `filter_properties`, `notion_sorts` → Notion sorts. Rows stream one 100-row page per batch with the Notion cursor kept as scan state.

vgi.example_queries.description: Open tasks due from November on, with the status and date filters pushed into Notion
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT "Name", "Status", "Due".start AS due FROM notion.main.query_data_source('1a2b3c4d-0000-4000-8000-00000000d501') WHERE "Status" <> 'Done' AND "Due".start >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01 00:00:00+00' ORDER BY due

vgi.example_queries.description: Task count and estimate total per status
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT "Status", count(*) AS tasks, sum("Estimate") AS points FROM notion.main.query_data_source('1a2b3c4d-0000-4000-8000-00000000d501') GROUP BY "Status" ORDER BY tasks DESC

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
Columns are computed from the data source's schema when the query is bound: `id`, then one column per property named exactly as in Notion (`data_source_schema(id)` lists each column's name and type; a `<name>__json` sibling follows each title / rich_text property, and a name colliding with another column gets a `_2` suffix), then the page metadata columns.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| id | VARCHAR | Page id of the row. |
| <title / rich_text property> | VARCHAR | Plain text. |
| <title / rich_text property>__json | JSON | Raw rich text (marks, links, mentions). |
| <number property> | DOUBLE | The number. |
| <checkbox property> | BOOLEAN | Ticked or not. |
| <select / status property> | VARCHAR | Option name. |
| <multi_select property> | VARCHAR[] | Option names. |
| <people / relation property> | VARCHAR[] | User ids / related page ids. |
| <date property> | STRUCT("start" TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE, "end" TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE, time_zone VARCHAR, has_time BOOLEAN) | Date or range; all-day dates at 00:00 UTC. |
| <created_time / last_edited_time property> | TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE | The instant. |
| <created_by / last_edited_by property> | VARCHAR | User id. |
| <url / email / phone_number property> | VARCHAR | The value. |
| <files property> | STRUCT("name" VARCHAR, "type" VARCHAR, url VARCHAR, expiry_time TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE)[] | Attached files. |
| <unique_id property> | BIGINT | The number (prefix in data_source_schema). |
| <formula property, text result> | VARCHAR | Formula result. |
| <formula property, boolean result> | BOOLEAN | Formula result. |
| <formula / rollup property, number result> | DOUBLE | Result (rollups: count, sum, average, …). |
| <rollup property, show_original / show_unique> | VARCHAR[] | The rolled-up values as text. |
| <formula / rollup property, date result> | STRUCT("start" TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE, "end" TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE, time_zone VARCHAR, has_time BOOLEAN) | Date result. |
| <other property types> | JSON | Raw value. |
| url | VARCHAR | Page URL in the Notion app. |
| created_time | TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE | When the page (row) was created. |
| last_edited_time | TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE | When the page was last edited (Notion rounds to the minute). |
| created_by | VARCHAR | User id of the page's creator. |
| last_edited_by | VARCHAR | User id of the last editor. |
| in_trash | BOOLEAN | true when the page is in the trash. |

Example: the Tasks data source the examples query (`1a2b3c4d-0000-4000-8000-00000000d501`) returns `id`, these property columns, then the metadata columns above.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Name | VARCHAR | title: the task name. |
| Name__json | JSON | Raw rich text of Name. |
| Status | VARCHAR | status: Not started, In progress or Done. |
| Priority | VARCHAR | select: High, Medium or Low. |
| Tags | VARCHAR[] | multi_select option names. |
| Assignee | VARCHAR[] | people: user ids. |
| Due | STRUCT("start" TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE, "end" TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE, time_zone VARCHAR, has_time BOOLEAN) | date (or range). |
| Estimate | DOUBLE | number. |
| Blocked | BOOLEAN | checkbox. |
| Project | VARCHAR[] | relation: page ids in the Projects data source. |
| Notes | VARCHAR | rich_text. |
| Notes__json | JSON | Raw rich text of Notes. |
| URL_2 | VARCHAR | url property 'URL' (renamed: it collides with the url column). |
| Owner email | VARCHAR | email. |
| Attachments | STRUCT("name" VARCHAR, "type" VARCHAR, url VARCHAR, expiry_time TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE)[] | files. |
| Task ID | BIGINT | unique_id number (prefix TASK). |
| Created | TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE | created_time. |
| Edited by | VARCHAR | last_edited_by user id. |
| Score | DOUBLE | formula with a number result. |
| Label | VARCHAR | formula with a text result. |
| Project count | DOUBLE | rollup count of Project. |
| Project names | VARCHAR[] | rollup show_original of the projects' names. |
