functions.name: query_database
functions.comment: Rows of a single-source Notion database (the database id from its URL) as a typed table

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Same as query_data_source, but takes a database id or the database's notion.so URL (what users copy from the browser) and queries its only data source. A database with several data sources is an error that lists them: use query_data_source with one of their ids. Rows (pages) of a Notion data source as a typed table: one column per property, named exactly as in Notion (quote names with spaces or capitals: "Status", "Due date"), plus id, url, created_time, last_edited_time, created_by, last_edited_by and in_trash. Types: title / rich_text `VARCHAR` plain text (+ "<name>__json" raw rich text `JSON`), number `DOUBLE`, checkbox `BOOLEAN`, select / status `VARCHAR`, multi_select `VARCHAR[]`, people / relation `VARCHAR[]` of ids (join users or another data source), date `STRUCT("start", "end" TIMESTAMPTZ, time_zone, has_time)` (filter with "Due".start), created / last edited time `TIMESTAMPTZ`, files `STRUCT(name, type, url, expiry_time)[]`, unique_id `BIGINT`, formula / rollup by result type. Call data_source_schema(id) first to see the exact column names and types. WHERE on properties pushes down into Notion's filter (equality, ranges, IN, LIKE '%…%' / contains / suffix, list_contains, IS NULL, AND/OR); only the columns you select are downloaded. Ids may be given as notion.so URLs.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## query_database(database_id, notion_filter := NULL, notion_sorts := NULL, rich_text_json := true)

The rows of a database that has one data source (most do). Each row is a page of the data source; each property becomes a typed column. `data_source_schema(id)` lists the columns. Pushdown: WHERE → Notion filter object (`and`/`or`, property conditions by type, `created_time`/`last_edited_time` timestamp filters), projection → `filter_properties`, `notion_sorts` → Notion sorts. Rows stream one 100-row page per batch with the Notion cursor kept as scan state.

vgi.example_queries.description: Tasks tagged 'search', addressing the database by its URL
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT "Name", "Tags" FROM notion.main.query_database('https://www.notion.so/acme/Tasks-1a2b3c4d00004000800000000000d001') WHERE list_contains("Tags", 'search') ORDER BY "Name"

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
Columns are computed from the data source's schema when the query is bound: `id`, then one column per property named exactly as in Notion (`data_source_schema(id)` lists each column's name and type; a `<name>__json` sibling follows each title / rich_text property, and a name colliding with another column gets a `_2` suffix), then the page metadata columns.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| id | VARCHAR | Page id of the row. |
| <title / rich_text property> | VARCHAR | Plain text. |
| <title / rich_text property>__json | JSON | Raw rich text (marks, links, mentions). |
| <number property> | DOUBLE | The number. |
| <checkbox property> | BOOLEAN | Ticked or not. |
| <select / status property> | VARCHAR | Option name. |
| <multi_select property> | VARCHAR[] | Option names. |
| <people / relation property> | VARCHAR[] | User ids / related page ids. |
| <date property> | STRUCT("start" TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE, "end" TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE, time_zone VARCHAR, has_time BOOLEAN) | Date or range; all-day dates at 00:00 UTC. |
| <created_time / last_edited_time property> | TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE | The instant. |
| <created_by / last_edited_by property> | VARCHAR | User id. |
| <url / email / phone_number property> | VARCHAR | The value. |
| <files property> | STRUCT("name" VARCHAR, "type" VARCHAR, url VARCHAR, expiry_time TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE)[] | Attached files. |
| <unique_id property> | BIGINT | The number (prefix in data_source_schema). |
| <formula property, text result> | VARCHAR | Formula result. |
| <formula property, boolean result> | BOOLEAN | Formula result. |
| <formula / rollup property, number result> | DOUBLE | Result (rollups: count, sum, average, …). |
| <rollup property, show_original / show_unique> | VARCHAR[] | The rolled-up values as text. |
| <formula / rollup property, date result> | STRUCT("start" TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE, "end" TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE, time_zone VARCHAR, has_time BOOLEAN) | Date result. |
| <other property types> | JSON | Raw value. |
| url | VARCHAR | Page URL in the Notion app. |
| created_time | TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE | When the page (row) was created. |
| last_edited_time | TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE | When the page was last edited (Notion rounds to the minute). |
| created_by | VARCHAR | User id of the page's creator. |
| last_edited_by | VARCHAR | User id of the last editor. |
| in_trash | BOOLEAN | true when the page is in the trash. |

Example: the Tasks data source the examples query (`1a2b3c4d-0000-4000-8000-00000000d501`) returns `id`, these property columns, then the metadata columns above.

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Name | VARCHAR | title: the task name. |
| Name__json | JSON | Raw rich text of Name. |
| Status | VARCHAR | status: Not started, In progress or Done. |
| Priority | VARCHAR | select: High, Medium or Low. |
| Tags | VARCHAR[] | multi_select option names. |
| Assignee | VARCHAR[] | people: user ids. |
| Due | STRUCT("start" TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE, "end" TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE, time_zone VARCHAR, has_time BOOLEAN) | date (or range). |
| Estimate | DOUBLE | number. |
| Blocked | BOOLEAN | checkbox. |
| Project | VARCHAR[] | relation: page ids in the Projects data source. |
| Notes | VARCHAR | rich_text. |
| Notes__json | JSON | Raw rich text of Notes. |
| URL_2 | VARCHAR | url property 'URL' (renamed: it collides with the url column). |
| Owner email | VARCHAR | email. |
| Attachments | STRUCT("name" VARCHAR, "type" VARCHAR, url VARCHAR, expiry_time TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE)[] | files. |
| Task ID | BIGINT | unique_id number (prefix TASK). |
| Created | TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE | created_time. |
| Edited by | VARCHAR | last_edited_by user id. |
| Score | DOUBLE | formula with a number result. |
| Label | VARCHAR | formula with a text result. |
| Project count | DOUBLE | rollup count of Project. |
| Project names | VARCHAR[] | rollup show_original of the projects' names. |

## blocks(block_id, max_depth := 10, include_child_pages := false)

Every block under a page, depth-first, with plain text. `ORDER BY path` restores document order.

workers.title: National Weather Service
workers.tagline: National Weather Service APIs, radar grids, and NOAA products as TypeScript VGI SQL functions
workers.subtitle: Explore US weather alerts, observations, forecast grids, bulletins, and river conditions.
workers.summary: US National Weather Service forecasts, alerts, observations and bulletins, river gauges and flood forecasts, plus NOAA outlook maps, buoys, space weather and MRMS radar grids, as SQL tables. No API key needed.
workers.doc_md:
# NWS and NWPS for DuckDB

Read US National Weather Service (NWS) and National Water Prediction Service (NWPS) data, plus related NOAA products, as SQL tables. The worker covers four kinds of data: weather (alerts, observations, gridded forecasts, original text bulletins, zones and forecast-office assets); rivers and floods (NWPS gauges, stage/flow forecasts, flood thresholds and impacts, rating curves, low-water information and National Water Model reaches); spatial products from the NOAA/NWS GIS map services (SPC, WPC and CPC outlook polygons, winter and hazard outlooks, observed and analyzed rainfall, soil moisture, snow and air-quality rasters, storm reports); and other NOAA feeds (NDBC buoys, SWPC space weather, NHC tropical products, AviationWeather.gov and native MRMS radar grids). How the parts fit: start from a latitude/longitude with the point lookup to find the forecast office, grid cell and nearby stations, or pass a known station, office, zone or NWPS gauge ID directly. Readers with an _at suffix intersect a product with one point; their unsuffixed counterparts return the whole product. Discovery functions list GIS layers, API operations, buoy files and MRMS products so generic readers can fetch them. Positional arguments accept columns and correlated LATERAL calls; named options inside a LATERAL call need DuckDB 2.0.1 or later. No API key is required. Times are UTC `TIMESTAMPTZ`, missing data is NULL, and grid, river and gauge-datum units are kept as published. Network readers include source_url and fetched_at, honor upstream HTTP caching and raise HTTP errors rather than silently returning no rows. Outlook probabilities and categories are forecast products, not active warnings. The upstream APIs serve current and recent data, not comprehensive historical archives.

Set NWS_USER_AGENT to an identifying application/contact string. See [NWS documentation](https://www.weather.gov/documentation/services-web-api) and [NWPS documentation](https://api.water.noaa.gov/nwps/v1/docs/).

## Sources and references

- [NWS API Web Service](https://www.weather.gov/documentation/services-web-api): forecasts, alerts, observations, zones and bulletins (api.weather.gov).
- [National Water Prediction Service API](https://api.water.noaa.gov/nwps/v1/docs/): river gauges, stage/flow forecasts, flood thresholds and National Water Model reaches.
- [NOAA/NWS GIS map services](https://mapservices.weather.noaa.gov/vector/rest/services): the ArcGIS REST services behind the outlook, map and raster readers.
- [Space Weather Prediction Center](https://www.swpc.noaa.gov/), [National Data Buoy Center](https://www.ndbc.noaa.gov/), [AviationWeather.gov Data API](https://aviationweather.gov/data/api/) and the [MRMS product server](https://mrms.ncep.noaa.gov/): the remaining upstreams read by the space weather, buoy, aviation and MRMS functions.

example_queries.description: Compare the RMDV2 forecast crest with the gauge's flood thresholds: the highest category reached (NULL when below action stage), the next category above the crest, and the feet of headroom left
example_queries.sql: WITH crest AS (SELECT gauge_id, primary_unit, max(primary_value) AS peak_stage FROM nws.main.stageflow('RMDV2', product := 'forecast') GROUP BY gauge_id, primary_unit) SELECT c.gauge_id, c.peak_stage, c.primary_unit AS unit, max_by(t.category, t.stage) FILTER (WHERE t.stage <= c.peak_stage) AS category_reached, min_by(t.category, t.stage) FILTER (WHERE t.stage > c.peak_stage) AS next_category, min(t.stage) FILTER (WHERE t.stage > c.peak_stage) - c.peak_stage AS headroom FROM crest c JOIN nws.main.flood_thresholds('RMDV2') t ON t.gauge_id = c.gauge_id AND t.stage_unit = c.primary_unit GROUP BY c.gauge_id, c.peak_stage, c.primary_unit ORDER BY c.gauge_id

example_queries.description: Read the latest observation from the three stations nearest Charlottesville, ranking the point's observation stations by approximate distance in kilometres
example_queries.sql: SELECT s.station_id, s.name, round(111.2 * sqrt((s.latitude - 38.0293) ^ 2 + ((s.longitude + 78.4767) * cos(radians(38.0293))) ^ 2), 1) AS distance_km, o.observed_at, o.temperature_c, o.wind_speed_m_s FROM nws.main.stations_at(38.0293, -78.4767) s, LATERAL nws.main.latest_observation(s.station_id) o ORDER BY distance_km, s.station_id LIMIT 3

example_queries.description: Resolve Charlottesville to the name and website of its forecast office and the name of its forecast zone
example_queries.sql: SELECT p.office_id, f.name AS office_name, f.website, p.forecast_zone, z.name AS zone_name FROM nws.main.point(38.0293, -78.4767) p, LATERAL nws.main.office(p.office_id) f, LATERAL nws.main.zone('forecast', p.forecast_zone) z ORDER BY p.office_id

example_queries.description: Find the forecast office and zone serving Charlottesville, Virginia
example_queries.sql: SELECT office_id, forecast_zone, grid_x, grid_y FROM nws.main.point(38.0293, -78.4767)

example_queries.description: Review active weather hazards in Virginia
example_queries.sql: SELECT event, severity, headline, expires FROM nws.main.alerts(area := 'VA') ORDER BY sent DESC

example_queries.description: Count the alerts that covered a garden in Charlottesville over the past week and list their event names; 0 alerts means no alert covered the point
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS alerts, list(DISTINCT event ORDER BY event) AS events, max(sent) AS latest_sent FROM nws.main.alerts_at(38.0293, -78.4767, active := false)

example_queries.description: Read full details for current Virginia alert identifiers
example_queries.sql: SELECT d.event, d.headline, d.description FROM nws.main.alerts(area := 'VA') a, LATERAL nws.main.alert(a.id) d LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Discover freeze-related alert event names
example_queries.sql: SELECT event FROM nws.main.alert_types() WHERE event ILIKE '%freeze%' ORDER BY event

example_queries.description: Discover weather observation stations for a location
example_queries.sql: SELECT station_id, name, elevation_m FROM nws.main.stations_at(38.0293, -78.4767) ORDER BY station_id

example_queries.description: Inspect Charlottesville airport observation station
example_queries.sql: SELECT station_id, name, elevation_m FROM nws.main.station('KCHO')

example_queries.description: Summarize recent temperatures from a station
example_queries.sql: SELECT min(temperature_c) AS minimum_c, max(temperature_c) AS maximum_c FROM nws.main.observations('KCHO')

example_queries.description: Inspect the latest temperature and wind observation
example_queries.sql: SELECT observed_at, temperature_c, wind_speed_m_s FROM nws.main.latest_observation('KCHO')

example_queries.description: Review the upcoming day/night forecast
example_queries.sql: SELECT start_time, temperature_c, short_forecast FROM nws.main.forecast(38.0293, -78.4767) ORDER BY start_time

example_queries.description: Inspect hourly garden temperatures
example_queries.sql: SELECT start_time, temperature_c, short_forecast FROM nws.main.forecast_hourly(38.0293, -78.4767) ORDER BY start_time

example_queries.description: Inspect minimum temperature intervals without assuming hourly samples
example_queries.sql: SELECT valid_from, valid_to, value, unit FROM nws.main.grid_series(38.0293, -78.4767, variable := 'minTemperature') ORDER BY valid_from

example_queries.description: Retrieve the forecast zone boundary for Albemarle County
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, geometry_json FROM nws.main.zone('forecast', 'VAZ037')

example_queries.description: Count the winter precipitation features covering Charlottesville and list their original categories or units; 0 features and NULL details mean no published area covers the point
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS features, list({'hazard': hazard, 'threshold_inches': threshold_inches, 'category': category, 'probability_min_pct': probability_min_pct, 'probability_max_pct': probability_max_pct, 'valid_from': valid_from} ORDER BY object_id) AS details FROM nws.main.winter_precipitation_at(38.0293, -78.4767, day := 1)

example_queries.description: Find current local weather story graphics
example_queries.sql: SELECT title, download_url FROM nws.main.weather_stories('LWX')

example_queries.description: Count the weather hazards features covering Charlottesville and list their original categories or units; 0 features and NULL details mean no published area covers the point
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS features, list({'period': period, 'hazard_group': hazard_group, 'hazard': hazard, 'valid_from': valid_from, 'valid_to': valid_to} ORDER BY object_id) AS details FROM nws.main.weather_hazards_at(38.0293, -78.4767)

example_queries.description: Count recent local storm reports by event type
example_queries.sql: SELECT event, count(*) AS reports FROM nws.main.storm_reports(lookback_hours := 72) GROUP BY event ORDER BY event

example_queries.description: Compare available observed and forecast peaks without mixing units
example_queries.sql: SELECT product, max(primary_value) AS peak, primary_unit FROM nws.main.stageflow('RMDV2') GROUP BY product, primary_unit ORDER BY product

example_queries.description: Inspect current and forecast NOAA space-weather scales without losing native probabilities
example_queries.sql: SELECT record_key, record_json FROM nws.main.space_weather_rows('products/noaa-scales.json') ORDER BY record_key

example_queries.description: Discover current GOES space-weather feeds
example_queries.sql: SELECT product_id, kind FROM nws.main.space_weather_products(folder := 'json/goes/primary') ORDER BY product_id

example_queries.description: Inspect modeled near-surface soil saturation at Charlottesville
example_queries.sql: SELECT region, saturation_pct, soil_depth_cm, valid_at FROM nws.main.soil_moisture_at(38.0293,-78.4767) ORDER BY region, raster_id

example_queries.description: Count the published severe outlook features and list their original categories or units; 0 features and NULL details mean none is currently published
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS features, list({'day': day, 'hazard': hazard, 'category': category, 'probability_pct': probability_pct, 'valid_from': valid_from, 'valid_to': valid_to} ORDER BY object_id) AS details FROM nws.main.severe_outlook(day := 1)

example_queries.description: Count the river flood outlook features covering Charlottesville and list their original categories or units; 0 features and NULL details mean no published area covers the point
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS features, list({'outlook': outlook, 'product': product, 'valid_from': valid_from, 'valid_to': valid_to} ORDER BY object_id) AS details FROM nws.main.river_flood_outlook_at(38.0293, -78.4767)

example_queries.description: Count the published river flood outlook features and list their original categories or units; 0 features and NULL details mean none is currently published
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS features, list({'outlook': outlook, 'product': product, 'valid_from': valid_from, 'valid_to': valid_to} ORDER BY object_id) AS details FROM nws.main.river_flood_outlook()

example_queries.description: List the NHC coastal watch and warning breakpoints with their original name, position and state fields

example_queries.description: Inspect current analyzed snow depth and water equivalent near Boulder
example_queries.sql: SELECT variable, raw_value, raw_unit, value_mm, valid_at FROM nws.main.snow_analysis_at(40,-105) ORDER BY variable, raster_id

example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS features, list({'period': period, 'contour_value': contour_value, 'unit': unit, 'valid_from': valid_from, 'valid_to': valid_to} ORDER BY object_id) AS details FROM nws.main.precipitation_forecast_at(38.0293, -78.4767, period := 'day1')

Start with point to discover a forecast office and grid, or use a station ID, office ID, or NWPS gauge ID directly. Positional inputs accept correlated LATERAL joins. Use land _at readers for modeled soil saturation, rainfall anomalies and analyzed snowpack, and storm_reports_near for radius searches of recent local reports. Use GIS outlook _at readers for point intersections, gauges_near for geographic river discovery, and alerts_at for zone-aware point alerts; use latest_product for complete bulletin text. Each network reader includes source_url and fetched_at; grid and river units remain explicit.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Weather, water, and reference functions

The main schema exposes weather, spatial outlook, and river readers plus the offline parse_valid_time interval helper. Start with point to discover a forecast office and grid, or use a station ID, office ID, or NWPS gauge ID directly. Positional inputs accept correlated LATERAL joins. Use land _at readers for modeled soil saturation, rainfall anomalies and analyzed snowpack, and storm_reports_near for radius searches of recent local reports. Use GIS outlook _at readers for point intersections, gauges_near for geographic river discovery, and alerts_at for zone-aware point alerts; use latest_product for complete bulletin text. Each network reader includes source_url and fetched_at; grid and river units remain explicit.

Weather readers preserve upstream missing values, timestamps, alert zones, and forecast intervals. River readers expose native units and gauge datums. Use parse_valid_time for an offline interval example.

vgi.example_queries.description: Compare the RMDV2 forecast crest with the gauge's flood thresholds: the highest category reached (NULL when below action stage), the next category above the crest, and the feet of headroom left
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH crest AS (SELECT gauge_id, primary_unit, max(primary_value) AS peak_stage FROM nws.main.stageflow('RMDV2', product := 'forecast') GROUP BY gauge_id, primary_unit) SELECT c.gauge_id, c.peak_stage, c.primary_unit AS unit, max_by(t.category, t.stage) FILTER (WHERE t.stage <= c.peak_stage) AS category_reached, min_by(t.category, t.stage) FILTER (WHERE t.stage > c.peak_stage) AS next_category, min(t.stage) FILTER (WHERE t.stage > c.peak_stage) - c.peak_stage AS headroom FROM crest c JOIN nws.main.flood_thresholds('RMDV2') t ON t.gauge_id = c.gauge_id AND t.stage_unit = c.primary_unit GROUP BY c.gauge_id, c.peak_stage, c.primary_unit ORDER BY c.gauge_id

vgi.example_queries.description: Read the latest observation from the three stations nearest Charlottesville, ranking the point's observation stations by approximate distance in kilometres
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT s.station_id, s.name, round(111.2 * sqrt((s.latitude - 38.0293) ^ 2 + ((s.longitude + 78.4767) * cos(radians(38.0293))) ^ 2), 1) AS distance_km, o.observed_at, o.temperature_c, o.wind_speed_m_s FROM nws.main.stations_at(38.0293, -78.4767) s, LATERAL nws.main.latest_observation(s.station_id) o ORDER BY distance_km, s.station_id LIMIT 3

vgi.example_queries.description: Resolve Charlottesville to the name and website of its forecast office and the name of its forecast zone
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT p.office_id, f.name AS office_name, f.website, p.forecast_zone, z.name AS zone_name FROM nws.main.point(38.0293, -78.4767) p, LATERAL nws.main.office(p.office_id) f, LATERAL nws.main.zone('forecast', p.forecast_zone) z ORDER BY p.office_id

functions.name: storm_reports
functions.comment: Read recent NWS Local Storm Reports with locations, native magnitudes/units, and remarks. These are preliminary reports, which may include estimates, corrections, or duplicate observations of the same event; they are not a complete verified event archive. Select one rolling 24/48/72-hour layer; overlapping windows are not additive. Event/state filters apply to each fetched page. No matching reports does not establish that no event occurred. Optionally restrict by WGS84 bbox, including dateline-crossing bounds; empty bbox scans the selected layer.

Select one rolling 24/48/72-hour layer; overlapping windows are not additive. Event/state filters apply to each fetched page. No matching reports does not establish that no event occurred. Optionally restrict by WGS84 bbox, including dateline-crossing bounds; empty bbox scans the selected layer.

Use the source_url and fetched_at columns for provenance. Units and missing values are retained. No API key is needed.

See [NWS API documentation](https://www.weather.gov/documentation/services-web-api).

vgi.example_queries.description: Compare the RMDV2 forecast crest with the gauge's flood thresholds: the highest category reached (NULL when below action stage), the next category above the crest, and the feet of headroom left
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH crest AS (SELECT gauge_id, primary_unit, max(primary_value) AS peak_stage FROM nws.main.stageflow('RMDV2', product := 'forecast') GROUP BY gauge_id, primary_unit) SELECT c.gauge_id, c.peak_stage, c.primary_unit AS unit, max_by(t.category, t.stage) FILTER (WHERE t.stage <= c.peak_stage) AS category_reached, min_by(t.category, t.stage) FILTER (WHERE t.stage > c.peak_stage) AS next_category, min(t.stage) FILTER (WHERE t.stage > c.peak_stage) - c.peak_stage AS headroom FROM crest c JOIN nws.main.flood_thresholds('RMDV2') t ON t.gauge_id = c.gauge_id AND t.stage_unit = c.primary_unit GROUP BY c.gauge_id, c.peak_stage, c.primary_unit ORDER BY c.gauge_id

functions.name: space_weather_rows
functions.comment: Read SWPC data records or original forecast/alert bulletin text. Object arrays emit native records; header-row tables become objects without changing native string/number/null values. NOAA-scale horizon keys remain record_key. Aurora grids emit one longitude/latitude/aurora row with original model timing and format in context_json. No physical units, missing codes or risk category are invented; consult native fields and the product's documentation. Explicit native UTC time_tag and aurora timestamps are exposed when available. Pages retain a source-content fingerprint and fail if the file changes mid-read. This is current published space-weather data, not a comprehensive archive.

functions.name: soil_moisture_at
functions.comment: Sample National Water Model near-surface soil moisture saturation for the top 40 cm. This is modeled saturation, not volumetric water content, a garden sensor reading, or an irrigation prescription. Native 0–1 fractions are preserved in raw_value and explicitly converted to saturation_pct. Auto checks all four published regional layers and retains their actual coverage. Raw NoData within a raster becomes NULL; no raster footprint emits no rows. Source valid, issue, file, and retrieval times remain separate. Each overlapping raster is a separate row; use its name and provenance, never sum overlaps. The service is not a historical archive.

Each overlapping raster is a separate row; use its name and provenance, never sum overlaps. The service is not a historical archive.

Use the source_url and fetched_at columns for provenance. Units and missing values are retained. No API key is needed.

functions.name: tropical_features
functions.comment: Read NHC/CPHC tropical development areas, forecast tracks/points/cones, watches and warnings, past tracks, wind radii/swaths, wind arrival contours, wind probability contours, peak storm surge features and coastal breakpoints. Resolve current layer IDs by exact source names. Native attributes retain product-specific units, probability ranges, wind thresholds, advisory identifiers and time wording; shared storm/advisory fields are exposed where present. A wallet is a reusable source slot, not a permanent cyclone ID. The cone describes track uncertainty, not the entire impact area; wind/probability contours overlap and must not be summed. Empty active-storm layers are legitimate. For surge inundation/tidal-mask pixels and static surge-risk scenarios, discover Mosaic Layers using map_layers and read with map_raster_at; static scenario maps are not live storm forecasts.

functions.name: snow_analysis_at
functions.comment: Sample NOHRSC analyzed snow depth and snow water equivalent for the conterminous US. These analyses combine model estimates and assimilated observations; these are current snowpack quantities, not new snowfall or forecasts. Native GRIB snow depth is metres and snow water equivalent is kg per square metre. value_mm converts depth to millimetres or water equivalent to millimetres of liquid water (1 kg/m² = 1 mm). Read variable with every value and do not sum depth with water equivalent. Native pixels differ from the inches shown in the map legend. Each variable retains its own valid time. Raw NoData within a raster becomes NULL; no raster footprint emits no rows. Source valid, issue, file, and retrieval times remain separate. Each overlapping raster is a separate row; use its name and provenance, never sum overlaps. The service is not a historical archive.

functions.name: precipitation_anomaly_at
functions.comment: Read RFC precipitation normals and comparisons with PRISM normals: normal amount, observed departure from normal, or percent of normal. Default all returns three separate metrics. Negative departure indicates a deficit; 100 percent means the normal amount, not a rain probability. Read the published pixels directly, without dividing by a potentially zero normal or inferring the climatological baseline years. Periods use the source's 12Z daily accounting, not local midnight. Different rasters may have different publication times. Raw NoData within a raster becomes NULL; no raster footprint emits no rows. Source valid, issue, file, and retrieval times remain separate. Each overlapping raster is a separate row; use its name and provenance, never sum overlaps. The service is not a historical archive.

functions.name: mesoscale_discussions_at
functions.comment: Read current SPC mesoscale discussion areas for developing severe thunderstorms or hazardous winter weather. Native discussion identifiers, descriptive information and popup HTML are preserved. Popup HTML includes the source discussion link; original bulletin text is also accessible through the worker's text-product readers. NoArea placeholder polygons are omitted. These are forecaster discussions, not warnings. Each discussion may have a different publication time. Returns every polygon intersecting the point, including boundaries; no match means no published intersecting feature, not a guarantee of no hazard.

functions.name: map_features_at
functions.comment: Read a discovered NWS Feature Layer as rows with native attributes and optional WGS84 GeoJSON. Supports all public NWS GIS product families, including sea ice, river breakup, fire spot forecasts, tropical and coastal layers. Resolve current layer IDs and field meanings with map_layers/map_fields. Pagination orders by the layer's declared object ID and supports dateline bounds. A live layer is not a transactional snapshot or a historical archive; independently issued features retain their own timestamps. Missing intersection does not establish absence of risk.

functions.name: winter_precipitation
functions.comment: Read WPC day 1–3 snow and ice accumulation probability bands. Snow thresholds are 4, 8, or 12 inches; ice uses 0.25 inches. functions.name: storm_reports_near
functions.comment: Read recent NWS Local Storm Reports with locations, native magnitudes/units, and remarks. These are preliminary reports, which may include estimates, corrections, or duplicate observations of the same event; they are not a complete verified event archive. Select one rolling 24/48/72-hour layer; overlapping windows are not additive. Event/state filters apply to each fetched page. No matching reports does not establish that no event occurred. Geographic bounds are followed by an exact great-circle radius filter, including dateline and polar locations. Order by distance_km for nearest reports.

functions.name: long_range_flood_outlook
functions.comment: Read three-month probabilistic river flood outlooks at NWS forecast gauges. Emits a row for each minor/moderate/major flood category, preserving censored probabilities such as <0.05 as bounds and explicit inclusivity flags. The map threshold selects the source classification layer and does not change the native category probabilities. target_period is native season text; exact dates are not inferred. Availability is limited to locations with probabilistic forecasts. State/gauge filters continue through every page.

functions.name: tropical_features_at
functions.comment: Read NHC/CPHC tropical development areas, forecast tracks/points/cones, watches and warnings, past tracks, wind radii/swaths, wind arrival contours, wind probability contours, peak storm surge features and coastal breakpoints. Resolve current layer IDs by exact source names. Native attributes retain product-specific units, probability ranges, wind thresholds, advisory identifiers and time wording; shared storm/advisory fields are exposed where present. A wallet is a reusable source slot, not a permanent cyclone ID. The cone describes track uncertainty, not the entire impact area; wind/probability contours overlap and must not be summed. Empty active-storm layers are legitimate. For surge inundation/tidal-mask pixels and static surge-risk scenarios, discover Mosaic Layers using map_layers and read with map_raster_at; static scenario maps are not live storm forecasts.

functions.name: weather_hazards
functions.comment: Read WPC/CPC days 3–7 or 8–14 weather-hazard outlooks. Native layer groups include temperature, precipitation, and wildfire/drought; the temperature group can also contain high winds, so interpret each hazard label. Labels are not invented probabilities or active warnings. Native start/end dates are retained at source precision; date-only end dates are inclusive. NoArea placeholder features are omitted. Optionally restrict results with bbox; intersecting polygons are returned without clipping.

functions.name: map_image_at
functions.comment: Sample every matching native raster in a NWS ImageServer at a point, preserving temporal slices and separate bands. Enumerates the image catalog and samples explicitly locked raster IDs in bounded pages, avoiding the service's silent mosaic limit. Optional dates filter native validity intervals. Native pixel values are not guaranteed physical measurements: some radar services contain color bands. No units, probabilities, or missing timestamps are invented. This is the currently published catalog, not a historical archive. Changes between catalog enumeration and sampling fail explicitly.

functions.name: fire_outlook_at
functions.comment: Read SPC day 1–8 fire-weather outlooks for wind/low humidity or dry thunderstorms. Days 1–2 use categorical codes; days 3–8 use native probability fractions, converted to percent separately. A zero code means no delineated probability area, not zero risk. These are not active fire perimeters or warnings. Returns every polygon intersecting the point, including boundaries; no match means no published intersecting feature, not a guarantee of no hazard.

functions.name: beach_forecast_at
functions.comment: Read NWS marine/beach forecast areas for day 1 or day 2. Rip/swim risk, surf, water temperature, UV, weather and wind wording are preserved as source text, because ranges and units vary by office. Unavailable values such as N/A remain distinguishable from measured zero. The service can include locations with no current forecast; has_forecast identifies usable product-date records. This does not supply a continuous coastal ocean model. Returns every polygon intersecting the point, including boundaries; no match means no published intersecting feature, not a guarantee of no hazard.

functions.name: air_quality_at
functions.comment: Read NWS air-quality forecast rasters at a point, covering all published PM2.5, ozone, smoke and dust service variants. Native values and complete currently published time slices are preserved. PM2.5 and surface dust use micrograms/m³ and ozone uses ppb according to service descriptions. Smoke and column-integral descriptions contain ambiguous units, so unit remains NULL and source_description/interpretation_note retain that uncertainty. No AQI, health category, or unit conversion is inferred. Product averaging periods and daily maxima are separate choices; native validity times remain authoritative. The hr01 bias-corrected PM2.5 service has conflicting legacy averaging prose, explicitly noted in output.

Native probability contour percentages are retained; they are not exact interpolated point probabilities. forecast_hour selects a published rolling 24-hour window ending at lead 24–168 hours in six-hour increments; zero returns every published window. Returns every polygon intersecting the point, including boundaries; no match means no published intersecting feature, not a guarantee of no hazard.

functions.name: mrms_at
functions.comment: Download and decode a native MRMS GRIB2 grid to return the nearest grid-cell value, not a rendered color. Uses native ECMWF ecCodes for regular latitude/longitude GRIB2 grids and the packing codecs enabled in that build, including PNG. Requires grib_ls and grib_get on PATH or in NWS_ECCODES_BIN. Defaults to the latest retained file and lowest available native file level; specify file_time and level to reproduce a listed file. Returns physical units and distinct missing/no-coverage/range-folded codes from NOAA's parameter table, preserving raw_value. Zero remains numeric even when a source table uses ambiguous zero codes, which are labeled. Unknown parameter codes retain raw values and NULL units. Outside the grid emits no rows. Unsupported/corrupt encodings fail explicitly. Each call reads a complete source grid: compressed downloads are bounded to 32 MiB, GRIB messages to 64 MiB, and grids to 64 million points. Native decoding is serialized per worker process with a 30-second limit per ecCodes command. Shared HTTP caching reduces repeated downloads; use GIS QPE sampling for lightweight routine rainfall queries.

functions.name: climate_outlook_at
functions.comment: Read CPC 6–10 day, 8–14 day, monthly, or seasonal temperature/precipitation outlooks. Seasonal leads 1–13 select successive three-month windows; monthly and seasonal target_period text is retained without inventing exact timestamps. Probabilities refer to the published above/near/below-normal category, not temperature values, rainfall amounts, or the chance of any rain. Forecast dates have day precision; the last validity date is inclusive. Returns every polygon intersecting the point, including boundaries; no match means no published intersecting feature, not a guarantee of no hazard.

functions.name: beach_forecast
functions.comment: Read NWS marine/beach forecast areas for day 1 or day 2. Rip/swim risk, surf, water temperature, UV, weather and wind wording are preserved as source text, because ranges and units vary by office. Unavailable values such as N/A remain distinguishable from measured zero. The service can include locations with no current forecast; has_forecast identifies usable product-date records. This does not supply a continuous coastal ocean model. Optionally restrict results with bbox; intersecting polygons are returned without clipping.

functions.name: api_rows
functions.comment: Read actual records from an operation discovered through api_endpoints, retaining all native JSON or original aviation text. GeoJSON features and standard collections emit one row per record; hierarchical products emit one complete JSON record, preserving their nested units and times. Follow NWS pagination to completion. Aviation has no pagination: responses reaching 400 records fail so filters can be narrowed. Missing aviation data (HTTP 204) emits no rows. Requests are limited to trusted official roots; schema constraints and parameter names are checked. Use dedicated typed readers where available and JSON extraction for less common products. Native geometry is not reprojected.

functions.name: mesoscale_discussions
functions.comment: Read current SPC mesoscale discussion areas for developing severe thunderstorms or hazardous winter weather. Native discussion identifiers, descriptive information and popup HTML are preserved. Popup HTML includes the source discussion link; original bulletin text is also accessible through the worker's text-product readers. NoArea placeholder polygons are omitted. These are forecaster discussions, not warnings. Each discussion may have a different publication time. Optionally restrict results with bbox; intersecting polygons are returned without clipping.

functions.name: buoy_measurements
functions.comment: Read NDBC realtime measurements as long-form rows with native variable names, units, timestamps and original value tokens. Supports all 15 current realtime formats, including directional wave spectra and DART seconds. MM and documented spectral/continuous-wind missing codes become NULL; zero remains zero and categorical text remains available. Each spectral bin has frequency_hz; ADCP bin names and quality fields remain distinct. Source files normally cover recent observations, not a complete historical archive. File content changes during paging raise an error. DART water-column heights are raw measurements, not tsunami warnings.

functions.name: flash_flood_guidance_at
functions.comment: Sample RFC gridded flash flood guidance: estimated rainfall over a selected duration that could cause small streams to flood under current soil/stream conditions. Native GRIB FFLDG values are kg/m², numerically equivalent to millimetres of water; inches are explicitly converted, never taken from a color class. Durations 1/3/6 hours have broad CONUS coverage; 12-hour guidance is regional. The discontinued 24-hour layer is rejected even if still listed. Coverage and RFC methods vary. This is guidance, not a forecast rainfall amount or an active warning. NoData remains NULL and no footprint emits no rows.

workers.title: OData v2/v4 Reader
workers.tagline: Query OData v2/v4 services as tables in DuckDB (Go)
workers.subtitle: Read OData v2/v4 REST services from SQL, with $filter pushdown, automatic paging and metadata discovery.
workers.summary: Query OData v2/v4 services and return their entities as rows
workers.doc_md:
# OData v2/v4 Reader for DuckDB

**Query any OData v2 or v4 REST service directly in SQL** — discover its entity sets, read entities as rows, and inspect `$metadata`, all without writing a line of HTTP or JSON-parsing code.

OData (the Open Data Protocol) is the JSON-over-REST standard behind a huge slice of enterprise data: Microsoft Dynamics 365 and Dataverse, SAP Gateway (S/4HANA and NetWeaver), Microsoft Graph, and countless in-house APIs all speak it. This extension turns those services into queryable tables, so analysts and data engineers can join live OData entities against the rest of their warehouse using plain SQL. It is a *generic* OData reader, not a vendor-specific connector, so the same three functions work against TripPin, Northwind, Dynamics, SAP, or any spec-compliant service.

Under the hood the worker speaks OData over HTTP using only the Go standard library — no heavyweight SDK — and streams results to DuckDB over Apache Arrow. It transparently follows server-driven paging (the v4 `@odata.nextLink` and the v2 `d.__next` cursor), pushes `$filter`, `$select`, `$orderby`, and `$top` down to the service so the server does the work, and understands both response shapes: v4 (`value` / `@odata.nextLink`) and v2 (`d.results` / `d.__next`). Protected services are supported via an optional bearer token argument.

The `main` schema exposes a small set of read functions covering the whole workflow: discovering the entity sets a service advertises in its service document, reading an entity set as rows of raw JSON (with `$filter`/`$select`/`$orderby`/`$top` pushdown, automatic nextLink paging, and a configurable row cap), and parsing an entity type's properties and EDM types from its `$metadata` (EDMX) document — namespace-agnostically across both EDM 3.0 (v2) and EDM 4.0 (v4). It also ships a browsable registry of well-known auth-free public services so you can start querying without a URL in hand. The catalog's executable examples and per-object example queries provide ready-to-run SQL, and the usual path is discover → inspect → read.

## Learn more

- [OData protocol homepage](https://www.odata.org)
- [OData official documentation](https://www.odata.org/documentation/)
- [Microsoft OData documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/odata/)
- [vgi-odata source code](https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-odata)
- [vgi-go SDK](https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-go)

example_queries.description: Discover the entity sets the TripPin OData service exposes.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name FROM odata.main.odata_entity_sets('https://services.odata.org/V4/TripPinService') ORDER BY name;

example_queries.description: Read the first 5 People entities and pull a field out of the raw JSON.
example_queries.sql: SELECT seq, json_extract_string(entity, '$.FirstName') AS first_name FROM odata.main.odata_query('https://services.odata.org/V4/TripPinService', 'People', top := '5') ORDER BY seq;

example_queries.description: Inspect the properties and EDM types of the Person entity type from $metadata.
example_queries.sql: SELECT property, type FROM odata.main.odata_metadata('https://services.odata.org/V4/TripPinService') WHERE entity_type = 'Person' ORDER BY property;

example_queries.description: Read the first 5 People entities and project a field out of the raw JSON.
example_queries.sql: SELECT seq, json_extract_string(entity, '$.FirstName') AS first_name FROM odata.main.odata_query('https://services.odata.org/V4/TripPinService', 'People', top := '5')

example_queries.description: Inspect the Person entity type's properties and EDM types from $metadata.
example_queries.sql: SELECT property, type FROM odata.main.odata_metadata('https://services.odata.org/V4/TripPinService') WHERE entity_type = 'Person'

example_queries.description: Profile data completeness: for every property the Person entity type declares in $metadata, count how many TripPin People entities carry a non-empty value (not null, an empty string, or an empty collection), least-populated first.
example_queries.sql: SELECT m.property, m.type, count(*) FILTER (WHERE coalesce(json_extract(p.entity, '$.' || m.property)::VARCHAR, 'null') NOT IN ('null', '""', '[]')) AS populated, count(*) AS people FROM odata.main.odata_metadata('https://services.odata.org/V4/TripPinService') AS m CROSS JOIN odata.main.odata_query('https://services.odata.org/V4/TripPinService', 'People') AS p WHERE m.entity_type = 'Person' GROUP BY m.property, m.type ORDER BY populated, m.property

example_queries.description: Summarise every numeric column of the Northwind Products entity set: take the Product properties $metadata declares as Edm.Int16/Int32/Decimal/Double and compute each one's min, max and average across all products.
example_queries.sql: WITH product_values AS (SELECT m.property, m.type, TRY_CAST(json_extract_string(p.entity, '$.' || m.property) AS DOUBLE) AS amount FROM odata.main.odata_metadata('https://services.odata.org/V4/Northwind/Northwind.svc') AS m CROSS JOIN odata.main.odata_query('https://services.odata.org/V4/Northwind/Northwind.svc', 'Products') AS p WHERE m.entity_type = 'Product' AND m.type IN ('Edm.Int16', 'Edm.Int32', 'Edm.Decimal', 'Edm.Double')) SELECT property, type, min(amount) AS min_value, max(amount) AS max_value, round(avg(amount), 2) AS avg_value FROM product_values GROUP BY property, type ORDER BY property

example_queries.description: Join two entity sets client-side: the five Northwind customers with the most orders, matching Orders to Customers on CustomerID and pushing $select down so only the needed fields are fetched.
example_queries.sql: SELECT json_extract_string(c.entity, '$.CompanyName') AS company, json_extract_string(c.entity, '$.Country') AS country, count(*) AS orders FROM odata.main.odata_query('https://services.odata.org/V4/Northwind/Northwind.svc', 'Customers', "select" := 'CustomerID,CompanyName,Country') AS c JOIN odata.main.odata_query('https://services.odata.org/V4/Northwind/Northwind.svc', 'Orders', "select" := 'OrderID,CustomerID') AS o ON json_extract_string(o.entity, '$.CustomerID') = json_extract_string(c.entity, '$.CustomerID') GROUP BY company, country ORDER BY orders DESC, company LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: List the auth-free public OData v4 services this worker ships, newest-style first.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, service_url FROM odata.main.odata_public_services WHERE odata_version = 'v4' ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Count the registered public services grouped by OData protocol version.
example_queries.sql: SELECT odata_version, count(*) AS services FROM odata.main.odata_public_services GROUP BY odata_version ORDER BY odata_version

example_queries.description: Count the German customers in the public Northwind OData v4 sample, pushing the predicate down to the service via the OData $filter option.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM odata.main.odata_query('https://services.odata.org/V4/Northwind/Northwind.svc', 'Customers', "filter" := 'Country eq ''Germany''', max_rows := 1000);

## odata_public_services

A curated registry of **well-known, public, authentication-free OData services** you can query immediately — no credentials, no setup.

### Overview

Every row is a real OData service root plus its protocol version and a short description. Use it as the zero-argument starting point for exploration: pick a `service_url`, then pass it to `odata_entity_sets` to see what the service exposes, `odata_metadata` to inspect an entity type's schema, or `odata_query` to read rows. Because the view is a static in-worker registry, it scans instantly and works offline even when a listed service is unreachable.

### Columns

- `name` (`VARCHAR`) — short human-friendly service name.
- `service_url` (`VARCHAR`) — the service root URL; feed it to the OData functions.
- `odata_version` (`VARCHAR`) — `v2`, `v3`, or `v4`; pass `version := 'v2'` to `odata_query` for a v2 service.
- `description` (`VARCHAR`) — what the service contains.

### Notes

The registry is a convenience sample of stable public reference services, not an exhaustive directory — this worker can query any spec-compliant OData v2/v4 endpoint, not only these.

## odata_metadata

Inspect an OData service's **`$metadata` (EDMX) schema**.

### Overview

Fetches and parses the service's `$metadata` (EDMX/CSDL) document and returns one row per entity-type property: the entity type name, the property name, and the property's EDM type. Use it to learn the shape and column types of an entity before querying it with `odata_query`.

### Result

One row per entity-type property, with `entity_type`, `property`, and `type` (the property's EDM type) columns. Filter by `entity_type` to inspect a single type. See this function's example queries for ready-to-run SQL against the public TripPin service.

### Notes

- Parsing is namespace-agnostic, so both OData v2 (EDM 3.0) and v4 (EDM 4.0) documents are supported.
- Pass `token := '<bearer>'` for protected services; a NULL `service_url` yields zero rows.

## odata_entity_sets

List the **entity sets** an OData service exposes.

### Overview

Push $filter/$select/$orderby/$top down to the service as system query options, and authenticate with an optional bearer token. ## odata_query

Read an **OData v2/v4 entity set** as rows of raw JSON.

### Overview

Fetches an entity set from an OData service and returns one row per entity, following `@odata.nextLink` (v4) or `d.__next` (v2) paging automatically until the set is exhausted or `max_rows` is reached.

### Result

Each row has `seq` (0-based position of the entity across all fetched pages) and `entity` (the entity's raw JSON object text). Project individual fields with DuckDB's `json_extract` / `json_extract_string`. See this function's example queries for ready-to-run SQL against the public TripPin service.

### Notes

- Push `$filter`/`$select`/`$orderby`/`$top` down to the service with the matching named arguments; `"filter"` and `"select"` must be quoted (SQL keywords).
- Pass `version := 'v2'` for OData v2 services and `token := '<bearer>'` for protected services.
- A NULL `service_url` or `entity_set` yields zero rows rather than an error.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT seq, json_extract_string(entity, '$.FirstName') AS first_name FROM odata.main.odata_query('https://services.odata.org/V4/TripPinService', 'People', top := '5');

vgi.example_queries.description: Join two entity sets client-side: the five Northwind customers with the most orders, matching Orders to Customers on CustomerID and pushing $select down so only the needed fields are fetched.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT json_extract_string(c.entity, '$.CompanyName') AS company, json_extract_string(c.entity, '$.Country') AS country, count(*) AS orders FROM odata.main.odata_query('https://services.odata.org/V4/Northwind/Northwind.svc', 'Customers', "select" := 'CustomerID,CompanyName,Country') AS c JOIN odata.main.odata_query('https://services.odata.org/V4/Northwind/Northwind.svc', 'Orders', "select" := 'OrderID,CustomerID') AS o ON json_extract_string(o.entity, '$.CustomerID') = json_extract_string(c.entity, '$.CustomerID') GROUP BY company, country ORDER BY orders DESC, company LIMIT 5

vgi.example_queries.description: Summarise every numeric column of the Northwind Products entity set: take the Product properties $metadata declares as Edm.Int16/Int32/Decimal/Double and compute each one's min, max and average across all products.
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH product_values AS (SELECT m.property, m.type, TRY_CAST(json_extract_string(p.entity, '$.' || m.property) AS DOUBLE) AS amount FROM odata.main.odata_metadata('https://services.odata.org/V4/Northwind/Northwind.svc') AS m CROSS JOIN odata.main.odata_query('https://services.odata.org/V4/Northwind/Northwind.svc', 'Products') AS p WHERE m.entity_type = 'Product' AND m.type IN ('Edm.Int16', 'Edm.Int32', 'Edm.Decimal', 'Edm.Double')) SELECT property, type, min(amount) AS min_value, max(amount) AS max_value, round(avg(amount), 2) AS avg_value FROM product_values GROUP BY property, type ORDER BY property

workers.title: Okta Workforce Identity
workers.tagline: Okta users, groups, apps, policies and System Log as SQL in DuckDB (TypeScript)
workers.subtitle: Okta users, groups, apps, policies, admin roles, devices and System Log events as SQL tables.
workers.summary: Okta Workforce Identity as SQL: users, groups, apps, policies, admin roles, devices and the System Log, read-only from the Okta Management API.
workers.doc_md:
# Okta

Query an Okta Workforce Identity org from DuckDB: users, groups and memberships, app assignments, MFA factors, policies, admin roles, devices, network zones and the System Log. Read-only.

Create an `okta` secret with your org URL (`ORG_URL`) and either an SSWS API token (`API_TOKEN`) or an OAuth 2.0 service app (`CLIENT_ID` + `PRIVATE_KEY`). Filters are translated into Okta's search/filter syntax and the System Log time window, so only matching rows cross the network; Link header paging and Okta's rate-limit headers are handled for you.

### Sources and references

- [Okta Management API](https://developer.okta.com/docs/api/openapi/okta-management/guides/overview/) — the endpoints this worker reads
- [Users API](https://developer.okta.com/docs/api/openapi/okta-management/management/tag/User/) and [search syntax](https://developer.okta.com/docs/api/#filter)
- [System Log API](https://developer.okta.com/docs/api/openapi/okta-management/management/tag/SystemLog/) — since/until/filter/q
- [Pagination](https://developer.okta.com/docs/api/#pagination) and [rate limits](https://developer.okta.com/docs/reference/rl-best-practices/)
- [API tokens](https://help.okta.com/en-us/content/topics/security/api.htm) and [OAuth 2.0 service apps](https://developer.okta.com/docs/guides/implement-oauth-for-okta-serviceapp/main/)
workers.readme_sql:
CREATE SECRET okta (TYPE okta, ORG_URL 'https://acme.okta.com', API_TOKEN '00a…');

-- Active engineers who have not signed in for 90 days (one Okta search request).
SELECT login, display_name, last_login
FROM okta.main.users()
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE' AND department = 'Engineering'
  AND (last_login IS NULL OR last_login < now() - INTERVAL 90 DAY);

-- Failed sign-ins in the last day, by user (since/until + filter pushed to /api/v1/logs).
SELECT actor_alternate_id, count(*) AS failures
FROM okta.main.system_log()
WHERE published > now() - INTERVAL 1 DAY
  AND event_type = 'user.session.start' AND outcome_result = 'FAILURE'
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY failures DESC;

example_queries.title: users_columns
example_queries.description: The users() result columns (binds only; attach an okta secret and drop LIMIT 0 for rows)
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, login, status, account_enabled, last_login FROM okta.main.users() LIMIT 0;

example_queries.title: system_log_columns
example_queries.description: The system_log() result columns (binds only; attach an okta secret and drop LIMIT 0 for rows)
example_queries.sql: SELECT published, event_type, actor_alternate_id, outcome_result FROM okta.main.system_log() LIMIT 0;

example_queries.description: Active engineers (both predicates become one Okta search)
example_queries.sql: SELECT login, display_name, department FROM okta.main.users() WHERE status = 'ACTIVE' AND department = 'Engineering' ORDER BY login

example_queries.description: User count by lifecycle status
example_queries.sql: SELECT status, count(*) AS users FROM okta.main.users() GROUP BY status ORDER BY users DESC

example_queries.description: Status and last sign-in of one user
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, status, last_login FROM okta.main.user('ada@example.com')

example_queries.description: Group names for one user
example_queries.sql: SELECT display_name FROM okta.main.user_groups(user_id := 'ada@example.com') ORDER BY display_name

example_queries.description: Users by number of group memberships
example_queries.sql: SELECT u.login, count(*) AS groups FROM okta.main.user_groups() g JOIN okta.main.users() u ON u.id = g.user_id GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY groups DESC

example_queries.description: Factors one user has enrolled
example_queries.sql: SELECT factor_type, status FROM okta.main.user_factors(user_id := 'ada@example.com') ORDER BY factor_type

example_queries.description: MFA adoption by factor type
example_queries.sql: SELECT factor_type, count(DISTINCT user_id) AS users FROM okta.main.user_factors() WHERE status = 'ACTIVE' GROUP BY factor_type ORDER BY users DESC

example_queries.description: Okta-mastered groups and when their membership last changed
example_queries.sql: SELECT display_name, last_membership_updated FROM okta.main.groups() WHERE group_type = 'OKTA_GROUP' ORDER BY display_name

example_queries.description: Groups by type
example_queries.sql: SELECT group_type, count(*) FROM okta.main.groups() GROUP BY group_type ORDER BY group_type

example_queries.description: Active members of one group (group_id pushes down)
example_queries.sql: SELECT login, status FROM okta.main.group_members() WHERE group_id = '00g2eng' AND account_enabled ORDER BY login

example_queries.description: Member count per group
example_queries.sql: SELECT g.display_name, count(*) AS members FROM okta.main.group_members() m JOIN okta.main.groups() g ON g.id = m.group_id GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY members DESC

example_queries.description: Broken group rules
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, expression FROM okta.main.group_rules() WHERE status = 'INVALID' ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Blocklisted zones and their CIDRs
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, gateways FROM okta.main.network_zones WHERE usage = 'BLOCKLIST' ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Active policies in evaluation order
example_queries.sql: SELECT type, name, priority FROM okta.main.policies WHERE status = 'ACTIVE' ORDER BY type, priority

example_queries.description: Password policies only (one API call)
example_queries.sql: SELECT name FROM okta.main.policies WHERE type = 'PASSWORD' ORDER BY priority

example_queries.description: Every global session policy rule
example_queries.sql: SELECT p.name AS policy, r.name AS rule, r.status FROM okta.main.policy_rules() r JOIN okta.main.policies p ON p.id = r.policy_id WHERE p.type = 'OKTA_SIGN_ON' ORDER BY ALL

example_queries.description: Whether each rule of one policy requires MFA
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, priority, actions->'signon'->>'requireFactor' AS mfa FROM okta.main.policy_rules(policy_id := '00p1signon') ORDER BY priority

example_queries.description: Users with the most failed sign-ins since a date (window and filters pushed to Okta)
example_queries.sql: SELECT actor_alternate_id, count(*) AS failures FROM okta.main.system_log() WHERE published >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01 00:00:00+00' AND event_type = 'user.session.start' AND outcome_result = 'FAILURE' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY failures DESC LIMIT 20

example_queries.description: Latest policy changes in the last 7 days
example_queries.sql: SELECT published, event_type, display_message FROM okta.main.system_log(sort_order := 'DESCENDING') WHERE starts_with(event_type, 'policy.') ORDER BY published DESC LIMIT 50

example_queries.description: Active devices by platform
example_queries.sql: SELECT operating_system, count(*) AS devices FROM okta.main.devices() WHERE status = 'ACTIVE' GROUP BY operating_system ORDER BY devices DESC

example_queries.description: Macs without secure hardware
example_queries.sql: SELECT display_name, os_version FROM okta.main.devices() WHERE operating_system = 'MACOS' AND NOT secure_hardware_present ORDER BY display_name

example_queries.description: Names of the groups assigned to an app
example_queries.sql: SELECT a.group_id, g.display_name FROM okta.main.app_groups(app_id := '0oa1salesforce') a JOIN okta.main.groups() g ON g.id = a.group_id ORDER BY g.display_name

example_queries.description: Active authorization servers and their next key rotation
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, issuer, signing_next_rotation FROM okta.main.authorization_servers() WHERE status = 'ACTIVE' ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: How many users hold each admin role
example_queries.sql: SELECT role_type, count(DISTINCT principal_id) AS admins FROM okta.main.admin_role_assignments() GROUP BY role_type ORDER BY admins DESC

example_queries.description: Super administrators by login
example_queries.sql: SELECT u.login, r.assignment_type FROM okta.main.admin_role_assignments() r JOIN okta.main.users() u ON u.id = r.principal_id WHERE r.role_type = 'SUPER_ADMIN' ORDER BY u.login

example_queries.description: Active apps and their sign-on mode
example_queries.sql: SELECT label, sign_on_mode FROM okta.main.apps() WHERE status = 'ACTIVE' ORDER BY label

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Okta Management API collections as SQL. Org-wide collections are table functions with optional named arguments (a raw Okta `search := ` expression, keyword `q := `, `page_size := `) or plain tables when they take none. Per-parent collections (memberships, assignments, factors, rules) accept the parent id as a named argument or a pushed `= / IN` filter on that id column and otherwise read every parent, one extra API call each. The System Log is time-windowed: filter on published to choose the window (default lookback 7 days, Okta retains 90). All objects need an `okta` secret.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

Okta Management API collections: the directory, applications and their assignments, security configuration and the System Log.

Org-wide collections are table functions (or tables when they take no arguments). Per-parent collections take the parent id as a named argument or a pushed filter and otherwise read every parent.

All objects need an `okta` secret; filters push down into Okta's search and filter syntax.

functions.name: system_log
functions.comment: Okta System Log events, with time window and filters pushed down

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Okta System Log events (GET /api/v1/logs) — sign-ins, MFA, admin changes, provisioning. Columns: uuid (also id), published (also created_date_time), event_type, display_message, severity, actor (id, type, alternate_id, display_name; user_principal_name when the actor is a user), outcome_result (also status) and outcome_reason, client ip_address / user agent / OS / browser / zone, geo city/state/country/lat/lon, app_display_name (first AppInstance target), targets (list of structs), transaction_id, external_session_id and debug_data JSON. ALWAYS filter on published: `published >= / > / < / <=` become Okta's since/until; without one the last `lookback_days` (default 7) are read. Okta retains 90 days, so older lower bounds are clamped to the retention window. Filters on event_type (eq / IN / starts_with), actor_id, actor_alternate_id, actor_type, outcome_result / status, severity, ip_address, transaction_id and uuid become Okta's `filter` expression; `q := 'word'` adds keyword search and `filter_expr := '…'` a raw filter expression.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## system_log(q := NULL, filter_expr := NULL, lookback_days := 7, sort_order := 'ASCENDING', page_size := 1000)

Okta System Log events. Columns align with the Entra sign-in/audit workers (`created_date_time`, `user_principal_name`, `app_display_name`, `ip_address`, `status`).

**Pushdown:** `published`/`created_date_time` ranges → `since`/`until` (clamped to 90-day retention; always bounded by the scan start); `event_type` (eq, IN, starts_with), `actor_id`, `actor_alternate_id`, `actor_type`, `outcome_result`/`status`, `severity`, `ip_address`, `transaction_id`, `uuid`/`id` → `filter`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Users with the most failed sign-ins since a date (window and filters pushed to Okta)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT actor_alternate_id, count(*) AS failures FROM okta.main.system_log() WHERE published >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01 00:00:00+00' AND event_type = 'user.session.start' AND outcome_result = 'FAILURE' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY failures DESC LIMIT 20

vgi.example_queries.description: Latest policy changes in the last 7 days
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT published, event_type, display_message FROM okta.main.system_log(sort_order := 'DESCENDING') WHERE starts_with(event_type, 'policy.') ORDER BY published DESC LIMIT 50

workers.title: Open-Meteo Weather
workers.tagline: Open-Meteo weather API family as queryable DuckDB table functions (VGI worker)
workers.summary: Weather, air-quality, marine, flood, climate, geocoding & elevation (Open-Meteo)
workers.doc_md:
## Open-Meteo weather for DuckDB

[Open-Meteo](https://open-meteo.com) is a free, high-resolution weather API. This catalog wraps it
as SQL table functions so you can query weather, climate and geospatial data directly from DuckDB.

### What you can ask

Point-based **forecasts** (hourly, daily, current), **historical** reanalysis back to 1940, **air quality**, **marine** waves and swell, **flood** river-discharge, and downscaled **climate** projections. A **geocoding** search maps place names to coordinates, and an **elevation** lookup returns terrain height. Inline **decoding macros** turn raw coded columns into labels (weather code → text/emoji, wind direction → compass, AQI and UV → categories).

### Conventions

Every function takes a `latitude`/`longitude` (geocoding takes a `name`). Timestamps are always returned in UTC; a `timezone` argument only controls how daily aggregates are bucketed. Commercial customers can pass an `apikey` at ATTACH time to use the paid endpoints.

attach_options.name: apikey
attach_options.description: Open-Meteo commercial API key. Omit for the free tier. When set, requests use the customer-* API hosts.

example_queries.title: elevation_echoes_coordinate
example_queries.description: elevation() echoes the requested coordinate and adds terrain height.
example_queries.sql: SELECT latitude, longitude FROM open_meteo.main.elevation(52.52, 13.41);

example_queries.title: geocoding_resolves_place_name
example_queries.description: geocoding() turns a place name into the coordinate the weather functions want — the starting point for anyone who has a city rather than a latitude.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, country_code FROM open_meteo.main.geocoding('Tokyo', count := 1);

example_queries.description: Current conditions in Berlin, weather code decoded to text.
example_queries.sql: SELECT temperature_2m, open_meteo.main.weather_code_text(weather_code) AS conditions FROM open_meteo.main.forecast_current(52.52, 13.41)

example_queries.description: Geocode a place name; its coordinates feed the forecast functions.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, latitude, longitude FROM open_meteo.main.geocoding('Paris', count := 1)

example_queries.description: The usual starting point: a place name joined straight through to its current weather.
example_queries.sql: SELECT g.name, w.temperature_2m, open_meteo.main.weather_code_text(w.weather_code) AS conditions FROM open_meteo.main.geocoding('Paris', count := 1) AS g, LATERAL open_meteo.main.forecast_current(g.latitude, g.longitude) AS w

example_queries.description: A column of place names geocoded and forecast in one query, each city's days in its own local time ('auto' is resolved from each row's coordinates).
example_queries.sql: SELECT p.city, d.time, d.temperature_2m_max FROM (VALUES ('Berlin'), ('Tokyo')) AS p(city), LATERAL open_meteo.main.geocoding(p.city, count := 1) AS g, LATERAL open_meteo.main.forecast_daily(g.latitude, g.longitude, forecast_days := 3, timezone := 'auto') AS d ORDER BY p.city, d.time

example_queries.description: Label a forecast by joining to the code table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT f.time, w.description, w.emoji FROM open_meteo.main.forecast_hourly(52.52, 13.41, forecast_days := 1) f JOIN open_meteo.main.weather_codes w ON w.code = f.weather_code ORDER BY f.time

example_queries.description: Same, for a place named rather than located: geocode, forecast, then label.
example_queries.sql: SELECT g.name, f.time, w.description, w.emoji FROM open_meteo.main.geocoding('Oslo', count := 1) AS g, LATERAL open_meteo.main.forecast_hourly(g.latitude, g.longitude, forecast_days := 1) AS f JOIN open_meteo.main.weather_codes w ON w.code = f.weather_code ORDER BY f.time

example_queries.description: Browse the lookup on its own — no arguments needed.
example_queries.sql: SELECT code, description, emoji FROM open_meteo.main.weather_codes ORDER BY code

example_queries.description: Hourly forecasts from successive earlier model runs, for scoring forecast skill by lead time (Berlin).
example_queries.sql: SELECT time, temperature_2m, temperature_2m_previous_day1 FROM open_meteo.main.previous_runs_hourly(52.52, 13.41) ORDER BY time

example_queries.description: Next 3 days, daily buckets in the location's local time zone.
example_queries.sql: SELECT time, temperature_2m, temperature_2m_previous_day1 FROM open_meteo.main.previous_runs_hourly(52.52, 13.41, forecast_days := 3, timezone := 'auto') ORDER BY time

example_queries.description: The past 7 days instead of the forecast window.
example_queries.sql: SELECT time, temperature_2m, temperature_2m_previous_day1 FROM open_meteo.main.previous_runs_hourly(52.52, 13.41, past_days := 7, forecast_days := 0) ORDER BY time

example_queries.description: Imperial units (°F, mph).
example_queries.sql: SELECT time, temperature_2m, temperature_2m_previous_day1 FROM open_meteo.main.previous_runs_hourly(52.52, 13.41, temperature_unit := 'fahrenheit', wind_speed_unit := 'mph') ORDER BY time

example_queries.description: Many locations in one query — coordinates supplied by a column.
example_queries.sql: SELECT c.city, w.time, w.temperature_2m FROM (VALUES ('Berlin', 52.52, 13.41), ('Tokyo', 35.69, 139.69)) AS c(city, lat, lon), LATERAL open_meteo.main.previous_runs_hourly(c.lat, c.lon) AS w

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The main schema holds the full Open-Meteo function family. It groups point-based weather into forecast (hourly/daily/current), historical reanalysis, air-quality, marine, flood and climate-projection categories, plus two helpers: geocoding to resolve place names to coordinates and elevation to look up terrain height. All functions share one calling convention — a WGS84 latitude/longitude and named optional arguments (timezone, units, forecast_days, date ranges, model for forecast/history, models for specialist functions) — and emit UTC timestamps. Positional arguments accept columns, so use a LATERAL join over a bounded coordinates table for multi-location queries or to chain geocoding into weather. The schema also provides inline SQL decoding macros in its 'helpers' category — weather_code_text and weather_code_emoji (WMO code), wind_compass (degrees to a 16-point compass), us_aqi_category / european_aqi_category, and uv_index_category — that turn the raw coded columns into human-readable labels; call them schema-qualified, e.g. weather_code_text(weather_code).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Open-Meteo functions

Point-based weather, climate and geospatial functions from [Open-Meteo](https://open-meteo.com), organized into forecast, historical, air-quality, marine, flood and climate categories, plus geocoding and elevation helpers.

Every function shares one calling convention: a WGS84 `latitude`/`longitude` (geocoding takes a `name`), named optional arguments, and UTC timestamps. Positional arguments may be columns: use a bounded `LATERAL` join for several locations, or chain `geocoding(...)` directly into a weather function in one query.

### Decoding helpers

Several columns come back as raw codes. The schema's `helpers` category adds inline SQL macros that decode them — `weather_code_text` / `weather_code_emoji`, `wind_compass`, `us_aqi_category` / `european_aqi_category`, and `uv_index_category`. They expand inline (no round-trip); call them schema-qualified alongside the functions (applying, say, `weather_code_text` to the `weather_code` column). The browsable `weather_codes` view lists every WMO code with its text and emoji. See each object's example queries for runnable SQL.

vgi.example_queries.description: Current conditions in Berlin, weather code decoded to text.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT temperature_2m, open_meteo.main.weather_code_text(weather_code) AS conditions FROM open_meteo.main.forecast_current(52.52, 13.41)

vgi.example_queries.description: Geocode a place name; its coordinates feed the forecast functions.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, latitude, longitude FROM open_meteo.main.geocoding('Paris', count := 1)

vgi.example_queries.description: The usual starting point: a place name joined straight through to its current weather.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT g.name, w.temperature_2m, open_meteo.main.weather_code_text(w.weather_code) AS conditions FROM open_meteo.main.geocoding('Paris', count := 1) AS g, LATERAL open_meteo.main.forecast_current(g.latitude, g.longitude) AS w

vgi.example_queries.description: A column of place names geocoded and forecast in one query, each city's days in its own local time ('auto' is resolved from each row's coordinates).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT p.city, d.time, d.temperature_2m_max FROM (VALUES ('Berlin'), ('Tokyo')) AS p(city), LATERAL open_meteo.main.geocoding(p.city, count := 1) AS g, LATERAL open_meteo.main.forecast_daily(g.latitude, g.longitude, forecast_days := 3, timezone := 'auto') AS d ORDER BY p.city, d.time

## weather_codes

The complete WMO 4677 weather-code table (`code`, `description`, `emoji`). Unlike the weather functions it needs no arguments, so it is directly browsable, and it is the lookup behind the `weather_code_text` / `weather_code_emoji` macros. JOIN it to a forecast's `weather_code` column, or query it on its own. See its example queries for runnable SQL.

vgi.example_queries.description: Label a forecast by joining to the code table.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT f.time, w.description, w.emoji FROM open_meteo.main.forecast_hourly(52.52, 13.41, forecast_days := 1) f JOIN open_meteo.main.weather_codes w ON w.code = f.weather_code ORDER BY f.time

vgi.example_queries.description: Same, for a place named rather than located: geocode, forecast, then label.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT g.name, f.time, w.description, w.emoji FROM open_meteo.main.geocoding('Oslo', count := 1) AS g, LATERAL open_meteo.main.forecast_hourly(g.latitude, g.longitude, forecast_days := 1) AS f JOIN open_meteo.main.weather_codes w ON w.code = f.weather_code ORDER BY f.time

vgi.example_queries.description: Browse the lookup on its own — no arguments needed.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT code, description, emoji FROM open_meteo.main.weather_codes ORDER BY code

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## previous_runs_hourly

Hourly forecasts from successive earlier model runs, for scoring forecast skill by lead time.

Pass `latitude` and `longitude` in WGS84 degrees. The function returns one row per hour; every timestamp is emitted in UTC. Notes: the window is set with forecast_days / past_days; units are configurable (temperature_unit, wind_speed_unit, precipitation_unit); specific models can be selected with the models argument; timezone only shifts where the window starts and how daily buckets are aligned — instants stay UTC; use timezone := 'auto' to resolve the zone from each row's coordinates; the provider holds one UTC offset across a response.

If you have a place name rather than a coordinate, resolve it with `geocoding(...)` and join its `latitude`/`longitude` straight in — the positional arguments take column references, so name → weather stays one query.

Returned columns are `time` plus `temperature_2m`, `temperature_2m_previous_day1`, `temperature_2m_previous_day2` and more — see the result schema for the full set with types. Runnable queries live in this function's example queries rather than inline here.

## marine_daily

Daily marine forecast (wave/swell maxima) for a coordinate.

Pass `latitude` and `longitude` in WGS84 degrees. The function returns one row per day; every timestamp is emitted in UTC. Notes: the window is set with forecast_days / past_days; timezone only shifts where the window starts and how daily buckets are aligned — instants stay UTC; use timezone := 'auto' to resolve the zone from each row's coordinates; the provider holds one UTC offset across a response.
