## us_aqi_category

Maps a US AQI number to its EPA health category. Apply it to the `us_aqi` column of an air_quality function; see this macro's example queries for a runnable form.

vgi.example_queries.description: US AQI category for current conditions in Los Angeles.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT us_aqi, open_meteo.main.us_aqi_category(us_aqi) AS category FROM open_meteo.main.air_quality_current(34.05, -118.24)

vgi.example_queries.description: Same city by name — geocode, then band the AQI.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT g.name, a.us_aqi, open_meteo.main.us_aqi_category(a.us_aqi) AS category FROM open_meteo.main.geocoding('Los Angeles', count := 1) AS g, LATERAL open_meteo.main.air_quality_current(g.latitude, g.longitude) AS a

arguments.name: aqi
arguments.description: US Air Quality Index value from an air_quality function (us_aqi column).

examples: SELECT us_aqi, open_meteo.main.us_aqi_category(us_aqi) AS category FROM open_meteo.main.air_quality_current(34.05, -118.24)

SELECT g.name, a.us_aqi, open_meteo.main.us_aqi_category(a.us_aqi) AS category FROM open_meteo.main.geocoding('Los Angeles', count := 1) AS g, LATERAL open_meteo.main.air_quality_current(g.latitude, g.longitude) AS a
functions.macro_definition: CASE  WHEN ((aqi IS NULL)) THEN (NULL) WHEN ((aqi <= 50)) THEN ('Good') WHEN ((aqi <= 100)) THEN ('Moderate') WHEN ((aqi <= 150)) THEN ('Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups') WHEN ((aqi <= 200)) THEN ('Unhealthy') WHEN ((aqi <= 300)) THEN ('Very Unhealthy') ELSE 'Hazardous' END

functions.name: weather_code_text
functions.comment: Translate a WMO weather_code into an English description (e.g. 61 → 'Slight rain').

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Maps a WMO 4677 weather_code (the raw number returned by forecast_* and historical_* functions) to a short English description such as 'Clear sky', 'Slight rain' or 'Thunderstorm with heavy hail'. Expands inline as SQL — no round-trip. Unknown codes return 'Unknown (<code>)'.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## weather_code_text

Turns the raw WMO `weather_code` (an integer) into an English description. Apply it to the `weather_code` column of any forecast or historical function; see this macro's example queries for a runnable form.

vgi.example_queries.description: Decode the current weather code to text.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT weather_code, open_meteo.main.weather_code_text(weather_code) AS conditions FROM open_meteo.main.forecast_current(52.52, 13.41)

vgi.example_queries.description: Same, starting from a place name: geocode, then decode.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT g.name, open_meteo.main.weather_code_text(w.weather_code) AS conditions FROM open_meteo.main.geocoding('Lisbon', count := 1) AS g, LATERAL open_meteo.main.forecast_current(g.latitude, g.longitude) AS w

arguments.name: code
arguments.description: WMO weather-interpretation code from a forecast/historical function.

examples: SELECT weather_code, open_meteo.main.weather_code_text(weather_code) AS conditions FROM open_meteo.main.forecast_current(52.52, 13.41)

SELECT g.name, open_meteo.main.weather_code_text(w.weather_code) AS conditions FROM open_meteo.main.geocoding('Lisbon', count := 1) AS g, LATERAL open_meteo.main.forecast_current(g.latitude, g.longitude) AS w
functions.macro_definition: CASE  WHEN ((code = 0)) THEN ('Clear sky') WHEN ((code = 1)) THEN ('Mainly clear') WHEN ((code = 2)) THEN ('Partly cloudy') WHEN ((code = 3)) THEN ('Overcast') WHEN ((code = 45)) THEN ('Fog') WHEN ((code = 48)) THEN ('Depositing rime fog') WHEN ((code = 51)) THEN ('Light drizzle') WHEN ((code = 53)) THEN ('Moderate drizzle') WHEN ((code = 55)) THEN ('Dense drizzle') WHEN ((code = 56)) THEN ('Light freezing drizzle') WHEN ((code = 57)) THEN ('Dense freezing drizzle') WHEN ((code = 61)) THEN ('Slight rain') WHEN ((code = 63)) THEN ('Moderate rain') WHEN ((code = 65)) THEN ('Heavy rain') WHEN ((code = 66)) THEN ('Light freezing rain') WHEN ((code = 67)) THEN ('Heavy freezing rain') WHEN ((code = 71)) THEN ('Slight snowfall') WHEN ((code = 73)) THEN ('Moderate snowfall') WHEN ((code = 75)) THEN ('Heavy snowfall') WHEN ((code = 77)) THEN ('Snow grains') WHEN ((code = 80)) THEN ('Slight rain showers') WHEN ((code = 81)) THEN ('Moderate rain showers') WHEN ((code = 82)) THEN ('Violent rain showers') WHEN ((code = 85)) THEN ('Slight snow showers') WHEN ((code = 86)) THEN ('Heavy snow showers') WHEN ((code = 95)) THEN ('Thunderstorm') WHEN ((code = 96)) THEN ('Thunderstorm with slight hail') WHEN ((code = 99)) THEN ('Thunderstorm with heavy hail') ELSE (('Unknown (' || code) || ')') END

functions.name: weather_code_emoji
functions.comment: Map a WMO weather_code to a representative weather emoji (e.g. 95 → ⛈️).

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Maps a WMO 4677 weather_code to a single representative weather emoji (☀️ clear, ⛅ partly cloudy, 🌧️ rain, 🌨️ snow, ⛈️ thunderstorm, 🌫️ fog). Handy for compact, human-facing dashboards. Unknown codes return ❓.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## weather_code_emoji

Maps the raw WMO `weather_code` to one weather emoji — a compact companion to `weather_code_text` for display. See this macro's example queries for a runnable form.

vgi.example_queries.description: Weather emoji for the current conditions.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT weather_code, open_meteo.main.weather_code_emoji(weather_code) AS icon FROM open_meteo.main.forecast_current(52.52, 13.41)

vgi.example_queries.description: A dashboard row per named city, geocoded in the same query.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT p.city, w.temperature_2m, open_meteo.main.weather_code_emoji(w.weather_code) AS icon FROM (VALUES ('Berlin'), ('Tokyo'), ('Cairo')) AS p(city), LATERAL open_meteo.main.geocoding(p.city, count := 1) AS g, LATERAL open_meteo.main.forecast_current(g.latitude, g.longitude) AS w

arguments.name: code
arguments.description: WMO weather-interpretation code from a forecast/historical function.

examples: SELECT weather_code, open_meteo.main.weather_code_emoji(weather_code) AS icon FROM open_meteo.main.forecast_current(52.52, 13.41)

SELECT p.city, w.temperature_2m, open_meteo.main.weather_code_emoji(w.weather_code) AS icon FROM (VALUES ('Berlin'), ('Tokyo'), ('Cairo')) AS p(city), LATERAL open_meteo.main.geocoding(p.city, count := 1) AS g, LATERAL open_meteo.main.forecast_current(g.latitude, g.longitude) AS w
functions.macro_definition: CASE  WHEN ((code = 0)) THEN ('☀️') WHEN ((code = 1)) THEN ('🌤️') WHEN ((code = 2)) THEN ('⛅') WHEN ((code = 3)) THEN ('☁️') WHEN ((code IN (45, 48))) THEN ('🌫️') WHEN ((code IN (51, 53, 55, 56, 57))) THEN ('🌦️') WHEN ((code IN (61, 63, 65, 66, 67, 80, 81, 82))) THEN ('🌧️') WHEN ((code IN (71, 73, 75, 77, 85, 86))) THEN ('🌨️') WHEN ((code IN (95, 96, 99))) THEN ('⛈️') ELSE '❓' END

functions.name: wind_compass
functions.comment: Convert a bearing in degrees to a 16-point compass abbreviation (e.g. 315 → 'NW').

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Converts a bearing in degrees (0–360, meteorological — the direction the flow comes from) into a 16-point compass abbreviation like N, ENE or SW. Works for wind_direction_10m, the daily dominant direction, and marine wave/swell directions. NULL in, NULL out.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## wind_compass

Converts a degree bearing to a 16-point compass point (`N`, `NNE`, … `NNW`). Apply it to a `wind_direction_*` or wave-direction column; see this macro's example queries for a runnable form.

vgi.example_queries.description: Current wind direction as a compass point.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT wind_direction_10m, open_meteo.main.wind_compass(wind_direction_10m) AS from_dir FROM open_meteo.main.forecast_current(52.52, 13.41)

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT g.name, w.wind_speed_10m, open_meteo.main.wind_compass(w.wind_direction_10m) AS from_dir FROM open_meteo.main.geocoding('Wellington', count := 1) AS g, LATERAL open_meteo.main.forecast_current(g.latitude, g.longitude) AS w

arguments.name: degrees
arguments.description: Wind (or wave) bearing the flow comes from, in meteorological degrees.

examples: SELECT wind_direction_10m, open_meteo.main.wind_compass(wind_direction_10m) AS from_dir FROM open_meteo.main.forecast_current(52.52, 13.41)

workers.title: Opendatasoft Open Data
workers.tagline: Query any Opendatasoft open-data portal with ODSQL pushdown in DuckDB (Python)
workers.subtitle: Any Opendatasoft (Huwise) portal's catalog and records as SQL, with ODSQL pushdown.
workers.summary: Any Opendatasoft (Huwise) open-data portal as SQL: search dataset catalogs and read typed records, with filters, projections and aggregates pushed down as ODSQL. No API key needed for public data.
workers.doc_md:
# Opendatasoft open-data portals in DuckDB

Query **any [Opendatasoft (Huwise)](https://www.opendatasoft.com) portal** with SQL: Paris, public.opendatasoft.com, the data.opendatasoft.com hub and hundreds of European cities, regions and utilities. No API key is needed for public data.

Filters, projections and `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` run on the portal as ODSQL, large results stream from the export endpoint, and aggregations can run server-side. Columns get real DuckDB types, including points as `STRUCT(lon, lat)` and shapes as GeoJSON `JSON`.
workers.readme_sql:
-- Paris's first four arrondissements: the filter and the columns are sent to the portal
SELECT l_aroff AS arrondissement, round(surface / 1000000, 2) AS km2
FROM opendatasoft.main.records('opendata.paris.fr', 'arrondissements')
WHERE c_ar <= 4 ORDER BY c_ar;

example_queries.description: The ten most prolific publishers on the Paris open-data portal
example_queries.sql: SELECT publisher, count(*) AS datasets, sum(records_count) AS records FROM opendatasoft.main.datasets('opendata.paris.fr') GROUP BY publisher ORDER BY datasets DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Recently updated population datasets with more than 1,000 records
example_queries.sql: SELECT dataset_id, title, records_count FROM opendatasoft.main.datasets('public.opendatasoft.com', q := 'population') WHERE modified >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2025-01-01' AND records_count > 1000 ORDER BY records_count DESC

example_queries.description: The columns of the Paris arrondissements dataset and their types
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, label, ods_type, duckdb_type FROM opendatasoft.main.fields('opendata.paris.fr', 'arrondissements') ORDER BY position

example_queries.description: Which GeoNames fields can be used as facets
example_queries.sql: SELECT name FROM opendatasoft.main.fields('public.opendatasoft.com', 'geonames-all-cities-with-a-population-1000') WHERE is_facet ORDER BY position

example_queries.description: How many Paris datasets each theme has
example_queries.sql: SELECT value AS theme, count AS datasets FROM opendatasoft.main.facets('opendata.paris.fr', facet := 'theme') ORDER BY count DESC

example_queries.description: Countries with the most cities above 1,000 inhabitants, counted by the portal
example_queries.sql: SELECT value AS country, count AS cities FROM opendatasoft.main.facets('public.opendatasoft.com', dataset_id := 'geonames-all-cities-with-a-population-1000', facet := 'cou_name_en') ORDER BY count DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Name and area of Paris's first four arrondissements
example_queries.sql: SELECT l_aroff AS arrondissement, round(surface / 1000000, 2) AS km2 FROM opendatasoft.main.records('opendata.paris.fr', 'arrondissements') WHERE c_ar <= 4 ORDER BY c_ar

example_queries.description: The five most populous French cities, sorted and limited by the portal

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The `main` schema holds every function: catalog discovery (dataset search with theme, keyword and publisher filters; a dataset's field list with types; facet value counts) and data access (typed records with ODSQL pushdown, and raw server-side ODSQL aggregation). `portal` is a domain such as 'opendata.paris.fr' or a URL. tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

Everything this worker offers lives in one schema, grouped in two categories.

**Catalog** functions search a portal's datasets, list a dataset's fields with the DuckDB type each one gets, and count facet values (themes, publishers, keywords or a dataset's own facet fields).

**Data** functions read a dataset's records with filters, projections and Top-N sorts pushed to the portal, or run an ODSQL aggregate on the portal and return only the summary.

functions.name: records
functions.comment: Rows of one Opendatasoft dataset, typed from its schema, with ODSQL pushdown

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Read the rows of one dataset of an Opendatasoft portal, given the portal and dataset_id. Columns are the dataset's fields (see fields(portal, dataset_id)), typed: int `BIGINT`, double `DOUBLE`, date `DATE`, datetime `TIMESTAMPTZ`, geo_point_2d `STRUCT(lon, lat)`, geo_shape GeoJSON geometry `JSON`, file `STRUCT(id, filename, format, url, ...)`, json_blob `JSON`, multivalued text `VARCHAR[]`, everything else `VARCHAR`. Selected columns become the ODSQL `select`; filters (= <> IN IS NULL starts_with on text; ranges on numbers, dates, datetimes) become `where`; ORDER BY <number/date column> LIMIT n is sorted and limited by the portal. Up to 10,000 matching rows are paged from the records API; larger results are streamed from the export endpoint automatically, so filter first. Optional: filter := raw ODSQL (e.g. geo distance), q := full-text search, refine := 'facet:value'. For server-side GROUP BY use odsql().
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## records(portal, dataset_id, filter :=, q :=, refine :=)

All rows of a dataset, with columns typed from the dataset schema.

**Pushdown.** Projections, filters and `ORDER BY ... LIMIT n` on numeric/date columns run on the portal. Results above 10,000 rows (the records API cap) are streamed from the export endpoint instead of paged.

functions.name: odsql
functions.comment: Run a server-side ODSQL query (aggregates, group_by) on an Opendatasoft dataset

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Run an ODSQL query on the portal and return its rows. Arguments: the portal, the dataset_id, an ODSQL `select` list, and the named arguments filter (an ODSQL condition), group_by (grouping expressions, aliases allowed), order_by (an alias or field, optionally DESC) and max_rows (default 1000). The `select` list may use ODSQL aggregates (count(*), sum(x), avg(x), min, max, percentile) and functions (year(date), ...) with AS aliases; result columns are named by alias (or the expression text) and typed from the dataset fields or the returned values. Use it to summarize large datasets without downloading them: one request instead of streaming every record. group_by returns at most 20,000 groups, otherwise 10,000 rows.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## odsql(portal, dataset_id, select_list, ...)

A server-side ODSQL query, e.g. counts per country over a 170,000-row dataset in one request. Column types come from the dataset schema and the returned values.

workers.title: Open Graph Metadata
workers.tagline: Parse Open Graph, Twitter Card & link-preview metadata from HTML or URLs in DuckDB (TypeScript)
workers.subtitle: Parse Open Graph, Twitter Card and HTML link-preview metadata from HTML text or URLs.
workers.summary: Link-preview metadata from web pages: Open Graph, Twitter Card and plain HTML fallbacks such as title, description, canonical URL and favicon, parsed from HTML you already hold or fetched from URLs with per-row HTTP errors.
workers.doc_md:
# Open Graph metadata for DuckDB

**Parse [Open Graph](https://ogp.me), Twitter Card and HTML link-preview metadata in SQL**, from HTML text or straight from URLs.

- Parse HTML you already have (crawl tables, saved pages) with no network access.
- Or fetch pages directly: redirects followed, only the `<head>` read, failures reported per row in an `error` field.
- Sensible fallbacks: missing `og:*` tags fall back to `twitter:*`, then `<title>`, `<meta name=description>` and `<link rel=canonical>`.
- Relative image and page URLs resolved to absolute ones.

## Sources and references

- [The Open Graph protocol](https://ogp.me): the `og:*`, `article:*` and `product:*` properties the parser reads.
- [oEmbed](https://oembed.com/): the embed-discovery `<link>` format reported alongside the tags.
- [HTML `<meta>` element (WHATWG)](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/semantics.html#the-meta-element): the plain-HTML `name`/`content` metadata used as the fallback.

A [Query.Farm](https://query.farm) [VGI](https://query.farm/vgi) worker.

example_queries.description: Pull the title and preview image out of an HTML document
example_queries.sql: SELECT og.title, og.image FROM (SELECT opengraph.main.parse_opengraph('<html lang="en"><head><title>Fallback</title><meta property="og:title" content="Rock & Roll"><meta property="og:image" content="/cover.png"></head></html>') AS og)

example_queries.description: Resolve a relative og:image against the page URL
example_queries.sql: SELECT opengraph.main.parse_opengraph('<html lang="en"><head><title>Fallback</title><meta property="og:title" content="Rock & Roll"><meta property="og:image" content="/cover.png"></head></html>', 'https://example.com/music/').image AS image

example_queries.description: Build article preview cards from crawled HTML: title and absolute image from parse_opengraph(html, base_url), plus the article:tag keywords (not in the summary) collected from opengraph_tags
example_queries.sql: WITH pages(page_url, html) AS (VALUES ('https://blog.example.com/posts/duckdb', '<title>Blog</title><meta property="og:title" content="Why DuckDB"><meta property="og:image" content="/img/duck.png"><meta property="article:tag" content="duckdb"><meta property="article:tag" content="sql">'), ('https://blog.example.com/posts/hello', '<title>Hello, world</title><meta property="article:tag" content="intro">')) SELECT page_url, og.title, og.image, article_tags FROM (SELECT page_url, opengraph.main.parse_opengraph(html, page_url) AS og, [t.content FOR t IN opengraph.main.opengraph_tags(html) IF t.property = 'article:tag'] AS article_tags FROM pages) ORDER BY page_url

example_queries.description: Unnest the raw meta tags of a document
example_queries.sql: SELECT t.property, t.content FROM (SELECT unnest(opengraph.main.opengraph_tags('<meta property="og:type" content="article"><meta property="article:author" content="Ada">')) AS t) ORDER BY t.property

example_queries.description: Audit where each page's preview title comes from: check the raw tags from opengraph_tags for og:title or twitter:title, else parse_opengraph fell back to the <title> element
example_queries.sql: WITH pages(page_url, html) AS (VALUES ('https://shop.example.com/a', '<title>Shop A</title><meta property="og:title" content="Spring Sale">'), ('https://shop.example.com/b', '<title>Shop B</title><meta name="twitter:title" content="B on Twitter">'), ('https://shop.example.com/c', '<title>Shop C</title>')) SELECT page_url, preview_title, CASE WHEN list_contains(props, 'og:title') THEN 'og:title' WHEN list_contains(props, 'twitter:title') THEN 'twitter:title' ELSE '<title> fallback' END AS title_source FROM (SELECT page_url, opengraph.main.parse_opengraph(html).title AS preview_title, [t.property FOR t IN opengraph.main.opengraph_tags(html)] AS props FROM pages) ORDER BY page_url

example_queries.description: Unfurl a link the way a chat app would
example_queries.sql: SELECT og.title, og.site_name, og.image FROM (SELECT opengraph.main.fetch_opengraph('https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb') AS og) WHERE og.error IS NULL

example_queries.description: A relative og:image becomes absolute
example_queries.sql: SELECT opengraph.main.parse_opengraph('<html lang="en"><head><title>Fallback</title><meta property="og:title" content="Rock & Roll"><meta property="og:image" content="/cover.png"></head></html>', 'https://example.com/music/').image AS image ORDER BY ALL;

agent_tasks: Using the opengraph worker, what is the Open Graph title of this HTML: <head><title>Home</title><meta property="og:title" content="Spring Sale"></head>
A page at https://shop.example.com/items/42 contains <meta property="og:image" content="../img/42.jpg">. Using the opengraph worker, what is the absolute URL of its preview image?

Using the opengraph worker, how many article:tag meta properties does this HTML have: <meta property="article:tag" content="duckdb"><meta property="article:tag" content="sql"><meta property="og:type" content="article">

The parse category works on HTML text with no network: a summary `STRUCT` of a page's preview metadata (optionally resolving relative URLs against the page URL), or the full list of <meta> property/content pairs for unnest-and-filter work. The fetch category downloads pages by URL and returns the same summary plus final_url, http_status, content_type and error; a bad URL yields an error value, not a failed query. All are scalars over whole columns, so they compose with any table of HTML or URLs.

## main

Open Graph / Twitter Card / HTML link-preview metadata extraction, as vectorized scalars that run over a whole column.

- **Parse**: from HTML text you already hold (crawl tables, saved pages), offline. Returns a summary `STRUCT`, or every `<meta>` property/content pair as a list.
- **Fetch**: from URLs over HTTP(S), following redirects and reading only the `<head>`. Failures come back in an `error` field instead of failing the query.

functions.name: parse_opengraph
functions.comment: Parse Open Graph, Twitter Card and basic HTML metadata from an HTML document into a `STRUCT`.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Same as parse_opengraph(html) but takes the page's own URL as a second argument and returns every URL-valued field (url, image, images, video, audio, canonical_url, favicon_url, oembed_url) as an absolute URL. Use it when you stored crawled HTML next to its URL: `parse_opengraph(body, page_url)`. A <base href> in the document overrides base_url. Fields: title, description, type, url, site_name, locale, image, image_alt, image_width, image_height, images (list), video, audio, twitter_card, twitter_site, twitter_creator, canonical_url, favicon_url, oembed_url. Fallbacks: title = og:title → twitter:title → <title>; description = og:description → twitter:description → <meta name=description>; url = og:url → <link rel=canonical>; image = first og:image → twitter:image; locale = og:locale → <html lang>. The first occurrence of a property wins. Values are entity-decoded and whitespace-trimmed; absent values are NULL (images is an empty list).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## parse_opengraph(html, base_url)

functions.name: parse_opengraph
functions.comment: Parse Open Graph metadata from HTML, resolving relative URLs against the page's URL.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Same as parse_opengraph(html) but takes the page's own URL as a second argument and returns every URL-valued field (url, image, images, video, audio, canonical_url, favicon_url, oembed_url) as an absolute URL. Use it when you stored crawled HTML next to its URL: `parse_opengraph(body, page_url)`. A <base href> in the document overrides base_url. Fields: title, description, type, url, site_name, locale, image, image_alt, image_width, image_height, images (list), video, audio, twitter_card, twitter_site, twitter_creator, canonical_url, favicon_url, oembed_url. Fallbacks: title = og:title → twitter:title → <title>; description = og:description → twitter:description → <meta name=description>; url = og:url → <link rel=canonical>; image = first og:image → twitter:image; locale = og:locale → <html lang>. The first occurrence of a property wins. Values are entity-decoded and whitespace-trimmed; absent values are NULL (images is an empty list).

functions.name: fetch_opengraph
functions.comment: Download a web page and return its Open Graph metadata as a STRUCT, with HTTP status and error.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Fetch each URL over HTTP(S) (following redirects, reading only the document head) and return the same `STRUCT` as parse_opengraph plus final_url (after redirects; relative URLs are resolved against it), http_status `INTEGER`, content_type and error. A page that can't be read does NOT fail the query: its row has error set (e.g. 'HTTP 404 Not Found', 'timed out after 10000 ms', 'not an HTML page …') and NULL metadata, so filter with `WHERE og.error IS NULL`. URLs in one batch are fetched concurrently (8 at a time) and duplicates are fetched once; 429/5xx responses are retried. Tune with the environment variables OPENGRAPH_TIMEOUT_MS, OPENGRAPH_MAX_BYTES, OPENGRAPH_CONCURRENCY and OPENGRAPH_USER_AGENT. Results depend on the live web; if you already have the HTML, use parse_opengraph(html, base_url) instead.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Return a `LIST(STRUCT(property VARCHAR, content VARCHAR))` with every <meta> tag that has a property= or name= attribute and a content= attribute, in document order, duplicates kept. property is lower-cased (og:title, og:image:width, article:published_time, twitter:card, description, …); content is entity-decoded. workers.title: OpenLineage Lineage
workers.tagline: OpenLineage events and Marquez lineage, runs and column lineage as SQL in DuckDB (Python)
workers.subtitle: OpenLineage events and Marquez lineage as DuckDB tables: runs, datasets, column lineage.
workers.summary: OpenLineage lineage as SQL: query raw RunEvent, DatasetEvent and JobEvent JSON files or a Marquez server's namespaces, datasets, jobs, runs and lineage graph from DuckDB.
workers.doc_md:
# OpenLineage

Query [OpenLineage](https://openlineage.io) lineage from DuckDB: the runs, datasets, schemas and column-level lineage that Airflow, Spark, dbt, Dagster and other integrations emit.

**Event files** (schema `main`) need nothing but the events: point a table function at a file, glob, directory or URL of what the OpenLineage `file` or `http` transport wrote.

**Marquez** (schema `marquez`) reads a [Marquez](https://marquezproject.ai) API server: namespaces, datasets and their versions, jobs, runs and facets, the lineage graph, column lineage and search. Create a secret of type `marquez` with the server's `BASE_URL` first.

**Unified** (schema `unified`) puts Marquez runs in the column layout shared by the Query.Farm orchestrator workers, ready for `UNION ALL`.

example_queries.description: Count RunEvents by eventType
example_queries.sql: SELECT event_type, count(*) AS events FROM openlineage.main.read_events('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-openlineage/v0.1.0/test/fixtures/all-events.ndjson') WHERE event_kind = 'run' GROUP BY event_type ORDER BY events DESC

example_queries.description: The latest FAIL events with their error message
example_queries.sql: SELECT job_name, event_time, run_facets->>'$.errorMessage.message' AS error FROM openlineage.main.read_events('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-openlineage/v0.1.0/test/fixtures/all-events.ndjson') WHERE event_type = 'FAIL' ORDER BY event_time DESC LIMIT 20

example_queries.description: Failed runs with the error message from the errorMessage facet
example_queries.sql: SELECT job_name, ended_at, error_message FROM openlineage.main.runs('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-openlineage/v0.1.0/test/fixtures/all-events.ndjson') WHERE status = 'failed' ORDER BY ended_at DESC

example_queries.description: The ten slowest jobs by average successful run time
example_queries.sql: SELECT job_name, count(*) AS runs, round(avg(duration_seconds), 1) AS avg_seconds FROM openlineage.main.runs('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-openlineage/v0.1.0/test/fixtures/all-events.ndjson') WHERE status = 'success' GROUP BY job_name ORDER BY avg_seconds DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Which jobs write each dataset
example_queries.sql: SELECT dataset_namespace, dataset_name, list(job_name ORDER BY job_name) AS writers FROM openlineage.main.job_io('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-openlineage/v0.1.0/test/fixtures/all-events.ndjson') WHERE direction = 'output' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY dataset_name

example_queries.description: Column lists of every dataset with a schema facet
example_queries.sql: SELECT dataset_name, count(*) AS columns, list(field_name ORDER BY ordinal) AS fields FROM openlineage.main.dataset_schema('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-openlineage/v0.1.0/test/fixtures/all-events.ndjson') GROUP BY dataset_name ORDER BY dataset_name

example_queries.description: Where each column of one table comes from
example_queries.sql: SELECT output_field, input_dataset, input_field, transformation_subtype FROM openlineage.main.column_lineage('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-openlineage/v0.1.0/test/fixtures/all-events.ndjson') WHERE output_dataset = 'analytics.orders_enriched' ORDER BY output_field, input_field

example_queries.description: Processing engine and version per job
example_queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT job_name, facet->>'$.name' AS engine, facet->>'$.version' AS version FROM openlineage.main.facets('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-openlineage/v0.1.0/test/fixtures/all-events.ndjson') WHERE facet_name = 'processing_engine' ORDER BY job_name

example_queries.description: Every dataset upstream of analytics.customers
example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, name, hops FROM openlineage.main.lineage('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-openlineage/v0.1.0/test/fixtures/all-events.ndjson', 'analytics.customers', depth := 10, direction := 'upstream') WHERE node_type = 'dataset' AND hops > 0 ORDER BY hops, name

example_queries.description: Impact analysis: jobs downstream of a source table
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, hops FROM openlineage.main.lineage('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-openlineage/v0.1.0/test/fixtures/all-events.ndjson', 'dataset:postgres://db.internal:5432:shop.public.orders', direction := 'downstream') WHERE node_type = 'job' ORDER BY hops, name

example_queries.description: Run counts by orchestrator and normalized status
example_queries.sql: SELECT orchestrator, status, count(*) AS runs FROM openlineage.main.unified_runs('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-openlineage/v0.1.0/test/fixtures/all-events.ndjson') GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY orchestrator, status

example_queries.description: The latest failed task runs with their attempt number
example_queries.sql: SELECT task_name, status, attempt, duration_seconds FROM openlineage.main.unified_task_runs('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-openlineage/v0.1.0/test/fixtures/all-events.ndjson') WHERE status = 'failed' ORDER BY started_at DESC LIMIT 20

example_queries.description: Events per orchestrator in a hand-loaded NDJSON file
example_queries.sql: SELECT openlineage.main.orchestrator(producer) AS orchestrator, count(*) AS events FROM read_json('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-openlineage/v0.1.0/test/fixtures/all-events.ndjson', format = 'newline_delimited') GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY events DESC

example_queries.description: Events per normalized status in a hand-loaded NDJSON file
example_queries.sql: SELECT openlineage.main.run_status(eventType) AS status, count(*) AS events FROM read_json('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-openlineage/v0.1.0/test/fixtures/all-events.ndjson', format = 'newline_delimited') GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY status

example_queries.description: Classify an Airflow provider and the Spark integration
example_queries.sql: SELECT openlineage.main.orchestrator('https://github.com/apache/airflow/tree/providers-openlineage/1.14.0') AS a, openlineage.main.orchestrator('https://github.com/OpenLineage/OpenLineage/tree/1.24.2/integration/spark') AS b;

example_queries.description: Normalize every OpenLineage eventType
example_queries.sql: SELECT t, openlineage.main.run_status(t) AS status FROM (VALUES ('START'), ('RUNNING'), ('COMPLETE'), ('FAIL'), ('ABORT'), ('OTHER')) v(t) ORDER BY t;

example_queries.description: Namespaces in the order Marquez first saw them
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, created_at FROM openlineage.marquez.namespaces ORDER BY created_at

example_queries.description: Every source and its connection URI
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, connection_url FROM openlineage.marquez.sources ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Datasets in one namespace with their column counts

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Table functions over raw OpenLineage event JSON; no credentials. The first argument `path` is a file, a directory (every .json/.ndjson/.jsonl[.gz] inside, recursively), a glob such as '/var/log/ol/**/*.ndjson', or an http(s) URL. A source can hold one event object, a JSON array, NDJSON lines or a Marquez `{"events": [...]}` page; `ignore_errors := true` skips malformed lines. Each call re-reads the sources, so point it at the files once and join the results freely.

Run state rules: START/RUNNING mean running, COMPLETE success, FAIL failed, ABORT cancelled, and a run with only OTHER events is queued; a terminal event wins over a START that arrives later. A run with a parent facet is a task run. The orchestrator comes from the jobType facet's integration, then the processing_engine facet, then the producer URI. Inputs and outputs are `LIST` of `STRUCT(namespace, name)`; facets are `JSON`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main: OpenLineage event files

Every function reads `path`: a file, directory, glob or http(s) URL of OpenLineage events (single objects, JSON arrays or NDJSON, optionally gzipped).

Results cover single events, run state, job inputs and outputs, schemas, column lineage, facets and multi-hop lineage, plus the shared orchestrator run shape.

functions.name: lineage
functions.comment: Walk the job/dataset lineage graph upstream or downstream from one node, N hops

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Breadth-first walk of the bipartite job <-> dataset graph built from the events in `path` (dataset -> job for inputs, job -> dataset for outputs). `node` is 'dataset:<namespace>:<name>', 'job:<namespace>:<name>' or a unique dataset/job name. Named args: depth := 5 (max hops, 1-100), direction := 'upstream' | 'downstream' | 'both'. Returns node_id, node_type ('dataset'/'job'), namespace, name, direction ('start' for the node itself), hops (edges from the start: a dataset's writer job is 1 hop, the datasets that job reads are 2) and reached_from (the neighbour it was reached through).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## lineage(path, node, depth := 5, direction := 'both')

Everything upstream and/or downstream of a dataset or job, with the hop count.

vgi.example_queries.description: Every dataset upstream of analytics.customers

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Tables and functions over a Marquez API server (the OpenLineage reference backend). They need one DuckDB secret of type `marquez`: `BASE_URL` (the API root, e.g. 'http://localhost:5000'), optional `API_KEY` (sent as a bearer token) and optional `PAGE_SIZE` (default 100). Lists are paged with Marquez's limit/offset and the cursor travels with the scan.

Pushdown: `namespace` equality on datasets, jobs and runs, `job_name` on runs, and `event_time` ranges on the raw event table (Marquez after/before). Marquez prefixes child job names with the parent job, e.g. 'etl_orders.extract'. Lineage node ids are 'dataset:<ns>:<name>', 'job:<ns>:<name>' and 'datasetField:<ns>:<dataset>:<field>'. Columns are `LIST` of `STRUCT` values; facets are `JSON`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## marquez: a Marquez API server

Namespaces, sources, datasets, jobs, runs and raw events as tables; versions, run facets, the lineage graph, column lineage and search as functions.

Create a secret of type `marquez` with the server's `BASE_URL` (and `API_KEY` if it sits behind an auth proxy) before querying.

vgi.example_queries.description: Jobs whose latest run failed
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, name, latest_run_state FROM openlineage.marquez.jobs WHERE latest_run_state = 'FAILED' ORDER BY namespace, name

vgi.example_queries.description: Failed runs in one namespace
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT job_name, state, duration_ms FROM openlineage.marquez.runs WHERE namespace = 'airflow-prod' AND state = 'FAILED' ORDER BY ended_at DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: FAIL events since a point in time
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT job_name, event_type, event_time FROM openlineage.marquez.lineage_events WHERE event_time >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-03 00:00:00+00' AND event_type = 'FAIL' ORDER BY event_time

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Marquez runs in the column layout shared by every Query.Farm orchestrator worker, so `UNION ALL` with dagster.unified.runs, airflow.unified.runs etc. works. Top-level runs are runs without an OpenLineage parent facet (DAG runs, dbt invocations, standalone jobs); task runs carry a parent facet (Airflow tasks, dbt models, Spark jobs launched by a task), and their run_id is the root (or parent) run. The orchestrator comes from the jobType facet's integration, the processing_engine facet or Airflow facets ('unknown' when Marquez stored none). Needs the `marquez` secret. For event files use the `unified_runs(path)` and `unified_task_runs(path)` table functions in schema `main`.

workers.title: OpenMetadata Catalog
workers.tagline: OpenMetadata tables, columns, lineage, tests and usage as SQL in DuckDB (Python)
workers.subtitle: OpenMetadata and Collate assets, ownership, glossary, lineage and data quality as SQL tables.
workers.summary: OpenMetadata and Collate metadata catalog (assets, governance, lineage, data quality) as SQL tables.
workers.doc_md:
# OpenMetadata

Query an [OpenMetadata](https://open-metadata.org) or Collate catalog from DuckDB: data assets, ownership, tags and glossary terms, domains, lineage, data-quality tests and their results, profiles and usage.

Connect with an `openmetadata` secret holding the API root (`HOST_PORT`, e.g. `http://localhost:8585/api`) and a bot JWT (`TOKEN`).

Read-only. Filters push down into OpenMetadata's search `query_filter`, REST query parameters and time ranges.

example_queries.description: Tables per schema in one service (service pushes into the search query_filter)
example_queries.sql: SELECT schema, count(*) AS tables FROM openmetadata.main.datasets WHERE service = 'snowflake_prod' GROUP BY schema ORDER BY tables DESC

example_queries.description: Columns tagged PII.Sensitive
example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, column_name FROM openmetadata.main.columns WHERE list_contains(tags, 'PII.Sensitive') ORDER BY qualified_name, column_name

example_queries.description: Database services per platform
example_queries.sql: SELECT platform, count(*) AS services FROM openmetadata.main.database_services GROUP BY platform ORDER BY services DESC

example_queries.description: Databases of one service (service pushes down)
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, owners FROM openmetadata.main.databases WHERE service = 'snowflake_prod' ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Schemas of one database (database_fqn pushes down)
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, description FROM openmetadata.main.database_schemas WHERE database_fqn = 'snowflake_prod.analytics' ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Dashboards of one BI service by chart count
example_queries.sql: SELECT display_name, len(charts) AS charts FROM openmetadata.main.dashboards WHERE service = 'looker_prod' ORDER BY charts DESC

example_queries.description: Charts per chart type
example_queries.sql: SELECT chart_type, count(*) AS charts FROM openmetadata.main.charts GROUP BY chart_type ORDER BY charts DESC

example_queries.description: Pipelines whose latest run failed
example_queries.sql: SELECT fqn, last_run_at FROM openmetadata.main.pipelines WHERE last_run_status = 'Failed' ORDER BY last_run_at DESC

example_queries.description: Topics by partition count with retention in days
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, partitions, retention_ms / 86400000 AS retention_days FROM openmetadata.main.topics ORDER BY partitions DESC

example_queries.description: ML models with their algorithm and feature count
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, algorithm, len(features) AS features FROM openmetadata.main.ml_models ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: How many tables each user or team owns
example_queries.sql: SELECT owner_name, count(*) AS tables FROM openmetadata.main.owners WHERE entity_type = 'table' GROUP BY owner_name ORDER BY tables DESC

example_queries.description: Human users and their teams
example_queries.sql: SELECT username, teams FROM openmetadata.main.users WHERE NOT is_bot ORDER BY username

example_queries.description: Teams by size
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, team_type, user_count FROM openmetadata.main.teams ORDER BY user_count DESC

example_queries.description: Classifications and how many tags each has
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, term_count FROM openmetadata.main.classifications ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: PII tags by how often they are applied
example_queries.sql: SELECT fqn, usage_count FROM openmetadata.main.tags WHERE classification = 'PII' ORDER BY usage_count DESC

example_queries.description: Glossaries with their size and reviewers
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, term_count, reviewers FROM openmetadata.main.glossaries ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Glossary terms still awaiting approval
example_queries.sql: SELECT fqn, status FROM openmetadata.main.glossary_terms WHERE status <> 'Approved' ORDER BY fqn

example_queries.description: Tables per domain
example_queries.sql: SELECT d.fqn, count(t.id) AS tables FROM openmetadata.main.domains d LEFT JOIN openmetadata.main.datasets t ON t.domain = d.fqn GROUP BY d.fqn ORDER BY tables DESC

example_queries.description: Data products of the Sales domain by size
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, asset_count FROM openmetadata.main.data_products WHERE domain = 'Sales' ORDER BY asset_count DESC

example_queries.description: Tables feeding one table directly (downstream_fqn pushes down)
example_queries.sql: SELECT upstream_qualified_name FROM openmetadata.main.lineage_edges WHERE downstream_fqn = 'snowflake_prod.analytics.marts.fct_orders' AND level = 'dataset' ORDER BY upstream_qualified_name

example_queries.description: Tables with failing tests
example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, failed, test_count FROM openmetadata.main.test_suites WHERE suite_type = 'basic' AND failed > 0 ORDER BY failed DESC

example_queries.description: Currently failing tests
example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, name, last_result FROM openmetadata.main.assertions WHERE last_status = 'Failed' ORDER BY qualified_name, name

example_queries.description: Failure counts per table since a date (run_at pushes down as startTs)
example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'Failed') AS failures, count(*) AS runs FROM openmetadata.main.assertion_results WHERE run_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01 00:00:00+00' GROUP BY qualified_name ORDER BY failures DESC

example_queries.description: Open incidents, oldest first
example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, test_case_fqn, assignee FROM openmetadata.main.incidents WHERE state <> 'Resolved' ORDER BY updated_at

example_queries.description: Largest profiled tables in one service
example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, row_count, size_bytes FROM openmetadata.main.dataset_profiles WHERE service = 'snowflake_prod' ORDER BY size_bytes DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: The ten most-queried tables over the last month
example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, monthly_query_count FROM openmetadata.main.usage ORDER BY monthly_query_count DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Slowest queries touching one table
example_queries.sql: SELECT query, duration_ms FROM openmetadata.main.queries WHERE list_contains(used_in, 'snowflake_prod.analytics.marts.fct_orders') ORDER BY duration_ms DESC LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Every table a table depends on, nearest first
example_queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT upstream_qualified_name, degree FROM openmetadata.main.lineage('snowflake_prod.analytics.marts.fct_orders', downstream_depth := 0) WHERE level = 'dataset' ORDER BY degree, upstream_qualified_name

example_queries.description: Tier 1 tables matching 'orders'
example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, score FROM openmetadata.main.search('orders', tier := 'Tier.Tier1') ORDER BY score DESC

example_queries.description: Distinct sample values per non-PII column
example_queries.sql: SELECT column_name, count(DISTINCT value) AS distinct_values FROM openmetadata.main.sample_data('snowflake_prod.analytics.marts.fct_orders') GROUP BY column_name ORDER BY column_name

example_queries.description: Most-consumed upstream tables by qualified name
example_queries.sql: SELECT openmetadata.main.fqn_qualified_name(upstream_fqn) AS source, count(*) AS consumers FROM openmetadata.main.lineage_edges WHERE level = 'dataset' AND upstream_type = 'table' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY consumers DESC

example_queries.description: Test cases per database service
example_queries.sql: SELECT openmetadata.main.split_fqn(fqn)[1] AS service, count(*) AS tests FROM openmetadata.main.assertions GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY tests DESC

example_queries.description: Mostly-NULL columns
example_queries.sql: SELECT p.qualified_name, c.column_name, c.null_proportion FROM openmetadata.main.dataset_profiles p, unnest(p.column_profiles) AS u(c) WHERE c.null_proportion > 0.5 ORDER BY c.null_proportion DESC

example_queries.description: Daily usage history of one table
example_queries.sql: SELECT usage_date, query_count FROM openmetadata.main.usage WHERE table_fqn = 'snowflake_prod.analytics.marts.fct_orders' ORDER BY usage_date

example_queries.description: Tier 1 tables and their owners
example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, owners FROM openmetadata.main.datasets WHERE tier = 'Tier.Tier1' ORDER BY qualified_name

example_queries.description: Test definitions used on one table (table_fqn pushes down as entityLink)
example_queries.sql: SELECT test_definition, count(*) AS tests FROM openmetadata.main.assertions WHERE table_fqn = 'snowflake_prod.analytics.marts.fct_orders' GROUP BY test_definition ORDER BY tests DESC

example_queries.description: Schema of one table (table_fqn fetches only that table)
example_queries.sql: SELECT column_name, data_type, nullable FROM openmetadata.main.columns WHERE table_fqn = 'snowflake_prod.analytics.marts.fct_orders' ORDER BY ordinal_position

example_queries.description: Column-level lineage into one table
example_queries.sql: SELECT upstream_column, downstream_column, transformation FROM openmetadata.main.lineage_edges WHERE downstream_fqn = 'snowflake_prod.analytics.marts.fct_orders' AND level = 'column' ORDER BY downstream_column

example_queries.description: Every kind of asset mentioning revenue
example_queries.sql: SELECT entity_type, fqn FROM openmetadata.main.search('revenue', entity_type := 'all') ORDER BY entity_type, fqn

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The `main` schema mirrors an OpenMetadata catalog, one table per concept: assets, governance, lineage, data quality, profiles and usage. Start from the datasets table (one row per OpenMetadata table, keyed by id and fqn = service.database.schema.table, with owners, tags, tier, glossary terms and domain) and join out by id or fqn. Multi-hop lineage and full-text search are table functions; sample rows are returned only on request and never for PII-tagged columns. Ids are OpenMetadata UUIDs; fqn columns are fully-qualified names. Filter a quality-result time range to push it down.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

OpenMetadata assets, governance metadata, lineage, data quality, profiles and usage, one table per concept.

Column names follow the shared data-catalog vocabulary (`catalog_tool`, `id`, `qualified_name`, `platform`, `description`, `updated_at`, `url`), so results combine with the DataHub worker's tables through `UNION ALL BY NAME`.

Filters on ids, FQNs, services, tiers, domains, tags and owners are pushed into OpenMetadata's REST parameters and search `query_filter`; time ranges on results and incidents become `startTs` / `endTs`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Tables per schema in one service (service pushes into the search query_filter)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT schema, count(*) AS tables FROM openmetadata.main.datasets WHERE service = 'snowflake_prod' GROUP BY schema ORDER BY tables DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Columns tagged PII.Sensitive
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, column_name FROM openmetadata.main.columns WHERE list_contains(tags, 'PII.Sensitive') ORDER BY qualified_name, column_name

vgi.example_queries.description: Database services per platform
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT platform, count(*) AS services FROM openmetadata.main.database_services GROUP BY platform ORDER BY services DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Databases of one service (service pushes down)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, owners FROM openmetadata.main.databases WHERE service = 'snowflake_prod' ORDER BY name

vgi.example_queries.description: Schemas of one database (database_fqn pushes down)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, description FROM openmetadata.main.database_schemas WHERE database_fqn = 'snowflake_prod.analytics' ORDER BY name

vgi.example_queries.description: Dashboards of one BI service by chart count
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT display_name, len(charts) AS charts FROM openmetadata.main.dashboards WHERE service = 'looker_prod' ORDER BY charts DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Charts per chart type
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT chart_type, count(*) AS charts FROM openmetadata.main.charts GROUP BY chart_type ORDER BY charts DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Pipelines whose latest run failed
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT fqn, last_run_at FROM openmetadata.main.pipelines WHERE last_run_status = 'Failed' ORDER BY last_run_at DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: How many tables each user or team owns
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT owner_name, count(*) AS tables FROM openmetadata.main.owners WHERE entity_type = 'table' GROUP BY owner_name ORDER BY tables DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Human users and their teams
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT username, teams FROM openmetadata.main.users WHERE NOT is_bot ORDER BY username

vgi.example_queries.description: Teams by size
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, team_type, user_count FROM openmetadata.main.teams ORDER BY user_count DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Classifications and how many tags each has
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, term_count FROM openmetadata.main.classifications ORDER BY name

vgi.example_queries.description: PII tags by how often they are applied
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT fqn, usage_count FROM openmetadata.main.tags WHERE classification = 'PII' ORDER BY usage_count DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Glossaries with their size and reviewers
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, term_count, reviewers FROM openmetadata.main.glossaries ORDER BY name

vgi.example_queries.description: Glossary terms still awaiting approval
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT fqn, status FROM openmetadata.main.glossary_terms WHERE status <> 'Approved' ORDER BY fqn

vgi.example_queries.description: Tables per domain
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT d.fqn, count(t.id) AS tables FROM openmetadata.main.domains d LEFT JOIN openmetadata.main.datasets t ON t.domain = d.fqn GROUP BY d.fqn ORDER BY tables DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Data products of the Sales domain by size
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, asset_count FROM openmetadata.main.data_products WHERE domain = 'Sales' ORDER BY asset_count DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Tables feeding one table directly (downstream_fqn pushes down)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT upstream_qualified_name FROM openmetadata.main.lineage_edges WHERE downstream_fqn = 'snowflake_prod.analytics.marts.fct_orders' AND level = 'dataset' ORDER BY upstream_qualified_name

vgi.example_queries.description: Tables with failing tests
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, failed, test_count FROM openmetadata.main.test_suites WHERE suite_type = 'basic' AND failed > 0 ORDER BY failed DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Currently failing tests
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, name, last_result FROM openmetadata.main.assertions WHERE last_status = 'Failed' ORDER BY qualified_name, name

vgi.example_queries.description: Failure counts per table since a date (run_at pushes down as startTs)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'Failed') AS failures, count(*) AS runs FROM openmetadata.main.assertion_results WHERE run_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01 00:00:00+00' GROUP BY qualified_name ORDER BY failures DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Open incidents, oldest first
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, test_case_fqn, assignee FROM openmetadata.main.incidents WHERE state <> 'Resolved' ORDER BY updated_at

vgi.example_queries.description: Largest profiled tables in one service
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, row_count, size_bytes FROM openmetadata.main.dataset_profiles WHERE service = 'snowflake_prod' ORDER BY size_bytes DESC LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: The ten most-queried tables over the last month
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, monthly_query_count FROM openmetadata.main.usage ORDER BY monthly_query_count DESC LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: Slowest queries touching one table
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT query, duration_ms FROM openmetadata.main.queries WHERE list_contains(used_in, 'snowflake_prod.analytics.marts.fct_orders') ORDER BY duration_ms DESC LIMIT 5

vgi.example_queries.description: Every table a table depends on, nearest first
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT upstream_qualified_name, degree FROM openmetadata.main.lineage('snowflake_prod.analytics.marts.fct_orders', downstream_depth := 0) WHERE level = 'dataset' ORDER BY degree, upstream_qualified_name

vgi.example_queries.description: Tier 1 tables matching 'orders'
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT qualified_name, score FROM openmetadata.main.search('orders', tier := 'Tier.Tier1') ORDER BY score DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Distinct sample values per non-PII column
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT column_name, count(DISTINCT value) AS distinct_values FROM openmetadata.main.sample_data('snowflake_prod.analytics.marts.fct_orders') GROUP BY column_name ORDER BY column_name

vgi.example_queries.description: Most-consumed upstream tables by qualified name
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT openmetadata.main.fqn_qualified_name(upstream_fqn) AS source, count(*) AS consumers FROM openmetadata.main.lineage_edges WHERE level = 'dataset' AND upstream_type = 'table' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY consumers DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Test cases per database service
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT openmetadata.main.split_fqn(fqn)[1] AS service, count(*) AS tests FROM openmetadata.main.assertions GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY tests DESC

tables.name: lineage_edges
tables.comment: Direct table- and column-level lineage edges recorded in OpenMetadata

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per direct lineage edge into an OpenMetadata table: level ('dataset' for the entity edge, 'column' for each fromColumn -> toColumn pair of its columnsLineage), upstream_id / _type / _fqn / _name / _qualified_name / _column, the same for downstream, pipeline_fqn, transformation, sql_query, lineage_source, created_at, updated_at. Pushdown: downstream_fqn = / IN asks /v1/lineage/table/name/{fqn} for those tables' upstream edges only; upstream_fqn = / IN (without downstream_fqn) asks for those tables' downstream edges. Unfiltered, every table's upstream edges are fetched (one lineage call per table), so edges into non-table entities (dashboards, ML models) appear only with an upstream_fqn filter or through lineage(). For multi-hop traversal use lineage(fqn, ...).
tags.vgi.doc_md: Direct lineage edges, table- and column-level.

vgi.example_queries.description: Tables feeding one table directly (downstream_fqn pushes down)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT upstream_qualified_name FROM openmetadata.main.lineage_edges WHERE downstream_fqn = 'snowflake_prod.analytics.marts.fct_orders' AND level = 'dataset' ORDER BY upstream_qualified_name

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT upstream_column, downstream_column, transformation FROM openmetadata.main.lineage_edges WHERE downstream_fqn = 'snowflake_prod.analytics.marts.fct_orders' AND level = 'column' ORDER BY downstream_column

workers.title: OR-Tools Optimization
workers.tagline: Constraint solving & optimization in DuckDB with SQL — CP-SAT, vehicle routing (VRP/TSP), assignment, scheduling, flows, knapsack and bin-packing via Google OR-Tools. A VGI worker.
workers.subtitle: Compute optimal assignments, vehicle routes, schedules, network flows and packings, or solve constraint models, with Google OR-Tools.
workers.summary: Google OR-Tools optimization / constraint solving as SQL functions.
workers.doc_md:
# Optimization & Constraint Solving in SQL (Google OR-Tools)

**Prescriptive compute inside DuckDB: constraint programming, vehicle routing, scheduling, assignment, network flow, and packing as plain SQL functions.**

This catalog turns [Google OR-Tools](https://developers.google.com/optimization) into DuckDB table and scalar functions, so an operations, logistics, or planning team that already lives in DuckDB can solve optimization problems next to their data instead of standing up a separate Python optimization microservice with its own deploy, data copy, and ETL round-trip.

## When to reach for it

Use it when a question is a *decision* problem rather than an aggregation -- matching supply to demand at least cost, sequencing work under precedence and resource limits, routing a fleet under capacity and time windows, maximizing the throughput of a network, or any hand-built constraint model mixing the global constraints (all-different, no-overlap, cumulative, circuit) that LP/MIP solvers such as the community `highs` extension stop short of. It is the decision-making complement to the predictive ML workers.

## How it works

Build the cost, distance, demand, or capacity matrices using ordinary SQL joins and `array_agg`, hand them to a solver as integer list arguments (OR-Tools is an integer engine -- scale fractional data first), and get the optimal or best-found solution back as rows you can join straight back into the warehouse. Every solver returns a `status` column, and a problem with no solution returns exactly one status row rather than an empty result.

## Data residency

The worker makes **no outbound network calls** -- pure local CPU, no API keys, no rate limits, no data egress. Your problem instances never leave the box. OR-Tools is Apache-2.0; the worker is MIT.

example_queries.description: Least-cost assignment of three workers to three tasks (returns each worker's chosen task and its cost).
example_queries.sql: SELECT worker, task, cost FROM ortools.main.solve_assignment(cost := [[0,0,90],[0,1,76],[0,2,75],[1,0,35],[1,1,85],[1,2,55],[2,0,125],[2,1,95],[2,2,90]]::BIGINT[][], maximize := false) ORDER BY worker

example_queries.description: Optimal travelling-salesperson tour over a 5-node distance matrix, in visit order.
example_queries.sql: SELECT seq, node, arrival FROM ortools.main.solve_tsp(distance := [[0,2,9,10,1],[1,0,6,4,8],[15,7,0,8,3],[6,3,12,0,5],[9,8,4,7,0]]::BIGINT[][], start := 0) ORDER BY seq

example_queries.description: List the bundled OR-Tools / solver component versions.
example_queries.sql: SELECT component, version FROM ortools.main.solver_info ORDER BY component

example_queries.description: Arc criticality: for each arc carrying flow in the 0->3 max-flow solution, re-solve with that arc removed (max_flow_value) and report the throughput lost. Losing arc 2->3 drops the max flow from 30 to 10; each of the other flow-carrying arcs costs 10.
example_queries.sql: SELECT f."from", f."to", f.flow, ortools.main.max_flow_value(list_filter([[0,1,20],[0,2,30],[1,2,10],[1,3,10],[2,3,20]]::BIGINT[][], lambda a: NOT (a[1] = f."from" AND a[2] = f."to")), 0, 3) AS flow_without_arc, ortools.main.max_flow_value([[0,1,20],[0,2,30],[1,2,10],[1,3,10],[2,3,20]]::BIGINT[][], 0, 3) - flow_without_arc AS flow_lost FROM ortools.main.max_flow(arcs := [[0,1,20],[0,2,30],[1,2,10],[1,3,10],[2,3,20]]::BIGINT[][], source := 0, sink := 3) AS f ORDER BY flow_lost DESC, f."from", f."to"

example_queries.description: Ship 12 units from node 0 to node 3 at minimum cost (68), and compare against the network's maximum 0->3 throughput from max_flow_value over the same arcs' capacities (17), leaving 5 units of headroom.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sum(flow) FILTER (WHERE "from" = 0) AS shipped, sum(cost) AS total_cost, ortools.main.max_flow_value(list_transform([[0,1,10,2],[0,2,8,5],[1,2,6,1],[1,3,5,4],[2,3,12,2]]::BIGINT[][], lambda a: a[1:3]), 0, 3) AS max_shippable, max_shippable - shipped AS headroom FROM ortools.main.min_cost_flow(arcs := [[0,1,10,2],[0,2,8,5],[1,2,6,1],[1,3,5,4],[2,3,12,2]]::BIGINT[][], supplies := [[0,12],[3,-12]]::BIGINT[][]) ORDER BY total_cost

example_queries.description: Fetch just the status of the most recent solve.
example_queries.sql: SELECT value FROM ortools.main.last_solve_stats WHERE metric = 'status'

SELECT metric, value FROM ortools.main.last_solve_stats ORDER BY metric;

example_queries.description: Capacitated VRP: 1 depot, 3 stops of demand 1, 2 vehicles of capacity 2 (optimal distance 6).
example_queries.sql: SELECT route_id, seq, node, arrival, load_0 FROM ortools.main.solve_vrp(distance := [[0,1,1],[0,2,1],[0,3,2],[1,0,1],[1,2,1],[1,3,2],[2,0,1],[2,1,1],[2,3,1],[3,0,2],[3,1,2],[3,2,1]]::BIGINT[][], demand := [[1,1],[2,1],[3,1]]::BIGINT[][], num_vehicles := 2, vehicle_capacity := 2, depot := 0, time_limit_s := 1.0) ORDER BY route_id, seq

example_queries.description: Same problem from the sparse `[from, to, meters]` edge-list form (build it with `array_agg([f, t, m])`) instead of a dense matrix -- here a complete 4-node graph.

example_queries.sql: SELECT item, chosen FROM ortools.main.solve_knapsack(item_values := [10,20,30,40,50]::BIGINT[], weights := [[5],[10],[15],[20],[25]]::BIGINT[][], capacities := [40]::BIGINT[]) ORDER BY item

example_queries.description: 0/1 knapsack as a CP-SAT model: maximize value within a weight budget (optimum 40).
example_queries.sql: SELECT var, value, status, objective FROM ortools.main.solve_cpsat(model := '{"version":1,"variables":[{"kind":"bool","name":"a"},{"kind":"bool","name":"b"},{"kind":"bool","name":"c"}],"constraints":[{"type":"linear","expr":{"sum":[{"coef":5,"var":"a"},{"coef":10,"var":"b"},{"coef":15,"var":"c"}]},"op":"<=","rhs":20}],"objective":{"sense":"maximize","terms":[{"coef":10,"var":"a"},{"coef":20,"var":"b"},{"coef":30,"var":"c"}]}}') ORDER BY var

example_queries.description: Single-machine no-overlap schedule minimizing makespan (optimum 10).
example_queries.sql: SELECT objective, status FROM ortools.main.solve_cpsat(model := '{"version":1,"variables":[{"kind":"int","name":"s0","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"int","name":"e0","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"int","name":"s1","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"int","name":"e1","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"int","name":"s2","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"int","name":"e2","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"interval","name":"i0","start":{"var":"s0"},"size":{"const":3},"end":{"var":"e0"}},{"kind":"interval","name":"i1","start":{"var":"s1"},"size":{"const":5},"end":{"var":"e1"}},{"kind":"interval","name":"i2","start":{"var":"s2"},"size":{"const":2},"end":{"var":"e2"}},{"kind":"int","name":"makespan","lb":0,"ub":20}],"constraints":[{"type":"no_overlap","intervals":["i0","i1","i2"]},{"type":"max_equality","target":{"var":"makespan"},"exprs":[{"var":"e0"},{"var":"e1"},{"var":"e2"}]}],"objective":{"sense":"minimize","terms":[{"coef":1,"var":"makespan"}]}}', time_limit_s := 5.0) LIMIT 1

agent_tasks: Three workers must each be assigned to a distinct task. The cost of a (worker, task) pair is given by these [worker, task, cost] arcs: [[0,0,90],[0,1,76],[0,2,75],[1,0,35],[1,1,85],[1,2,55],[2,0,125],[2,1,95],[2,2,90]]. Assign every worker to exactly one task so the total cost is as small as possible, and return that minimum total cost as a single number.
A directed network has [from, to, capacity] arcs [[0,1,20],[0,2,30],[1,2,10],[1,3,10],[2,3,20]]. What is the maximum flow that can be routed from node 0 to node 3? Return a single number.

Route 20 units from node 0 to node 4 over a network whose [from, to, capacity, unit_cost] arcs are [[0,1,15,4],[0,2,8,4],[1,2,20,2],[1,3,4,2],[2,3,15,1],[2,4,4,3],[3,4,20,2],[4,2,5,3]], with node supplies [[0,20],[4,-20]], minimizing total cost. Return the minimum total cost as a single number.

Schedule a job shop whose [job, task, machine, duration] operations are [[0,0,0,3],[0,1,1,2],[1,0,1,2],[1,1,0,4]], minimizing the makespan (the finish time of the last operation). Return the optimal makespan as a single number.
Pack items of sizes [3,5,2,7,1,4] into bins that each hold at most 10. What is the fewest number of bins needed? Return a single number.

A salesperson must visit every location exactly once and return to location 0, over the distance matrix [[0,2,9,10,1],[1,0,6,4,8],[15,7,0,8,3],[6,3,12,0,5],[9,8,4,7,0]]. How many distinct locations does the computed optimal tour visit? Return a single number.

A network has [from, to, capacity, unit_cost] arcs [[0,1,7,3],[0,2,5,1],[1,3,6,2],[2,1,3,1],[2,3,4,4],[3,4,9,1],[1,4,2,6]]. Ship 9 units from node 0 to node 4 at minimum total cost. tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Optimization and constraint-solving table and scalar functions backed by Google OR-Tools, organized into constraint programming, routing, assignment, scheduling, network flow, packing, and introspection categories.

Problems are passed as scalar integer list arguments built by `array_agg`, or -- for the general constraint solver -- as a versioned JSON model. Every solver returns a `status` column, and an unsolved problem yields exactly one status row rather than an empty result.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## OR-Tools Solvers

Prescriptive optimization and constraint-solving functions backed by Google OR-Tools, covering:

- **Constraint programming** -- a general CP-SAT model expressed as versioned JSON
- **Routing** -- shortest tours and capacitated, time-windowed vehicle routing
- **Assignment** -- least-cost matching of workers to tasks
- **Scheduling** -- job-shop and resource-constrained project scheduling
- **Network flow** -- minimum-cost and maximum flow
- **Packing** -- knapsack and bin packing
- **Introspection** -- solver versions and last-solve statistics

Every solver takes its problem as scalar integer list arguments (or a JSON model) and returns rows carrying a `status` column; a problem with no solution yields a single status row, never an empty result.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The statistics of the **most recent solve** handled by this worker process, as `(metric, value)` rows: `status`, `objective`, `best_bound`, `wall_time`, `num_branches`, `num_conflicts`, `num_booleans`, `deterministic_time`. A convenience mirror of the solve metadata; every `value` is NULL until the first solve runs. This is per-process, not strictly per-connection -- the authoritative, race-free source is the metadata columns on each solver's own result rows.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## last_solve_stats

A browsable table of the most recent solve's metrics, one row per metric: `status`, `objective`, `best_bound`, `wall_time`, `num_branches`, `num_conflicts`, `num_booleans`, `deterministic_time`. Scan it after a solve; every `value` is NULL until the first solve runs. It reflects the last solve on this worker *process*, so for a race-free per-query value prefer the metadata columns on the solver's own result rows.

**Reference:** [OR-Tools documentation](https://developers.google.com/optimization/cp/cp_solver)

functions.name: solve_vrp
functions.comment: Vehicle routing problem: route a fleet from a depot to serve stops at minimum total distance, with optional capacity dimensions, time windows, service/travel time, pickup-delivery pairs, droppable stops, and route balancing. OR-Tools routing library.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `solve_vrp`

Route a **fleet of vehicles** from a depot to serve a set of stops at **minimum total distance**, with the full routing surface: multi-dimension **capacity** (`demand` + `vehicle_capacity`), **time windows** (`time_windows` + `service_time` / `travel_time`), **pickup-delivery** pairs (same vehicle + precedence), droppable stops (`allow_dropping` + `drop_penalty`), route balancing (`span_cost_coefficient`), and the OR-Tools `first_solution_strategy` / `local_search_metaheuristic`.

**Inputs.** `distance` (sparse `[from, to, meters]` or dense `n x n`); `demand` = `[node, d0, d1, ...]` (the number of demand columns sets the number of capacity dimensions and therefore the `load_0` .. `load_k` output columns); `num_vehicles`; `vehicle_capacity`; `depot`. Advanced shapes -- per-vehicle / per-dimension capacities, per-vehicle `[start, end]` depots -- go through `settings_json`.

**Outputs.** One row per stop: `route_id` (vehicle), `seq`, `node`, `arrival`, `departure`, `load_0` .. `load_k`, `is_dropped`, `status`. A dropped node appears as a single row with `is_dropped = true` and NULL `route_id`. An unsolved instance returns one status row.

**Determinism.** Governed by the fixed `first_solution_strategy` / `local_search_metaheuristic`. The output `load_*` column count is fixed at bind time from the `demand` argument, so pass `demand` as a literal or a session VARIABLE that is set before the query binds.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# solve_vrp

Capacitated, time-windowed vehicle routing.

**Reference:** [OR-Tools documentation](https://developers.google.com/optimization/routing/cvrp)

vgi.example_queries.description: Capacitated VRP: 1 depot, 3 stops of demand 1, 2 vehicles of capacity 2 (optimal distance 6).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT route_id, seq, node, arrival, load_0 FROM ortools.main.solve_vrp(distance := [[0,1,1],[0,2,1],[0,3,2],[1,0,1],[1,2,1],[1,3,2],[2,0,1],[2,1,1],[2,3,1],[3,0,2],[3,1,2],[3,2,1]]::BIGINT[][], demand := [[1,1],[2,1],[3,1]]::BIGINT[][], num_vehicles := 2, vehicle_capacity := 2, depot := 0, time_limit_s := 1.0) ORDER BY route_id, seq

vgi.executable_examples.description: Capacitated VRP: 1 depot, 3 stops of demand 1, 2 vehicles of capacity 2 (optimal distance 6).
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT route_id, seq, node, arrival, load_0 FROM ortools.main.solve_vrp(distance := [[0,1,1],[0,2,1],[0,3,2],[1,0,1],[1,2,1],[1,3,2],[2,0,1],[2,1,1],[2,3,1],[3,0,2],[3,1,2],[3,2,1]]::BIGINT[][], demand := [[1,1],[2,1],[3,1]]::BIGINT[][], num_vehicles := 2, vehicle_capacity := 2, depot := 0, time_limit_s := 1.0) ORDER BY route_id, seq

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
The number of `load_d` columns is fixed at bind time from the `demand` argument (one per capacity dimension), so the output schema varies by call. For `k+1` capacity dimensions the columns are:

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| route_id | INTEGER | Vehicle index (NULL on a dropped-node row). |
| seq | INTEGER | 0-based stop order on the vehicle. |
| node | BIGINT | Node id (depot at seq 0 and last). |
| arrival | BIGINT | Cumulative time/distance at arrival. |
| departure | BIGINT | Arrival + service time. |
| load_0 | BIGINT | Cumulative load for capacity dimension 0. |
| load_k | BIGINT | Cumulative load for capacity dimension k (one load_d column per dimension). |
| is_dropped | BOOLEAN | True on the row emitted for a dropped node. |
| status | VARCHAR | OPTIMAL / FEASIBLE / INFEASIBLE / UNKNOWN / MODEL_INVALID. |

functions.name: solve_tsp
functions.comment: Travelling salesperson: shortest single-vehicle tour visiting every node once and returning to the start, over a distance matrix. OR-Tools routing library.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `solve_tsp`

Find the **shortest single-vehicle tour** that visits every node once and returns to `start`, over a distance matrix.

**Inputs.** `distance` is either sparse `[from, to, meters]` integer triples (build with `array_agg([f, t, m])`) or a dense `n x n` matrix; `start` is the depot node. **Outputs.** The tour in visit order: `seq`, `node`, `arrival` (cumulative distance), `status`. The tour rotation / direction may vary but the length is optimal.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `solve_knapsack`

Choose a subset of items to **maximize total value** subject to one or more **capacity dimensions** (multi-dimensional 0/1 knapsack).

**Inputs.** `item_values` = `[v0, v1, ...]`; `weights` = `[[w0_d0, w0_d1, ...], ...]` (one row per item, one column per capacity dimension); `capacities` = `[c_d0, c_d1, ...]`. **Outputs.** One row per item with `chosen` (`BOOLEAN`) and `status`.

functions.name: solve_jobshop
functions.comment: Job-shop scheduling: schedule the tasks of several jobs on shared machines (tasks of a job run in order, one task per machine at a time) to minimize the makespan. CP-SAT.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `solve_jobshop`

Schedule the tasks of several **jobs** onto shared **machines** to minimize the **makespan** (the time the last task finishes). Within a job, tasks run in `task` order; each machine runs one task at a time.

**Inputs.** `tasks` = `[job, task, machine, duration]` integer rows. Optional `horizon` (defaults to the sum of durations), `time_limit_s`, `random_seed`.

**Outputs.** One row per task with its `start` / `end`, the optimal `makespan` (repeated on every row), and `status`. An infeasible / unsolved instance returns a single status row.

functions.name: solve_cpsat
functions.comment: Solve an arbitrary CP-SAT constraint-programming model expressed as a versioned JSON document (variables, constraints, objective). Returns one row per variable plus solve metadata. The general escape hatch for constraints highs/LP cannot express.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `solve_cpsat`

Solve an **arbitrary CP-SAT constraint-programming model** handed in as a **versioned JSON document** -- the general escape hatch for everything the per-domain builders and the `highs` LP/MIP extension cannot express (global constraints like `all_different`, `no_overlap`, `cumulative`, `circuit`, reification, intervals).

**The model.** A JSON object with `version` (must be 1), `variables` (each `int` / `bool` / `interval` with a unique `name`), `constraints`, and an optional `objective`. All numeric domains are **integers** -- a fractional bound / coefficient / constant is rejected with a clear error (scale floats to integers first). The full grammar is in the README (section A).

**Outputs.** One row per variable: `var`, `value`, plus the solve metadata (`status`, `objective`, `best_bound`, `wall_time`, `num_branches`) repeated on every row so a single SELECT is self-describing. Interval variables expand to `<name>.start` / `.size` / `.end` (and `.presence` for optional intervals).

**The empty-vs-infeasible contract.** A model with no solution still returns **exactly one row** carrying `status` in {`INFEASIBLE`, `MODEL_INVALID`, `UNKNOWN`} with NULL `var`/`value`; a solve is never an empty result set. Test `WHERE status='INFEASIBLE'`, never `count(*)=0`.

**Determinism.** Single-threaded by default (`num_workers := 0`) with a fixed `random_seed`, so the objective and assignment are reproducible.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# solve_cpsat

Solve a hand-built **CP-SAT** model expressed as a versioned JSON document.

See the README (section A) for the full JSON dialect: `variables` (int / bool / interval), `constraints` (linear, all_different, element, table, no_overlap, cumulative, circuit, reservoir, mult/div/abs/min/max equality, bool_or/and/xor, implication, with optional `enforce` reification), and an optional `objective`.

All numeric domains are integers. A no-solution model returns a single status row.

**Reference:** [OR-Tools documentation](https://developers.google.com/optimization/cp/cp_solver)

vgi.example_queries.description: 0/1 knapsack as a CP-SAT model: maximize value within a weight budget (optimum 40).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT var, value, status, objective FROM ortools.main.solve_cpsat(model := '{"version":1,"variables":[{"kind":"bool","name":"a"},{"kind":"bool","name":"b"},{"kind":"bool","name":"c"}],"constraints":[{"type":"linear","expr":{"sum":[{"coef":5,"var":"a"},{"coef":10,"var":"b"},{"coef":15,"var":"c"}]},"op":"<=","rhs":20}],"objective":{"sense":"maximize","terms":[{"coef":10,"var":"a"},{"coef":20,"var":"b"},{"coef":30,"var":"c"}]}}') ORDER BY var

vgi.example_queries.description: Single-machine no-overlap schedule minimizing makespan (optimum 10).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT objective, status FROM ortools.main.solve_cpsat(model := '{"version":1,"variables":[{"kind":"int","name":"s0","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"int","name":"e0","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"int","name":"s1","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"int","name":"e1","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"int","name":"s2","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"int","name":"e2","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"interval","name":"i0","start":{"var":"s0"},"size":{"const":3},"end":{"var":"e0"}},{"kind":"interval","name":"i1","start":{"var":"s1"},"size":{"const":5},"end":{"var":"e1"}},{"kind":"interval","name":"i2","start":{"var":"s2"},"size":{"const":2},"end":{"var":"e2"}},{"kind":"int","name":"makespan","lb":0,"ub":20}],"constraints":[{"type":"no_overlap","intervals":["i0","i1","i2"]},{"type":"max_equality","target":{"var":"makespan"},"exprs":[{"var":"e0"},{"var":"e1"},{"var":"e2"}]}],"objective":{"sense":"minimize","terms":[{"coef":1,"var":"makespan"}]}}', time_limit_s := 5.0) LIMIT 1

vgi.executable_examples.description: 0/1 knapsack as a CP-SAT model: maximize value within a weight budget (optimum 40).
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT var, value, status, objective FROM ortools.main.solve_cpsat(model := '{"version":1,"variables":[{"kind":"bool","name":"a"},{"kind":"bool","name":"b"},{"kind":"bool","name":"c"}],"constraints":[{"type":"linear","expr":{"sum":[{"coef":5,"var":"a"},{"coef":10,"var":"b"},{"coef":15,"var":"c"}]},"op":"<=","rhs":20}],"objective":{"sense":"maximize","terms":[{"coef":10,"var":"a"},{"coef":20,"var":"b"},{"coef":30,"var":"c"}]}}') ORDER BY var

vgi.executable_examples.description: Single-machine no-overlap schedule minimizing makespan (optimum 10).
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT objective, status FROM ortools.main.solve_cpsat(model := '{"version":1,"variables":[{"kind":"int","name":"s0","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"int","name":"e0","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"int","name":"s1","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"int","name":"e1","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"int","name":"s2","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"int","name":"e2","lb":0,"ub":20},{"kind":"interval","name":"i0","start":{"var":"s0"},"size":{"const":3},"end":{"var":"e0"}},{"kind":"interval","name":"i1","start":{"var":"s1"},"size":{"const":5},"end":{"var":"e1"}},{"kind":"interval","name":"i2","start":{"var":"s2"},"size":{"const":2},"end":{"var":"e2"}},{"kind":"int","name":"makespan","lb":0,"ub":20}],"constraints":[{"type":"no_overlap","intervals":["i0","i1","i2"]},{"type":"max_equality","target":{"var":"makespan"},"exprs":[{"var":"e0"},{"var":"e1"},{"var":"e2"}]}],"objective":{"sense":"minimize","terms":[{"coef":1,"var":"makespan"}]}}', time_limit_s := 5.0) LIMIT 1

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## `max_flow`

Compute the **maximum flow** that can be pushed from `source` to `sink` over a capacitated network (the max-flow / min-cut value).

**Inputs.** `arcs` = `[from, to, capacity]` integer arcs; `source` and `sink` node ids. **Outputs.** One row per arc with positive flow: `from`, `to`, `flow`, `status`. Use the scalar `max_flow_value(arcs, source, sink)` when you only need the total.

# max_flow
