workers.title: Perpetual Futures Across Venues
workers.tagline: US-regulated perpetual futures data (funding, marks, order books, premiums, OI) normalized across Kalshi, Coinbase & Bitnomial in DuckDB (Python)
workers.subtitle: Funding, marks, books and carry for US-regulated perps, benchmarked against offshore venues.
workers.summary: Normalized market data for US-regulated perpetual futures on Kalshi, Coinbase Derivatives and Bitnomial, with Hyperliquid, Binance and Bybit as an offshore benchmark: funding, marks, order books, trades and carry analytics. Read-only, no API key needed.
workers.doc_md:
# Perpetual futures, normalized across venues

Funding, marks, books, trades and bars for **US-regulated perpetual futures** (Kalshi, Coinbase Derivatives, Bitnomial) next to an **offshore benchmark** (Hyperliquid, Binance USD-M, Bybit), in one schema.

**Conventions.** Prices are quote currency per one unit of the underlying (USD per BTC, per share, per troy ounce), whatever the venue's own quoting. Sizes are contracts, and `contract_size` is underlying units per contract. Funding rates are decimal fractions per interval with one sign convention: **positive means longs pay shorts**. Annualized rates are simple: `rate * 8760 / interval_hours`. Times are UTC `TIMESTAMPTZ`.

Each venue sits behind its own adapter; the venue documentation in the repository records how each venue's units and signs were mapped, with sources. Read-only public market data, no account or order endpoints. Market data belongs to the venues and is subject to their terms of use.

## Sources and references

- [Kalshi API](https://docs.kalshi.com/) — Kalshi perpetuals: markets, funding, books
- [Coinbase Advanced Trade API](https://docs.cdp.coinbase.com/coinbase-app/advanced-trade-apis/overview) — Coinbase Derivatives perpetual-style futures
- [Bitnomial REST API](https://bitnomial.com/exchange/docs/api/rest/overview) and the [OG.com public API](https://exchange-developer.crypto.com/fcm-b2c/v1/docs/api/rest-introduction) — the other US-regulated venues
- [Hyperliquid docs](https://hyperliquid.gitbook.io/hyperliquid-docs) — funding, liquidations and HIP-3 builder perps on the offshore benchmark
- [CCXT](https://github.com/ccxt/ccxt) — the library used for the Hyperliquid, Binance and Bybit public endpoints

example_queries.description: Which venues are reachable right now
example_queries.sql: SELECT venue, status, instrument_count, last_error FROM perps.main.venues() ORDER BY venue

example_queries.description: What Coinbase Derivatives does not serve publicly, and why
example_queries.sql: SELECT capability, support, notes FROM perps.main.capabilities(venue := 'coinbase') WHERE support <> 'supported' ORDER BY capability

example_queries.description: Every BTC perp: how much BTC one contract is and how often it funds
example_queries.sql: SELECT venue, symbol, contract_size, funding_interval_hours, funding_cap FROM perps.main.instruments(underlying := 'BTC') ORDER BY venue, contract_size

example_queries.description: Average annualized BTC funding per venue over the last week
example_queries.sql: SELECT venue, avg(rate_annualized) AS mean_apr, count(*) AS settlements FROM perps.main.funding(underlying := 'BTC', start_date := now() - INTERVAL 7 DAY) GROUP BY venue ORDER BY mean_apr DESC

example_queries.description: ETH perps side by side: price, premium, carry and size
example_queries.sql: SELECT venue, symbol, mark_price, premium_bps, funding_rate_annualized, open_interest_usd FROM perps.main.marks(underlying := 'ETH') ORDER BY open_interest_usd DESC NULLS LAST

example_queries.description: Notional resting in the top 25 levels of Kalshi's BTC perp, per side
example_queries.sql: SELECT side, max(cum_usd) AS depth_usd FROM perps.main.order_book('kalshi', 'KXBTCPERP', depth := 25) GROUP BY side ORDER BY side

example_queries.description: Aggressor buy vs sell notional on Kalshi BTC over 15 minutes
example_queries.sql: SELECT taker_side, count(*) AS n, sum(size_usd) AS usd FROM perps.main.trades('kalshi', 'KXBTCPERP', start_date := now() - INTERVAL 15 MINUTE) GROUP BY taker_side ORDER BY taker_side

example_queries.description: Two weeks of daily Kalshi BTC closes, volume and open interest
example_queries.sql: SELECT ts, close, volume_usd, open_interest_contracts FROM perps.main.candles('kalshi', 'KXBTCPERP', bar := '1d') ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 14

example_queries.description: Which BTC perp trades richest to its own index
example_queries.sql: SELECT venue, symbol, premium_bps FROM perps.main.premium(underlying := 'BTC') ORDER BY premium_bps DESC NULLS LAST

example_queries.description: The widest BTC funding carry between any two venues this week
example_queries.sql: SELECT venue_a, venue_b, spread_bps, carry_trade FROM perps.main.funding_spread('BTC') ORDER BY abs(spread_bps) DESC LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: What a $50k ETH clip costs on Kalshi
example_queries.sql: SELECT spread_bps, buy_cost_bps, sell_cost_bps, imbalance FROM perps.main.depth_metrics('kalshi', 'KXETHPERP', notional_usd := 50000)

example_queries.description: Estimated ETH liquidation bands on Hyperliquid with the default leverage mix
example_queries.sql: SELECT side, leverage, liquidation_price, cum_notional_usd FROM perps.main.liquidation_estimate('hyperliquid', 'ETH') WHERE feasible ORDER BY side, distance_pct

example_queries.description: Where the next BTC funding settlement is heading
example_queries.sql: SELECT weight_accrued, accrued_rate * 1e4 AS accrued_bps, projected_rate_annualized FROM perps.main.kalshi_funding_nowcast('KXBTCPERP')

example_queries.description: Kalshi crypto perps' funding deadbands
example_queries.sql: SELECT symbol, funding_deadband, funding_limit_unit FROM perps.main.raw_kalshi_markets() WHERE asset_class = 'Crypto' ORDER BY symbol

example_queries.description: Mean and worst BTC premium over the last half hour
example_queries.sql: SELECT avg(premium_bps) AS mean_bps, max(abs(premium_bps)) AS worst_bps FROM perps.main.raw_kalshi_premium_index('KXBTCPERP', start_date := now() - INTERVAL 30 MINUTE)

example_queries.description: Coinbase perps with the highest overnight margin
example_queries.sql: SELECT symbol, intraday_long_margin_rate, overnight_long_margin_rate FROM perps.main.raw_coinbase_products() ORDER BY overnight_long_margin_rate DESC LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Bitnomial perps with their size tier and margin rate
example_queries.sql: SELECT symbol, contract_size, product_group_margin_rate FROM perps.main.raw_bitnomial_products() ORDER BY symbol

example_queries.description: How much of its per-interval funding cap each BTC perp's current rate uses (marks joined to instruments; venues that publish no cap drop out)
example_queries.sql: SELECT m.venue, m.symbol, m.funding_rate, i.funding_cap, abs(m.funding_rate) / i.funding_cap AS cap_used FROM perps.main.marks(underlying := 'BTC') AS m JOIN perps.main.instruments(underlying := 'BTC') AS i USING (venue, symbol) WHERE i.funding_cap IS NOT NULL ORDER BY cap_used DESC, m.venue, m.symbol

example_queries.description: Venues that answer right now and serve a public order book, with the endpoint each uses
example_queries.sql: SELECT v.venue, v.status, c.notes FROM perps.main.venues() AS v JOIN perps.main.capabilities() AS c USING (venue) WHERE c.capability = 'order_book' AND c.support = 'supported' AND v.status = 'ok' ORDER BY v.venue

example_queries.description: Kalshi BTC perp, last week: each daily bar's open-to-close return next to the funding its three settlements charged longs, both in bps
example_queries.sql: WITH bars AS (SELECT ts, coalesce(lead(ts) OVER (ORDER BY ts), ts + INTERVAL 1 DAY) AS bar_end, (close / open - 1) * 1e4 AS return_bps FROM perps.main.candles('kalshi', 'KXBTCPERP', bar := '1d')) SELECT b.ts, b.return_bps, sum(f.rate_bps) AS funding_bps FROM bars AS b JOIN perps.main.funding(venue := 'kalshi', underlying := 'BTC') AS f ON f.funding_time > b.ts AND f.funding_time <= b.bar_end GROUP BY b.ts, b.return_bps HAVING count(*) = 3 ORDER BY b.ts

example_queries.description: The next Kalshi BTC settlement's projected annualized rate against the past week's settled average
example_queries.sql: SELECT n.funding_time, n.weight_accrued, n.projected_rate_annualized, h.week_mean_apr, n.projected_rate_annualized - h.week_mean_apr AS vs_week FROM perps.main.kalshi_funding_nowcast('KXBTCPERP') AS n CROSS JOIN (SELECT avg(rate_annualized) AS week_mean_apr FROM perps.main.funding(venue := 'kalshi', underlying := 'BTC')) AS h

example_queries.description: Per-minute traded notional on Coinbase's BTC perp
example_queries.sql: SELECT date_trunc('minute', ts) AS minute, sum(size_usd) AS usd FROM perps.main.trades('coinbase', 'BIP-20DEC30-CDE', max_trades := 2000) GROUP BY minute ORDER BY minute

example_queries.description: Where Coinbase charges shorts the most extra overnight margin
example_queries.sql: SELECT symbol, overnight_short_margin_rate - overnight_long_margin_rate AS short_premium FROM perps.main.raw_coinbase_products() ORDER BY short_premium DESC LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Today's price limits around settlement for Bitnomial's BTC perps
example_queries.sql: SELECT symbol, price_limit_lower, settlement_price, price_limit_upper FROM perps.main.raw_bitnomial_products() WHERE base_symbol LIKE 'BTC%' ORDER BY symbol

example_queries.description: Kalshi markets whose leverage shrinks most at $1m notional
example_queries.sql: SELECT symbol, json_extract(leverage_estimates, '$."1000000"') AS lev_at_1m FROM perps.main.raw_kalshi_markets() WHERE status = 'active' ORDER BY lev_at_1m LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Coinbase ETH perp trading range over the last day
example_queries.sql: SELECT max(high) - min(low) AS range_usd FROM perps.main.candles('coinbase', 'ETP-20DEC30-CDE', start_date := now() - INTERVAL 1 DAY)

example_queries.description: US ETH perps priced against Hyperliquid's oracle
example_queries.sql: SELECT venue, symbol, reference_source, premium_bps FROM perps.main.premium(underlying := 'ETH', reference := 'hyperliquid') ORDER BY venue

example_queries.description: Top five levels of Coinbase's nano BTC perp
example_queries.sql: SELECT side, level, price, size_usd FROM perps.main.order_book('coinbase', 'BIP-20DEC30-CDE', depth := 5) ORDER BY side, level

example_queries.description: Kalshi's active perps by asset class
example_queries.sql: SELECT asset_class, count(*) AS contracts FROM perps.main.instruments(venue := 'kalshi') GROUP BY asset_class ORDER BY contracts DESC

example_queries.description: Kalshi BTC bands under an assumed 5% maintenance margin
example_queries.sql: SELECT side, leverage, distance_pct FROM perps.main.liquidation_estimate('kalshi', 'KXBTCPERP', mm_rate := 0.05, leverages := '3,5,10', weights := '0.5,0.3,0.2') ORDER BY side, leverage

example_queries.description: Settlement if the BTC premium holds at 2 bps for the rest of the window
example_queries.sql: SELECT projected_rate_annualized FROM perps.main.kalshi_funding_nowcast('KXBTCPERP', assume_premium := 0.0002)

example_queries.description: Minute-averaged ETH premium over the last ten minutes
example_queries.sql: SELECT date_trunc('minute', ts) AS minute, avg(premium_bps) AS bps FROM perps.main.raw_kalshi_premium_index('KXETHPERP') GROUP BY minute ORDER BY minute

example_queries.description: How many venues fully support each capability
example_queries.sql: SELECT capability, count(*) FILTER (WHERE support = 'supported') AS venues_supported FROM perps.main.capabilities() GROUP BY capability ORDER BY capability

example_queries.description: Venues with a public order book
example_queries.sql: SELECT venue FROM perps.main.capabilities() WHERE capability = 'order_book' AND support = 'supported' ORDER BY venue;

example_queries.description: Kalshi's funding-history support
example_queries.sql: SELECT support, auth_required FROM perps.main.capabilities(venue := 'kalshi') WHERE capability = 'funding_history';

example_queries.description: Kalshi's ten largest perps by open-interest notional
example_queries.sql: SELECT underlying, open_interest_usd FROM perps.main.marks(venue := 'kalshi') ORDER BY open_interest_usd DESC NULLS LAST LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: 30-day ETH carry of Bitnomial against every other venue
example_queries.sql: SELECT symbol_a, symbol_b, spread_bps FROM perps.main.funding_spread('ETH', start_date := now() - INTERVAL 30 DAY) WHERE venue_a = 'bitnomial' OR venue_b = 'bitnomial' ORDER BY spread_bps

example_queries.description: Bitnomial's last nine ETH funding settlements with the mark-vs-index premium
example_queries.sql: SELECT funding_time, rate_bps, premium_bps FROM perps.main.funding(venue := 'bitnomial', underlying := 'ETH') ORDER BY funding_time DESC LIMIT 9

example_queries.description: Can Coinbase's BTC perp absorb a $1m market buy
example_queries.sql: SELECT venue, buy_cost_bps, fully_filled FROM perps.main.depth_metrics('coinbase', 'BIP-20DEC30-CDE', notional_usd := 1000000)

example_queries.description: US-regulated venues and how many capabilities each supports, without network calls
example_queries.sql: SELECT venue, venue_type, len(capabilities) AS n_capabilities FROM perps.main.venues(probe := false) WHERE venue_type = 'us_regulated' ORDER BY venue

## main

- **Reference**: venue health, the capability matrix, contract specifications.

- **Analytics**: premiums, carry spreads, depth costs, liquidation estimates.
- **Venue raw**: fields that only one venue publishes.

Sizes are contracts, and `contract_size` is underlying units per contract. Funding rates are decimal fractions per interval with one sign convention: **positive means longs pay shorts**. Annualized rates are simple: `rate * 8760 / interval_hours`. Times are UTC `TIMESTAMPTZ`.

vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH bars AS (SELECT ts, coalesce(lead(ts) OVER (ORDER BY ts), ts + INTERVAL 1 DAY) AS bar_end, (close / open - 1) * 1e4 AS return_bps FROM perps.main.candles('kalshi', 'KXBTCPERP', bar := '1d')) SELECT b.ts, b.return_bps, sum(f.rate_bps) AS funding_bps FROM bars AS b JOIN perps.main.funding(venue := 'kalshi', underlying := 'BTC') AS f ON f.funding_time > b.ts AND f.funding_time <= b.bar_end GROUP BY b.ts, b.return_bps HAVING count(*) = 3 ORDER BY b.ts

vgi.example_queries.description: The next Kalshi BTC settlement's projected annualized rate against the past week's settled average
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT n.funding_time, n.weight_accrued, n.projected_rate_annualized, h.week_mean_apr, n.projected_rate_annualized - h.week_mean_apr AS vs_week FROM perps.main.kalshi_funding_nowcast('KXBTCPERP') AS n CROSS JOIN (SELECT avg(rate_annualized) AS week_mean_apr FROM perps.main.funding(venue := 'kalshi', underlying := 'BTC')) AS h

functions.name: trades
functions.comment: Public trades for one contract in a time window, normalized price and USD size, with taker side

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Public trades for one contract: `trades('kalshi', 'KXBTCPERP', start_date := now() - INTERVAL 10 MINUTE)`. Venue and symbol are positional. Columns: `trade_id`, `ts`, `price` per underlying unit, `size_contracts`, `size_usd`, `taker_side` ('buy'/'sell'; Coinbase publishes the maker side, so it is inverted), `is_block_trade`. Default window is the last hour; `max_trades` caps the result (default 10,000). Pages stream in batches. Bitnomial trades are WebSocket-only and raise an error.

functions.name: instruments
functions.comment: Perpetual contract specifications per venue: underlying, contract size, tick, funding interval, cap, margin

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per perpetual contract. `symbol` is venue-native (pass it to order_book, trades, candles); `underlying` and `canonical_id` are shared across venues (join on them). `contract_size` is underlying units per contract, so notional = contracts * contract_size * price. `tick_size` is in quote currency per underlying unit. `funding_interval_hours`, `funding_cap` (decimal per interval), `max_leverage`, `initial_margin_rate`, `maintenance_margin_rate` (only where documented) and `margin_source`. Arguments: `venue := 'kalshi'`, `underlying := 'BTC'`, `include_inactive := true`. Kalshi lists crypto, single-stock, index, metal and energy perps; Coinbase lists perp-style futures. Hyperliquid includes its HIP-3 builder dexes: `symbol` keeps the prefix ('xyz:NVDA'), `underlying` drops it ('NVDA'), and `dex` names the builder dex.

functions.name: liquidation_estimate
functions.comment: ESTIMATE of liquidation price bands from open interest, an assumed leverage mix and the venue's maintenance margin

tags.vgi.doc_llm: An ESTIMATE, not venue data: splits a contract's open interest (both sides hold all of it) across an assumed leverage distribution and computes each bucket's liquidation price for an isolated linear position entered at the mark: X = entry * (side - 1/L) / (side - mm). `liquidation_estimate('hyperliquid', 'BTC')`; venue and symbol are positional. Parameters: `leverages` (default '2,3,5,10,20'), `weights` (default '0.30,0.25,0.20,0.15,0.10'), `mm_rate` (maintenance fraction), `entry_price`. With `mm_rate` NULL it uses the venue's documented maintenance margin and REFUSES venues that publish none (Kalshi, Coinbase, Bitnomial, Binance, Bybit): pass `mm_rate` to estimate them under your own assumption. Every row carries `estimate_method`, `mm_source` and `feasible`; `cum_notional_usd` accumulates per side nearest-first.

functions.name: kalshi_funding_nowcast
functions.comment: Kalshi funding for one window, computed from the per-second premium with Kalshi's linear time weights: accrued so far, projected to settlement, or reconstructed for a past window

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Forecast or reconstruct a Kalshi perp funding settlement: `kalshi_funding_nowcast('KXBTCPERP')` for the current window, `funding_time := TIMESTAMPTZ '...'` for a past one. Kalshi funding is the linear time-weighted mean of the per-second premium (second i of the window weighs i), set to 0 when its absolute value is below `funding_deadband` and clamped to `funding_cap`. `accrued_rate` is the weighted mean so far and equals Kalshi's own estimate; `weight_accrued` says how much of the final weight it represents (about 1.6% after the first hour of an 8-hour window). `projected_rate` fills the rest of the window with `assume_premium` (default: the mean of the last `recent_minutes`). For a past window `settled_rate` shows the published settlement next to the reconstruction. Rates are per interval; positive = longs pay.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## kalshi_funding_nowcast(symbol, funding_time := NULL, assume_premium := NULL, recent_minutes := 15)

Kalshi funding is `sum(i * p_i) / sum(i)` over the seconds `i` of the window, zeroed inside the deadband and capped. This returns the accrued value, a projection to settlement, and for a past window the settled rate.

vgi.example_queries.description: Where the next BTC funding settlement is heading
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT weight_accrued, accrued_rate * 1e4 AS accrued_bps, projected_rate_annualized FROM perps.main.kalshi_funding_nowcast('KXBTCPERP')

vgi.example_queries.description: Settlement if the BTC premium holds at 2 bps for the rest of the window
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT projected_rate_annualized FROM perps.main.kalshi_funding_nowcast('KXBTCPERP', assume_premium := 0.0002)

vgi.example_queries.description: The next Kalshi BTC settlement's projected annualized rate against the past week's settled average
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT n.funding_time, n.weight_accrued, n.projected_rate_annualized, h.week_mean_apr, n.projected_rate_annualized - h.week_mean_apr AS vs_week FROM perps.main.kalshi_funding_nowcast('KXBTCPERP') AS n CROSS JOIN (SELECT avg(rate_annualized) AS week_mean_apr FROM perps.main.funding(venue := 'kalshi', underlying := 'BTC')) AS h

tags.vgi.doc_llm: For one underlying (positional: `funding_spread('BTC')`), averages each contract's settled, annualized funding over the window (`start_date`/`end_date`, default last 7 days) and returns every pair of contracts on different venues: `annualized_a`, `annualized_b`, `spread_annualized` = a - b, `spread_bps`, observation counts and `carry_trade` ('short a / long b' collects a positive spread, because positive funding means longs pay). workers.title: PII Detection & Redaction
workers.tagline: PII detection, redaction & anonymization for DuckDB (Python, Microsoft Presidio)
workers.subtitle: Detect, redact, and mask personal data in text from SQL, using Microsoft Presidio.
workers.summary: PII detection + redaction for SQL, powered by Microsoft Presidio
workers.doc_md:
# PII Detection & Redaction in SQL

![Microsoft Presidio logo](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft/presidio/main/docs/assets/dps-icon.svg)

**Find, redact, and anonymize personally-identifiable information (PII) in free text directly from DuckDB SQL** — person names, email addresses, phone numbers, credit-card numbers, US SSNs, locations, URLs, IP addresses and more — powered by [Microsoft Presidio](https://microsoft.github.io/presidio/).

This extension brings privacy scrubbing, data-loss-prevention (DLP) checks, and PII auditing to your data warehouse without exporting a single row to an external service. It is built for data engineers, privacy and security teams, and analysts who need to sanitize logs, user-generated content, support transcripts, and other text columns before sharing, training, or archiving them. Every function runs in-process over Apache Arrow, so detection happens right next to your data and PII never leaves your environment.

Detection is powered by [Microsoft Presidio](https://github.com/microsoft/presidio) (its analyzer and anonymizer engines) backed by a [spaCy](https://spacy.io/) named-entity-recognition pipeline using the pinned `en_core_web_sm` model from the [spaCy models](https://github.com/explosion/spacy-models) collection. Presidio combines this NLP model with pattern recognizers and checksum validation (for example, Luhn validation of credit-card numbers) to flag a broad catalog of entity types, each with a confidence score and character offsets you can inspect or threshold.

## What you can do

Two complementary capabilities are grouped in the `main` schema. *Detection* answers whether text holds sensitive data, which categories it holds, and exactly where each value sits (with a confidence score you can threshold). *Redaction* rewrites the text so the sensitive values are gone -- either labelled by the kind of value that was there, or masked so even the shape is hidden. Detection powers filtering, alerting, and auditing; redaction powers safe sharing, export, and archival. Every operation accepts an optional ISO language argument (defaulting to English) and treats NULL or blank input gracefully.

```sql
SELECT pii.main.redact('Call John Smith at john@example.com');
-- 'Call <PERSON> at <EMAIL_ADDRESS>'
```

Learn more from the [Presidio documentation](https://microsoft.github.io/presidio/), the [Presidio source repository](https://github.com/microsoft/presidio), and the [spaCy NLP library](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy).

example_queries.description: Flag whether text contains any PII (a boolean predicate for filtering).
example_queries.sql: SELECT pii.main.has_pii('Call John Smith at john@example.com')

example_queries.description: Replace each PII entity with a <TYPE> tag naming its kind.
example_queries.sql: SELECT pii.main.redact('Call John Smith at john@example.com')

example_queries.description: Mask each PII entity's characters with '*'.
example_queries.sql: SELECT pii.main.anonymize('Call John Smith at john@example.com')

example_queries.description: List the distinct PII entity types present in text.
example_queries.sql: SELECT pii.main.pii_types('Call John Smith at john@example.com')

example_queries.description: Enumerate every detected PII entity with its offsets and confidence.
example_queries.sql: SELECT entity_type, text, start, end_pos, score FROM pii.main.detect_pii('Call John Smith at john@example.com') ORDER BY start

example_queries.description: Discover which entity types the analyzer can detect.
example_queries.sql: SELECT entity_type FROM pii.main.supported_entities() ORDER BY entity_type

example_queries.description: Scrub a ticket column: keep only tickets where has_pii fires, and show each one's tag-redacted text next to the sorted list of PII types found in it (the clean printer ticket is filtered out).
example_queries.sql: WITH tickets(id, body) AS (VALUES (1, 'Hi, this is John Smith, my email is john.smith@example.com'), (2, 'Please charge my card 4111-1111-1111-1111 today'), (3, 'The printer on floor 3 is jammed again'), (4, 'Jane Doe can be reached at jane@example.org')) SELECT id, pii.main.redact(body) AS redacted, pii.main.pii_types(body) AS pii_found FROM tickets WHERE pii.main.has_pii(body) ORDER BY id

example_queries.description: PII prevalence report: for every entity type the analyzer recognises (the entity_types table), count how many tickets contain it according to pii_types, most common first; recognizable types never seen report 0.
example_queries.sql: WITH tickets(id, body) AS (VALUES (1, 'Hi, this is John Smith, my email is john.smith@example.com'), (2, 'Please charge my card 4111-1111-1111-1111 today'), (3, 'The printer on floor 3 is jammed again'), (4, 'Jane Doe can be reached at jane@example.org')), found AS (SELECT id, unnest(pii.main.pii_types(body)) AS entity_type FROM tickets) SELECT e.entity_type, count(DISTINCT f.id) AS tickets FROM pii.main.entity_types AS e LEFT JOIN found AS f USING (entity_type) GROUP BY e.entity_type ORDER BY tickets DESC, e.entity_type

example_queries.description: Tune the confidence threshold: list the entity types pii_types finds at the default 0.5 threshold that detect_pii no longer reports at score_threshold := 0.9 (here the 0.85-confidence PERSON and the 0.5-confidence URL; the 1.0 EMAIL_ADDRESS survives).
example_queries.sql: SELECT unnest(pii.main.pii_types('Hi, this is John Smith, my email is john.smith@example.com')) AS entity_type EXCEPT SELECT entity_type FROM pii.main.detect_pii('Hi, this is John Smith, my email is john.smith@example.com', score_threshold := 0.9) ORDER BY entity_type

example_queries.description: Count how many PII entity types the analyzer recognises.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS n FROM pii.main.entity_types

example_queries.description: Check whether the analyzer recognises credit-card numbers.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) > 0 AS detects_cards FROM pii.main.entity_types WHERE entity_type = 'CREDIT_CARD'

example_queries.description: Find which detectable entity types relate to payment cards.
example_queries.sql: SELECT entity_type FROM pii.main.supported_entities() WHERE entity_type LIKE '%CARD%' ORDER BY entity_type

example_queries.description: Count how many entity types the analyzer supports.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pii.main.supported_entities()

example_queries.description: Keep only high-confidence detections via score_threshold.
example_queries.sql: SELECT entity_type, text FROM pii.main.detect_pii('Email john@example.com', score_threshold := 0.8)

example_queries.description: Detect whether text contains any PII.
example_queries.sql: SELECT pii.main.has_pii('Call John Smith at john@example.com') AS has_pii;

example_queries.description: Tag-redact each PII entity with its <TYPE> label.
example_queries.sql: SELECT pii.main.redact('Call John Smith at john@example.com') AS redacted;

example_queries.description: Mask each PII entity's characters with '*'.
example_queries.sql: SELECT pii.main.anonymize('Call John Smith at john@example.com') AS masked;

example_queries.description: List the distinct PII entity types present in text.
example_queries.sql: SELECT pii.main.pii_types('Call John Smith at john@example.com') AS types;

example_queries.description: Expand text into one row per detected PII entity.
example_queries.sql: SELECT entity_type, text, start, end_pos FROM pii.main.detect_pii('Call John Smith at john@example.com') ORDER BY start;

example_queries.description: Count how many PII entity types the analyzer supports.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS n FROM pii.main.supported_entities();

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## main

The main schema groups every PII capability in the pii catalog. Reach for it whenever you need to find, scrub, or audit personally-identifiable information in a text column. Two kinds of work live here.

- **Detection** tells you about the PII in a value without changing it: whether any is present (a boolean predicate for filtering), which distinct entity types occur (as a sorted array), the full per-occurrence detail (one row per entity with its type, character offsets, and confidence score you can threshold), and which entity types the analyzer is able to recognise at all.
- **Redaction** rewrites the text so the sensitive values are removed -- either replaced by a tag naming the kind of value that was there, or masked character-for-character so even the shape is hidden.

The per-row operations are scalars usable inline in any projection or predicate; the per-occurrence and discovery operations are table functions. Every operation takes an optional ISO language argument (defaulting to English). Detection is powered by Microsoft Presidio with a spaCy NLP model; NULL or blank input is handled gracefully (NULL or no rows). Detection tags a broad set of entity types (PERSON, EMAIL_ADDRESS, PHONE_NUMBER, CREDIT_CARD, US_SSN, LOCATION, URL, IP_ADDRESS, and more), each with a confidence score you can raise via the `score_threshold` argument to trade recall for precision.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# main

PII detection and redaction over free text, exposed as DuckDB scalar and table functions.

## Detection vs. redaction

The schema offers two complementary kinds of operation. **Detection** inspects text without changing it -- flag whether any PII is present, summarise which entity types occur, enumerate each occurrence with its character offsets and confidence score, and introspect which entity types the analyzer can recognise. **Redaction** rewrites text so the sensitive values are removed -- either tagged by the kind of value or masked so even its shape is hidden.

## Notes

Per-row operations are scalars (usable inline in any projection or predicate) and take an optional trailing `language`; the per-occurrence and discovery operations are table functions that accept named arguments (`language :=`, `score_threshold :=`). Raise `score_threshold` on the table functions to keep only high-confidence detections, and pass `language` to scan non-English text. Powered by [Microsoft Presidio](https://microsoft.github.io/presidio/).

## entity_types

A browsable discovery **table** listing every PII entity type this worker's analyzer can recognise (for the default English configuration), one type per row. Read it with a plain `SELECT` -- no arguments required -- to learn the exact vocabulary that `detect_pii.entity_type` and `pii_types` can produce, e.g. to validate a filter, build a picker, or document coverage.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## detect_pii

A table function that returns **one row per detected PII entity** in the input text, with the matched substring, its character offsets, the entity type, and the detection confidence. Use it when you need the full, per-occurrence detail -- e.g. to highlight spans, build a redaction map, or audit exactly what was found and where.

- **Arguments:** `text` (positional `VARCHAR`); optional named `language := 'en'` and `score_threshold := 0.5` (minimum confidence in `[0, 1]`).
- **Returns:** rows of `(entity_type, text, start, end_pos, score)`. `end_pos` is exclusive (named with a `_pos` suffix because `end` is a SQL keyword).
- **Edge cases:** `NULL`, empty, or whitespace-only text yields **no rows**; raising `score_threshold` drops low-confidence guesses.

For a per-row boolean or a list of types, use the `has_pii` / `pii_types` scalars instead. Backed by Microsoft Presidio.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# detect_pii

Expand text into one row per detected PII entity, with offsets and confidence.

## Signature

`detect_pii(text[, language := 'en'][, score_threshold := 0.5])` — the single positional `text` argument is required; `language` and `score_threshold` are optional named arguments.

## Result columns

Each row is `(entity_type, text, start, end_pos, score)`: the entity type, the matched substring, its inclusive start and exclusive end character offsets, and the detection confidence in `[0, 1]`.

## Notes

`end_pos` is the exclusive end offset (the column is named `end_pos` because `end` is a SQL keyword). NULL/blank text returns no rows. Raise `score_threshold` to keep only high-confidence detections. See this function's example queries for runnable demonstrations.

## has_pii

Return `true` when the input text contains **any** personally-identifiable information (PII) entity, otherwise `false`. Use it as a fast boolean predicate to flag or filter rows that need privacy handling, before deciding to redact or anonymize them.

- **Input:** a `VARCHAR` of free text; an optional second argument is the ISO language code (defaults to `'en'`).
- **Output:** `BOOLEAN` -- `true` if at least one entity (PERSON, EMAIL_ADDRESS, PHONE_NUMBER, CREDIT_CARD, US_SSN, LOCATION, URL, IP_ADDRESS, ...) is detected.
- **Edge cases:** `NULL`, empty, or whitespace-only input returns `NULL`.

Backed by Microsoft Presidio (analyzer) with the `en_core_web_sm` spaCy model.

A scalar predicate that answers a single question: *does this text contain PII?* Call it inline in a projection to tag rows, or in a `WHERE` clause to keep only the rows that need privacy handling before they are shared, exported, or archived.

- `NULL`, empty, or whitespace-only input yields `NULL` rather than `false`.

See this function's example queries for a runnable demonstration.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## redact

Return the input text with every detected PII span replaced by a tag naming its entity type, e.g. `<PERSON>` or `<EMAIL_ADDRESS>`. Use it when you want a human-readable, *self-documenting* scrub that preserves which kind of value was removed (useful for audit, debugging, and downstream classification).

- **Input:** a `VARCHAR` of free text; an optional second argument is the ISO language code (defaults to `'en'`).
- **Output:** `VARCHAR` -- the same text with each entity replaced by `<TYPE>`.
- **Example:** `'Call John Smith at john@example.com'` -> `'Call <PERSON> at <EMAIL_ADDRESS>'`.
- **Edge cases:** `NULL`, empty, or whitespace-only input returns `NULL`; text with no PII is returned unchanged.

Contrast with `anonymize`, which masks characters (`****`) instead of labelling them. Backed by Microsoft Presidio (analyzer + anonymizer).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# redact

Replace each PII entity in text with a tag that names its type, leaving the surrounding text intact.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT pii.main.redact('Call John Smith at john@example.com');
-- 'Call <PERSON> at <EMAIL_ADDRESS>'
```

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## redact

Return the input text with every detected PII span replaced by a tag naming its entity type, e.g. `<PERSON>` or `<EMAIL_ADDRESS>`. Use it when you want a human-readable, *self-documenting* scrub that preserves which kind of value was removed (useful for audit, debugging, and downstream classification).

- **Input:** a `VARCHAR` of free text; an optional second argument is the ISO language code (defaults to `'en'`).
- **Output:** `VARCHAR` -- the same text with each entity replaced by `<TYPE>`.
- **Example:** `'Call John Smith at john@example.com'` -> `'Call <PERSON> at <EMAIL_ADDRESS>'`.
- **Edge cases:** `NULL`, empty, or whitespace-only input returns `NULL`; text with no PII is returned unchanged.

Contrast with `anonymize`, which masks characters (`****`) instead of labelling them. Backed by Microsoft Presidio (analyzer + anonymizer).

## anonymize

Return the input text with every detected PII span overwritten character-for-character by a `*` mask, so the value is hidden but its length/position is preserved. Use it for display or export where the *shape* of the data can remain but the value must not.

- **Input:** a `VARCHAR` of free text; an optional second argument is the ISO language code (defaults to `'en'`).

- **Edge cases:** `NULL`, empty, or whitespace-only input returns `NULL`; text with no PII is returned unchanged.

Contrast with `redact`, which labels each entity with a `<TYPE>` tag. Backed by Microsoft Presidio (analyzer + anonymizer).

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## pii_types

Return the **distinct** PII entity types present in the input text as a sorted `VARCHAR[]`. Use it to summarise what categories of sensitive data a value contains -- e.g. to drive routing, alerting, or per-type handling -- without needing the per-span detail of `detect_pii`.

- **Input:** a `VARCHAR` of free text; an optional second argument is the ISO language code (defaults to `'en'`).
- **Output:** `VARCHAR[]` -- the sorted, de-duplicated set of detected entity type names, e.g. `['EMAIL_ADDRESS', 'PERSON', 'URL']`.
- **Edge cases:** `NULL`, empty, or whitespace-only input returns `NULL`; text with no PII returns an empty list. Every detection above the threshold counts, including overlapping ones: an email address also yields `URL` for its domain (`redact` keeps only the `<EMAIL_ADDRESS>` tag).

For one row per occurrence (with offsets and confidence) use the `detect_pii` table function instead. Backed by Microsoft Presidio.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# pii_types

Return the set of PII entity types found in text, sorted and de-duplicated, as a `VARCHAR[]`.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT pii.main.pii_types('Call John Smith at john@example.com');
-- ['EMAIL_ADDRESS', 'PERSON', 'URL']
```

## Notes

This is a compact summary; for per-occurrence detail (matched text, offsets, confidence) use `detect_pii`. Accepts an explicit language as the second argument. NULL/blank input yields NULL; PII-free text yields an empty list.

vgi.example_queries.description: List the distinct PII types in text (-> ['EMAIL_ADDRESS', 'PERSON', 'URL']).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT pii.main.pii_types('Call John Smith at john@example.com')

vgi.example_queries.description: List the distinct PII types with an explicit ISO language.

vgi.example_queries.description: PII prevalence report: for every entity type the analyzer recognises (the entity_types table), count how many tickets contain it according to pii_types, most common first; recognizable types never seen report 0.
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH tickets(id, body) AS (VALUES (1, 'Hi, this is John Smith, my email is john.smith@example.com'), (2, 'Please charge my card 4111-1111-1111-1111 today'), (3, 'The printer on floor 3 is jammed again'), (4, 'Jane Doe can be reached at jane@example.org')), found AS (SELECT id, unnest(pii.main.pii_types(body)) AS entity_type FROM tickets) SELECT e.entity_type, count(DISTINCT f.id) AS tickets FROM pii.main.entity_types AS e LEFT JOIN found AS f USING (entity_type) GROUP BY e.entity_type ORDER BY tickets DESC, e.entity_type

workers.subtitle: Read cells and sheets from .xls/.xlsx workbooks and export query results to .xlsx, powered by Apache POI.
workers.summary: Read and write Microsoft Excel spreadsheets (.xls / .xlsx) as DuckDB SQL functions, backed by Apache POI.
workers.doc_md:
# Excel Spreadsheet Read & Write in SQL

![Apache POI logo](https://poi.apache.org/images/project-header.png)

**Query Microsoft Excel workbooks (`.xls` and `.xlsx`) directly from DuckDB SQL — read every cell with its value, type, and formula, and export any query result to a downloadable `.xlsx` file — powered by [Apache POI](https://poi.apache.org/).**

This extension turns spreadsheets into first-class SQL data sources. It is built for data engineers, analysts, and application developers who need to ingest Excel files, inspect workbook structure, or hand results back to spreadsheet users — without leaving SQL or writing glue code in Python or a BI tool. Both the legacy binary `.xls` format (OLE2 / HSSF) and the modern Office Open XML `.xlsx` format (OOXML / XSSF) are supported, and inputs may be supplied either as a file path or as raw `BLOB` bytes already loaded into DuckDB.

Under the hood the worker embeds [Apache POI](https://github.com/apache/poi), the mature, battle-tested Java library for reading and writing Microsoft Office file formats. POI parses the workbook, evaluates formulas, and preserves cell typing (numbers, dates, booleans, strings, and errors), while the worker streams the results back to DuckDB over Apache Arrow. Untrusted spreadsheets are opened behind zip-bomb and decompression-ratio defenses, and external workbook links are never resolved, so importing arbitrary `.xlsx` files stays safe. See the [Apache POI spreadsheet documentation](https://poi.apache.org/components/spreadsheet/) and the [HSSF/XSSF quick guide](https://poi.apache.org/components/spreadsheet/quick-guide.html) for format details.

## Key concepts

- **Rich, cell-level reads.** A workbook is surfaced not as opaque rows but cell by cell, each with its worksheet, position, A1 reference, evaluated value, data type, and (for formula cells) the underlying formula text — so numbers, dates, booleans, strings, errors, and computed values are all preserved and distinguishable.
- **Structure before data.** You can inspect a workbook's worksheet directory — names and dimensions — cheaply, without materializing every cell, then drill into a single sheet.
- **Path or bytes.** Reader inputs may be a filesystem path the worker opens, or raw `BLOB` bytes already loaded into DuckDB, so the same function works on files on disk and on content that arrived over the wire.
- **Round-tripping to Excel.** Any query result can be serialized back into a downloadable `.xlsx` workbook, and raw bytes can be sniffed to confirm their format.

## When to use it

Reach for this worker when you need to ingest spreadsheet exports into an analytical pipeline, audit the sheets and formulas inside a workbook, validate untrusted uploads by content rather than file extension, or hand polished Excel deliverables back to spreadsheet users — all without leaving SQL or writing glue code in Python or a BI tool.

example_queries.description: Read a workbook's non-blank cells (passed as inline bytes).
example_queries.sql: SELECT sheet, cell_ref, value, type FROM excel.main.read_excel(from_base64('')) ORDER BY cell_ref;

example_queries.description: Export a query result to an .xlsx workbook BLOB and confirm bytes were produced.
example_queries.sql: SELECT octet_length(xlsx) > 0 AS produced FROM excel.main.write_xlsx((SELECT 1 AS id, 'Ada' AS name), sheet_name := 'People');

example_queries.description: Round-trip: detect that the written bytes are an .xlsx workbook.
example_queries.sql: SELECT excel.main.detect_excel(xlsx) AS fmt FROM excel.main.write_xlsx((SELECT 1 AS id, 'Ada' AS name));

example_queries.description: Audit a workbook sheet by sheet: join the worksheet directory to its cells to report each sheet's used-range size next to how many non-blank cells and formula cells it holds (the inline workbook: Numbers 2x3 with 4 cells / 1 formula; a blank sheet would show 0 cells).
example_queries.sql: SELECT s.idx, s.name, s.rows, s.cols, count(c.cell_ref) AS cells, count(c.formula) AS formulas FROM excel.main.excel_sheets(from_base64('')) AS s LEFT JOIN excel.main.read_excel(from_base64('')) AS c ON c.sheet = s.name GROUP BY s.idx, s.name, s.rows, s.cols ORDER BY s.idx;

example_queries.description: Export a query result to an .xlsx workbook BLOB on a named sheet and size the bytes.
example_queries.sql: SELECT octet_length(xlsx) AS bytes FROM excel.main.write_xlsx((SELECT 1 AS id, 'Ada' AS name), sheet_name := 'People');

example_queries.description: Detect the format of a file's bytes — 'xls' for this legacy workbook ('xlsx' for OOXML, NULL for anything else).
example_queries.sql: SELECT excel.main.detect_excel(content) AS fmt FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-poi/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/sample.xls');

example_queries.description: Triage a batch of files by content, not extension: detect each file's Excel format and look it up in the formats view to see whether read_excel can read it (sample.xls -> xls, sample.xlsx -> xlsx, both readable; the non-Excel garbage.bin gets NULL). For a local folder, read_blob takes a glob pattern.
example_queries.sql: SELECT parse_filename(b.filename) AS file, excel.main.detect_excel(b.content) AS fmt, f.readable FROM read_blob(['https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-poi/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/sample.xls', 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-poi/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/sample.xlsx', 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-poi/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/garbage.bin']) AS b LEFT JOIN excel.main.formats AS f ON f.format = excel.main.detect_excel(b.content) ORDER BY file;

example_queries.description: Browse every Excel format the worker understands with its container.
example_queries.sql: SELECT format, description, container FROM excel.main.formats ORDER BY format;

example_queries.description: List only the formats write_xlsx can produce.
example_queries.sql: SELECT format FROM excel.main.formats WHERE writable ORDER BY format;

example_queries.description: Build a formula-audit deliverable: read a workbook's formula cells (sheet, cell, formula text, evaluated value) and export them to a new .xlsx workbook with a header row, confirming the output is detected as 'xlsx'.
example_queries.sql: SELECT octet_length(xlsx) > 0 AS produced, excel.main.detect_excel(xlsx) AS fmt FROM excel.main.write_xlsx((SELECT sheet, cell_ref, formula, value FROM excel.main.read_excel(from_base64('')) WHERE formula IS NOT NULL ORDER BY sheet, cell_ref), sheet_name := 'Formulas', header := true);

example_queries.description: List every worksheet of a workbook (passed as inline bytes) with its dimensions.
example_queries.sql: SELECT idx, name, rows, cols FROM excel.main.excel_sheets(from_base64('')) ORDER BY idx;

example_queries.description: Detect the format of a workbook's bytes — returns 'xlsx' for an OOXML workbook.
example_queries.sql: SELECT excel.main.detect_excel(from_base64('')) AS fmt;

example_queries.description: Non-Excel bytes return NULL, so a NULL check tells you the BLOB is not a workbook.
example_queries.sql: SELECT excel.main.detect_excel('not a spreadsheet'::BLOB) IS NULL AS not_excel;

Reach for it to turn a workbook (a file path or raw `BLOB` bytes) into rows of typed, evaluated cells with their A1 references and formula text, to inspect a workbook's worksheet layout, to export a query result as a downloadable .xlsx `BLOB`, or to classify untrusted bytes as Excel without trusting a file name. tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Excel functions

Read and write Microsoft Excel workbooks (`.xls` and `.xlsx`) directly in SQL over Apache Arrow, powered by [Apache POI](https://poi.apache.org/).

The functions in this schema cover three areas:

- **Reading** — stream a workbook's non-blank cells as rows (with type, A1 reference, evaluated value, and formula text), and list its worksheet directory with per-sheet dimensions.
- **Writing** — serialize any SQL relation into a downloadable `.xlsx` workbook returned as a `BLOB`.
- **Detection** — sniff raw bytes to classify them as `.xlsx`, `.xls`, or neither, without trusting a file name.

Reader inputs are polymorphic: pass a filesystem path the worker opens, or a raw `BLOB` of workbook bytes already loaded into DuckDB. Formula cells are evaluated, cell typing is preserved, and a corrupt or non-spreadsheet input yields no rows (or `NULL`) rather than failing the query.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT s.idx, s.name, s.rows, s.cols, count(c.cell_ref) AS cells, count(c.formula) AS formulas FROM excel.main.excel_sheets(from_base64('')) AS s LEFT JOIN excel.main.read_excel(from_base64('')) AS c ON c.sheet = s.name GROUP BY s.idx, s.name, s.rows, s.cols ORDER BY s.idx;
vgi.example_queries.description: Audit a workbook sheet by sheet: join the worksheet directory to its cells to report each sheet's used-range size next to how many non-blank cells and formula cells it holds (the inline workbook: Numbers 2x3 with 4 cells / 1 formula; a blank sheet would show 0 cells).

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT octet_length(xlsx) AS bytes FROM excel.main.write_xlsx((SELECT 1 AS id, 'Ada' AS name), sheet_name := 'People');
vgi.example_queries.description: Export a query result to an .xlsx workbook BLOB on a named sheet and size the bytes.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT excel.main.detect_excel(content) AS fmt FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-poi/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/sample.xls');
vgi.example_queries.description: Detect the format of a file's bytes — 'xls' for this legacy workbook ('xlsx' for OOXML, NULL for anything else).

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT parse_filename(b.filename) AS file, excel.main.detect_excel(b.content) AS fmt, f.readable FROM read_blob(['https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-poi/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/sample.xls', 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-poi/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/sample.xlsx', 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-poi/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/garbage.bin']) AS b LEFT JOIN excel.main.formats AS f ON f.format = excel.main.detect_excel(b.content) ORDER BY file;
vgi.example_queries.description: Triage a batch of files by content, not extension: detect each file's Excel format and look it up in the formats view to see whether read_excel can read it (sample.xls -> xls, sample.xlsx -> xlsx, both readable; the non-Excel garbage.bin gets NULL). For a local folder, read_blob takes a glob pattern.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Supported Excel formats

A curated, zero-argument reference relation you can browse to learn which Excel formats this worker handles — no file or credential required.

Each row describes one workbook format:

- **format** — the exact tag `detect_excel` returns (`xlsx` or `xls`).
- **description** — the format's full name and Apache POI backend (XSSF for OOXML, HSSF for legacy OLE2).
- **container** — how the bytes are packaged on disk.
- **readable** / **writable** — whether `read_excel` / `excel_sheets` can parse it and whether `write_xlsx` can produce it.

Both formats are readable; only the modern `.xlsx` format is writable. Query this relation to branch on format capabilities before reading or writing a workbook.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT format, description, container FROM excel.main.formats ORDER BY format;
vgi.example_queries.description: Browse every Excel format the worker understands with its container.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT format FROM excel.main.formats WHERE writable ORDER BY format;
vgi.example_queries.description: List only the formats write_xlsx can produce.

tags.vgi.title: Supported Excel Formats

functions.name: write_xlsx
functions.comment: Serialize an input relation into an .xlsx workbook BLOB with typed cells and an optional bold header row (Apache POI).

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## write_xlsx

A **table-in-out** function that consumes an input relation and emits a single-column (`xlsx` `BLOB`) result carrying that relation serialized as an `.xlsx` (OOXML) workbook. Named arguments: `sheet_name := 'Sheet1'` sets the worksheet name and `header := true` writes a **bold first row** of the input column names.

Cells are typed from the input columns: numeric columns become numeric cells, booleans become boolean cells, date/timestamp columns become date-formatted cells, and everything else is written as text. Because DuckDB rejects `length()` on a `BLOB`, use `octet_length(xlsx)` to size the result.

**Streaming caveat**: the table-in-out transport delivers input batches with no separate finalize signal, so the workbook-so-far is emitted after each input batch. A typical single-batch input yields exactly one `BLOB` row containing the whole relation; an input large enough to span multiple Arrow batches yields one row per batch, the **last** of which is the complete workbook. Pair it with `detect_excel` to validate the output.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Serializes a SQL relation into a downloadable Microsoft Excel `.xlsx` workbook, returned as a `BLOB`, with typed cells and an optional bold header row.

**Usage**: wrap the relation you want to export as the input subquery, optionally set `sheet_name` and toggle `header`, then read back the `xlsx` `BLOB` column and size it with `octet_length`. Runnable, fully-qualified examples are attached to this object's metadata.

**Notes**: numeric/boolean/date columns keep their Excel cell types; use `octet_length` (not `length`) on the `BLOB`; for a multi-batch input the last emitted row is the complete workbook.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT octet_length(xlsx) > 0 AS produced FROM excel.main.write_xlsx((SELECT 1 AS id, 'Ada' AS name), sheet_name := 'People');
vgi.example_queries.description: Export a one-row query result to an .xlsx workbook BLOB on a named sheet and confirm bytes were produced.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT excel.main.detect_excel(xlsx) AS fmt FROM excel.main.write_xlsx((SELECT 1 AS id, 'Ada' AS name));
vgi.example_queries.description: Round-trip check: the BLOB written by write_xlsx is detected as an 'xlsx' workbook.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT octet_length(xlsx) > 0 AS produced, excel.main.detect_excel(xlsx) AS fmt FROM excel.main.write_xlsx((SELECT sheet, cell_ref, formula, value FROM excel.main.read_excel(from_base64('')) WHERE formula IS NOT NULL ORDER BY sheet, cell_ref), sheet_name := 'Formulas', header := true);
vgi.example_queries.description: Build a formula-audit deliverable: read a workbook's formula cells (sheet, cell, formula text, evaluated value) and export them to a new .xlsx workbook with a header row, confirming the output is detected as 'xlsx'.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: xlsx
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: The generated .xlsx workbook bytes (one row per input batch; the last row is the complete workbook).

tags.vgi.title: Write Relation To Xlsx Workbook

functions.name: read_excel
functions.comment: Read every non-blank cell of an Excel workbook (.xls or .xlsx) as rows with type, A1 reference, evaluated value, and formula text (Apache POI).

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## read_excel

Reads an Excel workbook into SQL as **one row per non-blank cell**. Accepts a `.xlsx` (OOXML/XSSF) or legacy `.xls` (OLE2/HSSF) file **path** *or* the raw workbook **bytes** as a `BLOB`. The optional named argument `sheet := '<name>'` restricts output to a single worksheet. The whole workbook is parsed into memory and returned as a single result set (it buffers rather than incrementally streams), so cardinality scales with the workbook size.

Each row carries the worksheet name, 0-based `row`/`col`, the A1-style `cell_ref` (e.g. `B3`), the cell `value`, the cell `type`, and the raw `formula` text for formula cells. `type` is one of `NUMERIC`, `STRING`, `BOOLEAN`, `FORMULA`, or `ERROR` — **blank cells are skipped entirely**, so `BLANK` never appears.

**`value` is always `VARCHAR` text**, so cast it to work with it numerically or temporally. The rendering rules are: numbers with no fraction drop the trailing `.0` (`3.0` -> `3`); date-formatted numeric cells render as ISO-8601 `yyyy-MM-ddTHH:mm:ss`; booleans render as `true`/`false`; error cells render as the Excel error string (e.g. `#DIV/0!`). For a `FORMULA` cell, `formula` holds the expression text (without a leading `=`) and `value` holds the **evaluated** result rendered by these same rules; external-workbook links are never resolved (the cached value or an error is used).

Use it to ingest spreadsheet data, audit formulas, or flatten a workbook for further SQL. A corrupt or non-spreadsheet input yields **zero rows** (logged to stderr) rather than an error, and a NULL document yields no rows. Table-function arguments must be **literals** — pass bytes as a `BLOB` literal, not a subquery.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Reads a Microsoft Excel workbook (`.xls` or `.xlsx`) and returns one row for every non-blank cell, including its worksheet, position, A1 reference, evaluated value, type, and (for formula cells) the formula text. `value` is always `VARCHAR` — numbers render without a trailing `.0`, dates as ISO-8601, booleans as `true`/`false` — so cast it (`value::DOUBLE`, `value::TIMESTAMP`) to compute on it. The `type` column is one of `NUMERIC`, `STRING`, `BOOLEAN`, `FORMULA`, or `ERROR`; blank cells are omitted rather than returned.

**Usage**: point it at a filesystem path to an `.xls`/`.xlsx` file, add the named `sheet` argument to restrict output to one worksheet, or hand it the raw workbook bytes as a `BLOB` literal. Runnable, fully-qualified examples are attached to this object's metadata.

**Notes**: formulas are evaluated and the result lands in `value`; both `.xls` (HSSF) and `.xlsx` (XSSF) are supported; a hostile or corrupt input returns no rows instead of failing the scan.

functions.name: excel_sheets
functions.comment: List the worksheets of an Excel workbook (.xls or .xlsx) with index, name, row count, and column count (Apache POI).

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## excel_sheets

Returns the **worksheet directory** of an Excel workbook — one row per sheet — without reading any cell data. Accepts a `.xlsx` or legacy `.xls` file **path** *or* the raw workbook **bytes** as a `BLOB`.

Each row gives the sheet's 0-based ordinal (`idx`), its `name`, the `rows` count (last row index + 1) and the maximum `cols` count across the sheet. Use it to discover sheet names before calling `read_excel(..., sheet := '<name>')`, or to gauge a workbook's size and shape cheaply.

A corrupt or non-spreadsheet input yields **zero rows** (logged to stderr) rather than an error. Table-function arguments must be **literals** — pass bytes as a `BLOB` literal, not a subquery.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Lists the worksheets of a Microsoft Excel workbook (`.xls` or `.xlsx`), returning each sheet's ordinal, name, row count, and column count.

**Usage**: give it a filesystem path to an `.xls`/`.xlsx` file, or the raw workbook bytes as a `BLOB` literal, and it returns one row per worksheet ordered by ordinal. Runnable, fully-qualified examples are attached to this object's metadata.

**Notes**: a lightweight companion to `read_excel` for discovering sheet names and dimensions; supports both `.xls` (HSSF) and `.xlsx` (XSSF); inputs may be a file path or raw bytes.

functions.name: detect_excel
functions.comment: Detect whether a BLOB is an Excel workbook: returns 'xlsx', 'xls', or NULL (Apache POI).

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## detect_excel

A scalar that classifies a `BLOB` as `'xlsx'` (a modern OOXML/XSSF workbook), `'xls'` (a legacy OLE2/HSSF workbook), or `NULL`. It is a **two-stage** check, not merely a magic-byte peek: it first matches the leading signature (`PK\x03\x04` for OOXML, the OLE2 header `D0 CF 11 E0` for `.xls`), then **actually opens the bytes with Apache POI** to confirm they parse as a spreadsheet. That second stage is why a plain `.zip`, a `.docx`, or a `.pptx` — all of which share the `PK` prefix — correctly return `NULL` instead of a false `'xlsx'`.

`NULL` is returned for every non-workbook input, and the distinct paths that produce it are: the input is `NULL`; the `BLOB` is shorter than the 8-byte minimum; the leading signature matches no known format; or the signature matches but POI fails to open the bytes as a workbook (truncated, corrupt, or a different `PK`/OLE2 format). All of these collapse to a single `NULL` result — the function never raises. Detection is **content-based** and ignores any file name or extension, so it works on bytes that arrived over the wire or from another function. Use it to validate untrusted uploads before calling `read_excel`, to branch on workbook format, or to confirm that `write_xlsx` produced a valid workbook.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Identifies whether a `BLOB` is a Microsoft Excel workbook by matching its leading signature and then opening it with Apache POI to confirm, returning `'xlsx'`, `'xls'`, or `NULL`. Because it opens the bytes (rather than trusting the `PK`/OLE2 prefix alone), a plain `.zip` or a `.docx` returns `NULL`, not a false `'xlsx'`.

**Usage**: pass it any `BLOB` — a file's bytes loaded with `read_blob`, an upload, or the output of `write_xlsx` — and it classifies the content, so a non-NULL result guards a workbook before you read it. Runnable, fully-qualified examples are attached to this object's metadata.

**Notes**: detection is by content, not extension; legacy `.xls` (OLE2) and modern `.xlsx` (OOXML) are distinguished; anything else yields `NULL`.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT excel.main.detect_excel(from_base64('')) AS fmt;
vgi.example_queries.description: Detect the format of a workbook's bytes — returns 'xlsx' for an OOXML workbook.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT excel.main.detect_excel('not a spreadsheet'::BLOB) IS NULL AS not_excel;
vgi.example_queries.description: Non-Excel bytes return NULL, so a NULL check tells you the BLOB is not a workbook.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT parse_filename(b.filename) AS file, excel.main.detect_excel(b.content) AS fmt, f.readable FROM read_blob(['https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-poi/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/sample.xls', 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-poi/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/sample.xlsx', 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-poi/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/garbage.bin']) AS b LEFT JOIN excel.main.formats AS f ON f.format = excel.main.detect_excel(b.content) ORDER BY file;
vgi.example_queries.description: Triage a batch of files by content, not extension: detect each file's Excel format and look it up in the formats view to see whether read_excel can read it (sample.xls -> xls, sample.xlsx -> xlsx, both readable; the non-Excel garbage.bin gets NULL). For a local folder, read_blob takes a glob pattern.

tags.vgi.title: Detect Excel File Format

arguments.name: doc
arguments.description: The candidate workbook content to inspect. Its leading signature is matched and then the bytes are opened with POI to confirm, classifying the content as an OOXML/.xlsx or legacy-OLE2/.xls workbook; anything else (including NULL or bytes too short to classify) yields NULL.

examples: SELECT excel.main.detect_excel(from_base64('')) AS fmt;
SELECT excel.main.detect_excel('not a spreadsheet'::BLOB) IS NULL AS not_excel;

workers.title: Polymarket Prediction Markets
workers.tagline: Read-only VGI connector exposing Polymarket prediction-market data to DuckDB/SQL
workers.subtitle: Live odds, order books, trades and on-chain holders, read-only
workers.summary: What the crowd thinks a future event is worth, priced as a probability — read-only Polymarket data, including who holds each position
workers.doc_md:
Polymarket is a prediction market where each outcome of a question trades as its own token. A token pays $1 if its outcome happens and $0 otherwise, so its price is the market's implied probability of that outcome.

### The two identifiers — read this first

Polymarket has two keys and its own URLs call both of them `market`. They are not interchangeable, and passing one where the other belongs usually returns an empty result rather than an error:

| Key | Looks like | Names | Used by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `condition_id` | `0x` + 64 hex | a whole market | the trade tape, the holder list, the market lookup |
| `token_id` | a long decimal string | one outcome of it | resting depth, live quotes, price history |

Every market row carries an `outcomes` list holding each outcome's `token_id`, so unnesting that column is how you get from one key to the other. Each function's own docs say which it takes.

Getting it wrong fails differently by direction: a market key passed where an outcome key belongs is an HTTP 404 in one place and an empty price series in another, and an outcome key passed to the trade tape is an HTTP 400. The empty price series is indistinguishable from 'nothing traded'.

### How the data is shaped

- **Tag** — a topic such as Crypto or Politics. The filter almost everything accepts, and the only axis that covers the whole site.
- **Series** — a recurring question that opens a new event each occurrence. Many markets belong to no series.
- **Event** — the markets that resolve together: one game, or one election.
- **Market** — one question, named by its `condition_id`.
- **Outcome** — one answer to that question, trading as its own token and named by its `token_id`.

### Reading prices

Every price column is USDC per share between 0 and 1, so a midpoint of 0.62 is a 62% implied probability — **provided the spread is tight**. Displayed outcome prices are normalised to sum to 1, so a thin market can look like a coherent forecast while nobody would trade at it; the quote and order-book functions document how to check. Prices are `DECIMAL`, never `DOUBLE`: however Polymarket encodes money (decimal strings, JSON floats, arrays nested inside strings), it is recovered exactly.

### Access

No credentials are needed and none are accepted. The whole market-data surface is public; only order placement requires a wallet signature, and this worker exposes no such endpoint. It is read-only by construction, not by configuration.

### Rate limits and cost

The public APIs answer roughly 20 requests a second without throttling, and the worker batches the expensive per-outcome reads, so a correlated `LATERAL` over many rows stays practical. Origin cache directives are forwarded; live book and quote endpoints declare none and stay uncached.

### Sources

- [Polymarket](https://polymarket.com) — the prediction market this data comes from.
- [Polymarket API documentation](https://docs.polymarket.com/api-reference) — the three public read APIs this worker calls:
  - [Gamma API](https://docs.polymarket.com/api-spec/gamma-openapi.yaml) (`gamma-api.polymarket.com`) — tags, series, events, markets and search.
  - [CLOB API](https://docs.polymarket.com/api-spec/clob-openapi.yaml) (`clob.polymarket.com`) — order books, quotes, midpoints and price history.
  - [Data API v2](https://data-api.polymarket.com/v2/docs) (`data-api.polymarket.com/v2`) — trades, holders, positions and wallet activity.
- [Market data overview](https://docs.polymarket.com/market-data/overview) — how Polymarket organizes events, markets and outcome tokens.

No API key or account is needed for any of them.

### Terms of use

The market data is Polymarket's, not covered by this worker's MIT license, and is subject to the [Polymarket Terms of Use](https://polymarket.com/tos). This worker is not affiliated with or endorsed by Polymarket.

ATTACH 'polymarket' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'uvx --from git+https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-polymarket@v0.1.3 vgi-polymarket');
SELECT count(*) FROM polymarket.tags;

example_queries.title: tags_catalog_is_populated
example_queries.description: The tag catalog streams thousands of topics.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) > 500 FROM (SELECT tag_id FROM polymarket.main.tags LIMIT 600);

example_queries.title: tags_and_scan_function_agree
example_queries.description: The `tags` table and the `all_tags` function behind it are the same rows.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT tag_id FROM polymarket.main.tags LIMIT 200)) = (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT tag_id FROM polymarket.main.all_tags() LIMIT 200));

example_queries.title: series_and_scan_function_agree
example_queries.description: The `series` table and the `all_series` function behind it are the same rows.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT series_id FROM polymarket.main.series LIMIT 100)) = (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT series_id FROM polymarket.main.all_series() LIMIT 100));

example_queries.title: a_limit_stops_the_scan_early
example_queries.description: A paged scan yields its first rows without walking every page — the property that keeps a LIMIT over a large catalog from wedging the client.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT question FROM polymarket.main.markets() LIMIT 5);

example_queries.title: prices_are_exact_decimals
example_queries.description: Money comes back as DECIMAL, never a float.
example_queries.sql: SELECT typeof(volume_24hr) FROM polymarket.main.markets() LIMIT 1;

example_queries.title: outcomes_carry_their_tokens
example_queries.description: Every outcome is zipped with the CLOB token that trades it — the join key the order book needs.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bool_and(o.token_id IS NOT NULL) FROM (SELECT outcomes FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false') LIMIT 20) m, LATERAL (SELECT unnest(m.outcomes, recursive := true)) o;

example_queries.title: closed_filter_is_applied_by_the_origin
example_queries.description: The closed filter reaches Gamma rather than being applied after the fact.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bool_and(NOT closed) FROM (SELECT closed FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false') LIMIT 100);

example_queries.title: orderbook_sides_are_bid_or_ask
example_queries.description: A book flattens to labelled sides, or to nothing when it is empty.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bool_and(side IN ('bid', 'ask')) IS NOT FALSE FROM (SELECT b.side FROM (SELECT o.token_id FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') m, LATERAL (SELECT unnest(m.outcomes, recursive := true)) o LIMIT 5) t, LATERAL polymarket.main.orderbook(t.token_id) b LIMIT 50);

example_queries.title: a_quote_is_ordered_bid_then_ask
example_queries.description: best_ask is never below best_bid, which pins the BUY/SELL naming.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bool_and(q.best_ask >= q.best_bid) IS NOT FALSE FROM (SELECT o.token_id FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') m, LATERAL (SELECT unnest(m.outcomes, recursive := true)) o LIMIT 5) t, LATERAL polymarket.main.quote(t.token_id) q;

example_queries.title: prices_read_as_probabilities
example_queries.description: Every outcome price sits between 0 and 1, so it reads as a probability.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bool_and(o.price BETWEEN 0 AND 1) IS NOT FALSE FROM (SELECT outcomes FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false') LIMIT 50) m, LATERAL (SELECT unnest(m.outcomes, recursive := true)) o WHERE o.price IS NOT NULL;

example_queries.description: Find the topic you want, then its id
example_queries.sql: SELECT tag_id, label, slug FROM polymarket.main.tags WHERE label ILIKE '%crypto%' ORDER BY label

example_queries.description: The busiest open markets right now, with their implied probabilities
example_queries.sql: SELECT question, outcomes, volume_24hr FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') LIMIT 20

example_queries.description: Every outcome of every crypto market, one row per outcome
example_queries.sql: SELECT m.question, o.outcome, o.price, o.token_id FROM polymarket.main.markets(tag_id => '21', closed => 'false') m, LATERAL (SELECT unnest(m.outcomes, recursive := true)) o ORDER BY m.volume_24hr DESC LIMIT 50

example_queries.description: Live top-of-book for every outcome in a topic, via LATERAL
example_queries.sql: SELECT m.question, o.outcome, q.midpoint, q.spread FROM polymarket.main.markets(tag_id => '21', closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') m, LATERAL (SELECT unnest(m.outcomes, recursive := true)) o, LATERAL polymarket.main.quote(o.token_id) q LIMIT 40

example_queries.description: Total resting size on each side of a topic's books
example_queries.sql: SELECT b.side, sum(b.size) AS resting FROM polymarket.main.markets(tag_id => '21', closed => 'false') m, LATERAL (SELECT unnest(m.outcomes, recursive := true)) o, LATERAL polymarket.main.orderbook(o.token_id) b GROUP BY b.side

example_queries.description: A week of hourly implied probability for the busiest open market
example_queries.sql: SELECT h.ts, h.price FROM (SELECT o.token_id FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') m, LATERAL (SELECT unnest(m.outcomes, recursive := true)) o LIMIT 1) t, LATERAL polymarket.main.price_history(t.token_id, '1w', 60) h ORDER BY h.ts

example_queries.description: This week's movers: each outcome of the five busiest open markets, from the first point of its past-week hourly history to its live midpoint
example_queries.sql: WITH tokens AS (SELECT m.question, o.outcome, o.token_id FROM (SELECT question, outcomes FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') LIMIT 5) m, LATERAL (SELECT unnest(m.outcomes, recursive := true)) o), week AS (SELECT t.question, t.outcome, t.token_id, arg_min(h.price, h.ts) AS first_price FROM tokens t, LATERAL polymarket.main.price_history(t.token_id, '1w', 60) h GROUP BY t.question, t.outcome, t.token_id) SELECT w.question, w.outcome, w.first_price, q.midpoint, q.midpoint - w.first_price AS change FROM week w, LATERAL polymarket.main.quote(w.token_id) q ORDER BY abs(change) DESC NULLS LAST, w.question, w.outcome

example_queries.description: The most recent prints on the busiest open market, with who traded
example_queries.sql: SELECT t.ts, t.side, t.outcome, t.price, t.size, t.trader_name FROM (SELECT condition_id FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') LIMIT 1) m, LATERAL polymarket.main.trades(m.condition_id, 100, '') t ORDER BY t.ts DESC

example_queries.description: Who holds the biggest positions in the busiest open market
example_queries.sql: SELECT h.outcome_index, h.holder_name, h.amount FROM (SELECT condition_id FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') LIMIT 1) m, LATERAL polymarket.main.holders(m.condition_id, 20) h ORDER BY h.amount DESC

example_queries.description: What the busiest open market's largest holders' stakes are worth at each outcome's live midpoint
example_queries.sql: SELECT h.outcome_index, h.holder_name, h.amount, q.midpoint, h.amount * q.midpoint AS marked_value FROM (SELECT condition_id FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') LIMIT 1) m, LATERAL polymarket.main.holders(m.condition_id, 20) h, LATERAL polymarket.main.quote(h.token_id) q ORDER BY marked_value DESC

example_queries.description: Follow the biggest holder in a busy market to everything else they hold
example_queries.sql: SELECT p.title, p.outcome, p.size, p.cash_pnl FROM (SELECT h.proxy_wallet FROM (SELECT condition_id FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') LIMIT 1) m, LATERAL polymarket.main.holders(m.condition_id, 20) h ORDER BY h.amount DESC LIMIT 1) w, LATERAL polymarket.main.positions(w.proxy_wallet, 100) p ORDER BY p.current_value DESC

example_queries.description: The biggest open events, and the markets under one of them
example_queries.sql: SELECT m.question, m.volume_24hr FROM (SELECT event_id FROM polymarket.main.events(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') LIMIT 1) e, LATERAL polymarket.main.event_markets(e.event_id) m ORDER BY m.volume_24hr DESC NULLS LAST

example_queries.description: Find events by subject, then the markets under the best match
example_queries.sql: SELECT m.question, m.outcomes FROM (SELECT event_id FROM polymarket.main.search('bitcoin') LIMIT 1) e, LATERAL polymarket.main.event_markets(e.event_id) m

example_queries.description: How the biggest holder in a busy market built their position
example_queries.sql: SELECT a.ts, a.activity_type, a.side, a.price, a.size FROM (SELECT h.proxy_wallet FROM (SELECT condition_id FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') LIMIT 1) m, LATERAL polymarket.main.holders(m.condition_id, 20) h ORDER BY h.amount DESC LIMIT 1) w, LATERAL polymarket.main.activity(w.proxy_wallet, 500, '') a ORDER BY a.ts DESC

example_queries.description: Pre-fee displayed-book cost of 5,000 shares in the ten busiest open markets, against what the touch advertises
example_queries.sql: SELECT m.question, o.outcome, q.midpoint, f.avg_price, f.slippage, f.fully_filled FROM (SELECT question, outcomes, volume_24hr FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') LIMIT 10) m, LATERAL (SELECT unnest(m.outcomes, recursive := true)) o, LATERAL polymarket.main.quote(o.token_id) q, LATERAL polymarket.main.fill_price(o.token_id, 'buy', 5000) f ORDER BY m.volume_24hr DESC, o.outcome_index

example_queries.description: Active recurring series by recent volume
example_queries.sql: SELECT slug, title, recurrence, volume_24hr FROM polymarket.main.series WHERE active AND NOT closed ORDER BY volume_24hr DESC NULLS LAST LIMIT 20

example_queries.description: Topics read from the scan function behind the tags table
example_queries.sql: SELECT tag_id, label FROM polymarket.main.all_tags() WHERE label ILIKE '%politics%'

example_queries.description: Series read from the scan function behind the series table
example_queries.sql: SELECT slug, title FROM polymarket.main.all_series() WHERE recurrence = 'daily' LIMIT 20

example_queries.description: The event behind the busiest open market

example_queries.description: The question behind a market, by its on-chain id
example_queries.sql: SELECT m.question, m.volume_24hr FROM (SELECT condition_id FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') LIMIT 1) t, LATERAL polymarket.main.market(t.condition_id) m

example_queries.description: How many series run at each cadence
example_queries.sql: SELECT recurrence, count(*) AS series_count FROM polymarket.main.series GROUP BY recurrence ORDER BY series_count DESC

example_queries.description: Topics whose tags were published most recently
