example_queries.description: The widest spreads among the 50 busiest open markets — where liquidity is thin
example_queries.sql: SELECT m.question, o.outcome, q.spread FROM (SELECT question, outcomes FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') LIMIT 50) m, LATERAL (SELECT unnest(m.outcomes, recursive := true)) o, LATERAL polymarket.main.quote(o.token_id) q WHERE q.spread IS NOT NULL ORDER BY q.spread DESC LIMIT 20

example_queries.description: How far each outcome moved over the last day
example_queries.sql: SELECT o.outcome, max(h.price) - min(h.price) AS swing FROM (SELECT outcomes FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') LIMIT 3) m, LATERAL (SELECT unnest(m.outcomes, recursive := true)) o, LATERAL polymarket.main.price_history(o.token_id, '1d', 60) h GROUP BY o.outcome ORDER BY swing DESC

example_queries.description: How that holder's book is doing overall
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS positions, sum(p.current_value) AS value, sum(p.cash_pnl) AS unrealised FROM (SELECT h.proxy_wallet FROM (SELECT condition_id FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') LIMIT 1) m, LATERAL polymarket.main.holders(m.condition_id, 20) h ORDER BY h.amount DESC LIMIT 1) w, LATERAL polymarket.main.positions(w.proxy_wallet, 100) p

example_queries.description: Join a market's trade tape back to its question
example_queries.sql: SELECT m.question, count(*) AS prints FROM (SELECT condition_id FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') LIMIT 3) s, LATERAL polymarket.main.market(s.condition_id) m, LATERAL polymarket.main.trades(s.condition_id, 100, '') t GROUP BY m.question

example_queries.description: Open interest of the events behind the busiest markets
example_queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT e.title, e.open_interest FROM (SELECT event_id FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') LIMIT 5) m, LATERAL polymarket.main.event(m.event_id) e ORDER BY e.open_interest DESC NULLS LAST

example_queries.description: Full depth on both sides of one actively traded outcome's book
example_queries.sql: WITH t AS (SELECT o.token_id FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') m, LATERAL (SELECT unnest(m.outcomes, recursive := true)) o LIMIT 10), books AS (SELECT t.token_id, b.side, b.price, b.size FROM t, LATERAL polymarket.main.orderbook(t.token_id) b) SELECT side, price, size FROM books WHERE token_id = (SELECT min(token_id) FROM books) ORDER BY side, price DESC

example_queries.description: Volume-weighted average price by outcome, from the tape
example_queries.sql: SELECT t.outcome, sum(t.price * t.size) / sum(t.size) AS vwap FROM (SELECT condition_id FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') LIMIT 1) m, LATERAL polymarket.main.trades(m.condition_id, 100, '') t GROUP BY t.outcome

example_queries.description: The biggest open events by 24-hour volume
example_queries.sql: SELECT slug, title, volume_24hr, liquidity FROM polymarket.main.events(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') LIMIT 20

example_queries.description: Which topics an event is filed under, one row per tag
example_queries.sql: SELECT e.title, (unnest(e.tags)).label AS topic FROM polymarket.main.events(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') e LIMIT 40

example_queries.description: Find the tag id for a topic, read from the scan function
example_queries.sql: SELECT tag_id, label, slug FROM polymarket.main.all_tags() WHERE label ILIKE '%crypto%' ORDER BY label

example_queries.description: How concentrated each side of a market is
example_queries.sql: SELECT h.token_id, count(*) AS holders, sum(h.amount) AS shares, max(h.amount) / sum(h.amount) AS top_holder_share FROM (SELECT condition_id FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') LIMIT 1) m, LATERAL polymarket.main.holders(m.condition_id, 20) h GROUP BY h.token_id

example_queries.description: Every candidate market under the biggest open event
example_queries.sql: SELECT m.question, m.outcomes, m.volume_24hr FROM (SELECT event_id FROM polymarket.main.events(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') LIMIT 1) e, LATERAL polymarket.main.event_markets(e.event_id) m ORDER BY m.volume_24hr DESC NULLS LAST

example_queries.description: How many markets each of the busiest events carries

example_queries.description: Displayed-book cost of 5,000 shares on the busiest market, before fees
example_queries.sql: SELECT f.side, f.avg_price, f.touch_price, f.slippage, f.fully_filled FROM (SELECT o.token_id FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') m, LATERAL (SELECT unnest(m.outcomes, recursive := true)) o LIMIT 1) t, LATERAL polymarket.main.fill_price(t.token_id, 'buy', 5000) f

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The whole read-only Polymarket surface, in one schema. Work top-down: the `tags` table lists every topic and needs no arguments, so start there and take a tag id. That id filters the market catalog. Each market then leads two different ways with two different keys — its outcomes' token ids for anything about price or resting liquidity, and its own condition id for anything about who traded or who holds. Both keys live on the same row, which is what lets a single query span the catalog, the order book and the chain.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One schema holding the whole read-only Polymarket surface.

### Finding your way in

The unkeyed `tags` table is the way in: it lists every topic, and a tag id is the filter the two catalog browsers accept. From a market you reach two different things with two different keys — its outcomes' token ids for anything about price, and its own condition id for anything about who traded.

### What composes under LATERAL, and what does not

The point-lookup functions are blended: one registration serves both a literal call and a correlated `LATERAL`, so a per-row lookup becomes a set-based query without a second registration. The two catalog browsers are streaming scans instead — a `LIMIT` over them stops early, but they cannot be the inner side of a LATERAL, so drive a join from them rather than into them. The point lookups exist for that direction.

### Unnesting outcomes

A market's outcomes arrive as a list of structs, so reaching one outcome's token needs `LATERAL (SELECT unnest(m.outcomes, recursive := true)) o`. The `recursive := true` is what exposes the struct's fields as columns; without it the alias carries a single column named `unnest` and `o.token_id` will not bind.

### The one real trap

Two identifiers, both called `market` in Polymarket's own URLs. A condition id names the whole market; a token id names one outcome. Unnesting the outcomes column converts between them. See the catalog notes for how the wrong one fails.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The catalog of recurring question series — about 2,400 rows. A series opens a new event each occurrence, like `nfl` opening one per game, so this is the level to start from for anything periodic. Take a `slug` and pass it to `events()` as `series_slug`. Note that many of Polymarket's biggest markets are one-offs belonging to no series, so use `tags` when you want coverage of the whole site.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Every recurring series Polymarket lists, as an ordinary table — no argument required.

### What a series is, and is not

A series groups events that recur: `nfl` opens an event per game, and each of those events carries a market per outcome. Plenty of the biggest markets on the site are one-offs that belong to no series at all, so this is a view of the recurring part of Polymarket rather than of all of it — `tags` is the axis that covers everything.

### Where to go next

Take a `slug` and pass it to `events()` as `series_slug` for that series' occurrences.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The catalog of every topic on Polymarket — around 7,300 rows, small and slow-changing. This is the discovery entry point: `tag_id` is the filter `markets()` and `events()` both accept, and this is where you find one. Match on `label` or `slug` for a topic like Crypto, Politics or Sports.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Every topic tag Polymarket uses, as an ordinary table — no argument required.

### Why this is a table and most things are functions

It has no required key and changes slowly. The market-data functions are neither, which is why they take a key.

### The long tail is real

A few dozen tags carry nearly all the volume, and the rest are narrow one-off labels left over from individual events. Search `label` for the topic you want rather than browsing.

### Where to go next

Take a `tag_id` and pass it to `markets()` for the tradeable questions, or to `events()` for the groupings above them.

functions.name: quote
functions.comment: Current best bid, best ask, midpoint and spread for one outcome

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The current top of book for ONE OUTCOME TOKEN, in a single row: best bid, best ask, midpoint and spread. Takes a `token_id` from a market's `outcomes` list. This is the cheapest way to ask 'what is this outcome trading at right now' — prefer it over `orderbook()` when you do not need depth, and over the price columns on `markets()` when you need the number to be live rather than as of Gamma's last refresh.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per token, assembled from the CLOB's batched quote endpoints.

### Midpoint is the number you usually want — if the spread is tight

`midpoint` sits halfway between best bid and best ask and is what Polymarket displays as the price. Because a share pays $1 if its outcome happens, it reads as an implied probability: 0.62 is 62%.

**Check `spread` before believing it.** A midpoint is only a forecast to the extent that someone is willing to trade near it. On a thin market the two sides can be almost unrelated — a real book quoted 0.020 bid against 0.990 ask, whose midpoint of 0.505 is not a coin flip but the average of two numbers nobody would trade at. That is why this function returns `spread` alongside `midpoint` rather than only the price: a wide spread means the number above it is noise, and `orderbook()` will show how little is resting behind it.

### Naming

The CLOB reports quotes as `BUY` and `SELL`, and the mapping is the opposite of the obvious one: `BUY` is the best **bid** and `SELL` is the best **ask**, verified against the raw book. They are renamed here to the side of the book they actually sit on, so `best_ask >= best_bid` always holds and `spread` is never negative.

### Cost under LATERAL

Two batched requests per 200 tokens regardless of how many rows drive it, so a quote across a whole topic is cheap.

### Freshness

The CLOB declares no cacheability on quotes, so nothing here is cached. That is the honest policy for a top-of-book read: the number is only worth having if it is current.

functions.name: price_history
functions.comment: How one outcome's price moved over time, as a sampled series

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The historical price series for ONE OUTCOME TOKEN — the time-series view. Reach for it to chart or backtest how an outcome's implied probability moved, rather than where it stands now. Takes a `token_id` from a market's `outcomes` list. Passing a condition id instead returns an EMPTY SERIES with no error, so an empty result usually means the wrong identifier rather than an untraded market.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
A sampled price curve for one outcome token.

### It takes a token id, and the failure is silent

The underlying parameter is called `market`, but it wants a **token id**. A condition id is answered with HTTP 200 and an empty history — indistinguishable from an outcome that never traded. Get the token from `unnest(markets.outcomes)`.

### Not OHLC

Polymarket publishes one price per sampled instant, so each row is a single `price` rather than a bar. `fidelity` is the gap between samples in minutes; `period` is how far back to look.

### Window and caching

Every call ends at the present and requires both `period` and `fidelity`. The series therefore contains a still-forming final point and follows the origin's 90-second cache lifetime. Explicit start/end windows are not part of the SQL surface.

Repeated observations with the same timestamp and exact numeric price within one response are returned once, preserving their first position. Conflicting prices at the same timestamp raise an error; the worker does not choose one. This normalization is local to each token response, without merging separate calls or rounding prices.

### Prices are probabilities

Each `price` is USDC per share between 0 and 1, so the curve reads as the market's implied probability over time. These are traded prices rather than a normalised display figure, so a flat stretch means nothing traded — not that the market held an opinion steady. Pair it with `quote()` if you need to know whether there is a market behind the curve right now.

functions.name: positions
functions.comment: Every open position one wallet holds, with its profit and loss

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Every open position one wallet holds, with entry price, current value and unrealised P&L. Takes a wallet address — a THIRD key, distinct from both market identifiers — which you get from `holders()` or from the trader columns on `trades()`. This is the reverse of `holders()`: that answers 'who is in this market', this answers 'what else is this person in'. Reach for it to follow a large or successful trader across the whole site.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per open position, keyed on the holder's wallet.

### The third key

This is the only function here keyed on a wallet address rather than on a market or an outcome. Get one from `holders()` (who is in this market) or from the `proxy_wallet` column of `trades()` (who just traded).

### Closing the loop

`holders()` goes market to wallet; this goes wallet to market. Chaining them is how you get from 'this market moved' to 'here is who moved it and what else they hold' — which is possible only because Polymarket settles on a public chain.

### Reading the P&L

`cash_pnl` is unrealised profit in USDC and `percent_pnl` is the same as a percentage — a percentage, not a fraction, so -44.5 means down 44.5%. `avg_price` against `cur_price` gives the direction directly, and both are probabilities between 0 and 1. `redeemable` marks a resolved market whose position can be cashed out.

### Cross-API lifecycle

The Data API can retain a position after Gamma retires its catalog record. In that case the row remains valid here, but passing its `condition_id` to `market()` returns no row; use the denormalised `title` and `event_slug` carried by the position itself.

### Freshness

Polymarket declares `max-age=5` here, the shortest TTL it publishes anywhere, because a position's value moves with the market price.

functions.name: market
functions.comment: Look up one Polymarket market by its on-chain condition id

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A single market's current snapshot, by exact condition id. Use this when you already have a condition id — from a trade row, say — and want the question behind it; use `markets()` when you want to browse or filter. Same columns as `markets()`, so the two are interchangeable downstream, and unlike `markets()` this composes under a correlated LATERAL.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row for one market, looked up by `condition_id`.

### When to use this instead of `markets()`

`markets()` is the browse path and streams a catalog; this is the point lookup, and it is the one that works as the inner side of a `LATERAL`. It is the natural way back from a trade or a holding to the question being traded.

### Cost

Requests are batched behind the scenes: Gamma accepts up to 60 condition ids per call, so a join over hundreds of markets costs a handful of requests, not hundreds.

### An unknown id returns nothing

Gamma answers a filter that matches nothing with an empty list rather than a 404, so a condition id that does not exist produces no rows — the same as one that does exist but was filtered away.

functions.name: event
functions.comment: Look up one Polymarket event by its Gamma id

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A single event by its exact Gamma id, with the same columns `events()` returns. Use this when you already hold an `event_id` — every market row carries one — and want the event's aggregate volume, its resolution date or its topic tags. `events()` is the browse path; this is the lookup, and this is the one that works under a correlated LATERAL.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row for one event.

### When to use this instead of `events()`

`events()` streams a catalog and cannot be the inner side of a `LATERAL`. This fetches one event and can, so it is the way to go from a set of markets back up to the events they belong to.

### What it does not return

Gamma's response also carries the event's markets — usually most of the payload. They are not returned here: `event_markets()` is the way to ask for those, and it reshapes them to the same columns `markets()` returns.

### One request per row

Unlike `market()`, this endpoint has no batch form, so a LATERAL costs one request per input row, so drive it from a bounded set rather than a whole catalog.

functions.name: orderbook
functions.comment: Resting order-book depth for one outcome, one row per side and price level

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Resting order-book depth for ONE OUTCOME TOKEN, flattened to one row per side and price level so it aggregates and joins like an ordinary table. Takes a `token_id` from a market's `outcomes` list — NOT a condition id, which is a 404 here. Reach for this to see liquidity behind the best quote: spread, depth at a price, or the shape of one side. For just the top of book use `quote()`, which is one row instead of many.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
The CLOB returns a book as nested `bids` and `asks`; this flattens it to one row per (side, price level).

### It takes a token id

Each outcome of a market trades as its own token with its own book. Get the `token_id` from `unnest(markets.outcomes)`. A condition id here is an HTTP 404 — which at least fails loudly, unlike `price_history()`, where the same mistake returns an empty series.

### Reading the two sides

`bid` rows are buyers, `ask` rows are sellers, and the outcomes of a binary market mirror each other: a Yes bid at 0.40 is economically a No ask at 0.60. There is no `depth` argument: the batched endpoint returns the whole book either way, and SQL caps it exactly — `QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY side ORDER BY CASE WHEN side = 'bid' THEN -price ELSE price END) <= 5`. The side-aware ordering matters: best bids are highest, while best asks are lowest.

### Cost under LATERAL

Books are fetched in batches of up to 200 tokens per request, which is what makes a join across a whole topic affordable: measured at 12.85s for 100 books individually against 0.16s batched. No query change is needed; it happens automatically.

### An empty result

A token with no resting orders contributes no rows, and so does a token the batch endpoint omits — both mean 'nothing is resting here'.

vgi.example_queries.description: Full depth on both sides of one actively traded outcome's book
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH t AS (SELECT o.token_id FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') m, LATERAL (SELECT unnest(m.outcomes, recursive := true)) o LIMIT 10), books AS (SELECT t.token_id, b.side, b.price, b.size FROM t, LATERAL polymarket.main.orderbook(t.token_id) b) SELECT side, price, size FROM books WHERE token_id = (SELECT min(token_id) FROM books) ORDER BY side, price DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Total resting size per side across a whole topic, in one query
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT b.side, sum(b.size) AS resting FROM polymarket.main.markets(tag_id => '21', closed => 'false') m, LATERAL (SELECT unnest(m.outcomes, recursive := true)) o, LATERAL polymarket.main.orderbook(o.token_id) b GROUP BY b.side

functions.name: markets
functions.comment: Browse Polymarket's tradeable questions with their prices and volume

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The entry point to Polymarket's market data: one row per tradeable question, with its current price, volume and lifecycle state. Reach for this to browse or filter — start from a `tag_id` out of the `tags` table, or pass `order_by => 'volume24hr'` to see what is busy right now. The `outcomes` column is the important one: it carries each outcome's `token_id`, which is what `orderbook()`, `quote()` and `price_history()` key on. The `condition_id` column is a DIFFERENT key, and is what `trades()` and `holders()` take. Passing one where the other belongs usually returns an empty result rather than an error. Without `closed`, only OPEN markets come back, even for a `slug` or `condition_id` lookup: pass `closed => 'true'` to see resolved ones, or use `market()`, which checks both.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Markets are the tradeable questions on Polymarket. Each has two or more outcomes, and each outcome trades as its own CLOB token.

### The two identifiers

This is the thing to get right, because getting it wrong is usually silent:

- `condition_id` (`0x` + 64 hex) identifies the **market**. `trades()` and `holders()` take it.
- `token_id` (a long decimal string, inside `outcomes`) identifies **one outcome**. `orderbook()`, `quote()` and `price_history()` take it.

Both are called `market` in Polymarket's own URLs, which is where the confusion comes from.

### Open markets unless asked otherwise

Gamma's market catalog treats a missing `closed` as `closed => 'false'`. A call without it returns open markets only, and that includes a `slug` or `condition_id` lookup (or a `WHERE` on either column): a resolved market comes back only with `closed => 'true'`. There is no single call for both; `UNION ALL` the two, or use `market()`, which finds a condition id whether or not its market has closed. `events()` differs: without `closed` it returns running and finished events together.

### Reading `outcomes`

Polymarket sends outcome names, prices and token ids as three separate JSON-encoded strings whose only relationship is positional. They are zipped here into one list of structs so the correspondence cannot be got wrong. Reach the individual outcomes by unnesting that column in a LATERAL — the shipped example queries show the exact form, which needs `recursive := true` to expose the struct's fields as columns.

### Prices are probabilities, where the market is liquid

Every price column is USDC per share between 0 and 1, and a share pays $1 if its outcome happens — so a price of 0.62 reads as a 62% implied probability. They are `DECIMAL`, never `DOUBLE`.

The prices inside `outcomes` are Polymarket's displayed figures, normalised to sum to 1 across a market's outcomes. That means they always *look* like a coherent forecast, even when nothing is resting on the book. Before treating one as a probability, check the real quote: `quote()` returns the `spread` and `orderbook()` the size behind it. A market quoting 0.02 bid against 0.99 ask has a displayed price and no market.

### Streaming

Rows arrive one API page at a time, so a `LIMIT` stops early instead of paying for the whole catalog. The cost is that this cannot be the inner side of a correlated `LATERAL` — drive a join from it, not into it. Use `market()` for the per-row lookup.

vgi.example_queries.description: The busiest open markets right now, with their implied probabilities
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT question, outcomes, volume_24hr FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') LIMIT 20

vgi.example_queries.description: Every outcome of every crypto market, one row per outcome
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT m.question, o.outcome, o.price, o.token_id FROM polymarket.main.markets(tag_id => '21', closed => 'false') m, LATERAL (SELECT unnest(m.outcomes, recursive := true)) o ORDER BY m.volume_24hr DESC LIMIT 50

functions.name: trades
functions.comment: Executed trades on one Polymarket market, with the trader behind each

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Individual executed trades on ONE MARKET — the public tape, newest first. Takes a `condition_id`, NOT a token id: a token id here is rejected with an error. Reach for this when you need actual prints rather than quotes: trade-by-trade flow, taker direction, a volume-weighted price, or WHO traded — each row carries the counterparty's wallet and profile name, because Polymarket settles on a public chain.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per execution, with the trader attached.

### It takes a condition id

This is the Data API, which keys on the market rather than the outcome. A token id is rejected with HTTP 400 (`invalid condition id`). Each row's `token_id` column tells you which outcome changed hands.

### Public counterparties

`proxy_wallet`, `trader_name` and `pseudonym` identify the taker. This is ordinary public chain data, and it is what makes flow analysis possible here in a way it is not on a conventional exchange.

### Volume

An active market can have a very long tape, which is why `max_rows` is required rather than defaulted — the call should say how much it wants, up to 10,000 trades per call.

### Prices arrive as floats

The Data API sends price and size as JSON numbers rather than strings. They are recovered to exact `DECIMAL` through the shortest round-tripping representation, so a 0.955 print reads as 0.955 and not as 0.9549999999.

vgi.example_queries.description: The most recent prints on the busiest open market
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT t.ts, t.side, t.outcome, t.price, t.size, t.trader_name FROM (SELECT condition_id FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') LIMIT 1) m, LATERAL polymarket.main.trades(m.condition_id, 100, '') t ORDER BY t.ts DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Volume-weighted average price by outcome, from the tape
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT t.outcome, sum(t.price * t.size) / sum(t.size) AS vwap FROM (SELECT condition_id FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') LIMIT 1) m, LATERAL polymarket.main.trades(m.condition_id, 100, '') t GROUP BY t.outcome

functions.name: events
functions.comment: Browse the events that group Polymarket's markets by resolution

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The layer between a topic and its markets: one row per event, with its aggregate volume, liquidity, open interest and topic tags. Reach for this to find a specific `event_id` — which `event_markets()` takes to return that event's markets — or to compare whole events rather than individual questions. An event groups the markets that resolve together: one NFL game, or one election with a market per candidate.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
An event groups the markets that resolve together. A single-question event has one market under it; an election event has one per candidate.

### Narrowing from here

Take an `event_id` and pass it to `event_markets()` to get that event's markets. There is deliberately no `event_slug` filter on `markets()`: `/markets/keyset` has no such parameter, and Gamma answers an unrecognised filter by ignoring it and returning everything, so offering one would silently return the wrong rows.

### Tags stay nested

`tags` is a list of `{tag_id, label, slug}` structs — flattening it would fan every event out into one row per tag. `unnest` the column when you do want that shape.

### Money is float-encoded here

Gamma sends event-level volume and liquidity as JSON numbers where the market level sends the same quantities as strings. Both are carried to `DECIMAL` through the same converter, so the two levels compare exactly.

### Paging

Rows stream a page at a time, so a `LIMIT` stops early. Gamma clamps the page size to 100 silently rather than erroring on a larger request.

vgi.example_queries.description: The biggest open events by 24-hour volume
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT slug, title, volume_24hr, liquidity FROM polymarket.main.events(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') LIMIT 20

vgi.example_queries.description: Which topics an event is filed under, one row per tag
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT e.title, (unnest(e.tags)).label AS topic FROM polymarket.main.events(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') e LIMIT 40

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Every topic tag on Polymarket, as a function. Prefer the `tags` table, which scans this and reads as plain SQL; this form exists for the rare case you want the scan itself. Either way it is the discovery starting point: `tag_id` is the filter both `markets()` and `events()` accept, and it is the only way to ask for 'everything about crypto' rather than naming markets one at a time.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Polymarket's topic axis — roughly 7,300 tags, streamed a page at a time.

### Prefer the table

The `tags` catalog table is backed by this function, so it can be selected from directly, without parentheses. This function returns exactly the same rows; it is named `all_tags` only so that the function and the table it backs can coexist in one schema.

### The long tail is real

A few dozen tags carry nearly all the volume (`Crypto`, `Politics`, `Sports`), and the rest are narrow one-off labels left over from individual events. Match on `label` or `slug` when you know the topic you want; scanning for a tag by eye is not rewarding.

### Where to go next

Take a `tag_id` and pass it to `markets()` or `events()`.

functions.name: holders
functions.comment: Who holds the largest positions in one Polymarket market

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The largest position holders in ONE MARKET, one row per holder per outcome. Takes a `condition_id`, like `trades()` and unlike the order book. This has no equivalent on a conventional exchange: Polymarket settles on a public chain, so who is holding what is public. Reach for it to ask who is on each side of a question, or how concentrated a position is.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per holder per outcome, ranked by size.

### Why this exists at all

Positions are on-chain, so the holder list is public data rather than something an exchange chooses to publish. There is no equivalent on Kalshi or a conventional venue.

### Shape

The API groups holders under each outcome token; that grouping is flattened here and the `token_id` stamped onto every row, so a holder row can say which side of the question it is a position in. `amount` is shares of that outcome, and each share pays $1 if the outcome happens.

### Concentration

Summing `amount` by `token_id` and comparing the top holder to the rest is the usual way to ask whether a price is one whale's opinion or a crowd's.

vgi.example_queries.description: The biggest positions in the busiest open market
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT h.outcome_index, h.holder_name, h.amount FROM (SELECT condition_id FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') LIMIT 1) m, LATERAL polymarket.main.holders(m.condition_id, 20) h ORDER BY h.amount DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: How concentrated each side of a market is
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT h.token_id, count(*) AS holders, sum(h.amount) AS shares, max(h.amount) / sum(h.amount) AS top_holder_share FROM (SELECT condition_id FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') LIMIT 1) m, LATERAL polymarket.main.holders(m.condition_id, 20) h GROUP BY h.token_id

vgi.example_queries.description: What the busiest open market's largest holders' stakes are worth at each outcome's live midpoint
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT h.outcome_index, h.holder_name, h.amount, q.midpoint, h.amount * q.midpoint AS marked_value FROM (SELECT condition_id FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') LIMIT 1) m, LATERAL polymarket.main.holders(m.condition_id, 20) h, LATERAL polymarket.main.quote(h.token_id) q ORDER BY marked_value DESC

functions.name: event_markets
functions.comment: Every tradeable market grouped under one Polymarket event

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The markets under one event, by event id — an election's candidates, a game's outcomes. Returns exactly the columns `markets()` does, so it is interchangeable downstream, and unlike `markets()` it composes under a correlated LATERAL. This is the ONLY way to get an event's markets: `markets()` has no event filter, because Gamma's market endpoint does not offer one.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per market under one event, in `markets()`' columns.

### Why this is a separate function

`/markets/keyset` has no event parameter. Gamma ignores query parameters it does not recognise and answers with the unfiltered first page, so an `event_slug` argument on `markets()` would return the wrong rows with no error at all. The event's own payload carries its markets, so they are read from there instead.

### Composing

Drive it from `events()` to expand a set of events into their markets, then `unnest(outcomes)` to reach the tokens the order book keys on.

### One request per row

There is no batch form, so a LATERAL costs one request per event. Pass a bounded set of events rather than a whole catalog.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT m.question, m.outcomes, m.volume_24hr FROM (SELECT event_id FROM polymarket.main.events(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') LIMIT 1) e, LATERAL polymarket.main.event_markets(e.event_id) m ORDER BY m.volume_24hr DESC NULLS LAST

functions.name: fill_price
functions.comment: Displayed-book fill price and slippage for a given order size, before fees

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The price a given order size would actually get, having consumed the resting book level by level. Takes a `token_id`, a side, and a share count. Reach for this instead of `quote()` whenever size matters: a market can quote a one-tick spread and hold fifteen shares behind it, so the midpoint is a real price at which almost nothing trades. `avg_price` is what the position costs per share, `slippage` is what the size cost over the touch, and `fully_filled` says whether the book could cover the request at all. Values are pre-fee: this function models displayed liquidity, not venue fees.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per request, computed from the same batched book `orderbook()` returns — so it costs no extra call when driven alongside it.

### Why the touch is not enough

Spread measures the distance between the best bid and the best ask. It says nothing about how much is standing there. A live market quoted a 0.001 spread on 15 shares; another quoted 0.97 on a book with one order a side. Neither number tells you what a position would cost, and this does.

### Reading the result

`avg_price` is size-weighted across every level consumed. `slippage` is the distance from the touch, signed so that it is always the cost of size rather than a direction — never negative. `fully_filled = false` means the book ran out: the row prices the portion that could fill, and the rest of the order would move the price further than this reports. `notional` and `avg_price` are computed from displayed book levels before any applicable venue fees.

### Sizing a strategy

Comparing `avg_price` across candidates at the size you actually intend to trade is a different ranking from comparing midpoints, and it is the one that survives contact with the book.

vgi.example_queries.description: Displayed-book cost of 5,000 shares on the busiest market, before fees
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT f.side, f.avg_price, f.touch_price, f.slippage, f.fully_filled FROM (SELECT o.token_id FROM polymarket.main.markets(closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') m, LATERAL (SELECT unnest(m.outcomes, recursive := true)) o LIMIT 1) t, LATERAL polymarket.main.fill_price(t.token_id, 'buy', 5000) f

vgi.example_queries.description: Which outcomes in a topic can absorb real size, and which cannot
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT m.question, o.outcome, f.avg_price, f.filled_size, f.fully_filled FROM polymarket.main.markets(tag_id => '21', closed => 'false', order_by => 'volume24hr', ascending => 'false') m, LATERAL (SELECT unnest(m.outcomes, recursive := true)) o, LATERAL polymarket.main.fill_price(o.token_id, 'buy', 10000) f WHERE NOT f.fully_filled LIMIT 20

functions.name: all_series
functions.comment: Every Polymarket series (the scan backing the `series` table)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Every recurring question series on Polymarket, as a function. Prefer the `series` table, which scans this. A series is a question that opens a new event each occurrence — 'NFL' opens one per game — so this is the level to start from for anything periodic. Take a `slug` and pass it to `events()` as `series_slug`. Note that most one-off markets belong to no series at all, so this is a view of the recurring part of the site rather than of all of it.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Polymarket's recurring question series — about 2,400 rows, streamed a page at a time.

### Prefer the table

The `series` catalog table is backed by this function and reads as plain SQL. This function returns exactly the same rows; the `all_` prefix exists only so that the function and the table can coexist in one schema.

### What a series is, and is not

A series groups events that recur: `nfl` opens an event per game, and each of those events carries a market per outcome. Plenty of Polymarket's biggest markets are one-offs that belong to no series, so this does **not** enumerate the site — `tags` is the axis that covers everything.

### Cost

Each series inlines every event beneath it, and those events inline their markets: 50 series come to 1.73 MB with the events and 31.6 KB without. This scan asks Gamma to exclude them, which is the difference between ~83 MB and ~1.5 MB for the whole catalog.

functions.name: activity
functions.comment: One wallet's history of trades, redemptions, yield and rebates

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Everything one wallet has done, newest first — the history counterpart to `positions()`, which reports only what it holds now. Takes a wallet address, the same key `positions()` takes. Reach for it to reconstruct how a trader built a position, or when they got out. Note the feed is broader than a trade tape: on a long-lived wallet most entries are `YIELD` accruals, so filter on `activity_type = 'TRADE'` when you want executions.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One row per event in a wallet's history.

### Wider than a trade tape

`activity_type` distinguishes `TRADE` from `REDEEM` (cashing out a resolved market), `YIELD` (interest accrued on collateral), `MAKER_REBATE` and `TAKER_REBATE`, and the `SPLIT`/`MERGE` operations that convert between a dollar and a full set of outcome shares. Only `TRADE` rows carry a price and a side; the rest leave those NULL rather than reporting a misleading zero. Across a sample of active wallets, trades were roughly 92% of all entries.

### Completing the chain

`holders()` goes market to wallet, `positions()` goes wallet to its current markets, and this goes wallet to everything it has ever done. All three are public because Polymarket settles on a public chain.

### Volume

An active wallet has a very long history, so `max_rows` is required and capped at 5,000 entries per call.

functions.name: search
functions.comment: Find events by searching their text, the way the site's search box does

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Full-text search over events — the way in when you know the subject but not the tag or the slug. Reach for this FIRST for any question phrased in words ('markets about the Fed', 'anything on Bitcoin'), because no other object here searches text: filtering `markets()` on a title predicate downloads the whole catalog to do it. Returns the same columns `events()` does, so chain it into `event_markets()` to reach the tradeable questions.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Gamma's search endpoint, returning events with the same columns `events()` gives.

### Why this exists

It is the only text search in the catalog. Gamma's other filters match ids, slugs and tags — never free text — so a `WHERE title ILIKE '%bitcoin%'` on `events()` cannot be pushed down and pages the entire catalog over the network to filter locally. This asks the search index instead.

### Where to go next

Take an `event_id` and pass it to `event_markets()` for the markets beneath, then unnest their outcomes to reach prices and books.

### Paging

Results stream a page at a time and are ranked by relevance, so a `LIMIT` takes the best matches rather than an arbitrary slice.

vgi.example_queries.description: Find the events matching a subject, best matches first
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT event_id, title, volume_24hr FROM polymarket.main.search('bitcoin') LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: Search for a subject, then the tradeable markets under the best match
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT m.question, m.outcomes FROM (SELECT event_id FROM polymarket.main.search('federal reserve') LIMIT 1) e, LATERAL polymarket.main.event_markets(e.event_id) m

workers.title: PostHog Product Analytics
workers.tagline: PostHog events, persons and HogQL queries as SQL in DuckDB, with HogQL pushdown (Python)
workers.subtitle: PostHog events, persons, sessions and HogQL as SQL, plus flags, experiments and insights.
workers.summary: PostHog product analytics as SQL: run HogQL through the Query API, read events, persons, sessions and groups with filters pushed into HogQL, and list feature flags, experiments, insights and other project resources. Works with US Cloud, EU Cloud and self-hosted PostHog.
workers.doc_md:
# PostHog

PostHog product analytics in DuckDB SQL: run HogQL through PostHog's [Query API](https://posthog.com/docs/api/queries) and get typed columns back, read events, persons, sessions and groups with your `WHERE` clause translated into HogQL, and list feature flags, experiments, insights, dashboards, cohorts and definitions.

Credentials come from a DuckDB secret of type `posthog`, created **after** `ATTACH`:

```sql
-- US Cloud (default host https://us.posthog.com)
CREATE SECRET ph (TYPE posthog, PERSONAL_API_KEY 'phx_...', PROJECT_ID '12345');
-- EU Cloud or self-hosted
CREATE SECRET ph (TYPE posthog, PERSONAL_API_KEY 'phx_...', PROJECT_ID '12345',
                  HOST 'https://eu.posthog.com');
```

Use a *personal* API key (Settings → Personal API keys) with read scopes for Query and the resources you list, not the `phc_` project key.
workers.readme_sql:
-- Which pages did pro-plan users view last week, and how often?
SELECT current_url, count(*) AS views
FROM posthog.main.events_where(event := '$pageview', properties := '{"plan": "pro"}',
                               after := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-08', before := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-15')
GROUP BY current_url ORDER BY views DESC LIMIT 10;

example_queries.description: Event counts for one day (the timestamp range runs in HogQL)
example_queries.sql: SELECT event, count(*) AS n FROM posthog.main.events WHERE timestamp >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01 00:00:00+00' AND timestamp < TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-02 00:00:00+00' GROUP BY event ORDER BY n DESC

example_queries.description: Identified persons and their email property
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, properties->>'email' AS email, created_at FROM posthog.main.persons WHERE is_identified ORDER BY created_at

example_queries.description: Persons with more than one distinct id
example_queries.sql: SELECT person_id, list(distinct_id ORDER BY distinct_id) AS ids FROM posthog.main.person_distinct_ids GROUP BY person_id HAVING count(*) > 1

example_queries.description: Bounce rate and median duration per channel for November
example_queries.sql: SELECT channel_type, avg(is_bounce::INT) AS bounce_rate, median(duration_seconds) AS median_s FROM posthog.main.sessions WHERE start_timestamp >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01 00:00:00+00' GROUP BY channel_type ORDER BY bounce_rate DESC

example_queries.description: Companies by seat count
example_queries.sql: SELECT g.group_key, g.properties->>'name' AS name, (g.properties->>'seats')::INT AS seats FROM posthog.main.groups g JOIN posthog.metadata.group_types t USING (group_type_index) WHERE t.group_type = 'company' ORDER BY seats DESC

example_queries.description: Event counts computed in PostHog, with the date bound as a placeholder
example_queries.sql: SELECT event, n FROM posthog.main.hogql('SELECT event, count() AS n FROM events WHERE timestamp >= {since} GROUP BY event', values := '{"since": "2026-11-01"}') WHERE n > 1 ORDER BY n DESC

example_queries.description: Revenue from purchases by pro-plan users (property filter runs in HogQL)
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS purchases, sum((properties->>'amount')::DOUBLE) AS revenue FROM posthog.main.events_where(event := 'purchase', properties := '{"plan": "pro"}')

example_queries.description: A named ClickHouse tuple becomes a DuckDB STRUCT
example_queries.sql: SELECT posthog.main.clickhouse_type_to_duckdb('Tuple(label String, rank UInt8)') AS duckdb_type

example_queries.description: Pageviews per URL for one user
example_queries.sql: SELECT current_url, count(*) AS views FROM posthog.main.events WHERE event = '$pageview' AND distinct_id = 'user-1' GROUP BY current_url ORDER BY views DESC

example_queries.description: Revenue per plan from purchase events
example_queries.sql: SELECT plan, sum(revenue) AS revenue FROM posthog.main.hogql('SELECT properties.plan AS plan, toFloat(properties.amount) AS revenue FROM events WHERE event = {ev}', values := '{"ev": "purchase"}') GROUP BY plan ORDER BY revenue DESC

example_queries.description: The 20 latest events of one user
example_queries.sql: SELECT timestamp, event, current_url FROM posthog.main.events_where(distinct_id := 'user-1', max_rows := 20, newest_first := true) ORDER BY timestamp DESC

example_queries.description: How common HogQL result types land in DuckDB
example_queries.sql: SELECT t, posthog.main.clickhouse_type_to_duckdb(t) AS duckdb_type FROM (VALUES ('Nullable(String)'), ('DateTime64(6, ''UTC'')'), ('Array(UInt8)'), ('Decimal(18, 4)')) AS v(t) ORDER BY t;

example_queries.description: Projects the key can read
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, name, timezone FROM posthog.metadata.projects ORDER BY id

example_queries.description: Group type names
example_queries.sql: SELECT group_type_index, group_type FROM posthog.metadata.group_types ORDER BY 1

example_queries.description: Verified events by 30-day volume
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, volume_30_day, last_seen_at FROM posthog.metadata.event_definitions WHERE verified ORDER BY volume_30_day DESC NULLS LAST

example_queries.description: Numeric event properties
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, property_type FROM posthog.metadata.property_definitions WHERE definition_type = 'event' AND is_numerical ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Actions and the events their steps match
example_queries.sql: SELECT a.name, s.event, s.selector FROM posthog.metadata.actions a, unnest(a.steps) AS u(s) ORDER BY a.name

example_queries.description: Dynamic cohorts by size
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, count, last_calculation FROM posthog.metadata.cohorts WHERE NOT is_static AND NOT deleted ORDER BY count DESC NULLS LAST

example_queries.description: Active flags and their rollout
example_queries.sql: SELECT key, rollout_percentage, is_multivariate FROM posthog.metadata.feature_flags WHERE active AND NOT deleted ORDER BY key

example_queries.description: Running experiments
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, feature_flag_key, start_date FROM posthog.metadata.experiments WHERE start_date IS NOT NULL AND end_date IS NULL AND NOT archived ORDER BY start_date

example_queries.description: Launched surveys and their size
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, type, question_count FROM posthog.metadata.surveys WHERE start_date IS NOT NULL ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Saved insights per query kind
example_queries.sql: SELECT query_kind, count(*) AS insights FROM posthog.metadata.insights WHERE saved AND NOT deleted GROUP BY query_kind ORDER BY insights DESC

example_queries.description: Pinned dashboards
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, name FROM posthog.metadata.dashboards WHERE pinned ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Deploy annotations
example_queries.sql: SELECT date_marker, content FROM posthog.metadata.annotations WHERE creation_type = 'GIT' ORDER BY date_marker

example_queries.description: Insights on each dashboard

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Analytics data of the secret's PostHog project, read through the Query API in HogQL. Typed tables cover captured events, persons and the distinct ids merged into them, web sessions and group-analytics entities; equality, range, IN and NULL predicates on their typed columns run inside PostHog, so bound the timestamp to keep scans small. JSON property predicates cannot be pushed from SQL and are applied by DuckDB after reading; the events_where table function pushes property equality and a row cap instead. The hogql table function runs any HogQL query, with constants passed as named placeholders bound from a JSON values argument, and returns at most 50,000 rows per call. Events link to persons through person_id and to sessions through session_id.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

Analytics data through PostHog's Query API, in HogQL.

`WHERE` predicates on typed columns become HogQL and scans page with a keyset cursor; bound the timestamp to keep them small.

JSON property filters are applied by DuckDB; use the property-filter table function to push them, or write the HogQL yourself.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Every captured event of the project, read from HogQL's events table ordered by (timestamp, uuid) with keyset pagination. Columns: uuid, event, timestamp (`TIMESTAMPTZ` UTC), distinct_id, person_id, session_id ($session_id), current_url ($current_url), properties (JSON), elements_chain, created_at. Pushed into HogQL: =, <>, <, <=, >, >=, IN and IS [NOT] NULL on event, timestamp, created_at, distinct_id, person_id, uuid, session_id, current_url and elements_chain, with AND/OR; only the needed columns are selected; ORDER BY <column> LIMIT n with no WHERE becomes one HogQL ORDER BY ... LIMIT n. Always bound timestamp. JSON property filters are applied by DuckDB; use events_where() to push property equality.

functions.name: hogql
functions.comment: Run a HogQL query through PostHog's Query API and return its typed result

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Run a HogQL SELECT (PostHog's SQL dialect over ClickHouse; tables events, persons, sessions, groups; property access as properties.$browser or person.properties.email) through PostHog's Query API and return its columns with DuckDB types mapped from the ClickHouse types in the response: String becomes `VARCHAR`, DateTime64 `TIMESTAMPTZ`, Array a `LIST`, Map a `MAP`, Tuple a `STRUCT`, Decimal a `DECIMAL`, UInt64 `UBIGINT` (clickhouse_type_to_duckdb shows the mapping). Pass constants in values as a JSON object and reference them as {name} placeholders instead of quoting them, and alias every computed column. The query is wrapped so DuckDB's projection and simple predicates on the result run in PostHog, capped at max_rows (default and PostHog maximum 50,000; 0 sends the query verbatim, where PostHog's default of 100 rows applies unless it has a LIMIT). There is no OFFSET paging: aggregate in HogQL, or read large row sets from the events table. refresh 'async' or 'force_async' runs the query asynchronously and the worker polls until it completes.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Runs any HogQL `SELECT` and returns typed columns. Bind constants with `values` and `{name}` placeholders instead of quoting them. At most 50,000 rows per query (PostHog's cap).

vgi.example_queries.description: Event counts computed in PostHog, with the date bound as a placeholder
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT event, n FROM posthog.main.hogql('SELECT event, count() AS n FROM events WHERE timestamp >= {since} GROUP BY event', values := '{"since": "2026-11-01"}') WHERE n > 1 ORDER BY n DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Revenue per plan from purchase events
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT plan, sum(revenue) AS revenue FROM posthog.main.hogql('SELECT properties.plan AS plan, toFloat(properties.amount) AS revenue FROM events WHERE event = {ev}', values := '{"ev": "purchase"}') GROUP BY plan ORDER BY revenue DESC

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
The columns are the HogQL query's own output columns, in order, named as PostHog names them (alias computed columns), all nullable. Each column's type follows the ClickHouse type PostHog reports (`clickhouse_type_to_duckdb` shows the mapping). For example, the query `SELECT event, count() AS n, max(timestamp) AS last_seen FROM events GROUP BY event` returns:

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| event | VARCHAR | ClickHouse String: the event name. |
| n | UBIGINT | ClickHouse UInt64: count() of events. |
| last_seen | TIMESTAMPTZ | ClickHouse DateTime64(6, 'UTC'): latest event time. |

functions.comment: DuckDB column type that hogql() produces for a ClickHouse type string from a HogQL response

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Return the DuckDB type name that hogql() gives a column of the given ClickHouse type, as PostHog reports it in a HogQL response's types: 'String' gives `VARCHAR`, "DateTime64(6, 'UTC')" gives `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE`, 'Array(String)' gives `VARCHAR[]`, 'Map(String, String)' gives `MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)`, named tuples become `STRUCT`, 'UInt64' gives `UBIGINT`. Nullable and LowCardinality wrappers are unwrapped (every hogql() column is nullable); unknown types fall back to `VARCHAR`. Runs locally, no PostHog connection or secret needed. NULL in, NULL out.

workers.title: pprof Profile Decoder
workers.tagline: Decode pprof profiles in DuckDB with SQL — flatten samples/stacks/functions for bulk profile diffing and CI gates. A VGI worker.
workers.subtitle: Decode Go, gperftools, Parca and py-spy pprof profiles into SQL rows for flamegraph diffs and CI performance-regression gates.
workers.summary: Decode pprof (profile.proto) CPU/heap/alloc/mutex profiles into SQL rows for bulk profile diffing and CI performance-regression gates.
workers.doc_md:
# pprof

Decode **pprof** profiles — the gzip-wrapped `profile.proto` produced by Go, gperftools, Parca, Pyroscope, py-spy, and friends — into rows so SRE and performance teams can **bulk-diff profiles in SQL** and wire up CI performance-regression gates. `go tool pprof` is interactive and single-file; this worker lets you load hundreds of profiles at once and ask "which function regressed across this deploy?"

The headline is a **flattened, flamegraph-ready view**: one row per sample with its call stack already resolved — the per-type measured values (a `BIGINT[]` aligned to the profile's sample value types), the sample labels as a `MAP`, and the call stack as a leaf-first list of `(function, filename, line, address)` frames, with inlined frames expanded and unsymbolized frames keeping their raw address. A flamegraph diff across many profiles then needs no manual join.

The underlying `profile.proto` graph is also exposed for ad-hoc joins, with the profile's original ids passed through verbatim, alongside a one-row profile summary (sample value types, sampling period, duration). A loaded binary's build id is emitted verbatim so the addresses of unsymbolized native frames can be resolved by a downstream symbolizer.

Reach for this worker whenever you need to **compare or aggregate profiles at scale** — across a fleet, a deploy, or a CI run — rather than inspecting one at a time. Each source is decoded independently — a **path** (which may be a glob like `/profiles/*.pb.gz`), a **list of paths**, or **inline profile bytes** — so a malformed or zero-byte profile produces a single **error row** (every data column NULL) rather than failing the whole scan.

## Sources and references

- [google/pprof](https://github.com/google/pprof) — the pprof tool and format
- [profile.proto](https://github.com/google/pprof/blob/main/proto/profile.proto) — the protobuf schema this worker decodes
- [profile.proto README](https://github.com/google/pprof/blob/main/proto/README.md) — field semantics and conventions
workers.readme_sql:
INSTALL vgi FROM community; LOAD vgi;
ATTACH 'pprof' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'github-auto://Query-farm/vgi-pprof@v0.4.3');
SET search_path = 'pprof.main';

-- top self-time functions across a directory of your CPU profiles: the source
-- may be a path, a glob, a list of paths, or inline BLOB bytes
-- (value[2] is cpu/nanoseconds; value[1] is samples/count — see pprof.meta)
SELECT frame[1].function AS fn, sum(value[2]) AS cpu_ns
FROM pprof.stacks('/profiles/*.pb.gz')
WHERE error IS NULL
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 20;

-- regression diff: candidate build vs baseline
WITH base AS (
  SELECT frame[1].function AS fn, sum(value[2]) AS ns
  FROM pprof.stacks('baseline.pb.gz') WHERE error IS NULL GROUP BY 1),
cand AS (
  SELECT frame[1].function AS fn, sum(value[2]) AS ns
  FROM pprof.stacks('candidate.pb.gz') WHERE error IS NULL GROUP BY 1)
SELECT cand.fn, cand.ns - COALESCE(base.ns, 0) AS delta
FROM cand LEFT JOIN base USING (fn) ORDER BY delta DESC;

-- symbolization hand-off: hottest unsymbolized leaf addresses as
-- (binary, build_id, offset-in-binary), joining samples → locations → mappings
SELECT m.filename AS binary_path, m.build_id,
       printf('0x%x', l.address - m.memory_start + m.file_offset) AS binary_offset,
       sum(s.value[2]) AS cpu_ns
FROM pprof.samples('native.pb.gz') s
JOIN pprof.locations('native.pb.gz') l ON l.location_id = s.location_ids[1]
JOIN pprof.mappings('native.pb.gz') m ON m.mapping_id = l.mapping_id
WHERE s.error IS NULL
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY cpu_ns DESC, binary_offset;

example_queries.description: Top self-time functions summed across two CPU profiles (a baseline and a candidate run, passed inline as BLOBs; with profiles on disk, pass a path glob or a list of paths).
example_queries.sql: SELECT fn, sum(cpu_ns) AS cpu_ns FROM (SELECT frame[1].function AS fn, value[2] AS cpu_ns FROM pprof.main.stacks(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL UNION ALL SELECT frame[1].function, value[2] FROM pprof.main.stacks(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL) GROUP BY fn ORDER BY cpu_ns DESC, fn LIMIT 20

example_queries.description: A heap profile's sample value types, sampling period, and duration.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_types, period, duration_nanos FROM pprof.main.meta(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL

example_queries.description: Mappings that carry a build id (the binaries still to symbolize).
example_queries.sql: SELECT mapping_id, filename, build_id FROM pprof.main.mappings(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL AND build_id IS NOT NULL

example_queries.description: Total a heap profile's default sample type (inuse_space) per leaf function, finding the value slot by name from pprof.main.meta instead of hard-coding value[N], so the same query works unchanged on a CPU profile (where it totals cpu).
example_queries.sql: WITH m AS (SELECT default_sample_type AS sample_type, list_position([t.type FOR t IN sample_types], default_sample_type) AS slot FROM pprof.main.meta(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL) SELECT m.sample_type, s.frame[1].function AS fn, sum(s.value[m.slot]) AS total FROM pprof.main.stacks(from_base64('')) s, m WHERE s.error IS NULL GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY total DESC, fn

example_queries.description: Hottest unsymbolized leaf addresses as symbolizer-ready (binary, build_id, offset in the binary) rows, weighted by CPU time: each sample's leaf location id is joined to pprof.main.locations and on to pprof.main.mappings.
example_queries.sql: SELECT m.filename AS binary_path, m.build_id, printf('0x%x', l.address - m.memory_start + m.file_offset) AS binary_offset, sum(s.value[2]) AS cpu_ns FROM pprof.main.samples(from_base64('')) s JOIN pprof.main.locations(from_base64('')) l ON l.location_id = s.location_ids[1] JOIN pprof.main.mappings(from_base64('')) m ON m.mapping_id = l.mapping_id WHERE s.error IS NULL GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY cpu_ns DESC, binary_offset

example_queries.description: Show what the compiler inlined: for every location whose line table has more than one entry, name each function folded into that address (depth 1 = innermost) by joining the line table to pprof.main.functions.
example_queries.sql: WITH l AS (SELECT location_id, address, unnest(lines) AS ln, generate_subscripts(lines, 1) AS depth FROM pprof.main.locations(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL AND len(lines) > 1) SELECT l.location_id, l.address, l.depth, f.name AS function_name, f.filename, l.ln.line AS line FROM l JOIN pprof.main.functions(from_base64('')) f ON f.function_id = l.ln.function_id ORDER BY l.location_id, l.depth

example_queries.description: Look up which value slot holds CPU time for a Go CPU profile (and in what unit).
example_queries.sql: SELECT value_index, sample_type, unit FROM pprof.main.sample_type_guide WHERE producer = 'Go' AND profile_kind = 'cpu' ORDER BY value_index

example_queries.description: Raw samples with their leaf location id.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, location_ids[1] AS leaf_loc, value FROM pprof.main.samples(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL;

example_queries.description: Inspect the per-sample labels (e.g. a heap profile's size_class tag) carried alongside the values.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, labels, value FROM pprof.main.samples(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL LIMIT 5;

example_queries.description: Inspect a heap profile's sample value types and duration, from a profile passed inline as BLOB bytes.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_types, period, duration_nanos, default_sample_type FROM pprof.main.meta(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL;

example_queries.description: The sample types and duration of a profile.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_types, duration_nanos, default_sample_type FROM pprof.main.meta(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL;

example_queries.description: The sampling period and what it counts (read this to convert raw counts to time), plus the wall-clock duration covered.
example_queries.sql: SELECT period, period_type, duration_nanos FROM pprof.main.meta(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL;

example_queries.description: Every loaded binary/segment in a profile with its address range (memory_start .. memory_limit).
example_queries.sql: SELECT mapping_id, filename, memory_start, memory_limit FROM pprof.main.mappings(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL ORDER BY mapping_id;

example_queries.description: Locations with their line table (inlined frames).
example_queries.sql: SELECT location_id, address, mapping_id, lines FROM pprof.main.locations(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL ORDER BY location_id;

example_queries.description: Locations with their line table (inlined frames).
example_queries.sql: SELECT location_id, address, mapping_id, lines FROM pprof.main.locations(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL ORDER BY location_id LIMIT 10;

example_queries.description: The most heavily inlined locations (longest line table = deepest inlining the compiler folded into one address).
example_queries.sql: SELECT location_id, address, len(lines) AS inline_depth FROM pprof.main.locations(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL ORDER BY inline_depth DESC, location_id LIMIT 5;

example_queries.description: List the functions defined in a profile.
example_queries.sql: SELECT function_id, name, filename, start_line FROM pprof.main.functions(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL ORDER BY function_id;

example_queries.description: List the functions in a profile.
example_queries.sql: SELECT function_id, name, filename, start_line FROM pprof.main.functions(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL ORDER BY function_id LIMIT 10;

example_queries.description: Which source files contribute the most symbols (functions) to a profile.
example_queries.sql: SELECT filename, count(*) AS fns FROM pprof.main.functions(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL GROUP BY filename ORDER BY fns DESC, filename LIMIT 5;

example_queries.description: Flatten a profile passed inline as BLOB bytes (self-contained): each sample's leaf frame and per-type values.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, frame[1].function AS leaf, value FROM pprof.main.stacks(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL;

example_queries.description: Top self-time functions in a CPU profile (value[2] = cpu/nanoseconds).
example_queries.sql: SELECT frame[1].function AS fn, sum(value[2]) AS cpu_ns FROM pprof.main.stacks(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 20;

agent_tasks: The file data/go_cpu.pb.gz is a Go CPU profile. Which leaf function has the most total CPU time? CPU nanoseconds is the second sample value. Return one row with a column named fn and a column named cpu_ns.
data/go_heap.pb.gz is a Go heap profile. How many distinct sample value types does it carry? Return one row with a single column named n.
data/native.pb.gz is an unsymbolized native profile. List the build ids of its mappings that have one, so they can be symbolized. Return a column named build_id.

Compare two CPU profiles data/go_cpu.pb.gz (baseline) and data/go_cpu2.pb.gz (candidate): for the busiest leaf function in the candidate, return its name and the CPU-nanosecond delta (candidate minus baseline). Return columns fn and delta.
data/go_cpu.pb.gz is a Go CPU profile. How many samples (recorded stack traces) does it contain? Return one row with a single column named n.
How many rows does the function table of data/go_cpu.pb.gz have (the number of distinct symbolized functions in the profile)? Return one row with a single column named n.

In data/go_cpu.pb.gz, across all locations, what is the greatest number of line-table entries on any single location (the deepest inlining the compiler folded into one instruction address)? Return one row with a single column named max_inline.

Using the worker's built-in reference guide of pprof sample value types, which value index carries CPU time measured in nanoseconds for a Go 'cpu' profile? Return one row with a single column named value_index.

data/native.pb.gz is an unsymbolized native CPU profile (value[2] is CPU nanoseconds). For each loaded binary, identified by its mapping's build id, how much CPU time was spent with that binary anywhere on the stack (inclusive time: count each sample at most once per binary, even if several of its frames fall in the same binary)? Return one row per build id with columns build_id (VARCHAR) and cpu_ns (the summed nanoseconds).

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Decode a pprof profile into SQL rows. The headline is a flattened, flamegraph-ready view — one row per sample with its per-type values (a list of BIGINTs aligned to the profile's sample value types), its labels as a `MAP`, and its call stack pre-resolved leaf-first as frame structs — so a flamegraph diff is a GROUP BY over frames with a SUM and no join. The underlying protobuf graph is also exposed for ad-hoc joins with the profile's original ids passed through verbatim, alongside a one-row summary of the sample value types, sampling period, and duration. The profile source is a path, a glob, a list of paths, or inline bytes; a bad file becomes one error row rather than aborting the scan.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## pprof · main

The single schema for the `pprof` worker — the catalog name matches the `ATTACH` name, so calls qualify as `pprof.main.<fn>(...)`.

It decodes a pprof profile into SQL rows across three groups: a flattened, flamegraph-ready view of samples with their call stacks pre-resolved (the headline), the raw `profile.proto` graph for ad-hoc joins, and a one-row profile summary of the sample value types, sampling period, and duration.

Every table takes the same overloaded profile source — a path, a glob, a list of paths, or inline bytes — and appends `file` and `error` columns for per-file provenance and error capture, so a bad file in a glob becomes one error row instead of aborting the scan.

vgi.example_queries.description: Top self-time functions summed across two CPU profiles (a baseline and a candidate run, passed inline as BLOBs; with profiles on disk, pass a path glob or a list of paths).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT fn, sum(cpu_ns) AS cpu_ns FROM (SELECT frame[1].function AS fn, value[2] AS cpu_ns FROM pprof.main.stacks(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL UNION ALL SELECT frame[1].function, value[2] FROM pprof.main.stacks(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL) GROUP BY fn ORDER BY cpu_ns DESC, fn LIMIT 20

vgi.example_queries.description: A heap profile's sample value types, sampling period, and duration.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_types, period, duration_nanos FROM pprof.main.meta(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL

vgi.example_queries.description: Mappings that carry a build id (the binaries still to symbolize).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT mapping_id, filename, build_id FROM pprof.main.mappings(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL AND build_id IS NOT NULL

vgi.example_queries.description: Total a heap profile's default sample type (inuse_space) per leaf function, finding the value slot by name from pprof.main.meta instead of hard-coding value[N], so the same query works unchanged on a CPU profile (where it totals cpu).
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH m AS (SELECT default_sample_type AS sample_type, list_position([t.type FOR t IN sample_types], default_sample_type) AS slot FROM pprof.main.meta(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL) SELECT m.sample_type, s.frame[1].function AS fn, sum(s.value[m.slot]) AS total FROM pprof.main.stacks(from_base64('')) s, m WHERE s.error IS NULL GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY total DESC, fn

vgi.example_queries.description: Hottest unsymbolized leaf addresses as symbolizer-ready (binary, build_id, offset in the binary) rows, weighted by CPU time: each sample's leaf location id is joined to pprof.main.locations and on to pprof.main.mappings.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT m.filename AS binary_path, m.build_id, printf('0x%x', l.address - m.memory_start + m.file_offset) AS binary_offset, sum(s.value[2]) AS cpu_ns FROM pprof.main.samples(from_base64('')) s JOIN pprof.main.locations(from_base64('')) l ON l.location_id = s.location_ids[1] JOIN pprof.main.mappings(from_base64('')) m ON m.mapping_id = l.mapping_id WHERE s.error IS NULL GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY cpu_ns DESC, binary_offset

vgi.example_queries.description: Show what the compiler inlined: for every location whose line table has more than one entry, name each function folded into that address (depth 1 = innermost) by joining the line table to pprof.main.functions.
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH l AS (SELECT location_id, address, unnest(lines) AS ln, generate_subscripts(lines, 1) AS depth FROM pprof.main.locations(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL AND len(lines) > 1) SELECT l.location_id, l.address, l.depth, f.name AS function_name, f.filename, l.ln.line AS line FROM l JOIN pprof.main.functions(from_base64('')) f ON f.function_id = l.ln.function_id ORDER BY l.location_id, l.depth

tables.name: sample_type_guide
tables.comment: Reference table of common pprof sample value-type conventions: which sample_type and unit each value[N] slot carries per (producer, profile_kind). VALUES-backed, so it scans with no file or credential.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A browsable reference table mapping common pprof `(producer, profile_kind, value_index)` conventions to the `sample_type` and `unit` that each `value[N]` slot carries — e.g. for a Go 'cpu' profile value[1] is samples/count and value[2] is cpu/nanoseconds. Read it to know which `value` index to sum in pprof.stacks / pprof.samples without decoding a file first; the authoritative per-profile answer is pprof.meta(src).sample_types. Backed by a VALUES list, so it scans with no file, network, or credential.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Reference table of common pprof sample value-type conventions: `producer`, `profile_kind`, `value_index`, `sample_type`, `unit`, `meaning`. Tells you which `value[N]` slot to read (e.g. Go CPU time is value[2], nanoseconds).

vgi.example_queries.description: Look up which value slot holds CPU time for a Go CPU profile (and in what unit).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT value_index, sample_type, unit FROM pprof.main.sample_type_guide WHERE producer = 'Go' AND profile_kind = 'cpu' ORDER BY value_index

arguments.description: Where to read the pprof profile(s) to decode. Pass a filesystem path to one gzip-wrapped or raw `profile.proto` file; a path containing glob wildcards such as '/profiles/*.pb.gz' expands to every match in sorted order. A LIST value is read as several such paths scanned together; a BLOB value is read as inline profile bytes. Each file is decoded on its own so that a profile which is absent or fails to decode becomes a single error row (data columns NULL, `file` and `error` set) instead of failing the scan.

examples: SELECT location_id, address, mapping_id, lines FROM pprof.main.locations(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL ORDER BY location_id;

WITH l AS (SELECT location_id, address, unnest(lines) AS ln, generate_subscripts(lines, 1) AS depth FROM pprof.main.locations(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL AND len(lines) > 1) SELECT l.location_id, l.address, l.depth, f.name AS function_name, f.filename, l.ln.line AS line FROM l JOIN pprof.main.functions(from_base64('')) f ON f.function_id = l.ln.function_id ORDER BY l.location_id, l.depth

SELECT location_id, address, mapping_id, lines FROM pprof.main.locations(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL ORDER BY location_id LIMIT 10;

SELECT location_id, address, len(lines) AS inline_depth FROM pprof.main.locations(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL ORDER BY inline_depth DESC, location_id LIMIT 5;

WITH l AS (SELECT location_id, address, unnest(lines) AS ln, generate_subscripts(lines, 1) AS depth FROM pprof.main.locations(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL AND len(lines) > 1) SELECT l.location_id, l.address, l.depth, f.name AS function_name, f.filename, l.ln.line AS line FROM l JOIN pprof.main.functions(from_base64('')) f ON f.function_id = l.ln.function_id ORDER BY l.location_id, l.depth;

result_columns.name: location_id
result_columns.description: The location's unique id within the profile (verbatim); referenced by pprof.samples.location_ids.

result_columns.name: address
result_columns.description: Instruction address for this location (0 if unavailable); within its mapping's memory range.

result_columns.name: mapping_id
result_columns.description: Id of the pprof.mappings row this location belongs to (0 if unknown).

result_columns.name: lines
result_columns.description: The line table, innermost inlined frame first; function_id joins to pprof.functions.function_id. Empty for an unsymbolized location.

result_columns.name: file
result_columns.description: Source path the row came from (NULL when the profile was passed as inline BLOB bytes).

result_columns.name: error
result_columns.description: NULL on success; otherwise this is an error row for a file that could not be read or decoded, with every data column NULL and the failure message here.

functions.name: stacks
functions.comment: Flatten a pprof profile into flamegraph-ready stack rows

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Flatten a pprof profile into one row per sample with the call stack pre-resolved: `value` is a `LIST(BIGINT)` aligned to meta.sample_types, `labels` is a `MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)`, and `frame` is a `LIST(STRUCT(function, filename, line, address))` ordered leaf-first (inlined frames expanded, unsymbolized frames keep their address). This is the 90% view: a flamegraph diff across many profiles is a GROUP BY frame … SUM(value) with no manual location/function join. `src` may be a file path, a glob, a list of paths, or inline `BLOB` bytes; a bad file yields one error row.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Flatten a pprof profile into flamegraph-ready rows: `sample_id`, `value` (a `LIST(BIGINT)` aligned to the sample types), `labels` (a `MAP`), and `frame` (a `LIST(STRUCT(function, filename, line, address))`, leaf first). Use it to diff profiles in SQL.

vgi.example_queries.description: Flatten a profile passed inline as BLOB bytes (self-contained): each sample's leaf frame and per-type values.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, frame[1].function AS leaf, value FROM pprof.main.stacks(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL;

vgi.example_queries.description: Top self-time functions in a CPU profile (value[2] = cpu/nanoseconds).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT frame[1].function AS fn, sum(value[2]) AS cpu_ns FROM pprof.main.stacks(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 20;

vgi.example_queries.description: Total a heap profile's default sample type (inuse_space) per leaf function, finding the value slot by name from pprof.main.meta instead of hard-coding value[N], so the same query works unchanged on a CPU profile (where it totals cpu).
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH m AS (SELECT default_sample_type AS sample_type, list_position([t.type FOR t IN sample_types], default_sample_type) AS slot FROM pprof.main.meta(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL) SELECT m.sample_type, s.frame[1].function AS fn, sum(s.value[m.slot]) AS total FROM pprof.main.stacks(from_base64('')) s, m WHERE s.error IS NULL GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY total DESC, fn

vgi.executable_examples.description: Top self-time functions summed across two CPU profiles (a baseline and a candidate run, passed inline as BLOBs; with profiles on disk, pass a path glob or a list of paths).
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT fn, sum(cpu_ns) AS cpu_ns FROM (SELECT frame[1].function AS fn, value[2] AS cpu_ns FROM pprof.main.stacks(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL UNION ALL SELECT frame[1].function, value[2] FROM pprof.main.stacks(from_base64('')) WHERE error IS NULL) GROUP BY fn ORDER BY cpu_ns DESC, fn LIMIT 20
