workers.title: Prefect Orchestration
workers.tagline: Prefect 3 flows, flow runs, task runs, deployments and logs as SQL in DuckDB (Python)
workers.subtitle: Prefect 3 flows, runs, logs, deployments, work pools and events as SQL tables
workers.summary: Prefect 3's REST API, from Prefect Cloud or a self-hosted server, as read-only SQL tables for auditing flows, runs, logs, infrastructure and events, plus cross-orchestrator unified runs.
workers.doc_md:
# Prefect

Audit a Prefect 3 workspace with SQL: failed and late runs, what they logged, which work pools and workers pick them up, and what the event feed recorded. Works with Prefect Cloud and self-hosted Prefect servers, and is read-only.

Credentials come from a DuckDB secret of type `prefect`, created **after** `ATTACH`:

```sql
-- Prefect Cloud: the workspace's API URL and an API key
CREATE SECRET pf (TYPE prefect,
  API_URL 'https://api.prefect.cloud/api/accounts/<account_id>/workspaces/<workspace_id>',
  API_KEY 'pnu_...');
-- Self-hosted Prefect server (AUTH_STRING only if the server sets PREFECT_SERVER_API_AUTH_STRING)
CREATE SECRET pf (TYPE prefect, API_URL 'http://localhost:4200/api', AUTH_STRING 'admin:...');
```

Filters on names, ids, states, tags and time ranges become Prefect's own `POST /…/filter` bodies, so a query for one flow's failed runs last week reads only those runs. The `unified` schema lines Prefect up with the other Query.Farm orchestrator workers for cross-tool reporting.
workers.readme_sql:
-- Which flows failed or crashed this month, and how long did those runs take?
SELECT flow_name, count(*) AS failures, round(avg(total_run_time), 1) AS avg_s
FROM prefect.main.flow_runs
WHERE state_type IN ('FAILED', 'CRASHED') AND start_time >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01'
GROUP BY flow_name ORDER BY failures DESC;

example_queries.description: Failed or crashed runs of one flow in November 2026 (flow, state types and the range reach the API)
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, state_name, start_time, state_message FROM prefect.main.flow_runs WHERE flow_name = 'broken-import' AND state_type IN ('FAILED', 'CRASHED') AND start_time >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01' ORDER BY start_time

example_queries.description: Task runs that needed a retry
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, run_count, max_retries, state_name FROM prefect.main.task_runs WHERE run_count > 1 ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Deployments per work pool and whether they are paused
example_queries.sql: SELECT work_pool_name, flow_name, name, paused, status FROM prefect.main.deployments ORDER BY work_pool_name, flow_name, name

example_queries.description: Flow-run state changes in a window (occurred and the prefix reach the API)
example_queries.sql: SELECT event, count(*) AS n FROM prefect.main.events WHERE starts_with(event, 'prefect.flow-run.') AND occurred >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-15' AND occurred < TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-16' GROUP BY event ORDER BY n DESC

example_queries.description: Error lines logged by flow runs (level is sent to the API)
example_queries.sql: SELECT flow_run_id, timestamp, message FROM prefect.main.flow_run_logs WHERE level_name = 'error' ORDER BY timestamp

example_queries.description: Non-secret variable values
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, value FROM prefect.main.variable_values(reveal := true) WHERE NOT is_masked ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Variable names, types and tags (values masked)
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, value_type, tags FROM prefect.main.variables ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Named blocks per type (values are never read)
example_queries.sql: SELECT block_type_slug, list(name ORDER BY name) AS blocks FROM prefect.main.block_documents GROUP BY block_type_slug ORDER BY block_type_slug

example_queries.description: Enabled automations and the events they expect
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, trigger_type, trigger_definition->>'$.posture' AS posture, trigger_definition->'$.expect' AS expects FROM prefect.main.automations WHERE enabled ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Concurrency limits and their slot usage
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, kind, "limit", active_slots FROM prefect.main.concurrency_limits ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Flows with a given tag
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, created FROM prefect.main.flows WHERE list_contains(tags, 'etl') ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Flow-run outcomes per flow
example_queries.sql: SELECT f.name, r.state_type, count(*) AS runs FROM prefect.main.flows f JOIN prefect.main.flow_runs r ON r.flow_id = f.id GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY f.name, r.state_type

example_queries.description: Workers and their last heartbeat
example_queries.sql: SELECT work_pool_name, name, status, last_heartbeat_time FROM prefect.main.workers ORDER BY work_pool_name, name

example_queries.description: Work pools by type and status
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, type, status, is_paused FROM prefect.main.work_pools ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Why each failed task run failed
example_queries.sql: SELECT t.name, l.timestamp, l.message FROM prefect.main.task_runs t JOIN prefect.main.task_run_logs l ON l.task_run_id = t.id WHERE l.level >= 40 ORDER BY l.timestamp

example_queries.description: Block types by slug
example_queries.sql: SELECT slug, name FROM prefect.main.block_types WHERE NOT is_protected ORDER BY slug LIMIT 20

example_queries.description: Slowest completed tasks
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, total_run_time FROM prefect.main.task_runs WHERE state_type = 'COMPLETED' ORDER BY total_run_time DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Latest rows of a table artifact
example_queries.sql: SELECT created, data FROM prefect.main.artifacts WHERE key = 'orders-summary' ORDER BY created DESC LIMIT 1

example_queries.description: Run count and median run time per flow and state
example_queries.sql: SELECT flow_name, state_type, count(*) AS runs, median(total_run_time) AS median_s FROM prefect.main.flow_runs GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY flow_name, state_type

example_queries.description: Queues per pool in priority order
example_queries.sql: SELECT work_pool_name, name, priority, status, last_polled FROM prefect.main.work_queues ORDER BY work_pool_name, priority

example_queries.description: Active cron schedules with their deployment
example_queries.sql: SELECT deployment_name, cron, timezone FROM prefect.main.deployment_schedules WHERE active AND cron IS NOT NULL ORDER BY deployment_name

example_queries.description: Runs per status
example_queries.sql: SELECT status, count(*) AS runs FROM prefect.unified.runs GROUP BY status ORDER BY status

example_queries.description: Task outcomes joined to their runs
example_queries.sql: SELECT r.pipeline, t.status, count(*) AS tasks FROM prefect.unified.task_runs t JOIN prefect.unified.runs r USING (run_id) GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY r.pipeline, t.status

example_queries.description: Task runs per unified status
example_queries.sql: SELECT prefect.unified.unified_status(state_type) AS status, count(*) AS task_runs FROM prefect.main.task_runs GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY status

example_queries.description: Failure rate per pipeline since November
example_queries.sql: SELECT pipeline, avg((status = 'failed')::INT) AS failure_rate FROM prefect.unified.runs WHERE started_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01' GROUP BY pipeline ORDER BY failure_rate DESC

example_queries.description: Normalize every Prefect state type
example_queries.sql: SELECT s AS state_type, prefect.unified.unified_status(s) AS status FROM (VALUES ('COMPLETED'), ('CRASHED'), ('CANCELLING'), ('SCHEDULED'), ('cancelled')) t(s) ORDER BY s;

example_queries.description: A missing state counts as queued
example_queries.sql: SELECT prefect.unified.unified_status(NULL::VARCHAR) AS status;

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Prefect's native resources, one table per REST collection, with Prefect's own ids and column names so results line up with the Prefect UI and API. Resources form a hierarchy: a flow has deployments (with schedules) and flow runs, a flow run has task runs, and both levels emit log lines and artifacts; work pools own queues and workers. Each table's description lists its join keys and the predicates it pushes down. state_type is Prefect's upper-case StateType and state_name its display name (Late, AwaitingRetry, ...). Pushdown covers equality and IN on ids and names, state filters, list_contains(tags, 'x') and timestamp ranges; anything else is filtered locally after the API returns, so narrow by flow, state and time first. Configuration objects are exposed without their secrets: variable values are masked unless a non-secret value is explicitly revealed, and block documents carry names and types only.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

Prefect's REST resources as tables, in Prefect's own vocabulary. A flow has deployments and flow runs, a flow run has task runs, and both emit logs and artifacts.

Filter by flow, state and a time range wherever you can: those predicates become Prefect filter bodies, so the worker reads only the matching runs instead of the whole history. Each table's own description lists its join keys and pushed-down columns.

Secrets stay in Prefect. Variable values are masked unless you ask for non-secret ones, and block documents are listed by name and type only.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Cross-orchestrator tables with columns identical across the Airflow, Dagster, Prefect, Temporal, Databricks, dbt and GitHub workers, for UNION ALL. runs(orchestrator, run_id, pipeline, status, raw_status, trigger, queued_at, started_at, ended_at, duration_seconds, url) and task_runs(orchestrator, run_id, task_run_id, task_name, status, raw_status, attempt, started_at, ended_at, duration_seconds, url). status is one of queued, running, success, failed, cancelled, skipped, derived from Prefect's state type (CRASHED counts as failed; SCHEDULED and PENDING as queued; PAUSED and CANCELLING as running). raw_status is the state name. runs.run_id is the flow-run id and pipeline the flow name; task_runs.run_id joins runs.run_id. Filters on run_id, pipeline, status, raw_status and started_at/ended_at ranges are pushed to the API.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## unified

Flow runs and task runs in the shape every Query.Farm orchestrator worker shares, so you can `UNION ALL` Prefect with Airflow, Dagster, Temporal and others.

`status` comes from Prefect's state type (a crashed run counts as `failed`); `raw_status` keeps the state name such as `Late` or `AwaitingRetry`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Runs per status
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT status, count(*) AS runs FROM prefect.unified.runs GROUP BY status ORDER BY status

vgi.example_queries.description: Task outcomes joined to their runs
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT r.pipeline, t.status, count(*) AS tasks FROM prefect.unified.task_runs t JOIN prefect.unified.runs r USING (run_id) GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY r.pipeline, t.status

vgi.example_queries.description: Task runs per unified status
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT prefect.unified.unified_status(state_type) AS status, count(*) AS task_runs FROM prefect.main.task_runs GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY status

tags.vgi.doc_llm: unified_status(state_type) maps a Prefect StateType to the shared orchestrator vocabulary used by the unified schema: COMPLETED→success, FAILED and CRASHED→failed, CANCELLED→cancelled, RUNNING, PAUSED and CANCELLING→running, SCHEDULED and PENDING→queued. workers.title: PROJ transforms
workers.tagline: CRS transforms & geodesic distance for DuckDB (Python, pyproj/PROJ)
workers.subtitle: Reproject coordinates between CRSs and measure geodesic distances on the WGS84 ellipsoid.
workers.summary: CRS transforms (always_xy) + WGS84 geodesic distance/bearing via pyproj/PROJ.
workers.doc_md:
# Coordinate Reference System Transforms & Geodesic Distance in SQL

![PROJ logo](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OSGeo/PROJ/master/docs/images/logo.png)

**Reproject coordinates between any two CRSs and measure accurate ellipsoidal distance and bearing directly in DuckDB SQL** -- EPSG transforms, UTM and Web Mercator projection, and WGS84 geodesic geometry, powered by [PROJ](https://proj.org/) through [pyproj](https://pyproj4.github.io/pyproj/stable/).

The `proj` extension brings industry-standard geospatial coordinate math into your queries, so you never have to export points to a GIS tool or a Python notebook just to change projection or compute a great-circle distance. It is built for analysts, data engineers, and mapping developers who work with longitude/latitude points, EPSG-coded geometries, tile coordinates, or survey data and need correct, repeatable coordinate transformations next to the rest of their SQL. Every transformation is identified by a standard EPSG code or CRS string (for example `EPSG:4326` for WGS84 longitude/latitude and `EPSG:3857` for Web Mercator), so results match what PostGIS, QGIS, and other PROJ-based tools produce.

Under the hood the extension calls [pyproj](https://github.com/pyproj4/pyproj), the Python binding for the [PROJ](https://github.com/OSGeo/PROJ) C library that is the de-facto standard for cartographic projections and datum transformations. The pyproj binary wheel bundles PROJ together with its data grids, so there is no separate native install and no external services or API keys -- the worker is fully offline and hermetic. Building a PROJ transformer is comparatively expensive, so transformers are cached and the common WGS84 <-> Web Mercator pipelines are warmed at startup, keeping per-row transforms fast. All coordinate input and output uses `always_xy` axis order `(x/easting/longitude, y/northing/latitude)` regardless of a CRS's declared native axis order, eliminating the classic lon/lat swap.

## Capabilities

The worker's functions fall into a few capability areas: general CRS-to-CRS reprojection identified by EPSG code; convenience conversions to and from the Web Mercator tile projection and into a point's automatically selected UTM zone; accurate WGS84-ellipsoid geodesic distance and initial bearing between two longitude/latitude points; and lookups of a CRS's human-readable name and axis units alongside the bundled PROJ library version. Reprojection results come back as typed `STRUCT` coordinates, while the geodesic and metadata functions return plain metres, degrees, or strings. Because every CRS is named by its standard EPSG code and all transforms share the same `always_xy` axis convention, results line up with what PostGIS, QGIS, and other PROJ-based tools produce.

NULL or non-finite (and, where applicable, out-of-range) coordinates yield NULL, while an unknown CRS raises a clear query error.
workers.readme_sql:
INSTALL vgi FROM community; LOAD vgi;
ATTACH 'proj' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'uvx --from git+https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-proj@v0.4.1 vgi-proj-worker');

SELECT proj.transform(-122.42, 37.77, 'EPSG:4326', 'EPSG:3857'); -- STRUCT(x, y)
SELECT proj.to_webmercator(-122.4194, 37.7749);                  -- STRUCT(x, y) metres
SELECT proj.from_webmercator(-13627665, 4547675);                -- STRUCT(lon, lat)
SELECT proj.to_utm(-122.42, 37.77);                              -- STRUCT(easting, northing, zone, hemisphere, epsg)
SELECT proj.to_utm(-122.42, 37.77).zone;                         -- 10
SELECT proj.geodesic_distance(-74.006, 40.7128, -0.1276, 51.5074); -- ~5,585,000 m (NYC -> London)
SELECT proj.geodesic_bearing(-74.006, 40.7128, -0.1276, 51.5074);  -- ~51 deg
SELECT proj.crs_name('EPSG:4326');                               -- 'WGS 84'
SELECT proj.crs_units('EPSG:3857');                              -- 'metre'

example_queries.description: Reproject British National Grid (EPSG:27700) easting/northing sites to WGS84 lon/lat and rank them by geodesic distance from the London Eye (Cardiff Castle 212.6 km, York Minster 281.5 km, Edinburgh Castle 535.0 km).
example_queries.sql: WITH eye AS (SELECT proj.main.transform(530600.0, 179700.0, 'EPSG:27700', 'EPSG:4326') AS o), sites(site, easting, northing) AS (VALUES ('Edinburgh Castle', 325160.0, 673490.0), ('Cardiff Castle', 318080.0, 176540.0), ('York Minster', 460350.0, 452230.0)), ll AS (SELECT site, proj.main.transform(easting, northing, 'EPSG:27700', 'EPSG:4326') AS p FROM sites) SELECT site, round(p.x, 4) AS lon, round(p.y, 4) AS lat, round(proj.main.geodesic_distance(o.x, o.y, p.x, p.y) / 1000, 1) AS km_from_london_eye FROM ll CROSS JOIN eye ORDER BY km_from_london_eye

example_queries.description: Check straight-line UTM grid distances against the true WGS84 geodesic distance for three San Francisco survey segments (all in UTM zone 10): the grid figure runs 2.4-3.0 m short over these 6.6-7.9 km segments because of UTM's scale factor near the central meridian.
example_queries.sql: WITH segments(segment, lon1, lat1, lon2, lat2) AS (VALUES ('Ferry Building -> Golden Gate Bridge', -122.3937, 37.7955, -122.4783, 37.8199), ('Ferry Building -> Twin Peaks', -122.3937, 37.7955, -122.4477, 37.7544), ('Twin Peaks -> Golden Gate Bridge', -122.4477, 37.7544, -122.4783, 37.8199)), u AS (SELECT segment, lon1, lat1, lon2, lat2, proj.main.to_utm(lon1, lat1) AS a, proj.main.to_utm(lon2, lat2) AS b FROM segments) SELECT segment, a.zone AS utm_zone, round(sqrt(power(b.easting - a.easting, 2) + power(b.northing - a.northing, 2)), 1) AS utm_grid_m, round(proj.main.geodesic_distance(lon1, lat1, lon2, lat2), 1) AS geodesic_m FROM u ORDER BY segment

example_queries.description: Measure the true ground length of segments stored in Web Mercator (EPSG:3857) metres by converting their endpoints back to lon/lat: the same 5,000 Mercator metres is ~5,000 m near the equator (Quito) but only ~2,513 m at Oslo (lat 59.9).
example_queries.sql: WITH segments(segment, x1, y1, x2, y2) AS (VALUES ('Quito, 5 km east', -8738000.0, -24600.0, -8733000.0, -24600.0), ('Oslo, 5 km east', 1194000.0, 8381000.0, 1199000.0, 8381000.0)), ll AS (SELECT segment, x1, y1, x2, y2, proj.main.from_webmercator(x1, y1) AS a, proj.main.from_webmercator(x2, y2) AS b FROM segments) SELECT segment, round(a.lat, 2) AS lat, round(sqrt(power(x2 - x1, 2) + power(y2 - y1, 2))) AS mercator_m, round(proj.main.geodesic_distance(a.lon, a.lat, b.lon, b.lat)) AS geodesic_m FROM ll ORDER BY segment

example_queries.description: Distance (km) and initial compass bearing (degrees) from New York to five world cities, nearest first (London 5,585 km at 51 deg ... Sydney 15,988 km at 266 deg).
example_queries.sql: WITH destinations(city, lon, lat) AS (VALUES ('London', -0.1276, 51.5074), ('Paris', 2.3522, 48.8566), ('Tokyo', 139.6917, 35.6895), ('Sydney', 151.2093, -33.8688), ('Sao Paulo', -46.6333, -23.5505)) SELECT city, round(proj.main.geodesic_distance(-74.006, 40.7128, lon, lat) / 1000) AS distance_km, round(proj.main.geodesic_bearing(-74.006, 40.7128, lon, lat)) AS initial_bearing_deg FROM destinations ORDER BY distance_km

tags.vgi.doc_md:
# main

Coordinate-reference-system (CRS) transform and WGS84 geodesic functions, served over Apache Arrow and backed by pyproj/PROJ (PROJ and its data grids are bundled in the pyproj wheel, so there is no separate native install).

## Capabilities

Reproject coordinates between CRSs identified by EPSG code -- including shorthands for the Web Mercator tile projection and a point's auto-selected UTM zone -- returning typed `STRUCT` outputs. Measure accurate ellipsoidal (WGS84) geodesic distance in metres and initial bearing in degrees between two longitude/latitude points. Look up CRS metadata such as a system's display name and axis units to confirm a code resolves to the CRS you expect before interpreting its coordinates.

## Conventions

All coordinate I/O uses `always_xy` axis order `(x/easting/longitude, y/northing/latitude)` regardless of the CRS's declared native axis order. NULL/non-finite (and, where applicable, out-of-range) coordinates yield NULL; an unknown CRS raises a clear query error.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# to_utm

Project a WGS84 `(lon, lat)` point into its **auto-selected** Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) zone, returning the easting/northing in metres plus the chosen zone and hemisphere.

**When to use:** when you want a locally-accurate metric coordinate for a point without picking the zone yourself -- ideal for measuring distances or areas in metres near a single location.

**Inputs:** `lon` (-180..180 degrees), `lat` (-90..90 degrees).

**Output:** `STRUCT(easting DOUBLE, northing DOUBLE, zone INT32, hemisphere VARCHAR, epsg INT32)`; `hemisphere` is `'N'` or `'S'`, and `epsg` is the target UTM CRS's EPSG code (`326xx` north / `327xx` south) which you can use as a constant `transform` CRS (e.g. `'EPSG:32610'`; `transform`'s CRS arguments must be constants, so it cannot be passed per row). The zone is derived from the longitude (`floor(lon/6)+31`).

**Edge cases:** NULL, non-finite, or out-of-range (`|lat| > 90` / `|lon| > 180`) coordinates yield a NULL struct.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## to_utm(lon, lat)

Project WGS84 lon/lat into the point's automatically-selected UTM zone.

### Usage

```sql
SELECT proj.to_utm(-122.42, 37.77);        -- full struct
SELECT proj.to_utm(-122.42, 37.77).zone;   -- 10
```

It can also be applied per row over a lon/lat column, reading `.easting`, `.northing`, `.zone`, `.hemisphere`, or `.epsg` off the returned struct.

### Notes

- Returns `STRUCT(easting, northing, zone, hemisphere, epsg)` with metres for easting/northing.
- The zone is chosen from the longitude; the hemisphere is `'N'`/`'S'`.
- `epsg` is the target UTM CRS code (`326xx`/`327xx`) — use it as a constant `transform` CRS (e.g. `'EPSG:32610'`) to reproject in or out of that zone; `transform`'s CRS arguments must be constants, not per-row columns.
- Out-of-range or NULL coordinates produce a NULL struct.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# geodesic_bearing

Compute the **initial geodesic bearing** (forward azimuth) in degrees from point 1 toward point 2 on the WGS84 ellipsoid, normalized to `[0, 360)` where 0 = north, 90 = east.

**When to use:** to find the compass direction to travel from one location to another along the shortest path -- navigation, heading indicators, directional filters.

**Inputs:** `lon1, lat1` (origin) and `lon2, lat2` (destination) in degrees.

**Output:** initial forward azimuth in degrees, `[0, 360)` (`DOUBLE`).

**Edge cases:** NULL/non-finite or out-of-range coordinates yield NULL. It is the *initial* bearing -- along a geodesic the bearing changes continuously, so the arrival bearing differs from this value.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## geodesic_bearing(lon1, lat1, lon2, lat2)

Initial forward azimuth (compass heading) in degrees `[0, 360)` from point 1 toward point 2 on the WGS84 ellipsoid.

### Usage

```sql
SELECT proj.geodesic_bearing(-74.006, 40.7128, -0.1276, 51.5074);
```

It can also be applied per row over origin/destination columns to derive a heading for each leg of a route.

### Notes

- 0 deg = north, 90 deg = east; result is normalized to `[0, 360)`.
- This is the *initial* bearing; along a geodesic it changes en route.
- NULL, non-finite, or out-of-range coordinates yield NULL.

functions.comment: Accurate ellipsoidal (WGS84) geodesic distance between two points, in metres

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# geodesic_distance

Compute the **accurate ellipsoidal (WGS84) geodesic distance** in metres between two `(lon, lat)` points. Unlike a spherical haversine, this uses the WGS84 ellipsoid (via PROJ's `Geod`), so it is correct to the metre over global distances.

**When to use:** for true great-circle / shortest-path distances on Earth -- routing, proximity filters, nearest-neighbour queries -- where accuracy matters more than a flat-plane approximation.

**Inputs:** `lon1, lat1` (point 1) and `lon2, lat2` (point 2) in degrees.

**Output:** distance in metres (`DOUBLE`).

**Edge cases:** any NULL/non-finite or out-of-range coordinate (`|lat| > 90` / `|lon| > 180`) yields NULL. The result is ~0.3% different from a spherical haversine because it is ellipsoidal.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## geodesic_distance(lon1, lat1, lon2, lat2)

Accurate WGS84-ellipsoid geodesic distance, in metres, between two geographic points.

### Usage

```sql
SELECT proj.geodesic_distance(-74.006, 40.7128, -0.1276, 51.5074);
```

It is often used in a predicate over a table of points -- for example to keep only rows within a given number of metres of a reference location.

### Notes

- Ellipsoidal (WGS84), so it differs from spherical haversine by ~0.3%.
- NULL, non-finite, or out-of-range coordinates yield NULL.
- Returns metres regardless of input units (inputs are always degrees).

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# from_webmercator

Inverse of `to_webmercator`: convert **Web Mercator** `(x, y)` metres (`EPSG:3857`) back to WGS84 `(lon, lat)` degrees (`EPSG:4326`).

**When to use:** to turn tile/pixel-derived Web Mercator coordinates back into geographic lon/lat, e.g. after reading map-tile geometry.

**Inputs:** `x` (easting metres), `y` (northing metres).

**Output:** `STRUCT(lon DOUBLE, lat DOUBLE)` in WGS84 degrees.

**Edge cases:** NULL/non-finite input yields a NULL struct. This pairs exactly with `to_webmercator` for a round-trip.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## from_webmercator(x, y)

Convenience wrapper for `transform(x, y, 'EPSG:3857', 'EPSG:4326')`, returning `STRUCT(lon, lat)` in WGS84 degrees.

### Usage

```sql
SELECT proj.from_webmercator(-13627665.27, 4547675.35);
```

It can also be applied per row over an easting/northing column, reading `.lon` or `.lat` off the returned struct.

### Notes

- Inverse of `to_webmercator`; round-trips back to the original lon/lat (within PROJ precision).
- Uses `always_xy` axis order.
- NULL or non-finite coordinates produce a NULL struct.

# crs_units

Return the **unit name of a CRS's first axis** -- e.g. `'degree'` for a geographic CRS like `EPSG:4326`, or `'metre'` for a projected CRS like `EPSG:3857`.

**When to use:** to discover whether a CRS is angular (degrees) or linear (metres/feet) before deciding how to interpret or transform its coordinates.

**Inputs:** `crs` -- an EPSG code/string (e.g. `'EPSG:3857'`).

**Output:** the axis unit name as `VARCHAR`.

**Edge cases:** NULL input yields NULL; an unknown/invalid CRS raises a clear query error.

SELECT proj.crs_units('EPSG:4326');  -- 'degree'

- NULL input yields NULL; an unknown CRS raises a query error.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# to_webmercator

Shorthand for the most common reprojection: WGS84 `(lon, lat)` (`EPSG:4326`) to **Web Mercator** `(x, y)` metres (`EPSG:3857`), the CRS used by web map tiles (Google/OSM/Mapbox slippy maps).

**When to use:** to place lon/lat points onto a web map or tile grid, or whenever you need the Web Mercator metric coordinate without spelling out the EPSG codes.

**Inputs:** `lon`, `lat` in WGS84 degrees.

**Output:** `STRUCT(x DOUBLE, y DOUBLE)` in Web Mercator metres.

**Edge cases:** NULL/non-finite input yields a NULL struct. Web Mercator is undefined near the poles (|lat| ~> 85.06 deg), where values grow unbounded -- this is a property of the projection, not an error.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## to_webmercator(lon, lat)

Convenience wrapper for `transform(lon, lat, 'EPSG:4326', 'EPSG:3857')`, returning `STRUCT(x, y)` in Web Mercator metres.

### Usage

```sql
SELECT proj.to_webmercator(-122.4194, 37.7749);
```

It can also be applied per row over a lon/lat column, reading `.x` or `.y` off the returned struct.

### Notes

- Equivalent to a `transform` call into `EPSG:3857`, with `always_xy` axis order.
- The projection is undefined near the poles; expect very large values above ~85.06 degrees latitude.
- NULL or non-finite coordinates produce a NULL struct.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# transform

Reproject a single `(x, y)` coordinate pair from one coordinate reference system (CRS) to another, identified by **EPSG** code/string (e.g. `EPSG:4326` WGS84 lon/lat, `EPSG:3857` Web Mercator).

**When to use:** any time you need to convert between map projections or geographic systems in SQL -- e.g. WGS84 lon/lat to a metric projection for distance/area work, or between two national grids.

**Inputs:** `x` (longitude/easting in `from_crs`), `y` (latitude/northing in `from_crs`), `from_crs`, `to_crs`. The CRS arguments must be constants (folded at plan time); a per-row CRS column is a bind error.

**Output:** `STRUCT(x DOUBLE, y DOUBLE)` in the target CRS.

**Axis order:** always `always_xy` -- inputs/outputs are `(x/easting/longitude, y/northing/latitude)` regardless of the CRS's declared native axis order.

**Edge cases:** a NULL or non-finite coordinate yields a NULL struct; an unknown/invalid CRS raises a clear query error.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## transform(x, y, from_crs, to_crs)

General CRS-to-CRS reprojection returning `STRUCT(x, y)` in the target system.

### Usage

```sql
SELECT proj.transform(-122.42, 37.77, 'EPSG:4326', 'EPSG:3857');
```

It can also be applied per row over a coordinate column, reading `.x` or `.y` off the returned struct.

### Notes

- Uses `always_xy` axis order: `(x/easting/longitude, y/northing/latitude)`.
- NULL or non-finite coordinates produce a NULL struct.
- An unknown CRS raises a DuckDB query error rather than crashing.

workers.subtitle: PromQL queries, typed samples with pushdown, metadata and server status from any Prometheus-compatible API.
workers.summary: Query Prometheus-compatible HTTP APIs (Prometheus, Thanos, Mimir, VictoriaMetrics, Grafana Cloud) from DuckDB: PromQL instant and range queries, typed samples with filter pushdown, series metadata, server status and offline PromQL tools.
workers.doc_md:
# Prometheus in DuckDB

Run PromQL against any Prometheus-compatible HTTP API and get typed rows back: labels as a `MAP` of label names to values plus hoisted `metric`, `job` and `instance` columns, `TIMESTAMPTZ` times and `DOUBLE` values (NaN and Inf kept), with native histograms as a typed struct.

- **query / query_range**: arbitrary PromQL; long ranges are split under the 11,000-point limit without changing the step.
- **samples**: one metric's samples; SQL filters on labels and `ts` become PromQL matchers and the request window.
- **Metadata and status**: series, label names and values, metric metadata, targets, rules, alerts, Alertmanagers, TSDB cardinality, build info.
- **PromQL tools**: validate, explain, canonicalize and audit PromQL with no server.

Credentials come from a `prometheus` DuckDB secret (bearer token or basic auth, optional tenant header).

example_queries.description: Current temperature of every node at one site at a fixed time
example_queries.sql: SELECT instance, value FROM prometheus.main.query('fixture_temperature_celsius{site="ams"}', time := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:15:00+00') ORDER BY instance

example_queries.description: How many targets are up per job right now
example_queries.sql: SELECT labels['job'] AS job, value AS targets_up FROM prometheus.main.query('sum by (job) (up)') ORDER BY job

example_queries.description: Six-hour average and peak temperature per node at one-minute resolution
example_queries.sql: SELECT instance, avg(value) AS avg_c, max(value) AS max_c FROM prometheus.main.query_range('fixture_temperature_celsius', TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00', TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 06:00:00+00', 60) GROUP BY instance ORDER BY instance

example_queries.description: Hourly request rate by status code from a five-minute rate()
example_queries.sql: SELECT date_trunc('hour', ts) AS hour, labels['code'] AS code, avg(value) AS req_per_s FROM prometheus.main.query_range('sum by (code) (rate(fixture_requests_total[5m]))', TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00', TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 06:00:00+00', 300) GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY hour, code

example_queries.description: Raw samples for two nodes over one hour; the job/instance filters and the ts range are pushed into the PromQL selector and request window
example_queries.sql: SELECT instance, count(*) AS samples, min(value) AS lo, max(value) AS hi FROM prometheus.main.samples('fixture_temperature_celsius') WHERE job = 'fixture' AND instance IN ('node-a:9100', 'node-b:9100') AND ts >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00' AND ts < TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 01:00:00+00' GROUP BY instance ORDER BY instance

example_queries.description: Five-minute resampled averages per environment and site, with env exposed as a pushdown column
example_queries.sql: SELECT env, site, avg(value) AS avg_c FROM prometheus.main.samples('fixture_temperature_celsius', label_columns := 'env,site', step_seconds := 300) WHERE env LIKE 'prod%' AND ts BETWEEN TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00' AND TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 06:00:00+00' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY ALL

example_queries.description: Cardinality audit: series per metric for one job
example_queries.sql: SELECT metric, count(*) AS series FROM prometheus.main.series('{job="fixture"}', start_date := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00', end_date := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 06:00:00+00') GROUP BY metric ORDER BY series DESC, metric

example_queries.description: How many temperature series each environment contributes
example_queries.sql: SELECT labels['env'] AS env, count(*) AS series FROM prometheus.main.series('fixture_temperature_celsius', start_date := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00') GROUP BY env ORDER BY env

example_queries.description: Which labels the temperature metric carries
example_queries.sql: SELECT label FROM prometheus.main.label_names(match := 'fixture_temperature_celsius', start_date := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00') ORDER BY label

example_queries.description: How many distinct label names the server knows
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS label_names FROM prometheus.main.label_names()

example_queries.description: Every fixture metric name
example_queries.sql: SELECT value AS metric FROM prometheus.main.label_values('__name__', match := '{job="fixture"}', start_date := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00') WHERE value LIKE 'fixture_%' ORDER BY value

example_queries.description: The instances reporting temperature
example_queries.sql: SELECT value AS instance FROM prometheus.main.label_values('instance', match := 'fixture_temperature_celsius', start_date := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00') ORDER BY value

example_queries.description: Type and help text of every fixture metric
example_queries.sql: SELECT metric, type, help FROM prometheus.main.metric_metadata() WHERE metric LIKE 'fixture_%' ORDER BY metric

example_queries.description: How many metrics of each type the server has seen
example_queries.sql: SELECT type, count(*) AS metrics FROM prometheus.main.metric_metadata() GROUP BY type ORDER BY metrics DESC, type

example_queries.description: Target health per scrape pool
example_queries.sql: SELECT scrape_pool, health, count(*) AS targets FROM prometheus.main.targets(state := 'active') GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY ALL

example_queries.description: Down targets and why
example_queries.sql: SELECT job, instance, last_error FROM prometheus.main.targets() WHERE health = 'down' ORDER BY job, instance

example_queries.description: Every alerting rule with its state
example_queries.sql: SELECT group_name, rule_name, state, active_alerts FROM prometheus.main.rules(rule_type := 'alert') ORDER BY group_name, rule_name

example_queries.description: Rule health summary
example_queries.sql: SELECT rule_type, health, count(*) AS rules FROM prometheus.main.rules() GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY ALL

example_queries.description: Active alerts with severity
example_queries.sql: SELECT alert_name, state, labels['severity'] AS severity FROM prometheus.main.alerts() ORDER BY alert_name

example_queries.description: Firing alerts per severity
example_queries.sql: SELECT labels['severity'] AS severity, count(*) AS alerts FROM prometheus.main.alerts() WHERE state = 'firing' GROUP BY severity ORDER BY alerts DESC

example_queries.description: How many Alertmanagers are active and dropped
example_queries.sql: SELECT state, count(*) AS alertmanagers FROM prometheus.main.alertmanagers() GROUP BY state ORDER BY state

example_queries.description: Where alerts are being sent
example_queries.sql: SELECT url FROM prometheus.main.alertmanagers() WHERE state = 'active' ORDER BY url

example_queries.description: The five metrics with the most head series
example_queries.sql: SELECT name AS metric, value AS series FROM prometheus.main.tsdb_status(top_n := 5) WHERE section = 'series_count_by_metric_name' ORDER BY series DESC, metric

example_queries.description: Head-block totals
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, value FROM prometheus.main.tsdb_status() WHERE section = 'head' ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Which Prometheus version the secret points at
example_queries.sql: SELECT version, go_version FROM prometheus.main.build_info()

example_queries.description: Check the server is Prometheus 3.x
example_queries.sql: SELECT version LIKE '3.%' AS is_v3 FROM prometheus.main.build_info()

example_queries.description: Rules whose expression no longer parses with the current PromQL grammar
example_queries.sql: SELECT rule_name, query FROM prometheus.main.rules() WHERE NOT prometheus.main.is_valid(query)

example_queries.description: Why each broken rule fails to parse
example_queries.sql: SELECT rule_name, prometheus.main.parse_error(query) AS problem FROM prometheus.main.rules() WHERE prometheus.main.parse_error(query) IS NOT NULL

example_queries.description: Rules that are the same expression written differently
example_queries.sql: SELECT prometheus.main.format_expr(query) AS canonical, count(*) AS rules FROM prometheus.main.rules() GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*) > 1

example_queries.description: Which metrics the most rules depend on
example_queries.sql: SELECT m AS metric, count(*) AS rules FROM prometheus.main.rules(), unnest(prometheus.main.metric_names(query)) u(m) GROUP BY m ORDER BY rules DESC

example_queries.description: Spread a one-minute budget over each scrape pool's targets
example_queries.sql: SELECT scrape_pool, prometheus.main.duration_seconds('1m') / count(*) AS seconds_per_target FROM prometheus.main.targets() GROUP BY scrape_pool

example_queries.description: Errors for a broken and a valid expression
example_queries.sql: SELECT e, prometheus.main.parse_error(e) AS problem FROM (VALUES ('up'), ('sum(rate(x[5m])')) t(e) ORDER BY e;

example_queries.description: Check three expressions
example_queries.sql: SELECT e, prometheus.main.is_valid(e) AS ok FROM (VALUES ('rate(x[5m])'), ('rate(x[5m]'), ('sum by (job) (up)')) t(e) ORDER BY e;

example_queries.description: Two spellings, one canonical form
example_queries.sql: SELECT DISTINCT prometheus.main.format_expr(e) AS canonical FROM (VALUES ('sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m]))by(job)'), ('sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))')) t(e);

example_queries.description: Convert durations
example_queries.sql: SELECT d, prometheus.main.duration_seconds(d) AS seconds FROM (VALUES ('1h30m'), ('5m'), ('250ms'), ('1d'), ('soon')) t(d) ORDER BY d;

example_queries.description: Metrics read by a ratio query
example_queries.sql: SELECT prometheus.main.metric_names('sum(rate(errors_total[5m])) / sum(rate(requests_total[5m])) > on() group_left vector(0.1) or errors_total') AS metrics;

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The main schema holds every function. Table functions that call the server take an optional secret_name named argument (default: the prometheus secret whose scope matches). Time arguments are named start_date/end_date (range queries take them positionally) and step arguments step_seconds. Rows are long: one row per series and timestamp. Read a label with labels['name'] or, in the samples table, list it in label_columns to get a pushdown column. The PromQL scalars take one `VARCHAR` expression and need no secret.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

Table functions call the Prometheus HTTP API named by a `prometheus` secret (bearer token or basic auth, optional `X-Scope-OrgID` tenant); pass `secret_name` to choose between several. Scalars run the PromQL parser locally and need no secret.

Conventions: rows are long (one per series and timestamp) with `metric`, `job` and `instance` hoisted and every label in a `labels` map; times are `TIMESTAMPTZ`, values `DOUBLE` with NaN and Inf kept, and windows are `start_date`/`end_date` with steps in `step_seconds`. Range evaluation keeps the step you ask for and splits long windows into requests under Prometheus's 11,000-point limit.

Reach for `samples` when you want SQL filters on labels and `ts` pushed into the PromQL selector and request window, and for the query functions when you need arbitrary PromQL such as `rate()` or aggregations.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Evaluate a PromQL expression at one instant (GET /api/v1/query) and return one row per result series. Positional arg: the PromQL text. Named args: time (`TIMESTAMPTZ`; omitted = now on the server), secret_name (pick a named prometheus secret). functions.name: samples
functions.comment: Stored or resampled samples of one metric as typed rows; label and time filters push down into the PromQL selector

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Read one metric's samples as typed rows, with SQL WHERE filters pushed down. Positional arg: metric name or series selector. Named: label_columns (comma-separated labels to expose as `VARCHAR` columns, e.g. 'env,region'), step_seconds (0 = raw stored samples, default; > 0 = evaluate at a fixed step), start_date/end_date (alternative to a WHERE ts range), chunk_seconds (raw mode request size, default 3600), max_points_per_chunk (step mode, default 11000), secret_name. Columns: metric, job, instance, one column per label_columns entry, labels `MAP(VARCHAR,VARCHAR)`, ts `TIMESTAMPTZ`, value `DOUBLE`, histogram (native histograms). Pushdown: =, <>, IN, OR of equalities on one column, IS [NOT] NULL, LIKE, NOT LIKE, prefix, suffix and contains on metric/job/instance/label columns become PromQL label matchers; ts comparisons/BETWEEN become the request window. DuckDB does not push regexp_matches or ILIKE to the worker, so put a regex matcher in the selector argument instead (e.g. 'up{instance=~"node-[ab].*"}'). A lower time bound is required (WHERE ts >= ... or start_date :=). Filters on labels['x'] are applied in DuckDB, so list the label in label_columns to push it.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## samples(metric, label_columns := '', step_seconds := 0, ...)

Typed rows for one metric. SQL filters on label columns compile into the PromQL selector and `ts` ranges into the request window; every filter is also re-applied exactly by the worker, so results always match the SQL. A lower time bound is required (`WHERE ts >= ...` or `start_date :=`).

vgi.example_queries.description: Raw samples for two nodes over one hour; the job/instance filters and the ts range are pushed into the PromQL selector and request window
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT instance, count(*) AS samples, min(value) AS lo, max(value) AS hi FROM prometheus.main.samples('fixture_temperature_celsius') WHERE job = 'fixture' AND instance IN ('node-a:9100', 'node-b:9100') AND ts >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00' AND ts < TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 01:00:00+00' GROUP BY instance ORDER BY instance

vgi.example_queries.description: Five-minute resampled averages per environment and site, with env exposed as a pushdown column
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT env, site, avg(value) AS avg_c FROM prometheus.main.samples('fixture_temperature_celsius', label_columns := 'env,site', step_seconds := 300) WHERE env LIKE 'prod%' AND ts BETWEEN TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00' AND TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 06:00:00+00' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY ALL

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
The result always has `metric`, `job`, `instance`, then one `VARCHAR` column per name in `label_columns` (in the order given), then `labels`, `ts`, `value` and `histogram`.

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `metric` | VARCHAR | The __name__ label. |
| `job` | VARCHAR | The job label (NULL when absent). |
| `instance` | VARCHAR | The instance label (NULL when absent). |
| `<label>` | VARCHAR | One per label_columns entry, e.g. `env`; NULL when the series lacks the label. |
| `labels` | MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR) | Every label of the series. |
| `ts` | TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE | Sample time. |
| `value` | DOUBLE | Float value (NaN/Inf kept); NULL for native histograms. |
| `histogram` | STRUCT | Native-histogram sample; NULL for float samples. |
tags.vgi.title: Metric Samples With Pushdown

arguments.name: metric
arguments.description: Metric name (e.g. 'node_load1') or a full series selector (e.g. 'up{job="api"}'); SQL filters add matchers to it.

arguments.name: label_columns
arguments.description: Comma-separated label names to expose as their own columns (in addition to metric/job/instance) so they can be filtered and pushed down, e.g. 'env,region'.

arguments.name: step_seconds
arguments.description: 0 (default) returns raw stored samples; > 0 evaluates the selector at this fixed step (query_range).

arguments.name: start_date
arguments.description: Window start when not given by a WHERE ts >= ... predicate.

arguments.name: end_date
arguments.description: Window end (inclusive) when not given by WHERE ts <= ...; default: now.

arguments.name: chunk_seconds
arguments.description: Raw mode: seconds of data fetched per request.

arguments.name: max_points_per_chunk
arguments.description: Step mode: evaluation points per request (Prometheus rejects more than 11000).

arguments.name: secret_name
arguments.description: Name of the prometheus secret to use when several exist.

SELECT env, site, avg(value) AS avg_c FROM prometheus.main.samples('fixture_temperature_celsius', label_columns := 'env,site', step_seconds := 300) WHERE env LIKE 'prod%' AND ts BETWEEN TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00' AND TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 06:00:00+00' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY ALL

functions.name: query_range
functions.comment: Evaluate a PromQL expression over a time range at a fixed step, chunked under the server's point limit

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Evaluate a PromQL expression at every step between two times (/api/v1/query_range) and return long-format rows: one per series per step. Positional args: promql, start (`TIMESTAMPTZ`), end (inclusive), step_seconds (`DOUBLE` > 0). Named: max_points_per_chunk (default 11000), secret_name. Ranges longer than the server's 11,000-points-per-series limit are split into consecutive chunks automatically; the step is never changed, so a chunked pull returns exactly the rows an unchunked one would. Same columns as query(); result_type is 'matrix'. Use query() for a single instant and samples() for raw stored samples with SQL filter pushdown.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## query_range(promql, start, end, step_seconds, max_points_per_chunk := 11000)

Range PromQL evaluation (`/api/v1/query_range`) as long-format rows, chunked under the 11,000-point limit with a resumable cursor.

functions.name: parse_error
functions.comment: The PromQL parser's error message (with position) for an expression, or NULL when it parses

tags.vgi.doc_llm: parse_error(expr) returns the parser's message for PromQL text that does not parse, prefixed with the position (e.g. '1:11: parse error: unclosed left parenthesis'), and NULL when it parses or the input is NULL. Pair it with is_valid to report what is wrong with stored rules. Runs Prometheus's own PromQL parser inside the worker: no server, no secret, no network.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## parse_error(expr)

`NULL` when the PromQL parses; otherwise `line:column: message` from the upstream parser.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT rule_name, prometheus.main.parse_error(query) AS problem FROM prometheus.main.rules() WHERE prometheus.main.parse_error(query) IS NOT NULL

vgi.executable_examples.description: Errors for a broken and a valid expression
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT e, prometheus.main.parse_error(e) AS problem FROM (VALUES ('up'), ('sum(rate(x[5m])')) t(e) ORDER BY e

tags.vgi.title: Explain PromQL Parse Error

arguments.name: expr
arguments.description: PromQL expression text, e.g. 'sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))'. NULL gives NULL.

examples: SELECT rule_name, prometheus.main.parse_error(query) AS problem FROM prometheus.main.rules() WHERE prometheus.main.parse_error(query) IS NOT NULL
SELECT e, prometheus.main.parse_error(e) AS problem FROM (VALUES ('up'), ('sum(rate(x[5m])')) t(e) ORDER BY e;
functions.return_type_bound_from: SELECT prometheus.main.parse_error(query) FROM prometheus.main.rules() WHERE (prometheus.main.parse_error(query) IS NOT NULL)

functions.name: is_valid
functions.comment: True when a PromQL expression parses, false otherwise

tags.vgi.doc_llm: is_valid(expr) returns true when the PromQL text parses and false when it does not (NULL for NULL). Use it to lint PromQL kept in SQL tables, such as alert or recording rules, before sending it to a server; parse_error(expr) says why one fails. Runs Prometheus's own PromQL parser inside the worker: no server, no secret, no network.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## is_valid(expr)

`true` when the PromQL parses, `false` when it does not, `NULL` for `NULL`.

Uses the upstream Prometheus parser, so experimental functions are accepted.

vgi.example_queries.description: Rules whose expression no longer parses with the current PromQL grammar

vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT e, prometheus.main.is_valid(e) AS ok FROM (VALUES ('rate(x[5m])'), ('rate(x[5m]'), ('sum by (job) (up)')) t(e) ORDER BY e

tags.vgi.title: Validate PromQL

arguments.name: expr
arguments.description: PromQL expression text, e.g. 'sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))'. NULL gives NULL.

SELECT e, prometheus.main.is_valid(e) AS ok FROM (VALUES ('rate(x[5m])'), ('rate(x[5m]'), ('sum by (job) (up)')) t(e) ORDER BY e;

functions.name: format_expr
functions.comment: Canonical single-line text of a PromQL expression (NULL when it does not parse)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: format_expr(expr) parses PromQL and prints it back in Prometheus's canonical form: normalized spacing, grouping clauses after the aggregation, quoted label values. Two spellings of the same query give the same text, so it is the key for deduplicating or diffing rules and dashboard queries. NULL when the text does not parse or is NULL. Runs Prometheus's own PromQL parser inside the worker: no server, no secret, no network.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## format_expr(expr)

The expression as Prometheus prints it (`String()` of the parsed AST), or `NULL` when it does not parse.

vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT DISTINCT prometheus.main.format_expr(e) AS canonical FROM (VALUES ('sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m]))by(job)'), ('sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))')) t(e)

tags.vgi.title: Canonicalize PromQL

arguments.name: expr
arguments.description: PromQL expression text, e.g. 'sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))'. NULL gives NULL.

examples: SELECT prometheus.main.format_expr(query) AS canonical, count(*) AS rules FROM prometheus.main.rules() GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*) > 1
SELECT DISTINCT prometheus.main.format_expr(e) AS canonical FROM (VALUES ('sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m]))by(job)'), ('sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))')) t(e);

functions.name: duration_seconds
functions.comment: Seconds in a Prometheus duration string such as '5m' or '1h30m' (NULL when invalid)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: duration_seconds(d) converts a Prometheus duration ('30s', '5m', '1h30m', '2d', '1w', '1y', or '0') to seconds as a double, using the same grammar as Prometheus configuration and PromQL range selectors. NULL for NULL or an invalid duration. Use it to compare scrape intervals or rule `for` clauses, or to turn a range into a step_seconds value. Runs Prometheus's own PromQL parser inside the worker: no server, no secret, no network.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## duration_seconds(d)

workers.doc_md:
# Google Cloud Pub/Sub in DuckDB

Inventory and troubleshoot Pub/Sub from SQL with typed columns: durations as `DOUBLE` seconds, times as `TIMESTAMPTZ`, labels and attributes as `MAP`.

- **Resources**: topics (retention, schema, CMEK, ingestion), subscriptions (type, ack deadline, dead-letter, retry, exactly-once, filter; push endpoint host only), snapshots, schemas and revisions.
- **IAM**: resource policies flattened to role/member rows, with unreadable policies reported, not hidden.
- **Backlog**: Cloud Monitoring series (`labels`, `ts`, `value`) and the current consumer lag per subscription.
- **Messages**: opt-in replay of retained messages through a temporary subscription that the worker deletes. Existing subscriptions are never pulled from.

Credentials come from a `gcp_pubsub` DuckDB secret (service account key or access token).

Upstream references: the [Pub/Sub REST API](https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/reference/rest), [Pub/Sub monitoring metrics](https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/monitoring) via the [Cloud Monitoring API](https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/api/v3), [Pub/Sub access control](https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/access-control), and the [Pub/Sub emulator](https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/emulator).

attach_options.name: use_application_default_credentials
attach_options.description: Opt in to Google Application Default Credentials (GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS, gcloud user credentials, or the GCE/GKE metadata server) when the gcp_pubsub secret has no SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON or ACCESS_TOKEN. Off by default: the worker never reads local credentials unless this is true.

example_queries.description: Every topic with its retention, schema and owning team label
example_queries.sql: SELECT topic, message_retention_seconds / 86400 AS retention_days, schema, labels['team'] AS team FROM pubsub.main.topics() ORDER BY topic

example_queries.description: Topics with neither CMEK nor retention (cannot be replayed)
example_queries.sql: SELECT topic FROM pubsub.main.topics() WHERE kms_key_name IS NULL AND message_retention_seconds IS NULL ORDER BY topic

example_queries.description: Every subscription with its delivery type, ack deadline and dead-letter topic
example_queries.sql: SELECT subscription, type, ack_deadline_seconds, dead_letter_topic, enable_exactly_once_delivery FROM pubsub.main.subscriptions() ORDER BY subscription

example_queries.description: Subscriptions per topic: topics with zero subscriptions drop every message
example_queries.sql: SELECT t.topic, count(s.name) AS subscriptions FROM pubsub.main.topics() t LEFT JOIN pubsub.main.subscriptions() s ON s.topic = t.name GROUP BY t.topic ORDER BY subscriptions, t.topic

example_queries.description: Snapshots by expiry (the soonest to disappear first)
example_queries.sql: SELECT snapshot, topic, expire_time FROM pubsub.main.snapshots() ORDER BY expire_time

example_queries.sql: SELECT schema, type, revision_id, length(definition) AS definition_chars FROM pubsub.main.schemas() ORDER BY schema

example_queries.sql: SELECT s.schema, count(t.name) AS topics FROM pubsub.main.schemas() s LEFT JOIN pubsub.main.topics() t ON t.schema = s.name GROUP BY s.schema ORDER BY topics DESC, s.schema

example_queries.description: The revision history of a schema, newest first
example_queries.sql: SELECT revision_id, revision_create_time, definition FROM pubsub.main.schema_revisions('order-avro') ORDER BY revision_create_time DESC

example_queries.description: Public grants on any topic, subscription, snapshot or schema
example_queries.sql: SELECT resource_type, resource, role, member FROM pubsub.main.iam_policies() WHERE member IN ('allUsers', 'allAuthenticatedUsers') ORDER BY resource

example_queries.description: Which principals hold which roles on topics
example_queries.sql: SELECT member, list(DISTINCT role ORDER BY role) AS roles FROM pubsub.main.iam_policies(resource_type := 'topic') WHERE error IS NULL AND member IS NOT NULL GROUP BY member ORDER BY member

example_queries.description: Peak backlog per subscription over a day
example_queries.sql: SELECT subscription, max(value) AS peak_backlog FROM pubsub.main.time_series('subscription/num_undelivered_messages', start_time := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00', end_time := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-02 00:00:00+00') GROUP BY subscription ORDER BY peak_backlog DESC

example_queries.description: Publish requests to a topic per 5 minutes by response code (last hour)
example_queries.sql: SELECT ts, labels['response_code'] AS response_code, value FROM pubsub.main.time_series('topic/send_request_count', topic := 'orders', alignment_seconds := 300) ORDER BY ts, response_code

example_queries.description: Which subscriptions are furthest behind right now
example_queries.sql: SELECT subscription, undelivered_messages, oldest_unacked_age_seconds / 60 AS lag_minutes FROM pubsub.main.subscription_backlog() ORDER BY oldest_unacked_age_seconds DESC NULLS LAST

example_queries.description: Backlogged subscriptions with their dead-letter settings
example_queries.sql: SELECT s.subscription, s.dead_letter_topic, b.undelivered_messages FROM pubsub.main.subscriptions() s JOIN pubsub.main.subscription_backlog() b ON b.subscription = s.subscription WHERE b.undelivered_messages > 1000 ORDER BY b.undelivered_messages DESC

example_queries.description: Short subscription ids next to their topic

example_queries.description: Subscriptions per project of their topic (cross-project subscriptions show up here)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The main schema holds every function; all are table functions taking project := (default the secret's PROJECT_ID) and secret_name := (default the gcp_pubsub secret whose scope matches). Resource names are accepted as ids ('orders') or full names ('projects/p/topics/orders'); name columns hold full names, so join subscriptions.topic = topics.name. Durations are `DOUBLE` seconds, times `TIMESTAMPTZ`, labels and message attributes `MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)`. read_messages shares the messaging columns of the other VGI messaging workers: timestamp (publish time), key (ordering key), payload `BLOB`, payload_text, payload_bytes, headers (attributes). Monitoring functions need roles/monitoring.viewer.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

A read-only view of one Google Cloud project's Pub/Sub deployment, for platform engineers auditing configuration and on-call engineers chasing a lagging consumer. Resource listings are read-only GETs against the Pub/Sub REST API; time series come from Cloud Monitoring and need `roles/monitoring.viewer`.

Every function takes `project` (default: the secret's `PROJECT_ID`) and `secret_name` (default: the matching `gcp_pubsub` secret). Names are accepted as short ids or full resource names, and name columns always hold full names, so joins between resources work without string surgery.

Message contents are never read from an existing subscription. Replaying retained messages is an explicit opt-in that creates a temporary subscription and deletes it afterwards; nothing else changes the project.

functions.name: read_messages
functions.comment: Replay a topic's retained messages through a temporary subscription (opt-in; never touches existing subscriptions)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Read a topic's retained messages through a TEMPORARY subscription — only with allow_temporary_subscription := true (required opt-in). Positional arg: topic. Named: allow_temporary_subscription, start_time (seek; default the oldest retained message), end_time, snapshot := (seek to a snapshot instead), filter := (Pub/Sub attribute filter, server-side), max_messages (default 100), wait_seconds (default 10), truncate, project, secret_name. Pub/Sub has no read-only peek: pulling from an existing subscription would hide its messages from the real subscribers until the ack deadline, count delivery attempts toward dead-lettering, and acking would drop them. read_messages therefore never pulls from an existing subscription. With allow_temporary_subscription := true it creates a temporary subscription (vgi-temp-<time>-<random>, label vgi-temp=true, 24 h expiration), seeks it to start_time or a snapshot, pulls and acks on it only, and deletes it at the end (also on error). That needs pubsub.subscriptions.create/delete and pubsub.topics.attachSubscription, is visible in audit logs, and only replays what the topic retains (topic message retention) or the snapshot captured. Columns (shared messaging vocabulary): project, topic, subscription (the temporary one), sequence (always NULL), timestamp (publish time), key (ordering key), payload `BLOB`, payload_text, payload_bytes, headers `MAP` (attributes), message_id, delivery_attempt.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## read_messages(topic, allow_temporary_subscription := true, start_time := NULL, snapshot := NULL)

Replays a topic's **retained** messages through a temporary subscription that the worker creates, seeks, drains and deletes. Existing subscriptions are never pulled from. Opt-in only, because it creates (and removes) a subscription.

vgi.example_queries.description: Replay retained messages of a topic through a temporary subscription (opt-in)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT timestamp, key, headers['tenant'] AS tenant, payload_text::JSON->>'order_id' AS order_id FROM pubsub.main.read_messages('orders', allow_temporary_subscription := true, start_time := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00', max_messages := 50) ORDER BY timestamp, message_id

vgi.example_queries.description: What a snapshot's captured backlog contains, without touching the subscription it was taken from
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT headers['event'] AS event, count(*) AS messages, max(payload_bytes) AS largest FROM pubsub.main.read_messages('orders', allow_temporary_subscription := true, snapshot := 'before-deploy', max_messages := 1000) GROUP BY event ORDER BY messages DESC

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: project
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Project of the topic.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: topic
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Topic id the message was published to.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: subscription
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: The temporary subscription (vgi-temp-...) the message was read through; it is deleted when the read ends.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: sequence
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Position of the message in its source. Always NULL: Pub/Sub has no offsets (kept for the shared messaging columns; use timestamp and message_id).

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: timestamp
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Publish time assigned by Pub/Sub (publishTime).

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: key
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Ordering key the message was published with; NULL when none.

arguments.name: topic
arguments.description: Topic to read (id or full name). Messages are read through a new temporary subscription; existing subscriptions are never touched.

arguments.name: allow_temporary_subscription
arguments.description: Required opt-in. true acknowledges that the read CREATES a temporary subscription on the topic (vgi-temp-..., label vgi-temp=true, 24 h expiration), seeks it, pulls and acks on it only, and DELETES it at the end. Never pulls from an existing subscription.

arguments.name: start_time
arguments.description: Replay messages published at or after this time (seek). Default: the oldest the topic retains (now minus its message retention). Needs topic message retention.

arguments.name: end_time
arguments.description: Drop messages published after this time.

arguments.name: snapshot
arguments.description: Instead of start_time, seek the temporary subscription to this snapshot (id or full name) and read the backlog it captured.

arguments.name: filter
arguments.description: Pub/Sub filter set on the temporary subscription (server-side), e.g. 'attributes.tenant = "a"'. Only attributes can be filtered.

arguments.name: max_messages
arguments.description: Stop after this many messages.

arguments.name: wait_seconds
arguments.description: Upper bound on the time spent pulling; the read also stops once the subscription is drained.

arguments.name: truncate
arguments.description: Return at most this many bytes of each message (payload_bytes still gives the full size).

arguments.name: project
arguments.description: Google Cloud project id; default the gcp_pubsub secret's PROJECT_ID.

arguments.name: secret_name
arguments.description: Name of the gcp_pubsub secret to use when several exist.

examples: SELECT timestamp, key, headers['tenant'] AS tenant, payload_text::JSON->>'order_id' AS order_id FROM pubsub.main.read_messages('orders', allow_temporary_subscription := true, start_time := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00', max_messages := 50) ORDER BY timestamp, message_id

SELECT headers['event'] AS event, count(*) AS messages, max(payload_bytes) AS largest FROM pubsub.main.read_messages('orders', allow_temporary_subscription := true, snapshot := 'before-deploy', max_messages := 1000) GROUP BY event ORDER BY messages DESC

workers.title: PySAL Spatial Analysis
workers.tagline: A VGI worker exposing PySAL spatial datasets, weights, autocorrelation, classification, and spatial regression to DuckDB/SQL
workers.subtitle: Spatial weights, autocorrelation tests, map classification, inequality measures, and spatial regression from PySAL, callable from SQL.
workers.summary: PySAL spatial statistics for SQL: datasets, weights, autocorrelation, classification, and regression.
workers.doc_md:
# PySAL spatial analysis for SQL

This worker exposes the [PySAL](https://pysal.org/) Python spatial analysis library as DuckDB table functions. Load a bundled example dataset or pass any query with a numeric value and a geometry, and the worker builds spatial weights from the geometries and returns the statistic as rows: global and local spatial autocorrelation, map classification, inequality measures and spatial regression. Permutation p-values depend on the permutation count and seed; all computation is local.

## Sources and references

- [PySAL](https://pysal.org/): the Python Spatial Analysis Library federation this worker wraps.
- [libpysal](https://pysal.org/libpysal/stable/): spatial weights and the bundled example datasets.
- [esda](https://pysal.org/esda/): Moran's I, Geary's C and local (LISA) autocorrelation statistics.
- [spreg](https://pysal.org/spreg/), [mapclassify](https://pysal.org/mapclassify/stable/) and [inequality](https://pysal.org/inequality/): spatial regression, choropleth classification and inequality measures.

example_queries.description: Spatial lag of columbus crime: join the row-standardised queen weights edge list to the dataset and average each neighbourhood's neighbours' crime; the five highest-lag neighbourhoods, with their own crime and neighbour count
example_queries.sql: WITH c AS (SELECT id, crime FROM pysal.main.columbus()) SELECT w.focal::BIGINT AS id, own.crime AS crime, round(sum(w.weight * nb.crime), 2) AS neighbour_crime, count(*) AS neighbours FROM pysal.main.weights((SELECT id, geom FROM pysal.main.columbus()), w_type => 'queen', id => 'id') AS w JOIN c AS own ON own.id = w.focal::BIGINT JOIN c AS nb ON nb.id = w.neighbor::BIGINT GROUP BY w.focal, own.crime ORDER BY neighbour_crime DESC, id LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Profile local Moran crime clusters: join local_moran back to columbus by id and compare average crime, income, and house value per cluster type (high-high clusters are the poorer, lower-value neighbourhoods)
example_queries.sql: SELECT lm.cluster, count(*) AS neighbourhoods, round(avg(c.crime), 1) AS avg_crime, round(avg(c.inc), 1) AS avg_income, round(avg(c.hoval), 1) AS avg_house_value FROM pysal.main.local_moran((SELECT id, crime AS y, geom FROM pysal.main.columbus()), w_type => 'queen', id => 'id') AS lm JOIN pysal.main.columbus() AS c USING (id) GROUP BY lm.cluster ORDER BY avg_crime DESC

example_queries.description: Average columbus crime per household-income quintile: classify income with quantiles, join the classes back to the dataset by id, and aggregate crime per class
example_queries.sql: SELECT q.class AS income_quintile, round(max(q.upper_bound), 2) AS income_upper_bound, count(*) AS neighbourhoods, round(avg(c.crime), 1) AS avg_crime FROM pysal.main.quantiles((SELECT id, inc AS y FROM pysal.main.columbus()), value => 'y', k => 5, id => 'id') AS q JOIN pysal.main.columbus() AS c USING (id) GROUP BY q.class ORDER BY income_quintile

agent_tasks: Using queen-contiguity spatial weights between the Mexican states in the built-in mexico dataset (row-standardised, the default transform), compute each state's spatial lag of 2000 per-capita GDP (pcgdp2000) — the weighted average over its neighbours. Which state has the highest spatial lag? Return one column: the state name.

Run a Getis-Ord G_i* hot-spot analysis of crime on the built-in columbus neighbourhoods using 8-nearest-neighbour weights. How many neighbourhoods does the worker label as crime hot spots, and what is their average house value (hoval)? Return two columns: the hot-spot count (integer) and the average house value rounded to 1 decimal place.
