workers.doc_md:
# Quantitative Finance Math in SQL

![QuantLib logo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/74/QL-title.jpg)

**Price options, compute Black-Scholes Greeks, value fixed-rate bonds, and do day-count and discounting math directly in DuckDB SQL** — no spreadsheets, no external pricing service, no round-trips to Python. The `quant` catalog turns industry-standard quantitative-finance calculations into ordinary SQL functions you can call inline in any query.

This extension is for analysts, quants, risk teams, and data engineers who keep their market data in DuckDB and want option pricing, implied volatility, bond analytics, and rate-risk math to live right next to the data. Because the calculations are exposed as scalar functions, you can value a whole portfolio in a single `SELECT`, filter on a computed risk measure in a `WHERE` clause, or join model output back onto your positions — all with the speed of DuckDB's vectorized engine over Apache Arrow.

## Key concepts

- **Per-row vs. constant arguments.** Market inputs (spot, strike, rate, volatility, price, coupon, yield, dates) are per-row columns, while the option kind, the bond coupon frequency, and the day-count convention are constant (literal) arguments fixed at planning time. That split lets you value an entire table of positions in one pass.
- **Analytic and deterministic.** Option values use the closed-form Black-Scholes model (no dividend yield — carry equals the risk-free rate); bond analytics use a fixed-rate bond priced on a pinned evaluation date. Results are reproducible run to run.
- **NULL vs. error.** Any NULL input yields a NULL result, but a genuinely invalid non-NULL input (a non-positive time to maturity, a negative volatility, an unknown convention) raises a clear error rather than silently returning a wrong number.

## When to reach for it

Use `quant` whenever you need theoretical option premia and their risk sensitivities, want to convert between bond prices and yields or measure interest-rate risk, or need consistent day-count and present-value math alongside your data — without exporting to a separate analytics stack. Because every calculation is a deterministic, closed-form function, results are reproducible and cheap enough to run across a whole portfolio in a single query.

## Backed by QuantLib

Under the hood the math is backed by [QuantLib](https://www.quantlib.org/), the widely used open-source library for quantitative finance, which provides the analytic option pricing, the fixed-rate bond pricing and yield solvers, and the day-count conventions this worker exposes. See the QuantLib [source code on GitHub](https://github.com/lballabio/QuantLib), the [official documentation](https://www.quantlib.org/docs.shtml), and the [Python bindings reference](https://quantlib-python-docs.readthedocs.io/) for the underlying models and conventions.
workers.readme_sql:
INSTALL vgi FROM community; LOAD vgi;
ATTACH 'quant' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'uvx --from git+https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-quant@v0.5.1 vgi-quant-worker');

SELECT quant.bs_price(100, 100, 0.05, 0.2, 1, 'call');        -- ~10.4506
SELECT quant.bs_delta(100, 100, 0.05, 0.2, 1, 'call');        -- ~0.6368
SELECT quant.bs_vega(100, 100, 0.05, 0.2, 1, 'call');         -- ~37.524 (per 1.00 vol)
SELECT quant.implied_vol(10.4506, 100, 100, 0.05, 1, 'call'); -- ~0.20
SELECT quant.bond_price(100, 0.05, 0.05, 10, 2);              -- ~100 (par bond)
SELECT quant.bond_yield(100, 100, 0.05, 10, 2);               -- ~0.05
SELECT quant.bond_duration(100, 0.05, 0.05, 10, 2);           -- ~7.80 (modified)
SELECT quant.bond_convexity(100, 0.05, 0.05, 10, 2);          -- ~73.65
SELECT quant.year_fraction(DATE '2026-01-01', DATE '2026-07-01', 'ACT/360'); -- 181/360
SELECT quant.discount_factor(0.05, 1);                        -- exp(-0.05) ~0.9512
SELECT quant.present_value(100, 0.05, 1);                     -- ~95.123
SELECT * FROM quant.day_count_conventions();

example_queries.description: Black-Scholes fair value of an at-the-money 1-year European call.
example_queries.sql: SELECT quant.main.bs_price(100, 100, 0.05, 0.2, 1, 'call') AS call_price

example_queries.description: Delta (hedge ratio) of that same at-the-money call.
example_queries.sql: SELECT quant.main.bs_delta(100, 100, 0.05, 0.2, 1, 'call') AS delta

example_queries.description: Recover the implied volatility (~0.20) from a quoted call price.
example_queries.sql: SELECT quant.main.implied_vol(10.45, 100, 100, 0.05, 1, 'call') AS iv

example_queries.description: Clean price of a 10-year 5% semiannual par bond (prices to 100).
example_queries.sql: SELECT quant.main.bond_price(100, 0.05, 0.05, 10, 2) AS clean_price

example_queries.description: Invert a par price back to the bond's yield to maturity (~0.05).
example_queries.sql: SELECT quant.main.bond_yield(100, 100, 0.05, 10, 2) AS ytm

example_queries.description: Day-count year fraction of a half-year span under ACT/360 (181/360).
example_queries.sql: SELECT quant.main.year_fraction(DATE '2026-01-01', DATE '2026-07-01', 'ACT/360') AS yf

example_queries.description: One-year continuously-compounded discount factor at 5% (~0.9512).
example_queries.sql: SELECT quant.main.discount_factor(0.05, 1) AS df

example_queries.description: List the supported day-count convention names, alphabetically.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name FROM quant.main.day_count_conventions() ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Gold cash-and-carry: futures carry over the 3-month T-bill rate.
example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(quant.main.implied_carry_rate(4000, 4050, 0.25) - quant.main.tbill_rate(0.0412, 91), 4) AS excess_carry

example_queries.description: Short perp at the 1 bp/8h funding floor, hedged with a long future.
example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(quant.main.funding_rate_annual(0.0001, 8) - quant.main.implied_carry_rate(4000, 4050, 0.25), 4) AS net_carry

example_queries.description: Back out implied vol for three quoted 6-month calls, then compute each strike's delta at its own implied vol (implied_vol feeding bs_delta); the vol skews down as strike rises.
example_queries.sql: WITH quotes(strike, price) AS (VALUES (90, 14.50), (100, 8.20), (110, 3.90)), smile AS (SELECT strike, quant.main.implied_vol(price, 100, strike, 0.05, 0.5, 'call') AS iv FROM quotes) SELECT strike, ROUND(iv, 4) AS iv, ROUND(quant.main.bs_delta(100, strike, 0.05, iv, 0.5, 'call'), 4) AS delta FROM smile ORDER BY strike

example_queries.description: Value a small call book dated 2026-06-15: each expiry date becomes an ACT/365 time to maturity via year_fraction, which feeds bs_price and bs_delta summed by position size.
example_queries.sql: WITH book(qty, strike, expiry) AS (VALUES (10, 100, DATE '2026-09-18'), (-10, 110, DATE '2026-09-18'), (5, 100, DATE '2026-12-18')), priced AS (SELECT qty, strike, quant.main.year_fraction(DATE '2026-06-15', expiry, 'ACT/365') AS ttm FROM book) SELECT ROUND(SUM(qty * quant.main.bs_price(100, strike, 0.05, 0.2, ttm, 'call')), 4) AS book_value, ROUND(SUM(qty * quant.main.bs_delta(100, strike, 0.05, 0.2, ttm, 'call')), 4) AS book_delta FROM priced

example_queries.description: Shock a 10-year 5% semiannual par bond up 100bp: the full bond_price reprice (-7.44) versus the duration-only (-7.80) and duration-plus-convexity (-7.43) estimates.
example_queries.sql: WITH base AS (SELECT quant.main.bond_price(100, 0.05, 0.05, 10, 2) AS p0, quant.main.bond_duration(100, 0.05, 0.05, 10, 2) AS dur, quant.main.bond_convexity(100, 0.05, 0.05, 10, 2) AS cvx) SELECT ROUND(quant.main.bond_price(100, 0.05, 0.06, 10, 2) - p0, 4) AS actual_change, ROUND(-p0 * dur * 0.01, 4) AS duration_estimate, ROUND(p0 * (-dur * 0.01 + 0.5 * cvx * 0.0001), 4) AS duration_convexity_estimate FROM base

example_queries.description: Present value of a 2-year 5% semiannual coupon schedule settled 2026-06-15, discounting each cash flow at 4.5% continuous over its ACT/365 year_fraction (~100.84).
example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(SUM(quant.main.present_value(CASE WHEN n = 4 THEN 102.5 ELSE 2.5 END, 0.045, quant.main.year_fraction(DATE '2026-06-15', CAST(DATE '2026-06-15' + to_months(6 * n) AS DATE), 'ACT/365'))), 4) AS pv FROM range(1, 5) AS t(n)

example_queries.description: List the supported day-count convention names, alphabetically.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name FROM quant.main.day_count_conventions ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Count how many day-count conventions are supported.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS n FROM quant.main.day_count_conventions

example_queries.description: Show only the actual/actual-family conventions.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name FROM quant.main.day_count_conventions WHERE name LIKE 'ACT%' ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Count how many day-count conventions the worker supports.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS n FROM quant.main.day_count_conventions()

example_queries.description: Two-year discount factor at 5% is exp(-0.10) (~0.9048).
example_queries.sql: SELECT quant.main.discount_factor(0.05, 2) AS df

example_queries.description: 5% continuous over six months is ~5.06% simple.
example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(quant.main.continuous_to_simple(0.05, 0.5), 4) AS simple

example_queries.description: Dollar carry on $100,000 held 3 months at the gold futures carry rate.
example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(100000 * quant.main.continuous_to_simple(quant.main.implied_carry_rate(4000, 4050, 0.25), 0.25) * 0.25, 2) AS dollars

example_queries.description: Gold 3-month future at 4050 and 6-month at 4110 imply ~5.88%/yr between them.
example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(quant.main.calendar_spread_rate(4050, 4110, 0.25, 0.5), 4) AS fwd_rate

example_queries.description: Every leg of a futures curve, using LEAD over expiries.
example_queries.sql: SELECT ttm, ROUND(quant.main.calendar_spread_rate(px, nx_px, ttm, nx_ttm), 4) AS leg_rate FROM (SELECT ttm, px, LEAD(px) OVER (ORDER BY ttm) AS nx_px, LEAD(ttm) OVER (ORDER BY ttm) AS nx_ttm FROM (VALUES (0.1, 4020.0), (0.25, 4050.0), (0.5, 4110.0)) c(ttm, px)) WHERE nx_px IS NOT NULL ORDER BY ttm

example_queries.description: Round-trip: price a call, then invert that price back to its vol.
example_queries.sql: SELECT quant.main.implied_vol(quant.main.bs_price(100, 100, 0.05, 0.2, 1, 'call'), 100, 100, 0.05, 1, 'call') AS iv

example_queries.description: Convexity of a 10-year 5% semiannual par bond; near 73.65 and positive.
example_queries.sql: SELECT quant.main.bond_convexity(100, 0.05, 0.05, 10, 2) AS convexity

example_queries.description: Theta (per year) of an at-the-money 1-year European call; negative.
example_queries.sql: SELECT quant.main.bs_theta(100, 100, 0.05, 0.2, 1, 'call') AS theta

example_queries.description: Convert to per-calendar-day time decay by dividing by 365.
example_queries.sql: SELECT quant.main.bs_theta(100, 100, 0.05, 0.2, 1, 'call') / 365 AS theta_per_day

example_queries.description: Price the matching European put (same spot, strike, rate, vol, maturity).
example_queries.sql: SELECT quant.main.bs_price(100, 100, 0.05, 0.2, 1, 'put') AS put_price

example_queries.description: Gamma of an at-the-money 1-year European call (identical for the put).
example_queries.sql: SELECT quant.main.bs_gamma(100, 100, 0.05, 0.2, 1, 'call') AS gamma

example_queries.description: A 1000-wide SPX box costing 989 with 3 months left lends at ~4.42%/yr.
example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(quant.main.box_spread_rate(989, 5000, 6000, 0.25), 4) AS box_rate

example_queries.description: Price the box from its four legs, then take its rate.
example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(quant.main.box_spread_rate(c_lo - c_hi + p_hi - p_lo, 5000, 6000, 0.25), 4) AS box_rate FROM (VALUES (1050.0, 210.0, 160.0, 11.0)) l(c_lo, c_hi, p_hi, p_lo)

example_queries.description: The same span under 30/360 is exactly 0.5 (six 30-day months).
example_queries.sql: SELECT quant.main.year_fraction(DATE '2026-01-01', DATE '2026-07-01', '30/360') AS yf

example_queries.description: Black-Scholes price of an at-the-money 1y European call.
example_queries.sql: SELECT quant.main.bs_price(100, 100, 0.05, 0.2, 1, 'call') AS price;

example_queries.description: 5% simple over six months is ~4.94% continuous.
example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(quant.main.simple_to_continuous(0.05, 0.5), 4) AS cont

example_queries.description: Round trip through continuous_to_simple returns the input.
example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(quant.main.continuous_to_simple(quant.main.simple_to_continuous(0.05, 0.5), 0.5), 6) AS back

example_queries.description: A price below par implies a yield above the 5% coupon.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Quant — the `main` schema

The single schema of the `quant` catalog. It groups every quantitative-finance calculation the worker exposes over Apache Arrow into one namespace.

## What lives here

Four families of functionality:

- **Options** — closed-form Black-Scholes pricing and the full set of first- and second-order Greeks, plus inversion of a market price back to implied volatility.
- **Fixed-rate bonds** — clean pricing from a yield, the inverse yield-to-maturity solve, and interest-rate risk measures (modified duration and convexity).
- **Day-count & discounting** — year fractions under the common day-count conventions and continuously-compounded discount factors and present values, with a discovery listing of the accepted convention strings.
- **Carry** — the annual financing rate implied by a futures basis, a futures calendar spread, a box spread, a T-bill discount quote or a perp funding rate, all on one continuous basis, plus simple/continuous rate conversion.

## When to use it

Use this schema for option pricing and risk sensitivities, bond price/yield conversion and rate-risk analytics, and day-count or present-value math directly in SQL. Every object is a deterministic scalar (or the one discovery table), so the math composes inline in projections, `WHERE` filters, and joins over your positions.

vgi.example_queries.description: Black-Scholes fair value of an at-the-money 1-year European call.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT quant.main.bs_price(100, 100, 0.05, 0.2, 1, 'call') AS call_price

vgi.example_queries.description: Clean price of a 10-year 5% semiannual par bond (prices to 100).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT quant.main.bond_price(100, 0.05, 0.05, 10, 2) AS clean_price

vgi.example_queries.description: Invert a par price back to the bond's yield to maturity (~0.05).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT quant.main.bond_yield(100, 100, 0.05, 10, 2) AS ytm

vgi.example_queries.description: Day-count year fraction of a half-year span under ACT/360 (181/360).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT quant.main.year_fraction(DATE '2026-01-01', DATE '2026-07-01', 'ACT/360') AS yf

vgi.example_queries.description: One-year continuously-compounded discount factor at 5% (~0.9512).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT quant.main.discount_factor(0.05, 1) AS df

vgi.example_queries.description: List the supported day-count convention names, alphabetically.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name FROM quant.main.day_count_conventions() ORDER BY name

vgi.example_queries.description: Gold cash-and-carry: futures carry over the 3-month T-bill rate.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(quant.main.implied_carry_rate(4000, 4050, 0.25) - quant.main.tbill_rate(0.0412, 91), 4) AS excess_carry

vgi.example_queries.description: Short perp at the 1 bp/8h funding floor, hedged with a long future.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(quant.main.funding_rate_annual(0.0001, 8) - quant.main.implied_carry_rate(4000, 4050, 0.25), 4) AS net_carry

vgi.example_queries.description: Back out implied vol for three quoted 6-month calls, then compute each strike's delta at its own implied vol (implied_vol feeding bs_delta); the vol skews down as strike rises.
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH quotes(strike, price) AS (VALUES (90, 14.50), (100, 8.20), (110, 3.90)), smile AS (SELECT strike, quant.main.implied_vol(price, 100, strike, 0.05, 0.5, 'call') AS iv FROM quotes) SELECT strike, ROUND(iv, 4) AS iv, ROUND(quant.main.bs_delta(100, strike, 0.05, iv, 0.5, 'call'), 4) AS delta FROM smile ORDER BY strike

vgi.example_queries.description: Value a small call book dated 2026-06-15: each expiry date becomes an ACT/365 time to maturity via year_fraction, which feeds bs_price and bs_delta summed by position size.
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH book(qty, strike, expiry) AS (VALUES (10, 100, DATE '2026-09-18'), (-10, 110, DATE '2026-09-18'), (5, 100, DATE '2026-12-18')), priced AS (SELECT qty, strike, quant.main.year_fraction(DATE '2026-06-15', expiry, 'ACT/365') AS ttm FROM book) SELECT ROUND(SUM(qty * quant.main.bs_price(100, strike, 0.05, 0.2, ttm, 'call')), 4) AS book_value, ROUND(SUM(qty * quant.main.bs_delta(100, strike, 0.05, 0.2, ttm, 'call')), 4) AS book_delta FROM priced

vgi.example_queries.description: Shock a 10-year 5% semiannual par bond up 100bp: the full bond_price reprice (-7.44) versus the duration-only (-7.80) and duration-plus-convexity (-7.43) estimates.
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH base AS (SELECT quant.main.bond_price(100, 0.05, 0.05, 10, 2) AS p0, quant.main.bond_duration(100, 0.05, 0.05, 10, 2) AS dur, quant.main.bond_convexity(100, 0.05, 0.05, 10, 2) AS cvx) SELECT ROUND(quant.main.bond_price(100, 0.05, 0.06, 10, 2) - p0, 4) AS actual_change, ROUND(-p0 * dur * 0.01, 4) AS duration_estimate, ROUND(p0 * (-dur * 0.01 + 0.5 * cvx * 0.0001), 4) AS duration_convexity_estimate FROM base

vgi.example_queries.description: Present value of a 2-year 5% semiannual coupon schedule settled 2026-06-15, discounting each cash flow at 4.5% continuous over its ACT/365 year_fraction (~100.84).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(SUM(quant.main.present_value(CASE WHEN n = 4 THEN 102.5 ELSE 2.5 END, 0.045, quant.main.year_fraction(DATE '2026-06-15', CAST(DATE '2026-06-15' + to_months(6 * n) AS DATE), 'ACT/365'))), 4) AS pv FROM range(1, 5) AS t(n)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## discount_factor

Compute the continuously-compounded **discount factor** `exp(-rate * ttm)` -- the present value today of one unit of currency received at a future time.

**Signature:** `discount_factor(rate, ttm)` -- `rate` is the continuously-compounded annual rate; `ttm` is the time horizon in years.

**Output:** a `DOUBLE` in `(0, 1]` for non-negative rates. Multiply a future cash flow by it to discount (or use `present_value`). NULL in -> NULL out.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Continuous Discount Factor

Continuously-compounded discount factor `exp(-rate * ttm)`.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT quant.discount_factor(0.05, 1);  -- exp(-0.05) ~ 0.9512
```

## Notes

- Continuous compounding (not periodic).
- Multiply a future amount by this to get its present value.

functions.comment: Convert a continuous annual rate to a simple rate over ttm years: (exp(rate*ttm)-1)/ttm

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## continuous_to_simple

Converts a continuously compounded annual rate (what the carry functions return) into a simple annual rate over a holding period: `(exp(rate * ttm) - 1) / ttm`.

**Signature:** `continuous_to_simple(rate, ttm)`; `ttm` in years (> 0).

**Use:** turn a carry rate into the simple return of a trade held for `ttm`, e.g. dollars earned = notional * result * ttm.

**Output:** a `DOUBLE` simple annual rate. NULL in -> NULL out.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Continuous to Simple Rate

```sql
SELECT quant.continuous_to_simple(0.05, 0.5);  -- ~0.0506
```

- Inverse of `simple_to_continuous` for the same `ttm`.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## calendar_spread_rate

The forward financing rate implied by two futures on the same underlying: `ln(far_price / near_price) / (far_ttm - near_ttm)`.

**Signature:** `calendar_spread_rate(near_price, far_price, near_ttm, far_ttm)`; prices > 0, `near_ttm >= 0`, `far_ttm > near_ttm`, both in years from today.

**Use:** read a futures curve as a strip of forward rates, e.g. the Dec->Feb and Feb->Apr legs of the gold curve, without needing a spot price.

**Output:** a `DOUBLE` continuously compounded annual rate (0.05 = 5%/yr). NULL in -> NULL out.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Calendar Spread Rate

Forward rate between two futures expiries.

```sql
SELECT quant.calendar_spread_rate(4050, 4110, 0.25, 0.5);  -- ~0.0588
```

- `far_ttm` must be later than `near_ttm`.
- Use `LEAD()` over a curve ordered by expiry to get every leg.

vgi.example_queries.description: Gold 3-month future at 4050 and 6-month at 4110 imply ~5.88%/yr between them.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(quant.main.calendar_spread_rate(4050, 4110, 0.25, 0.5), 4) AS fwd_rate

vgi.example_queries.description: Every leg of a futures curve, using LEAD over expiries.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ttm, ROUND(quant.main.calendar_spread_rate(px, nx_px, ttm, nx_ttm), 4) AS leg_rate FROM (SELECT ttm, px, LEAD(px) OVER (ORDER BY ttm) AS nx_px, LEAD(ttm) OVER (ORDER BY ttm) AS nx_ttm FROM (VALUES (0.1, 4020.0), (0.25, 4050.0), (0.5, 4110.0)) c(ttm, px)) WHERE nx_px IS NOT NULL ORDER BY ttm

functions.name: implied_vol
functions.comment: Black-Scholes implied volatility reproducing an option price (raises if not invertible)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## implied_vol

Invert the Black-Scholes model: given an observed option **price**, solve for the volatility that reproduces it.

**Signature:** `implied_vol(price, spot, strike, rate, ttm, opt_type)` -- note `price` comes **first** and there is no `vol` argument (that is what is solved for). `opt_type` is the literal `'call'`/`'put'`.

**Output:** annualized volatility as a `DOUBLE` (e.g. `0.20` for 20%). Use it to back out market-implied vol from quoted prices. NULL in -> NULL out; a non-invertible price (e.g. below intrinsic value) raises a clear error.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Black-Scholes Implied Volatility

Solves for the volatility consistent with an observed option price.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT quant.implied_vol(10.45, 100, 100, 0.05, 1, 'call');  -- ~0.20
```

## Notes

- Argument order is `(price, spot, strike, rate, ttm, opt_type)`.
- Round-trips `bs_price`: feeding its output recovers the vol.
- Raises if the price is not invertible (e.g. below intrinsic).

## bond_convexity

Compute the **convexity** of a fixed-rate bond at a given yield -- the second-order sensitivity of price to yield that refines the duration estimate.

**Signature:** `bond_convexity(face, coupon_rate, yield_rate, years, freq)` -- same inputs as `bond_price`; `freq` is the literal coupon frequency (`1`/`2`/`4`/`12`).

**Output:** convexity as a `DOUBLE` (positive for plain bonds). Combine with `bond_duration` for a second-order price-change approximation under large yield moves. NULL in -> NULL out; invalid inputs raise.

# Fixed-Rate Bond Convexity

Convexity -- second-order price sensitivity to yield.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT quant.bond_convexity(100, 0.05, 0.05, 10, 2);  -- ~73.65
```

## Notes

- Positive for plain vanilla bonds.
- Refines the duration-based price-change estimate.
- Larger for longer maturities and lower coupons.

functions.comment: Black-Scholes price of a European option ('call'|'put')

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## bs_price

Compute the analytic **Black-Scholes** fair value of a European option.

**Signature:** `bs_price(spot, strike, rate, vol, ttm, opt_type)`

**Inputs:** `spot` and `strike` are prices (> 0); `rate` is the continuously-compounded annual risk-free rate; `vol` is annualized volatility (>= 0, e.g. `0.2` for 20%); `ttm` is time to maturity in years (> 0); `opt_type` is the **literal** `'call'` or `'put'`.

**Output:** a `DOUBLE` option premium in the same currency as `spot`.

Use this when you need a theoretical option premium per row. There is no dividend yield (carry equals `rate`). Any NULL input yields NULL; `ttm <= 0`, negative `vol`, non-positive `spot`/`strike`, or an unknown `opt_type` raise a clear error. Pair with `implied_vol` to invert a market price back to volatility.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Black-Scholes Option Price

Prices a European option with the closed-form Black-Scholes model.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT quant.bs_price(100, 100, 0.05, 0.2, 1, 'call');  -- ~10.45
```

## Notes

- `opt_type` must be a literal `'call'` or `'put'`.
- No dividend yield is modeled; carry equals the risk-free `rate`.
- At-the-money 1y example above returns roughly `10.4506`.

functions.name: box_spread_rate
functions.comment: Annual rate implied by a European box spread: ln((high-low)/box_price)/ttm

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## box_spread_rate

The lending/borrowing rate implied by a European box spread. A box is long a call and short a put at `low_strike` plus short a call and long a put at `high_strike`; it pays `high_strike - low_strike` at expiry regardless of the underlying, so it is a zero-coupon loan.

**Signature:** `box_spread_rate(box_price, low_strike, high_strike, ttm)`. `box_price` is the net cost of the four legs: `call(low) - call(high) + put(high) - put(low)`, in the same units as the strikes (not multiplied by the contract multiplier).

**Use:** buying a box lends at this rate; selling one borrows at it. Compare with `tbill_rate` and `implied_carry_rate`. Only European-style options (e.g. SPX) are safe from early assignment.

**Output:** a `DOUBLE` continuously compounded annual rate (0.05 = 5%/yr). NULL in -> NULL out.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Box Spread Rate

Implied rate of a European box spread.

```sql
SELECT quant.box_spread_rate(989, 5000, 6000, 0.25);  -- ~0.0442
```

- `box_price = call(low) - call(high) + put(high) - put(low)`.
- Use European-exercise options; American legs can be assigned early.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(quant.main.box_spread_rate(989, 5000, 6000, 0.25), 4) AS box_rate

Compute the **year fraction** between two dates under a day-count convention -- the accrual basis used to prorate interest and discount factors.

functions.name: implied_carry_rate
functions.comment: Annual cost of carry implied by a spot and a futures price: ln(forward/spot)/ttm

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## implied_carry_rate

The annual rate implied by the gap between a spot price and a forward or futures price on the same underlying: `ln(forward / spot) / ttm`.

**Signature:** `implied_carry_rate(spot, forward, ttm)`; prices > 0, `ttm` in years.

**Meaning:** the net cost of carry, i.e. financing minus any income the underlying pays (dividends, lease rate, convenience yield). For gold, income is roughly zero, so this is the financing rate a cash-and-carry trade earns: buy spot, sell the future. Compare it with `tbill_rate` or `box_spread_rate`.

**Output:** a `DOUBLE` continuously compounded annual rate (0.05 = 5%/yr). NULL in -> NULL out.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Implied Carry Rate

Annualized basis between spot and a future, `ln(forward / spot) / ttm`.

```sql
SELECT quant.implied_carry_rate(4000, 4050, 0.25);  -- ~0.0497
```

- Continuously compounded; convert with `continuous_to_simple`.
- Negative when the future trades below spot (backwardation).

vgi.example_queries.description: Gold at 4000 spot with the 3-month future at 4050 implies ~4.97%/yr of carry.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(quant.main.implied_carry_rate(4000, 4050, 0.25), 4) AS carry

vgi.example_queries.description: Carry over a 3-month T-bill: what a cash-and-carry earns above cash.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(quant.main.implied_carry_rate(4000, 4050, 0.25) - quant.main.tbill_rate(0.0412, 91), 4) AS excess

tags.vgi.title: Implied Carry Rate

arguments.name: spot
arguments.description: Spot price of the underlying (> 0).

arguments.name: forward
arguments.description: Forward or futures price (> 0).

arguments.name: ttm
arguments.description: Time to maturity in years (> 0), e.g. days / 365.

examples: SELECT ROUND(quant.main.implied_carry_rate(4000, 4050, 0.25), 4) AS carry
SELECT ROUND(quant.main.implied_carry_rate(4000, 4050, 0.25) - quant.main.tbill_rate(0.0412, 91), 4) AS excess

functions.name: bond_price
functions.comment: Clean price of a fixed-rate bond at a given yield (par bond prices to face)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## bond_price

Compute the **clean** price of a fixed-rate coupon bond at a given yield.

**Signature:** `bond_price(face, coupon_rate, yield_rate, years, freq)` -- `face` is par value (> 0); `coupon_rate` and `yield_rate` are annual decimals (e.g. `0.05`); `years` is whole years to maturity (> 0); `freq` is the **literal** coupon frequency (`1`=annual, `2`=semiannual, `4`=quarterly, `12`=monthly).

**Output:** clean price as a `DOUBLE`. A par bond (coupon == yield) prices to ~`face`. Inverse of `bond_yield`. NULL in -> NULL out; `years <= 0` or an unknown `freq` raise.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Fixed-Rate Bond Price

Clean price of a fixed-rate bond given its yield to maturity.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT quant.bond_price(100, 0.05, 0.05, 10, 2);  -- ~100 (par)
```

## Notes

- `freq` must be a literal `1`, `2`, `4`, or `12`.
- Uses ActualActual(ISDA), compounded at the coupon frequency.
- A par bond (coupon == yield) prices to face value.

vgi.example_queries.description: Clean price of a 10-year 5% semiannual par bond (coupon == yield) is 100.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT quant.main.bond_price(100, 0.05, 0.05, 10, 2) AS clean_price

vgi.example_queries.description: When yield exceeds the coupon the bond trades at a discount (price < face).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT quant.main.bond_price(100, 0.05, 0.07, 10, 2) AS discount_price

tags.vgi.title: Fixed-Rate Bond Price

functions.name: present_value
functions.comment: Present value amount * exp(-rate * ttm) (continuous compounding)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## present_value

Compute the **present value** of a future cash amount under continuous compounding: `amount * exp(-rate * ttm)`.

**Signature:** `present_value(amount, rate, ttm)` -- `amount` is the future cash flow; `rate` is the continuously-compounded annual discount rate; `ttm` is the time horizon in years.

**Output:** the discounted value today as a `DOUBLE`. Equivalent to `amount * discount_factor(rate, ttm)`. NULL in -> NULL out.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Continuous Present Value

Present value of a future amount, `amount * exp(-rate * ttm)`.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT quant.present_value(100, 0.05, 1);  -- ~95.12
```

## Notes

- Continuous compounding.
- Equals `amount * discount_factor(rate, ttm)`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Present value of 100 due in one year, discounted continuously at 5% (~95.12).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT quant.main.present_value(100, 0.05, 1) AS pv

vgi.example_queries.description: Present value of 1000 due in two years at 5% is 1000 * exp(-0.10) (~904.84).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT quant.main.present_value(1000, 0.05, 2) AS pv

vgi.example_queries.description: Present value of a 2-year 5% semiannual coupon schedule settled 2026-06-15, discounting each cash flow at 4.5% continuous over its ACT/365 year_fraction (~100.84).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(SUM(quant.main.present_value(CASE WHEN n = 4 THEN 102.5 ELSE 2.5 END, 0.045, quant.main.year_fraction(DATE '2026-06-15', CAST(DATE '2026-06-15' + to_months(6 * n) AS DATE), 'ACT/365'))), 4) AS pv FROM range(1, 5) AS t(n)

tags.vgi.title: Continuous Present Value

functions.name: funding_rate_annual
functions.comment: Continuous annual rate equivalent to a perpetual-futures funding rate

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## funding_rate_annual

Annualizes a perpetual-futures funding rate onto the same continuous basis as the other carry functions: `ln(1 + rate) * 8760 / interval_hours`.

**Signature:** `funding_rate_annual(rate, interval_hours)`; `rate` is the per-interval rate as a decimal (0.0001 = 1 bp), `interval_hours` how often it is paid (8 on most venues, 1 on Hyperliquid).

**Sign:** positive means longs pay shorts, so it is what a short earns. A short perp plus a long future earns `funding_rate_annual(...) - implied_carry_rate(...)`.

**Output:** a `DOUBLE` continuously compounded annual rate (0.05 = 5%/yr). NULL in -> NULL out.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Annualized Funding Rate

Perp funding to a continuous annual rate.

```sql
SELECT quant.funding_rate_annual(0.0001, 8);  -- the 1 bp/8h floor, ~0.1095
```

- Treats each payment as compounding; the simple `rate * 1095` differs only slightly at normal rates.

vgi.example_queries.description: The common 1 bp per 8 hours funding floor is ~10.95%/yr.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(quant.main.funding_rate_annual(0.0001, 8), 4) AS annual

vgi.example_queries.description: A short perp hedged with a long future: funding minus futures carry.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(quant.main.funding_rate_annual(0.0001, 8) - quant.main.implied_carry_rate(4000, 4050, 0.25), 4) AS net_carry

tags.vgi.title: Annualized Funding Rate

arguments.name: rate
arguments.description: Funding rate per interval as a decimal (> -1).

arguments.name: interval_hours
arguments.description: Hours between funding payments (> 0).

examples: SELECT ROUND(quant.main.funding_rate_annual(0.0001, 8), 4) AS annual
SELECT ROUND(quant.main.funding_rate_annual(0.0001, 8) - quant.main.implied_carry_rate(4000, 4050, 0.25), 4) AS net_carry

functions.name: bs_delta
functions.comment: Black-Scholes delta d(value)/d(spot) of a European option

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## bs_delta

First-order Greek: the sensitivity of a European option's value to the underlying spot price, `d(value)/d(spot)`.

**Signature:** `bs_delta(spot, strike, rate, vol, ttm, opt_type)` -- same arguments as `bs_price`; `opt_type` is the literal `'call'`/`'put'`.

**Output:** a unitless `DOUBLE` in roughly `[0, 1]` for calls and `[-1, 0]` for puts. Use it for hedge ratios and directional exposure. NULL in -> NULL out; invalid inputs raise.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Black-Scholes Option Delta

Delta -- the rate of change of option value with respect to spot.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT quant.bs_delta(100, 100, 0.05, 0.2, 1, 'call');  -- ~0.637
```

## Notes

- Calls have positive delta (0..1); puts negative (-1..0).
- Commonly used as a hedge ratio against the underlying.

vgi.example_queries.description: Delta (hedge ratio) of an at-the-money 1-year European call; near 0.64.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT quant.main.bs_delta(100, 100, 0.05, 0.2, 1, 'call') AS call_delta

vgi.example_queries.description: Delta of the matching European put is negative (call delta minus 1).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT quant.main.bs_delta(100, 100, 0.05, 0.2, 1, 'put') AS put_delta

functions.comment: Modified duration of a fixed-rate bond at a given yield

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## bond_duration

Compute the **modified duration** of a fixed-rate bond at a given yield -- the first-order sensitivity of price to yield, in years.

**Signature:** `bond_duration(face, coupon_rate, yield_rate, years, freq)` -- same inputs as `bond_price`; `freq` is the literal coupon frequency (`1`/`2`/`4`/`12`).

**Output:** modified duration in years as a `DOUBLE`. A 1% (100 bp) yield rise drops price by roughly `duration%`. Duration is less than maturity for a coupon bond. NULL in -> NULL out; invalid inputs raise.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Fixed-Rate Bond Modified Duration

Modified duration -- price sensitivity to yield, in years.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT quant.bond_duration(100, 0.05, 0.05, 10, 2);  -- ~7.80
```

## Notes

- Modified (not Macaulay) duration.
- A 1% yield rise drops price by roughly `duration%`.
- Always less than maturity for a coupon-paying bond.

functions.name: tbill_rate
functions.comment: Continuous annual rate of a T-bill quoted on the bank-discount basis (ACT/360)

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## tbill_rate

Converts a Treasury bill's bank-discount quote into a continuously compounded annual rate, so it can be compared with the other carry functions.

**Signature:** `tbill_rate(discount_rate, days)`; `discount_rate` as a decimal (0.0412 for 4.12%), `days` to maturity (> 0). Price per 1 of face is `1 - discount_rate * days / 360`; the result is `-ln(price) / (days / 365)`.

**Use:** the risk-free benchmark. Yahoo's `^IRX` and Treasury's daily bill rates are discount quotes for the 13-week (91-day) bill.

**Output:** a `DOUBLE` continuously compounded annual rate (0.05 = 5%/yr). NULL in -> NULL out.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Treasury Bill Rate

Bank-discount T-bill quote to a continuous annual rate.

```sql
SELECT quant.tbill_rate(0.0412, 91);  -- ~0.0420
```

- Discount yields understate the true rate; this corrects for that and for ACT/360.

vgi.example_queries.description: A 91-day bill quoted at a 4.12% discount is ~4.20%/yr continuous.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ROUND(quant.main.tbill_rate(0.0412, 91), 4) AS bill_rate

vgi.example_queries.description: Bill-equivalent rates for a few quotes and tenors.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT days, ROUND(quant.main.tbill_rate(d, days), 4) AS rate FROM (VALUES (0.0412, 28), (0.0412, 91), (0.0400, 182)) q(d, days) ORDER BY days

tags.vgi.title: Treasury Bill Rate

arguments.name: discount_rate
arguments.description: Bank-discount yield as a decimal (0.0412 = 4.12%).

arguments.name: days
arguments.description: Days to maturity (> 0).

SELECT days, ROUND(quant.main.tbill_rate(d, days), 4) AS rate FROM (VALUES (0.0412, 28), (0.0412, 91), (0.0400, 182)) q(d, days) ORDER BY days

workers.title: VGI RabbitMQ Worker
workers.tagline: RabbitMQ broker state, queues, bindings and non-destructive stream reads as SQL in DuckDB (Go)
workers.subtitle: RabbitMQ broker state via the Management API, plus non-destructive stream reads.
workers.summary: RabbitMQ broker state as SQL tables through the Management HTTP API (queues, exchanges, bindings, connections, nodes, policies, permissions, health checks) plus non-destructive stream reads.
workers.doc_md:
# RabbitMQ in DuckDB

Query a RabbitMQ cluster's state with SQL and join it with anything else DuckDB reads.

- **Broker**: overview, nodes with memory/disk alarms and partitions, virtual hosts.
- **Topology**: queues (depth, consumers, rates, type, policy, arguments), exchanges, bindings.
- **Clients**: connections, channels, consumers.
- **Access**: users (no password hashes), permissions, topic permissions.
- **Config**: policies, operator policies, runtime parameters with masked credentials, shovels, definitions summary.
- **Health**: health checks, feature flags, deprecated features in use.
- **Messages**: `stream_messages` reads streams without consuming them; `peek_messages` peeks classic/quorum queues only with `peek_requeue := true`, because it re-queues what it fetches.

Credentials come from a `rabbitmq` DuckDB secret. Everything is read-only except the opt-in re-queueing peek.

example_queries.description: Cluster name, version and message backlog at a glance
example_queries.sql: SELECT cluster_name, rabbitmq_version, messages_ready, messages_unacknowledged, queues, connections FROM rabbitmq.main.overview()

example_queries.description: Resource alarms, memory headroom and partitions per node
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, mem_alarm, disk_free_alarm, round(100.0 * mem_used / mem_limit, 1) AS mem_pct, fd_used, len(partitions) AS partitions FROM rabbitmq.main.nodes() ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Virtual hosts ordered by backlog
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, default_queue_type, messages_ready, messages_unacknowledged FROM rabbitmq.main.vhosts() ORDER BY messages_ready DESC NULLS LAST, name

example_queries.description: Queues with a backlog, largest first
example_queries.sql: SELECT vhost, name, type, messages_ready, messages_unacknowledged, consumers FROM rabbitmq.main.queues() WHERE messages_ready > 0 ORDER BY messages_ready DESC, vhost, name

example_queries.description: User-declared exchanges in one vhost
example_queries.sql: SELECT vhost, name, type FROM rabbitmq.main.exchanges(vhost := 'shop') WHERE name NOT LIKE 'amq.%' AND name <> '' ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: The routing graph of one vhost (default-exchange bindings left out)
example_queries.sql: SELECT source, routing_key, destination_type, destination FROM rabbitmq.main.bindings(vhost := 'shop') WHERE source <> '' ORDER BY source, destination

example_queries.description: Connections per user and client library
example_queries.sql: SELECT user, client_product, count(*) AS connections FROM rabbitmq.main.connections() GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY connections DESC, user

example_queries.description: Channels holding unacknowledged messages
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, user, prefetch_count, messages_unacknowledged FROM rabbitmq.main.channels() WHERE messages_unacknowledged > 0 ORDER BY messages_unacknowledged DESC, name

example_queries.description: Consumers and combined prefetch per queue
example_queries.sql: SELECT vhost, queue, count(*) AS consumers, sum(prefetch_count) AS total_prefetch FROM rabbitmq.main.consumers() GROUP BY vhost, queue ORDER BY consumers DESC, vhost, queue

example_queries.description: Administrators
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, tags FROM rabbitmq.main.users() WHERE list_contains(tags, 'administrator') ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Users with full permissions on a vhost
example_queries.sql: SELECT user, vhost FROM rabbitmq.main.permissions() WHERE configure = '.*' AND write = '.*' AND read = '.*' ORDER BY user, vhost

example_queries.description: Routing-key restrictions on topic exchanges
example_queries.sql: SELECT user, vhost, exchange, write, read FROM rabbitmq.main.topic_permissions() ORDER BY user, vhost, exchange

example_queries.description: Policies with their message TTL
example_queries.sql: SELECT vhost, name, pattern, apply_to, definition['message-ttl'] AS ttl_ms FROM rabbitmq.main.policies() ORDER BY vhost, priority DESC, name

example_queries.description: Operator policies (limits users cannot override)
example_queries.sql: SELECT vhost, name, pattern, definition FROM rabbitmq.main.operator_policies() ORDER BY vhost, name

example_queries.description: Dynamic shovels and where they move messages (credentials masked)
example_queries.sql: SELECT vhost, name, json_extract_string(value, '$."src-queue"') AS src_queue, json_extract_string(value, '$."dest-uri"') AS dest_uri FROM rabbitmq.main.parameters(component := 'shovel') ORDER BY vhost, name

example_queries.description: The cluster name as stored in the global parameters
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, value FROM rabbitmq.main.global_parameters() WHERE name = 'cluster_name'

example_queries.description: Shovels that are not running and why
example_queries.sql: SELECT vhost, name, state, reason FROM rabbitmq.main.shovels() WHERE state <> 'running' ORDER BY vhost, name

example_queries.description: How many of each object the broker's definitions export holds
example_queries.sql: SELECT object_type, object_count FROM rabbitmq.main.definitions_summary() ORDER BY object_type

example_queries.description: Failing health checks and why
example_queries.sql: SELECT check_name, status, reason FROM rabbitmq.main.health_checks() WHERE NOT ok ORDER BY check_name

example_queries.description: Feature flags not yet enabled (must be enabled before upgrading)
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, stability FROM rabbitmq.main.feature_flags() WHERE state <> 'enabled' ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Deprecated features in use that block a future upgrade
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, deprecation_phase, doc_url FROM rabbitmq.main.deprecated_features() WHERE in_use ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Read a stream from the beginning without consuming it
example_queries.sql: SELECT sequence, key, payload_text::JSON->>'order_id' AS order_id, headers['tenant'] AS tenant FROM rabbitmq.main.stream_messages('shop', 'events') ORDER BY sequence

example_queries.description: Look at the first five messages of a classic queue (re-queues them: opt-in)
example_queries.sql: SELECT message_id, key, payload_text, headers['trace'] AS trace FROM rabbitmq.main.peek_messages('shop', 'orders.created', count := 5, peek_requeue := true)

example_queries.description: Which destinations a message published to the orders topic exchange with key orders.created.eu reaches
example_queries.sql: SELECT destination FROM rabbitmq.main.bindings(vhost := 'shop') WHERE source = 'orders' AND rabbitmq.main.topic_matches(routing_key, 'orders.created.eu') ORDER BY destination

example_queries.description: Shovel source URIs with credentials masked (parameters already masks; this works on any text)
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, rabbitmq.main.mask_uri(json_extract_string(value, '$."src-uri"')) AS src FROM rabbitmq.main.parameters(component := 'shovel') ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: How many users are restricted on each topic exchange
example_queries.sql: SELECT exchange, count(*) AS users FROM rabbitmq.main.topic_permissions(vhost := 'shop') GROUP BY exchange ORDER BY exchange

example_queries.description: Message counts per routing key from offset 2 on
example_queries.sql: SELECT key, count(*) AS messages, sum(payload_bytes) AS bytes FROM rabbitmq.main.stream_messages('shop', 'events', start_offset := '2', max_messages := 100000) GROUP BY key ORDER BY messages DESC, key

example_queries.description: Users with no permission on any vhost
example_queries.sql: SELECT u.name FROM rabbitmq.main.users() u ANTI JOIN rabbitmq.main.permissions() p ON p.user = u.name ORDER BY u.name

example_queries.description: Shovels by state
example_queries.sql: SELECT state, count(*) AS shovels FROM rabbitmq.main.shovels() GROUP BY state ORDER BY state

example_queries.description: Which queues each policy applies to
example_queries.sql: SELECT p.name AS policy, q.name AS queue FROM rabbitmq.main.policies(vhost := 'shop') p JOIN rabbitmq.main.queues(vhost := 'shop') q ON q.policy = p.name ORDER BY p.name, q.name

example_queries.description: Vhosts that are not running on every node
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, map_keys(cluster_state) AS nodes FROM rabbitmq.main.vhosts() WHERE len(list_filter(map_values(cluster_state), lambda s: s <> 'running')) > 0 ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Order queues in the shop vhost (vhost and regex pushed to the API) with their dead-letter exchange
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, type, arguments['x-dead-letter-exchange'] AS dlx, policy FROM rabbitmq.main.queues(vhost := 'shop', name := '^orders\.', use_regex := true) ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Queues piling up with no consumer
example_queries.sql: SELECT vhost, name FROM rabbitmq.main.queues() WHERE consumers = 0 AND messages_ready > 0 ORDER BY vhost, name

example_queries.description: Who can do what in one vhost
example_queries.sql: SELECT user, configure, write, read FROM rabbitmq.main.permissions(vhost := 'shop') ORDER BY user

example_queries.description: What kinds of messages sit in a dead-letter queue
example_queries.sql: SELECT content_type, count(*) AS messages, max(payload_bytes) AS largest FROM rabbitmq.main.peek_messages('shop', 'orders.dlq', count := 100, peek_requeue := true) GROUP BY content_type ORDER BY messages DESC

example_queries.description: Runtime parameters by component
example_queries.sql: SELECT component, count(*) AS parameters FROM rabbitmq.main.parameters() GROUP BY component ORDER BY component

example_queries.description: Nodes that need attention
example_queries.sql: SELECT name FROM rabbitmq.main.nodes() WHERE mem_alarm OR disk_free_alarm OR len(partitions) > 0 OR NOT running ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Feature flags by stability and state
example_queries.sql: SELECT stability, state, count(*) AS flags FROM rabbitmq.main.feature_flags() GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY stability, state

example_queries.description: Deprecated features by phase
example_queries.sql: SELECT deprecation_phase, count(*) AS features FROM rabbitmq.main.deprecated_features() GROUP BY deprecation_phase ORDER BY deprecation_phase

example_queries.description: Channels and consumers per vhost
example_queries.sql: SELECT vhost, count(*) AS channels, sum(consumer_count) AS consumers FROM rabbitmq.main.channels() GROUP BY vhost ORDER BY vhost

example_queries.description: Every global parameter's name
example_queries.sql: SELECT name FROM rabbitmq.main.global_parameters() ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Connections blocked by a resource alarm in one vhost

example_queries.description: Each queue's backlog next to who consumes it

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The main schema holds every function. Each table function takes an optional secret_name named argument (default: the rabbitmq secret whose scope matches). Most listings take vhost := (pushed into the API path); queues, exchanges, connections and channels also take name := (case-insensitive substring, or a regex with use_regex := true) and page_size := (max 500). Arguments, policy definitions and headers are `MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)` with values as text: read one with arguments['x-queue-type']. Times are `TIMESTAMPTZ`, counters `BIGINT`, rates `DOUBLE` per second. stream_messages and peek_messages share the messaging columns sequence, timestamp, key, payload (`BLOB`), payload_text, headers. Two offline scalars (topic pattern matching and URI credential masking) need no secret.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

Management functions call the Management HTTP API named by a `rabbitmq` secret (username/password or an OAuth 2 bearer token, optional TLS client certificates) with read-only GETs, so results reflect that user's tags and vhost permissions. `stream_messages` reads streams over AMQP (the secret's `AMQP_URL`) from an offset spec without consuming them. `peek_messages` is the one exception to read-only: it fetches from a classic or quorum queue and re-queues what it took (marking it redelivered), so it runs only with `peek_requeue := true`.

Conventions: `vhost :=` and `name :=` filters are pushed into the API, listings page with an externalized cursor, arguments and headers are `MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)`, times `TIMESTAMPTZ`, rates per second. Passwords are never returned and credentials inside URIs are masked.

Start with `overview()` and `queues()`; use `bindings()` to follow routes and `health_checks()` for alarms.

functions.name: stream_messages
functions.comment: Read a stream's messages from an offset or time without consuming them (non-destructive)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Read messages from a RabbitMQ stream (queue type stream) without consuming them: streams are append-only logs, so reading never removes or reorders anything. Uses AMQP 0-9-1 (the secret's AMQP_URL) with x-stream-offset. Positional: vhost, stream. Named: start_offset ('first' default, 'last', 'next' or a numeric offset), start_timestamp (`TIMESTAMPTZ`, overrides start_offset), max_messages (default 1000), batch_size (default 500), idle_timeout_ms (default 1000: the scan ends when the tail is reached), secret_name. Columns: vhost, queue, sequence (stream offset), timestamp, key (routing key), exchange, payload `BLOB`, payload_text, payload_bytes, headers `MAP`, redelivered and AMQP properties. The next offset is the externalized cursor, so long reads resume across batches. Refuses non-stream queues (use peek_messages for those).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## stream_messages(vhost, stream, start_offset := 'first', start_timestamp := NULL, max_messages := 1000)

Non-destructive read of a stream over AMQP from an offset spec; the stream is never consumed.

functions.name: peek_messages
functions.comment: Fetch and re-queue messages from a classic or quorum queue (opt-in: peek_requeue := true)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: WARNING: classic and quorum queues have no read-only peek. peek_messages fetches with ackmode reject_requeue_true, so every fetched message is re-queued: it is marked redelivered, a quorum queue counts a delivery attempt against its delivery-limit (a message can be dead-lettered or dropped), and with active consumers the order can change. Use stream_messages for streams (truly non-destructive). Fetches up to count messages from the head of a classic or quorum queue with POST /api/queues/{vhost}/{queue}/get. Positional: vhost, queue. Named: count (default 10), peek_requeue (must be true, default false = error), truncate (body bytes, default 50000), secret_name. Columns as stream_messages; sequence is NULL.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## peek_messages(vhost, queue, count := 10, peek_requeue := false)

**WARNING: classic and quorum queues have no read-only peek. peek_messages fetches with ackmode reject_requeue_true, so every fetched message is re-queued: it is marked redelivered, a quorum queue counts a delivery attempt against its delivery-limit (a message can be dead-lettered or dropped), and with active consumers the order can change. ** It refuses to run unless you pass `peek_requeue := true`. Prefer `stream_messages` for streams.

vgi.example_queries.description: Look at the first five messages of a classic queue (re-queues them: opt-in)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT message_id, key, payload_text, headers['trace'] AS trace FROM rabbitmq.main.peek_messages('shop', 'orders.created', count := 5, peek_requeue := true)

vgi.example_queries.description: What kinds of messages sit in a dead-letter queue
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT content_type, count(*) AS messages, max(payload_bytes) AS largest FROM rabbitmq.main.peek_messages('shop', 'orders.dlq', count := 100, peek_requeue := true) GROUP BY content_type ORDER BY messages DESC

functions.name: health_checks
functions.comment: Run the broker's health checks (alarms, certificate expiry, quorum criticality, readiness)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Runs the management health-check endpoints and returns one row per check: alarms (cluster-wide resource alarms), local_alarms, certificate_expiration (listener certificates expiring within cert_within cert_unit), node_is_quorum_critical (stopping this node would lose quorum), virtual_hosts, is_in_service, below_node_connection_limit and ready_to_serve_clients. Columns: check_name, ok, status, reason, http_status, details JSON. A failed check (HTTP 503) is a row with ok=false, never an error. Checks a broker does not have (older versions) are omitted. Named args: cert_within (default 1), cert_unit (days|weeks|months|years, default months), secret_name.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## health_checks(cert_within := 1, cert_unit := 'months')

Every health check as a row; failures are rows with `ok = false`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Failing health checks and why
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT check_name, status, reason FROM rabbitmq.main.health_checks() WHERE NOT ok ORDER BY check_name

vgi.example_queries.description: One healthy/unhealthy verdict, with certificates checked 30 days ahead
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT bool_and(ok) AS healthy, count(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT ok) AS failing FROM rabbitmq.main.health_checks(cert_within := 30, cert_unit := 'days')

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: check_name
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Check name: alarms, local_alarms, certificate_expiration, node_is_quorum_critical, virtual_hosts, is_in_service, below_node_connection_limit, ready_to_serve_clients.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: ok
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: true when the check passed (HTTP 200).

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: status
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: The check's status: 'ok' or 'failed'.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: reason
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Why the check failed (or a note when it passed, e.g. 'single node cluster'); NULL otherwise.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: http_status
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: HTTP status of the check endpoint (200 ok, 503 failed).

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: details
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: The full check response as JSON (alarm lists, expiring certificates, critical queues).

tags.vgi.title: Health Checks

arguments.name: cert_within
arguments.description: certificate_expiration fails when a listener certificate expires within this many cert_unit.

arguments.name: cert_unit
arguments.description: Unit of cert_within.

arguments.name: secret_name

examples: SELECT check_name, status, reason FROM rabbitmq.main.health_checks() WHERE NOT ok ORDER BY check_name
SELECT bool_and(ok) AS healthy, count(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT ok) AS failing FROM rabbitmq.main.health_checks(cert_within := 30, cert_unit := 'days')

workers.summary: Transactional SQL tables stored as RDF in an Oxigraph dataset, so the same data can be queried as ordinary SQL rows or with local SPARQL and graph traversal.
workers.doc_md:
## RDF database worker

Persistent SQL tables backed by an Oxigraph RDF dataset. Supports SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, CREATE/DROP TABLE, schemas, RETURNING, defaults, NOT NULL, primary/unique keys and immediate foreign keys. Native SQL runs in the host engine; data and table definitions persist as RDF. Transactions use immutable snapshots and reject concurrent writer conflicts. Attach with database set to a durable directory, or omit it for a temporary database. Query the same data as typed SQL rows or RDF terms using local read-only SPARQL and bounded graph traversal. Stable resource identities connect the two query models. Foreign keys produce transactional resource-to-resource RDF edges. The backend enforces CHECK constraints, but the tested SQL engines cannot send native CHECK definitions.

SQL data and definitions live in an Oxigraph dataset. The database directory contains immutable committed generations and private transaction workspaces. Commit publishes a complete generation; rollback discards private writes.

## Sources and references

- [Oxigraph](https://github.com/oxigraph/oxigraph) and its Python binding [pyoxigraph](https://pyoxigraph.readthedocs.io/) — the RDF store and SPARQL engine underneath
- [RDF 1.1 Concepts](https://www.w3.org/TR/rdf11-concepts/) — the IRI, literal, datatype and language-tag model the stored rows and returned terms follow
- [SPARQL 1.1 Query Language](https://www.w3.org/TR/sparql11-query/) — the query language `rdf_sparql` accepts

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## SQL tables and RDF graphs

Create application tables here and query them with ordinary SQL. Schema names and quoted identifiers retain their spelling.

Query relationships with local read-only SPARQL or bounded graph traversal. Stable row IRIs connect ordinary typed SQL rows to RDF terms without losing literal datatypes or language tags. Foreign-key edges share SQL transaction boundaries; external named graphs can hold imported RDF. Choose SQL for tabular analysis and graph queries for paths and neighborhoods.

functions.name: rdf_reachable
functions.comment: Traverse RDF relationships with cycle detection and bounded minimum-depth results

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Breadth-first RDF traversal starting from node. Returns each reachable node once with depth equal to the minimum number of edges from the start, excluding the start itself even when cycles exist. max_depth defaults to 8 and cannot exceed 64. graph_iri, predicate_iri and direction have the same meaning as rdf_neighbors. The default graph contains SQL foreign-key relationships. Traversal has row, examined-edge and wall-time limits; exceeding a limit raises an error. Order results explicitly, for example ORDER BY depth, node.

## rdf_quads()

Use `graph_iri := 'urn:vgi:rdf:catalog'` to select one graph, or omit it to read all graphs. Read the actual RDF storage as four `VARCHAR` columns: `subject`, `predicate`, `object`, `graph`. Read an existing SQL table with ordinary typed columns plus __rdf_iri containing its stable RDF row IRI. Supply raw schema and table names separately. If a user column already has that name, underscores are appended until it is unique. Identities survive updates but disappear on DELETE; replacement tables get new identities. Use these identifiers to join relational rows with graph queries. Requires a user-created table; the executable examples create and roll back a small people/orders dataset first.

### Operation

The function reads the current attachment and participates in its SQL transaction. Use explicit SQL ordering when row order matters. A failure returns an error; retry the whole transaction after a serialization conflict. SQL examples are listed separately.

functions.name: rdf_sparql
functions.comment: Query RDF with bounded local SPARQL and join the results with SQL tables

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Execute local read-only SPARQL SELECT, ASK, CONSTRUCT or DESCRIBE. SELECT variables become SQL columns of `STRUCT(kind, value, datatype, language)`, preserving unbound values as NULL; use column.value for an IRI or literal lexical value. ASK returns answer `BOOLEAN`; graph results return subject, predicate, object term structs. SERVICE and remote access are disabled. Use GRAPH clauses, or union_default := true. Results are frozen once per statement. max_rows (default 10000) and timeout_ms (default 30000) are hard bounds; operator ceilings also apply. A limit error fails the query instead of returning incomplete results.

workers.title: Item Recommender
workers.tagline: Collaborative-filtering recommendations (ALS) for DuckDB (Python, implicit)
workers.subtitle: Recommend items and find similar items from user interaction data.
workers.summary: Collaborative-filtering recommendation worker (implicit-feedback ALS) for DuckDB via VGI.
workers.doc_md:
# Recommender: Collaborative-Filtering Recommendations in SQL

Generate personalized product and content recommendations directly in DuckDB SQL with implicit-feedback **Alternating Least Squares (ALS)** collaborative filtering -- no separate ML pipeline, notebook, or model server required.

This VGI worker turns a single relation of `(user, item, value)` interactions -- clicks, purchases, plays, ratings, or any engagement signal -- into top-N recommendations, item-to-item similarity, and per-user suggestions. It is built for data engineers, analysts, and application developers who want a fast, reproducible recommender system they can call from a query instead of standing up a dedicated service. Because it runs as a DuckDB attachment, you can join recommendations straight back to your catalog tables, filter them, and ship them to downstream tables or dashboards in a single statement.

Under the hood the worker fits an implicit-feedback ALS matrix-factorization model with the [`implicit`](https://github.com/benfred/implicit) library by Ben Frederickson -- a fast, Cython/BLAS-accelerated implementation of the classic ALS algorithm for implicit datasets. Each call buffers the whole interaction relation, learns latent user and item factors, and scores candidates by the dot product (recommendations) or the cosine of the item factors (similarity). Results are deterministic (pinned `random_state`, single-threaded BLAS), and `value` is treated as the interaction confidence, defaulting to `1.0` when the value column is omitted. See the [implicit documentation](https://benfred.github.io/implicit/) and the [collaborative filtering overview](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collaborative_filtering) for background on the method.

## Function surface

The worker covers the three everyday collaborative-filtering workloads: personalized top-N recommendations for the whole user base at once, on-demand recommendations for a single target user, and item-to-item nearest-neighbour lookups (the classic *"people who liked X also liked Y"* / related-items surface).

Every recommendation function takes the interaction relation as a positional `(user, item, value)` subquery (`Arg(0)`) and accepts the column roles and hyperparameters as named arguments (`user := ...`, `item := ...`, `value := ...`, `n := ...`, `factors := ...`). The relation's columns are the data; the named arguments just declare which column plays the user, item, and confidence role, so the same query works over any interaction table by pointing the roles at its columns.

example_queries.description: Top-3 recommended items per user (recommend_all), ranked best-first.
example_queries.sql: SELECT user, item, rank FROM recommender.main.recommend_all((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('u1','A',1.0),('u1','B',1.0),('u1','C',1.0),('u2','A',1.0),('u2','B',1.0),('u2','C',1.0),('u3','A',1.0),('u3','B',1.0),('u4','A',1.0),('u4','B',1.0)) AS events(u, i, v)), user := 'u', item := 'i', value := 'v', n := 3) ORDER BY user, rank

example_queries.description: Top-2 nearest-neighbour items per item (similar_items) by ALS cosine.
example_queries.sql: SELECT item, similar_item, rank FROM recommender.main.similar_items((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('u1','A',1.0),('u1','B',1.0),('u1','C',1.0),('u2','A',1.0),('u2','B',1.0),('u2','C',1.0),('u3','A',1.0),('u3','B',1.0),('u4','A',1.0),('u4','B',1.0)) AS events(u, i, v)), user := 'u', item := 'i', value := 'v', n := 2) ORDER BY item, rank

example_queries.description: Top-2 recommendations for one target user (recommend_for), ranked best-first.
example_queries.sql: SELECT item, rank FROM recommender.main.recommend_for((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('u1','A',1.0),('u1','B',1.0),('u1','C',1.0),('u2','A',1.0),('u2','B',1.0),('u2','C',1.0),('u3','A',1.0),('u3','B',1.0),('u4','A',1.0),('u4','B',1.0)) AS events(u, i, v)), user := 'u', item := 'i', value := 'v', target_user := 'u3', n := 2) ORDER BY rank

example_queries.description: Explain each viewer's top recommendation (recommend_all) with the title they already watched that is most similar to it (similar_items), e.g. cal gets Matrix because of Dune.
example_queries.sql: WITH plays AS (SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('ana','Alien',3.0),('ana','Dune',2.0),('ana','Matrix',4.0),('ben','Alien',1.0),('ben','Dune',5.0),('ben','Matrix',2.0),('ben','Blade Runner',3.0),('cal','Dune',2.0),('cal','Blade Runner',4.0),('dee','Notebook',5.0),('dee','Titanic',2.0),('dee','Amelie',3.0),('eve','Notebook',2.0),('eve','Titanic',4.0),('fay','Titanic',3.0),('fay','Amelie',2.0),('fay','Alien',1.0)) AS t(viewer, title, n_plays)), recs AS (SELECT user AS viewer, item AS title FROM recommender.main.recommend_all((SELECT viewer, title, n_plays FROM plays), user := 'viewer', item := 'title', value := 'n_plays', n := 1)), sims AS (SELECT item, similar_item, similarity FROM recommender.main.similar_items((SELECT viewer, title, n_plays FROM plays), user := 'viewer', item := 'title', value := 'n_plays', n := 10)) SELECT r.viewer, r.title AS recommended, arg_max(s.similar_item, s.similarity) AS because_you_watched, round(max(s.similarity), 3) AS similarity FROM recs r JOIN plays p ON p.viewer = r.viewer JOIN sims s ON s.item = r.title AND s.similar_item = p.title GROUP BY r.viewer, r.title ORDER BY r.viewer

example_queries.description: Score viewer eve's top-3 ALS recommendations (recommend_for) by their summed item-item similarity to the titles eve watched (similar_items) -- a second, item-based signal to compare or blend with the ALS ranking.
example_queries.sql: WITH plays AS (SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('ana','Alien',3.0),('ana','Dune',2.0),('ana','Matrix',4.0),('ben','Alien',1.0),('ben','Dune',5.0),('ben','Matrix',2.0),('ben','Blade Runner',3.0),('cal','Dune',2.0),('cal','Blade Runner',4.0),('dee','Notebook',5.0),('dee','Titanic',2.0),('dee','Amelie',3.0),('eve','Notebook',2.0),('eve','Titanic',4.0),('fay','Titanic',3.0),('fay','Amelie',2.0),('fay','Alien',1.0)) AS t(viewer, title, n_plays)), recs AS (SELECT item AS title, score, rank FROM recommender.main.recommend_for((SELECT viewer, title, n_plays FROM plays), user := 'viewer', item := 'title', value := 'n_plays', target_user := 'eve', n := 3)), sims AS (SELECT item, similar_item, similarity FROM recommender.main.similar_items((SELECT viewer, title, n_plays FROM plays), user := 'viewer', item := 'title', value := 'n_plays', n := 10)) SELECT r.rank, r.title, round(r.score, 3) AS als_score, round(sum(s.similarity), 3) AS item_similarity_support FROM recs r JOIN plays p ON p.viewer = 'eve' JOIN sims s ON s.item = r.title AND s.similar_item = p.title GROUP BY r.rank, r.title, r.score ORDER BY r.rank

example_queries.description: Top recommendation per user from the built-in sample dataset (recommend_all over sample_interactions), joined back to the dataset to count how many users already interacted with the recommended item: u3 and u4 both get C, which 2 users already have.
example_queries.sql: WITH recs AS (SELECT "user", item FROM recommender.main.recommend_all((SELECT * FROM recommender.main.sample_interactions), n := 1)) SELECT r."user", r.item, count(DISTINCT s."user") AS users_already_interacted FROM recs r JOIN recommender.main.sample_interactions s ON s.item = r.item GROUP BY r."user", r.item ORDER BY r."user"

tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Recommendation Functions

Collaborative-filtering recommendation table functions powered by implicit-feedback **Alternating Least Squares (ALS)**. Each function takes a single relation of `(user, item, value)` interactions as a subquery and fits a matrix-factorization model over the whole user x item matrix before emitting results.

## Key concepts

- **Interaction relation** -- one row per user/item interaction; `value` is the interaction confidence and defaults to `1.0` when omitted.
- **Latent factors** -- ALS learns dense user and item vectors; scores are dot products (recommendations) or cosines (item similarity).
- **Determinism** -- a pinned `random_state` and single-threaded BLAS make every call reproducible.

## When to use

Reach for these functions to generate personalized recommendations, build 'people who liked X also liked Y' related-item surfaces, or score a single user on demand -- all directly in SQL, without a separate ML service or feature pipeline.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT user, item, rank FROM recommender.main.recommend_all((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('u1','A',1.0),('u1','B',1.0),('u1','C',1.0),('u2','A',1.0),('u2','B',1.0),('u2','C',1.0),('u3','A',1.0),('u3','B',1.0),('u4','A',1.0),('u4','B',1.0)) AS events(u, i, v)), user := 'u', item := 'i', value := 'v', n := 3) ORDER BY user, rank

vgi.example_queries.description: Top-2 nearest-neighbour items per item (similar_items) by ALS cosine.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT item, similar_item, rank FROM recommender.main.similar_items((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('u1','A',1.0),('u1','B',1.0),('u1','C',1.0),('u2','A',1.0),('u2','B',1.0),('u2','C',1.0),('u3','A',1.0),('u3','B',1.0),('u4','A',1.0),('u4','B',1.0)) AS events(u, i, v)), user := 'u', item := 'i', value := 'v', n := 2) ORDER BY item, rank

vgi.example_queries.description: Top-2 recommendations for one target user (recommend_for), ranked best-first.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT item, rank FROM recommender.main.recommend_for((SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('u1','A',1.0),('u1','B',1.0),('u1','C',1.0),('u2','A',1.0),('u2','B',1.0),('u2','C',1.0),('u3','A',1.0),('u3','B',1.0),('u4','A',1.0),('u4','B',1.0)) AS events(u, i, v)), user := 'u', item := 'i', value := 'v', target_user := 'u3', n := 2) ORDER BY rank

vgi.example_queries.description: Explain each viewer's top recommendation (recommend_all) with the title they already watched that is most similar to it (similar_items), e.g. cal gets Matrix because of Dune.
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH plays AS (SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('ana','Alien',3.0),('ana','Dune',2.0),('ana','Matrix',4.0),('ben','Alien',1.0),('ben','Dune',5.0),('ben','Matrix',2.0),('ben','Blade Runner',3.0),('cal','Dune',2.0),('cal','Blade Runner',4.0),('dee','Notebook',5.0),('dee','Titanic',2.0),('dee','Amelie',3.0),('eve','Notebook',2.0),('eve','Titanic',4.0),('fay','Titanic',3.0),('fay','Amelie',2.0),('fay','Alien',1.0)) AS t(viewer, title, n_plays)), recs AS (SELECT user AS viewer, item AS title FROM recommender.main.recommend_all((SELECT viewer, title, n_plays FROM plays), user := 'viewer', item := 'title', value := 'n_plays', n := 1)), sims AS (SELECT item, similar_item, similarity FROM recommender.main.similar_items((SELECT viewer, title, n_plays FROM plays), user := 'viewer', item := 'title', value := 'n_plays', n := 10)) SELECT r.viewer, r.title AS recommended, arg_max(s.similar_item, s.similarity) AS because_you_watched, round(max(s.similarity), 3) AS similarity FROM recs r JOIN plays p ON p.viewer = r.viewer JOIN sims s ON s.item = r.title AND s.similar_item = p.title GROUP BY r.viewer, r.title ORDER BY r.viewer

vgi.example_queries.description: Score viewer eve's top-3 ALS recommendations (recommend_for) by their summed item-item similarity to the titles eve watched (similar_items) -- a second, item-based signal to compare or blend with the ALS ranking.
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH plays AS (SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('ana','Alien',3.0),('ana','Dune',2.0),('ana','Matrix',4.0),('ben','Alien',1.0),('ben','Dune',5.0),('ben','Matrix',2.0),('ben','Blade Runner',3.0),('cal','Dune',2.0),('cal','Blade Runner',4.0),('dee','Notebook',5.0),('dee','Titanic',2.0),('dee','Amelie',3.0),('eve','Notebook',2.0),('eve','Titanic',4.0),('fay','Titanic',3.0),('fay','Amelie',2.0),('fay','Alien',1.0)) AS t(viewer, title, n_plays)), recs AS (SELECT item AS title, score, rank FROM recommender.main.recommend_for((SELECT viewer, title, n_plays FROM plays), user := 'viewer', item := 'title', value := 'n_plays', target_user := 'eve', n := 3)), sims AS (SELECT item, similar_item, similarity FROM recommender.main.similar_items((SELECT viewer, title, n_plays FROM plays), user := 'viewer', item := 'title', value := 'n_plays', n := 10)) SELECT r.rank, r.title, round(r.score, 3) AS als_score, round(sum(s.similarity), 3) AS item_similarity_support FROM recs r JOIN plays p ON p.viewer = 'eve' JOIN sims s ON s.item = r.title AND s.similar_item = p.title GROUP BY r.rank, r.title, r.score ORDER BY r.rank

# sample_interactions

A small, static, built-in interaction dataset -- 10 `(user, item, value)` rows -- exposed as a browsable view so you can see the exact input shape the recommendation functions expect without supplying your own data. `SELECT` from it freely (it fits no model and touches no network), then feed it straight into `recommend_all`, `similar_items`, or `recommend_for` as their interaction relation. Its columns are named `user`, `item`, and `value`, which are exactly the functions' default role arguments, so `recommend_all((SELECT * FROM recommender.main.sample_interactions))` works with no role arguments at all.

## Contents
A deliberately rigged signal: users `u1`/`u2` interacted with items `A`, `B`, and `C`; `u3`/`u4` with only `A` and `B`. Collaborative filtering therefore recommends the unseen item `C` to `u3` and `u4`, and treats `A` and `B` as each other's nearest neighbours -- handy for a first, self-contained end-to-end call.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## sample_interactions

A built-in, static `(user, item, value)` interaction dataset (10 rows) exposed as a browsable view. Use it to learn the input shape the recommendation functions expect and as a ready-made relation to try them on -- no data of your own required.

### Columns

- `user` -- interacting user id (`VARCHAR`).
- `item` -- interacted item id (`VARCHAR`).
- `value` -- interaction strength / confidence (`DOUBLE`, all `1.0` here).

### Notes

The column names match the functions' default role arguments, so the whole view can be passed as the interaction relation with no `user :=` / `item :=` / `value :=` arguments. The rows carry a planted signal: `C` is the novel recommendation for `u3`/`u4`, and `A`/`B` are mutual nearest neighbours.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# recommend_for

Single-user collaborative-filtering recommender. Fits implicit-feedback ALS over the supplied `(user, item, value)` interaction relation and returns the **top-N recommended items for one target user** (`target_user`, a named scalar argument), excluding items that user has already interacted with.

## When to use
Use this for an on-demand 'recommended for you' list for a specific user. For the whole user base in one pass use `recommend_all`; for item-to-item neighbours use `similar_items`.

## Inputs
- `Arg(0)`: a `(SELECT user, item, value)` subquery -- the interaction relation.
- `user`, `item`, `value`: names of the columns playing each role.
- `target_user`: the id of the single user to recommend for (named scalar).
- `n`: number of recommendations (default 10).
- `factors`: ALS latent-factor count (default 50, clamped on tiny matrices).

## Output
Rows of `(item, score, rank)`; `score` is the ALS dot-product score and `rank` is 1-based (1 = best).

## Behavior & edge cases
An unknown `target_user` yields zero rows (not an error). Already-seen items are excluded. `value` is interaction confidence and defaults to 1.0 when absent. Deterministic (pinned random_state, single-threaded BLAS).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## recommend_for

Top-N collaborative-filtering recommendations for a **single target user**, computed with implicit-feedback ALS over the supplied interaction relation.

### Usage

Pass the interaction relation as the positional `(user, item, value)` subquery, name the role columns, and set `target_user` to the id of the one user to score (plus `n`, the number of recommendations). Each output row is `(item, score, rank)`, ordered by `rank`. A ready-to-run demonstration lives in this function's example queries.

### Notes

- `target_user` is a named scalar argument naming the one user to score.
- An unknown `target_user` returns an empty result rather than raising.
- Already-seen items are never recommended; `value` (confidence) defaults to 1.0 if the column is missing.

# recommend_all

Batch collaborative-filtering recommender. Consumes a whole relation of `(user, item, value)` interactions, fits an implicit-feedback Alternating Least Squares (ALS) model over the entire user x item matrix, and returns the **top-N recommended items for every user** that appears in the input.

## When to use
Use this when you want personalized recommendations for the full user base in one pass -- e.g. precomputing a 'recommended for you' shelf for every user. For a single user prefer `recommend_for`; for item-to-item neighbours prefer `similar_items`.

## Inputs
- `Arg(0)`: a `(SELECT user, item, value)` subquery -- the interaction relation.
- `user`, `item`, `value`: names of the columns playing each role.
- `n`: recommendations per user (default 10).
- `factors`: ALS latent-factor count (default 50, clamped on tiny matrices).

## Output
Rows of `(user, item, score, rank)`; `score` is the ALS dot-product score and `rank` is 1-based within each user (1 = best).

## Behavior & edge cases
Items the user has already interacted with are excluded. `value` is the interaction confidence and defaults to 1.0 when the value column is absent. Results are deterministic (pinned random_state, single-threaded BLAS).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## recommend_all

Top-N collaborative-filtering recommendations for **all** users, computed with implicit-feedback ALS over the supplied interaction relation.

### Usage

Pass the interaction relation as the positional `(user, item, value)` subquery and name the role columns plus `n` (recommendations per user). Each output row is `(user, item, score, rank)`; order by `user` then `rank` for a stable, per-user ranked list. A ready-to-run demonstration lives in this function's example queries.

### Notes

- One ALS model is fit over the entire matrix, so the whole relation is buffered before any rows are emitted.
- Already-seen items are never recommended back to a user.
- `value` (confidence) defaults to 1.0 if the column is missing; `factors` is auto-clamped on small matrices.
