workers.title: Sigma Detection-Rule Evaluation
workers.tagline: Evaluate Sigma detection rules over log rows in DuckDB (Python)
workers.subtitle: Match log events against Sigma detection rules, check that rules compile, and list the fields they use.
workers.summary: Evaluate Sigma detection rules against log/event rows for SQL, powered by pySigma
workers.doc_md:
# Sigma Detection Rules in SQL

![Sigma logo](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SigmaHQ/sigma/master/images/Sigma_0.3.png)

Run [Sigma](https://sigmahq.io) detection rules — the open, vendor-neutral standard for **detection-as-code** — directly over your log and event tables in SQL, powered by [pySigma](https://github.com/SigmaHQ/pySigma).

This extension brings SIEM-style threat detection and threat hunting into DuckDB. If you have events as rows (Windows Security logs, EDR telemetry, cloud audit trails, web/proxy logs, or any JSON records), you can take a Sigma rule and ask, per row, "does this event match?" — without exporting data to a separate SIEM. It is built for detection engineers, threat hunters, incident responders, and data engineers who want to test, triage, and measure detection coverage where the data already lives. It is a defensive security tool and part of Query Farm's cyber analytics cluster alongside YARA, IOC, CVE, PE, and X.509 workers.

Under the hood, each rule's YAML is parsed and compiled once by pySigma — the reference Sigma implementation maintained by [SigmaHQ](https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma) — into a boolean condition tree, then evaluated against every row. Compilation is cached by rule text, so a constant rule scanned across a whole log column compiles a single time and only the per-row match runs hot, keeping column scans cheap. The evaluator honors Sigma field modifiers (contains, startswith, endswith, regex, and the rest), wildcard string matching, numeric, boolean and null values, and the full selector grammar (`1 of selection_*`, `all of them`, and friends). Rules and their metadata, including [MITRE ATT&CK](https://attack.mitre.org) tags, are read straight from the rule text.

The workflow is deliberately simple: keep your events as rows, express detection logic as Sigma YAML, and evaluate one against the other as an ordinary SQL predicate. Because a constant rule compiles once and only the boolean match runs per row, applying a detection across a whole log column stays cheap enough to run interactively. Beyond matching, the catalog also lets you validate a rule library before you trust it, and introspect a rule's header metadata and referenced fields for triage, index planning, and coverage analysis — so a single attached worker covers the detect / validate / plan loop of detection engineering.

A typical hunt applies a matcher predicate per row over a log table (for example in a `WHERE` clause against `to_json(row)`), while separate helpers validate that a rule library compiles and introspect rule metadata and referenced fields for planning. A browsable discovery table lists the field modifiers the evaluator supports.

Learn more from the [Sigma documentation](https://sigmahq.io/docs/), the [pySigma reference docs](https://sigmahq-pysigma.readthedocs.io), and the [pySigma source repository](https://github.com/SigmaHQ/pySigma).

INSTALL vgi FROM community; LOAD vgi;
ATTACH 'sigma' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'uvx --from git+https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-sigma@v0.4.2 vgi-sigma-worker');

-- The headline: which log rows match a rule?
SELECT *
FROM windows_security_log AS t
WHERE sigma.sigma_match(
    to_json(t),
    'title: Failed Network Logon
logsource: {product: windows, service: security}
detection:
  selection:
    EventID: 4625
    LogonType: 3
  condition: selection');

example_queries.sql: WITH rules(rule_name, rule) AS (VALUES ('encoded_powershell', '{title: Encoded PowerShell, level: high, logsource: {product: windows, category: process_creation}, detection: {selection: {Image|endswith: \powershell.exe, CommandLine|contains: " -enc "}, condition: selection}}'), ('failed_network_logon', '{title: Failed Network Logon, level: medium, logsource: {product: windows, service: security}, detection: {selection: {EventID: 4625, LogonType: 3}, condition: selection}}'), ('ssh_to_internal_net', '{title: SSH To Internal Network, level: low, logsource: {category: network_connection}, detection: {selection: {DestinationIp|cidr: 10.0.0.0/8, DestinationPort: 22}, condition: selection}}')), used AS (SELECT rule_name, unnest(regexp_extract_all(rule, '\|(\w+)', 1)) AS modifier FROM rules WHERE NOT sigma.main.sigma_check(rule)) SELECT rule_name, list(DISTINCT modifier ORDER BY modifier) AS unsupported_modifiers FROM used WHERE modifier NOT IN (SELECT modifier FROM sigma.main.supported_modifiers) GROUP BY rule_name ORDER BY rule_name

## sigma.main

The single schema of the `sigma` catalog, bringing SIEM-style 'detection-as-code' into SQL. Use it to compile a [Sigma](https://sigmahq.io) rule once and test it against an entire log/event table, all without leaving the database.

**What it's for.** The schema spans the everyday loop of detection engineering: match events against a rule to hunt for a known threat, validate that a rule library parses and compiles before you trust it, and introspect a rule's header metadata and the fields it keys on for triage, index planning, and MITRE ATT&CK coverage analysis. Matching is the hot path and the usual entry point; validation and introspection support it around the edges.

**Notes.** Every rule must include a non-empty `logsource:` block. Rules compile once per distinct text (cached), then evaluate per row, so a constant rule over a column is cheap. Events are supplied as JSON object strings (e.g. from `to_json(row)`).

# sigma.main

Sigma detection-rule evaluation for SQL, powered by [pySigma](https://github.com/SigmaHQ/pySigma).

## What it covers

This schema turns Sigma 'detection-as-code' into ordinary SQL. It supports the everyday detection-engineering loop directly over your log tables:

- **Detect** — test log/event rows against a rule to hunt for a known threat.
- **Validate** — confirm a rule library parses and compiles before you rely on it.
- **Plan** — introspect a rule's header metadata and the fields it references for triage, index planning, and coverage analysis.

List the schema to browse the individual functions; each ships its own documentation and runnable examples. A browsable discovery table lists the Sigma field modifiers the evaluator understands, so you can review them before authoring a rule.

## Typical use

Apply a matcher predicate per row over a log table (typically in a `WHERE` clause against `to_json(row)`), and use the validation and introspection helpers to check a rule library and plan coverage. Every attached example query is fully catalog-qualified and runnable.

Every example rule carries a non-empty `logsource:` block, which pySigma requires.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: A ready-to-scan **discovery table** of every Sigma field modifier this worker's evaluator understands, so you can check what a rule may use before authoring or trusting it. Browse the view directly (no arguments): the `modifier` column holds the keyword written after a pipe in a rule field (e.g. `CommandLine|contains`), with the `plain` row standing for the default modifier-free comparison; `kind` groups them into `equality`, `affix`, `startswith`/`endswith` style, `regex`, and the `all` `combiner`; and `description` explains the matching semantics. A rule that uses any modifier absent from this table is rejected by `sigma_check` and raises from `sigma_match`, so this is the authoritative capability list. Rows are generated from the evaluator's own registry, so the view can never drift from actual behaviour. Runnable browse and filter queries are attached as examples.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# supported_modifiers (view)

Every Sigma field modifier the evaluator implements, as a plain browsable table.

The `modifier` column is the keyword written after a pipe on a rule field (`CommandLine|contains`, `Image|endswith`); the `plain` row is the default modifier-free comparison. The `kind` column groups modifiers into `equality`, `affix`, `regex`, and `combiner` families, and `description` explains the matching semantics. A rule using any modifier not listed here is rejected by `sigma_check` and raises from `sigma_match`, so this view is the authoritative capability list. The rows are generated from the evaluator's own registry, so they stay in lockstep with behaviour: filter by `kind` to review a family, or probe for a specific `modifier` before authoring a rule that uses it.

## sigma_rule_info(rule_yaml)

Parses a [Sigma](https://sigmahq.io) rule (YAML) and returns a single row of its header metadata: `title`, `id`, `level`, `status`, `description`, logsource `product`/`service`, and the rule's `tags` (a `VARCHAR[]`, typically MITRE ATT&CK references like `attack.t1110`).

**When to use it.** Triage and catalog rules without evaluating them against events -- e.g. build an inventory of a rule repository, filter by severity `level`, group by logsource `product`, or expand `tags` with `UNNEST` to map coverage against MITRE ATT&CK.

**Inputs.** `rule_yaml` -- a complete Sigma rule (positional). Like every rule here it needs a non-empty `logsource:` block.

**Output & edge cases.** A table function returning exactly one row. A NULL rule yields **no rows**; a malformed rule raises a clear parse error (this is an introspection helper run against a known rule, not a per-row scan). Header fields absent from the rule come back NULL.

# sigma_rule_info

Returns one row of header metadata for a Sigma rule -- the human-facing fields you would show in a rule catalog or triage view.

## Usage

Pass a rule and project the header columns you need (`title`, `level`, ...), or expand the `tags` list with `UNNEST` to map MITRE ATT&CK coverage. Fully runnable, catalog-qualified queries are attached as example queries.

## Notes

- One row per rule; a NULL rule yields no rows.
- A malformed rule raises a clear parse error.

vgi.example_queries.description: Turn matches into alerts: label every event the rule matches with the rule's title, severity level and MITRE ATT&CK tags read from its header (-> events 1 and 3).

## sigma_match_fields(rule_yaml)

Returns one row per distinct event field that a [Sigma](https://sigmahq.io) rule keys on (e.g. `EventID`, `LogonType`, `Image`). It answers 'what columns does this rule actually look at?' without evaluating the rule against any data.

**When to use it.** Plan indexes and storage coverage: discover which log fields must be present and indexed for a rule to be evaluable, audit a fleet of rules for a common field set, or detect rules that reference fields your pipeline does not collect.

**Inputs.** `rule_yaml` -- a complete Sigma rule (positional), with a non-empty `logsource:` block.

**Output & edge cases.** A table function emitting one `field` row per referenced field. A NULL rule yields **no rows**; a malformed rule raises a clear parse error. Bare-keyword conditions (which match anywhere in the event rather than a named field) contribute no field rows.

# sigma_match_fields

Lists the event fields a Sigma rule references, one per row -- the input for index and coverage planning.

## Usage

Pass a rule to get the distinct event field names it keys on, so you know which log columns must be present and indexed. Fully runnable, catalog-qualified queries are attached as example queries.

## Notes

## sigma_check(rule_yaml)

Returns `true` when a [Sigma](https://sigmahq.io) rule (YAML) parses and compiles successfully using only features this worker supports, and `false` otherwise. Unlike `sigma_match`, it **never raises** -- it is the safe, boolean-returning gate you run before trusting a rule.

**When to use it.** Validate rules in bulk -- e.g. lint a column of candidate rules, filter a detection-rule repository down to the ones this engine can actually evaluate, or guard a pipeline with `WHERE sigma.sigma_check(rule_text)` before feeding rules to `sigma_match`.

**Inputs.** `rule_yaml` -- a complete Sigma rule. Remember that pySigma requires a non-empty `logsource:` block; a rule missing it (or with `logsource: {}`) is invalid and returns `false`.

**Output & edge cases.** Returns `BOOLEAN`; NULL in, NULL out. It returns `false` for malformed YAML, a missing `logsource:`, a missing `condition`, or any unsupported modifier. Because it swallows errors into `false`, use `sigma_rule_info` if you need the specific parse error surfaced.

# sigma_check

A non-raising validator: returns `true` when a Sigma rule parses and compiles with only supported features, `false` otherwise.

## Usage

## sigma_match(event_json, rule_yaml)

Tests whether a single log/event row, supplied as a JSON object string, matches a [Sigma](https://sigmahq.io) detection rule supplied as YAML. This is the headline function of the catalog: it turns 'detection-as-code' into a SQL predicate so you can hunt for a known threat across an entire log table.

**When to use it.** Apply it per row over a log column to find matching events, typically in a `WHERE` clause: `WHERE sigma.sigma_match(to_json(t), :rule)`. The rule is parsed and compiled exactly once per distinct rule string (the engine is `lru_cache`-d), so scanning one constant rule across millions of rows compiles a single time and then evaluates the boolean condition tree per row.

**Inputs.** `event_json` — the event as a JSON object string (e.g. from `to_json(row)`); `rule_yaml` — a complete Sigma rule, which must include a non-empty `logsource:` block and a `detection:` section with a `condition`.

**Output & edge cases.** Returns `BOOLEAN`. A NULL input row yields NULL. A malformed *event* JSON yields `false` (one bad log row is a non-match, never a crash), but a malformed or unsupported *rule* raises a clear error so you never silently mis-evaluate. Supported leaf forms include field/value comparisons (equals, contains, startswith, endswith, regex, wildcards) and bare keyword searches; selector forms like `1 of selection_*` and `all of them` are expanded by pySigma and work for free.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# sigma_match

Returns `true` when a JSON event matches a Sigma detection rule. It is the core matcher for SIEM-style threat detection directly in SQL.

## Usage

Apply it per row over a log column -- typically in a `WHERE` clause against `to_json(row)` -- to keep only the events a rule matches. Fully runnable, catalog-qualified queries are attached as example queries.

## Arguments

| name | type | description |
|---|---|---|
| `event_json` | VARCHAR | The event as a JSON object string. |
| `rule_yaml` | VARCHAR | A Sigma rule (YAML) with a non-empty `logsource:`. |

## Notes

- A malformed *event* returns `false`; a malformed *rule* raises a clear error.
- NULL in, NULL out.
- The rule compiles once per distinct string, then evaluates per row, so a constant rule over a whole column is cheap.

vgi.example_queries.description: A failed-logon event matches a rule requiring EventID 4625.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT sigma.main.sigma_match('{"EventID": 4625, "LogonType": 3}', '{title: Failed Network Logon, logsource: {service: security}, detection: {selection: {EventID: 4625}, condition: selection}}')

vgi.example_queries.description: Hunt per row over an inline log table, keeping only matching events.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT event FROM (VALUES ('{"EventID": 4625, "LogonType": 3}'), ('{"EventID": 1}')) AS logs(event) WHERE sigma.main.sigma_match(event, '{title: Failed Network Logon, logsource: {service: security}, detection: {selection: {EventID: 4625, LogonType: 3}, condition: selection}}')

vgi.example_queries.description: Run a small rule library over an event log: keep only the rules sigma_check accepts (dropping the cidr rule the engine cannot evaluate), then join each event to every usable rule it matches (-> event 1 failed_network_logon, event 3 encoded_powershell).
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH rules(rule_name, rule) AS (VALUES ('encoded_powershell', '{title: Encoded PowerShell, level: high, logsource: {product: windows, category: process_creation}, detection: {selection: {Image|endswith: \powershell.exe, CommandLine|contains: " -enc "}, condition: selection}}'), ('failed_network_logon', '{title: Failed Network Logon, level: medium, logsource: {product: windows, service: security}, detection: {selection: {EventID: 4625, LogonType: 3}, condition: selection}}'), ('ssh_to_internal_net', '{title: SSH To Internal Network, level: low, logsource: {category: network_connection}, detection: {selection: {DestinationIp|cidr: 10.0.0.0/8, DestinationPort: 22}, condition: selection}}')), logs(event_id, event) AS (VALUES (1, '{"EventID": 4625, "LogonType": 3, "TargetUserName": "admin"}'), (2, '{"EventID": 4625, "LogonType": 2, "TargetUserName": "alice"}'), (3, '{"EventID": 1, "Image": "C:\\Windows\\System32\\WindowsPowerShell\\v1.0\\powershell.exe", "CommandLine": "powershell.exe -nop -enc SQBFAFgA"}'), (4, '{"EventID": 1, "Image": "C:\\Windows\\explorer.exe", "CommandLine": "explorer.exe"}')), usable AS (SELECT rule_name, rule FROM rules WHERE sigma.main.sigma_check(rule)) SELECT l.event_id, u.rule_name FROM logs AS l JOIN usable AS u ON sigma.main.sigma_match(l.event, u.rule) ORDER BY l.event_id, u.rule_name

vgi.executable_examples.description: A failed-logon event (EventID 4625, network logon type 3) matches a brute-force detection rule.
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT sigma.main.sigma_match('{"EventID": 4625, "LogonType": 3}', '{title: Failed Network Logon, logsource: {service: security}, detection: {selection: {EventID: 4625, LogonType: 3}, condition: selection}}') AS matched

vgi.executable_examples.description: An unrelated process-creation event does not match the same rule.
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT sigma.main.sigma_match('{"EventID": 1}', '{title: Failed Network Logon, logsource: {service: security}, detection: {selection: {EventID: 4625, LogonType: 3}, condition: selection}}') AS matched

vgi.executable_examples.description: Apply the matcher per row over an inline log table -- the headline hunting pattern.
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT event, sigma.main.sigma_match(event, '{title: Failed Network Logon, logsource: {service: security}, detection: {selection: {EventID: 4625, LogonType: 3}, condition: selection}}') AS matched FROM (VALUES ('{"EventID": 4625, "LogonType": 3}'), ('{"EventID": 1}')) AS logs(event) ORDER BY matched

# Singer taps in DuckDB

Run any [Singer](https://hub.meltano.com/singer/spec) tap and query its streams with SQL.

Taps are installed into isolated, cached environments; their configs come from DuckDB secrets; JSON Schema becomes real DuckDB types; and Singer STATE drives resumable, incremental scans.

Attach a tap together with its Singer catalog to see every stream as a table, or read saved Singer JSONL output directly.

attach_options.name: tap
attach_options.description: Tap executable name, e.g. 'tap-csv'. With catalog, every stream becomes a table.

attach_options.name: catalog
attach_options.description: Singer catalog for the tap: a file path or the catalog JSON itself.

attach_options.name: pip_url
attach_options.description: pip requirement the tap is installed from into an isolated cached environment.

attach_options.name: executable
attach_options.description: Path to an already installed tap executable; skips installation.

attach_options.name: python
attach_options.description: Python version for the tap's environment, e.g. '3.12'.

attach_options.name: secret_name
attach_options.description: Name of the singer secret with the tap config; empty uses the 'singer://<tap>' scope.

attach_options.name: timeout_seconds
attach_options.description: Stop a tap that prints nothing for this many seconds; 0 waits forever.

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
One column per top-level property of the stream's JSON Schema, in schema order, all nullable. The type depends on the property's schema:

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| integer property | BIGINT | `type: integer` |
| number property | DOUBLE | `type: number` (or integer and number) |
| boolean property | BOOLEAN | `type: boolean` |
| string property | VARCHAR | `type: string` without a known format |
| date-time property | TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE | `format: date-time`; offset-less values are UTC |
| date property | DATE | `format: date` |
| time property | TIME | `format: time` |
| object property | STRUCT(city VARCHAR, zip VARCHAR) | e.g. `properties` city and zip declared, no extra keys allowed, up to 4 levels deep |
| array property | VARCHAR[] | e.g. `items: {type: string}`; items are mapped by the same rules |
| open property | JSON | open objects, mixed types, or no type |

One column per top-level property of the stream's JSON Schema, in schema order, all nullable. The type depends on the property's schema:

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| integer property | BIGINT | `type: integer` |
| number property | DOUBLE | `type: number` (or integer and number) |
| boolean property | BOOLEAN | `type: boolean` |
| string property | VARCHAR | `type: string` without a known format |
| date-time property | TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE | `format: date-time`; offset-less values are UTC |
| date property | DATE | `format: date` |
| time property | TIME | `format: time` |
| object property | STRUCT(city VARCHAR, zip VARCHAR) | e.g. `properties` city and zip declared, no extra keys allowed, up to 4 levels deep |
| array property | VARCHAR[] | e.g. `items: {type: string}`; items are mapped by the same rules |
| open property | JSON | open objects, mixed types, or no type |

workers.subtitle: Read Slack channels, people and messages, and post messages, from DuckDB SQL.
workers.summary: Slack workspace data as SQL tables: channels, people, channel history and threads, read through the Slack Web API with a bot token, plus posting messages from a query.
workers.doc_md:
# Slack for DuckDB

**Query Slack channels, people and messages, and post messages, from SQL.**

Attach with a bot token: `ATTACH 'slack' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION '/abs/path/bin/vgi-slack-worker', token getenv('SLACK_BOT_TOKEN'))`. The token is declared secret, so DuckDB redacts it from `duckdb_databases()` and never logs it.

Bot token scopes: `channels:read`, `groups:read`, `channels:history`, `groups:history`, `users:read` (plus `users:read.email` for emails) and `chat:write`. Invite the bot to every channel it should read or post in.

## Sources and references

- [Slack Web API](https://docs.slack.dev/apis/web-api/): the HTTP API every function calls, with the [method reference](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/methods) for `conversations.*`, `users.list`, `auth.test` and `chat.postMessage`.
- [Slack apps](https://api.slack.com/apps): create an app and install it to get the bot token; [token types](https://docs.slack.dev/authentication/tokens) explains bot tokens.
- [OAuth scopes](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/scopes): what each scope above grants.

attach_options.name: token
attach_options.description: Slack bot token (xoxb-...). Pass it as an expression to keep it out of the SQL text: token getenv('SLACK_BOT_TOKEN').

attach_options.name: api_url
attach_options.description: Slack Web API root URL. Change it only for a proxy or a test server.

example_queries.description: Check which workspace and bot the token is for
example_queries.sql: SELECT team, user, bot_id FROM slack.main.auth_info()

example_queries.description: The ten largest channels the bot is in
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, num_members FROM slack.main.channels() WHERE is_member ORDER BY num_members DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Count public and private channels, including archived ones
example_queries.sql: SELECT is_private, count(*) AS channels FROM slack.main.channels(exclude_archived := false) GROUP BY is_private

example_queries.description: Who created each channel the bot can see, oldest channel first (include_deleted keeps creators who have left)
example_queries.sql: SELECT c.name, u.real_name AS created_by, c.created_at FROM slack.main.channels() c LEFT JOIN slack.main.users(include_deleted := true) u ON u.id = c.creator ORDER BY c.created_at

example_queries.description: Where the workspace's people are, by time zone
example_queries.sql: SELECT tz, count(*) AS people FROM slack.main.users() WHERE NOT is_bot GROUP BY tz ORDER BY people DESC

example_queries.description: Most active people in #general since the start of 2026
example_queries.sql: SELECT u.real_name, count(*) AS messages FROM slack.main.messages('#general', oldest := TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01') m JOIN slack.main.users() u ON u.id = m.user_id GROUP BY u.real_name ORDER BY messages DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: The twenty latest messages in a channel, by ID
example_queries.sql: SELECT posted_at, text FROM slack.main.messages('C0123ABCD') ORDER BY posted_at DESC LIMIT 20

example_queries.description: Read one thread in order
example_queries.sql: SELECT posted_at, user_id, text FROM slack.main.replies('#general', '1700000000.000100') ORDER BY posted_at

example_queries.description: Read a thread (parent message first, then replies) with each author's real name instead of a user ID
example_queries.sql: SELECT r.posted_at, coalesce(u.real_name, r.user_id) AS author, r.text FROM slack.main.replies('#general', '1767225900.000100') r LEFT JOIN slack.main.users(include_deleted := true) u ON u.id = r.user_id ORDER BY r.posted_at

example_queries.description: Announce a deploy and keep the message ts
example_queries.sql: SELECT channel_id, ts FROM slack.main.post_message('#deploys', 'Deployed *v1.2* :rocket:')

example_queries.description: Reply in an existing thread
example_queries.sql: SELECT ts FROM slack.main.post_message('#deploys', 'Rollback finished', thread_ts := '1700000000.000100')

example_queries.description: Dry run: an empty input posts nothing (no token or network needed)
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS posted FROM slack.main.post_messages((SELECT '#alerts' AS channel, 'never sent' AS text WHERE false))

example_queries.description: Post an alert per down host and count them
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS posted FROM slack.main.post_messages((SELECT '#alerts' AS channel, 'Host ' || h || ' is down' AS text FROM (VALUES ('web-1'), ('web-2')) t(h)))

example_queries.description: Reply in the thread of every unanswered message people posted in #general in the last day, and count the nudges
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS nudged FROM slack.main.post_messages((SELECT channel_id AS channel, 'Bumping this: is anyone looking at it?' AS text, ts AS thread_ts FROM slack.main.messages('#general', oldest := now()::TIMESTAMP - INTERVAL 1 DAY) WHERE reply_count IS NULL AND subtype IS NULL AND bot_id IS NULL))

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Everything Slack lives in `main`. Readers stream Slack's paginated Web API one page per batch, so SQL `LIMIT` stops paging early, and time-bounded history should use the reader's own time arguments rather than a `WHERE` on the timestamp, which would page through the whole channel first. Writers post real messages and return the new message's `ts`. Message rows join to people on `user_id` and to channels on `channel_id`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

Readers for the workspace (channels, people, the token's identity) and for conversations (channel history, threads), plus writers that post messages.

Readers page through the Slack API as DuckDB asks for rows, so `LIMIT` is cheap. Bound history with the reader's time arguments instead of filtering afterwards.

Writers post real messages: run them deliberately.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Post one message to Slack with chat.postMessage and return one row describing it. Positional arguments: `channel` (ID like 'C0123ABCD' or name like '#general') and `text` (Slack mrkdwn). Named argument `thread_ts` (default NULL) replies in the thread of that parent message. Every call posts a real message; to post one message per row of a query use post_messages(). Needs the chat:write scope, and the bot must be in the channel (or have chat:write.public for public channels).

functions.name: post_messages
functions.comment: Post one Slack message per input row (columns channel, text, optional thread_ts)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Post one Slack message for every row of a subquery, in order. Pass the subquery as the only argument; it must have `VARCHAR` columns `channel` (ID or '#name') and `text`, and may have `thread_ts` to reply in a thread (NULL for a top-level message). Returns one row per posted message. Returns `channel_id`, `ts` (the new message's ID; pass it as `thread_ts` to reply), `posted_at`, `thread_ts` and `text`. A NULL or empty channel or text fails the query. Rate limits are respected by retrying with Slack's Retry-After. Needs the chat:write scope.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## post_messages((SELECT channel, text [, thread_ts] ...))

Post one message per row of a subquery, for example one alert per failing host.

workers.title: SNMP Devices
workers.tagline: SNMP v1/v2c/v3 device queries — GET, walk & MIB tables as typed rows — for DuckDB (Python, pysnmp)
workers.subtitle: Query SNMP v1/v2c/v3 devices from SQL: GET, WALK and MIB tables as typed rows.
workers.summary: Queries SNMP v1, v2c and v3 network devices such as routers, switches, servers and printers, returning variable bindings and MIB tables as typed rows, with offline lookups over the bundled IETF and Net-SNMP MIB modules.
workers.doc_md:
# SNMP for DuckDB

**Read SNMP devices with SQL.** GET instances, walk subtrees and read MIB tables such as `ifXTable` or `hrStorageTable` as typed rows, over SNMP v1, v2c or v3.

MIB names resolve offline against the bundled IETF and Net-SNMP MIB modules, and table schemas come from the MIB, so `DESCRIBE` works without contacting a device.

Credentials come from a `snmp` DuckDB secret scoped by host, so they stay out of queries.

## Sources and references

- [RFC 3416](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3416): SNMPv2 protocol operations (GET, GETNEXT, GETBULK) and [RFC 3414](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3414): the SNMPv3 User-based Security Model behind v3 authentication and privacy.
- [RFC 2863](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2863): IF-MIB, the interface tables (`ifTable`, `ifXTable`) most device queries read.
- [Net-SNMP](http://www.net-snmp.org/): source of the bundled UCD-SNMP-MIB and NET-SNMP-MIB modules.
- [PySNMP](https://docs.lextudio.com/pysnmp/): the SNMP engine the worker runs on.

example_queries.description: Identify a device by its system group
example_queries.sql: SELECT object, value FROM snmp.main.snmp_get('192.0.2.10', 'sysName.0', 'sysDescr.0', 'sysLocation.0') ORDER BY object

example_queries.description: Uptime in days from sysUpTime (hundredths of a second)
example_queries.sql: SELECT round(value_int / 8640000.0, 1) AS uptime_days FROM snmp.main.snmp_get('192.0.2.10', 'sysUpTime.0', community := 'monitor')

example_queries.description: One row per device: its name and its platform, the sysObjectID OID named offline with snmp_oid_name (for example 'NET-SNMP-MIB::netSnmpAgentOIDs.10' for a Linux Net-SNMP agent)
example_queries.sql: SELECT max(value) FILTER (WHERE object = 'sysName') AS sys_name, snmp.main.snmp_oid_name(max(value) FILTER (WHERE object = 'sysObjectID')) AS platform FROM snmp.main.snmp_get('192.0.2.20', 'sysName.0', 'sysObjectID.0')

example_queries.description: List interface names by ifIndex
example_queries.sql: SELECT instance AS if_index, value AS interface FROM snmp.main.snmp_walk('192.0.2.10', 'ifDescr') ORDER BY instance::INTEGER

example_queries.description: Which MIB-2 objects does a device populate most?
example_queries.sql: SELECT object, count(*) AS instances FROM snmp.main.snmp_walk('192.0.2.10', 'mib-2') GROUP BY object ORDER BY instances DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Current values of the system-group objects an SNMP SET can change (sysContact, sysName, sysLocation), by joining the walk to the MIB's MAX-ACCESS
example_queries.sql: SELECT w.object, w.value, o.syntax FROM snmp.main.snmp_walk('192.0.2.20', 'system') w JOIN snmp.main.snmp_mib_objects(module := 'SNMPv2-MIB', kind := 'scalar') o ON o.name = w.object WHERE o.access = 'read-write' ORDER BY string_split(w.oid, '.')::INTEGER[]

example_queries.description: The five busiest interfaces by received octets
example_queries.sql: SELECT ifName, ifHCInOctets, ifHCOutOctets FROM snmp.main.snmp_table('192.0.2.10', 'ifXTable') ORDER BY ifHCInOctets DESC LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Disk and memory utilisation from HOST-RESOURCES-MIB
example_queries.sql: SELECT hrStorageDescr, round(100.0 * hrStorageUsed / nullif(hrStorageSize, 0), 1) AS pct_used FROM snmp.main.snmp_table('192.0.2.10', 'hrStorageTable') ORDER BY pct_used DESC NULLS LAST

example_queries.description: Storage areas labelled by type (hrStorageRam, hrStorageFixedDisk, ...) by decoding the hrStorageType OID with snmp_oid_name, with used space in GB (used units times allocation units)
example_queries.sql: SELECT split_part(snmp.main.snmp_oid_name(hrStorageType), '::', 2) AS storage_type, hrStorageDescr, round(hrStorageUsed * hrStorageAllocationUnits / 1e9, 2) AS used_gb, round(100.0 * hrStorageUsed / nullif(hrStorageSize, 0), 1) AS pct_used FROM snmp.main.snmp_table('192.0.2.20', 'hrStorageTable') ORDER BY storage_type, hrStorageDescr

example_queries.description: The numeric OID of the 64-bit input octet counter column
example_queries.sql: SELECT snmp.main.snmp_oid('IF-MIB::ifHCInOctets') AS oid

example_queries.description: Resolve a column of names; unknown names give NULL
example_queries.sql: SELECT n, snmp.main.snmp_oid(n) AS oid FROM (VALUES ('sysName.0'), ('hrStorageUsed'), ('notAnObject')) t(n) ORDER BY n

example_queries.description: Name the sysUpTime instance
example_queries.sql: SELECT snmp.main.snmp_oid_name('1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0') AS name

example_queries.description: Name a column of OIDs, including an unknown vendor OID
example_queries.sql: SELECT oid, snmp.main.snmp_oid_name(oid) AS name FROM (VALUES ('1.3.6.1.2.1.25.2.3.1.6.1'), ('1.3.6.1.4.1.9.1.1')) t(oid) ORDER BY oid

example_queries.description: Decode numeric OIDs from a trap or log: name each with snmp_oid_name, then join snmp_mib_objects for the object's syntax and UNITS clause (NULL when the MIB declares none)
example_queries.sql: WITH named AS (SELECT oid, snmp.main.snmp_oid_name(oid) AS name FROM (VALUES ('1.3.6.1.2.1.31.1.1.1.15.3'), ('1.3.6.1.2.1.25.2.3.1.4.1'), ('1.3.6.1.2.1.31.1.1.1.6.3')) t(oid)) SELECT n.oid, n.name, o.syntax, o.units FROM named n JOIN snmp.main.snmp_mib_objects() o ON o.module = split_part(n.name, '::', 1) AND o.name = split_part(split_part(n.name, '::', 2), '.', 1) ORDER BY string_split(n.oid, '.')::INTEGER[]

example_queries.description: Which loaded MIB modules define the most tables?
example_queries.sql: SELECT module, count(*) AS tables FROM snmp.main.snmp_mib_objects(kind := 'table') GROUP BY module ORDER BY tables DESC

example_queries.description: Net-SNMP memory statistics available with snmp_get
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, syntax, units FROM snmp.main.snmp_mib_objects(module := 'UCD-SNMP-MIB', kind := 'scalar') WHERE name LIKE 'mem%' ORDER BY oid

example_queries.description: The 64-bit counters in IF-MIB
example_queries.sql: SELECT name FROM snmp.main.snmp_mib_objects(module := 'IF-MIB', kind := 'column') WHERE syntax = 'Counter64' ORDER BY name LIMIT 3;

example_queries.description: Columns of hrStorageTable
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS columns FROM snmp.main.snmp_mib_objects(module := 'HOST-RESOURCES-MIB', kind := 'column') WHERE oid LIKE '1.3.6.1.2.1.25.2.3.1.%';

example_queries.description: Resolve a column instance
example_queries.sql: SELECT snmp.main.snmp_oid('IF-MIB::ifInOctets.3') AS oid;

example_queries.description: Resolve system group scalars
example_queries.sql: SELECT n, snmp.main.snmp_oid(n) AS oid FROM (VALUES ('sysDescr.0'), ('sysUpTime.0')) t(n) ORDER BY n;

example_queries.description: Name an interface counter instance
example_queries.sql: SELECT snmp.main.snmp_oid_name('1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.10.3') AS name;

Which column of the snmp worker's single-instance GET results holds a counter's exact integer value, and what is its DuckDB type? Answer without contacting a device.

I need to poll interface ifIndex 7 with a tool that only takes numeric OIDs. Using the snmp worker's MIBs, list every IF-MIB column whose syntax is Counter64 together with the numeric OID of its instance for ifIndex 7. Return two columns: name and oid, in OID order.
How many columns does the snmp worker's subtree walk return? Answer without contacting a device.

vgi.categories.description: Table functions that query SNMP agents on the network (GET, WALK, tables).

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The `main` schema holds the SNMP functions. Device queries take the agent address as their first argument and share the named arguments `version`, `community`, `port`, `timeout`, `retries` and `context`; raw results have the columns host, oid, name, object, instance, type, value, value_int and value_bytes, and table results have typed columns named after the MIB objects plus `_index`, the row's instance suffix. OIDs are written numerically or as MIB names, optionally module-qualified, with an instance suffix for scalars ('sysUpTime.0'). The offline MIB lookups return NULL for NULL or unresolvable input and are how to discover table and column names. OIDs are `VARCHAR`, so sort them numerically by casting string_split(oid, '.') to `INTEGER[]`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

Device queries send SNMP GET, GETNEXT and GETBULK requests to the agent named by their first argument, using SNMP v1, v2c or v3.

MIB lookups work offline against the bundled MIB modules: translate names and OIDs, and find the tables and columns a device query can name.

vgi.example_queries.description: Identify a device by its system group
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT object, value FROM snmp.main.snmp_get('192.0.2.10', 'sysName.0', 'sysDescr.0', 'sysLocation.0') ORDER BY object

vgi.example_queries.description: Uptime in days from sysUpTime (hundredths of a second)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT round(value_int / 8640000.0, 1) AS uptime_days FROM snmp.main.snmp_get('192.0.2.10', 'sysUpTime.0', community := 'monitor')

vgi.example_queries.description: One row per device: its name and its platform, the sysObjectID OID named offline with snmp_oid_name (for example 'NET-SNMP-MIB::netSnmpAgentOIDs.10' for a Linux Net-SNMP agent)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT max(value) FILTER (WHERE object = 'sysName') AS sys_name, snmp.main.snmp_oid_name(max(value) FILTER (WHERE object = 'sysObjectID')) AS platform FROM snmp.main.snmp_get('192.0.2.20', 'sysName.0', 'sysObjectID.0')

vgi.example_queries.description: List interface names by ifIndex
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT instance AS if_index, value AS interface FROM snmp.main.snmp_walk('192.0.2.10', 'ifDescr') ORDER BY instance::INTEGER

vgi.example_queries.description: Which MIB-2 objects does a device populate most?
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT object, count(*) AS instances FROM snmp.main.snmp_walk('192.0.2.10', 'mib-2') GROUP BY object ORDER BY instances DESC LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: Current values of the system-group objects an SNMP SET can change (sysContact, sysName, sysLocation), by joining the walk to the MIB's MAX-ACCESS
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT w.object, w.value, o.syntax FROM snmp.main.snmp_walk('192.0.2.20', 'system') w JOIN snmp.main.snmp_mib_objects(module := 'SNMPv2-MIB', kind := 'scalar') o ON o.name = w.object WHERE o.access = 'read-write' ORDER BY string_split(w.oid, '.')::INTEGER[]

vgi.example_queries.description: The five busiest interfaces by received octets
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ifName, ifHCInOctets, ifHCOutOctets FROM snmp.main.snmp_table('192.0.2.10', 'ifXTable') ORDER BY ifHCInOctets DESC LIMIT 5

vgi.example_queries.description: Disk and memory utilisation from HOST-RESOURCES-MIB
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT hrStorageDescr, round(100.0 * hrStorageUsed / nullif(hrStorageSize, 0), 1) AS pct_used FROM snmp.main.snmp_table('192.0.2.10', 'hrStorageTable') ORDER BY pct_used DESC NULLS LAST

vgi.example_queries.description: Storage areas labelled by type (hrStorageRam, hrStorageFixedDisk, ...) by decoding the hrStorageType OID with snmp_oid_name, with used space in GB (used units times allocation units)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT split_part(snmp.main.snmp_oid_name(hrStorageType), '::', 2) AS storage_type, hrStorageDescr, round(hrStorageUsed * hrStorageAllocationUnits / 1e9, 2) AS used_gb, round(100.0 * hrStorageUsed / nullif(hrStorageSize, 0), 1) AS pct_used FROM snmp.main.snmp_table('192.0.2.20', 'hrStorageTable') ORDER BY storage_type, hrStorageDescr

vgi.example_queries.description: The numeric OID of the 64-bit input octet counter column
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT snmp.main.snmp_oid('IF-MIB::ifHCInOctets') AS oid

vgi.example_queries.description: Resolve a column of names; unknown names give NULL
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT n, snmp.main.snmp_oid(n) AS oid FROM (VALUES ('sysName.0'), ('hrStorageUsed'), ('notAnObject')) t(n) ORDER BY n

vgi.example_queries.description: Name the sysUpTime instance
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT snmp.main.snmp_oid_name('1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0') AS name

vgi.example_queries.description: Name a column of OIDs, including an unknown vendor OID
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT oid, snmp.main.snmp_oid_name(oid) AS name FROM (VALUES ('1.3.6.1.2.1.25.2.3.1.6.1'), ('1.3.6.1.4.1.9.1.1')) t(oid) ORDER BY oid

vgi.example_queries.description: Decode numeric OIDs from a trap or log: name each with snmp_oid_name, then join snmp_mib_objects for the object's syntax and UNITS clause (NULL when the MIB declares none)
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH named AS (SELECT oid, snmp.main.snmp_oid_name(oid) AS name FROM (VALUES ('1.3.6.1.2.1.31.1.1.1.15.3'), ('1.3.6.1.2.1.25.2.3.1.4.1'), ('1.3.6.1.2.1.31.1.1.1.6.3')) t(oid)) SELECT n.oid, n.name, o.syntax, o.units FROM named n JOIN snmp.main.snmp_mib_objects() o ON o.module = split_part(n.name, '::', 1) AND o.name = split_part(split_part(n.name, '::', 2), '.', 1) ORDER BY string_split(n.oid, '.')::INTEGER[]

vgi.example_queries.description: Which loaded MIB modules define the most tables?
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT module, count(*) AS tables FROM snmp.main.snmp_mib_objects(kind := 'table') GROUP BY module ORDER BY tables DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Net-SNMP memory statistics available with snmp_get
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, syntax, units FROM snmp.main.snmp_mib_objects(module := 'UCD-SNMP-MIB', kind := 'scalar') WHERE name LIKE 'mem%' ORDER BY oid

tags.vgi.title: SNMP Functions

functions.name: snmp_walk
functions.comment: Walk an SNMP subtree (GETBULK/GETNEXT) and return every instance under it

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Walk every instance below the subtree `oid` on the agent at `host` and return one row per instance, in OID order: `host, oid, name, object, instance, type, value, value_int, value_bytes`. `oid` is numeric or a MIB name without instance suffix ('system', 'ifTable', 'ifHCInOctets', 'hrStorageTable'). Rows stream in batches, so LIMIT stops the walk early. Uses GETBULK with `max_repetitions` (named, default 25) on v2c/v3 and GETNEXT on v1. Use snmp_table instead when you want one row per table row with typed columns; use snmp_walk for raw subtrees, vendor MIBs this worker does not know, or discovery. Connection named arguments: `version` ('1', '2c' or '3'; default '3' when a v3 user is configured, else '2c'), `community`, `port` (default 161; 'host:port' also works), `timeout` (seconds per attempt, default 2), `retries` (default 1) and `context` (SNMPv3 context name). Credentials come from the `community` argument, else from a DuckDB secret of type `snmp` whose SCOPE is a prefix of 'snmp://<host>:<port>', else from the SNMP_COMMUNITY, SNMP_USER, SNMP_AUTH_PROTOCOL, SNMP_AUTH_KEY, SNMP_PRIV_PROTOCOL and SNMP_PRIV_KEY environment variables, else the community 'public'. A v3 secret looks like:

```sql
CREATE SECRET (TYPE snmp, SCOPE 'snmp://10.0.0.', USER 'monitor', AUTH_PROTOCOL 'sha256',
  AUTH_KEY 'auth-passphrase', PRIV_PROTOCOL 'aes', PRIV_KEY 'priv-passphrase');
```

A timeout or wrong credentials raise an error that names the agent.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## snmp_walk(host, oid, max_repetitions := 25)

Every instance under a subtree, like `snmpbulkwalk`.

Rows stream in OID order, so `LIMIT` ends the walk early.

**Connection:** `version := '1' | '2c' | '3'`, `community := '...'`, `port := 161`, `timeout := 2.0`, `retries := 1`, `context := ''`. Credentials can also come from a `snmp` secret scoped to `snmp://<host>` or from `SNMP_*` environment variables; see the README.

vgi.example_queries.description: Current values of the system-group objects an SNMP SET can change (sysContact, sysName, sysLocation), by joining the walk to the MIB's MAX-ACCESS

functions.name: snmp_table
functions.comment: Read an SNMP MIB table (ifTable, hrStorageTable, ...) as typed rows, one per table row

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Read a MIB conceptual table from the agent at `host`, one row per table row, with one typed column per readable MIB column. The table can be named by the table, its entry, one of its columns or its numeric OID. Column names are the MIB object names (ifDescr, ifOperStatus, ifHCInOctets). Enumerations become their labels ('up', 'down'), Counter64 becomes `UBIGINT`, other integers `BIGINT`, and everything else `VARCHAR` display text. `_index` is the row's instance suffix, and the INDEX objects (such as ifIndex) are decoded from it. Only the columns the query uses are fetched. The schema comes from the MIB, so describing the query lists the columns without contacting the agent, and the MIB object listing shows which tables exist. Tables that augment another (ifXTable augments ifTable) share its index and combine by `_index`. For tables of MIBs this worker does not load, walk the subtree instead. Connection named arguments: `version` ('1', '2c' or '3'; default '3' when a v3 user is configured, else '2c'), `community`, `port` (default 161; 'host:port' also works), `timeout` (seconds per attempt, default 2), `retries` (default 1) and `context` (SNMPv3 context name). Credentials come from the `community` argument, else from a DuckDB secret of type `snmp` whose SCOPE is a prefix of 'snmp://<host>:<port>', else from the SNMP_COMMUNITY, SNMP_USER, SNMP_AUTH_PROTOCOL, SNMP_AUTH_KEY, SNMP_PRIV_PROTOCOL and SNMP_PRIV_KEY environment variables, else the community 'public'. A v3 secret looks like:

```sql
CREATE SECRET (TYPE snmp, SCOPE 'snmp://10.0.0.', USER 'monitor', AUTH_PROTOCOL 'sha256',
  AUTH_KEY 'auth-passphrase', PRIV_PROTOCOL 'aes', PRIV_KEY 'priv-passphrase');
```

A timeout or wrong credentials raise an error that names the agent.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## snmp_table(host, table, max_repetitions := 25)

A MIB table as rows with typed columns, like `snmptable`. Only projected columns are walked.

**Connection:** `version := '1' | '2c' | '3'`, `community := '...'`, `port := 161`, `timeout := 2.0`, `retries := 1`, `context := ''`. Credentials can also come from a `snmp` secret scoped to `snmp://<host>` or from `SNMP_*` environment variables; see the README.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT ifName, ifHCInOctets, ifHCOutOctets FROM snmp.main.snmp_table('192.0.2.10', 'ifXTable') ORDER BY ifHCInOctets DESC LIMIT 5

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT hrStorageDescr, round(100.0 * hrStorageUsed / nullif(hrStorageSize, 0), 1) AS pct_used FROM snmp.main.snmp_table('192.0.2.10', 'hrStorageTable') ORDER BY pct_used DESC NULLS LAST

vgi.example_queries.description: Storage areas labelled by type (hrStorageRam, hrStorageFixedDisk, ...) by decoding the hrStorageType OID with snmp_oid_name, with used space in GB (used units times allocation units)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT split_part(snmp.main.snmp_oid_name(hrStorageType), '::', 2) AS storage_type, hrStorageDescr, round(hrStorageUsed * hrStorageAllocationUnits / 1e9, 2) AS used_gb, round(100.0 * hrStorageUsed / nullif(hrStorageSize, 0), 1) AS pct_used FROM snmp.main.snmp_table('192.0.2.20', 'hrStorageTable') ORDER BY storage_type, hrStorageDescr

The columns depend on the `table` argument and come from its MIB definition: `_index`, then the INDEX objects decoded from it, then one column per readable column object. Counter64 is `UBIGINT`, other integers `BIGINT`, enumerations and everything else `VARCHAR`. Common tables:

**`table` = 'IF-MIB::ifXTable'**:

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| _index | VARCHAR | Instance suffix |
| ifIndex | BIGINT | InterfaceIndex |
| ifName | VARCHAR | DisplayString |
| ifInMulticastPkts | BIGINT | Counter32 |
| ifInBroadcastPkts | BIGINT | Counter32 |
| ifOutMulticastPkts | BIGINT | Counter32 |
| ifOutBroadcastPkts | BIGINT | Counter32 |
| ifHCInOctets | UBIGINT | Counter64 |
| ifHCInUcastPkts | UBIGINT | Counter64 |
| ifHCInMulticastPkts | UBIGINT | Counter64 |
| ifHCInBroadcastPkts | UBIGINT | Counter64 |
| ifHCOutOctets | UBIGINT | Counter64 |
| ifHCOutUcastPkts | UBIGINT | Counter64 |
| ifHCOutMulticastPkts | UBIGINT | Counter64 |
| ifHCOutBroadcastPkts | UBIGINT | Counter64 |
| ifLinkUpDownTrapEnable | VARCHAR | Integer32 |
| ifHighSpeed | BIGINT | Gauge32 |
| ifPromiscuousMode | VARCHAR | TruthValue |
| ifConnectorPresent | VARCHAR | TruthValue |
| ifAlias | VARCHAR | DisplayString |
| ifCounterDiscontinuityTime | BIGINT | TimeStamp |


**`table` = 'HOST-RESOURCES-MIB::hrStorageTable'**:

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| _index | VARCHAR | Instance suffix |

tags.vgi.doc_llm: List every named object in the MIB modules this worker has loaded, offline: module, name, oid, kind (scalar/table/row/column/notification/node), syntax, access, status, units and description. Filter with the named arguments `module := 'IF-MIB'` and `kind := 'table'`. Use it to discover which tables snmp_table can read and which columns they have (a column's oid starts with its row's oid), and which scalars snmp_get can read (append '.0').

functions.name: snmp_get
functions.comment: Read specific SNMP instances (GET) from an agent, one row per OID

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Send one SNMP GET to the agent at `host` for every OID listed after it and return one row per OID, in argument order: `host, oid, name, object, instance, type, value, value_int, value_bytes`. OIDs are numeric ('1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5.0') or MIB names with an instance suffix ('sysName.0', 'IF-MIB::ifHCInOctets.2'); scalars need the '.0' suffix. A missing object is a row with type 'noSuchObject' or 'noSuchInstance' and NULL values, not an error. Use `value` for display text (enum labels, MAC addresses), `value_int` for arithmetic on counters/gauges/TimeTicks (TimeTicks are hundredths of a second). Connection named arguments: `version` ('1', '2c' or '3'; default '3' when a v3 user is configured, else '2c'), `community`, `port` (default 161; 'host:port' also works), `timeout` (seconds per attempt, default 2), `retries` (default 1) and `context` (SNMPv3 context name). Credentials come from the `community` argument, else from a DuckDB secret of type `snmp` whose SCOPE is a prefix of 'snmp://<host>:<port>', else from the SNMP_COMMUNITY, SNMP_USER, SNMP_AUTH_PROTOCOL, SNMP_AUTH_KEY, SNMP_PRIV_PROTOCOL and SNMP_PRIV_KEY environment variables, else the community 'public'. A v3 secret looks like:

```sql
CREATE SECRET (TYPE snmp, SCOPE 'snmp://10.0.0.', USER 'monitor', AUTH_PROTOCOL 'sha256',
  AUTH_KEY 'auth-passphrase', PRIV_PROTOCOL 'aes', PRIV_KEY 'priv-passphrase');
```

A timeout or wrong credentials raise an error that names the agent.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## snmp_get(host, oid, ...)

One row per requested instance. Missing instances come back as `noSuchObject` / `noSuchInstance` rows.

Scalars need the `.0` instance suffix: `sysName.0`, not `sysName`.

**Connection:** `version := '1' | '2c' | '3'`, `community := '...'`, `port := 161`, `timeout := 2.0`, `retries := 1`, `context := ''`. Credentials can also come from a `snmp` secret scoped to `snmp://<host>` or from `SNMP_*` environment variables; see the README.

functions.name: snmp_oid
functions.comment: Resolve a MIB name such as 'IF-MIB::ifInOctets.3' to its numeric OID

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Translate a MIB name to a dotted numeric OID, offline, like `snmptranslate -On`. Accepts 'sysDescr', 'sysDescr.0', 'IF-MIB::ifInOctets.3' or an already numeric OID (returned normalized without a leading dot). Returns NULL for NULL input and for names not in the loaded MIBs. Vectorized: works over a column of names.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## snmp_oid(name)

`snmp_oid('IF-MIB::ifInOctets.3')` returns `'1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.10.3'`. NULL for unknown names.

functions.name: snmp_oid_name
functions.comment: Name a numeric OID, e.g. '1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0' becomes 'SNMPv2-MIB::sysUpTime.0'

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Translate a dotted numeric OID to 'MODULE::object.instance' using the loaded MIBs, offline. The deepest named ancestor is used, so an unknown vendor OID still gets a prefix such as 'SNMPv2-SMI::enterprises.9.1.1'. Returns NULL for NULL, non-numeric input, or OIDs outside every loaded MIB.

## snmp_oid_name(oid)

`snmp_oid_name('1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.10.3')` returns `'IF-MIB::ifInOctets.3'`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Decode numeric OIDs from a trap or log: name each with snmp_oid_name, then join snmp_mib_objects for the object's syntax and UNITS clause (NULL when the MIB declares none)
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH named AS (SELECT oid, snmp.main.snmp_oid_name(oid) AS name FROM (VALUES ('1.3.6.1.2.1.31.1.1.1.15.3'), ('1.3.6.1.2.1.25.2.3.1.4.1'), ('1.3.6.1.2.1.31.1.1.1.6.3')) t(oid)) SELECT n.oid, n.name, o.syntax, o.units FROM named n JOIN snmp.main.snmp_mib_objects() o ON o.module = split_part(n.name, '::', 1) AND o.name = split_part(split_part(n.name, '::', 2), '.', 1) ORDER BY string_split(n.oid, '.')::INTEGER[]

workers.title: World Football (Soccer) Data
workers.tagline: Premier League, La Liga, Bundesliga, Serie A, Champions League & World Cup football data in DuckDB (Python)
workers.subtitle: League tables, scores, match events, xG and player statistics for 200+ competitions as SQL.
workers.summary: Read-only world football data: league tables, fixtures, results, match detail and player statistics from ESPN, plus open World Cup (openfootball) and German league (OpenLigaDB) data
workers.doc_md:
# World football data

Query league tables, fixtures and results, match events, box scores, play-by-play with expected goals, squads, leaderboards and player season lines for 200+ competitions, plus every men's World Cup since 1930 and German league data from OpenLigaDB.

## Data model

Competitions are addressed by ESPN league slug (`eng.1`, `uefa.champions`, `fifa.world`; list them in `leagues`). Seasons are start years. Matches carry an `event_id` that keys every `match_*` function.

## Sources and terms

Data is fetched on demand and never rehosted. ESPN endpoints are undocumented and subject to ESPN's terms; openfootball is CC0; OpenLigaDB is community open data. This worker is not affiliated with ESPN, Disney, FIFA, UEFA or any league.

- [ESPN soccer](https://www.espn.com/soccer/): leagues, matches, box scores and players (endpoints undocumented; [Disney terms of use](https://disneytermsofuse.com/)).
- [openfootball/worldcup.json](https://github.com/openfootball/worldcup.json): every men's World Cup, released under [CC0 1.0](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/).
- [OpenLigaDB](https://www.openligadb.de/) and its [API](https://api.openligadb.de/): Bundesliga tables and matches.

example_queries.title: leicester_2015_title
example_queries.description: Leicester City won the 2015-16 Premier League with 81 points.
example_queries.sql: SELECT team_name, points FROM soccer.main.standings(league := 'eng.1', season := 2015) WHERE rank = 1;

example_queries.description: Argentina won the 2022 World Cup final on penalties.
example_queries.sql: SELECT winner, team1_penalties, team2_penalties FROM soccer.main.world_cup_matches(2022) WHERE round = 'Final';

example_queries.sql: SELECT league_name FROM soccer.main.leagues WHERE league_slug = 'eng.1';

example_queries.description: The current tables cover all five leagues.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(DISTINCT league_slug) AS leagues FROM soccer.main.current_standings;

example_queries.description: The current Premier League table.
example_queries.sql: SELECT rank, team_name, games_played, goal_difference, points FROM soccer.main.current_standings WHERE league_slug = 'eng.1' ORDER BY rank

example_queries.description: Leaders of each big-five league.
example_queries.sql: SELECT league_name, team_name, points FROM soccer.main.current_standings WHERE rank = 1 ORDER BY points DESC

example_queries.description: 2023-24 Premier League top ten scorers with their club's final league position and points, joining stat_leaders to standings on team_id.
example_queries.sql: SELECT l.rank, l.player_name, l.team_name, l.goals, s.rank AS team_rank, s.points FROM soccer.main.stat_leaders(league := 'eng.1', season := 2023) AS l JOIN soccer.main.standings(league := 'eng.1', season := 2023) AS s USING (team_id) WHERE l.category = 'goals' ORDER BY l.rank, l.player_name LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Top ten players by shot xG in Manchester United 4-4 Aston Villa, with their shots and goals, joining match_plays to match_player_stats on athlete_id.
example_queries.sql: WITH shot_xg AS (SELECT athlete_id, count(*) AS shots, round(sum(expected_goals), 2) AS xg FROM soccer.main.match_plays(401879240) WHERE expected_goals IS NOT NULL GROUP BY athlete_id) SELECT p.team_name, p.player_name, x.shots, x.xg, p.goals FROM soccer.main.match_player_stats(401879240) AS p JOIN shot_xg AS x USING (athlete_id) ORDER BY x.xg DESC, p.player_name LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: 2018 World Cup knockout results after extra time, with shoot-out scores and every goal scorer in minute order (own goals marked), joining world_cup_matches to world_cup_goals.
example_queries.sql: SELECT m.round, m.team1, coalesce(m.team1_extra_time, m.team1_goals) AS team1_score, coalesce(m.team2_extra_time, m.team2_goals) AS team2_score, m.team2, m.team1_penalties, m.team2_penalties, string_agg(g.player_name || ' ' || g.minute_display || CASE WHEN g.own_goal THEN ' (og)' ELSE '' END, ', ' ORDER BY g.minute, g.stoppage_minute) AS scorers FROM soccer.main.world_cup_matches(2018) AS m LEFT JOIN soccer.main.world_cup_goals(2018) AS g ON g.round = m.round AND g.team IN (m.team1, m.team2) AND g.opponent IN (m.team1, m.team2) WHERE m.group_name IS NULL GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY min(m.match_number)

example_queries.description: Bundesliga matchday 10 of 2025-26 with each club's final 2025-26 table position, joining bundesliga_matches to bundesliga_table on team_id for home and away side.
example_queries.sql: SELECT m.team1_name, h.position AS team1_position, m.team1_goals, m.team2_goals, m.team2_name, a.position AS team2_position FROM soccer.main.bundesliga_matches(2025, matchday := 10) AS m JOIN soccer.main.bundesliga_table(2025) AS h ON h.team_id = m.team1_id JOIN soccer.main.bundesliga_table(2025) AS a ON a.team_id = m.team2_id ORDER BY least(h.position, a.position)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Start with leagues to find a league_slug, current_standings for today's big-five tables, current_matches for today's matches and event_ids, and current_stat_leaders for top scorers. Parameterized functions cover any league, past seasons (start year), single-match detail by event_id, squads, player season lines, World Cup history and OpenLigaDB German data.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## World football analytical data

Rows are explicitly league-, team-, match-, player-, event- or goal-grain. Current tables serve the common questions; parameterized functions reach any competition and season ESPN covers.

Find a competition's `league_slug` in `leagues`, take an `event_id` from `scoreboard()` or `schedule()`, and pass it to the `match_*` functions for box scores, line-ups, key events, commentary and play-by-play with expected goals.

vgi.example_queries.description: The current Premier League table.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT rank, team_name, games_played, goal_difference, points FROM soccer.main.current_standings WHERE league_slug = 'eng.1' ORDER BY rank

vgi.example_queries.description: Leaders of each big-five league.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT league_name, team_name, points FROM soccer.main.current_standings WHERE rank = 1 ORDER BY points DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: 2023-24 Premier League top ten scorers with their club's final league position and points, joining stat_leaders to standings on team_id.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT l.rank, l.player_name, l.team_name, l.goals, s.rank AS team_rank, s.points FROM soccer.main.stat_leaders(league := 'eng.1', season := 2023) AS l JOIN soccer.main.standings(league := 'eng.1', season := 2023) AS s USING (team_id) WHERE l.category = 'goals' ORDER BY l.rank, l.player_name LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: Top ten players by shot xG in Manchester United 4-4 Aston Villa, with their shots and goals, joining match_plays to match_player_stats on athlete_id.
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH shot_xg AS (SELECT athlete_id, count(*) AS shots, round(sum(expected_goals), 2) AS xg FROM soccer.main.match_plays(401879240) WHERE expected_goals IS NOT NULL GROUP BY athlete_id) SELECT p.team_name, p.player_name, x.shots, x.xg, p.goals FROM soccer.main.match_player_stats(401879240) AS p JOIN shot_xg AS x USING (athlete_id) ORDER BY x.xg DESC, p.player_name LIMIT 10

vgi.example_queries.description: 2018 World Cup knockout results after extra time, with shoot-out scores and every goal scorer in minute order (own goals marked), joining world_cup_matches to world_cup_goals.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT m.round, m.team1, coalesce(m.team1_extra_time, m.team1_goals) AS team1_score, coalesce(m.team2_extra_time, m.team2_goals) AS team2_score, m.team2, m.team1_penalties, m.team2_penalties, string_agg(g.player_name || ' ' || g.minute_display || CASE WHEN g.own_goal THEN ' (og)' ELSE '' END, ', ' ORDER BY g.minute, g.stoppage_minute) AS scorers FROM soccer.main.world_cup_matches(2018) AS m LEFT JOIN soccer.main.world_cup_goals(2018) AS g ON g.round = m.round AND g.team IN (m.team1, m.team2) AND g.opponent IN (m.team1, m.team2) WHERE m.group_name IS NULL GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY min(m.match_number)

vgi.example_queries.description: Bundesliga matchday 10 of 2025-26 with each club's final 2025-26 table position, joining bundesliga_matches to bundesliga_table on team_id for home and away side.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT m.team1_name, h.position AS team1_position, m.team1_goals, m.team2_goals, m.team2_name, a.position AS team2_position FROM soccer.main.bundesliga_matches(2025, matchday := 10) AS m JOIN soccer.main.bundesliga_table(2025) AS h ON h.team_id = m.team1_id JOIN soccer.main.bundesliga_table(2025) AS a ON a.team_id = m.team2_id ORDER BY least(h.position, a.position)

vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH shot_xg AS (SELECT athlete_id, count(*) AS shots, round(sum(expected_goals), 2) AS xg FROM soccer.main.match_plays(401879240) WHERE expected_goals IS NOT NULL GROUP BY athlete_id) SELECT p.team_name, p.player_name, x.shots, x.xg, p.goals FROM soccer.main.match_player_stats(401879240) AS p JOIN shot_xg AS x USING (athlete_id) ORDER BY x.xg DESC, p.player_name LIMIT 10

functions.name: world_cup_matches
functions.comment: Every match of one men's FIFA World Cup, 1930-2026 (openfootball, CC0)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Results of every match at one men's World Cup (positional year). team1_goals/team2_goals are the 90-minute score; extra-time and shoot-out columns are filled only when played; winner resolves all three. group_name is null for knockout games.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Results of every match at one men's World Cup (positional year). team1_goals/team2_goals are the 90-minute score; extra-time and shoot-out columns are filled only when played; winner resolves all three. group_name is null for knockout games.

**Source:** the openfootball worldcup.json project on GitHub, dedicated to the public domain (CC0). Player names are as published and occasionally vary in spelling.

vgi.example_queries.description: The 2022 World Cup knockout rounds, including extra time and penalties.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT round, team1, team2, team1_goals, team2_goals, team1_extra_time, team2_extra_time, team1_penalties, team2_penalties, winner FROM soccer.main.world_cup_matches(2022) WHERE group_name IS NULL ORDER BY match_number

vgi.example_queries.description: 2018 World Cup knockout results after extra time, with shoot-out scores and every goal scorer in minute order (own goals marked), joining world_cup_matches to world_cup_goals.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT m.round, m.team1, coalesce(m.team1_extra_time, m.team1_goals) AS team1_score, coalesce(m.team2_extra_time, m.team2_goals) AS team2_score, m.team2, m.team1_penalties, m.team2_penalties, string_agg(g.player_name || ' ' || g.minute_display || CASE WHEN g.own_goal THEN ' (og)' ELSE '' END, ', ' ORDER BY g.minute, g.stoppage_minute) AS scorers FROM soccer.main.world_cup_matches(2018) AS m LEFT JOIN soccer.main.world_cup_goals(2018) AS g ON g.round = m.round AND g.team IN (m.team1, m.team2) AND g.opponent IN (m.team1, m.team2) WHERE m.group_name IS NULL GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY min(m.match_number)

workers.subtitle: Any Socrata (Tyler Data & Insights) portal's catalog and datasets as SQL, with SoQL pushdown.
workers.summary: Any Socrata (Tyler Data & Insights) open-data portal as SQL: search portal catalogs and read typed dataset rows, with filters, projections and aggregates pushed down as SoQL. No key needed for public data.
workers.doc_md:
# Socrata open-data portals in DuckDB

Query **any Socrata (Tyler Data & Insights) open-data portal** with SQL: New York City, Chicago, Washington State, the CDC and thousands more US and European government portals. No key is needed for public data.

Filters, projections, `count(*)` and `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` run on the portal as SoQL, rows are paged with a resumable keyset cursor, and aggregations can run server-side. Columns get real DuckDB types, including timestamps, decimals, booleans, GeoJSON points and location structs.
workers.readme_sql:
-- NYC 311 complaints in Brooklyn in the first ten minutes of 2024. The filter and the columns are
-- sent to the portal as SoQL, so 40 million rows become one small request.
SELECT complaint_type, count(*) AS requests
FROM socrata.main.dataset('data.cityofnewyork.us', 'erm2-nwe9')
WHERE created_date >= TIMESTAMP '2024-01-01 00:00:00' AND created_date < TIMESTAMP '2024-01-01 00:10:00'
  AND borough = 'BROOKLYN'
GROUP BY complaint_type ORDER BY requests DESC;

example_queries.description: The five most viewed NYC datasets about 311 service requests
example_queries.sql: SELECT dataset_id, title, page_views_last_month FROM socrata.main.datasets('data.cityofnewyork.us', q := '311 service requests') ORDER BY page_views_last_month DESC, dataset_id LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Datasets per category on the Dutch vehicle authority (RDW) portal, an EU portal
example_queries.sql: SELECT category, count(*) AS datasets FROM socrata.main.datasets('opendata.rdw.nl') GROUP BY category ORDER BY datasets DESC, category

example_queries.description: Ten police use-of-force datasets from any US portal
example_queries.sql: SELECT portal, dataset_id, title FROM socrata.main.search_datasets('police use of force', max_rows := 10) ORDER BY portal, dataset_id

example_queries.description: Which European portals publish datasets about vehicles ('voertuigen')
example_queries.sql: SELECT portal, count(*) AS datasets FROM socrata.main.search_datasets('voertuigen', region := 'eu', max_rows := 50) GROUP BY portal ORDER BY datasets DESC, portal

example_queries.description: Field names and types of NYC 311 service requests
example_queries.sql: SELECT field_name, data_type, duckdb_type FROM socrata.main.dataset_columns('data.cityofnewyork.us', 'erm2-nwe9') WHERE NOT is_system ORDER BY position

example_queries.description: How many columns of each Socrata type the Chicago crimes dataset has
example_queries.sql: SELECT data_type, count(*) AS columns FROM socrata.main.dataset_columns('data.cityofchicago.org', 'ijzp-q8t2') GROUP BY data_type ORDER BY columns DESC, data_type

example_queries.description: NYC 311 complaint types in Brooklyn in the first ten minutes of 2024 (filters run on the portal)
example_queries.sql: SELECT complaint_type, count(*) AS requests FROM socrata.main.dataset('data.cityofnewyork.us', 'erm2-nwe9') WHERE created_date >= TIMESTAMP '2024-01-01 00:00:00' AND created_date < TIMESTAMP '2024-01-01 00:10:00' AND borough = 'BROOKLYN' GROUP BY complaint_type ORDER BY requests DESC, complaint_type

example_queries.description: Chicago public library branches whose name starts with 'Ch', with website and coordinates
example_queries.sql: SELECT branch_, website.url AS website, location.latitude, location.longitude FROM socrata.main.dataset('data.cityofchicago.org', 'x8fc-8rcq') WHERE starts_with(branch_, 'Ch') ORDER BY branch_

example_queries.description: NYC 311 requests per borough on 1 January 2024, counted by the portal
example_queries.sql: SELECT borough, requests::BIGINT AS requests FROM socrata.main.soql('data.cityofnewyork.us', 'erm2-nwe9', 'SELECT borough, count(*) AS requests WHERE created_date >= ''2024-01-01T00:00:00'' AND created_date < ''2024-01-02T00:00:00'' GROUP BY borough ORDER BY borough') ORDER BY borough

example_queries.description: The five crime types with the most arrests in Chicago on 1 January 2024
example_queries.sql: SELECT primary_type, arrests::BIGINT AS arrests FROM socrata.main.soql('data.cityofchicago.org', 'ijzp-q8t2', 'SELECT primary_type, count(*) AS arrests WHERE arrest = true AND date >= ''2024-01-01T00:00:00'' AND date < ''2024-01-02T00:00:00'' GROUP BY primary_type ORDER BY arrests DESC, primary_type LIMIT 5') ORDER BY arrests DESC, primary_type

example_queries.description: Quote a value containing an apostrophe for a SoQL condition
example_queries.sql: SELECT socrata.main.soql_quote('O''Brien') AS literal

example_queries.description: Use a quoted literal inside a raw SoQL condition
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS requests FROM socrata.main.dataset('data.cityofnewyork.us', 'erm2-nwe9', soql_where := 'agency = ' || socrata.main.soql_quote('NYPD') || ' AND created_date >= ''2024-01-01T00:00:00'' AND created_date < ''2024-01-01T00:10:00''')

example_queries.description: Escape LIKE wildcards in a literal value
example_queries.sql: SELECT socrata.main.soql_like_escape('100%_done') AS pattern

example_queries.description: NYC 311 noise complaints in the first hour of 2024, matched on the portal
example_queries.sql: SELECT descriptor, count(*) AS requests FROM socrata.main.dataset('data.cityofnewyork.us', 'erm2-nwe9', soql_where := 'upper(descriptor) like ' || socrata.main.soql_quote('%' || socrata.main.soql_like_escape('NOISE') || '%') || ' AND created_date >= ''2024-01-01T00:00:00'' AND created_date < ''2024-01-01T01:00:00''') GROUP BY descriptor ORDER BY requests DESC, descriptor

example_queries.description: Build a quoted contains-pattern for a SoQL like
example_queries.sql: SELECT socrata.main.soql_quote('%' || socrata.main.soql_like_escape('50%') || '%') AS pattern;

example_queries.description: Build a SoQL condition for each value of a column
example_queries.sql: SELECT 'borough = ' || socrata.main.soql_quote(b) AS condition FROM (VALUES ('BRONX'), ('QUEENS')) t(b) ORDER BY b;

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Everything for Socrata portals lives in this one schema, in three groups: catalog discovery (the Discovery API's dataset listings for one portal or a federated search, and a dataset's column metadata), data access (typed rows with SoQL pushdown, and full server-side SoQL queries for aggregates), and helpers that quote values for hand-written SoQL. Every portal-facing function takes the portal domain first (e.g. 'data.cityofnewyork.us') and, for a dataset, its four-by-four id. Look up field names before filtering (display names differ from field names); filter in SQL so the portal does the work; for GROUP BY over millions of rows let the portal aggregate.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

Everything this worker offers lives in one schema, grouped in three categories.

**Catalog** functions search one portal's datasets or every portal at once through the Socrata Discovery API, and list a dataset's columns with the DuckDB type each one gets.

**Data** functions read a dataset's rows with filters, projections and Top-N sorts pushed to the portal as SoQL, or run a SoQL aggregate on the portal and return only the summary.

**SoQL helpers** quote values for hand-written SoQL.

functions.name: soql
functions.comment: Run a server-side SoQL query (aggregates, GROUP BY) on a Socrata dataset

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
Run a full SoQL query on the portal and return its rows, typed. Arguments: the portal, the dataset_id (four-by-four) and a SoQL query, which is like a SQL query without a FROM clause, for example:

```sql
SELECT borough, count(*) AS n WHERE created_date >= '2024-01-01T00:00:00' GROUP BY borough
```

SoQL string literals use single quotes; timestamps compare with text literals such as '2024-01-01T00:00:00'; useful functions include count, sum, avg, min, max, date_trunc_ym, upper, starts_with and within_circle. Result columns are named by alias (an unaliased count is 'count') and typed from the portal's own type report (numbers `DECIMAL(28,10)`, timestamps `TIMESTAMP`, text `VARCHAR`). A query without a limit may return at most max_rows (default 10,000) rows, otherwise it fails. Use it to summarize huge datasets in one request instead of reading every row with dataset().
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## soql(portal, dataset_id, query, max_rows :=)

A server-side SoQL query, e.g. NYC 311 requests per borough over 40 million rows in one request. Column types come from the portal (`X-SODA2-Types`).

vgi.example_queries.description: NYC 311 requests per borough on 1 January 2024, counted by the portal
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT borough, requests::BIGINT AS requests FROM socrata.main.soql('data.cityofnewyork.us', 'erm2-nwe9', 'SELECT borough, count(*) AS requests WHERE created_date >= ''2024-01-01T00:00:00'' AND created_date < ''2024-01-02T00:00:00'' GROUP BY borough ORDER BY borough') ORDER BY borough

vgi.example_queries.description: The five crime types with the most arrests in Chicago on 1 January 2024
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT primary_type, arrests::BIGINT AS arrests FROM socrata.main.soql('data.cityofchicago.org', 'ijzp-q8t2', 'SELECT primary_type, count(*) AS arrests WHERE arrest = true AND date >= ''2024-01-01T00:00:00'' AND date < ''2024-01-02T00:00:00'' GROUP BY primary_type ORDER BY arrests DESC, primary_type LIMIT 5') ORDER BY arrests DESC, primary_type

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
One column per SELECT expression, named by its alias (or the portal's generated name, e.g. 'count' for count(*)), typed from the portal's report:

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| <text expression> | VARCHAR | Text results and group keys. |
| <count / sum / avg / number expression> | DECIMAL(28,10) | Numeric results. |
| <timestamp expression, e.g. date_trunc_ym(created_date)> | TIMESTAMP | Floating timestamps. |
| <checkbox expression> | BOOLEAN | Booleans. |
| <point / polygon expression> | JSON | GeoJSON geometry. |

For the NYC 311 per-borough example:

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| borough | VARCHAR | The borough (group key). |
| requests | DECIMAL(28,10) | count(*) per borough. |

For the Chicago arrests example:

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| primary_type | VARCHAR | Crime type (group key). |
| arrests | DECIMAL(28,10) | count(*) of arrests. |

functions.name: dataset
functions.comment: Rows of one Socrata dataset, typed from its metadata, with SoQL pushdown

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Read the rows of one dataset of a Socrata (Tyler Data & Insights) portal, given the portal domain and the dataset's four-by-four id (e.g. 'erm2-nwe9'; find it with datasets()). Columns are the dataset's columns (see dataset_columns(portal, dataset_id)) plus soda_row_id, typed: number/money/percent `DECIMAL(28,10)`, double `DOUBLE`, checkbox `BOOLEAN`, calendar_date and floating_timestamp `TIMESTAMP` (local time, no zone), fixed_timestamp `TIMESTAMPTZ`, point/line/polygon GeoJSON `JSON`, location `STRUCT(latitude, longitude, address, city, state, zip)`, url `STRUCT(url, description)`, text and others `VARCHAR`. Selected columns become SoQL `$select`; WHERE filters (= <> IN IS NULL starts_with on text; ranges on numbers and timestamps; = on checkbox) become `$where`; ORDER BY <number or timestamp column> LIMIT n (with no WHERE) is sorted and limited by the portal. Rows are paged with a keyset cursor on :id (page_rows := rows per request, default 1000), so filter first on big datasets. soql_where := adds a raw SoQL condition (within_circle, like, cross-column OR). For server-side GROUP BY use soql().
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## dataset(portal, dataset_id, soql_where :=, page_rows :=)

All rows of a dataset, with columns typed from its metadata.

**Pushdown.** Projections, filters and `ORDER BY ... LIMIT n` (without `WHERE`) on numeric and timestamp columns run on the portal as SoQL. Paging uses a keyset cursor on the system `:id` column (never deep `$offset`), carried in the scan state so long scans resume.

vgi.example_queries.description: NYC 311 complaint types in Brooklyn in the first ten minutes of 2024 (filters run on the portal)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT complaint_type, count(*) AS requests FROM socrata.main.dataset('data.cityofnewyork.us', 'erm2-nwe9') WHERE created_date >= TIMESTAMP '2024-01-01 00:00:00' AND created_date < TIMESTAMP '2024-01-01 00:10:00' AND borough = 'BROOKLYN' GROUP BY complaint_type ORDER BY requests DESC, complaint_type

vgi.example_queries.description: Chicago public library branches whose name starts with 'Ch', with website and coordinates
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT branch_, website.url AS website, location.latitude, location.longitude FROM socrata.main.dataset('data.cityofchicago.org', 'x8fc-8rcq') WHERE starts_with(branch_, 'Ch') ORDER BY branch_

One column per dataset column, named by its field name as in dataset_columns(portal, dataset_id); the type follows the Socrata data type:

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| <number / money / percent column> | DECIMAL(28,10) | Exact number; NULL if it needs more than 18 integer digits. |
| <double column> | DOUBLE | Floating-point number. |
| <checkbox column> | BOOLEAN | Checkbox. |
| <calendar_date / floating_timestamp column> | TIMESTAMP | Local (floating) date and time. |
| <fixed_timestamp column> | TIMESTAMPTZ | Absolute timestamp, UTC. |
| <point / line / polygon / multi* column> | JSON | GeoJSON geometry (use ST_GeomFromGeoJSON). |
| <location column> | STRUCT(latitude DOUBLE, longitude DOUBLE, address VARCHAR, city VARCHAR, state VARCHAR, zip VARCHAR) | Legacy location. |
| <url column> | STRUCT(url VARCHAR, description VARCHAR) | Link. |
| <phone column> | STRUCT(phone_number VARCHAR, phone_type VARCHAR) | Phone number. |
| <text column> | VARCHAR | Text and any other type. |
| soda_row_id | VARCHAR | System row id (:id), the paging cursor. |
