functions.name: soql_like_escape
functions.comment: Escape %, _ and backslash so text matches literally inside a SoQL like pattern

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Escape the LIKE wildcards `%` and `_` (and the escape character backslash) in `text` with a backslash, so it matches literally inside a SoQL `like` pattern. Combine with soql_quote: 'descriptor like ' || soql_quote('%' || soql_like_escape(t) || '%'). NULL in, NULL out. Runs locally. DuckDB never pushes LIKE/ILIKE into dataset() scans, so a server-side substring match must be written as soql_where := or inside soql().
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## soql_like_escape(text)

`soql_like_escape('100%_done')` returns `100\%\_done`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Escape LIKE wildcards in a literal value
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT socrata.main.soql_like_escape('100%_done') AS pattern

vgi.example_queries.description: NYC 311 noise complaints in the first hour of 2024, matched on the portal
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT descriptor, count(*) AS requests FROM socrata.main.dataset('data.cityofnewyork.us', 'erm2-nwe9', soql_where := 'upper(descriptor) like ' || socrata.main.soql_quote('%' || socrata.main.soql_like_escape('NOISE') || '%') || ' AND created_date >= ''2024-01-01T00:00:00'' AND created_date < ''2024-01-01T01:00:00''') GROUP BY descriptor ORDER BY requests DESC, descriptor

functions.name: soql_quote
functions.comment: Quote text as a SoQL string literal for soql_where := and soql() queries

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Return `value` as a SoQL string literal: wrapped in single quotes with embedded single quotes doubled and backslashes doubled (SoQL literals treat backslash as an escape), ready to concatenate into a `soql_where :=` condition of dataset() or a soql() query, e.g. 'borough = ' || soql_quote(b). NULL in, NULL out. Runs locally without contacting any portal. SQL WHERE clauses on dataset() do not need it: those are translated and quoted automatically.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## soql_quote(value)

Quote text for use inside raw SoQL.

`soql_quote('O''Brien')` returns `'O''Brien'`.

workers.doc_md:
# sourcemap

Decode **JavaScript Source Map v3** (`.map`) files and resolve minified `(line, col)` positions back to original `source:line:col:name`, directly in DuckDB SQL. Nothing else in DuckDB reads source maps — `read_json` gives you the wrapper object but not the decoded Base64-VLQ `mappings` grammar. This worker performs that decode and exposes both the raw mapping rows and resolved original positions, so a column of production RUM / error-tracking frames can be de-minified in bulk with a single JOIN.

The heavy lifting (Base64-VLQ decode, index maps via `sections`, inline `sourcesContent`, the nearest-preceding lookup) is done by the Sentry `sourcemap` crate; this worker is a thin Arrow adapter over it. A map is supplied as a **path** to a `.map` file, the raw map **JSON text** (e.g. `(SELECT content FROM read_text(...))`), or map `BLOB` bytes — so data-URI inline maps decode via the text/bytes mode.

## Semantics

- All line/column numbers are **0-indexed** (Source Map v3); browser stack frames are usually 1-indexed, so subtract one before resolving.
- Position resolution is **nearest-preceding** (the greatest mapping `<=` the requested position), so an exact `(line, col)` match isn't required.
- Per-row resolution is **tolerant**: a NULL, malformed, or empty map — or a position with no match — yields NULL rather than failing the query, so one bad frame never aborts a scan.

## When to use

Reach for it whenever you have minified positions (deployed bundle line/column) and the corresponding source map, and you want the original file, line, column, and symbol name back — one frame at a time or a whole error table at once.

## Sources and references

- [ECMA-426 Source map format specification](https://tc39.es/ecma426/) — the standardized Source Map v3 format (`mappings`, `sources`, `names`, index-map `sections`) this worker decodes.
- [Sentry `sourcemap` crate](https://github.com/getsentry/rust-sourcemap) ([API docs](https://docs.rs/sourcemap)) — the decoder and lookup engine the worker wraps.

The first output column is the **passthrough id** — it takes the exact name and type of the input `id` column (whatever you named via `id :=`), so results join back to the originating row. It is followed by four fixed resolution columns. For an input relation whose id column is a `BIGINT` named `id`, the result columns are:

| `src_col` | BIGINT | 0-indexed original column, or NULL when unresolved. |
| `name` | VARCHAR | Original symbol name, or NULL if the mapping carries none. |

workers.doc_md:
# statsmodels: Regression & Statistical Inference in SQL

![statsmodels logo](https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/_images/statsmodels-logo-v2-horizontal.svg)

Run regression with full statistical inference and classic hypothesis tests directly in DuckDB SQL: fit OLS, logistic, and generalized linear models and get coefficient tables complete with standard errors, t/z-statistics, p-values, and 95% confidence intervals — no Python notebook required.

This extension brings the proven statistics of the [statsmodels](https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/index.html) library ([source on GitHub](https://github.com/statsmodels/statsmodels)) to anyone who already speaks SQL. It is built for data analysts, data scientists, and engineers who want trustworthy estimation and inference — effect sizes, significance, model fit, and stationarity checks — without exporting data to a separate stats environment. Every function takes a whole input relation as a `(SELECT ...)` subquery, so you model the result of any DuckDB query: joins, filters, window functions, and aggregates all flow straight into the fit.

Under the hood each call buffers the input relation, builds the design matrices from a [Patsy](https://patsy.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) ([source on GitHub](https://github.com/pydata/patsy)) `formula` (for the regressions) or from named column roles (for the tests), then runs the corresponding statsmodels routine once and returns the results as an ordinary SQL table you can join, filter, and persist. The familiar R-style formula syntax (`y ~ x1 + x2 + C(group)`) makes specifying interactions, transformations, and categorical encodings concise and readable.

The capabilities group into three areas. **Regression** estimates how predictors drive an outcome — linear for continuous responses, logistic for binary events, and generalized linear models for counts and other exponential-family outcomes — always returning coefficients with standard errors, t- or z-statistics, p-values, and 95% confidence intervals. **Model fit** reports whole-model diagnostics such as R-squared, adjusted R-squared, the F-test, AIC/BIC, and log-likelihood so you can judge how well a linear model explains the data. **Hypothesis tests** compare two group means and check a time series for a unit root (stationarity). Together they let you ask, in SQL alone, which predictors matter and by how much, whether an effect is significant, how well a model fits, and whether a series is stationary.

example_queries.description: Fit y ~ x by OLS and read each term's coefficient and p-value.
example_queries.sql: SELECT term, round(coef, 3) AS coef, round(p_value, 6) AS p_value FROM statsmodels.main.ols((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1,5.1),(2,7.9),(3,11.2),(4,13.8)) AS t(x, y)), formula := 'y ~ x') ORDER BY term

example_queries.description: Report the R-squared goodness-of-fit for an OLS model of y on x.
example_queries.sql: SELECT round(value, 4) AS r_squared FROM statsmodels.main.model_stats((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1,5.1),(2,7.9),(3,11.2),(4,13.8)) AS t(x, y)), formula := 'y ~ x') WHERE statistic = 'r_squared'

example_queries.description: Fit a Poisson GLM of count y on x and read the log-rate coefficient on x.
example_queries.sql: SELECT term, round(coef, 3) AS coef FROM statsmodels.main.glm((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1,1),(2,2),(3,2),(4,4),(5,5),(6,7),(7,9),(8,12)) AS t(x, y)), formula := 'y ~ x', family := 'poisson') WHERE term = 'x'

example_queries.description: Two-sample t-test of v across groups; read the p-value and mean difference.
example_queries.sql: SELECT round(p_value, 6) AS p_value, round(mean_diff, 2) AS mean_diff FROM statsmodels.main.ttest((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (10,'a'),(11,'a'),(20,'b'),(22,'b')) AS t(v, g)), "column" := 'v', "group" := 'g')

example_queries.description: Regress sales on ad spend and price with ols, and attach model_stats' adjusted R-squared and overall F-test verdict to every coefficient row
example_queries.sql: WITH ads AS (SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1,8.5,12.6),(2,10.0,12.7),(3,10.4,15.6),(4,8.1,24.8),(5,8.6,28.7),(6,11.7,26.0),(7,8.3,35.2),(8,8.5,40.6),(9,11.8,36.6),(10,10.5,41.2),(11,9.5,50.5),(12,10.0,51.7)) AS t(spend, price, sales)), fit AS (SELECT max(value) FILTER (WHERE statistic = 'adj_r_squared') AS adj_r_squared, max(value) FILTER (WHERE statistic = 'f_pvalue') AS f_pvalue FROM statsmodels.main.model_stats((SELECT * FROM ads), formula := 'sales ~ spend + price')) SELECT o.term, round(o.coef, 3) AS coef, round(o.p_value, 6) AS p_value, round(fit.adj_r_squared, 4) AS adj_r_squared, fit.f_pvalue < 0.001 AS model_significant FROM statsmodels.main.ols((SELECT * FROM ads), formula := 'sales ~ spend + price') AS o CROSS JOIN fit ORDER BY o.term

example_queries.description: Compare a linear and a quadratic model of the same data side by side on adjusted R-squared, AIC and BIC (the quadratic wins: higher adj R-squared, lower AIC/BIC)
example_queries.sql: WITH curve AS (SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1,2.0),(2,4.8),(3,7.6),(4,10.2),(5,14.0),(6,20.4),(7,27.0),(8,32.4),(9,39.2),(10,48.4)) AS t(x, y)), lin AS (SELECT statistic, value FROM statsmodels.main.model_stats((SELECT * FROM curve), formula := 'y ~ x')), quad AS (SELECT statistic, value FROM statsmodels.main.model_stats((SELECT * FROM curve), formula := 'y ~ x + I(x**2)')) SELECT lin.statistic, round(lin.value, 4) AS linear, round(quad.value, 4) AS quadratic FROM lin JOIN quad USING (statistic) WHERE lin.statistic IN ('adj_r_squared', 'aic', 'bic') ORDER BY lin.statistic

example_queries.description: Cointegration check in the Engle-Granger style: fit y ~ x with ols, then run adfuller on the regression residuals; a small p-value means the two trending series move together

## Regression & inference over SQL relations

This schema fits statistical models and runs classic hypothesis tests directly over DuckDB relations, powered by [statsmodels](https://www.statsmodels.org/). Every function takes a whole input relation as a `(SELECT ...)` subquery plus either a Patsy formula (`y ~ x1 + x2`) or named column roles, buffers the rows, runs the routine once, and returns a coefficient or statistic table you can join, filter, and persist.

It covers three areas:

- **Regression** — linear, logistic, and generalized linear fits that return a coefficient table with standard errors, t/z-statistics, p-values, and 95% confidence intervals.
- **Model fit** — whole-model diagnostics for a linear fit, such as R-squared, the F-test, and AIC/BIC.
- **Hypothesis tests** — compare two group means, and test a time series for a unit root (stationarity).

Reach for it to estimate effects, judge model fit, compare two groups, or check a series for stationarity — all without leaving SQL.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# glm_families

A small browsable reference view listing the **GLM error families** the `glm` function accepts as its `family` argument. Each row pairs a family name with its default link function, the kind of outcome it models, and a concrete example use.

**Use it** to discover valid `family` values before calling `glm`: the `family` column is exactly what you pass as `glm(<relation>, formula := '...', family := '<family>')`. Four families are available: `gaussian` (identity link, equals OLS), `binomial` (logit link, for binary/proportion outcomes), `poisson` (log link, for counts), and `gamma` (inverse link, for positive right-skewed responses). The view is a fixed in-memory table, so it scans instantly with no arguments.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## GLM error families

A reference view of the four error families the [statsmodels](https://www.statsmodels.org/) GLM fit supports, exposed so you can browse valid `family` values before calling `glm`.

Each row gives the `family` name (what you pass as `glm(..., family := '<family>')`), its default `link` function, the `typical_outcome` it models, and an `example_use`. The families are `gaussian` (identity link, equivalent to OLS), `binomial` (logit link, binary or proportion outcomes), `poisson` (log link, count outcomes), and `gamma` (inverse link, positive right-skewed outcomes).

It is a fixed four-row table, so it always scans instantly.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# model_stats

Fit the same **OLS** model as `ols` but return the **whole-model fit statistics** instead of the per-term coefficient table. Pass the data as a `(SELECT ...)` subquery and a Patsy `formula` named argument.

**Use it** to judge how well a linear model explains the data: the result is one `(statistic, value)` row per metric, covering `r_squared`, `adj_r_squared`, `f_statistic`, `f_pvalue`, `aic`, `bic`, `log_likelihood`, `nobs`, `df_model`, and `df_resid`. Reach for `ols` (same formula) when you need individual coefficients and their significance instead.

**Edge cases:** a bad formula, a missing or non-numeric column, empty input, or a singular design raises a clean `StatsError`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## OLS model fit statistics

Whole-model goodness-of-fit metrics for an OLS regression, powered by [statsmodels](https://www.statsmodels.org/). Same inputs as `ols` (a `(SELECT ...)` relation and a Patsy `formula`), but the output describes the model as a whole rather than each term.

Returns one row per statistic: R-squared and adjusted R-squared, the overall F-test (`f_statistic`, `f_pvalue`), `aic`/`bic`, log-likelihood, and the observation / degrees-of-freedom counts.

Call it as `model_stats(<relation>, formula := 'y ~ x')` and filter by `statistic`; a ready-to-run version is in this function's example queries.

functions.comment: Logistic (binary-outcome) regression with full inference: emits (term, coef, std_err, z_value, p_value, ci_lower, ci_upper, odds_ratio). Response must be binary. Pass a Patsy formula.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# logit

Fit a **binary logistic regression** over a whole SQL relation and return its coefficient table on the log-odds scale, with full inference and a convenience odds ratio per term. Pass the data as a `(SELECT ...)` subquery and a Patsy `formula` named argument; the response on the left of the formula must be binary (two distinct values, e.g. 0/1).

**Use it** when the outcome is a yes/no event and you want to know how each predictor shifts the odds: each row is one model term with its log-odds coefficient, standard error, Wald z-statistic, p-value, 95% confidence interval, and `odds_ratio` (= `exp(coef)`; >1 raises the odds, <1 lowers them).

**Edge cases:** a non-binary response, perfect separation, a singular design, a bad formula, a missing/non-numeric column, or empty input raises a clean `StatsError`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Logistic regression

Binary logistic (logit) regression over a SQL relation, powered by [statsmodels](https://www.statsmodels.org/). Pass the data as a `(SELECT ...)` subquery and the model as a Patsy `formula` whose response is binary.

Returns one row per model term with the log-odds coefficient, standard error, Wald z-value, p-value, 95% confidence interval, and the odds ratio `exp(coef)`.

Call it as `logit(<relation>, formula := 'y ~ x')` with a binary response; a ready-to-run version is in this function's example queries.

vgi.example_queries.description: Logistic fit of binary y on x; read the x log-odds coefficient and odds ratio
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT term, round(coef, 3) AS coef, round(odds_ratio, 3) AS odds_ratio FROM statsmodels.main.logit((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1,0),(2,0),(3,0),(4,1),(5,0),(6,1),(7,0),(8,1),(9,1),(10,1),(11,1),(12,1)) AS t(x, y)), formula := 'y ~ x') WHERE term = 'x'

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# glm

Fit a **generalized linear model** over a whole SQL relation with a selectable error `family`, returning a coefficient table on the link scale with full inference. Pass the data as a `(SELECT ...)` subquery, a Patsy `formula`, and `family := 'gaussian' | 'binomial' | 'poisson' | 'gamma'` (default `gaussian`).

**Use it** for outcomes that aren't plain continuous Gaussian: `poisson` for counts (log link), `binomial` for binary/proportion outcomes (logit link), `gamma` for positive skewed responses, and `gaussian` to reproduce OLS. Each row is one model term with its coefficient, standard error, Wald z-statistic, p-value, and 95% confidence interval.

**Edge cases:** an unknown family name, a family/data mismatch, a singular design, a bad formula, a missing/non-numeric column, or empty input raises a clean `StatsError`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Generalized linear model

GLM regression over a SQL relation with a configurable error family, powered by [statsmodels](https://www.statsmodels.org/). Pass the data as a `(SELECT ...)` subquery, a Patsy `formula`, and a `family`.

Call it as `glm(<relation>, formula := 'y ~ x', family := 'poisson')`; a ready-to-run version is in this function's example queries.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# ols

Fit an **ordinary least squares** linear regression over a whole SQL relation and return its coefficient table with full statistical inference. The first positional argument is the data, passed as a `(SELECT ...)` subquery; the model is given as a Patsy `formula` named argument such as `'y ~ x1 + x2'`. Every column of the relation is available to the formula by name.

**Use it** to estimate how continuous predictors drive a continuous outcome and to judge which terms matter: each row is one model term (predictors plus the `Intercept`) with its coefficient, standard error, t-statistic, two-sided p-value, and 95% confidence interval. For whole-model fit quality (R-squared, F-test, AIC/BIC) use `model_stats` with the same formula.

**Edge cases:** a malformed formula, a missing or non-numeric column, empty input, or a singular (rank-deficient) design raises a clean `StatsError` rather than crashing.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## OLS regression

Ordinary least squares regression over a SQL relation, powered by [statsmodels](https://www.statsmodels.org/). Pass the data as a `(SELECT ...)` subquery and the model as a Patsy `formula`.

Returns one row per model term (`Intercept` and each predictor) with the estimated coefficient, standard error, t-value, p-value, and 95% confidence bounds.

Call it as `ols(<relation>, formula := 'y ~ x')`; a ready-to-run version is in this function's example queries. See `model_stats` for whole-model fit statistics on the same formula.

vgi.example_queries.description: Fit y ~ x by OLS and read each term's coefficient and p-value
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT term, round(coef, 3) AS coef, round(p_value, 6) AS p_value FROM statsmodels.main.ols((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1,5.1),(2,7.9),(3,11.2),(4,13.8),(5,17.1),(6,19.9),(7,23.2),(8,25.8)) AS t(x, y)), formula := 'y ~ x') ORDER BY term

vgi.example_queries.description: Regress sales on ad spend and price with ols, and attach model_stats' adjusted R-squared and overall F-test verdict to every coefficient row
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH ads AS (SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1,8.5,12.6),(2,10.0,12.7),(3,10.4,15.6),(4,8.1,24.8),(5,8.6,28.7),(6,11.7,26.0),(7,8.3,35.2),(8,8.5,40.6),(9,11.8,36.6),(10,10.5,41.2),(11,9.5,50.5),(12,10.0,51.7)) AS t(spend, price, sales)), fit AS (SELECT max(value) FILTER (WHERE statistic = 'adj_r_squared') AS adj_r_squared, max(value) FILTER (WHERE statistic = 'f_pvalue') AS f_pvalue FROM statsmodels.main.model_stats((SELECT * FROM ads), formula := 'sales ~ spend + price')) SELECT o.term, round(o.coef, 3) AS coef, round(o.p_value, 6) AS p_value, round(fit.adj_r_squared, 4) AS adj_r_squared, fit.f_pvalue < 0.001 AS model_significant FROM statsmodels.main.ols((SELECT * FROM ads), formula := 'sales ~ spend + price') AS o CROSS JOIN fit ORDER BY o.term

functions.name: adfuller
functions.comment: Augmented Dickey-Fuller unit-root (stationarity) test over an already-ordered series; emits one row (statistic, p_value, used_lag, n_obs). Pass an ORDER BY'd relation so rows are in time order. Small p_value => reject unit root => stationary.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# adfuller

Run the **Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) unit-root test** to decide whether a time series is stationary. Pass the series as a `(SELECT ...)` subquery and the series column as `column`. Because `column` is a SQL reserved word, **double-quote the argument name**: `"column" := 'v'`.

**Ordering matters:** SQL has no inherent row order, so the input must already be time-ordered — pass `(SELECT v FROM series ORDER BY t)`. The function treats the rows in the order it receives them.

**Use it** for stationarity checks before ARIMA / regression on time series. The result is a single row: the test `statistic`, the MacKinnon `p_value` (small => reject the unit-root null => the series is stationary), the number of lags chosen by AIC (`used_lag`), and the observation count after lagging/differencing (`n_obs`).

**Edge cases:** a missing/non-numeric column, empty input, or a series too short for the chosen lag raises a clean `StatsError`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Augmented Dickey-Fuller test

Stationarity (unit-root) test for a time series over a SQL relation, powered by [statsmodels](https://www.statsmodels.org/).

The input must be time-ordered — pass an `ORDER BY`'d subquery, since SQL rows have no inherent order. `column` is a SQL keyword, so the argument name must be double-quoted.

Returns a single row: the test statistic, the MacKinnon p-value (small means the series is stationary), the lag count chosen by AIC, and the effective observation count.

Call it as `adfuller(<ordered-relation>, "column" := 'v')` with the argument name double-quoted and the rows already time-ordered; a ready-to-run version is in this function's example queries.

vgi.example_queries.description: ADF stationarity test on an ordered series; read the lag, n_obs, and p-value
Cointegration check in the Engle-Granger style: fit y ~ x with ols, then run adfuller on the regression residuals; a small p-value means the two trending series move together

functions.name: ttest
functions.comment: Two-sample (pooled-variance) t-test of 'column' across the two levels of 'group'; emits one row (statistic, p_value, df, mean_diff). 'column' and 'group' are SQL keywords -- double-quote both arg names in SQL.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# ttest

Run a **two-sample (pooled-variance) t-test** comparing the mean of a numeric column across the two levels of a grouping column. Pass the data as a `(SELECT ...)` subquery, the value column as `column`, and the grouping column as `group`. Because `column` and `group` are SQL reserved words, **double-quote both argument names** at the call site: `"column" := 'v', "group" := 'g'`.

**Use it** to answer 'do these two groups differ in mean?'. The result is a single row: the t-statistic, the two-sided p-value for equal means, the degrees of freedom, and `mean_diff` (mean of the first group minus the second). A small p-value is evidence the group means differ.

**Edge cases:** a grouping column that does not have exactly two levels, a missing/non-numeric value column, or empty input raises a clean `StatsError`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Two-sample t-test

Pooled-variance two-sample t-test over a SQL relation, powered by [statsmodels](https://www.statsmodels.org/). Compares the mean of a value column across the two levels of a grouping column.

Note that `column` and `group` are SQL keywords, so both argument names must be double-quoted in SQL.

Returns a single row: the t-statistic, the two-sided p-value, the degrees of freedom, and the difference in group means.

Call it as `ttest(<relation>, "column" := 'value', "group" := 'arm')` with both argument names double-quoted; a ready-to-run version is in this function's example queries.

workers.subtitle: Every Steampipe plugin's tables as DuckDB tables, with key-column pushdown and secret-held credentials.
workers.summary: Host Steampipe plugins and query their tables from DuckDB: each plugin named at ATTACH becomes a schema, each plugin table a table, with key-column filters pushed down. No Steampipe CLI or Postgres needed.
workers.doc_md:
# Steampipe plugins in DuckDB

Hosts [Steampipe](https://steampipe.io) plugins and turns their tables into DuckDB tables, talking to each plugin directly over the steampipe-plugin-sdk gRPC protocol: no Steampipe CLI, no embedded Postgres. Name plugins in the `plugins` ATTACH option; each becomes a schema, and its tables are queried like any other.

- **Plugins**: OCI images from ghcr.io (fetched once, sha256-verified, cached) or local binaries.
- **Credentials**: a DuckDB secret of type `steampipe`, never the ATTACH string.
- **Pushdown**: key-column filters become plugin quals, and only the selected columns are hydrated.

attach_options.name: plugins
attach_options.description: Comma-separated Steampipe plugins to host, each `[schema=]ref`. A ref is an OCI image (`csv`, `csv@1.3.0`, `turbot/aws`, `ghcr.io/org/repo/name:tag`, `name@sha256:<digest>`) or a local plugin binary path. Each plugin becomes a schema named after it (or `schema`), holding one table per plugin table.

attach_options.name: config
attach_options.description: Non-secret connection settings, one HCL block per schema (`csv { paths = ["/data/*.csv"] }`) or a JSON object keyed by schema. Used to discover tables at ATTACH and for every query. Never put credentials here: use CREATE SECRET (TYPE steampipe, ...).

attach_options.name: cache_dir
attach_options.description: Directory for plugins fetched from a registry (default: <user cache dir>/vgi-steampipe/plugins). Binaries are stored by verified sha256 digest and reused offline.

attach_options.name: registry
attach_options.description: OCI registry for plugin refs that name none (default https://ghcr.io); for mirrors and tests.

example_queries.description: Read a plugin table directly, filtering on a key column
example_queries.sql: SELECT category, count(*) AS items FROM steampipe.main.scan('fixture', 'fixture_item') WHERE id <= 12 GROUP BY category ORDER BY category

example_queries.description: Ask the plugin for at most 10 rows (Steampipe's limit pushdown)
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS fetched FROM steampipe.main.scan('fixture', 'fixture_item', max_rows := 10)

example_queries.description: The attached plugins and how many tables each serves
example_queries.sql: SELECT schema_name, plugin, plugin_version, table_count FROM steampipe.main.plugin ORDER BY schema_name

example_queries.description: Tables that need a WHERE filter, and on which columns
example_queries.sql: SELECT schema_name, table_name, required_filters FROM steampipe.main.plugin_table WHERE required_filters IS NOT NULL ORDER BY ALL

example_queries.description: Columns each table can filter on through the plugin's API

example_queries.sql: SELECT table_name, column_name, call FROM steampipe.main.plugin_key_column WHERE require = 'required' ORDER BY ALL;

example_queries.description: Tables of the fixture plugin that need a filter
example_queries.sql: SELECT table_name, required_filters FROM steampipe.main.plugin_table WHERE required_filters IS NOT NULL ORDER BY table_name;

example_queries.sql: SELECT schema_name, plugin, sdk_version, table_count FROM steampipe.main.plugin ORDER BY schema_name;

## main

Introspection of the plugins this ATTACH hosts: what the `plugins` option resolved to, which tables exist, which filters each table needs and which filters the plugin's API can apply.

The plugin tables themselves live in one schema per plugin. When a plugin's tables depend on credentials that only a secret holds, read them with `scan` instead.

tables.name: plugin_key_column
tables.comment: The key columns of every attached plugin table: the filters the plugin pushes to its API, and which are required.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per key column per table and call: schema_name, table_name, column_name, call ('get' looks one row up, 'list' filters a listing), require ('required', 'optional', or 'any_of' meaning at least one of the table's any_of columns) and operators (the comparisons the plugin accepts: =, <>, <, <=, >, >=; IN is sent as =, IS NULL as is null). Filtering on a key column with one of its operators makes the plugin's API do the filtering, which is much faster and cheaper than filtering a full listing. sp_connection_name, which every table has, is listed too.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Read one table of an attached Steampipe plugin: scan(schema, table_name, max_rows := 0). schema is a plugin schema of this ATTACH (see the plugin table), table_name a table of that plugin (see plugin_table). The output columns are the plugin table's own columns. WHERE filters on key columns are sent to the plugin as quals and every filter is applied exactly; tables with required key columns need a WHERE filter on them. max_rows is the plugin-side row limit, applied before filters that are not key-column quals. The tables in each plugin schema are the usual way to query; call scan() directly when a plugin's tables only appear once the credentials held in a secret are applied.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## scan(schema, table_name, max_rows := 0)

Reads one plugin table; the output columns are the table's own. The tables in each plugin schema are backed by this function, so you rarely need it, except for plugins whose tables only appear once the credentials in a secret are applied.

The output columns are the plugin table's own columns, as listed for the table in its plugin schema: Steampipe BOOL, INT, DOUBLE, STRING, JSON and TIMESTAMP columns become BOOLEAN, BIGINT, DOUBLE, VARCHAR, JSON and TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE; INET, CIDR and LTREE columns are VARCHAR. Every table also has the two columns below. For example, scan('fixture', 'fixture_greeting') returns:

| Name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| name | VARCHAR | The name greeted (the table's required key column). |
| message | VARCHAR | The greeting. |
| sp_connection_name | VARCHAR | The plugin schema the row came from. |
| sp_ctx | JSON | Steampipe connection context (connection name, SDK version). |

workers.doc_md:
# Stripe

Query a Stripe account from DuckDB: charges, PaymentIntents, refunds, disputes, balance transactions, payouts, customers, invoices, subscriptions, the product catalog, Connect transfers and the event feed. Read-only.

Create a `stripe` secret with an API key — a **restricted key** with read permissions is recommended. Filters on time ranges, ids, status and type become Stripe list parameters; filters only Stripe Search understands use the Search API. Amounts come both as Stripe's minor-unit integers and as exact decimals. Pagination, rate limits (429 + `Stripe-Should-Retry`) and Connect (`Stripe-Account`) are handled for you.

### Every endpoint

The curated `main` schema covers everyday analysis. For everything else, one schema per Stripe product area is generated from Stripe's OpenAPI spec with a table function for every read endpoint, nested lists included, and `api.get(path)` returns any single object as raw JSON. Sigma's scheduled query runs are listed there (running Sigma SQL is not part of the API). Products not enabled on the account answer with a clear "not enabled" error.

### Sources and references

- [Stripe API reference](https://docs.stripe.com/api) — the endpoints this worker reads
- [Pagination](https://docs.stripe.com/api/pagination) and [Search](https://docs.stripe.com/search) (query language, eventual consistency)
- [Expanding responses](https://docs.stripe.com/expand) and [API versioning](https://docs.stripe.com/api/versioning)
- [Restricted API keys](https://docs.stripe.com/keys#limit-access) and [rate limits](https://docs.stripe.com/rate-limits)
- [Currencies and minor units](https://docs.stripe.com/currencies#minor-units)
- [stripe/openapi](https://github.com/stripe/openapi) — the spec the test fixtures are checked against
workers.readme_sql:
CREATE SECRET stripe (TYPE stripe, API_KEY 'rk_live_…');   -- a restricted, read-only key

-- Net revenue after Stripe fees, by currency, this month (created range pushed down;
-- projecting fee/net expands each charge's balance transaction in the same requests).
SELECT currency, sum(amount_decimal) AS gross, sum(fee_decimal) AS fees, sum(net_decimal) AS net
FROM stripe.main.charges()
WHERE status = 'succeeded' AND created >= date_trunc('month', now())
GROUP BY currency ORDER BY gross DESC;

-- What was in a payout?
SELECT type, sum(net_decimal) AS net
FROM stripe.main.balance_transactions(payout := 'po_1QxY…')
GROUP BY type;

-- Who is churning? (every status, canceled included)
SELECT cancellation_reason, count(*) FROM stripe.main.subscriptions()
WHERE status = 'canceled' AND canceled_at >= now() - INTERVAL 30 DAY GROUP BY ALL;

## api

Raw GET access to the Stripe API for single objects by id and for fields the typed functions do not flatten.

### Safety

Only paths that match a GET in the vendored OpenAPI spec are accepted, so nothing can be written; credentials are redacted from responses.

### When to use

Reach for the typed schemas first; use this for one object or a verbatim field.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Escape hatch: GET any documented Stripe v1 read endpoint and return the response as one row (path, object, body JSON with credentials redacted). tags.vgi.doc_llm: Money movement endpoints of the Stripe API: the balance and its settings, balance transactions, payouts and top-ups, and currency reference data. Generated from Stripe's OpenAPI spec (API 2026-09-30.endive, stripe/openapi a045100cf4af), one table function per GET endpoint. Columns use Stripe's field names (ids for expandable references, `TIMESTAMPTZ` for Unix times, `BIGINT` minor units plus exact `*_decimal` amounts, `MAP` metadata, `JSON` for deeper objects, `raw` with credentials redacted). Documented list parameters push down: equality / IN on ids, status and type, boolean flags, `created`-style time ranges, `ids[]`, and `id = …` becomes a retrieve. Other query parameters are named arguments, and `params := MAP {…}` passes any documented one. Nested lists take the parent id as a named argument or a pushed `= / IN` filter, or fan out over every parent (one request per parent). For everyday analysis prefer the curated functions in stripe.main. All need a `stripe` secret.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## balance

Money movement endpoints of the Stripe API: the balance and its settings, balance transactions, payouts and top-ups, and currency reference data.

Generated from Stripe's OpenAPI spec (API 2026-09-30.endive, stripe/openapi a045100cf4af), one table function per GET endpoint. Families covered: balance & payouts, reference data.

### Pushdown

List parameters, time ranges and retrieve-by-id are pushed to Stripe; every other filter runs in DuckDB. Nested lists fan out over their parent unless you name the parent.

### Credentials

## billing

Every billing read endpoint of the Stripe API: customers and their sub-resources, invoices, credit notes, quotes, subscriptions, the product catalog, usage-based billing, entitlements and the portal.

Generated from Stripe's OpenAPI spec (API 2026-09-30.endive, stripe/openapi a045100cf4af), one table function per GET endpoint. Families covered: customers, invoicing, subscriptions, product catalog, usage-based billing, entitlements.

### Pushdown

List parameters, time ranges and retrieve-by-id are pushed to Stripe; every other filter runs in DuckDB. Nested lists fan out over their parent unless you name the parent.

### Credentials

All functions need a `stripe` secret; secrets in responses are redacted.

## connect

Connect endpoints of the Stripe API: your account, connected accounts and their people, capabilities and external accounts, transfers and reversals, application fees and fee refunds.

Generated from Stripe's OpenAPI spec (API 2026-09-30.endive, stripe/openapi a045100cf4af), one table function per GET endpoint. Families covered: accounts, transfers & fees.

### Pushdown

List parameters, time ranges and retrieve-by-id are pushed to Stripe; every other filter runs in DuckDB. Nested lists fan out over their parent unless you name the parent.

### Credentials

All functions need a `stripe` secret; secrets in responses are redacted.

## issuing

Stripe Issuing endpoints: cards, cardholders, authorizations, transactions, disputes, tokens, settlements, personalization designs and physical bundles. Needs Issuing enabled on the account.

Generated from Stripe's OpenAPI spec (API 2026-09-30.endive, stripe/openapi a045100cf4af), one table function per GET endpoint. Families covered: cards & cardholders, spend.

### Pushdown

List parameters, time ranges and retrieve-by-id are pushed to Stripe; every other filter runs in DuckDB. Nested lists fan out over their parent unless you name the parent.

### Credentials

All functions need a `stripe` secret; secrets in responses are redacted.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Returns a list of Issuing Authorization objects. The objects are sorted in descending order by creation date, with the most recently created object appearing first. Endpoint: GET /v1/issuing/authorizations (Stripe API 2026-09-30.endive), one row per issuing.authorization object (paged 100 at a time). Columns are Stripe's own field names: expandable references are ids, Unix times are `TIMESTAMPTZ`, minor-unit amounts beside a currency are `BIGINT` with an exact `*_decimal` major-unit companion, metadata is a `MAP`, deeper objects are `JSON`, and `raw` holds the whole object with credentials redacted. Pushdown: `cardholder` (= / IN), `status` (= / IN) → list parameters; time ranges on `created` → [gt/gte/lt/lte]; `id` = / IN (≤25) → one GET /v1/issuing/authorizations/{authorization} per id; named arguments `card` → Stripe parameters (card). Every filter is re-applied exactly by DuckDB/the SDK. Needs a `stripe` secret.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Stripe API collections as table functions, one per list endpoint (stripe.main.charges(), customers(), invoices(), …). Every function takes the named arguments stripe_account := (read a Connect account) and expand := [...] (raw Stripe expand paths into the raw JSON column); searchable resources (charges, customers, invoices, payment_intents, prices, products, subscriptions) also take search := (a Stripe search query). Child collections (invoice_line_items, subscription_items, payment_methods) take the parent id as a named argument or a pushed `= / IN` filter, and otherwise read every parent. All need a `stripe` secret.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

The hand-tuned Stripe functions: one table function per core list endpoint, with money as `BIGINT` minor units plus exact `*_decimal` amounts, Unix times as `TIMESTAMPTZ` and metadata as a `MAP`.

### Arguments

Every function takes `stripe_account :=` (read a Connect account) and `expand := [...]` (Stripe expand paths into the `raw` JSON column). Searchable resources (charges, customers, invoices, payment_intents, prices, products, subscriptions) also take `search :=`, a Stripe search query.

### Pushdown

`created`-style time ranges, ids, status and type filters are sent to Stripe; other filters run in DuckDB. Child collections (invoice_line_items, subscription_items, payment_methods) take the parent id as a named argument or a pushed `= / IN` filter, and otherwise read every parent (one request each).

### Credentials

All functions need a `stripe` secret holding an API key; a restricted `rk_...` read-only key is enough. For endpoints not covered here, use the generated schemas or `stripe.api.get`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Funds available to pay out, per currency
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT currency, amount_decimal FROM stripe.main.balance() WHERE bucket = 'available' ORDER BY currency

vgi.example_queries.description: Fees and net by transaction type since 1 November (the date range is pushed down)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT type, currency, sum(fee_decimal) AS fees, sum(net_decimal) AS net FROM stripe.main.balance_transactions() WHERE created >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY type, currency

vgi.example_queries.description: Paid payouts arriving since 1 November (both filters push down)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id, amount_decimal, currency, arrival_date FROM stripe.main.payouts() WHERE status = 'paid' AND arrival_date >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01' ORDER BY arrival_date

vgi.example_queries.description: Gross volume per currency (status uses Stripe Search)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT currency, count(*) AS charges, sum(amount_decimal) AS gross FROM stripe.main.charges() WHERE status = 'succeeded' GROUP BY currency ORDER BY currency

vgi.example_queries.description: Charges with Stripe fee and net (projecting fee expands the balance transaction)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id, amount_decimal, fee_decimal, net_decimal FROM stripe.main.charges() WHERE created >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01' ORDER BY id

vgi.example_queries.description: PaymentIntent funnel since 1 November
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT status, count(*) AS intents FROM stripe.main.payment_intents() WHERE created >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01' GROUP BY status ORDER BY intents DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Refunded amount by reason and currency
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT reason, currency, sum(amount_decimal) AS refunded FROM stripe.main.refunds() WHERE status = 'succeeded' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY reason, currency

vgi.example_queries.description: Disputes awaiting a response, by deadline
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id, reason, amount_decimal, currency, evidence_due_by FROM stripe.main.disputes() WHERE status IN ('needs_response', 'warning_needs_response') ORDER BY evidence_due_by

vgi.example_queries.description: Actionable early fraud warnings by fraud type
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT fraud_type, count(*) AS warnings FROM stripe.main.early_fraud_warnings() WHERE actionable GROUP BY fraud_type ORDER BY fraud_type

vgi.example_queries.description: Checkout conversion: complete vs expired sessions
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT status, count(*) AS sessions FROM stripe.main.checkout_sessions() WHERE created >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01' GROUP BY status ORDER BY status

vgi.example_queries.description: Look a customer up by exact email (list API email parameter)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id, name, created FROM stripe.main.customers() WHERE email = 'ada@example.com'

vgi.example_queries.description: Customers by country
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT address_country, count(*) AS customers FROM stripe.main.customers() GROUP BY address_country ORDER BY customers DESC

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Events (GET /v1/events): every change Stripe recorded in the last 30 days — type (charge.succeeded, customer.subscription.updated, invoice.paid …), created, object_type and object_id of the affected object, data_object (the object's state after the change, JSON), previous_attributes (changed fields' old values, JSON), api_version, request_id and idempotency_key (what API request caused it; NULL for automatic changes), pending_webhooks and account (Connect). `starts_with(type, 'invoice.')` pushes down as the `invoice.*` wildcard. object_id is filtered locally (Stripe cannot filter events by object).
tags.vgi.doc_md:

vgi.example_queries.description: Event volume by type since 1 November
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT type, count(*) AS events FROM stripe.main.events() WHERE created >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01' GROUP BY type ORDER BY events DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Invoice events only (pushed down as the invoice.* wildcard)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT created, type, object_id FROM stripe.main.events() WHERE starts_with(type, 'invoice.') ORDER BY created

functions.name: payment_methods
functions.comment: Customers' saved payment methods: type, card brand, last4 and expiry (never full numbers)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: PaymentMethods attached to customers (GET /v1/customers/{id}/payment_methods): id, customer, type (card, us_bank_account, sepa_debit, link …), card brand / last4 / exp_month / exp_year / funding / country / wallet, billing name/email/postal code, allow_redisplay, created and metadata. Only these card fields are exposed; Stripe never returns full card numbers. `customer_id := 'cus_…'` or a pushed `customer = / IN` reads just those customers; otherwise every customer is listed and read in turn (one call per customer).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## payment_methods(customer_id := NULL, expand := NULL)

Saved payment methods per customer.

**Pushdown:** `customer` (=, IN) or `customer_id :=` → one call per customer; otherwise fans out over all customers. `type` → `type`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Saved cards that expire by the end of 2026
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT customer, card_brand, card_last4, card_exp_month, card_exp_year FROM stripe.main.payment_methods() WHERE type = 'card' AND card_exp_year <= 2026 ORDER BY customer

functions.name: customers
functions.comment: Customers with contact details, balance, delinquency and address

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Every customer (GET /v1/customers or /search): email, name, phone, description, currency, balance (credit balance, + balance_decimal), delinquent, default_source, invoice_prefix, tax_exempt, address (country/state/city/postal code), preferred_locales, test_clock, created and metadata. `email = '…'` uses the list API's exact (case-sensitive) email parameter; name / phone filters and starts_with / contains on email or name use Search (substring, eventually consistent).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## customers(search := NULL, expand := NULL)

Customers and their contact details.

**Pushdown:** `created` ranges, `email` (=, IN), `test_clock` → list parameters; `name`, `phone` (=) and starts_with/contains on `name` or `email` (3+ characters, as `~` substring) → Stripe Search.

vgi.example_queries.description: Look a customer up by exact email (list API email parameter)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id, name, created FROM stripe.main.customers() WHERE email = 'ada@example.com'

vgi.example_queries.description: Customers by country
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT address_country, count(*) AS customers FROM stripe.main.customers() GROUP BY address_country ORDER BY customers DESC

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Every balance transaction (GET /v1/balance_transactions): one row per movement of funds — charges, refunds, adjustments, payouts, transfers, application fees, Stripe fees — with amount, fee, net (each also as an exact *_decimal major-unit `DECIMAL`), currency, type, reporting_category, status, source id, created and available_on. The authoritative ledger for fee and net-revenue analysis. `payout := 'po_…'` lists only the transactions settled in that automatic payout (payout reconciliation). available_on is filtered locally (Stripe has no list parameter for it).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## balance_transactions(payout := NULL)

The balance ledger: amount, fee and net per movement of funds.

**Pushdown:** `created` ranges → `created[gte|lte]`; `type`, `source`, `currency` (=, IN as one request per value) → list parameters; `payout :=` → `payout`. `available_on` is filtered locally.

vgi.example_queries.description: Fees and net by transaction type since 1 November (the date range is pushed down)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT type, currency, sum(fee_decimal) AS fees, sum(net_decimal) AS net FROM stripe.main.balance_transactions() WHERE created >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY type, currency

functions.name: charges
functions.comment: Charges: card and other payments with amounts, outcome, card brand/last4 and refunds

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Every charge (GET /v1/charges, or /v1/charges/search): status (succeeded, pending, failed), amount, amount_captured, amount_refunded (each with *_decimal major units), currency, customer, payment_intent, captured / paid / refunded / disputed flags, failure_code and message, Radar outcome (type, risk level and score), card brand / last4 / expiry / funding / country, billing details, receipt, created and metadata. fee, net, settlement_currency and available_on come from the expanded balance transaction and are fetched only when projected. Filters on status, amount, currency, refunded, disputed, card_last4 or billing_postal_code use the eventually consistent Search API (seconds-to-minutes lag); `search :=` adds a raw query such as 'metadata["order_id"]:"6735"'.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## charges(search := NULL, expand := NULL)

Charges with their outcome, card details and refund state.

**Pushdown:** `created` ranges, `customer`, `payment_intent`, `transfer_group` → list parameters. `status`, `amount` (=, <, >, …), `currency`, `refunded`, `disputed`, `card_last4`, `billing_postal_code` → Stripe Search (with created/customer) when no list-only filter is present. Projecting fee, net, settlement_currency or available_on adds expand[]=data.balance_transaction to each page request: the same number of requests, larger and slower responses.

vgi.example_queries.description: Gross volume per currency (status uses Stripe Search)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT currency, count(*) AS charges, sum(amount_decimal) AS gross FROM stripe.main.charges() WHERE status = 'succeeded' GROUP BY currency ORDER BY currency

vgi.example_queries.description: Charges with Stripe fee and net (projecting fee expands the balance transaction)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id, amount_decimal, fee_decimal, net_decimal FROM stripe.main.charges() WHERE created >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01' ORDER BY id

Generated from Stripe's OpenAPI spec (API 2026-09-30.endive, stripe/openapi a045100cf4af), one table function per GET endpoint. Columns use Stripe's field names (ids for expandable references, `TIMESTAMPTZ` for Unix times, `BIGINT` minor units plus exact `*_decimal` amounts, `MAP` metadata, `JSON` for deeper objects, `raw` with credentials redacted). Documented list parameters push down: equality / IN on ids, status and type, boolean flags, `created`-style time ranges, `ids[]`, and `id = …` becomes a retrieve. Other query parameters are named arguments, and `params := MAP {…}` passes any documented one. Nested lists take the parent id as a named argument or a pushed `= / IN` filter, or fan out over every parent (one request per parent). For everyday analysis prefer the curated functions in stripe.main. All need a `stripe` secret.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## payments

Every payments read endpoint of the Stripe API: charges, PaymentIntents, SetupIntents, payment methods and their configuration, Checkout, Payment Links, Radar and payment records.

Generated from Stripe's OpenAPI spec (API 2026-09-30.endive, stripe/openapi a045100cf4af), one table function per GET endpoint. Families covered: payments, payment methods, checkout & payment links, radar.

### Pushdown

List parameters, time ranges and retrieve-by-id are pushed to Stripe; every other filter runs in DuckDB. Nested lists fan out over their parent unless you name the parent.

### Credentials

All functions need a `stripe` secret; secrets in responses are redacted.

## platform

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## treasury

Stripe Treasury endpoints: financial accounts and their features, money movements in and out, reversals, received credits and debits, transactions and entries. Needs Treasury enabled.

Generated from Stripe's OpenAPI spec (API 2026-09-30.endive, stripe/openapi a045100cf4af), one table function per GET endpoint. Families covered: financial accounts, money movement.

### Pushdown

List parameters, time ranges and retrieve-by-id are pushed to Stripe; every other filter runs in DuckDB. Nested lists fan out over their parent unless you name the parent.

### Credentials

All functions need a `stripe` secret; secrets in responses are redacted.

workers.title: Survival analysis
workers.tagline: Survival analysis — Kaplan-Meier, Cox PH & log-rank for DuckDB (Python, lifelines)
workers.subtitle: Estimate survival curves, hazard ratios and log-rank tests from time-to-event data.
workers.summary: Survival / time-to-event analysis (Kaplan-Meier, Cox PH, log-rank, median survival) for SQL.
workers.doc_md:
# Survival & Time-to-Event Analysis in SQL

![lifelines logo](https://i.imgur.com/EOowdSD.png)

**Run Kaplan-Meier survival curves, Cox proportional-hazards regression, and the log-rank test directly in DuckDB SQL** — no Python notebook, no data export, no glue code. The `survival` catalog brings rigorous time-to-event statistics to your data warehouse over Apache Arrow.

## What it does

Survival analysis answers *time-until-something-happens* questions: how long until a patient relapses, a customer churns, a machine fails, or a subscription lapses. This extension takes a cohort of subjects — each with a follow-up **duration** and a 0/1 **event** indicator (`1` = the event of interest occurred, `0` = the subject was right-censored, i.e. still event-free when observation ended) — and computes the standard estimators of survival analysis, all from a SQL query. It is built for analysts, data scientists, and engineers working on clinical trials, customer churn and retention, hardware reliability, and any cohort whose outcome is *time until an event*.

## How it works

Every estimator is powered by [lifelines](https://github.com/CamDavidsonPilon/lifelines), the widely used, MIT-licensed Python survival-analysis library (see the [lifelines documentation](https://lifelines.readthedocs.io/)). The worker buffers the entire input relation, hands it to the appropriate lifelines estimator once, and streams the result back as Arrow rows — so the numbers match lifelines exactly. Every function is a **table function**: it consumes a whole `(SELECT ...)` relation as its first argument, and you name which columns play which role using named string arguments such as `duration := 't'` and `event := 'e'`.

## When to reach for it

Reach for the `survival` catalog whenever your question is *time until an event* and your data has a follow-up duration plus a 0/1 censoring indicator: charting how an event-free population decays over time, quantifying how covariates raise or lower risk, testing whether two arms differ, or reducing a cohort to a single headline survival number. It fits [Kaplan-Meier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaplan%E2%80%93Meier_estimator) curves, [Cox proportional-hazards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proportional_hazards_model) regression, and the [log-rank test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logrank_test).

## Notes

Event coding is `1`/true = event occurred, `0`/false = right-censored — get this backwards and every curve and hazard ratio inverts. Cox treats every column besides duration/event as a covariate, so select exactly the covariate columns you want. Because `group` is a SQL keyword, double-quote it at the `logrank_test` call site: `"group" := 'arm'`.
workers.readme_sql:
INSTALL vgi FROM community; LOAD vgi;
ATTACH 'survival' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'uvx --from git+https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-survival@v0.4.1 vgi-survival-worker');

-- cohort(t, e, arm, age): follow-up time, event (1 = event, 0 = censored),
-- treatment arm ('control' / 'treated'), and a numeric covariate

-- Kaplan-Meier survival curve
SELECT * FROM survival.kaplan_meier((SELECT t, e FROM cohort),
                                    duration := 't', event := 'e')
ORDER BY time;

-- Cox proportional-hazards: one hazard ratio per covariate column
-- (every column besides duration/event is a covariate, so select only numeric ones)
SELECT * FROM survival.cox_hazard_ratios((SELECT t, e, age FROM cohort),
                                         duration := 't', event := 'e');

-- Log-rank test comparing arms ("group" is double-quoted: it's a SQL keyword)
SELECT * FROM survival.logrank_test((SELECT t, e, arm FROM cohort),
                                    duration := 't', event := 'e', "group" := 'arm');

-- Median survival time
SELECT * FROM survival.median_survival((SELECT t, e FROM cohort),
                                       duration := 't', event := 'e');

-- Combine them: each arm's median survival next to the log-rank p-value
SELECT mc.median_survival AS median_control, mt.median_survival AS median_treated,
       lr.p_value AS logrank_p_value
FROM survival.median_survival((SELECT t, e FROM cohort WHERE arm = 'control'),
                              duration := 't', event := 'e') AS mc
CROSS JOIN survival.median_survival((SELECT t, e FROM cohort WHERE arm = 'treated'),
                                    duration := 't', event := 'e') AS mt
CROSS JOIN survival.logrank_test((SELECT t, e, arm FROM cohort),
                                 duration := 't', event := 'e', "group" := 'arm') AS lr;

example_queries.description: Kaplan-Meier survival curve for a small cohort, projected and ordered by time
example_queries.sql: SELECT time, survival, at_risk FROM survival.main.kaplan_meier((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (5,1),(8,0),(12,1),(3,1),(9,0)) AS c(t, e)), duration := 't', event := 'e') ORDER BY time

example_queries.description: Cox hazard ratio and Wald p-value for a single covariate
example_queries.sql: SELECT covariate, hazard_ratio, p_value FROM survival.main.cox_hazard_ratios((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (5,1,1.0),(8,0,0.0),(12,1,2.0),(3,1,3.0),(9,0,0.0),(6,1,1.0)) AS c(t, e, prio)), duration := 't', event := 'e') ORDER BY covariate

example_queries.description: Log-rank test comparing survival between two treatment arms
example_queries.sql: SELECT test_statistic, p_value, degrees_freedom FROM survival.main.logrank_test((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (5,1,'a'),(8,0,'a'),(12,1,'b'),(3,1,'b'),(9,0,'a'),(6,1,'b')) AS c(t, e, arm)), duration := 't', event := 'e', "group" := 'arm')

example_queries.description: Median survival time as a single headline number
example_queries.sql: SELECT median_survival FROM survival.main.median_survival((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (5,1),(8,0),(12,1),(3,1),(9,0)) AS c(t, e)), duration := 't', event := 'e')

example_queries.description: Treatment-effect headline for a two-arm trial: the log-rank p-value comparing the arms next to the Cox hazard ratio (with 95% CI and Wald p-value) of treated vs control, one row from the same cohort
example_queries.sql: WITH cohort AS (SELECT * FROM (VALUES (2,1,'control'),(3,1,'control'),(4,1,'control'),(5,0,'control'),(6,1,'control'),(8,1,'control'),(9,0,'control'),(11,1,'control'),(4,1,'treated'),(7,0,'treated'),(9,1,'treated'),(12,1,'treated'),(14,0,'treated'),(15,1,'treated'),(18,1,'treated'),(20,0,'treated')) AS c(t, e, arm)) SELECT round(lr.p_value, 4) AS logrank_p_value, round(cx.hazard_ratio, 3) AS hazard_ratio, round(cx.ci_lower, 3) AS hr_ci_lower, round(cx.ci_upper, 3) AS hr_ci_upper, round(cx.p_value, 4) AS cox_p_value FROM survival.main.logrank_test((SELECT t, e, arm FROM cohort), duration := 't', event := 'e', "group" := 'arm') AS lr CROSS JOIN survival.main.cox_hazard_ratios((SELECT t, e, (arm = 'treated')::INTEGER AS treated FROM cohort), duration := 't', event := 'e') AS cx ORDER BY cx.covariate

example_queries.description: Median survival time of each trial arm side by side with the log-rank p-value testing whether the arms differ (control 6.0, treated 15.0, p = 0.0199)
example_queries.sql: WITH cohort AS (SELECT * FROM (VALUES (2,1,'control'),(3,1,'control'),(4,1,'control'),(5,0,'control'),(6,1,'control'),(8,1,'control'),(9,0,'control'),(11,1,'control'),(4,1,'treated'),(7,0,'treated'),(9,1,'treated'),(12,1,'treated'),(14,0,'treated'),(15,1,'treated'),(18,1,'treated'),(20,0,'treated')) AS c(t, e, arm)) SELECT mc.median_survival AS median_control, mt.median_survival AS median_treated, round(lr.p_value, 4) AS logrank_p_value FROM survival.main.median_survival((SELECT t, e FROM cohort WHERE arm = 'control'), duration := 't', event := 'e') AS mc CROSS JOIN survival.main.median_survival((SELECT t, e FROM cohort WHERE arm = 'treated'), duration := 't', event := 'e') AS mt CROSS JOIN survival.main.logrank_test((SELECT t, e, arm FROM cohort), duration := 't', event := 'e', "group" := 'arm') AS lr ORDER BY median_control

example_queries.description: Landmark survival table: each arm's Kaplan-Meier survival probability at t = 6 and t = 12, read off the step curves with an ASOF join
example_queries.sql: WITH cohort AS (SELECT * FROM (VALUES (2,1,'control'),(3,1,'control'),(4,1,'control'),(5,0,'control'),(6,1,'control'),(8,1,'control'),(9,0,'control'),(11,1,'control'),(4,1,'treated'),(7,0,'treated'),(9,1,'treated'),(12,1,'treated'),(14,0,'treated'),(15,1,'treated'),(18,1,'treated'),(20,0,'treated')) AS c(t, e, arm)), landmarks AS (SELECT * FROM (VALUES (6.0), (12.0)) AS l(landmark)) SELECT l.landmark, round(kc.survival, 3) AS control_survival, round(kt.survival, 3) AS treated_survival FROM landmarks AS l ASOF JOIN survival.main.kaplan_meier((SELECT t, e FROM cohort WHERE arm = 'control'), duration := 't', event := 'e') AS kc ON kc.time <= l.landmark ASOF JOIN survival.main.kaplan_meier((SELECT t, e FROM cohort WHERE arm = 'treated'), duration := 't', event := 'e') AS kt ON kt.time <= l.landmark ORDER BY l.landmark

example_queries.description: List every regression method with the question it answers
example_queries.sql: SELECT method, question, returns FROM survival.main.methods WHERE category = 'regression' ORDER BY method

example_queries.description: Count the available survival methods per category
example_queries.sql: SELECT category, count(*) AS n_methods FROM survival.main.methods GROUP BY category ORDER BY category

example_queries.description: Kaplan-Meier survival at the first observed event time for a small cohort (one death at t=3 among 5 at risk gives S=0.8)
example_queries.sql: SELECT time, survival, at_risk FROM survival.main.kaplan_meier((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (5,1),(8,0),(12,1),(3,1),(9,0)) AS c(t, e)), duration := 't', event := 'e') WHERE time = 3;

agent_tasks: A cohort has a follow-up time column `t` and an event indicator `e` (1 = the event occurred, 0 = right-censored), with rows (5,1), (8,0), (12,1), (3,1), (9,0). Return the Kaplan-Meier survival curve as two columns — the observed time and the survival probability S(t) — ordered by time ascending.

Fit a Cox proportional-hazards model to a cohort with follow-up time `t`, event indicator `e` (1 = event, 0 = censored), and a single covariate `prio`, with rows (5,1,1.0), (8,0,0.0), (12,1,2.0), (3,1,3.0), (9,0,0.0), (6,1,1.0). Return the covariate name and its hazard ratio.

Two treatment arms are labelled in column `arm`; each subject has a follow-up time `t` and an event indicator `e` (1 = event, 0 = censored), with rows (5,1,'a'), (8,0,'a'), (12,1,'b'), (3,1,'b'), (9,0,'a'), (6,1,'b'). Use the log-rank test to compare survival between the arms and return the test statistic, the p-value, and the degrees of freedom.
A cohort has a follow-up time column `t` and an event indicator `e` (1 = the event occurred, 0 = right-censored), with rows (5,1), (8,0), (12,1), (3,1), (9,0). Return the median survival time.

Subscribers have a tenure in months `tenure`, a churn indicator `churned` (1 = churned, 0 = still subscribed, i.e. censored), and a `plan` ('monthly' or 'annual'), with rows (1,1,'monthly'), (2,1,'monthly'), (3,0,'monthly'), (3,1,'monthly'), (5,1,'monthly'), (6,1,'monthly'), (8,0,'monthly'), (9,1,'monthly'), (3,1,'annual'), (6,0,'annual'), (10,1,'annual'), (12,1,'annual'), (12,0,'annual'), (15,1,'annual'), (18,1,'annual'), (24,0,'annual'). Return one row per plan with three columns: the plan name, that plan's median survival (tenure) time, and the log-rank test p-value comparing the two plans (the same p-value on both rows). Order the rows by plan name ascending.

Hardware units have run-time `hours`, a failure indicator `failed` (1 = failed, 0 = still running, i.e. censored), and a `model` ('old' or 'new'), with rows (120,1,'old'), (200,1,'old'), (250,0,'old'), (310,1,'old'), (400,1,'old'), (450,1,'old'), (500,0,'old'), (180,1,'new'), (350,0,'new'), (420,1,'new'), (600,1,'new'), (650,0,'new'), (700,1,'new'), (800,0,'new'). Return a single row with two columns: the log-rank test p-value comparing the two models, and the Cox proportional-hazards hazard ratio for the new model, fitted with a single 0/1 covariate that is 1 for 'new' and 0 for 'old'.

This catalog exposes several survival / time-to-event methods and also provides a browsable relation that lists them. Using that registry of methods, return the name of every method whose category is regression.

## main

The single schema of the `survival` catalog. It holds the survival / time-to-event table functions over Apache Arrow, powered by lifelines — grouped into estimation, regression, and comparison categories.

### Usage

Pass your cohort as a parenthesised subquery and name the role columns — the follow-up `duration` and the 0/1 `event` indicator, plus a grouping column for the comparison test. Each estimator ships a ready-to-run example query; browse the schema's objects to copy one.

### Notes

Event coding is `1` = event occurred, `0` = right-censored. The grouping argument of the group-comparison test collides with the SQL `GROUP` keyword, so quote it at the call site: `"group" := 'arm'`.

vgi.example_queries.description: Kaplan-Meier survival curve for a small cohort, projected and ordered by time
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT time, survival, at_risk FROM survival.main.kaplan_meier((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (5,1),(8,0),(12,1),(3,1),(9,0)) AS c(t, e)), duration := 't', event := 'e') ORDER BY time

vgi.example_queries.description: Cox hazard ratio and Wald p-value for a single covariate
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT covariate, hazard_ratio, p_value FROM survival.main.cox_hazard_ratios((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (5,1,1.0),(8,0,0.0),(12,1,2.0),(3,1,3.0),(9,0,0.0),(6,1,1.0)) AS c(t, e, prio)), duration := 't', event := 'e') ORDER BY covariate

vgi.example_queries.description: Log-rank test comparing survival between two treatment arms
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT test_statistic, p_value, degrees_freedom FROM survival.main.logrank_test((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (5,1,'a'),(8,0,'a'),(12,1,'b'),(3,1,'b'),(9,0,'a'),(6,1,'b')) AS c(t, e, arm)), duration := 't', event := 'e', "group" := 'arm')

vgi.example_queries.description: Median survival time as a single headline number
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT median_survival FROM survival.main.median_survival((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (5,1),(8,0),(12,1),(3,1),(9,0)) AS c(t, e)), duration := 't', event := 'e')

vgi.example_queries.description: Treatment-effect headline for a two-arm trial: the log-rank p-value comparing the arms next to the Cox hazard ratio (with 95% CI and Wald p-value) of treated vs control, one row from the same cohort
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH cohort AS (SELECT * FROM (VALUES (2,1,'control'),(3,1,'control'),(4,1,'control'),(5,0,'control'),(6,1,'control'),(8,1,'control'),(9,0,'control'),(11,1,'control'),(4,1,'treated'),(7,0,'treated'),(9,1,'treated'),(12,1,'treated'),(14,0,'treated'),(15,1,'treated'),(18,1,'treated'),(20,0,'treated')) AS c(t, e, arm)) SELECT round(lr.p_value, 4) AS logrank_p_value, round(cx.hazard_ratio, 3) AS hazard_ratio, round(cx.ci_lower, 3) AS hr_ci_lower, round(cx.ci_upper, 3) AS hr_ci_upper, round(cx.p_value, 4) AS cox_p_value FROM survival.main.logrank_test((SELECT t, e, arm FROM cohort), duration := 't', event := 'e', "group" := 'arm') AS lr CROSS JOIN survival.main.cox_hazard_ratios((SELECT t, e, (arm = 'treated')::INTEGER AS treated FROM cohort), duration := 't', event := 'e') AS cx ORDER BY cx.covariate

vgi.example_queries.description: Median survival time of each trial arm side by side with the log-rank p-value testing whether the arms differ (control 6.0, treated 15.0, p = 0.0199)
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH cohort AS (SELECT * FROM (VALUES (2,1,'control'),(3,1,'control'),(4,1,'control'),(5,0,'control'),(6,1,'control'),(8,1,'control'),(9,0,'control'),(11,1,'control'),(4,1,'treated'),(7,0,'treated'),(9,1,'treated'),(12,1,'treated'),(14,0,'treated'),(15,1,'treated'),(18,1,'treated'),(20,0,'treated')) AS c(t, e, arm)) SELECT mc.median_survival AS median_control, mt.median_survival AS median_treated, round(lr.p_value, 4) AS logrank_p_value FROM survival.main.median_survival((SELECT t, e FROM cohort WHERE arm = 'control'), duration := 't', event := 'e') AS mc CROSS JOIN survival.main.median_survival((SELECT t, e FROM cohort WHERE arm = 'treated'), duration := 't', event := 'e') AS mt CROSS JOIN survival.main.logrank_test((SELECT t, e, arm FROM cohort), duration := 't', event := 'e', "group" := 'arm') AS lr ORDER BY median_control

vgi.example_queries.description: Landmark survival table: each arm's Kaplan-Meier survival probability at t = 6 and t = 12, read off the step curves with an ASOF join
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH cohort AS (SELECT * FROM (VALUES (2,1,'control'),(3,1,'control'),(4,1,'control'),(5,0,'control'),(6,1,'control'),(8,1,'control'),(9,0,'control'),(11,1,'control'),(4,1,'treated'),(7,0,'treated'),(9,1,'treated'),(12,1,'treated'),(14,0,'treated'),(15,1,'treated'),(18,1,'treated'),(20,0,'treated')) AS c(t, e, arm)), landmarks AS (SELECT * FROM (VALUES (6.0), (12.0)) AS l(landmark)) SELECT l.landmark, round(kc.survival, 3) AS control_survival, round(kt.survival, 3) AS treated_survival FROM landmarks AS l ASOF JOIN survival.main.kaplan_meier((SELECT t, e FROM cohort WHERE arm = 'control'), duration := 't', event := 'e') AS kc ON kc.time <= l.landmark ASOF JOIN survival.main.kaplan_meier((SELECT t, e FROM cohort WHERE arm = 'treated'), duration := 't', event := 'e') AS kt ON kt.time <= l.landmark ORDER BY l.landmark

# methods

A browsable registry of every survival table function in this catalog — a discovery aid so an agent can pick the right method before guessing a function's arguments.

## Columns

`method` (the function name), `category` (estimation / regression / comparison), `question` (the time-to-event question it answers), `signature` (its fully-qualified call shape), and `returns` (a one-line result summary).

## Usage

Filter by category to list the estimators, or read a row's signature to learn a method's role arguments. The relation is VALUES-backed, so it returns instantly with no network access or credentials.

## Notes

This registry only names the methods; call the listed function itself to run the analysis. Event coding across every method is `1` = event occurred, `0` = right-censored.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Run the multivariate log-rank test to ask whether survival differs across two or more groups. Pass the cohort as `(SELECT ...)` with `duration`, `event` (0/1), and a `group` column, and name those roles. Returns a single row: the chi-squared test statistic, the p-value, and the degrees of freedom (number of groups minus one). A small p-value (e.g. < 0.05) indicates the survival curves of the groups differ. Use it to compare treatment arms, segments, or cohorts. Note the `group` argument collides with the SQL `GROUP` keyword, so quote it at the call site as `"group" := 'arm'`.

# logrank_test

Multivariate **log-rank test** comparing survival across a grouping column.

## Usage

Pass your cohort as the first argument — a parenthesised subquery projecting the follow-up time, the 0/1 event column, and the grouping column — and name the `duration := 't'`, `event := 'e'`, and `"group" := 'arm'` roles. Because `group` is a SQL keyword it must be double-quoted at the call site. A ready-to-run example is attached to this function.

## Returns

Exactly one row: `test_statistic`, `p_value`, and `degrees_freedom`. A small `p_value` means the groups' survival curves differ.

## Notes

Needs at least two distinct groups. `group` is a SQL keyword, so double-quote it at the call site (`"group" := 'arm'`). Event coding is `1` = event, `0` = censored.

# kaplan_meier

Non-parametric **Kaplan-Meier** estimate of the survival function S(t) over a buffered cohort relation.

## Usage

Pass your cohort as the first argument — a parenthesised subquery projecting the follow-up time and 0/1 event columns — and name those roles with `duration := 't'` and `event := 'e'`. Order the result by `time` to read the curve top to bottom. A ready-to-run example is attached to this function.

## Returns

One row per distinct observed follow-up time (ordered by `time`): the survival probability `survival`, its `ci_lower`/`ci_upper` 95% confidence band, and the `at_risk` count.

## Notes

Event coding is `1` = event occurred, `0` = right-censored. The curve begins at 1.0 and never increases. The result can be long (one row per distinct time).

Pass the cohort as `(SELECT ...)` containing `duration`, `event` (0/1; 1 = event occurred), and one or more numeric covariate columns; every column that is not the duration or event is treated as a covariate. # cox_hazard_ratios

Fit a **Cox proportional-hazards** model and return per-covariate hazard ratios.

## Usage

Pass your cohort as the first argument — a parenthesised subquery projecting the follow-up time, the 0/1 event column, and one or more numeric covariate columns — and name the `duration := 't'` and `event := 'e'` roles. Project only the covariate columns you want fitted. A ready-to-run example is attached to this function.

## Returns

One row per covariate: the `coef`, the `hazard_ratio` (`exp(coef)`), its `ci_lower`/`ci_upper` band, and the Wald `p_value`.

## Notes

Every column besides `duration`/`event` becomes a covariate, so `SELECT` only the columns you want fitted (non-numeric covariates raise an error). A relation with no covariate column raises a clear error.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT covariate, hazard_ratio, p_value FROM survival.main.cox_hazard_ratios((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (5,1,1.0),(8,0,0.0),(12,1,2.0),(3,1,3.0),(9,0,0.0),(6,1,1.0)) AS c(t, e, prio)), duration := 't', event := 'e') ORDER BY covariate

vgi.example_queries.description: Treatment-effect headline for a two-arm trial: the log-rank p-value comparing the arms next to the Cox hazard ratio (with 95% CI and Wald p-value) of treated vs control, one row from the same cohort
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH cohort AS (SELECT * FROM (VALUES (2,1,'control'),(3,1,'control'),(4,1,'control'),(5,0,'control'),(6,1,'control'),(8,1,'control'),(9,0,'control'),(11,1,'control'),(4,1,'treated'),(7,0,'treated'),(9,1,'treated'),(12,1,'treated'),(14,0,'treated'),(15,1,'treated'),(18,1,'treated'),(20,0,'treated')) AS c(t, e, arm)) SELECT round(lr.p_value, 4) AS logrank_p_value, round(cx.hazard_ratio, 3) AS hazard_ratio, round(cx.ci_lower, 3) AS hr_ci_lower, round(cx.ci_upper, 3) AS hr_ci_upper, round(cx.p_value, 4) AS cox_p_value FROM survival.main.logrank_test((SELECT t, e, arm FROM cohort), duration := 't', event := 'e', "group" := 'arm') AS lr CROSS JOIN survival.main.cox_hazard_ratios((SELECT t, e, (arm = 'treated')::INTEGER AS treated FROM cohort), duration := 't', event := 'e') AS cx ORDER BY cx.covariate

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Compute the median survival time from a cohort relation: the time at which the Kaplan-Meier survival function S(t) first drops to 0.5. Pass the cohort as `(SELECT ...)` and name the `duration` and `event` (0/1; 1 = event occurred) columns. Returns a single row with one `median_survival` value. When the survival curve never reaches 0.5 (e.g. under heavy censoring) the result is `inf`, not NULL. Use it when you want a single headline number summarizing a cohort's survival rather than the whole curve.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# median_survival

The **median survival time**: where the Kaplan-Meier curve S(t) first reaches 0.5.

## Usage

Pass your cohort as the first argument — a parenthesised subquery projecting the follow-up time and 0/1 event columns — and name the `duration := 't'` and `event := 'e'` roles. The result is a single row. A ready-to-run example is attached to this function.

## Returns

Exactly one row with the single `median_survival` value.

## Notes

If S(t) never reaches 0.5 the value is `inf` (median undefined), passed through as a float rather than NULL. Event coding is `1` = event, `0` = right-censored.
