workers.title: Native Symbolication
workers.tagline: Native stack symbolication in DuckDB with SQL — resolve (build_id, address) to function/file/line from DWARF and PDB debug info, with a stateful cache. A VGI worker.
workers.subtitle: Resolve stack-frame addresses to function names, source lines and inlined call chains using DWARF and PDB debug info.
workers.summary: Native (DWARF/PDB) symbolication as a bulk SQL JOIN over (build_id, address) frames, backed by a persistent build-id-keyed debug-info cache.
workers.doc_md:
# symbols

Native **symbolication** as a SQL JOIN: turn a column of `(build_id, address)` stack frames into `function` + `file` + `line` plus the **inlined call chain**, by parsing DWARF (ELF / Mach-O / dSYM) and Windows PDB — the same resolution as `addr2line` / `llvm-symbolizer`, but over millions of frames in-engine and backed by a **persistent, build-id-keyed debug-info cache** so each debug module is parsed exactly once.

Reach for it to make stack traces, CPU/heap profiles, and crash dumps readable directly in SQL. Addresses are **module-relative** (the caller subtracts the load base); local symbol sources are zero-egress while remote ones (`debuginfod` / `s3` / `http`) are opt-in and off by default; and resolution is total — a missing or malformed module yields a per-row status, never a dropped row. The upstream feeders are `vgi-minidump`, `vgi-pprof`, and `vgi-perf`.

## Sources and references

- [DWARF Debugging Information Format](https://dwarfstd.org/) — the debug-info standard read from ELF, Mach-O and dSYM files.
- [The PDB File Format (LLVM)](https://llvm.org/docs/PDB/index.html) — the Windows program-database format used for PE modules.
- [debuginfod](https://sourceware.org/elfutils/Debuginfod.html) — the build-id-keyed debug-info server protocol behind the opt-in `debuginfod` source kind.
- [`addr2line`](https://docs.rs/addr2line) / [`gimli`](https://docs.rs/gimli) and [`pdb-addr2line`](https://docs.rs/pdb-addr2line) — the Rust DWARF and PDB resolvers the engine is built on.

example_queries.description: Register a local, zero-egress directory of debug files and capture its source_id.
example_queries.sql: SELECT source_id FROM symbols.main.add_source('dir', path => '/srv/debug')

example_queries.description: Symbolicate one module-relative frame to its function name and resolution status.
example_queries.sql: SELECT (symbols.main.symbolicate('e4c1f2b9', 303600)).function AS function, (symbols.main.symbolicate('e4c1f2b9', 303600)).status AS status

example_queries.description: Bulk-symbolicate a frame column: resolve each (build_id, address) to its innermost function name for a flamegraph or GROUP BY key.
example_queries.sql: SELECT f.build_id, f.address, symbols.main.function_name(f.build_id, f.address) AS function FROM stack_frames f

example_queries.description: Demangle a raw Itanium C++ linkage name to its readable form.
example_queries.sql: SELECT symbols.main.demangle('_ZN3foo3barEv') AS name

example_queries.description: Watch the build-id-keyed cache: the hottest resident debug modules first.
example_queries.sql: SELECT debug_id, name, bytes_resident FROM symbols.main.cache_status() ORDER BY bytes_resident DESC

example_queries.description: Find the local, zero-egress source kinds that are not registered yet (source_kinds anti-joined to sources()), with the add_source argument each one needs; returns dir and glob on a fresh worker, and only glob once a dir source is added.
example_queries.sql: SELECT k.kind, k.locator_arg FROM symbols.main.source_kinds AS k WHERE k.egress = false AND k.kind NOT IN (SELECT s.kind FROM symbols.main.sources() AS s) ORDER BY k.kind

example_queries.description: List the local, zero-egress source kinds and the add_source argument that locates each.
example_queries.sql: SELECT kind, locator_arg FROM symbols.main.source_kinds WHERE egress = false ORDER BY kind

example_queries.description: Show every source kind with whether registering it crosses the trust boundary.
example_queries.sql: SELECT kind, locality, egress FROM symbols.main.source_kinds ORDER BY egress, kind

example_queries.description: Audit the registered symbol sources in resolve order, including whether each is enabled and whether using it crosses the trust boundary (egress). Returns no rows until a source is registered with add_source; pass enabled_only => true to list only active sources.
example_queries.sql: SELECT source_id, kind, location, enabled, egress FROM symbols.main.sources();

example_queries.description: Deregister the symbol source with id 'src0'; dropped is false if no such source was registered.
example_queries.sql: SELECT dropped FROM symbols.main.drop_source('src0')

example_queries.description: List the debug modules the worker has parsed and the manifest knows about, hottest first. Returns no rows on a cold worker (nothing parsed yet); pass resident_only => true to skip evicted/manifest-only entries.
example_queries.sql: SELECT debug_id, name, bytes_resident, rows_resolved FROM symbols.main.cache_status() ORDER BY bytes_resident DESC;

example_queries.description: Clear the entire resident cache (keeping the manifest) and report the bytes reclaimed; 0 on a cold worker with nothing resident.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bytes_freed FROM symbols.main.cache_evict()

example_queries.description: Triage a debug file by filesystem path: save a committed Mach-O dSYM fixture to the current directory, then inspect it by path (one row; zero rows if the path is missing or not a debug file).
example_queries.sql:
COPY (SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-symbols/v0.4.2/crates/symbols-core/tests/fixtures/macho_inline.dwarf')) TO 'macho_inline.dwarf' (FORMAT blob);
SELECT format, debug_id, has_line_table FROM symbols.main.module_info('macho_inline.dwarf');

example_queries.description: Check that a downloaded debug file belongs to the build that crashed: compare its module_info debug_id with the debug-ids a crash report lists. One verdict row per crash module: matches is true for the build the file was produced from and false for any other build.
example_queries.sql:
SET VARIABLE symbols_debug_file = (SELECT content FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-symbols/v0.4.2/crates/symbols-core/tests/fixtures/macho_inline.dwarf'));
SELECT crash.crash_module, coalesce(d.debug_id = crash.debug_id, false) AS matches, d.debug_id AS debug_file_debug_id, d.format, d.arch, d.has_line_table FROM (VALUES ('compute', '4930eb84c7b63ef6a97fbdcdd473f5a30'), ('inline', '76ff8518da153e64a8403892fcbf11250')) AS crash(crash_module, debug_id) LEFT JOIN symbols.main.module_info(getvariable('symbols_debug_file')) AS d ON true ORDER BY crash.crash_module;

example_queries.description: Get the length of the inlined call chain (innermost-first, physical frame excluded) at module-relative address 303600 in build-id 'e4c1f2b9'; 0 until the address has both symbols and inlining.
example_queries.sql: SELECT length(symbols.main.inline_frames('e4c1f2b9', 303600)) AS inline_depth

example_queries.description: Resolve a frame (build-id 'e4c1f2b9', module-relative address 303600) to just its innermost function name; returns NULL until a symbol source for that build-id is registered with add_source.
example_queries.sql: SELECT symbols.main.function_name('e4c1f2b9', 303600) AS function

agent_tasks: Using the worker's demangle function, turn the mangled Itanium C++ linkage name '_ZN3foo3barEv' into its readable name (it should read 'foo::bar'). Return only the single demangled string.
The demangle function returns any name that is not actually mangled unchanged. Show what it returns for the plain name 'main'.

This worker has no symbol sources registered yet, so nothing can be resolved. Symbolicate the frame with build_id 'deadbeef' and module-relative address 4096 and report just the resolution status of the result (it will be 'not_found' because no matching debug file is available).
With no symbol sources registered, resolving any address yields no name. Resolve the innermost function name for build_id 'deadbeef' at module-relative address 4096 — the result should be NULL.

The inline_frames function returns just the inlined call chain (a list) at a frame. With no symbol sources registered, the chain for build_id 'deadbeef' at module-relative address 4096 is empty. Report the length of that list (it should be 0).

Use the module_info table function to inspect the debug file at the path '/no/such/file.debug'. Because that path does not exist, module_info returns no rows. Report how many rows it returns (it should be 0).

The worker exposes a browsable reference table of the symbol-source kinds add_source accepts. Using it, count how many source kinds are local (they do not cross the trust boundary, i.e. egress is false). Return the count.
How many symbol sources are currently registered on this freshly attached worker? List them with the sources function and return the count (it should be 0 until add_source is called).

This worker keeps a persistent, build-id-keyed debug-info cache. Using the cache_status table function, confirm the cache is queryable and report how many debug modules are currently cached (it may well be zero on a freshly attached worker).
Clear the worker's entire resident debug-info cache using cache_evict (with no argument) and report how many bytes were freed. On a cold worker with nothing resident this is 0.
Try to drop a symbol source whose id is 'no_such_source'. Since no source with that id was registered, report whether one was actually removed (it should be false).

Register a local, zero-egress directory symbol source pointing at the directory '/srv/debug' so the worker can find debug files there. Use the add_source function with the appropriate kind and locator argument, then confirm a source is now registered.

## `source_kinds`

A browsable, credential-free registry of the five symbol-source kinds `add_source` accepts — read it to discover valid inputs before registering a source.

Each row is one kind:

- **kind** — `dir`, `glob`, `debuginfod`, `s3`, or `http`.
- **locality** — `local` (zero-egress filesystem) or `remote` (opt-in network).
- **egress** — true when using the kind crosses the trust boundary.
- **locator_arg** — the `add_source` named argument that locates it (`path` / `url` / `bucket`).
- **description** — a one-line explanation.

Filter `egress = false` for the local kinds, or read `locator_arg` to learn which argument a kind needs.

functions.name: sources
functions.comment: List the registered symbol sources (source_id, kind, location, enabled, egress)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: List the registered symbol sources in resolve order: `source_id`, `kind`, `location` (the path / url / bucket), `enabled`, and `egress` (whether using the source crosses the trust boundary). functions.name: add_source
functions.comment: Register a symbol source (dir/glob/debuginfod/s3/http); returns its source_id

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Register where debug files live so `symbolicate` can find them, returning the assigned `source_id`. Sources are tried in the order added; the first debug-id match wins. Local, zero-egress kinds: `dir` (`path =>` a directory of symbol files) and `glob` (`path =>` a recursive glob like '/builds/**/*.{debug,pdb,dSYM}'). Remote, egress kinds (opt-in, default disabled): `debuginfod` (`url =>`), `http` (`url =>`), and `s3` (`bucket =>`) — pass `enabled => true` to turn one on; credentials come from the SDK secret provider via `secret =>`, never inline. The default posture is air-gap-safe: with no remote source enabled there is zero network egress.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Register a symbol source and get its source_id. `add_source('dir', path => '/srv/debug')` or `add_source('glob', path => '/b/**/*.debug')`; remote kinds (debuginfod/s3/http) are opt-in (`enabled => true`) with secrets via `secret =>`.

vgi.executable_examples.description: Register a local, zero-egress directory of symbol files and capture its assigned source_id (use `add_source('glob', path => '/builds/**/*.{debug,pdb}')` for a recursive glob, or a remote kind like 'debuginfod'/'s3'/'http' with `enabled => true`).
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT source_id FROM symbols.main.add_source('dir', path => '/srv/debug')

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: source_id
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: The id assigned to the new source (e.g. src0). Pass it to drop_source to remove it.

functions.name: cache_status
functions.comment: Report the parsed/resident debug modules (the build-id-keyed cache state)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Report what debug modules are parsed and resident right now (the stateful heart of this worker): one row per known debug-id — both modules resident in RAM and manifest-only entries (evicted or proven-missing). Columns: `debug_id`, `name` (debug file), `format`, `arch`, `bytes_resident` (0 if not resident), `rows_resolved` (cumulative addresses resolved against it), `last_used`, `origin` (where it came from), and `resident`. Order by `bytes_resident DESC` to see the hot modules. Use it to watch the parse-once / LRU behavior of the cache.
tags.vgi.doc_md: List the resident + known debug modules: debug_id, name, format, arch, bytes_resident, rows_resolved, last_used, origin, resident. The cache-observability surface.

vgi.executable_examples.description: List the debug modules the worker has parsed and the manifest knows about, hottest first. Returns no rows on a cold worker (nothing parsed yet); pass resident_only => true to skip evicted/manifest-only entries.
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT debug_id, name, bytes_resident, rows_resolved FROM symbols.main.cache_status() ORDER BY bytes_resident DESC

functions.name: cache_evict
functions.comment: Force-evict one module (or the whole resident set) from the cache; returns bytes freed

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Force whole-module eviction from the resident debug-info cache, returning the number of bytes freed. With `debug_id =>` set, evict just that module (e.g. after its symbol file was updated on disk); with no argument, clear the entire resident set. Either way the manifest entry is kept, so a later address re-parses the module from its origin rather than re-discovering it. Use it to reclaim RAM or to pick up an updated symbol file.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Evict from the resident cache and return bytes freed: `cache_evict(debug_id => '…')` evicts one module, `cache_evict()` clears the resident set (manifest kept).

vgi.example_queries.description: Clear the entire resident cache (keeping the manifest) and report the bytes reclaimed; 0 on a cold worker with nothing resident.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT bytes_freed FROM symbols.main.cache_evict()

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: bytes_freed
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Resident bytes reclaimed by the eviction (0 if the module was not resident, or the cache was already empty).

tags.vgi.title: Cache Evict

arguments.name: debug_id
arguments.description: The normalized debug-id (or build-id alias) to evict. Omit to clear the whole resident set. The manifest entry is kept either way.

examples: SELECT bytes_freed FROM symbols.main.cache_evict()

result_columns.name: bytes_freed
result_columns.description: Resident bytes reclaimed by the eviction (0 if the module was not resident, or the cache was already empty).

functions.name: module_info
functions.comment: Inspect a debug file given inline as a BLOB (format, debug-id, line info) without resolving

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Inspect a debug file named by a single filesystem `path` argument without resolving any frames: returns one row describing the container `format` ('ELF' / 'MachO' / 'PE' / 'PDB' / 'dSYM' / 'Breakpad'), the CPU `arch`, the raw per-format `build_id` hex and the normalized `debug_id` cache key (so you can check whether this file matches the frames you have), the `code_id`, the `has_dwarf` / `has_pdb` / `has_line_table` capability flags, the `symbol_count` / `file_count` / `byte_size`, and the image's preferred `image_base`. It is the triage tool — 'does this file actually have line info, and does its debug-id match?' — answered header-only, without paying the parse-into-cache cost. Zero rows if the input is not a recognizable debug file.

functions.name: inline_frames
functions.comment: Resolve a (build_id, address) frame to its inline chain only (a list of STRUCT(function, file, line))

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Resolve a `(build_id, address)` frame to just its inlined call chain — a `LIST(STRUCT(function, file, line))` ordered innermost-first, **excluding** the physical frame. Empty list when the address has no inlining (or no symbols). Useful to reconstruct a logically-deeper stack than the captured frame count. `build_id` is the normalized debug-id or raw build-id hex; `address` is the MODULE-RELATIVE virtual address (caller subtracts the load base). workers.doc_md:
# SymPy Symbolic Math (CAS) for DuckDB

![SymPy logo](https://www.sympy.org/static/images/logo.png)

**Do computer algebra in SQL** — simplify, expand, factor, differentiate, integrate, and solve symbolic expressions stored as text columns, powered by the [SymPy](https://www.sympy.org/) computer algebra system and exposed as DuckDB scalar functions.

## What it does

This VGI worker turns DuckDB into a symbolic calculator that works with *symbols*, not just numbers. Instead of shelling out to Python notebooks or a separate CAS, you can run algebra and calculus directly inside a query — manipulating formulas held in `VARCHAR` columns. It is built for data engineers, scientists, educators, and anyone who needs to normalize, transform, or verify mathematical expressions at scale alongside the rest of their SQL pipeline. Every function returns canonical, deterministic output that is stable across runs, so results are safe to materialize, diff, and join.

## How it works

The catalog wraps [SymPy](https://www.sympy.org/) — the pure-Python, BSD-licensed computer algebra library ([documentation](https://docs.sympy.org/latest/index.html), [source](https://github.com/sympy/sympy)) — behind a set of per-row Arrow scalar functions. Expression strings are never passed to `eval` or `sympify`: each one runs through a hardened allow-list parser (a `tokenize`-based screen plus a restricted namespace with empty `__builtins__`), so a malformed or hostile string is rejected or returns `NULL`, never executed. SymPy itself produces a canonical string form for results, which is why outputs are reproducible and worth pinning in tests.

## When to use it

Reach for this catalog whenever a value in your data is a *formula* rather than a number and you need to reason about it: canonicalize free-form formula columns so equivalent inputs collapse to one representation, grade student or model answers against a key, derive derivatives and antiderivatives for a scientific pipeline, solve equations row by row, or render expressions for display. Because every transform is a per-row scalar that yields `NULL` on invalid or unsafe input (rather than aborting the scan), it drops into an ordinary projection or predicate and composes over messy, semi-structured text without special-casing.

```sql
SELECT sympy.main.simplify('sin(x)**2 + cos(x)**2');  -- '1'
SELECT sympy.main.differentiate('x**3', 'x');         -- '3*x**2'
```

## Notes

Invalid or unsafe expressions yield `NULL` rather than erroring (except `evaluate`, which raises on a structurally wrong `vars_json`), so the transforms compose cleanly over messy columns. Parsing is sandboxed: hostile strings are rejected before any evaluation happens.
workers.readme_sql:
INSTALL vgi FROM community; LOAD vgi;
ATTACH 'sympy' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'uvx --from git+https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-sympy@v0.4.1 vgi-sympy-worker');

SELECT sympy.simplify('sin(x)**2 + cos(x)**2');      -- '1'
SELECT sympy.expand('(x + 1)**2');                   -- 'x**2 + 2*x + 1'
SELECT sympy.factor('x**2 - 1');                     -- '(x - 1)*(x + 1)'
SELECT sympy.differentiate('x**3', 'x');             -- '3*x**2'
SELECT sympy.integrate('2*x', 'x');                  -- 'x**2'
SELECT sympy.solve('x**2 - 4', 'x');                 -- ['-2', '2']
SELECT UNNEST(sympy.solve('2*x = 10', 'x'));         -- 5
SELECT sympy.evaluate('x**2 + y', '{"x":3,"y":1}');  -- 10.0
SELECT sympy.to_latex('x**2');                       -- 'x^{2}'
SELECT sympy.symbolic_equal('2*(x+1)', '2*x+2');     -- true
SELECT sympy.sympy_version(1);                       -- e.g. '1.13.3'

example_queries.description: Differentiate x**3 with respect to x.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sympy.main.differentiate('x**3', 'x')

example_queries.description: Integrate 2*x with respect to x (no constant of integration).
example_queries.sql: SELECT sympy.main.integrate('2*x', 'x')

example_queries.description: Solve a quadratic equation for x, returning a VARCHAR[] of roots.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sympy.main.solve('x**2 - 4', 'x')

example_queries.description: Substitute x=3, y=1 into an expression and evaluate to a DOUBLE.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sympy.main.evaluate('x**2 + y', '{"x":3,"y":1}')

example_queries.description: Test that two different-looking expressions are symbolically equal.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sympy.main.symbolic_equal('2*(x+1)', '2*x+2')

example_queries.description: Find the stationary points of x**3 - 3*x by solving its derivative for zero, then evaluate the function at each one: a local maximum of 2.0 at x = -1 and a local minimum of -2.0 at x = 1.
example_queries.sql:
WITH crit AS (
  SELECT UNNEST(sympy.main.solve(sympy.main.differentiate('x**3 - 3*x', 'x'), 'x')) AS root
), pts AS (
  SELECT root, sympy.main.evaluate(root, '{}') AS x_value FROM crit
)
SELECT root, x_value,
       sympy.main.evaluate('x**3 - 3*x', '{"x": ' || x_value || '}') AS f_value
FROM pts
ORDER BY x_value

example_queries.description: Integrate each integrand, then verify the antiderivative by differentiating it back and testing symbolic equality with the original (all four rows are verified TRUE, even where the round-tripped string looks different).
example_queries.sql:
SELECT integrand,
       sympy.main.integrate(integrand, 'x') AS antiderivative,
       sympy.main.symbolic_equal(
         sympy.main.differentiate(sympy.main.integrate(integrand, 'x'), 'x'), integrand) AS verified
FROM (VALUES ('x*exp(x)'), ('1/(1 + x**2)'), ('sin(x)**2'), ('log(x)')) AS t(integrand)
ORDER BY integrand

example_queries.description: Grade free-form answers against the key (x + 1)**2: render each answer as LaTeX for display and mark it correct when it is symbolically equal to the key (only x**2 + 1 is wrong).
example_queries.sql:

       sympy.main.to_latex(answer) AS latex,
       sympy.main.symbolic_equal(answer, '(x + 1)**2') AS correct
FROM (VALUES ('x**2 + 2*x + 1'), ('(1 + x)*(x + 1)'), ('x**2 + 1'), ('x*(x + 2) + 1')) AS t(answer)
ORDER BY answer

example_queries.description: Show each polynomial's factorization over the rationals beside its roots: x**3 - 6*x**2 + 11*x - 6 factors into (x - 3)*(x - 2)*(x - 1) with roots 1, 2, 3, while x**2 - 2 comes back unfactored because its roots -sqrt(2) and sqrt(2) are irrational.

ORDER BY poly

Compute the definite integral of x**2 with respect to x from x = 0 to x = 3 symbolically (find the antiderivative, then take its value at the upper bound minus its value at the lower bound). Return exactly one row with a single DOUBLE column holding the result.

Find the slope of the curve y = x**3 - 2*x at x = 2 by symbolically differentiating it with respect to x and evaluating the derivative there. Return exactly one row with a single DOUBLE column holding the slope.

## Symbolic-math scalar functions (SymPy)

The `main` schema groups every computer-algebra scalar in this worker, organized into algebraic transforms, calculus, equation solving, numeric evaluation, and diagnostics (see the schema's category registry to browse them).

Each function takes expression strings (and, where relevant, a variable name or a JSON of variable values) and returns a SymPy-canonical string, a list of solutions, a number, or a boolean. The transforming functions return `NULL` for invalid or unsafe input so they can be applied across columns of free-form formulas without aborting a scan. Reach for this schema whenever you need algebra or calculus on symbolic expressions inside SQL — for example to canonicalize formula columns, grade answers against a key, or derive derivatives row by row.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# main — symbolic math

Computer-algebra scalar functions over [SymPy](https://www.sympy.org/).

## Organization

The functions fall into algebraic **transforms** (simplify, expand, factor, to_latex), **calculus** (differentiate, integrate), **equation** solving (solve, symbolic_equal), numeric **evaluation** (evaluate), and worker **diagnostics** (sympy_version), grouped by the schema's `vgi.categories` registry.

## Usage

Inputs are expression strings such as `'(x + 1)**2'`. Outputs are SymPy-canonical strings (stable across runs), a `VARCHAR[]` of solutions, a `DOUBLE`, or a `BOOLEAN`.

## Notes

Invalid/unsafe expressions become `NULL` (composes cleanly over messy columns); parsing is sandboxed and never evaluates hostile input.

## to_latex(expr)

For example `'x**2'` becomes `'x^{2}'` and `'sqrt(x)'` becomes `'\sqrt{x}'`. The expression is parsed and simplified to SymPy's internal form first, then pretty-printed as LaTeX.

functions.name: simplify

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## simplify(expr)

Apply SymPy's general-purpose algebraic **simplification** to a single expression string and return a canonical, simplified form as `VARCHAR`.

Use it to collapse trig identities (`sin(x)**2 + cos(x)**2` -> `1`), cancel common factors, and normalize equivalent forms to one representation. The result is SymPy's stable canonical string, so it is safe to compare or store.

**Input:** one expression string. **Output:** simplified string, or `NULL` when the input is `NULL`, invalid, unsafe, or too complex — so it composes over messy columns.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# simplify

Algebraically simplifies an expression to a canonical form.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT sympy.simplify('sin(x)**2 + cos(x)**2');  -- '1'
SELECT sympy.simplify('(x**2 - 1)/(x - 1)');     -- 'x + 1'
```

## Notes

Returns `NULL` for `NULL`, invalid, or unsafe input. Simplification is heuristic: it aims for a simpler form, not a guaranteed minimal one.

functions.name: factor
functions.comment: Factored form of an expression, e.g. '(x - 1)*(x + 1)', or NULL if invalid

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## factor(expr)

**Factor** an expression into a product of irreducible factors over the rationals and return that form as `VARCHAR`.

It is the inverse direction of `expand`: `x**2 - 1` becomes `(x - 1)*(x + 1)`. Use it to reveal roots, find common factors, or rewrite a polynomial as a product before cancellation.

**Input:** one expression string. **Output:** factored string, or `NULL` for `NULL`, invalid, or unsafe input. Expressions with no nontrivial factorization come back unchanged.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# factor

Factors an expression into a product of irreducible factors.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT sympy.factor('x**2 - 1');         -- '(x - 1)*(x + 1)'
SELECT sympy.factor('x**2 + 2*x + 1');   -- '(x + 1)**2'
```

## Notes

The opposite of `expand`. Already-irreducible inputs return unchanged; `NULL`/invalid/unsafe input returns `NULL`.

       sympy.main.solve(poly, 'x') AS roots
FROM (VALUES ('x**3 - 6*x**2 + 11*x - 6'), ('x**2 - 2')) AS t(poly)
ORDER BY poly

functions.name: integrate
functions.comment: Indefinite integral of an expression w.r.t. a variable (no +C), or NULL if invalid or no closed form is found

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## integrate(expr, var)

Compute the symbolic **indefinite integral** (antiderivative) of an expression with respect to a named variable and return it as `VARCHAR`. The constant of integration `+C` is **not** included.

For example `integrate('2*x', 'x')` returns `'x**2'`. It is the inverse of `differentiate`.

**Inputs:** an expression string and a variable name (both positional). **Output:** the antiderivative string, or `NULL` if either input is `NULL`/invalid/unsafe, or if no closed-form antiderivative exists (the result still contains an unresolved `Integral`).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# integrate

Symbolic indefinite integration (antiderivative, no `+C`).

## Usage

```sql
SELECT sympy.integrate('2*x', 'x');   -- 'x**2'
SELECT sympy.integrate('cos(x)', 'x'); -- 'sin(x)'
```

## Notes

The inverse of `differentiate`. Returns `NULL` when no closed form is found, or for `NULL`/invalid/unsafe input. No constant of integration is added.

vgi.example_queries.sql:
SELECT integrand,
       sympy.main.integrate(integrand, 'x') AS antiderivative,
       sympy.main.symbolic_equal(
         sympy.main.differentiate(sympy.main.integrate(integrand, 'x'), 'x'), integrand) AS verified
FROM (VALUES ('x*exp(x)'), ('1/(1 + x**2)'), ('sin(x)**2'), ('log(x)')) AS t(integrand)
ORDER BY integrand

## expand(expr)

Algebraically **expand** an expression — multiply out products and powers — and return the expanded polynomial form as `VARCHAR`.

It is the inverse direction of `factor`: `(x + 1)**2` becomes `x**2 + 2*x + 1`. Use it to flatten nested products before pattern matching, term counting, or comparison.

**Input:** one expression string. **Output:** expanded string, or `NULL` for `NULL`, invalid, or unsafe input.

# expand

Multiplies out products and powers into a flat polynomial form.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT sympy.expand('(x + 1)**2');     -- 'x**2 + 2*x + 1'
SELECT sympy.expand('(x + y)*(x - y)'); -- 'x**2 - y**2'
```

## Notes

The opposite of `factor`. Returns `NULL` for `NULL`/invalid/unsafe input.

functions.name: symbolic_equal
functions.comment: True if two expressions are symbolically equivalent (simplify(a-b)==0), or NULL if either is invalid

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## symbolic_equal(a, b)

Test whether two expressions are **symbolically equivalent** and return a `BOOLEAN`.

Equivalence is decided by simplifying the difference: `a` and `b` are equal when `simplify(a - b) == 0`. This catches forms that are textually different but mathematically the same, e.g. `'2*(x+1)'` and `'2*x+2'` are equal.

**Inputs:** two expression strings (positional). **Output:** `TRUE`/`FALSE`, or `NULL` when either input is `NULL`/invalid/unsafe. Use it instead of string equality to compare expressions whose canonical form you don't want to pin.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# symbolic_equal

Returns `TRUE` when two expressions are mathematically equivalent.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT sympy.symbolic_equal('2*(x+1)', '2*x+2'); -- true
SELECT sympy.symbolic_equal('sin(x)', 'cos(x)'); -- false
```

## Notes

Compares via `simplify(a - b) == 0`, so different-looking but equal forms match. Returns `NULL` if either side is invalid/unsafe.

vgi.example_queries.description: Grade free-form answers against the key (x + 1)**2: render each answer as LaTeX for display and mark it correct when it is symbolically equal to the key (only x**2 + 1 is wrong).
vgi.example_queries.sql:
SELECT answer,
       sympy.main.to_latex(answer) AS latex,
       sympy.main.symbolic_equal(answer, '(x + 1)**2') AS correct
FROM (VALUES ('x**2 + 2*x + 1'), ('(1 + x)*(x + 1)'), ('x**2 + 1'), ('x*(x + 2) + 1')) AS t(answer)
ORDER BY answer

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## evaluate(expr, vars_json)

Substitute numeric values into an expression and **evaluate** it to a `DOUBLE`.

The second argument is a JSON object mapping variable names to numbers, e.g. `'{"x":3,"y":1}'`. After substitution `evaluate('x**2 + y', '{"x":3,"y":1}')` returns `10.0`.

**Output:** a `DOUBLE`. Returns `NULL` when free symbols remain after substitution or the result is non-real. Unlike the transforms, it **raises an error** when `vars_json` is structurally wrong (not a JSON object, or a non-numeric value), since that is a caller mistake rather than dirty data.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# evaluate

Substitutes numeric values from a JSON object and evaluates to a `DOUBLE`.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT sympy.evaluate('x**2 + y', '{"x":3,"y":1}'); -- 10.0
SELECT sympy.evaluate('2*pi', '{}');                  -- 6.283...
```

## Notes

`NULL` if free symbols remain or the result isn't real. **Errors** (not NULL) when `vars_json` is not a JSON object of numbers.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## differentiate(expr, var)

Compute the symbolic **derivative** of an expression with respect to a named variable and return it as `VARCHAR`.

For example `differentiate('x**3', 'x')` returns `'3*x**2'`. The second argument names the variable to differentiate by; other symbols are treated as constants.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
# differentiate

Symbolic differentiation with respect to a variable.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT sympy.differentiate('x**3', 'x');     -- '3*x**2'
SELECT sympy.differentiate('sin(x)', 'x');   -- 'cos(x)'
```

## Notes

Variables other than `var` are held constant. Returns `NULL` for `NULL`/invalid/unsafe input.

vgi.example_queries.description: Find the stationary points of x**3 - 3*x by solving its derivative for zero, then evaluate the function at each one: a local maximum of 2.0 at x = -1 and a local minimum of -2.0 at x = 1.
vgi.example_queries.sql:
WITH crit AS (
  SELECT UNNEST(sympy.main.solve(sympy.main.differentiate('x**3 - 3*x', 'x'), 'x')) AS root
), pts AS (
  SELECT root, sympy.main.evaluate(root, '{}') AS x_value FROM crit
)
SELECT root, x_value,
       sympy.main.evaluate('x**3 - 3*x', '{"x": ' || x_value || '}') AS f_value
FROM pts
ORDER BY x_value

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## solve(equation, var)

**Solve** an equation for a variable and return all solutions as a `VARCHAR[]` (list of expression strings).

The first argument is either `'lhs = rhs'` (the single `=` is split before parsing) or a bare expression assumed equal to zero. The second argument names the variable to solve for. Results are **sorted by string** for order-independence — in SQL use `UNNEST(...)` to fan them into rows.

**Output:** a list of solution strings; an **empty list** when there are no solutions, or `NULL` when either input is `NULL`/invalid/unsafe.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# solve

Solves an equation for a variable, returning a `VARCHAR[]` of solutions.

## Usage

```sql
SELECT sympy.solve('x**2 - 4', 'x');      -- ['-2', '2']
SELECT UNNEST(sympy.solve('2*x = 10', 'x')); -- 5
```

## Notes

Accepts `'lhs = rhs'` or a bare expression (assumed `= 0`). Solutions are sorted by string. Empty list = no solutions; `NULL` = invalid/unsafe input.

workers.doc_md:
# Tableau

Query a Tableau Cloud or Tableau Server site from DuckDB: dashboards and worksheets with view counts, workbooks, projects, published data sources and their connections, users, groups, favorites, subscriptions, alerts, extract refreshes, jobs, Prep flows, revisions, and Metadata API lineage. Read-only.

Create a `tableau` secret with `SERVER_URL`, `SITE_CONTENT_URL` and a personal access token (`PAT_NAME`, `PAT_SECRET`) or a connected app (`CLIENT_ID`, `SECRET_ID`, `SECRET_VALUE`, `USERNAME`). Filters become Tableau REST `filter=` expressions, paging and rate limits are handled for you, and passwords are never returned.

### Sources and references

- [Tableau REST API reference](https://help.tableau.com/current/api/rest_api/en-us/REST/rest_api_ref.htm) — the endpoints this worker reads
- [Filtering and sorting](https://help.tableau.com/current/api/rest_api/en-us/REST/rest_api_concepts_filtering_and_sorting.htm) and [paging](https://help.tableau.com/current/api/rest_api/en-us/REST/rest_api_concepts_paging.htm)
- [Metadata API (GraphQL)](https://help.tableau.com/current/api/metadata_api/en-us/index.html) — lineage
- [Personal access tokens](https://help.tableau.com/current/online/en-us/security_personal_access_tokens.htm) and [connected apps (direct trust)](https://help.tableau.com/current/online/en-us/connected_apps_direct.htm)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Tableau site collections as SQL tables (no arguments; filter with WHERE). Two kinds of table live here: BI-vocabulary tables (dashboards, worksheets, view usage, projects as folders, published data sources, connections, users, custom SQL) that share columns with the other Query.Farm BI workers so they UNION, and Tableau-native tables for workbooks, groups, favorites, subscriptions and alerts, schedules, extract refreshes, jobs, Prep flows, revisions and Metadata API lineage. Per-item collections read only the items named by a pushed `= / IN` filter on their key column, otherwise every item (one extra call each). Other WHERE filters push down into Tableau's REST `filter=` syntax and are re-checked exactly. All tables need a `tableau` secret.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

Tableau site content, people, usage, operations and lineage as tables.

Per-item collections (connections, revisions, group members, favorites) take their parent id from a pushed filter and otherwise read every parent. All tables need a `tableau` secret.

workers.tagline: BM25 full-text search with stemming & tokenization for DuckDB (Rust, tantivy)
workers.subtitle: Rank documents by BM25 relevance, tokenize text, and stem words with Snowball stemmers for many languages.
workers.summary: Full-text search (BM25 ranking), tokenization, and Snowball stemming, powered by the tantivy search engine.
workers.doc_md:
# tantivy — Full-Text Search & Text Analysis in SQL

![tantivy logo](https://tantivy-search.github.io/logo/tantivy-logo.png)

Add **BM25 full-text search**, relevance ranking, and query-time text analysis (tokenization and Snowball stemming) directly to DuckDB SQL — no separate search service, index server, or ETL pipeline required. The `tantivy` worker is a standalone VGI worker that DuckDB attaches over Apache Arrow, exposing lexical (keyword) search and text-normalization functions you can call inline from any query.

## How it works

Every function is powered by [tantivy](https://github.com/quickwit-oss/tantivy), the fast full-text search engine written in Rust (the library behind Quickwit), documented at [docs.rs/tantivy](https://docs.rs/tantivy/latest/tantivy/). For each `bm25_search` / `bm25_score` call the worker builds a fresh in-RAM tantivy index, registers the appropriate per-language analyzer (simple tokenizer + lowercasing + a Snowball stemmer), indexes your documents, runs the query through tantivy's query parser and top-docs collector, and drops the index when the call returns. Nothing is persisted or shared between calls, so results are fully deterministic and there is no external state to manage. Relevance is computed with the industry-standard [Okapi BM25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okapi_BM25) ranking model, and stemming uses the [Snowball](https://snowballstem.org/) algorithms.

## Key concepts

Corpora are passed **inline as constant JSON** rather than as table references, because the ranking function binds its corpus at query-bind time: assemble a text column into a JSON payload with `json_group_array`, materialize it with `SET VARIABLE`, and pass `getvariable(...)` (a subquery is not accepted as a table-function argument). Multi-term queries match documents containing every term; use `a OR b` for any-term matching. Relevance is lexical (keyword/BM25), not semantic — there is no embedding model or vector store. Text analysis is language-aware through Snowball stemming, so word variants collapse to a shared root; the set of stemmer languages is discoverable at runtime.

## Who it's for

Reach for this worker whenever you want lightweight, embedded lexical search and relevance ranking inside an analytical SQL workflow — log triage, document shortlisting, fuzzy keyword matching, or normalizing text before joins and grouping — without standing up Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, or a dedicated indexing service. Every index is built in RAM **per call** and dropped immediately, and corpora are passed inline as constant JSON, so queries run with no external state.

example_queries.description: Rank a small JSON corpus by BM25 relevance to a query, best score first.
example_queries.sql: SELECT doc_id, score FROM tantivy.main.bm25_search('["the cat sat","dogs bark","stock crash"]', 'cat') ORDER BY score DESC, doc_id

example_queries.description: Compute the ad-hoc BM25 score of a single document against a query.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tantivy.main.bm25_score('the cat sat on the mat', 'cat') AS score

example_queries.description: Tokenize text into lowercased word tokens (no stemming).
example_queries.sql: SELECT tantivy.main.tokenize('Running quickly, CATS!') AS tokens

example_queries.description: Tokenize and Snowball-stem text for a language.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tantivy.main.tokenize('Running quickly', 'english') AS tokens

example_queries.description: Snowball-stem a single word to its root for a language.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tantivy.main.stem('running', 'english') AS root

example_queries.description: List the first few supported Snowball stemmer languages, alphabetically.
example_queries.sql: SELECT lang FROM tantivy.main.supported_languages ORDER BY lang LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Rank product titles for 'running OR shoes' with bm25_search, join the hits back to the titles by id, and use tokenize(…, 'english') to list which stemmed query terms each hit contains.
example_queries.sql: SELECT p.title, round(h.score, 3) AS score, list_sort(list_intersect(tantivy.main.tokenize(p.title, 'english'), tantivy.main.tokenize('running shoes', 'english'))) AS matched_terms FROM tantivy.main.bm25_search('[{"id":1,"text":"Trail running shoes"},{"id":2,"text":"Leather dress shoes"},{"id":3,"text":"Runners guide to the marathon"},{"id":4,"text":"Cast iron skillet"},{"id":5,"text":"Running socks"}]', 'running OR shoes') AS h JOIN (VALUES (1, 'Trail running shoes'), (2, 'Leather dress shoes'), (3, 'Runners guide to the marathon'), (4, 'Cast iron skillet'), (5, 'Running socks')) AS p(id, title) ON p.id = h.doc_id ORDER BY h.score DESC, p.title

example_queries.description: Tokenize a sentence (no stemming), then stem each token with stem() to group the word variants under their English Snowball root, most frequent root first.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tantivy.main.stem(tok, 'english') AS root, list(DISTINCT tok ORDER BY tok) AS variants, count(*) AS occurrences FROM unnest(tantivy.main.tokenize('Runners were running; the runner runs and ran a run.')) AS u(tok) GROUP BY root ORDER BY occurrences DESC, root

example_queries.description: Stem the word 'connections' with every supported Snowball stemmer (one row per language from supported_languages) and keep only the languages whose stemmer changes it.
example_queries.sql: SELECT lang, tantivy.main.stem('connections', lang) AS root FROM tantivy.main.supported_languages WHERE tantivy.main.stem('connections', lang) <> 'connections' ORDER BY lang

example_queries.description: Check whether a specific language is supported.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) > 0 AS supported FROM tantivy.main.supported_languages WHERE lang = 'english'

example_queries.description: List the first few supported Snowball stemmer languages, alphabetically.
example_queries.sql: SELECT lang FROM tantivy.main.supported_languages() ORDER BY lang LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Check whether a specific language is supported.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) > 0 AS supported FROM tantivy.main.supported_languages() WHERE lang = 'english'

example_queries.description: Rank a small JSON corpus by BM25 relevance to a query, best score first.
example_queries.sql: SELECT doc_id, score FROM tantivy.main.bm25_search('["the cat sat","dogs bark","a cat and a dog"]', 'cat') ORDER BY score DESC, doc_id

example_queries.description: Rank a corpus carrying explicit {id,text} document ids.
example_queries.sql: SELECT doc_id, score FROM tantivy.main.bm25_search('[{"id":10,"text":"the cat sat"},{"id":20,"text":"stock crash"}]', 'cat')

agent_tasks: Given exactly these three documents, in this order — 'the cat sat', 'dogs bark', and 'a cat and a dog' — rank them by BM25 relevance to the query 'cat'. Return every matching row as (doc_id, score), best score first, exactly as the worker produces them.

Rank this corpus, whose documents carry explicit ids, by BM25 relevance to the query 'cat': the document with id 10 is 'the cat sat', id 20 is 'stock crash', and id 30 is 'the cat and the dog'. Return the matching rows as (doc_id, score).

Run the worker to compute the ad-hoc BM25 relevance score of the single document 'the cat sat on the mat' against the query 'cat'. Execute the function against these exact inputs and return the numeric score it outputs — do not estimate it or reuse a value from documentation.

Use this worker to split the text 'Running quickly, CATS!' into lowercased word tokens WITHOUT any stemming (the plain 1-argument tokenizer). Run the function and return the resulting array of tokens exactly as produced.

Use this worker to tokenize the text 'Running quickly' and additionally apply the English Snowball stemmer to each token (the 2-argument tokenizer). Return the resulting array of tokens exactly as produced.
List every Snowball stemmer language this worker supports, ordered alphabetically. Return the full list of language ids.

Using this worker's single-word stemming function, reduce the individual English word 'running' to its Snowball root. Return exactly one row holding a single scalar text value — the stemmed root word itself (a plain string, not a list or array).

Stem the single word 'nationalities' with every Snowball stemmer language this worker supports, then group the languages by the root they produce. Return two columns (root VARCHAR, languages BIGINT) — each distinct root and how many languages produce it — ordered by languages descending, then root ascending.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## tantivy.main

The single schema of the `tantivy` worker, grouping its full-text search, relevance-scoring, and text-analysis capabilities into three areas.

### What lives here

**Search & ranking** covers BM25 relevance over a document corpus that you pass inline as a constant JSON payload, plus an ad-hoc single-document scorer. **Text analysis** provides language-aware tokenization and Snowball stemming for normalizing text before matching, grouping, or building search keys. **Discovery** lets you introspect which stemmer languages are available and which engine version is in use.

### How it behaves

Every function is deterministic given its inputs and needs no persisted state — indexes are built in a RAM directory per call and dropped when the call returns.

functions.name: bm25_search
functions.comment: BM25 full-text ranking of a JSON document corpus against a query, as (doc_id, score) rows

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Rank a corpus of documents against a full-text query by BM25 relevance, using an ephemeral in-RAM tantivy index built per call (English stemmer). The corpus is a constant JSON payload: a JSON array of strings (doc_id = array index) or of {id,text} objects (explicit doc_id); a subquery is not accepted as an argument, so materialize one with SET VARIABLE and pass getvariable(...). Multi-term queries are conjunctive (every term must match); write 'a OR b' to match any term. Returns one (doc_id, score) row per matching document, best score first. NULL/empty corpus or blank query → no rows; malformed JSON or an unparseable query is a clear error.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Rank a JSON document corpus by BM25 relevance to a query, returning `(doc_id, score)` rows best-first, e.g. `bm25_search('["the cat sat","dogs bark"]', 'cat')`.

functions.name: tokenize
functions.comment: Tokenize text into VARCHAR[]; 1-arg form only splits+lowercases (no stemming)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Split text into normalized word tokens, returned as a `VARCHAR` array. Two forms: `tokenize(text)` applies the default analyzer only — unicode word segmentation, lowercasing, and dropping of overly long tokens, with NO stemming (e.g. 'Running quickly, CATS!' → ['running','quickly','cats']); `tokenize(text, lang)` does the same and additionally Snowball-stems each token for the given language, collapsing word variants to a shared root (e.g. 'Running quickly' with 'english' → ['run','quickli']). NULL text (or NULL language in the 2-arg form) → NULL; an unknown language is a clear error.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Tokenize text into a `VARCHAR` array of normalized terms. The 1-arg form `tokenize(text)` only tokenizes and lowercases (no stemmer), e.g. `tokenize('Running quickly, CATS!')` → `['running','quickly','cats']`. The 2-arg form `tokenize(text, lang)` additionally Snowball-stems each token, e.g. `tokenize('Running quickly', 'english')` → `['run','quickli']`.

workers.subtitle: Temporal workflow executions, histories, activities, schedules and task queues as SQL.
workers.summary: Temporal workflow executions, event histories, pending activities, schedules, task queues and batch operations as SQL, from self-hosted Temporal or Temporal Cloud. Read-only.
workers.doc_md:
# Temporal

Query a [Temporal](https://temporal.io) cluster from DuckDB: workflow executions with server-side visibility filtering, counts by status, full event histories, pending activities, schedules, task queue pollers and backlog, search attributes and batch operations. Works with self-hosted Temporal and Temporal Cloud (API key or mTLS). Read-only: nothing can be started, signalled or terminated.

Connect with a `temporal` secret holding `HOST`, `NAMESPACE` and either `API_KEY` (Temporal Cloud) or `CLIENT_CERT`/`CLIENT_KEY` (mTLS). Without a secret the worker talks to a local `temporal server start-dev`.

The `unified` schema exposes runs and task runs in the shape shared by the Query.Farm orchestrator workers.

example_queries.description: Failed or timed-out runs per workflow type since January (filters run server-side)
example_queries.sql: SELECT workflow_type, count(*) AS failures FROM temporal.main.workflow_executions() WHERE status IN ('Failed', 'TimedOut') AND start_time >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01' GROUP BY workflow_type ORDER BY failures DESC

example_queries.description: The oldest open workflows on one task queue
example_queries.sql: SELECT workflow_id, start_time FROM temporal.main.workflow_executions() WHERE status = 'Running' AND task_queue = 'orders' ORDER BY start_time LIMIT 20

example_queries.description: How many executions are in each status
example_queries.sql: SELECT status, count FROM temporal.main.count_workflow_executions() ORDER BY count DESC

example_queries.description: Total runs of one workflow type
example_queries.sql: SELECT count FROM temporal.main.count_workflow_executions(query := 'WorkflowType = ''OrderWorkflow''', group_by_status := false)

example_queries.description: Walk the history of the latest run of one workflow
example_queries.sql: SELECT event_id, event_type, event_time, failure_message FROM temporal.main.workflow_history('order-123') ORDER BY event_id

example_queries.description: Each activity of a run with its final attempt and outcome
example_queries.sql: SELECT s.activity_type, st.attempt, c.event_type AS outcome FROM temporal.main.workflow_history('order-123') s JOIN temporal.main.workflow_history('order-123') c ON c.scheduled_event_id = s.event_id AND c.event_type LIKE 'ActivityTask%' AND c.event_type <> 'ActivityTaskStarted' LEFT JOIN temporal.main.workflow_history('order-123') st ON st.scheduled_event_id = s.event_id AND st.event_type = 'ActivityTaskStarted' WHERE s.event_type = 'ActivityTaskScheduled' ORDER BY s.event_id

example_queries.description: Why is this workflow stuck?
example_queries.sql: SELECT activity_type, state, attempt, last_failure_message FROM temporal.main.pending_activities('order-123') ORDER BY attempt DESC

example_queries.description: Every schedule with its next run
example_queries.sql: SELECT schedule_id, workflow_type, paused, next_action_times[1] AS next_run FROM temporal.main.schedules() ORDER BY schedule_id

example_queries.description: Recent runs started by schedules
example_queries.sql: SELECT schedule_id, a.workflow_id, a.status FROM temporal.main.schedules(), UNNEST(recent_actions) AS r(a) ORDER BY a.actual_time DESC

example_queries.description: Workers and backlog of one task queue
example_queries.sql: SELECT task_queue_type, poller_count, approximate_backlog_count FROM temporal.main.task_queues('orders') ORDER BY task_queue_type

example_queries.description: Custom search attributes of the namespace
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, type FROM temporal.main.search_attributes() WHERE is_custom ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Recent bulk actions and why they ran
example_queries.sql: SELECT job_id, operation_type, state, complete_operation_count, reason FROM temporal.main.batch_operations() ORDER BY start_time DESC

example_queries.description: Every namespace with its retention
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, retention_days, state FROM temporal.main.namespaces ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Run counts per workflow type in the cross-orchestrator status vocabulary
example_queries.sql: SELECT workflow_type, temporal.main.unified_run_status(status) AS status, count(*) AS runs FROM temporal.main.workflow_executions() GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY workflow_type, status

example_queries.description: Normalize a few Temporal statuses
example_queries.sql: SELECT s, temporal.main.unified_run_status(s) AS status FROM (VALUES ('TimedOut'), ('ContinuedAsNew'), ('Canceled'), ('running'), ('WORKFLOW_EXECUTION_STATUS_TERMINATED'), ('bogus')) t(s) ORDER BY s;

example_queries.description: Failure counts per workflow type in the shared shape
example_queries.sql: SELECT pipeline, count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed') AS failures, count(*) AS runs FROM temporal.unified.runs WHERE queued_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01' GROUP BY pipeline ORDER BY failures DESC

example_queries.description: Activities of recent failed runs, most-retried first
example_queries.sql: SELECT t.task_name, t.attempt, t.status FROM temporal.unified.task_runs t WHERE t.run_id IN (SELECT run_id FROM temporal.unified.runs WHERE status = 'failed' AND queued_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01') ORDER BY t.attempt DESC

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Schema main reads Temporal's own objects for one namespace at a time (the secret's NAMESPACE, or a namespace := argument). Start from the execution listing and filter it with WHERE on workflow id, run id, workflow type, status, task queue, start/close/execution time, history length or a custom search attribute column: those filters become a Temporal visibility query and run server-side, so a narrow WHERE is cheap even in a namespace with millions of runs. Status values are Temporal's spelling (Running, Completed, Failed, Canceled, Terminated, ContinuedAsNew, TimedOut). To explain one execution, read its event history (one row per event, with activity, timer, child workflow and failure fields hoisted) or its pending activities (attempt, backoff and last failure of whatever it is waiting on). Counting by status is done server-side without listing. The remaining objects describe the namespace: schedules, task queue pollers and backlog, search attributes and batch operations.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

Temporal's own objects for one namespace: workflow executions (with visibility-query pushdown and typed custom search attribute columns), server-side counts by status, event histories and pending activities.

Namespace-level operations live here too: namespaces, schedules with their spec and recent actions, task queue pollers and backlog, search attributes and batch operations.

Statuses use Temporal's spelling; `unified_run_status` maps them to the cross-orchestrator vocabulary.

vgi.example_queries.description: Failed or timed-out runs per workflow type since January (filters run server-side)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT workflow_type, count(*) AS failures FROM temporal.main.workflow_executions() WHERE status IN ('Failed', 'TimedOut') AND start_time >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01' GROUP BY workflow_type ORDER BY failures DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: The oldest open workflows on one task queue
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT workflow_id, start_time FROM temporal.main.workflow_executions() WHERE status = 'Running' AND task_queue = 'orders' ORDER BY start_time LIMIT 20

vgi.example_queries.description: How many executions are in each status
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT status, count FROM temporal.main.count_workflow_executions() ORDER BY count DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Total runs of one workflow type
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT count FROM temporal.main.count_workflow_executions(query := 'WorkflowType = ''OrderWorkflow''', group_by_status := false)

vgi.example_queries.description: Walk the history of the latest run of one workflow
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT event_id, event_type, event_time, failure_message FROM temporal.main.workflow_history('order-123') ORDER BY event_id

vgi.example_queries.description: Each activity of a run with its final attempt and outcome
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT s.activity_type, st.attempt, c.event_type AS outcome FROM temporal.main.workflow_history('order-123') s JOIN temporal.main.workflow_history('order-123') c ON c.scheduled_event_id = s.event_id AND c.event_type LIKE 'ActivityTask%' AND c.event_type <> 'ActivityTaskStarted' LEFT JOIN temporal.main.workflow_history('order-123') st ON st.scheduled_event_id = s.event_id AND st.event_type = 'ActivityTaskStarted' WHERE s.event_type = 'ActivityTaskScheduled' ORDER BY s.event_id

vgi.example_queries.description: Why is this workflow stuck?
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT activity_type, state, attempt, last_failure_message FROM temporal.main.pending_activities('order-123') ORDER BY attempt DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Every schedule with its next run
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT schedule_id, workflow_type, paused, next_action_times[1] AS next_run FROM temporal.main.schedules() ORDER BY schedule_id

vgi.example_queries.description: Recent runs started by schedules
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT schedule_id, a.workflow_id, a.status FROM temporal.main.schedules(), UNNEST(recent_actions) AS r(a) ORDER BY a.actual_time DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Workers and backlog of one task queue
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT task_queue_type, poller_count, approximate_backlog_count FROM temporal.main.task_queues('orders') ORDER BY task_queue_type

vgi.example_queries.description: Custom search attributes of the namespace
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, type FROM temporal.main.search_attributes() WHERE is_custom ORDER BY name

vgi.example_queries.description: Recent bulk actions and why they ran
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT job_id, operation_type, state, complete_operation_count, reason FROM temporal.main.batch_operations() ORDER BY start_time DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Every namespace with its retention
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, retention_days, state FROM temporal.main.namespaces ORDER BY name

vgi.example_queries.description: Run counts per workflow type in the cross-orchestrator status vocabulary
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT workflow_type, temporal.main.unified_run_status(status) AS status, count(*) AS runs FROM temporal.main.workflow_executions() GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY workflow_type, status

tags.vgi.doc_llm: workflow_history(workflow_id, run_id := NULL, namespace := NULL) returns every history event of one workflow run (the latest run when run_id is omitted) via GetWorkflowExecutionHistory, paged. Columns: workflow_id, run_id, event_id, event_type (e.g. WorkflowExecutionStarted, ActivityTaskScheduled, ActivityTaskStarted, ActivityTaskCompleted, ActivityTaskFailed, TimerFired, ChildWorkflowExecutionCompleted, WorkflowExecutionSignaled), event_time, task_id, then hoisted fields: activity_id and activity_type (on Scheduled events), scheduled_event_id / started_event_id (link later activity/child events back to their Scheduled event), attempt (ActivityTaskStarted carries the final attempt number), timer_id, child_workflow_id/type/run_id, signal_name, task_queue, identity, failure_message, and attributes (full JSON with payloads decoded). tags.vgi.doc_llm: workflow_executions(namespace := NULL, query := NULL) lists workflow executions (one row per run) of a namespace via ListWorkflowExecutions. Columns: namespace, workflow_id, run_id, workflow_type, status (Running, Completed, Failed, Canceled, Terminated, ContinuedAsNew, TimedOut - capitalized as Temporal spells them), start_time, execution_time, close_time, execution_duration_seconds, task_queue, history_length, history_size_bytes, state_transition_count, parent/root workflow and run ids, first_run_id, scheduled_by_id, memo JSON, search_attributes JSON, url, then one typed column per custom search attribute named exactly like the attribute (Keyword/Text `VARCHAR`, Int `BIGINT`, Double `DOUBLE`, Bool `BOOLEAN`, Datetime `TIMESTAMPTZ`, KeywordList `VARCHAR[]`). schemas.name: unified
schemas.comment: runs and task_runs in the shape shared by every orchestrator worker.

vgi.categories.name: unified
vgi.categories.title: Unified Orchestrator Shape
vgi.categories.description: runs / task_runs with the columns shared by every orchestrator worker.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Schema unified has two tables with the exact columns the airflow, dagster, prefect, dbt, databricks and github workers also expose, for UNION ALL across orchestrators. runs: one row per Temporal workflow run (pipeline = workflow type). task_runs: one row per activity execution, derived from each run's event history (one history read per workflow run), so filter run_id or join from a filtered runs query first.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## unified

`runs` and `task_runs` in the column layout shared by every Query.Farm orchestrator worker, so Temporal workflows can be reported next to Airflow DAG runs, Dagster runs or Prefect flow runs with a plain `UNION ALL`.

Statuses are normalized to queued, running, success, failed, cancelled and skipped; the Temporal status is kept in `raw_status`. Task runs are Temporal activity executions, read from each run's event history, so filter `run_id` before scanning them.

vgi.example_queries.description: Failure counts per workflow type in the shared shape
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT pipeline, count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed') AS failures, count(*) AS runs FROM temporal.unified.runs WHERE queued_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01' GROUP BY pipeline ORDER BY failures DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Activities of recent failed runs, most-retried first
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT t.task_name, t.attempt, t.status FROM temporal.unified.task_runs t WHERE t.run_id IN (SELECT run_id FROM temporal.unified.runs WHERE status = 'failed' AND queued_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01') ORDER BY t.attempt DESC

tags.vgi.title: Unified Orchestrator Runs

tables.name: task_runs
tables.comment: Temporal activity executions in the cross-orchestrator task_runs shape, derived from event histories

tags.vgi.doc_llm: unified.task_runs has columns orchestrator ('temporal'), run_id, task_run_id, task_name (activity type), status (queued/running/success/failed/cancelled), raw_status, attempt, started_at, ended_at, duration_seconds, url - the same columns as the other orchestrator workers' unified.task_runs. Each row is one activity execution; attempt is the final (or current) attempt, since Temporal retries inside one execution. Rows are derived from each workflow run's event history - one history read per run - so always filter run_id (pushed down) or join from a filtered unified.runs query; an unfiltered scan reads every history in the namespace.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## unified.task_runs

workers.doc_md:
# ATP and WTA tennis

Rankings, tournament calendars, full draw results, Grand Slam finals, player profiles and player season logs, fetched on demand and returned as typed Arrow tables.

## Sources and ids

WTA data comes from the official [WTA](https://www.wtatennis.com/) API (the same data behind its [rankings](https://www.wtatennis.com/rankings/singles) and [tournaments](https://www.wtatennis.com/tournaments) pages). ATP data, live scoreboards and Grand Slam finals come from [ESPN tennis](https://www.espn.com/tennis/)'s undocumented endpoints, subject to the [Disney terms of use](https://disneytermsofuse.com/). Player and tournament ids are specific to their `source`.

## Scores

`score` reads from the winner's side with the tiebreak loser's points in parentheses, e.g. `7-6(5) 6-3`. `sets` holds per-set games for side 1 and side 2.

example_queries.title: current_rankings_cover_both_tours
example_queries.description: Singles rankings are present for both the ATP and WTA.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(DISTINCT tour) AS tours FROM tennis.main.current_rankings;

example_queries.title: each_tour_has_a_number_one
example_queries.description: Each tour has exactly one player ranked first.
example_queries.sql: SELECT bool_and(n = 1) AS ok FROM (SELECT tour, count(*) AS n FROM tennis.main.current_rankings WHERE ranking = 1 GROUP BY tour);

example_queries.title: current_matches_are_typed
example_queries.description: Every current match has an id and a known status.
example_queries.sql: SELECT coalesce(bool_and(match_id IS NOT NULL AND status IN ('scheduled','in_progress','completed','retired','walkover','other')), true) AS ok FROM tennis.main.current_matches;

example_queries.title: ao_2026_womens_champion
example_queries.description: Elena Rybakina won the 2026 Australian Open women's singles final.
example_queries.sql: SELECT winner_name FROM tennis.main.tournament_matches('WTA', 901, 2026) WHERE draw_type = 'singles' AND round = 'Final';

example_queries.description: The top ten of each tour.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tour, ranking, player_name, country, points FROM tennis.main.current_rankings WHERE ranking <= 10 ORDER BY tour, ranking

example_queries.description: Biggest climbers in the latest ATP release.
example_queries.sql: SELECT ranking, player_name, movement FROM tennis.main.current_rankings WHERE tour = 'ATP' ORDER BY movement DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: This week's completed ATP singles matches won by the lower-ranked player, joining current_matches to current_rankings for both players (ATP ids are ESPN ids on both sides; players outside the top 150 drop out).
example_queries.sql: SELECT m.tournament_name, m.round, m.winner_name, w.ranking AS winner_rank, m.loser_name, l.ranking AS loser_rank, m.score FROM tennis.main.current_matches AS m JOIN tennis.main.current_rankings AS w ON w.tour = 'ATP' AND w.player_id = if(m.winner_side = 1, m.side1_player_id, m.side2_player_id) JOIN tennis.main.current_rankings AS l ON l.tour = 'ATP' AND l.player_id = if(m.winner_side = 1, m.side2_player_id, m.side1_player_id) WHERE m.tour = 'ATP' AND m.draw_type = 'singles' AND m.status = 'completed' AND w.ranking > l.ranking ORDER BY w.ranking - l.ranking DESC, m.match_id

example_queries.description: Elena Rybakina's 2026 singles wins against players now in the WTA top 10, joining player_matches to current_rankings on the WTA opponent id.
example_queries.sql: SELECT p.opponent_name, r.ranking AS current_rank, count(*) AS wins FROM tennis.main.player_matches('WTA', 324166, season := 2026) AS p JOIN tennis.main.current_rankings AS r ON r.tour = 'WTA' AND r.player_id = p.opponent_id WHERE p.draw_type = 'singles' AND p.result = 'W' AND r.ranking <= 10 GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY current_rank

example_queries.description: Every 2026 tournament where Elena Rybakina lost a singles match: the round, who beat her, and the event's eventual singles champion from the WTA calendar.
example_queries.sql: SELECT p.tournament_name, p.round, p.opponent_name AS lost_to, t.singles_champion FROM tennis.main.player_matches('WTA', 324166, season := 2026) AS p JOIN tennis.main.tournaments('WTA', season := 2026) AS t ON t.tournament_id = p.tournament_id WHERE p.draw_type = 'singles' AND p.result = 'L' ORDER BY p.tournament_start_date

example_queries.description: Each 2026 Grand Slam singles champion with their current ranking and points, joining grand_slam_results to current_rankings by tour and player name (Slam finals carry no player ids).
example_queries.sql: SELECT g.tournament_name, g.draw, g.champion, r.ranking AS current_rank, r.points FROM tennis.main.grand_slam_results(2026) AS g LEFT JOIN tennis.main.current_rankings AS r ON r.tour = g.tour AND r.player_name = g.champion WHERE g.draw IN ('Men''s Singles', 'Women''s Singles') ORDER BY g.final_date, g.draw

example_queries.description: Completed singles results this week.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tournament_name, round, winner_name, loser_name, score FROM tennis.main.current_matches WHERE status = 'completed' AND draw_type = 'singles' ORDER BY scheduled_at DESC

example_queries.description: Match count and completion by tournament and draw.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tournament_name, draw, count(*) AS matches, count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'completed') AS completed FROM tennis.main.current_matches GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY tournament_name, draw

example_queries.description: Read the top three of each tour from the backing scan.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tour, ranking, player_name, country, points FROM tennis.main.all_current_rankings() WHERE ranking <= 3 ORDER BY tour, ranking

example_queries.description: The 2026 men's Grand Slam finals.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tournament_name, draw, champion, runner_up, score FROM tennis.main.grand_slam_results(2026, tour := 'ATP') ORDER BY final_date, draw

example_queries.description: Australian Open 2026 women's singles semifinals and final.
example_queries.sql: SELECT round, winner_name, loser_name, score FROM tennis.main.tournament_matches('WTA', 901, 2026) WHERE draw_type = 'singles' AND NOT qualifying AND round IN ('Semifinal', 'Final')

example_queries.description: Matches on Wimbledon 2026 men's final day.
example_queries.sql: SELECT draw, round, winner_name, loser_name, score FROM tennis.main.matches_on('ATP', DATE '2026-07-12') ORDER BY scheduled_at

example_queries.description: Carlos Alcaraz's ESPN profile.
example_queries.sql: SELECT player_name, birth_date, height_inches, plays, debut_year FROM tennis.main.player('ATP', 3782)

example_queries.description: Elena Rybakina's 2026 singles results.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tournament_name, round, opponent_name, result, score FROM tennis.main.player_matches('WTA', 324166, season := 2026) WHERE draw_type = 'singles'

example_queries.description: The WTA doubles top 20.
example_queries.sql: SELECT ranking, player_name, country, points, movement FROM tennis.main.rankings('WTA', ranking_type := 'doubles', max_rank := 20) ORDER BY ranking

example_queries.description: 2026 WTA Grand Slams and WTA 1000s with champions.
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, level, surface, start_date, singles_champion FROM tennis.main.tournaments('WTA', season := 2026) WHERE level IN ('Grand Slam', 'WTA 1000') ORDER BY start_date

example_queries.description: Latest completed matches from the backing scan.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tour, tournament_name, draw, round, winner_name, loser_name, score FROM tennis.main.all_current_matches() WHERE status = 'completed' ORDER BY scheduled_at DESC LIMIT 20

## Professional tennis

Rows are player-, tournament- or match-grain. Current tables need no arguments; functions take a tour ('ATP' or 'WTA') as their first, positional argument except `grand_slam_results(season)`.

vgi.example_queries.description: The 2026 men's Grand Slam finals.

vgi.example_queries.description: Each 2026 Grand Slam singles champion with their current ranking and points, joining grand_slam_results to current_rankings by tour and player name (Slam finals carry no player ids).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT g.tournament_name, g.draw, g.champion, r.ranking AS current_rank, r.points FROM tennis.main.grand_slam_results(2026) AS g LEFT JOIN tennis.main.current_rankings AS r ON r.tour = g.tour AND r.player_name = g.champion WHERE g.draw IN ('Men''s Singles', 'Women''s Singles') ORDER BY g.final_date, g.draw

functions.name: player_matches
functions.comment: One ATP or WTA player's match results for a season

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per match a player played in a season, from the player's point of view: tournament, round, partner, opponent, result W/L, score and status. WTA rows add entry rankings, ranking points and prize money earned at that tournament. Positional: player_matches('WTA', 324166, season := 2026). Byes are omitted.
tags.vgi.doc_md: A player's season, one row per match. WTA uses the official WTA API and ids; ATP (and WTA with `source := 'espn'`) scans ESPN's season scoreboards for the ESPN id.

vgi.example_queries.description: Elena Rybakina's 2026 singles results.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT tournament_name, round, opponent_name, result, score FROM tennis.main.player_matches('WTA', 324166, season := 2026) WHERE draw_type = 'singles'

vgi.example_queries.description: Every 2026 tournament where Elena Rybakina lost a singles match: the round, who beat her, and the event's eventual singles champion from the WTA calendar.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT p.tournament_name, p.round, p.opponent_name AS lost_to, t.singles_champion FROM tennis.main.player_matches('WTA', 324166, season := 2026) AS p JOIN tennis.main.tournaments('WTA', season := 2026) AS t ON t.tournament_id = p.tournament_id WHERE p.draw_type = 'singles' AND p.result = 'L' ORDER BY p.tournament_start_date

vgi.example_queries.description: Elena Rybakina's 2026 singles wins against players now in the WTA top 10, joining player_matches to current_rankings on the WTA opponent id.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT p.opponent_name, r.ranking AS current_rank, count(*) AS wins FROM tennis.main.player_matches('WTA', 324166, season := 2026) AS p JOIN tennis.main.current_rankings AS r ON r.tour = 'WTA' AND r.player_id = p.opponent_id WHERE p.draw_type = 'singles' AND p.result = 'W' AND r.ranking <= 10 GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY current_rank
