workers.doc_md:
# HCP Terraform

Query [HCP Terraform](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cloud-docs) and Terraform Enterprise from DuckDB: workspaces, runs, plans and applies, policy results, cost estimates, state versions, outputs, resources, variables, teams, agents, the private registry and drift-detection results. Read-only: the worker only sends GET requests, and sensitive variables and outputs are never returned.

Connect with a `terraform` secret (add `HOSTNAME` for Terraform Enterprise):

```sql
CREATE SECRET (TYPE terraform, TOKEN '...', ORGANIZATION 'acme');
```

Schema `files` reads `terraform.tfstate` files and `terraform show -json` plans offline, with no credentials, for OpenTofu and Terraform alike. Schema `unified` holds runs in the shape shared by the Query.Farm orchestrator workers.

example_queries.description: Resource types in a state file
example_queries.sql: SELECT type, count(*) AS instances FROM terraform.files.read_state('sample:basic.tfstate') GROUP BY type ORDER BY type

example_queries.description: Instances that hold sensitive attributes
example_queries.sql: SELECT address, sensitive_attributes FROM terraform.files.read_state('/path/to/terraform.tfstate') WHERE len(sensitive_attributes) > 0 ORDER BY address

example_queries.description: Non-sensitive outputs
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, value FROM terraform.files.state_outputs('sample:basic.tfstate') WHERE NOT sensitive ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: What forces each replacement
example_queries.sql: SELECT address, action_reason, replace_paths FROM terraform.files.read_plan('sample:change.plan.json') WHERE action = 'replace' ORDER BY address

example_queries.description: Count planned actions
example_queries.sql: SELECT action, count(*) AS resources FROM terraform.files.read_plan('sample:change.plan.json') GROUP BY action ORDER BY action

example_queries.description: Outputs whose value is only known after apply
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, action FROM terraform.files.plan_outputs('sample:change.plan.json') WHERE unknown ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Outputs that change in the bundled plan
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, action, unknown FROM terraform.files.plan_outputs('sample:change.plan.json') WHERE action <> 'no-op' ORDER BY name;

example_queries.description: Which attribute forces each replacement
example_queries.sql: SELECT address, replace_paths[1] AS forced_by FROM terraform.files.read_plan('sample:change.plan.json') WHERE action = 'replace' ORDER BY address;

example_queries.description: Sensitive attributes are masked
example_queries.sql: SELECT address, attributes->>'result' AS result FROM terraform.files.read_state('sample:basic.tfstate') WHERE type = 'random_password';

example_queries.description: Outputs of the bundled state, sensitive ones masked
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, sensitive, value IS NULL AS masked FROM terraform.files.state_outputs('sample:basic.tfstate') ORDER BY name;

example_queries.description: Organizations and their default execution mode
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, default_execution_mode, cost_estimation_enabled FROM terraform.main.organizations ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Projects by workspace count
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, workspace_count FROM terraform.main.projects() ORDER BY workspace_count DESC

example_queries.description: Workspaces whose latest run errored
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, terraform_version, current_run_id FROM terraform.main.workspaces() WHERE current_run_status = 'errored' ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Resources under management per project
example_queries.sql: SELECT project_id, count(*) AS workspaces, sum(resource_count) AS resources FROM terraform.main.workspaces() GROUP BY project_id ORDER BY resources DESC

example_queries.description: Errored runs per workspace
example_queries.sql: SELECT workspace_name, count(*) AS errored_runs, max(created_at) AS latest FROM terraform.main.runs() WHERE status = 'errored' GROUP BY workspace_name ORDER BY errored_runs DESC

example_queries.description: Resources destroyed per workspace by applied runs
example_queries.sql: SELECT workspace_name, sum(resource_destructions) AS destroyed FROM terraform.main.runs() WHERE status = 'applied' GROUP BY workspace_name ORDER BY destroyed DESC

example_queries.description: Plans that would destroy resources
example_queries.sql: SELECT workspace_name, run_id, resource_destructions FROM terraform.main.plans() WHERE resource_destructions > 0 ORDER BY run_created_at DESC

example_queries.description: Failed applies
example_queries.sql: SELECT workspace_name, run_id, finished_at FROM terraform.main.applies() WHERE status = 'errored' ORDER BY run_created_at DESC

example_queries.description: Runs that raise monthly cost by more than $100
example_queries.sql: SELECT workspace_name, run_id, delta_monthly_cost FROM terraform.main.cost_estimates() WHERE delta_monthly_cost > 100 ORDER BY delta_monthly_cost DESC

example_queries.description: Hard-failed policies of a run
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, hard_failed, soft_failed FROM terraform.main.policy_checks('run-abc123') WHERE hard_failed > 0

example_queries.description: Blocking OPA evaluations of a run
example_queries.sql: SELECT stage, status, mandatory_failed FROM terraform.main.policy_evaluations('run-abc123') WHERE policy_kind = 'opa' AND mandatory_failed > 0

example_queries.description: State versions written outside of runs
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, serial, created_at FROM terraform.main.state_versions('prod-network') WHERE run_id IS NULL ORDER BY serial DESC

example_queries.description: Current outputs of a workspace
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, value FROM terraform.main.state_version_outputs(workspace_id := 'ws-abc123') WHERE NOT sensitive ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Resource types in a workspace
example_queries.sql: SELECT provider_type, count(*) AS n FROM terraform.main.workspace_resources('ws-abc123') GROUP BY provider_type ORDER BY n DESC

example_queries.description: Non-sensitive Terraform variables of a workspace
example_queries.sql: SELECT key, value FROM terraform.main.variables('ws-abc123') WHERE category = 'terraform' AND NOT sensitive ORDER BY key

example_queries.description: Global variable sets
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, var_count FROM terraform.main.variable_sets() WHERE global ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Environment variables a variable set injects
example_queries.sql: SELECT key, sensitive FROM terraform.main.varset_variables('varset-abc123') WHERE category = 'env' ORDER BY key

example_queries.description: Teams that can manage workspaces
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, users_count FROM terraform.main.teams() WHERE organization_access->>'manage-workspaces' = 'true' ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Teams with admin access to a workspace
example_queries.sql: SELECT a.team_id, t.name FROM terraform.main.team_access('ws-abc123') a JOIN terraform.main.teams() t ON t.id = a.team_id WHERE a.access = 'admin'

example_queries.description: Agent pools by size
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, agent_count FROM terraform.main.agent_pools() ORDER BY agent_count DESC

example_queries.description: Agents that are not idle or busy
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, status, last_ping_at FROM terraform.main.agents('apool-abc123') WHERE status NOT IN ('idle', 'busy') ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Modules with their number of versions
example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, name, provider, len(versions) AS version_count FROM terraform.main.registry_modules() ORDER BY version_count DESC

example_queries.description: Private providers
example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, name FROM terraform.main.registry_providers() WHERE registry_name = 'private' ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Drifted workspaces
example_queries.sql: SELECT workspace_name, created_at FROM terraform.main.assessments() WHERE drifted ORDER BY workspace_name

example_queries.description: Enabled destinations notified on drift
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, destination_type FROM terraform.main.notification_configurations('ws-abc123') WHERE enabled AND list_contains(triggers, 'assessment:drifted')

example_queries.description: Failed deployments per workspace
example_queries.sql: SELECT pipeline, count(*) AS failures FROM terraform.unified.runs WHERE status = 'failed' GROUP BY pipeline ORDER BY failures DESC

example_queries.description: Average plan and apply duration
example_queries.sql: SELECT task_name, avg(duration_seconds) AS avg_seconds FROM terraform.unified.task_runs WHERE status = 'success' GROUP BY task_name ORDER BY task_name

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Reads the JSON form of a saved plan (the output of `terraform show -json plan.bin` or `tofu show -json plan.bin`; path positional, or sample:change.plan.json): one row per resource instance with action (create, update, delete, replace, read, no-op), the raw actions list, action_reason, replace_paths (the attributes that force a replacement), changed_attributes (top-level attributes that change or become unknown), and before / after / after_unknown as JSON. One row per resource change of a `terraform show -json` plan: action, action reason, `replace_paths` (what forces a replacement), changed attributes and masked before/after values.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Reads a Terraform / OpenTofu state file (format version 4, written by Terraform 0.12+ and OpenTofu) from the worker's filesystem: one row per resource instance (address, type, name, count/for_each key, provider, attributes as JSON, dependencies, tainted flag). path is positional; sample:basic.tfstate is a bundled example. Every attribute the state lists in sensitive_attributes is replaced by "(sensitive value)" and its path is listed in the sensitive_attributes column. Extract attribute values with attributes->>'id'. No credentials needed. Outputs are in state_outputs(path).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## read_state(path)

One row per resource instance in a `terraform.tfstate` (v4) file: address, module, mode, type, name, index key, provider, attributes (JSON, sensitive values masked), dependencies, tainted and deposed flags.

`sample:basic.tfstate` is bundled for trying it out.

vgi.example_queries.description: Resource types in a state file
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT type, count(*) AS instances FROM terraform.files.read_state('sample:basic.tfstate') GROUP BY type ORDER BY type

vgi.example_queries.description: Instances that hold sensitive attributes
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT address, sensitive_attributes FROM terraform.files.read_state('/path/to/terraform.tfstate') WHERE len(sensitive_attributes) > 0 ORDER BY address

vgi.executable_examples.description: Count instances per resource type in the bundled state
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT type, count(*) AS instances FROM terraform.files.read_state('sample:basic.tfstate') GROUP BY type ORDER BY type

vgi.executable_examples.description: Sensitive attributes are masked
vgi.executable_examples.sql: SELECT address, attributes->>'result' AS result FROM terraform.files.read_state('sample:basic.tfstate') WHERE type = 'random_password'

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Schema main is the live HCP Terraform / Terraform Enterprise API v2, for questions about what infrastructure runs are doing: which runs errored or would destroy resources, what policy checks and cost estimates said, what a workspace's current state and outputs hold, who has access, and which workspaces have drifted. Auth: the terraform secret's TOKEN, optional HOSTNAME for Terraform Enterprise, and ORGANIZATION as the default organization. Objects follow the API hierarchy organization -> project -> workspace -> run -> plan / apply: organization-scoped functions accept organization := to override the secret's default, workspace-scoped ones take the workspace positionally (its ws-... id, or its name for state history), and run-scoped ones take a run id. Start from the workspace and run listings and join down by id. WHERE filters on run status, source, workspace and creation time, and on workspace project, name and current-run status, push down to the API; other predicates filter locally after paging. Read-only: only GET requests are sent, sensitive variable and output values are always NULL, and webhook URLs are reduced to their host.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

The HCP Terraform / Terraform Enterprise API v2, read with the `terraform` secret's token.

Objects follow the API hierarchy: organization, project, workspace, run, then the run's plan and apply. Functions below the organization take the parent's id as an argument.

WHERE filters on run status, source, workspace and creation time, and on workspace project, name and current-run status, are sent to the API. Sensitive variable and output values are never returned.

vgi.example_queries.description: Organizations and their default execution mode
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, default_execution_mode, cost_estimation_enabled FROM terraform.main.organizations ORDER BY name

vgi.example_queries.description: Projects by workspace count
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, workspace_count FROM terraform.main.projects() ORDER BY workspace_count DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Workspaces whose latest run errored
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, terraform_version, current_run_id FROM terraform.main.workspaces() WHERE current_run_status = 'errored' ORDER BY name

vgi.example_queries.description: Resources under management per project
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT project_id, count(*) AS workspaces, sum(resource_count) AS resources FROM terraform.main.workspaces() GROUP BY project_id ORDER BY resources DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Errored runs per workspace
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT workspace_name, count(*) AS errored_runs, max(created_at) AS latest FROM terraform.main.runs() WHERE status = 'errored' GROUP BY workspace_name ORDER BY errored_runs DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Resources destroyed per workspace by applied runs
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT workspace_name, sum(resource_destructions) AS destroyed FROM terraform.main.runs() WHERE status = 'applied' GROUP BY workspace_name ORDER BY destroyed DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Plans that would destroy resources
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT workspace_name, run_id, resource_destructions FROM terraform.main.plans() WHERE resource_destructions > 0 ORDER BY run_created_at DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Failed applies
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT workspace_name, run_id, finished_at FROM terraform.main.applies() WHERE status = 'errored' ORDER BY run_created_at DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Runs that raise monthly cost by more than $100
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT workspace_name, run_id, delta_monthly_cost FROM terraform.main.cost_estimates() WHERE delta_monthly_cost > 100 ORDER BY delta_monthly_cost DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Hard-failed policies of a run
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id, hard_failed, soft_failed FROM terraform.main.policy_checks('run-abc123') WHERE hard_failed > 0

vgi.example_queries.description: Blocking OPA evaluations of a run
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT stage, status, mandatory_failed FROM terraform.main.policy_evaluations('run-abc123') WHERE policy_kind = 'opa' AND mandatory_failed > 0

vgi.example_queries.description: State versions written outside of runs
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id, serial, created_at FROM terraform.main.state_versions('prod-network') WHERE run_id IS NULL ORDER BY serial DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Current outputs of a workspace
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, value FROM terraform.main.state_version_outputs(workspace_id := 'ws-abc123') WHERE NOT sensitive ORDER BY name

vgi.example_queries.description: Resource types in a workspace
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT provider_type, count(*) AS n FROM terraform.main.workspace_resources('ws-abc123') GROUP BY provider_type ORDER BY n DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Non-sensitive Terraform variables of a workspace
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT key, value FROM terraform.main.variables('ws-abc123') WHERE category = 'terraform' AND NOT sensitive ORDER BY key

vgi.example_queries.description: Global variable sets
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, var_count FROM terraform.main.variable_sets() WHERE global ORDER BY name

vgi.example_queries.description: Environment variables a variable set injects
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT key, sensitive FROM terraform.main.varset_variables('varset-abc123') WHERE category = 'env' ORDER BY key

vgi.example_queries.description: Teams that can manage workspaces
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, users_count FROM terraform.main.teams() WHERE organization_access->>'manage-workspaces' = 'true' ORDER BY name

vgi.example_queries.description: Teams with admin access to a workspace
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT a.team_id, t.name FROM terraform.main.team_access('ws-abc123') a JOIN terraform.main.teams() t ON t.id = a.team_id WHERE a.access = 'admin'

vgi.example_queries.description: Agent pools by size
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, agent_count FROM terraform.main.agent_pools() ORDER BY agent_count DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Agents that are not idle or busy
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, status, last_ping_at FROM terraform.main.agents('apool-abc123') WHERE status NOT IN ('idle', 'busy') ORDER BY name

vgi.example_queries.description: Modules with their number of versions
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, name, provider, len(versions) AS version_count FROM terraform.main.registry_modules() ORDER BY version_count DESC

vgi.example_queries.description: Private providers
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT namespace, name FROM terraform.main.registry_providers() WHERE registry_name = 'private' ORDER BY name

vgi.example_queries.description: Drifted workspaces
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT workspace_name, created_at FROM terraform.main.assessments() WHERE drifted ORDER BY workspace_name

vgi.example_queries.description: Enabled destinations notified on drift
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT name, destination_type FROM terraform.main.notification_configurations('ws-abc123') WHERE enabled AND list_contains(triggers, 'assessment:drifted')

functions.name: runs
functions.comment: Runs of a workspace or a whole organization, newest first, with plan add/change/destroy counts.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per run, newest first: of one workspace (workspace_id := 'ws-...') or of the whole organization (organization :=, default the secret's ORGANIZATION). Pushdown: status = / IN (...) becomes filter[status], source = becomes filter[source], workspace_name = / IN becomes filter[workspace_names] (organization listing), and created_at >= / > a timestamp stops paging once older runs are reached, so 'runs in the last 7 days' reads only those pages. The plan's resource_additions / resource_changes / resource_destructions / resource_imports come with the run. The API omits speculative plan-only runs from workspace listings. The run listing is rate-limited by HCP Terraform to 30 requests per minute; the worker retries 429 responses.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## runs(workspace_id := ..., organization := ...)

Runs, newest first, with status, source, trigger, destroy/plan-only flags, status timestamps and the plan's resource counts.

vgi.example_queries.description: Resources destroyed per workspace by applied runs

workers.title: Terrain analysis
workers.tagline: vgi-terrain — Query Farm VGI worker with executable SQL notebook examples
workers.subtitle: DEM visibility, viewsheds, slope and aspect from SQL.
workers.summary: Terrain analysis over projected digital elevation models: line-of-sight visibility between tower, building or other point pairs, accounting for earth curvature, plus per-cell elevation, slope and aspect. A synthetic ridge DEM and sample tower pairs are included.
workers.doc_md:
## GIS analysis

Evaluate terrain visibility between query-supplied tower/building pairs and inspect DEM elevation, slope and aspect. Distances and heights are metres. Input coordinates have an explicit CRS; DEMs must be projected in metres. Missing terrain yields unknown visibility. Synthetic sample assets ship in the wheel. The main schema exposes visibility, dem_cells and the ridge_tower_pairs sample table.

### SQL workflow

Pass query results to the main schema functions, retaining IDs for joins. Use bundled synthetic data to try the executable examples without network access. CRS, coverage, inference limits and resource bounds are explicit function parameters.

## Sources and references

- [Rasterio](https://rasterio.readthedocs.io/) on [GDAL](https://gdal.org/): reads and samples the DEM rasters.
- [OGC GeoTIFF](https://www.ogc.org/standards/geotiff/): the georeferenced raster format expected for DEM inputs such as the bundled `demo://ridge.tif`.
- [pyproj](https://pyproj4.github.io/pyproj/stable/) ([PROJ](https://proj.org/)): coordinate transforms from endpoint CRSs into the DEM's projected metre CRS.
workers.readme_sql:
SELECT split_part(v.pair_id, ':', 1) AS tower,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE v.visible) AS visible_cells,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT v.visible) AS blocked_cells
FROM terrain.main.visibility((
    SELECT t.pair_id || ':' || c.cell_id AS pair_id, t.source_x, t.source_y,
           c.x AS target_x, c.y AS target_y, t.source_height_m, 2.0 AS target_height_m
    FROM terrain.main.ridge_tower_pairs AS t
    CROSS JOIN terrain.main.dem_cells('demo://ridge.tif') AS c)) AS v
GROUP BY tower
ORDER BY tower;

example_queries.description: Inspect the two tower heights
example_queries.sql: SELECT pair_id, source_height_m FROM terrain.main.ridge_tower_pairs ORDER BY pair_id

example_queries.description: A tall tower clears the ridge; a low tower is blocked
example_queries.sql: SELECT pair_id, visible, status FROM terrain.main.visibility((SELECT * FROM terrain.main.ridge_tower_pairs)) ORDER BY pair_id

example_queries.description: Viewshed per tower: cross join each ridge_tower_pairs tower with every dem_cells cell centre, run visibility on the 242 sight lines, and count visible vs blocked cells (80 m tower 99/22, 2 m tower 55/66 of 121)
example_queries.sql: SELECT split_part(v.pair_id, ':', 1) AS tower, count(*) FILTER (WHERE v.visible) AS visible_cells, count(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT v.visible) AS blocked_cells FROM terrain.main.visibility((SELECT t.pair_id || ':' || c.cell_id AS pair_id, t.source_x, t.source_y, c.x AS target_x, c.y AS target_y, t.source_height_m, 2.0 AS target_height_m FROM terrain.main.ridge_tower_pairs AS t CROSS JOIN terrain.main.dem_cells('demo://ridge.tif') AS c)) AS v GROUP BY tower ORDER BY tower

example_queries.description: Locate what blocks each blocked pair: snap the visibility obstruction point to the nearest dem_cells cell centre (the 2 m tower's line passes 28 m under the 30 m ridge crest cell 60)
example_queries.sql: SELECT v.pair_id, round(v.min_clearance_m, 2) AS min_clearance_m, c.cell_id, c.x, c.y, c.elevation_m FROM terrain.main.visibility((SELECT * FROM terrain.main.ridge_tower_pairs)) AS v CROSS JOIN terrain.main.dem_cells('demo://ridge.tif') AS c WHERE v.status = 'blocked' QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY v.pair_id ORDER BY (c.x - v.obstruction_x) ^ 2 + (c.y - v.obstruction_y) ^ 2, c.cell_id) = 1 ORDER BY v.pair_id

example_queries.description: Tower height sweep: re-run the ridge_tower_pairs 'low' pair through visibility at heights 40-70 m in 5 m steps; heights up to 55 m are blocked by the ridge and 60 m is the first that clears it (+1.0 m)
example_queries.sql: WITH candidates AS (SELECT 'low@' || h.height_m AS pair_id, h.height_m, d.source_x, d.source_y, d.target_x, d.target_y, h.height_m::DOUBLE AS source_height_m, d.target_height_m FROM terrain.main.ridge_tower_pairs AS d CROSS JOIN range(40, 75, 5) AS h(height_m) WHERE d.pair_id = 'low') SELECT c.height_m, v.status, round(v.min_clearance_m, 2) AS min_clearance_m FROM terrain.main.visibility((SELECT * FROM candidates)) AS v JOIN candidates AS c USING (pair_id) ORDER BY c.height_m

example_queries.description: Count cells and find the ridge elevation
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*), max(elevation_m) FROM terrain.main.dem_cells('demo://ridge.tif')

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Terrain visibility

Evaluate terrain visibility between query-supplied tower/building pairs and inspect DEM elevation, slope and aspect. Distances and heights are metres. Input coordinates have an explicit CRS; DEMs must be projected in metres. Missing terrain yields unknown visibility. Synthetic sample assets ship in the wheel. The main schema exposes visibility, dem_cells and the ridge_tower_pairs sample table. Heights are above the DEM surface. This is sampled terrain visibility, not a radio propagation model. Nodata produces NULL visible; invalid inputs fail.

vgi.example_queries.description: A tall tower clears the ridge; a low tower is blocked
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT pair_id, visible, status FROM terrain.main.visibility((SELECT * FROM terrain.main.ridge_tower_pairs)) ORDER BY pair_id

vgi.example_queries.description: Viewshed per tower: cross join each ridge_tower_pairs tower with every dem_cells cell centre, run visibility on the 242 sight lines, and count visible vs blocked cells (80 m tower 99/22, 2 m tower 55/66 of 121)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT split_part(v.pair_id, ':', 1) AS tower, count(*) FILTER (WHERE v.visible) AS visible_cells, count(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT v.visible) AS blocked_cells FROM terrain.main.visibility((SELECT t.pair_id || ':' || c.cell_id AS pair_id, t.source_x, t.source_y, c.x AS target_x, c.y AS target_y, t.source_height_m, 2.0 AS target_height_m FROM terrain.main.ridge_tower_pairs AS t CROSS JOIN terrain.main.dem_cells('demo://ridge.tif') AS c)) AS v GROUP BY tower ORDER BY tower

vgi.example_queries.description: Locate what blocks each blocked pair: snap the visibility obstruction point to the nearest dem_cells cell centre (the 2 m tower's line passes 28 m under the 30 m ridge crest cell 60)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT v.pair_id, round(v.min_clearance_m, 2) AS min_clearance_m, c.cell_id, c.x, c.y, c.elevation_m FROM terrain.main.visibility((SELECT * FROM terrain.main.ridge_tower_pairs)) AS v CROSS JOIN terrain.main.dem_cells('demo://ridge.tif') AS c WHERE v.status = 'blocked' QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY v.pair_id ORDER BY (c.x - v.obstruction_x) ^ 2 + (c.y - v.obstruction_y) ^ 2, c.cell_id) = 1 ORDER BY v.pair_id

vgi.example_queries.description: Tower height sweep: re-run the ridge_tower_pairs 'low' pair through visibility at heights 40-70 m in 5 m steps; heights up to 55 m are blocked by the ridge and 60 m is the first that clears it (+1.0 m)
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH candidates AS (SELECT 'low@' || h.height_m AS pair_id, h.height_m, d.source_x, d.source_y, d.target_x, d.target_y, h.height_m::DOUBLE AS source_height_m, d.target_height_m FROM terrain.main.ridge_tower_pairs AS d CROSS JOIN range(40, 75, 5) AS h(height_m) WHERE d.pair_id = 'low') SELECT c.height_m, v.status, round(v.min_clearance_m, 2) AS min_clearance_m FROM terrain.main.visibility((SELECT * FROM candidates)) AS v JOIN candidates AS c USING (pair_id) ORDER BY c.height_m

workers.title: Threat Intelligence
workers.tagline: Enrich IPs/domains/hashes against reputation feeds for DuckDB (Go)
workers.subtitle: Classify IPs, domains, URLs, and file hashes offline, then enrich them against threat-intel reputation feeds.
workers.summary: Enrich cyber indicators against threat-intel reputation sources; classify offline
workers.doc_md:
# Threat Intelligence

**Enrich and classify cyber threat indicators — IPs, domains, URLs, and file hashes — against threat-intelligence reputation feeds directly in SQL.** This VGI worker turns DuckDB into a threat-hunting and indicator-of-compromise (IoC) triage engine: parse and type any indicator offline, screen out private/reserved IPs, then look up reputation verdicts (malicious flag, score, categories, source) from a pluggable feed — all without leaving your query.

It is built for SOC analysts, threat hunters, incident responders, and detection engineers who want to enrich and prioritize indicators in place rather than juggling separate enrichment scripts and spreadsheets. The worker is a **defensive** security tool intended for **authorized use only**, and it composes with sibling VGI workers such as `vgi-ioc`, `vgi-cve`, `vgi-yara`, and `vgi-sigma` to build a full SQL-native threat-intelligence stack.

Under the hood the worker is a standalone process that [DuckDB](https://duckdb.org) attaches over Apache Arrow via the [vgi-go SDK](https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-go). It deliberately hard-codes no single feed: it speaks a simple **normalized reputation JSON** over `GET {base_url}?indicator=<value>`, so you point it at any adapter that maps a provider's response into that shape. Popular feeds plug in behind this one interface, including [AlienVault OTX](https://otx.alienvault.com/api), [abuse.ch URLhaus](https://urlhaus-api.abuse.ch/), [abuse.ch ThreatFox](https://threatfox.abuse.ch/api/), and [VirusTotal](https://docs.virustotal.com/) — each with its own API key, rate limits, and terms of use.

## SQL functions

Two offline scalars triage indicators with **no network call**: `indicator_type` classifies a string as `ipv4`/`ipv6`/`domain`/`url`/`md5`/`sha1`/`sha256` (or NULL when unrecognized), and `is_private_ip` flags private/reserved IP addresses that should never be sent to an external feed. The `reputation` table function then enriches a single indicator against the configured source — selected with `base_url` plus optional `api_key` and `timeout_ms` — and returns at most one verdict row with the `malicious` flag, `score`, `categories`, `source`, and `last_seen`.

A typical workflow first triages a whole column of indicators with the two offline scalars — `indicator_type` to classify each observable and `is_private_ip` to screen out internal hosts — and then enriches only the survivors with `reputation('1.2.3.4')`. Private/reserved IPs and unknown indicators return zero rows with no error, so enrichment stays cheap and safe. See the [vgi-threatintel source repository](https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-threatintel) for adapter examples and the full normalized-feed contract.
workers.readme_sql:
INSTALL vgi FROM community; LOAD vgi;

ATTACH 'threatintel' AS threatintel (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'github-auto://Query-farm/vgi-threatintel@v0.4.1');

-- Offline indicator typing / triage (no network):
SELECT threatintel.indicator_type('1.2.3.4');        -- ipv4
SELECT threatintel.indicator_type('evil.example');   -- domain
SELECT threatintel.is_private_ip('10.0.0.1');        -- true  (skip the lookup)
SELECT threatintel.is_private_ip('8.8.8.8');         -- false

-- Triage a batch: type each indicator, describe the type, flag what needs a lookup:
WITH iocs(ioc) AS (VALUES ('185.220.101.1'), ('10.0.0.5'), ('malware-c2.example'), ('not-an-indicator!!'))
SELECT i.ioc, t.indicator_type, t.description,
       t.indicator_type IS NOT NULL AND NOT threatintel.is_private_ip(i.ioc) AS needs_lookup
FROM iocs AS i
LEFT JOIN threatintel.indicator_types AS t
  ON t.indicator_type = threatintel.indicator_type(i.ioc)
ORDER BY i.ioc;

-- Reputation lookup against a threat-intel source:
SELECT indicator, type, malicious, score, categories, source, last_seen
FROM threatintel.reputation('185.220.101.1');

example_queries.description: Classify an IPv4 address string into its indicator (IoC) type.
example_queries.sql: SELECT threatintel.main.indicator_type('8.8.8.8') AS kind

example_queries.description: Flag a private/reserved (RFC1918) IP that should never be sent to an external reputation feed.
example_queries.sql: SELECT threatintel.main.is_private_ip('10.0.0.5') AS is_private

example_queries.description: Enrich a single indicator against the configured reputation source, projecting the verdict fields.
example_queries.sql: SELECT indicator, malicious, score, categories FROM threatintel.main.reputation('1.2.3.4')

example_queries.description: Look up an indicator against an explicit reputation adapter with an API key, keeping only the malicious flag, score, and categories.
example_queries.sql: SELECT malicious, score, categories FROM threatintel.main.reputation('evil.example.com', base_url := 'https://my-reputation-adapter.internal/reputation', api_key := 'YOUR_KEY')

example_queries.description: Triage a mixed batch of indicators: classify each with indicator_type, attach the type's description from the indicator_types view, flag private IPs with is_private_ip, and mark which rows need a reputation lookup (4 of the 6 here: the private 10.0.0.5 and the unrecognized string do not).
example_queries.sql:
WITH iocs(ioc) AS (
  VALUES ('185.220.101.1'), ('10.0.0.5'), ('malware-c2.example'),
         ('https://good.example/login'), ('44d88612fea8a8f36de82e1278abb02f'), ('not-an-indicator!!')
), typed AS (
  SELECT ioc,
         threatintel.main.indicator_type(ioc) AS kind,
         threatintel.main.is_private_ip(ioc) AS is_private
  FROM iocs
)
SELECT typed.ioc, typed.kind, t.description, typed.is_private,
       typed.kind IS NOT NULL AND NOT typed.is_private AS needs_lookup
FROM typed
LEFT JOIN threatintel.main.indicator_types AS t ON t.indicator_type = typed.kind
ORDER BY needs_lookup DESC, typed.ioc

example_queries.description: Count a batch of indicators per IoC type, listing every type in the indicator_types view (types absent from the batch show 0; the unrecognized string matches no type and is not counted).
example_queries.sql:
WITH iocs(ioc) AS (
  VALUES ('185.220.101.1'), ('8.8.8.8'), ('10.0.0.5'), ('malware-c2.example'),
         ('44d88612fea8a8f36de82e1278abb02f'),
         ('e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855'), ('not-an-indicator!!')
)
SELECT t.indicator_type, count(i.ioc) AS n_indicators
FROM threatintel.main.indicator_types AS t
LEFT JOIN iocs AS i ON threatintel.main.indicator_type(i.ioc) = t.indicator_type
GROUP BY t.indicator_type
ORDER BY t.indicator_type

example_queries.description: Sanity-check a reputation adapter: compare the type the feed reports for a looked-up indicator with the offline indicator_type classification (types_agree is false when the adapter mislabels it). Requires a reachable base_url; returns no rows when the feed does not know the indicator.
example_queries.sql:
SELECT r.indicator, r.type AS feed_type,
       threatintel.main.indicator_type(r.indicator) AS offline_type,
       r.type = threatintel.main.indicator_type(r.indicator) AS types_agree
FROM threatintel.main.reputation('malware-c2.example',
       base_url := 'https://my-reputation-adapter.internal/reputation') AS r
ORDER BY r.indicator

example_queries.description: Classify a 64-hex-character file hash as sha256.
example_queries.sql: SELECT threatintel.main.indicator_type('e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855') AS kind;

example_queries.sql: SELECT threatintel.main.is_private_ip('8.8.8.8') AS private;

example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS n FROM threatintel.main.reputation('10.0.0.5');

Using the worker's indicator_types reference view, how many distinct indicator (IoC) types does this worker recognize?

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## `threatintel.main`

The single schema of the **threatintel** worker. It groups two complementary capability families for working with cyber indicators (IoCs) directly in SQL:

- **Offline triage** — pure, deterministic scalars that run with no network access: classify an indicator string into its type and screen out private/reserved IP addresses that should never be sent to an external feed.
- **Reputation enrichment** — a table function that looks up a single indicator against a normalized threat-intel reputation source and returns a verdict row (malicious flag, score, categories, source, last_seen).

The usual pattern is to triage a whole column of indicators with the offline scalars first, then enrich only the survivors so lookups stay cheap and safe.

vgi.example_queries.description: Classify an IPv4 address string into its indicator (IoC) type.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT threatintel.main.indicator_type('8.8.8.8') AS kind

vgi.example_queries.description: Flag a private/reserved (RFC1918) IP that should never be sent to an external reputation feed.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT threatintel.main.is_private_ip('10.0.0.5') AS is_private

vgi.example_queries.description: Enrich a single indicator against the configured reputation source, projecting the verdict fields.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT indicator, malicious, score, categories FROM threatintel.main.reputation('1.2.3.4')

vgi.example_queries.description: Look up an indicator against an explicit reputation adapter with an API key, keeping only the malicious flag, score, and categories.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT malicious, score, categories FROM threatintel.main.reputation('evil.example.com', base_url := 'https://my-reputation-adapter.internal/reputation', api_key := 'YOUR_KEY')

vgi.example_queries.description: Triage a mixed batch of indicators: classify each with indicator_type, attach the type's description from the indicator_types view, flag private IPs with is_private_ip, and mark which rows need a reputation lookup (4 of the 6 here: the private 10.0.0.5 and the unrecognized string do not).
vgi.example_queries.sql:
WITH iocs(ioc) AS (
  VALUES ('185.220.101.1'), ('10.0.0.5'), ('malware-c2.example'),
         ('https://good.example/login'), ('44d88612fea8a8f36de82e1278abb02f'), ('not-an-indicator!!')
), typed AS (
  SELECT ioc,
         threatintel.main.indicator_type(ioc) AS kind,
         threatintel.main.is_private_ip(ioc) AS is_private
  FROM iocs
)
SELECT typed.ioc, typed.kind, t.description, typed.is_private,
       typed.kind IS NOT NULL AND NOT typed.is_private AS needs_lookup
FROM typed
LEFT JOIN threatintel.main.indicator_types AS t ON t.indicator_type = typed.kind
ORDER BY needs_lookup DESC, typed.ioc

vgi.example_queries.description: Count a batch of indicators per IoC type, listing every type in the indicator_types view (types absent from the batch show 0; the unrecognized string matches no type and is not counted).
vgi.example_queries.sql:
WITH iocs(ioc) AS (
  VALUES ('185.220.101.1'), ('8.8.8.8'), ('10.0.0.5'), ('malware-c2.example'),
         ('44d88612fea8a8f36de82e1278abb02f'),
         ('e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855'), ('not-an-indicator!!')
)
SELECT t.indicator_type, count(i.ioc) AS n_indicators
FROM threatintel.main.indicator_types AS t
LEFT JOIN iocs AS i ON threatintel.main.indicator_type(i.ioc) = t.indicator_type
GROUP BY t.indicator_type
ORDER BY t.indicator_type

vgi.example_queries.description: Sanity-check a reputation adapter: compare the type the feed reports for a looked-up indicator with the offline indicator_type classification (types_agree is false when the adapter mislabels it). Requires a reachable base_url; returns no rows when the feed does not know the indicator.
vgi.example_queries.sql:
SELECT r.indicator, r.type AS feed_type,
       threatintel.main.indicator_type(r.indicator) AS offline_type,
       r.type = threatintel.main.indicator_type(r.indicator) AS types_agree
FROM threatintel.main.reputation('malware-c2.example',
       base_url := 'https://my-reputation-adapter.internal/reputation') AS r
ORDER BY r.indicator

workers.tagline: NOAA tides, water levels and tidal currents as VGI SQL functions
workers.subtitle: NOAA CO-OPS tide and current stations, predictions and observations for marine analysis.
workers.summary: NOAA CO-OPS tide and current stations, tide predictions, observed water levels, and predicted and observed tidal currents as SQL tables, with heights in metres on a chosen datum and speeds in m/s. No API key needed.
workers.doc_md:
# NOAA Tides

NOAA CO-OPS tide and current stations, predictions and observations in SQL. Table functions return typed Arrow columns with UTC timestamps, source URLs and retrieval times. No API key is needed. Missing measurements become NULL; invalid arguments and unexpected upstream responses fail explicitly. Data is retrieved when a query executes. Use SQL to filter, aggregate and join stations to measurements. Water levels are metres relative to the returned datum, default MLLW. Current velocities are converted from cm/s to m/s. Time-series dates are inclusive UTC days, at most 366 days; requests are automatically chunked. Tide predictions are astronomical and current slack is a separate product.

## Data access

Use the main schema to discover stations and retrieve observations. Each response preserves its source URL and UTC retrieval time. Missing sensor values remain NULL.

## Sources and references

- [NOAA Tides & Currents (CO-OPS)](https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/): the upstream station network, predictions and observations.
- [CO-OPS Data Retrieval API](https://api.tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/api/prod/): the data getter used for predictions, water levels and currents.
- [CO-OPS Metadata API](https://api.tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/mdapi/prod/): the station directory used by stations().
- [Tidal datums](https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum_options.html): what MLLW, MSL, NAVD88 and the other datum choices mean.

example_queries.description: Find tide prediction stations in New York
example_queries.sql: SELECT station_id, name, latitude, longitude FROM tides.main.stations() WHERE state = 'NY' ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Inspect tide predictions in UTC
example_queries.sql: SELECT time, height_m FROM tides.main.tide_predictions('8518750', '2026-01-01', '2026-01-02') ORDER BY time

example_queries.description: Compare each predicted high tide at The Battery on 1–3 January 2026 with the highest observed water level within an hour of it; surge_m is observed peak minus predicted height
example_queries.sql: SELECT p.time AS predicted_high, p.height_m AS predicted_m, max(o.height_m) AS observed_peak_m, round(max(o.height_m) - p.height_m, 3) AS surge_m FROM tides.main.tide_predictions('8518750', '2026-01-01', '2026-01-03') AS p JOIN tides.main.water_levels('8518750', '2026-01-01', '2026-01-03') AS o ON o.time BETWEEN p.time - INTERVAL 1 HOUR AND p.time + INTERVAL 1 HOUR WHERE p.event_type = 'H' GROUP BY p.time, p.height_m ORDER BY p.time

example_queries.description: Inspect observed water levels in UTC
example_queries.sql: SELECT time, height_m FROM tides.main.water_levels('8518750', '2026-01-01', '2026-01-02') ORDER BY time

example_queries.description: Daily range of the storm-surge residual (observed minus predicted water level, metres) at The Battery for 1–7 January 2026, joining six-minute observations to six-minute tide predictions on time; days follow the session time zone (set UTC)
example_queries.sql: SELECT CAST(o.time AS DATE) AS obs_day, round(max(o.height_m - p.height_m), 3) AS max_residual_m, round(min(o.height_m - p.height_m), 3) AS min_residual_m, count(o.height_m) AS samples FROM tides.main.water_levels('8518750', '2026-01-01', '2026-01-07') AS o JOIN tides.main.tide_predictions('8518750', '2026-01-01', '2026-01-07', step := '6') AS p USING (time) GROUP BY obs_day ORDER BY obs_day

example_queries.description: Inspect tidal current predictions in UTC
example_queries.sql: SELECT time, velocity_major_mps FROM tides.main.current_predictions('ACT0956', '2026-01-01', '2026-01-02') ORDER BY time

example_queries.description: Check each predicted slack, maximum flood and maximum ebb at the Chesapeake Bay entrance (cb0102, bin 4) on 1 January 2026 against the mean observed speed within 15 minutes of the event
example_queries.sql: SELECT p.time, p.event_type, round(abs(p.velocity_major_mps), 2) AS predicted_speed_mps, round(avg(o.speed_mps), 2) AS observed_speed_mps, count(o.speed_mps) AS observations FROM tides.main.current_predictions('cb0102', '2026-01-01', '2026-01-01', bin := 4) AS p JOIN tides.main.currents('cb0102', '2026-01-01', '2026-01-01', bin := 4) AS o ON o.time BETWEEN p.time - INTERVAL 15 MINUTE AND p.time + INTERVAL 15 MINUTE GROUP BY p.time, p.event_type, p.velocity_major_mps ORDER BY p.time

example_queries.description: Inspect observed currents in UTC
example_queries.sql: SELECT time, speed_mps FROM tides.main.currents('cb0102', '2026-01-01', '2026-01-02') ORDER BY time

example_queries.description: Mean and peak observed current speed by sensor depth at Cape Henry (cb0102) on 1 January 2026, joining all-bin observations to the current-meter bin depths
example_queries.sql: SELECT b.bin, b.depth_m, round(avg(c.speed_mps), 3) AS mean_speed_mps, round(max(c.speed_mps), 3) AS max_speed_mps FROM tides.main.currents('cb0102', '2026-01-01', '2026-01-01') AS c JOIN tides.main.current_bins('cb0102') AS b USING (bin) GROUP BY b.bin, b.depth_m ORDER BY b.bin

example_queries.description: Inspect the observation depths at Cape Henry
example_queries.sql: SELECT bin, depth_m FROM tides.main.current_bins('cb0102') ORDER BY bin

example_queries.description: Supported CO-OPS products and the units returned by this worker
example_queries.sql: SELECT sql_function, output_units FROM tides.main.products WHERE output_units = 'm/s' ORDER BY sql_function

Time-series dates are inclusive UTC days, at most 366 days; requests are automatically chunked. Tide predictions are astronomical and current slack is a separate product.

### Query patterns

Discover station IDs first, retrieve measurements, then join or aggregate the resulting rows. Use the reference table for measurement units and supported products.

vgi.example_queries.description: Find tide prediction stations in New York
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT station_id, name, latitude, longitude FROM tides.main.stations() WHERE state = 'NY' ORDER BY name

vgi.example_queries.description: Inspect tide predictions in UTC
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT time, height_m FROM tides.main.tide_predictions('8518750', '2026-01-01', '2026-01-02') ORDER BY time

vgi.example_queries.description: Compare each predicted high tide at The Battery on 1–3 January 2026 with the highest observed water level within an hour of it; surge_m is observed peak minus predicted height
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT p.time AS predicted_high, p.height_m AS predicted_m, max(o.height_m) AS observed_peak_m, round(max(o.height_m) - p.height_m, 3) AS surge_m FROM tides.main.tide_predictions('8518750', '2026-01-01', '2026-01-03') AS p JOIN tides.main.water_levels('8518750', '2026-01-01', '2026-01-03') AS o ON o.time BETWEEN p.time - INTERVAL 1 HOUR AND p.time + INTERVAL 1 HOUR WHERE p.event_type = 'H' GROUP BY p.time, p.height_m ORDER BY p.time

vgi.example_queries.description: Inspect observed water levels in UTC
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT time, height_m FROM tides.main.water_levels('8518750', '2026-01-01', '2026-01-02') ORDER BY time

vgi.example_queries.description: Daily range of the storm-surge residual (observed minus predicted water level, metres) at The Battery for 1–7 January 2026, joining six-minute observations to six-minute tide predictions on time; days follow the session time zone (set UTC)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT CAST(o.time AS DATE) AS obs_day, round(max(o.height_m - p.height_m), 3) AS max_residual_m, round(min(o.height_m - p.height_m), 3) AS min_residual_m, count(o.height_m) AS samples FROM tides.main.water_levels('8518750', '2026-01-01', '2026-01-07') AS o JOIN tides.main.tide_predictions('8518750', '2026-01-01', '2026-01-07', step := '6') AS p USING (time) GROUP BY obs_day ORDER BY obs_day

vgi.example_queries.description: Inspect tidal current predictions in UTC
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT time, velocity_major_mps FROM tides.main.current_predictions('ACT0956', '2026-01-01', '2026-01-02') ORDER BY time

vgi.example_queries.description: Check each predicted slack, maximum flood and maximum ebb at the Chesapeake Bay entrance (cb0102, bin 4) on 1 January 2026 against the mean observed speed within 15 minutes of the event
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT p.time, p.event_type, round(abs(p.velocity_major_mps), 2) AS predicted_speed_mps, round(avg(o.speed_mps), 2) AS observed_speed_mps, count(o.speed_mps) AS observations FROM tides.main.current_predictions('cb0102', '2026-01-01', '2026-01-01', bin := 4) AS p JOIN tides.main.currents('cb0102', '2026-01-01', '2026-01-01', bin := 4) AS o ON o.time BETWEEN p.time - INTERVAL 15 MINUTE AND p.time + INTERVAL 15 MINUTE GROUP BY p.time, p.event_type, p.velocity_major_mps ORDER BY p.time

vgi.example_queries.description: Inspect observed currents in UTC
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT time, speed_mps FROM tides.main.currents('cb0102', '2026-01-01', '2026-01-02') ORDER BY time

vgi.example_queries.description: Mean and peak observed current speed by sensor depth at Cape Henry (cb0102) on 1 January 2026, joining all-bin observations to the current-meter bin depths
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT b.bin, b.depth_m, round(avg(c.speed_mps), 3) AS mean_speed_mps, round(max(c.speed_mps), 3) AS max_speed_mps FROM tides.main.currents('cb0102', '2026-01-01', '2026-01-01') AS c JOIN tides.main.current_bins('cb0102') AS b USING (bin) GROUP BY b.bin, b.depth_m ORDER BY b.bin

vgi.example_queries.description: Inspect the observation depths at Cape Henry
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT bin, depth_m FROM tides.main.current_bins('cb0102') ORDER BY bin

## Observed Currents

Read current speed and direction from NOAA current-meter stations. Requires station_id, start_date and end_date (inclusive UTC dates, YYYY-MM-DD). Returns speed_mps with typed UTC timestamps, station_id, source_url and fetched_at. Speeds are m/s converted from NOAA cm/s. Current predictions describe flow, and slack must not be inferred from high or low tide.  Requests are split into non-overlapping chunks of at most seven days; all-bin observations use one-day chunks. Missing measurements become NULL and observation flags remain unmodified. Explicit NOAA no-data responses produce no rows; other API errors fail. NULL arguments are rejected. No API key required.

### Result columns

| Column | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| station_id | NOAA station identifier; retain as text, including leading zeroes. |
| time | UTC timestamp of the current observation. |
| speed_mps | Observed current speed in m/s, converted from NOAA cm/s. |
| direction_deg | Direction toward which the current flows, degrees from true north. |
| bin | Observed depth-bin identifier; use current_bins for deployed sensor depths. |
| flags | Unmodified NOAA quality flags, when available. |
| source_url | Exact NOAA request URL; identifies the data product and request parameters. |
| fetched_at | UTC time the NOAA response was retrieved; not the observation time. |

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Read predicted slack, flood and ebb events or interval major-axis currents. Requires station_id, start_date and end_date (inclusive UTC dates, YYYY-MM-DD). Returns velocity_major_mps with typed UTC timestamps, station_id, source_url and fetched_at. Speeds are m/s converted from NOAA cm/s. Current predictions describe flow, and slack must not be inferred from high or low tide. velocity_major_mps is signed along the major axis; mean flood/ebb directions are not instantaneous bearings. Default step=max_slack; bin=1.  Requests are split into non-overlapping chunks of at most seven days; all-bin observations use one-day chunks. Missing measurements become NULL and observation flags remain unmodified. Explicit NOAA no-data responses produce no rows; other API errors fail. NULL arguments are rejected. No API key required.

## Tidal Current Predictions

Read predicted slack, flood and ebb events or interval major-axis currents. Requires station_id, start_date and end_date (inclusive UTC dates, YYYY-MM-DD). Returns velocity_major_mps with typed UTC timestamps, station_id, source_url and fetched_at. Speeds are m/s converted from NOAA cm/s. Current predictions describe flow, and slack must not be inferred from high or low tide. velocity_major_mps is signed along the major axis; mean flood/ebb directions are not instantaneous bearings. Default step=max_slack; bin=1.  Requests are split into non-overlapping chunks of at most seven days; all-bin observations use one-day chunks. Missing measurements become NULL and observation flags remain unmodified. Explicit NOAA no-data responses produce no rows; other API errors fail. NULL arguments are rejected. No API key required.

| Column | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| station_id | NOAA station identifier; retain as text, including leading zeroes. |
| time | UTC timestamp of the current prediction. |
| velocity_major_mps | Signed velocity along the major axis in m/s: positive flood, negative ebb; NOAA cm/s divided by 100. |

| depth_m | NOAA prediction-bin depth in metres. |
| source_url | Exact NOAA request URL; identifies the data product and request parameters. |
| fetched_at | UTC time the NOAA response was retrieved; not the observation time. |

## Tide Predictions

Read predicted high/low tides or interval water levels from NOAA. Requires station_id, start_date and end_date (inclusive UTC dates, YYYY-MM-DD). | Column | Meaning |

| station_id | NOAA station identifier; retain as text, including leading zeroes. |
| time | UTC timestamp of the predicted tide or observed water level. |

| datum | Requested vertical reference, such as MLLW; compare heights only on compatible datums. |

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Read preliminary or verified six-minute water levels with NOAA quality flags. Requires station_id, start_date and end_date (inclusive UTC dates, YYYY-MM-DD). Returns height_m with typed UTC timestamps, station_id, source_url and fetched_at. Heights are metres relative to the named datum (default MLLW). Predictions are astronomical, not weather-adjusted water levels.  Requests are split into non-overlapping chunks of at most seven days; all-bin observations use one-day chunks. Missing measurements become NULL and observation flags remain unmodified. Explicit NOAA no-data responses produce no rows; other API errors fail. NULL arguments are rejected. No API key required.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Observed Water Levels

Read preliminary or verified six-minute water levels with NOAA quality flags. Requires station_id, start_date and end_date (inclusive UTC dates, YYYY-MM-DD). Returns height_m with typed UTC timestamps, station_id, source_url and fetched_at. Heights are metres relative to the named datum (default MLLW). Predictions are astronomical, not weather-adjusted water levels.  Requests are split into non-overlapping chunks of at most seven days; all-bin observations use one-day chunks. Missing measurements become NULL and observation flags remain unmodified. Explicit NOAA no-data responses produce no rows; other API errors fail. NULL arguments are rejected. No API key required.

### Result columns

| Column | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| station_id | NOAA station identifier; retain as text, including leading zeroes. |
| time | UTC timestamp of the predicted tide or observed water level. |
| height_m | Water level in metres relative to the datum column; NULL for a missing value. |
| datum | Requested vertical reference, such as MLLW; compare heights only on compatible datums. |
| event_type | H for high tide, L for low tide; NULL for interval samples or observations. |
| sigma_m | Standard deviation in metres for observed water levels; NULL for predictions. |
| quality | NOAA observation quality code: p preliminary or v verified; NULL for predictions. |
| flags | Unmodified NOAA comma-separated observation quality flags; NULL when absent. |
| source_url | Exact NOAA request URL; identifies the data product and request parameters. |
| fetched_at | UTC time the NOAA response was retrieved; not the observation time. |

workers.title: Apache Tika Document Extraction
workers.tagline: Document & OCR text/metadata extraction for DuckDB (Java, Apache Tika)
workers.subtitle: Pull text and metadata out of PDFs, Office files and other documents, detect their type and language, and OCR scanned images.
workers.summary: Document text, metadata, and OCR extraction (Apache Tika)
workers.doc_md:
# Apache Tika Document & OCR Text Extraction in SQL

![Apache Tika logo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/74/Apache_Tika_Logo.svg)

Extract plain text, document metadata, language, page counts, and OCR directly in DuckDB SQL from PDF, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, HTML, email, and image files — powered by [Apache Tika](https://tika.apache.org/) ([source](https://github.com/apache/tika)).

## What it does

The **tika** extension turns DuckDB into a document-parsing engine: point it at a file path or a `BLOB` of document bytes and get back searchable plain text plus a rich metadata map, all without leaving SQL. It is built for data engineers, analysts, and AI/RAG pipelines that need to mine unstructured documents — contracts, invoices, reports, slide decks, spreadsheets, web pages, and scanned images — and join the extracted content against the rest of their warehouse. Because it runs as a VGI worker over Apache Arrow, extraction happens close to your data with no external service calls and no manual file shuffling.

## How it works

Every function is backed by [Apache Tika](https://tika.apache.org/), the battle-tested Apache content-detection and analysis toolkit that ships more than a thousand parsers (PDFBox for PDF, Apache POI for Microsoft Office, and many more). Tika auto-detects each document's media type and dispatches it to the right parser, so a single call handles dozens of formats. Scanned PDFs and images are run through [Tesseract OCR](https://github.com/tesseract-ocr/tesseract) when the Tesseract binary is available; when it is not, OCR results return `NULL` rather than failing the query. See the official [Apache Tika documentation](https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/TIKA) for the full parser and metadata catalog.

## When to use it

Reach for this worker whenever unstructured documents need to become queryable rows: building a full-text or vector index over a document store, routing or filtering files by their true media type, detecting the language of a body of text, or pulling structured metadata (author, title, creation date, page count) out of office and PDF files. Inputs are always either a `VARCHAR` filesystem path the worker opens or a `BLOB` of the raw document bytes, so documents already living in a table column can be processed in place without shuffling files around.

## Navigating the functions

The worker's functions are organized into navigable categories — text and metadata extraction (single-document and whole-column batch), content detection (media type and language), and optical character recognition — each carrying its own runnable examples and documented return columns.

example_queries.description: Extract the plain-text body and detected media type from a single document.
example_queries.sql: SELECT content, mime FROM tika.main.extract_text('A plain-text body.'::BLOB)

example_queries.description: Read a document's media type and page count without extracting its body text.
example_queries.sql: SELECT mime, n_pages FROM tika.main.metadata('Some document bytes.'::BLOB)

example_queries.description: Detect the media (MIME) type of a document from its raw bytes.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tika.main.detect_mime('Plain text.'::BLOB)

example_queries.description: Detect the natural-language code of a body of text.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tika.main.detect_lang('The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.')

example_queries.description: Batch-extract a whole column of documents, passing an id column through onto every output row.
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, content FROM tika.main.extract_all((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1, 'Body bytes.'::BLOB)) AS t(id, body)), id := 'id', doc_column := 'body')

example_queries.description: Language breakdown of a document corpus: extract every body with extract_all, tag it with detect_lang, and send bodies whose detect_lang_conf is below 0.5 (or undetectable) to 'und'. Returns en [1, 4] and und [5, 6] (2 docs each), then de [3] and fr [2].
example_queries.sql: SELECT CASE WHEN tika.main.detect_lang_conf(content) >= 0.5 THEN tika.main.detect_lang(content) ELSE 'und' END AS language, count(*) AS docs, list(id ORDER BY id) AS ids FROM tika.main.extract_all((SELECT id, body FROM (VALUES (1, 'The quarterly report shows strong growth across every region this year.'::BLOB), (2, 'Le rapport trimestriel montre une forte croissance dans toutes les regions.'::BLOB), (3, 'Der Quartalsbericht zeigt ein starkes Wachstum in allen Regionen.'::BLOB), (4, 'Our customers renewed their contracts early and expanded their usage.'::BLOB), (5, 'OK'::BLOB), (6, 'PO-88213'::BLOB)) AS t(id, body)), id := 'id', doc_column := 'body') GROUP BY language ORDER BY docs DESC, language

example_queries.description: Triage a mixed inbox of raw bytes: detect_mime sniffs each blob so only the HTML pages go through extract_all (the PNG, id 2, is skipped), then each page's <title> is read from the metadata map and its body language tagged with detect_lang (1 'Q3 Update' en, 3 'Point trimestriel' fr).
example_queries.sql:
WITH inbox(id, body) AS (VALUES (1, 'Q3 Update

Revenue grew in every region this quarter and margins improved.

'::BLOB), (2, '\x89PNG\x0D\x0A\x1A\x0A\x00\x00\x00\x0DIHDR'::BLOB), (3, 'Point trimestriel

Le chiffre d''affaires a progresse dans toutes les regions ce trimestre.

'::BLOB)) SELECT x.id, x.meta['dc:title'] AS title, tika.main.detect_lang(x.content) AS language FROM tika.main.extract_all((SELECT id, body FROM inbox WHERE tika.main.detect_mime(body) = 'text/html'), id := 'id', doc_column := 'body') AS x ORDER BY x.id

example_queries.description: Extract the body text, MIME type, and page count of a single document.
example_queries.sql: SELECT content, mime, n_pages FROM tika.main.extract_text('A short plain-text body.'::BLOB);

example_queries.description: Split a document into one row per page (leading `page` column).
example_queries.sql: SELECT page, content FROM tika.main.extract_text('Single page body.'::BLOB, by_page := true);

example_queries.description: Extract from document bytes (a BLOB) and read a metadata key from the `meta` MAP.
example_queries.sql: SELECT meta['Content-Type'] AS ct FROM tika.main.extract_text('Some bytes.'::BLOB);

example_queries.description: Extract the body text and MIME type of inline document bytes.
example_queries.sql: SELECT content, mime FROM tika.main.extract_text('Hello from a plain-text document body.'::BLOB);

example_queries.description: Read a single key from the Tika metadata MAP of a document.
example_queries.sql: SELECT meta['Content-Type'] AS content_type FROM tika.main.extract_text('Some document bytes.'::BLOB);

example_queries.description: Read a document's MIME type, page count, and language without extracting the body text.
example_queries.sql: SELECT mime, n_pages, lang FROM tika.main.metadata('A short document body.'::BLOB);

example_queries.description: Read a single metadata field from the `meta` MAP.
example_queries.sql: SELECT meta['Content-Type'] AS ct FROM tika.main.metadata('Some bytes.'::BLOB);

example_queries.description: Extract every document in an inline column of bytes, keeping the source `id` on each output row to join results back.
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, content, mime FROM tika.main.extract_all((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1, 'First body.'::BLOB), (2, 'Second body.'::BLOB)) AS t(id, body)), id := 'id', doc_column := 'body');

example_queries.description: Extract from a BLOB column (`body`) of inline document bytes, with the `id` column passed through.
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, content FROM tika.main.extract_all((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1, 'Inline document bytes.'::BLOB)) AS t(id, body)), id := 'id', doc_column := 'body');

example_queries.description: Detect the language of an extracted document's body text.
example_queries.sql: SELECT content, tika.main.detect_lang(content) AS lang FROM tika.main.extract_text('Bonjour le monde, ceci est un texte en francais.'::BLOB);

example_queries.description: Detect the MIME type of inline document bytes (returns 'text/plain').
example_queries.sql: SELECT tika.main.detect_mime('Hello, plain text body.'::BLOB);

example_queries.description: Detect the MIME type of a PDF read as bytes with read_blob() (returns 'application/pdf'); a local file path works the same.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tika.main.detect_mime(content) FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-tika/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/hello.pdf');

example_queries.description: OCR a scanned image read as bytes with read_blob(), using the default English model; returns the card's text starting 'LIBRARY RETURN CHECKLIST' (NULL if Tesseract is not installed).
example_queries.sql: SELECT tika.main.ocr(content) FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-tika/fbe9bce2524010aa5b0ec8f4456c05f4082fa1b5/notebooks/assets/scan-card.png');

example_queries.description: Split the OCR'd text of a scanned card into its non-blank lines, one row per line (4 rows; no rows if Tesseract is not installed).
example_queries.sql: SELECT line FROM (SELECT unnest(string_split(tika.main.ocr(content), chr(10))) AS line FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-tika/fbe9bce2524010aa5b0ec8f4456c05f4082fa1b5/notebooks/assets/scan-card.png')) WHERE trim(line) <> '';

example_queries.description: Confidence (0.0-1.0) of the top detected language for a piece of text.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tika.main.detect_lang_conf('The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.');

example_queries.description: Report the detected language and its confidence for an extracted document body.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tika.main.detect_lang(content) AS lang, tika.main.detect_lang_conf(content) AS conf FROM tika.main.extract_text('The annual report covers quarterly results.'::BLOB);

I have three documents as raw bytes: id 1 is 'The quarterly report shows strong growth across every region this year.', id 2 is 'Invoice 4471-B', and id 3 is 'Le rapport trimestriel montre une forte croissance dans toutes les regions.'. Extract the body text of each document and find the one whose language detection is least confident. Return a single row with one INTEGER column named id.

I have three HTML pages as raw bytes: id 1 is 'Pricing

Our plans are billed monthly and you can cancel at any time.

', id 2 is 'Preise

Unsere Tarife werden monatlich abgerechnet und sind jederzeit kuendbar.

', and id 3 is 'About us

We are a small team building tools for analysts around the world.

'. Return the HTML title, as reported in the extracted document metadata, of every page whose extracted body text is in English. Return one VARCHAR column named title, ordered by title ascending.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
# tika.main

Apache Tika document text, metadata, language, and OCR extraction, exposed as DuckDB SQL functions over Apache Arrow.

## Concepts

Each function takes a document as either a `VARCHAR` filesystem path (the worker opens it) or a `BLOB` of the raw bytes, and Tika auto-detects the media type before dispatching to the right parser. Text extraction returns the plain-text body alongside a `MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)` of Tika's full metadata bag; per-row error capture keeps a single corrupt document from failing an entire query.

## Categories

The functions are organized into navigable categories — text and metadata extraction (single-document and batch), content detection (media type and language), and optical character recognition — so agents and users can discover the right tool for a task. See each function's own documentation and examples for exact inputs, options, and returned columns.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT content, mime FROM tika.main.extract_text('A plain-text body.'::BLOB)
vgi.example_queries.description: Extract the plain-text body and detected media type from a single document.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT mime, n_pages FROM tika.main.metadata('Some document bytes.'::BLOB)
vgi.example_queries.description: Read a document's media type and page count without extracting its body text.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT tika.main.detect_mime('Plain text.'::BLOB)
vgi.example_queries.description: Detect the media (MIME) type of a document from its raw bytes.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT tika.main.detect_lang('The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.')
vgi.example_queries.description: Detect the natural-language code of a body of text.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id, content FROM tika.main.extract_all((SELECT * FROM (VALUES (1, 'Body bytes.'::BLOB)) AS t(id, body)), id := 'id', doc_column := 'body')
vgi.example_queries.description: Batch-extract a whole column of documents, passing an id column through onto every output row.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT CASE WHEN tika.main.detect_lang_conf(content) >= 0.5 THEN tika.main.detect_lang(content) ELSE 'und' END AS language, count(*) AS docs, list(id ORDER BY id) AS ids FROM tika.main.extract_all((SELECT id, body FROM (VALUES (1, 'The quarterly report shows strong growth across every region this year.'::BLOB), (2, 'Le rapport trimestriel montre une forte croissance dans toutes les regions.'::BLOB), (3, 'Der Quartalsbericht zeigt ein starkes Wachstum in allen Regionen.'::BLOB), (4, 'Our customers renewed their contracts early and expanded their usage.'::BLOB), (5, 'OK'::BLOB), (6, 'PO-88213'::BLOB)) AS t(id, body)), id := 'id', doc_column := 'body') GROUP BY language ORDER BY docs DESC, language
vgi.example_queries.description: Language breakdown of a document corpus: extract every body with extract_all, tag it with detect_lang, and send bodies whose detect_lang_conf is below 0.5 (or undetectable) to 'und'. Returns en [1, 4] and und [5, 6] (2 docs each), then de [3] and fr [2].

vgi.example_queries.sql:
WITH inbox(id, body) AS (VALUES (1, 'Q3 Update

Revenue grew in every region this quarter and margins improved.

'::BLOB), (2, '\x89PNG\x0D\x0A\x1A\x0A\x00\x00\x00\x0DIHDR'::BLOB), (3, 'Point trimestriel

Le chiffre d''affaires a progresse dans toutes les regions ce trimestre.

'::BLOB)) SELECT x.id, x.meta['dc:title'] AS title, tika.main.detect_lang(x.content) AS language FROM tika.main.extract_all((SELECT id, body FROM inbox WHERE tika.main.detect_mime(body) = 'text/html'), id := 'id', doc_column := 'body') AS x ORDER BY x.id
vgi.example_queries.description: Triage a mixed inbox of raw bytes: detect_mime sniffs each blob so only the HTML pages go through extract_all (the PNG, id 2, is skipped), then each page's <title> is read from the metadata map and its body language tagged with detect_lang (1 'Q3 Update' en, 3 'Point trimestriel' fr).

functions.name: extract_text
functions.comment: Extract text, metadata, language, and page count from a document (PDF, DOCX, PPTX, XLSX, HTML, EML, RTF, ODF, images) via Apache Tika.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## extract_text

Parse a single document with Apache Tika and return its plain-text body together with detected metadata. Handles PDF, DOCX, PPTX, XLSX, HTML, EML/MSG, RTF, ODF, and image formats.

**Input** — an `any`-typed `doc` argument: a `VARCHAR` filesystem path the worker opens, or a `BLOB` of the document bytes. Named options: `by_page := true` emits one row per page (real per-page splitting for PDFs, a single fallback row for other formats); `lang` sets the OCR language; `ocr := true` forces OCR; `strict := true` re-raises parse errors instead of capturing them.

**Output** — one row (or one per page) with `content`, `mime`, `n_pages`, `lang`, a `meta` `MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)`, and an `error` column.

**Error handling** — a corrupt or unsupported document yields a row with `NULL` content and a populated `error` message rather than failing the whole query, unless `strict := true`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# extract_text

Extracts text, metadata, language, and page count from a single document.

## Usage

Pass a file path or document bytes. Use `by_page := true` to fan a PDF out into per-page rows, `ocr := true` for image-only content, and `strict := true` to fail loudly on parse errors.

## Notes

- Per-row error capture: failures surface in the `error` column (NULL `content`) unless `strict`.
- The `meta` column is a `MAP(VARCHAR, VARCHAR)` of Tika's full metadata bag.
- See the returned-columns table below for the exact output shape.

## metadata

Like `extract_text`, but returns only a document's metadata — its MIME type, page count, language, and the full Tika metadata bag — without the (potentially large) body text. One row per call.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## extract_all

A table-in-out function that runs `extract_text` over a whole column of documents at once. Stream a relation whose column holds either filesystem paths (`VARCHAR`) or document bytes (`BLOB`); the function emits one extract row per input row.

**Input** — a table argument plus named options: `doc_column` selects the document column (defaults to the first non-id column); `id` names a passthrough column that is excluded from parsing and copied verbatim onto every output row so results join back to the source; `ocr` and `lang` control OCR as in `extract_text`.

**Output** — the `extract_text` column set (`content`, `mime`, `n_pages`, `lang`, `meta`, `error`), optionally prefixed by the `id` passthrough column.

**Error handling** — per-row: a failed document yields `NULL` content and an `error` message; the rest of the batch still processes. Use this to bulk-extract a corpus referenced by a SQL relation.

functions.name: detect_lang
functions.comment: Detect the ISO-639 language code of a piece of text (Apache Tika language detection).

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## detect_lang

Identify the dominant natural language of a piece of text and return its ISO-639 code (e.g. `en`, `fr`, `de`), using Apache Tika's Optimaize n-gram language detector.

**Input** — a `VARCHAR` of text (often the `content` column produced by `extract_text`).

**Output** — a short ISO-639 language code, or `NULL` when the input is `NULL`/blank or no language can be detected confidently.

Pair it with `detect_lang_conf` to threshold on detection confidence. Detection is most reliable on at least a sentence or two of text; very short strings may return `NULL`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# detect_lang

Returns the ISO-639 language code of a text string.

## Usage

Feed it any `VARCHAR` text — typically extracted document bodies — to tag rows by language for filtering or routing.

## Notes

- Returns `NULL` for `NULL`, blank, or low-confidence input.
- Backed by the Optimaize models bundled with Tika; accuracy improves with longer text.
- Use `detect_lang_conf` for the matching confidence score.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT tika.main.detect_lang('The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.');

functions.name: detect_mime
functions.comment: Detect a document's MIME type from its bytes or a file path (Apache Tika).

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## detect_mime

Sniff the media (MIME) type of a document using Apache Tika's container-aware detector, working from the document's magic bytes rather than its file extension.

**Input** — a single `any`-typed argument resolved at runtime: a `BLOB` of the raw document bytes, or a `VARCHAR` filesystem path the worker opens.

**Output** — a `VARCHAR` media type such as `application/pdf`, `application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.wordprocessingml.document`, or `text/plain`; `NULL` for a `NULL` input.

Use it to route, filter, or validate documents by type before calling the heavier `extract_text` / `metadata` table functions.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# detect_mime

Returns the detected media type of a document as a `VARCHAR`.

## Usage

Pass either a `BLOB` of document bytes or a `VARCHAR` file path; detection is content-based (Tika reads the leading bytes), so it does not rely on the file name.

## Notes

- Returns `NULL` for a `NULL` input.
- Office formats are correctly disambiguated by inspecting the OOXML/ODF container, not just the ZIP signature.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT tika.main.detect_mime('Hello, plain text body.'::BLOB);
vgi.example_queries.description: Detect the MIME type of inline document bytes (returns 'text/plain').

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT tika.main.detect_mime(content) FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-tika/v0.4.0/test/sql/data/hello.pdf');
vgi.example_queries.description: Detect the MIME type of a PDF read as bytes with read_blob() (returns 'application/pdf'); a local file path works the same.

vgi.example_queries.sql:
WITH inbox(id, body) AS (VALUES (1, 'Q3 Update

Revenue grew in every region this quarter and margins improved.

Le chiffre d''affaires a progresse dans toutes les regions ce trimestre.

'::BLOB)) SELECT x.id, x.meta['dc:title'] AS title, tika.main.detect_lang(x.content) AS language FROM tika.main.extract_all((SELECT id, body FROM inbox WHERE tika.main.detect_mime(body) = 'text/html'), id := 'id', doc_column := 'body') AS x ORDER BY x.id
vgi.example_queries.description: Triage a mixed inbox of raw bytes: detect_mime sniffs each blob so only the HTML pages go through extract_all (the PNG, id 2, is skipped), then each page's <title> is read from the metadata map and its body language tagged with detect_lang (1 'Q3 Update' en, 3 'Point trimestriel' fr).

functions.name: ocr
functions.comment: OCR an image or scanned PDF (bytes or path) via Tika's Tesseract parser; returns NULL when Tesseract is unavailable.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## ocr

Run optical character recognition over an image or a scanned PDF using Apache Tika's Tesseract parser, returning the recognized text.

**Input** — an `any`-typed document argument (`BLOB` bytes or `VARCHAR` path) plus an optional `lang` setting. `lang` is a `+`-joined list of Tesseract trained-data languages, e.g. `'eng'` (default) or `'eng+deu'`.

**Output** — a `VARCHAR` of the OCR'd text.

**Important** — OCR requires the system `tesseract` binary on `PATH`. When it is absent the function returns `NULL` for every row instead of failing the query, so pipelines stay resilient. Use this for image-only documents where `extract_text` returns little or no text.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# ocr

Returns text recognized from an image or scanned PDF as a `VARCHAR`.

## Usage

Pass image bytes or a path; optionally set `lang` to a `+`-joined trained-data list (`'eng+deu'`) to recognize multiple scripts.

## Notes

- Requires the `tesseract` system binary; returns `NULL` when it is not installed rather than raising.
- Returns `NULL` for a `NULL` input.
- For born-digital documents prefer `extract_text`; reach for `ocr` when the content is rasterized.

vgi.example_queries.description: OCR a scanned image read as bytes with read_blob(), using the default English model; returns the card's text starting 'LIBRARY RETURN CHECKLIST' (NULL if Tesseract is not installed).

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT line FROM (SELECT unnest(string_split(tika.main.ocr(content), chr(10))) AS line FROM read_blob('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Query-farm/vgi-tika/fbe9bce2524010aa5b0ec8f4456c05f4082fa1b5/notebooks/assets/scan-card.png')) WHERE trim(line) <> '';
vgi.example_queries.description: Split the OCR'd text of a scanned card into its non-blank lines, one row per line (4 rows; no rows if Tesseract is not installed).
