functions.name: detect_lang_conf
functions.comment: Confidence (0.0-1.0) of the top detected language for a piece of text (Apache Tika language detection); the companion score to detect_lang.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## detect_lang_conf

Return the detector's confidence in the top language it found for a piece of text, as a continuous score in `0.0`–`1.0`. This is the companion to `detect_lang`: that function gives the ISO-639 code, this one gives how sure the model is.

**Input** — a `VARCHAR` of text.

**Output** — a `DOUBLE` raw probability (`0.0`–`1.0`), or `NULL` when the input is `NULL`/blank or no language is detected (mirroring `detect_lang`'s `NULL`).

Tika exposes language confidence as a coarse `NONE`/`LOW`/`MEDIUM`/`HIGH` enum; this function surfaces the underlying raw score so callers can apply their own threshold (e.g. keep rows where confidence `> 0.5`).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
# detect_lang_conf

Returns the confidence (`0.0`–`1.0`) of the top detected language as a `DOUBLE`.

## Usage

Run it alongside `detect_lang` to keep only high-confidence language tags, or to rank ambiguous rows.

## Notes

- Returns `NULL` for `NULL`, blank, or undetected input.
- The score is the model's raw probability, not Tika's coarse enum.
- Longer text yields more reliable confidence.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT tika.main.detect_lang_conf('The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.');
vgi.example_queries.description: Confidence (0.0-1.0) of the top detected language for a piece of text.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT tika.main.detect_lang(content) AS lang, tika.main.detect_lang_conf(content) AS conf FROM tika.main.extract_text('The annual report covers quarterly results.'::BLOB);
vgi.example_queries.description: Report the detected language and its confidence for an extracted document body.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT CASE WHEN tika.main.detect_lang_conf(content) >= 0.5 THEN tika.main.detect_lang(content) ELSE 'und' END AS language, count(*) AS docs, list(id ORDER BY id) AS ids FROM tika.main.extract_all((SELECT id, body FROM (VALUES (1, 'The quarterly report shows strong growth across every region this year.'::BLOB), (2, 'Le rapport trimestriel montre une forte croissance dans toutes les regions.'::BLOB), (3, 'Der Quartalsbericht zeigt ein starkes Wachstum in allen Regionen.'::BLOB), (4, 'Our customers renewed their contracts early and expanded their usage.'::BLOB), (5, 'OK'::BLOB), (6, 'PO-88213'::BLOB)) AS t(id, body)), id := 'id', doc_column := 'body') GROUP BY language ORDER BY docs DESC, language
vgi.example_queries.description: Language breakdown of a document corpus: extract every body with extract_all, tag it with detect_lang, and send bodies whose detect_lang_conf is below 0.5 (or undetectable) to 'und'. Returns en [1, 4] and und [5, 6] (2 docs each), then de [3] and fr [2].

workers.title: Tiktoken Tokenizer
workers.tagline: Count LLM tokens & chunk text for RAG in DuckDB (Rust, tiktoken)
workers.subtitle: Count, tokenize, truncate and chunk text using exact OpenAI BPE token counts.
workers.summary: Exact LLM token counting and token-aware text chunking, powered by tiktoken-rs.
workers.doc_md:
# tiktoken — Count LLM Tokens & Chunk Text in SQL

![OpenAI logo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a0/OpenAI_wordmark_2017.svg/330px-OpenAI_wordmark_2017.svg.png)

**Count LLM tokens, tokenize text, and split documents into token-bounded chunks directly in DuckDB SQL** — exact OpenAI-compatible BPE token counting and token-aware text chunking for prompt budgeting, API cost estimation, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), with no Python and no network calls.

This extension is for anyone who needs to know exactly how many tokens a piece of text will consume before sending it to a large language model. Instead of approximating with character or word counts, `tiktoken` computes the *real* token count using the same byte-pair-encoding (BPE) vocabularies that OpenAI's GPT models use. That makes it ideal for staying within context-window limits, estimating the cost of an API call, deduplicating or filtering rows by token length, and preparing large corpora for embedding pipelines — all from ordinary SQL over your existing tables.

Under the hood the worker wraps the Rust crate [`tiktoken-rs`](https://github.com/zurawiki/tiktoken-rs) ([docs](https://docs.rs/tiktoken-rs)), a fast, pure-Rust port of OpenAI's [`tiktoken`](https://github.com/openai/tiktoken) tokenizer. The BPE encodings are **bundled into the binary** and built lazily on first use, so token counting works fully offline with no model download. The supported encodings cover every modern OpenAI model family: `cl100k_base` (GPT-4 / GPT-3.5), `o200k_base` (GPT-4o), `p50k_base`, `r50k_base`, and `o200k_harmony`. Results are exact and deterministic, so the same text always yields the same count and the same token-id sequence.

The worker exposes a small, composable set of scalar SQL functions in the `tiktoken.main` schema, covering the everyday token-oriented tasks: getting an exact token count for a string, returning the raw BPE token ids as an `INTEGER[]`, mapping a model name (e.g. `'gpt-4o'`) to its encoding name, clipping text to a fixed token budget, and splitting text into token-bounded, optionally overlapping windows that make ideal RAG chunks before embedding. Each text function offers a default-encoding form (`cl100k_base`) and a model-aware form that accepts a model or encoding name; unknown model names return `NULL`, and `NULL` input flows through to `NULL`. Built and maintained by [Query.Farm](https://query.farm).

example_queries.description: Count the GPT-4/3.5 (cl100k_base) tokens in a sentence.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tiktoken.main.count_tokens('The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.');

example_queries.description: Count tokens with a specific model's encoding (gpt-4o uses o200k_base).
example_queries.sql: SELECT tiktoken.main.count_tokens('Summarize this prompt.', 'gpt-4o');

example_queries.description: Get the raw BPE token ids of a string under the default encoding.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tiktoken.main.tokenize('tiktoken is great!');

example_queries.description: Look up which tiktoken encoding a model uses.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tiktoken.main.encoding_for_model('gpt-4o');

example_queries.description: Clip text to its first 5 cl100k_base tokens, decoded back to a string.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tiktoken.main.truncate_to_tokens('The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.', 5);

example_queries.description: Split a document into non-overlapping 8-token chunks for embedding.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tiktoken.main.chunk_by_tokens('A long document to split before embedding.', 8);

example_queries.description: Split a document into 8-token chunks (cl100k_base), number them in order with WITH ORDINALITY, and count the tokens in each chunk to confirm it fits the budget (4 chunks of 8, 8, 8 and 5 tokens).
example_queries.sql: SELECT c.chunk_no, c.chunk, tiktoken.main.count_tokens(c.chunk) AS tokens FROM unnest(tiktoken.main.chunk_by_tokens('Retrieval augmented generation splits long documents into token-bounded chunks, embeds each chunk, and retrieves the most relevant ones at query time.', 8)) WITH ORDINALITY AS c(chunk, chunk_no) ORDER BY c.chunk_no;

example_queries.description: Compare what one multilingual sentence costs under three models, showing each model's encoding: gpt-4o (o200k_base) needs 20 tokens versus 24 for gpt-4 (cl100k_base) and 30 for text-davinci-003 (p50k_base).
example_queries.sql: SELECT m.model, tiktoken.main.encoding_for_model(m.model) AS encoding, tiktoken.main.count_tokens('Tokenizers differ: GPT-4o packs multilingual text such as こんにちは世界 into fewer tokens.', m.model) AS tokens FROM (VALUES ('gpt-4o'), ('gpt-4'), ('text-davinci-003')) AS m(model) ORDER BY tokens, m.model;

example_queries.description: Fit a table of prompts to a 10-token budget: report each prompt's original token count, the clipped text, and its token count after truncation (the 3-token prompt passes through unchanged; the 20-token one is cut to 10).
example_queries.sql: SELECT p.id, tiktoken.main.count_tokens(p.prompt) AS original_tokens, tiktoken.main.truncate_to_tokens(p.prompt, 10) AS clipped, tiktoken.main.count_tokens(tiktoken.main.truncate_to_tokens(p.prompt, 10)) AS clipped_tokens FROM (VALUES (1, 'Short question?'), (2, 'Please summarize the following quarterly report in three bullet points, focusing on revenue growth, margins and guidance.')) AS p(id, prompt) ORDER BY p.id;

example_queries.description: Tokenize text using a specific model's encoding (gpt-4o uses o200k_base).
example_queries.sql: SELECT tiktoken.main.tokenize('hello world', 'gpt-4o');

example_queries.description: Count tokens with the encoding for a specific model (gpt-4o uses o200k_base) to budget a context window.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tiktoken.main.count_tokens('Summarize this prompt for GPT-4o.', 'gpt-4o');

example_queries.description: Truncate text to a token budget using a specific model's encoding (gpt-4o uses o200k_base).
example_queries.sql: SELECT tiktoken.main.truncate_to_tokens('The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.', 5, 'gpt-4o');

example_queries.description: Split a document into non-overlapping windows of at most 256 tokens (cl100k_base) for embedding.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tiktoken.main.chunk_by_tokens('A long document to split before embedding.', 256);

example_queries.description: Split a document into 256-token windows that share 32 overlapping tokens, preserving context across chunks for RAG.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tiktoken.main.chunk_by_tokens('A long RAG document to split into overlapping windows.', 256, 32);

example_queries.description: Count the GPT-4/3.5 (cl100k_base) tokens in a sentence.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tiktoken.main.count_tokens('The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.') AS n;

example_queries.description: Count tokens with a specific model's encoding (gpt-4o uses o200k_base).
example_queries.sql: SELECT tiktoken.main.count_tokens('Summarize this prompt.', 'gpt-4o') AS n;

example_queries.description: Get the BPE token ids for a string under the default encoding.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tiktoken.main.tokenize('tiktoken is great!') AS ids;

example_queries.description: Map a model name to its tiktoken encoding name.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tiktoken.main.encoding_for_model('gpt-4o') AS encoding;

example_queries.description: Truncate text to its first 5 tokens, decoded back to a string.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tiktoken.main.truncate_to_tokens('The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.', 5) AS clipped;

example_queries.description: Split a document into non-overlapping 8-token chunks for embedding.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tiktoken.main.chunk_by_tokens('A long document to split before embedding for retrieval augmented generation.', 8) AS chunks;

example_queries.description: Split a document into 8-token windows that share 2 overlapping tokens (RAG).
example_queries.sql: SELECT tiktoken.main.chunk_by_tokens('A long document to split into overlapping windows for retrieval.', 8, 2) AS chunks;

## tiktoken.main

The primary schema of the tiktoken worker. It brings **exact LLM token counting** and **token-aware text chunking** to DuckDB SQL over Apache Arrow, grouped into a few areas: **counting** tokens, **tokenizing** text into raw BPE ids, **shaping** text to fit a token budget, and **reference** lookups that map a model name to its encoding and report the worker build.

The default encoding is `cl100k_base` (GPT-4 / GPT-3.5); pass a model name (e.g. `gpt-4o`) to select another. Encodings are bundled into the binary, so token counting is exact, deterministic, and needs no network access.

workers.title: TLS Fingerprinting
workers.tagline: Compute TLS fingerprints in DuckDB with SQL — JA3, JA3S and JA4 (TLS-client) for clustering C2 and bot infrastructure. A VGI worker.
workers.subtitle: Compute JA3, JA3S, and JA4 TLS fingerprints from raw handshake bytes or extracted fields.
workers.summary: TLS client/server fingerprinting (JA3, JA3S, JA4 TLS-client) as pure SQL scalars over raw handshake bytes.
workers.doc_md:
# tlsfp — TLS Client/Server Fingerprinting in SQL

**Compute JA3, JA3S, and the base JA4 (TLS-client) fingerprints directly in DuckDB SQL** from raw `ClientHello`/`ServerHello` bytes — or from fields you already extracted with Zeek/pcap tooling. Apply a fingerprint to a column of captured handshakes and `GROUP BY` it to surface a C2 or bot family, then JOIN the resulting `VARCHAR` hashes to certificate and flow data to pivot from a fingerprint to the certs and flows behind it.

Every function is pure, deterministic compute — no network, no state. Each fingerprint offers two input modes: pass the **raw handshake record** (the worker parses it) or the **component fields**. Malformed or truncated bytes return `NULL` per row rather than failing the query, and an `is_tls_handshake(bytes)` guard scalar lets you filter first. The `*_string`/`*_raw` companions expose the pre-hash JA3 string and the un-hashed JA4_r form for audit and custom re-hashing, and `parse_client_hello` decodes the handshake into a struct of its fields.

**Licensing:** only the patent-free fingerprints are implemented — JA3/JA3S (BSD-3) and base JA4 TLS-client (BSD-3, patent-disclaimed). The JA4+ suite (JA4S/JA4H/JA4L/JA4X/JA4SSH, FoxIO License 1.1, patent-pending) and JARM are intentionally NOT implemented.

## Sources and references

- [JA3 / JA3S (Salesforce)](https://github.com/salesforce/ja3)
- [JA4 (FoxIO)](https://github.com/FoxIO-LLC/ja4) — see the [JA4 technical details](https://github.com/FoxIO-LLC/ja4/blob/main/technical_details/JA4.md)
- [RFC 8446](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446) — TLS 1.3 handshake messages
- [RFC 8701](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8701) — GREASE values, ignored by the fingerprints

example_queries.description: Cluster a set of captured ClientHellos by their JA3 and JA4 fingerprints, most frequent first — the headline threat-hunting query.
Compute the JA3S server fingerprint of a captured ServerHello.
Compute JA3 from ClientHello fields already parsed by a tool such as Zeek (no raw bytes needed).

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Pure TLS-fingerprint scalars in three families: Salesforce JA3 client and JA3S server fingerprints, the base FoxIO JA4 client fingerprint, and ClientHello parsing with a cheap is-this-a-handshake guard. Each fingerprint takes either the raw handshake record or the already-extracted fields (for example from Zeek), and both modes share the same builders so they agree; pre-hash/raw companions let you audit a hash. tags.vgi.doc_md:
The single schema (`main`) for the `tlsfp` worker — its whole surface of pure TLS-fingerprint scalars.

Each fingerprint offers two input modes: pass the **raw handshake record** and let the worker parse it, or pass the **already-extracted fields** when a tool such as Zeek has parsed the handshake for you. Both modes share the same builders, so they always agree.

The functions group into a few families:

- **JA3 / JA3S** — Salesforce client and server fingerprints, with a pre-hash string companion for audit.
- **JA4** — the base FoxIO TLS-client fingerprint, with its un-hashed raw form for audit.
- **Parsing & guards** — decode a handshake into its component fields, and cheaply test whether raw bytes even look like a TLS handshake before fingerprinting.

Everything is deterministic compute with no network or state, and malformed or truncated input yields `NULL` per row rather than failing the query.

workers.title: Trading Calendar
workers.tagline: Stock-exchange trading calendars — sessions, market hours & schedules — for DuckDB (Python)
workers.subtitle: Find trading days, sessions and market hours for stock exchanges.
workers.summary: Stock-exchange trading-calendar math for SQL: sessions, market hours, and schedules
workers.doc_md:
# Trading-Day & Market-Hours Math in SQL

**`tcal` brings stock-exchange trading calendars directly into DuckDB SQL — no ETL, no Python glue, just `SELECT`.** Ask whether a date is a trading session, advance or count trading days, find the next or previous session, or check market open/close hours (including early closes) for the NYSE and ~100 other exchanges, all as ordinary SQL expressions and table functions.

This VGI worker is for analysts, data engineers, and application developers who need correct market-calendar logic close to their data: trading-day filtering, settlement (T+N) date math, session alignment of fills and ticks, and market-hours analytics. It exposes a single `tcal` catalog (schema `main`) over Apache Arrow, so every function streams results back to DuckDB with native types — `DATE`, `TIMESTAMP`, and `TIMESTAMPTZ` round-trip cleanly. Coverage is global, not US-centric: roughly a hundred exchange calendars are supported, and `'XNYS'` (NYSE) is merely the default argument, not a limit.

Trading calendars are provided by [exchange-calendars](https://github.com/gerrymanoim/exchange_calendars) ([tutorials](https://github.com/gerrymanoim/exchange_calendars/tree/master/docs/tutorials)), the maintained successor to Quantopian's `trading_calendars`, covering roughly a hundred exchanges including early closes and holiday sessions. A **session** is a trading day; `market_open` / `market_close` are timezone-aware **UTC** instants. Coverage is the library's default window (roughly two decades back to about a year ahead — future exchange holidays are only defined so far); a date outside that window resolves to `NULL` / no rows rather than raising.

Per-row questions are answered by scalar functions you can drop straight into a projection or predicate; set-returning questions — a range of trading sessions, an expanded per-session schedule — are table functions. The exchange is an ordinary argument that defaults to `'XNYS'`.

example_queries.title: is-market-open
example_queries.description: Whether a date is an NYSE trading session (New Year's Day is a holiday).
example_queries.sql: SELECT tcal.main.is_trading_day(DATE '2026-01-01') AS is_session;

example_queries.title: next-nyse-session
example_queries.description: The first NYSE session strictly after a given date.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tcal.main.next_trading_day(DATE '2026-01-01') AS next_session;

example_queries.title: list-exchanges
example_queries.description: A few of the supported exchange MIC codes.
example_queries.sql: SELECT code FROM tcal.main.exchanges ORDER BY code LIMIT 5;

example_queries.title: nyse-open-london-closed
example_queries.description: NYSE sessions in 2026 on which the London Stock Exchange is closed (UK bank holidays such as Easter Monday and the Boxing Day substitute) -- days a US/UK pairs desk trades only one leg.
example_queries.sql: SELECT s.session FROM tcal.main.trading_sessions(DATE '2026-01-01', DATE '2026-12-31') AS s WHERE NOT tcal.main.is_trading_day(s.session, 'XLON') ORDER BY s.session;

example_queries.description: Is 3 July 2026 (US Independence Day observed) a London Stock Exchange session?
example_queries.sql: SELECT tcal.main.is_trading_day(DATE '2026-07-03', 'XLON') AS is_session

example_queries.description: The last NYSE session strictly before 2 January 2026.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tcal.main.previous_trading_day(DATE '2026-01-02') AS prev_session

example_queries.description: Advance a trade date by 10 NYSE sessions (settlement-style date math).
example_queries.sql: SELECT tcal.main.add_trading_days(DATE '2026-01-02', 10) AS settle_date

example_queries.description: Count NYSE sessions in January 2026 via the half-open [start, end) interval.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tcal.main.trading_days_between(DATE '2026-01-01', DATE '2026-02-01') AS n_sessions

example_queries.description: NYSE market-open instant (UTC) for 2 January 2026.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tcal.main.market_open(DATE '2026-01-02') AS open_utc

example_queries.description: NYSE early close (UTC) the day after US Thanksgiving 2026.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tcal.main.market_close(DATE '2026-11-27') AS close_utc

example_queries.description: Flag the day after US Thanksgiving 2026 as an early-close half-day.
example_queries.sql: SELECT tcal.main.is_early_close(DATE '2026-11-27') AS early_close

example_queries.description: Count the NYSE trading sessions in January 2026.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS n_sessions FROM tcal.main.trading_sessions(DATE '2026-01-01', DATE '2026-01-31')

example_queries.description: Half-days in the NYSE Thanksgiving-week schedule, with their early close time.
example_queries.sql: SELECT session, market_close FROM tcal.main.trading_schedule(DATE '2026-11-25', DATE '2026-11-30') WHERE is_early_close

example_queries.description: T+1 settlement date for a trade on each NYSE session of Thanksgiving week 2026 -- the Wednesday trade settles on Friday because the Thanksgiving holiday is skipped.
example_queries.sql: SELECT s.session AS trade_date, tcal.main.add_trading_days(s.session, 1) AS settles_t1 FROM tcal.main.trading_sessions(DATE '2026-11-23', DATE '2026-11-30') AS s ORDER BY s.session

example_queries.description: Every NYSE early-close half-day in 2026 with its early close time (UTC) and when the market next opens -- how long positions sit over the holiday break.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sc.session, sc.market_close, tcal.main.next_trading_day(sc.session) AS next_session, tcal.main.market_open(tcal.main.next_trading_day(sc.session)) AS next_open FROM tcal.main.trading_schedule(DATE '2026-01-01', DATE '2026-12-31') AS sc WHERE sc.is_early_close ORDER BY sc.session

example_queries.description: Minutes of overlap between NYSE and London trading hours on sessions both trade in March-April 2026: usually 2 hours, widening to 3 hours for the weeks when the US has moved to daylight saving time and the UK has not.
example_queries.sql: SELECT date_diff('minute', greatest(ny.market_open, ln.market_open), least(ny.market_close, ln.market_close)) AS overlap_minutes, count(*) AS n_sessions, min(ny.session) AS first_session FROM tcal.main.trading_schedule(DATE '2026-03-01', DATE '2026-04-30') AS ny JOIN tcal.main.trading_schedule(DATE '2026-03-01', DATE '2026-04-30', exchange := 'XLON') AS ln USING (session) GROUP BY overlap_minutes ORDER BY first_session

example_queries.description: List all supported exchange MIC codes.
example_queries.sql: SELECT code FROM tcal.main.exchanges ORDER BY code

example_queries.description: Confirm the NYSE (XNYS) calendar is available.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS n FROM tcal.main.exchanges WHERE code = 'XNYS'

example_queries.description: The last London Stock Exchange sessions of January 2026 (26th onward).
example_queries.sql: SELECT session FROM tcal.main.trading_sessions(DATE '2026-01-01', DATE '2026-01-31', exchange := 'XLON') WHERE session >= DATE '2026-01-26'

example_queries.description: London open on 2026-01-02
example_queries.sql: SELECT tcal.main.market_open(DATE '2026-01-02', 'XLON')

example_queries.description: Christmas Eve is an early close on the LSE
example_queries.sql: SELECT tcal.main.is_early_close(DATE '2026-12-24', 'XLON')

example_queries.description: Is 2026-12-28 a London Stock Exchange session?
example_queries.sql: SELECT tcal.main.is_trading_day(DATE '2026-12-28', 'XLON')

example_queries.description: London close on 2026-01-02
example_queries.sql: SELECT tcal.main.market_close(DATE '2026-01-02', 'XLON')

example_queries.description: London sessions in January 2026
example_queries.sql: SELECT tcal.main.trading_days_between(DATE '2026-01-01', DATE '2026-02-01', 'XLON')

example_queries.description: Next Tokyo session after New Year's Day
example_queries.sql: SELECT tcal.main.next_trading_day(DATE '2026-01-01', 'XTKS')

example_queries.description: Last London session before New Year's Day
example_queries.sql: SELECT tcal.main.previous_trading_day(DATE '2026-01-01', 'XLON')

example_queries.description: Five London sessions after 2026-01-02
example_queries.sql: SELECT tcal.main.add_trading_days(DATE '2026-01-02', 5, 'XLON')

Using the tcal worker, is 3 July 2026 a trading session on the London Stock Exchange (MIC code 'XLON')? It is a US market holiday (observed Independence Day) but London is unaffected. Return a single boolean.
Using the tcal worker, what is the last New York Stock Exchange trading session strictly before 2 January 2026? Return a single date.
Using the tcal worker, at what UTC timestamp does the New York Stock Exchange open on 2 January 2026? Return a single timestamp.
Using the tcal worker, is 27 November 2026 (the day after US Thanksgiving) an early-close half-day session on the New York Stock Exchange? Return a single boolean.
Using the tcal worker, list the New York Stock Exchange trading sessions from 1 January 2026 through 31 January 2026 (inclusive) and return how many there are as a single integer.
Using the tcal worker, in the New York Stock Exchange schedule for 27 November 2026, is that session flagged as an early close? Return a single boolean.

Using the tcal worker, confirm the New York Stock Exchange (MIC code 'XNYS') is one of the supported exchange calendars by returning how many rows of the supported-exchanges list have that code (expect 1). Return a single integer.

Using the tcal worker, consider a trade executed on every New York Stock Exchange trading session in calendar year 2026 (1 January through 31 December inclusive), each settling T+1 (one NYSE trading session later). For how many of those trades is the settlement date more than one calendar day after the trade date (because a weekend or exchange holiday intervenes)? Return a single integer.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Trading-day & market-hours math

Stock-exchange trading-calendar functions over Apache Arrow, exposed as ordinary DuckDB SQL.

**Key concepts**

- Scalar functions answer one question per row and slot into a projection or predicate.
- Table functions return sets of rows: a range of trading sessions or an expanded per-session schedule.
- The exchange is an ordinary argument; `'XNYS'` (NYSE) is only a default, not a limit — coverage spans ~100 exchange calendars.
- A *session* is a trading day; `market_open` / `market_close` are timezone-aware **UTC** instants. `DATE`, `TIMESTAMP`, and `TIMESTAMPTZ` round-trip natively over Arrow.

**When to use it**

Reach for this schema for trading-day filtering, settlement (T+N) date math, session alignment of fills and ticks, and market-hours analytics.

vgi.example_queries.description: Is New Year's Day 2026 an NYSE trading session? (No — it is a holiday.)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT tcal.main.is_trading_day(DATE '2026-01-01') AS is_session

vgi.example_queries.description: Is 3 July 2026 (US Independence Day observed) a London Stock Exchange session?
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT tcal.main.is_trading_day(DATE '2026-07-03', 'XLON') AS is_session

vgi.example_queries.description: The first NYSE session strictly after New Year's Day 2026.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT tcal.main.next_trading_day(DATE '2026-01-01') AS next_session

vgi.example_queries.description: The last NYSE session strictly before 2 January 2026.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT tcal.main.previous_trading_day(DATE '2026-01-02') AS prev_session

vgi.example_queries.description: Advance a trade date by 10 NYSE sessions (settlement-style date math).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT tcal.main.add_trading_days(DATE '2026-01-02', 10) AS settle_date

vgi.example_queries.description: Count NYSE sessions in January 2026 via the half-open [start, end) interval.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT tcal.main.trading_days_between(DATE '2026-01-01', DATE '2026-02-01') AS n_sessions

vgi.example_queries.description: NYSE market-open instant (UTC) for 2 January 2026.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT tcal.main.market_open(DATE '2026-01-02') AS open_utc

vgi.example_queries.description: NYSE early close (UTC) the day after US Thanksgiving 2026.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT tcal.main.market_close(DATE '2026-11-27') AS close_utc

vgi.example_queries.description: Flag the day after US Thanksgiving 2026 as an early-close half-day.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT tcal.main.is_early_close(DATE '2026-11-27') AS early_close

vgi.example_queries.description: Count the NYSE trading sessions in January 2026.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS n_sessions FROM tcal.main.trading_sessions(DATE '2026-01-01', DATE '2026-01-31')

vgi.example_queries.description: Half-days in the NYSE Thanksgiving-week schedule, with their early close time.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT session, market_close FROM tcal.main.trading_schedule(DATE '2026-11-25', DATE '2026-11-30') WHERE is_early_close

vgi.example_queries.description: The first five supported exchange MIC codes, alphabetically.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT code FROM tcal.main.exchanges ORDER BY code LIMIT 5

vgi.example_queries.description: NYSE sessions in 2026 on which the London Stock Exchange is closed (UK bank holidays such as Easter Monday and the Boxing Day substitute) -- days a US/UK pairs desk trades only one leg.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT s.session FROM tcal.main.trading_sessions(DATE '2026-01-01', DATE '2026-12-31') AS s WHERE NOT tcal.main.is_trading_day(s.session, 'XLON') ORDER BY s.session

vgi.example_queries.description: T+1 settlement date for a trade on each NYSE session of Thanksgiving week 2026 -- the Wednesday trade settles on Friday because the Thanksgiving holiday is skipped.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT s.session AS trade_date, tcal.main.add_trading_days(s.session, 1) AS settles_t1 FROM tcal.main.trading_sessions(DATE '2026-11-23', DATE '2026-11-30') AS s ORDER BY s.session

vgi.example_queries.description: Every NYSE early-close half-day in 2026 with its early close time (UTC) and when the market next opens -- how long positions sit over the holiday break.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT sc.session, sc.market_close, tcal.main.next_trading_day(sc.session) AS next_session, tcal.main.market_open(tcal.main.next_trading_day(sc.session)) AS next_open FROM tcal.main.trading_schedule(DATE '2026-01-01', DATE '2026-12-31') AS sc WHERE sc.is_early_close ORDER BY sc.session

vgi.example_queries.description: Minutes of overlap between NYSE and London trading hours on sessions both trade in March-April 2026: usually 2 hours, widening to 3 hours for the weeks when the US has moved to daylight saving time and the UK has not.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT date_diff('minute', greatest(ny.market_open, ln.market_open), least(ny.market_close, ln.market_close)) AS overlap_minutes, count(*) AS n_sessions, min(ny.session) AS first_session FROM tcal.main.trading_schedule(DATE '2026-03-01', DATE '2026-04-30') AS ny JOIN tcal.main.trading_schedule(DATE '2026-03-01', DATE '2026-04-30', exchange := 'XLON') AS ln USING (session) GROUP BY overlap_minutes ORDER BY first_session

workers.title: VGI Trajectory Worker
workers.tagline: vgi-trajectory — Query Farm VGI worker with executable SQL notebook examples
workers.subtitle: Reconstruct visits, dwell and trips from GPS observations.
workers.summary: GPS track analysis: turns timestamped position fixes into geofence visits, trips and explicit observation gaps, interpolating crossings between fixes but never inferring visits across long gaps, implausible speeds or poor-accuracy fixes. Sample fixes and fences are included.
workers.doc_md:
## GIS analysis

Reconstruct visits and trips from timestamped GPS rows, including geofence crossings between fixes. The worker buffers within an explicit point budget, sorts by entity and UTC time, intersects each piecewise-linear track with polygons, and emits visits, trips, and explicit observation gaps. Long gaps, implausible speeds and poor-accuracy fixes never create inferred visits. Durations and paths describe the linear interpolation model, not unobserved ground truth.

### SQL workflow

Pass query results to the main schema functions, retaining IDs for joins. Use bundled synthetic data to try the executable examples without network access. CRS, coverage, inference limits and resource bounds are explicit function parameters.

## Sources and references

- [Shapely](https://shapely.readthedocs.io/): the geometry engine behind track/geofence intersections and the WKB episode paths.
- [pyproj](https://pyproj4.github.io/pyproj/stable/) ([PROJ](https://proj.org/)): coordinate transforms from the input CRS into a projected metre CRS for distances and speeds.
- [OGC Simple Feature Access](https://www.ogc.org/standards/sfa/): the WKB geometry encoding used for fences and returned paths.

example_queries.description: Count observations per synthetic entity
example_queries.sql: SELECT entity_id, count(*) FROM trajectory.main.sample_fixes GROUP BY entity_id ORDER BY entity_id

example_queries.description: Recover a visit even though neither recorded fix is inside the fence
example_queries.sql: SELECT entity_id, duration_s, fix_count FROM trajectory.main.episodes((SELECT * FROM trajectory.main.sample_fixes)) WHERE episode_type='visit' ORDER BY entity_id

example_queries.description: ASOF-join each reconstructed visit back to the last sample_fixes fix at or before its entry: the crossing entity entered the yard 30 seconds after its last fix and has zero fixes inside, while the stopped entity's visit starts at a recorded fix
example_queries.sql: SELECT v.entity_id, v.fence_id, v.started_at, f.observed_at AS last_fix_at, date_diff('second', f.observed_at, v.started_at) AS seconds_after_fix, v.fix_count FROM trajectory.main.episodes((SELECT * FROM trajectory.main.sample_fixes)) AS v ASOF JOIN trajectory.main.sample_fixes AS f ON v.entity_id = f.entity_id AND v.started_at >= f.observed_at WHERE v.episode_type = 'visit' ORDER BY v.entity_id, v.started_at

example_queries.description: Share of each entity's observed span (first to last sample_fixes fix) spent in fence visits: crossing spends 60 of 120 seconds in the yard (0.5), stopped all 600 seconds (1.0)
example_queries.sql: WITH span AS (SELECT entity_id, date_diff('second', min(observed_at), max(observed_at)) AS observed_s FROM trajectory.main.sample_fixes GROUP BY entity_id), visits AS (SELECT entity_id, sum(duration_s) AS visit_s FROM trajectory.main.episodes((SELECT * FROM trajectory.main.sample_fixes)) WHERE episode_type = 'visit' GROUP BY entity_id) SELECT span.entity_id, span.observed_s, coalesce(visits.visit_s, 0) AS visit_s, round(coalesce(visits.visit_s, 0) / span.observed_s, 3) AS visit_share FROM span LEFT JOIN visits USING (entity_id) ORDER BY span.entity_id

functions.comment: Reconstruct visits, dwell, trips and gaps from timestamped GPS rows

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Reconstruct visits and trips from timestamped GPS rows, including geofence crossings between fixes. The worker buffers within an explicit point budget, sorts by entity and UTC time, intersects each piecewise-linear track with polygons, and emits visits, trips, and explicit observation gaps. Long gaps, implausible speeds and poor-accuracy fixes never create inferred visits. Durations and paths describe the linear interpolation model, not unobserved ground truth. Identical duplicate fixes are collapsed; conflicting positions at one timestamp fail. Fence boundaries count as inside. A tangent with zero residence time does not produce a visit. Censored endpoints and interpolated boundaries are explicit. Input/output state uses invocation-scoped VGI storage, so entity histories survive multiple batches and parallel producers.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: entity_id
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Input device/vehicle identity.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: episode_id
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Stable chronological episode number within an entity for the supplied query.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: episode_type
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: visit, trip, or gap. Overlapping fences produce independent visit rows.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: fence_id
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Visited fence identity, or NULL for trips and gaps.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: started_at
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: UTC episode start; inferred boundary time when a segment crosses a fence.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: ended_at
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: UTC episode end; inferred boundary time when a segment exits a fence.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: duration_s
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Elapsed seconds under the piecewise-linear interpolation model.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: distance_m
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Length of reconstructed projected track in metres; NULL for unknown movement gaps.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: fix_count
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Number of observation timestamps inside this episode's time interval; may be zero for a between-fix visit.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: interpolated_boundaries
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: True if at least one episode boundary occurs between recorded GPS fixes.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: left_censored
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: True if the episode was already in progress at the start of available continuous observations.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: right_censored
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: True if the episode may continue past the end of available continuous observations.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: status
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: linear_interpolation, long_gap, implausible_speed, or poor_accuracy.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: geometry_wkb
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Reconstructed episode LineString WKB in analysis_crs; NULL for gaps.

vgi.result_columns_schema.name: analysis_crs
vgi.result_columns_schema.description: Projected metre CRS used for lengths and reconstructed geometry.

arguments.description: Rows with entity_id, observed_at, x and y; optional accuracy_m. Unsorted and interleaved entities are accepted.

arguments.name: analysis_crs
arguments.description: Suitable local projected metre CRS for segment interpolation and distances.

arguments.name: fence_buffer_m
arguments.description: Explicit outward polygon tolerance for GPS jitter, metres; changes the spatial definition of visits.

arguments.name: fence_crs
arguments.description: Explicit CRS of fence coordinates; use EPSG:4326 for standard GeoJSON.

arguments.name: fences
arguments.description: Local FeatureCollection JSON path with unique feature id or properties.fence_id and Polygon/MultiPolygon geometry.

arguments.name: input_crs
arguments.description: CRS of GPS XY input coordinates; always XY axis order.

arguments.name: max_accuracy_m
arguments.description: Optional accuracy_m values above this bound prevent interpolation through that fix.

arguments.name: max_episodes
arguments.description: Maximum reconstructed episodes, including visits later removed by min_dwell_s.

arguments.name: max_fence_vertices
arguments.description: Maximum total fence coordinates after projection and optional buffering.

arguments.name: max_fences
arguments.description: Maximum geofence polygons in the collection.

arguments.name: max_gap_s
arguments.description: Maximum seconds between fixes permitting movement interpolation; longer intervals become gap rows.

arguments.name: max_input_bytes
arguments.description: Maximum total Arrow bytes of used input columns before global reconstruction.

arguments.name: max_json_bytes
arguments.description: Maximum bytes in the geofence JSON file.

arguments.name: max_path_vertices
arguments.description: Maximum coordinates stored across reconstructed paths, including overlapping visits.

arguments.name: max_points
arguments.description: Hard input-point budget before global sorting; partition large histories by entity and time with overlap.

arguments.name: max_segment_splits
arguments.description: Maximum distinct boundary cut positions along one GPS segment.

arguments.name: max_speed_m_s
arguments.description: Maximum plausible straight-line speed; faster intervals become gaps.

arguments.name: min_dwell_s
arguments.description: Exclude visit episodes shorter than this duration; trips are not merged across excluded visits.

examples: SELECT entity_id, duration_s, fix_count FROM trajectory.main.episodes((SELECT * FROM trajectory.main.sample_fixes)) WHERE episode_type='visit' ORDER BY entity_id

SELECT v.entity_id, v.fence_id, v.started_at, f.observed_at AS last_fix_at, date_diff('second', f.observed_at, v.started_at) AS seconds_after_fix, v.fix_count FROM trajectory.main.episodes((SELECT * FROM trajectory.main.sample_fixes)) AS v ASOF JOIN trajectory.main.sample_fixes AS f ON v.entity_id = f.entity_id AND v.started_at >= f.observed_at WHERE v.episode_type = 'visit' ORDER BY v.entity_id, v.started_at

WITH span AS (SELECT entity_id, date_diff('second', min(observed_at), max(observed_at)) AS observed_s FROM trajectory.main.sample_fixes GROUP BY entity_id), visits AS (SELECT entity_id, sum(duration_s) AS visit_s FROM trajectory.main.episodes((SELECT * FROM trajectory.main.sample_fixes)) WHERE episode_type = 'visit' GROUP BY entity_id) SELECT span.entity_id, span.observed_s, coalesce(visits.visit_s, 0) AS visit_s, round(coalesce(visits.visit_s, 0) / span.observed_s, 3) AS visit_share FROM span LEFT JOIN visits USING (entity_id) ORDER BY span.entity_id
SELECT entity_id, duration_s, fix_count FROM trajectory.main.episodes((SELECT * FROM trajectory.main.sample_fixes)) WHERE episode_type='visit' ORDER BY entity_id;

result_columns.name: entity_id
result_columns.description: Input device/vehicle identity.

result_columns.name: episode_id
result_columns.description: Stable chronological episode number within an entity for the supplied query.

result_columns.name: episode_type
result_columns.description: visit, trip, or gap. Overlapping fences produce independent visit rows.

result_columns.name: fence_id
result_columns.description: Visited fence identity, or NULL for trips and gaps.

result_columns.name: started_at
result_columns.description: UTC episode start; inferred boundary time when a segment crosses a fence.

result_columns.name: ended_at
result_columns.description: UTC episode end; inferred boundary time when a segment exits a fence.

result_columns.name: duration_s
result_columns.description: Elapsed seconds under the piecewise-linear interpolation model.

result_columns.name: distance_m
result_columns.description: Length of reconstructed projected track in metres; NULL for unknown movement gaps.

result_columns.name: fix_count
result_columns.description: Number of observation timestamps inside this episode's time interval; may be zero for a between-fix visit.

result_columns.name: interpolated_boundaries
result_columns.description: True if at least one episode boundary occurs between recorded GPS fixes.

result_columns.name: left_censored
result_columns.description: True if the episode was already in progress at the start of available continuous observations.

result_columns.name: right_censored
result_columns.description: True if the episode may continue past the end of available continuous observations.

result_columns.name: status
result_columns.description: linear_interpolation, long_gap, implausible_speed, or poor_accuracy.

result_columns.name: geometry_wkb
result_columns.description: Reconstructed episode LineString WKB in analysis_crs; NULL for gaps.

result_columns.name: analysis_crs
result_columns.description: Projected metre CRS used for lengths and reconstructed geometry.

workers.summary: Local neural machine translation and language detection for DuckDB/SQL.
workers.doc_md:
# Offline Machine Translation & Language Detection in SQL

![Argos Translate logo](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argosopentech/argos-translate/master/img/icon.png)

Translate text between languages and identify the language of any string directly in DuckDB SQL — fully offline, with no API keys, no rate limits, and no data ever leaving your machine. This VGI extension brings local **neural machine translation (NMT)** and **language detection** to your queries, so multilingual text processing, localization (i18n), and content normalization become ordinary SQL.

Translation is powered by [Argos Translate](https://github.com/argosopentech/argos-translate) ([project site & docs](https://www.argosopentech.com/)), an open-source (MIT-licensed) offline translation library built on the [OPUS-MT](https://github.com/Helsinki-NLP/Opus-MT) neural models trained on the [OPUS](https://opus.nlpl.eu/) parallel corpora. Language packages install lazily on first use and are cached per worker process, so a model loads once and then serves every subsequent query at full speed with zero network access. Because Argos Translate and the OPUS-MT models are permissively licensed, this default backend is **commercial-safe** (the CC-BY-NC NLLB-200 models are intentionally not the default). Language detection uses [py3langid](https://github.com/adbar/py3langid), a fast BSD-licensed identifier that ships its own model and runs entirely offline.

The catalog exposes a small, focused function surface. The scalar `translate(text, target)` translates a string into an ISO 639-1 target language while auto-detecting the source per row, and the `translate(text, target, source)` overload lets you pin an explicit source language. `detect_lang(text)` returns the detected ISO 639-1 language code of each value. For high-throughput workloads, the table function `translate_all(rows, id, target, source)` streams a whole table of rows through the model in batches — reusing the cached model across the entire scan and carrying an `id` column through so results join straight back to the source. Typical uses include translating user-generated content, normalizing multilingual product catalogs and support tickets, building localization pipelines, and routing or filtering rows by detected language. Source, issues, and full documentation live in the [project repository](https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-translate).

example_queries.description: Translate an English sentence into Spanish (auto-detecting the source).
example_queries.sql: SELECT translate.main.translate('The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.', 'es')

example_queries.description: Translate a Spanish string back into English with an explicit source.
example_queries.sql: SELECT translate.main.translate('Hola, mundo.', 'en', 'es')

example_queries.description: Detect the ISO 639-1 language code of a French phrase.
example_queries.sql: SELECT translate.main.detect_lang('Bonjour le monde')

example_queries.description: Batch-translate a table of rows, projecting the id and its translation.
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, translation FROM translate.main.translate_all((SELECT 1 AS id, 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.' AS body), id := 'id', target := 'es', source := 'en')

example_queries.description: Look up the ISO 639-1 code for a language by its English name.
example_queries.sql: SELECT code FROM translate.main.languages WHERE name = 'Spanish'

example_queries.description: Detect the language of each message and label it with its English name from the languages reference view (returns fr/French, de/German, es/Spanish, en/English).
example_queries.sql: WITH detected AS (SELECT id, body, translate.main.detect_lang(body) AS code FROM (VALUES (1, 'Bonjour le monde, comment allez-vous ce matin?'), (2, 'Guten Morgen, wie geht es Ihnen heute?'), (3, 'Hola, mucho gusto en conocerte.'), (4, 'The weather is lovely today.')) AS messages(id, body)) SELECT d.id, d.code, l.name AS language FROM detected AS d LEFT JOIN translate.main.languages AS l ON l.code = d.code ORDER BY d.id

example_queries.description: Use detect_lang to pick out the Spanish rows of a mixed-language review table and translate only those into English with an explicit 'es' source (the English review is filtered out; reviews 1 and 3 come back translated).
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, body, translate.main.translate(body, 'en', 'es') AS english FROM (VALUES (1, 'El envío llegó tarde y la caja estaba dañada.'), (2, 'Great product, works as described.'), (3, 'Muy buena calidad, lo recomiendo.')) AS reviews(id, body) WHERE translate.main.detect_lang(body) = 'es' ORDER BY id

example_queries.description: Normalize a mixed Spanish/English review table to English in one batch, auto-detecting each row's source and naming it via the languages view (Spanish rows are translated; the English row passes through unchanged).
example_queries.sql: SELECT t.id, l.name AS source_language, t.text, t.translation FROM translate.main.translate_all((SELECT id, body FROM (VALUES (1, 'El envío llegó tarde y la caja estaba dañada.'), (2, 'Great product, works as described.'), (3, 'Muy buena calidad, lo recomiendo.')) AS reviews(id, body)), id := 'id', target := 'en', source := 'auto') AS t LEFT JOIN translate.main.languages AS l ON l.code = t.src_lang ORDER BY t.id

example_queries.description: Count how many reference languages are listed.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS n FROM translate.main.languages

example_queries.description: Detect the language of a German greeting (returns 'de').
example_queries.sql: SELECT translate.main.detect_lang('Guten Morgen')

example_queries.description: Translate an English sentence into Spanish (auto-detect source).
example_queries.sql: SELECT translate.main.translate('The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.', 'es') AS es;

example_queries.description: Translate a Spanish string back into English with an explicit source.
example_queries.sql: SELECT translate.main.translate('Hola, mundo.', 'en', 'es') AS en;

example_queries.description: Detect the ISO 639-1 language code of a French phrase.
example_queries.sql: SELECT translate.main.detect_lang('Bonjour le monde') AS lang;

## Machine Translation & Language Detection

Offline neural machine translation and language identification exposed as SQL over Apache Arrow. Everything runs locally — no API keys and no per-query network once a language package is cached.

**What you can do here**

- Translate a string into a target language, with the source auto-detected or supplied explicitly.
- Detect the ISO 639-1 language code of any text.
- Batch-translate a whole column of rows in one streamed pass, reusing a single cached model and carrying an id column through.

See each function's own documentation for arguments, worked examples, and output columns.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# languages

A browsable reference of common **ISO 639-1** language codes and their English names, so you can discover the valid `source` / `target` values for `translate`, `translate_all`, and the codes `detect_lang` returns without guessing.

**Columns**
- `code` (`VARCHAR`): the two-letter ISO 639-1 code, e.g. `'es'`, `'fr'`, `'de'`.
- `name` (`VARCHAR`): the English name of the language.

**When to use**: browse it to find a code, or join it to a `detect_lang` result to label detected rows with a human-readable language name.

**Note**: this is a curated, representative list of languages the default Argos / OPUS-MT backend commonly supports — not an exhaustive catalog, and not a guarantee that every `source -> target` pair has an installable package (that is resolved lazily at translate time).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## languages

- The list is representative, not exhaustive; package availability for a specific pair is resolved at translate time.

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# translate_all

Batched, table-in / table-out translation: stream a table of `(id, text)` rows through the local neural model and emit `(id, text, translation, src_lang)`. This is the **throughput path** — it batches whole Arrow record batches and reuses the per-process model cache, so a single language-package load serves the entire scan.

**Inputs (named arguments)**
- `data` (table): a subquery selecting exactly one text column plus, optionally, the id column.
- `target` (`VARCHAR`, required): ISO 639-1 target language code.
- `source` (`VARCHAR`, default `'auto'`): ISO 639-1 source code, or `'auto'` to detect per row.
- `id` (`VARCHAR`, optional): name of a passthrough id column carried through unchanged so the result joins back to the source.

**Output columns**: `id` (only when `id :=` given), `text`, `translation`, `src_lang`.

**When to use**: translating an entire column/table efficiently. Prefer this over the `translate` scalar for anything beyond a few rows.

**Behavior & edge cases**: the input must contain exactly one non-id text column (errors otherwise); `NULL` text yields `NULL` translation and `src_lang`; `target` is required.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## translate_all(data, id, target, source)

Batch-translate a streamed table, carrying an id column through so the result joins back to the source. The high-throughput counterpart to the `translate` scalar.

### Usage

Call it in a `FROM` clause over a subquery of rows, passing the named arguments `id := 'id', target := 'es', source := 'auto'`. See this function's example queries for complete, runnable statements.

### Notes

- Named arguments are `id`, `target`, `source` (not `to`/`from`, which are SQL reserved words).
- The input must have exactly one non-id text column.
- See the returned columns documented below.

vgi.example_queries.description: Batch-translate a table of rows from English to Spanish, carrying the id through and projecting just the id and its translation.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id, translation FROM translate.main.translate_all((SELECT 1 AS id, 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.' AS body), id := 'id', target := 'es', source := 'en')

vgi.example_queries.description: Normalize a mixed Spanish/English review table to English in one batch, auto-detecting each row's source and naming it via the languages view (Spanish rows are translated; the English row passes through unchanged).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT t.id, l.name AS source_language, t.text, t.translation FROM translate.main.translate_all((SELECT id, body FROM (VALUES (1, 'El envío llegó tarde y la caja estaba dañada.'), (2, 'Great product, works as described.'), (3, 'Muy buena calidad, lo recomiendo.')) AS reviews(id, body)), id := 'id', target := 'en', source := 'auto') AS t LEFT JOIN translate.main.languages AS l ON l.code = t.src_lang ORDER BY t.id

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
The result always contains `text`, `translation`, and `src_lang`. When an `id :=` column is given it is prepended as a passthrough column so the output joins straight back to the source; otherwise the result begins at `text`.

### With an `id :=` passthrough column

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| id | BIGINT | Passthrough id column, copied unchanged so the result joins back to the source. Its type mirrors the input id column (shown here as `BIGINT`). |
| text | VARCHAR | The original source text. |
| translation | VARCHAR | The translated text. |
| src_lang | VARCHAR | Source language used (detected when `source := 'auto'`). |

### Without an id column

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| text | VARCHAR | The original source text. |
| translation | VARCHAR | The translated text. |
| src_lang | VARCHAR | Source language used (detected when `source := 'auto'`). |

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# detect_lang

Detect and return the **ISO 639-1 language code** of each input string using a bundled, fully-offline language-identification model (`py3langid`). No download, ever.

**Inputs**
- `text` (`VARCHAR`): the string whose language to identify. `NULL` passes through as `NULL`.

**Output**: `VARCHAR` — a two-letter ISO 639-1 code such as `'en'`, `'fr'`, `'de'`; empty/whitespace-only input yields `'und'` (undetermined).

**When to use**: route, filter, or tag rows by language before translating, or to populate a language column. Detection is per row and most reliable on longer text; very short strings can be ambiguous.

**Behavior & edge cases**: deterministic and offline; pair with `translate` (passing the detected code as the source) for an explicit-source translation pipeline.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## detect_lang(text)

Return the **ISO 639-1** language code of a string using a bundled offline identifier (`py3langid`, BSD). Never downloads.

### Usage

```sql
SELECT translate.main.detect_lang('Bonjour le monde'); -- fr
```

### Notes

- Empty/whitespace input returns `und` (undetermined).
- `NULL` input yields `NULL`.
- Most reliable on longer text; short strings can be ambiguous.

AS messages(id, body)) SELECT d.id, d.code, l.name AS language FROM detected AS d LEFT JOIN translate.main.languages AS l ON l.code = d.code ORDER BY d.id

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
# translate (explicit source)

Translate a text value from a **known source language** into a target language using a local neural machine-translation model. This is the three-argument overload `translate(text, target, source)`.

**Inputs**
- `text` (`VARCHAR`): the string to translate. `NULL` passes through as `NULL`.
- `target` (`VARCHAR` constant): ISO 639-1 target language code.
- `source` (`VARCHAR` constant): ISO 639-1 source language code, or `'auto'` to detect per row.

**Output**: `VARCHAR` translated text.

**When to use**: prefer this overload when the source language is known (skips detection and avoids mis-detection on short strings). Pass `'auto'` as the third argument to fall back to detection (scalar arguments are positional; `source := 'auto'` does not bind). For large tables use the `translate_all` table function instead.

**Behavior & edge cases**: the first call for a language pair lazily installs and caches the Argos package; subsequent calls are offline.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## translate(text, target, source)

Translate a string from an **explicit** `source` language into `target`. Skips language detection, which is faster and more reliable for short strings of a known language.

### Usage

```sql
SELECT translate.main.translate('Hola, mundo.', 'en', 'es'); -- Hello, world.
```

### Notes

- `source` / `target` are ISO 639-1 codes; pass `'auto'` as the third argument to detect instead (arguments are positional).
- `NULL` input yields `NULL`.

workers.tagline: Python VGI worker for US Treasury debt, cash balances, fiscal statements and interest rates
workers.subtitle: Query federal debt, operating cash, deposits, withdrawals and public debt transactions, and discover Fiscal Data endpoint fields.
workers.summary: US Treasury Fiscal Data as SQL tables, covering federal debt, operating cash, deposits and withdrawals, public debt transactions, monthly statements and average interest rates, with exact decimal amounts. No API key needed.
workers.doc_md:
# vgi-treasury

Query federal debt, operating cash, deposits, withdrawals and public debt transactions, and discover Fiscal Data endpoint fields. Treasury Fiscal Data is public and needs no upstream API key. Dates and currency amounts are typed, including exact decimals. Use date arguments and filters_json to reduce upstream work. page_size controls request size and max_rows=0 retrieves all matches. NULL arguments are rejected. Missing optional response fields return NULL. Upstream errors fail the query; SQL WHERE filters are local.

Queries use bounded HTTP responses and retries. Credentials stay out of continuation state. See README.md for deployment and operational limits.

## Sources and references

- [U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data](https://fiscaldata.treasury.gov/)
- [Fiscal Data API documentation](https://fiscaldata.treasury.gov/api-documentation/)
- [Fiscal Data dataset catalog](https://fiscaldata.treasury.gov/datasets/)

example_queries.title: debt_to_penny_endpoint
example_queries.description: Look up the Fiscal Data endpoint behind debt_to_penny in the worker's curated dataset catalog (no network request)
example_queries.sql: SELECT dataset, endpoint FROM treasury.main.datasets() WHERE dataset = 'debt_to_penny';

example_queries.description: Discover fiscal datasets
example_queries.sql: SELECT dataset, endpoint, amount_units FROM treasury.main.datasets() ORDER BY dataset

example_queries.description: Inspect endpoint fields
example_queries.sql: SELECT field_name, source_type, source_format FROM treasury.main.fields('v2/accounting/od/debt_to_penny') ORDER BY field_name

example_queries.description: Read arbitrary fiscal records
example_queries.sql: SELECT record_date, record_json FROM treasury.main.records('v2/accounting/od/debt_to_penny', start_date := '2024-01-02', end_date := '2024-01-03') ORDER BY record_date

example_queries.description: Label every field of one raw record from an uncurated endpoint (the second line of Monthly Treasury Statement Table 9 for January 2024, Individual Income Taxes): fields() supplies each source field's label and type, records() the original JSON value as text
example_queries.sql: SELECT f.field_name, f.label, f.source_type, r.record_json ->> f.field_name AS source_value FROM treasury.main.records('v1/accounting/mts/mts_table_9', start_date := '2024-01-31', end_date := '2024-01-31', page_size := 1, start_page := 2, max_rows := 1) AS r CROSS JOIN treasury.main.fields('v1/accounting/mts/mts_table_9') AS f ORDER BY f.field_name

example_queries.description: Federal debt to the penny
example_queries.sql: SELECT record_date, tot_pub_debt_out_amt FROM treasury.main.debt_to_penny(start_date := '2024-01-02', end_date := '2024-01-03') ORDER BY record_date

example_queries.description: Reconcile each day's change in total public debt (debt_to_penny, exact dollars) with the Daily Treasury Statement's issues minus redemptions (public_debt_transactions, USD millions scaled to dollars); the gap stays within a few million dollars because statement amounts are rounded
example_queries.sql: WITH debt AS (SELECT record_date, tot_pub_debt_out_amt - lag(tot_pub_debt_out_amt) OVER (ORDER BY record_date) AS debt_change_usd FROM treasury.main.debt_to_penny(start_date := '2024-01-02', end_date := '2024-01-12')), flows AS (SELECT record_date, sum(CASE transaction_type WHEN 'Issues' THEN transaction_today_amt ELSE -transaction_today_amt END) * 1000000 AS net_issuance_usd FROM treasury.main.public_debt_transactions(start_date := '2024-01-03', end_date := '2024-01-12') GROUP BY record_date) SELECT f.record_date, f.net_issuance_usd, d.debt_change_usd, d.debt_change_usd - f.net_issuance_usd AS gap_usd FROM flows AS f JOIN debt AS d USING (record_date) ORDER BY f.record_date

example_queries.description: Operating cash balance
example_queries.sql: SELECT record_date, account_type, open_today_bal FROM treasury.main.operating_cash_balance(start_date := '2024-01-02', end_date := '2024-01-02') ORDER BY record_date, src_line_nbr

example_queries.description: Compare the Treasury General Account closing cash balance (operating_cash_balance; since April 2022 the closing balance is the open_today_bal of the Closing Balance row, in USD millions) with total public debt outstanding (debt_to_penny) for each business day, as a percentage of debt
example_queries.sql: WITH tga AS (SELECT record_date, open_today_bal * 1000000 AS tga_close_usd FROM treasury.main.operating_cash_balance(start_date := '2024-01-02', end_date := '2024-01-12') WHERE account_type = 'Treasury General Account (TGA) Closing Balance') SELECT d.record_date, d.tot_pub_debt_out_amt, t.tga_close_usd, round(100 * t.tga_close_usd / d.tot_pub_debt_out_amt, 2) AS tga_pct_of_debt FROM treasury.main.debt_to_penny(start_date := '2024-01-02', end_date := '2024-01-12') AS d JOIN tga AS t USING (record_date) ORDER BY d.record_date

example_queries.description: Cash deposits and withdrawals
example_queries.sql: SELECT transaction_type, transaction_catg, transaction_today_amt FROM treasury.main.deposits_withdrawals(start_date := '2024-01-02', end_date := '2024-01-02') ORDER BY src_line_nbr

example_queries.description: Public debt transactions
example_queries.sql: SELECT transaction_type, security_type, transaction_today_amt FROM treasury.main.public_debt_transactions(start_date := '2024-01-02', end_date := '2024-01-02') ORDER BY src_line_nbr

example_queries.description: Monthly Treasury receipts and outlays
example_queries.sql: SELECT classification_desc, current_month_gross_rcpt_amt, current_month_gross_outly_amt FROM treasury.main.monthly_statement(start_date := '2024-01-31', end_date := '2024-01-31') WHERE data_type_cd='D' ORDER BY src_line_nbr

example_queries.description: Average interest rates
example_queries.sql: SELECT security_desc, avg_interest_rate_amt FROM treasury.main.average_interest_rates(start_date := '2024-01-31', end_date := '2024-01-31') ORDER BY security_desc

Using the Treasury worker, compare two measures for the week of 2024-01-08 to 2024-01-12: the Daily Treasury Statement's net public debt issuance (all Issues minus all Redemptions across every security type, summed over those five business days) and the change in total public debt outstanding from its 2024-01-05 value to its 2024-01-12 value. Return one row with exactly the columns net_issuance_musd and debt_change_musd, both in whole USD millions as BIGINT (round the debt change to the nearest million).

# TSA checkpoint throughput

Passenger volumes screened at Transportation Security Administration checkpoints, from [tsa.gov](https://www.tsa.gov/travel/passenger-volumes):

- **National daily counts** since 2019, from TSA's passenger-volumes pages.
- **Hourly counts per airport checkpoint**, parsed from the weekly throughput PDFs in TSA's [FOIA reading room](https://www.tsa.gov/foia/readingroom).

Nothing here is real time: the national daily count is posted with a lag of about one to three days, and the hourly checkpoint reports arrive as weekly PDFs one to two weeks after the week ends.

Data is fetched when a query needs it and cached on disk. TSA publications are U.S. government works and in the public domain.
workers.readme_sql:
-- Thanksgiving week, nationwide, against the same days a year earlier.
SELECT date, travelers,
       lag(travelers, 364) OVER (ORDER BY date) AS same_weekday_last_year
FROM tsa.main.daily_throughput
WHERE date >= DATE '2024-11-01'
QUALIFY date >= DATE '2025-11-20' AND date < DATE '2025-12-03'
ORDER BY date;

-- Which weeks of hourly data exist?
SELECT start_date, end_date FROM tsa.main.throughput_reports ORDER BY end_date DESC LIMIT 3;

-- When are JFK's checkpoints busiest? (downloads and parses one ~5 MB PDF on first use)
SELECT hour, sum(throughput) AS passengers
FROM tsa.main.checkpoint_throughput(DATE '2026-11-01', DATE '2026-11-07', airport := 'JFK')
GROUP BY hour ORDER BY hour;

attach_options.name: cache_dir
attach_options.description: Directory for cached tsa.gov pages and parsed weekly reports (about 1 MB of Parquet per week). Default: the per-user cache directory, e.g. ~/.cache/vgi-tsa or ~/Library/Caches/vgi-tsa.

attach_options.name: base_url
attach_options.description: Where pages and PDFs are fetched from: https://www.tsa.gov (default), a mirror URL, or a local directory laid out like tsa.gov (travel/passenger-volumes/index.html, travel/passenger-volumes/<year>/index.html, foia/readingroom/page-<n>.html, sites/default/files/foia-readingroom/<report>.pdf).

attach_options.name: user_agent
attach_options.description: User-Agent sent to tsa.gov (default 'vgi-tsa/0.1 (+https://query.farm)').

attach_options.name: max_reports
attach_options.description: Most weekly report PDFs one checkpoint_throughput query may download and parse (default 8; each is ~5 MB and ~15 s). Cached weeks do not count.

attach_options.name: offline
attach_options.description: Never touch the network: use only what is cached, even if stale (default false).

example_queries.description: The ten airports that screened the most passengers in the week of 1 November 2026
example_queries.sql: SELECT airport, sum(throughput) AS passengers FROM tsa.main.checkpoint_throughput(DATE '2026-11-01', DATE '2026-11-07') GROUP BY airport ORDER BY passengers DESC LIMIT 10

example_queries.sql: SELECT hour, sum(throughput) AS passengers FROM tsa.main.checkpoint_throughput(DATE '2026-11-01', DATE '2026-11-07', airport := 'JFK') GROUP BY hour ORDER BY hour

example_queries.description: Confirm a weekly report parsed cleanly: 0 rejects means every row passed validation
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS rejects, count(DISTINCT reason) AS reasons, min(page) AS first_page FROM tsa.main.checkpoint_throughput_rejects(DATE '2026-11-01', DATE '2026-11-07')

example_queries.sql: SELECT date, travelers, round(avg(travelers) OVER (ORDER BY date ROWS 6 PRECEDING)) AS seven_day_avg FROM tsa.main.daily_throughput WHERE date >= DATE '2025-11-01' AND date < DATE '2025-12-15' ORDER BY date

example_queries.description: The five most recent weekly checkpoint reports

tags.vgi.doc_llm: TSA passenger screening volumes at two grains. The national grain is one count per day of everyone screened at TSA checkpoints, back to 2019; it is cheap to read (one HTML page per year) and is the right source for nationwide trends, holidays and year-over-year comparisons. The checkpoint grain is passengers per hour per airport checkpoint, parsed from TSA's weekly FOIA PDF reports (2017 onward, about 420 airports); each week costs a ~5 MB download and ~15 s of parsing on first use, and the max_reports ATTACH option (default 8) caps how many uncached weeks one query may fetch, so ask for short date ranges and check which weeks exist before asking for recent ones. Airports are IATA codes, states USPS codes, hours local airport time. Rows the PDF parser cannot validate are counted and inspectable, never silently dropped. Nothing here is real time: the national daily count is posted with a lag of about one to three days, and the hourly checkpoint reports arrive as weekly PDFs one to two weeks after the week ends.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per weekly 'TSA Throughput' PDF in TSA's FOIA reading room (about 510 weeks, 2017 onward, plus two January 2015 files), newest posting first in the source. Columns: start_date and end_date (the week covered, parsed from the title; NULL if the title cannot be read), title, url, listed_size_mb, cached (already parsed locally), parsed_rows and rejected_rows (NULL until parsed). Use max(end_date) to find the latest week checkpoint_throughput() can return; TSA posts each week one to two weeks after it ends, and some weeks are missing. A filter like `end_date >= DATE '2026-01-01'` is pushed down and stops paging through the index early; the full listing reads all ~27 index pages once, then is cached for 6 hours.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per day since 2019-01-01: date (`DATE`) and travelers (`BIGINT`), the number of people TSA screened at checkpoints nationwide, as listed on tsa.gov/travel/passenger-volumes. TSA updates it on weekdays, usually 1-3 days behind, so the newest dates are missing and recent days can be revised; it is not real time. Comparisons on date (=, <, <=, >, >=, BETWEEN) are pushed down and decide which yearly pages are fetched; use them instead of year(date) for speed. The current year is cached for 3 hours, past years for 30 days. For hourly or per-airport detail use checkpoint_throughput().

functions.name: checkpoint_throughput
functions.comment: Hourly passengers screened per airport checkpoint from TSA's weekly FOIA reports (weeks late)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: checkpoint_throughput(start_date `DATE`, end_date `DATE`, airport := 'ATL', state := 'GA') returns one row per date, hour (0-23, local airport time as printed), airport (IATA), checkpoint, with airport_name, city, state (USPS), throughput (people screened that hour) and report_url. Data comes from the weekly 'TSA Throughput' PDFs in TSA's FOIA reading room (2017 onward, about 420 airports): the newest week is usually one to two weeks old, so check max(end_date) in throughput_reports first. Each week not yet cached is downloaded and parsed on first use (~5 MB, ~15 s); one query may need at most max_reports uncached weeks (ATTACH option, default 8), otherwise it fails with a message saying how many it needs. airport and state filter rows before they leave the worker. Rows whose cells fail validation are left out and counted in throughput_reports.rejected_rows; see them with checkpoint_throughput_rejects().
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## checkpoint_throughput(start_date, end_date, airport := , state := )

Hourly passengers screened per checkpoint, parsed from TSA's weekly [FOIA throughput reports](https://www.tsa.gov/foia/readingroom). Reports appear one to two weeks after the week ends. The first query for a week downloads and parses its PDF (~15 s); `max_reports` (ATTACH option, default 8) bounds how many a query may fetch.

workers.title: TypeSafe System One
workers.tagline: A VGI worker exposing TypeSafe System One questions (choice, noul, score) to DuckDB/SQL as LATERAL-joinable table functions
workers.subtitle: Classify rows, answer yes/no questions and score text from SQL with calibrated confidence
workers.summary: TypeSafe System One questions (choice, noul, score) as LATERAL-joinable table functions
workers.doc_md:
TypeSafe evaluates typed questions against a *state* — the content being judged — and answers with structured values rather than prose.

### The two things you write

A **state** is what you are judging: a piece of text, a struct built from several columns, a whole row, or a list. Descriptive field names help, because they tell the model how the parts relate.

A **question** has a type, an instruction, and usually criteria. There are three types. A *choice* picks one option from a set you define and reports a probability for every option. A *noul* answers yes or no as a probability between 0 and 1, where 0.5 means genuinely undecided. A *score* places the state on an ordered scale you define, and returns a probability-weighted position rather than a single rung.

### Reading an answer

Every judgment except a noul carries a `confidence`: how concentrated the probability distribution was. It is the field to filter on when you want to route the clear cases automatically and send the rest to a person. A noul needs no such field, because a probability near 0.5 already says the model could not decide.

### Authentication

Credentials come from a redacted DuckDB secret; its optional `base_url` field points the worker at another endpoint, such as the bundled mock server (`uv run vgi-typesafe-mock`). See a question function's examples for the statement.

### Cost

One API request per distinct piece of work in an input batch — a state together with the questions asked of it — however many questions that is, so asking five things about a row costs the same as asking one. Requests within a batch run concurrently; rate-limit and overload responses are retried with backoff.

### Sources and references

- [TypeSafe](https://typesafe.ai) — the service that produces the judgments.
- [TypeSafe documentation](https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction) and the [System One model](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/system-one) the questions run on.
- [Quickstart](https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction/quickstart) — how to create the API key the `typesafe` secret holds.

example_queries.title: ask_shapes_its_columns_from_the_questions
example_queries.description: The result columns are built from the `questions` argument at bind time — one typed STRUCT per question, then `usage`. DESCRIBE only binds, so this runs without an API key and issues no request.
example_queries.sql: DESCRIBE SELECT * FROM typesafe.main.ask('a lost package', questions => {'dept': {'type': 'choice', 'instructions': 'Which team?', 'criteria': {'shipping': 'Delays and lost packages', 'billing': 'Invoices'}}, 'urgent': {'type': 'noul', 'instructions': 'Does this need a reply today?'}});

example_queries.description: Route, flag and grade every row in one request each
example_queries.sql: SELECT t.id, a.dept.choice, a.urgent.noul FROM (VALUES (1, 'My package is lost')) t(id, body), LATERAL typesafe.main.ask(t.body, questions => {'dept': {'type': 'choice', 'instructions': 'Which team?', 'criteria': {'shipping': 'Lost packages', 'billing': 'Invoices'}}, 'urgent': {'type': 'noul', 'instructions': 'Needs a reply today?'}}) a

example_queries.description: Classify one text column with the single-question shorthand
example_queries.sql: SELECT choice, confidence FROM typesafe.main.choice('I was charged twice', instructions => 'Which team should handle this?', criteria => MAP {'shipping': 'Lost packages', 'billing': 'Invoices'})

example_queries.description: Rate one text column on an ordered scale
example_queries.sql: SELECT score, confidence FROM typesafe.main.score('The whole site is down', instructions => 'How severe is this?', criteria => ['minor question', 'disruptive delay', 'critical outage'])

example_queries.description: Keep only the rows a yes/no question is true of
example_queries.sql: SELECT t.body FROM (VALUES ('My package never arrived'), ('Thanks for the quick refund')) t(body) WHERE typesafe.main.is_true(t.body, 'Is this message about a lost package?') > 0.5

example_queries.description: List the models a question may name
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, description, release_date FROM typesafe.main.models() ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Rate how bad each delivery problem is, for only the messages confidently routed to shipping
example_queries.sql: WITH routed AS (SELECT t.body, c.choice, c.confidence FROM (VALUES ('My package never arrived'), ('The delivery is delayed and the package looks lost'), ('Delivery status says delayed by a week'), ('I was charged twice on my invoice')) t(body), LATERAL typesafe.main.choice(t.body, instructions => 'Which team should handle this?', criteria => MAP {'shipping': 'Delivery status, delays, lost packages', 'billing': 'Charges, invoices, payment problems'}) c) SELECT r.body, s.score, s.confidence FROM routed r, LATERAL typesafe.main.score(r.body, instructions => 'How bad is this delivery problem?', criteria => ['short delay', 'long delay', 'lost package']) s WHERE r.choice = 'shipping' AND r.confidence > 0.8 ORDER BY s.score DESC, r.body

example_queries.description: Route every message to a team, then keep only the billing messages that ask for a refund
example_queries.sql: WITH routed AS (SELECT t.body, c.choice, typesafe.main.is_true(t.body, 'Is the customer asking for a refund?') AS refund FROM (VALUES ('I was charged twice, please refund me'), ('My invoice shows a wrong charge'), ('My package never arrived')) t(body), LATERAL typesafe.main.choice(t.body, instructions => 'Which team should handle this?', criteria => MAP {'shipping': 'Delivery status, delays, lost packages', 'billing': 'Charges, invoices, payment problems'}) c) SELECT body, refund FROM routed WHERE choice = 'billing' AND refund > 0.5 ORDER BY refund DESC, body

example_queries.description: Route each message, then ask it the follow-up question that belongs to the team it was routed to
example_queries.sql: WITH routed AS (SELECT t.body, c.choice FROM (VALUES ('My package never arrived'), ('I was charged twice, please refund me'), ('My invoice shows a wrong charge')) t(body), LATERAL typesafe.main.choice(t.body, instructions => 'Which team should handle this?', criteria => MAP {'shipping': 'Delivery status, delays, lost packages', 'billing': 'Charges, invoices, payment problems'}) c), follow_ups(team, questions) AS (VALUES ('shipping', '{"lost": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Is the package lost?"}}'), ('billing', '{"refund": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Is the customer asking for a refund?"}}')) SELECT r.body, r.choice AS team, a.answers FROM routed r JOIN follow_ups f ON f.team = r.choice, LATERAL typesafe.main.ask_dynamic(r.body, f.questions) a ORDER BY r.body
