example_queries.description: Ask each row the questions that row carries
example_queries.sql: SELECT t.id, a.answers->'dept'->>'choice' AS dept, a.answers->'urgent'->>'noul' AS urgent FROM (VALUES (1, 'My package is lost and delivery is delayed', '{"dept": {"type": "choice", "instructions": "Which team should handle this?", "criteria": {"shipping": "Delivery status, delays, lost packages", "billing": "Charges, invoices, payment problems"}}}'), (2, 'Thanks, just one routine question', '{"urgent": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Does this need a reply today?"}}')) t(id, body, questions), LATERAL typesafe.main.ask_dynamic(t.body, t.questions) a ORDER BY t.id

agent_tasks: Route this support message to the right team — shipping, billing or returns — and tell me how confident the model was: 'My package never arrived and the tracking has not updated in a week.'

For the message 'I was charged twice and nobody has replied to me in three days', I want three things at once: which team should handle it, whether the customer sounds angry, and how severe it is on a three-point scale. Do it without paying for three separate API calls.

My queue stores the question it wants asked alongside each row, and they are not all the same kind of question — one row wants its ticket routed to a team, the next wants a yes/no. I cannot hard-code one fixed set of questions for the whole query. How do I ask each row the question it carries, and read the answers back?

Classify these two messages into shipping or billing — 'my package is lost in delivery' and 'my invoice shows a wrong charge' — but only keep the rows the model was confident about, so the rest can go to a human.
I have rows where several columns matter together — a message, a customer tier and an order id. Ask one yes/no question about the whole row rather than just the message column.
Before I run this against real data: what columns and types come back if I ask a choice question and a yes/no question about the same row?

For these two messages — 'My package never arrived and nobody has replied in three days' and 'Thanks, just a routine question' — I do not want a yes or a no. I want to know how likely each one is to need a reply today, so I can pick my own cut-off later.
Rate 'The whole site is down and no orders can be placed' on a three-point severity scale running from a minor question up to a critical outage, and tell me how sure the model was.

From these two messages — 'My package never arrived' and 'Thanks for the quick refund' — keep only the ones about a lost package. I want the AI judgment inline in the WHERE clause, not joined in as a separate table.

Route these five messages to the shipping team (delivery status, delays, lost packages) or the billing team (charges, invoices, payment problems): 'I was charged twice, please refund me', 'My invoice shows a wrong charge', 'Please refund the duplicate charge on my invoice', 'My package never arrived and I want a refund' and 'My package never arrived'. Then tell me, per team, how many of its messages are more likely than not asking for a refund. Return one row per team with two columns: team (VARCHAR) and refund_requests (BIGINT).
I do not want to be stuck on whatever model is the default. Which models can I actually name here, and when was each one published?

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Turn a row into a typed judgment with a calibrated confidence, instead of into prose. You supply the content being judged — a text column, a struct built from several columns, or the whole row — and one or more questions. A question either picks an option from a set you define, answers yes/no as a probability, or places the row on a scale you define. Ask several things about the same row together and they cost one request, not one each. Everything here takes the content as its first argument, so it composes under a correlated LATERAL to judge a whole table; filter on the reported confidence to route the clear cases and leave the rest to a person. Requires a `typesafe` secret.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Typed judgments over rows, backed by TypeSafe's System One models.

### Choosing a shape

Asking several things about the same row is cheaper as one call than as several — the cost is one request per state, whatever it carries — so prefer the combined form when you want more than one judgment. Reach for a single-question form when you want one judgment and flat columns rather than a `STRUCT` to unpack. Reach for the scalar when the judgment is a yes/no probability you want to drop straight into a predicate: it is the same request either way, so this is about how the SQL reads, not what is possible.

One form goes further and takes the questions themselves as a per-row column, so different rows can be asked different things. It pays for that by returning its answers as JSON rather than as typed columns, which makes it the one to reach for last — and only when the questions genuinely vary.

### What they share

All of them take the content as their first argument, which makes them blended table functions: one registration serves a literal call, an implicit lateral and an explicit one alike. Each produces exactly one output row per input row; a NULL input is never sent and answers NULL; identical inputs within a batch are asked once; and an API failure raises rather than quietly becoming NULL, which would be indistinguishable from a NULL input.

### Before you spend anything

A question written as a plan-time argument is validated when the query is planned, so a malformed one fails before a single row is billed. A question that arrives as data can only be checked as each row is read, and its errors say which row. `DESCRIBE` a call to see its result columns without issuing a request at all.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Ask TypeSafe questions that are chosen per row rather than fixed for the whole query, and read each row's answers back as JSON. Both positional arguments are per-row input columns, so a column of questions may carry a different set — different names, different types, different criteria — on every row. That flexibility costs the typed columns `ask()` gives you: because no shape is known when the query is planned, all of a row's answers arrive inside one JSON value that DuckDB's JSON functions take apart. Prefer `ask()` whenever the questions are the same for every row; reach for this only when they genuinely vary, such as a rules table joined to the rows it governs. The question types and their answers are `ask()`'s: a choice reports the chosen option with a confidence and a distribution, a noul reports a probability, a score reports a position on the scale. Cost is one request per distinct pairing of content and questions. Needs a `typesafe` secret.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Per-row questions, answered as JSON.

### When to reach for this instead of `ask()`

`ask()` is almost always the one you want. Its questions are fixed when the query is planned, so it can give you one typed column per question — a `STRUCT` whose fields suit that question's type, readable with a dot. `ask_dynamic()` trades those typed columns away. Here the questions are a per-row input column, so two rows in one scan may ask entirely different things, and nothing about the result shape can be known at plan time. Everything a row was told therefore comes back inside one JSON column that you take apart yourself.

That makes this the more awkward of the two, and it should not be anyone's default. Use it when the questions genuinely vary per row: a rules table joined to the rows it governs, a work queue where each item carries its own rubric, questions assembled by an application. If every row asks the same thing, use `ask()` and keep the typed columns.

### The two positional arguments

Both are per-row input columns. The first is the content being judged, in the same shapes `ask()` accepts: text, a `STRUCT` (the row alias itself works), a `LIST` or a `MAP`, sent to the API as the equivalent JSON object or array.

The second carries that row's questions, in either of two forms.

- JSON text is the form to prefer when the questions really differ: each row carries its own shape verbatim, and nothing is reconciled against any other row.
- A `STRUCT` or `MAP` column works too, and reads better when the questions vary only in their wording. DuckDB unifies a column's type across rows, though, so a question only some rows ask is padded onto all of them as NULL. Those NULLs are dropped before the request, so that much is harmless — but two rows that give one question name two different criteria shapes cannot be unified at all, and DuckDB rejects the query before this worker sees it.

`model =>` and `concurrency =>` stay named, because a blended function's positional arguments are input columns rather than plan-time constants.

### Reading the answers

The `answers` column is a JSON object keyed by question name, and each value is the answer object for that question's type:

| Question type | Answer object |
| --- | --- |
| choice | `choice`, `confidence`, and `probabilities` keyed by option |
| noul | `noul`, a probability where near 1 is yes and 0.5 is genuinely undecided |
| score | `score`, `confidence`, and `probabilities` keyed by level number, where 0 is the first criterion |

Keys in JSON are text, so a score level reads back as the digits of its number. DuckDB's JSON operators and the `json_extract` family are what take all this apart; this function's example queries show the exact spelling.

What a row cost does not vary in shape, so it stays in real columns beside the JSON rather than inside it: `model`, `input_tokens` and `output_tokens`.

### Row semantics

Strictly one output row per input row. A NULL state — or a struct or list holding no non-null content — answers NULL and makes no request; its questions are not examined, because nothing is being asked of it. Any other row that carries no questions is an error that names the row and quotes what it held, since a per-row argument cannot be checked when the query is planned.

Repeated work is collapsed on the pair, not on the content alone: two rows asking the same thing of the same content share one request, while the same content asked two different things is two requests. Errors raise — only a NULL input answers NULL, so a failure can never be mistaken for one.

### Authentication

Credentials come from a `typesafe` secret, or from `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` in the worker's environment.

functions.name: choice
functions.comment: Classify each row into one of a set of options with a TypeSafe choice question

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Classify text into exactly one of a fixed set of options using TypeSafe's System One model. Pass the text as the positional argument — a literal, or a column under LATERAL to classify a whole table — and describe the question once with the named `instructions` and `criteria` arguments. Returns one row per input row: the chosen option, a 0-1 confidence, and the full probability distribution as a `MAP`. Filter on `confidence` to route uncertain rows to review. Needs a `typesafe` secret.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One TypeSafe choice question, asked of every input row.

### Arguments

- `state` (positional): the content to evaluate. A literal, or a column.
- `instructions =>`: the question, e.g. `'Which team should handle this?'`.
- `criteria =>`: a `MAP` from option name to a description of when it applies. Up to 255 options; include an `'other'` option when the list may be incomplete.
- `model =>`: defaults to `jev-latest`.
- `concurrency =>`: in-flight requests per batch (default 8).

### Row semantics

Strictly one output row per input row. A NULL state yields a row of NULLs and makes no request. Identical states within a batch are asked once.

### Errors

An API failure raises — it never degrades to NULL, which would be indistinguishable from a NULL input. 429 and 529 are retried with backoff first.

### Authentication

Add `base_url` to the secret to target the bundled mock endpoint. `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` in the worker's environment is the fallback.

```sql
CREATE SECRET (TYPE typesafe, api_key '...');
```

functions.name: noul
functions.comment: Answer a yes/no question about each row as a calibrated probability, not a verdict

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Ask one yes/no question about each row using TypeSafe's System One model, and get the probability that the answer is yes rather than a bare boolean. Pass the text as the positional argument — a literal, or a column under LATERAL to judge a whole table — and the question as the named `instructions` argument. Returns a `DOUBLE` between 0 and 1 per row: near 1 is yes, near 0 is no, 0.5 means the model genuinely cannot tell. Compare it against a threshold you choose, which is the point of getting a probability instead of a verdict. Optional `criteria` describes what a yes and a no look like. A noul answer has no separate confidence, because the number is already the whole answer. Use `is_true()` when you want the same number as a plain expression, and `ask()` when the row needs more than one question. Needs a `typesafe` secret.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One TypeSafe yes/no question, asked of every input row.

### Arguments

- `state` (positional): the content to evaluate. A literal, or a column.
- `instructions =>`: the question, phrased so that yes and no both make sense.
- `criteria =>`: optional. A `MAP` with a `'true'` entry describing what a yes looks like and a `'false'` entry describing what a no looks like. Either may be given on its own, and no other key is accepted — a noul has exactly two outcomes, so this is a rubric rather than a set of things to choose between.
- `model =>`: defaults to `jev-latest`.
- `concurrency =>`: in-flight requests per batch (default 8).

### Reading the answer

`noul` is a probability, not a verdict: near 1 is yes, near 0 is no, and 0.5 is the model saying the content does not decide the question. That is why there is no `confidence` column here as there is on `choice()` and `score()` — a one-number answer carries its own certainty, and 0.5 is exactly what low confidence looks like. Pick the threshold that suits the cost of being wrong, and keep the rows near 0.5 for a human.

### Row semantics

Strictly one output row per input row. A NULL state yields a row of NULLs and makes no request. Identical states within a batch are asked once.

### Errors

An API failure raises — it never degrades to NULL, which would be indistinguishable from a NULL input. 429 and 529 are retried with backoff first.

### Authentication

Add `base_url` to the secret to target the bundled mock endpoint. `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` in the worker's environment is the fallback.

```sql
CREATE SECRET (TYPE typesafe, api_key '...');
```

functions.name: score
functions.comment: Place each row on an ordered scale you describe, as a probability-weighted position

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Rate each row on an ordered scale using TypeSafe's System One model. Pass the text as the positional argument — a literal, or a column under LATERAL to rate a whole table — and describe the scale once with the named `instructions` and `criteria` arguments, where `criteria` is an ordered list of level descriptions with the lowest first. Returns one row per input row: `score`, the probability-weighted position on that scale where 0 is the first level; a 0-1 `confidence`; and the full distribution as a `MAP` keyed by level number. Because the score is weighted rather than rounded, a row the model reads as between two levels lands between them, which is what makes the column sortable. Reach for `choice()` instead when the options have no order, and `ask()` when one row needs several questions. Needs a `typesafe` secret.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One TypeSafe score question, asked of every input row.

### Arguments

- `state` (positional): the content to evaluate. A literal, or a column.
- `instructions =>`: the question, e.g. `'How severe is this?'`.
- `criteria =>`: the scale, as an ordered list of level descriptions with the lowest first. A scale needs at least two rungs, and the API caps it at ten. A level may be a plain description or a fuller rubric; what matters is that neighbouring rungs are told apart by something the content can actually show.
- `model =>`: defaults to `jev-latest`.
- `concurrency =>`: in-flight requests per batch (default 8).

### Reading the answer

`score` is a position, not a level: the probability-weighted average of the level numbers, so a row the model reads as halfway between the first and second rung scores 0.5. Round it to snap to a rung, or leave it alone to rank rows against each other. `probabilities` is keyed by level number rather than by the level's text, so the key stays meaningful when two levels read similarly. `confidence` says how concentrated that distribution was — a row spread evenly across the whole scale lands mid-scale with a low confidence, which is a different fact from a row the model is sure belongs in the middle.

### Row semantics

Strictly one output row per input row. A NULL state yields a row of NULLs and makes no request. Identical states within a batch are asked once.

### Errors

An API failure raises — it never degrades to NULL, which would be indistinguishable from a NULL input. 429 and 529 are retried with backoff first.

### Authentication

Add `base_url` to the secret to target the bundled mock endpoint. `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` in the worker's environment is the fallback.

```sql
CREATE SECRET (TYPE typesafe, api_key '...');
```

functions.name: ask
functions.comment: Ask several TypeSafe questions (choice, noul, score) about each row in one request

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Ask any number of TypeSafe questions about each row and get one typed `STRUCT` column per question, for the cost of a single API request per row. Three question types: `choice` picks one option (-> choice, confidence, probabilities), `noul` is a yes/no probability (-> noul, 0-1), `score` places the row on an ordered scale (-> score, confidence, probabilities by level). Pass the content as the positional argument — a string, a struct, or the whole row alias under LATERAL — and the questions as a struct keyed by the column name you want. Prefer this over several `choice()` calls.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
Several questions about each row, answered in one request.

### State (positional)

- `VARCHAR` is sent as a string.
- `STRUCT`, `LIST` and `MAP` are sent as the equivalent JSON object or array. The row alias itself works: `ask(t, ...)` sends every column of `t`.
- A DuckDB `JSON` column is plain text to the worker; pass `parse_json => true` to send it structured.

TypeSafe recommends an object for most requests: descriptive field names tell the model how the parts relate.

### Questions (`questions =>`)

A struct keyed by question name. Each value has `type`, `instructions`, and:

- `choice` — `criteria`: struct or `MAP` of option -> description (1-255 options).
- `score` — `criteria`: ordered list of 2-10 level descriptions, lowest first.
- `noul` — optional `criteria` with `'true'` and/or `'false'` descriptions.

`instructions` and every criterion may be a plain string or a structured object — TypeSafe accepts both, and a rubric (`{what, not_for, examples}` for a choice option, `{summary, signals}` for a score level) is what separates options a model keeps confusing. A JSON string or a `MAP` is accepted in place of the struct. Questions are validated at bind, before any row is sent.

### Output

One `STRUCT` column per question, named after it:

| Type | Fields |
| --- | --- |
| choice | `choice VARCHAR`, `confidence DOUBLE`, `probabilities MAP(VARCHAR, DOUBLE)` |
| noul | `noul DOUBLE` — near 1 is yes, near 0 is no, 0.5 is genuinely undecided |
| score | `score DOUBLE`, `confidence DOUBLE`, `probabilities MAP(INTEGER, DOUBLE)` keyed by level (0 = first) |

then `usage STRUCT(model, input_tokens, output_tokens)`. Strictly one output row per input row. A NULL state — or a struct/list with no non-null content — yields NULL answers and makes no request. Identical states in a batch are asked once. API errors raise — they never become NULL.

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
The result carries one column per entry in `questions`, named after that entry, followed by a `usage` column. A question column's type is decided by its `type` field, so there are three variants.

### A `choice` question

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <question name> | STRUCT(choice VARCHAR, confidence DOUBLE, probabilities MAP(VARCHAR, DOUBLE)) | The chosen option, how concentrated the distribution was, and every option's probability in criteria order. |

### A `noul` question

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <question name> | STRUCT(noul DOUBLE) | Probability between 0 and 1 that the answer is yes; 0.5 is genuinely undecided. |

### A `score` question

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <question name> | STRUCT(score DOUBLE, confidence DOUBLE, probabilities MAP(INTEGER, DOUBLE)) | Probability-weighted position on the scale, its confidence, and each level's probability keyed by level number (0 is the first criterion). |

### Always present

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| usage | STRUCT(model VARCHAR, input_tokens BIGINT, output_tokens BIGINT) | The model that answered and the tokens billed for this row's request. |

functions.name: is_true
functions.comment: Probability that a yes/no question is true of the given content, as a plain expression usable in WHERE, CASE and ORDER BY

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Ask TypeSafe one yes/no question about a value and get back a single `DOUBLE`: the probability that the answer is yes, where near 1 is yes, near 0 is no and 0.5 is genuinely undecided. It is a scalar, so it goes wherever an expression goes — a `WHERE` predicate, a `CASE` arm, an `ORDER BY` key, the right-hand side of an `UPDATE`. Compare it against a threshold; it is a probability, not a boolean. One request per distinct non-null value, and a NULL costs nothing and answers NULL. Use `noul()` instead when you need `criteria`, a specific model, or the token usage, and `ask()` when one row needs several questions at once. Needs a `typesafe` secret.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
One yes/no question, answered as a number you can put in an expression.

### What it cannot do

A scalar takes no named arguments in DuckDB, so this is the whole signature: the default model, no criteria, no usage columns, and a question that is constant for the whole query. `noul()` is the same judgment with all of those, in table-function form.

### Reading the answer

The result is the probability that the answer is yes: near 1 is yes, near 0 is no, and 0.5 is the model saying the content does not decide the question. So it is compared against a threshold rather than used as a bare predicate — see this function's example queries for the shape. Pick the threshold to suit the cost of being wrong, and keep the rows near 0.5 for a human.

### Why it exists

A noul answer is one number, so a scalar loses nothing by returning just that, and the query stops needing a join to reach it. `noul()` can express the same filters and orderings through a `LATERAL` join or a scalar subquery — this is shorter, not more capable.

### Cost and row semantics

One API request per distinct non-null value in each chunk, issued concurrently; repeated values are asked once. A NULL value answers NULL and makes no request. An API failure raises rather than becoming NULL, which would be indistinguishable from that NULL input. 429 and 529 are retried with backoff first.

### Authentication

Add `base_url` to the secret to target the bundled mock endpoint. `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` in the worker's environment is the fallback.

```sql
CREATE SECRET (TYPE typesafe, api_key '...');
```

AS refund FROM (VALUES ('I was charged twice, please refund me'), ('My invoice shows a wrong charge'), ('My package never arrived')) t(body), LATERAL typesafe.main.choice(t.body, instructions => 'Which team should handle this?', criteria => MAP {'shipping': 'Delivery status, delays, lost packages', 'billing': 'Charges, invoices, payment problems'}) c) SELECT body, refund FROM routed WHERE choice = 'billing' AND refund > 0.5 ORDER BY refund DESC, body

workers.doc_md:
# UFC fight data

Query official UFC rankings, event calendars, fight cards, results, judges' scorecards, and round-by-round fight statistics directly from SQL.

## Sources and ids

* **UFC live-data feed** (official): cards, results, per-round statistics. Event and fight ids are sequential integers; discover them with `feed_events()`.
* **[ufc.com/rankings](https://www.ufc.com/rankings)** (official): current rankings; the [UFC events page](https://www.ufc.com/events) lists the same cards.
* **[ESPN MMA](https://www.espn.com/mma/)** (unofficial, undocumented; [Disney terms of use](https://disneytermsofuse.com/)): calendars for UFC, PFL and Bellator, bout results, and fighter profiles, histories and per-fight statistics. ESPN ids differ from UFC ids.

All data is fetched on demand, cached briefly in process, and never rehosted. This worker is not affiliated with UFC, TKO Group, ESPN, or Disney.

example_queries.title: rankings_have_champions
example_queries.description: The official rankings list a champion in every weight class.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) >= 8 AS has_champions FROM ufc.main.current_rankings WHERE is_champion AND NOT pound_for_pound;

example_queries.title: current_season_has_events
example_queries.description: ESPN lists UFC events for the current year.
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) > 0 AS populated FROM ufc.main.current_season_events;

example_queries.title: feed_event_1291_main_event
example_queries.description: The UFC feed records Gabriel Bonfim's KO/TKO win in the 2025-11-08 main event.
example_queries.sql: SELECT winner_name, method, ending_round FROM ufc.main.fight_results(1291) WHERE fight_order = 1;

example_queries.description: The current lightweight top 15.
example_queries.sql: SELECT division, rank, fighter_name, rank_change FROM ufc.main.current_rankings WHERE division = 'Lightweight' ORDER BY rank

example_queries.description: Every current UFC champion.
example_queries.sql: SELECT division, fighter_name, is_interim_champion FROM ufc.main.current_rankings WHERE is_champion ORDER BY division_order

example_queries.description: Fight 12000 round by round: significant strikes landed by each corner next to how many judges scored the round for each corner (red-corner Navajo Stirling outlanded Ivan Erslan 31-12 in round 1 but won it on only one of three cards).
example_queries.sql: WITH strikes AS (SELECT round_number, max(sig_strikes_landed) FILTER (WHERE corner = 'Red') AS red_landed, max(sig_strikes_landed) FILTER (WHERE corner = 'Blue') AS blue_landed FROM ufc.main.fight_round_stats(12000) GROUP BY round_number), votes AS (SELECT round_number, count(*) FILTER (WHERE red_score > blue_score) AS judges_for_red, count(*) FILTER (WHERE blue_score > red_score) AS judges_for_blue FROM ufc.main.fight_scorecards(12000) GROUP BY round_number) SELECT round_number, red_landed, blue_landed, judges_for_red, judges_for_blue FROM strikes JOIN votes USING (round_number) ORDER BY round_number

example_queries.description: Every result on UFC feed event 1291 with the winner's reach advantage over the loser in inches (negative when the shorter-reach fighter won), from fight_results joined to card_fighters.
example_queries.sql: SELECT r.fight_order, r.winner_name, r.loser_name, r.method, w.reach_in - l.reach_in AS winner_reach_edge_in FROM ufc.main.fight_results(1291) AS r JOIN ufc.main.card_fighters(1291) AS w ON w.fight_id = r.fight_id AND w.fighter_id = r.winner_fighter_id JOIN ufc.main.card_fighters(1291) AS l ON l.fight_id = r.fight_id AND l.fighter_id = r.loser_fighter_id ORDER BY r.fight_order

example_queries.description: Fighters on the UFC 324 card (2026-01-24, UFC feed event 1294) who hold a current ufc.com ranking, matched on ufc_athlete_url; a fighter appears once per list they are ranked on.
example_queries.sql: SELECT c.fighter_name, r.division, r.rank FROM ufc.main.card_fighters(1294) AS c JOIN ufc.main.current_rankings AS r USING (ufc_athlete_url) ORDER BY r.rank, r.division, c.fighter_name

tags.vgi.doc_md:
## UFC analytical data

Rows are explicitly ranking-, event-, bout-, fighter-, fight-fighter- or fight-fighter-round-grain. Current tables need no arguments; functions take a season, an ESPN id, or a UFC feed id.

ESPN identifiers (events and athletes) and UFC live-data feed identifiers (events, fights and fighters) are separate numbering systems. Match across them by event date and fighter name, not by id.

Use the ESPN side for calendars, other promotions and career histories; use the UFC feed side for official per-fight and per-round statistics and scorecards.

functions.name: feed_events
functions.comment: List UFC live-data feed events whose ids fall in a range (event-id discovery)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: UFC's official live-data feed numbers events with sequential integers that cannot be searched by name. feed_events(first_id, last_id) probes an inclusive id range (at most 100 ids) and returns one row per existing event with name, start time, status, venue and fight count; missing ids are skipped. Anchors: 1252 = UFC 315 (2025-05-10), 1291 = 2025-11-08, 1320 = 2026-07-18, 1343 = 2026-11-07, 1350 = UFC 336 (2027-01-30). Ids are roughly but not strictly chronological, so scan a window around the date you want and filter by event_name or start_time.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Event-id discovery for the UFC feed. Each id in the range is one upstream request (cached), so keep ranges tight. Use the returned `event_id` with `fight_card()`, `card_fighters()` and `fight_results()`.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per fight on a UFC feed event with the official result: winner and loser (UFC fighter ids and names), outcome (win, Draw, NC), method (KO/TKO, Submission, Decision - Unanimous/Split/Majority), ending round and time, total fight seconds, finishing strike/target/position or submission hold, judges' totals winner-first, Fight of the Night and Performance of the Night bonuses, and referee. tags.vgi.doc_md: Official UFC results for a card. `judges_scores` lists each judge's total as winner-loser; per-round scoring is in `fight_scorecards(fight_id)`.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT r.fight_order, r.winner_name, r.loser_name, r.method, w.reach_in - l.reach_in AS winner_reach_edge_in FROM ufc.main.fight_results(1291) AS r JOIN ufc.main.card_fighters(1291) AS w ON w.fight_id = r.fight_id AND w.fighter_id = r.winner_fighter_id JOIN ufc.main.card_fighters(1291) AS l ON l.fight_id = r.fight_id AND l.fighter_id = r.loser_fighter_id ORDER BY r.fight_order

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per judge per round for a UFC feed fight_id, with the red and blue corner scores under the 10-point must system. Finishes have no scorecards and return no rows. Sum red_score and blue_score by judge for the judge's total.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Per-round judging for a decision. Finished fights return an empty result.

vgi.example_queries.description: How each judge scored every round of fight 12000.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT judge_name, round_number, red_fighter_name, red_score, blue_fighter_name, blue_score FROM ufc.main.fight_scorecards(12000) ORDER BY judge_name, round_number

vgi.example_queries.description: Fight 12000 round by round: significant strikes landed by each corner next to how many judges scored the round for each corner (red-corner Navajo Stirling outlanded Ivan Erslan 31-12 in round 1 but won it on only one of three cards).
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH strikes AS (SELECT round_number, max(sig_strikes_landed) FILTER (WHERE corner = 'Red') AS red_landed, max(sig_strikes_landed) FILTER (WHERE corner = 'Blue') AS blue_landed FROM ufc.main.fight_round_stats(12000) GROUP BY round_number), votes AS (SELECT round_number, count(*) FILTER (WHERE red_score > blue_score) AS judges_for_red, count(*) FILTER (WHERE blue_score > red_score) AS judges_for_blue FROM ufc.main.fight_scorecards(12000) GROUP BY round_number) SELECT round_number, red_landed, blue_landed, judges_for_red, judges_for_blue FROM strikes JOIN votes USING (round_number) ORDER BY round_number

workers.title: United Nations Data
workers.tagline: United Nations SDG, UNESCO, World Heritage, population, refugee and WHO statistics in DuckDB (Python)
workers.subtitle: UN SDG, UNESCO, World Heritage, World Population Prospects, UNHCR and WHO data as tidy tables.
workers.summary: Curated United Nations statistics as tidy country-year tables: SDG indicators, UNESCO education data, the World Heritage List, World Population Prospects, UNHCR refugee figures and WHO health indicators.
workers.doc_md:
# United Nations data

**Curated UN statistics as tidy `(country, year, indicator, value)` tables in DuckDB.** Each schema talks to one UN system portal's own JSON API and pushes indicator, country and year filters into it:

| Schema | Source |
|---|---|
| `sdg` | [UN SDG Global Database](https://unstats.un.org/sdgs/dataportal) (UN Statistics Division) |
| `uis` | [UNESCO Institute for Statistics](https://databrowser.uis.unesco.org/) data API |
| `heritage` | [UNESCO World Heritage List](https://data.unesco.org/explore/dataset/whc001/) |
| `population` | [UN DESA World Population Prospects](https://population.un.org/dataportal/) |
| `refugees` | [UNHCR Refugee Population Statistics](https://www.unhcr.org/refugee-statistics/) |
| `health` | [WHO Global Health Observatory](https://www.who.int/data/gho) |

Countries are joined on ISO 3166-1 alpha-3 codes (`country_iso3`); the bundled [UN M49 standard](https://unstats.un.org/unsd/methodology/m49/overview/) maps M49 numeric codes. Data belongs to the publishing organisations and is used under their terms: UNdata terms (SDG, M49), CC BY-SA 4.0 (UIS, World Heritage), CC BY 3.0 IGO (WPP), CC BY 4.0 (UNHCR) and the WHO data terms. This worker is not affiliated with or endorsed by the United Nations.
workers.readme_sql:
-- Extreme poverty in India over time (SDG 1.1.1)
SELECT year, value FROM un.sdg.data('SI_POV_DAY1')
WHERE country_iso3 = 'IND' AND sex = 'BOTHSEX' AND age = 'ALLAGE' AND location = 'ALLAREA'
ORDER BY year;

-- Where Syrian refugees lived at the end of 2023
SELECT asylum_name, value FROM un.refugees.populations
WHERE origin_iso3 = 'SYR' AND year = 2023 AND measure = 'refugees'
ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 5;

-- Life expectancy by WHO region, joined through the bundled M49 table
SELECT m.region_name, round(avg(d.value), 1) AS life_expectancy
FROM un.health.data('WHOSIS_000001') d JOIN un.main.m49_countries m ON m.iso_alpha3 = d.country_iso3
WHERE d.year = 2019 AND d.sex = 'SEX_BTSX' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY ALL;

attach_options.name: base_url
attach_options.description: Where requests go. Empty (default): each organisation's public API. An http(s) URL: a mirror or proxy serving <base_url>/<schema>/<api path>. A local directory: recorded responses (see test/fixtures), for offline use and tests.

attach_options.name: user_agent
attach_options.description: User-Agent sent upstream (default 'vgi-un/0.1 (+https://query.farm)').

example_queries.description: Life expectancy at birth in India by sex, 2015-2021
example_queries.sql: SELECT year, sex, value FROM un.health.data('WHOSIS_000001') WHERE country_iso3 = 'IND' AND year BETWEEN 2015 AND 2021 ORDER BY year, sex

example_queries.description: Life expectancy in 2019 in three South Asian countries, with M49 names
example_queries.sql: SELECT d.country_iso3, m.country_or_area, d.value FROM un.health.data('WHOSIS_000001') d JOIN un.main.m49_countries m ON m.iso_alpha3 = d.country_iso3 WHERE d.country_iso3 IN ('BGD', 'IND', 'PAK') AND d.year = 2019 AND d.sex = 'SEX_BTSX' ORDER BY d.value DESC

example_queries.description: Decode the SEX dimension
example_queries.sql: SELECT code, title FROM un.health.dimension_values('SEX') ORDER BY code

example_queries.description: Find the life expectancy indicators
example_queries.sql: SELECT indicator_code, name FROM un.health.indicators WHERE name ILIKE '%life expectancy%' ORDER BY indicator_code

example_queries.description: Number of countries in each WHO region
example_queries.sql: SELECT who_region, count(*) AS countries FROM un.health.countries GROUP BY who_region ORDER BY who_region

example_queries.description: Dimensions about age
example_queries.sql: SELECT dimension, title FROM un.health.dimensions WHERE title ILIKE '%age%' ORDER BY dimension

example_queries.description: Sites on the List of World Heritage in Danger, by category
example_queries.sql: SELECT category, count(*) AS sites FROM un.heritage.sites() WHERE in_danger GROUP BY category ORDER BY category

example_queries.description: World Heritage sites in Syria with their inscription year and criteria
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, year_inscribed, criteria FROM un.heritage.sites(country := 'SYR') ORDER BY year_inscribed, name

example_queries.description: Convert SDG-style M49 area codes to ISO alpha-3 (regions give NULL)
example_queries.sql: SELECT code, un.main.iso3_from_m49(code) AS iso3 FROM (VALUES ('4'), ('356'), ('150')) t(code) ORDER BY code

example_queries.description: Convert ISO alpha-3 codes to M49 (unknown codes give NULL)
example_queries.sql: SELECT iso3, un.main.m49_from_iso3(iso3) AS m49 FROM (VALUES ('AFG'), ('bra'), ('XXX')) t(iso3) ORDER BY iso3

example_queries.description: Countries and small island developing states in each Oceania sub-region
example_queries.sql: SELECT subregion_name, count(*) AS countries, count(*) FILTER (WHERE sids) AS sids FROM un.main.m49_countries WHERE region_name = 'Oceania' GROUP BY subregion_name ORDER BY subregion_name

example_queries.description: Least developed countries per region
example_queries.sql: SELECT region_name, count(*) AS ldcs FROM un.main.m49_countries WHERE ldc GROUP BY region_name ORDER BY region_name;

example_queries.description: Look up India by its ISO code
example_queries.sql: SELECT m49, country_or_area, subregion_name FROM un.main.m49_countries WHERE iso_alpha3 = 'IND';

example_queries.description: India's total population (thousands), 2020-2025 (needs a un_population secret)
example_queries.sql: SELECT year, value AS population_thousands FROM un.population.data('49') WHERE country_iso3 = 'IND' AND year BETWEEN 2020 AND 2025 AND sex = 'Both sexes' ORDER BY year

example_queries.description: Data Portal indicators per topic
example_queries.sql: SELECT topic, count(*) AS indicators FROM un.population.indicators GROUP BY topic ORDER BY topic

example_queries.description: Data Portal ids of India and Nigeria
example_queries.sql: SELECT location_id, name FROM un.population.locations WHERE country_iso3 IN ('IND', 'NGA') ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Refugees from Syria living in Germany at the end of 2023
example_queries.sql: SELECT value AS refugees FROM un.refugees.populations WHERE origin_iso3 = 'SYR' AND asylum_iso3 = 'DEU' AND year = 2023 AND measure = 'refugees'

example_queries.description: The five countries hosting the most Syrian refugees in 2023
example_queries.sql: SELECT asylum_name, value FROM un.refugees.populations WHERE origin_iso3 = 'SYR' AND year = 2023 AND measure = 'refugees' ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Syrian asylum applications in Germany in 2023 by procedure stage
example_queries.sql: SELECT decision_level, sum(value) AS applications FROM un.refugees.asylum_applications WHERE origin_iso3 = 'SYR' AND asylum_iso3 = 'DEU' AND year = 2023 GROUP BY decision_level ORDER BY decision_level

example_queries.description: Outcomes of Syrian asylum claims decided in Germany in 2023
example_queries.sql: SELECT measure, sum(value) AS decisions FROM un.refugees.asylum_decisions WHERE origin_iso3 = 'SYR' AND asylum_iso3 = 'DEU' AND year = 2023 GROUP BY measure ORDER BY measure

example_queries.description: Where Syrian refugees returning home in 2023 came back from
example_queries.sql: SELECT asylum_name, value FROM un.refugees.solutions WHERE origin_iso3 = 'SYR' AND year = 2023 AND measure = 'returned_refugees' ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 5

example_queries.description: Countries whose UNHCR code differs from the ISO code
example_queries.sql: SELECT unhcr_code, country_iso3, name FROM un.refugees.countries WHERE unhcr_code <> country_iso3 ORDER BY unhcr_code LIMIT 10

example_queries.description: Share of India's population below the international poverty line, by year
example_queries.sql: SELECT year, value FROM un.sdg.data('SI_POV_DAY1') WHERE country_iso3 = 'IND' AND sex = 'BOTHSEX' AND age = 'ALLAGE' AND location = 'ALLAREA' ORDER BY year

example_queries.description: Average poverty rate of India and Bangladesh by year, labelled with the M49 region
example_queries.sql: SELECT d.year, m.region_name, round(avg(d.value), 1) AS avg_poverty_pct FROM un.sdg.data('SI_POV_DAY1') d JOIN un.main.m49_countries m ON m.iso_alpha3 = d.country_iso3 WHERE d.country_iso3 IN ('IND', 'BGD') AND d.year BETWEEN 2004 AND 2022 AND d.age = 'ALLAGE' AND d.location = 'ALLAREA' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY ALL

example_queries.description: All 17 goals in numeric order
example_queries.sql: SELECT goal, title FROM un.sdg.goals ORDER BY goal::INTEGER

example_queries.description: Number of targets under each goal
example_queries.sql: SELECT goal, count(*) AS targets FROM un.sdg.targets GROUP BY goal ORDER BY goal::INTEGER

example_queries.description: Indicators under target 1.1 and the series that measure them
example_queries.sql: SELECT indicator, description, series_codes FROM un.sdg.indicators WHERE target = '1.1' ORDER BY indicator

example_queries.description: Series that measure indicator 1.1.1 (extreme poverty)
example_queries.sql: SELECT series_code, description FROM un.sdg.series WHERE list_contains(indicators, '1.1.1') ORDER BY series_code

example_queries.description: Countries versus regional groupings in the SDG area list
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE country_iso3 IS NOT NULL) AS countries, count(*) FILTER (WHERE country_iso3 IS NULL) AS other_areas FROM un.sdg.geoareas

example_queries.description: Primary completion rate in Brazil and the United States, 2015-2020
example_queries.sql: SELECT geo_unit, year, round(value, 1) AS completion_rate FROM un.uis.data(indicator := 'CR.1') WHERE country_iso3 IN ('BRA', 'USA') AND year BETWEEN 2015 AND 2020 ORDER BY geo_unit, year

example_queries.description: Every UIS indicator value for Brazil in 2020, with indicator names
example_queries.sql: SELECT d.indicator_code, i.name, d.value FROM un.uis.data(geo_unit := 'BRA') d JOIN un.uis.indicators i USING (indicator_code) WHERE d.year = 2020 ORDER BY d.indicator_code

example_queries.description: Number of UIS indicators per theme
example_queries.sql: SELECT theme, count(*) AS indicators FROM un.uis.indicators GROUP BY theme ORDER BY theme

example_queries.description: Regional groupings and how many regions each defines
example_queries.sql: SELECT region_group, count(*) AS regions FROM un.uis.geo_units WHERE type = 'REGIONAL' GROUP BY region_group ORDER BY regions DESC

example_queries.description: The current default UIS data version
example_queries.sql: SELECT version, publication_date FROM un.uis.versions WHERE is_default

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Observations of one WHO Global Health Observatory indicator. `indicator` (positional, required) is a code from `health.indicators`, e.g. 'WHOSIS_000001' (life expectancy at birth). One row per area x period x disaggregation. Filter with WHERE `country_iso3 = 'IND'` (or IN), `spatial_dim` for regions ('SEAR', 'GLOBAL') and `year` ranges; these become an OData $filter. Countries have spatial_dim_type 'COUNTRY'; regions and income groups have country_iso3 NULL. `sex` is SEX_BTSX (both sexes), SEX_FMLE or SEX_MLE when the indicator is broken down by sex; other breakdowns are in dim1..dim3 (decode with `health.dimension_values`). `value` is the numeric value with `low`/`high` bounds.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The `main` schema holds reference data shared by every source: the UN M49 standard (country or area name, 3-digit M49 code, ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 and alpha-3 codes, region / sub-region / intermediate region codes and names, and LDC / LLDC / SIDS flags), bundled with the worker so it needs no network. Use it to turn SDG M49 area codes into ISO alpha-3 codes, to group countries by region, or to filter least developed countries. M49 codes are `VARCHAR` with leading zeros ('004' Afghanistan).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

The [UN M49 standard](https://unstats.un.org/unsd/methodology/m49/overview/) of country and area codes for statistical use, bundled, plus scalar converters between M49 and ISO alpha-3 codes.

*Source and terms:* United Nations Statistics Division, UNdata terms of use (free reuse with citation).

vgi.example_queries.description: Convert SDG-style M49 area codes to ISO alpha-3 (regions give NULL)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT code, un.main.iso3_from_m49(code) AS iso3 FROM (VALUES ('4'), ('356'), ('150')) t(code) ORDER BY code

vgi.example_queries.description: Convert ISO alpha-3 codes to M49 (unknown codes give NULL)
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT iso3, un.main.m49_from_iso3(iso3) AS m49 FROM (VALUES ('AFG'), ('bra'), ('XXX')) t(iso3) ORDER BY iso3

vgi.example_queries.description: Countries and small island developing states in each Oceania sub-region
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT subregion_name, count(*) AS countries, count(*) FILTER (WHERE sids) AS sids FROM un.main.m49_countries WHERE region_name = 'Oceania' GROUP BY subregion_name ORDER BY subregion_name

tags.vgi.title: UN Reference Codes

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The UN M49 standard (bundled, no network): one row per country or area (248) with `m49` ('004'), `country_or_area`, `iso_alpha2`, `iso_alpha3`, the region / sub-region / intermediate region codes and names, and boolean `ldc`, `lldc`, `sids` flags. Join any source's `country_iso3` to `iso_alpha3`, or SDG `m49` to `m49`, to group by region.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: World Population Prospects estimates (to 2023) and projections (to 2100) from the UN DESA Population Division Data Portal. tags.vgi.doc_llm: The `refugees` schema reads UNHCR's Refugee Population Statistics API. Every observation function is in long format (year, origin, asylum country, measure, value) and is a table: filter with WHERE on `origin_iso3`, `asylum_iso3` (ISO alpha-3) and `year`, which are pushed into the API. Unfiltered origins or asylum countries come back one row each (not summed). Values are people (or applications and decisions).
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## refugees

[UNHCR Refugee Population Statistics](https://www.unhcr.org/refugee-statistics/) in tidy long format.

*Source and terms:* UNHCR Refugee Population Statistics Database, [CC BY 4.0](https://www.unhcr.org/terms-use-datasets) (cite as 'UNHCR Refugee Population Statistics Database').

vgi.example_queries.description: Refugees from Syria living in Germany at the end of 2023
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT value AS refugees FROM un.refugees.populations WHERE origin_iso3 = 'SYR' AND asylum_iso3 = 'DEU' AND year = 2023 AND measure = 'refugees'

vgi.example_queries.description: The five countries hosting the most Syrian refugees in 2023
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT asylum_name, value FROM un.refugees.populations WHERE origin_iso3 = 'SYR' AND year = 2023 AND measure = 'refugees' ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 5

vgi.example_queries.description: Syrian asylum applications in Germany in 2023 by procedure stage
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT decision_level, sum(value) AS applications FROM un.refugees.asylum_applications WHERE origin_iso3 = 'SYR' AND asylum_iso3 = 'DEU' AND year = 2023 GROUP BY decision_level ORDER BY decision_level

vgi.example_queries.description: Outcomes of Syrian asylum claims decided in Germany in 2023
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT measure, sum(value) AS decisions FROM un.refugees.asylum_decisions WHERE origin_iso3 = 'SYR' AND asylum_iso3 = 'DEU' AND year = 2023 GROUP BY measure ORDER BY measure

vgi.example_queries.description: Where Syrian refugees returning home in 2023 came back from
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT asylum_name, value FROM un.refugees.solutions WHERE origin_iso3 = 'SYR' AND year = 2023 AND measure = 'returned_refugees' ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 5

vgi.example_queries.description: Countries whose UNHCR code differs from the ISO code
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT unhcr_code, country_iso3, name FROM un.refugees.countries WHERE unhcr_code <> country_iso3 ORDER BY unhcr_code LIMIT 10

tags.vgi.doc_llm: The `sdg` schema reads the UN Statistics Division SDG Global Database API. Catalog tables describe the framework (goals -> targets -> indicators -> data series); observations are published per data series, so look up a `series_code` and pass it to the observations function, filtering by `country_iso3` and `year`. ## sdg

The [SDG Global Database](https://unstats.un.org/sdgs/dataportal): the indicator framework and country, regional and global observations.

*Source and terms:* UN Statistics Division, [SDG Global Database](https://unstats.un.org/sdgs/dataportal); free to copy and redistribute with citation under the [UNdata terms of use](https://data.un.org/Host.aspx?Content=UNdataUse).

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT d.year, m.region_name, round(avg(d.value), 1) AS avg_poverty_pct FROM un.sdg.data('SI_POV_DAY1') d JOIN un.main.m49_countries m ON m.iso_alpha3 = d.country_iso3 WHERE d.country_iso3 IN ('IND', 'BGD') AND d.year BETWEEN 2004 AND 2022 AND d.age = 'ALLAGE' AND d.location = 'ALLAREA' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY ALL

functions.comment: SDG Global Database observations for one or more data series, by area, year and dimension

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Observations of one or more SDG data series from the UN SDG Global Database, one row per area x year x dimension combination. `series` (positional, required) is a series code such as 'SI_POV_DAY1' or a comma-separated list; find codes in `sdg.series` or `sdg.indicators.series_codes`. Filter with WHERE: `country_iso3 = 'IND'` (ISO alpha-3), `m49 = '356'` or `area_code = '356'`, and `year = 2022` / `year BETWEEN 2015 AND 2022`; these are pushed into the API request. Many series are disaggregated: `sex` ('BOTHSEX', 'FEMALE', 'MALE'), `age` ('ALLAGE', '15-24' ...), `location` ('ALLAREA', 'URBAN', 'RURAL') and `reporting_type` ('N' national, 'G' UN global estimate); pick the totals (BOTHSEX, ALLAGE, ALLAREA) to avoid double counting, and see `dimensions` for any other breakdown. `value` is `DOUBLE` (NULL when the published text is not numeric; `value_text` keeps it), `unit` is the units code. Regions have country_iso3 NULL.

workers.title: Unit Conversion
workers.tagline: Physical unit conversion & dimensional analysis (14 dimensions) for DuckDB (Rust)
workers.subtitle: Convert measurements between units, normalize them to SI, and check that two quantities are comparable.
workers.summary: Runtime, string-driven physical-unit conversion and dimensional analysis.
workers.doc_md:
# Units — Physical Unit Conversion & Dimensional Analysis in SQL

**Convert physical quantities between units and run dimensional analysis directly in DuckDB SQL** — length, mass, time, energy, temperature, pressure, data sizes, and more, all resolved at query time. The `units` worker brings runtime, string-driven unit conversion to your queries: units are named by ordinary strings (`'mi'`, `'GiB'`, `'°C'`, `'kWh'`), so you can normalize measurements, check that two quantities are comparable, and reduce values to their SI base unit without leaving SQL.

This extension is for data engineers, analysts, and scientists who deal with messy, mixed-unit measurement data — energy bills in kWh, distances in miles and kilometers, storage in GiB and GB, sensor readings in mixed temperature scales. Instead of hard-coding conversion factors into every query or pipeline, you call a single well-tested function and get consistent, documented results. Because unit names are plain strings evaluated per row, it works naturally over columns of dirty real-world data, returning `NULL` for unrecognized units rather than aborting a scan.

Under the hood the worker is powered by a **curated internal unit table** rather than an external dependency: each unit string maps to a `(dimension, factor, offset)` triple, and every conversion is an exact affine round-trip through the SI base unit of its dimension (`base = value * factor + offset`). Offsets are used only by the temperature scales (°C/°F/K/°R) so that 0 °C = 273.15 K = 32 °F comes out right; all other factors are the exact agreed SI constants (e.g. inch = 0.0254 m, pound = 0.45359237 kg, atm = 101325 Pa, calorie = 4.184 J, IEC binary prefixes as 1024ⁿ vs decimal 1000ⁿ). The factors follow the official SI definitions maintained by the [BIPM](https://www.bipm.org/en/measurement-units) and the [NIST reference on constants, units, and uncertainty](https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/Units/).

**When to reach for it.** Use this worker whenever a query must reconcile measurements recorded in different units, confirm that two quantities are even comparable before combining them, reduce heterogeneous values to a common SI base so they can be aggregated, or turn free-text quantity strings into structured numeric values. It fits reporting pipelines that mix imperial and metric sources, scientific workloads that must normalize before doing math, and data-cleaning steps that quarantine unrecognized units as NULL rather than failing.
workers.readme_sql:
LOAD vgi;
ATTACH 'units' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'github-auto://Query-farm/vgi-units@v0.4.1');
SET search_path = 'units.main';

SELECT convert(1, 'mi', 'km');        -- 1.609344
SELECT convert(0, 'C', 'F');          -- 32.0
SELECT convert(1, 'GiB', 'byte');     -- 1073741824.0
SELECT dimension('mi');               -- 'length'
SELECT compatible('mi', 'kg');        -- false
SELECT to_base(1, 'km');              -- 1000.0   (SI base unit of the dimension)
SELECT (parse_quantity('5 km')).*;    -- (value := 5.0, unit := 'km')
SELECT * FROM supported_units();      -- discovery: unit, dimension, base_unit
SELECT convert_strict(0, '°C', '°F'); -- 32.0     (invalid input raises an ERROR)
SELECT convert_difference_strict(10, '°C', '°F'); -- 18.0 (a temperature change)
SELECT * FROM unit_catalog;           -- factors, offsets and versions

example_queries.description: Convert a marathon distance from miles to kilometres.
example_queries.sql: SELECT units.main.convert(26.2, 'mi', 'km') AS km

example_queries.description: Reduce 1 GiB to bytes via the SI base unit.
example_queries.sql: SELECT units.main.to_base(1, 'GiB') AS bytes

example_queries.description: Look up the physical dimension of a unit.
example_queries.sql: SELECT units.main.dimension('kWh') AS dim

example_queries.description: Check whether two units can be converted between.
example_queries.sql: SELECT units.main.compatible('mi', 'km') AS ok

example_queries.description: Parse a free-text quantity string into a (value, unit) struct.
example_queries.sql: SELECT units.main.parse_quantity('5 km') AS q

example_queries.description: List the recognized units in the length dimension.
example_queries.sql: SELECT unit, base_unit FROM units.main.supported_units WHERE dimension = 'length' ORDER BY unit

example_queries.description: Parse free-text readings, group them by physical dimension, and total each group in its SI base unit; '7 furlongs' is not a recognized unit, so it parses to NULL and is skipped.
example_queries.sql: WITH r AS (SELECT units.main.parse_quantity(txt) AS q FROM (VALUES ('5 km'), ('3 mi'), ('800 m'), ('2 kg'), ('12 lb'), ('7 furlongs')) AS t(txt)) SELECT units.main.dimension((q).unit) AS dim, count(*) AS readings, round(sum(units.main.to_base((q).value, (q).unit)), 4) AS total_si FROM r WHERE q IS NOT NULL GROUP BY dim ORDER BY dim

example_queries.description: Normalize mixed free-text readings to SI and label each with its base unit by joining the parsed unit to supported_units (e.g. '98.6 °F' becomes 310.15 K).
example_queries.sql: WITH r AS (SELECT txt, units.main.parse_quantity(txt) AS q FROM (VALUES ('5 km'), ('2 GiB'), ('1 kWh'), ('98.6 °F')) AS t(txt)) SELECT r.txt, units.main.to_base((r.q).value, (r.q).unit) AS base_value, s.base_unit FROM r JOIN units.main.supported_units AS s ON s.unit = (r.q).unit ORDER BY r.txt

example_queries.description: Express one mile in every length unit the worker recognizes, largest number first.
example_queries.sql: SELECT unit, units.main.convert(1, 'mi', unit) AS one_mile FROM units.main.supported_units WHERE dimension = 'length' ORDER BY one_mile DESC, unit

example_queries.description: Guard a conversion: convert each row to kilograms only when its unit is compatible with kg, so the length row ('m') yields NULL instead of an incompatible-dimension error.
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, qty, unit, CASE WHEN units.main.compatible(unit, 'kg') THEN units.main.convert(qty, unit, 'kg') END AS kg FROM (VALUES (1, 150.0, 'lb'), (2, 2.5, 'kg'), (3, 3.0, 'm'), (4, 16.0, 'oz')) AS t(id, qty, unit) ORDER BY id

example_queries.description: Report each reactor's final temperature in °F with convert_strict and its rise in °F with convert_difference_strict: the 15 °C rise of reactor_a is 27 °F, not the 59 °F an absolute conversion would give.
example_queries.sql: SELECT sensor, round(units.main.convert_strict(end_c, '°C', '°F'), 2) AS end_f, round(units.main.convert_difference_strict(end_c - start_c, '°C', '°F'), 2) AS rise_f FROM (VALUES ('reactor_a', 20.0, 35.0), ('reactor_b', 18.5, 21.0)) AS t(sensor, start_c, end_c) ORDER BY sensor

example_queries.description: Audit strict temperature conversions: convert 100 of each unit with convert_strict and recompute the same result from the factor and offset published in unit_catalog ((value * f.factor + f.offset - t.offset) / t.factor).

tags.vgi.doc_md:
# Units — main schema

The single namespace for the `units` worker, bringing runtime, string-driven physical-unit conversion and dimensional analysis to SQL.

Its capabilities are organized into a few areas:

- **Conversion** — convert and normalize numeric quantities between units of the same dimension, including reduction to the SI base unit.
- **Analysis** — look up a unit's physical dimension and test whether two units are compatible for conversion.
- **Parsing** — turn free-text quantity strings such as `5 km` into a structured value and unit.
- **Discovery** — browse the catalog of every recognized unit string, its dimension, and its SI base unit.

Reach for this schema whenever a query must reconcile mixed-unit measurements, confirm that two quantities are comparable, or normalize values to a common base before aggregating.

vgi.example_queries.description: Parse free-text readings, group them by physical dimension, and total each group in its SI base unit; '7 furlongs' is not a recognized unit, so it parses to NULL and is skipped.
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH r AS (SELECT units.main.parse_quantity(txt) AS q FROM (VALUES ('5 km'), ('3 mi'), ('800 m'), ('2 kg'), ('12 lb'), ('7 furlongs')) AS t(txt)) SELECT units.main.dimension((q).unit) AS dim, count(*) AS readings, round(sum(units.main.to_base((q).value, (q).unit)), 4) AS total_si FROM r WHERE q IS NOT NULL GROUP BY dim ORDER BY dim

vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH r AS (SELECT txt, units.main.parse_quantity(txt) AS q FROM (VALUES ('5 km'), ('2 GiB'), ('1 kWh'), ('98.6 °F')) AS t(txt)) SELECT r.txt, units.main.to_base((r.q).value, (r.q).unit) AS base_value, s.base_unit FROM r JOIN units.main.supported_units AS s ON s.unit = (r.q).unit ORDER BY r.txt

# unit_catalog

Versioned, authoritative unit definitions for administrative approval of strict conversions. One row per exact unit string with `unit`, `dimension`, `base_unit`, `quantity_space`, `factor`, `offset` (`base = value * factor + offset`; differences use `factor` only), `implementation_version` and `contract_version`. Quote the `"offset"` column, which is a SQL keyword.

columns.name: unit
columns.comment: The exact recognized unit string, e.g. 'km', 'MB', '°C'. Case-significant.

columns.name: dimension
columns.comment: The physical dimension the unit measures, e.g. 'length' or 'temperature'.

columns.name: base_unit
columns.comment: The SI base unit of the dimension that conversions pass through, e.g. 'm'.

columns.name: quantity_space
columns.comment: 'affine' for temperature units (offsets apply to absolute values and cancel for differences); 'linear' for every other dimension.

columns.name: contract_version
columns.comment: The strict-conversion contract version these definitions satisfy.

# supported_units

The discovery table of every recognized unit string. One row per unit, with columns `unit` (the string, e.g. `km`), `dimension` (e.g. `length`), and `base_unit` (the SI base unit of that dimension, e.g. `m`). Use it to find valid unit inputs for the scalar functions, or `WHERE dimension = '…'` to browse a single dimension.

vgi.example_queries.description: Normalize mixed free-text readings to SI and label each with its base unit by joining the parsed unit to supported_units (e.g. '98.6 °F' becomes 310.15 K).
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH r AS (SELECT txt, units.main.parse_quantity(txt) AS q FROM (VALUES ('5 km'), ('2 GiB'), ('1 kWh'), ('98.6 °F')) AS t(txt)) SELECT r.txt, units.main.to_base((r.q).value, (r.q).unit) AS base_value, s.base_unit FROM r JOIN units.main.supported_units AS s ON s.unit = (r.q).unit ORDER BY r.txt

tags.vgi.title: Convert to SI Base Unit

arguments.name: value
arguments.description: The quantity to express in its SI base unit, given in the unit named by `unit` (e.g. 100 for 100 centimetres).

arguments.name: unit
arguments.description: The unit the value is given in, e.g. 'GiB'. Must be recognized by the worker; an unknown unit yields NULL.

examples: SELECT units.main.to_base(100, 'cm') AS metres
SELECT units.main.to_base(1, 'GiB') AS bytes

WITH r AS (SELECT txt, units.main.parse_quantity(txt) AS q FROM (VALUES ('5 km'), ('2 GiB'), ('1 kWh'), ('98.6 °F')) AS t(txt)) SELECT r.txt, units.main.to_base((r.q).value, (r.q).unit) AS base_value, s.base_unit FROM r JOIN units.main.supported_units AS s ON s.unit = (r.q).unit ORDER BY r.txt

functions.name: compatible
functions.comment: Whether two units share a dimension (i.e. can be converted between). Unknown units are never compatible

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Return TRUE when two units share the same physical dimension and can therefore be converted between one another (e.g. 'mi' and 'km'), and FALSE otherwise. Unknown units are never compatible. Returns NULL when either operand is NULL.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Check whether two units share a dimension (are convertible), e.g. `compatible('mi', 'km')` → true.

vgi.example_queries.description: Check whether two units can be converted between (true).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT units.main.compatible('mi', 'km') AS ok

vgi.example_queries.description: Guard a conversion: convert each row to kilograms only when its unit is compatible with kg, so the length row ('m') yields NULL instead of an incompatible-dimension error.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id, qty, unit, CASE WHEN units.main.compatible(unit, 'kg') THEN units.main.convert(qty, unit, 'kg') END AS kg FROM (VALUES (1, 150.0, 'lb'), (2, 2.5, 'kg'), (3, 3.0, 'm'), (4, 16.0, 'oz')) AS t(id, qty, unit) ORDER BY id

tags.vgi.title: Units Compatible?

arguments.name: unit_a
arguments.description: The first unit to compare, e.g. 'mi'. The result is whether it shares a dimension with unit_b (and is therefore convertible).

arguments.name: unit_b
arguments.description: The second unit to compare, e.g. 'km'. Compared against unit_a to test dimensional compatibility.

examples: SELECT units.main.compatible('mi', 'km') AS ok

SELECT id, qty, unit, CASE WHEN units.main.compatible(unit, 'kg') THEN units.main.convert(qty, unit, 'kg') END AS kg FROM (VALUES (1, 150.0, 'lb'), (2, 2.5, 'kg'), (3, 3.0, 'm'), (4, 16.0, 'oz')) AS t(id, qty, unit) ORDER BY id

workers.doc_md:
# Unity Catalog

Query the metadata of a Unity Catalog metastore with SQL, whether it is an open-source [Unity Catalog](https://www.unitycatalog.io) server or a Databricks workspace: catalogs, schemas, tables and their columns, views and their SQL, volumes, functions, registered models, external locations, storage credentials (by name), grants and owners, and, on Databricks, connections, Delta Sharing, tags and lineage. Read-only.

Connect with a DuckDB secret of type `unity_catalog`, created **after** `ATTACH`:

```sql
-- open-source Unity Catalog server (no authorization, or a bearer TOKEN)
CREATE SECRET uc (TYPE unity_catalog, HOST 'http://localhost:8080');
-- Databricks: personal access token
CREATE SECRET uc (TYPE unity_catalog, HOST 'https://dbc-a1b2c3d4-e5f6.cloud.databricks.com', TOKEN 'dapi...');
-- Databricks: OAuth machine-to-machine (service principal)
CREATE SECRET uc (TYPE unity_catalog, HOST 'https://adb-123.7.azuredatabricks.net',
                  CLIENT_ID '...', CLIENT_SECRET '...');
```

The fields match the `databricks` secret of vgi-databricks.

Tables use the same columns as the DataHub and OpenMetadata workers (`datasets`, `columns`, `owners`, `tags`, `lineage_edges`), so catalogs can be compared with `UNION ALL`.

example_queries.description: The metastore id and region
example_queries.sql: SELECT metastore_id, cloud, region FROM unity_catalog.main.metastores

example_queries.description: Catalogs by type and owner
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, catalog_type, owner FROM unity_catalog.main.catalogs ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Schemas of one catalog (catalog_name is sent to the API)
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, owner, description FROM unity_catalog.main.schemas WHERE catalog_name = 'sales' ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Tables per type and format in one catalog (only that catalog's schemas are listed)
example_queries.sql: SELECT table_type, data_source_format, count(*) AS tables FROM unity_catalog.main.datasets WHERE catalog_name = 'sales' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY tables DESC

example_queries.description: Views that read a given table
example_queries.sql: SELECT id FROM unity_catalog.main.views WHERE view_definition ILIKE '%sales.raw.orders%' ORDER BY id

example_queries.description: Partition columns of one table (fetched with one GET /tables call)
example_queries.sql: SELECT column_name, native_data_type, partition_index FROM unity_catalog.main.columns WHERE dataset_id = 'sales.raw.orders' AND partition_index IS NOT NULL ORDER BY partition_index

example_queries.description: External volumes and where their files live
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, storage_location FROM unity_catalog.main.volumes WHERE volume_type = 'EXTERNAL' ORDER BY id

example_queries.description: SQL functions and their parameter counts
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, len(parameters) AS params, full_data_type FROM unity_catalog.main.functions WHERE routine_body = 'SQL' ORDER BY id

example_queries.description: Registered models per catalog
example_queries.sql: SELECT catalog_name, count(*) AS models FROM unity_catalog.main.registered_models GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY ALL

example_queries.description: Latest ready version of each model
example_queries.sql: SELECT model_id, max(version) AS latest FROM unity_catalog.main.model_versions WHERE status = 'READY' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY model_id

example_queries.description: External locations and their credentials
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, url, credential_name FROM unity_catalog.main.external_locations ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Storage credentials by kind
example_queries.sql: SELECT credential_type, count(*) AS credentials FROM unity_catalog.main.storage_credentials GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY ALL

example_queries.description: Federated connections and their hosts
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, connection_type, options['host'] AS host FROM unity_catalog.main.connections ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Delta Sharing shares and owners
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, owner, created_at FROM unity_catalog.main.shares ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Recipients that have not activated
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, authentication_type FROM unity_catalog.main.recipients WHERE NOT activated ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Who can SELECT from tables in one catalog
example_queries.sql: SELECT securable_name, principal FROM unity_catalog.main.grants WHERE securable_type = 'table' AND catalog_name = 'sales' AND privilege = 'SELECT' ORDER BY ALL

example_queries.description: Inherited privileges on one table
example_queries.sql: SELECT principal, privilege, inherited_from_type, inherited_from_name FROM unity_catalog.main.effective_grants WHERE securable_type = 'table' AND securable_name = 'sales.raw.orders' ORDER BY ALL

example_queries.description: Objects owned per principal
example_queries.sql: SELECT owner_id, entity_type, count(*) AS objects FROM unity_catalog.main.owners GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY objects DESC

example_queries.description: Governed tags and their allowed values
example_queries.sql: SELECT name, allowed_values FROM unity_catalog.main.tags ORDER BY name

example_queries.description: Columns tagged as PII in one catalog
example_queries.sql: SELECT entity_id, column_name, tag_value FROM unity_catalog.main.tag_assignments WHERE entity_type = 'column' AND catalog_name = 'sales' AND tag_key = 'pii' ORDER BY ALL

example_queries.description: What feeds one table (only that table's lineage is requested)
example_queries.sql: SELECT upstream_id, upstream_type FROM unity_catalog.main.lineage_edges WHERE level = 'dataset' AND downstream_id = 'sales.marts.daily_revenue' ORDER BY ALL

example_queries.description: Look a table up by a name typed in any case
example_queries.sql: SELECT d.id, d.owner FROM unity_catalog.main.datasets d WHERE d.qualified_name = unity_catalog.main.uc_qualified_name('Sales.Raw.Orders')

example_queries.description: Who can read which table, with the privilege typed as in a GRANT statement
example_queries.sql: SELECT securable_name, principal FROM unity_catalog.main.grants WHERE securable_type = 'table' AND privilege = unity_catalog.main.uc_privilege('select') ORDER BY ALL

example_queries.description: Columns whose comment mentions PII
example_queries.sql: SELECT dataset_id, column_name FROM unity_catalog.main.columns WHERE catalog_name = 'sales' AND description ILIKE '%pii%' ORDER BY ALL

example_queries.description: Column-level impact of changing one table
example_queries.sql: SELECT upstream_column, downstream_id, downstream_column FROM unity_catalog.main.lineage_edges WHERE level = 'column' AND upstream_id = 'sales.raw.orders' ORDER BY ALL

example_queries.description: External tables without a comment
example_queries.sql: SELECT id, storage_location FROM unity_catalog.main.datasets WHERE table_type = 'EXTERNAL' AND description IS NULL ORDER BY id

example_queries.description: Privileges held by one user across the metastore
example_queries.sql: SELECT securable_type, securable_name, privilege FROM unity_catalog.main.grants WHERE principal = 'alice@example.com' ORDER BY ALL

example_queries.description: Open-source and SQL spellings of two privileges
example_queries.sql: SELECT unity_catalog.main.uc_privilege('USE CATALOG') AS use_catalog, unity_catalog.main.uc_privilege(' read volume ') AS read_volume;

example_queries.description: Join keys of a mixed-case and a backtick-quoted three-part name
example_queries.sql: SELECT unity_catalog.main.uc_qualified_name('Sales.RAW.Orders') AS plain, unity_catalog.main.uc_qualified_name('`sales`.`raw`.`daily revenue`') AS quoted;

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Schema main holds the whole metastore's metadata, one table per Unity Catalog collection, for inventory, access reviews, ownership audits and impact analysis. Objects follow Unity Catalog's hierarchy: metastore > catalog > schema > securable, and every id is the object's full name ('catalog', 'catalog.schema', 'catalog.schema.object'), so joins are on full names; each table's description names its own join keys. Asset and governance tables use the column names of the shared data-catalog vocabulary (catalog_tool, qualified_name, entity_type/entity_id) for UNION ALL with the DataHub and OpenMetadata workers. Pushdown: catalog_name / schema_name and = / IN on ids decide which catalogs and schemas the worker lists, and the permission, ownership, tagging and lineage tables call the API once per object in scope, so always narrow by catalog and schema on large metastores. Some collections exist only on Databricks; on an open-source server those tables raise 'not implemented by this server', as each such table's description says. Secrets are never returned: credentials appear by name and kind only, connection options are masked.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

Everything a Unity Catalog metastore knows about its objects, who can use them, who owns them and how data flows between them, as read-only tables. A metastore holds catalogs, a catalog holds schemas, and a schema holds the securables; ids are full names throughout.

Filter by `catalog_name` and `schema_name` whenever you can: those predicates decide which schemas the worker lists, and the permission, ownership, tag and lineage lookups cost one API call per object in scope.

Secrets stay in Unity Catalog: storage credentials are listed by name and kind, connection options are masked and Delta Sharing recipient tokens are never read.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Databricks only (Data Lineage API). Direct edges: level 'dataset' (table to table, or between a table and the notebook / job / query / dashboard / pipeline that reads or writes it, as '<workspace_id>/<id>') and 'column' (column to column). via lists the notebooks / jobs on a table-to-table edge. Pushed down: downstream_id / downstream_qualified_name (that table's upstreams), upstream_id / upstream_qualified_name (that table's downstreams), level. workers.doc_md:
# US Congress in DuckDB

Members, votes and legislation of the United States Congress, joined on **bioguide_id**.

| Upstream | What it covers | Key |
|---|---|---|
| [unitedstates/congress-legislators](https://github.com/unitedstates/congress-legislators) (CC0) | every member since 1789, terms, IDs | none |
| [Voteview](https://voteview.com/data) (Lewis, Poole, Rosenthal et al.) | all roll calls since 1789, member votes, DW-NOMINATE | none |
| [Senate roll-call votes](https://www.senate.gov/legislative/votes_new.htm) | the newest Senate votes, member by member | none |
| [Congress.gov API v3](https://github.com/LibraryOfCongress/api.congress.gov) | bills, laws, amendments, committees, nominations, treaties, House votes | [free api.data.gov key](https://api.congress.gov/sign-up/) |

Bulk files are downloaded on first use into a per-user cache and revalidated after a TTL (24 hours by default). The Congress.gov API is read live, 250 rows per request, with congress, type and date filters pushed into the request.

```sql
CREATE SECRET (TYPE us_congress, API_KEY 'your-api.data.gov-key');
```

Please cite Voteview as: Lewis, Jeffrey B., Keith Poole, Howard Rosenthal, Adam Boche, Aaron Rudkin, and Luke Sonnet. *Voteview: Congressional Roll-Call Votes Database*. https://voteview.com/
workers.readme_sql:
-- Which senators broke with their party most often in the 118th Congress?
WITH v AS (
  SELECT v.bioguide_id, v.rollnumber, v.vote, i.party_name
  FROM us_congress.main.member_votes(118, chamber := 'senate') v
  JOIN us_congress.main.member_ideology(118, chamber := 'senate') i USING (bioguide_id)
  WHERE v.vote IN ('Yea', 'Nay')
), party AS (
  SELECT rollnumber, party_name, mode(vote) AS party_vote FROM v GROUP BY ALL
)
SELECT m.full_name, v.party_name, round(avg((v.vote <> p.party_vote)::INT) * 100, 1) AS pct_against_party
FROM v JOIN party p USING (rollnumber, party_name)
JOIN us_congress.main.members m USING (bioguide_id)
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY pct_against_party DESC LIMIT 10;

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Everything here joins on bioguide_id. People come first: the members table has one row per person since 1789 with cross-walk IDs, and member_terms has one row per term with chamber, dates, state, district and party; filter terms on start_date/end_date to find who served when. Voting behaviour has three layers: Voteview's per-Congress files for every roll call since 1789, each member's position and DW-NOMINATE ideology (pass the Congress number and chamber := 'house' or 'senate' to download only what you need); senate.gov's XML for Senate votes taken today; and Congress.gov's beta House vote endpoint from the 118th Congress on. Legislation (bills and their actions, cosponsors, subjects, summaries and text; laws; amendments; committees; nominations; treaties) comes live from the Congress.gov API and needs an API key secret of type us_congress; congress, bill type and update_date filters are pushed into those requests. Prefer the keyless relations when they can answer the question.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## main

- **Members**: who served, when, for which state and party, with ideology scores.
- **Votes**: every roll call since 1789 from Voteview, the newest Senate votes from senate.gov, and House votes from Congress.gov.
- **Legislation**: bills, laws, amendments, committees, nominations and treaties from Congress.gov (API key required).

Join everything on `bioguide_id`.

tables.name: cache_files
tables.comment: The bulk files (legislators, Voteview, Senate XML) this worker has downloaded, with source and freshness.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per file in the worker's download cache: cache_dir, path, url, bytes, fetched_at, etag, last_modified, sha256. Files are downloaded on first use by members, member_terms, the Voteview functions and the Senate functions, and revalidated after the cache TTL (ATTACH option cache_ttl_hours, default 24). Set ATTACH option cache_dir to move the cache. Use it to see how fresh the data is or how much disk it uses. Reading it makes no network requests.

tables.name: member_terms
tables.comment: Every term served in the House or Senate since 1789: chamber, dates, state, district and party.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: One row per term served by a member of Congress since 1789 (about 45,500 rows), keyed by (bioguide_id, term_number). chamber is 'house' or 'senate'; start_date and end_date are DATEs (House terms run two years, Senate six; end_date is earlier when a member left early). state is the USPS code; district is the House district (0 at-large or delegate, -1 historic unknown, NULL for senators); senate_class is 1-3. party is the party at the start of the term. To find who served on a date D, filter start_date <= D AND end_date >= D; for a Congress N use the window starting January 3 of year 1789 + 2*(N-1). is_current marks terms in progress today. Join to members on bioguide_id. No API key needed.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## member_terms

One row per term served, with chamber, dates, state, district, senate class, party and office contact details. Source: [unitedstates/congress-legislators](https://github.com/unitedstates/congress-legislators) (CC0 public domain), downloaded on first scan and cached; refreshed after the cache TTL.

vgi.example_queries.description: Senators serving California on January 1, 2000
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT bioguide_id, party, start_date, end_date FROM us_congress.main.member_terms WHERE chamber = 'senate' AND state = 'CA' AND DATE '2000-01-01' BETWEEN start_date AND end_date ORDER BY bioguide_id

vgi.example_queries.description: Size of each party's House delegation in the 1st Congress
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT party, count(DISTINCT bioguide_id) AS members FROM us_congress.main.member_terms WHERE chamber = 'house' AND start_date < DATE '1791-03-04' AND end_date > DATE '1789-03-04' GROUP BY party ORDER BY members DESC

tags.vgi.title: Terms Served in Congress
