functions.name: read_270
functions.comment: Shaped positional view of X12 transaction set 270

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Shaped, relational view of X12 transaction set 270 (read_270) — a 270 eligibility / benefit inquiry. The single `input` argument takes a file path or glob (e.g. '/data/*.270'), or inline `VARCHAR`/`BLOB` content (auto-detected by the ISA/UNA/UNB prefix). Every row carries the five envelope keys (interchange_ctrl, group_ctrl, transaction_ctrl, transaction_type, source_path), then this set's positional columns — for example hl_id, hl_level_code, entity_name, eb_service_type. Columns are named by the PUBLIC segment ID and element position only (e.g. hl_level_code = HL03); raw codes are surfaced verbatim, so code-value translation needs your own licensed X12 reference. Each HL parent starts a logical row group; repeating children fan out to one row each sharing the parent's keys, so re-aggregate with GROUP BY on the parent id. Structural / positional only — no TR3 loop or code-set rules.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Shaped positional view of X12 `270` (a 270 eligibility / benefit inquiry). Carries the five envelope keys plus positional columns named by public segment ID and element position (e.g. hl_level_code = HL03) — such as hl_id, hl_level_code, entity_name, eb_service_type; raw codes verbatim. Reads a file path/glob, inline `VARCHAR` content, or a `BLOB`.

arguments.name: input
arguments.description: The EDI to parse, overloaded across three auto-detected input modes: a file path or glob (e.g. '/data/claims/*.837'), or a list of paths — the streaming hot path, read locally in sorted order; OR an inline interchange string; OR inline interchange bytes. Use `mode =>` to force path versus content.

functions.name: envelope
functions.comment: One row per ST transaction: ISA/GS/ST envelope metadata + structural validity flags

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Summarize ANSI ASC X12 EDI file(s) as one row per ST transaction set — the routing / triage view. The single `input` argument is a file path/glob or inline content (auto-detected by the ISA/UNA/UNB magic prefix). Columns expose the ISA interchange header (control number, sender/receiver qualifiers + IDs, date/time, version, P/T usage indicator), the GS functional group header (functional id, app sender/receiver, date, GS08 version), the ST header (control number, transaction type, impl reference), the actual ST..SE segment_count, and the structural validity flags se_count_ok / ge_count_ok / iea_count_ok / se_ctrl_match / ge_ctrl_match / iea_ctrl_match (NULL when the matching trailer is absent — e.g. a truncated interchange). This is structural validation only (segment counts + control-number matching) — no loop or code-set rules.
tags.vgi.doc_md: One row per X12 transaction set with ISA/GS/ST metadata and the SE/GE/IEA structural count + control-match validity flags. Reads a file path/glob or inline content.

vgi.example_queries.description: Summarize an inline 837 interchange as one envelope row with structural validity flags.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT interchange_ctrl, transaction_type, segment_count, se_count_ok FROM x12.main.envelope('ISA*00*          *00*          *ZZ*SENDER         *ZZ*RECEIVER       *240101*1200*^*00501*000000001*0*P*:~GS*XX*SEND*RECV*20240101*1200*1*X*005010~ST*837*0001~BHT*0019*00*REF01*20240101*1200*CH~CLM*ACCT777*500***11:B:1*Y~SV1*HC:99213*200*UN*1~SE*5*0001~GE*1*1~IEA*1*000000001~')

vgi.example_queries.description: Reconcile a sent three-transaction 837 batch (envelope) against the partner's 997 acknowledgment (read_997), matched on group and transaction control numbers: 0001 has AK5 status A, 0002 has AK5 status R with one AK3 segment error, and 0003 is NOT ACKNOWLEDGED because the 997 has no AK2 for it.
vgi.example_queries.sql: WITH sent AS (SELECT group_ctrl, transaction_type, transaction_ctrl FROM x12.main.envelope('ISA*00*          *00*          *ZZ*CLINIC         *ZZ*PAYER          *240101*1200*^*00501*000000101*0*P*:~GS*HC*CLINIC*PAYER*20240101*1200*1*X*005010X222A1~ST*837*0001~BHT*0019*00*REF01*20240101*1200*CH~CLM*ACCT777*500***11:B:1*Y~SE*4*0001~ST*837*0002~BHT*0019*00*REF02*20240101*1200*CH~CLM*ACCT778*1000***11:B:1*Y~SE*4*0002~ST*837*0003~BHT*0019*00*REF03*20240101*1200*CH~CLM*ACCT779*250***11:B:1*Y~SE*4*0003~GE*3*1~IEA*1*000000101~')), acks AS (SELECT ak1_group_control, ak2_transaction_set_id, ak2_transaction_control, any_value(ak5_status) AS ak5_status, count(ak3_segment_id) AS segment_errors FROM x12.main.read_997('ISA*00*          *00*          *ZZ*PAYER          *ZZ*CLINIC         *240101*1300*^*00501*000000501*0*P*:~GS*FA*PAYER*CLINIC*20240101*1300*5*X*005010~ST*997*0001~AK1*HC*1~AK2*837*0001~AK5*A~AK2*837*0002~AK3*CLM*3**8~AK4*2*782*1~AK5*R*5~AK9*P*3*2*1~SE*10*0001~GE*1*5~IEA*1*000000501~') GROUP BY ALL) SELECT s.transaction_ctrl, coalesce(a.ak5_status, 'NOT ACKNOWLEDGED') AS ack_status, coalesce(a.segment_errors, 0) AS segment_errors FROM sent AS s LEFT JOIN acks AS a ON a.ak1_group_control = s.group_ctrl AND a.ak2_transaction_set_id = s.transaction_type AND a.ak2_transaction_control = s.transaction_ctrl ORDER BY s.transaction_ctrl;

functions.name: copy_x12
functions.comment: Import and export complete X12 segment rows through the catalog's COPY format.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Import and export X12 with the alias-scoped x12 COPY format. FROM emits the complete read_x12 schema. TO consumes ordered segment_id, elements, element_separator, and segment_terminator columns. Paths are worker-local. The writer validates complete ASCII envelopes and publishes only after validation; recalculate_counts updates trailer counts without changing control numbers. Use read_x12 for ordinary SELECT queries.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## X12 COPY format

The registered handler is invoked by DuckDB's COPY machinery. It cannot be called directly as a table function; name it as `FORMAT '<alias>.x12'` (`'x12.x12'` when attached as `x12`).

**Import.** Create the destination table from the schema of `read_x12(input)` with zero rows, then import a worker-local file or glob. Column names, order, and types must match. Reads retain malformed segments for inspection and materialize the input in memory.

**Export.** Supply the four named columns `segment_id`, `elements`, `element_separator`, and `segment_terminator`, ordered by document and segment index. Other columns are informational. ISA11 and ISA16 preserve repetition and component delimiters. Empty element strings are retained; NULL values are rejected.

**Validation and publication.** The writer checks ASCII text, fixed-width ISA, envelope nesting, counts, and control matches across batches. The explicit `recalculate_counts` option updates SE01/GE01/IEA01 only. A same-directory temporary file replaces the target after validation completes; failure preserves the old target. Empty input writes an empty file. This is structural validation; transaction-specific content rules remain outside scope. Formatting whitespace is normalized. EDIFACT and binary payloads are unsupported. See the repository README for the complete edit-and-export workflow.

vgi.example_queries.description: Export an X12 interchange's segment rows to a file through the X12 COPY format, in document and segment order.
vgi.example_queries.sql: COPY (SELECT * FROM x12.main.read_x12('ISA*00*          *00*          *ZZ*SENDER         *ZZ*RECEIVER       *240101*1200*^*00501*000000001*0*P*:~GS*XX*SEND*RECV*20240101*1200*1*X*005010~ST*997*0001~AK1*PO*1~AK9*A*1*1*1~SE*4*0001~GE*1*1~IEA*1*000000001~') ORDER BY document_index, segment_index) TO 'acknowledgment.x12' (FORMAT 'x12.x12');

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Explode UN/EDIFACT interchange file(s) into one row per element. The input is a file path/glob or inline content (auto-detected by the ISA/UNA/UNB prefix). The delimiters come from the optional UNA service-string advice (overriding the EDIFACT defaults), and the release/escape byte (default '?') is un-escaped so an escaped delimiter is treated as data. functions.name: read_999
functions.comment: Shaped positional view of X12 transaction set 999

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Shaped, relational view of X12 transaction set 999 (read_999) — a 999 implementation acknowledgment. The single `input` argument takes a file path or glob (e.g. '/data/*.999'), or inline `VARCHAR`/`BLOB` content (auto-detected by the ISA/UNA/UNB prefix). Every row carries the five envelope keys (interchange_ctrl, group_ctrl, transaction_ctrl, transaction_type, source_path), then this set's positional columns — for example ak2_transaction_control, ik5_status, ik3_segment_id, ak9_status. Columns are named by the PUBLIC segment ID and element position only (e.g. ik5_status = IK501); raw codes are surfaced verbatim, so code-value translation needs your own licensed X12 reference. Each AK2 parent starts a logical row group; repeating children fan out to one row each sharing the parent's keys, so re-aggregate with GROUP BY on the parent id. Structural / positional only — no TR3 loop or code-set rules.

functions.name: read_x12
functions.comment: Read complete X12 segment rows, including envelopes, ordering, and delimiter metadata.

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Read every X12 segment, including ISA/GS/GE/IEA envelopes, with positional elements, document/segment ordering, source offsets, and per-interchange delimiters. Envelope keys apply only to the current scope (NULL outside it). Accepts paths/globs, inline content, or bytes. Use this representation for COPY FROM/TO FORMAT 'x12.x12'. Order by document_index, segment_index before writing. Text round trips preserve element values, empty elements, and ISA padding, but normalize inter-segment whitespace. The reader is permissive; the writer requires complete, structurally valid ASCII X12. Shaped read_* projections cannot reconstruct an interchange.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## Complete X12 segments

Use this reader to edit or inspect an entire interchange before COPY export. Unlike the transaction-only segments view, every ISA, GS, GE, and IEA row remains available.

**Ordering.** Each invocation assigns a document_index to each resolved input and a document-wide segment_index to every row. Order by both when exporting. Keep a separate import identifier when appending several calls to one staging table.

**Values and delimiters.** Positional elements retain empty strings, padding, composites, and repetitions as unsplit text. The row carries its element separator and segment terminator; ISA11 and ISA16 retain the other delimiters. A new ISA starts a new delimiter scope, including concatenated interchanges with different separators.

**Envelope keys.** Keys are NULL outside their scope. A trailer carries the keys of the scope it closes. Source paths are NULL for inline content; byte offsets refer to the original document and become informational after edits.

**Round trips.** The reader is permissive and materializes its input. COPY export checks complete ASCII envelopes and control numbers, with optional trailer-count recalculation. Inter-segment whitespace is normalized; binary payloads and EDIFACT writing are unsupported.

vgi.example_queries.description: Read all segments of an inline X12 interchange, including its envelopes.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT segment_index, segment_id, elements FROM x12.main.read_x12('ISA*00*          *00*          *ZZ*SENDER         *ZZ*RECEIVER       *240101*1200*^*00501*000000001*0*P*:~GS*XX*SEND*RECV*20240101*1200*1*X*005010~ST*837*0001~CLM*ACCT1*500~SE*3*0001~GE*1*1~IEA*1*000000001~')

functions.name: delimiters
functions.comment: Sniff the X12/EDIFACT delimiters from inline content into a STRUCT(element, segment, component, repetition)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Discover the delimiter bytes governing an inline X12 or UN/EDIFACT interchange and return them as a `STRUCT(element, segment, component, repetition)`, each a 1-char `VARCHAR`. For X12 the bytes are read deterministically from the fixed-width ISA (element = byte after 'ISA', component = ISA16, segment = byte after ISA16, repetition = ISA11 or NULL for the version-4010 'U' placeholder); for EDIFACT they come from the optional UNA service-string advice (or the EDIFACT defaults). `repetition` is NULL when no repetition separator is in use. Content that is not a recognizable interchange returns a NULL struct (never an error). Pass the content from a column, e.g. via read_text().
tags.vgi.doc_md: Sniff the EDI delimiters from inline content into a `STRUCT(element, segment, component, repetition)`; `repetition` is NULL when unused, and unrecognized content returns NULL.

vgi.example_queries.description: Sniff the element separator (ISA byte-3) from a canonical ISA header.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT (x12.main.delimiters('ISA*00*          *00*          *ZZ*SENDER         *ZZ*RECEIVER       *240101*1200*^*00501*000000001*0*P*:~')).element AS element_sep;

arguments.name: content
arguments.description: Inline interchange content whose delimiters to sniff — e.g. the first bytes of an ISA or UNA/UNB header. Typically the content column from read_text(...). NULL or unrecognized content yields a NULL struct.

examples: SELECT (x12.main.delimiters('ISA*00*          *00*          *ZZ*SENDER         *ZZ*RECEIVER       *240101*1200*^*00501*000000001*0*P*:~')).element AS element_sep;

functions.name: transaction_type
functions.comment: Detect the transaction type (first ST01, or EDIFACT UNH02 message type) of inline content

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Detect the transaction set type of inline X12 or UN/EDIFACT content without fully parsing the body: returns the first X12 ST01 transaction set identifier ('835', '837', '270', '271', '850', '997', '999', …) or, for an EDIFACT interchange, the UNH02 message type ('ORDERS', 'INVOIC', …). Useful for routing / triage. Returns NULL when no transaction header is found or the content is unrecognized (never an error). Pass the content from a column, e.g. via read_text().
tags.vgi.doc_md: Detect the EDI transaction type of inline content — first X12 ST01 or EDIFACT UNH02 message type; NULL when none is found.

''UNB+UNOA:1+SENDER+RECEIVER+240102:1200+REF1''UNH+MSG1+ORDERS:D:96A:UN''BGM+220+PO12345+9''UNT+3+MSG1''UNZ+1+REF1''')) AS inbox(filename, content) LEFT JOIN x12.main.transaction_sets AS t ON t.transaction_set = x12.main.transaction_type(inbox.content) ORDER BY inbox.filename;

workers.title: X.509 & TLS
workers.tagline: Parse X.509 certificates & inspect TLS endpoints for DuckDB (Go)
workers.subtitle: Read subjects, expiry and fingerprints from certificates, fetch TLS chains, and find every logged certificate for a domain.
workers.summary: Parse X.509 certificates, inspect TLS endpoints and search Certificate Transparency logs
workers.doc_md:
# X.509 Certificate & TLS Inspection for DuckDB

**Parse X.509 certificates and inspect live TLS endpoints directly in SQL** — read subjects, issuers, validity windows, SHA-256 fingerprints, and subject alternative names (SANs) from PEM or DER certificates, and pull the certificate chain a TLS server presents, all without leaving DuckDB.

This is a defensive security and compliance toolkit for anyone who works with certificates at scale: SREs auditing certificate expiry across a fleet, security engineers triaging TLS configurations, and compliance teams reporting on certificate authorities, key algorithms, and signature algorithms. Certificate Transparency search adds the outside view: every certificate a public CA has logged for your domains, including ones you did not know were issued. Instead of shelling out to `openssl` and parsing text by hand, you query certificates and endpoints as ordinary SQL columns and rows, then filter, join, and aggregate them like any other DuckDB data.

It is powered entirely by the Go standard library's battle-tested [`crypto/x509`](https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/x509) and [`crypto/tls`](https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/tls) packages — no third-party parsing code. The only external service is the free, keyless [crt.sh](https://crt.sh/) index of the public Certificate Transparency logs, used only for Certificate Transparency search. The worker speaks the VGI protocol over Arrow, so DuckDB attaches it as a catalog and certificate parsing runs in-process at native speed. Certificate inputs are accepted as **PEM text** (`VARCHAR`) or **DER bytes** (`BLOB`); the format is sniffed from the content at runtime, so one query works for both.

## When to reach for it

Reach for this worker whenever certificates or TLS endpoints show up in your data and you want to treat them as structured columns rather than opaque blobs: auditing expiry windows across a fleet, pinning or comparing SHA-256 fingerprints, checking key and signature algorithms against a policy, expanding a certificate into a row per attribute for ad-hoc inspection, or pulling the chain a live server presents to confirm what it actually serves. Offline certificate parsing runs entirely in-process; live endpoint inspection **opens a network connection, so use it against AUTHORIZED endpoints only.**

## Typical uses

A few patterns recur. To flag soon-to-expire certificates, apply `cert_not_after` to a column of PEM or DER certificates and keep the rows whose expiry falls inside your renewal window, reporting each certificate's `cert_subject` alongside. To audit cryptographic hygiene across a fleet, group a certificate table by `cert_key_algorithm` and `cert_signature_algorithm` and count the weak ones. To confirm what a server actually serves, call the `tls_inspect` table function on an **authorized** `host:port` and read back the presented chain. To find every certificate issued for your domain, search the public Certificate Transparency logs with a `'%.example.com'` pattern (a passive lookup via crt.sh that never contacts your hosts) and download the logged certificates for the parsing scalars. Browse the `cert_fields` registry view to discover every attribute the worker can read and the scalar that returns each; ready-to-run, fully qualified statements live in the `x509.main` schema's example queries.

Learn more about the underlying library in the [Go `crypto/x509` documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/x509) and the [Go source on GitHub](https://github.com/golang/go/tree/master/src/crypto/x509). Source for this worker lives at [github.com/Query-farm/vgi-x509](https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-x509).

example_queries.description: Certificate Transparency audit of a domain: list every certificate logged for its subdomains (ct_search), download each one (ct_certificate) and read its key and signature algorithms with the cert_* scalars. example_queries.description: List the certificate fields whose scalar function returns a BOOLEAN, with the function name.
example_queries.sql: SELECT field, scalar_function FROM x509.main.cert_fields WHERE result_type = 'BOOLEAN' ORDER BY field

example_queries.description: List the unexpired certificates logged for every subdomain of the sample domain, one row per certificate (the reserved vgi-x509.example domain is answered offline from the worker's sample log).

tags.vgi.doc_llm: X.509 certificate parsing and TLS inspection functions: read subject, issuer, serial, validity window, key/signature algorithms, SHA-256 fingerprint, CA flag, expiry status, and subject alternative names from a PEM/DER certificate; dump all fields in long format; fetch the certificate chain presented by a live TLS host:port; and search Certificate Transparency logs (crt.sh) for the certificates issued for a domain.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
## x509.main

Defensive **X.509 certificate** parsing and **TLS endpoint** inspection, exposed as DuckDB SQL functions over Apache Arrow.

### Two ways to work

Scalar functions take one certificate and return a single field (subject, issuer, serial, key and signature algorithms, SHA-256 fingerprint, validity window, CA flag, or subject alternative names) — ideal for filtering, joining, and aggregating certificate columns. Table functions expand a certificate or endpoint into rows: one dumps every attribute of a certificate for ad-hoc inspection, the other connects to a live TLS endpoint (**AUTHORIZED endpoints only**) and returns the presented chain, and a third searches the public Certificate Transparency logs through crt.sh (a passive lookup that never contacts the hosts searched for); a companion scalar downloads a logged certificate for the parsing scalars.

### Usage

Certificate inputs accept **PEM text** (`VARCHAR`) or **DER bytes** (`BLOB`); the content is sniffed at runtime. NULL certificate input yields NULL (scalars) or zero rows.

functions.name: ct_search
functions.comment: Search Certificate Transparency logs (crt.sh) for the certificates issued for a domain or %.domain pattern

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Search the public Certificate Transparency (CT) logs through the free, keyless crt.sh JSON API and return one row per logged certificate: crt.sh id, issuing CA id and name, common name, the SAN names as a `VARCHAR[]`, serial number (lowercase hex, as crt.sh reports it), validity window and log entry time as UTC `TIMESTAMP`s, newest first. The query is an exact domain (`example.com`) or a SQL LIKE pattern (`%.example.com` for every subdomain). `exclude_expired` and `deduplicate` map to crt.sh's exclude=expired and deduplicate=Y (without deduplicate a certificate usually appears twice: its precertificate and the final certificate). `include_certificate := true` also downloads each certificate into the `pem` column (otherwise NULL), which feeds straight into the cert_* scalars; `ct_certificate(id)` does the same per row. This is a PASSIVE lookup of public log data: it never contacts the hosts being searched for. crt.sh is a shared, often slow service that rate-limits, so each request is bounded by `timeout_ms` and retried on HTTP 429 / 5xx with exponential backoff (`max_retries`); keep wildcard queries narrow. The reserved sample domain vgi-x509.example is answered offline from the worker's two sample certificates. NULL query yields zero rows.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Search Certificate Transparency logs via crt.sh for the certificates issued for a domain or `%.domain` pattern: id, issuer, names, serial, validity, log time (passive, public data).

vgi.example_queries.description: List the unexpired certificates logged for every subdomain of the sample domain, one row per certificate (the reserved vgi-x509.example domain is answered offline from the worker's sample log).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id, common_name, sans, not_after FROM x509.main.ct_search('%.vgi-x509.example', exclude_expired := true, deduplicate := true) ORDER BY id;

vgi.example_queries.description: Certificate Transparency audit of a domain: list every certificate logged for its subdomains (ct_search), download each one (ct_certificate) and read its key and signature algorithms with the cert_* scalars. On the sample domain the expired legacy certificate shows RSA-1024 with an ECDSA-SHA1 signature.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT c.common_name, c.not_after, x509.main.cert_key_algorithm(x509.main.ct_certificate(c.id)) AS key_algorithm, x509.main.cert_signature_algorithm(x509.main.ct_certificate(c.id)) AS signature_algorithm FROM x509.main.ct_search('%.vgi-x509.example', deduplicate := true) AS c ORDER BY c.not_after

vgi.example_queries.description: Newest five unexpired certificates crt.sh has logged for example.com (live query to the public crt.sh service, which can be slow).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT id, issuer_name, common_name, not_before, not_after FROM x509.main.ct_search('example.com', exclude_expired := true, deduplicate := true, max_results := 5) ORDER BY not_before DESC;

tags.vgi.title: Certificate Transparency Search

arguments.name: query
arguments.description: Domain to search the Certificate Transparency logs for: an exact name such as example.com or a SQL LIKE pattern such as %.example.com for every subdomain

arguments.name: exclude_expired
arguments.description: Drop certificates whose validity window has already ended (crt.sh exclude=expired)

arguments.name: deduplicate
arguments.description: Return one row per certificate instead of a precertificate plus its final certificate (crt.sh deduplicate=Y)

arguments.name: max_results
arguments.description: Keep only the newest N entries by crt.sh id (0 = all)

arguments.name: include_certificate
arguments.description: Also download each certificate into the pem column (one extra crt.sh request per row so keep the result small with max_results)

arguments.name: timeout_ms
arguments.description: Timeout for each crt.sh HTTP attempt in milliseconds

arguments.name: max_retries
arguments.description: How many times to retry a crt.sh answer of HTTP 429 or 5xx or a network error with exponential backoff

arguments.name: base_url
arguments.description: Override the crt.sh endpoint (a mirror or test server); empty means https://crt.sh/

SELECT id, issuer_name, common_name, not_before, not_after FROM x509.main.ct_search('example.com', exclude_expired := true, deduplicate := true, max_results := 5) ORDER BY not_before DESC;

functions.name: tls_inspect
functions.comment: Connect to a TLS host:port and return the presented certificate chain (AUTHORIZED endpoints only)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Connect to a live TLS endpoint given as host:port and return the certificate chain the server presents, one row per certificate (seq, subject, issuer, validity window, CA flag, SHA-256 fingerprint). functions.name: cert_key_algorithm
functions.comment: Public-key algorithm with size/curve (e.g. RSA-2048, ECDSA-P256, Ed25519)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Return the certificate's subject public-key algorithm together with its key size or curve, as a `VARCHAR` built by this worker (not Go's bare algorithm name). The value follows a fixed convention: RSA keys render as `RSA-<bits>` where <bits> is the modulus size, typically `RSA-2048`, `RSA-3072` or `RSA-4096`; ECDSA keys render as `ECDSA-<curve>` with the curve name stripped of its hyphen, i.e. `ECDSA-P256`, `ECDSA-P384`, `ECDSA-P521`; Edwards keys render as the single token `Ed25519`, and X25519, X448 and Ed448 keys as `X25519`, `X448`, `Ed448`. Any other key type Go recognises falls back to Go's public-key algorithm name (e.g. `DSA`, `ML-DSA`); an unrecognised key algorithm yields `Unknown`. For a security audit, RSA moduli below 2048 bits are considered weak. Accepts PEM text (`VARCHAR`) or DER bytes (`BLOB`); NULL input yields NULL. Example: the committed fixture certificate carries a P-256 ECDSA key and returns `ECDSA-P256`.

functions.name: ct_certificate
functions.comment: Download the certificate crt.sh logged under an id, as PEM text

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Download the certificate that crt.sh logged under a crt.sh id (the `id` column of ct_search) and return it as PEM text (`VARCHAR`), ready for the cert_* scalars: e.g. `cert_key_algorithm(ct_certificate(id))`. Calls crt.sh's `?d=<id>` endpoint once per distinct id, with a 60-second timeout and up to 3 retries with exponential backoff on HTTP 429 / 5xx. A passive lookup of public CT log data. An id crt.sh does not know yields NULL; NULL input yields NULL. The two-argument form `ct_certificate(id, base_url)` targets a crt.sh mirror or test server. Sample-log ids (from ct_search over the reserved vgi-x509.example domain) are answered offline. For many rows prefer `ct_search(..., include_certificate := true)`.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Download a logged certificate by crt.sh id as PEM text (passive, public CT data).

vgi.example_queries.description: Download a logged certificate by its crt.sh id and read its subject (the sample-log id used here is answered offline; real ids come from ct_search).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT x509.main.cert_subject(x509.main.ct_certificate(9100000000000000002)) AS subject;

vgi.example_queries.description: Certificate Transparency audit of a domain: list every certificate logged for its subdomains (ct_search), download each one (ct_certificate) and read its key and signature algorithms with the cert_* scalars. On the sample domain the expired legacy certificate shows RSA-1024 with an ECDSA-SHA1 signature.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT c.common_name, c.not_after, x509.main.cert_key_algorithm(x509.main.ct_certificate(c.id)) AS key_algorithm, x509.main.cert_signature_algorithm(x509.main.ct_certificate(c.id)) AS signature_algorithm FROM x509.main.ct_search('%.vgi-x509.example', deduplicate := true) AS c ORDER BY c.not_after

functions.name: cert_signature_algorithm
functions.comment: Certificate signature algorithm (Go crypto/x509 canonical name, e.g. ECDSA-SHA256)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Return the algorithm the issuing CA used to sign this certificate, as a `VARCHAR`. The value is Go crypto/x509's canonical name for the algorithm and is drawn from a fixed vocabulary: for RSA PKCS#1 v1.5, `SHA256-RSA`, `SHA384-RSA`, `SHA512-RSA` (and the legacy `SHA1-RSA`, `MD5-RSA`); for RSA-PSS, `SHA256-RSAPSS`, `SHA384-RSAPSS`, `SHA512-RSAPSS`; for ECDSA, `ECDSA-SHA256`, `ECDSA-SHA384`, `ECDSA-SHA512` (and legacy `ECDSA-SHA1`); for DSA, `DSA-SHA1`, `DSA-SHA256`; `Ed25519`; and `ML-DSA-44`, `ML-DSA-65`, `ML-DSA-87`. An unrecognised OID, including the obsolete MD2-RSA, yields `Unknown`. Note the ordering convention differs by family — RSA/DSA render as hash-then-key (`SHA256-RSA`) while ECDSA renders as key-then-hash (`ECDSA-SHA256`) — so match on the whole token, not a positional split. For a security audit, the SHA-1 and MD5 variants (and `Unknown`) are considered weak/deprecated and are the ones worth flagging. Accepts PEM text (`VARCHAR`) or DER bytes (`BLOB`); NULL input yields NULL. Example: the committed fixture certificate is P-256 ECDSA and returns `ECDSA-SHA256`.
tags.vgi.doc_md: Read the certificate signature algorithm as Go crypto/x509's canonical name (e.g. `ECDSA-SHA256`, `SHA256-RSA`, `Ed25519`). The value comes from a fixed vocabulary; the SHA-1/MD5 variants are weak and worth flagging in an audit.

workers.title: XGBoost
workers.tagline: XGBoost for DuckDB/SQL — train/predict model registry, hyperparameter search, native categoricals, feature importance and SHAP, exposed as a VGI worker
workers.subtitle: Train, tune, score and explain gradient-boosted tree models on your tables with plain SQL.
workers.summary: XGBoost train/predict model registry, datasets, and interpretation for DuckDB/SQL
workers.doc_md:
# XGBoost for SQL

Exposes [XGBoost](https://xgboost.ai) to DuckDB/SQL as VGI functions:

- **Datasets** — toy datasets and generators
- **Models** — `fit`/`predict`, typed `fit_<estimator>`, cross-validation, grid/randomized search
- **Interpretation** — feature importance, SHAP `explain`, partial dependence, permutation importance

Models are stored as reusable BLOBs in a registry; native UBJSON serialization.

example_queries.description: Load the built-in iris dataset.
example_queries.sql: SELECT * FROM xgboost.main.iris LIMIT 5;

example_queries.description: Fit an XGBoost classifier on iris, then predict with the fitted model.
example_queries.sql:
SET VARIABLE iris_model = (SELECT model FROM xgboost.main.fit((SELECT * FROM xgboost.main.iris), estimator := 'xgb_classifier', target := 'target', id := 'sample_id'));
SELECT sample_id, prediction FROM xgboost.main.predict((SELECT * FROM xgboost.main.iris), model := getvariable('iris_model'), id := 'sample_id') LIMIT 5;

example_queries.description: Three-fold cross-validated accuracy of an XGBoost classifier on iris.
example_queries.sql: SELECT fold, score FROM xgboost.main.cross_val_score((SELECT * EXCLUDE (target_name) FROM xgboost.main.iris), estimator := 'xgb_classifier', target := 'target', cv := 3);

example_queries.description: Grid-search an XGBoost classifier on iris over a tiny grid (3-fold).
example_queries.sql: SELECT params, mean_test_score, rank FROM xgboost.main.grid_search((SELECT * EXCLUDE (target_name) FROM xgboost.main.iris), target := 'target', cv := 3, estimator := union_value(xgb_classifier := {'n_estimators': [25, 50], 'max_depth': [3]})) ORDER BY rank;

example_queries.description: Out-of-fold confusion matrix for an XGBoost iris classifier: 5-fold cross_val_predict on the species name, joined back to the iris table by sample_id and counted per (actual, predicted) species pair. Only non-empty cells are returned; the off-diagonal rows are the held-out misclassifications, almost all of them versicolor/virginica mix-ups.
example_queries.sql: SELECT i.target_name AS actual_species, cv.prediction AS predicted_species, count(*) AS n_flowers FROM xgboost.main.cross_val_predict((SELECT sample_id, sepal_length_cm, sepal_width_cm, petal_length_cm, petal_width_cm, target_name FROM xgboost.main.iris), estimator := 'xgb_classifier', target := 'target_name', id := 'sample_id', cv := 5) AS cv JOIN xgboost.main.iris AS i USING (sample_id) GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY actual_species, predicted_species;

example_queries.description: Fit an XGBoost classifier on iris and return the training summary
example_queries.sql: SELECT estimator, task, n_samples, n_features, train_score FROM xgboost.main.fit((SELECT * FROM xgboost.main.iris), estimator := 'xgb_classifier', target := 'target', id := 'sample_id')

example_queries.description: Where does an XGBoost regressor miss? 5-fold out-of-fold predictions on diabetes joined back to the patients, with the held-out mean absolute error and mean progression score per BMI quartile (1 = lowest BMI).
example_queries.sql: SELECT d.bmi_quartile, count(*) AS patients, round(avg(abs(cv.prediction - d.target)), 1) AS oof_mae, round(avg(d.target), 1) AS mean_progression FROM xgboost.main.cross_val_predict((SELECT * FROM xgboost.main.diabetes), estimator := 'xgb_regressor', target := 'target', id := 'sample_id', cv := 5) AS cv JOIN (SELECT sample_id, target, ntile(4) OVER (ORDER BY bmi, sample_id) AS bmi_quartile FROM xgboost.main.diabetes) AS d USING (sample_id) GROUP BY d.bmi_quartile ORDER BY d.bmi_quartile

example_queries.description: How many models are saved
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS model_count FROM xgboost.main.list_models

example_queries.description: Class balance
example_queries.sql: SELECT target_name, count(*) FROM xgboost.main.breast_cancer GROUP BY target_name

example_queries.description: Target range
example_queries.sql: SELECT min(target), max(target), round(avg(target), 1) FROM xgboost.main.diabetes

example_queries.description: Average value by latitude band
example_queries.sql: SELECT round(latitude) AS lat, round(avg(target), 2) FROM xgboost.main.california_housing GROUP BY lat ORDER BY lat

example_queries.description: Average alcohol per cultivar
example_queries.sql: SELECT target_name, round(avg(alcohol), 2) FROM xgboost.main.wine GROUP BY target_name

example_queries.description: Row count per species
example_queries.sql: SELECT target_name, count(*) FROM xgboost.main.iris GROUP BY target_name

example_queries.description: Train an XGBoost classifier on iris and store it as 'iris_clf'
example_queries.sql: SELECT model_name, task, n_samples, n_features, train_score FROM xgboost.main.fit((SELECT sample_id, sepal_length_cm, sepal_width_cm, petal_length_cm, petal_width_cm, target FROM xgboost.main.iris()), model_name => 'iris_clf', estimator => 'xgb_classifier', target => 'target', id => 'sample_id')

example_queries.description: Patient count and mean disease-progression score
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS n, round(avg(target), 1) AS mean_progression FROM xgboost.main.diabetes()

example_queries.description: 5-fold accuracy of an XGBoost classifier on iris
example_queries.sql: SELECT fold, score FROM xgboost.main.cross_val_score((SELECT sepal_length_cm, sepal_width_cm, petal_length_cm, petal_width_cm, target FROM xgboost.main.iris()), estimator => 'xgb_classifier', target => 'target')

example_queries.description: Predict with the stored 'iris_clf' model
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, prediction FROM xgboost.main.predict((SELECT * FROM xgboost.main.iris()), model_name => 'iris_clf', id => 'sample_id')

example_queries.description: Tumour count and mean nucleus radius by diagnosis
example_queries.sql: SELECT target_name, count(*) AS n, round(avg(mean_radius), 2) AS avg_mean_radius FROM xgboost.main.breast_cancer() GROUP BY target_name ORDER BY target_name

example_queries.description: Top three features by gain for a stored model
example_queries.sql: SELECT feature, importance, rank FROM xgboost.main.feature_importance('iris_clf', importance_type => 'gain') WHERE rank <= 3

example_queries.description: Show one stored model's training metadata
example_queries.sql: SELECT estimator, task, target, n_features, train_score FROM xgboost.main.model_info('iris_clf')

example_queries.description: Train a xgb_rf_regressor with named hyperparameters
example_queries.sql: SELECT n_samples, n_features, train_score FROM xgboost.main.fit_xgb_rf_regressor((SELECT * FROM xgboost.main.iris()), target := 'target', id := 'sample_id', n_estimators := 200, max_depth := 6)

example_queries.description: Explain each row's prediction with per-feature contributions
example_queries.sql: SELECT feature, round(avg(abs(shap_value)), 3) AS mean_abs_shap FROM xgboost.main.explain((SELECT * FROM xgboost.main.diabetes()), model_name => 'diab_reg', id => 'sample_id') GROUP BY feature ORDER BY mean_abs_shap DESC

example_queries.description: Train a xgb_classifier with named hyperparameters
example_queries.sql: SELECT n_samples, n_features, train_score FROM xgboost.main.fit_xgb_classifier((SELECT * FROM xgboost.main.iris()), target := 'target', id := 'sample_id', n_estimators := 200, max_depth := 6)

example_queries.description: Rank iris features by permutation importance for a stored model
example_queries.sql: SELECT feature, importance_mean, rank FROM xgboost.main.permutation_importance((SELECT * EXCLUDE (target_name) FROM xgboost.main.iris()), model_name := 'iris_clf', target := 'target') ORDER BY importance_mean DESC

example_queries.description: 5-fold out-of-fold predictions on iris
example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, prediction FROM xgboost.main.cross_val_predict((SELECT sample_id, sepal_length_cm, sepal_width_cm, petal_length_cm, petal_width_cm, target FROM xgboost.main.iris()), estimator => 'xgb_classifier', target => 'target', id => 'sample_id')

example_queries.description: Train a xgb_rf_classifier with named hyperparameters
example_queries.sql: SELECT n_samples, n_features, train_score FROM xgboost.main.fit_xgb_rf_classifier((SELECT * FROM xgboost.main.iris()), target := 'target', id := 'sample_id', n_estimators := 200, max_depth := 6)

example_queries.description: Grid-search an XGBoost classifier on iris
example_queries.sql: SELECT params, mean_test_score, rank FROM xgboost.main.grid_search((SELECT * FROM xgboost.main.iris()), target := 'target', id := 'sample_id', estimator := union_value(xgb_classifier := {'n_estimators': [50, 100], 'max_depth': [3, 5]})) ORDER BY rank

example_queries.description: Partial dependence of 'iris_clf' on petal length
example_queries.sql: SELECT class, feature_value, partial_dependence FROM xgboost.main.partial_dependence((SELECT * FROM xgboost.main.iris()), model_name := 'iris_clf', feature := 'petal_length_cm') ORDER BY feature_value

example_queries.description: Samples per iris species
example_queries.sql: SELECT target_name, count(*) AS n FROM xgboost.main.iris() GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY target_name

example_queries.description: Mean petal length per species
example_queries.sql: SELECT target_name, avg(petal_length_cm) FROM xgboost.main.iris() GROUP BY target_name

example_queries.description: Stored models with their estimator and training score
example_queries.sql: SELECT model_name, estimator, train_score FROM xgboost.main.list_models() ORDER BY model_name

example_queries.description: Train a xgb_regressor with named hyperparameters
example_queries.sql: SELECT n_samples, n_features, train_score FROM xgboost.main.fit_xgb_regressor((SELECT * FROM xgboost.main.iris()), target := 'target', id := 'sample_id', n_estimators := 200, max_depth := 6)

example_queries.description: Class balance of 500 generated rows with 5 features and 3 classes
example_queries.sql: SELECT target, count(*) AS n FROM xgboost.main.make_classification(n_samples => 500, n_features => 5, n_classes => 3) GROUP BY target ORDER BY target

example_queries.description: Size and target spread of 500 generated rows with 4 features
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS n, round(stddev(target), 2) AS target_sd FROM xgboost.main.make_regression(n_samples => 500, n_features => 4, noise => 5.0)

example_queries.description: Randomized-search an XGBoost classifier on iris
example_queries.sql: SELECT params, mean_test_score, rank FROM xgboost.main.randomized_search((SELECT * FROM xgboost.main.iris()), target := 'target', id := 'sample_id', n_iter := 4, estimator := union_value(xgb_classifier := {'n_estimators': [50, 100, 200], 'max_depth': [3, 5, 8]})) ORDER BY rank

example_queries.description: Delete a stored model and report whether it existed
example_queries.sql: SELECT model_name, dropped FROM xgboost.main.drop_model('iris_clf')

example_queries.description: Mean alcohol content per wine cultivar
example_queries.sql: SELECT target_name, round(avg(alcohol), 2) AS mean_alcohol FROM xgboost.main.wine() GROUP BY target_name ORDER BY target_name

example_queries.description: District count and mean house value (downloads on first use)
example_queries.sql: SELECT count(*) AS n_districts, round(avg(target), 3) AS mean_value_100k FROM xgboost.main.california_housing()

agent_tasks: Before deploying a tumor-screening model, I want an honest estimate of how accurately gradient boosting distinguishes malignant from benign breast tumors on unseen data. Using the built-in Wisconsin breast-cancer dataset and all 30 cell-nucleus features, run 5-fold cross-validation with an XGBoost classifier and report the mean held-out accuracy across the folds. Return a single row with one column named mean_cv_accuracy.

I'm tuning an XGBoost classifier on Fisher's iris dataset. Run a 5-fold cross-validated grid search over n_estimators (30, 60, 90) and max_depth (2, 4, 6), and report the best mean cross-validated accuracy across all those hyperparameter combinations. Return a single row with one column named best_cv_accuracy.

Train a gradient-boosted regressor on the diabetes dataset (predict target from the baseline measurements), then use the fitted model to predict on those same rows and report the root-mean-squared error between the predictions and the actual target. The predictions come back keyed by sample_id, so join them back to the data by sample_id. Round to 2 decimals and return a single row with one column named train_rmse.

Train a gradient-boosted regressor on the diabetes dataset, compute gain-based feature importances, and count how many features have a gain importance strictly greater than the mean gain importance across all features. Return a single row with one column named n_above_mean.
How many samples are in the built-in wine recognition dataset? Return a single row with one column named n.
How many districts are in the built-in California housing dataset? Return a single row with one column named n.
Generate a synthetic classification dataset with 120 samples, 3 classes, and random_state 42, then report how many rows it has. Return a single row with one column named n.
Generate a synthetic regression dataset with 90 samples and random_state 42, then report how many rows it has. Return a single row with one column named n.

Using the typed classifier fitter, train an XGBoost classifier on the iris dataset (target column 'target', id column 'sample_id') and report the training summary's sample and feature counts. Return one row with columns named n_samples and n_features.

Using the typed regressor fitter, train an XGBoost regressor on the diabetes dataset (target column 'target', id column 'sample_id') and report the training summary's sample and feature counts. Return one row with columns named n_samples and n_features.

Using the typed random-forest classifier fitter, train an XGBoost RF classifier on the iris dataset (target 'target', id 'sample_id') and report the training summary's sample and feature counts. Return one row with columns named n_samples and n_features.

Using the typed random-forest regressor fitter, train an XGBoost RF regressor on the diabetes dataset (target 'target', id 'sample_id') and report the training summary's sample and feature counts. Return one row with columns named n_samples and n_features.

Using 5-fold out-of-fold cross-validated predictions from an XGBoost classifier on the iris dataset (target 'target', id 'sample_id'), compute the overall accuracy of those out-of-fold predictions against the true labels (join by sample_id). Round to 4 decimals and return a single column named oof_accuracy.

Train an XGBoost regressor on the diabetes dataset, then use SHAP contributions (via the explain function) to identify the single most influential feature overall — the one with the largest mean absolute SHAP value. Return one row with a column named feature.

Train an XGBoost regressor on the diabetes dataset, then compute a partial-dependence curve for the 'bmi' feature over a 20-point grid, and report the minimum and maximum predicted value along the curve, each rounded to 2 decimals. Return one row with columns named min_pd and max_pd.

Train an XGBoost regressor on the diabetes dataset, then use permutation importance (5 repeats, random_state 42) to find the single most important feature by mean importance. Return one row with a column named feature.

Train an XGBoost classifier on the built-in iris dataset with the generic fit function (estimator xgb_classifier, target column 'target', id column 'sample_id') and report its in-sample training accuracy rounded to 4 decimals. Return a single row with one column named train_accuracy.

Train an XGBoost classifier on the wine dataset (target 'target', id 'sample_id') and save it in the model registry under the name 'wine_clf'. Then look that saved model up in the registry and report which target column it was trained on and how many features it uses. Return one row with columns named target and n_features.

Train an XGBoost regressor on the diabetes dataset (target 'target', id 'sample_id') and save it in the model registry as 'diab_saved'. Then list the stored models and return the registry entry for that model only. Return one row with columns named model_name, estimator and task.

Train an XGBoost classifier on iris (target 'target', id 'sample_id'), save it in the model registry as 'scratch_clf', then delete it from the registry and report whether a model was actually removed. Return one row with one column named dropped.

Tune an XGBoost classifier on the iris dataset with a randomized hyperparameter search: sample 4 combinations (random seed 0) from n_estimators (25, 50, 100) and max_depth (2, 3, 4), scoring each by 3-fold cross-validation, using only the four measurement columns as features. Report the best mean cross-validated accuracy, rounded to 4 decimals. Return a single row with one column named best_cv_accuracy.

For a tumor-screening review I need to know how many cancers a gradient-boosted model would have missed on data it never trained on. Using the built-in Wisconsin breast-cancer dataset with its 30 cell-nucleus measurements as the features, get 5-fold out-of-fold predictions from an XGBoost classifier and count the malignant tumours (target 0) that were predicted benign (target 1). Return a single row with one BIGINT column named n_missed_malignant.

tags.vgi.doc_md:
# `main` schema

Every XGBoost function lives here, grouped by family:

- **datasets** — toy/generated data as table functions
- **models** — `fit`/`predict`, typed `fit_<estimator>`, cross-validation, grid/randomized search
- **interpretation** — feature importance, SHAP `explain`, partial dependence, permutation importance

Fit returns a reusable model `BLOB`; predict aligns features by name.

vgi.example_queries.description: Fit an XGBoost classifier on iris and return the training summary
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT estimator, task, n_samples, n_features, train_score FROM xgboost.main.fit((SELECT * FROM xgboost.main.iris), estimator := 'xgb_classifier', target := 'target', id := 'sample_id')

vgi.example_queries.description: Out-of-fold confusion matrix for an XGBoost iris classifier: 5-fold cross_val_predict on the species name, joined back to the iris table by sample_id and counted per (actual, predicted) species pair. Only non-empty cells are returned; the off-diagonal rows are the held-out misclassifications, almost all of them versicolor/virginica mix-ups.
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT i.target_name AS actual_species, cv.prediction AS predicted_species, count(*) AS n_flowers FROM xgboost.main.cross_val_predict((SELECT sample_id, sepal_length_cm, sepal_width_cm, petal_length_cm, petal_width_cm, target_name FROM xgboost.main.iris), estimator := 'xgb_classifier', target := 'target_name', id := 'sample_id', cv := 5) AS cv JOIN xgboost.main.iris AS i USING (sample_id) GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY actual_species, predicted_species

vgi.example_queries.description: Where does an XGBoost regressor miss? 5-fold out-of-fold predictions on diabetes joined back to the patients, with the held-out mean absolute error and mean progression score per BMI quartile (1 = lowest BMI).
vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT d.bmi_quartile, count(*) AS patients, round(avg(abs(cv.prediction - d.target)), 1) AS oof_mae, round(avg(d.target), 1) AS mean_progression FROM xgboost.main.cross_val_predict((SELECT * FROM xgboost.main.diabetes), estimator := 'xgb_regressor', target := 'target', id := 'sample_id', cv := 5) AS cv JOIN (SELECT sample_id, target, ntile(4) OVER (ORDER BY bmi, sample_id) AS bmi_quartile FROM xgboost.main.diabetes) AS d USING (sample_id) GROUP BY d.bmi_quartile ORDER BY d.bmi_quartile

functions.name: fit
functions.comment: Fit an XGBoost estimator and store it in the model registry

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Buffers a training table, fits an XGBoost estimator (`estimator :=` one of `xgb_classifier`, `xgb_regressor`, `xgb_rf_classifier`, `xgb_rf_regressor`), and returns a one-row training summary whose `model` column is a self-contained `BLOB` (estimator + metadata). Name the label column with `target :=`; every other column except an optional `id :=` passthrough becomes a feature (strings/missing values handled natively). Hyperparameters go in a JSON `params :=` string. Pass `model_name :=` to also persist the model to the registry; otherwise it lives only in the returned `BLOB`. Feed that `BLOB` to `predict`/`explain`/`feature_importance` via `SET VARIABLE` + `getvariable()`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**Fit an XGBoost model** — train and return a reusable model `BLOB`.

- Input: a training table `(SELECT ...)`; name the label with `target :=`, optionally an `id :=` passthrough
- `estimator :=` `xgb_classifier` | `xgb_regressor` | `xgb_rf_classifier` | `xgb_rf_regressor`; hyperparameters via JSON `params :=`
- Returns one row: `estimator`, `task`, `n_samples`/`n_features`/`n_classes`, `train_score`, `features`, and the `model` `BLOB`
- `model_name :=` also persists to the registry; classification labels may be any dtype (string/int/bool) and are decoded back on predict

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT model_name, task, n_samples, n_features, train_score FROM xgboost.main.fit((SELECT sample_id, sepal_length_cm, sepal_width_cm, petal_length_cm, petal_width_cm, target FROM xgboost.main.iris()), model_name => 'iris_clf', estimator => 'xgb_classifier', target => 'target', id => 'sample_id')
vgi.example_queries.description: Train an XGBoost classifier on iris and store it as 'iris_clf'

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Runs k-fold cross-validation and returns the held-out score for each fold (one `(fold, score)` row), without storing any model. - Returns `(fold, score)` — the held-out score for each fold

Default scorer is the estimator's own (accuracy / R^2). Take `avg(score)` for a single cross-validated estimate.

functions.name: predict
functions.comment: Score a table through a stored model, emitting predictions

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Streams a table through an already-fit XGBoost model and emits its predictions. Identify the model with either `model_name :=` (a registry name) or `model :=` (a `BLOB` from `fit`, passed via `SET VARIABLE` + `getvariable()` since a table function has only one subquery slot). Features are matched by name (order-independent; extra columns ignored; missing ones error at bind). The default output is the decoded `prediction` (the original label dtype for classifiers, value for regressors); the mutually exclusive modes `with_proba`, `output_margin`, and `pred_leaf` switch to per-class probabilities, the raw margin, or per-tree leaf indices respectively. Name an `id :=` column to carry it through.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**Predict with a stored model** — score a table row by row.

- Identify the model with `model_name :=` *or* `model :=` (a `fit` `BLOB`)
- Features aligned by name; an optional `id :=` is carried through
- Default output: `prediction` (label or value)
- `with_proba := true` → one `proba_<class>` column per class; `output_margin := true` → a `margin` `DOUBLE`; `pred_leaf := true` → a `leaf` `INTEGER[]` (one index per tree) — the three modes are mutually exclusive

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, prediction FROM xgboost.main.predict((SELECT * FROM xgboost.main.iris()), model_name => 'iris_clf', id => 'sample_id')
vgi.example_queries.description: Predict with the stored 'iris_clf' model

tags.vgi.result_dynamic_columns_md:
If `id :=` names a column it is carried through first. The prediction column depends on the model task and on the prediction mode; `with_proba := true` on a classifier adds one `proba_<class>` `DOUBLE` column per class.

### Classifier (default)

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| sample_id | BIGINT | Column named by `id :=` (here `sample_id`), carried through first as-is. |
| prediction | BIGINT | Predicted class label (`VARCHAR` for string labels). |

### Regressor (default)

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| sample_id | BIGINT | Column named by `id :=` (here `sample_id`), carried through first as-is. |
| prediction | DOUBLE | Predicted value. |

### output_margin := true

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| sample_id | BIGINT | Column named by `id :=` (here `sample_id`), carried through first as-is. |
| margin | DOUBLE | Raw (untransformed) margin score. |

### pred_leaf := true

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| sample_id | BIGINT | Column named by `id :=` (here `sample_id`), carried through first as-is. |
| leaf | INTEGER[] | Leaf index reached in each tree, one element per tree. |
tags.vgi.title: Predict

functions.name: feature_importance
functions.comment: Per-feature importance (weight/gain/cover) for a stored model, ranked

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Returns the booster's built-in per-feature importance for a stored model, one ranked row per feature (`feature`, `importance`, `rank`; rank 1 = most important, already sorted descending). Identify the model positionally by name (`feature_importance('m')`) or with `model :=` (a `BLOB`). Choose the `importance_type :=` — `gain` (default; average loss reduction), `weight` (split count), `cover`, `total_gain`, or `total_cover`. Features never used in a split report importance 0. A fast, model-native ranking; for a model-agnostic alternative use `permutation_importance`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**Booster feature importance** — model-native, ranked.

- Identify the model by name (`feature_importance('m')`) or `model :=` `BLOB`
- `importance_type :=` `gain` (default) | `weight` | `cover` | `total_gain` | `total_cover`
- Returns `(feature, importance, rank)`, sorted by importance descending

Unused features score 0. See `permutation_importance` for a model-agnostic measure.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT feature, importance, rank FROM xgboost.main.feature_importance('iris_clf', importance_type => 'gain') WHERE rank <= 3

functions.name: fit_xgb_rf_regressor
functions.comment: Fit a xgb_rf_regressor with typed hyperparameters; returns/stores the model

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Buffers a training table and fits a **random-forest regressor** built on XGBoost (`XGBRFRegressor`) — a single boosting round of bagged trees with its key hyperparameters exposed as typed, named SQL arguments (`n_estimators`, `max_depth`, `learning_rate`, `subsample`, `colsample_bytree`, `min_child_weight`, `gamma`, `reg_alpha`, `reg_lambda`, ...), each defaulting to XGBoost's own documented default. Equivalent to `fit(estimator := 'xgb_rf_regressor', ...)` but discoverable and type-checked in the catalog instead of a JSON `params` blob. Name the regression label with `target :=`, optionally carry an `id :=` through; every other column is a feature (strings/missing values handled natively). functions.name: explain
functions.comment: Per-row SHAP feature contributions, long format (row, [class], feature, shap_value, base_value)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Streams a table through a stored model and emits SHAP-style per-row prediction contributions (XGBoost's `pred_contribs`) in long format: one row per (input row, feature) with `feature`, `shap_value` (how much that feature pushed this row's raw margin away from the model's base), and `base_value` (the expected margin). Identify the model with `model_name :=` or `model :=` (a `BLOB`); name an `id :=` to tag every emitted row. For multiclass models an extra `class` column appears (one row per (row, class, feature)). Sum `shap_value` over a row's features and add `base_value` to recover the raw margin. Use it for local, per-prediction explanations.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**SHAP explanations** — per-row feature contributions, long format.

- Identify the model with `model_name :=` or `model :=`; optional `id :=` passthrough
- One row per (input row, feature): `feature`, `shap_value`, `base_value`
- Multiclass adds a `class` `BIGINT` column (one row per (row, class, feature))

`sum(shap_value) + base_value` = the row's raw margin. Local, per-prediction explanation.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT feature, round(avg(abs(shap_value)), 3) AS mean_abs_shap FROM xgboost.main.explain((SELECT * FROM xgboost.main.diabetes()), model_name => 'diab_reg', id => 'sample_id') GROUP BY feature ORDER BY mean_abs_shap DESC
vgi.example_queries.description: Explain each row's prediction with per-feature contributions

functions.name: permutation_importance
functions.comment: Model-agnostic feature importance: the drop in score when each feature is shuffled

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Computes model-agnostic permutation importance over an evaluation table: for each feature, shuffle its values `n_repeats :=` times and measure the resulting drop in the model's score; a larger drop means a more important feature. Returns one ranked row per feature (`feature`, `importance_mean`, `importance_std`, `rank`; rank 1 = most important). Identify the model with `model_name :=` or `model :=`, name the held-out `target :=` column, and optionally set `scoring :=` and `random_state :=`. Unlike `feature_importance` this measures impact on real predictions and respects feature correlations, but it needs labelled data and is slower.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**Permutation importance** — model-agnostic, ranked.

- Identify the model with `model_name :=` or `model :=`; name the `target :=` column
- `n_repeats :=` shuffles per feature, optional `scoring :=`, `random_state :=`
- Returns `(feature, importance_mean, importance_std, rank)`, sorted descending

Measures impact on real predictions (needs labels; slower than `feature_importance`).

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT feature, importance_mean, rank FROM xgboost.main.permutation_importance((SELECT * EXCLUDE (target_name) FROM xgboost.main.iris()), model_name := 'iris_clf', target := 'target') ORDER BY importance_mean DESC
vgi.example_queries.description: Rank iris features by permutation importance for a stored model

functions.name: cross_val_predict
functions.comment: Out-of-fold cross-validated predictions (no model is stored)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Computes out-of-fold cross-validated predictions for a training table without persisting any model. Each row is predicted by a model trained on the other folds (`cv :=` folds, default 5), so the result is an honest, leakage-free prediction per row — ideal for building a held-out prediction column to score with metrics or to stack. Name the label with `target :=`, pick the `estimator :=`, optionally carry an `id :=` through, and tune via JSON `params :=`. Classification labels of any dtype are decoded back to the original values.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**Cross-validated out-of-fold predictions** — no model is stored.

- Each row is predicted by a model fit on the *other* folds (`cv :=`, default 5)
- `estimator :=`, `target :=`, optional `id :=` passthrough, JSON `params :=`
- Returns one `prediction` per input row (label or value), leakage-free

Use it to make a held-out prediction column for metrics or model stacking.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT i.target_name AS actual_species, cv.prediction AS predicted_species, count(*) AS n_flowers FROM xgboost.main.cross_val_predict((SELECT sample_id, sepal_length_cm, sepal_width_cm, petal_length_cm, petal_width_cm, target_name FROM xgboost.main.iris), estimator := 'xgb_classifier', target := 'target_name', id := 'sample_id', cv := 5) AS cv JOIN xgboost.main.iris AS i USING (sample_id) GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY actual_species, predicted_species
vgi.example_queries.description: Out-of-fold confusion matrix for an XGBoost iris classifier: 5-fold cross_val_predict on the species name, joined back to the iris table by sample_id and counted per (actual, predicted) species pair. Only non-empty cells are returned; the off-diagonal rows are the held-out misclassifications, almost all of them versicolor/virginica mix-ups.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT d.bmi_quartile, count(*) AS patients, round(avg(abs(cv.prediction - d.target)), 1) AS oof_mae, round(avg(d.target), 1) AS mean_progression FROM xgboost.main.cross_val_predict((SELECT * FROM xgboost.main.diabetes), estimator := 'xgb_regressor', target := 'target', id := 'sample_id', cv := 5) AS cv JOIN (SELECT sample_id, target, ntile(4) OVER (ORDER BY bmi, sample_id) AS bmi_quartile FROM xgboost.main.diabetes) AS d USING (sample_id) GROUP BY d.bmi_quartile ORDER BY d.bmi_quartile
vgi.example_queries.description: Where does an XGBoost regressor miss? 5-fold out-of-fold predictions on diabetes joined back to the patients, with the held-out mean absolute error and mean progression score per BMI quartile (1 = lowest BMI).

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT sample_id, prediction FROM xgboost.main.cross_val_predict((SELECT sample_id, sepal_length_cm, sepal_width_cm, petal_length_cm, petal_width_cm, target FROM xgboost.main.iris()), estimator => 'xgb_classifier', target => 'target', id => 'sample_id')
vgi.example_queries.description: 5-fold out-of-fold predictions on iris

functions.name: grid_search
functions.comment: Cross-validated grid search over an XGBoost estimator's hyperparameters

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Runs scikit-learn's `GridSearchCV` over a training table and returns the cross-validation leaderboard — one row per hyperparameter combination tried, with its `params` (JSON), `mean_test_score`, `std_test_score`, and `rank` (1 = best). The estimator and its grid are one tagged-union argument: `estimator := union_value(<estimator> := {param: [values], ...})`, where the union tag picks the estimator and each member exposes only that estimator's hyperparameters; omitted params stay at their default. Set `target :=`, `cv :=` folds, optional `scoring :=`. The refit best model rides as a `model` `BLOB` on the rank-1 row — grab it with `WHERE model IS NOT NULL`; pass `model_name :=` to also persist it.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**Cross-validated grid search** — exhaustive hyperparameter sweep.

- `estimator := union_value(<estimator> := {param: [values], ...})` (a discriminated union; only that estimator's params are exposed)
- `target :=`, `cv :=` folds, optional `scoring :=`, optional `model_name :=`
- Returns the leaderboard: `params`, `mean_test_score`, `std_test_score`, `rank`

The refit best model is a `model` `BLOB` on the rank-1 row — `WHERE model IS NOT NULL`.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT params, mean_test_score, rank FROM xgboost.main.grid_search((SELECT * FROM xgboost.main.iris()), target := 'target', id := 'sample_id', estimator := union_value(xgb_classifier := {'n_estimators': [50, 100], 'max_depth': [3, 5]})) ORDER BY rank

functions.name: partial_dependence
functions.comment: How a stored model's average prediction changes as one feature varies over a grid

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Computes the partial-dependence curve for one numeric feature: sweeps `feature :=` over a grid of `grid_resolution :=` points and reports the model's average prediction at each value, holding the rest of the buffered background table fixed. Returns `(feature_value, class, partial_dependence)` ordered along the grid; `class` is NULL for regression and the single binary curve, and is the class index (one curve per class) for multiclass. Identify the model with `model_name :=` or `model :=`. Numeric features only (categorical features raise a clear error). Use it to see the marginal effect and shape of a feature on the prediction.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**Partial dependence** — marginal effect of one feature.

- `feature :=` (numeric only) swept over `grid_resolution :=` points
- Identify the model with `model_name :=` or `model :=`; input is the background table
- Returns `(feature_value, class, partial_dependence)` along the grid

`class` is NULL for regression/binary, the class index for multiclass (one curve each).

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT class, feature_value, partial_dependence FROM xgboost.main.partial_dependence((SELECT * FROM xgboost.main.iris()), model_name := 'iris_clf', feature := 'petal_length_cm') ORDER BY feature_value

functions.name: fit_xgb_regressor
functions.comment: Fit a xgb_regressor with typed hyperparameters; returns/stores the model

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Buffers a training table and fits a gradient-boosted decision-tree **regressor** (XGBoost's `XGBRegressor`) with its key hyperparameters exposed as typed, named SQL arguments (`n_estimators`, `max_depth`, `learning_rate`, `subsample`, `colsample_bytree`, `min_child_weight`, `gamma`, `reg_alpha`, `reg_lambda`, ...), each defaulting to XGBoost's own documented default. Equivalent to `fit(estimator := 'xgb_regressor', ...)` but discoverable and type-checked in the catalog instead of a JSON `params` blob. Name the regression label with `target :=`, optionally carry an `id :=` through; every other column is a feature (strings/missing values handled natively). Returns the same one-row summary with a reusable `model` `BLOB`, and persists to the registry when `model_name :=` is given. Feed the `BLOB` to `predict`/`explain`/`feature_importance`.
tags.vgi.doc_md:
**`fit_xgb_regressor`** — fit a gradient-boosted decision-tree **regressor** (XGBoost's `XGBRegressor`) with typed hyperparameters.

- Input: a training table `(SELECT ...)`; name the label with `target :=`, optional `id :=` passthrough
- Hyperparameters are named, typed SQL args (`n_estimators`, `max_depth`, `learning_rate`, `subsample`, `reg_lambda`, ...) at XGBoost's real defaults
- Returns the standard fit summary plus a reusable `model` `BLOB`; `model_name :=` also persists it

The discoverable, type-checked alternative to `fit(estimator := 'xgb_regressor', ...)`.

vgi.example_queries.sql: SELECT n_samples, n_features, train_score FROM xgboost.main.fit_xgb_regressor((SELECT * FROM xgboost.main.iris()), target := 'target', id := 'sample_id', n_estimators := 200, max_depth := 6)

tags.vgi.doc_llm: Table function that synthesises a random n-class classification problem (scikit-learn's `make_classification`). Control the shape with `n_samples`, `n_features`, `n_informative`, `n_classes`, and `random_state`; the output schema has a `sample_id`, one `feature_<i>` `DOUBLE` column per feature, and an integer `target`. tags.vgi.doc_md:

- `target :=`, `cv :=` folds, optional `scoring :=`, optional `model_name :=`

workers.title: XSLT and XQuery
workers.tagline: XSLT 3.0 / XQuery 3.1 / XPath 3.1 over XML for DuckDB (Python, SaxonC-HE)
workers.subtitle: Transform and query XML documents from SQL with XSLT, XQuery and XPath.
workers.summary: XSLT 3.0 / XQuery 3.1 / XPath 3.1 over XML for SQL (SaxonC-HE).
workers.doc_md:
# XSLT, XQuery & XPath for XML in SQL

![Saxonica SaxonC-HE logo](https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/3630933?s=240&v=4)

Transform, query, and shred XML directly in DuckDB SQL with full **XSLT 3.0**, **XQuery 3.1**, and **XPath 3.1** support, powered by the production-grade Saxon processor.

This extension turns DuckDB into an XML processing engine. Instead of exporting data to a separate XSLT/XQuery toolchain, you can apply stylesheets, evaluate XPath expressions, run XQuery FLWOR programs, and explode XML documents into relational rows without ever leaving SQL. It is built for data engineers and analysts who land XML in columns -- SOAP/EDI payloads, RSS/Atom feeds, OOXML and SVG fragments, scientific and financial document formats -- and need to extract, reshape, or validate that markup at query time, row by row, with NULLs passed through cleanly.

## Key concepts

- **Per-row scalars vs. set-returning table functions.** Scalars compute one value per row (a string, boolean, number, or list); table functions and the array-plus-UNNEST pattern explode a single document into many rows -- the natural way to *shred* XML into a relational result.
- **Transform, query, and validate.** XSLT reshapes documents, XPath and XQuery pull values out of them, and a well-formedness check lets you filter malformed rows before processing.
- **NULL / invalid / error.** A NULL input yields NULL output (or no rows); malformed XML or a bad stylesheet/expression raises a clean DuckDB error, so bad data never crashes the worker.

## When to use it

Reach for this worker whenever XML lands in a DuckDB column and you need to read a value out of it, transform it into another shape, or normalize its repeated structure into rows for downstream SQL.

## Under the hood

The worker is backed by [SaxonC-HE](https://www.saxonica.com/), the free Home Edition of [Saxonica](https://www.saxonica.com/)'s Saxon processor -- the reference implementation for XSLT 3.0 / XQuery 3.1 / XPath 3.1 -- via the [saxonche](https://pypi.org/project/saxonche/) Python bindings. A single native Saxon processor is booted once per worker and reused; compiled stylesheets and queries are cached on their source text, so a constant stylesheet applied down a column compiles once and transforms many rows. Note that SaxonC-HE is not schema-aware, so there is no XSD validation; the well-formedness check provides the strongest guarantee the free edition offers.

## Learn more

- [Saxonica homepage](https://www.saxonica.com/)
- [Saxon documentation](https://www.saxonica.com/documentation/index.html)
- [Saxon-HE source on GitHub](https://github.com/Saxonica/Saxon-HE)
- [`saxonche` on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/saxonche/)
- W3C specs: [XSLT 3.0](https://www.w3.org/TR/xslt-30/), [XPath 3.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/xpath-31/), [XQuery 3.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/xquery-31/)
workers.readme_sql: INSTALL vgi FROM community; LOAD vgi; ATTACH 'xslt' (TYPE vgi, LOCATION 'uvx --from git+https://github.com/Query-farm/vgi-xslt@v0.4.2 vgi-xslt-worker'); SELECT xslt.xpath_string('x', '//a'); -- 'x' SELECT xslt.xpath_boolean('', 'count(//a) = 1'); -- true SELECT xslt.xpath_number('42', 'number(//n)'); -- 42.0 SELECT UNNEST(xslt.xpath_array('ab', '//i')); -- 'a','b' ← shred! SELECT xslt.xquery('ab', 'string-join(//i, ",")'); -- 'a,b' SELECT xslt.is_well_formed(''); -- true SELECT * FROM xslt.xpath_nodes('ab', '//i'); -- (seq, value) rows SELECT version, schema_aware FROM xslt.saxon_info; -- engine capabilities

example_queries.description: Pull the string value of an XPath match out of a document.
example_queries.sql: SELECT xslt.main.xpath_string('x', '//a')

example_queries.description: Test an XPath count predicate as a boolean.
example_queries.sql: SELECT xslt.main.xpath_boolean('<r><a/></r>', 'count(//a) = 1')

example_queries.description: Read a numeric value out of a document via XPath.
example_queries.sql: SELECT xslt.main.xpath_number('<r><n>42</n></r>', 'number(//n)')

example_queries.description: Shred every XPath match into rows with UNNEST.
example_queries.sql: SELECT UNNEST(xslt.main.xpath_array('ab', '//i')) AS item

example_queries.description: Join matched values into one string with an XQuery string-join.
example_queries.sql: SELECT xslt.main.xquery('ab', 'string-join(//i, ",")')

example_queries.description: Filter to only well-formed candidate documents.
example_queries.sql: SELECT xslt.main.is_well_formed('') AS well_formed

example_queries.description: Explode a document into numbered (seq, value) rows in document order.
example_queries.sql: SELECT seq, value FROM xslt.main.xpath_nodes('ab', '//i') ORDER BY seq

example_queries.description: Explode a catalog into one serialized <book> per row with xquery_rows, then pull each book's title, lang attribute and numeric price out of that row with xpath_string and xpath_number (Dune/en/9.99, Candide/fr/7.5, Emma/en/12.0).
example_queries.sql: SELECT r.seq, xslt.main.xpath_string(r.value, '/book/title') AS title, xslt.main.xpath_string(r.value, 'string(/book/@lang)') AS lang, xslt.main.xpath_number(r.value, '/book/price') AS price FROM xslt.main.xquery_rows('<catalog><book lang="en"><title>Dune</title><price>9.99</price></book><book lang="fr"><title>Candide</title><price>7.5</price></book><book lang="en"><title>Emma</title><price>12</price></book></catalog>', 'for $b in /catalog/book return serialize($b)') AS r ORDER BY r.seq

example_queries.description: Skip malformed documents with is_well_formed, then read each remaining order's id attribute and customer with xpath_string and its total (sum of qty * price over its lines) with xpath_number; the malformed order C3 is dropped (A1/acme/21.5, B7/globex/38.0).
example_queries.sql: WITH docs(id, doc) AS (VALUES (1, '<order id="A1"><customer>acme</customer><line sku="bolt" qty="2" price="9.5"/><line sku="nut" qty="10" price="0.25"/></order>'), (2, '<order id="B7"><customer>globex</customer><line sku="bolt" qty="4" price="9.5"/></order>'), (3, '<order id="C3"><customer>initech</order>')) SELECT id, xslt.main.xpath_string(doc, 'string(/order/@id)') AS order_id, xslt.main.xpath_string(doc, '/order/customer') AS customer, xslt.main.xpath_number(doc, 'sum(//line/(@qty * @price))') AS total FROM docs WHERE xslt.main.is_well_formed(doc) ORDER BY id

example_queries.description: Shred the lines of a column of order documents with two position-aligned UNNEST(xpath_array(...)) calls, tag each line with its order's customer via xpath_string, and total the quantity per SKU (bolt 6 from acme,globex; nut 10 from acme).
example_queries.sql: WITH docs(id, doc) AS (VALUES (1, '<order id="A1"><customer>acme</customer><line sku="bolt" qty="2"/><line sku="nut" qty="10"/></order>'), (2, '<order id="B7"><customer>globex</customer><line sku="bolt" qty="4"/></order>')), lines AS (SELECT xslt.main.xpath_string(doc, '/order/customer') AS customer, UNNEST(xslt.main.xpath_array(doc, '//line/@sku')) AS sku, CAST(UNNEST(xslt.main.xpath_array(doc, '//line/@qty')) AS INTEGER) AS qty FROM docs) SELECT sku, CAST(SUM(qty) AS BIGINT) AS total_qty, string_agg(customer, ',' ORDER BY customer) AS customers FROM lines GROUP BY sku ORDER BY sku

example_queries.description: Normalize a feed with an XSLT stylesheet (one upper-cased <item> per <entry>), then shred the transformed output into numbered rows with xpath_nodes (1 A, 2 B).
example_queries.sql: SELECT seq, value FROM xslt.main.xpath_nodes(xslt.main.xslt('<feed><entry><t>a</t></entry><entry><t>b</t></entry></feed>', '<xsl:stylesheet version="3.0" xmlns:xsl="http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform"><xsl:template match="/"><items><xsl:for-each select="//entry"><item><xsl:value-of select="upper-case(t)"/></item></xsl:for-each></items></xsl:template></xsl:stylesheet>'), '//item') ORDER BY seq

example_queries.description: Read the engine version and whether XSD validation is available.
example_queries.sql: SELECT version, schema_aware FROM xslt.main.saxon_info

example_queries.description: Confirm the XSLT and XQuery language levels the engine implements.
example_queries.sql: SELECT xslt_version, xquery_version FROM xslt.main.saxon_info

example_queries.description: Explode an XQuery FLWOR result into numbered rows.
example_queries.sql: SELECT seq, value FROM xslt.main.xquery_rows('12', 'for $x in //i return $x*2') ORDER BY seq

example_queries.description: Check whether a string is well-formed XML.

example_queries.description: First matching node's string value.

example_queries.description: Shred all matching nodes into rows with UNNEST.
example_queries.sql: SELECT UNNEST(xslt.main.xpath_array('ab', '//i'))

example_queries.description: Apply an XSLT 3.0 stylesheet, lifting an inner element value into a new wrapper element.
example_queries.sql: SELECT xslt.main.xslt('<doc><n>hi</n></doc>', '<xsl:stylesheet version="3.0" xmlns:xsl="http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform"><xsl:template match="/"><out><xsl:value-of select="//n"/></out></xsl:template></xsl:stylesheet>')

tags.vgi.doc_md:
# main

XSLT 3.0 / XQuery 3.1 / XPath 3.1 processing over XML, backed by SaxonC-HE.

The functions in this schema group into four capabilities:

- **Transform** an XML document with an XSLT 3.0 stylesheet.
- **Query** a document with XPath or XQuery to pull out a string, boolean, or numeric value.
- **Shred** a document into relational rows -- per row via an array you UNNEST, or via a set-returning table function.
- **Validate** that text is well-formed XML before you process it.

## saxon_info (table)

A single-row, directly-browsable table describing the SaxonC engine bundled with this worker — its version and edition, the XSLT/XQuery/XPath language levels it implements, and whether it is schema-aware.

**When to use:** learn the engine's capabilities before relying on them. The `schema_aware` column is the key signal: it is always false on the Home Edition, so there is no XSD validation. The table has no arguments and a single row of engine facts, so it is directly browsable.

**Columns:** `version`, `edition`, `xslt_version`, `xquery_version`, `xpath_version` (all `VARCHAR`) and `schema_aware` (`BOOLEAN`).

tags.vgi.doc_llm:
## xpath_nodes

Explode a single XML document into rows: emit **one `(seq, value)` row per XPath 3.1 match**, in document order.

**When to use:** shred one constant document into a relational result — turn `//item` matches into a numbered table you can join, filter, and aggregate. For shredding a *column* of documents instead, use the `xpath_array` scalar with `UNNEST`.

**Inputs:** `xml` (the document) and `expr` (an XPath 3.1 expression). Both `VARCHAR`; table-function named-argument syntax (`name := value`) is supported.

**Output columns:** `seq` (`BIGINT`, 1-based position) and `value` (`VARCHAR`, the match's string value).

**Behavior & edge cases:** no matches -> zero rows. Malformed XML or XPath raises a clean DuckDB error.

# xpath_nodes

Table function: one `(seq, value)` row per XPath 3.1 match in one document.

## Usage
